### In-hall: rooms strung on a walk, the interior trail

The out-trail strings beats on a spine outdoors; a hall strings rooms on a walk indoors, the first rung of the rooms'
ladder (hall → section → floor) that the out-trail's header reserved. A stage recipe's `hall` is read against a card the
way a trail is, planned into rooms, links and two ports, built by the stage as any rooms are, and held by laws.

- **The card** (`era/in-hall.js` `IN_HALL`): an explorer's walk indoors (4.5 m/s, a run of 8–20 s, 60–150 s to explore),
  and the beats as rooms, each with its width, its depth along the walk, its share of the hall's height, its dwell and
  its words: `squeeze` (a low narrow passage), `reveal` (a tall wide room through a narrow door), `landmark` (the set
  piece's room, at the end of the sightline), `pocket` (a side room off the walk, a dead end), `rest` (an even room).
  `crossing`, `pit`, `stair` and `gate` are named and refused until the stage lays their geometry.
- **The grammar** (`hallOrderFaults`, `drawHallBeats`): never two alike together, a reveal always out of a squeeze
  (compression, then release), the landmark neither first nor past the middle (the mouth sees it), a pocket off the
  room before it; drawn by the seed when the recipe names none, a reveal, a landmark and a pocket always.
- **The plan** (`planInHall`): a straight spine from the mouth, each room centred on one axis with an even width, so
  every doorway stands on it; the heartbeat swings each beat's height and width, no ceiling under 3.5 m (`IN_HALL.floor`:
  a squeeze's doorway stays a full metre over the walker's eye); the spine's depths drawn in their
  ranges and scaled together to the run; a pocket off the side of the room before it, no deeper than its host; the
  landmark's link last, so the kit's dressing seats its set piece there; a mouth through the first room's `-y` and an
  exit through the last's `+y` (`exit: 'none'`, a dead end ending at its landmark). `mouth` and `exit` say how each is
  entered (`arch`, `door`, `portal`, `cave`), for the threshold that will read them.
- **The laws** (`inHallLaws`, on the stage's own plan): run, explore, order, release (every reveal half again as tall as
  its squeeze), landmark (the mouth's eye to the landmark's room through every doorway, under its head), ports (each
  through an outside wall), reach (every room from the mouth), fit (every beat laid).
- **Built by the stage** (`stage: { hall }`, `withHall`): the hall writes the rooms, links and ways (a recipe with a hall
  names none of them), in the recipe's kit or its cube's interior's bones (`geocubeBones`); the payload carries the
  hall's anchors (`beat`, `port`, tagged `hall: 'in-hall:<id>'`) and `hall: { beats, ports, laws }`. A recipe with no
  hall is as it was.
- **The geocube kind's `show: 'hall'`**: the cube's interior (its room, or an inside domain) walked as a hall from the
  seed, its kit dressed (the crypt's set piece in the landmark's room), the cube's accent on the landmark room's far wall
  unless the kit's dressing made it its own. Gen-7 lights it as any room.
- **Halls to walk** (`scripts/spikes/hall/halls.mjs`): limestone-crags' room and temple hall rolled as halls and one
  written on the crypt kit, each a walkable page in both eras beside its plan plate (the rooms by beat, the doorways, the
  ports, the sightline, each ceiling) and its laws, captured from the mouth and from the squeeze into the reveal. Every
  law holds on all three.

### Juice fidelity: the venue's and the era's drawing, and the platformer's and pinball's movement juice

A game's effects were composed from a register (how they look) and a game type (how they play). They now also have a
FIDELITY: how finely they are drawn, read from the venue and the era. A voxel stadium's blast is a heap of tumbling
blocks; the sixth generation paints a flash's light on the ground; the seventh throws it on the lit world and blooms
round the hot core. The platformer and pinball also gain movement juice on the hero: what the world shows round a jump,
a landing and a run at speed. No fidelity word: every effect as it was.

- **The floor's fidelity** (`scene/juice-style.js` `JUICE_FIDELITIES`, an `fxStyle`'s `fidelity`):
  - **`voxel`:** every particle a cube, drawn on twos. No thrown light: the flash is a flat square of light on the
    ground.
  - **`paint`, the sixth generation:** the flash's light laid on the ground as a soft pool, because a paint world takes
    no lamp.
  - **`form`, the seventh generation:** more light thrown on the lit world, a bloom halo round every hot core, more
    sparks.
  - **`era`:** drawn at the read's era (gen-6 paint, gen-7 form), so the same recipe renders at either.
  - An explosion carries its `pool` and its `bloom`, and its length covers them.
  - The page's events channel emits the cube glyph, the pool and the bloom only when a floor uses them, beams' sparks
    included.
- **A machine's juice at its fidelity** (`car-designer/juice.js` `rigFidelity`, `bakeJuice`'s `fidelity`):
  - Racers' and supercars' smoke, dust and sparks are drawn as:
    - tumbling blocks at a voxel kit or a voxel stadium;
    - flat cel discs at an anime stadium (banded);
    - hot cores in a wide bloom when read in the seventh generation.
  - The paint tier is the page's own soft sprite, written as no key. A world's composed floor wins over the venue.
- **The hero's movement juice** (`gameworld/feel/hero-juice.js`):
  - Rows for the page's rig juice (the racer's engine), at the body's feet, middle and head. They are baked onto a hero
    resolved under a composed floor of that game type.
  - **The platformer:** a puff at the take-off; dust and a squash ring on a landing, more the harder the fall; a ring of
    air under an air jump; skid dust on a hard stop; stars from a stomp or a boop; the buster's charge in its three
    colours; a white flash on a hit and the mercy's flicker after it.
  - **Pinball:** a trail of light at the feet past running pace; the air streaking past near the top speed; speed lines
    on the screen in a surge; a ring of air thrown back as a boost starts; the spin dash's sparks revving in its
    colours; ricochet stars off a bumper; the body glowing while it revs.
  - **Realistic and action:** no movement juice; their effects are the floor's.
  - **Facts:** the page reads the platform rule's facts for a hero's juice only. Its speed comes from how far it went,
    because the rule moves a body directly. The facts are a jump's frame, an air jump's, the landing and its speed, a
    hard stop, the charge, a blow taken and a bump.
- **A gameworld stamps its fidelity** (`gameworld/juice.js`): `voxel` for a voxel stadium (its quick words' venue) or a
  voxel kit, else `era`. The operator's word wins over both, and the readout says where it came from.
- **Held:**
  - `juice-fidelity.test.js`:
    - the word read and refused;
    - each fidelity's composition, and none without one;
    - the pool and the bloom;
    - the page's emission;
    - a machine's fidelity from the floor, the venue and the era;
    - the hero's rows by game type at the body's anchors;
    - the hero's facts emitted only with its juice;
    - the gameworld's stamp.
  - `hero-juice.live.test.js` (e2e, real browser): a platform body runs, jumps, air-jumps and lands. The platformer's
    take-off puff and landing dust fire, pinball's trail runs at speed, and no fidelity raises a page error.
- **Seen:** the proving ground's blast at each fidelity (`proving-ground.mjs --juice material:action:<fidelity>`).
  Voxel reads as blocks with a square pool; paint and form differ at the flash (its pool, its bloom). The hero's juice
  was checked by the live test's numbers, not by eye. The eyes gate is open.
- **Not built, said:**
  - Juice inside the sports pages (the contest channel's ball, its hits and its points).
  - Smoke lit by the key, soft particles, heat haze.
  - The voxel tier's particles stepped on twos in the rig juice: its blocks tumble but move every frame.

### Named heroes and their marks

A hero can carry marks of its own (a logo, an emblem, an insignia) pasted as an SVG path, and a game that adopts it
keeps them. A hero can be named: its name its own on this machine, its emblem worn on whatever body, and a game adopts
it by name. An identity that travels with the row into any game on this machine.

- **A mark** (`polygonizer/field-paint.js`): a field-paint shape `{ path: '<an SVG path d>' }`.
  - The path is drawn as pasted: every outline and its holes (even-odd), its curves, and its arcs as arcs.
  - It is fitted into the entry's `size` by its larger side, with its y turned up, then simplified to a millimetre on
    a chest emblem (`MARK`) and cut as convex pieces (`markPolys`).
  - It is refused by name when it does not read as a path, when a key stands beside it, or when it would take more
    pieces than a cut holds.
  - One colour per path: a two-colour emblem is two entries, the charge after the field.
- **Part words**: field paint's `part` takes a suffix (`'*_torso'`: every layer worn over the torso). So
  `['torso', '*_torso']` is the chest whatever is worn on it, the top or the suit or a catsuit's painted skin, and
  the outermost layer shows. Seen on the tiered and the realistic bodies.
- **Arcs**: `parseSvgPath` draws an arc along the arc when asked (`arcs: true`, `carve-solid.js` `arcPoints`). A carved
  solid's arcs are still read as lines, so its bytes never move.
- **An adopted hero keeps its marks when equipped.** A game equips a hero it adopted (or one edited by hand) over the
  hero's own row. It used to rebuild that copy from the door's words alone, dropping the row's `fieldPaint`, `strokes`,
  `bake`, `rim` and `hullShade` (`gameworld/runner.js`). They now ride; a hero the run makes has none of its own.
- The `layered` manual card names the mark and the suffix.
- **A named hero** (`polygonizer/hero-emblem.js`): two of the hero door's words, `name` and `emblem`, inside `spec`, so
  no tool's schema changes.
  - `name` is the hero's own on this machine. A second hero is refused the same name, case and spacing aside, naming
    the hero that holds it, however it is named: the door's mint (`create_character`, `mint_solid`), `update_character`
    or an `update_sketch` patch on `/hero/name` (`assertHeroNameFree`, `SketchRepository.heroByName`).
  - The row is titled by the name, and a rename retitles a row titled by its old name or the door's.
  - `emblem: { layers: [{ path, role?, color? }], at?, size?, offset? }` is its mark, each layer one SVG path. A layer's
    colour is its role's from the hero's palette (`field`, `charge`, `outline`, each its own palette group with the
    suit's colours it falls back to), or a fixed `color` of its own. It is worn on the chest (the default) or the back.
  - The emblem is kept as given and lowered at every read to field paint under the row's own, on the torso and every
    layer worn over it (`heroFieldPaint`), so a body or a palette edit redraws it. The mint's readout counts it.
  - **A game adopts a named hero by name**: `design_game` with `characters.hero.name` (or a quick game's
    `hero: { name }`) writes the hero's ref beside the name and plays it as an adopted hero, its emblem with it. A name
    no hero holds is refused.
  - The `revise-character` routing card and a `hero-identity` section of the `layered` manual say both words.
- Found and not fixed: the anime head's character light draws no field-paint cells, so a mark on an anime hero is not
  seen. The light splits each face into its lit and shade pieces; the cells must be cut first.

### Race machines: the streamlined supercar, the gloss racer, and the seventh generation's light on them

The race machines' visual quality taken up a generation: the supercar's body streamlined and detailed, the cartoon
racer finished in gloss, and both drawn in the form render (gen-7: a surface carries its material and its form, and
the renderer lights it) instead of with their light baked in. Stored races keep their bytes; a race minted from now
takes all of it.

- **The streamlined supercar** (`car-designer/vehicle-odm-surface.js`, `surface.line: 'streamline'`; `classic`, the
  line as it was, when absent):
  - **The body flows.** The fender swells broadly over its wheel instead of humping. The shoulder runs as one line
    rising to the rear haunch. The sill tucks under a character line a third of the way up. The deck is a wedge, low at
    the nose. The tail draws in to a boat tail. The arches sit closer round the tyres.
  - **Wider, staggered tyres.** The rear is wider than the front, set inward about its outer face so the wheel stays
    inside the classic envelope.
  - **A finer mesh.** Its own sampling (`STREAMLINE_LODS`) and ceilings (`STREAMLINE_BUDGETS`: 15k, 32k and 64k
    triangles).
  - **The details.** A splitter, skirts, diffuser strakes, polished exhaust tips with dark bores (where the figure's
    flames already come out), brake calipers in the language's colour, a light bar across the tail between the lamps,
    split spokes. A lamp is held under its own deck edge so it fits the wedge.
  - `scripts/render-supercars.mjs` takes the line as its last argument.
- **The gloss racer** (`car-designer/racer.js`, `shade: 'gloss'`): the smooth finish with its tyres turned on a lathe.
  `buildBlock`'s new opt-in `lathe` draws the wheel primitive as a tyre (a crowned tread, a rounded shoulder, its
  sidewalls down to the bead, 24 to 48 sides) instead of a prism. The laws judge the plain machine and the physics are
  the plain machine's, so a finish never changes how it drives. `scripts/render-karts.mjs` renders every finish and the
  lit review of each finished one.
- **The form render** (`vehicle-designer/vehicle-rig.js` `packFormMesh`, `car-designer/form-light.js`):
  - **What it carries.** A vehicle figure carries each bone's material slot, its albedo (no light in it) and its
    crease-aware normals, quantized and grouped by slot. Its lamps stay as they shine, on the bones the status lights.
  - **Who carries it.** A supercar with `light: 'form'`, a finished (smooth or gloss) racer with `light: 'form'`, and
    either read in gen-7 (`world-scene.js`: the read's era). A cel racer is a look of its own and stays as it is drawn.
  - **How the page draws it** (the controllable channel, gated on a form figure: a page without one is byte-identical):
    - a physical material per slot: paint under clearcoat, glass, polished alloy, rubber, carbon and the emissive
      lamps, the finish's own response (`VEHICLE_MATERIALS`, `KART_MATERIALS`);
    - an environment made of the world's sky (zenith, horizon, ground and the sun's disc), so the clearcoat and the
      glass reflect the sky they are raced under;
    - the shadow lights the page already casts with take the key's colour and strength (they were white and lit
      nothing), so the car shadows itself and takes the world's shadows; a hemisphere of the sky over the ground fills
      it;
    - a filmic curve in its own shader, since the painted world is not tone-mapped;
    - the race's mood (golden, dusk, night, rain) its key, its ambient and its sky.
- **Minted now** (`gameworld/quick.js`, `car-designer/roster.js`): a quick race's supercars are written streamlined in
  the form render, and its racers in gloss in the form render unless an entry names its own `shade` or `light`
  (`paint` bakes the light, as before). The race card says so.
- **Held** (`race-machines.test.js`, `form-render.live.test.js` in the e2e tier): the streamlined line within its ceiling
  at every quality, its kit, its pipes at the flames' anchors, its tyres wider and still inside the envelope, its bytes
  the same for the same words; the form mesh's groups, unit normals and linear albedo; a supercar's and a racer's form
  when asked or read in gen-7, never a cel racer's, `light: 'paint'` byte-identical to no word, the gloss racer's physics
  the plain machine's; the page's form path present only with a form figure. In Chromium, a streamlined supercar and a
  gloss racer drawn with physical materials, their lamps baked, every shader compiled, the shadow lights at the key and
  the car drawn lit. Seen in machine screenshots (the four presets in both lines, baked and lit; four racers in every
  finish, cel against gloss in the form render); the eyes gate is open.
- **Not built, said:**
  - The cartoon racer's parts themselves: the wheel faces' two-spoke bar reads as a stub at an angle. It is part data
    every finish shares.
  - Bloom on the lamps, motion blur, a reflection of the track itself (the environment is the sky).
  - The form render for the realistic fleet's cars and the other vehicle rigs.
  - A light tier for the form render (a phone draws it as a screen does).

### Race of Champions: a duel's two lanes inside a stadium

A stadium race, as the Race of Champions runs one: two cars side by side on mirrored lanes that swap once over a
crossover bridge, so both drive the same distance, head to head, inside a stadium's bowl.

- **The duel** (`roads/course.js` `designDuel`, the `race-of-champions` preset, a course spec's `duel: true`): one closed
  alignment round the stadium twice. Lane one runs from the start to the crossover, cuts across onto lane two, and lane
  two runs back round to the start: the first car's lap, half the alignment. The second car starts a lane over, half the
  alignment on. The base loop's second half is its first turned half a turn about the middle, so each car drives one
  lane-half of each side and one diagonal, and the two laps come out equal (`duel.fair`, millimetres on the preset). The
  crossover is a short S in the middle of the far straight, steep enough that the lanes meet only where the figure of
  eight's bridge has lifted one clear of the other. `twist` dents a chicane into each long side. A lap shorter than the
  corners fit is advised.
- **The stadium class** (`roads/classes.js`, `TRACK_TEMPLATES`): a Race of Champions' lane, 8 m of asphalt between
  concrete walls, no run-off, a crossover steeper than a circuit's. A raised road's side is concrete, not an
  embankment (a template's new `skirt`, earth unless it says).
- **Its stadium** (`scape.venue`, `stadium/stadium.js` `trackVenue`): a stadium preset or a stadium's words. Its bowl,
  masts and skyline wrap the track's whole footprint, drawn in the track's kit on its pole, and stand on the track's
  own ground (`bowlFaces`' new `ground: false`: no infield, apron or plaza). The bowl is the whole dressing: no arena
  plan, surrounds or set pieces. The driver's eye meets its four sides.
- **The contract's duel** (`roads/contract.js`): both starts, the grid lane by lane (lane two's slot first, the rival's;
  lane one's the player's), and each leg's checkpoints, as many in each and none on the crossover; a car's lap is one
  leg and its next the other. Each start line is painted.
- **The race on it** (`gameworld/quick.js`, `game/mechanics.js`): a quick race on a duel puts you in lane one and one
  rival in lane two, on its own checkpoints through the `laps` mechanic's new `rivalCheckpoints` (a rival's own ring, as
  many as the player's: the place is counted in passes; absent, a rival runs the player's, as before). Laps are 1 or an
  even number (two, the default, is the whole loop); more than one rival is refused, teaching.
- **The words** (`trackscape-compose.js`): "race of champions", "stadium race", "stadium track", "head to head" in the
  football ground; "olympic stadium", "colosseum" and "dome" name the venue. A duel's course has no hills, ramps or
  crossing of its own; a point-to-point stage is never a duel.
- **Held** (`roads/duel.test.js`): one crossing over a deck that clears the lower lane, and no near pass anywhere else,
  plain and chicaned; equal laps, the second start a lane over and the same way; the contract's duel; a rival in lane
  two racing the whole loop from the contract alone, its own checkpoints in order, never backing off a wall, the
  player on the grid second; the words; the bowl clear of the footprint and no arena or surrounds. Seen in machine
  screenshots, the track bare and in the football and anime stadiums; the eyes gate is open.
- **Not built, said:** the knockout (heats in a bracket, the winner on to the next: nothing plays heats as levels
  yet), race control and the broadcast on the duel's page (the stopping point below), a wall shared by the two lanes
  (each lane keeps its own, a metre apart), the crowd's cars and a podium.

### Racing arenas: the stadium's primitives at the circuit, the broadcast at the race

A racing venue's stands were one set piece of boxes and a panel roof. They are now built from the battle city stadium's
own parts, so a stand beside a track reads as a stadium's does; and the race has a referee whose calls and timing tower
the broadcast package can cover, as it covers a contest.

- **The stand** (`stadium/stand.js`): the bowl's section (`stadium/bowl.js`) swept along a straight instead of round a
  ring. From the front: a wall of hoardings, raked tiers two rows a step with aisles, the crowd a mosaic on the treads
  (never figures), a concourse and a band of glass boxes under an upper tier, a parapet, the back wall in a facade card
  between pilasters, a canopy cantilevered from the back with its truss and rafters, a screen on the rim facing the
  track. Both ends are closed by the section itself. A class's stand is fitted to the arena plan's stand zone: a
  circuit's two tiers under a canopy behind glass, a kart track's one covered tier, a rally's open bank.
  - **Painted in the track's kit:** the concrete and the steel are the kit's materials on its pole (material, banded,
    shaded). The seats, the crowd and the hoardings are a stadium livery's tints, lit as paint (a new `tint` on the
    track kit, and `paintPiece` honours a face's `tint`; a face without one is painted as before).
  - **In the local area** (`roads/local-area.js`): the stand zone's elements on every pole but the voxel's (its cubes
    keep the block), set back from the zone's front. A debris fence stands at that front, its posts painted and its mesh
    drawn translucent so the lower rows read from the track. A new law, `in-zone`: the stand stays on its zone's
    footprint.
  - **The word:** `scape.stands`: `'block'` (the set piece, when absent), `'bowl'`, or `{ rows?: [lower, upper?],
    roof?: none | canopy, facade?: none | glass | brick | metal, crowd?: 0..1, screens?: 0 | 1, livery? }` over the
    class's. A gameworld roadway level reads it too. A track from words (`composeTrack`) is stamped `stands: 'bowl'` at
    mint on every pole but the voxel's, so a row minted before keeps its bytes.
  - **Held:** the words read and refused; the section rises away from the track to its depth and eye, every face four
    corners at most and wound to its side, the ends closed, the canopy, facade and screen where the words say, the
    crowd's share; the stands on their footprints and off the road in a local area, the fence seen through; the voxel
    pole and a scape without the word byte-identical, every other zone unmoved. Every roadway, track and emit byte pin
    stands unchanged. Seen in machine screenshots on a realistic GT circuit, a cartoon kart track and a shaded one; the
    eyes gate is open.
- **Race control** (`roads/race-control.js`): the race's referee, the contest kernel's discipline (one self-contained
  closure, `buildRaceControl`, pure and seeded, a page runs it from its own source). It reads what the timing loops saw
  (a car crossed timing line j, only its next one counting) and calls every place:
  - the five red lights a second apart and out after a held beat the dice choose, or a rolling start; a car that rolls
    first a jump start and its penalty;
  - each sector and lap timed (purple the best of all, green a car's own), the fastest lap, the last lap when the
    leader begins it, an overtake on the line it was made, a yellow, a retirement;
  - the chequered flag at the full distance, every car after it home at its next crossing, a lapped car classified its
    laps down; the result with the penalties in it.
  - `display` is the timing tower: the running order, the gap to the leader and the interval at the same line (or a lap
    or more down), the last and best laps, the race clock, the leader's lap.
  - **Held** on written-out crossings: the lights, the jump start, the laps and the fastest, a pass, the gaps and a
    lapped car, the field home after the flag, a retirement, a line out of order ignored, the same facts the same race,
    no state mutated, the closure run from its own source.
- **Stopping point:** the race page. The broadcast does not yet cover a race: its cues (`CALL_CUES`) gain race control's
  calls, its client a `best` tone (the timing screens' purple) and the tower's feed, and the controllable page inlines
  both when a race carries `broadcast`, feeding race control the checkpoint zones' enters. Each re-pins the contest pages
  that inline the client, so it is its own step. The voxel pole's stands, a stadium section the track runs through and the
  pit building's suites are not built.

### The realistic wardrobe: the legendary merc

The realistic register's character and clothing raised toward the seventh generation at its best: a middle-aged
legendary mercenary in tactical gear, face and hair showing, as the game model (the skinned GLB an engine plays). Then
the same man in a leather jacket. The eyes gate is the operator's.

- **Hair as alpha cards** (realistic laws 7, `REALISTIC_LAWS_VERSION`). The scalp's blades and the beard's locks were
  opaque ribbons (the grass hat): up close they drew as shards. They are now cards that carry a strand texture.
  - A card runs full width to its end (`HAIR_CARD.tip` of its root, never a point), each point its place across and
    along it (`hair-depict.js` `stripMesh` `card`), carried through the pin and the compile to the mesh's provenance.
  - The texture (`epidermis/hair-strands.js` `strandPage`): fine white strands, each tapering, waving and ending at a
    length of its own, filled at the root, with alpha between them. A card draws one of its cells by its index.
  - The texture is a strip under the head's page on the skin's atlas (`dermal-hero.js` `heroSkinPaint` `cardUV`), so
    the figure stays one material; a card's colour is its band's, the root darker than the tip, as before.
  - The figure's material is alpha tested (`alphaMode: 'MASK'`, cutoff 0.4, double sided) when its atlas carries the
    strip, on the GLB (`scene-gltf.js`) and the World page.
  - The strands are the hero's own: most are its pigment, a share (its `grey`) the cards' mean colour, so a greying man
    reads salt and pepper. The mean alone washed every strand grey once the cards showed it lit.
  - A hero minted before keeps its grass hat: the cards are its laws'.
- **`face.scalp`**: the realistic face's cut by word (a style such as `long`, `ponytail` or `crop`, `{ style, …its
  groom }`, or `'none'`) in place of the one its ancestry rolls. Before, the cut could not be named.
- **The kit as pieces** (realistic laws 8, `polygonizer/body-relational-kit.js`). The authored kernel made each piece
  a slab lifted off the skin's envelope. It never saw the tailor's cloth (it looked for a garment by a name the tailor
  no longer gives), so straps and pouches sat inside the shirt, and the belt was two of the cloth's rings copied, so it
  rippled with them. Now each is made as the thing it is, on what the body wears:
  - **A belt is one mass** (`beltOn`): its section read off everything worn at its height across its whole width,
    the hollows spanned as a cinched belt spans them (the section's hull), the same section top to bottom, its edges
    rounded. Its buckle is a frame (`frameBuckle`: four bars, a tongue, the belt's tail through it, a keeper loop).
    It is fitted over what is under it (the piece it is on, the trunk's cloth inside that, the belts before it, the
    skin): a garment wider than it there is worn over it and clears it, as before, and a sleeve hanging beside the waist
    is no girth. A belt within a hand's width of one already made shares its height, cinched over it: a duty belt rides
    over the trousers' belt, never a band of its own above it.
  - **A pouch is a piece** (`pouchOn`): a body with rounded corners and a bevelled front, its back pressed flat to
    whatever stands out most under its footprint, a lid flap over its top with a rounded fold, a closure tab and its
    snap, a seam bead down each front edge. It hangs on its own belt (its top a little over the belt's) and rides it
    rigidly. A thigh rig hangs from the belt above it by a strap down the hip.
  - **Webbing lies on the cloth** (`webbingOn`): along its path, each point lifted over the farthest thing worn within
    the strap's width, the lift eased along, so it lies on the outermost layer (the shirt, a belt) and never stands off
    or sinks. An end that runs to a belt is fastened to it: carried down the body to just over the belt, a ladder lock
    there and a tab over the belt's face. A strap along a path one is already laid on is that strap (a rig's shoulder
    straps and a harness worn with it).
  - **A rig's X is anchored to a waist strap**: straps whose two ends meet at the waist (a harness's) end on a band of
    the same webbing round the body just over the belt, made once for every strap that ends at its height. Each strap
    is cut where it first comes down to the band (never run along it), set onto it and locked there. Its ends had hung
    open at the sides.
  - **A gun harness** (an outfit's vest `cut: 'holster'`, `outfit-plan.js`): the harness's straps, a pistol holstered
    level under the off arm and a double magazine carrier level under the draw arm (`side` the draw hand's), in place
    of the rig's magazine pouches across the chest. On the realistic body the pieces (`holsterOn`: the holster tapering
    to the muzzle's end, the pistol's slide and its grip raked down and forward out of its mouth, a retention strap and
    its snap, a hanger up to the harness; the magazines two pouches turned level, flaps forward); elsewhere the authored
    kernel's boxes. A piece on the trunk lies on the trunk: an arm hanging beside it is no surface (a holster pressed
    to it had ridden on the arm).
  - Each frame a piece is laid by is read out from its part's own axis: an address's normal comes from its neighbours'
    handedness, which a reshaped part can turn over, and a pouch laid along it went into the body.
  - A band round a thigh is a belt on that leg's cloth, read off that leg alone, no higher than a hand under the crotch.
- **The cloth's folds** (realistic laws 8, `polygonizer/body-relational-folds.js`): the folds a game draws, not a
  simulation's, a few broad ridges that keep reading as the body moves (each rides the cloth's own weights, so a bend
  closes the crescents it shows). Crescents inside the elbows and behind the knees, stacked rolls over the boots and at
  the cuffs, the shirt bloused over its belt with gathers under it and flat where the belt cinches. A ridge only ever
  stands out from the cloth, its crease side sharp and its other side soft, its size the cloth's weight by the
  garment's role (`FOLD_CLOTH`: a knit small, canvas sharper, a heavy layer broad, leather broadest). The cloth is
  refined where a fold lies, its new rings' weights mixed from their neighbours; a piece a garment is worn over is left.
- **The man's hips** (realistic laws 9, `body-relational-builds.js` `MALE_HIPS`). The male build narrowed the
  shoulders (its tune, 0.8) but stood on the heroic cast's hip joints, 22 cm apart, the pelvis's skin carried out to
  them. So every male physique had a pinched waist over wide hips, waist to hip 0.76 … 0.79, inside the female band
  (`hero-core-measures.js` `CORE_BANDS`), and from behind and in profile a turntable read a woman. The door warned "the
  waist is narrow for the hips" on every male realistic hero. The hip sockets now come in with the narrowed frame
  (`hipSpan` 0.78, about 17 cm apart), the knees under them as they were, before the slice reads the rig: waist to hip
  0.85 … 0.91 across the physiques (athletic 0.88), the hips 4 to 5 cm narrower. The female build is as it was. The
  hero's `tune.hips` widens the pelvis's girth only, never the sockets.
- **A man's run** (`hero-gaits.js` `HERO_RUN_POLE`): the jog and the sprint as stamped for a man land on a wider base
  (feet about 9 cm apart, legs never crossing), the pelvis turning and swaying less, the shoulders more against it. The
  run as minted (feet nearly on one line, the pelvis turning 8°) read as a woman's on
  a man. The woman keeps it. Stamped where a hero is written, as the walk's pole is: a hero stored before keeps its run.
- **The jacket as built** (`polygonizer/body-relational-jacket.js`), from an outfit's outer garment words, on the
  realistic body. The tailor's jacket was a closed tube whose opening was painted on it (the cloth taken in and coloured
  as what shows there), so an open jacket did not open and its collar stayed a closed ring round the neck.
  - **A real opening** (`openFront`): each ring of the jacket's body a C in section, the inner face round to a front
    edge, the edge turned, the outer face back a leather's thickness out, so the two fronts are edges with a real gap
    between them; the ends turned in and drawn small inside the body, where the tube's caps close them. Its collar is
    opened with it. Each new point carries the weights of the cloth point it was made from.
  - **The construction words** on `language.outer`: `front: 'zip'` (closed on a zip in the gap: its tape behind the
    edges, its teeth, its pull; no V, no lapels, no buttons), `collar: 'shirt'` (the collar's points snapped to the
    chest), `rib: 'cuffs' | 'waist' | 'both'` (knit bands cinched round what is under them, the body and the sleeves
    bloused over them, the card's `Rib` tone), `pockets: 'flap'` (a patch pocket low on each front under a flap with a
    snap, each inside its own front), `epaulettes: true` (a strap over each shoulder, laid by the shoulder's own slope,
    buttoned at the collar), `cloth: 'leather'` or a cloth word (how it folds). `open: true` hangs the fronts apart.
  - Its pieces lie on its own outer face (`faceAt`, `patchOn`: a slab following the curve, not a flat box).
  - **A flight jacket**: the `flight` style card (the A-2), brown leather to the belt on rib bands.
- The principles of the kit and the folds are written down: [garment-principles.md](../docs/garment-principles.md) has
  them as rules, the realistic body's contract points at them, and `/garment-design` reads a piece against them.
- **The lids rest on the eyes** (realistic laws 11, `head-relational-eye.js` `SEAT`). The one skin's opening was a
  tunnel cut straight back to the globe through skin that stood proud of it: the lower lid was the cheek's shelf, 16 to
  17 mm ahead of the globe just under the margin, and toward the corners the upper lid stood out as a thin plate where
  its lid space is shallow. Every realistic face showed a dark void between the lids and the eye. Now the skin within a
  reach of each margin is cut back to the lid shell and rises out of it with the distance from the margin, cut with a
  wide blend so the lid rolls into the cheek rather than kinking. The lower lid stands as far off the globe as the
  upper (about 6 mm with its thickness, where it stood 16), and its margin is rounded by its rim as the upper's is.
  Above the crease the fold now rises to the brow as a pad (`SEAT.fold`): forward out of the crease, which keeps its
  shadow, then near upright under the brow, the brow's underside trimmed to it and the cap at its top blended rather
  than cut hard. It used to stand at the lid's depth well up under the brow, a cove facing down that read near-black
  under any light from above; a straight lean faced it down its whole height. Its ends rise toward the nose and the
  temple. The fit keeps `seat`, so the skin's bake, the hair, the jewellery and the face rig rebuild the same seated
  head.
- **The brow lower, the eye forward** (realistic laws 11, `SEAT.brow`, `SEAT.forward`). The brow's arc hangs 3.7 mm
  lower and the brow's ties 2.8 mm lower, so the eyebrows come down with the fold's arch. A deep-set eye (its globe,
  lids and lashes; the socket and the skin about it stay) comes forward a third of the way from the cornea toward the
  nose's tip, its cornea kept at least 6 mm behind the glabella: about 7 mm on the male pole, none on the female,
  whose eye already sits near the brow's line and would stand proud of her face at the full share.
- **The lower lashes on a seated lid** (`epidermis.js` `SEATED_LOWER`). Out of the tunnel that cut most of their length
  off, they hung from under the lid's band as a long fringe. On a seated lid they root up the margin's front, just
  under the eye, a quarter shorter, nearer level and curled less. A head that is not seated grows them as before.
- A hero minted before keeps what its laws made; a hero minted now is stamped laws 11 (`REALISTIC_LAWS_VERSION`): laws 10 is the hair as its main shapes (`1028-realistic-hair`), the seat after it.

### Table RPG: a pen-and-paper game played in text, its game book, its cast and its arms

#### Table RPG: a pen-and-paper game played in text first
A tabletop role-playing game as a recipe, the concept layer: a module (a rules card, a party rolled from it, a world, its
dungeons, foes, items, tables, beats and a goal) played fully in text, every die rolled in the open, before any page
or picture. The map, the research behind it and what each part is composed from: [docs/table-rpg.md](../docs/table-rpg.md).
No MCP surface changes in this theme; the game type it becomes is the next theme.

- **Rules as procedures** (`lib/graph/table-rpg/table-rpg-systems.js`): a rules card is a resolution procedure and its
  numbers (a d20 against a target, a d20 rolled under, 2d6 in bands, fudge dice for shifts, d100 under a score, a d6
  against two d10), with its abilities, generation methods (rolled in order, rolled and placed by the class, an array,
  points bought), modifiers, hit points, foe ranks, progression and classes. Mojulo ships one generic starter per
  procedure, in its own words and numbers, and no published game: one the person names is written out as a card by
  their model from the rules they supply, checked by the kernel, its `attribution` (if it carries one) printed by the
  referee packet.
- **The kernel** (`table-rpg-kernel.js`): one closure a page can emit by `toString()` (held equal by a test), pure and
  seeded. Dice notation (NdS, d%, dF, keep and drop, exploding), every procedure read as one band, character sheets
  on their own stream per member, the point-crawl world and its days of road, dungeon rooms and links (locked, secret,
  one way, forced), traps, searches, fights (the system's initiative; foes that roll, or players who roll every die and
  take harm on the bands the system says cost), experience, marks on a miss or milestones, rests, tables, a yes/no
  oracle and a dice tape. `legal` / `parse` / `apply` give a typed game its moves; the command list is the save.
- **Portable words**: a module names a faculty, a difficulty word, a foe's rank and a member's role, and the card
  says each in its own numbers, so one scenario plays under every card. The test module (`fixtures/sunken-chapel.js`:
  a village, a road, a chapel with a loop, a lock and its key, a hidden way, a trap, a wandering table) is played to
  its goal under each procedure.
- **Composed with the rest of mojulo**: a member's persona from the egocube (the sheet `create_character { egocube }`
  draws a body from), the party lowered to the live RPG's `play.rpg` and fought by its battle kernel
  (`table-rpg-party.js`), a dungeon drawn from a building's program (`table-rpg-program.js`), the world lowered to the
  epoch map (`table-rpg-world.js`), a dungeon read for whether it plays (`table-rpg-dungeon.js`: reach with keys, a
  key behind its own lock, a lock with no key, the goal, the way back, loops and dead ends, advisory), and the referee
  packet an agent runs a game from in prose (`table-rpg-module.js`).
- **`scripts/table-rpg.mjs`**: the module at a terminal prompt, its referee packet, or a command list's transcript.

Machine gate: the table RPG suites (the dice, each generation method, each procedure's bands, the whole module under
each procedure, the closure against the live copy, the dungeon findings on sound and broken graphs, a program's
dungeon per plan shape, the epoch map through `readMapSpec`, the live party through `readRpg` and a round of the
battle kernel). Eyes gate not run: the author read the transcripts and the packet under every system.

#### Books: a press, a style library, and the game book printed to PDF
A book mojulo makes is one self-contained page that reads on a screen and prints as a book, and headless Chromium
prints it to PDF: the first PDF the export stack writes. The table RPG's game book is the first book on it. The map:
[docs/books.md](../docs/books.md).

- **The style library** (`lib/graph/book/book-style.js`): a style is a look (a presentation theme token, the words
  decks and charts already use; recoloured by a `palette`), a format (one column held in the hand, two columns on a
  full page, one landscape sheet in three panels, a form a page), a paper, and faces for text, titles and tables (font
  shelf keys); presets compose them (`tome`, `zine`, `dossier`, `pamphlet`, `screen`). A dark look printed is advised
  against, never refused.
- **The press** (`book-press.js`): `@page` sets the paper, margins, running title and page numbers; text flows in the
  format's columns; keyed entries, stat blocks, roll tables, boxed notes and figures stay whole across a break; the
  faces the style uses are inlined as `@font-face`, only theirs (a style's page carries no other face's bytes). Pure.
- **The printer** (`book-pdf.js`): `printPdf(html)` through `scene/chromium.js` (consent to fetch, never under the
  plugin profile): the page's own paper, the colours printed, tagged, the headings as the outline.
- **Faces on the shelf**: Crimson Text (a book's text), Courier Prime (its typewriter) and IM Fell English vendored
  from google/fonts, unmodified, each beside its OFL text, in `fonts/LICENSES.md` and `NOTICE`; `fontFaceCss(key,
  styles)` gives a book a vendored face. IM Fell English was already a shelf face falling back to the host's: a cover
  naming `im-fell` (the novel cover's title) now carves in it everywhere, its letters changing once, to the face the
  recipe always meant.
- **The game book** (`lib/graph/table-rpg/table-rpg-book.js`, `table-rpg-maps.js`): a module as a book — the title
  page, how the rules run in the card's numbers, the world and its point-crawl map, each dungeon's flowchart map and
  its rooms keyed by the map's own numbers, the foes as stat blocks, the tables, the party's sheets a page each, the
  dice tape, the colophon (a card's attribution when it carries one). A one-sheet format keeps what the table needs in
  play: the one-page adventure. `scripts/table-rpg.mjs --book out.html --pdf out.pdf --style <preset>`.

Machine gate: the press and style suites (presets, formats, refusals, the faces inlined per role and only the used
ones, the blocks kept whole), the maps (every room once with its key's number, every link by its kind, every road with
its days), the book (keys, sheets, the tape, a card's own words, the one-sheet cut), and the live suite in the e2e tier
printing a book and a one-sheet pamphlet (the pages, the faces embedded). Eyes gate not run: the author printed every
preset and read the pages (fixing four column and map faults on the way); the operator has not.

#### Table RPG: the game type, its page, its export and character creation
The table game becomes a game type beside the board games: `create_game({ table_rpg })`, engine `table-rpg`, its own
page and its own book, no store and no levels. One property on the door, no new tool; the flat tools/list payload's
pin rises 212,300 → 212,500 for it (measured 212,353). The map: [docs/table-rpg.md](../docs/table-rpg.md).

- **The row** (`lib/graph/table-rpg/table-rpg-manifest.js`): `{ kind: 'game', engine: 'table-rpg', title, tableRpg }`,
  the module's keys and a `book` style; the page, the book and the sheets regenerate from it; `update_sketch` plays an
  edit through the kernel first (refused, `Invalid table game`, when it cannot play).
- **The starter** (`table-rpg-starter.js`): `starter: { use: 'crypt' }` makes a whole game from a building's program —
  a town, the road and its table, the dungeon with its loop, lock and key, minions and the boss guarding the prize, a
  wandering table, the goal; what the module writes itself wins.
- **Character creation**: the party rolled by the card's method, each member on its own dice, `egocube` rolling who
  they are (a persona, a name rolled from syllables when none, the role when none); three rolled when no party is
  named. The mint's answer says every sheet as rolled and how it was made, and the checks' findings (advice).
- **The page** (`table-rpg-page.js`): the kernel's own closure on one self-contained page in the book's look and
  faces, the transcript, the moves offered as buttons and typed, every die in the open; the moves kept in the player's
  browser are the save, replayed on load.
- **Where it is**: `/api/sketches/<ref>/game` the page; `/bible` the game book (`?parts=party` the characters' sheets
  alone, `?style=`); the game rail's exits play, book and characters; playtest refuses (no levels to open).
- **Export**: `export_game` writes `game.html`, `book.html`, `characters.html`, and `book.pdf` and `characters.pdf`
  through a browser already on the machine (an export never fetches one: without it the pages print from any browser,
  and the answer says so), with the recipe and a README.
- **Cards**: `get_game_vocab({ id: 'table-rpg' })` (the grammar, every starter, character creation and the book's
  styles, read from their tables); the routing card `table-rpg` with pen-and-paper phrasings and collision rows
  against the live RPG. `scripts/table-rpg.mjs --parts party` prints the characters alone.

Machine gate: the door's suite (a starter's mint and its sheets, the page and the book from the row, a module written
out, refusals, the checks advising, the update gate, the export with a printer injected and without one, the card),
the starter and naming tests, the routing-card and tool-description suites, and two live suites in the e2e tier (the
page in a browser playing Node's game line for line and replaying its kept moves on reload; the book printed). Eyes
gate not run: the author looked at the page and a characters print; the operator has not.

#### Table RPG: the party made characters, photographed into the book
- **The character loop at mint**: `create_game({ table_rpg })` makes each party member rolled on the egocube a real
  character — an egocube row from the very roll its persona came from, then `create_character { egocube }`, children
  of the game's ref, as the fight goal makes its fighters — and records it on the member (`character: <ref>`, the roll
  kept as `egocube: { roll }` so the stored party reads back the same persona). `characters: false` skips it; a member
  may name a character already made. The answer names each member's character
  (`lib/mcp/tools/table-rpg-portraits.js`).
- **Portraits**: the book photographs each character's World page in headless Chromium (the character bible's colour
  turnaround: its palette, its light), a three-quarter figure framed by its height and a bust at the head and
  shoulders, on the book's own paper, kept per character revision; the party lined up on the title page, each bust
  heading its sheet (`tableRpgBook`'s `portraits`). The `/bible` route and `export_game` take them; without a browser
  the sheets print without, and the export names who was not photographed.
- A persona now rolls on the member's own seed (`memberSeed`) with the default path, the roll an egocube row stores.

Machine gate: the door's suite (a member made a character: its sheet and body rows, the member recording it, the stored
roll reading back the persona; the export with photographs injected), the book's (the line-up and the busts placed,
none without), and a live suite in the e2e tier photographing a made character (a figure and a bust, read again from
memory). Eyes gate not run: the author read a starter game's printed book with its three characters; the operator has
not.

#### Table RPG: factioned encounters from the egocube's cast
- **Factions, standing and talk in the kernel**: a module's `factions` (standing −2 hostile … 2 allied, allies,
  rivals) and a foe's `faction`, `heeds` and `scorns`. A fight is spoken to through its leader, the highest-ranked
  foe standing: `parley` (presence), `threaten` (might) or `bribe <treasure>` (presence), once a fight, the standing
  setting the difficulty and what the leader heeds or scorns a step. Talked aside, the foes stand aside and their
  experience is earned; a parley or a bribe warms the faction, a threat cools it, a fumble cools it. Beaten, a
  faction's foes cool it and its allies and warm its rivals. Allied foes stand aside unasked. The `factions` move says
  where the party stands (`table-rpg-kernel.js`).
- **The cast** (`table-rpg-cast.js`): `cast: true | { seed?, as? }` rolls the journey's antagonists on the egocube
  (`rollCast`) and writes them as the mastermind's faction (leader, lieutenant, troops; wary) and the rival's (the
  rival and its hands; neutral), rivals of each other, each foe a persona with what it listens to read from its
  motivation and order. `as` lays the parts on the module's own foes, a starter's boss, minions and bandits unasked;
  what the module writes wins. A foe's `egocube: true` rolls it a persona alone.
- **In print and in the answer**: the book's Factions chapter (a diagram of the party and the factions, the talk and
  the standing ladder in the card's numbers, each faction's people by rank), the referee packet's Factions section,
  and `create_game`'s answer naming the factions and their people, advising on any placed in no room and on no table.

Machine gate: the factions suite (a faction it cannot read refused; the difficulty by standing and by what the leader
heeds or scorns, hostile unheard; a parley, a threat and a bribe that land, each on a seed found in code; standing after
a fight won across allies and rivals; allied foes standing aside; no factions move without factions; the cast's parts,
ranks, factions and determinism; `as` and the starter; the chapter, the diagram and the packet) and the door's (a cast
on a starter: the factions named, the unplaced advised). Eyes gate not run: the author looked at the chapter's page;
the operator has not.

#### Table RPG: the cast's leaders made characters, human or not, photographed into the book
- **Any body**: `cast.people: { <part>: { body?, species?, brief?, facets?, mascot? } }` says what a part of the cast
  is, in the egocube cast's own member words: a person (the default), a beast-kin, a beast (a real species) or a
  mascot. Each foe's persona is read from its body and its temperament (`persona.body`, `persona.species`).
- **Made at mint**: the cast is stored as an egocube cast row (`castRequestOf`: the very request the game reads), and
  the mastermind, the lieutenant and the rival are made characters by their member paths through `create_character`
  (the hero, creature and animal doors, a mascot as a creature), as is a foe rolled alone on the egocube; each
  recorded as its foe's `character: <ref>`, named in the answer's factions. A body the loop cannot make is advised and
  the game goes on (`makeTableCharacters`, formerly `makePartyCharacters`). The game writes its egocube rows from the
  roll or the cast it has already rolled (checked by the kind and rolled where they are written), not resolved as a world
  at mint: a cast's line-up preview mints every member, a minute's work, and is drawn when the row is opened.
- **Photographed**: the foes that are characters are photographed as the party is, framed by the body's own extent (a
  long body by its length between its 2nd and 98th percentiles, a mascot's bust its whole head); the Factions chapter
  lines the leaders up and puts each bust in its entry, a foe of no faction gets its bust over its stat block. The
  `/bible` route and `export_game` take them (`foePortraits`).

Machine gate: the factions suite (each body's persona; an unknown body word refused; the chapter's line-up and busts
placed, none without), the door's (a cast row, the three leaders made with a beast among them, recorded on their foes,
the game reading the beast as its lieutenant), and the live suite photographing a beast-kin, a wolf and a mascot (a
figure and a bust each). Eyes gate not run: the author looked at the six photographs and a beast-kin's; the operator
has not.

#### Table RPG: the cast's beasts made game creatures by the mutagen
- **The egocube cast carries an ooze**: a beast member (`body: 'beast'`) takes `ooze`, the mutagen's words, carried to
  the animal door when it is made (`egocube/cast.js`, `egocube/kind.js`): the species made a game creature, its limbs
  and rig its own. Absent, the animal as it was.
- **The table game uses it**: a beast among the cast's leaders is a creature unless it says otherwise: its own `ooze`,

- **A beast's bust at its head**: framed where its plan seats the head (forward of `neckTop`), not at its highest
  point, which a wing or a horn can be.

Machine gate: the cast and kind suites (an ooze refused off a beast and unknown; carried to the animal door's spec, none

#### Table RPG: arms and artifacts, made by the equipment kernel
- **In the rules**: items of kind `weapon` and `armour` are artifacts with a portable `bonus` (1 to 3; a weapon's
  `faculty` the one it strikes with), taken up with `equip <item> [by <member>]` (the arm replaced goes back to the
  bag), or held from the start (`arms` on a member). A weapon's bonus rides the attack and the harm under every
  resolution procedure; an armour's the defence where the card counts one, else it turns that much of each blow.
- **In the look** (`table-rpg-gear.js`): an item's `build` is the equipment kernel's words, checked by it; `gear: {
  style, foes }` the game's arms language. At mint each item with a build is minted as an equipment item (`artifact:
  <ref>`); a member made a character holds its class's weapon as the kernel makes it (`WEAPON_GEAR`) or the artifact it
  starts with, in the game's style; a person of the cast its role's arms (`ROLE_ARMS`) in the foes' style.
- **The starter** arms its people in its building's style and leaves an artifact with its key (a crypt's barrow blade,
  a keep's warden's shield, a temple's rite staff …). Its foes and items now sit beside the module's, merged by id (a
  character recorded on the starter's boss no longer drops the starter's other foes).
- **The book's Arms and artifacts chapter**: each artifact photographed as an object, its rules, its look in words and
  where it is found; the Sunken Chapel's ossuary hides the bone knife.

Machine gate: the arms suite (artifacts refused that cannot be read; equip, its swap and its words; the weapon's bonus
in the roll under three procedures; the armour on the defence and turning a blow; the builds checked by the equipment
kernel, the class weapon and the starting artifact held, the cast's role arms; the starter's relic with the key, its
style and the merge by id; the chapter), the door's (a member holding a celestial sword, the relic minted as an
equipment item), and the live suite (the armed member and the relic photographed). Eyes gate not run: the author
looked at the armed member and the relic; the operator has not.

#### Table RPG: loot, arms of every kind, and the equipment kernel's hafts and blade heads
- **The equipment kernel** (`equipment/items.js`): the staff takes three blade heads, `spear` (a point, the sword's
  own blade loft in the `blade` word's outline), `axe` (a bearded blade and a poll at the haft's top) and `halberd`
  (the axe's blade low on the head, a point through it, a spike behind), none carrying a stone, and a `reach`: `long`

- **Loot** (`table-rpg-loot.js`): a table written as loot words (`n`, `rank`, `era`, `style`, `forms`) is rolled out
