### The relational creature head: a beast's head the seventh generation's way

Every beast-kin wore a head from the creature library, built for the creature biped: a skull lofted from seven rows of
seven slots, flat-shaded at its facets (it splits at the light's 35° crease), sized for the biped's neck. Measured
against the tiered person's head, it had more triangles (2,464 on the wolf-kin, 1,176 on the person) and less shape: they
went to its eyes, teeth and lids. This theme builds its successor on the realistic hero's head's construction
(`head-relational.js`): points placed by relations, masses as vajras between them, one skin over them.

- **The head** (`creature-heads/relational.js` `relationalCreatureHead`; `CREATURE_RELATIONS`, a preset per skull in
  `CREATURE_HEADS`). In the relational head's frame and units (V, the head's height; the field in STAND units at a
  1.8 m figure). Its relations name a skull's measures:
  - the vault's length and breadth (`craniumLength`, `cephalic`), the crown, the brow;
  - the stop; the muzzle's length, breadth, depth, taper and drop, the nose's pad and the whisker pads;
  - the mouth's line, the gape, the jaw's depth, the chin; the cheek arch's breadth and mass;
  - the eyes' size, set (to the side … ahead), height, pupil (round | slit) and iris; the ears' size, width, set, tilt
    and point.

  The muzzle is two masses meeting at the mouth, as a real one is: the upper (the maxilla and the upper lip, its
  underside the mouth's line) and the lower jaw (narrower, its chin set back, its top on that line), so a mouth can read.
  The ears are blades: a cone squashed through its own facing. The skin is the masses' soft union in two layers: the
  body's masses melted three nearest at a time at a wide blend, then each small feature (the nose, the whisker pads, the
  chin) joined at its own narrow one. A sum over every mass (`−k log Σ e^(−d/k)`, the human head's superposition, which it
  answers by solving its beads deeper) swelled the cat's muzzle a seventh of the head forward where eight masses overlap
  and drowned every feature; a blend picked per nearest pair cracked where the pair changed. The eyes, the nose's pad and
  the mouth's line are SEATED on the skin: each marched out from inside to where the skin crosses, then set (a globe in a
  socket that hugs it as lids do; the pad standing proud; the groove along the surface, never a chord under it).
- **The first two skulls**: the wolf (a long, deep, tapering muzzle off a clear stop, oblique eyes, tall pointed ears
  high on the vault) and the cat (a round vault, a short broad muzzle under a shallow stop, full whisker pads and a small
  chin, wide cheeks, big forward eyes with slit pupils and the iris filling them, broad ears to the top's sides).

- **Worn on the tiered neck** (`beast.head: { relational: 'wolf' | 'felid', relations? }`; `creature-heads/worn.js`
  `creatureHeadOn`, the plan's half in `beast/head.js` `creatureHeadPlan`). Opt-in: a kin still wears its library head by
  default, so no pin moves.
  - **The fit**: the head's STAND units times the figure's height (an ooze's head growth on it). The nape's foot sits
    down the neck's top ring, so the neck runs into the back of the skull. The neck leans 24° under it, and the head is
    raised until the ring below the top stands clear, so the neck keeps two rings.
  - **The skin**: netted as ONE SKIN on the realistic hero's route (`hero-one-skin.js` `oneSkinHead`), joined smoothly
    to the neck's column and sealed point for point to the neck's highest ring that stands clear of it. Its lips are cut
    along the mouth's line, from the front back along the muzzle's sides to the corners, and turned in along the skin's
    own facing. The nose's pad is painted.
  - **The new options** (each default the human head's, which stays byte for byte): how far back the cut reaches, which
    way the lips turn in, which rim is the seam's (the one nearest the ring: a slanted ring's low side
    held a pinch's hole lower than its middle) and where a globe's edges are found (along each slot, so a slit pupil is
    ringed as the lens it now is).
  - **The bind**: the jaw bone carries the lower lip, the chin and the throat ahead of the ramus; the crown stays the
    head's. The rig's jaw is hinged at the condyle with its tip at the chin; its head top is on the crown.
  - **The eyes and the ears**: the globes are their own parts in rounded sockets (the lid's rim a fold the net resolves).
    The ears are their own closed parts netted from their blades, their inner faces painted. The face's colours come from
    the kin's library head, toned to its coat.
  - **The coat's cover on the head**: the skin and the ears take the cover's tile by a box chart (`coverChart`, a mesh
    part's way: `beast/cover.js`), so the fur runs onto the head with no seam at the neck.
  - **Teeth and gums** (`creature-heads/dentition.js`). The arch is the mouth's line carried in by the lip's thickness.
    Along it the teeth are placed by a relation, `dentition` (canid | felid; `fang` the canines' length): incisors, the
    canine, premolars, the carnassial, a molar, each a small cone (a chisel, a round fang, a blade) rooted in a ringed gum.
    The upper row and gum are the head's, the lower the jaw's, so they part as the jaw opens. The gum lines sit a little
    past the mouth's line, so parted, the crowns stand clear of the lips. Shut, all of it lies inside the skin: a tooth
    that would stand out of it is moved in, then shortened, until it fits. The mouth's seated line, which the arch is
    built from, had two points seated on the wrong side of a narrow muzzle (their march started past its far side), and
    the groove kinked there; each march now starts no further over than the midline. hero-live gained a Mouth view.
  - **The mouth's lining** (`creature-heads/mouth.js`), in place of the one skin's closed bag. The bag's band between
    its head half and its jaw half stretched into a flat wall across the wolf's long side opening. The lining is an upper
    shell (the cheek walls and the palate, the head's) and a lower one (the cheek walls and the floor, the jaw's), open
    along the lips and joined only at the back by the throat, which stretches facing the eye as a throat does. A thin
    veil down the midline, from the palate to the floor, closes the view through from one side's opening to the other's
    (a long gape's two openings line up); edge on from the front, it never hides the teeth. The teeth and the gums stand
    inside the lining, so the whole row shows when the mouth opens. (Its first build bound the floor to the head: a point
    id carrying a dot is read as a station and a slot, so its jaw blend never applied.)
  - **A beast's head opens its jaw in a clip** (the door's `jaw` key), the library head's too: both carried the jaw bone,
    and the door refused the key on them.

  Not yet: the other kin as presets, the sheet's head and the lexicon on relations, and the expression actions. The
  coat's pattern atlas does not reach the head yet (it charts ringed parts; the head is a mesh). The head has no tongue. The cat's mouth is a straight line (its cleft under the nose is a lip
  relation to come). A head costs some seconds to net, so worn heads are kept by what a build reads.

Machine gate (`creature-heads/relational.test.js`): one closed skin; a relation moves what it names (the muzzle the
nose's tip, the cephalic the vault's sides); no swelling past the beads; the eyes and the nose seated (a globe breaks the
skin, the pad stands proud and paints); the skulls told apart by their relations; deterministic. Eyes: the wolf and the
cat surface-netted in clay from six sides (the operator's to judge). Worn (`creature-heads/worn.test.js`): the word swaps
the library head for the skin, its globes, a mouth and its ears, and without it the kin keeps its skull; the skin is
sealed to each point of the neck's last ring; the jaw bone carries the chin and the lower lip, never the crown or the
upper lip, and the rig's jaw tip is the chin; the cover runs onto the skin and the ears, not the eyes or the nose's pad;
the word is refused by name; the teeth and the gums are a row on each bone, every point inside the shut skin, the canines
the longest pair, the felid's rows shorter; the mouth's lining lies inside the shut skin and no face of it joins a head
point to a jaw point but the throat's. Eyes: the wolf-kin and the cat-kin through hero-live, the library heads beside them, at
rest and with the jaw open (the operator's to judge).

### Scene composer: a game's intent resolved into one composed interior

An interior's look is composed, not picked: the registers (a hangar, a warehouse, a lab, an office) become presets on
four axes the composer resolves from a game's intent (construction, palette, light plot, dressing), one best guess
stored in the recipe as numbers. Built so far:

- **The axes** (`era/style/bay-axes.js`): a register card split into its construction, palette, plot and dressing, each
  a table of its own; a register is a preset naming a value on each. Every bay page byte for byte as it was.
- **The intent reader** (`era/compose.js`): a stage's `compose`, words (`'a cold lab with military greys under sodium
  light'`) or `{ words?, register?, construction?, palette?, plot?, dressing? }`, read into a value on each axis: an axis
  its words name takes that value, the rest take the register the words lean to (a place's words count twice), else the
  kit's register. A named axis is pinned. The longest phrase is heard first and taken out, so the words inside it are
  not heard again. Read once at authoring time (`create_sketch` / `update_sketch`) and stored as `{ intent, resolved,
  said }`; the stage builds on `bayKitOf(resolved)` and never re-reads the words.
- **The rooms' roles** (`era/compose-roles.js`): a composed stage's plan carries `compose: { axes, roles }`, each room's
  part in the walk read from the plan's own graph (a program's building, a hall and a hand-laid stage alike): the goal the
  climax, the first way in the arrival, a stair's room and a long narrow room passages, the biggest room the landmark when
  it stands well over the rest, the deepest dead ends pockets (two a storey at most: a corridor building has a dead end at
  every door), the rest rests. Each names its set piece and its FOCUS, where the room is built to be looked at: the way on
  from an arrival or a passage, straight across from the doorway come in by elsewhere. `compose.roles` pins a room's.
  A stage not composed carries none of it.
- **Any palette on any construction**: a swatch that leaves a catalog material its own face lends that face (`own`, the
  catalog's colour) to a dressed cut laid in its place; a program is laid for the kit it composes (a construction with
  wider doors widens the corridors). A deep sweep composes every pairing of the four axes.
- **The light plot** (`era/compose-plot.js`): a composed room lit from its role. The mood (`even` 2:1, `drama` 4:1,
  `noir` 8:1; read from the words, the darkest heard, or `compose.mood`) sets the ratio of the light at each room's focus
  over the room's mean and thins the shell's lamps into fill; a KEY hangs over each focus, its colour the plot's own that
  stands farthest in warmth from the fill, its intensity solved for the ratio by each role's weight (the goal and the
  landmark the whole ratio, the way on 0.8, a pocket's find a glint, a still room none). Measured by the seventh
  generation's falloff without walls (a model of the bake) and reported on the stage as `compose.plot`. Seen in a hangar
  suite in gen-7: the rooms darken by about a third from even to noir while the focus holds its light; on screen that is
  about 1.3 to 1, not the model's 8 (the key lands on the doorway's floor and jambs, no set piece standing there yet, and
  the page tone-maps); gen-6 dims the whole room, the key flattened by its bake's shoulder. `scripts/spikes/bay/moods.mjs`.
- **Bake or live, per light** (`compose-plot.js` BEATS, `scene/channels/form.js`): a key a beat changes, an `alarm` (a
  beacon's sweep in the register's signal colour), a `pulse` (a slow breath) or a `flicker` (a failing lamp, mostly on),
  is solved with the room's lamps but laid by none of its corners in the seventh generation's bake: the page lights it
  whole (its falloff and its cosine on the face, no shadow) and swings its key in time (`__mojForm.at` holds a moment for
  a capture). By role and mood: the goal pulses in drama and sounds its alarm in noir, a pocket's find flickers in noir;
  `compose.beats` pins one to a room, or `'none'`. The sixth generation bakes it steady. A room without a beat emits the
  form channel byte for byte as before. Seen (`scripts/spikes/bay/beats.mjs`): a noir hall's alarm swings the wall round
  its focus from 73 to 86 in mean luminance, peak to trough, with no page errors.
- **The report, measured on the bake** (`era/compose-report.js`): a composed stage reports `compose.report`, each room's
  focus over its room's mean read from the seventh generation's baked corners (`cornerLight`: the ambient, every steady
  lamp where it sees the corner, its bounce), a beat's room at its peak, and laws that advise: `focus` (every keyed room's
  focus reads brighter than its room), `way-on` (the way on lit over the dead ends), `lit` (no room dark against the
  rooms' mean), `palette` (the colour theorist's targets reached). Without that bake (the sixth generation) it reads the
  plot's model and says `measured: 'model'`. A storeyed building's storeys keep the roles the whole building gave them,
  and their reports merge, the laws read across every storey.
- **Keys tuned on the bake** (`compose-plot.js` keyTuner, `formLightFaces`'s `tune`): measured on the bake, the plot's
  model fell well short (a hangar hall's landmark 0.86 of its room in even, asked 2; 2.1 in noir, asked 8: the model lit
  points in the air, the bake lights surfaces, with shadows, bounce and the ambient). Each key is now scaled on the bake's
  own shares so its focus holds the ratio, at most ten times the middle fill lamp's light before the mood thinned it
  (past that a key burns its focus out); a room it cannot bring there is reported `short`. The reach a focus is read by
  scales with its room (a fixed one covered half a small room's floor, and no key lifts that much). Seen in the hangar
  suite in gen-7: even reaches its ratios, drama within a tenth, noir about half (3.4 and 4.8 of 6.4 and 8): one key does
  not make a spot eight times its room without burning it out. On screen the doorway over the walls reads 1.03, 1.33 and
  1.52 from even to noir (0.93, 1.08 and 1.31 before the keys were tuned).
- **The dressing** (`era/compose-dress.js`, `era/compose-lay.js`): a composed room's things, laid as a sane default the
  operator then changes. Each is an item in the recipe (`props: [{ id, kind, room, at, facing, level?, scale? }]`), laid
  once at authoring time (`create_sketch` / `update_sketch`) and read by the build; its id is its place
  (`hall/+y/crate-2`, `hall/focus/generator`), and update_sketch's own patch edits it by id (`remove`, `set`, `add` into
  `props`: manifest-patch.js learned the list), the room keeping the rest where they stood. `props: 'reroll'` lays them
  again, `props: false` lays none. A set piece where a role names one (a register's great object at a landmark's focus,
  scaled with its room; a find in a pocket, a prize at the goal, a sign over the way in), clusters of the dressing's
  pieces along the walls by role and mood (a passage left clear, a noir pocket cluttered), stacked where a piece stacks,
  and never in a keep-out: a doorway's approach, a stair with its foot and head, a doorway's sightline to its room's
  focus (a set piece the approach takes moves to the nearest clear place). Pieces are rows (`PIECES`, a set per
  dressing: crates, ammo cans, drums and tool chests; racking and carts; benches, a fume hood and instrument racks;
  desks, filing and lockers), built of boxes and prisms painted with the kit's own surfaces, so they take the composed
  palette. Each thing is named on its faces, has a collider and an anchor (a `prop` of its piece's class), so
  breakability takes it by the game's degree: the words name it (`firefight` cover, `demolition` world; the recipe's
  `destruction` where it sets none, `compose.destruction` pinned) and an item's own `breakable` wins. The dressing's laws
  (keep-outs, sightlines, the count per room) on the stage's `compose.dress`. Seen (`scripts/spikes/bay/dress.mjs`): a
  hangar, a warehouse, a lab and an office, every law holding, no page errors.

### Scenes in the seventh generation

- **A new scene is drawn in gen-7.** A walkable scene minted through `create_sketch`'s geocube kind (`words`, or `show:
  'path'` / `'trail'` written) has its cube's `era` stamped `gen-7` at mint (`era/geocube.js` stampSceneEra, beside the
  solid stamp in `lib/mcp/tools/sketch-mint.js`): its land, stones, grass, trees and bushes read as form under the cube's
  light, its plants in the wind. New is a scene with no seed yet (a path or a trail draws its seed at its first mint), so a
  row already minted, or one restored from its export through `create_sketch`, keeps the era it renders in; a cube that
  names its era keeps it (`cube.era: 'gen-6'` is the painted render). The `scene` routing card and the geocube manual say
  so. Of seventeen scene phrases from the card, fourteen land on island-noon (meadow, alpine, desert, grove flora) and
  draw wholly in gen-7; the three on jungle-haze ("a forest walk", "a jungle path", "a bamboo grove") wholly so too since
  bamboo has a form of its own (below).
- **Fixed on the way:** the form flora read a cube's whole `colour` as colours; a stamped cube carries its `shade` hue
  there too (`form/flora-read.js` reads only the colours it uses, as hex or bytes).
- **Gen-7 bamboo** (`form/bamboo-form.js`). A culm the vegetation library grows (vegetation/bamboo.js growCulm: jointed,
  tapering, nodding under its leaves, its branches alternating sides) read as form: its culm a tube through its nodes, a
  darker band at each (its colour its age's), its branches thin tubes; its leaves gathered into cells of 0.7 m, a clump of
  narrow `lance` leaves each facing out of the culm and up, and two sprays from each clump's heart inside its rim near the
  eye (the outline kept). A bamboo card's culms (era/isekai.js bambooItems) grow on the trail as Moso, the running grove's
  straight culm (`FLORA_BAMBOO`), three templates each a culm of its own at the clump's middle height, every culm turned
  to lean out of its clump's middle; its wood waxy and smooth in its own colours; in the wind it bends from its foot, more
  than a tree's limbs (`culmPhi`: it has no trunk, it flexes). Measured on a "bamboo grove in the morning" scene
  (jungle-haze): 53 plants, 0.21M to 0.25M triangles. A spray's twig strip now takes the leaf a shade darker (its brown
  over the leaf's green had tinted it pink).
- **The bamboo in the level's colours, and the painted copies gone.** A culm took its species' own green and stood out
  of the cube's palette (teal on jungle-haze's olive): it is now tinted 70% of the way to the level's foliage
  (`CULM_TO_LEAF`), and less glossy. The painted culms and leaf sprays still showed in the same places: a group drawn in
  several meshes (its faces split by their tiles) is one name in the page's `meshes`, and only the last was hidden; with
  the form's plants on the page every mesh of the groups it replaces is hidden (no plants: the page as it was).

### Snow and footprints in gen-7

- **Snow drawn by the form render** (`era/snow.js` snowMap, `scene/channels/form-land.js`). The gen-7 page drew a level's
  snow as the painted surface it reads nothing of, with stepped bands at the trail's edge. Read for the form render (the
  read's `ctx.form`), a level lays no snow faces over its ground: it hands the page a map of where the snow lies (the
  snow field, read on the ground's own normal, half a metre a texel), and the layered ground lays the snow over whatever
  is beneath, held per pixel only where the ground is level enough (a rock's ledge white, its face bare), its edge
  wandering in and out over a metre and finer. It buries the ground's own detail (deeper, more), swells in soft drifts a
  couple of metres across and glitters (a grain in fifty, polished, lit through the light); on the trail it is trodden,
  packed and greyed, the soil showing through as far as it is shallow. Its colour is the snow's own (snowAlbedo) solved
  under the cube's light as the palette's colours are (`snowBase`). The grass thins in it by the cube of the share its
  depth leaves standing (the near blades stand their full height), and the plants carry it: a leaf turned up past its cap
  (capOf) takes it, a share of them by the depth, where the map says it lies. The stones' painted caps stay as they were.
- **Footprints** (`scene/channels/form-land.js`, `PRINTS`; window.__formPrints). The walker's steps press into the sand of
  a land with dunes and into its snow: a sole (heel and ball, a tread, its rim pushed up) every 0.8 m, left and right, on
  a map 12 m across that moves with the walker; the ground reads it a march along the view into the print (its far wall
  seen, its near one hidden), lights its walls from their slopes, erases the ripples and the drifts where the foot
  pressed and shades its inside (a snow print holds the sky's blue). A sand print is 3.5 cm deep and the wind fills it
  back over a minute; a snow print is as deep as the snow lets it (to 12 cm) and lasts ten. Under the form render the
  gen-6 snow's footprint bed (`channels/snow-prints.js`) is not laid; gen-6 pages keep it. A land with neither dunes nor
  snow carries none of this: the same page to the byte.

### The trail's ground allotted

- **Grass in sections** (`form/land-read.js`, `scene/channels/form-grass.js`). The sward has three lengths, each in
  areas of its own: tall, medium and short. Near the eye the medium grass was drawn under the tall grass; now each
  length draws only where the sward is that length. The medium is the same clump lower on a finer grid. A long sward
  (`'tall'`, the default) lays a share of its grass medium (`SWARD_MEDIUM`, 45%, a field of stretches about 11 m across)
  between its tall ones. A biocube names its own shares with `flora.grass.sward: { short?, medium? }`.
- **Nothing through anything** (`era/isekai.js` `ALLOT`, `form/land-read.js`, `form/land-stones.js`). In the form
  render each thing on a trail claims its ground: a stone its footprint, a trunk its foot, a bush or an arrangement its
  reach. No grass grows in a claim, thinning and shortening toward it so no blade leans into a boulder or a trunk, and
  no ground stone lies in one. No tree stands in a stone's ground. The plants carry their claims (`plants.clear`).
- **A clear overlook** (`form/flora-read.js` `viewHeld`). A raised view, a camera whose eye stands 5 m or more over
  what it looks at, claims what it looks over: a crown rising over its eye within 25 m ahead of it is held back. The
  trail's cliff-top view sees the trail again past the taller trees. The rest of the trees keep the heights they had.
- The gen-6 renders are unchanged: the claims, the sections and the held trees are the form render's alone.

### The 7G anime head: the hero's acting, read as drawings

The anime hero acts with the realistic hero's acting (its beats, emotions, gaze, lines and recordings), read as anime
draws it: a library of drawings per layer (eyes, lids, brows, gaze, mouth), each a real form on the head that reads
from any angle, and a timing grammar (keys, holds on twos and threes, snaps, in-betweens). The default anime hero's
head first, in one style. It is a higher setting of the anime head, at home from T3 (a late PS3 / PS4 hero): asked
for, it is built at any tier; unset, a take at T3 or higher gets it and below T3 is lowered to the four channels. A
hero with no take and no setting is today's head, byte for byte. The eyes gate is the operator's.

- **The drawings** (`polygonizer/anime-drawings.js`): the vocabulary, by layer: the brows (raised, low, angry, worried),
  the lids' shapes at the open eye (angry, sad, wide; the closures stay the head's knots), the gaze's positions (left,
  right, up, down; pupils shrunk in shock) and the mouth (the vowels A I U E O, the shout, the frown, the cat's ω, the
  wavy line, the small mouth, the smirk), each with the words a 2D brief draws it by and the four-channel face it lowers
  to. A face is one drawing per layer: the brows, the lids and the mouth share no vertex and add exactly; the gaze is
  drawn at its positions, since the lids clip the lenses.
- **The studio's new words** (`anime-form.js` `drawing`, through `animeHead`): the brow block raised, its inner end
  raised or knit down toward the nose; the upper lid lowered at either end or raised whole, its aperture, white, lens
  clip and lid band following one outline; the lenses slid and the pupil scaled; the mouth's outline opened per lip,
  widened, its corners lifted or dropped, squared, drawn as ω or as a wave. Each keeps the head's topology and turns no
  face over, within ranges measured on the default head. A head with no drawing is the studio's, byte for byte.
- **The eye's socket** (sculpt `orbit`, a depth of the head's height): the socket cut as planes, so the face breaks into
  blocks in profile and at three-quarter: the brow's plane runs back to an apex just over the eye and the cheekbone's
  comes forward from it (a "<"), and the nose's side walls angle in down along the bridge, setting the brow and nose apart
  from the cheekbones. The planes meet in soft fillets, and an eye in a socket is built with more rings about it, so no
  streak or raised rim shows around it. The eye, its lids, its lenses and its brow sit in the socket and act as before. A
  head without it keeps its bytes.
- **The pyramid nose** (sculpt `noseShape: 'pyramid'`; `round`, the graphic base's, unchanged): a ridge between two flat
  side planes, its root at the eye's line where the lids meet and set back a little there, the bridge rising straight to
  a tip no further out than the round nose's, its underside cut back to the lip: in profile the centre line's "<" (the
  brow, back to the root, out to the tip) keeps step with the socket's, so the nose reads by its bridge, not by sticking
  out. The tip and dorsum words still size it.
- **The jaw curved in** (sculpt `jawHollow`, a depth of the head's height; none at 0): below the cheekbone the lower face
  narrows toward the jaw's edge and on through its underside, gently at first and more toward the edge, every point by
  its own distance from the middle, so the jaw's side turns down and away from a side light instead of rounding out
  into it, and its edge turns under with no lip. The centre line, the chin's point and the cheekbones keep their place.
- **The lips flat** (sculpt `flatLips`, 0 to 1; none at 0): the rim the studio raised round the mouth, which read as
  lips, laid flat on the face, so the mouth reads drawn, shut or open, in every drawing. The skin round it and the
  mouth's own outline stay where they were.
- **The anime head's form by default** (hero laws 19, `anime-looks.js` `ANIME_FORM`): an anime hero minted now wears the
  socket (`orbit` 0.025), the pyramid nose, the jaw curved in (`jawHollow` 0.02) and the lips flat (`flatLips` 1), under
  every other sculpt layer, so its own words move or undo each (`flatLips: -1` the studio's rim again). Each base wears
  its own beside it (`ANIME_FORM_POLE`): the male's head narrower (`width` 0.95) and his jaw turned under by half as
  much, so less of a plane shows under its edge; the female's chin shorter (`chinHeight` 0.9). The bases' feature bands
  hold under it, each nudged back inside: the male's opening a hair taller, the female's nose tip a hair further out and
  higher, her lip line a hair higher.
- **The anime face smooth in an engine** (`export_model`, the lit, skinned export of an anime hero minted under laws
  19): its corners carry the studio's welded shading normals and no baked shade, so the engine's light shades the face
  as one smooth form, a painted figure's, instead of its triangles; the realistic body's path. A hero minted before
  keeps its export, byte for byte. Each base keeps its feature bands under it (`ANIME_FORM_POLE`): the male's opening a
  hair taller, since the socket reads his lid band a hair heavier, and the female's tip a hair further out, since the
  pyramid sets it nearer the face; so the default hero is advised nothing. A hero minted before keeps its head, byte for
  byte; the child's round face and the studio's own face (`sculpt: false`) do not wear it.
- **The anime hero performs** (the door's `perform` on `head: 'anime'`; `acting: 'full' | 'basic'` on the anime head):
  the same takes the realistic hero plays, each a face-only clip in an export (`face:<take>`), its recorded lines inside
  the GLB and beside an engine pack's scene. Unset, a take on a target of T3 or higher draws the 7G, below it the four
  channels; `full` draws it at any target and `basic` never.
- **The reading** (`face-acting/anime-read.js`): a take read frame by frame as drawings, one per layer (each eye's brow
  and lid, the gaze, the mouth): anger's knit brows and narrowed lids, surprise's raised brows and wide lids, sadness's
  worried brows, happiness's smile, a thought's turned gaze; every layer held on twos but a spoken closure, the mouth in
  kuchipaku (a, i, u, e, o, shut on m, b and p), the gaze stepped. Keyed STEP, so a drawing snaps instead of melting
  through its neighbour; lowered, the same frames weigh the four channels.
- **The 7G rig** (`anime-face-rig.js` `sevenG`): beside the four channels' targets, kept as they were, each drawing is a
  target differenced from the exact head built at it, a brow and a lid per side and the sided mouths per side, with the
  correctives for the pairs that do not add (a lid's shape over a turned gaze, a brow over its shut eye), so a face drawn
  per layer is the exact build of its drawings. Its cost is stamped on the rig (`meta.sevenG`), and a hero whose layout
  moves its vertices skips it with the reason.
- **The pyramid nose points up** (`anime-form.js` PYRAMID): the tip stands out past the face and turns up, its line
  hollowed from the bridge and its underside cut back from a point set above the pronasale to the lip, so the side
  profile reads by it; the face gains a row halfway in each gap through the nose's band, so the tip and its underside
  are drawn by rows, not one edge. The pyramid draws no nose line: its shade plane carries it. A new word raises its
  root toward the brow (`bridgeRoot`), the bridge then rising from between the brows with a shallower dip.
- **The anime face's principles** ([docs/anime-face-principles.md](../../../../docs/anime-face-principles.md)), built
  into the head: the brow never covers the eye (sculpt `browClear`: over the eye the brow is held above the widest lid
  any drawing draws, so a lid's drawing never moves it; the form wears 0.05), the socket follows the brow (its recess
  rises to the brow's middle at rest, and its rim warps with the brow as it acts, raised with it, drawn down at the inner
  end with a knit, never below the lash band; the 7G rig adds a corrective per brow over each lid where the warped rim
  meets the lid's rings), no line where the form carries it, the profile read
  by its blocks, no deformation, drawings snap. The formed head's feature bands are its own (`ANIME_FORM_POLE` bands:
  its nose stands out, its brow held off the eye), a style's over them.
- **The open smile** (`mouth.beam`, a 7G mouth drawing): the top lip held level on the lip line, the bottom dropped
  into a U under it and the corners lifted, so a smile can open without its top line moving; the reading draws an
  open jaw under a smile with it (a laugh), where it drew a plain "a" and lost the smile.

### Caverns: building into the rock

A cave is the room of building against the rock: two cliffs with a ceiling. Cut into a trail's cliff on the geocube's own
rock (its walls the cliff's rock, its floor scree, a ceiling under the land), lit by what its mouth lets in.

- **The cave** (`era/cave.js`, a trail's `ground.caves: [{ y, depth?, width?, height?, along?, mouth? }]`): a centreline
  from the cliff's foot at station `y` into the rock, then along behind its face (a gallery), held inside the site's back
  edge. The trail's grid is cut to its floor (rising a little inward) and only cut, the land before the cliff left as it
  lay; its sides fall steep, so its walls are the cliff's own rock faces, and its floor is the land's soil with rock at the
  walls' feet, nothing growing on it. A LID of rock is laid over it wherever the land stood above its ceiling: the
  ceiling under it (a dome springing at the walls), the land as it stood on top, a skirt where its edge shows, the cells
  at its edge cut along the line the land meets the ceiling on. The mouth is where the cliff's face falls below the
  ceiling; `mouth` a taller entrance, the ceiling flaring down from it over a width in, opening as a cleft where it
  stands taller than the rock over it. Each cave an anchor (`kind: 'cave'`).
- **Its light** (`caveLight`): each face under a lid lit by what it sees of the day against what an open face of its tilt
  would: the sky through the mouth (the polygon form factor, strip by strip where the line to it stays in the cave), the
  sunlit land before the mouth, and the glow of its cross-sections (every half its width along it, each giving back the
  rock's share of what reaches it), so light is carried in and round a bend and a big cave lights as a small one of its
  shape does; the sun its own (the lid casts with the land), its share kept for the live sun; never darker than a floor.
- **Lined with the geocube's rock** (`caveRocks`): the land's own boulders (`isekai.js` boulderFaces, broken edges and
  all) along each wall and across its far end in two staggered rows up to where its ceiling springs, and slabs hung
  upside down across its ceiling from where a taller mouth has come down; the cut and the lid behind them the rock they
  are set in. No grass hat on any; never in the walkway (at a bend a wall of one leg is the way into the next).
- **Rock behind the cliff** (`trail.ground.behind`, 0 to 80 m): the land over the far cliff that much deeper, the cliff
  where it was, for a deep cave or a mountain's base; with `ground.cliff.height` a cave big enough to drive an elephant
  through (22 m wide, a 24 m mouth, in a 34 m cliff) lights and lines as a small one does.
- **Its register** (a cave's `light`, `CAVE_LIGHTS`): the same rock a base's, a temple's or a grotto's by what lights it
  past its daylight. `fluorescent` hangs tubes along its crown (two rows in a wide cave), cold white; `torch` sets
  sconces on both walls in front of their rock, warm; `bio` grows glowing clusters at the walls' feet and from the
  ceiling, cyan-green, faint. Each fixture is drawn bright, its own light; each lamp lays its colour on the faces that
  can see it (in the cave, under its ceiling), falling with the square past its near distance, added to what the day
  lays, the same at any hour (against a darker hour's bake, the more). A register is laid for a cave 8 m across and
  scaled with the cave (`lampScale`): in a hall its tubes are high-bay floods and its sconces braziers.
- **The cavern** (`era/cavern.js`, a trail's `ground.cavern: true | { height?, skylight?, formations?, light?, cracks?,
  ends? }`): a whole trail underground, a level could be set in one. The land is the geocube's, closed in: the open side
  and the ends raised to the far cliff's top, the walk's notch through each end kept, under a pretend ceiling of the
  cliff's rock (a lumped dome over the site, its rim over the walls' tops, a skirt round its edge down into the land, or
  to a lintel over the walk with `ends: 'open'`, a passage out). Nothing grows in it: no grass, no tree, no far layers,
  no biocube flora; its floor soil and scree, its water a trail's. Its formations stand off the walk and out of the
  water: stalagmites, stalactites hung over them and on their own, columns where a pair nearly meets, the land's rock.
  It is lit by its dark (the page's sky a room's), the CRACKS in its ceiling (`cracks`: jagged slits of day drawn bright,
  their light falling to the floor), a `skylight` (a hole over the walk: the day's sky through it, the sun's shaft), its
  register's lamps along the walk (`light`: torch by default) and the bounce of all of it round the hall (the rock's share
  of the mean light on its floor). An anchor (`kind: 'cavern'`); `scripts/spikes/caves/cavern.mjs` captures it.
- **Its floor, soil and scree** (`floorKind`, `floorDress`): a cavern's ground is soil, its walk packed earth and the
  floor off it a darker dirt; scree lies round its rocks (its walls' feet, its formations, its boulders, the bigger
  stones strewn on it; a pebble sheds none), rubble nearest; its walk is broken by stretches of the rock it runs through
  (worn bedrock, a limestone pavement; natural flagstones; plates) and patched with gravel, its edge frayed into the
  dirt. The surfaces are smooth fields taking the floor in order (`floorFields`), each face cut along their contours
  (`floorPieces`), so they meet in rounded lines, never along the land's cells; each surface a tile in the cube's own soil or rock, each face lit by the cavern's own light at its corners
  (`cavernLightAt`). Only the hall's floor: the walls' tops and the plateau under the ceiling stay the rock's. Its edges
  are strewn as a dirt trail's are (`local-meru/broken-land.js` strewEdge, now taking its numbers, EDGE's by default),
  heaped evenly both sides with more and bigger stones reaching further out and in (`CAVERN_EDGE`), so no line shows
  between the walk and the floor; no grass hat on any stone underground. It is still a trail: its beats and its walk as
  any trail's, a level's section as any is.
- **Its wall rocks** (`wallRocks`): small rocks (0.3 to 1.1 m, most small) heaped along the foot of every wall, the far
  cliff's and the open side's, one to three a step, found where the land lies level past the wall's face, out of the
  walk: the land's boulders, no hat.
- **Its colour key** (`era/cavern-key.js` `cavernKey`, the colour theorist's offer to a cave, as `flora-colours.js` is to
  trees): one key the cavern is painted and lit in, solved from the world's own palette and its register. The register
  names a family of light and the world turns it inside it, never out (a torch toward the world's soil, a tube toward its
  sky, a growth's glow toward its nearest accent); the shade is the temperature opposite the key's (a warm key, a cool
  shade), taken by its dark and half by its bounce, so light given back keeps some of the key's warmth; the cracks and
  the skylight let in the world's daylight; the formations are the rock lifted toward the soil, paler than the walls;
  the set's accent is the world's accent farthest round the wheel from the key; what a set is built of (metal, stone,
  wood, a drab, cloth) is in the key. Its laws (temperature, family, accent apart, formations lifted) are measured and
  read out on the cavern's anchor (`key`); advice, none refuses. A cave's lamps take a key where one is given, and a
  lamp may carry its own light (`era/cave.js` lampLight); a cave without one lights as before.
- **Its set** (`era/cavern-set.js`, a cavern's `set: true | 'base' | 'temple' | 'grotto' | { use?, mood? }`): the set
  designer in a cave, the scene composer's reading of a walk laid on the trail's beats, one room each (the trailhead the
  arrival, a pinch or a crossing a passage, the landmark the landmark, a pocket a pocket, a reveal or a rest a rest, the
  exit the climax). Each beat's set piece stands at its focus off the walk (`true`, the register's use: a base's
  generator, a temple's altar, a grotto's geode at the landmark, scaled to the hall where it fits; a prize, a reliquary
  or a great crystal at the exit; a find in a pocket's middle; a barrier, or standards either side of the walk, at the
  way in), on a stone plinth where the land falls under it; clusters of the use's pieces beside the walk (the rooms'
  crates, ammo crates, drums and tool chests, stacked where they stack; the cave's own urns, braziers, crystals and
  fungus), never in the walk, the water, on a rock or a formation, a passage left clear. Every piece is painted in the
  key (a set piece's paint its accent) and lit by the cavern; a brazier's fire and a crystal's glow are lamps of their
  own in the key's light. The LIGHT PLOT hangs a key light over each focus the role weighs (`compose-plot.js`
  LIGHT_PLOT.roles), a tight pool across the temperature from the cave's light (a cool shaft of day in a torch-lit temple
  or a glowing grotto, a warm sodium in a fluorescent base), its strength solved so the focus stands at the mood's ratio
  over the walk round it.
  Each piece is a prop anchor (a collider; the set's own marked); the cavern's anchor reads the set out (its use, mood,
  plot and laws: every piece off the walk, every focus at its ratio). Opt-in: a cavern without `set` holds none.
- **The meru's rock**: a trail with caves, or a cavern, wears the meru's gen-7 rock fabric, strata and joints near the eye, inside and
  out.
- **The geocube card** says it; `scripts/spikes/caves/cave.mjs` captures a cave from the approach, wide, at the mouth,
  from its far end and up at its ceiling.

### Cloth relief: the realistic wardrobe as PBR material

Operator: "for 7th gen and higher resolution, can we add textures on clothing via parallax? creases on leather, cloth like
PBR for anything that uses that kind of lighting". The realistic hero's clothes carried no surface of their own to an
engine: no UVs (every garment corner on the atlas's one white texel), a colour per face, and one material for the whole
figure (roughness 0.85, no metal), so a leather jacket, a wool suit and a brass buckle shone alike and the creases were
geometry only.

- **The clothes' relief on the lit engine export (realistic laws 13; `epidermis/cloth-relief.js`).** On the lit skinned
  GLB (and so Godot, Unreal, Blender and Unity's glTFast) each garment's tube is unrolled onto a cloth page of the skin's
  atlas, under the strands: around by its rings' own arc from its back (the wrap out of sight), along by its middles'
  path, in metres, so the map's tangent space is the tube's own. A height is baked there and read into the figure's
  normal map beside the head's: creases where the body bends (an elbow's crook, behind the knee, the hip's lap, the
  armpit, the cloth stacked at a wrist and broken at an ankle, each joint creasing only the tubes that cross it), seams
  (a limb's inner seam and a leg's outseam, a trunk's side seams, an outer layer's centre back, placed between slots by
  angle and eased along the tube), hems, leather's wear (short creases everywhere it is worn), the cloth's grain and a
  knit's rib. Every feature is at least a texel and a half wide at the skin's rung (2 mm at L2, 4 at L1, 8 at L0).
- **Each cloth's roughness and metalness** (`CLOTHS`): the cloth the outer names, else read off the outfit's language
  by its layer (a knit top jersey, a woven one cotton, trousers twill, a skirt and a tailored jacket wool), else its
  group's (leather shoes and belts, rubber soles, steel buckles, brass, horn buttons, a silk tie). An ORM map beside the
  normal map, written as the material's `metallicRoughnessTexture` and `occlusionTexture`, its roughness factor so the
  skin's texels are the export's own roughness: leather satin and polished on its crests, wool dull, a buckle metal,
  the creases' valleys occluded. The hard goods too small to chart lie on their cloth's swatch.
- `dermal-hero.js` `heroSkinPaint` takes the chart (`cloth`) and lays the cloth faces' corners on its page (`clothUV`);
  `dermal-relief.js` `heroRelief` bakes the page into the map, the cloth faces' tangents from their own UVs, and returns
  the ORM; the rig pack carries it (`ormTex`); `outfit/expand.js` `outfitLanguage` reads a build's language. The recipe
  is laws 12's: a hero minted before, an unlit export and the World page carry none, byte for byte.
- Unreal: the lit master is `M_MojuloLitCloth`, the relief's master with an `OrmTex` input (its red the ambient
  occlusion, its green times Roughness, its blue times Metal, which is 0 where a figure carries no ORM); a project's
  `M_MojuloLitRelief` from an import before is left as it was. Godot binds the ORM as its glTF import does, said in its
  ledger.
- `/hero-live`: a shot's `relief` sets the normal map's strength on the figure (0 off, more to read it).
- **The clothes in depth: parallax** (operator: "go ahead with the parallax"). The cloth relief's depth map (white the
  surface, black 1 cm under it, every texel no cloth's white so the skin never shifts; in the finest island's texels so
  one metre's UVs march every island) rides the GLB as a texture the figure material's extras name (`mojulo.relief`: its
  index, its depth, the UVs a metre spans across and along the atlas). Godot's kernel (0.31.0) marches it:
  `level.gd` `_fix_parallax` puts `figure_parallax.gdshader` on the figure's material, its textures carried across, the
  map written beside the GLB as `figure_depth.png` and named in `score.figure_parallax` (Godot's own heightmap takes one
  scale for both axes, and the atlas is not square). Unreal's master `M_MojuloLitCloth` marches it in a custom
  `ParallaxUV` node (`HeightTex`, `ParallaxDepth` 0 by default, `ParallaxPerM`), the importer importing the map beside the
  GLB. `/hero-live`'s viewer marches it too (a shot's `parallax` its strength). Advisory where the engines are absent.
- **Knits: a sweater's lines and its yarn** (operator: "sweater lines and yarn"). `cloth: 'knit'`, stockinette: its
  stitches in columns down the garment, each a V of two legs of round yarn with a ply's twist, under the surface so the
  parallax marches into the gaps; `cloth: 'cable'`, ropes of two strands crossing down it between purl channels; a rib's
  purl sunk between its columns. A knit's island is baked at half the page's texel, so a stitch reads at every rung.
- **Patterns** (operator: "use this principle to create wool patterns, herringbone, into coats hats pants, and other
  related things that can be applied patterns to"). `pattern` on the top, the bottom, the outer and the waistcoat (a name,
  or `{ kind, scale, contrast }`): herringbone, houndstooth, plaid, gingham, pinstripe, chalkstripe, corduroy, quilted,
  waffle, tweed. Each its relief (into the normal map and the depth) and its colour, a grey the base colour's cloth page
  multiplies the cloth's own by (a motif darkens its ground; the ground is the palette's); a colour weave made as it is
  woven, warp and weft coloured by their order and the 2/2 twill showing one or the other; a stripe drawn by its share
  of a pixel. The language takes `cloth` on every layer (`CLOTH_WORDS`: the outer's words and twill, jersey, knit,
  cable, silk) and `pattern` (`PATTERN_WORDS`), and refuses an unknown one. Lapels, ties and belts are charted as
  ribbons (their cloth and their pattern, no seams); a waistcoat takes its own words, else the outer's.
- The tube is unrolled from each ring's point facing straight back, in the ring's own plane (a foot's, straight down),
  found between slots, kept continuous down the tube (an opened front passes the back twice), and each slot's share of
  the turn eased along it: the tailor's folds, written into the rings, had slid every slot past them and kinked a stripe
  at each.
- Not yet: a hat (the outfit has no word for one), a garment painted on the skin (`fit: 'skin'`), a second colour in a
  motif (a pattern darkens its ground), the weave finer than a stitch.

### Clothes fitting: the realistic wardrobe's construction on the game body

The game body (the authored and the tiered hero) wears its kit as the realistic body does: each piece the thing it is,
fitted over what is worn under it (docs/garment-principles.md, the kit as pieces). Before, it laid the kit as slabs lifted
off the body's envelope, and its buckle was four bars round a point.

- **A belt is one mass, its buckle a frame** (`polygonizer/authored-kit.js`, run by `expandPlan`'s `kit` hook after the
  garments and before the adornment bake). A belt (a band wrapped round the trunk, or a skirt's waist, carrying a
  buckle or a boss) is one section read off everything worn at its height (`beltOn`, sampled round the body 24 ways,
  not the cloth's 12), the hollows spanned, its edges rounded; its buckle a frame with its tongue, the tail through it
  and a keeper (`frameBuckle`). Belts within a hand's width share a height, the later cinched over the earlier. Cloth
  worn over a belt (a jacket's or a tunic's) is carried out over it and eased back within 2 cm.
- **The kit's pieces** (`kitPieces`): a pouch is a body with a flap, a tab, a snap and seams, hung on its belt and riding
  it rigidly; a harness's straps are webbing on the outermost layer, fastened to the belt by a ladder lock and a tab,
  an X anchored to a waist strap; a gun harness carries its holster and pistol and its magazine pouches; a thigh rig's
  band is a belt on that leg's cloth. The kernel's shells for them are left off.
- Every piece takes the weights of the cloth under it, read by ring as the game body's weights are (`bindNearest`'s
  `rings`; `beltOn` and `kitPieces` take `{ around, rings }`), so the kit bends with the body as the realistic kit does.
- A pouch on a leg rides the leg (a belt slung on the hips above it is not its carrier) and hangs below a pouch already
  hung above it, never through it; a pouch finds its own belt (the duty belt its kit came with) up to 15 cm off, since a
  game body's short pelvis puts its window in from the belt (`kitPieces`, on both bodies). On the game body a belt rides
  no lower than the hips' widest and is fitted over the legs' tops it spans.
- **A waistband has no ease** (outfit law 2; docs/garment-principles.md). Trousers sat 2 to 3 cm off the body all round
  at the waist on both bodies, which read as bulk and put the belt on a ledge. Now the band sits on what it is worn over,
  a hair off the skin, and a tail tucked under it is pressed flat with it; the cloth takes its own ease back by the hips'
  widest. The game body's kernel takes it as a piece's `waistband` (the station its band starts at: body-garment.js),
  set by the expander on the trousers' seat; the realistic tailor as `waistbandOf` and `cinchWaist`
  (body-relational-tailor.js), the layers tucked under the band cinched first, in the order worn. Measured on the male
  tactical hero: the game body's waist from 2.8 cm to under 1 cm over the skin (a tucked shirt under it), the realistic
  body's untucked trousers from about 2.5 cm to 0.35 cm.
- **The kit follows the live dials** (`followDials`): each piece's stations take ids of their own and the piece joins
  every dial that moves the body part it lies on, weighted as that surface is at its height (a pouch, a holster, one
  weight: it moves whole). A belt widens with what it is round (`bulk`, `stance`) and never swings with a hinge (`lean`),
  spanning the hinge's pivot. The ranger's belt, pinned to the torso's hem, had sunk into the pelvis at `bulk` 0.8 (the
  door's warning); it no longer does.
- An armour build is the plate kernel's still: its straps and its ridge stack over its plates, and the kit hook leaves it.
- The door's dress readout counts the kit's pieces (`dress.parts.kit`), and a pouch made as pieces (`<id>Body_kit` …) is
  worn, never listed `unworn` (it was, on the realistic body too).
- Pins moved, each with its reason in its header: the outfit laws' pin (version 1 rewritten in place, unreleased, for
  the waistband), the statue characterization's draped and belted cases, the adult-form chibi's ranger recipe.
- **The jacket opens on the game body** (`polygonizer/authored-jacket.js`, from the kit hook, which now runs for a plan
  with a tailoring as well as one with adornments). An outfit naming a jacket's construction (`front: 'zip'`, `open`,
  `rib`, `pockets: 'flap'`, `epaulettes`, `collar: 'shirt'`: the `flight` card) was a closed tube on the game body with
  its opening painted on. Now its trunk pieces (`outer_torso`, `outerTail_pelvis`) and its collar are opened at the centre
  front in place (`openFront`, ten points a side: the game body's cloth is ring12), keeping their names and their
  stations, so what was placed on them and the dials still find them; their trims are carried across the opening. Its
  zip, rib waistband and cuffs, flapped pockets, collar points and epaulettes are laid on a view of the jacket as the
  realistic body makes it (its trunk one tube, `oneTube`), weighted by ring and following the dials (a zip and a rib
  waistband never swing with a hinge). The door no longer says the jacket's construction is the realistic body's.
- `jacketPieces` takes `{ rings, around }`, and its rib waistband lies on the first garment with a ring at the band's own
  height (on a game body the shirt's body ends above the band, its tail at it).
- **A pocket, a flap and a collar's point drew inside out** (`patchOn`, on both bodies): the compiler turns a part out by
  its first band face, which lay at the section's end, a pocket wide and 2.5 mm thick, and read either way, so they drew
  dark. The ring now starts at its outer face's middle.
- **The tailoring on the game body** (`polygonizer/authored-tailoring.js` over `polygonizer/tailored-front.js`). The
  realistic body's tailored front and shape (the V onto the shirt and tie, the lapels, the right front's edge and the
  quarters cut away below the last button, the buttons at the stance, a tie, a waistcoat's V, armholes and buttons,
  structured shoulders, a suppressed or a straight waist) moved out of `body-relational-wear.js` into
  `tailored-front.js`'s `tailorFronts`, every change made on each of a jacket's pieces and every read of one view of them;
  the realistic body calls it on its one tube and is byte for byte as it was. The game body calls it on its jacket's
  pieces densified IN PLACE (`densePiece`: 48 round, a ring every 1.5 cm, round the old ring's centre and never on its
  chords, keeping the pieces' names and their stations' ids, the new rings' dial blends, weights, trims and addresses
  mixed from their neighbours), what they are worn over read densified (`denseRead`). There a lapelled jacket is its
  lapels alone (`collars: false`: two bands to the gorge, none round the back of the neck), its stand collar and the
  shirt's under it taken off the recipe and the dials. The door no longer says the tailoring is the realistic body's.
- `tailored-front.js`: a surface with no cloth along a ray (a shirt's neckline cut lower at the front) is read at its
  ring's mean radius there (a tie's knot stood a metre out); the cut-away quarters show a skirt as they show trousers
  (they were painted skin on a skirt suit, on both bodies).
- **The jacket fitted on the game body** (`fitJacket`, operator: "tighten the fit on the jackets"): the outer layer's
  pieces on the trunk brought onto what they are worn over at a jacket's ease (`FIT`: 7.5 mm, a layer's step and about
  2.5 cm of girth), its sleeves square to the arm (6 mm), read densified; never let out. `cinchWaist` leaves a ray that
  reads nothing under it as it stands (it was drawn to the axis).
- **The shoulder under a jacket** (operator: "make the shoulder patches the same colour"): the tiered body's shoulder
  sockets (its ball, cone and web), which no garment covers and which are painted as the shirt, take the outermost
  sleeve's colour: the white patches at a suit's shoulders and the tee's green under a flight jacket are gone. A sleeve
  starting on the arm's first ring takes its shoulder cap out past the skin's by its own ease, and one worn under another
  the outer's colour on its cap and first bands (`sleeveSeams`).
- **The shirt's collar under a suit** (operator: "the shirt collar is the white shirt underneath, the suit jacket the
  blue above it; they are not the same and don't overlap"). The suit's jacket carries no collar, and the shirt's collar
  is back under it, all its own white (the trim an outfit spends on a collar's edge is the suit's colour, and read as a
  second, blue collar). It stood level up the neck's first third, no higher than the shirt's own neckline at the back,
  which tilts 7 cm up from the front, so the shirt and the jacket hid it there. Now it stands on the neckline
  (`standCollar`, authored-jacket.js, on every collared shirt on the game body): its rings follow the neckline round,
  from 1.2 cm under it to 2.6 cm over it in front and 3 cm behind, 5 mm off the neck, and it shows over the jacket at
  the back and the sides, on the male suit and the female skirt and trouser suits.
- **The V's edge a seam, not a row of teeth** (operator: "fix these tooth things along the inner part of the top of the
  jacket"). The V was cut slot by slot on each ring, and where it crosses a ring's slots on the slant each ring's edge
  stepped a slot on from the next one's, a face between them running from the shirt out to the jacket: a tooth. On the
  game body (`cutV`'s `seam`) the same slots now lie in the V on every ring it crosses, eight a side of the front and the
  front's own, spread from one roll line to the other, the rest over the jacket beyond them; a double front's V, off
  the middle, the same. At its foot the V is taken in over 5 cm, its slots drawn together from as wide as they stood,
  and the rings under it turn toward the apex, so no band fans across a bust or dives under the shirt. And the V is
  read at each point's own height (`at`): the game body's rings at the neckline tilt 10 cm front to back, and read at
  the ring's middle a point low on its ring was taken in to where the skin is 3 cm above it and stood through the shirt
  as navy shards; it is taken under the nearest of the trunk, the neck and the shirt there. The realistic body's V is
  as it was, byte for byte.
- Pins moved, each with its reason in its header: the outfit laws' rings (the tucked shirt's collar; and, from the
  jacket's construction before, the sleeves' seam at the shoulder and the outer layer's fit, which had moved them
  unpinned), the statue characterization's draped cases (the sleeves' seam).
- Not yet: a waistcoat's V shows the shirt only below the chest, the waistcoat over it up to the collar (it did before,
  under the jacket's white walls).

### Compose geotown: block segments composed into neighbourhoods on a cube's hills, map first and levelled

A town on a geocube's own land (the geocube kind's `show: 'geotown'`, `lib/graph/geotown/`): its map comes first, and
it is LEVELLED: its streets keep the land's grade, each building a level pad over its walk. A game evokes a town
rather than laying it out: a BLOCK SEGMENT is the unit (a few buildings, each designed on its own), four or more make a
NEIGHBOURHOOD, and neighbourhoods are a geocity graph's nodes (each one's `ports`); every plot to scale is `metro`.

- **The map** (`geotown/design.js`): a frame of blocks on the board (A1 the south-west), the right-of-way round each
  (road, kerb, boulevard, walk; a road cross and walked corners at each crossing), each block two rows of plots back
  to back, semis in pairs about their party wall and detached houses by the pattern's mix, a corner plot wider for its
  flank. Each plot's surface is allocated: front yard (the setback a block face holds), path, the house's envelope,
  side yards, back yard. Every square metre of the frame is one surface and the LEDGER sums them per block and for
  the town; a block's plots roll their own dice, so a block changed moves no other. A block may be a park (its paths
  across the land as it lies) or laid but not built.
- **Levelled on the land**: the cube's hills read from a painted landscape (`hills: { height, span }`), smoothed into
  the streets' ground so they keep its grade; each house a pad over the walk at its front, in risers, a semi pair one
  pad. The front yard is a bank from the walk to the pad, its path's steps set in it; a retaining face stands where
  pads meet (along a row, at a corner's flank, at a block's back line). The land under the town is never drawn: a
  pad is one quad.
- **Evoked** (`evoke`: `segment`, the default, one block segment; `neighbourhood`, four or more composed; `metro`
  every plot to scale): an evoked row is cut by a count of its buildings, on a window of the town to scale's land; its
  `evokes` law holds its houses' plot shares (house, front, side, back, the semis' share) to that town's. A segment's
  kind (`segment`, pattern.js SEGMENTS): `houses` six or eight back to back; `main-street` shops built to the main
  street's walk, their service yards behind, houses backing onto them; `apartments` a walk-up and its lot among houses;
  `park`. Each house is a TYPE of its pattern's (`geotown/houses.js`: the pattern's style changed, spoken as its own
  language, its material words laid as tiles whatever the cube's grit), never its neighbour's, a semi pair one building
  mirrored; its FRONT a canted or square bay with framed lights and a porch at the door or across the house
  (`geotown/fronts.js`). Each shop its own brick, sign and awning over a mullioned shopfront; the walk-up a canopy over
  its door. Each back yard its own PLAN (`geotown/yards.js`), a feature in each of three zones, each given its depth
  in order from the house and never its row neighbour's in that zone: by the back door a patio (a table under a
  parasol, or a grill and loungers) or a deck (its rail, steps and planters); in its middle a lawn and its tree, garden
  beds, a swing with a sandbox or a slide, a trampoline (its mat, padded rim and net posts), a mansion's pool; by its
  back fence a shed, a kitchen garden and compost bin, or a large shade tree (the pattern's `grow.shade`) ringed in
  mulch over a bench. A feature without its room is lawn, the back fence's first. A share of houses (`yards.balcony`)
  keep a balcony off an upper floor at the back, its rail and brackets, its reach the house's in the trees' room. Each
  yard behind its own fence (board, picket, hedge); a shop's service yard its bins and now and then a car, a walk-up's
  lot its painted stalls and cars.
- **The midtown mansion** (`pattern.mansion`): a houses segment holds at most two (`evoke.mansions`), each a much
  larger property taking houses' frontage: set back further on a wide lawn, its drive (the pattern's `drive` finish)
  along one side yard to a garage at the back, its yard a pool in its coping and terrace, a garden or a lawn behind a
  hedge, its house a revival of its own (`mansion.types`: Tudor, half-timbered over a stone ground storey under clay
  tiles; Georgian, brick under a hip with a fanlight and quoins; Richardsonian, rubble stone round-arched under a
  porch), three storeys, never its neighbour's. Its `mansions` law holds each at least twice a house's plot, at most
  two a block; the ledger counts the garage's footprint; a `mansion` view.
- **A neighbourhood** (`neighbourhood`: the pattern's `annex`, `main-street`, `quiet-streets`, or a written `{ layout,
  main }`, rows of letters north to south): its streets ranked, a MAIN street wider with its walk paved to the kerb and
  its trees in pits (`pattern.main`); each segment's rows turned to their streets (a main-street segment's shops face
  its main street) and TUNED to its cell: each column as wide and each row of cells as long as its segments need, a row
  its cell stretches past the pattern's `evoke.stretch` recut by count, then spread to fill it, its rows' depths shared
  out (its `fits` law). The ledger counts the buildings' footprints by use; `ports` are its perimeter streets, their
  ranks and their ends' heights, where a geocity graph joins neighbourhoods.
- **Sites** (`geotown/sites.js`): a block given to one program, evoked as the houses are. `school` (letter S) a brick
  school of three storeys on its own lot facing its street (a canopy over its doors, a flagpole), a schoolyard of
  courts and hoops behind it, a staff lot beside it, its field behind round a track where the field holds one;
  `sports` (F) a local field: a softball diamond (its dirt, bases, mound, backstop, outfield fence), a pitch under its
  lights and beside its bleachers, tennis courts in their fence, a field house and a lot; `park` (P) now its playground
  on its chips, a pavilion and its picnic tables, benches along its paths. A school or a sports field is two segments'
  ground: `segment: 'school'` lays two cells as one block, and in a layout wide letters side by side are one block, no
  street through it (its crossings walk across). Each site is proportioned to the block it is given: alone it takes
  its pattern's rails (`pattern.sites`), composed it yields to its neighbours' cells, to scale it takes the block it is
  laid on, fronting its long side or a main street; its `sites` law holds it near its rails and its grounds' shares
  (building, lot, playing ground, green, paved) near the site to scale's. Its ground is one level (the land under it,
  held to its walks), retaining faces round it and its school's lot; its fields and courts grow nothing, its lawns
  their trees, each held to its room. Every square metre is still one surface: the new `grounds`, `field`, `court`,
  `track`, `infield`, `play`; a part drawn round (a track, a diamond's dirt) carries its own area. The `apart` law: two
  playing fields never side by side across one street. The pattern's neighbourhood `school-and-field`.
- **The edge** (letter E, `segment: 'edge'`): a neighbourhood's edge on a MAJOR street (the pattern's `major` section:
  four lanes, a narrower walk, its trees in pits, sparse; a layout's `major` lines, a lone edge's south street). Its
  AVENUE row faces the major street: two-storey buildings each a type (`rows.avenue.types`: a shop with a flat over it, a
  small office under its canopy, a shop behind its forecourt of parking, a house turned to business on its lawn), no two
  neighbours alike, each at its type's setback and frontage; a public LANE behind them (the `lane` surface), and the
  houses behind it facing their quiet street, some with a garage off the lane (counted in `parking`). The pattern's
  neighbourhood `edges`: quiet streets between two major ones.
- **Its flora as the seventh generation grows it**: read by gen-7 (a page in the form render), the town hands its
  lawns, boulevards, back yards, parks, sites' lawns and fields to the form's land as its ground (`isekai:ground`,
  geotown/scene.js FORM_GROUND) and its trees to the form's plants: real blades of mown grass (the short sward, no
  meadow's drifts) on them under the cube's light, its trees grown as form (bark, crowns, the litter round their feet),
  each its own species (`form/flora-read.js`: a tree may name its `species`; `treeSizes` the height and reach the form
  grows each at), each held to its room by the form's own crown, a tree without room not planted. No trail's dress: no
  rubble, dust, clay or patches, no moss, and no tree held for a raised view. The ground under a yard's or a park's
  things (a patio, a deck, a shed, a pool, beds, chips) is claimed from the grass. Any other generation: as it was.
- **Streets by their lanes** (`pattern.street`, `main`, `major`: `lanes`, `lane`, `park` m): a local street two lanes and
  a parked side each way, four cars across tightly; a main or major street four lanes and parking each side, parked
  both sides whatever the streetscape; BIKE lanes on some (`pattern.bikes`: the share a rank's lines get them by their
  dice, a layout's `bike` lines always), kerb, parking, bike lane, travel. Painted: a local street's dashed yellow
  centre, a serious street's double yellow and its dashed white lane lines, the travel lanes' edge lines, a bike
  lane's green and its marks.
- **Fences of more materials** (`yards.js` FENCES, `pattern.fences` their weights): a stained board fence (its boards'
  tile), a board fence under a band of lattice, horizontal slats, chain-link on its posts and rail, an iron railing, a
  low brick wall under its coping (brick's tile), a fieldstone wall (rubble's tile), a picket, a hedge; each its own
  paint, stain or brick.
- **Shared entries and rear garages** (`pattern.access`): each houses segment's access by its dice: a rear LANE, its
  houses backing onto it and most keeping a garage off it; MUTUAL drives, a shared drive straddling two buildings'
  side yards (never within a semi pair), from the walk across their front yards and down between them to a garage at
  each one's back corner, no fence down it, the yard laid beside it; or none. The garages count in `parking`; a
  house's coverage is read less its half of the drive and a corner's flank.
- **Back doors and walkouts**: every house's back wall its door to the yard: a walkout onto its deck or patio
  (sliding glass doors; a mansion's french doors), else a door over a stoop and its steps; a split house's lower
  flat's under its stair's landing.
- **The street's own furniture** (the fractal city's kit at the micro scale): a local street's lamps hung on wooden
  hydro poles, their crossarms and three sagging wires on to the next pole; a blue street-name sign at each crossing;
  a hydrant on each block face; a main street's bins, post-and-ring bike stands and a post box (`pattern.furniture`);
  a bus shelter on each block face of a major street. A segment's face budget 13.5k for its streets' paint and kit.
 (`pattern.houseplants`): read by the seventh generation, a yard's garden and
  kitchen beds grow hostas, ferns and heather, a deck's planters box, the front hedges and the hedge fences are rows of
  box, and a share of front yards keep foundation plantings by the porch (forsythia, juniper, box, a flowering shrub in
  bloom): the library's bushes and shrubs (`form/bush-form.js` habits, grown by the form's plants), their ground
  claimed from the grass, the trees' litter on the lawns under them. Any other generation keeps its painted boxes.
- **Split duplex semis**: more of the houses semis (the pattern's mix), and a share of the pairs (`pattern.duplex`)
  split into two flats each: two doors side by side at the porch, a porch over a porch (the upper flat's, its own door
  onto it), a steel stair at the back from the yard to the upper flat's landing and door, the yard by the back door
  left to it; the households are flats (counted by the `parking` law, the ledger's `units`).
- **Storefronts, each its own** (`pattern.shopfronts`): a shop's sign a band across, a board over its door, a blade
  off the wall, lettering on its glass, or none; its awning sloped canvas, a flat metal canopy, a rounded one, or none;
  its frame's paint, its sign's and its awning's colours its own, its kick plate's height, its facade now and then
  painted; never its neighbour's sign and awning both.
- **Low-rise apartments** (letter L, `segment: 'lowrise'`): rows of four-storey low-rises on their lawns, each its own
  brick, balconies stacked over their fronts (`fronts.js` `balconies`), a canopy at the door, their lots behind.
- **Alleys behind storefronts**: a main-street segment's shops back onto a narrow alley (the `lane` surface, the
  pattern's `alley` width), not a parking yard: their lots shallower, a strip for bins behind each; the houses behind
  back onto the alley too.
- **Mansions away from the main street**: none on a block that touches a main or major street (the `mansions` law).
- **The pad's step** is measured past the walk's own fall between two fronts: a long frontage on a slope falls with its
  street.
- **Street furniture** (`d.traffic`, parametric): streetlights at a stride along each block-facing walk (both sides of a
  main or major street, staggered on a local one), clear of drives; each crossing controlled by its streets' ranks:
  signals every `signals` crossings along a main or major street (two-way stops on the minor street between them),
  all-way stops at a share (`stops`) of the local crossings; crosswalks at every controlled crossing (zebras at
  signals, two lines at stops), stop lines, stop signs, signal poles with their heads (a mast arm over a wide road).
  A streetscape sets them and a recipe changes them: `streetscape: { lights: m, signals: n, stops: share }`.
- **Streetscapes** (`streetscape`, the pattern's `streetscapes`): how close a neighbourhood is to the city, read from
  its sidewalk. `leafy` (the default) the Annex: a wide boulevard of maples, deep front lawns, a parked side, a gate
  here and there; `snug` closer to the city: a narrow strip of grass by the kerb and a tree here and there, narrow
  lots of semis near their walks, more of them to a segment, cars both sides, most fronts gated; `urban` the walk
  paved to the kerb, no street trees, row-tight lots with stoops a metre or two from the walk, every front behind its
  railing. Each changes the street's section, the street trees' stride and share, the plots' and houses' sizes, the
  SETBACK (how far a house stands from its walk; a deeper one asked deepens the block), PARKING and GATES; a recipe
  changes those four over its streetscape (`{ from, setback, gates, parking, trees }`). Parking is surface: a lane
  along the kerb on one side or both (the ledger's `parking`, out of the road), its stalls clear of every drive and
  cars parked in most, a front pad (the `drive` surface) where a front yard is deep and near level, a car on it now
  and then; the `parking` law counts stalls a household. A gated front: an iron railing, a low brick wall with its
  piers, or a picket, along the front line, a gate at the path; a mansion's stone piers and iron gates at its drive.
  A house's front is fitted to its setback (a porch across it where the yard holds one, else at the door, else a
  stoop; a bay raised over the door where it would stand on the walk); every street tree still stands twice a
  person's height or is not planted, so a tight street loses trees rather than growing short ones. A dense
  evocation's face budget is at least a building's share a building.
- **Finishes** (`pattern.finishes`): the ground laid in material words as tiles: the road's asphalt, the walk's scored
  concrete, a main street's brick furnishing strip and its trees' grates, brick paths, gravel side yards, a stone kerb.
- **Trees only in the town, held to their room**: no belt round the town and none on a perimeter street's outer side
  (the margin is a bare border); each tree's CROWN starts at least twice a person's height up (the geocube's walk,
  `era/out-ikebana.js` WALK.body): its crown raised as a street tree's is (`vegetation/pool.js` `clear`, opt-in: the
  whole crown carried up a clear trunk to that share of its height), so a tree stands at least as tall as that asks;
  held lower where its crown (its species' widest over its height, measured on its raised variants) would reach within
  0.6 m of a building's footprint, porches, bays and awnings in it; one without room to stand that tall is not planted
  (the `room` law), so a tight street loses trees rather than growing low ones.
- **What grows where** (`geotown/pattern.js` SURFACES): street trees on the boulevards at their stride, trees in back
  yards and parks, none on a road, walk, path or side yard; the trees grown variants stamped as repeats under a
  budget, each species its share.
- **The pattern** `bay-and-gable` (a Victorian and Edwardian streetcar suburb, a Toronto Annex) and its styles, three
  starters (`era/arch-style.js`): `bay-and-gable` (red brick, a steep slate gable to the street, sash lights on stone
  sills under stone lintels, a panelled door under its transom), `main-street` (brick shops, a cornice over a flat roof)
  and `walk-up` (four banded storeys under a deep cornice). Its house types: the gable, the Annex house (a
  sandstone ground storey with round-arched lights under a hip, a porch across it, an oriel over), the Edwardian (buff
  brick under a low hip), shingle over brick, painted brick.
- **The laws** advise, never refuse: the budget closes, a back yard every house, coverage (its rail's low end eased
  for an evoked row run deeper to fill its cell), frontage, the setback held, the street's grade, the pad's step, the
  green share (to scale), `fits`, `evokes`, nothing growing on a hard surface, `room`, the faces under their budget (to
  scale one budget; an evocation's a segment's times its segments).
- **The sheet** (`geotown/sheet.js`): the surface-area map from above, each pad shaded by its height, the crossings'
  heights, the ledger and the laws: the town map judged before anything is built. `scripts/spikes/geotown/geotown.mjs`
  writes it and captures the town at each hour (a street from its walk, a house, the back yards, a yard from its
  house's back window, over the block).
- `city/plan/look.js` now holds `hourSky` (the city scene imports it from there, unchanged).

### Compose scene, integrated: a designed building stands in an outdoor map

A building the scene composer designs (a military base's barracks, armoury or comms building) seated on an outdoor
map and walked into on the same map, its windows open on the land and its rooms lit by the land's own sun. The look and
the placement first; no game in it yet.

- **A base's building on the land is composed** (`era/stage-buildings.js`): a base use on an outdoor stage's
  `buildings`, or any bay building given `look: { construction?, palette? }`, is built on its bay kit and composed as
  a building level is, so its rooms are stocked (`era/stocking.js`), its `tone` laid, its plan's `storeys`, `wings`,
  `loading` and `bays` its own, its program's own ways out kept beside the front. Entered by its door, its inside is
  composed too (`gameworld/levels.js` `interiorStage`). Every other building is laid as it was.
- **Its windows open on the land**: the shell is cut at each glazed opening, with a reveal across to the room's wall,
  where the room on its own stood a painted sky card; the land shows through the glass and the open door. The land's
  sun at its hour lays the windows' sun patches (`_sun`, turned into the plan's frame); a sky with no sun (a dusk under
  its moon, a night) lays none, and its day dims the daylight at the windows.
- **It wears its construction outside** (`era/style/bay-exterior.js`): corrugated sheeting under a low standing-seam
  roof (military), board-formed concrete to a parapet (the bunker), painted block (utility), sheet panels (science)
  or a floated coat (everyday), coloured by the palette unless the material keeps its own; a flat roof behind a
  parapet; a wall rising over a lower room's roof where they meet.
- **A yard before its front** (8 m) is kept clear of what grows; a building that finds no place clear of the trail's
  beats, the stage's edge and the other buildings says so.
- **The game-building card** says it; `scripts/spikes/outpost/outpost.mjs` captures one on a cube's trail at each
  hour, from the approach, wide, the yard and inside looking out.
- **A building set into its slope** (`embed: true | { up }` on an outdoor stage's building): its way in a walkout on the
  low land, a door out of its upper storey's back onto the high land behind (a way out of an upper storey is allowed
