### Engine handoff: assets, animation and levels at the polygon level, on gen 7's form

Mojulo makes single-player and couch-multiplayer games, for two audiences. A solo creator gets the whole game, end to
end, on the web: `export_game` to the browser or the desktop app, unchanged. Developers and teams get a handoff, with the
recipe and its bible as their design source, the web build as the prototype that validated the loop, and a re-handoff
that keeps their own wiring, so more of a team can make prototypes and iterate on them: one export, `export_model { engine }`, gives Godot, Unity, Unreal and Blender every
surface as a gen-7 material (base colour, normal, occlusion and roughness, relief for parallax, the land's layers, the
plants and the scree's stones as instances), every rig with its clips and faces, and every level as layout, light,
colliders and named markers (the spawn, the foes, triggers, doors and keys, the critical path, the shots), for a
developer to wire and finish there. The form render's data is the bridge: it already holds a surface's material and
form and never its light, which is how every engine lights a scene.

It supersedes every engine export before it. The game runtimes ported into the engines (Godot's GDScript kernel, Unity's
C# runtime, Roblox's Luau kernel) and the conformance machinery that held them to the web are culled, Roblox is dropped as
a target, and "plays in an engine" stops being a measure: the hillclimb page loses its engine columns, and the engine
marks become one handoff ledger of what each export carried and what stayed the web's.

Built so far:

- **The runtimes are frozen.** The engine game runtimes take no new ports while the handoff replaces them.
- **A real Godot in CI.** The workflow's `godot` job fetches a pinned Godot (4.7.2, from the builds repository, checked
  against the release's SHA512 sums and cached), names it as `MOJULO_GODOT`, and runs the Godot legs the handoff keeps:
  a figure's import with its engine skeleton, BoneMap, retarget and clips.
- **The form data is pinned.** The land read's payload (a small meru island with its grass map) is hashed painted fresh
  and memoized, the two must agree, and the hash is held on every reference leg, so a run, a process or a CPU that paints
  a different byte fails before anything is handed off from it.
- **The handoff's contract, first slice.** `scene/handoff.js` reads a world unshaded in the form render (gen-7) and hands
  it off lit: every surface a glTF metal-rough material in its own colour with no light baked in, the water a smooth
  translucent one, and the form render's scree stones as instances, each standing on its ground's normal as the page
  stands it. A ledger says what was carried and what stays the web's for now (the land's layers, the stones' skin, the
  plants and grass, the light). Every other export is byte for byte as it was.
- **The plants.** Each plant leaves as a copy of its template: its wood on its bark (the bark's own colour, its relief's
  normal, occlusion and roughness, and its height for parallax) and its crown, its leaf clumps merged as the page merges
  them, each leaf's normal bent toward the crown's outside so the crown takes the sun as one volume. Each plant's own
  tint, the wind, the sprays near the eye, the far levels of detail and a conifer's needles stay the web's for now.
- **The dressed faces.** Every tile the matte painter painted from relief (a bay kit's floors, walls, columns, crowns and
  soffits, a crypt's ashlar, a house's render and tiles) leaves as the material it was painted from: its colour under no
  light, its relief's normal, its occlusion and roughness, and its height for parallax, instead of the tile with the
  light painted in. A tile painted any other way leaves as its paint, and the ledger counts both.
- **The land as form.** The island's and the trail's ground leaves as the form render draws it, in place of its painted
  faces: each ground class a mesh of its own, shaded smooth, each corner its palette-solved colour, and on the layered
  ground each corner's four layers' weights with the layers' textures alongside, for an engine's terrain shader to blend
  as the page does. The cliff's rock relief leaves as geometry, cut and pushed as the page pushes it, meeting the land
  round it without a gap.
- **A room's lamps.** A room under the form render leaves with its surfaces in their solved colours under no light and
  its lamps as point lights at the levels the solve gives them, so the engine's lamps light it as the page's bake does.
- **The level a developer wires.** A level's handoff carries a record of what its web prototype validated: its
  environment (the sky, the sun at its hour, the ambient), its markers (the spawn, every entity by its node's name with
  its part in the loop: the pilot, a seat's body, a foe with its rank and skill, a thing; the anchors; the cameras), its
  contract (what it produces, consumes and audits, synthesized from its mechanics as the game resolves it), its seats
  (each seat's number, colour, body and spawn, the screen they share, their lives) and its reference (the web build and
  the bible pages of the same recipe). Every name comes from the recipe, so handing off a changed level keeps the names
  of what did not change, and an engine can take the new version without losing a developer's own wiring.
- **The Godot adapter, first slice.** A handoff becomes a Godot 4 project: the GLB, a `handoff.json` with the level
  record and what glTF has no slot for (each material's height map, the terrain's atlases), and a post-import script
  that, on every import, gives the materials their colours and parallax, the static meshes their collision, the level
  its sky, ambient, occlusion and shadowed sun, and stands every marker and seat as a node carrying its record. The
  developer's `project.godot` and `level.tscn` are written once and kept: a re-handoff replaces mojulo's folder, Godot
  reimports, and whatever the developer wired stays. CI's Godot job imports a couch level and a dressed bay and probes
  what the importer built.
- **The cast travels.** A level's rigged bodies (its hero, its creatures) leave as their figures, skinned with every clip
  they play, on their entities' nodes; a primitive body (a box, a sphere) leaves as its mesh on its entity's node, so
  moving the entity in the engine moves the body. Found in the first Godot runs, with three more: a dressed face's
  relief lit by its normal map (its parallax bound but off: at the relief's real depth it reads as nothing), the haze's
  density taken so Godot's fog reaches half at the page's distance, and a default sun, background and camera.

- **The layered ground in Godot.** A form land's ground leaves Godot looking as it does on the World page: the page's
  layered-ground shader ported to Godot's shading language (each layer along the face's dominant axis, raised by its own
  height, the trail's powder and clay, the scree thinned by its stones, the ledges' dirt, the moss, the undergrowth, the
  pebbles, cracked earth and plates, the wet sand line), bound on import to every layered part with its layers as
  texture arrays. The corners' weights ride the GLB twice over the same bytes, as `_SPLAT` and as two UV sets an engine
  that drops an application attribute keeps, and the handoff now carries everything the page's ground reads (the trail's
  mask, the scree's dice, the dress, the bases, the wet line) for every engine. Found beside it: a cube's sky reached the
  record as colour bytes and broke Godot's environment (now hex, as the rest of the record), and the environment now
  lights as the page does (its tone curve, its solved ambient alone, the haze's colour as the page shows it, the sky
  clear of the fog). CI's Godot job imports a trail too, and fails on any script or shader error in the import.
- **The sea as the engine's own water.** Where a land has a sea's depth, its sea leaves as one plane at the water's
  height over the bed, see-through and fading to nothing toward the shore by the depth under it, in place of the painted
  sheet; in Godot it takes a water shader ported from the page's (the sea's colour lit, the shore's fade, the level's
  sky in its reflection), so the cliff's cut faces below the waterline no longer show through. The haze in Godot now
  follows the page's curve (faint near, closing late) instead of matching it at one distance only.
- **Hand a world to Godot from the agent.** `export_model { engine: 'godot' }` writes the handoff as a Godot 4 project in
  the world's outcome folder (`godot-handoff/`): open it and play `level.tscn`. Handing off a changed recipe again
  replaces mojulo's folder and keeps the developer's project and scene; `what: 'asset'` hands off a thing without its
  level. The result says what travelled, what stayed the web's, and the command that checks the import in a headless
  Godot. A desktop app built from the same outcome folder now leaves every engine pack out (Godot's handoff, Unreal's
  and Blender's packs had been packed into it).
- **One door to a team's engine.** `export_model`'s `engine` takes Godot, Unreal and Blender: a world or a game to
  Godot (a game's levels each its own project), a character or a solid to Unreal (lit: the engine lights it), a world
  to Blender as an art pack. `export_game` is the game itself, a web folder or a desktop app, and no longer offers the
  engine translations; a finished game's share offer hands its levels to Godot. Every pointer the agent reads (the
  routing card, the tool lines, the export dispatch, the vocab cards) points at the one door.
- **The engine runtimes retire.** Mojulo no longer translates a game into an engine: the Godot, Unity and Roblox game
  runtimes, their conformance corpora and the per-engine marks that measured them are gone (about 38,000 lines). The
  web build is the game, alone or on the desktop; a team's engine gets the handoff. `export_game`'s engine targets
  refuse with that move, a stored world's engine target is read as none, design_game no longer asks for one, and the
  hillclimb page measures what the web build makes. The Godot handoff and a humanoid figure's import are checked in a
  real Godot on CI.
- **Every engine on the handoff.** `export_model { engine }` now hands a world, a game's levels or an asset to Godot,
  Unity, Unreal (levels too, not only assets) and Blender, each as a project the team opens: every surface a material
  the engine lights, the layered ground and the sea on shaders ported from the page, the sun, lamps, sky, ambient and
  haze set to reproduce the page's look (each engine's light units measured, not assumed), the markers and seats as
  objects carrying their records, and the developer's own scene kept across a re-handoff. Held to the World page at
  the same cameras, each engine reads within a few levels a channel on most of the land. Godot's room lamps were
  three times too bright, and are fixed.
- **How close each engine is to the web build, measured.** A visual gate renders a level's own cameras on the World
  page and in each engine on the machine, scores every shot (structure and colour, region by region) and writes a
  contact sheet: the page beside each engine, the scores and a map of where they differ. It advises and never
  refuses. `mojulo script visual-gate --ref <level>` runs it; a level's engine export names the command.
- **The engines closer to the page.** A level's figures now stand in Godot, Unreal and Unity as the web build stands
  them when it starts (a walker in its walk's first step, as Blender already had it, not at the rig's rest), so a
  camera at the hero's eye no longer looks out through the inside of its head. The near sea in every engine now takes the sky's light on its colour as
  the page does, and is no longer 15 to 30 levels darker. Godot's sea is now solid past its depth map like the other
  engines' sea, which removes a faint line where the shallows end.
- **The copy.** The README, the docs, the plugin and the agent's own self-description say what is true now: the game
  plays in the browser or as a desktop app, and a team's engine gets a handoff of its levels and assets to wire.

### Meta Quest controllers: two sticks that go straight

Operator: "create sensible mapping of the WASD and game controls to meta quest devices … the controls are not consistent,
they don't always go straight … since there are 2 knobs, we can do 2 axis controls where move and rotate is possible so
the user doesn't have to rotate their head to turn". The headset walk (`xr` on a World, `?xr=1`) had three causes of a
bent path: it re-read the gaze every frame (a glance aside steered the walk), its dead zone was square (a worn stick's
drift, or a thumb a few degrees off true, leaked sideways), and its snap turn swung the rig about the play-space origin
rather than the player's head.

- **The xr family has its driver** (`controls/xr-driver.js`, `devices.js` `driver: 'webxr-gamepad'`): an XR session's
  input sources read by hand in the xr-standard mapping (Quest Touch, Touch Plus on the Quest 3 / 3S, Touch Pro), and
  the thumbstick shaping a headset walks through: a radial dead zone, the travel past it rescaled, a push within 12° of a
  cardinal snapped onto it. Its own closure and module, so only a page that can open a session carries it; the controls
  kernel, in every game page, is unchanged.
- **The headset reads the pilot scheme** (`scene/channels/xr.js`): forward, back, strafe and turn are the scheme's own xr
  bindings, read through the kernel and the driver, so the headset and the controls card agree and `xr.bind` remaps them.
  - Feet, body, head: the feet go where the body points (the left stick, forward, back and sideways to it) and the
    head is a camera that looks without steering. What turns the body is the stance:
    - `move: 'seated'`, the default (the operator: "the sitting in couch action game mode"): the right stick alone.
    - `move: 'standing'` (the operator: "a game that cares about physical body rotation rather than right stick"):
      the player turns it by turning. WebXR tracks no torso, so it is estimated as an avatar's is: the point between
      the controllers held out in front leads it; with the hands down it catches up to where the head has stayed
      (about a second, so a glance barely moves it); the head never sits more than `neck` (50°) off it. The right
      stick snap-turns on top by default (a play space and a cable run out); `turn: 'off'` removes it.
    - For comparison, head-steered: `move: 'latch'` takes the gaze when a push begins and holds it, `move: 'head'`
      steers by the gaze every frame (the old way), `move: 'hand'` walks where the left controller points.
    Every mode goes straight.
  - Forward is where the body faces after a right-stick turn (the operator, on a Quest 3S: walking north, turned east,
    forward still walked north): the gaze is read from the frame's own viewer pose carried through the rig, not off
    three's XR camera, and the test's headset reports its pose rig-local as a real one does.
  - Turns on the right stick about the head: smooth by default (`turnSpeed`, 120°/s), or `turn: 'snap'` (`snap`
    degrees; `{ snap }` alone still means snap turning).
  - `?xr=` takes the mode words for an A/B in a headset without a re-mint: `?xr=standing`, `?xr=seated,snap`, `?xr=standing,off`, `?xr=head`.
    The live route applies them, and the page reads them itself too, so a downloaded or statically hosted copy takes them.
- **Test pages for a headset** (`scripts/xr-test-pages.mjs <out-dir>`): a Quest browser opens a WebXR session only over
  https, so the script writes static pages (three from the pinned CDN) for a host such as GitHub Pages: a course (a
  straight lane down +X with a post every 5 m and a goal at its end, the opening view standing on it) and the walkable
  fractal city, with an index linking each mode.
- **The xr rows of the other schemes**: the action game, the same verb on the same control as the pilot's (left stick
  moves and its click sprints, the triggers hold attack (right) and guard (left), A jumps, B dodges, X dashes like the
  pilot's tackle, Y switches, the right grip shoots, the right stick's click locks, the left grip stays the hands' use),
  the grid
  puzzle and the tactics board (the left stick moves the cursor, the right turns and zooms the view), with their legend
  rows. The pilot scheme's rows are as they were: they ride every game page, and no game page reads a headset yet.
- Gates: machine — the driver and the shaping, and the emitted block run against three's math with a fake session (a
  push with drift and a glance aside walks a straight line; a turn leaves the head where it stood; a remap swaps the
  hands). The two xr fixtures' byte pins moved; every other page is byte-identical. Eyes — the operator's Quest 3S, not
  yet run.
- Not yet: a game's hero is not driven in a headset (the rig replaces the hero's step on entering VR), and the session has
  no wall collision.

### The realistic face squeezes its squint

- **The squint's squeeze on the realistic face** (realistic laws 15, `relational-face-rig.js` `SQUINT_SQUEEZE`, the
  head's `squeeze` relation): as the anime head's squint slides its brow's mass down onto the eye (`anime-sockets.js`
  `rise`), the realistic squint slides the mass over each eye, the brow and the forehead's foot, 3 mm down and a touch
  forward, so the skin between the brow and the lid's crease gathers while the lids, their corners and the lashes stay
  as the squint draws them; the brows' hairs ride it. The eyeSquint target and its sides carry it. A slide weighed about
  each globe rather than a drive through the head's field: the brow pad's dip moved the eye's inner corner, a valley
  where the pad meets the lid, four times as far as the brow, and the skin folded there. A row stamped before laws 15
  squints as it did.
- **hero-live's clay on the realistic hero**: the clay toggle swaps in a material of its own instead of stripping the
  painted one, whose parallax shader samples its colour map (stripped, the shader failed and the figure vanished).
- **The lateral periorbital fill** (realistic laws 16, `head-relational.js`, the `periorbital` relation): a soft mass
  over the lateral orbital rim, from beside the brow's outer end down past the outer canthus into the cheek under the
  lower lid's outer third, so the skin beside each eye stands at the canthus's depth and wraps the globe's side up to the
  corner (it fell back a centimetre behind the canthus, and the globe's side showed bare from 3/4 and the side). Its beads
  stand outside the globe's limb and inside the face's outline: the eye and the front's silhouette keep. A row stamped
  before laws 16 keeps its face.

### The view cone

- **The cone, not a ring** (`scene/channels/view-cone.js`, emitted by the form channel). Full detail is where the
  screen can show it: the camera's frustum, cut off at a reach. `window.__mojCone` holds the eye, the frustum, the reach
  in metres and the pixel at a metre, set before each frame's render list is built, so what the cone does not see is
  left undrawn the same frame. The reach is the screen's by default: the distance at which a tall grass blade's width
  covers `VIEW_CONE.px` pixels, at the camera's field of view and the canvas's height, so a bigger screen sees real
  grass further. It replaces the grass's third-of-the-map rule.
- **The reach adjustable**: a geocube outside's `cone` fixes it in metres (`cone: 40`; refused indoors or out of
  range); live, `[` and `]` shrink and grow it, and `\` returns it to the screen's. `window.__mojCone.set(m | null)`
  does the same from a script.
- **The grass reads the cone** (`scene/channels/form-grass.js` `POV_GRASS`): real grass inside it, thinning over its last
  half, strands past it; a tile is drawn only if the frustum sees it and its band of distance reaches it. The aerial
  camera still draws the whole field.
- **The far field** (`scene/channels/far-field.js`): past the cone's reach the grass is its colour on the ground,
  nothing standing, in the ground's own shader: the grass's (a standing drift's where one holds the cell), offset by each
  cell's dice, lit and shadowed as the ground is, and speckled with world-anchored specks about a pixel and a half at
  their distance (the grain snapped to powers of two, so it holds while the eye walks): a flower's colour where flowers
  grow, a weed's head in the weeds' patches, a lighter or a darker fleck. No draw, no triangle. F toggles it.
- **The far trees** (`scene/channels/form-flora.js` `FLORA_FAR`): a plant has two rungs, by the screen's own rule: whole
  inside the cone's reach (where its old hand-set 25 m was) and until its card's texel is under the cone's grain, then
  its card. The card is itself from that side, solved from the recipe rather than rendered: its near crown's own leaves
  (each clump's turned as the tree's recipe turns them, so the leaf mass lies the way its clusters do, gaps kept, no
  volume the leaves do not hold) and its wood's own triangles, baked once a template from eight bearings at 128 × 192
  texels, POINT-SAMPLED as the screen samples the tree (a texel is leaf where its centre falls on a leaf, nothing grown,
  so the card is no thicker than the tree it replaces), lit as the near crown's leaves are by each leaf's clump's facing,
  at each leaf's own tone, casting its silhouette from the sun's side. Every far plant is one draw. No far form between
  the rungs: the old one, a share of the crown's clumps grown, read as a bubble there and gone as the eye walked; a
  crossed crown's half-leaved far bundles (`farGeo`) are gone from the payload too. A needled crown and a culm keep their
  own far form; an aerial camera's reach is `FLORA_LOD.mid`.
- **The stones on the same ladder** (`scene/channels/form-land.js` `STONE_LADDER`): the scree's stones, every one drawn
  chipped or as its block at any distance before, are chipped inside the cone's reach (a stone big enough to cast),
  their block past it, and gone once the whole stone is under a pixel, where the ground's own scree and pebbles carry
  it. The meadow's cameras draw about 300k fewer triangles each, looking the same.
- **The far structures** (`scene/channels/far-structures.js`): what stands on a form page that is not the land or a
  plant (a town's buildings, fences, poles, cars), painted a mesh a group across the whole level, is drawn instead as a
  batch a group (`BatchedMesh`, one draw as before on a GPU with multi-draw) of 16 m tiles, each shown or left out on its
  own, and each tile has its card: itself from that side, baked once from its own triangles and colours from eight
  bearings, turned to the eye and casting from the sun's side. A tile is its card past the cone's reach where its card's
  texel is under a pixel. What stands is a triangle more than half a metre over the land's own height and under 60 m, so
  roads, kerbs, terrain and clouds stay live. A pass that swaps its own material onto each mesh (the creases' and the
  occlusion's prepass) draws the merged mesh in its place; the cards, the trees' too, sit it out.
  `scripts/runnability.mjs` counts a multi-draw's triangles.
  A page without the form render (a geocity) carries the view cone and its far structures when its world asks
  (`cone: true` for the screen's reach, or metres), the land's height there its lowest surface in each cell. A level
  whose standing plan holds more than 128 tiles is left as it was and says so (`window.__formStructures().skipped`): at
  a metro's size a tile's card is too coarse to stand in inside it, and its finer cards wait for baking ahead of the eye.
- **No strands past the reach** (`scene/channels/form-grass.js`): the 0.45 m strand rows and their meshes are gone; a
  far map, one strand a cell of the grass map (its height, colour slot and dice), is what the far field paints from
  (`window.__formFar`).
- **The surveyor** (`form/survey.js`, `scripts/far-survey.mjs`): what an eye sees of a sketch's form land, solved from
  its recipe rather than rendered. Each sample of the image is a ray over the land's triangles, read against the grass
  map: sky, inside the reach, or past it as grass, bare, outside the grass map, or the contour, counted by land class and
  charted as text, camera by camera. And what it hands the art (`surveyRegions`): the far field as regions of one
  substance (grass where the map covers it, else the land's class), each with its main colour, its horizontal bounds,
  and column by column its upper bound (the land's top from the eye, less what stands on it: the grass's height there in
  pixels at its distance) and its lower bound (where the far field begins).
  Its contour scan (`contourScan`: from a point of view, on each bearing of a full turn, where the ground peaks against
  the sky or ground well past it) is kept for what stands past the reach, trees, rocks and buildings, not the grass.
- **An exported page walks at the scene's eye** (`mcp/tools/sketch-model-export.js` `htmlWalk`): `export_model format:
  'html'` turned a scene's own walk (its spawn, eye and speed) into a bare `true`, so the page took the walk's defaults
  off the whole scene's bounds: over a gen-7 meadow, whose sky and hills are wide, an eye of 15 m, a 6 m stride and walls
  a body could not pass. It keeps the scene's walk now, as the /world route always did.
- **The gen-7 sky** (`scene/channels/form-sky.js`, emitted by the form channel): a geocube's gen-7 outside draws the sky as
  the light that lights its land, in place of the stage's painted sky. The air's level is the solved sky light's (its
  cosine-weighted average over the dome, by luminance), its hue and gradient the cube's zenith and horizon, more air at
  the horizon, the sky's scattering round the sun and the forward glow at it; the sun a disc where the solved sun stands,
  at its light. Clouds are a layer over the eye, its cover the recipe's `clouds` (clear, fair, overcast, storm, haze,
  high, and its cover; absent, fair where the stage painted clouds, clear where it painted none), lit by the solved sun
  through their own depth with a silver edge toward it and by the sky from below, passing over as the eye walks and
  drifting with the page's wind. The haze takes the air where the far land stands, and the stage's painted far land
  takes it too. All through the land's own tone curve; a night's stars and moon stay.
  A gen-7 geocube page without the form render (a geocity) carries the same sky (`formSky`), its light the cube's own
  sky colours and its sun the page's; a recipe naming no clouds over a stage that painted none has a few fair-weather
  clouds, not an empty sky.
- **The far land** (`scene/channels/form-land.js` `FAR_LAND`, `form/land-read.js` `FAR_GROUPS`): the stage's far ring, its
  ridges past the level (standing curtains, layer behind layer, up to a skyline), was left painted on a gen-7 page, a
  pale backdrop shimmering with its tiles. The read gives it its own range (`far`) and the form draws it as land, in
  facets lit as the land is: the trail's own grass low on it rising into its stone toward the peaks, each facet a shade
  its own, under the sky's air (the new sky's, where the far land stands), more of it the farther its layer. What the
  read cannot class otherwise (a town's own buildings) stays painted.
- **The plants' budget** (`form/flora-read.js` `FLORA_BUDGET`): a plant on a gen-7 page spends at most 300 triangles a
  square metre of its side's silhouette (its crown's width × its height). Over it, it gives up its sprays (the crown
  holds the outline), then its leaves' outlines (a leaf one width, four triangles: `leafClump` `lean`), then clumps by
  rank, each kept clump grown to hold the crown's cover; every template carries what it spends (`budget`). A garden's
  spray bush, 1.2 m tall, drew about 3,800 triangles a crown and 192 sprays near: it draws 516 now. In a town's garden
  bed the plants drawn near fell from about 261k triangles to 102k (the bushes from about 200k to 30k); the trees keep
  their own, well within theirs.
- **One grain past the reach** (`scene/channels/view-cone.js` `VIEW_CONE.grain`): everything past the cone's reach is its
  impression at one grain, at most a pixel and a half a texel: a tree its card, a tile of buildings its card, as the grass
  is its colour there, its specks about a pixel (`FAR_FIELD.speck.px`); a tree turns to its card where its card's texel is
  under that grain, so a meadow's grown trees show their leaf-built cards from about 45 m, smaller ones sooner.
- **No bubble left in a gen-7 trail** (`era/isekai.js` `plantItems` `skirt`, `form/flora-read.js` `SKIRT_FLAG`): the stage's
  clumps of trees out on the skirt, three faceted blobs a tree, stood past the plants' box and were drawn as faceted land
  (the `crown` class). The trail hands them over as data now (each tree's foot, its crown's reach, its kind) and the form
  grows them as the level's own trees, each as wide as the crown it stands for, a card at that distance; no litter round
  them and never brushed. A bamboo or a blossom card keeps its painted clumps. And what stands is read once the form has
  hidden what it draws in its place (`scene/channels/form-land.js`): a painted crown, trunk or rock had been taken for a
  structure, batched near and carded far, so a crown the form had grown over showed again as a ghost card past the reach
  and was gone inside it.

### The arms library: modern and future guns and knives, drawn for the seventh generation

The equipment kernel gains an arms library (`control/lib/graph/equipment/arms/`): pistols (service, compact, heavy,
revolver), the carbine, rifles (assault, marksman, bullpup), the submachine gun, shotguns (pump, tactical) and knives
(combat, tanto, dagger, karambit), each in the modern, the future or the near line and a finish card, every part tunable by word.
Generic forms, no make or model. They are drawn by eight laws for the gen-7 look (a live key over materials told apart
by how they reflect): every major part a side outline pushed through its width; every edge chamfered to its part's
thickness so the key draws a highlight along it; bare or coated metal, a finish and the grip as three responses, a
future arm's one glow hue; the bore one line with the grip raked 18°; detail in three tiers, fewer and bigger as it
stylizes; a trigger guard's finger opening; the future line a transform of the same mechanics (facets, a shell gap, a
lit conduit, an emitter, a cell), so a blaster is held as a pistol; a blade read by its grind and a brighter edge bevel.
The machine gate (`stats.equipment.arms`) reads the laws back; the eyes gate is the operator's.

- **The build** (`mint_solid` workbench `build`, a hero's `gear`): `{ item, model?, line?, style?, parts?, dials? }`.
  Items `pistol`, `carbine`, `shotgun`, and the new `rifle`, `smg`, `knife`. Parts: `barrel` (a word or cm), `stock`,
  `magazine`, `optic` (irons, red dot, holographic, scope), `muzzle` (crown, flash hider, brake, suppressor, emitter),
  `rail`, `underbarrel` (foregrip, light, bipod), a shotgun's `grip`; a knife's `blade`, `length`, `guard`, `handle`,
  `serrations`. Finishes: black, fde, od, stainless, walnut (modern); white, gunship, titan, hazard (future); the
  firearm samples' `service` and `future` read as black and white.
- **Opt-in, byte for byte.** A `pistol`, `carbine` or `shotgun` build naming none of model, line, parts or an arms finish
  is the earlier firearm proxy, unchanged; the workbench mint and the hero's gear record stamp the item's default model
  on a new one, so rows minted before keep their bytes and new guns are the library's.
- **The hero holds them.** A rifle and an smg at low ready or slung like the carbine (no hip); a knife as a blade, on the
  hip at the left side.
- **Review:** `node scripts/render-arms.mjs <dir> [presets]` draws each arm side-on and from the front three-quarter
  with its triangles and its laws readout (a third-person pistol about 1.7k triangles, a marksman rifle about 7k).
- **The near line** (law 9: futuristic, styled real; `line: 'near'`): each new part shows what it does in a form a
  factory could make, shells are moulded and read by their parting lines and vent rows, and light appears only on a
  display. Its own models, each inspired by a modern design: the `smart` pistol (a moulded shroud, a recessed crown, an
  ammo counter), the `pdw` (a top-fed translucent magazine, a thumbhole), the `caseless` rifle (a monolithic shell, a
  top-loaded cassette, a sight on posts), the `coilgun` (countable copper coils in a skeleton of rails, a capacitor bank
  with its cells bare, a cable) and the `breacher` (a drum-fed shotgun). Any model takes the line (a smart sight, a
  seam, a round counter), every gun's optic takes `smart`, and four finishes carry it: slate, sand, ranger, arctic.
- Manual: the equipment card's modern and future arms section; the hero card's gear line.

### The airport: one plan, a miniature of the whole and a wing at scale

An airport planned at its real figures from the transport hub's grammar, drawn whole as a miniature on a plinth, and,
from the same plan, one wing at full scale for a level.

- **The plan in true metres** (`airport/plan.js`, `planAirport`): the transport hub's grammar re-laid at an airport's
  figures.
  - The terminal is linear (a processor along the frontage and its piers reaching airside) or radial (a rotunda and
    its arms).
  - Each pier is 20 m wide and hooks at its tip as the old grammar's do, in one rotational sense. Each top-level
    concourse is a wing, and its branches are the wing's.
  - The stands are nose-in along both flanks, sized to the craft shelf's liners (the bizjet up to the jumbo). They are
    filled by a weighted fleet, then by the largest class that fits, each tested against every pier and every other
    stand.
  - Each stand's jet bridge runs from a rotunda off the pier's face to the aircraft's first left door, at its sill.
  - The apron and its taxilane, a parallel taxiway and a 2.8 km runway sit at their separations, with their
    connectors. The tower is landside, the maintenance hangar at the apron's end, and a forecourt and car park
    landside.
- **The miniature** (`airport/miniature.js`): the whole plan as an architect's presentation model, 1:1000 by default
  (1:250 to 1:4000), on a walnut plinth on a gallery floor.
  - The ground is in printed layers: grass mown in bands, the apron's concrete, the asphalt with the runway's edges,
    centreline, thresholds and touchdown zones, and the yellow taxi and lead-in lines.
  - The terminal's long-span roof sits over glass, or a rotunda under its dome. The piers are glazed boxes under white
    roofs and skylights.
  - The jet bridges run from their rotundas to each door. The tower has a flared cab, and the hangar a vault and its
    doors.
  - The fleet is the registry's stylised nets at each aircraft's true length, each in a seeded livery.
- **Composable:** the `/world` kind `airport` (`show: 'miniature'`; an orbited object) is minted by the transport
  hub's door (`compose_world` base `transport-hub`, `overrides: { mode: 'airport', show: 'miniature', stands?, scale? }`).
  Without `show`, the airport mode is the CSS diorama it always was.
- **The jet bridge** (`airport/jet-bridge.js`), at full scale in the hull kit's language and posed by the plan's stand:
  - the fixed glazed link from the pier to the rotunda's drum on its column;
  - two telescoping tunnel sections with window bands, sloping to the door's sill;
  - the lift columns on a wheeled bogie;
  - the cab square to the fuselage, its dark bellows at the door.

  The plan swings each bridge in from a rotunda 13 m along the pier, past the door's side, and gives none where the
  door is under a bridge cab's lowest (a turboprop or a bizjet boards by its own airstairs).
- **The wing at full scale** (`airport/wing.js`, `show: 'wing'`): one concourse of the same plan.
  - Its piers are in a modern pier's language: a concrete base and service doors, a full-height curtain wall (its
    mullions, transom and spandrel), a white roof slab proud of the glass on its fascia, a skylight and roof plant, a
    glazed tip.
  - The apron is concrete in 7.5 m slabs, with the taxilane's line and each stand's lead-in line, stop bar, painted
    number and red equipment line.
  - Each stand's aircraft is off the craft shelf in the form render, made, in an airline look the seed picks, with its
    jet bridge. At the stands `crews` busies (`busy`, `all`, `none`), its ground crew stands round it, all but the
    stairs, since the bridge has the door.
  - It is minted by the same door (`overrides: { mode: 'airport', show: 'wing', wing?, crews? }`).

### The airside ground crew: realistic support vehicles

The airfield's support vehicles, built at their true numbers in the hull kit's language, and set to work round a parked
aircraft.

- **Three classes at their true numbers** (`roads/vehicles.js`, each a class and not a replica):
  - `cateringTruck`, a catering hi-loader: 8.6 m long, 3.9 m tall.
  - `beltLoader`, a belt loader: 7.5 m long, its belt's nose 1.45 m up on the road.
  - `stairTruck`, a passenger stair truck: 8.2 m long, its platform 2.65 m up.

  The registry's `catering truck`, `belt loader` and `boarding stairs` rows now name them. Their realistic builds are
  live: previewed, parked, driven and exported to GLB like the field's vehicles. Their old scenery nets stay for the
  transport hub.
- **Their bodies** (`car-designer/road-airside.js`, in the hull kit's language):
  - the catering truck:
    - a cab-over cab, its frame and axles;
    - the galley body (ribbed sides, corner posts, roof lamps, a service door, the double doors to the aircraft, a
      rear shutter) on a two-stage scissor lift and its rams;
    - stabiliser jacks, down on their pads when it is raised;
    - the platform at its front, folded up against it on the road and laid out over the cab, rails up, once the
      body clears the cab.
  - the belt loader:
    - a low chassis, the driver's open station on the left (seat, wheel, dash) and the engine's cover behind it;
    - the conveyor over the right: its channel, belt and cleats, rollers, rubber nose, work lamps and handrail;
    - a strut at its tail and two rams ahead.
  - the stair truck:
    - a cab-over cab, the platform over it on two telescoping columns, its rails;
    - the flight down past the frame to its foot, its treads level at every height, its stringers and handrails.
- **How high each reaches** (`reach`: the galley's floor, the belt's nose, the platform):
  - stowed on the road;
  - `raised` in a brief sets it to a single-aisle airliner's door, or its hold for the belt;
  - a number (`pose.reach` to the compiler, `reach` in a loft's recipe) sets it, clamped to its range.

  The census measures each stowed.
- **Their look:**
  - the airside's white and a fleet number unless a livery is named; a camo on a base;
  - hazard stripes on the bumpers and edges, an amber beacon;
  - smooth tyres (`mil-wheel.js`, `lugs: 0`);
  - kept clean unless a wear is asked.

  A livery or wear given to `mint_solid vehicle` for one of them picks its realistic body.
- **The haulers** (`car-designer/road-airside-haul.js`; the shared kit and the reach table are in `airside-kit.js`):
  four new classes and their registry rows.
  - `baggageTug`, the baggage tug: a low tow tractor, its bonnet and ballast, the driver's seat under a roof on four
    posts, the hitch's jaw and pin.
  - `baggageCart`, a baggage cart: a bed on a turntable its drawbar steers, a canopy on posts, canvas curtains folded
    down its sides. Parked, not driven.
  - `pushbackTug`, the towbarless pushback tug: a low U, its beams either side of the nose-wheel cradle (its plate,
    clamps, pusher and ramp), the engine's deck and the sunk cab. `coupled` lifts the cradle and closes the clamps.
  - `fuelTruck`, the refueller, on three axles: an elliptical tank with dished heads on its saddles, its walkway,
    manholes, vents, folded rails and ladder; the hose cabinet with its reel and nozzle; lockers, pipework and
    placards.

  Their rows are `baggage tug` (tow tractor), `baggage cart` (baggage dolly), `pushback tug` (aircraft tug,
  towbarless tug) and `fuel truck` (refueller).
- **The turnaround** (`vehicle-registry/turnaround.js`): a parked craft's `crew` (true for its role's, or a list of
  the ground crew) sets them to work round it. Each is placed and posed to the aircraft's own geometry, read off its
  form: its doors' sills and the skin's reach at them, its holds low in the belly, its nose gear, what of its wing and
  engines stands over a band.
  - The stairs and the catering truck go to the first door, left and right, raised to its sill.
  - A belt loader goes to each hold.
  - The baggage train stands beyond the forward belt.
  - The refueller stands clear ahead of the wing.
  - The pushback stands ahead of the nose gear.

  A vehicle a door is out of reach of is left off. A camo'd aircraft's crew wears the field's camo. The crew follows
  the craft in the level's parked list, each its own figure and collider.
- **A parked airside vehicle takes `reach`.** The catering platform, laid out, telescopes past the cab so its rubber
  meets a door first. The lifts' ranges reach a twin-aisle's doors.

### Civil airliners: the made finish, the airline looks, the jumbo

The shelf's civil aircraft (the bizjet, the regional turboprop, the single-aisle and the twin-aisle) in the treatment
the fighter and the helicopters have, and a four-engined jumbo.

- **The airliner's made finish** (`craft-shelf/liner-made.js`, with `made`). A civil hull, one with a glazed flight
  deck and a windowed cabin, gets:
  - its flight deck's frame (sill, head, posts and centre post);
  - pitot probes and angle-of-attack vanes under it;
  - red beacons over and under the cabin;
  - the APU's exhaust at the tail cone;
  - each door's viewport, handle and hinge line;
  - the cargo holds' doors on the right, their outline, hinge and handle following the skin. They come from a new hull
    word, `holds`, which the single-aisle and the twin-aisle carry.

  A fighter's hull keeps the fighter's finish, and an airliner carries no IFF blades or heat bands.
- **A turbofan, made:** its nacelle and lip open, so the intake reads as a hole down to a fan face behind the blades,
  in place of the disc that stood in front of them. Its spinner carries a swirl. The fan nozzle's trailing edge and
  the core cowl step down to the plug, and the latches sit along the cowl's foot.
- **The turnaround** reads a row's own holds where it names them.
- **The airline looks** (`craft-shelf/liner-looks.js`): a third look family, `liner`, for an airliner's or a courier's
  fixed wing. Its cards are generic schemes, never a real airline's:
  - `white`;
  - `tail`, its colour and a disc on the tail;
  - `cheatline`, dark and gold lines under the windows, a polished belly and a gold sweep;
  - `bellied`, a coloured belly up to the windows and a chevron;
  - `bold`, one strong body colour, grey wings and an accent tail;
  - `freighter`, its windows plugged.

  A card's scheme sets the tail's, engines' and wings' colours, cuts a belly or cheatlines into the hull by height,
  lays an emblem on both sides of the fin and carries the tail's colour to the winglets. A look is taken by
  `assembleCraft`, `craftForm`, a world's craft figure and a parked craft.
- **A fixed wing's civil registration** is aft, under its tail, where an airliner's is; a helicopter's stays at its
  boom's root.
- **The jumbo** (archetype `jumbo`, a class and not a replica): a four-engined twin-aisle with an upper deck over its
  forward third.
  - Its hull is `fus-jumbo`: its stations raise the hump and fair it into the main deck's barrel. Its windows run in a
    row per deck, since a hull's `windows` may now be a list; the first row's ids stay a single row's, so every other
    hull is unchanged. It has main-deck doors, an upper-deck door and two holds.
  - Its wing carries inner and outer engines on their own pylons, and winglets.
  - Its tailplane and fin are its own.
  - It stands on four-wheel wing and body bogies and its own nose leg.

  It measures within a few percent of its reference. The registry's new `jumbo jet` row (jumbo, quad jet, four-engine
  airliner) names it, and the twin-aisle keeps `widebody` and `long-haul jet`.
- **The turnaround** calls a jumbo's whole crew, and the fuel truck waits clear of every engine and pylon by their
  layout's ids (a jumbo's inner and outer pairs). Its craft read loops over a big craft's corners rather than spreading
  them into an argument list.

### The crust softened: the impressions past the view cone's reach read as distance

- **`cone: { reach?, soften? }`** (`scene/channels/view-cone.js` `readCone`, drawn by `scene/channels/frame-pass.js`): past
  the cone's reach a gen-7 page draws impressions (a tree its card, a tile of buildings its card, the grass its colour
  speckled at a pixel's grain); `soften` spreads them by their distance past it, none at the reach and its most (`true`, a
  pixel and a half, the impressions' grain; or 0.5 to 4 css pixels) at three reaches, the sky at its most, so the far reads
  as the same world seen far off, with or without any air. A near thing never spreads onto the far behind it; nothing
  inside the reach is softened. The geotown and the micro-city take `cone` too (a geotown, drawn by the form render, was
  already on the cone at the screen's reach).
- **One frame pass** (`scene/channels/frame-pass.js`): the air's blur (`air.blur`, channels/atmosphere.js) moved into it, so
  the air and the soften share one target and one composite, each pixel taking the larger. `window.__mojFrame` is its probe
  ({ air, soften, passes, set }); `__mojAir.set({ blur })` reaches it.
- **A cavern's page draws again** (`form/land-read.js`, `scene/channels/form-land.js`): an underground trail has no sky
  colours, and the form land built its reflections' dome and the gen-7 sky from them, so every gen-7 cavern page threw
  before its view cone, its air or its soften could start. A land with no sky now carries `sky: null`: no gen-7 sky over
  it, its reflections in the rock's dark.

### Drone parts: a library of drone parts on the craft shelf

In progress. Drone parts as new kinds on the craft shelf:
- the frame, the arms, the motors, the rotors, the guards, the payloads and the masts;
- with the shelf's own fuselages, wings, tails, engines and gear at drone sizes for the fixed-wing ones.

Drones of many kinds assemble from them as layouts:
- multirotors: a camera quad, a racer, an inspection quad, heavy lifters, a crop sprayer, a delivery drone;
- fixed wings: a hand-launched pusher, a twin-boom, a long-endurance recon drone, a flying-wing combat drone;
- hybrids: a quadplane, a loitering munition, modelled and never fired.

Civilian or military by a look card. Drawn in the aircraft's language: the made finish, the form render, camo,
markings and wear.

- **The kinds and the first quad** (`craft-shelf/drone-odm.js`, `drone-parts.js`, `drone-archetypes.js`, merged into
  the shelf's inventory, builders and archetypes).
  - **The kinds:**
    - `drone-frame`: a moulded shell lofted nose to tail, its sensors' windows in the nose, tail and belly, the
      battery's cover, vents along its sides.
    - `drone-arm`: a beam to the motor's pad, its hinge's knuckle, a LED (green right, red left, or a status light), a
      foot the drone stands on. It folds about the vertical by the craft's `fold`.
    - `drone-motor`: an outrunner's base, its bell and cooling slots, the prop adapter; or a starship drone's lift
      vent.
    - `drone-rotor`: its hub and cap, blades with their pitch washing out and swept tips. Handed, so a mirrored pair
      counter-rotates. Spun by `pose.rotor`.
    - `drone-guard`: a prop guard's rings on spokes.
    - `drone-payload`: a three-axis gimbal camera, or a starship drone's sensor eye.
    - `drone-mast`: a GPS mast and puck.
  - **The layout's `yaw`:** degrees about the vertical, composed with `roll`, absent adding nothing. A multirotor's arms
    are radial: a quad is two mirrored pairs.
  - **The folding camera quad** (`cameraQuad`): the rear pair wears the counter-handed rotor, so its diagonals turn
    alike. It stands on its four feet and its arms fold.
  - **Its starship twin, the sentry probe** (`sentryProbe`), on four lift vents with a sensor eye. With it the new
    `survey` role holds a craft in each realm.
  - **On the roster:** `camera drone` (quadcopter, camera quad, quad drone, consumer drone) and `sentry probe`, each
    with its live craft build; the roster's role `survey`.
  - **A palette:** `droneConsumer`, a light grey moulding with its dark plastics.
  - **Held:**
    - `drone.test.js`:
      - every drone kind a row, each the same twice;
      - the arms radial and mirrored;
      - a pair handed opposite, the diagonals alike;
      - four feet on the ground;
      - the arms folding;

### Fantasy arms: truer proportions, hilts apart from ends, a held idle that clears the body

A sweep of the fantasy arms (every item in its styles, side and front three-quarter, through the workbench's own scene
so a barked shaft shows) found oversized crescent and winged guards on short blades, polearm heads too small for their
poles, pommels that outgrew their grips and a grip band floating off a grown staff. Equipment laws 2 fixes them and
separates what the hand holds from what does the work; the hero holds laws-2 gear without wearing it through the body.
Rows minted under laws 1 keep their bytes (their pins hold, now stamped). The eyes gate is the operator's.

- **Hilts and ends** (`control/lib/graph/equipment/compose.js`): `parts.hilt` (dagger, one-hand, hand-and-half,
  two-hand; wand, arm, long, pole) and `parts.end` (a blade of any outline, or any staff head), with `hiltLength` and
  `endLength` in cm. The item names are presets of the two, so a glaive, a longsword, a sword-hilted mace or a long axe
  is a word away. The staff's heads are now one function any hilt carries (`items.js staffHead`).
- **Laws 8–11** (`principles.js`): the grip counted in hands; the guard sized by its blade and its rise bounded by its
  span; the pommel balancing the blade within the grip's bounds; a head sized by its haft, a band and a collar on the
  shaft however it wanders.
- **Handling** (`control/lib/graph/polygonizer/hero-hold.js`): each laws-2 item (and every arm) is fitted in the hand
  so it clears the body's capsules at rest and through the poses it rides (a haft rolls out past the head, a blade or a
  gun turns off the thigh, a shield stands off the arm); the idle breathes through the weapon by its class and a haft
  stays upright by its wrist; every key of the stand, the idle and the walk is solved clear. The readout's
  `hero.gear.<slot>.clearance` says how near each item comes per clip.
- **Staves and clubs** (`equipment/heads.js`, laws 2's own ends on any hilt): club, spiked club, flanged mace, war
  hammer, maul, bone club, crook, orb, quarterstaff (an iron cap), trident and scythe, each sized by its haft.
- **Curved and paneled shields** (`equipment/shields.js`): the scutum, the tower, the oval and the buckler; a barrel
  bend or a dished dome (`curve`, `bend`); planks with their seams, bands and nails, or panels framed by riveted straps
  (`construction`). A laws-2 shield naming none of them is the laws-1 shield.
- **The armory** (`equipment/armory.js`): generic arms for a crowd in the new `grave` card (rusted iron, grey wood,
  verdigris, chipped edges), a roster by name and kits by role (rabble, soldier, archer, warden, brute, captain). An
  armed undead minted now is stamped (`undead.armory`) and draws its arms from its card's kit on its own seed, so a host
  of skeletons is armed variously; one minted before keeps its card's arms, under equipment laws 1.
- **A frozen copy of a held staff** (the World page, `scene-three.js`): a hero playing its clips hides its static solid,
  but the solid's textured faces (a barked staff, a printed board) kept no group tag and stayed, so a hero holding a
  barked staff stood beside a still copy of it. A previewed figure's hidden group now hides its textured faces too (a
  page with no textured face in that group is byte for byte as before). The live figure draws held gear in its colours,
  not its bark: a limit kept.
- **Review:** `scripts/render-arms.mjs` now draws through the workbench scene (textures included) and turns every
  hilted item flat to the camera.

### Four game breakers: the flight page, the arenas' outcomes, the foes patch, the tiebreak

Four defects an end-to-end sweep of the game types found, each one line where it broke and each held by a test.

- **The flight page plays.** An airspace level (a flight sim, air combat) drew a black page: the terrain LOD and the
  touch pad a game made for a screen carries both declared `__tShown` at the page script's top level, a SyntaxError
  before the first frame. The terrain LOD's is `__lodShown` now. `scene/channels/page-scope.test.js` holds the pair to
  one scope (no shared top-level name, and the two parse as one module); the emit fixture matrix has no terrain or
  screen fixture to catch it.
- **An arena's outcome is saved.** The contests (court, pitch, meet, turns, innings), the versus fighter and the holo
  table posted their outcome without `contractVersion`, so the play shell refused it at the end of every match ("the
  level's outcome could not be applied, so nothing was saved from this run"). Each envelope now opens with its wire's
  version. `game/arena-outcomes.test.js` reads every arena client for the envelopes it posts (a text reader in
  `scripts/test-changed.mjs`).
- **The casting call's patch applies as handed out.** `design_game`'s `next` foes suggestion wrote `{ op: 'add', path }`,
  which the patch door refuses (`add` is `{ into, entry }`, an entry appended to a list of ids); it writes `set` now, and
  the game book card says what `add` takes. The foe cast test applies the proposal through `applyManifestPatch`.
- **A tennis set ends.** A set tied at six all played on without end (a computer exhibition reached 61–61). The contest
  kernel's ladder takes `tiebreak: { at, to, by? }` on a unit above the lowest: tied at `at`, the unit is decided by one
  more of the unit below, counted plainly to `to` ahead by `by`, its serve changing hands after the first point and every
  two after. Tennis (the book's and the arcade rules') breaks its set at six all with a game to seven by two. A ladder
  without one plays as it did; a minted tennis match plays as before until a set reaches six all.

### The body rails: what kind of body a game puts in it

A small table of what body a kind of game puts in it (`control/lib/graph/gameworld/game-bodies.js`), as the underlayer
rails are what a world's setting makes a person wear: a new kind of body is a row. Each rail names the games it is for
(their genres, feel templates and quick goals) and, per role (the hero, the henchman a cast fields), the hero-door words
it lowers, in a style the world's own primitives choose. Heads and light are not a rail's. The book hero, the casting call and
the quick games read it.

- **The rails**: `comic` (superheroes and their henchmen: a city stalker, a brawler), `realistic` (people as they are: a
  story, survival horror, stealth, a shooter, a dungeon crawler, tactics), `muscular` (the fighters) and `mascot` (the
  platformer's: a collectathon, a runner, a racer).
- **The styles**: the anime tradition draws on the anime frame's bodies (Shonen High's for a realistic lead, Toji and
  Mizuki the grown base, Armstrong and Kale the hulking); the western on the tiered builds (a comic drawn in ink) or the
  realistic body (a material look, a realistic or a fighting game); a pixel world's mascot on the lowpoly register.
- **The muscle shirt is optional**: an anime role names the definition it would wear, and it is put on only when the
  world asks (`muscle: true`, or a definition).
- **Shonen High's body is a body codename** (`animeBody: 'shonen-high'`, either pole, its tune read from the style), so a
  game can put the lead's lean body under any anime head; under its own head it draws as the default always has.
- **The book hero takes its game's body** (opt-in): `characters.direction.body` names a rail, `'game'` (the rail its feel,
  genre or quick goal reads) or `{ rail, style?, muscle? }`. The rail's words are laid under the body page, which now
  also takes `form`, `physique`, `animeBody` and `muscleShirt`; the page's own words win, each departure in the ledger.
  The character bible's body page says the rail, its style and why. A world with a book and no body is proposed one by
  design_game (`next: [{ step: 'body', suggest: 'game' }]`), never given one; a world that names none is composed as before.
- **The henchmen take their game's body**: a dress (`foes/dress.js`) takes `rail` (and `muscle`), the henchman's words
  over the grunt's in the game's tradition: on the anime frame its codename (Armstrong or Kale, by the grunt's pole),
  western on the realistic body for a realistic or a fighting game, a mascot's frame; drawn in ink, the crew's own builds
  stand. The casting call dresses its crew with the rail the book's `direction.body` reads; a book that names none
  dresses it as before. A people foe rolled on the Egocube (not dressed) takes the same body: the words the rail
  changes over the sheet's person are laid over it when its character is made (`create_character { egocube, spec }`,
  a word set to null left off).
- **Quick games take a body**: `quick.body` (a rail, `'game'` for the one its goal reads, or `{ rail, style?, muscle? }`)
  lays the rail's hero under the hero spec's own words (a cast word naming the pole; the anime frame's codename takes the
  anime head where the spec names none) and its henchman under each foe, gunner, tower and guard the run rolls; a
  farmhand or an athlete stands as rolled, a hero by ref or a mascot is its own. Absent, every step as before.
- **The head fitted to the body**: each body codename has a home head (Toji, Mizuki, Armstrong and Kale Z-Fighter's;
  Satoru, Maki and Shonen High's own Shonen High's), and a head worn from another style is scaled half the way toward the
  home head's size (`anime-bodies.js` `headFit`): the body keeps the proportion it was drawn to, the style half its own
  (a School-Kid Hero head is still the big one). A style's head size is one number against Shonen High's per pole
  (`HEAD_SIZE`, measured: two heads' ratio is the same on every body to half a percent), held to the measure by its test.
  The NECK follows the head it carries (`neckFit`): its girth half the fitted head's remaining departure from the home
  head's size, so a bigger head stands on a thicker neck and a smaller on a slimmer, the join nearer the home pair's.
  The fit rides the body's stamp with the style it was fitted under, and fits again when the style changes; a row minted
  before, its stamp without a fit, is drawn as it was.

### The pose rails: how a game's people stand when they are shown

A character shown by a game no longer always takes the same tilted rest. A small table beside the body rails
(`control/lib/graph/gameworld/game-poses.js`) says which pose a context takes, by the game's rail and the role, from
the poses the door already has. The creator's own stand wins wherever it is said.

- **The cover**: the character bible's cover is a plate of the hero striking a showcase pose its rail picks (a comic hero
  `heroHips` or `fistToSky`, a fighter `fistCrush`, a person `pocketsCool`, a mascot `peaceWink`, a henchman crossing its
  arms), the world's seed choosing among the rail's own, photographed three-quarter.
- **The live stand and idle**: the bible's live page and its turnaround stand the hero in its rail's stand and play the
  rail's idle in place of the form's one breathing loop: a fighter's guard bouncing at the knees, a hero planted wide with
  the chest out, a person settling its weight side to side, a mascot bobbing with its head cocked. A world with no rail is
  drawn as before.
- **A showcase word as the stand**: the hero door's `gesture` takes a showcase pose (`heroHips`, `crossedArms`, …, each
  `…Left`) and holds its hit, solved on the rig with the hands on the body's own surfaces.
- **The cast lineup**: a cast's preview stands each member striking the showcase its role picks (the hero's side the
  rail's hero poses, a rival pointing the challenge, a mastermind turning its back or looking down its arms, the rank and
  file squaring up), no two neighbours alike, the right half mirrored so the line frames toward its middle. Stamped on a
  cast when it is first written (`lineup: 'showcase'`); a cast written before stands as it did.
- **The foes' portraits**: the cast sheet photographs each person foe striking the showcase its rank picks on the game's
  rail (a boss, an elite, a grunt), in memory: the foe as made never changes; a beast stands as made.

### Game type layers: from a sentence to a game that plays as its type

The sentence door (`design_game({ compose: { prompt } })`) reads a genre and lays the same walks for most of them, while
the kernels that play each type sit behind other doors (a `quick` goal, a kit, the pixelizer). This theme makes the
door reach them, one layer at a time, measured on the door people use.

- **The yardstick: the door probes** (`lib/graph/gameworld/door-probes.js`). One probe a kernel family (race, shoot,
  defend, battle, contest, tabletop, pixel, platform, sneak, fly, seats, and a blocked type), never one a genre: a
  sentence a person says, the hillclimb genre it stands for, and the concept the made game must hold, read from what
  the run would make (`runner.js` `runSteps`: each level's `compose_world` order, nothing minted). Each probe records
  what the door makes `now`; when the probes landed every family's was `not`.
  - `door-probes.e2e.test.js` (the e2e tier) runs each sentence through `design_game`'s own `composedWorld` (exported for
    it) and the run's steps, and holds each probe to its `now`: a door that starts making a family's game, or stops,
    fails until the table says so.
  - `door-probes.test.js` holds each concept to the door that makes its family's game today (its `reference`, a book
    world or a quick goal) and against a bare walk, so a concept that could never hold is caught.
  - The hillclimb page's genre probes gain a **from a sentence** column beside the registry's verdict, read from the
    table (`npm run tool-surface`).
- **The door lays a genre's levels in its book form** (`lib/graph/gameworld/genre-forms.js`, read by `compose.js`). The
  quick door stays the one-level outcome door; a game sentence is laid as a book world, its levels in the form its
  kernel plays.
  - **Flight:** a flight sim, air combat or a space shooter is laid as airspace levels: a runway and a gate course, in
    a trainer, a jet or a space fighter (an asteroid field). No walk, no town. The brief says so (`brief.levelForm`).
  - **Hand-off:** a match-3 saga is said to be the pixelizer's (`create_pixelizer_game({ reducer: 'stone-saga' })`),
    and nothing is laid.
  - **Refusal:** a genre the registry cannot make yet (the cosmos dry run's verdict: co-op kitchen, party mash,
    split-screen deathmatch, driver and gunner, the co-op scroller) is refused with the values it waits on and the
    makeable genres the same words point at. Nothing is laid in its place; it used to be laid as single-player walks.
  - The genres the book lays in its own walks and buildings are laid as before.
  - **Racing waits on the vehicle registry's ride.**
- **A genre's own name is a clear read on its own** (`intent.js` `readGenre`): "metroidvania", "tennis" or "tower
  defence" said once writes the genre, ahead of another genre's plain words. Plain words still need two, and two
  genres' names said alike are a tie. "stealth guards and a race with cars" reads as stealth now.
- The fly, pixel and blocked probes hold (`now: 'type'`). The fly probe's reference is a book world. The hillclimb
  column says "refused" and "handed off" where that is the right answer.
- **A genre the book cannot lay from a sentence yet is refused until its form lands** (`genre-forms.js` `PENDING`), not
  laid as walks. Each refusal says what it waits on and the one level it plays alone today (`design_game({ quick: { goal } })`):
  - racing and kart racing: a ride the book drives
  - the arena shooter: its deathmatch as a book level
  - tower defence, RTS, tactics, farming, rhythm, roguelike, the puzzles, the versus fighter and the sports: the
    kernel as a book level
  - Laid as before: the genres of the book's own walks and buildings (dungeon crawler, collectathon, top-down adventure,
    metroidvania, survival horror, story), and the ones a hero completes (stealth's guards, a co-op platformer's side
    camera and seats, a party's battles).
- **A genre on foot is laid with a hero, its camera and its screen** (`genre-forms.js` `heroFrameOf`, read by
  `compose.js`). Where the genre's cube asks a hero, the sentence's world has one, said in the brief (`brief.hero`):
  - its body the game's (`characters.direction.body: 'game'`, the body rails) in the world's own tradition, moving
    by the genre's vibe;
  - no powers, said: `actions: { none: true }`, an answer the actions page now takes (no system, idiom or
    progression; nothing open), so an autonomous run makes the hero and then its levels in one call;
  - the camera the cube asks (side for a metroidvania or a co-op platformer, fixed for survival horror; third person
    is the hero's own chase), with no climbs under a side camera and no side-scroller laid indoors;
  - a monitor's screen (16:9), except a runner's phone.
  A dungeon crawler, a collectathon, a metroidvania, survival horror, stealth, a party's battles and a co-op
  platformer's seats are now played by a body from their sentence, not by a bodiless first-person walker.
- **The endless runner and the city stalker are laid in their forms with that hero**: runner levels, and city levels
  played by the stalker with the wall and the line (`moves: ['wall', 'swinger']`). They are no longer refused.
- **A building level takes the world's camera**: top-down plays its rooms under the overhead camera, moving in the
  screen's frame; fixed stands a camera over each room; a side camera is refused there (no lane). Absent, the chase as
  before.
- **A city level carries the world's screen** (`city/plan/card.js` takes `screen` as a world channel); a city level
  with one was refused.
- **A guard holds a post it cannot see the start from** (`quick.js` `guardPosts`): guards stand only on the beats past a
  guard's sight from the spawn (its narrow beam, 14 m, and a step), where the way has any. On a short way the first
  guard faced the spawn from inside its beam, and the level was lost before the hero moved. A way whose beats all lie
  within it is posted as before.
- The battle, platform, sneak and seats probes hold. The battle probe reads a battle or a party's encounters (a level's
  bag is a play block too).
- **The hero fights with what it carries.** An adornment item may serve the body's own verbs beside the powers
  (`adornment.js` `BASIC_VERBS`): `serves: ['strike']` (it is swung) or `['shoot']` (it is fired). A hero with no powers
  still carries what it fights with, and the page leaves nothing open. The page takes any item the gear door takes,
  the firearms and the arms library's included (`GEAR_ITEMS`); the equipment table keeps the myth's classes, and a
  firearm is built from the item itself.
  - **The strike** (`levels.js`): a hero carrying a right-hand item for its strike takes the runtime's own contact
    window on its pilot rule where no feel names one, on a trail and in a building. The page arms the rule with what
    the figure holds (the held strike: its reach, seconds and damage), and the controls say `click  strike`. Seen in a
    composed crawler's exported page: three swings of the sword took a grunt from 20 to 14.
  - **The shot**: a hero carrying a right-hand firearm for its shot fires it as the quick shooter's player does (a
    pistol the handgun's numbers, a long gun the rifle's, from the eye; its body hittable). A third-person hero is
    played over the shoulder, its rounds converging on the crosshair. The controls say `click  fire`.
  - A hero carrying nothing for either is played as before, byte for byte.
- **A sentence's hero is armed by its genre**: a sword for a genre that fights in melee (dungeon crawler, top-down
  adventure, metroidvania, the brawlers), a carbine for one that fights only at range (a first-person shooter, played
  from the armed hero's eyes) and a pistol for survival horror. A composed world whose hero fights is cast:
  `design_game`'s compose writes the casting call's proposal (the foes, each level's stand; `brief.foes` names the
  roles), where it used to be only suggested. A fighting genre's "guards" are its foes, not watchers the level is lost
  to (the sneak keeps those). The shooter, the arena brawler and the co-op brawler are laid from a sentence, no longer
  refused.
- **A building's hero starts a step into its entry room** (2.5 m along its heading, where the room holds it). At the
  door, with the wall at its back, its chase was pulled in until the hero's back filled the frame. The level's ends stay
  at the door.
- The strike probe (a hero swinging what it holds, with foes to strike: the composed crawler) joins the table and holds;
  the shoot probe holds.

### The air of a gen-7 geocube

- **A fog by its visibility** (`scene/channels/atmosphere.js`, the recipe's `air` on the `geocube` kind, every gen-7 show:
  the path and trail, the geocity, a hall, a room, a cavern). `haze`, `mist`, `fog`, `true` (haze), or `{ kind, visibility,
  clear, height, glow, blur }` over a kind. Its extinction is Beer-Lambert's, set by a VISIBILITY in metres (where a dark
  thing's contrast against the air falls to 2%) past a clear distance at the eye. Outside it lies low: its density falls
  with height over the walk's ground by a scale height (`height`, false to lie even), each ray's optical depth integrated
  in closed form, so a mist sits at the walker's feet and a hill top stands over it; toward the sun it glows (`glow`).
  Each word has a trail's measures, a metro's (a geocity: the same haze seeing kilometres, in a deeper layer) and a room's;
  inside (no sun: a hall, a room, a cavern) it lies even, its colour a room's own light (its ambient and a share of its
  lamps over its void, `roomAirColour`), a cavern keeping its page's dark. It is three's own fog chunk, patched once
  before any material compiles, so every surface that took the page's fog takes it (the form's land, grass and far field,
  the trees and their cards, the far structures' tiles, a room's baked surfaces); its colour stays the page's (the form
  sky's haze, the city's air; a room's its own light, below), and `scene.fog.density` is its extinction, so the weather still
  thickens and thins it. A painted (gen-6) page and the unshaded export keep their haze; the word is read on any geocube.
- **The sky veiled to it**: the gen-7 dome takes the air at its horizon, in a band as thick as the air (`band`, the kind's),
  so the land and the sky meet in one colour where the fog swallows the land.
- **The far softened** (`blur`, css pixels at its most, 3 by default; false for none): the frame drawn to a target with its
  depth, then laid on the canvas with each pixel spread over a golden-angle disc by how much air lies between it and the
  eye (the same optical depth, rebuilt from the depth), only past the view cone's reach (where the impostors begin: the
  trees' and the buildings' cards, the far field's colour), never nearer than a fifth of the visibility. A near thing never spreads
  onto the far behind it, and nothing near is softened. The target holds what the canvas would (tone-mapped and encoded as
  on screen); a renderer without half-float targets, a non-perspective camera and an XR session keep the plain frame.
  `window.__mojAir` is the probe (`set({ blur })` live).
- **Its own colour** (`colour`, #rrggbb): the air as the eye sees it where it is not the page's (a neon night's glow over
  its streets); a room's own light otherwise, as above.
- **Every show takes it**: the geocity's, the geotown's and the micro-city's own settings gates take `air` (they refused it),
  and inside is what the page is (a room's form, a cavern) rather than the sun's absence, so a night outside keeps the
  outside's measures and lies low.
- An engine export draws its own fog (`godot-marks.js` `air`); absent `air`, the page is byte for byte as it was.

### The heavy utility vehicle: a buffed-up jeep in the field's language

A heavy utility 4x4, a class and not a replica: wide, low and heavy-tyred, a four-door hard top or a two-door cab with
a canvas-covered bed.

- **The class** (`heavy4x4`, `roads/vehicles.js`): 4.6 m long, 2.16 m wide, 1.83 m tall, its wheels 3.3 m apart on
  0.47 m tyres at its body's corners. Governed as its manual is; the sheet reads it a truck on a ladder frame.
- **The body** (`car-designer/road-military.js`, kind `heavyUtility`, in the hull kit's language):
  - a slab side to the class's width, its wheel openings arched and lipped in rubber;
  - a floor, the frame low between the wheels, the axles' housings;
  - a wide flat bonnet over the whole nose, its grille slotted between round lamps and their markers;
  - heavy bumpers;
  - a four-door cab: a raked two-pane screen in its frame, its wipers, the pillars, glass inset from the body's side
    over a ledge, the doors' shut lines, handles and hinges, a roof with an empty ring and its hatch, a rear wall and
    its window;
  - a short deck behind the cab, its tailgate, its tail lamps.

  The side skin stands a little in from the class's width, so its handles, hinges and lips stay inside it.
- **`cargo`** (a brief's cargo, troop, bed, canvas, pickup: `heavyWords`): a two-door cab and a long bed under bows and
  a canvas tilt.
- **Its kit:** cans and tools on its deck's sides, the whip, grab bars, mud flaps, shackles, the pintle, mirrors, a
  tarp maybe.
- **The registry:** `heavy utility vehicle` (humvee, heavy jeep, high mobility vehicle, wide jeep, military SUV),
  role transport, driven, crewed, parked and in traffic. Its realistic body is live. "Humvee" is a word here, said of
  any such vehicle, as "jeep" is.
- **Held** (`road-military.test.js`):
  - both bodies at the class's size, its axles its wheelbase apart;
  - its openings arched and lipped, what stands proud of its side inside the width;
  - four doors and no tilt for a hard top, two doors and the bows and canvas for `cargo`;
  - its words;
  - within its budget (under 25k triangles plain, 60k in camo and used);
  - the same twice;
  - found by its words, live.

  The engines' sweep builds its GLB, valid by the Khronos validator.
- **Also:** `parked.test.js`'s room for every field body side by side is as deep as they are, since the field grows a
  class at a time.
- **Seen** (machine gate only; the eyes gate is open): both bodies in woodland, used, from three quarters, the front,
  behind and the side.

### Helicopters: rotorcraft on the craft shelf, military and civilian

Helicopters on the craft shelf:
- **Their rotor systems:**
  - a main rotor's head, swashplate, pitch links and drooped, handed blades, folding aft;
  - a tail rotor or a ducted fan.

  Both spin in the figure as the drones' rotors do.
- **Their cowlings, exhausts and kit.**
- **Their airframes:**
  - a light civilian helicopter;
  - a medium utility machine that is a medevac or an assault transport by its look;
  - an armoured tandem attack helicopter (its weapons modelled, never fired);
  - a heavy tandem-rotor transport.
- **The APC's language on the military hulls:** chamfered faceted armour, plates and bolt rows.
- **Civilian or military by a look card.**

- **The rotor systems and the light helicopter** (`craft-shelf/heli-odm.js`, `heli-parts.js`, `heli-archetypes.js`,
  merged into the shelf's inventory, builders and archetypes).
  - **A main rotor** (`heli-rotor`):
    - its head: the mast, the swashplate's fixed lower ring and turning upper ring, a pitch link from the upper ring to
      each blade's horn (leading it), the scissors, the hub and its cap, each blade's grip and elastomeric bearing;
    - its blades: long, cambered, washing out from root to tip, drooping toward their tips as a rotor at rest does,
      their tips swept back and banded.

    Handed; spun by `pose.rotor` about its hub. Its blades swing aft about their grips by the craft's `fold`, lying
    along the boom.
  - **A tail** (`heli-tail`):
    - a tail rotor: its gearbox out to the side, its hub, its blades turning about the craft's x, its pitch spider;
    - or a ducted fan: the shroud's walls open with its lips round both faces, its hub, its blades spaced unevenly, its
      stators, a fin's root on its top.
  - **A roof cowling** (`heli-cowl`): its intakes' grilles each side, its exhaust (or two), the transmission's fairing
    round the mast, the mast's point on top.
  - **The light single-engine helicopter** (`lightHeli`):
    - a low tub forward under a glass bubble, the cabin full height behind it with its doors, the boom tapering aft;
    - the cowling and the three-blade rotor on the cabin's roof;
    - the stabilizer with its end plates, the fin, the ventral fin;
    - the tail rotor;
    - skids.

    The shelf's own kinds (fuselage, canopy, stabilizer, fin) and the drones' skid as new rows. A palette:
    `heliCivil`. On the roster: `light helicopter` (news, police and private helicopter, light chopper).
  - **Spinning:** `spins` take a helicopter's rotors: the main rotor about its mast's top, the tail rotor about the
    craft's x. A rotorcraft's figure gets its `spin` clip, as a drone's does.
  - **Held** (`heli.test.js`):
    - the head's parts per blade;
    - the blades drooping to the rotor's radius, spun about a still hub, folded aft along the boom;
    - both tails spinning about the craft's x, the fan's shroud open;
    - a tail rotor's thrust against its main rotor's torque (a rotor turning anticlockwise from above turns its fuselage
      nose right; its tail rotor pushes the tail right);
    - the helicopter on its skids, level, its rotor clear above, at its figures;
    - its rotors' bones at their hubs;
    - within 50k triangles, the same twice, found by its words.

    The shelf's char test pins the new builder paths; no other pin moved. The deep sweep builds every part closed and
    assembles the helicopter at its figures.
  - **Seen** (machine gate only; the eyes gate is open): the helicopter from three quarters, the side and the front, its
    rotor head close up, its cabin.
- **The cockpit, a part of its own** (`craft-shelf/cockpit-parts.js`, the shelf's new kind `craft-cockpit`, the
  operator having seen the bubble empty). Drawn by default wherever a craft's glass lets one see in, sized by its row
  and seated on a hull point at the cabin's floor.
  - **Layouts:** `side` (side by side: one panel across, a centre console between) or `tandem` (down the centreline, the
    rear seat raised, a panel before each).

    - `parked.test.js`:
      - the word helicopter a live craft that stands parked;
