      - a craft's words read and refused (another family's look, a fold out of range, a pad too big, a craft word on a
        car);
      - its figure a craft's, its box its body's, turned with its heading, narrower than its rotor's disc;
      - in a world, its figure compiled with its helipad and its box beside the level's colliders;
      - a base folding helicopters into its hangar in the air's nearest camo, refusing one that does not fit.
    - `heli.test.js`: the GLB.
  - **Seen** (machine gate only; the eyes gate is open): a world with four parked: the medevac and the police
    helicopter each on a helipad, the attack helicopter in desert camo, the tandem with its blades folded.
  - **Not done:** flying them (a hover model, the rotor's thrust), and a cabin seen through an open side door.

### Worn objects of your own: anything made, worn on a bone

The hero wears what no catalogue has. `attach: [{ object | ref, at, … }]` on the hero door
(`control/lib/graph/polygonizer/hero-attach.js`) puts an object of the operator's own on a bone: a workbench recipe
inline (lathes, extrudes, sweeps, lofts, fields, shells, a program, cuts: the workbench's whole language), or a solid
already made with `mint_solid { kind: 'workbench' }` by its `ref`, copied in at the door so the hero stays its own recipe
(a later edit of the solid never moves it until the ref is set again). It is the protoform figure's attachment seam,
brought to the hero and carried the way held gear is.

- **Placed by words**: `at` a rig joint or a pair with `t` along it, riding the bone that starts there (or `bone` by id);
  `size` in metres along `fit`, or the object's own size; `anchor`, `rotate`, `align: 'bone'`, `offset`; `mirror: true`
  wears a reflected twin on the other side.
- **Carried everywhere gear is**: rigid on its bone at rest, so the stand, the clips, the rig preview and the skinned GLB
  carry it; the spend counts it with the gear; the readout's `hero.attach` names each object's bone, length and share of
  the figure's height. It layers over whatever the hero wears.
- **Refused clearly, never broken**: an attachment is checked at the door (one object or ref, a joint, the placing
  words; an object that draws nothing, or a ref that is not a workbench solid, is refused); at render a joint the rig lacks
  wears nothing. A hero without `attach` is byte for byte as it was. Manual: the layered card's `hero-attach` section.

### The manual manipulator's controllers: hands in the headset

The headset's controllers become the player's hands: their poses are input, the game runs in the headset, the hero's
own hands, and what they hold, are drawn where the controllers are, and a swing or a shot from them lands in the game,
so a saber rhythm level, a gun held as a gun or VR boxing can be made. Played on a Quest by no one yet: the eyes gate
is the operator's.

- **Poses are input** (`controls/xr-driver.js`): the `xr` family carries the poses OpenXR names (`head`, each hand's
  `grip` and `aim`) beside its buttons and sticks; `xrPoses` reads them from a frame and `poseToWorld` carries one from
  the headset's y-up play space into the z-up world through the rig, so a recorded pose stream replays in Node.
- **The headset plays the game** (`scene/channels/xr.js`): on a page with a pilot, entering the headset no longer
  stops the game. The controllers read through the pilot scheme's `xr` bindings as a pad does (the left stick walks,
  the right turns, the right trigger fires, A jumps, the left grip uses), the pilot walks and turns on the body the
  headset estimates and looks where the head looks, a step in the play space moves the pilot (a wall stops it), the
  view stands where the pilot stands, and the pilot's body is hidden (first person). Any game level's live page takes it
  with `?xr=1`. A page without a pilot walks as before; a page without `xr` is unchanged byte for byte.
- **The hero's hands on the controllers** (`polygonizer/hero-xr-hands.js`): in the headset the hero's own hands are drawn
  where the controllers are, each on its grip pose (the hand's grip centre on the grip's origin, through the fist toward
  the thumb along its −Z, the back of the right hand along its +X, as WebXR defines the grip), its fingers following
  the controller: the grip closes the middle, ring and little fingers and points the index, the trigger closes the
  index, and the thumb comes down while it rests on a thumb button. The hands reuse the body's own bone meshes (no new
  geometry on the page); what rides the hero's figure is a small table per finger, its bones at seven curls, played as
  the page plays any clip, and it rides only a world a headset plays (its `xr`, or `?xr=` on the live page). A hero
  with mitten hands, or a page without a headset, is unchanged.
- **What the hands hold, and a shot from them**: a hero's held item (its `gear` right or left) is drawn in the headset
  apart from the hand that holds it, re-held for a controller: a blade comes out of the fist past the thumb, its edge
  leading with the knuckles; a gun is presented, its grip through the fist and its bore along the hand, raked a little
  toward the thumb; a bow or a long staff keeps the hero's own hold. A hand that holds something closes round it from
  the grip. The ranged weapon takes an opt-in aim (`input.aim`, `worlds/controllable/combat-ranged.js`): in the headset
  the round leaves from the held gun's muzzle along its bore, or, where the hand holds no gun, along the controller's
  own ray, so the controller is the gun whatever the body or the head faces. A game without a headset fires as before.
- **A hit from a swing** (`worlds/controllable/sweep.js`): in the headset, what each hand strikes with is handed to the
  game each frame (a held blade from its guard to its tip, an empty hand its fist's knuckles, the controller itself
  where the hero's hands are not drawn), and whatever it crosses as it moves is struck: the first hittable body its path
  meets, moving at a swing's pace (a blade resting in a body strikes nothing), once a pass. The blow lands as melee's
  does (the flash, the damage, the stagger, a spark at the point of contact), and the game hears the CUT, its
  direction in the player's view (up, down, left, right), its speed and the hand, as `cut` and `cut:<id>` beside the
  hit. The pass is composed only into a page a headset plays; every other page keeps every byte.
- **Notes to cut on the beat** (the `notes` mechanic, `game/mechanics.js`; its card `mechanic-cards/notes.md`): a rhythm
  chart played by note bodies the level mints asleep, a small pool per lane, each floating at its lane's height. A note
  wakes `lead` beats before its own at its lane's far end and walks in at the pace that puts it on the cutting line on
  its beat (the music's clock says a beat early, so it walks that much longer); a cut in its direction and with its
  hand scores it and sends it away, a wrong one leaves it walking, and one that passes the line, or that something stops
  on its walk, is a miss. Every note scored or missed wins; `misses` can lose. A pool too small for its chart is
  refused, naming the lane.
- **A saber level, as a concept** (the notes card, `mechanic-cards/notes.md`): a saber rhythm level is parts on any
  stage level, written out in the card: the level played in a headset, the hero holding two light blades (the `saber`
  equipment style: a neon blade, its own glow, out of a short machined hilt; red in the left hand, blue in the right),
  note blocks minted asleep per lane and cut (the glyph forms `note-up`, `note-down`, `note-left`, `note-right`,
  `note-any`: a cube with its arrow on every side; a glyph body now keeps its other fields, `hittable` and `egg`), a
  club score with its seed fixed so its beat is the chart's, and `notes` with `score`. And `xr` at the world (and the
  quick game's) level, carried onto every stage level, so any game's pages open a session that plays it.
- **The HUD in the headset** (`scene/channels/xr.js`): a game played in a headset shows its HUD there. The page's HUD is
  drawn on a panel in the play space, low on the floor ahead of the player and tilted up to the eye, under where a
  game's things come at the player: its left slots on the left, its right on the right, the rest in the middle, each
  widget its own text in its own colour and fade. It is the HUD the game already has (a saber game's notes and score, a
  shooter's rounds, a toast, a banner), not its keyboard legend; it is drawn again only when what it says changes.
  `xr: { hud: false }` leaves it out.

### The manual manipulator: arms that hit targets, hands that grasp by role

The realistic hero's arms and hands, solved from targets rather than picked from a pose library. This lands the
studies, the arm's and the hand's servos, the arm solver with the body joining in and its target drill, the wider hand
and the hand solver. Still to come: the arm and the hand moving as one, and the words a person asks for them by; until
then none of it is reachable from the hero door (the scripts under `control/scripts/spikes/manipulator/` drive it).

- **Space boxer (the arm).** The shoulder, elbow, forearm and wrist as servos (a hard range, a comfortable range, a
  rest and a speed each, from published adult norms), and an exact solver that brings a chosen surface of the hand
  (knuckles, palm heel, the little-finger edge, the back of the fist, the fingertips) to a target along a straight line
  or an arc. When the arm alone cannot reach, the girdle, the trunk, the hips and then a step join in, in that order.
  First result: a seeded target drill, the hero hitting targets around it at different distances.
- **Octopus boxer (the hand).** Each finger and the thumb solved as its own small reacher from a palm treated as a box
  with named faces, with roles (the thumb opposes, the index triggers or points, the other three wrap and support), so a
  hand grips a haft around its own size and forms shapes such as a crane beak, a tiger claw or sword fingers.
- **Opt-in, byte for byte.** The hand words `relaxed`, `open`, `fist`, `point` and `grip` run exactly as before, and
  every hero and clip minted before is unchanged.
- **The studies** (`control/scripts/spikes/manipulator/`): `hand-measures.mjs` (the hand's controls, each word's bends,
  the thumb's path, opposition tip to tip) and `arm-envelope.mjs` (seeded targets through today's arm solver from the
  guard: error, elbows, the punch line, time). The baseline: today's thumb curls in a fixed arc 29–46 mm in front of
  the palm and cannot meet the middle finger; the arm reaches within about a millimetre at most distances but takes
  about 0.2 s a solve, misses some cross-body and high targets at full reach, and lands near targets with the forearm
  45–66° off the line a straight punch needs.
- **The arm's servos** (`lib/graph/polygonizer/hero-servo.js`): the shoulder read as swing and rotation off the posed
  skeleton (a plane of elevation and an elevation held to a cone that reaches differently by direction, the rotation
  external +), the girdle's turn, the elbow and the wrist each with a hard range and an ease range from adult norms
  (estimates marked), and the speeds the hero's own strikes and swings reach. `servoRead` reads a pose and
  `servoReport` a clip; advisory, nothing refuses. Read over every stance, strike, guard and swing
  (`scripts/spikes/manipulator/servo-audit.mjs`): the shoulder's rotation is the joint the clips push past its range
  most (a thrust's rear arm thrown back about 35° past it), then the forearm's turn in three sword guards; no clip
  bends an elbow past its stop.
- **Space boxer, the arm** (`lib/graph/polygonizer/hero-reach.js`): a target is reached by bringing a surface of the
  hand (knuckles, the back of the fist, the palm heel, the knife edge, the fingertips) to it, facing along its approach,
  the arm held to its servos. The solve keeps hero-grip's way (the hand placed first, the arm solved to serve it) and
  adds the hand's roll, its aim and the force line (the wrist as its surface wants it, so a fist lands with the forearm
  behind it). Each strike tries a straight, a hook and an uppercut and keeps the cheapest, so a near target is hooked
  or uppercut and a far one punched straight without being told. From the guard, against today's arm solver on the
  same targets: every target within reach landed within a millimetre (today's within 5 mm for about four in five,
  missing by up to 8 cm), the forearm a median 5–9° off the line of the strike (today's 22–67°); but about twice as slow
  cold.
- **The body joins in** when the arm cannot land a target, a rung at a time and only as far as it must: the shoulders'
  girdle turns, then the trunk turns, leans and bows, then the hips turn and the weight shifts over the feet (held
  inside them) with the knees bending, then the striking side's foot steps toward the target. Targets a tenth past the
  arm's reach now land within 2 mm (they fell 5–8 cm short); a target past what a step can bring in is reported as
  missed, not stretched to.
- **The target drill** (`targetDrill`; `scripts/spikes/manipulator/drill.mjs`): seeded targets around the shoulder, each
  struck and recovered to the guard, timed by the servos' speeds, and checked on the clip as played (the contact, the
  facing, the servos, how close the hand keeps to its drive, the balance). A straight drives along its line; a hook and
  an uppercut along an arc that meets the target along its approach, the trunk coiling into it; a step lifts the foot
  and sets it down. `--page` writes a review page that plays the drill's skeleton with the targets and their drives
  drawn.
- **The wider hand** (the rig's `fingers<S>`): a digit may be given as an object, each joint by its own angle (the
  knuckle, the middle joint and the last, a middle joint alone bringing the last at two thirds), each finger spread
  away from the middle, and the thumb turned across the palm and in toward it on a second axis. A number or a word is
  the curl it always was, to the bit, and nothing is added to the rig, so every hero minted before is unchanged. With
  it the thumb meets every fingertip, the middle's included, which the one-curl thumb could not reach.
- **The hand's servos** (`hero-servo.js` `handRead`): each finger joint's angle, its spread and the thumb's read off the
  posed hand in its own frame, held to adult norms (estimates marked); every hand word lies within them.
- **Octopus boxer, the hand** (`lib/graph/polygonizer/hero-digits.js`): each digit reaches a point with its pad or tip,
  or closes onto an object knuckle first, then the middle joint, then the last, each until it touches, the hand's
  servos held throughout. A haft laid in the palm is held round its own size: on hafts from 12 to 40 mm every phalanx
  ends on the surface, and a thinner haft closes the hand further. Hand shapes are compositions of those goals: crane
  beak, tiger claw, sword fingers, leopard fist, phoenix eye, vertical palm, pinch, OK, fist, grip and point (plain
  aliases resolve). Each solves into the rig's own finger channel, so it plays and exports as any hand word does. The
  existing hand words' thumbs turn out to run through the curled fingers; the solved fist keeps its thumb clear.
- **Fixed in the studies:** the arm envelope now stands in the guard (it stood at rest), the servo audit plays swings
  with the elbows-down roll and reads the wrist as anatomy.

### Military aircraft: the field's visual language on the craft shelf

In progress. The craft shelf's aircraft drawn in the field's language:
- the form render's material slots and the setting's light;
- camo, panel lines and markings cut in as geometry;
- wear (soot, streaks, chipped edges, patched panels);
- kit as cards.

New military aircraft on new flight primitives (a helicopter's rotors, a reconnaissance drone), parked in a base and
exported to a valid GLB.

- **The craft in the form render** (`craft-shelf/craft-form.js`): the shelf's own craft, the same faces and size,
  handed to the page instead of baked.
  - **From the lowered build:** the assembler lowered under the flat light (raw albedo), each face kept with its item
    (the hull, each wing, the engine, the canopy, the gear, the stores) as its part.
  - **Its slot:**
    - its palette role where its colour is one;
    - else its material's signature: a light rough and lit, glass smooth, bare metal metallic, rubber dark and rough;
    - else the nearer of paint and trim.

    A light is told by its hue: port red, starboard green, an exhaust's glow.
  - **`AIR_MATERIALS`:** a semi-gloss paint and its trim, bare and hot metal, a canopy's tinted glass, the rubber, the
    nav lights and the glow.
  - **Its form:** corner normals smoothed within each item and slot at a crease, so a lofted hull reads round and a
    trailing edge stays sharp.
  - **The figure** (`craftFormFigure`, and `craftFigure(archetype, { light: 'form' })`): one bone per item, still,
    lit by its world's sky (`skyMood`) or noon. Without the word, the baked figure as it always was.
  - **Held** (`craft-form.test.js`):
    - the shelf's size and items;
    - every face a slot, an albedo, unit normals; the slots an aircraft has, nav lights both sides;
    - the hull round;
    - a bone per item, in the form render, dimmer at night;
    - the same twice; the baked figure unchanged;
    - its GLB valid by the Khronos validator.
  - **Seen** (machine gate only; the eyes gate is open): the multirole fighter at noon and under a golden sun, and the
    close-support jet at noon, in the page's own light and shadows.

- **The study** (after the craft in the form render): the aircraft, close up, were nowhere near the vehicles' made
  detail.
  - **What they lacked:** smooth lofts with ring seams only; an opaque canopy; a smooth scoop; hinge lines that barely
    read; box petals; a torus tyre; a plastic sheen; the mirrored half of every pair shading as its underside.
  - **The breakdown:** what each part kind must carry, the recomposition's order (the plan).
- **The aircraft detail kit:**
  - **The skin** (`craft-shelf/air-kit.js`). Panel lines laid on each item's own faces along the planes they lie on:
    - a ribbon a centimetre and a half wide, a millimetre proud, a quad on each face a line crosses;
    - darker than the paint and in its slot, so a livery's cut passes it by.

    By part kind:
    - **A tube** (a fuselage, a nacelle, an intake, a store): its frames round it, closer over its forward third; its
      longerons (the spine, the chines, the waterline, the keel); its access panels outlined, their fasteners set on
      the skin where a ray from the axis meets it.
    - **A wing or a tailplane:** its ribs across the span, its front and rear spars.
    - **A fin:** the same, up its span.

    `craftForm(archetype, { made: true })` lays them. The fighter's made skin costs about 7.5k triangles.
  - **The parts** (`craft-shelf/air-kit-parts.js`), the shelf's own monomers for the builders' made finish (the
    recomposition, next):
    - a rolled lip;
    - a hinge line and its knuckles;
    - a door with its hinge and actuator;
    - a gear's well (boxed, ribbed, its plumbing);
    - a treaded tyre on its hub and brake disc;
    - a petal nozzle (petals with gaps, their rods, the flameholder's rings and spray bars inside, a heat-tinted
      throat);
    - a light in its clear cover;
    - a blister;
    - a raked blade.

    Their tints give their materials through the shelf's own finish.
  - **The light:**
    - the paint's sheen lowered;
    - the canopy's glass seen into (transparent);
    - a big figure's own shadow bias (the form's `normalBias`, the page taking the deeper of its own and the
      figure's);
    - every form face wound to agree with its normal. The page draws both sides and turns a back face's normal round,
      so a mirrored part's faces, wound against theirs, shaded as their underside.
  - **Held** (`air-kit.test.js`):
    - the seams laid on the hull, the wings and the fin, darker, in their slot, on the skin;
    - the fasteners;
    - every face wound to its normal;
    - the made fighter within 40k triangles, the same twice;
    - each kit part lowering in its tints at its size (a tyre's tread ribbed, a nozzle's petals);
    - the light's materials and bias.
  - **Seen** (machine gate only; the eyes gate is open): the made fighter whole and from above (the spine's bay and its
    fasteners, the wing's ribs and spars, the mirrored wing lit), and the nose.
- **The cockpit** (the operator saw the glass empty). A fighter's cockpit under its canopy (`air-kit-parts.js`
  `cockpit`), the hull's own under the made finish, so it stays put when the canopy opens.
  - **Built up from a dark deck over the hull's top:** the hull is a closed skin, and what is under it is never seen.
  - **Fitted to the canopy's own section where each piece stands.** The layout hands the hull the canopy it sets on
    it, and a bubble narrows and drops toward its nose.
  - **Its pieces:**
    - the coaming and its glare shield over the instrument panel, its two displays and its dials;
    - the HUD's combiner on its posts;
    - low side consoles;
    - the stick;
    - the ejection seat: its pan, its raked back, its headrest under the roof, the yellow pull handle, its rails.
  - **The canopy's own glass,** made, the smoky gold of its coating.
  - **Threaded:** `made` runs through `assembleCraft`, the layout and `resolveCraftPart` to a builder (absent, its
    recipe as it was).
  - **Held** (`air-kit.test.js`): the seat, its handle, the HUD's glass, all inside the canopy and under its roof; the
    gold glass when made; none without the word or on a craft with no canopy.
  - **Seen** (machine gate only; the eyes gate is open): from the side and from over the nose.
- **The fighter recomposed, part by part** (`craft-shelf/air-made.js`). The made finish each of the shelf's builders adds
  under the word, drawn with the kit's parts. Earth craft only: a spacecraft's language is its own. By part kind:
  - **The hull:**
    - the radome's dark break ring;
    - the angle-of-attack vanes and the IFF blades;
    - the bands the engine's heat leaves over its end (straw, blue, brown, a tint over the paint).
  - **The gear's wells and doors, the airframe's:**
    - The layout hands the hull the parts set on its hardpoints. Each retracting leg's well is laid on the hull's own
      skin: its roof in primer, ribbed, its plumbing. Its doors hang open with the leg down and lie shut with it up.
    - A leg standing in a chin intake's duct has its well under the duct.
    - A well lies the way its leg folds where the belly (or the duct) stays flat over it. Where it would run off the
      nose or the duct, it lies the other way.
  - **The canopy's frame:** its sill rails, the windscreen's bow (where the row names none), its aft frame, moving with
    it as it opens.
  - **The intake:**
    - a polished rolled lip;
    - its duct opened and lined dark back to a deep face, so the mouth reads deep;
    - a side intake's splitter plate on its struts.
  - **The afterburning engine:** the petal nozzle (its petals, rods, flameholder and spray bars) in place of the turned
    one, the engine's face dark behind it.
  - **The gear:** treaded tyres on hubs that show inside the sidewall, the brake disc, a brake line down each leg, the
    nose leg's taxi light.
  - **The wings and the tail:**
    - each control surface's hinge gap on both faces;
    - actuator fairings under a wing's surfaces;
    - the leading-edge flap's line;
    - the nav light in its clear cover;
    - a fin's cap and its beacon.
  - **A missile:** its warhead's and motor's bands, its seeker's dome, its canards.
  - **Fittings, not skin.** Every made piece carries its monomer's group to its faces (`fitting`), so the skin's panel
    lines, its fasteners and a livery pass it by.
  - **Budget:** the made fighter about 43k triangles, within the plan's 80k.
  - **Held** (`air-made.test.js`):
    - each part kind's pieces on the fighter;
    - the wells on the hull, not the swinging leg;
    - the doors open down and shut up;
    - the nose well under the chin duct;
    - a spacecraft's parts and the fighter without the word carrying none of it;
    - a folding-wing fighter made, within budget, the same twice.

    `air-kit.test.js` holds a seam to the made hull's own skin of its slot.
  - **Seen** (machine gate only; the eyes gate is open): the fighter close up before and after (the nose, the intake,
    the canopy, the wing, the tail, the gear and their wells from below), and the other military rows made.
- **The surface: camo, markings and wear** (`craft-shelf/air-surface.js`). `craftForm(archetype, { livery, wear })`, each
  absent adding nothing, all of it geometry and slots.
  - **The livery:** a pattern word or `{ pattern, colours?, scale?, seed?, marks? }`.
    - **Graded** (counterShaded, naval): by the hull's height, the line softened by noise; a wing by its face, darker
      above.
    - **Blotched** (wraparound, desert, arctic): a warped field cut into the paint (`cutByField`), each band its share
      of the craft's painted area.
    - **Splinter:** plan-view lines across the craft, each face split exactly where one crosses it, a shard's colour
      from its side of every line.

    A control surface keeps its shade in its band's colour. A store keeps its own paint. The camo is cut before the
    made skin's seams, so a seam is the camo's colour darkened. The heat's bands tint the camo under them.
  - **The marks** (generic, never a nation's), low-visibility against the paint: a tail number on both sides of each
    fin, a side number on the nose, a disc or bar emblem on the fuselage's sides and the wings (one up, one down), the
    red ejection warning by the canopy, the walkways by the wing roots.
    - Each is a conforming decal (`decal`): convex shapes clipped onto every skin face turned toward them, on its plane,
      a millimetre or two proud.
    - `marks: { number?, emblem?, warnings? }`, or false.
  - **The wear** (`pristine | used | battered`, the field's words): the sun's fade on what faces up and the engine's soot
    over the hull's end, per corner; as decals, the gun's soot plume beside its muzzle, repainted panels, grime streaks
    running aft, and chips to bare metal along the leading edges and the intake's lip.
  - **Fixed in the kernel** (`worlds/workbench-assembler.js`): an item turned or mirrored was relit without the flat
    light's `flat` marker. Under the unshaded light a mirrored part (a left wing, its stabilizer, its gear, its missile)
    lowered shaded where its twin was raw albedo, and the form render slotted it as trim. Now the marker is kept.
  - **Budget:** every military row in any pattern, battered, under 130k triangles (the fighter about 46k to 53k).
  - **Held** (`air-surface.test.js`):
    - a pair's two sides alike;
    - the livery's words;
    - graded darker on top and on a wing's upper face;
    - blotched in every band, the first the most;
    - splinter's shards, the stores spared;
    - seams the camo darkened;
    - the marks on the skin's planes, both sides of the fin, low-visibility, the warning red;
    - a decal only on faces turned toward it;
    - wear more battered than used, chips on what faces ahead, soot over the engine's end;
    - pristine and absent words adding nothing;
    - within budget, wound, the same twice.
  - **Seen** (machine gate only; the eyes gate is open): the fighter in each pattern from above and the side, and
    battered close up (the tail, the wing's leading edge, the gun).

### Military vehicles: the field's 4x4, truck and carrier, drawn realistic from a hull kit

Field vehicles a realistic game can put beside a realistic soldier. A field vehicle is made, not styled: flat plates with
rolled edges, bent tube, a frame you can see under it, fittings bolted and welded on. This theme builds them in the form
render, from a kit of those solids, at their classes' true numbers.

- **The rows** (`vehicle-registry/roster.js`):
  - `utility-4x4`, the military utility vehicle. People say "jeep" for any light military 4x4, so the word is kept
    here, the one maker's name the roster keeps. Its role is a new one, `scout`.
  - `cargo-truck`, the military cargo truck (canvas truck, troop truck, six by six), role `transport`.
  - `apc` relabelled the armoured personnel carrier, its old words kept, and now parked as well as driven.
- **The classes** (`roads/vehicles.js`):
  - `utility4x4`, `cargo6x6` and `apc8x8`, from public spec ranges, rounded.
  - Each has all-wheel drive on cross-country tyres (less grip on asphalt, more rolling) and is governed as its manual
    says.
  - The vehicle sheet takes them as classes (`car-designer/facets.js`, `channels.js`). The truck and the carrier are
    `UNBUILT` until their bodies are (`sheet.js`): named, searchable and drawn as their concept, never rolled.
- **The hull kit** (`car-designer/mil-hull.js`):
  - **Plate:** a convex section extruded along an axis, every edge rounded: the Minkowski sum of a smaller prism and a
    sphere. Its corner normals are worked out, not averaged. A big flat panel keeps its own normal to the corner, so it
    reads flat, and its round turns through the exact normals, so the edge catches a line of light as a real plate's
    rolled edge does. A round is tagged `edge` for the wear to come.
  - **Tube:** a polyline swept by a circle and carried without twisting, its bends rounded (`bend`), its normals radial.
  - **Bolts:** hex heads.
  - **Weld:** a bead rippled as a run of tacks is.
  - **Slab:** armour, the convex solid inside its outline seen from the front, the side and above (the three prisms
    intersected, plane by plane), each face flat. Every edge sharper than a crease is chamfered by taking the same
    width off each face it joins, so a sharp edge's chamfer is broad and a shallow crease's a sliver, tagged `edge` for
    the wear. A face the body leaves off (inside another slab) is not drawn and its edges are not chamfered.
- **The utility 4x4** (`car-designer/road-military.js`, compiled by `car-designer/military.js` in the realistic
  compile's shape):
  - **Underneath:** a ladder frame, its axles and differentials.
  - **Bumpers:** channel beams bolted to the frame.
  - **Bonnet:** a flat bonnet on a piano hinge, held by rubber latches. Its face is a slotted grille between round lamps
    in wire guards, over blackout markers.
  - **Fenders:** flat over open wheels, with a turned-down flange and a lip, welded to the cowl.
  - **Windscreen:** a split pane in its frame, its fold hinges, the wipers hung from the top.
  - **Tub:** open, its sides and doorways rimmed by a rolled edge, the rear wheels in wheelhouses under rimmed openings.
    Rivets run along its foot, welds up its rear corners, and the rear panel carries its lamps.
  - **Inside:** canvas seats, a dash and its gauges, the wheel on its column.
  - **Roll bar:** braced to the rear, its feet bolted down.
  - **Wheels:** the field's own (below).
  - **Materials:** the field's own slots (`MIL_MATERIALS`): matte paint with no clearcoat, canvas, bare steel, weld, and
    the frame's dark steel.
- **The field's wheel** (`car-designer/mil-wheel.js` `milWheel`):
  - **The tyre:** a cross-country tyre. Its carcass is lathed and sits a lug's depth under the tread. Its tread lugs
    are geometry: chevron blocks proud of the crown, two rows offset half a pitch and angled opposite, running out over
    the shoulder.
  - **The rim:** a split steel rim in the vehicle's paint. A flange and its ring, a pressed dish, the beadlock bolts
    round it, the wheel nuts, and the tyre-inflation hub's cap and valve.
  - **Any axis:** it faces along the axis asked, so the same wheel is a spare on a panel or lying on a bonnet
    (`mil-hull.js` `place`).
- **The fittings as cards** (`car-designer/mil-fittings.js`). A card builds in the frame of an anchor a body declares
  (its point, its outward normal, its up), and refuses an anchor of a kind it does not fit. A new fitting is a card.
  - **What it carries:** the spare on its carrier; jerry cans (each with its pressed X, three handles and a spout) in a
    rack with its tray, posts, strap and buckle; a shovel and an axe in their clips; a saddle fuel tank, strapped on its
    cradle, its filler capped.
  - **On its ends:** a D-ring through its tab, painted red; the pintle hook on its block, its latch red.
  - **On its sides:** a whip antenna on a sprung base; grab bars; a holed tread step; mud flaps on their bars; a round
    mirror on its arm; a rolled tarp, strapped.
- **The 4x4's kit** (`road-military.js` `KITS`):
  - **On the hull:** the spare on the bonnet, a can racked each side of the rear panel, the shovel and axe along the
    left flank, the whip at the right rear, grab bars beside the doorways, the steps under them.
  - **On the ends and underneath:** red D-rings on the front bumper, the pintle behind, mud flaps behind the rear
    wheels, a saddle tank under the right doorway.
  - **At the top:** a mirror on the screen post, and a rolled tarp on the rear panel, which most carry.
  - **The seed's dice:** a can's tone (olive or sand), the whip's length, and whether it carries the tarp.
  - **The census:** it measures the hull against the class, since the fittings hang off it as a mirror does a car. The
    rear panel stands short of the tail, so the cans and the pintle hang inside the class's length.
  - **The budget:** about 21.6k triangles with its kit and its four lugged wheels and the spare.
- **The livery, cut** (`car-designer/livery-cut.js`). A field vehicle's paint as words, the pattern cut into its painted
  faces as geometry, with no texture, so every engine gets it as drawn. It is the supercar's livery idea
  (`vehicle-livery.js`, cut at planes), cut at contours too.
  - **The words:** `livery: '<pattern>' | { pattern, colours?, scale?, angle?, seed?, marks? }`.
    - `pattern` is `mono` or a camo: woodland, desert, tiger stripe, winter, urban or digital (`CAMO`).
    - `colours` go over the pattern's own in band order, the base first; `scale` is the blotch's size in metres.
    - `marks` are a stencilled number (from the seed by default) and an emblem, a chevron or a bar.
  - **The camo:**
    - **The field:** a seeded two-octave field over the vehicle's own space, warped, stretched per pattern (a tiger's
      stripes long along the hull).
    - **The cut:** each painted face is divided finely only where a band's edge crosses it; a thin strip (a tube's side,
      a plate's round) is sliced along its length only. Each piece is cut exactly where the field crosses a band's
      level, and one edge is cut at one point from either face.
    - **The bands:** each band's level is set from this vehicle's own painted area, so each colour takes its share.
    - **Seams:** the pattern runs on over seams, plates and fittings, as a sprayed one does.
    - **Exceptions:** what faces the ground is one colour, unseen. Digital is cut exactly at its cells' planes, each
      cell one colour.
  - **On the 4x4:**
    - The camo is cut into the hull and its fittings at once, so the spare's carrier, the grab bars and the tools'
      clips are painted with it.
    - The rims take the base colour, and the frame a shade of it.
    - Stencils go on its mark anchors: the number on each side and on the front bumper, the emblem on the rear panel and
      the bonnet's sides. They are dark on a pale camo and pale on a dark one, and read left to right as one faces them.
    - Its size is unchanged.
  - **Camo by setting:**
    - **At mint:** a new quick world whose ride is a field vehicle is stamped with its setting's camo when the operator
      names none (`vehicle-registry/ride.js` `settingLivery`). It is read from the world's kit and words: a jungle's
      tiger stripe, a desert's sand, the snow's white wash, a city's greys, an alien world's cells, a green land's
      woodland (`camoForSetting`).
    - **Before:** a world minted before carries none and stays olive.
  - **The doors:**
    - **The quick game:** `quick.livery` (a field vehicle's only; another build is refused, naming the rows it paints).
    - **The level:** the figure's `loft.livery`.
    - **The grid:** `mint_solid({ kind: 'vehicle', spec: { vehicle: 'jeep', livery: 'desert' } })`.
  - **Not yet moved:** the road cars' sheet liveries and the supercar's keep their own words, unchanged.
  - **The budget:** under 40k triangles in camo (woodland about 30k for the body and its kit, digital about 24k), and
    under 25k plain.
- **The wear** (`car-designer/mil-wear.js`). A field vehicle's history on its surface, after its livery. It is one word,
  the vehicle sheet's own: `pristine | used | battered`, or `{ level, soil? }`. A field vehicle is `used` unless the
  operator's word or its brief's (a beat-up jeep) says otherwise.
  - **Caked mud:** cut into the body as geometry, in its own rough `mud` slot. Its line runs about 0.15 m under the
    wear's mud top (a used vehicle's to its sills, a battered one's halfway up its flanks), broken up and down by the
    field's noise, and in a ring round each arch where the tyres throw it.
  - **Chips:** the paint off to bare steel (`worn`) cut into the top edges that are seen (the plates' rounds that face up
    or out on the upper body) and wherever a hand or a boot goes: the grab bars, the steps, the latches, the rim, the
    bumper and the carriers.
  - **Per corner** (`cornerAlbedo`, carried to the page, the GLB and now the studio grid's bake):
    - dust rising from the ground and settling on what faces up, broken by the field;
    - sun fade on what faces the sky;
    - grounding, laid at every wear, pristine too: the wells round the wheels, under the body, the tub's inside, and
      what faces down.
  - **The wheels:** the rubber darkened with the soil's mud (the tread most) and the rims dusted.
  - **The soil:** the setting's, read from the livery's camo (a desert's dust, the snow's slush, a city's ash-grey grit,
    a green land's mud), unless the wear names its own. The dried mud is lighter than the paint it cakes, so it reads on
    a dark camo.
  - **The doors:** `quick.wear` (a field vehicle's only), the loft's `wear`, and `mint_solid`'s `wear` beside the
    vehicle's word. A road car's wear stays its sheet's, and a wear's words on one are refused.
  - **The budget:** under 45k triangles at `used` (about 38k plain), under 55k in camo (woodland used about 47k,
    battered about 46k), and under 25k pristine.
  - **The packer:** `vehicle-rig.js` `packFormMesh` now takes a mesh's bounds by a loop, not by spreading every
    corner, which overflowed the stack on a large mesh. Its output is the same.
- **The light of the setting.** Until now a realistic vehicle carried noon's light, and the page lit it so (its key's
  colour and strength over the world's shadow lights). A jeep in a night world was lit at noon.
  - **The sky's light** (`car-designer/form-light.js` `skyMood`): a field vehicle a world draws is lit by that world's
    own sky (its zenith, horizon, day and sun), passed in by `world-scene.js` as the loft's `setting`:
    - by day, a full warm key;
    - as the sun sinks, the key toward the horizon's colour;
    - at night, a dim moonlight in the zenith's cool, an eighth of the day's;
    - the ambient the sky's share of it, the reflected sky the world's own, its travel the world's sun when it is up.
  - **Ground bounce:** the hemisphere bounces the soil's colour up under it (`formLight`'s `ground`; `groundOf`).
  - **Wet:** in a world whose weather is of the wet family (drizzle, rain, downpour, storm), its slots take the rain:
    the paint glossier under a thin coat of water, the rubber glossier, and the mud and canvas soaked darker
    (`wetMaterials`, `wetFaces`).
  - **Only the field's:** a road car and a supercar keep their noon or their race's mood, so no existing world's
    vehicle changes. With no world (the studio grid, an export), a field vehicle is lit at noon as before.
  - **The shadow's stripes:** the page's shadow lights now carry a normal bias for a physical body
    (`channels/controllable/index.js`). A flat plate turned from the sun wore its own shadow's stripes, the shadow map's
    depth steps laid on it; that is gone for every realistic vehicle.
- **The canvas truck** (`road-military.js` `cargo`; the six-wheeled class's realistic body, no longer waiting): the hull
  kit's second body, built on what the first taught.
  - **Underneath:** a ladder frame on three axles (the front under the bonnet, a tandem behind), each on stacked leaf
    springs, with its differentials.
  - **The front:**
    - a heavy bumper with a winch behind it, its cable wound and its fairlead in the bumper;
    - a long bonnet, louvred at its sides, its grille behind a tube guard;
    - flat fenders with round lamps on their noses, in wire guards, beside blackout markers.
  - **The cab:**
    - a steel box on the frame: its doors' shut lines, framed glass and the screen's two panes in rubber;
    - the wipers parked, the door handles and hinges, a round roof hatch, a small rear window;
    - an exhaust stack up its back corner, sooted, under its shield.
  - **The bed and the tilt:**
    - plank drop sides between stakes, a headboard and a chained tailgate, the floor on its bearers, the rear fenders
      over the tandem;
    - five bows, and the canvas tilt over them: its section a rounded box, sagging between the bows (the roof down, the
      sides in), smoothed as a cloth, roped and tied along its foot, its rear flap rolled and strapped.
  - **Its kit** (new card: `stowageBox`, a box hung on brackets, its lid latched):
    - the spare behind the cab and two cans on the bed's front corner;
    - a saddle tank and a stowage box on the rails;
    - the tools on the bed's side, and the whip on the cab;
    - grab bars and steps at the doors, mud flaps behind each axle group;
    - the D-rings, the pintle, and mirrors on both posts.
  - **Composed with the rest:**
    - the field's wheel on six bones;
    - its livery, with the camo's blotches as much bigger than the 4x4's as its wheels are, unless the operator names
      their size (`paintLivery`'s `size`);
    - its wear, its heights by the same size (`weather`'s `scale`: a truck's mud climbs as far up its wheels);
    - its setting's light;
    - its stencils on the doors, the bumper, the bonnet and the tailgate.
  - **The registry:** its realistic build is live, and `ride: 'a canvas truck'` drives it.
  - **The figure's wheelbase** runs to its rear axles' middle (the jeep's unchanged).
  - **The budget:** about 30k triangles kept, 60k used, 72k in woodland, six lugged wheels included.
  - **Robustness:** the census and the figure's height take their extremes by a loop (`realistic.js` `most`,
    `least`), the spread of a large mesh's corners having overflowed the stack. The output is the same.
- **The armoured carrier** (`road-military.js` `carrier`; the eight-wheeled class's realistic body, no longer waiting):
  the hull kit's third body, its hull three slabs.
  - **The hull:**
    - a narrow lower hull between the wheels, its belly a shallow V, its nose plate raked back under the glacis;
    - the troop compartment over it: sponsons out over the wheels, an upright band for the bins, the sides raked in to
      the roof;
    - ahead of it, a step lower, the driver's and the engine's roof and the glacis down to a nose with its corners cut;
    - welds at the step, the glacis's top and the rear corners.
  - **Underneath:** four axles in two pairs, each hub on its arms to the hull and a damper up to the sponson.
  - **Openings:**
    - the rear ramp on its hinges, the door in it with its vision block and handle;
    - the driver's hatch and its three blocks over the glacis;
    - the commander's cupola, six blocks round it, its lid, hinge and handle;
    - two troop hatches on the roof, their hinges, handles and the stops an open lid rests on;
    - a hatch in each raked side, its block, hinges and handle.
  - **On the hull:**
    - an empty mount ring, bolted, its well dark (weapons are mounts only);
    - bins along both sponsons, their lids lipped and latched;
    - the engine's grille deck, bolted;
    - an access plate bolted on the glacis, the lamps on their stems in wire guards, the blackout markers;
    - the exhaust's sooty louvred shield on the right, the tow cable looped and clamped on the left;
    - grab rails on the roof, tail lamps in their guards.
  - **Vision blocks** in their own slot (`MIL_MATERIALS.vision`: dark, deep, a small hard highlight).
  - **Its kit:**
    - a jerry can each side of the ramp, the tools on the right side;
    - two whips at the rear corners, grab bars by the driver;
    - steps at the nose, mud flaps behind the last axle;
    - four tow shackles and the pintle, mirrors at the front corners;
    - a rolled tarp on the roof (most carry one).
  - **Composed with the rest:** the field's wheel on eight bones, its livery, wear and setting's light; its stencils on
    the front bins, the ramp and the glacis.
  - **The registry:** its realistic build is live, and `ride: 'an apc'` drives it.
  - **The figure's wheelbase** is its first axle to its last, as its sheet quotes it.
  - **The budget:** about 30k triangles kept, 48k used, 63k in woodland, eight wheels included.
  - **The wear's cut** (`livery-cut.js`): a thin face of more than four corners (a chamfer whose ends are cut) is sliced
    along its length as a thin quad is, not shattered by bisection. The carrier's used hull went from 111k triangles to
    48k.
- **Parked, in a level** (`vehicle-registry/parked.js`):
  - A manifest's `parked: [{ vehicle, at, heading?, livery?, wear?, seed? }]` stands registry vehicles still. The world
    lowers each on read (`world-scene.js`) into its realistic loft as a static figure, and a box over its footprint
    (turned with its heading) added to the level's own colliders, so the walker goes round it. A livery and a wear are a
    field vehicle's; a road car's paint is its build's. Absent, byte-identical.
  - **A base parks its vehicles:** a building level's `building.parked` (true: a truck and a carrier; a list; or
    `{ vehicles?, livery?, wear? }`) lays them side by side in its hangar (else its largest room), noses to its doors,
    as many as it holds, stamped into the level's manifest.
  - **Painted by the faction:** its foes' crew colourway paints them (a camo it names, else its own colour flat), else
    the setting's camo, else the operator's `livery`. A crew in desert colours drives desert camo.
  - The walled-core dungeon card names the word beside a base's buildings (its ceiling re-pinned with the reason).
- **The engines:** each field body's GLB, in camo and worn, passes the Khronos glTF validator (`gltf-validator`, a
  devDependency) with no error and no warning: its camo and grime in `COLOR_0`, its slots its own materials (the
  paint, mud, worn steel, vision blocks). The Godot leg takes the same GLB; its own gate needs `MOJULO_GODOT`, absent
  here.
- **Composed:**
  - The quick race's card says a ride takes a registry vehicle (`'a jeep'`), its wording trimmed to keep the card
    under its ceiling now that the physics classes it lists have grown.
  - The class's realistic build is live: a quick game's `ride: 'a jeep'` drives it, `mint_solid({ kind: 'vehicle',
    spec: { vehicle: 'jeep' } })` shows it on the studio grid, and a world draws it in the form render or baked.
  - The registry says what the truck and the carrier need (`upscaleOf`).
- **Held:**
  - `road-military.test.js`:
    - a plate flat to its edge and round at it, its area the rounded box's;
    - a round shrunk to fit;
    - a tube's normals, a bolt's flats, a weld's ripple;
    - the wheel's lugs proud of the crown (two rows, five faces a block), its rim's materials, its face along the axis
      asked;
    - each fitting card built outward of an anchor it fits, and refusing one it does not;
    - a body's kit on the anchors it declares, its dice choosing among it;
    - the compile true to its class, every face a material the figure carries with unit normals, within its budget
      (25k triangles), the same twice, and the baked figure the same rig;
    - the word, the build, the ride, and a waiting class refused with what it needs;
    - in its livery: the camo cut into the hull and the fittings alike, the rims in the base, the stencils on, the size
      unchanged, within its budget.
  - `livery-cut.test.js`:
    - the words read whole and refused naming what they take;
    - a setting read to its camo;
    - a camo cut into the base paint only, each band its share, the area kept, the same twice, another seed another
      pattern;
    - a digital pattern cut at its cells;
    - mono a recolour;
    - the stencils read left to right.
  - `tier-ride.test.js`: the setting's camo stamped at mint, nothing where the setting says none, the operator's word
    kept, a livery refused on a ride it does not paint.
  - `preview-vehicle.test.js`: a field vehicle's livery and wear carried in its loft's recipe, refused on a road loft.
  - `mil-wear.test.js`:
    - the words and the soil read from a camo;
    - mud cut low and round the arch, more the harder the wear, the area kept;
    - chips only on seen edges and handled parts;
    - dust nearer the soil low than high, and grounding darker nearer the hub at every wear;
    - the same twice, another seed another way;
    - a wheel's rubber muddied.
  - `road-military.test.js`:
    - the wear a working vehicle's by default, a brief's word and the operator's over it, and refused on a road car;
    - in its setting: lit by its world's sky (full and warm by day, dim and cool at night, along the sun when it is up,
      noon with no world), its ground the soil's, wet in the rain (glossier, the mud darker, its size unchanged);
    - a road car keeps its noon;
    - a body on more than two axles: each axle's pair, its wheelbase to its rear axles' middle, at its class's size;
      its canvas sagging between its bows; within its budget; driven by its row;
    - the slab: the solid inside its outlines (its volume), closed and flat; its sharp edges chamfered narrow and a
      shallow crease nearly whole; a face left off not drawn, nor its edges chamfered;
    - the carrier: four pairs, its wheelbase first to last, at its class's size; a raked glacis and sides, chamfered;
      vision blocks in their slot, the mount ring empty; within its budget (40k kept, 60k used, 80k in camo); driven by
      its row.
  - `livery-cut.test.js`: a thin face of many corners sliced along its length, its area kept.
  - `parked.test.js`:
    - a word read through the registry, refused without a body that parks, a livery or wear refused on a road car;
    - laid in a room inside it, noses to +x, as many as it holds;
    - lowered: a static loft figure and a box over its footprint, turned with it; in a world its figure compiled and
      its box beside the level's own colliders; absent, nothing;
    - a faction's colourway to its paint; a base's word read; a hangar's vehicles in its setting's camo, or its foes'
      faction's; absent, the level as it was.
  - `scene-gltf.vehicle.test.js`: each field body's GLB valid by the Khronos validator, its colours and slots on.
  - The routing fixture: a muddy desert jeep to look at (`mint_solid`), a base with trucks and a carrier parked
    (`design_game`).
  - The form render in the page: each shadow light biased along the body's normals.
  - The quick game end to end: a night kit's jeep lit dimmer than the day valley's, under its world's own sky.
  - The form render in the page (`form-render.live.test.js`, e2e): the 4x4's shaders compile, it is drawn and lit, and
    its shadows are cast.
  - The quick game end to end (`design-game.quick.test.js`, e2e): `ride: 'a jeep'` written as its row, its level's
    figure the 4x4's in the field's materials.
- **Seen** (machine gate only; the eyes gate is open):
  - The 4x4 in a review sheet: the three-quarter, the side, the rear quarter, from above and from the front. With its
    kit, the spare on the bonnet, the racked cans, the red D-rings, the tools along the flank, the whip and the lugged
    tyres all read.
  - Its camos: woodland, tiger, desert, winter, urban and digital in the review sheet, and woodland in the page's own
    light. A desert 4x4 from behind shows its chevron between the cans, and from the front its bumper number.
  - Its wear: woodland used and battered, desert battered, and battered in the page's own light, low. The first pass was
    too faint (the mud dark on a dark camo and under the body), so the dried mud was made lighter and its line raised:
    a battered 4x4 carries a ragged mud line up its flanks, cowl and bumper.
  - In the page's own light, with shadows. The stripes of self-shadow on the flat plates turned from the sun are gone
    with the normal bias.
  - Its settings, a battered woodland 4x4 in the page under four skies:
    - noon;
    - a golden low sun, warm and raking, with long shadows;
    - an overcast rain, darker and glossy, the sky in its wet paint;
    - the alien night, a dim purple moonlight.
  - The canvas truck plain, from the three-quarter, the rear quarter and the side (the sag's wave along its roof), in
    woodland worn, and in desert under a golden sun.
  - The carrier plain, from the three-quarter, the side, the rear quarter and the nose; woodland used at noon and under a
    golden sun, desert battered under a golden sun.
  - A hangar-bay with `parked: true`: the truck and the carrier side by side in woodland, noses to the doors.
- **Not built yet, said:**
  - Streaks under the fittings (rain and rust runs).
  - A race mood (`golden`, `dusk`…) named on a field vehicle's loft: its light is its world's sky, read.
  - Lamps lit at night: the head and blackout lamps are emissive slots as always, not yet switched by the hour.
  - A camo on the canvas: the tilt is plain canvas, as most are.
  - A base's outdoor yard: a base has no outdoor stage yet, so its vehicles park in its hangar.
  - Parked vehicles lit indoors: they take the world's sky as their light, as outdoors (a hangar's own lamps do not
    light them yet).
  - The Godot gate on a machine with Godot.

### The missile launcher truck: a ballistic missile on a transporter-erector

A field vehicle of its class, not a replica: a V-2-class ballistic missile on a generic eight-wheeled
transporter-erector-launcher, stowed for the road or erect on its launch table. Modelled, never fired.

- **The class** (`launcher8x8`, `roads/vehicles.js`): 15.6 m on four axles (two steering under the cab, two driven aft),
  2.9 m wide. Its height is the truck's own, its cab's. The missile above it is its load, not its class. It is heavy,
  and the sheet's traits read it a truck on a ladder frame.
- **The body** (`car-designer/road-military.js`, kind `launcher`, in the hull kit's language):
  - a ladder frame on four axles and their springs;
  - a forward-control cab over the front axles: its raked face, a two-pane screen and wipers, its doors, a roof hatch, the
    grille under the screen, guarded lamps, the bumper;
  - the engine's louvred box behind the cab and its exhaust;
  - a deck on risers over the rear tyres;
  - the erector: a box beam hinged at its tail, three saddles and their straps, two telescoping rams;
  - the missile: 14 m, its boat-tail, body, ogive nose, nozzle and bands. Its fins are an X, so it rides inside the
    truck's width with its nose clear over the cab. It wears its own grey-green, which a camo leaves alone;
  - the launch table flat on the deck;
  - the rear jacks up;
  - its kit: a saddle tank, a stowage box, cans and tools on the engine box, the whip, grab bars and steps at the doors,
    mud flaps, shackles, mirrors.
- **Erect** (`launcherWords`: a brief's `erect`, `raised`, `upright`; `stowed` or nothing lays it down): the erector
  swings up 90° about its hinge, the rams run out, and the missile stands on its table, lowered on its legs behind the
  truck with its blast deflector under it. The jacks are down on their pads.
- **The census** measures the truck without its load (`military.js`), as it measures a tank without its gun: the
  missile, the erector and the table stand above it or behind it.
- **The registry:** `missile launcher truck` (missile launcher, launcher truck, missile truck, transporter erector
  launcher, mobile missile launcher, v2 launcher), role strike, driven, crewed and parked. Its realistic body is live.
- **Held** (`road-military.test.js`):
  - four pairs at its class's size, stowed or erect;
  - stowed: the missile inside the width, its nose clear over the cab (the test found it dipping 6 cm into the cab's
    roof; its axis raised), its fins an X, the jacks up, no legs;
  - erect: the missile upright on its table behind the truck, the rams out, the jacks on the ground;
  - its words;
  - the missile's finish left alone by a camo while the cab is cut;
  - the same twice;
  - within its budget: under 35k triangles plain, and under 100k in camo and used (twice a truck's length, the camo
    cutting its long frame and deck);
  - found by its words, live.

  The engines' sweep (`scene-gltf.vehicle.test.js`) builds its GLB, valid by the Khronos validator.
- **Seen** (machine gate only; the eyes gate is open): the launcher stowed and erect, in woodland and used, from three
  quarters, beside and behind.

### The realistic road look: the registry's realistic cars, trucks and buses in the form render

The vehicle registry's realistic road vehicles are the realistic pole's lofts, driven as a quick game's ride. They were
drawn with their light baked flat and no materials: the glass black, the paint matte, the tyres and rims one dark
mass. They are being brought up, panel by panel, to what the house draws now: the gen-7 form render, where a surface
carries its material and its form and the page lights it.

- **The albedo recorder** (`roads/road-faces.js` `withAlbedo`):
  - While it runs, every face `face` and `faceOut` make is noted in a side table with the colour it was asked in (no
    light in it) and its outward normal.
  - The faces themselves are unchanged, so the roadway, the tracks and the fleet keep their bytes.
  - The fleet's trim colours (`FLEET_TRIM`) and the lamps' smoked housing (`SMOKE`) are exported, for the compile to
    read them.
- **The loft named and smoothed** (`car-designer/road-form.js`):
  - **Parts by colour:** `roadPart` reads what a face is from the colour the fleet drew it in, giving each part its
    material:

    | Part | Material |
    | --- | --- |
    | glass | glass |
    | tyre | rubber |
    | rim (any hub style) and chrome | alloy |
    | head lamp | lamp |
    | tail lamp | tail |
    | lamp housing, grille, intake | carbon |
    | floor (the plastics facing the road), frame | seal |
    | box, and any other colour | paint |

    The paint takes its own part and colour from the compile: the body, a two-tone roof, the livery's marks.
  - **Smoothing:** `smoothForm` gives each face crease-aware corner normals. Coincident corners of one material whose
    faces turn less than 40° share a normal, so the paint curves across the loft's stations and a panel's edge stays an
    edge. A face with no area is left out.
  - **Materials:** `ROAD_MATERIALS` are the slots' response, a road car's paint a touch less glassy than a supercar's.
- **The realistic compile in the form render** (`compileRealistic(sheet, { form: true })`):
  - The body and every wheel carry their material form (`packFormMesh`), and the figure carries the form render's light
    (`formLight`).
  - Without `form` the compile is byte-identical.
  - A battered car's patch (one quad in 23 darkened, which the page's light reads as speckle) is drawn in the body's
    colour until the panels are a phase of their own.
- **The loft's `light`** (`race-families.js`):
  - `form` or `paint`, or a gen-7 read (`world-scene.js`), as a supercar's.
  - The realistic quick ride writes `light: 'form'`, so a realistic game's car, pickup or bus is drawn lit by the page.
- **The road wheel** (`car-designer/road-wheel.js`). In the form render a loft's wheel is lathed and given depth, in the
  supercar wheel's manner at a road tyre's proportions. The fleet's prism stays the wheel the census measures.
  - **The tyre:** lathed from bead to bead: a sidewall bulging past the rim, a rounded shoulder, a tread crowned across.
  - **The rim:** a lip proud at the bead, a barrel recessed behind it and closed at the back, a brake disc behind the
    face. The face is its style's:
    - `fiveSpokeAlloy`: five spokes, each a solid (its face and two flanks back into the dish);
    - `wireVintage`: many thin spokes to a bright centre;
    - `steelie`: a pressed dish with a ring of vents;
    - `heavyDuty`: a deep dish with a ring of studs;
    - a road car's six spokes when the sheet names none.

    A heavy class (a truck, a bus) takes the heavy dish unless its sheet names another.
  - **On the body**, so it never turns with the wheel: the arch's liner (a dark half-ring over the tyre, so the arch
    reads as a wheel well and not a gap to the sky) and the brake's caliper on the disc's trailing upper quarter.
  - **Normals:** every face takes Newell's normal over all its corners, so a corner repeated at the hub cannot zero it
    (it did, and the smoothing pass dropped the barrel's back: a hole through the wheel to the ground).
- **A pickup's arches over its wheels** (`roads/bodywork.js`): the fleet seats a pickup's axles 0.25 m back under its
  bed (`PICKUP_AXLE_SHIFT`, now one constant both read). The body language now cuts its arches there, not at the
  wheelbase's centre, where the wheels showed half behind the body. Only the realistic compile draws the language
  loft; the fleet's own pickup keeps its bytes.
- **The glasshouse** (`car-designer/road-glass.js` `glasshouse`). In the form render a loft's glass is parted, pillared
  and framed, read from the faces' own edges, so it holds for any loft:
  - **Panes:** each side's glass is parted along its length into panes about a door's length each (`GLASSHOUSE.pane`):
    a sedan's two, a short cab's one, a crossover's three, a van's several. A door pillar stands between them, black as
    the road's are, or in paint on a classic three-box.
  - **Pillars:** where two panes meet at a turn of more than 35° (the screen against the side glass, the rear glass
    against it), the joint is a pillar in the body's paint, the A and C pillars.
  - **Frames:** where glass meets paint (the roof's edge, the belt, the bonnet, the boot lid), a strip of the frame:
    black rubber, or chrome on a classic three-box. These are the roof's drip line, the belt's trim and the screen's
    border.
  - **Cuts and insets:** a pane is cut at a pillar's two planes with the cut's points shared exactly. An edge is inset
    along the pane's own sides, so neighbouring panes move a shared corner the same way. The glass's area is
    conserved: glass, frames and pillars cover what the glass covered.
- **The panels** (`car-designer/road-panels.js` `panels`). In the form render the body is parted into the panels a car
  is built from, with the fittings that sit on them, read from the faces after the glasshouse:
  - **Shut lines:** cut into the paint by planes (`road-glass.js` `cutPlane`, the glasshouse's cut made general). Each
    is a strip of the body's own surface, so it lies on it exactly and the paint's area is kept:
    - a door's front and rear edge down each side, at the glass's own joints (`paneJoints`, the glasshouse's rule,
      read by both);
    - the bonnet's gap at the cowl and along each fender;
    - the boot lid's at the rear glass and along each quarter.
  - **Door pulls:** one on each door, below the belt at its rear edge, a dark pocket (in chrome on a classic
    three-box), set on the side's own surface where it is.
  - **Mirrors:** a housing on each front door at the screen's foot, in the body's paint, its glass looking back.
  - **Number plates:** one on each end, low and centred, a plate's card (`plate`) just proud of the end's own face.
  - **A battered car's patched panel:** a whole front door in primer (`primer`: no clearcoat, no sheen), on one side
    by its seed. It replaces the speckle the old patch made.
  - **A cargo van:** its glass is its cab doors' alone (`glasshouse({ cargo })`), and its side behind them is a panel
    of the body.
- **The heavy classes** (`car-designer/road-heavy.js` `heavyBody`). In the form render a bus, a box truck and a semi are
  built as their own bodies, in place of the fleet's boxes, at the class's true numbers and round the fleet's own
  wheels. Their physics, their census and their wheels are the fleet's. The glasshouse and the panels read them as they
  read a car: the bus's window band is parted and framed, and a truck's cab doors are cut and fitted.
  - **Primitives:**
    - a plan rounded at its corners and sampled where it must be (an arch's stations, a door's edges);
    - a band extruding a plan between two heights, a material per edge and a foot that rises round each arch;
    - caps, boxes, cylinders, and plates set just proud of a face.
  - **The bus:** a skirt rising round its arches to the belt; a window band of side glass, with a flat screen between
    painted corners and the rear in paint; a roof edge, its bevel, the roof and a pod on it. On the kerb side, a door
    ahead of the front axle (as wide as the overhang lets it) and one between the axles, glazed full height. A
    destination sign lit over the screen (`sign`), head lamps and bumpers, a rear grille, a rear window and tail lamps.
    No car's doors, pulls or mirrors (`panels({ kind })`), and its door glass is its own pane (the glasshouse parts
    the window glass alone).
  - **The box truck:** a cab over its front wheels (a screen, a door's window each side, a grille between head lamps,
    a bumper) and its box. The box has panels between posts every 0.62 m, rails at its floor and its top, two rear
    doors with a seam and four lock bars, and amber marker lamps (`marker`). The frame is under it, mud flaps behind
    its rear wheels, and a lit underride bar.
  - **The semi:** a hood narrower than the cab, rising to the cowl, to a chrome grille with head lamps at its corners
    and a chrome bumper; the cab and its sleeper; two exhaust stacks, five marker lamps on the roof, chrome fuel tanks,
    the frame and flaps behind the drive axles. The trailer is a box as the truck's, with side skirts, landing gear,
    an underride guard and flaps.
- **The studio grid** (`road-form.js` `bakeForm`, `race-families.js` `loftInstanceFaces`). A loft's preview on the grid
  is what a game draws: its named faces, with the lathed wheels, the glasshouse and the panels, or a heavy class's own
  body. They are baked under the studio's light from their corner normals:
  - a lit slot (a lamp, a sign, a marker) in its own colour;
  - the glass with a touch of sky by how far it faces up;
  - the metal a touch brighter;
  - polygons fanned into triangles, since the grid draws a face's first four corners.

  The grid shows the form whatever the loft's own `light` says.
- **The engines** (`scene/scene-gltf.js`). A figure in the form render now carries its material slots into the GLB, for
  any form figure (the realistic lofts, the supercar, the gloss racer):
  - each form part is one primitive per slot, sharing its positions, its normals (decoded from the packed form, now
    carried) and its albedo as `COLOR_0`;
  - each slot is a real PBR material (`formMaterial`): its metalness and roughness, its clearcoat through
    `KHR_materials_clearcoat` (declared once), and its emissive in its own colour, with the emissive strength
    extension above 1;
  - one material per slot and response, shared across the figures that use it.

  A figure out of the form render keeps its one surface material. Godot's import fixup only turns the vertex colours
  on, so the slots' metal, roughness, clearcoat and emissive reach a Godot level as its importer reads them.
- **The compile returns its named faces** by bone (`form`) when asked for the form render, for a review to draw and
  an engine's materials to be read from.
- **Held** (`road-form.test.js`):
  - the recorder records every face and changes none, and is off outside its run;
  - each kind of trim named, the plastics by where they face, a wheel's own, an unrecorded mark turned outward;
  - a shallow joint smoothed, a crease kept, a face with no area left out;
  - the default compile unchanged;
  - a car's language loft and a heavy class's own build, each with its body's and every wheel's materials;
  - one group per material, unit normals, the same bytes for the same words;
  - the light word, the gen-7 read, and a word it does not know refused;
  - the wheel: a tyre lathed to its radius and width, its faces out of it; every face a material and a unit normal,
    the plates looking out of the wheel; a spoked style's spokes as solids and a dish as a plate; the liner facing the
    wheel and the caliper on the body; in the compile, the wheel bones rolling the wheel and the body keeping the
    liner;
  - the glasshouse, one case per rule on panes made in the test: a long side parted with a door pillar and its area
    kept, a short side left one pane, a pane framed against paint in rubber or a classic's chrome (its area kept), a
    turning joint painted as two pillar strips; in the compile, a car framed and pillared, every face a material;
  - the panels:
    - the shut lines cut in with the paint's area kept, and one pull a door (on panes made in the test);
    - in the compile, a car with shut lines each side, a mirror each side its glass looking back, a plate each end,
      and no primer when it is not battered;
    - a battered car's primer door on one side;
    - a cargo van glazed at its cab alone, its side behind a panel;
  - the heavy classes, one class a body plan found in code from the fleet:
    - every face of each with a material and a unit normal;
    - a bus's doors on the kerb side alone, its sign and lamps at the right ends, no skirt hanging below an arch's
      top, no car's pulls;
    - a truck's box (posts, lock bars, markers, grille, lamps, flaps) and a semi's rig (stacks, tanks, markers,
      skirts, grille, the trailer's posts);
    - a car's body still the loft's;
  - the grid: the named faces baked with a lit slot in its own colour, polygons fanned, a face at the key brighter than
    one away from it, and the loft's preview the same whatever its light;
  - the engines (`scene-gltf.vehicle.test.js`): a car's loft and a bus's body each export a primitive per slot, every
    one with its normals, the paint clearcoated (the extension declared) and a lit slot emissive; a figure out of the
    form render keeps its one material.

  End to end, the realistic ride's figure is in the form render.
- **Seen** (machine gate only; the eyes gate is open):
  - In headless Chrome, a realistic sedan, a pickup and a bus on a trail, chased and from the front, with no page
    errors. The paint carries the sky, the glass reads as glass, and the rims and tyres part.
  - The wheel close (the named faces under a static light): a sedan, a pickup and a box truck. The spokes stand off a
    dark barrel, the caliper shows through them, and the arch is a well; the pickup's wheels sit in their arches.
  - The glasshouse (the same review, and the sedan's level in the form render):
    - the sedan: a black B pillar between its doors' glass, the drip line along the roof, the belt's trim and the
      screen's border;
    - the crossover: its B and rear pillars;
    - the pickup: its short cab one framed pane;
    - in the level, the rear glass framed under the roof, with no page errors.
  - The panels:
    - the sedan close at its doors (the shut lines, a pull on each door, the mirror at the screen's foot) and from
      both quarters (the bonnet's and the boot lid's gaps, the plates);
    - the cargo van's side a panel behind its cab;
    - the sedan's level, its plate and boot lid reading from the chase, with no page errors.
  - The heavy classes, before and after (the same review):
    - the bus from the front and the kerb side, its sign, doors, arches and pod;
    - the truck from both quarters, its cab and its box;
    - the semi from both quarters;
    - the bus's and the semi's levels in the form render, with no page errors.
  - The studio grid's previews of a pickup and a bus, in the form render's geometry.
  - The Khronos glTF validator (`gltf-validator`, run from a scratch install, not a dependency) passes the GLB of a
    realistic sedan, a bus and a supercar with no errors and no warnings, the clearcoat extension declared.
- **Not built, said:**
  - **The glass set in:** pushed a few millimetres behind its frame, with the frame's reveal drawn.
  - **A crossover's third pane:** a rear quarter window, not a door, but it is given a pull as the doors are.
  - **A heavy class's mirrors:** a bus's on its arms, and a truck's larger than a car's (the panels give a truck's cab
    a car's).
  - **The head and tail lamps** as their own bones, lit by the page as status slots (moved again: they want the juice's
    status slots, a phase of their own).
  - **A validator in the suite:** the glTF validator is run by hand, not by a test (it is not a dependency).
  - **Unity and Unreal** read the GLB's slots as their importers do; neither was run here.

### The feature style, tuned: each animal's sizes and details by hand, and a seventh-generation detail tier

The feature style's animals (the mascot's `style: 'feature'`, docs/feature-style.md) take a `tune`: the operator's hand
on a model sheet, dialled by the style's own two halves, plus how much detail the model is made at. It rides the mascot
sheet, so every door that compiles a sheet carries it (`create_character({ as: 'mascot', spec: { tune } })`, a cast's
member, a quick game's hero). Code: `control/lib/graph/egocube/feature-tune.js`.

- **Structure.** `tune.structure` sizes the masses, each a multiplier on the species' designed size: `head`, `girth`,
  `legs`, `arms`, `hands`, `feet`, `tail`, `ears`, `muzzle`, `eyes`, `neck`.
  - The head grows about its own seat, its jaw kept on the neck. Its muzzle, its ears and its tufts grow with it.
  - The girth widens and deepens the trunk about its axis. The shoulders, the hips and the limbs' radii follow it.
  - The tail, the ears and the muzzle each grow as a module from their roots.
  - The function still holds. A quadruped's `legs` and `arms` are asks the all-fours fit honours as far as the floor
    allows. Where it keeps one longer, the mint says so (`mascot.tune.notes`).
- **Decoration.** `tune.decoration` sets the decoration dials (`tufts`, `crown`, `markings`, `horns`, `spines`, `mane`,
  `fins`): 0 to 3, where 1 is the designed amount and 0 leaves the structure bare. A dial never moves a mass.
- **Detail.** `tune.detail: 'gen7'` makes a hero model of the seventh console generation's HD era (`'game'` is the
  default game model):
  - a denser skin (about 21 to 27 thousand triangles, against 13 to 17 thousand; budget 34,000);
  - the fur's secondary clumps: a fuller cheek fan, a crown's two more locks, tufts at the shoulders, the elbows and
    the haunches, a ruff under a visible neck, a brush tail's fanned tip;
  - a wing's coverts, and a scaled back's second row of spines;
  - its light baked into its corners by the bake stack (`bake`, inline finishes): occlusion, a sky light, warm fur, wet
    eyes and nose, polished horns, hooves and beaks. Every lit export carries it as vertex colour.
- **Words.** A brief says the tune too: `big ears`, `big head`, `long legs`, `lanky`, `chubby`, `bushy tail`, `long
  snout`, `fluffy`, `shaggy`, `sleek`, `plain coat` and the rest of `TUNE_LEXICON`. Its tier is said with `7th gen`,
  `ps3`, `xbox 360`, `hd era` or `hero model`.
  - The words are read only in the feature style. A tier's word asks for the style; elsewhere a brief reads as it
    always has.
  - An explicit `tune` asks for the style too, and is refused under another named style.
- **The style's own words reach it.** `feature style`, `feature animation`, `stylized`, `stylised` and `cartoon
  realistic` now ask for the feature style. The brief reader did not know them before, though the style's first theme
  said it did.
- **Families' designed sizes.** `FAMILY_SIZES` sets five families' structure dials where the style's shared
  silhouettes misdrew them, multiplied under the operator's tune: a bear's head bigger, a canine's muzzle longer, a
  cat's shorter, a deer's and a horse's legs and necks longer.
- **Broader beaks.** Every bird's beak is broad at its root: side mandibles stand out from the middle of each mandible
  and converge on its tip. From the front it reads as a wedge, not a spike; in profile it keeps its species' shape (a
  hook, a needle, a deep beak). The breadth is capped by the beak's length, so an owl's short deep beak stays a beak. A
  bill is broadened too.
- **Wings that carry the profile.** A folded wing now reads as one bold shape on the bird's side:
  - it lies closer along the flank, and stands proud of it on thicker panels instead of sinking in;
  - its tone steps further from the body's (`WING_STEP`);
  - the hand turns at the wrist so its primaries lie back past the tail, in the hand panel's own plane. They no longer
    splay out sideways from the front, and no feather grazes the panel it springs from. That grazing tore the skin:
    on five birds measured, four carry fewer open edges in their skin (between 11 and 35% fewer), and the macaw 5% more.
    The open edges themselves are closed further down (Closed skins).
- **Birds rest bright, not droopy.** Every bird's default face read sad. Its eyes sit round the sides of its head, so
  the brow's outer end wrapped down over the eyeball, the upper lid sat heavy over the iris, and every bird's default
  sheet rolled `determined`. Now:
  - the bird plan has its own resting face (`BIRD_REST`): lids 12° more open, brows 12° higher off the lid, their outer
    ends lifted. It moves every expression alike, so the clips play the same and a blink still shuts;
  - a bird whose head is its own colour (an eagle's white, a mallard's green) wears that colour on its lids, instead of
    the body's dark bags under its eyes;
  - a feature bird whose face is not asked for rolls a bright one (`FEATURE_BIRD_LEAN`: mostly happy or grin); an asked
    face wins. Mammals roll as before.
- **Head tufts for every animal.** `tune.tuft` gives any feature-style animal a look for the top of its head, in place
  of its designed crown. That means furred, feathered, scaled and smooth animals alike: a crested pigeon, a spiky gecko, a
  frog with a topknot, a bear with a red mohawk.
  - The looks: `swept` (the designed fan), `cowlick`, `mohawk`, `spikes`, `crest`, `plume`, `fringe`, `mop`,
    `pompadour`, `none`.
  - Each look is a card of locks in `feature-tufts.js` (`HEAD_TUFTS`), placed on the skull by angle. It sits on any head
    and grows with a tuned head, and a new look is a card, not code.
  - Its colour is the coat's, pale, dark, the hair's, or any hex (a palette group `Tuft`); its `size` is a multiplier.
    The crown's decoration dial still rules it.
