  - A brief says it too: `mohawk`, `cowlick`, `crested`, `topknot`, `bangs`, `pompadour`, `quiff`, `spiky hair`, `mop
    top`.
  - Untuned animals keep their designed crown.
- **Rounder, bottom-heavy animals.** Every silhouette is rounded (`FEATURE_ROUND` in `feature-silhouettes.js`):
  - the lower masses (the belly, a pear's front, the haunches, a snake's coils) are fuller across and deep, and the
    chest is a little slimmer;
  - a leg that shows is fuller at the thigh;
  - every mass is less pointed and blends softer;
  - the pale belly follows the body.
  It is applied before the all-fours fit, so the function still holds. A tuned girth now lets the legs rise as far as
  the arms grow.
- **The frog, redesigned.** The squat silhouette is now a sitter: a wide pear on folded hind legs, each thigh forward
  along the side and its shin back under it.
  - The head is wide and flat (a frog head shape), with big eyes bulging on domes on top of it.
  - A new frog muzzle draws the mouth's line right across the face, over a pale throat and two small nostrils.
  - The webbed feet now sit on the ankle, with three round-padded toes. Before, they were discs lying apart from the
    leg, a bug for any webbed-footed animal.
  - Its thin arms end in four padded fingers, planted on the floor in front.
  - Its sitting pose is its own all fours, so it is no longer fitted to drop face down onto them (the known "frog faces
    the floor" issue).
  - A frog rests open-eyed like a bird and rolls a bright face when none is asked for.
- **Closed skins.** The skin's net pinches wherever two sheets of the surface pass within a cell: a crease under the
  jaw, a wing on its flank, an arm against the body. The pinch was let go and its hole left open, the slits PR #30
  listed as known. Now the holes are fanned shut on the surface (`skin-net.js closeHoles`, as the realistic hero's
  skin already did). On nine animals measured, with their colour zones cut in, every skin is closed: 0 open edges,
  where the raccoon had 151.
- **The horse and the deer read as their animals.** They read as a bear and a fox: the horse's kit gave it a short
  round muzzle and a mane of a few stubby spikes, and the deer's horns were a single curl. Each family now has its own
  modules, reached through its tuning's kit (`FAMILY_TUNE` `kit`), so every animal of the family gets them:
  - the horses (`equine`): a long face sloping down to a soft round nose with dark nostrils, a longer and narrower
    head, a flowing mane falling to one side from the poll to the withers with a forelock over the brow (its own
    colour, the roster's mane), a long hair tail in the same colour, and a longer neck. The zebra and the donkey keep a
    short upright mane and a tufted tail (`SPECIES_KIT`);
  - the deer (`cervid`): antlers (a beam each side curving forward, with three tines), big ears set out to the sides,
    a narrow snout tapering to a black nose over a pale chin, and a longer neck. The elk, the reindeer and the moose
    wear them too;
  - no pale cheek discs on a hoofed face. The horns' and the mane's decoration dials still rule the antlers and the
    mane.
- **Everything is attached.** A new rule (`feature-attach.js`): every shape on a feature animal is attached to the body
  or to something attached to it.
  - Two shapes count as one where the gap between their surfaces is narrow enough for the skin's blend to bridge.
  - Once the build is laid out, a piece apart is moved, whole, to the nearest attached shape and set into it: its design
    kept, its place corrected. The plan records what moved (`mascot.attached`).
  - It caught 14 of 57 species sampled (one or two per family). Thin tails stood off the rump (a cougar's, a mouse's, a
    wombat's, a platypus's), and the reptiles' and dinosaurs' dorsal spines floated above their backs. Each moved 0.3
    to 4.5 cm.
  - Every family's shapes are now one piece, as designed and at the gen7 tier, and every plan's minted skin is a single
    connected piece.
- **The giraffe's neck and the zebra's stripes.**
  - The long neck is slim now. It was one fat mass as wide as the chest, so the giraffe read as a tall body. It rises
    further (`FEATURE_PROPORTION.longNeck`), tapers up to the head, and its base no wider than the shoulders.
  - A head raised well clear of its body on a neck (`FEATURE_NECK_PIVOT`: a giraffe's, a horse's) turns at the top of
    that neck: the rig's neck bone spans the neck (it was 2 cm at its base, so a nod swung the whole neck stiffly from
    the shoulders). Other mascots' rigs are as they were.
  - A `stripes` coat (the zebra's, the tiger's) was six thin strokes on the flanks: a few scratches on a white coat. It
    is now bold rings round the standing figure, from the feet up the neck to just under the head, never across the
    face (`FEATURE_STRIPES`). The widths fall in rhythm, each ring leans a little the other way from the last, and the
    edges are notched.
  - The stripes are cut into the skin as a zone along their exact edges, not laid over it as a layer. So a zebra stays
    within the game model's triangle budget: 17,434 triangles, where the layer would have taken it to 24,767.
- **Stripes as a body wears them, and the giraffe's patches.** The rings went all the way round. Real stripes start at
  the spine and end at the belly. Now:
  - each body stripe starts at the spine (on an animal standing up, the middle of its back) and runs round each flank,
    widest at the spine, holding its width and pinching late to a point at the belly (an `arc` on the coat's `band`);
  - a zebra's points meet under it in chevrons, and a cat's (the tiger's) stop short of its pale belly and are
    thinner (FAMILY_TUNE `stripes`);
  - over the legs a stripe stays a ring.
- **The giraffe's patches.** A new `reticulated` coat is a network of big rounded patches parted by thin lines of the
  coat (`FEATURE_NETWORK`, the coat's `cells`). The seeds sit on a jittered lattice from seeded dice, and the patches
  take the roster's own brown (`Spot`), over the body, legs and neck to under the head. It is cut into the skin as a
  zone, the patches sized to keep the giraffe within budget (17,831 triangles).
- **The moose's palms and the cats' noses.**
  - A new `palmate` antler (the moose's, `SPECIES_KIT`): a short beam out from each side of the head carrying a broad
    flat palm, held up and out like an open hand, its broad face to the front, with points along its outer and upper
    rim. The moose had worn the deer's branching antlers.
  - A new `moose` muzzle: a long face ending in a big bulbous nose that overhangs and droops past the lip, fat at its
    foot, its big dark nostrils on its front, a small lip tucked under it. The moose had the deer's narrow snout. Its
    bell is not drawn: its head sits low on its shoulders, where a flap under the throat would never show.
  - A new `feline` muzzle for the cat family (tiger, lion, house cat, cougar): a bridge down from the brow, two puffy
    pale whisker pads and a pale chin, and an inverted triangle of a nose at the top of the pads in the roster's nose
    colour. The cats had a `button` nose, a small dot the tiger's orange swallowed.
- **The chunky rodents: the groundhog, the capybara, the beaver and their kind.**
  - Two new species in the fauna roster's rodent family (`fauna/families/rodent.js`, with their search cards, and the
    generated behaviour table regenerated). The groundhog is the beaver's build smaller and stouter, with plain
    digging feet, a short bushy tail and cream incisors. The capybara is a guinea pig's build grown big on longer legs,
    with a long boxy head, its eyes and ears set high, and no tail. They mint on the realistic door too.
  - In the feature style every rodent has BUCK TEETH (a kit word on the family, `teeth: 'buck'`): two incisors under
    the mouth in the roster's own tooth colour, a beaver's orange. The hedgehog, filed with the rodents but no rodent,
    has none.
  - The chunky ones (the beaver, groundhog, guinea pig, hamster, and the wombat though it is no rodent) wear a new
    `blunt` muzzle: a broad snout, puffy pale whisker pads and a chin, a small nose at the top of the pads. The capybara
    wears its own `capybara` muzzle: a long deep boxy snout ending square, a wide flat nose high on its front.
  - Each wears its own tail where they all had a rat's. The beaver has a dark flat scaly paddle lying on the ground
    (`ground` tails rest on the floor however high the body stands) and webbed feet. The groundhog has a short bushy
    stub. The capybara, guinea pig, hamster and wombat have none.
  - `SPECIES_TUNE`: a species' own tuning over its family's. The capybara's long boxy head, high-set eyes and coarse
    short coat (no crown, short tufts); the hamster's cheek pouches. The wombat is drawn as the barrel it is
    (`SILHOUETTE_OF`: its long low roster body read as a noodle).
- **Side hips, the round animals' default** (`tune.hips: 'below'` for the old way). A round animal's legs (the pear and
  the barrel silhouettes) are set on the sides of its ball at its centre's height, in place of legs from the bottom of the
  ball (`sideHips` in `feature-silhouettes.js`). On all fours the ball pitches about its own centre and rolls in place,
  instead of swinging forward and down over hips at the floor. On six round animals, against legs from the bottom:
  - the fit raises the legs about 0.31 head units, where it raised them about 0.57 (on the bent all-fours pose);
  - the belly's bottom sits 0.28 to 0.39 head units off the ground, where it sat 0.69 to 0.80: the butt low;
  - the arms lengthen as before; the function holds.
  A prototype first (opt-in), it was made the default once the operator saw it.
  - From the side each thigh is a DRUMSTICK (`SIDE_HIP_DRUM`): 2.4 times as deep as it is broad (its front-view
    breadth, the 1 : 4 : 1, untouched), round at the hip and tapering to a low knee, a fifth of the way up the hip, so
    its round end shows under the ball.
- **Standing straight, on all fours bent.** Standing, the legs are straight: a side-hipped animal's knee and ankle fall
  straight under its hip (`SIDE_HIP_REACH` 0), and the standing clips (the idle, the blink, the wave, the faces) bend
  no knee and stand the feet under the hips (a sturdy idle's wide stance had splayed a bear's straight legs out), a motion clip starting and ending on a straight stand (`straightened` in `feature-body.js`; a hop's or a
  squat's own crouch kept). On all fours the hind legs keep their natural bend (`FEATURE_FOURS.natural`, 0.3): the
  fours pose starts there, and the fit counts the hips that much lower when it clears the trunk.
- **Two balls in the trunk.** The round animals (the pear and the barrel silhouettes) are drawn as a rib ball over the
  waist, riding the torso, superposed on a pelvis ball under it, riding the pelvis, in place of one ball with a cap on
  it. The wedge's big rib ball is kept over the waist too. So the trunk can bend at the waist.
- **On all fours as a regular animal.** The all-fours pose is no longer the whole trunk tipped stiffly over the hips:
  - the hips tip 70°, the spine curls (`FEATURE_FOURS.curl`, as the rig's spine bends) and the core bends at the waist
    (`waist`, 15°), so the spine runs level from the hips to the neck's root and the rib ball comes down in front;
  - the head is carried out in front of the chest, turned up to look ahead (the neck back `FEATURE_FOURS.neck`, 30°,
    the head as far as it goes);
  - the fit (`foursOf`, `functional`) models that bent trunk segment by segment, as the rig poses it.
  - The rig takes a new pose word for it, `waist` (degrees, + the chest forward over the navel), in `figure-posing.js`.
    Absent, nothing changes.
- **The walk on all fours, and running on them** (`FEATURE_GAIT`). The hind feet take the biped's walk paths, and each
  foreleg plays its own side's hind foot's cycle a quarter of a cycle later: where that foot is fore and aft its paw is
  (from under the chest, the elbow folded, to its full reach), and as that foot lifts so does the paw. The walk on all
  fours (`prowl`) is a four-beat lateral sequence, left hind, left fore, right hind, right fore; a paw in stance rests on
  the floor; the head looks ahead and the tail is carried. An animal that goes on all fours RUNS on them: its `run` clip
  is the gallop; upright it only walks, slowly (`walk`). (A first slow trot was dropped; the trot below replaces it.) The paws' solve had mixed
  a unitless share to the side with metres, so a paw in stance stood a few centimetres off the floor: the share is now
  taken of the target's own length (the gallop's paws, too, now rest exactly on it).
- **Keyed clips play their keys** (`station-loft-rig.js` `layeredClip`, every packed and exported clip). Two channels were
  lost between a clip's keys and its packed frames:
  - a `feet` target, an array, was blended into an object the rig reads as no target at all. So, played or exported,
    no keyed gait's feet stepped: the mascots' walk and run, the walk on all fours and the gallop. The legs held their
    rest while the body bobbed. Now a target blends as a point, and a key without one holds the other's;
  - the waist: `resolvePose` turns `waist` into the raw `bend`, and the packer resolves a key twice, the second time
    dropping it. On all fours the chest rode 5 to 11 cm higher than its keys and the paws left the floor. The raw
    bend now flows through, as the raw spine and swivels do.
  The laws and the solvers pose the keys themselves, so neither showed in a test. `station-loft-rig.clip.test.js` now
  plays them.
- **The trot on all fours, from the horse study's mechanics** (a `trot` clip, `FEATURE_TROT` in `feature-trot.js`;
  `run` stays the gallop). The slow trot dropped before was laid on the biped run's paths, and its forelegs copied the
  hind feet by a share of their reach. So its forepaws travelled about half as far as the hind feet in the same stance
  and skated. This one is laid out as the horse study solves its gaits (`mount/`, branch 1102-horse-study), made
  dimensionless:
  - THE BEAT: a two-beat diagonal, each hind a moment before its fore (HILDEBRAND 1965, BACK 1995);
  - THE STRIDE: the reference horse's trot (CLAYTON 1994, HEGLUND 1974) at one Froude number (`froude` 0.6, a jog),
    scaled to the hip by dynamic similarity (Alexander & Jayes 1983) and cut to what the shorter pair of legs reaches.
    A raccoon-sized mascot trots at about three strides a second;
  - ONE GROUND: every planted foot, fore and hind, slides back at the one ground speed, so nothing skates. The swing
    is laid between the stance it leaves and the one it lands in: a quintic C1 at both ends (the horse study's
    `swingPath`), lifted by a bump peaking at 0.40 of the swing, the paw swung back to meet the ground;
  - THE BOUNCE: the heave integrated from the feet's half-sine forces (z'' = g·(ΣF − 1), two dips a stride), the
    trunk twisting between its girdles as the diagonals take the weight;
  - FOLLOW-THROUGH: the nod and the tail's swish as damped pendulums driven by the heave (the horse study's `NECK`),
    their frequency scaled to the leg;
  - THE CARRIAGE, the legs apart from the side: these bodies' arms were lengthened to reach the floor ahead, so they
    are long for the shoulders' height. Tipping the trunk up to stand the foreleg straight (the first cut, a hinge of
    57 to 60°) drew the forelegs back over the hind legs: on the round bodies they crossed. Leaning the trunk barely
    moves the shoulders forward (the shoulder stays about 0.22 of the height ahead of the hip at any hinge). So the
    trunk is tipped forward, near the all-fours pose (66 to 67°), until a standing foreleg, a COLUMN of `column` (0.97)
    of its arm, rakes `rake` (30°) ahead to the floor, and the hind stance is centred `back` (0.3 of the hip's height)
    behind the hips. From the side the forelegs clear the hind legs by 13 to 17% of the height in every key, where the
    raccoon's, the bear's and the pig's had crossed;
  - THE VAULT (the horse study's: a girdle over a stiff standing leg falls toward the ends of its stance): the trunk
    holds its lean, and the body as a whole rides over the standing foreleg (both girdles stand together in a trot).
    Its height is solved on the rig, key by key, where that foreleg is its column (the shoulder moves with its own
    arm's aim, so the arm is posed inside the solve), eased across the moments no forepaw stands, smoothed to the
    stride's low harmonics (`trotVault`) and given the bounce on top (`bounce` 1: a stylised 2.5 folded the foreleg
    to 73° at mid-stance). A standing foreleg's elbow stays at 29 to 41°. Tipping the trunk instead to hold the column
    rocked it 10° each step;
  - keyed at the packer's samples (12), so every packed frame is a key and nothing is blended between two;
    `mascot.trot` carries the cycle's seconds, ground speed, stride and duty.
  Every animal that goes on all fours trots (the leggy, barrel, wedge, pear and noodle silhouettes).
- **The standing walk, from the same mechanics** (the `walk` clip of every feature animal whose legs reach a stance,
  `FEATURE_WALK` in `feature-walk.js`). In this design language a slow walk is done on two legs and the trot on all
  fours is faster, so the walk is held under 0.7 of the animal's own trot: 0.35 to 0.45 m/s against the trot's 0.50
  to 0.68. It replaces the mascot walk on the feature style, which had 8 keys, a smoothstep swing that popped at lift-off
  and touchdown, and an energy's bob. The new walk has:
  - THE BEAT: the feet half a stride apart, each down 0.6 of it, both down twice a stride;
  - THE STRIDE: a person's stroll (Froude 0.15) at a cadence scaled to the leg by dynamic similarity (0.85 strides a
    second at a 0.9 m leg: a raccoon-sized mascot takes about 1.45). The stance is cut to what a near-straight leg
    reaches and to the trot's speed;
  - ONE GROUND: every planted foot slides back at the one ground speed, and the swing is laid C1 between stances (the
    trot's `swingPath`);
  - THE VAULT: the standing leg kept straight, as the style stands (its knee 13 to 19°, breaking to about 32° only to
    push off), the body riding over it. Solved on the rig as the least sink each standing leg needs, smoothed to the
    stride's low harmonics, its dips exaggerated (`bob`);
  - THE WADDLE: the body swung over the foot that bears it, an inverted pendulum driven by the feet's double-hump forces
    (the horse study's sway, MERKENS 1993's walk), so the wider the feet are set the further it swings. The walking feet
    are set closer in than the standing stance (`track`, 0.72 of it), so the sway is about 4.5% of the height. The trunk
    leans over the bearing foot, the pelvis turns with the reaching leg and the chest against it;
  - FOLLOW-THROUGH: the arms swing well fore and aft against the legs (`arms.swing` 0.5), a little late, each turned
    about its own side so it still clears the belly; the head nods after the bob. The tail is as designed, since standing it is not carried;
  - keyed at the packer's 12 samples. `mascot.walk` carries the cycle's seconds, ground speed, stride and duty. The
    walk on all fours (`prowl`) still takes the mascot walk's paths.
- **The downward dog, facing forward** (a `downDog` clip, `FEATURE_DOG`, `dogOf`): the hips high, the hind legs as
  straight as the forepaws allow (bent only as far as they need to reach the floor), the trunk tipped past level and
  bent down at the waist (the rib ball under the pelvis ball), the forepaws straight out in front on the floor, the face
  looking ahead. A quadruped's spine and neck bend further than the human ranges the rig's limits are set for, so the
  pose takes them 1.4 times (`unbound`): the waist bends 35°, and the neck and the head turn the face forward from a
  chest pitched down. The spine is not curled (a curl tips the neck's root down past where the head can look ahead).
  Every animal that goes on all fours takes it. Where a big rib ball on short legs cannot get under the pelvis ball (a
  gorilla's), the fit lengthens the legs until it does.
- **The gallop** (a `gallop` clip, `FEATURE_GALLOP`), the run on all fours, the forward-facing dog its base:
  - the hind feet take the biped run's paths as a half-bound, the left a key behind the right, its sink and lift kept;
  - the waist rounds as the hind feet come forward under the belly (the gather) and opens as they push (the extension);
  - each forepaw goes from under the chest (a quarter of its reach, the elbow folded, solved by the law of cosines) to
    its full reach (the arm straight): swung forward through the air, lifted most at mid-swing, STRIKING the floor at
    full reach, then swept back along it under the chest;
  - the hind legs are tilted back: their feet half the run's fore-aft span behind its paths, so they drive from behind
    the hips;
  - THE STRIKE: at full reach the trunk tips forward over the hips (up to 20° more, `FEATURE_GALLOP.pitch`, as far as
    the chest clears the floor: `dogOf` `strike`), easing in and out: the front low on both forepaws, the rump raised,
    the head ahead;
  - THE VAULT, a key of its own after the strike (`FEATURE_GALLOP.vault`): the trunk tipped 10° further (the spine 30°
    down to the front), the weight on both forepaws alone, the hind legs unsupported and stretched out behind, the head
    still looking ahead;
  - THE LANDING after it, the second impact (`FEATURE_GALLOP.land`): still on both forepaws, the elbows bent 35° their
    natural way to take the weight (the body lowered only where the bent forelegs would not reach the floor), the head
    ahead (the paws' solve keeps the landing's own elbow). The gallop is the run's keys, the vault and the landing;
  - at the gallop's most forward lean, the vault and the landing, every animal's hind legs are STRETCHED OUT BEHIND
    (a `feet` target each, 0.95 of the leg's length from its hip, 20° under level, never nearer the floor than the
    vault's clearance: `landed`, solved on the rig) with the feet POINTED BACK (the ankle turned −70°, the toes −160°),
    and the tail RAISED 30° (`FEATURE_CARRIAGE.leap`), so the hind legs show under it, not hidden along it. The tail's
    base is kept LOW ON THE RUMP: a `rump` chain turns the whole tail about the pelvis ball's middle (a round rump's
    rearmost point is behind its middle however it tips), so on all fours, walking, galloping and in the dog the root
    sits 25° under the rump's rearmost point (`FEATURE_TAIL_RUMP`), however far the hips tip (the strike's and the
    vault's tip had carried it 25 to 35° up the back). The skin about the root rides a `rump` bone (from the ball's
    middle to the root: wholly within 20°, none past 70°, `FEATURE_RUMP`): a ball turned about its middle maps onto
    itself, so the junction slides round the rump with the tail, never stretched into a web. The brush tail has a NECK
    (its base slim, the thick of it held out from the rump), so tail and body read as a figure eight, pinched where they
    meet, never a keel run on from the back. A tail is never dragged: carried low, it is lifted until its middle and
    its tip clear the floor by 0.12 of the height (`FEATURE_CARRIAGE.clear`, room for a brush's thickness). A tail's
    rings follow the skin's weights among the tail's own two bones (the rump's and the pelvis's dropped), so they bend
    with it and never tear at the middle joint. The thigh's
    skin blends into the pelvis's over a narrow hip (`FEATURE_SKIN.hip`, 0.4 of the usual width), so the haunch swings
    with its leg. A raccoon's hind leg is barely longer than its hip's reach to the rump, so its shin and pointed foot
    show past the rump and no more;
  - galloping, every tail is held back near level for balance (`FEATURE_CARRIAGE.run`, −25° to 10°), whatever its
    walking carriage: a cat's tail is up at a walk and back at a run;
  - and straightened: the tail rides two bones (`tail` from its root to its middle, `tailEnd` from there to its tip, each
    turned by its own chain; a tuft tail cut in two at its middle, `halved`, the halves continuing one another), and at
    a run the far half is turned in line with the near half, so a curled tip (a cat's) lies out straight behind.
    Standing and walking, the tail keeps its designed curl;
  - the raccoon's tail rings never stretch: the ring pattern, a layer over the skin, rides the tail's bones rigidly (each
    band the bone it sits on: a band's `bone`, feature-coat.js), where it had taken the skin's weights and smeared across
    the blend at the tail's root; and the tail's skin blends into the rump over a short collar (`FEATURE_SKIN.collar`, a
    third of the usual width), so the skin under a ring moves with it;
  - a zebra's and a tiger's stripes stretch less on the run. They are cut into the skin, so they stretch where it does:
    under a striped coat the skin is FIRM (`FEATURE_SKIN.firm`: the blend between any two bones half as wide, the stretch
    kept near the joints) and each stripe's points commit to the bones they ride (`FEATURE_SKIN.stripe`: their weights
    to the 4th power, renormalised), so the plain coat between the stripes takes the stretch. The stripe area stretched
    or shrunk past 1.5×, measured on the posed skin: the zebra's 4.2 / 8.7 / 6.5% (the gallop's strike, the walk on all
    fours, the downward dog) to 3.0 / 4.3 / 3.3%; the tiger's walk and dog 10.2 / 8.6% to 6.7 / 6.6%, its gallop 4.8 to
    5.7% (most of it the neck turned up to look ahead, stretching the stripes that run up it). Averaging each stripe's
    weights whole was tried and tore the mesh: a band is a cut across the whole standing figure, so one band spans legs,
    arms, trunk and tail;
  - the hips tip no further than 80° (`FEATURE_GALLOP.hinge`: the dog's tip past level carries the tail's root up the
    back), so running, the tail comes out of the rump;
  - the tail is carried as on all fours.
- **The head looking ahead on all fours** (`FEATURE_LOOK`): each key of the pose, the walk on it and the gallop turns the
  head up from the pitched trunk until its crown tips 15° ahead of upright (the face ahead, a little down), the head
  taking most of the turn and the neck the rest (a neck pulled far back tucked the head into the shoulders), solved on
  the rig. The gallop had taken the dog's full turn and pointed every face up.
- **The forepaws planted on the rig.** A clip's arm aim is read partly in the bent trunk's frame, so an aim written as
  a world direction landed the paws behind and above the floor, and splayed. Each key on all fours is now solved on the
  rig (`planted`, `FEATURE_PAWS`): the paw reaches the floor ahead, the arm straight forward in the downward dog and a
  little out round the belly on all fours, a walk's swing kept.
- **The tail carried as its animal carries it.** The tail rides its own bones (`tail` and `tailEnd`, chains turned from
  its root and its middle). On
  all fours, the walk on them and the downward dog, it is turned until its line rises at the species' carriage, read
  off the fauna roster's tail stations (`speciesTail`: a wolf's low, a cat's up; absent, −15°). It is carried a quarter
  of the way back toward where the mascot's own tail would point, a compromise between the regular animal and the
  mascot (`FEATURE_CARRIAGE`). Standing, the tail is as designed. Its root sits low on the round of the rump, 75° under
  the pelvis ball's middle, where the pelvis tipped on all fours turns it into the rump rather than up the back, and
  the tail is drooped back about it (`FEATURE_TAIL`), so standing it sweeps out behind.
- **A face worn from another species** (`face` in `SPECIES_KIT`): its nose and its pale muzzle and belly, the roster's
  colours, over the animal's own coat. The house cat wears the tiger's: a dark nose over bright whisker pads, where
  its own pink nose and dull pads blurred into its grey.
- **Thigh : body : thigh as 1 : 4 : 1 from the front.** A standing four-legged animal (the pear, barrel, wedge, leggy
  and noodle silhouettes) is proportioned across its hips within the width its body had (`fronted`, `FRONT_RATIO` in
  `feature-silhouettes.js`):
  - the body narrows to four sixths of that width (across only, its side view kept; never widened), the shoulders and
    the belly's shapes with it;
  - each thigh takes a sixth, never thinner than a round full leg (`FRONT_RATIO.least`: a body too slim for 1 : 4 keeps
    that floor and reads a little thicker), tucked against the body: its middle at the body's side, half of it over the
    belly (`FRONT_RATIO.overlap`);
  - the legs toed in, `\| |/` from the front: each tapers to 0.6 of its thigh at the ankle (`FRONT_RATIO.ankle`, was
    0.75) with its inner edge kept straight down, so it leans in toward the other; the feet still point ahead. Before, the
    thighs sat inside the body's outline, so from the front a wide body stood on thin legs; the legs' radius follows
    the thigh's;
  - the family's breadth is counted, so the ratio is the drawn one. Side hips keep the thigh's breadth.
  - A coat cut into the skin (stripes, the giraffe's patches) has the skin simplified further first
    (`FEATURE_CUT_SHARE`), so the figure stays within budget. The narrower giraffe had gone 151 triangles over.
- **QA.** `scripts/spikes/feature-roster.mjs` takes `--tune` (every species minted with it) and `--tunes` (each species
  once per tune, side by side).
- **Stored mascots keep their look.** A minted mascot stores its compiled plan. An untuned sheet compiles anew on
  a new mint: the five families above, the round animals' side hips, the front's proportion and the straight stand. A tuned mint records its tune in `plan.mascot.tune` and reads it back.

**Gates.**

- Machine: `feature-tune.test.js` holds these laws:
  - validation;
  - absent means nothing;
  - the words are read in the feature style alone;
  - no tuning phrase is a mascot lexicon phrase;
  - each structure dial moves its own mass;
  - on a tuned quadruped the paws still reach and the trunk still clears the floor;
  - decoration at 0 is bare;
  - the family sizes multiply;
  - gen7's clumps, coverts, denser skin within budget, and its bake (none on the game model);
  - and, in `feature-grammar.test.js`, a standing bird's wing panel out of its body, its primaries not splayed, its beak
    broader than deep; its default face rolled bright, its resting lids and brows higher, its brows' clips unchanged;
  - a frog sitting on its own all fours (hands planted, webbed feet on its ankles, eyes on domes, its own muzzle);
    every plan's minted skin closed and in one piece, and every family's shapes attached (`feature-body.test.js`);
  - under a striped coat, the stripe's points loose (no bone over 0.8) less than half as often as the plain coat's;
  - a long neck slim under its raised head and turning at its top; a striped coat's stripes from the feet to under
    the jaw (rings on the legs, arcs from the spine to the belly above them, a cat's stopping short), and a giraffe's
    seeded network of patches in its own colour, both cut into the skin within the budget, the markings' dial still
    ruling them;
  - thigh : body : thigh as 1 : 4 : 1 from the front for one species of each standing silhouette, the thighs alongside the
    body, never thinner than a full leg;
  - side hips as designed: a round animal's hips on its ball's sides at its centre, its legs straight and toed in
    (the inner edge straight, the ankle leaning in, the foot ahead), its thigh a drumstick (deeper than broad, its end under the ball), its belly lower than the legs-below build's, the fit's rise less than half and the trunk's travel under 0.7 of it, on
    all fours the natural bend, the function holding, a silhouette that is no ball untouched; no standing clip bends a
    knee or widens the stance and the fours clip bends one (`feature-body.test.js`);
  - everyone on all fours can downward dog (one species per silhouette, chosen in code): the rib ball at least
    `FEATURE_DOG.bow` under the pelvis ball, the trunk clear of the floor, the forepaws reaching it; on the rig the
    forepaws on the floor straight ahead (no share to the side), the hind feet planted, the chest under the hips, the
    face ahead (`feature-body.test.js`);
  - the walk on all fours on the rig: each foreleg lifted a quarter cycle after its own side's hind leg, a paw in stance
    on the floor; the `run` of an animal on all fours is its gallop;
  - the trot, PLAYED as packed: every foot on the floor in stance and clear of it in swing, sliding back at the one
    ground speed; each forepaw down with the other side's hind foot, the diagonals half a stride apart; a standing
    foreleg's elbow under 45°; the body bouncing and the head nodding; from the side, the forelegs clear in front of
    the hind legs in every key, the trunk's hinge held and within 6° of the all-fours pose's; and from the front, in every key, each foot on
    its own side under its girdle, the head on the middle, its crown ahead of upright and its eyes looking forward;
  - a keyed clip sampled at a key poses as the key (its feet's targets and its waist kept): `station-loft-rig.clip.test.js`;
  - the standing walk, PLAYED as packed: slower than the trot; each foot on the floor in stance, clear of it in swing,
    sliding back at the one ground speed; the feet half a stride apart, both down twice a stride; a leg bearing the
    weight alone near straight (its knee under 25°), every knee bent forward and never out; the body rising and falling
    a little; and from the front, the body over the foot that bears it alone and never past it, each foot on its own
    side, the eyes looking forward; the arms swinging; the tail as designed;
  - the gallop on the rig: the run's cycle, the waist working, the forepaw travelling fore and aft and reaching the
    floor in some keys and through the air in others, the hind feet behind the hips, the face ahead and a little down in
    every key (never up), the tail's root at the rump (never up the back) and the tail held back near level and
    straight (its two halves in line), the tail's ring layer each point on one tail bone, a strike key, the front
    tipped low on both forepaws, after it the vault, tipped further on the forepaws alone, and the landing, the elbows
    bent; in both the hind feet stretched out behind, off the floor and pointed back, the tail raised; the tail's root
    25° under the rump's rearmost point in every key on all fours, the skin about it on the `rump` bone, the tail clear
    of the floor;
  - on all fours on the rig: the spine level, the tail carried at the roster's carriage less the mascot's share, and no
    standing clip turning the tail;
  - a rodent's buck teeth (none on the hedgehog), a chunky rodent's blunt face on whisker pads, a beaver's flat paddle on
    the ground, a tailless rodent tailless, a capybara's longer head and short coat;
  - a moose's flat palms (broad face to the front, points on the rim, not the deer's tines) and its big droopy nose
    (past the end of its face and hanging below it, dark nostrils), and a cat's pointed nose
    on pale whisker pads;
  - a horse's long face, flowing mane, forelock and hair tail, and a deer's antlers, side-set ears and pale chin, with
    the dials still ruling them;
  - a head tuft worn by every plan in place of the crown, each card's locks rooted in the skull and standing out of it,
    its size and colour, `none` and the crown's dial at 0 bare, and the brief's word.
- Eyes: not passed. Sheets were shot for the operator: game against gen7, and one species tuned several ways.

**Known.**

- The gen7 look is vertex-baked light and denser geometry. The fur has no normal map yet: the skin has no UVs.

### Tracked vehicles: a light tank and a tracked carrier, drawn realistic on a track pair

The field's tracked vehicles drawn realistic from the military hull kit:
- running gear: a sprocket, an idler, road wheels on arms, return rollers, and a track of links as geometry;
- a light tank with a turret and a modelled gun (never fired);
- a tracked carrier.

Both carry the field's camo, wear and setting light, can be parked in a base and export to a valid GLB. Driving them
(skid steer) is a later theme.

- **The running gear** (`car-designer/mil-track.js`), one side at a time:
  - **The track** is links, not a band. Each link has a shoe, a grouser in two pads on the ground face, end connectors
    over the pins each side, and a guide horn standing in.
    - The links are laid as chords between pins spaced evenly along the track's path, so the track polygonizes round
      the sprocket and the idler as a real one does, and every link is one length.
    - The path is the lower hull of the sprocket, the road wheels and the idler: flat on the ground under the road
      wheels, straight up to the idler and down from the sprocket. Over the top it runs from the idler to the
      sprocket, resting on the return rollers and sagging between them.
  - **The drive sprocket:** two toothed rings either side of the horns, on a bolted hub, on its final drive.
  - **The idler:** a dual steel wheel on its tensioner arm.
  - **The road wheels:** dual and rubber-tyred, with dished discs, a hub cap and bolts. Each is on a trailing arm from
    its torsion bar's housing on the hull, with a bump stop over the arm.
  - **The return rollers:** on their brackets.
  - **What turns:** each road wheel, the sprocket, the idler and each roller is a spinner on its own hub, with its own
    radius (a bone each when a body uses them). The track stands still; its scroll waits for driving.
  - **The budget:** about 11k triangles a side.
  - **Held** (`mil-track.test.js`):
    - the path closed, anticlockwise and flat on the ground, resting on each roller, sagging between, clear of the
      wheels;
    - the links evenly pitched and closed, the grouser on the ground, the horns between the tyres;
    - the spinners on their hubs within their radii;
    - the left the right's mirror;
    - every face with a material;
    - the same twice;
    - within the budget.
  - **Seen** (machine gate only; the eyes gate is open): both sides round a stand-in hull, from the three-quarter and
    the side, and the sprocket and the idler close up.
- **The classes and the rows:**
  - **Physics classes** `lightTank` and `trackedCarrier` (`roads/vehicles.js`), from public spec ranges.
    `running: 'track'` says what they run on. Their wheelbase is the track's length on the ground and their wheel a
    road wheel; a tank's length is its hull's, its gun reaching past it.
  - **The sheet:** their traits in the sheet's tables, both heavy. Their bodies wait (`UNBUILT`), each naming what is
    built (the running gear) and what is not (the hull, the turret).
  - **The rows:** `light-tank` (scout, recon, airborne tank) and `tracked-carrier` (tracked APC, tracked carrier),
    role `armour`. The `tank` row stays the main battle tank, a concept.
  - **Not a ride:** a tracked class's realistic loft serves parked and watched, never driven. The registry says
    driving it needs skid steer, and `rideableRows` leaves them out.
  - **Held** (`mil-track.test.js`): each tracked class has its row, found by its words; never a ride; its waiting body
    refused by the sheet, naming what is built.
- **The light tank's hull** (`road-military.js` `lightTank`, on `trackedGear`'s stations):
  - **The hull:**
    - a lower hull between the tracks on a flat belly, its lower glacis raked to the nose;
    - a superstructure over it, its sides raked a little, its long shallow glacis and its raked rear plate;
    - welds at the glacis and the nose.
  - **The fenders** over the tracks, their fronts bent down. Side skirts in four bolted segments hang from them by the
    seed's dice (most carry them).
  - **On the hull:**
    - bins along the fenders, lipped and latched;
    - the turret's ring, bolted (the turret is phase 4);
    - the driver's hatch and its three vision blocks over the glacis;
    - the engine deck's two grilles, an access plate and the lifting eyes;
    - five spare track links racked across the glacis (`mil-track.js` `linkFaces`), the lamps in their guards and
      the blackout markers;
    - the exhausts' sooted louvred boxes and the tail lamps in their guards on the rear plate.
  - **Its kit:** two cans on the left fender, the tools on the right, two whips at the rear, grab handles, four
    shackles and the pintle.
  - **Compiled** (`military.js`): a tracked body's spinners are its bones, its road wheels first, with no wheel wells.
    Its wheelbase is its first road wheel to its last. Its camo and its mud are sized as its wheeled peer's (`sizeOf`:
    a tracked class's road wheels are small).
  - **Its glacis** faces forward before it faces up (a shallow glacis is not a roof).
  - **The budget:** about 35k triangles kept, 64k used and 65k in camo, before the turret.
  - **The sheet** still waits for its turret (`UNBUILT`).
  - **The wear's cutter** and the existing bodies are unchanged; their sizes and budgets hold.
  - **Held** (`mil-track.test.js`):
    - a bone each wheel, sprocket, idler and roller; its wheelbase and its length and width;
    - the fenders clear of the track; the glacis raked; chamfered;
    - the track bare steel and uncamouflaged;
    - skirted or not by its dice, the same length;
    - within its budget, kept, worn and in camo.
  - **Seen** (machine gate only; the eyes gate is open): plain from the three-quarter, the side, the rear quarter and
    the nose, skirted and bare; woodland used under a golden sun, desert battered at noon.
- **The light tank's turret and gun** (`road-military.js` `lightTank`), a bone of its own:
  - **The turret:** a slab with a wedged front, its cheeks cut, a bustle behind, its sides raked. It stands on the
    hull's ring as the `turret` bone, held still by the roll clip while the wheels turn.
  - **The gun** (geometry, never fired):
    - the mantlet and the coaxial port;
    - the barrel's sleeve, its thermal sleeve's bands and the bore evacuator, tapered at its ends;
    - the muzzle brake, its ports cut dark.

    It rides in the turret's bone and traverses with it. An elevation bone waits for a rig that parents bones.
  - **On the turret:**
    - the commander's cupola, six vision blocks round it, its lid and handle, and an empty pintle mount;
    - the loader's hatch with its hinges and handle; the gunner's sight, its block and hood;
    - four smoke-discharger cups a side on the cheeks, aimed out, forward and up;
    - grab rails along the sides;
    - a basket on the bustle carrying a rolled tarp (most do).
  - **Turning with it:** a face, a fitting or a mark carries its bone through the livery's and the wear's cuts (`bone`
    kept like `fitting`; absent, the bytes as they were). The camo and the turret's numbers turn with the turret.
  - **Measured:** the census measures the hull and the turret, not the gun, which reaches past the hull's length.
    L, W and H are within 1%.
  - **The sheet builds it** (no longer `UNBUILT`). The `light-tank` row's realistic build is live for parking,
    looking and export. It is still never a ride: driving needs skid steer.
  - **The budget:** about 38k triangles kept, 71k used and 74k in camo.
  - **Held** (`mil-track.test.js`):
    - the turret a bone on the ring, still while the wheels roll;
    - the gun, cupola, blocks, dischargers, basket and sight on it, the gun past the hull;
    - its camo and number turning with it;
    - the sheet builds it, never a ride;
    - within its budget.

    The GLB and parked sweeps take it too: its GLB is valid by the Khronos validator.
  - **Seen** (machine gate only; the eyes gate is open): plain from the three-quarter, the side, the rear quarter and
    above; woodland used under a golden sun; desert battered at noon.
- **The tracked carrier** (`road-military.js` `trackedCarrier`), a high troop box on the running gear:
  - **The running gear:** its sprocket forward by its engine and its idler aft under its ramp. `trackPath` wraps the
    track from the rear wheel's top, whichever that is.
  - **The hull:**
    - a lower hull, and a troop box with raked sides and a steep glacis, welded at its corners;
    - fenders and bins (fewer carriers wear skirts).
  - **The glacis:** a folded trim vane on its hinges, the engine's grille on the right, lamps in their guards.
  - **The roof:**
    - the driver's hatch and its blocks;
    - the commander's cupola, ringed by its blocks and by an empty mount rail on its posts;
    - the big troop hatch aft on its hinges, and grab rails.
  - **The rear:** the ramp, the door in it with its block and handle, the tail lamps in guards. The exhaust's louvred
    shield is on the right side, forward.
  - **Its kit:** cans each side of the ramp, the tools, two whips, four shackles, a tarp roll (half carry one).
  - **The sheet builds it.** Parked and watched, never a ride.
  - **The budget:** about 32k triangles kept, 47k used and 61k in camo. L, W and H are within 1%.
- **The light tank's variations, by its brief** (`trackedWords`: the sheet's unread words): "a short gun",
  "long gun", "skirts", "no skirts", "basket", "without basket".
  - What the brief does not say, the dice choose: most are skirted, most carry the long gun, every one its basket.
  - The short gun is stubbier and wider, its evacuator near the mantlet, its brake bigger.
  - A loft's `brief` carries the words, so `{ loft: { class: 'lightTank', brief: 'a short gun, no skirts' } }` draws
    that tank.
- **Shared:** the fenders, skirts and bins are one helper (`trackedFenders`). A kit's anchor that a body does not lay
  this time (a basket it does not carry) fits nothing.
- **Held** (`mil-track.test.js`):
  - a forward sprocket's track closed, flat and on its rollers;
  - the carrier's sprocket forward, its ramp, cupola, mount ring, trim vane, hatch and grille, no turret; at its size;
    within its budget; never a ride;
  - the brief's words read, and chosen on the tank (a shorter muzzle, no skirt, no basket); the dice choosing both
    guns among a dozen.

  The GLB and parked sweeps take the carrier too.
- **Seen** (machine gate only; the eyes gate is open): the carrier plain from the three-quarter, the side and the rear
  quarter, and desert used under a golden sun; the light tank from "a short gun, no skirts, no basket".
- **Composed:**
  - **The base:** a building's `parked` takes the tracked by name beside the wheeled (`['light tank', 'tracked
    carrier', 'apc']`). Each is laid in the hangar as its realistic loft in the faction's or the setting's paint,
    solid. The default stays a truck and an APC.
  - **The studio grid:** `mint_solid({ kind: 'vehicle', spec: { vehicle: 'light tank' } })` shows it. A loft's words
    beside the name without its class (`loft: { brief: 'a short gun' }`) take the row's own class.
  - **The engines:** each tracked body's GLB is valid by the Khronos validator, its turret its own node, so an
    engine can traverse it.
  - **Docs:** the vehicle card names the tracked and their words; a routing row ("a light tank with a short gun and
    no side skirts", `mint_solid`); the project's orientation names `mil-track.js`.
  - **Held:**
    - `parked.test.js`: a base parks a tank and a carrier beside the wheeled;
    - `preview-vehicle.test.js`: a brief beside the name takes the row's class;
    - `scene-gltf.vehicle.test.js`: the turret its own node.
- **Not built yet, said:**
  - Driving: a tracked physics class's skid steer, the track's scroll, a turret aimed by a player.
  - The gun's elevation as its own bone (the rig does not parent bones).
  - A main battle tank and a halftrack on the same parts.
  - Parked tracked vehicles lit indoors (as the wheeled: the world's sky).

### The urban pizza viewer: a city drawn by the view cone

- **A city on the cone** (`scene/channels/city-cone.js`): a geocity whose world asks for the view cone (`cone`: true for the
  screen's reach, or metres), read for the live page, draws its street as a gen-7 outside draws its land: in full where the
  screen can show it, an impression past it, nothing the cone cannot see. Its street was drawn in tiles within a 320 m ring
  of the eye, every tree at the one level the scene's bookmark cameras picked for it; on the cone:
  - **the trees** are grown twice, at their near level (`cone: 'in'`) and at L0 (`cone: 'out'`) on one grid of 48 m tiles:
    the page shows a tile's near level inside the cone's reach and its L0 past it, by the live eye. The two are
    complementary by construction (one distance, one reach): no tree is drawn twice and none goes missing;
  - **the kit** (lamps, signals, benches, scaffolding, a composed geotown's repeats; `cone: 'kit'`) is drawn while its height
    covers two pixels at the tile's nearest point;
  - **the air** (`air`, channels/atmosphere.js) leaves out a tile whose top lies under an optical depth of 6 (a quarter of
    a percent of contrast): the fog has already taken it. The air's probe answers the optical depth (`__mojAir.depth`);
  - all within the ring a tile without the cone keeps, so a high camera sees the street it saw.
  A lakeshore neighbourhood's street camera drew 1.63M triangles in 569 draws; on the cone 0.71M in 577, looking the same
  (its crossing 2.27M to 1.19M, its evocation's camera 2.28M to 1.11M); under a 150 m fog 0.58M in 348.
- **The air takes the far on every gen-7 page** (`ATMOSPHERE.cull`, an optical depth of 6; the air's probe answers
  `__mojAir.taken`): past it the far trees (`channels/form-flora.js`: whole or as their card) and the far structures'
  tiles (`channels/far-structures.js`: neither live nor carded, the ladder run again as the fog's density changes) are
  not drawn, nor do they cast, on a trail, a path and a geotown alike. A geotown neighbourhood's street camera under fog
  leaves out 333 of its plants and 34 of its tiles; its triangles hardly move (a far card is two of them), so outside the
  city this is the far kept tidy rather than a saving. A gen-7 geotown is drawn by the form render and so was already on
  the cone: its trees cards past the reach, its buildings tiles carded and culled.
- An export reads the geocity as before (one level a tree, the ring), and so does a page without `cone`: not a byte
  changes. Not yet: the micro-city and the geotown (`cone` is not their setting), and the far structures' 128-tile skip
  for a metro (its buildings are cheap massing).

### Vehicle registry: one front door for every vehicle, the old tables frozen behind it

A game's vehicles came from several tables that shared no names and read nothing of the game they were in: the city's
scenery nets, the physics classes, the highway fleet, the assembled rides, the race machines, the craft shelf, the fly
goal's flight models and a civilization's crafted technology. The registry names them once, the furnishings roster's
way. There is one row per vehicle, under the words people say, and each row claims its keys in each table. The tables
still measure, so no stored recipe changes by a byte.

- **The roster** (`vehicle-registry/roster.js`):
  - **A row:** a label, the words people say, where it goes (road, offroad, rail, water, air, space), what a game asks
    it for (a closed set of roles; rows that share a role stand in for each other), the world ages it belongs to (the
    casting call's eras), how a game meets it (driven, traffic, parked, watched, crewed), and its handles.
  - **Handles** are its keys into the tables that build it. Every row falls back to the technology crafter's concept,
    so a vehicle no table builds yet (a tank, a sailing ship, a helicopter) is still named, searchable and drawn as a
    concept.
  - **Words:** `resolveVehicle` (articles dropped, hyphens as spaces, plurals read), and one word names one vehicle (the
    index throws on a collision).
  - **Search:** `findVehicles({ words, realm, role, era, use })` ranks an exact name first, then the share of the words
    found, filtered by the facets. `suggestVehicles` gives a refusal the rows a word nearly names.
  - The brand and franchise names are left out: a row is a kind of vehicle, never a product.
- **Frozen** (`roster.test.js`):
  - Every key of every legacy table is claimed by exactly one row, every net through its scenery entry or as an
    orphan, and every vehicle concept the technology crafter draws by some row.
  - A key added to a legacy table without a row fails with "a new vehicle is a registry row first".
  - The rows agree with the legacy pairings: a ride is its assembly, and a fleet loft is its physics class.
- **Builds by tier** (`vehicle-registry/builds.js`). A build is a row at a tier (toy, stylised or realistic), made by
  the builder a handle points at.
  - **Each build says how far it reaches:**
    - `live`: a game or world draws it;
    - `preview`: the studio grid shows it, no game yet;
    - `asleep`: built, reached by nothing;
    - `concept`: the crafter's block plan.
  - **Each build says the uses it serves**, so a highway fleet's traffic loft is never mistaken for a car a hero drives.
  - **`buildOf(id, tier, { use })`** gives the tier's build, else the nearest tier's, else the concept, and says why when
    it fell.
  - **`upscaleOf(id)`** says what a row needs to be drawn realistic for the use that matters most: live already, a build
    to wire in, or a body to build. This is the upscale ledger for the old vehicles.
  - **`dimsOf(id)`** reads a row's size from the table that measures it, never retyped.
- **The realistic loft on the studio grid** (`car-designer/race-families.js` `loftInstanceFaces`, the family layer's
  `loft` instance):
  - A road class's realistic loft (`car-designer/realistic.js`, until now reached only by a render script) is shown at
    its true numbers in metres: `{ loft: { class, era?, brief?, seed? } }`.
  - It is the realistic build of every car, truck and bus with a loftable class.
  - An instance without the key keeps its bytes.
- **Every door reads a vehicle word through the registry:**
  - **`mint_solid({ kind: 'vehicle', spec: { vehicle, tier? } })`:**
    - Any word the registry names is read to its row, then to the build at the tier (or its first build the grid shows,
      for a parked vehicle).
    - The stored instance is that build's own keys plus `vehicle: <id>`, the row it was asked as.
    - A legacy `type` that is not a scenery key is read the same way. A scenery key keeps its own path byte for byte,
      with the registry beside it in the readout only.
    - A row the grid cannot show yet is refused with its builds; a word the registry does not know, with the rows it
      nearly names.
    - The readout's `registry` names the row, the build, every build and its upscale.
  - **The quick game's `ride`, `vehicle`, `craft` and the transformer's `vehicle.ride` / `vehicle.craft`:**
    - They take any word the registry names, written as the table's key at the door (`gameworld/quick.js` `quickWorld`,
      and design_game's patch ops on those pointers). A world asked as `ride: 'sedan'` stores exactly what
      `ride: 'car'` stores.
    - A row with no key in that table is refused with what it needs.
    - design_game's readout says what was read (`vehicles.registry`), only when something was.
  - **Retired:**
    - The dead `registerPreviewVehicleTools`, whose description told agents to commit new vehicles to the old table.
    - The `vehicle-smooth-box-net.js` re-export shim. Its test now reads the swept net it re-exported.
- **Docs:**
  - The `vehicle` solid card leads with the registry.
  - A generated `vehicles` card (`vehicle-registry/entries.js`) lists every vehicle by realm, with its build at each
    tier, for `get_solid_vocab` and `semantic_search`.
  - A `vehicle` routing card, with a fixture row for a vehicle by name.
  - The `design-vehicle-family` catalyst starts at the registry: a new vehicle is a row first.
- **Held** (`roster.test.js`, `doors.test.js`, `preview-vehicle.test.js`). Each concept is tested on a row chosen in
  code by what it carries:
  - the contract and the freeze;
  - the words, search and refusals;
  - one row per builder for its tier, status, uses and fallback;
  - the traffic loft against a driven one;
  - the quick words written as their keys (the world byte-identical), the patch ops, the legacy key and a spec without
    a vehicle word left as the same object;
  - the door's word, legacy type, tier and race-machine reads;
  - the tier read, one case per read and the stamp (`tier-ride.test.js`);
  - the ride at each tier: an assembled ride, its row's loft at the realistic tier, a loft-only row falling, and a row
    nothing drives refused;
  - end to end (`design-game.quick.test.js`, e2e tier): a realistic ride race stamped from the juice, its loft figure
    and its rival's, the class's rule and the rig resolved, and a pickup by name; the assembled ride and the kart race
    unchanged;
  - a scenery mint;
  - a loft minted at true dimensions and drawn by the world route;
  - a legacy mint's manifest unchanged.
- **The tier read** (`vehicle-registry/tier.js` `vehicleTierOf`): the fidelity a game's vehicles are drawn at, read
  from what the game already says, the first that speaks winning:
  - the game's own word (`quick.tier`);
  - a realistic hero (the quick hero's, the book's or an adopted hero's `form: 'realistic'`), or the people's body
    rail (the quick game's `body`, the book's direction: `gameworld/game-bodies.js`) laying the realistic body in the
    world's tradition and look;
  - the juice's written drawing (form → realistic, voxel → toy);
  - a shooter pole on the realistic side;
  - a voxel kit (→ toy);
  - a field of karts (→ toy);
  - else stylised.

  `stampedTier` gives what a new quick world is stamped with at mint, only when the read is not stylised. A world
  minted before carries no tier and drives what it always drove.
- **The realistic ride** (`vehicle-registry/ride.js` `rideOf`):
  - **Choosing the build:** a quick game's `ride` names a registry row, by its assembled ride's key (car, coupe, van)
    or by any row with a realistic loft (`ride: 'pickup'`, `'bus'`, `'box-truck'`; the door writes `'a pickup truck'`
    as `'pickup'`). The game's `tier` picks the build: the assembled ride, minted as its sketch as before, or the
    class's realistic loft.
  - **The loft in the game:** a figure the world compiles in place (`figures: { ride: { loft: { class, seed } } }`,
    `world-scene.js`, nothing to mint). It drives on its class's own physics row, which a quick `vehicle`, `tuning` and
    `conditions` still override, and is chased by a camera scaled to its length (a ride's `camera`, `levels.js`). Its
    rivals race in it.
  - **When the tier has none:** a row with no build at the tier drives the nearest and says so (a pickup has only its
    loft; a sedan has no toy build).
  - **The loft's status:** `live` in the registry, so every road row with a loftable class is drawn realistic for its
    driven use.
  - The cargo van's row is `cargo-van` (the word "van" still names it in the registry), since the ride key `van` is the
    minivan. A contract check holds that no row's id is another row's legacy ride key.
- **Seen** (machine gate only; the eyes gate is open):
  - The loft on the studio grid.
  - In headless Chrome, three trail levels, each followed from behind with no page errors: a stylised game's assembled
    car (as before), the same game at the realistic tier driving the midsize loft, and a pickup by name.
  - The lofts are at true size, and their look is plain (baked light, slab panels): the look work is not this
    wiring.
- **Not built, said:**
  - **Phase 2, search and the gaps page:** a generated `docs/vehicle-gaps.md` (realm × era, the wants ranked) and
    per-row cards.
  - **Phase 4's other half:** the fly goal's body from the craft shelf.
  - **The tier read's other inputs:** the setting's tradition and the levels' render era (gen-7). A gameworld's own
    record does not carry the era, so it is left out rather than guessed.
  - **Book worlds:** a vehicle word beside `quick` (`vehicles.tier`), with the fleet phases.
  - **Phase 5:** a civilization's technology vehicles resolved through the registry.
  - **Phase 6:** the city's traffic by tier.
  - **Phase 7:** the engines.
  - **Phase 8:** the wanted vehicles' own bodies.
  - The loft in the form render (gen-7 light), and the open frames' realistic bodies (kart, buggy, quad).

### The atlas: a gameworld drawn as an illustrated map

A gameworld's levels, trails and links can now be read as one illustrated map, at `/bible?book=atlas`
(`gameworld/atlas.js`, `gameworld/atlas-html.js`). The map is drawn from the world's own recipe:
- **The levels:** each is a province on one sheet, laid out from the hub (or the start) along its links, the first
  ways across the sheet and the rest round.
- **The ground:** grown as its land and words say: woods and hill bands massed from seeded noise, pines where its
  words are alpine, peaks where it climbs or a castle stands, a river from the heights to the sea.
- **The trails:** each level's trail winds through its stages, from where it is reached to where it leads. A stage
  shows as a dot, a climb as a wedge, a building as a square.
- **The places:** the hub ringed by its walls, its town, the castle.
- **The links:** each is drawn as its kind, a road a dashed track and a gate a dotted way with its arch, with a key
  where it is locked.
- **The sheet:** a cartouche, a compass and a scale.

The page is HTML and CSS alone, with no WebGL, canvas or library. The ground is SVG and the things on it are a layer of
sprites. Flat, it reads as a drawn map. On the table, a CSS-3D tilt lays the ground back, every sprite stands up off
it, and a drag turns the table.

Its looks are cards of paint only, and every look lays the same map:
- **painted:** the world's own solved colours on warm paper;
- **ink:** an engraving in one ink on cream;
- **night:** a star chart with glowing trails.

The world bible links it, and the next-moves card names it. The atlas is deterministic, from the world's seed alone.

**Depictions: the same map as different kinds of map.** The atlas page now draws a world's layout as a kind of map,
each kind with its own looks (`atlas-html.js` is the page; each depiction is its own module):
- **illustrated** (`atlas-illustrated.js`): the drawn map above, in painted, ink or night.
- **tactical** (`atlas-tactical.js`): a modern operations map, in three looks:
  - **ops:** a printed map, brown contours on white, blue water and grid, green woods, red roads, the control
    measures in black;
  - **nvg:** night-vision phosphor with a scan;
  - **command:** a dark command display, its corner brackets, amber roads, cyan friendly, the objective in red.

The tactical depiction draws:
- **Relief:** read off the land as a height field (the coast, the hills, the peaks), contoured by marching squares,
  every fifth line an index contour with its height.
- **Grid:** numbered in the margin.
- **Ground cover:** woods as a green tint, towns as built-up areas of blocks turned to their trail.
- **Each level:** an area of operations (AO) with its boundary and its name, its trail a track, its stages
  checkpoints numbered across the game in the order it reaches them.
- **The links:** each road with a phase line where it crosses into the next level, a gate a passage point, a locked
  way marked.
- **Places:** the start point, the base at the hub, the castle a fortified area, the objective at the deepest level.
- **The margin:** a title block, a north diagram and a scale in km.

On the table, the buildings, the mast, the fort's tower and the flags stand up. `?look=` takes any look of either
depiction, and every look lays the same map.

### Boat parts: the primitives watercraft are built from, on the craft shelf

In progress. Boats join the craft shelf as new part kinds, the way the drones did, so a variety of watercraft can be
assembled from one kit: a hull drawn from its lines, its drive, its fittings, floated at the waterline its weight sets.
The first boat is a small motor skiff; bigger and different boats follow from the same parts.

- **The kinds and the first boat** (`craft-shelf/boat-odm.js`, `boat-parts.js`, `boat-archetypes.js`, merged into the
  shelf's inventory, builders and archetypes; the shelf gains the `water` realm, its finish and a `skiffGreen` palette).
  - **`boat-hull`, drawn from its lines** the way a lines plan draws one: along its length the keel's height, the
    sheer's and the chine's heights and half-breadths, so the bottom's deadrise and the sides' flare follow from them.
    - An outer skin and an inner liner, each lofted as a U-shaped wall, painted outside and bare inside.
    - A plane clips the skin and the liner into a raked transom (its thickness the motor board's), and another clips
      the liner into the bow's deck. One mechanism, so a flat-bowed or decked hull is a different line or plane.
    - Benches lofted to the liner they sit in (each fits whatever hull it is in), ribs along the floor, strakes along
      the bottom, the gunwale rails, the transom's cap and motor pad, the keel strip up the stem, and the fittings: the
      bow eye, the bow handle, the stern cleats, the oarlocks, the drain plug and the transom's eyes.
    - Its points: the transom's motor point, where a tank stands on the floor, each seat's top.
  - **`boat-outboard`**, a tiller outboard:
    - the clamp bracket, raked to the transom, and its screws, with the tilt tube (they stay with the boat);
    - the swivel bracket (it tilts);
    - the cowl and its pan, the midsection, the anti-ventilation plate, and the gearcase's strut, torpedo, skeg and
      intake grilles;
    - a three-blade propeller, each blade's section pitched to the helix its pitch draws and raked aft, handed;
    - the tiller and its twist grip, the shift lever and the starter's handle.

    It tilts about its tilt tube (`pose.tilt`), steers about its swivel (`pose.yaw`, + to starboard) and its propeller
    turns (`pose.prop`), each a joint.
  - **`boat-tank`**: a portable fuel tank, its handle, cap, gauge and fitting.
  - **The motor skiff** (`motorSkiff`): a 14 ft aluminium V-bottom utility skiff with a 20 hp tiller outboard and its tank,
    in the water's own `utility` role (a boat's role holds boats; the flying roles still pair an earth craft with its
    starship).
- **Two more small boats from the same kit**, each by a word on a hull row, not a new builder:
  - **The jon boat** (`jonBoat`): a 12 ft flat-bottomed aluminium boat, marsh tan, with a 9.9 hp tiller. A flat bottom
    is its chine at its keel's height; its square bow (`bow: 'square'`) is where the bottom's rocker meets a small transom
    at the bow, its rail across it and its keel strip ending at its foot; runners along its bottom.
  - **The RIB tender** (`ribTender`): a 3.1 m deep-V moulded hull in its collar, with a 20 hp tiller, in a new `tender`
    role. Its `collar` is one tube from the transom round the rising bow and back, its cones run aft of the transom, its
    rubbing strake and lifeline along it, with no gunwale rails; its `sole` is a floor laid flat across the V (the liner
    clipped to a plane, as the deck and transom are), its locker under the bow, white inside (`tint`).
  - **A smaller outboard** (`outboard-10-tiller`): the tiller builder at the 9.9 hp class's cowl and propeller, its leg
    and gearcase drawn at `leg` of the 20 hp class's size, on the same shaft.
  - **A collar floats too:** its tubes' sections count in the hull's displacement once they are in the water, so a loaded
    RIB settles onto its tubes.
  - The registry's `jon-boat` and `rib` rows (john boat, flat bottom boat, duck boat …; rib, rigid inflatable, inflatable
    boat, yacht tender …), their craft builds asleep.
- **The centre console runabout** (`ccRunabout`): a 17 ft moulded deep-V hull, white with a navy stripe, a 90 hp remote
  outboard on a 25 in transom, its console and two cooler seats on the sole, in a new `runabout` role. Each new thing is
  a part or a word, absent adding nothing (the earlier boats' bytes held):
  - **`boat-console`** (`craft-shelf/boat-helm.js`): the body pushed from its side's outline (its front, its dash sloping
    aft to the helm); the access door; a windscreen in three panels (the middle and two wings swept aft) and its frame;
    a grab rail round it on bent posts; on the dash a screen, two gauges and a compass; the helm's pod and a wheel on an
    axis raked toward the helmsman (rim, hub, three spokes); the throttle's binnacle and lever on the starboard wall.
  - **`boat-seat`**: a cooler seat, its lid's seam, its rope handles, its cushion.
  - **The hull's new words:** `cap` (a moulded gunwale cap: the liner's top pulled inboard, level with the sheer),
    `points` (named points on the sole where a console or a seat stands), `stripe`, `stations` (a longer, more flared
    hull's station spacing, so a curved quad's twist stays under its skin), and fittings `bowRail` (stanchions and a
    rail round ahead of the stem), `navLights` (sidelights on the bow, green to starboard and red to port; an all-round
    light on a pole aft) and `rodHolders`. A moulded hull has no keel strip.
  - **The outboard's `remote` family:** no tiller, shift lever or starter; bolted through the transom; its rigging's boot
    and hose into the boat and a steering ram along its tilt tube; its brackets and swivel at its `leg` size, its pan
    `cowl.lift` over the clamp and its cowl's colour role `tint.cowl` (a white 90 hp).
  - It floats 1041 kg at a 30 cm draft with 34 cm of freeboard aft; tilted up, its cowl hangs in over the transom, clear
    of the sole and the helm's seat.
  - The registry's `center-console` row (centre console, runabout, bay boat, sport fishing boat …), its build asleep.
- **The motor well** (the hull's `well`): a notched transom and its splashwell, by the same planes the transom, the deck
  and the sole are clipped by.
  - **The notch:** across its `width` the transom steps down to the motor's height (`notch`), the quarters standing full
    height either side, their caps on them and the notch's cap and motor point down in it. Each layer (the skin's
    outside, its inside, the liner's inside) steps down and out by its own depth, so they stack in the notch as they do
    everywhere and every ring closes; each stepped run is arched by a millimetre and a half, so a stepped end's cap
    triangulates edge to edge.
  - **The splashwell:** the liner's floor at `floor` aft of the well's `length`, its bulkhead lofted to the skin's inside
    up to its `top`. Freeboard aft is measured at the notch, the lowest the water can come in.
  - The centre console now has a motor well and a 20 in shaft 90 hp (`outboard-90-remote-20`, its rigging hose into
    the well's bulkhead); the 25 in row stays for a full transom. Its well is long enough that the motor tilts up into
    it, clear of the transom's block and the bulkhead. It floats 1037 kg with 21 cm of freeboard at the notch.
- **The T-top** (`boat-top`, `tTop`; `ccTTop`, a second centre console that wears it):
  - four legs from feet on the sole beside the console, bent in to a frame under the top;
  - a front brace over the windscreen;
  - a moulded hardtop with its lip, overhanging aft over the helm with a standing helmsman's headroom;
  - rod holders raked aft along its back edge, spreader lights under it, the all-round light and an antenna on top.

  The boat's hull is the centre console's with `navLights: { pole: false }`, its all-round light moved to the top. The
  registry's `t-top-console` row, its build asleep.
- **The cuddy cabin** (`cuddyCabin`): a 19 ft moulded deep V, white with a sea-blue stripe and upholstery, a black
  150 hp remote on a 25 in shaft in its motor well, in the `runabout` role. Its new words each fit the hull they are on:
  - **`trunk`:** the cabin's top on the long foredeck, lofted bow-ward inboard of the sheer, its sides leaning in and its
    top falling toward the bow, its portlights along its sides, its hatch and grab rails on top.
  - **`companionway`:** the cabin's door in the deck's aft bulkhead.
  - **A hull's `windscreen`:** across the boat on the deck's edge, its wings running forward along the gunwales, raked
    aft, a walk-through in its middle to the cabin's door, its frame and posts.
  - **Points off the centreline** (`[s, x]`): a split dash (`dash-helm-19` to starboard with its wheel and throttle,
    `dash-passenger-19` to port with a grab handle and glovebox; the console builder now draws only the pieces a row
    names, the centre console's bytes held) and two bucket seats on pedestals (`boat-seat`'s `bucket`).
  - An aft bench with a `cushion`. It floats 1616 kg with 29 cm of freeboard at the notch; the 150 hp tilts into its
    well clear of the transom and the bulkhead.
  - The registry's `cuddy-cabin` row (cuddy, cabin runabout, weekender …), its build asleep.
- **Afloat by its weight** (`boat-parts.js` `hullVolume`, `hullFloat`). The hull's displacement is worked out from the
  same sections it is lofted from, so what floats is what is drawn. An assembled boat's readout says where it floats
  (`afloat`): its parts' mass and its payload, the draft that displaces them in fresh or salt water (`water`), the
  freeboard, and `waterline`, that line's height in the manifest's frame, where a level lays its water. The motor skiff
  carries 380 kg at a 15 cm draft with 25 cm of freeboard at its transom; the jon boat 311 kg at 10 cm; the RIB 319 kg
  at 24 cm, its tubes just in the water.
- **The registry:**
  - A `motor-skiff` row (skiff, motorboat, outboard boat, tinny, fishing boat …), its word taken off the rowboat row.
  - Its craft build is asleep: built and floated, and no door draws a boat yet.
  - A transformer's craft is refused a boat: it flies.
- **Review:** `node scripts/render-boats.mjs <dir> [boats] [--pose …] [--dry]` draws each boat from the side, the
  quarter, above and astern, on a sheet of water at its waterline (or `--dry`, out of it, to see its bottom).
- **Held** (`boat.test.js`; the shelf's pins and sweeps). Each concept is tested on a case chosen in code from the shelf:
  - every boat part the same twice;
  - the hull's envelope its dims, its halves mirrored, its transom raked, its benches inside it;
  - the waterline displacing its weight, deeper when heavier and shallower in salt water, swamped when overloaded;
  - the outboard's plate at the keel's height, its propeller under the water;
  - its tilt, steer and propeller each about its own axis;
  - the boat role filled by boats, the skiff by its words, its build asleep, a transformer refusing it;
  - each hull variation on the hull that carries it: a flat bottom level across, a square bow, a sole, a collar outboard
    of the sheer that floats the boat once it is in the water; a smaller outboard's slimmer leg on the same shaft.
  - a helm on the sole: the console and seats on the hull's points inside the cockpit, the wheel at a standing
    helmsman's hands; the gunwale's cap; the sidelights' colours and sides, the bow rail ahead of the stem; the remote
    outboard without a tiller, rigged, and clear of the transom tilted up.
  - a motor well: the notch at the motor's height and the quarters full, the splashwell's floor and the cockpit's sole,
    freeboard at the notch, the motor's plate at the keel on its shaft, tilted into the well and out of the transom's
    raked, notched block and the bulkhead; a T-top's feet on the sole beside the console, its hardtop over the helm with
    headroom, the all-round light moved to it.
  - a cuddy cabin: its cabin top inboard of the sheer standing its height over the deck, its ports; its windscreen inside
    the gunwales with its walk-through open and the cabin's door behind it; its split dash and bucket seats off the
    centreline, the passenger's dash without a helm.

  The shelf's new builder paths (the remote outboard, the console, the seat, the T-top, the bucket seat) are pinned, and
