    centreline and edges; the axial deck's line forward; four catapult tracks, a blast deflector hinged aft of each start
    (`pose.deflector` raises them); four arresting wires across the landing area on their posts; four deck-edge lifts
    outboard of its edge, the hangar's openings behind them (`pose.lift` lowers them to the hangar); sponsons under its
    edge, braced, carrying its weapons; its parking spots and the island's point.
  - **Its island:** the destroyer's superstructure and pyramid mast at an island's size on the deck's starboard edge, two
    bands of bridge windows.
  - **Its point defence:** three close-in weapons and two eight-cell launchers on the sponsons, modelled, never fired.
  - **Its aircraft:** `vehicle-registry/carry.js` `flightDeck(archetype)` says what its deck carries: the registry's
    carrier-role aircraft drawn on the shelf, each by its own assembled span spread and folded, its length and its
    weight, against its spots and its lifts. `render-boats.mjs --deck` parks them on its spots, wings folded, for review;
    a level lays them the same way.
  - It floats 90,800 t (its crew, air wing, stores and aviation fuel) at an 11.5 m draft, 69 m from its keel to its
    masthead, 98 m across its lifts.
  - Held: the deck on the hull's deck, flat, overhanging either side, its gallery; the angled deck's cant, the wires
    across it inside the landing area; each deflector flush at rest and raised by the pose, aft of its catapult's start;
    each lift outboard of the edge, lowered by its drop before its opening; the island to starboard with its mast; the
    weapons on sponsons outboard of the hull; four screws in two mirrored pairs; the field's carrier aircraft on its
    spots, a ship with no flight deck carrying none; its weight its waterline; its row in the registry. The flight deck's
    builder path is pinned, and no existing pin moved. The wear's salt and chips are laid on a flight deck too.
- **The submarine** (`attackSub`): a generic 110 m nuclear attack submarine in black, single screw, the registry's
  `submarine` row (attack submarine, nuclear submarine, hunter killer …) in the field's `armour` role and a new craft
  role, `submarine`. Its hull is a new family:
  - **`boat-hull`'s `round`** (`craft-shelf/boat-sub.js`): a body of revolution about its axis from its radius along its
    length (its stern's cone, its parallel middle, its rounded bow); its casing along its top with its hatches; the
    torpedo tubes' doors on its bow below the axis, shut; a row of missile hatches for a hull that carries them; its sail
    on the casing with its fairwater planes (`pose.planes`) and its masts housed in it (`pose.masts` raises them); its
    stern's four fins as a cross or an X, each a fixed fin and a moving flap, every flap turned by its share of the
    rudder (`pose.yaw`) and the rise (`pose.planes`) so all their trailing edges move one way; its skewed seven-bladed
    screw (`pose.prop`), its tips set in so no part of a blade passes its diameter. Modelled, never fired.
  - **Its hydrostatics:** a round hull's section is the circle of its radius at each station, so it floats by the same
    sections every hull floats by; its freeboard is its casing's deck over the water, and its readout's `afloat.ballast`
    is the water it floods to dive (its whole envelope less its weight: boat-parts.js `hullEnvelope`). A surface boat's
    readout carries no ballast and is unchanged.
  - It floats 6,600 t surfaced at an 8.4 m draft with 2.3 m of casing above the water, and floods 884 t to dive.
  - Held: its sections circles about its axis, its envelope its length and diameter; surfaced with its casing dry, its
    ballast its envelope less its weight, a surface boat with none; the sail on the casing, its masts housed and raised
    by their heights, its planes turning; a cross's and an X's flaps each moving their trailing edges one way for the
    rudder and the rise; the screw behind the stern inside its diameter and turning; the tubes' doors on the bow; its
    row in the registry. The round hull's builder path is pinned, and no existing pin moved.

### Object grip, balls: a hand that holds a ball by its size, throws and catches solved, a stick library for the ball games

The manual manipulator takes up balls. The hand closes on a ball of the ball card's own size by a grip a person names
(or the ball's own), a hero throws it in a technique timed so the ball leaves at the sport's real speed, and the
throws are baked into the stick the sports pages pose their athletes by, with the launch a sim gives the ball. Nothing
minted before moves. The eyes gate is the operator's: the throws were looked at only as stick figures in a review
page (`scripts/spikes/manipulator/throws.mjs --page`).

- **Ball grips** (`lib/graph/polygonizer/hero-ball-grip.js`): `power` (wrapped in the palm: a softball, a tennis ball),
  `fingertip` (a pitcher's: the index and the middle on top, the thumb under, the palm clear), `spread` (the fingers
  across a big ball, the palm a finger off it: a basketball, a handball, a football), `cradle` (on the open palm),
  `pinch` (thumb, index and middle pads: a golf ball, a table-tennis ball), `bowling` (the thumb and two fingers in the
  holes). Each digit closes until it touches (hero-digits), a digit the solve left in the ball is opened back onto its
  skin, and the laws read every named digit on the ball and none pressed in. `gripFor(ball)` picks a ball's own. A
  softball and a handball are held beside the ball card (`HAND_BALLS`: the sports' pages inline the card, so it is
  left as it was until a sport plays them).
- **Throws** (`lib/graph/polygonizer/hero-throw.js`, `THROWS`): overhand (a pitch), the quarterback's pass, sidearm,
  underhand, the bowling delivery, the chest pass, the set shot, the throw-in, the toss to serve. Each is a ball, a
  grip, a stance, one or two hands, keyed phases (the body's channels and each hand's place, way and palm) and a
  release cited from the sport (speed, elevation, spin). The hand is placed by the ball and the arm solved to it
  (holdArm, now with an optional seed so each key keeps the last key's way of reaching), a place past reach is drawn in
  toward the shoulder, a free hand goes by the arm alone, and the release is keyed as a drive along the launch line,
  re-timed until the played clip lets the ball go at the technique's speed. Checks: the hands on their places, the
  grip, the wrists at every key, the speed (within a tenth), the line, the drive's wobble (held where the drive is on
  screen: longer than a frame at 60 fps), the balance, and the servos' peak speeds as a report.
- **Where the throws stand:** overhand, sidearm, bowling, the chest pass and the toss hold every law. The quarterback's
  pass, the underhand and the set shot (a wrist at a key; the pass's and the shot's drive, which wanders off its line
  where the forearm stands near upright) and the throw-in (a wrist at a key, its drive) reach their release speed and
  hold the ball, and say which laws they miss.
- **Catches** (`lib/graph/polygonizer/hero-catch.js`, `CATCHES`): `high` (the hands' diamond above the chest), `low` (the
  basket below the waist), `chest` (taken into the body, the arms closing round it), `oneHand` (a bare hand at the
  shoulder), `skyball` (a high ball dropping steeply, taken by the eyes). The ball comes in along its line (its speed
  and its drop; a ball and a way in of the caller's own), the hands go out to meet it open, palms to it, close on it at
  the touch already moving back along its line at a share of its speed, and give with it until both stop, then bring
  it in. The readout gives the sting (the impulse at the touch), the give's distance, time and force. The throw's hand
  solver is shared (hero-throw.js `handsKit`). Checks: the hands, the grip, the wrists at every key, the palms to the
  ball, the hands' speed and way at the touch, the give on its line, the balance. `high`, `low`, `chest` and `oneHand`
  hold every law; `skyball` misses its wrist through the give.
- **Fixed: a throwing hand opening after the release** keyed the `open` word, a number per digit, where the grip's
  digits are objects; a clip's channels are its keys' numbers, so the thumb lost its joints through the whole throw.
  The hand now opens in the grip's own form (`openFingers`).
- **On the hero door**: motion words `throwOverhand`, `throwPass`, `throwSidearm`, `throwUnderhand`, `bowlRoll`,
  `chestPass`, `setShot`, `throwIn`, `tossServe` play a throw as a one-shot, the ball a prop of the throwing hand; the
  clip's readout names the release (when, how fast, along what line, and the library's launch for an engine to spawn
  the ball at). `catchHigh`, `catchLow`, `catchChest`, `catchOneHand`, `catchSkyball` play a catch; its ball carries no
  prop (it arrives at the touch: the readout's `contact` says when an engine puts it in the hand).
- **The stick library** (`lib/graph/contest/throw-sticks.js`, baked by `node scripts/throw-sticks.mjs` into
  `throw-sticks.data.js`): `throwStick(name, u, { at, face })` gives a sports page's stick at any moment of a throw,
  the ball in the hand until it leaves; `throwRelease(name, { at, face, power, toward })` the launch a sim gives the
  ball (speed, line and spin turned with the thrower, or the low arc through a point); `catchStick(name, u, …)` a catch
  the same way, the ball flying in and then held, and `catchOf(name)` its touch, its way in and its give, for a sim to
  time the hands to a ball it flies. The sports' sims still launch
  from their own fixed points: wiring them to these is next. A deep test holds the baked file to a fresh bake.
- **The review page** (`scripts/spikes/manipulator/throws.mjs --page out.html`): every throw and every catch as a looping
  stick figure, side on and from behind, a throw's ball held and then flown at its launch, a catch's flown in and given
  with, with a scrubber.

### A modern European old town, walked as a game

- **A modern European old town, a geotown pattern** (`geotown/pattern.js` `old-town`). Its streets are narrow setts
  lanes with flagged walks and no verge. Its town houses are rendered terraces three to five storeys high, built to the
  walk party wall to party wall. Its main street has shops on the ground floor, and the blocks behind hold gardens and
  courts. Each house has its own render (ochre, cream, terracotta, rose, stone, grey-blue under slate), its own
  shutters, and wrought balconies on some. It comes with one streetscape, `old-centre`, and two neighbourhoods:
  `old-centre` (terraced lanes round a main street of shops) and `market-street`. Where it does not differ it keeps
  the suburb's own: its fences, sites, furniture and houseplants. The suburb, `bay-and-gable`, is unchanged byte for
  byte (its design and scene hashed before and after) and stays the default.
- **The old-town house style** (`era/arch-style.js` `old-town`): lime render over an ashlar ground storey, tall
  shuttered casements in stone surrounds, a shallow clay-tiled hip behind a deep cornice, setts and flags.
- **A pattern's street furniture can be European.** `furniture.lamps: 'lantern'` lights every street with a lantern on
  a cast-iron post (no wooden pole, no arm, no wires). `furniture.paint: 'none'` leaves the lanes unpainted, with no
  yellow centre line. Neither is set for the suburb.
- **A square, a new site** (`geotown/sites.js` `square`, the segment letter `Q`). It is a paved piazza laid in the
  pattern's `piazza` finish. Its church stands on its own lot across the far side with its door to the square: a
  `church` row in the gothic-parish style, from a site plot that can now name its kind and where it stands (a school's
  lot still stands at its site's front corner, byte for byte). It has a stone fountain in its middle and café tables
  under parasols along its flanks, each parasol coloured from the pattern's awning colours. A square is not a playing
  field to the spacing law. The old town's third neighbourhood, `square`, sets the church and its piazza among the
  terraces. The new `piazza` surface enters a town's ledger only where one lies, so a town without a square keeps its
  ledger's bytes.
- **A game level can be a town.** `levels.<id>.geotown` takes the geocube kind's geotown: its pattern, streetscape, a
  segment or a neighbourhood. The town is the level's only ground, so it takes no walk, building, city, roadway,
  airspace, runner, places, ground or arena. It is drawn on the level's cube (a morning valley unless the style names
  one) and read in the seventh generation unless the cube names its era.
  - **Its stage:** one stage (`levels.js` `gameStages`). Its ends (`stageEnds`, through `geotownEnds`) set the hero
    down at the start of the walk round its first block, facing along it, with the exit at that walk's far side and
    beats along the way. Its ground is the town's ground faces, never a roof, and its colliders are its buildings'.
  - **On the page:** the geotown takes only its own settings, and the level's pilot and game are layered over it with
    no stand-in walker (`world-kinds.js`).
  - **In the books:** the world graph, the bible (the town's sheet), the atlas, the battles page and the review print
    each read it.
- **A quick game can walk a town.** `quick.geotown` is reached, collected along or survived. It refuses a building,
  climb, ride, run, roadway, runner or race beside it. With `hero: { form: 'realistic' }` its pilot is the realistic
  body.
- **Shutters with lines, as relief.** A building language's shutters take three more forms from the design library
  (`era/shutter-leaves.js`):
  - `persiana`: slats in a frame of stiles and rails.
  - `panelled`: two fielded panels.
  - `ledged`: boards, two ledges and a brace.

  Each leaf stays one box on the wall. Its front wears a painted tile of its form, and near the eye the World page marches
  the form's height along the view (parallax, `scene/channels/leaf-relief.js`). A street of shutters costs the faces it
  had. The old town hangs persiane, its rose houses ledged boards and its stone houses panels. `boards` and `louvred`
  draw as they did. A page with no leaf carries none of the channel.
- **A town's houses open at their doors.** A town level's `geotown.enter` names the uses entered at their door. The
  default is `['shop', 'hall', 'dwelling']` (a shop, an old town's church, a dwelling), and `[]` opens none. Of each
  use it takes the house whose door stands nearest the walk the hero is set down on.
  - Each door is a `door` mechanic on the town's page: its zone on the walk before the door, and the way back out a
    few steps further, facing away.
  - Each inside is a level of its own after the town, built from its use's program and linked by its door both ways.
  - A quick game walking a town gets them too.
- **A heavy level no longer loses the door it was entered by.** A hosted level waits 1.5 s for the shell's params,
  then plays its presets. That wait now counts real waiting, not a page busy building its world. A town page used to
  fire the fallback before the shell's answer was read, so a hero coming back out of a house stood at the town's
  start, not at its door (`scene/channels/game.js`).

### The cinematics department: one kind of actor plays a role from a script, in a style, and a director shoots it

In progress. One actor for every character a scene shows: a hero that plays a role from a script in a playing style,
its face, body and later its hands directed together on one clock, and its take played outside any game engine.

- **Cameras and cutscenes become Cinematics.** The studio's sixth department now directs scenes the way a film crew does:
  actors who play a role from a script in a style, speaking to each other and listening, walking their marks; the
  coverage a director would shoot; directed moments in the game; flythroughs and recorded runs; and a scene exported to
  Blender in a film look or an anime look. The README, the agent's one-breath answer and `CLAUDE.md` say so;
  the plugin's README says so at the next release, which raises its version (installed copies key on it).
  Its craft is written down as principles, each naming the code that holds it (`docs/cinematics.md`).
- **The director's notes** (`control/lib/graph/actor/notes.js`): suggestions read off a scene and its coverage, as a
  director, a script supervisor or an editor would give them, each with the principle it rests on and a change to the
  script that answers it:
  - a shot held too long on one framing;
  - a speaker facing away from whom it speaks to;
  - a cross that flips the line;
  - a scene where no one moves;
  - speakers too close or too far apart;
  - many lines and no close-up;
  - a speaking part played as background.

  They suggest and never refuse. The dailies and the Blender pack's `SCENE.md` carry them, and the scene export prints
  them.
- **One actor, three dials.** A role (who the character is: its resting state, its status, how it speaks; the
  persona's delivery registers are roles of speech), a style (how much it does and when: `thespian`, `action-star`,
  `anime-mocap`, `extra`, each a card tuned as `{ from, …overrides }`), and the keying and the look (continuous or on
  twos, film or anime), kept apart so any style can be shaded either way.
- **The persona is the actor.** A persona's spec takes a `style` and a `role`, for the whole persona or for one read
  (`create_character({ as: 'persona', spec: { hero, register, style: 'action-star', role: { status: 'high' }, reads }
  })`; `control/lib/graph/actor/`).
  - **The style** tunes the voice's rate and articulation and sets how strongly and how fast the face moves (eased in,
    or snapped into place). It decides how often a line opens with a brow flash, shows a tell or breaks for a glance
    off and back, and which moments a gesture marks, from which words. The extra never meets the lens.
  - **The role** sets the state of mind held under every line, a resting face, and a status: high keeps the head up
    and the eyes still, low drops the head and lets the eyes go.
  - **Absent, nothing changes.** A persona with neither reads byte for byte as before.
  - **The body waits.** Each style's body dials are carried, but the body plays them only from the next phase.
- **The body on the timeline.** The gestures a read names are played on the hero's rig
  (`control/lib/graph/actor/body.js`, `gestures.js`).
  - **The gestures**: a beat, an offered palm, a point, a shrug, a cheer, a clap, a hand to the chin, a nod, a
    headshake and a bow. Each is said as where the hand goes on the body (the chest, the belly, the chin), which way
    the fingers point and the palm faces, and the hand's shape, and is solved on the rig it plays on, so one word fits
    any proportions.
  - **The timing**: each gesture peaks just before its stressed word. It is wound up and let go at the style's pace,
    but never so fast that a joint turns faster than its limit. The shoulder, elbow, wrist and fingers arrive one
    after another. No two uses of a gesture are alike, and a gesture too close to the last on the same limbs is
    dropped or carries straight on from it.
  - **Near the trunk**: a hand there (a shrug, a hand to the chin, a clap, an offered palm) says where its elbow goes,
    so the arm goes round the chest rather than through it (`holdArm` takes the elbow's place, `elbowAt`). An arm keeps
    the place its solve found, whatever the style. A bigger style carries further past it at the apex and moves the
    head and the trunk more.
  - **The stand**: the actor stands with the preset's trunk and legs and its arms hanging at the sides, found on the
    rig it plays on (`standOf`). Between gestures it shifts its carriage every few seconds, less often the stiller the
    style.
  - **The machine gate**: the dailies read each body take law by law (the joints in order, the stroke on its word,
    the stand's life, the variation, the speeds and ranges). A dailies run beside a minted hero plays each take's body
    under its face in the hero-live viewer.
  - **The export**: a skinned export of a persona (`export_model({ format: 'glb', skinned: true })`) writes each read
    played in a style as `act:<read>` beside the face's `face:<read>`, on the same clock. It carries the joints alone,
    one-shot, with `moj:act` naming its style and each gesture's word, cause, hand and timing. The cue sheet names both
    clips, and the export's answer lists the acts. A read with no style is not acted, and the World page's payload is
    unchanged. The hero-live viewer plays a GLB's acts under their face takes.
  - **The vocabulary**: a style's gestures are the body's ten: `beat` and `offer` join the eight emote words, and a
    stressed word takes the baton where the register names none the style has.
- **Actors in a scene** (`control/lib/graph/actor/scene.js`, `screenplay.js`). A scene is a cast, the marks of a room
  and a screenplay.
  - **The screenplay**: `NAME: the line` (with the persona's markup), `NAME (worried): the line` for that line's face,
    and directions such as "Mara crosses to the table.", "Jon turns to Mara.", "Mara looks at the door.",
    "Jon waits 2 seconds.". Anything else is a note.
  - **The clock**: every line and direction is played in order on one clock.
  - **Looking and listening**: a speaker talks to whom it addresses, not to the lens. The others look at the speaker,
    listening, and nod on its stressed words as their style nods. While someone crosses, the others watch them go.
  - **Walking**: a cross turns the actor to its path and walks it with the hero's own walk cycle, the feet keeping
    their place on the floor, then the actor stands at the mark. A turn faces its target.
  - **Where it can be seen**: each actor's position and facing over time come with its take. The dailies draw the
    blocking from above and play each actor walking the floor in the hero-live viewer.
  - **Coverage** (`control/lib/graph/actor/coverage.js`): a scene comes with the shots a director would take. An
    establishing wide; over the listener's shoulder onto each speaker; a close on a line with a face of its own; the
    wide again for a cross. Every camera stays on one side of the actors' line as it turns. It is written as a shoot
    plan (cameras keyed in time, shots that cut between them), in the scenes card's own framings.
  - **Preview**: `control/scripts/spikes/actor/scene-film.mjs` plays a blocked scene beside a minted hero: both actors
    at once, each with its body and face, cut by its coverage, with captions.
- **Blender film export** (`control/scripts/export-scene-blender.mjs`, `control/lib/graph/actor/scene-film.js`). A scene
  is written as a Blender film pack:
  - **The actors**: each a skinned GLB of its hero with the scene's face take and act, a cross walked. The act's
    `moj:act` carries the actor's place over time.
  - **The cameras**: the coverage's cameras, keyed every frame and cut together as a world's film pack cuts a shoot
    plan's shots.
  - **The scripts**: `actors.py` hangs each actor under an empty keyed on its place and facing and binds its takes.
    `look.py` builds the look in Blender: `film` (Principled shading, a little subsurface on the skin, Cycles) or
    `anime` (cel bands shaded live from the scene's lights by Shader to RGB, a rim, an ink outline, EEVEE).
  - **The gate**: with a Blender found the export builds the film and verifies its cameras (advisory); without one it
    writes the pack and says the gate was skipped.
- **The dailies.** One page (`control/scripts/spikes/actor/dailies.mjs`) shows the takes side by side on one clock,
  each with its timeline and its readings law by law (`control/lib/graph/actor/readings.js`). The readings cover how
  much the face moves, the blinks, the pace, where the eyes rest, the gestures, and whether a gesture lands on its
  stressed word. In a scene they also cover how much each actor regards its partner and stays live while the other
  speaks. The baseline is the persona alone, with one speech for one speaker (`actor/baseline.js`) and a short scene
  for two, and its outputs are pinned. In that scene the persona never looks at its partner.
- **Opt-in, byte for byte.** A hero or persona with no actor data, and every clip minted before, is unchanged.

### The subway in the geocity

- **A subway line under a geocity's street** (`geocity.subway: true | { along?, stations?, plan?, line?, depth?, gap? }`,
  geocity/subway.js): an evocation's line under one of its arterials (the flatter spine over its span unless `along`
  names one: a line keeps to the contour where it can), its frame turned to the street's axis, its stations (two by
  default) in a row under the carriageway round the evocation's middle, each its depth (14 m) under the lowest street
  over it, the running tunnels between them graded no steeper than a rail's grade (a station let down where the street
  climbs faster). Each station's way out is a SIDEWALK entrance: a level cross passage out under the walk, a stair turning
  up along the street toward the station's middle, its well open in the walk behind open railings, a post with the
  line's roundel at its head; the city cuts its walk over each well and keeps its trees, lamps, poles and signs out of
  them. The subway's faces are lit by its own lamps (no sun); its stations, tunnels and entrances are anchors, with
  cameras down a platform, into a tunnel, at an entrance from the walk and down its stair; its readout is the city's
  `subway`. Walked along each platform, from one platform to the next and from a platform up to the sidewalk, both ways.
  A rail tunnel's fall over a landing is its ramp's, not a drop needing a stair. Absent, a city is as it was.
- **A streetcar across the subway** (geocity/streetcar.js): a city asked for a subway runs streetcars on its two-way
  spines, so one crosses the line over it; on each streetcar line crossing the subway's street along its run, a car
  stands at the stop each way past the crossing: the city metro's own streetcar (the car fractal-city's tram corridors
  run, vehicles/vehicles-css3d.js), at the metro's scale, on the street's ground; each held by its own box, a camera on
  the first from across its street. Each sidewalk entrance closes the walk's kerb along its stair's run, so
  nothing under the walk shows under its edge, and opens its well before the stair's ceiling nears the walk.
- **The subway meets the PATH: platforms lead into the network under the city** (`geocity: { under, subway }`): a
  line's stations are nodes of the network under the city beside its podiums' concourses, so a passage joins a
  concourse across the street to a station: from a side platform through a doorway in its wall (or a mezzanine's), up
  the passage's stair into the concourse, up the podium's stair and out of its lobby onto its plaza: a tower's lobby is
  a station's larger entrance from the street above. A station has several ways in: a sidewalk entrance from each side
  platform, on each side of the street, and a passage from each concourse that faces it; the network's laws count the
  stations reached from each other by their running tunnels, and no passage between two concourses runs through a
  station. A city's line is cut and cover by default (side platforms, 10 m under the street); an island lies deeper (14
  m). A line's station whose tracks do not run on at an end (the line's first or last) is closed there, its tracks at
  buffer stops (a through station had left a portal open onto nothing). Walked from a platform through the passage to
  the podium's plaza and back. A station takes its ways out (`exits`) and its mezzanine's reach (`mezzDepth`) from
  the line, and its open `ends`.
- **The streetcar's rails are the city metro's** (geocity/kit.js `rail`): every geocity streetcar track is laid as the
  city metro lays its own (city/roads.js streetcarTrack: a dark tie band between two steel rails standing proud of the
  street), at the metro's scale, on the city's own gauge and track lines.
- **A geocity's subway as a teleport, and a geocity played as a level** (`geocity.subway.tunnels: 'teleport'`; a
  geocube's `level`, geocity/subway.js withGeocitySubwayLevel, registered as the geocube's level kind): the city's line
  takes the teleport as a stage's does, its stubs and warps under the street (warp anchors in the city's frame,
  `subway.warps`, `subway.tunnels` the mode, `subway.runs` its running tunnels); a geocity with a subway asked to be a
  level is played from its first platform to the pavement outside its last station, through its tunnels or by its
  warps, each arrival shown over the walker's shoulder down the platform (network/subway.js levelOfLine, turned into
  the city's frame). A line is left by the way out on the platform the walker arrived on. A geocube that is not a
  geocity with a subway passes through.

### Subway elevation

- **An open rail run** (`passageOf({ …, open: true })`, network/passage.js): a rail or tube passage graded straight
  between its two ends, wherever they lie against the ground. Each span is built by where its track lies:
  - a TUNNEL where its ceiling stays under the ground;
  - a CUT where its track is under the ground but its roof would show: retaining walls up past the ground to a capped
    railing, open to the sky, its signals and cables still on its walls;
  - GRADE at the ground, between fences;
  - a VIADUCT over the ground: its deck on girders, parapets inside and out, column pairs on cross-heads every 12 m,
    each held, down to the ground; a deck too low to stand on columns sits on fill.

  Only a tunnel is roofed: its ceiling, soffit, lamps, columns and rings stop at the portal, and a tunnel's end face
  stands only where it ends underground. Its readout `runs` gives the metres of each. Its cover is measured on its full
  tunnel only, and a climb steeper than its section's grade is a finding. Walked from the tunnel up through the cut and
  out along the viaduct, and back. Without `open`, a passage is built as before, byte for byte.
- **Stations by elevation** (`station: { elevation: 'deep' | 'cut' | 'elevated' }`, network/station.js; `ground` its
  street over its track bed when a line lays it). Deep is the default, unchanged byte for byte.
  - A station in a CUT is open to the sky. Its walls are retaining walls that stop at a railing 1.1 m over the street,
    and a canopy in the line's band covers each platform. The canopy stands on its columns' posts, or hangs from the
    wall over a side platform, with a lamp strip under it. An island's mezzanine is a bridge across the cut at street
    level, its way out a gap in the railing. A side platform's way out is a stair up the wall to a landing at the
    street.
  - An ELEVATED station stands on its deck over the street, on paired piers with cross-heads every 12 m. It has
    parapets each side and canopies on steel posts. An island's stair goes down a railed well to a station house hung
    under its mezzanine end. Each way out is a flight down the station's outside to the street, with a landing halfway
    on a long one.
  - An open station's ways out are ports at the street (`street: true`), and its readout gives its elevation and
    street. A stage lays the street round it, open over a cut. Walked along each platform and out to the street, and
    back.
- **A line that rises out of the ground** (`subway.stations[].elevation`, network/subway.js). A station on a line can be
  `cut` or `elevated`. Its track bed is then stood against the street over its middle: a cut's mezzanine at the
  street, an elevated one's station house over it.
  - The gap to the next station is lengthened to what the rail's grade wants for the climb between them; the readout
    gives the `gaps` where they differ.
  - A run out of or into an open station is laid open: tunnel, cut, grade and viaduct where it lies, its `spans` in
    the readout. An open run also says where the ground must open over it (`openings`), and the street is opened over
    each cut, a station's and a run's.
  - An open station's ways out end at the street, so it takes no entrance; a deep station on the same line keeps its
    pavilions. A teleport's stubs out of an open station are laid open too.
  - New cameras: each open station from its street, and the line rising out of the ground.
  - Walked through every run, down the cut's stairs and the el's flights; played as a level from the deep platform
    to the street under the el. A line of deep stations is laid as before, byte for byte.
- **The el in the geocity** (`geocity.subway.elevation: 'elevated'`, or a list with one word a station, `'deep'` or
  `'elevated'`; geocity/subway.js). An elevated station stands over the avenue's carriageway on piers, each pier on the
  road under it where the street falls. Its flights stand out over the kerb (`flightGap`), so each lands on a sidewalk,
  their feet on the street there. Between two elevated stations the line is an el on its viaduct.
  - Where an el meets a deep station, the line dives through a cut in the road (the road opened over it) into its
    tunnel. The city's plan settles the line's spacing with the gaps lengthened to the rail's grade, and hands them to
    the line.
  - Nothing of the street's stands under the el: its lamps, poles, signs and a streetcar's wires are checked along their
    span, and trees by their crowns. An elevated station is no node of the network under the city.
  - New cameras `subway-el` (the el from the far sidewalk) and `subway-rise` (the dive, from over the kerb lane).
  - A station in a cut stays a stage's: a city's sloping street cannot keep a level retaining wall, and a cut is refused
    by name.
  - Walked along the el's platforms, its viaduct's walkway and down each flight to the sidewalk, and back; a line that
    dives from the el to a deep station is played as a level to the street. A deep line under the city is laid as before.
- **A line's track runs on past its ends** (`subway.runOn`, network/subway.js; a geocity's line always, up to 240 m each
  way as its land allows). The first and last stations open their outer ends (portals, the steps down to the
  walkway), and the track runs on out of what is shown:
  - from a deep station, a tunnel into the dark;
  - from an elevated one, an el on its viaduct to a buffer wall at its far end, held (passage.js: an open run's blind
    end).

  The readout's `runOn` gives each run-on's length and spans. A stage's line still ends at its buffers unless asked.
- **Levels and teleport over elevation.** A teleport's stations are joined by no track, so its gaps stay as asked and
  are not lengthened for a climb.
  - Each stub runs out of its station as the station stands: a tunnel out of a deep one, out of a cut one (a box deep
    enough to be a tunnel by its end), and an el out of an elevated one, to a buffer wall.
  - Each warp stands the walker on the next platform at its height: up from a deep stub onto the el, down into the cut.
    Its arrival is shown over the walker's shoulder down the el's platform.
  - Played as a level on the stage and in the geocity, a piece walked between each two warps, and won on the street
    under the el, or on a sidewalk down its flight. The warp up onto the el moves the walker in the page and fires its
    arrival scene (checked in headless Chrome).

### Subway tunnels
- **A subway's running tunnel** (network/sections.js `rail` and `tube`, network/passage.js's `rail` finish): `rail` a
  cut-and-cover box 9.6 m wide and 5.2 m high, two tracks with a line of columns between them; `tube` a bored tube, one
  track under a vault on its rings. Each track lies on a darker concrete bed with a drain, sleepers every 0.7 m, two
  running rails at standard gauge (a bright head on a dark web) and a third rail outboard on insulators under its cover
  board; a safety walkway runs a step up along the left wall, its edge lined yellow, a handrail on the wall over it; the
  walls are sooted to a man's height, cable trays run along them on brackets, bulkhead lamps between, a signal on the
  wall now and then; a box's soffit is dark. A section now takes a `profile` (`box`, or `vault`: its walls to their
  springing, an arch over them, met at a junction by the spandrel over it). A rail tunnel holds the line between its two
  track levels (deeper only where its cover wants it; a passage climbs toward the ground), takes no stair, and is
  walked along its walkway, on it where it is raised.
- **A subway station from its floor plan** (a stage recipe's `station`, network/station.js, network/station-plans.js):
  `{ kind: 'stage', station: { plan?, line?, length?, train? } }` lays a platform hall from a card: `island` (one
  platform between two tracks, a mezzanine across one end reached by a stair from the island, a tube to each track),
  `side` (a platform either side of two tracks, a column line between them, a doorway out through each platform's
  wall, one twin box), `terminus` (the island at the end of the line, its tracks ending at buffer stops under the
  mezzanine at its head); a new floor plan is a card. Its look is the original station's (its line's colours, a frieze
  with roundels, white subway tile, tiled columns with their capitals, tactile strips and a white lip at each platform
  edge, benches, bins and a sign, its train at a platform) with the network's panelling over it (back-painted glass
  between steel battens, a stainless kick, a glazed dado in the line's colour, lit glass strips, a coffered soffit, a
  marble mezzanine behind a glass balustrade). Its tracks are laid as a running tunnel's and run on through a portal
  at each open end: each portal is a port a running tunnel meets; each way out is a port a passage meets. Every
  platform is walked end to end and up to each way out, columns, benches, stair and train all standing.
- **A subway line: stations joined by running tunnels, each with its way up to the street** (a stage recipe's
  `subway`, network/subway.js): `{ kind: 'stage', subway: { stations: [{ id, plan?, line?, length?, train? }], gap?,
  depth?, line?, entrances? } }` lays its stations in a row under the street at a depth (14 m by default), joined by
  running tunnels a gap long (120 m by default): a tube to each track of an island (its walkway toward the island), one
  twin box over both tracks of side-platform stations (its walkway under a platform). The tunnels' tracks run on the
  stations' tracks; each station's portals open to the tunnel's width, and steps are cut in a platform's end down to
  the track bed where a tunnel's walkway meets it. Each station's way out climbs an inclined stair in a tiled tunnel to
  a glass pavilion on the street (its stairwell open under the glass behind a balustrade, a band of the line's colour
  round its eaves); `entrances: false` leaves them out. Every tunnel is walked from one platform to the next and every
  entrance from its doorway to the pavement, both ways; its laws (every station reached, cover, grade, run) are in its
  readout. A terminus only ends a line; a line is all tubes or all boxes, its stations' tracks lined up. A rail
  tunnel's walkway may run along either wall (`walkSide`), its finish mirrored.
- **A subway line played as a level, its tunnels real or a camera teleport** (a stage recipe's `subway` with a
  `level`; `subway.tunnels: 'real' | 'teleport'`): the walker starts on the first station's platform and wins on the
  street outside the last station's entrance; the route the audit walks runs along each platform, down the steps at
  its end, through each running tunnel and up onto the next platform. As a TELEPORT, each station's tunnel runs out of
  it as a 30 m stub into the dark, and a warp near the stub's end stands the walker on the next station's platform, on
  its walking lane facing into its hall; the arrival is shown, a shot over the walker's shoulder down the platform
  it has come out on (held 2.5 s, skippable). New mechanic `warp` (game/mechanics.js, its card): walking into its zone
  moves the walker to `to` (the bus's own warp, as a fall caught moves it) and says `then`, an event a scene starts
  on. Its stubs are held to the line's laws and its stations counted reached by their warps.

### The time map: a shot shows the world's time on the screen's time, and every channel plays the same map

A shot's time map says how the world's clock plays on the screen's. It covers a stretch slowed or sped up,
ramped in and out; an instant held; the camera moving on the screen's clock while the world holds (bullet time); and
the world on twos. One map, read by the camera, the world and the actors alike (`control/lib/graph/shoot/time.js`).

- **A shot's time map** (the shoot plan, `forge_motion({ shoot })`). Presentation, not simulation: the world steps as it
  always did, the screen shows it differently.
  - `time: [{ span: [t0, t1], speed, ramp? }]`: that stretch of the world at a speed. A `ramp` eases the speed down and
    back over its world seconds at each end (a speed ramp, the speed changing evenly on the screen's clock).
  - `time: [{ at, hold }]`: the world held at an instant for screen seconds, a freeze frame or an impact's beat
    (`frames` counts frames at the plan's fps). Holds sit anywhere, inside a ramp too.
  - `clock: 'screen'`: the camera's keys play on the screen's clock, so it moves at its own pace while the world holds
    or crawls: bullet time.
  - `grain: 'twos' | 'threes'`: the world shown on twos or threes, the camera on ones, as limited animation is keyed.
  - A shot's constant `speed` is the map's simplest case and plays as before.
- **Every clock reads it.**
  - The rendered film steps the world to each frame's `world_t` and frames the camera at its `camera_t` where the two
    part.
  - The World page's shoot channel runs the kernel's own function for the map, so the page and the film agree.
  - A live world plays on its own clock, so its page plays a map in real time, and the readout says so.
- **The edit and the readout.** `set_shot` takes `time`, `clock` and `grain` (null takes each away); `retime` moves a
  map's world instants with its span and keeps its holds. The readout gives each warped shot its world seconds, its
  slowest speed, the seconds it holds and its grain. The shoot manual says all of it in After Effects terms (time remap,
  speed ramp, freeze frame).
- **The actor scene plays on it** (the cinematics department).
  - **The screenplay**: `Slow motion.` (or `Slow motion 0.1.`) until `Real time.`; `Freeze.` (or `Freeze 2 seconds.`).
    They take none of the scene's time.
  - **The coverage** carries them onto the shots they fall in, cut at the shots' edges.
  - **The Blender film pack** lays the scene on the screen's clock. Each camera is keyed at its own clock, `scene.json`'s
    `clock` holds the scene's time each frame shows, each actor's place is keyed every frame, and `actors.py` plays each
    take through an NLA strip whose time is keyed to that clock. `export-scene-blender.mjs --grain twos` shows the
    scene on twos.
  - **The preview** (`scene-film.mjs --script`) plays the same map.
  - **A director's note, `slowed-line`**: slow motion over a line slows the picture, not the voice. Slow the move, the
    look or the silence, and play the words in real time.
  - `docs/cinematics.md` gains a section on time.
- **The cosmos cube's Time is also the camera's clock.** The Time facet gains three settings:
  - `tempo`: real time, slow, ramp, freeze, bullet;
  - `replay`: none, angles, replay;
  - `grain`: ones, twos, threes, mixed.

  Each is built offline (the shoot plan and the actor scene). In play each waits on the packages they are priced
  under: the world clock scale (`world-clock`: a live world's time slowed, ramped, held and replayed, the camera exempt)
  and keying (`keying`: a body's clips on twos in play, a grain a layer). A probe genre, `cinematic-action`, asks for
  them in the brief's words (bullet time, slow motion, a kill cam, set pieces). On the hillclimb page the world clock
  ranks second of all packages by worlds lifted per effort.
- **Absent, nothing changes.** A plan without a map normalizes, plays, lowers and emits its page byte for byte as
  before.

### The tool list, swept

A sweep of every registered tool for the ones nothing wires in: names an agent is told to call but cannot reach, doors
nothing points to, and aliases kept long past their release. This first wave fixes what agents were being sent to that
does not exist and deletes what was dead; it changes no door an agent can call. Built so far:

- **No dead pointers.** A tool registered unlisted and homed in no pack (a folded alias, a per-op name behind a door,
  a retired pack's member) cannot be called by a host that calls only what it lists, so a surface that names one sends
  the agent into a wall. A guard (`lib/mcp/no-dead-pointers.test.js`) reads what agents are handed (the catalysts, the
  routing cards, the vocab cards, and the prose the tools return: descriptions, `next` and `submit` hints, errors) and
  fails on any unreachable name; prose that says a name is retired is history and passes. What it found is fixed:
  - the doors' own hints: `mint_solid via:'packet'` handed back `submit_polygonizer_manifest`, the skin op handed back
    `skin_polygomer` and `get_skin_packet`, `capture_reference` and `semantic_search` named retired solid and world
    creators, and a sprite sheet, a scene forge and a keyframe card named the image handoff's per-op names. Each now
    names the door: `mint_solid` and its kind, `edit_solid` op `skin`, `compose_world` and its base, `render_handoff`
    and its op.
  - the catalysts, routing cards and sketch and view vocab cards that named them, and the plugin profile's edits of them;
  - the science views' and worlds' own errors, which still said `create_atom_view requires…` to a `create_view` caller;
  - the orientation gallery's lantern, minted live on a tour, now minted through `mint_solid` kind `workbench`;
  - the office wing's leftovers in live descriptions (the inventory, the catalyst shelf, plan mode, the stash's pointer
    type, the roles key), which pointed at the contextmap and the composer retired in 3.1.0.
  A few known pointers wait for their own change, listed in the guard and shrink-only: forward_context's office
  drawers, the Blender art pack's return step, and the figure-spec gate the character-from-dream catalyst runs on.
- **A cover takes its picture as a file.** `create_cover`'s `next` asked the operator to upload a picture on the
  dashboard, which is view only. `art: { path }` now takes a PNG, JPEG or WebP on this host, files it into a stash as
  an image item and maps it onto the illustration (the result's `art` says where); `art: { stash, item }` maps one
  already gathered, as before. And `capture_reference` no longer tells the agent to anchor a build with
  `bind_stash({ role: 'reference' })`: no build reads that link.
- **The pre-3.0 aliases are gone.** The per-kind names `mint_solid`, `edit_solid`, `compose_world` and `create_view`
  replaced in 1.0.0 and 1.1.0 (`create_figure`, `create_workbench`, `skin_polygomer`, `create_fractal_city`, the
  `create_*_view` family and the rest) were unlisted aliases for two majors; they are no longer registered,
  and a stored plan that names one compiles back to a draft that names it. With them go about a thousand lines of
  `register*Tools` functions nothing called. Every kind they made is made by its door, unchanged.

### Urban tunnelling: the geocity held, the first step under it

- **The geocity is solid** (`geocity/scene.js`): every mass a walker can reach is held by a box in the payload's
  `colliders` (`{ min, max, of: '<block>:<group>' }`), the analytic hull a game's pilot is blocked by, an engine builds
  as static boxes and the route audit pushes a walk out of. Each mass of a neighbourhood built at block scale (a tower,
  its podium, a slab, a midrise ring, a house under its gable, a shop, a building going up and its crane), each evoked
  lot, and the houses of each composed geotown, which the geocity used to drop, now in the metro's frame (a block
  town's cut to its block, so a front's steps the crop leaves out never stand on the metro's walk). The skyline's
  backdrop and a far town, never walked, carry none. A new law, `walk-clear`: the dummy's route round the seat's block
  and the walk's spawn stand in no box. The readout counts them (`counts.colliders`). The lakeshore test metro carries
  1,214 boxes (111 KB of its 12 MB payload); a segment evocation 337; the skyline none. The page's free walk already
  met the faces and is unchanged: a page without entities does not change by a byte.
- **A podium walked into** (`geocity.under: true | { at: '<block id>' }`, `geocity/podium.js`): in an evocation (a
  neighbourhood, a corridor or a segment: its blocks at a building's detail), a core tower or podium block's podium is
  entered from its plaza. A lobby on storey 1 stands level with the plaza at its door, and a concourse on storey 0 stands
  a storey under it, below grade, down a stair through the lobby's floor. It is the shape of a building set into its slope,
  placed by its lot: storeys stack from 0, so the concourse is storey 0 and the inside is lowered until the lobby meets
  the plaza. It is built on the everyday bay kit (an office's, a shop floor's) and baked in its own lamps, with no window
  (its concourse in the ground, its lobby inside the podium's mass). Its plan is the largest the lot holds inside its
  margin, clear of the towers that rise through the podium, its door as near the front's middle as it can stand.
  - Its facade is cut at the door (`cutFace`: each wall face in the door's plane the strips round the opening, its tile
    at the face's own rate). The ground under its footprint is cut round it (`groundLess`): the pad, and the land's own
    drape under the block, which would otherwise run through the concourse. The podium's box becomes its mass round the
    inside, plus the inside's own walls.
  - The payload carries the inside's lights, a `building` anchor (its door, floor, rise, rooms and `through`, the way in
    at the door, across the lobby, down the stair and along the concourse, each point at its floor), two cameras
    (`lobby`, from the plaza in at the door, and `concourse`, from the stair's foot) and a readout (`geocity.under`: the
    podium, its plan, rise, faces, colliders, lights, findings; or none and why). On a page taking the live sun, its
    faces take no sun share.
  - The machine gate: the way through walked by the page's ground probe over the payload's own faces and boxes, in and
    back out, no step taller than a riser, no wall crossed, no box entered. Refused by name: `under` on a metro drawn as
    massing, a malformed `under`, an `at` that is no evoked tower or podium. A recipe without `under` does not change.
- **The passages under the streets** (`geocity/tunnels.js`): `under: true` now walks into every evoked podium it can (a
  lobby opening on the podium's front, else another side, where the plaza before the door stands within a kerb of the
  podium's floor, so a lobby on a terraced block still meets its plaza), and joins their concourses below grade. A passage
  is laid between two concourses that face each other across one street, overlapping along it by a doorway and its
  frames, with no other block between (`tunnelEdges`); each concourse gets a way out for it in its wall (a stage way's
  new `along`, era/stage.js: the doorway's middle along its side; absent, the side's middle as before, not a byte
  changed). `{ at }` walks into one podium alone, with no passage.
  - A passage (`tunnelOf`) is its own lit box section, 4 m wide and 3 m high, in its concourse's tiles and at its floor's
    light, with lamps along its ceiling and a box down each wall. Its floor is the highest that keeps 1 m of cover under
    the street's land and 0.3 m under each block's plaza over its whole width, climbing no steeper than 1:12 (the
    constraint's envelope, slope-limited both ways); it leaves each concourse level for a landing, and takes a stair
    down where the envelope stands under the concourse's floor at the landing's end. Under its blocks the land's own
    drape is cut along its run; over a podium's footprint every ground face under the lobby's ceiling is cut, and the
    retaining faces between terraces with them (`wallLess`).
  - The network's laws (`networkLaws`): `under-reached` (every concourse from every other), `under-cover` (under the
    streets and the plazas), `under-grade` (the steepest ramp), `under-run` (the longest passage, 120 m). Advice: on the
    lakeshore neighbourhood five podiums, three passages (35 to 52 m, at least 1.03 m under a street and 0.41 m under a
    plaza, one meeting its concourse by a three-step stair), and one podium not reached: its concourse and its
    neighbour's do not overlap along the street between them (a passage with a dog-leg is not laid yet).
  - The payload carries a `tunnel` anchor a passage (its two podiums, its length, its middle walked), each podium's ways
    out (`ports`, each with its `reach` from the stair's foot) and its way `down` from the plaza, a `tunnel` camera, and
    `geocity.under.podia` and `.tunnels`. A podium's walks are planned round its stair's well and flight
    (a quarter-metre grid, pulled straight).
  - The walk gate is its own module (`geocity/walk-gate.js`, `walker`): the page's ground probe over a payload's faces,
    the walls it crosses (and which), the boxes it stands in. Each passage is walked from one podium's plaza, down its
    stair, along the passage, up the next podium's stair and out onto its plaza, and back.
- **The concourses dressed, and the light below grade** (`geocity/dress.js`): every concourse wears shopfronts in bays
  along its walls (a kick plate, lit glass, mullions, a frame and a sign band in its shop's colour, by its dice), never
  across a way out or against its stair. The concourse with the most ways out (the hub) seats a food court: tables and
  their stools, each a box the walk is held out of, on the cells a body's width and more clear of every walk through it,
  its counters' signs warmer. Wayfinding is a colour a route (`ROUTES`): north-south passages one, east-west the other,
  as a stripe down each passage's floor and a sign over each concourse's way out onto it. A passage now takes each
  surface's light from the concourse's own (the mean its corners are baked at, floor, wall and ceiling apart), its tiles
  the ones the concourse lays most at its own level, and lamps every 4.5 m: a passage is narrow, and the page's
  occlusion takes more of its light than of a concourse's. The page draws every face unlit (its corners' light is its
  light), so nothing of the sky reaches below grade; on a page taking the live sun, every face under the city carries a
  sun share of none, so a shadow on the street never reaches it. The payload gains a `food-court` camera and anchor and
  `geocity.under.dress` (the routes' colours, each concourse's shopfronts, the court's tables).
- **Glass and steel, as a mall builds them** (after `polygonizer/floorplan-mall.js`): a podium's lobby and concourse are
  now composed on the bay axes (`compose`: the clean construction, its terrazzo or poured floor and coffered ceiling, in
  the everyday palette's warm whites, lit and dressed as an everyday room; no props, no hazard band). A shopfront is the
  mall's glazed front: a translucent display pane (the page's glass pass) half a metre out from its lit display and
  shelves, a steel frame of real members (a dark kick plinth, a brushed head rail, slim mullions, end jambs), a deeper
  sign bulkhead in its shop's colour, dark steel returns; a body is held off it, and a bay a walk passes is left as
  wall. The walls between the fronts, and the lobby's round its door and its stair, are clad in large-format pale stone
  panels with steel reveals, a steel skirting and a steel band. A laylight runs down each concourse's middle (lit glass
  in a steel frame of edge beams and ribs), the stair's well in the lobby is behind glass under a steel cap, and a glass
  canopy on a steel frame, tied back to the facade, stands over each street door (in the sun, with the street). A
  passage is clad in back-painted glass panels between steel battens over a stainless kick band, a brushed steel frieze
  to its ceiling, a steel handrail each side following its floor, and a lit glass strip in a steel edge down its
  ceiling in place of its lamps.
- **The food court seated, and the concourses fitted** (`geocity/court-kit.js`): the furniture is turned where a hand or a
  hip meets it. The food court seats a mix of sets by its dice (`SETS`): round cafe tables on a pedestal with four chairs
  whose curved backs turn to them on slim steel legs, high round bistro tables with three tall round stools, long
  communal tables with rounded ends and a bench down each side, and booths (a table between two upholstered benches with
  high backs), in one upholstery and one table top a court. Every concourse is fitted (`FITTINGS`): a waste and a
  recycling bin side by side (round, coloured lids) beside each way out and at the court's corners, a lit wayfinding
  directory (its route's colour in a band) by the stair's foot, and slatted backless benches down its long middle between
  round steel planters of shrubs. Each set and fitting is a box the walk is held out of, laid where it stands clear of
  every walk, the shopfronts, the court and the stair. A shopfront now keeps 1.7 m from a way out's frame, room for its
  bins. The readout carries each concourse's fittings and the court's sets.
- **A network of passages, its own module** (`lib/graph/network/`): what the geocity's tunnels were, made general, the
  geocity its first client. `sections.js`: what a passage is, by what it carries, a row each (`passage`, the pedestrian
  passage under a downtown in glass and steel; `service`, a building's service tunnel in concrete with its conduits,
  edge lines and caged lamps, steeper; `vehicle`, a two-lane road tunnel with a raised walkway behind a kerb each side,
  a tiled band down each wall and its lamp lines, deep and gentle, no stair), each its box, its cover under open ground
  and its slab under a plaza or a floor, its grade, whether a stair may take it down, its lamps, its longest run and its
  finish; `readSection` takes a row or a row changed (`{ from, …changes }`). `edges.js`: which nodes a network joins and
  by what path: straight across a gap where two rooms overlap along it, a DOG-LEG where their sites face each other but
  their rooms do not (out of each to the gap's middle line and along it, the jog a section wide), never a run down a
  street to a site round a corner, never under another site. `passage.js`: one passage built to its section along a
  path of legs square to the axes, turning at square junctions held level (its floor the slope-limited envelope under
  its cover, levelled through each turn and limited again), its finish carried round each junction's outer walls.
  `laws.js` (reached, cover, grade, run, by a prefix and a noun), `walk-gate.js` (moved from the geocity). On the
  lakeshore neighbourhood every concourse is now reached: four passages, one a 62.6 m dog-leg with two turns.
- **A basement under any building of the core shape, and a building as a network's node** (`era/program-core.js`
  `basement`, `network/building.js`): `program: { …, basement: true }` (an office, a clinic, a lab, a warehouse, every one
  of a base's) lays a storey under the ground one, every storey above lifted one: the ground plate's twin room for room
  (a concourse under the lobby, the core's stair `core-0` climbing to `core-1`, a corridor under each corridor, a store
  under each wing room, an undercroft under an annex), so every ground room stands over one. `_program.under.ports` names
  the basement's walls that face out (none with a basement room against it: a double-loaded wing's front rooms flank the
  lobby): the concourse's, each corridor's far end, an annex's undercroft where its annex has ways out. Absent, a
  building is laid as it was. `buildingFit` sets such a building into a site (its front door at a point, facing a way),
  `buildingNode` builds it with its storey 1 at the ground and the network's ways out on its basement's walls, and hands
  back its faces, colliders and lights, each way out in the world, its way down from its door to its concourse and each
  way out's reach (the stage's own routes, which walk a switchback down cleanly). The network's edges now take a node's
  several rooms (`rooms: [{ id, rect, sides }]`, the pair facing each other straight across the gap first, the nearest of
  them), keep clear of a node's own other rooms (`solid`), and narrow a doorway to what a room's wall holds (a single
  door's at least: a basement corridor's end); a section names its `door` (a passage's 3.6 m, a service tunnel's 2 m, a
  vehicle tunnel's 8 m). A bay kit's hazard band is the floor at its doorways: taking it out left a hole (it is now
  repainted as the floor beside it, in the podium too). The walk gate reports where it found no floor (`gaps`). Two
  buildings across a yard are joined from their basements and walked door to door both ways.
- **A complex: buildings on one site, joined below grade, walked as one map** (a stage recipe's `complex`,
  `network/complex.js`): `{ kind: 'stage', complex: { buildings, network?, yard?, seed? } }`. Each building is of the core
  shape (an office, a clinic, a lab, a warehouse, a base's hangar, barracks, armoury, command …) with its basement, its
  storey 1 at the yard, placed where it says (`at: [x, y]`, its front door's middle) or BESIDE another (`{ beside, side,
  gap }`: its footprint a gap off that one's side, slid along it so a room of its basement faces one of the other's
  straight across the gap, else centred), turned by `facing`, finished by `look` (the bay axes). The network joins every
  pair that faces another across one gap (or only the pairs `network.links` names) by passages of one section (`service`
  by default). The yard is laid round them in cells, cut by each ground room's walls (a building's plan is an L or a T,
  its notches the yard's); each building wears its outside: its walls where no room of its storey stands against them, a
  band of glass a storey, its front door cut at its lobby's doorway, a flat roof over each top room over a plenum (what
  glows under its ceiling stays under its roof). The payload carries cameras (the site, each front door, the first
  passage, a basement), a `building` anchor a building (its door, rooms, way down and ways out) and a `tunnel` anchor a
  passage, and `complex` (its buildings, passages and laws: every building reached, cover, grade, run). Refused by name:
  a building standing on another, a link to a building it does not have, a ring of buildings beside each other.
- **A walled-core dungeon's spaces on one level, a complex** (a building level's `building: { complex: true | { buildings?,
  network?, yard?, from?, to? } }`): the dungeon's spaces that stand on the level become its buildings, in the critical
  path's order, each of its space's use in its space's look, stood beside the one before it; a door between two of them
  becomes the passage below grade that joins their basements (whatever its via, both ways); the level is played in at
  the first one's front door, down, through the passages, up the last one's stair to its program's goal room (the route
  the audit walks, a first-person walker that looks for its ground over its feet, or the world's hero). `buildings`
  stands its own instead (a building named for a space wears its look). Its network's laws (every building reached,
  cover, grade, run, and a way through from the building it is entered by to the one it is won in) advise in
  `design_game`'s `advice.wcd` beside the dungeon's (on their own, `advice.complex`, in a world with no dungeon). The
  book draws the level as a site plan (each building's ground floor, its front door, each passage, the way played
  through them) and the dungeon's rings call a door between two of its buildings a passage. A building level with
  several spaces on it takes the one of its use (the first was taken before, whatever its use), and one that names no
  use takes its space's. A gate does not yet hold a passage shut inside a level: its clearance is drawn and advised,
  not played.
- **A hospital, a campus by its name, and stocked buildings in a complex** (`network/campuses.js`, `era/programs.js`,
  `era/stocking.js`): three buildings of the core shape a hospital is made of, `emergency` (triage and resus by the way
  in, cubicles along the corridors, imaging at their ends, an ambulance bay off the end, the observation ward last),
  `ward-block` (wards along the corridors, the sluice and the nurses' station nearest, a day room at each wing's end, the
  ward office at the top) and `theatres` (the scrub and the anaesthetic rooms, theatres along a clean corridor, recovery,
  sterile services at the top), each stocked by its rooms' roles from a hospital's own table (a bed head to the wall, a
  row of waiting chairs, a scanner for the emergency department's great object; its lobby a waiting room, never a
  base's sandbags). `complex: { campus: 'hospital' | 'base' }` builds a complex by its name: its buildings, where each
  stands, the look each wears and what joins them (a new campus is a row). A complex's links may each name their own
  section (`{ between: [a, b], section }`): the hospital's patients walk a public passage, its plant's service tunnel
  comes in under the wards; the base's buildings are joined by the new `bunker` section (a hardened roof slab where it
  passes under a building). A building in a complex is now dressed when it wears a look or its use is a base's or a
  hospital's (its things laid from its plan on every read), its basement concourse kept a passage (no great object in
  the way through); every passage of both campuses is walked door to door, things and all. A complex is also held to
  `complex-distinct` (two buildings a passage joins differ in construction or palette), and a world's complex level
  takes `campus`.

### Wave Gauntlet: sealed in until nothing is left alive

The action game's held room: sealed in an arena until every foe of every wave is down, each wave coming when the last is
cleared, arenas one after another (N arenas × N waves). Static (the elevator fight, the arena lock, a Bloody Palace of a
hundred floors) or moving (a lockdown along the way). Named `wave-gauntlet`, its rooms `arenas`, apart from the gauntlet
that is a glove. Built so far:

- **The mechanic** `wave-gauntlet` (`game/wave-gauntlet.js`, its card), a terminal on the bus `waves` already uses (foes
  minted dormant, woken by the cast's spawn; a count of downs a wave and a watch on it; a sequence for each pause), no
  runtime of its own: `arenas: [{ waves: [{ foes, after? }] }]`, each wave woken only when the last is all down, arena
  after arena ("Arena a of A · Wave w of W"); the way out (`at`) sealed until the last wave is down, a walker turned
  away put `back`; without a way out, the clear wins at once (the elevator). Death (the gauntlet owns the player's `hp`,
  `hits` a hit) begins the arena again (its foes put away, its counts zeroed, hp full, the walker at `start`), or from
  the last `checkpoint` (every N arenas); `death: 'fail'` loses instead. Sounds and an engine sample.
- **A level goal** `goal: { gauntlet: { arenas: [{ waves: [{ <bestiary id>: <count> }], after? }], checkpoint? } }`
  (`gameworld/gauntlet.js`, `gameworld/gauntlet-cast.js`): the level's last stage an arena on the approach to its exit,
  the exit its sealed way out, in place of reach-exit. Its foes are the bestiary's, stood asleep in a ring round the arena
  (`foe-<id>-g<n>`, each as every hostile is: its class, figure and hp) and woken with their wave; they are fielded, so a
  run makes their figures. Refused beside a boss or health (the gauntlet owns the hero's hp and ends the level), and on a
  building (its arena is to come).
- **Laws, book and words**: its principles measured on the recipe, advice in `design_game`'s readout
  (`advice.gauntlet`, each named by its level): `escalates` (no wave lighter than the last in its arena, no arena
  lighter than the last), `breathes` (a pause before each arena after the first), `varied` (no three arenas in a row
  alike), `checkpointed` (more than ten arenas, a checkpoint). The book's wave gauntlets section
  (`gameworld/gauntlet-page.js`) draws each as its grid, arenas by waves, each cell its mix, the checkpoints marked, its
  laws beside. The foes card names the goal. A prompt's `horde` or `onslaught` holds the last level a boss does not end
  in a default gauntlet of two arenas (its last stage a trail, no health beside it); `gauntlet` and `waves` are not read
  from a prompt (a glove, a tower defence).
- **Proved** (machine gates, standing in for eyes): after a run, `design_game`'s readout carries `gauntlet_proof`
  (`gameworld/gauntlet-proof.js`): each gauntlet played on the bus on the level the run made, every foe given its fall
  as it wakes (said as assumed: the proof cannot fight). And in an exported page: a `design_game` world of one level, two
  arenas, three waves (2 walkers; 2 walkers and a charger; 2 walkers and 2 chargers), exported by `export_game` and
  played headless through its shell: the way out tried first was sealed and turned the walker back to the arena; each
  wave woke its own foes and no others until the cast's own kill downed them; after the ninth fall the seal lifted, the
  way out won (`success`) and the shell showed it cleared.
- **To overcome or to endure**: the same schedule, two settings. `pace: 'timed'` brings each wave `every` seconds
  whatever still stands (they stack: a holdout's pressure), `win: { outlast }` wins when the clock runs out with the
  player still standing (horde mode, survive the night; the seal lifts then), and `hold` names what must not fall (a
  generator, a payload: its fall loses the level). A gauntlet to endure fails on a death; a timed one cannot begin an
  arena again. As a level goal: `pace`, `every`, `outlast` (no checkpoints). A new law, `bounded`: a timed gauntlet never
  stands more than sixteen foes woken within half a minute (the worst case, none downed). The book's grid says when each
  timed wave comes; the proof plays its clock. A prompt's `holdout` lays the default to endure: one arena, four waves
  twenty seconds apart, ninety seconds to outlast. Tower defence stays `waves` (its path, base and leaks).
- **The holdout, proved in an exported page** (machine gate, standing in for eyes): a `design_game` world of one level
  held to endure (three waves eight seconds apart, thirty seconds to outlast), exported and played headless through its
  shell: the second wave came on the clock with the whole first still standing; with every wave down and thirteen
  seconds left the seal held and turned the walker back; at the clock's end the seal lifted and the way out won
  (`success`, the shell showing it cleared).

### Weapon grip and ranged play: hands on the real guns, the bow drawn, sights, scopes and switching in the shooters

The shooters (the quick `shoot` and `deathmatch` goals, first person or over the shoulder) and the hero's holds get the
arms kernel's own guns in their hands. A hero holds a rifle, a sniper rifle, a submachine gun or a handgun on the arm's
own stations, its fingers closed on the parts as drawn and the index on the trigger; a hero draws a bow to the anchor
and looses it; a player carries a kit of the latest arms, aims down their sights, looks through a scope, steadies it,
reloads and switches with the arm stowed and drawn, and moves and strafes while doing it. Every hero, clip and page
minted before is byte for byte as it was. The eyes gate is the operator's: the pages were driven in headless Chromium
and looked at in screenshots only.

- **Handling read off the arm** (`lib/graph/equipment/arms/handling.js`): `armHandling(build)` reads each part of an arm
  as the workbench draws it and gives its stations (the fist on the grip, the trigger's face, the index along the
  frame, the support hand's part: a vertical foregrip, a handguard, a pump, a guard's loop, or a handgun's wrap; the
  butt; the sight line: an optic's window, a scope's axis, its power and its eye relief, or a bead along the receiver;
  the magazine; the muzzle) and its handling (loaded mass, time to the eye, the switch's two halves, sway, recoil:
  class estimates, marked so). `armBoxes(build)` gives the arm as its parts' boxes.
- **A sniper rifle** (`equipment/arms/models.js`): `rifle` model `sniper`, the marksman's receiver on the longest
  barrel with a long scope read at 8×. No existing builder's bytes move.
- **Hands on the real guns** (`polygonizer/hero-carry.js`): new holds `rifleAim`, `rifleLowReady`, `sniperAim`,
  `sniperLowReady`, `smgAim`, `smgLowReady`, `handgunAim`, `handgunLowReady` hold the arms kernel's models on their
  own stations (the proxy-box samples' holds are unchanged). The fists close on the arm as drawn (hero-digits: the
  strong hand's fingers and thumb round the grip at its girth, the support hand round the handguard, the pump or up the
  foregrip, or wrapped over the strong fist on a handgun), the index's pad on the trigger at the aim (within 0.1 mm)
  and straight along the frame at the ready; a scope's eye relief is kept in the cheek weld. New checks: `grasp` (every
  closed digit on its part) and `trigger`. `heroHold(name, R, { arm })` puts another model of the class in the hold
  (a bullpup in `rifleAim`). The arm rides the hand as gear (`carryMounts`), so the clip's prop is the real arm.
- **The bow** (`polygonizer/hero-bow.js`, motion words `bowDraw` and `bowLoose`): side on to the mark, the nock at the
  corner of the mouth, the arrow from it to the mark, the bow arm straight at its own draw length, the bow hand closed
  round the grip, the drawing arm by the archer's rule (the elbow on the force line, the wrist straight, the three
  fingers hooked on the string). `bowDraw` nocks, raises and draws to the anchor and holds; `bowLoose` lets go (the
  hand thrown back along the jaw, the fingers open), follows through and comes back to the ready. The readout names
  the draw length and the nock's place per key; the bow is a rigid prop, so its string stays at brace on the model (a
  limit: an engine bends it from the readout).
- **The carried kit** (`gameworld/arms-kit.js`, the quick door's `arms: [...]` on `shoot` and `deathmatch`): up to five
  of `rifle`, `carbine`, `bullpup`, `smg`, `pdw`, `shotgun`, `breacher`, `marksman`, `sniper`, `coilgun`, `caseless`,
  `handgun`, `revolver`, `bow`, or an arm's build words. Each is a weapon row by its archetype (an assault rifle's
  automatic fire, a shotgun's wide cone thinning with range, a marksman's and a sniper's head multiple, a bolt's pull)
  scaled to the goal's base round, with its sights, its sway and its switch's halves from the arm's handling.
- **Gunplay in the world** (`worlds/controllable/gunplay.js`, opt-in, emitted only for a world that asks): the sights
  come up over the arm's aim time, tighten the cone and slow the feet (the body still moves, strafes and fires,
  wider on the move); the aim sways by the arm, more from the hip and on the move, and a scope's breath held steadies
  it for four seconds before the body wants air; R reloads a partly spent magazine; a first-person walker switches on
  the same keys with the switch's ready-time; a bow's arrow flies faster and harder the further it was drawn and falls
  as it flies. Deterministic: the sway is a curve of the world's clock.
- **The page** (`scene/channels/controllable/gunplay-view.js`, opt-in): right click aims, Shift steadies a scope, R
  reloads, the wheel and 1–5 switch, A and D strafe under a look camera. The view closes to the sight's power, a spray
  lifts it, a scope shows its picture (crosshair, marks, the breath's bar). In first person the arm is in hand as its
  parts' boxes (an optic an open hood), brought to the eye along its sight line, bobbing with the stride, lagging the
  look, kicking with each round, dipping to reload, and switched as two halves (lowered out, the next raised in); a
  bow's string draws back with the button held, and its arrows fly as shafts.

### The world clock: a live world's time slowed, held and ramped on what happens, the camera keeping real time

A world's `tempo` names moments that fire on what happens in play: a blow landing, a foe going down, the
last foe going down, a dodge. While one plays, the world steps slower or holds for a while and ramps back, and the
camera keeps real time, moving through the moment. That brings slow motion, the freeze and bullet time into play, on
the clock the impact cam will ride (`control/lib/graph/worlds/controllable/world-clock.js`).

- **The moments.** `tempo: { moments: [{ on, scale, hold, ramp?, cooldown? }] }`.
  - `on`: what fires a moment:
    - `strike`: a melee connect;
    - `down`: any body downed;
    - `down:foe`: a body other than the pilot downed;
    - `last-down`: the last foe downed, a finisher;
    - `dodge`: the pilot dodging;
    - any other name, fired from outside by the page.
  - `scale`: the world's speed, 0 (held) to 1.
  - `hold`, `ramp`, `cooldown`: real seconds.
  - A slower moment takes over a faster one, eased from where the world is. A cooldown keeps a multi-kill from
    ping-ponging the clock.
- **The words.** `finisher`, `kill-cam`, `impact` (a heavy blow holds the world for a beat, a foe going down slows it)
  and `bullet` (a dodge slows the world). A list mixes words and moments. The live world's manual says them.
- **The camera keeps real time.** The world steps at the scale and the camera's rule at the real step, so it moves
  through a held world. A freeze holds every body still while the camera goes on. A hitstop's frames run on the world's
  scaled clock.
- **The page.** A world with a tempo composes the clock into its page. The bodies, their clips and their effects step on
  the world's time; the camera, the HUD and the input step on real time. `window.__mojTempo` says where the clock is
  and fires a moment by name. The web page plays it.
- **A game's tempo** (`design_game`, `control/lib/graph/gameworld/tempo.js`). A gameworld's `tempo` (a word, moments,
  or `'auto'`) is laid on every level. `'auto'` is the game type's own: an action game slows on its finisher; the
  realistic, platformer and pinball flavors keep real time, where a blow's weight is the hitstop's. The gameworld's
  juice card names it.
- **The impact cam's bridge.** A moment that fires cues the live shoot plan's shot waiting on `tempo:<what fired it>`.
  A close-up with `on: 'tempo:last-down'` cuts in as the finisher slows the world.
- **A fix on the way.** A live world with a shoot plan stopped on its first frame. The world probed its ground through
  the camera gizmos, whose frustum has no lines until the camera is posed. A live plan's gizmos now take no raycast;
  every other plan's page is unchanged.
- **The cosmos cube.** The Time facet's `tempo` values (slow, ramp, freeze and bullet) are built for play on the web,
  through the world clock. A replay in play is the gap left: a recorded world clock, a moment shown again from another
