  camera. Its package (`replay`) replaces the world clock's on the hillclimb page.
  - Of 500 random worlds, 160 are now makeable (129 before).
  - Of 500 worlds near the genre probes, 344 are (330 before).
- **Absent, nothing changes.** A world without a tempo gets no state, and its page keeps every byte.

### The car shelf: personal and family cars, composed

The registry's personal and family cars, built from a shelf of composable choices: a body style, a design language, a
trim and its parts, and a paint, over a class's true numbers. Named configurations are cards in a library. The supercar
ODM's way (an archetype, a language, options, cards), for the cars people get about in. Each is a class, never a model.

- **Twelve car classes at their true numbers** (`roads/vehicles.js`, [E], each a class and not a model):
  - the small ones: `cityCar` (an A-segment city car), `keiCar` (a tall kei car), `microcar` (a two-seat microcar),
    `subcompact` (a B-segment supermini);
  - the bigger ones: `fullsize` (a full-size luxury saloon), `coupe` (a two-door coupe), `roadster` (a two-seat
    roadster), `muscle` (a V8 muscle coupe);
  - the tall ones: `minivan` (a people carrier), `midSuv` (a midsize three-row SUV), `largeSuv` (a full-size
    body-on-frame SUV), `offroader` (a short boxy off-roader).

  The vehicle sheet names them (`car-designer/channels.js`, their traits in `facets.js`), so a sheet's plain loft of
  one is its nearest body family's. Their rows draw their cards first.
- **The shelf** (`car-shelf/`). Each slot's words are in its own file; the language gives a slot's word, the trim
  overrides it, the card overrides that, and the composition's own parts override everything.
  - **Body styles** (`car-bodies.js`): sedan, hatchback, liftback, wagon, coupe, fastback, convertible, roadster,
    crossover, suv, boxy, minivan, tallBox, bubble. Each is stations along the length and heights over the class's
    height, plus what closes its back, whether it is open, and how upright it stands.
  - **Design languages** (`car-languages.js`):
    - `chrome`: the fifties and sixties;
    - `wedge`: the folded-paper eighties;
    - `jellybean`: the nineties;
    - `current`: the road today;
    - `aero`: an electric car;
    - `rugged`: an off-roader;
    - `cute`: a kei or city car.

    Each sets the section, the plan's rounding, bow and rake, the haunches over the wheels and the waist between them,
    round or square arches, and the default face and paint.
  - **Trims and parts** (`car-trims.js`): base, comfort, luxury, sport, offroad, eco. Each is a package of slots:
    - the face: lamps, grille;
    - the tail: tail lamps;
    - the body: bumpers, frames, strip, stripes, clad, flares, skirts, splitter, skid plate, fog lamps;
    - the roof: roof (solid, sunroof, glass, contrast, soft, open), spoiler, roof rails;
    - the running gear: wheel, tyre, exhausts, a spare wheel, the ride height and the wheel scale.
  - **Paints** (`car-paints.js`): each language's palette by name, or a hex, finished solid, metallic or pearl. A scheme
    lays a second colour on the roof and pillars or above the shoulder.
  - **The library** (`car-library.js`): `CAR_CARDS`, from a family sedan to a fifties cruiser, and `composeCar`. A card
    or a composition is solved at its class's numbers, every slot resolved, its paint picked, and its laws checked
    (the wheels inside the body, the track inside the width, the bonnet over the wheels, clearance, the roof the body
    takes). The laws advise.
- **The body** (`car-body.js`, `car-parts.js`, `car-wheels.js`, `car-figure.js`). A loft through sections round the half
  (the sill tucked under, the cladding's line, the widest line, the shoulder, the belt, the glass leaning in, the roof's
  edge and crown):
  - **The plan:** rounded, bowed at the corners and raked over the face. The sides swell over each wheel and draw in
    between them.
  - **An open body:** a tub with its seats, dash, steering wheel and a framed screen.
  - **Shared passes:** every face is named for the road loft's passes, so the glasshouse, the panels, the road wheel and
    its well and the crease-aware smoothing dress a composed car as they dress a loft.
  - **The parts sit on the body's own surface:**
    - on the end caps: lamps and grilles;
    - bands that follow the plan round a corner: bumpers, wrapping lamps, strips, flares;
    - on the roof: rails, a sunroof, stripes, spoilers;
    - at the tail: exhausts, a diffuser, a spare wheel on its carrier.

    Proud bumpers, a spare and flares stay inside the class's length and width.
  - **The wheels:** the road wheel in the shelf's styles (a chrome hubcap, a capped steelie, a flat eighties alloy, ten
    spokes, a dark sport wheel, an aero cover, an off-road dish). The tyres are road, whitewall, low profile, or the
    field's lugged all-terrain.
  - **`compileCar`** returns the realistic loft's shape (the rig, its baked faces, the form render's named faces and
    light, its census against the class), so every door that draws a loft draws it.
- **The road wheel** (`car-designer/road-wheel.js`) takes a style's own record and a rim share. A name and no rim draw
  as before.
- **The registry:**
  - A `car` handle (the library, one claim each), its first card the row's realistic build, listed before the class's
    plain loft. Its build is a loft with its card.
  - The sedan, compact, coupe, estate, crossover, suv and minivan rows take their cards. The coupe, suv and minivan get
    their classes, so their realistic build is live; their realistic ride was the stylised assembly until now.
  - New rows: supermini, city car, kei car, microcar, luxury sedan, electric car, hot hatch, convertible, roadster,
    muscle car, full-size suv, off-roader, classic car.
  - Words moved to the rows they name: 'roadster' from the sports car; 'subcompact', 'small car' and 'city car' from
    the compact; '4x4', 'four by four' and 'off-roader' from the suv.
- **The doors:**
  - **A loft's recipe:** `{ loft: { car, class?, seed?, light? } }` (`race-families.js`), with `car` a card's id or a
    composition. A sheet's words (era, brief, livery, wear, reach) are refused beside it.
  - **The studio grid** (`mint_solid` vehicle): a row's word draws its card, and `loft: { car }` beside the word
    composes another. A composition with no card is any car row's.
  - **A quick ride at the realistic tier** drives the row's card (`ride.js` `{ kind: 'loft', class, car }`).
  - **A level's parked vehicles** take `car` (`parked.js`). A car row stands as its card; a row the highway fleet lofts
    (the sedan, the compact, the crossover) keeps its plain loft unless it names a car.
  - **Kept as they were:** recipes minted before keep their bytes. The e2e pin of the realistic sedan's ride now expects
    its card. `parked.test.js` picks its concept-only row without a card.
- **Docs:** `docs/car-shelf.md`, the `vehicle` solid card, CLAUDE.md's pointer.
- **Held:**
  - `car-shelf.test.js`, one case a procedure chosen in code from the library:
    - the precedence of the slots, the spoiler's and the spare's rules, the open roof;
    - refusals, the car classes, the paint;
    - the census at the class, every face named and lit, the glass and panels dressed;
    - determinism, a part asked drawn and one not asked absent, the whitewall;
    - the registry's builds, the ride, the loft recipe and parking.
  - The registry's freeze (`roster.test.js`) holds every card to one row.
  - `car-shelf.deep.test.js` sweeps every card within its laws at its class's numbers, and every body in every
    language.
- **Seen** (machine gate only; the eyes gate is open): `scripts/render-cars.mjs` renders every card from the front
  quarter, the side, the rear quarter and above.

### The city's utility vehicles: civil support trucks, realistic

The vehicles that keep a city running, built at their true numbers in the hull kit's language, as the airside ground
crew are, and named in the vehicle registry. Each is a class, not a replica.

- **Eight classes at their true numbers** (`roads/vehicles.js`, [E], each a class and not a replica):
  - the works: `refuseTruck`, a rear-loading refuse truck on three axles, loaded; `snowPlow`, a plough truck and
    gritter, its width the angled blade's; `streetSweeper`, a truck-mounted street sweeper;
  - the emergency: `fireEngine`, a pumper; `ambulance`, a box ambulance on a van cab; `paramedicVan`, a high-roofed
    paramedic van;
  - the aerial lifts: `ladderTruck`, a rear-mount aerial ladder truck on three axles; `bucketTruck`, a utility's
    bucket truck.

  Each is drawn, worn, painted, previewed, parked and exported to GLB as the field's and the airside's vehicles are
  (`MILITARY_CLASSES`): the engines' sweep builds every one of them.
- **The civic kit** (`car-designer/civic-kit.js`, reusing the airside's cab-over cab, guards, lamps and stripes): a
  bonneted cab (its bonnet, grille, fenders, raked screen, doors and bumper), a crew cab (the cab-over lengthened, its
  rear doors, a raised roof), a light bar, reflective stripes and chevrons, a high-visibility chequer, roll-up lockers,
  outriggers, a frame on its axles with its under-run bars, and a hinge's turn.
- **The works** (`road-civic-works.js`):
  - the refuse truck: a cab-over cab; the ribbed compaction body, its band and number; the tailgate hinged at the body's
    top rear, with its hopper, sill, packer rams, bin lifter, chevrons and lamps; the crew's riding steps;
  - the plough truck: a bonneted cab, an amber light bar, plough lamps raised on stalks over the blade; the curved
    mouldboard angled to throw right, its cutting edge, ribs and markers, on its push frame and lift ram; the V-box
    spreader, its stiffeners, grate, chute and spinner;
  - the street sweeper: a cab-over cab; the hopper body and its rear door; the pickup head and its duct; two gutter
    brooms, a core and its bristles splayed to the road, on their arms.
- **The emergency vehicles** (`road-civic-emergency.js`, in no service's livery):
  - the fire engine: a crew cab, its raised roof white, its light bar; the pump panel set in from the body (gauges,
    discharges, caps); roll-up lockers down both sides, over and behind the rear wheels; the rub rail and reflective
    band; the hose bed and its hose; an extension ladder racked on the roof; the tailboard, chevrons and lamps;
  - the box ambulance: a bonneted van cab and the patient module behind and over it, its light bar and corner lights,
    a side door, rear doors and windows, its red band, its chevrons, its rear step;
  - the paramedic van: a high-roofed panel van, its raked screen, its cab, sliding and rear doors, its light bar and
    corner lights, a high-visibility chequer down its sides and across its doors.
- **The aerial lifts** (`road-civic-lifts.js`):
  - the ladder truck: a crew cab, lockers; the turntable over the tandem, its trunnion plates and console, the
    elevation rams; four nested truss sections bedded forward over the cab on a rest; four outriggers;
  - the bucket truck: a bonneted cab, a service body of compartments either side of its bed; the pedestal and turret
    at its tail; the lower boom and the insulated upper boom folded over it; the bucket at its tip; two outriggers.
- **How far each deploys** (`CIVIC_REACH`, `CIVIC_WORDS`, `reachOf`: metres, stowed on the road):
  - a brief's words deploy it: a refuse truck `tipping` (its tailgate's lower edge); a plough `plowing` (its blade on
    the road); a sweeper `sweeping` (its brooms down and swung out past its width, its head lowered); a ladder `raised`
    (its tip); a bucket `raised` (its floor);
  - a number sets it (`pose.reach`, `reach` in a loft's recipe or a parked vehicle), clamped to its range;
  - the ladder is elevated at its retracted length, then extended, then elevated to its limit (`ladderPose`); it is
    slewed by `pose.slew`;
  - the booms raise the lower boom first, unfold the upper, then telescope it (`bucketPose`); the bucket is held level;
  - a ladder or a bucket raised stands on its outriggers.
- **Their look:** each kind's plain livery (`CIVIC_LIVERY`: a fire appliance's red, a plough's orange, a municipal or
  medical white) and its fleet number, unless a livery is named. What is not paint is its own: the bands and chevrons,
  the lenses (each lit by its own colour: red, amber, blue or white), chrome, aluminium, rubber. Road tyres, smooth.
  Kept clean unless a wear is asked, as a road worker is (`roadWorker`).
- **The registry:**
  - the ambulance and fire engine rows take their classes and the words people say for them (pumper, fire tender,
    box ambulance);
  - new rows: garbage truck (refuse truck, bin lorry, dustcart), snowplow (snowplough, gritter, salt truck, snow
    removal truck), street sweeper (road sweeper), paramedic van (paramedic, van ambulance, medic unit; the word moved
    from the ambulance row), ladder truck (aerial ladder, turntable ladder, hook and ladder), bucket truck (cherry
    picker, elevator truck, aerial lift truck, aerial work platform).

  Role `service`; their realistic builds are live. A parked one takes a `reach` within its own range.
- **Held** (`road-civic.test.js`):
  - each body at its class's numbers stowed;
  - each that deploys to the height asked, by its words or a number, clamped to its range;
  - a tailgate turned on its hinge with the body left as it was; a blade wider than its truck and on the road; brooms
    inside the width stowed and past it sweeping; a ladder on its outriggers, elevated as its pose solves, slewed over
    the side by its run; a bucket held level at its floor;
  - the plain livery and a named one, the lenses lit by their colours, two-coloured chevrons and chequers;
  - the ambulance's module over its cab;
  - road tyres, clean unless asked, within budget (under 20k triangles), the same twice;
  - found by its words, realistic build live; parked with a reach in its range, refused one where it deploys nothing.
- **Also:** `parked.test.js` gives its room a centimetre's slack, so the depth's rounding does not leave the last
  vehicle out.
- **Seen** (machine gate; the eyes gate is open): `scripts/render-civic.mjs` renders each from the front quarter, the
  side, the rear quarter, and deployed.
- **The garbage truck's other models** (`car-designer/road-civic-refuse.js`), each read by its silhouette, beside the
  rear loader. Four new classes at their true numbers ([E]), their rows, their deployments and their liveries:
  - `frontLoader`, the front loader (front loader garbage truck, dumpster truck, commercial garbage truck; a bare "front loader" is the site's wheel loader): a cab well ahead of its
    set-back axle, narrower than the two arms that arch over it from the body's front corners to the forks ahead of its
    bumper; the hopper open in the body's roof. `lifting` swings the arms up and back over the cab (the reach: the
    forks' lowest point);
  - `sideLoader`, the automated side loader (side loader, automated garbage truck): a low-entry cab, a low hopper
    behind it open on the right, the body stepping up tall behind that; the arm under the hopper, its boom and its
    gripper on its track. `lifting` runs it out to the kerb and climbs it in over the hopper, a wheelie bin in its
    paddles tipped at the top (the reach: the gripper's foot);
  - `rollOff`, the roll-off truck (hook lift truck, container truck): a bonneted cab, the hook arm along its frame
    and its tower, the open-topped container on its rails, ribbed, its rollers. `tipping` turns the container and the
    arm together about the frame's tail (the reach: the container's nose);
  - `skipLoader`, the skip loader (skip lorry, skip truck): a cab-over cab, its bed and headboard, the portal arms
    pivoted at its tail, their beam and chains, the tapered skip, the stabiliser legs. `unloading` swings the arms
    back over the tail and sets the skip down behind it, the legs down (the reach: the skip's bottom).

  Their plain liveries: a municipal white, a green, a blue under an orange container, a white under a yellow skip.
- **Also:** `lowered` is the car sheet's own word (a stance), so it never reaches a body; it is no longer among the
  plough's, the sweeper's or the skip's deploying words.
- **Held** (`road-civic.test.js`):
  - each model at its numbers and deployed to its reach;
  - the front loader's arms over its cab, its forks ahead of the bumper, and up over the roof when lifting;
  - the side loader's hopper low between cab and body, its gripper out at the kerb low and in over the hopper high,
    a bin in it only when working;
  - the roll-off's container and tower tipped together, clear of the ground;
  - the skip carried on the bed and set down on the ground behind the tail, its legs down.
- **The delivery fleet** (`car-designer/road-civic-delivery.js`, in no carrier's livery), five classes at their true
  numbers ([E]), each read by its silhouette:
  - `mailTruck`, the mail truck (mail van, postal truck, post van): short and tall, a short bonnet under an upright
    screen, driven from the right; one roof over the cab and the cargo box, a kerbside sliding door, an up-and-over
    rear door, a blue band and a red pinstripe;
  - `courierVan`, the courier van (courier, parcel van, high roof van): a high-roofed panel van, blind behind its cab,
    a sliding door each side, its rear doors, amber bands;
  - `stepVan`, the walk-in step van, now the delivery truck row's realistic build (step van, parcel truck, walk-in
    van): one tall box from its drooped nose to its tail, rounded, its two-pane screen, a doorway over a step at the
    front of each side, a roll-up rear door;
  - `lightTruck`, the light box truck (small box truck, tail lift truck, luton van, refrigerated truck): a narrow
    cab-over cab, the box wider and taller behind it, corner posts and a red band, a tail lift; `refrigerated`
    (reefer, chilled) carries a fridge unit on the box's front over the cab;
  - `keiTruck`, the kei truck (mini truck, micro truck): a micro cab-over cab, an aluminium box; `flatbed` (drop
    side, pickup) gives it a bed with drop sides behind a mesh guard instead.
- **How they deploy:**
  - the mail truck and the courier van slide their kerbside door back when `delivering` (open);
  - the step van opens its doorways and rolls its rear door up (`delivering`, unloading; the reach: the rear door's
    foot);
  - the box truck lays its tail lift out at its floor and lowers it to the kerb (`unloading`; the reach: the platform,
    folded up against the doors at the floor's height on the road).

  Their plain liveries: white, the courier's charcoal.
- **Held** (`road-civic.test.js`):
  - each at its numbers and deployed to its reach;
  - a kerbside door slid back with its doorway dark on the right;
  - the step van's box to its roof over a low nose, its screen, its doorways open;
  - the tail lift folded on the road, laid flat at a height behind the truck, and a fridge unit only when refrigerated;
  - the kei truck's box, or its drop sides lower than the box would stand.

### The construction shelf: composable construction machines on the vehicle registry

In progress. The vehicle registry gains a handle, `construction`, into a new parts library for the machines that dig,
push, load, haul and lift on a site.
- **The machines:**
  - excavators (crawler, mini, wheeled);
  - the bulldozer;
  - the wheel loader;
  - the backhoe loader;
  - the skid steer and the compact track loader;
  - the telehandler and the forklift;
  - the tipper, the articulated dump truck, the haul truck and the mixer;
  - the mobile crane and the tower crane;
  - the road roller and the motor grader.
- **The structure:** each machine is layers on a shelf: a carrier, an upper, a front and a tool. The door swaps a tool
  or a carrier, and the laws read the machine as built.
- **The new capability:** a kinematic chain at assembly level. A part is placed on its parent's joint and inherits its
  angle. A hydraulic ram is solved between two bodies, and a linkage is closed as a four-bar.
- **Held:** reach, depth and dump height measured over the joints' ranges; rams within their strokes; tail swing;
  ground pressure; rated lift as a share of tipping.

- **The rows, the role and the classes** (`vehicle-registry/roster.js`, `roads/vehicles.js`,
  `construction-shelf/con-archetypes.js`):
  - **The role** `construction`: "it builds, digs, hauls or lifts on a site".
  - **The rows,** each under the words people say:
    - the excavator ('digger'), the mini excavator, the wheeled excavator;
    - the bulldozer ('dozer');
    - the wheel loader;
    - the backhoe loader ('backhoe');
    - the skid steer and the compact track loader;
    - the telehandler;
    - the tipper ('dump truck'), the mixer ('cement truck');
    - the articulated dump truck ('dumper'), the haul truck;
    - the mobile crane, the tower crane ('crane');
    - the road roller ('steamroller'), the motor grader.

    The forklift row takes its class. Each falls back to the crafter's tracked or truck concept until the shelf draws
    it. The tower crane never drives: it is parked and watched, and its size will be its own once built.
  - **Their classes,** with each machine's operator, [E]:
    - a 20 t crawler excavator, a 2.7 t mini, a 16 t wheeled one;
    - a 20 t dozer, a 15 t wheel loader, an 8.5 t backhoe loader;
    - a 3.3 t skid steer, a 4.3 t compact track loader;
    - a telehandler, a 2.5 t counterbalance forklift;
    - an 8x4 tipper and an 8x4 mixer, loaded;
    - a 30 t articulated dump truck and a 100 t rigid haul truck, loaded;
    - a five-axle all-terrain crane;
    - a 10 t tandem roller, a 17 t motor grader.

    A site machine's top speed is its published travel speed. A haul truck rolls on a haul road's resistance.
  - **How a class turns** (`STEERS`, `steerOf`): by its front wheels, its rear (the forklift), every axle (the
    telehandler, the crane), its frame bending (the loader, the dump truck, the roller, the grader), or skid (a skid
    steer, and every crawler). A word for the builders and the page; the drive rule does not read it. A skid-steered
    class is drawn and parked, as a tracked one is.
  - **The handle** `construction` → the shelf's `CON_ARCHETYPES`, empty until its first machine. The upscale ledger sends
    a site machine to the construction shelf.
  - **A site's class** says `site: true` (`siteClass`): its body is the construction shelf's. The car sheet refuses it as
    its class, naming where it is built, as it refuses a cycle's; its class dial stays the classes on axles that are not
    a site's.
  - **Held:**
    - `vehicles.test.js`: a crawler at its travel speed inside 2 s, a wheeled site machine 2.5–8 s to 20 km/h, a loaded
      tipper and mixer 35–65 s to 80, a loaded dump truck 40–80 s to 50; which tip before they slide; one class per way
      of turning.
    - `roster.test.js`: the handle's table frozen as every handle's is; a site machine's upscale.
    - `sheet.test.js`: the sheet refuses a site's class. `mil-track.test.js` reads the field's tracked classes only: a
      site's crawler is the shelf's.

    No byte pin moved.
- **The shelf, its chain and its first machine, the crawler excavator** (`construction-shelf/`: `con-common.js`,
  `con-odm.js`, `con-parts.js`, `con-chain.js`, `con-archetypes.js`, `con-laws.js`, `index.js`):
  - **The chain** (`con-chain.js`), the one new capability:
    - A layout entry sits `on` its parent's hardpoint, fixed or on a `joint` (a slew about the parent's +z, a hinge
      about its +x), and inherits the joint's angle. Every body is authored in its own frame, its pivot the origin, so
      a pose moves frames and never a part's geometry.
    - **A ram** is a barrel aimed from its base toward its eye and a rod aimed back, each a rigid body at its own length,
      so the rod slides in the barrel at every pose without being drawn again.
    - **A linkage** (the bucket's dogbones and H-link) is a four-bar the joint closes, its pin solved where its two
      links meet.
    - **A joint's range is its ram's:** where the ram's length lies between its closed length and its full stroke
      (derived, never stated), in the run the joint works `near`. Its ends are rounded inward.
  - **The parts of a 20 t excavator:**
    - the crawler (its track laid link by link on the military running gear's path and pins, `mil-track.js`, its
      sprockets, idlers, rollers and carriers, its frames and car body);
    - the slewing ring;
    - the upper (deck, hood, tank, the boom's foot);
    - the cab, with its glass, its lamps and its seat;
    - the counterweight, its tail an arc about the slew axis;
    - a banana mono boom, the stick and its heel, a digging bucket with its teeth;
    - the dogbones and the H-link;
    - the boom, stick and bucket rams.
  - **The machine** (`assembleMachine(archetype, { pose })`) at its named poses: rest (the bucket set down), travel,
    transport (folded for shipping), dig (the teeth at grade), dump, reach, slewed. A pose is a name, or joint values
    clamped into their ranges and said. A named pose is shares of each range, or `ground` (the joint lowered until the
    tool touches the ground).
  - **The laws, measured** (`con-laws.js`):
    - each joint's working arc;
    - the envelope swept over the ranges: reach along the ground, depth, cut height, dump height with the teeth plumb
      under the pin;
    - the counterweight's tail swing as built;
    - ground pressure;
    - the rated lift over the side at 6 m, 1.5 m up: 75% of tipping about the track's centreline, from every part's mass
      where it is built and posed (ISO 10567's share);
    - the parts' mass against the class's;
    - the bucket never entering the cab over the ranges;
    - the transport size folded (advisory).

    The 20 t machine reaches 9.56 m, digs 6.37 m, dumps at 6.94 m, cuts at 9.36 m, swings its tail at 2.85 m, stands at
    47 kPa and lifts a rated 2.8 t over the side.
  - **Found while building:**
    - The class's track gauge was a 20 t machine's too narrow (2.0 m): now 2.2 m, its width its shoes'.
    - The extruder reads an outline wound anticlockwise about its axis: a panel extruded toward −x, and a plan outline,
      now wind their own.
  - **The registry:** the excavator row claims the archetype. Its realistic build is the shelf's, asleep until a door
    draws it, parked and watched (a crawler is not driven until skid steer is built).
  - **Held:**
    - `construction-shelf.test.js`, the machine chosen in code by its linkage:
      - at every named pose each body on its parent's joint, each ram within its stroke with its rod's end on its eye,
        each link at its length;
      - each ram-driven joint's ends at its ram's closed and full lengths;
      - poses within their ranges and grounded;
      - the operator's joint clamped and said;
      - every law held;
      - a pose moving frames and never parts;
      - the slew turning the upper and never the undercarriage;
      - the words.
    - The char test pins every builder path, a ram's rod and the machine at rest.
    - The deep sweep walks every joint's range finely, and every named pose.
  - **Seen** (`scripts/render-construction.mjs`; machine gate only, the eyes gate is open): the excavator at rest, in
    travel, digging, dumping, at reach and slewed.
- **The chain grows, and the bulldozer:**
  - **The chain** (`con-chain.js`):
    - A pair of rams must both lie within their stroke: a range is where every side's does.
    - A `slide` joint moves a body along its parent's +y in metres; without a ram its range is its body's own travel.
    - A jointed entry may move a `scale` of its joint's value: a telescope's section, a mast's stage.
    - A `rocker` (a loader's bellcrank) is solved on its parent's pin from the coupler it drives.
    - A ram may be based on any body fixed to its joint's parent: the dozer's lift rams on its hull, its blade on the
      tracks' trunnions.
  - **The laws** read the excavator's envelope only on a machine with a boom, a stick and a tool. Any other front is
    held to its `measure`s: a named point swept over the joints it names, its highest or how far below the ground it
    goes.
  - **The 20 t bulldozer:**
    - the crawler, its sprocket larger and its grousers taller, its push arms' trunnions on its frames and no slew seat;
    - its hull (the mainframe, the hood narrowing to its grille, the lift rams' towers, the tank, the ripper's mount);
    - its cab;
    - a semi-U blade on its push arms (the curved moldboard, its end bits, its cutting edge);
    - a radial ripper (its beam, its shank and tooth);
    - two lift rams and the ripper's.

    At rest, travelling, dozing, ripping and at the top of its lift.
  - **Its laws:** its blade's lift (1.15 m) and its drop below the grade (0.52 m), its ripper's depth (0.67 m) and its
    clearance (0.54 m), its arcs, 61.9 kPa on its tracks, its mass, its transport size (its blade 3.4 m across).
  - The class's length takes the ripper (6.6 m). The bulldozer row claims it, asleep and undriven as the excavator is.
  - **Held:** the law tests walk one machine per procedure (a tool on a linkage, a front held to its measures). The
    char test pins the hull, the blade, the ripper and the machine; the deep sweep walks it.
- **The wheel loader, the skid steer and the compact track loader** (`con-wheeled.js`):
  - **The 15 t wheel loader:**
    - its rear frame (the engine, the hood, the counterweight, the cab's deck, its axle, the hitch) and its front frame
      (the towers, its axle), the front turned on the rear's hitch (a `slew` joint) by two steer rams, ±40°, both held
      to their stroke;
    - four site tyres on their rims, their lugs a chevron;
    - the lift arms on the towers, raised by two lift rams;
    - the bucket on the arms' tip, tilted through a Z-bar: the bellcrank (a `rocker`, solved on the cross tube's pin
      until its lower pin is the tilt link's length from the bucket's), the tilt link, the tilt ram from the arms to
      the bellcrank's upper pin.

    Its laws: its hinge pin at the top of its lift (3.94 m), its dump clearance with the bucket dumped (3.02 m), its
    arcs (the hitch 80°, the arms 64°, the bucket 120°), its mass, its tool clear of its cab, its transport size.
  - **The 3.3 t skid steer:** its chassis (the tub, the engine aft, the chain cases, the towers at its back) on four
    tyres; radial lift arms on the towers; a bucket tilted by two rams from the arms' cross member. Its hinge pin
    3.1 m, its dump clearance 2.52 m.
  - **The 4.3 t compact track loader, the carrier swap:** the skid steer on rubber tracks (`withCarrier(skidSteer,
    'tracks')`, `CON_CARRIERS`). The wheels taken off, the tracks put on at the chassis, its own class, its front
    untouched; 35 kPa on its tracks. The crawler draws a rubber belt (no rails, its lugs moulded on) in its `rubber`
    family.
  - **The laws:**
    - A measure may hold joints at a share of their ranges (`at`): the dump clearance's arms at full lift and its bucket
      dumped.
    - The tool-and-cab clearance sweeps whichever joints carry the tool, a slew or a hitch held where it rests.
  - **The registry:** the wheel-loader, skid-steer and compact-track-loader rows claim their machines, asleep; the
    skid-steered two undriven.
  - **Held:**
    - The law tests add a tool through a rocker and a machine on another carrier, chosen in code: the chain holds at
      every pose (the bellcrank on its pin, the tilt link at its length), every law, the carrier swap's front untouched
      and an unknown carrier refused.
    - The char test pins every new builder path and each machine; the deep sweep walks them all.
  - **Seen** (machine gate only, the eyes gate is open): the loader carrying, dumping and turned; the skid steer and
    the track loader carrying and dumping. The review renderer frames a tall pose by its height.
- **The forklift, the telehandler, the mini excavator and the backhoe loader** (`con-handlers.js`):
  - **The chain:**
    - A joint's ram may join any two bodies on it (a pair of stabiliser legs).
    - A slew may be turned its `zero` (a backhoe's swing frame faces aft); a hinge may turn about its own `axis` (a
      stabiliser about the machine's length); an entry's `scale` of −1 mirrors its joint (the left leg).
    - A ramless slide runs as far as its first stage runs out.
    - A pose may set several joints on the ground in turn, each lowering what it carries (its body and every body hung
      below it), from the end of its range that holds them highest.
    - A pose may hold a tool `level`: it turns back the hinges above it.
    - A value a rounding past its range's end is its end.
  - **A part at another size** (`S` in `con-odm.js`, `scaleDims`): another part's design at k times its lengths and k³
    its mass, drawn at the design's size and scaled. A chain's angles do not change with its size, so a scaled front
    keeps its arcs.
  - **A ram's allowances shrink on a short ram**, no more than a fifth of its length for its eye, its piston leaving
    5 cm at its base. No existing ram changed.
  - **The 2.5 t counterbalance forklift:**
    - its chassis (the counterweight, the overhead guard, the seat) on drive and steer tyres;
    - its mast tilted on the front axle by two rams (−6° to +10°);
    - its inner stage and its carriage each lifting half the extension, a duplex mast: the forks reach 3.31 m.
  - **The telehandler, 4 t to 14 m:**
    - its boom hinged at the chassis's back and raised by its ram (−3° to 70°);
    - its two inner sections sliding out half each of 7 m;
    - its fork carriage held level on the tip by its tilt ram;
    - its carriage pin at 13.44 m.

    The class's length is a 14 m machine's.
  - **The 2.7 t mini excavator:**
    - the 20 t front at 0.44 its size, its arcs the 20 t's;
    - on a swing post turned −50° to +75° by its swing ram;
    - its round upper, its canopy, its counterweight's tail inside its tracks (0.76 m);
    - a backfill blade on its rubber tracks.

    It reaches 4.78 m, digs 2.63 m and lifts a rated 0.4 t at 2.5 m.
  - **The 8.5 t backhoe loader:**
    - its loader's arms and bucket ahead;
    - its backhoe aft, the 20 t front at 0.62 its size on a swing frame turned ±90° by two rams, its reach read from the
      swing post (6.16 m), its depth 4.02 m;
    - its stabiliser legs folded up and swung down to the ground.
  - **The registry:** the forklift, telehandler, mini-excavator and backhoe-loader rows claim their machines, asleep.
  - **Held:**
    - The law tests add a machine with stages, one holding a tool level, one grounding several joints and one drawn at
      another size, each chosen in code: the stages each slide their share, a level tool stays level, each grounded
      joint's load touches the ground, a scaled part's hardpoints are its design's times its scale.
    - The chain test and the deep sweep read a slide's body along its axis.
    - The char test pins every new builder path and each machine.
  - **Seen** (machine gate only, the eyes gate is open): the forklift raised, the telehandler travelling and reaching,
    the mini digging and swung on its post, the backhoe digging, travelling and swung.
- **The door's swaps: a tool in the bucket's place, another carrier under the machine** (`con-tools.js`,
  `composeMachine`, `CON_MOUNTS`, `CON_CARRIERS`):
  - **The mounts:**
    - an excavator's pins (its bucket's and its link's) take a bucket, a ditching bucket, a breaker, a grapple and an
      auger;
    - a skid steer's plate takes a bucket, pallet forks, an auger and a sweeper.

    A tool's part number is its stem and the machine's size, so the excavator's tools come at the mini's and the
    backhoe's sizes too, drawn as the 20 t's at 0.44 and 0.62. Every tool of a mount hangs on its mount's pins, so it
    closes the machine's linkage and takes its rams.
  - **`assembleMachine(archetype, { tool, carrier })`**, or `composeMachine`, puts the tool on the machine's tool joint,
    or the carrier under it, under its own key (`crawlerExcavator+breaker`).
    - A carrier makes the machine it names: a skid steer on tracks the compact track loader, an excavator on wheels the
      wheeled excavator.
    - A tool the mount does not take, a carrier the machine does not list, or a machine whose tool is its own is
      refused, naming what it takes.
  - **The laws re-read the machine as built:**
    - its mass is the class's with the tool in its bucket's place;
    - its rated lift is read against tipping alone (it lifts something or nothing, and does not tip);
    - its tool's outline is swept against its cab;
    - a bucket's envelope bands are the bucket's, so another tool's envelope is read and not held to them.

    The 1.8 m ditching bucket can touch the 20 t's cab in one corner of its range: the clearance law says so.
  - **The 19 t wheeled excavator** is the 20 t excavator's upper and front on a wheeled chassis on twin tyres (the
    carrier swap, `withCarrier`; a carrier's parts set where the first part it drops stood). It reaches 9.49 m, digs
    6.06 m and lifts a rated 1.7 t over the side. Its class is 19 t. The wheeled-excavator row claims it, asleep.
  - **Held:**
    - The law tests: a tool its mount takes put in the bucket's place and nothing else changed; its laws re-read; a
      foreign tool, an unlisted carrier and a fixed tool refused; a carrier making its machine.
    - The deep sweep walks every machine and every tool on every machine whose mount takes it, over every joint's range.
    - The char test pins the tools, the wheeled chassis, the wheeled excavator and the excavator with its breaker.
    - The review renderer takes `--tool` and `--carrier`.
  - **Seen** (machine gate only, the eyes gate is open): the excavator with its breaker, its grapple and its auger;
    the skid steer with its forks and its sweeper; the wheeled excavator travelling.
- **The haulers** (`con-haulers.js`): a truck chassis of the shelf's own, its cab and its axles, carrying a body on a
  joint (a road truck's body cannot sit on a joint without changing its output, so the shelf's chassis is its own):
  - **The 8x4 tipper truck:** two steered axles and two driven on twin tyres, its body tipped on a telescopic hoist
    under its front. It tips through 50°. Its body holds 13.5 m³ struck: gravel to 1.15 times its rated 20 t. Its
    wheelbase is 5.43 m, and it is 2.89 m wide and 3.3 m high for the road.
  - **The 8x4 mixer truck:** the same chassis, its drum on its pedestal and rollers, turning freely about its tilted
    axis (a hinge with no ram and no range), its hopper and its chute at its back. Its drum holds 14 m³ gross, and the
    concrete it carries in its share of that is its rated 19 t.
  - **The 30 t articulated dump truck:** a front frame (its cab, its axle) steered at its hitch by two rams through
    90°, and a rear frame on two axles with the rock body on its two hoists. It tips through 70.8° and carries rock to
    its rated 30 t.
  - **The 100 t rigid haul truck:** its frame, its deck and stairs, its cab offset to one side, twin rear tyres, its
    body's canopy over the cab and its body on a three-stage hoist. It tips through 48.4° and holds 69.4 m³.
  - **The chain:** a telescopic ram, its stages nested between its barrel and its rod, each slid out its share of the
    extension so that each overlaps the tube outside it equally at full stroke. A ram's lengths are the chain's
    (`ramParts` moved to `con-chain.js`, unchanged for a two-stage ram). A hinge with no ram turns freely.
  - **The laws:** a body's struck volume (a drum's gross volume, turned from its profile) and its material's mass in it
    against its rated payload; the wheelbase as built against the class's; its tare, the class's loaded mass less its
    payload (`massShift`).
  - **The registry:** the tipper-truck, mixer-truck, articulated-dump-truck and haul-truck rows claim their machines,
    asleep.
  - **Held:**
    - The law tests pick, in code, a machine with a telescopic ram, one with a free hinge and one with a payload. A
      telescopic ram's tubes overlap at every named pose. A free hinge takes any turn unclamped and moves its body,
      never its parts. A payload is the weight off the class's mass.
    - The deep sweep walks the four haulers over their ranges and at every pose.
    - The char test pins the truck chassis, its cab, the three bodies, the drum, the dumper's frames, the haul
      truck's frame, the telescopic hoist and a stage of it, and the four machines. No existing pin moved.
  - **Seen** (machine gate only, the eyes gate is open): the tipper tipped, the mixer's drum turning, the dumper
    tipped and steered, the haul truck tipped.
- **The lifters** (`con-lifters.js`):
  - **The 60 t all-terrain crane:**
    - Its carrier rides on ten tyres on five axles. Its cab is at the front left. Four outrigger beams slide out of
      their boxes, the left two set turned round, and their jacks set their floats on the ground, 6.66 m apart.
    - Its superstructure turns on its slewing ring, with its operator's cab and its 8 t of counterweight slabs.
    - Its boom has five sections. One ram luffs it through 79.7°, and its four telescopes each slide a quarter of its
      33.6 m. Its head reaches 48.5 m up.
    - Its hook block hangs plumb from the head's sheaves on four falls, lowered to the ground or up to 1.2 m under
      the sheaves.
    - It carries its 60 t class's mass and folds to 2.92 m wide and 3.84 m high for the road.
  - **The tower crane, a 58 m hammerhead:**
    - A cross base and its 45 t of ballast blocks. Its mast is 1.8 m lattice sections 4 m long, built to the height
      under its hook the operator names (`assembleMachine('towerCrane', { height })`, a section at a time, 2 to 14
      sections). The default is ten, 40.4 m under its hook.
    - Its slewing unit carries its cab, its tower head and the pendants that hang its jib and its counter-jib.
    - The jib is a triangle of lattice panels: two bottom chords as the trolley's rails, and a top chord.
    - The counter-jib carries its winch, its cabinet, its walkway and its 20 t of ballast slabs.
    - The trolley runs 53.5 m along the jib, to a 57.4 m radius, its hook block plumb under it on two falls.
  - **The chain:**
    - An entry may be set turned about its parent's up (`turn`), its joint's axis turned with it: a left outrigger.
    - A body may hang plumb (`plumb`): its frame upright and facing its parent's heading, its slide along the
      machine's own down, whatever its parent turns.
    - A rope (`rope`) is drawn in lengths spread from its sheave to its hook block. A rope shorter than one length
      is drawn smaller. It counts once in the bill of materials.
    - A slide may say its travel and where it starts (`travel`, `from`): a hoist's, derived from the parts it is
      built of.
  - **The laws:**
    - **The load chart:** the crane's rated load over the side at 8, 12 and 20 m (34.1, 16.2 and 6.6 t), on the
      shortest boom that reaches each radius. It is 75% of the load that tips the crane over its floats, from every
      part's mass where it is posed. It is tipping only: a real chart's short radii are limited by the boom's
      strength, which is not modelled.
    - **The outriggers' spread.**
    - **The tower crane:**
      - its height under its hook within its mast's freestanding heights;
      - its radius;
      - its counter-jib's moment against its jib's own and half its rated 1.8 t at its tip (0.93);
      - its base's stability against that load, its upper's unbalance and a 20 m/s wind on its lattices (2.06).
    - A machine with no class to drive (the tower crane) states its class's mass.
  - **The registry:** the mobile-crane and tower-crane rows claim their machines, asleep. A machine with no class is
    parked and watched, never driven.
  - **Fixed:** the truck cab's bumper was a box of no length, its corners not numbers. It is now drawn across the cab,
    which re-pins the cab, the tipper and the mixer.
  - **Held:**
    - The law tests pick, in code, a crane with a plumb hook, one with a turned body, one built in sections and one
      held to a load chart.
      - The chain test reads each slide's axis turned or plumb, and each rope's lengths from its first point to its
        second.
      - The left outriggers reach as far as the right.
      - The hook hangs under its sheave by its hoist at every pose.
      - The rated load falls with the radius.
      - A height is built to the nearest section, held at the mast's most, and refused by a machine without sections.
    - The deep sweep walks both cranes, and the tower crane at its fewest and its most sections.
    - The char test pins the new builder paths and both cranes.
    - The review renderer takes `--height`.
  - **Seen** (machine gate only, the eyes gate is open): the all-terrain crane stowed and lifting on its outriggers;
    the tower crane at rest, lifting and with its hook on the ground; the tipper's bumper.
- **The finishers** (`con-finishers.js`):
  - **The 10 t tandem roller:**
    - Its two smooth 1.7 m drums are its wheels, each in its frame's yoke under a deck, a scraper and a sprinkler
      bar.
    - The rear frame carries the engine and the operator's platform (seat, console, wheel, canopy). The front frame
      carries the water tank.
    - The frames bend at the hitch on two rams, ±40°.
    - Its drums rest 24.9 kg/cm at the front and 30.8 kg/cm at the rear, from each part's mass where it is built.
    - Its wheelbase is 3.4 m, and it is 1.9 m wide and 3.05 m high for the road.
  - **The 17 t motor grader:**
    - Its rear frame carries the engine, the cab and two tandems.
    - Its front frame's gooseneck runs from the hitch, over the blade, to the front axle. The frames bend ±40° on two
      rams.
    - Its drawbar hangs from the ball under the nose and is lifted by two rams from the saddle.
    - Its circle turns under the drawbar.
    - Its moldboard (3.66 m) is pitched through 42° on its saddle by the tip ram and shifts 0.65 m either way along
      its rails.
    - Its blade lifts 0.38 m and cuts 0.64 m below the ground. Its wheelbase is 6.2 m, and it travels 2.52 m wide
      with its blade turned in.
  - **The chain:** a slide's `from` may lie below its zero, so a body slides both ways (the moldboard's side shift).
  - **The laws:**
    - A roller's linear load: each drum's share of the mass over its width.
    - The wheelbase reads a roller's drums as its wheels.
  - **The registry:** the road-roller and motor-grader rows claim their machines, asleep.
  - **Held:**
    - The law tests pick, in code, a machine on drums and a slide running both ways.
      - The drums' loads add up to the machine's mass.
      - The moldboard shifts its whole travel along its saddle.
    - The deep sweep walks both machines.
    - The char test pins their parts and both machines; no existing pin moved.
  - **Seen** (machine gate only, the eyes gate is open): the roller at rest and turned; the grader at rest, grading
    and travelling, from the side and above.
- **The doors, step 1: the studio grid and the level's figure** (`con-figure.js`):
  - **`mint_solid({ kind: 'vehicle', vehicle: 'excavator' })`** draws a site machine as its construction shelf
    machine, at true size on the studio grid. Beside its word:
    - `pose` poses it: a named pose (`'dump'`, `'rigged'`) or its joints' values (`{ boom: 20, slew: 90 }`).
    - `tool` puts a tool its mount takes on it (`'breaker'`).
    - `carrier` puts it on a carrier it lists (`'tracks'`).
    - `height` builds a tower crane to the height under its hook.
    - `palette` paints it.

    They are carried in its recipe (`{ construction: { archetype, pose?, tool?, carrier?, height?, palette? } }`) and
    regenerate on every read. A site's words on any other build are refused, naming whose they are.
  - **The family layer** builds a `construction` instance. **A level's figures map** takes a `construction` entry: the
    machine's rig, centred on its spot, with its footprint.
  - **The registry:** every site machine's realistic build is live for the studio grid and a level's parked vehicles.
    It is parked and watched, never driven: what one that drives needs is its ride (a skid steer's, skid steer).
  - **Held:** its words read and refused; its faces at a pose with a tool on; its figure centred, a tower crane at the
    height it is built to; the preview door minting a site machine at a pose and drawing it on the world page.
- **The doors, step 2: parked in a level** (`vehicle-registry/parked.js`):
  - A level's `parked` takes a site machine as its construction shelf machine. Beside its word:
    - `pose` (a crane's outriggers out and its floats down by its `'rigged'`);
    - `tool`;
    - `height` (a tower crane on its base, built to the height under its hook);
    - `palette`.
  - **Its box is over what it stands on at its pose:** its parts within 3 m of the ground, never a boom overhead. A
    crane rigged stands wider than one stowed, and a tower crane stands on its base. The figure is centred on that
    footprint (`conFootprint`, `conFigure`).
  - A site's words on any other vehicle are refused, naming whose they are.
  - **Held:** a crane parked stowed and rigged; a tower crane at a height; the words refused; a parked site machine
    compiled in a world at its pose, solid where it stands.
- **The doors, step 3: the cards.**
  - The vehicle vocab card (`solid-vocab/vehicle.md`) names every site machine and its words beside its word (`pose`
    by name or joint values, `tool`, `carrier`, `height`, `palette`). It also covers the `construction` family, the
    parked machine's words, and two worked examples (a breaker at work, a crane rigged).
  - The vehicle routing card says a site machine is a construction shelf machine, posed and fitted by its words.
  - The routing eval has a row for one ("an excavator with a breaker on, its boom raised" → `mint_solid`).
- **The doors, step 4: the geocity's building sites** (`geocity/scene.js`):
  - **The tower crane:** a site drawn in detail stands the construction shelf's tower crane at its corner, its jib over
    the building and its mast as many sections as clear the building's core. It is drawn within 1.5 km of the camera,
    a district's reach.
    - A site too tall for a freestanding mast keeps the massing crane, since a climbing crane is beyond the shelf.
    - The skyline's far sites keep the massing crane.
  - **The machines:** inside the hoarding, near the camera as the kit is, an excavator digging on the band beside the
    building, facing it, and a tipper waiting along its front.
  - **Lighting:** each machine is lowered under the city's own light, once per process for each light and height.
  - **`assembleMachine(…, { laws: false })`** draws a machine as scenery without reading its laws.
  - **Held:** a site drawn in detail stocked with its crane (one per site the counts name, drawn across its district)
    and its machines (near the camera only); every repeat still drawn by the near rule; the skyline none.
  - **Seen** (machine gate only, the eyes gate is open): two sites from the street corner, each crane over its rising
    building, a tipper in the hoarding, a taller core site keeping its massing crane.
- **The doors, step 5: the machines in a city's traffic** (`city/plan/traffic.js`, `worlds/world-kinds.js`):
  - A planned city's `cars: { machines: true }` puts the road's site machines among its moving cars: a tipper, a
    mixer and a mobile crane in transit.
    - Each is folded to drive (its `transport` pose) and baked as the city's cars are (`conTrafficMesh`): facing along
      its lane, at the bank's scale (a sedan baked at it against a midsize sedan's true length gives the units a
      metre).
    - They are one vehicle in five. The traffic's footprint is measured as before, so a crane's length is its own.
  - **Opt-in:** absent, the bank and every lane are as before, not a byte added.
  - **Held:** a city asked for them drives them (a machine longer than any car); one not asked for, none; the word
    refused when it is not true or false.
  - **Seen** (machine gate only, the eyes gate is open): a tipper in its lane down a street, beside a car.

### A character from the person's picture

The character-from-dream loop is gone, and a character creator from a picture the person gives the agent takes its place.
The old loop needed an image worker to dream a reference and refused anything it had not dreamed, so the Claude plugin
build left it out. It also tuned the old SVG figure, not the hero `create_character` mints. Now the agent reads the
person's own picture itself (a drawing, a photo, a figure, someone's OC): nothing is generated and no image is sent.

- **Retired: the dream loop.**
  - The tools `draft_figure_spec`, `get_figure_spec`, `resolve_figure_spec` and `build_figure_spec`, their spec store,
    the dream audit and the `character-from-dream` catalyst.
  - A figure's `dream_audit` now refuses, pointing at the new target. A figure minted with an audit still renders as
    it did.
  - A home's `data/figure-specs/` folder is left in place and never read.
- **Read the picture: `reference_protocol({ target: 'character' })`.** It tells the agent how to read the picture into
  the hero's own words, in this order: a thesis and its hook, proportions in head-heights, dress before body, hair and
  face, clothes as words, palette, which side the picture shows and what it does not, and what no word reaches.
  - A **look**: toon, anime, painterly anime, shonen, chibi, realistic or statue. Each look is a bundle of hero words
    with its own choices, such as the anime head casts and bodies, the realistic physique or the statue card.
  - A **register**: `round`, `lowpoly`, `chamfer` or `box`.
  - A look or register the person names wins. Otherwise the agent picks one from the picture and says why.
  - Every menu is read off the table that owns it, so a new cast or card is on it with no edit.
- **Make the hero: `capture_reference({ target: 'character', insights })`.** It mints the hero through `create_character`,
  so it is the hero those words make, and files the read in a reference stash.
  - A look's words win over the read's, except a choice the look offers. A word of the read that a look overrode is
    reported.
  - The answer shows the hero drawn at the picture's view, plus the back when the picture did not show it, one image
    per view. The same happens after every `update_character` on that hero, so the agent compares its render with the
    picture and moves one word at a time.
  - It draws with a browser already on the machine and never downloads one. Without one, it says so and gives the
    World page.
- **Likeness is the model's judgment.**
  - For identifiably trademarked work, the agent offers an "X-like" build: the spirit and the look are kept; the name,
    the emblems and the signature details are changed. It negotiates that with the person.
  - The hero carries the verdict as a `reference` word (`original` or `x-like`, what it is like, what changed). An
    x-like hero's readout captions it "X-like: inspired by …".
  - Nothing refuses on it. The person can edit the word or take it off.
- **Sculpting stays the person's.** After the capture, the hero is shaped prompt by prompt like any other. A second
  picture (`stash_ref`) refines it word by word, but never moves a word the person changed by hand since the last pass;
  `replace: true` takes the new read whole.
- **Non-human hair, coated like an animal.** The anime head's shaped hair now builds what no hair word reached, each
  style wearing a coat:
  - `gorgon`: thick bending tendrils, scaled like a snake;
  - `flame`: rising strands, hot at the root and pale at the tips;
  - `feathered`: swept, barred vanes with a crest;
  - `leafy`: cupped leaves;
  - `tentacled`: heavy curling falls with a pale, spotted underside;
  - `quilled`: raking, banded cones.

  Each is a `look` word any anime hero can wear, and the character target's protocol names them for non-human pictures.
  A coat is the beast-kin's own grammar read down each lock as down a tail: `coat: 'snake' | 'tiger' | 'barred' |
  'ember' | 'leaf' | 'banded'` on the shapes, a layer or a piece, or `{ from?, color?, cover?, pattern? }`. Covers are
  scales, fur, chitin or feathers, shading the lock on the page; patterns are stripes as rings, spots, a pale underside,
  dark tips, a line down the lock. The page draws the locks' coat beside the face's own paint. A hair with no coat
  draws exactly as before.
- **Xeno make-up: practical-effects alien appliances on any head.** A new hero word, `xenoHeaddress`, puts a make-up
  crew's pieces on the hero: sculpted, glued on with edges blended into the skin, and painted. It works on the landmark,
  the anime and the realistic head alike. Each piece is found on that head's own skin and pinned to it, so it turns and
  exports with the head.

  The quickest start is a STARTER SPECIES: `xenoSpecies` gives a skull, the appliances on it and the skin's colour in
  one word. The species are `grey-visitor`, `ridged-warrior`, `ridge-nosed`, `lekku-dancer`, `montral-hunter`,
  `crested-diplomat`, `plated-insectoid`, `cone-elder`, `brain-invader`, `domed-telepath` and `horn-crowned`, and the five
  below. Each says
  what it recalls. It also sets the eyes and the build in the words of the head the hero wears:
  - on the landmark head, its face (eye size and spacing, jaw, mouth) and a tune;
  - on the anime head, its face (eye width and height, iris, spacing, tilt) and an anime body for the hero's sex;
  - on the realistic head, the face's eye shape and a physique;
  - on every head, the eyes' colours: the sclera, the iris and the pupil (a grey's eyes all black, an insectoid's gold
    on dark).

  The person's own appliances, face, build and colours win over the species': their face is laid after the species'.
  The record keeps the species as one word, and the readout says what it gave on that head and what else reads it
  (markings, dress).

  The face has pieces of its own, on any head, found at its features:
  - markings, painted transfers flush with the skin, on the realistic head too: tear lines, brow chevrons, cheek
    stripes, a forehead mark, tribal lines, a pale mask, spot trails, a chin stripe;
  - ears: pointed or long tips glued to the top-back of the ear, long lobes, or no ears at all;
  - noses: a snout, flared or slit nostrils, a beak, a nose horn, with `nostrils` sizing the openings;
  - a third eye on the forehead: a lidded eye, an upright slit eye, a gem or a cluster of three, coloured by the eyes'
    own colours;
  - teeth: fangs, sabre fangs and tusks.

  Five more species use them: `pointed-eared`, `tusked-brute`, `three-eyed-seer`, `snouted-guard` and `beaked-avian`.
  The older ones gained markings and lost ears where their kind has none.

  A head that is not a person's shape starts from a SKULL: a cranial prosthetic glued over the actor's own, its edge
  feathered into the skin, over a bald cap. The skulls are `tall-cranium`, `cone-skull`, `bilobed-brain`, `domed-brow`,
  `keeled-skull`, `wide-temples` and `segmented-skull`. A hero wears one at most. It is laid first and every other card
  lands on it, so a ridged brow sits on a domed brow and horns rise from a cone.

  The other cards, named for what they are:
  - `forehead-ridges`: curving ridges up the forehead to the hairline;
  - `nose-ridges`: a stack of fine ridges across the nose's bridge;
  - `head-tails`: two thick tails from the back of the skull, over a bald cap;
  - `swept-horns`: two hollow horns rising from the top of the head and sweeping back;
  - `front-tails`: two head-tails from behind the temples, falling forward over the shoulders, over a bald cap;
  - `horned-tails`: swept horns, two front tails and one down the back, banded pale over dark, over a bald cap;
  - `chitin-crest`: two broad lobes off the brow that arch over the skull and fall beside the face to the shoulders
    like a hood. Each lobe's front is a hard, ribbed shell of plates, its back soft flesh, over a bald cap;
  - `cheek-ridges`: a fine ridge down each cheek.

  A protrusion no card names is written whole: `{ family: 'horn' | 'tail' | 'lobe', at: { az, el }, … }` grows a
  horn, a tail or a flat lobe from an address on the cap. It is shaped by its length, width and tip, a lift up or down off the skin, a sweep
  back, a spread out, and a droop under its own weight. Below the chin a tail falls on its own side of the body, held off
  it, and `pair` grows its mirror. `over` makes it hug the head first, carried over the cap a set distance off the skin.
  A lobe's `plates` lay hard ridges across its front: they wear the `shell` coat (chitin, say) and the lobe wears the
  soft `coat`. Every card is built in the same grammar.

  Each card says what screen alien it recalls, for the X-like stamp of a character read from a picture. `size` scales
  a card. `coat` paints it in the hair coat's grammar, the skin's own colour by default. `replaces: 'hair'` lays a bald
  cap that every head builds by its own rules; on the realistic skin, the scalp is painted bare (the dermis's
  `bareScalp`). The readout's `xeno` says what was placed where; the hero card's `hero-xeno` section and the character
  protocol name it.

  The coats of locks and appliances also draw in the World page's clip preview, on every head: alone on the landmark
  head, and stacked under the painted face's or the realistic skin's atlas on the others. An export's figure carries no
  coat yet.

### Fighter wiring: the muscular body under the realistic head, a boxer's basic moves, and a bout

The seams between the studio's fighter pieces, stitched so a fighting game's character can be made from the hero door: a
body codename and its muscle shirt under the realistic head, its skin painted and its face rigged, dressed, throwing a
boxer's basic punches. The test fighter is `control/scripts/spikes/fighter/` (its spec and how to play it in hero-live).
Every hero naming none of the new words is the hero it was. The eyes gate is the operator's.

- **A body codename under another head** (`anime-bodies.js`, `layered.js`): `animeBody` (Toji, Mizuki, Satoru, Maki,
  Armstrong, Kale, Shonen High) is worn under the landmark or the realistic head on the lofted body, as under the anime
  head: its tune laid under the hero's own, `muscleShirt` its card. It is worn on the frame it was drawn on (the anime
  frame, `proportions: 'anime'` stamped at mint unless the spec names proportions), since its ratios on the hero cast's
  thicker baseline stood a tenth heavier, the forearm a club over a narrow wrist and a hand not sized to it; the head
  keeps the hero cast's size, and the stamp's fit is null (no anime style sizes it). The realistic body refuses a
  codename by name (its build is its physique); a blank head refuses it.
- **The realistic head on the lofted body**: `head: 'relational'` without `form: 'realistic'` is swapped in on the
  lofted body as it stands after the muscle shirt (`relationalHeadWorn`, the realistic body's own swap, refactored out),
  with its face words, its `skin`, its scalp, its face's hair and its piercings; its realistic laws stamped as `headLaws`.
  The lofted neck (a dozen slots) stood as a faceted post under the head, whose skin is joined to the neck's column, so
  it is densified first on its smooth cage at the muscle shirt's grain (`musculature/passes.js densify`). Its skin is
  painted in an export and on the World page, its face rig plays, and it is lit as the realistic body is (the gates in
  `world-kinds.js` read the realistic skin, not the form).
- **A boxer's arced punches** (`polygonizer/hero-box.js`, the door's `motion`): `hook` (the lead hand), `uppercut` (the
  rear) and `bodyHook`, each `…Left`, beside `jab` and `cross`. Each is one strike of space boxer (`hero-reach.js`) at a
  MARK on an opponent from the guard: his chin or his ribs on the line between the fighters at the attacker's own
  heights, as far ahead as a share of the striking arm's reach (aimed off the shoulder instead, a bladed guard's turned
  trunk put the uppercut beside the opponent's head). The knuckles are driven along the family's arc into contact and
  carried 6 cm through it (`follow`), at the hero's own strike speed, a move between keys as short as 12 ms (`step`):
  the drill's touch held on the target and its 40 ms floor capped a hand at 2 m/s, so the hook had landed at a seventh
  of the jab's speed; it lands at about 6 m/s now. `seconds` stretches the timing. Its laws are its checks on the clip as
  played: landed within 5 mm, the knuckles square to the approach, no servo past a stop, balanced over the feet, the hand
  at contact two thirds of its fastest over its drive, the guarding arm out of the trunk. `targetDrill` takes `aimed`
  targets (a direction or a point), `follow` and `step`; a seeded drill draws and times as before.
- **Blows taken in the guard** (`hero-react.js`): `guardHitHigh`, `guardHitBody`, `guardHitLow`, `guardStagger`, the same
  blows out of the `guard` stance's held pose and back to it (its feet, its sink, its fists), the blow's shoulders whole;
  the plain words start and end on the relaxed stand, so a fighter dropped its hands before the punch landed.
- **Blocks** (`hero-react.js`): `block` (the high guard absorbing a punch: the gloves driven back toward the face, the
  chin tucked, the body rocked back, the knees giving) and `blockBody` (the elbows dropped onto the ribs, the trunk
  curled over them), each a change over the hero's own guard and home to it, as the fight's block is; with the guard's
  blows, their laws `solid`, `planted`, `ends`. A bout plays a block where a punch lands on a glove or a forearm.
- **Two bodies kept apart** (`polygonizer/hero-pushbox.js`, a fighting game's pushbox in the round): each fighter's body
  as capsules on its skeleton (the trunk, the head, the thighs, the shins, the upper arms; never the forearms and the
  gloves, which are meant to meet), each radius read off its own skin, and the least one must be pushed back along the
  line so none passes into the other's. No imports, so a page or an engine's runtime loads it as it is. The bout gives
  the defender a knockback on contact (less on a block) and the pushbox's push on top, never coming back in (folding
  over the body hook, his head had gone into the attacker's shoulder).
- **The body kept solid under its arms** (`polygonizer/hero-solid.js`): a clip's arm is never let deeper into the trunk
  than the stance it starts from holds it; past that, its shoulder is turned the least that brings it back, frame by
  frame (curved on their own, a shoulder's angles took a flung arm through the chest: the operator saw it in a bout).
  Worn by the blows taken in the guard and the arced punches' guarding arm, each with the law `solid`. The arm's
  clearance and the solver moved to a leaf module (`hero-lm.js`, re-exported by `hero-grip.js`) so the motion library
  can load it.
- **The bout** (`control/scripts/spikes/fighter/bout.mjs`, `bout-shot.mjs`): two minted fighters' GLBs squared up on one
  page, each punch into the defender's reaction, the defender stepped in until the glove's travel into contact meets
  his skin, his block or his hit by what it lands on, the knockback and the pushbox through the exchange (`--push off`
  to compare); the read says what each punch lands on, the range, the height, the speed, the reaction and how far the
  bodies would have passed into each other. A second fighter's spec:
  `test-opponent.json`.
- **A character's own strikes in the fight** (`versus/versus-hero.js`, the versus roster's `moves`): a fighter who is a
  character (`{ hero: { ref }, moves: 'hero' }`, or `{ <slot>: a strike }`) throws the punches it was made with in the
  fight sim's slots (the boxer's: `stand.L` the jab, `stand.M` the cross, `stand.H` the hook, `crouch.M` the body hook,
  `crouch.H` the uppercut) and stands in its own guard. Each strike is solved on the character's rig where it is
  measured, its skeleton seen from the side in the fight plane and read back as the sim's own pose angles (a segment
  seen end-on, the hook's forearm crossing the body, filled from where it is seen), and carried as a track; the
  compiler (`compileHeroNormal`) RETIMES it to the slot's frame data, as a fighting game's animation is authored to its
  frames, and lays its boxes on the fighter's body (the hurtboxes, the fist's hit box on the active frames). In the sim
  its jab hits a standing opponent and is blocked by one holding back, at the advantage it records. A fighter's walk is
  its guard's, the legs striding. Without `moves`, every fighter is compiled as before. The frame-data sheet:
  `control/scripts/spikes/fighter/frames.mjs` (each move's key frames, its boxes and its frame data, the tradition's
  keyed move beside the character's own).
- **The real models in the arena** (`versus-character.js` `characterBody`, `versus-arena.client.js`): a fighter throwing
  its own strikes is drawn as it was made, not as the arena's stand-in (rigid parts in flat vertex colours posed from the
  plane, inked; a realistic skin came out white). Its body is PLAYED: one skinned mesh of its parts (their joints and
  weights), its painted skin over it (the atlas and each part's UVs), and its own clips (the strikes, the guard, the
  blows and blocks taken in it, the knockdown and the rise), solved on its rig from the door's motion words laid onto
  its record for the bake (the row is not changed). Each frame the sim's state names the clip and its moment: a move
  its own clip at the share its compiled frame records (`u`, the retiming's), a blow or a block through the stun, a
  knockdown, else the guard held. What it has no clip of (a throw, a special) is the fight's own pose on its body.
- **Every style on its own body** (`versus-character.js` TRADITION_CLIPS, `versus-arena.client.js` `placeFromPose`): a
  character fighting with a tradition's keyed moves (karate, kung fu, …) is played in its own body too, not the posed
  rigid figure: its skinned, painted, lit pack, each bone riding its segment of the figure the fight's pose makes
  (`figureSegments`, as the rigid parts did), its hands (the wrist, the fingers) as its guard clip holds them on the
  forearm, so a fist stays a fist through a punch and a kick. The watch's CPUs fight at a level the picks name (`cpu`:
  novice | regular | veteran | ace; veteran as before). Two more test fighters: `test-karate.json` (Toji in a white
  gi) and `test-kungfu.json` (Mizuki in a red top and black martial trousers); `arena-gameplay.mjs` takes each one's
  tradition, name, the moves (`hero` | `tradition`) and the CPU's level. A character, drawn as it was made, pushes with
  its stance's legs whatever its moves (`bodyPush: 'legs'` on its recipe: a karateka's long stance had crossed the kung
  fu fighter's), and a body out cold lies on its back (`versus-react.js` LIMP: its rear arm had been turned into the
  floor, which propped the trunk 70 cm up on its fist, on the flat page as in the arena). And the arena's fight runs at
  its own speed: the page hands its frame step its clock in milliseconds (`__mojStep`, as the fx channel reads it), and
  the fight had read them as seconds, a drawn frame's 16 ms capped at 0.1 s, six fight frames a drawn frame: every
  arena fight had played at six times its speed (the court arena's stepper, `match-arena.client.js`, reads its clock
  the same way, not changed here).
- **The ring: an arena that shows its fighters as they were made** (`versus-arena.js` `set: 'ring'`, ARENA_SETS): a
  boxing ring the arena builds on its floor (a raised canvas, its apron, four corner posts and their pads, the ropes on
  three sides, the camera's side open as a ring is shot) in a nave fallen into the dark (a veil behind the far ropes:
  the hall's surfaces are baked and take no fog), the fight's walls the ropes' and its floor the canvas, the camera in
  close (a fighter near two thirds of the picture). A fight made now opens in it, before the plaza and the nave. A
  played body is drawn where the fight has it, but two are never drawn into each other: a knockdown's clip slides its
  root back to its origin from 0.8 m ahead (inside the opponent), and the fight flies the fall itself, so its slide is
  taken off; a body held in a throw (boxing's clinch, 36 cm off the thrower's pelvis in the fight) is drawn back to
  where the push boxes touch (the fight itself unchanged). A character standing in its own guard pushes with its legs
  too (`pushOf`, its lead knee and ankle ahead, its rear ones behind, a limb's radius beyond): a boxer's bladed stance
  puts the lead knee a third of a metre ahead of the pelvis, and two at the trunks' contact (61 cm apart) had their legs
  crossed; they stand 71 cm apart now, the lead legs passing on either side. A fighter in the tradition's stances
  pushes as before.
- **Fighters lit as an engine lights them**: a played fighter's pack is the lit export's (its albedo unshaded, each
  corner's normal, the skin's relief and its full-size atlas, `lit`), drawn in a lit material under the fighters' own
  lights (a warm key, a cool fill, a rim, a sky; on the ring a spot over the canvas); the page's pack had baked a studio
  light into its colours and drawn it unlit, so the muscles read flat and the seams between its parts showed.
- **A fighting game with your own characters, by default** (the quick `fight` goal's `strikes`): a fight made now is
  stamped `strikes: 'own'`, so a boxer (`tradition: 'boxing'`), a sheet the run makes into a character or one already
  made, throws its own punches (`moves: 'hero'` on its entry in the game's roster and each arena's); every other
  fighter keeps its style's or its tradition's moves (a grappler's own punches had overwritten five of its slots), and
  every character is played in its own body either way; `strikes: 'tradition'` keeps the keyed moves for all, a
  fighter's own `moves` win, and a fight minted before carries none and fights as it did. The fight goal's card says it.
- **The fighter's body rail**: `lowerBody` keeps the `muscular` rail's anime codename under a hero spec that names the
  realistic head (that pair was refused before), and leaves it off the landmark head as before.
- **Seen, not fixed**: the realistic head's neck on the codename's frame is an ordinary man's (386 mm on Toji; the anime
  head's neck form gives Toji 449 mm); the `guard` stand's lead forearm sinks about 2 cm into Toji's chest (the mint's
  advisory names it); `jab` and `cross` (stored clips, a laws bump away) aim at the attacker's shoulder height and dig
  the guarding arm up to 6 cm deeper into the trunk than the guard holds it; the pushbox and the knockback live in the
  bout page and the module, not yet in a game's runtime (the versus arena keeps its own); in the fight, a character's
  own strikes pay no reach tax yet (the tradition's keyed jab is a frame slower) and its crouch slots' strikes are
  thrown standing (it is drawn standing in a crouch too); a tradition's move on a real body is the fight's side-view
  pose turned into each segment's turn (no forearm roll the plane does not see; the hand held as the guard holds it,
  so an open-handed strike lands a fist).

### The game design studio, abstracted: the book in chapters, the compile bounded, each level checked a step at a time

A game book's run (`design_game` `run: true`) made every ready step in one call, and the last of them, the game, walked
every level in headless Chrome inside create_game. On the meadowmark reference book (five stages), one call took six
minutes, and the walks were 71% of it (a level's walk alone is 20–60 s). A book of ten levels could not finish inside one
tool call, so an agent session timed out on the compile. This is the first step of a larger change: the design steps
become chapters each department works alone, so the compile is one loop that makes what was designed.

- **A run has a budget** (`design-game.js` `RUN_BUDGET_MS`, about two minutes; `MOJULO_RUN_BUDGET_MS` sets it, 0 for
  none). Once it is spent, the run starts no new step. It says the steps it left as `pending`, keeps the record of what
  it made, and its next move is `{ step: 'run', pending }`. The next run takes up where it stopped. Each run makes at
  least one step, and no step is cut partway. The world a run leaves is the same however many calls it took.
- **Each level is walked in its own step, when a run checks.** The game is made at once (unaudited, create_game's
  waiver), and a run walks levels only when it asks (`check: true`, from the book-powers theme: a run compiles). After the
  game, a game
  whose levels the audit can prove (reach or survive) has one `audit-level-<level>-<n>` step per level
  (`gameworld/runner.js` `auditSteps`). Each walks that level (`create-game.js` `auditGameLevel`, in an installed browser,
  never a download) and keeps its verdict in the record (`made.<key>.verdict`). A level remade is walked again (a remade
  game was never re-audited before); a level that did not move is not. A walk that no browser could take is said as
  skipped and taken once a browser can. The readout counts them: `audits: { gate: 'machine', proved, of, unproved }`.
- **The first frame renders once a run.** It renders for the levels made or remade, or for all of them when something
  they all show moved. Before, create_game rendered every level and design_game rendered them all again.
- **Measured** on meadowmark with real Chrome: the compile now takes two calls, 224 s and 157 s, where it was one call of
  374 s (the same work, 381 s in all). A call holds its budget, the one step it started before the budget ran out (a
  walk is up to a minute) and the first frames of the levels it made, so its length no longer grows with the book.
- A game made before this is remade once on its next run, in place (its order no longer carries `auto_audit`), and its
  levels are walked after it. No level, hero or game kernel moved: the composed-world and meadowmark order pins hold as
  they were.
- **The book in chapters** (`gameworld/chapters.js`). Each page of the game book is a chapter, and each chapter sits in
  one of the studio's six departments. A chapter's contract names the recipe paths it owns, the review parts it answers,
  the steps a run makes for it, the cards it is written from, the chapters upstream it reads, and the rail outcome its
  parts are drawn under. It is derived from what the book already is (the guide's loop, the readers' parts, the runner's
  steps, the ready table), not a new rule. A guard test (`chapters.test.js`) gives every recipe key, every review part,
  every step a run lays (one world per procedure that lays its own) and every card exactly one chapter, so a new page
  that joins no department fails. The rail's grouping of parts is read from it (`partOutcome`), which now also shows the
  casting page (`characters:cast`), a part the rail used to leave out.
- **The readout says the chapters** (`design_game` `chapters`): each chapter the world holds, with its department, its
  state (open, advised, settled, or written for pages with no review of their own), how many of its parts are settled,
  the ones still open once some are, and the chapters upstream it `waits` on. The orchestrating agent reads the book a
