  chapter at a time and hands a department its own chapter; the `gameworld-next` card says so.
- **Fixed: a town's people kept in the record.** A run made a town's folk (`folk-<town>-<who>`), but the record reader
  refused the key, so a world with folk could not be read again after its run. The guard test found it.
- **A chapter's own readout** (`design_game({ ref, chapter })`, `gameworld/chapter-view.js`). The whole readout projected
  onto one chapter, so the two never disagree: its parts with their stamps and advice, its pages (the recipe at its
  paths, a deeper chapter's keys left to that chapter), the chapters upstream it reads as a digest (each one's state and
  the print of its pages, so a department sees when upstream moved without reading it), its own next moves (a review of
  its parts, a wait on it, a form ask for it; a run left pending is every chapter's), what a run made for it, its place
  in its bible, and the whole book as one word a chapter. On the meadowmark reference book a chapter's view is 0.8 to 2.6
  KB with its pages, where the whole readout is 7.2 KB without any. A write outside the chapter is written and said
  (`outside`), never refused. Every part of the book is in exactly one chapter's view (tested), and every next move the
  `gameworld-next` card documents belongs to a chapter. The tools/list payload holds under its pin.
- **A chapter's run** (`design_game({ ref, chapter, run: true })`, `chapters.js` `chapterSteps`). A department checks its
  chapter without making the whole book. The run makes the chapter's own steps and every step their orders name: a
  level's pilot, the foes and folk standing in it, a cast member's casting row, the hero the systems name. A step that
  waits on approvals is made ahead of them and says so (`ahead`: the parts it did not wait for). It is made at its own ref
  from its own order, so the build keeps it when its approvals come and the book has not moved, and remakes it when the
  book has (tested: a gated book's levels made ahead, then approved and built, are kept, not remade). A level can be
  checked, and its first frame read, before the characters are approved. The build is never a need (no game, no walks),
  and the build chapter's run is the whole run. A chapter's run does not report the compiler's resonance gaps, which
  belong to the whole run.
- **The pre-compile check** (`design-game-check.js`, the readout's `compile`, machine gate). It finds what a run would hit
  before anything is made, where it used to surface minutes into the run after the steps before it were made. It reads
  the run's plan, and each order as its door would read it where that check is cheap and needs nothing made:
  - every hero-door spec, for the hero, its cast, its foes and its folk;
  - every level's houses and bodies;
  - the game as create_game makes it, over the planned levels: its manifest, each level's contract dry-run against the
    game's store, its links and its menu;
  - every sketch an order names, which must be one a step makes or one that is stored (an adopted hero with no row, a
    building played by a ref that is gone).

  A refused plan is said on the chapter its field belongs to. Each blocker names its chapter: the build's view sees them
  whole, and each other chapter sees its own, with a `compile` next move. It also prices the build left (what a run makes
  now and what waits on approvals) at the step times measured on the reference book, divided by the run's budget, as
  `estimate: { seconds, calls }`: an order of size, not a promise. It runs on a run and on a chapter's view, never on a
  plain read; it advises, and a run goes ahead whatever it says. The world door's full resolve and the gear's workbench
  are not run, since they need what the run makes.
- **A climb's top is in reach** (`gameworld/levels.js` `climbLadders`). Two of the five meadowmark levels were never
  proved, and the reason was in the level, not the audit: each is a climb (a local meru) whose exit is its tower's
  deck, up a ladder. The meru draws a stand-in ladder ("until playscape's ladder stands there"), and the hero's platform
  rule climbs only a `climbable` entity, which nothing laid. So the hero could reach the summit but not the deck, and the
  level could not be finished. A climb's game level now lays, after its other entities, the climbable surface that
  playscape's ladder lowers for each climb site. A level with no climb is as it was. The reference books' order pins
  moved by the ladders alone, and each order without its ladders keeps the print it had (tested).
- **The audit walks a climb its own way up** (`levels.js` `climbRoute`, `motion/world-frames.js`). The walker steers by
  x,y, so a walk straight to a climb's top stood on a lower tier under it, and its leg "arrived". A level whose exit is
  off the ground is now walked by its climb's flights in height order, then by a climb leg for each ladder: stand off
  its foot on the climber's side, then walk into it until the climb rule mounts the lip. The climb leg is new in the
  traversal compiler. It runs Node-side, so no page changes, and the greedy walk leg's stuck check, which reads x,y
  progress, could not drive a climb. The audit steps take every level's walk again, once (their order names the walk).
  Measured with a real browser on the meadowmark book: all five levels proved (machine gate), where three were, in three
  calls of 186, 125 and 84 s.
- **An unproved walk says where it stopped** (`create-game.js` `auditGameLevel`, `auto-audit-runner.js` `runLevelWalk`):
  the leg that stopped and where, or, if every leg arrived, where the walker stood against the exit. A climb no walker can
  take is said as such.
- **A level that cannot be finished is said before the build** (the pre-compile check's `advises`, by chapter). A level
  whose exit is up a ladder, piloted first person (a world with no hero is walked by a walker, whose rule does not
  climb), is made but cannot be finished. The check says so on the levels chapter: give the world a hero, or end the
  level on a tier its stairs reach. The walker's climbing is the runtime's to add, and is not in this change.
- **A run that checks stays inside its budget.** The book-powers theme made checking opt-in (`check: true`), but a
  checking run still walked every level inside create_game's one call. Merged with this theme, a checking run walks
  each level as its own audit step, under the run's budget, its verdict kept. A run that does not check leaves the walks
  out, its earlier verdicts still read, and the pre-compile estimate does not price them. Each level's first frame is
  the book-powers theme's per-level record, judged again only when its row moves.
- **The studio card** (`gameworld-studio`, read after the guide; the guide's book line points at it). It teaches the agent
  how to work a game of several departments a chapter at a time, and it is generated from the chapter registry, so its
  order is the chapters' own. The waves (`chapters.js` `chapterWaves`) group the chapters so each wave reads only the
  waves before it: a wave's chapters can be worked side by side, a department or a subagent each, and the build is
  last. A chapter's session reads its view, writes its own pages, shows its bible section to the creator (the verdicts
  are the creator's: a subagent stops at the review and reports), proves its chapter with a chapter run, and is done
  when its state is settled and its blockers are cleared or said. The build reads the pre-compile check, runs until
  nothing is pending, and checks; the eyes gate is the creator playing it.
- **The cinematics department.** The registry's fifth department is renamed from cameras and cutscenes to `cinematics`,
  as the studio now names it. The story and camera chapters are its own, and a readout's `department` says
  `cinematics`.

### The rail shelf: primitives for locomotive transit, from the front of a train

- **The rail shelf** (`control/lib/graph/rail-shelf/`): primitives for locomotive transit, on the vehicle ODM's pattern
  (`car-designer/vehicle-odm.js`: a brief solved into a frame held to laws, compiled to named surfaces, composed by
  card). It starts at the front of a train, the cab car.
  - **The grammar** (`cab-odm.js`, `solveCabDesign`): an archetype, one per front form a train is drawn with (a metro
    car's flat front, a streetcar's rounded front over its low floor, a regional unit's raked crash nose, a high-speed
    power car's long nose, a box-cab electric locomotive's flat cab), solved into one frame (its length, width, height,
    floor, nose, wheels and axles, bogies) within each number's band, a seed exploring a small band and an explicit
    dimension winning. Its body's **section**: its half-width at each height above the rail, undercut from the skirt to
    the waist, leaning in by its tumblehome, round its cant rail, over its roof's crown. Its **front**: a field over that
    section, how far ahead of the nose's root it stands at each point (its side profile by height, its plan's corners
    by how square they are), meeting the body exactly at the side. Its laws: inside a generic loading gauge, the
    driver's eye inside the screen, the screen under the roof, the coupler at its height, the section ordered, the
    front ahead of its root, the wheels under the body.
  - **The surface** (`cab-surface.js`, `compileCabSurface`): the sides the section extruded, the front the field gridded
    on the same rows so every corner where they meet is shared, its rows, columns and stations snapped to every part's
    edge so each quad is one part: the screen (a mullion parting two panes), its frame and the dark mask round it, the
    lit destination sign, the livery band, the roof and the skirt; the driver's side window, a window band, bays or a
    locomotive's louvres, the doors and their windows and seams; headlamps and tail lamps on the front's own surface, a
    high lamp, wipers; the coupler (automatic, covered, or a buffer beam's buffers and hook), the anticlimber, a
    plough; the roof's units, the gangway at the far end; two bogies, each two wheelsets on the gauge with their axles,
    side frames, axle boxes, springs and bolster. Finished with materials by part (the vehicle ODM's, a lit sign over
    them), crease-aware normals and a census, at a game, studio or hero level of detail.
  - **The cards** (`cab-library.js`, `composeCab`): a metro cab car, a streetcar front module, a regional cab car, a
    high-speed power car and a box-cab locomotive, each in a generic livery.
  - `scripts/render-rail.mjs` draws each card on a stretch of track in the vehicle ODM's physically lit review page.
  - Held (`cab.test.js`): each front form solved within its laws; the seed's band, an explicit dimension winning, a
    number out of its band or an unknown word refused; the section continuous, widest at its waist, nothing at its top;
    the front meeting the sides at its root and ahead of it; the seams shared and the halves mirrored; the screen
    where the driver's eye is; the lamps on the front's surface below the screen; a mullion's panes; each coupler where
    its kind puts it; the wheels on the rail, on the gauge, inside the body; every face a named material; the same brief
    the same bytes; a finer level more triangles.
- **The bogies** (`bogie-odm.js`, `bogie-surface.js`): a bogie solved from a brief and compiled the same way as the cab.
  - **The grammar** (`solveBogieDesign`): an archetype (a metro motor and its trailer, a streetcar's, a regional motor,
    a high-speed, a freight car's three-piece truck, a locomotive's two-axle and three-axle) solved into its axles,
    wheel and wheelbase; the wheel's profile on the gauge (its back to back, its width, its flange, its tread's taper,
    scaled to the gauge asked for); its axle boxes, its frame (an H-frame over the boxes, dipping between the axles, or
    a three-piece's cast side frames), its primary and secondary suspension, its drive, brakes and dampers, and the
    pivot's height the body sits on. Its laws: the wheels on the gauge, the axles apart, the frame clear of the wheels
    and the rail, the envelope, the pivot over the frame.
  - **The surface** (`compileBogieSurface`): each wheel revolved from its profile (the tread named where it meets the
    rail, a mark on its web), the axles, the axle boxes and their covers; the side beams and transoms, or the side
    frames' members, columns and pedestal jaws and the bolster through them with its centre bowl; coil primaries as
    helices or a tram's rubber chevrons; air springs revolved from their bellows, coil pairs, a locomotive's
    flexicoils, a freight truck's spring nests and friction wedges; the pivot block; frame-mounted motors and their
    gearboxes or nose-suspended motors; brake discs and calipers, tread blocks, a tram's track brake shoes over the
    rails, a locomotive's sand pipes; vertical, lateral and yaw dampers; on a leading bogie its lifeguards. Poses: the
    wheels' `spin` (the marks and discs turning with them) and the bogie's `yaw` about its pivot; its hardpoints (the
    pivot, each wheel's contact with the rail, the axles).
  - **The cab car on them:** its two bogies drawn from the shelf on its seed, the leading one with its lifeguards, the
    trailing one turned end for end; its wheels and wheelbase the leading bogie's; a new law that its bogies' pivots sit
    under its floor (a low floor's bogies under its raised ends). `scripts/render-rail.mjs` takes a bogie's archetype as
    a preset and draws it alone on its track, swung and spun.
  - The shelf's geometry and finish (faces turned out, boxes, prisms, discs, solids of revolution about either axis,
    materials by part) are shared in `rail-geom.js`.
  - Held (`bogie.test.js`): each frame, axle count and drive solved within its laws, its axles spaced on its wheelbase;
    the wheels' back to back on any gauge and the tread's contact between the flange's root and the outer face; an
    explicit dimension winning, a number out of band or an unknown word refused; the treads meeting the rail at the
    gauge's half, the flanges inboard and below the rail's top; the frame clear of every wheel and of the rail; each
    archetype's springs, drive and brakes where it puts them; the lifeguards on a leading bogie alone; the spin turning
    the wheels and nothing else, the yaw turning the bogie about its pivot; the same brief the same bytes, a finer
    level more triangles; a cab car on its bogies under its floor, its wheels on the rail.
- **The pantographs** (`panto-odm.js`, `panto-surface.js`) and **the overhead line** (`catenary.js`).
  - **The grammar** (`solvePantoDesign`): a mainline single-arm pantograph, a streetcar's smaller arm, the older diamond,
    a trolley pole, each solved into its arms, its base on its insulators, its head (its width, its two carbon strips,
    their spacing, its horns) and its working range, held to laws: folded low on the roof, its range over its class's
    roof covering its class's wire band, its arms able to close, a single arm's head riding near over its hinge.
  - **The kinematics** (`pantoPose`): a pose's `raise` (folded to its highest), or `wire` (the head raised until its
    strips meet a contact wire that high, as far as its arms reach, saying whether it did): a single arm's knee where
    the circles of its two arms about the hinge and the head meet, leading; a diamond's knees its lozenge's sides; a
    pole's angle the one that reaches the wire.
  - **The surface** (`compilePantoSurface`): the insulators revolved with their sheds, the base frame, the drive (a single
    arm's air bellows, a diamond's springs, a pole's sprung swivel), the lower arm's converging tubes and its guide rod,
    the upper arm, the pan head's bar, its strips and its curled horns and the springs under it; a pole, its harp and its
    wheel. Its hardpoints (its mount, its contact), its joint (the raise); turned end for end by its facing.
  - **The catenary** (`compileCatenary`): a contact wire at its height over a stretch of track, staggered either side
    of the track's centre mast to mast (`wireAt`), its messenger sagging over it on droppers, the masts beside the track
    and their cantilevers and insulators; a tramway's a single wire on its spans.
  - **The cab car carries them:** each archetype's pantographs on its roof's crown at their places along it, facing
    their way (none on a metro car), raised by the cab's pose (`raise`, or `wire` over the rail), the roof's units kept
    clear of them; its laws now hold its pantographs folded inside an electrified gauge's pantograph zone and raised
    over their class's highest wire, and its bogies inside its body (which moved the high-speed car's bogie back from
    under its narrowing nose). `scripts/render-rail.mjs` runs a cab with pantographs under a catenary, its pantographs
    raised to it, and takes a pantograph's kind as a preset, folded, half raised and raised to its wire.
  - Held (`panto.test.js`): each kind within its laws, its range over its class's roof covering its band; a single
    arm's knee on both arms' circles and ahead of its head, the head rising with the raise; a diamond's sides its arms;
    a pole's tip its length out, trailing; a wire met when in reach, clamped and said when not; the strips' top at the
    contact, the insulators under the frame, the facing turning it end for end; folded and raised differing in the arms
    alone; the same pose the same bytes; a catenary's wire at its height, staggered mast to mast, a tramway's without a
    messenger; a cab car's pantographs folded inside the zone and raised to the wire, a car without them carrying none.
- **The cars behind the cab, and the train they make** (`solveCarDesign`, `compileCarSurface`, `composeTrain`): the
  rail shelf's cars on the cab car's pattern, a brief solved into one frame held to laws.
  - **The cars** (`car-odm.js`): a metro car, a streetcar's short module hung between its neighbours and its centre
    module on its own bogie, a regional car, a high-speed coach, a locomotive-hauled coach, and the freight wagons (a
    box wagon, a covered hopper, a tank wagon, a flat wagon with a container). A passenger car takes its body's section
    from its family's cab car of the same seed, so a train is one section from end to end; a coach and a wagon carry
    their own. Its doors spread along it, at its ends, near one end or in its middle; its bogies two at its overhangs,
    one under its middle, or none; its laws: the gauge, the doors on the body, the bogies under it and under its floor.
  - **The shell** (`body-shell.js`): the section's rows, the window lights between the ends and the doors, what a side's
    quad is (a door, its glass and its seams, a window, the band, the roof, the skirt), the sides extruded, a flat end,
    a streetcar's articulation ring; the cab car's body and the cars' are drawn by it alike.
  - **The surface** (`compileCarSurface`): a passenger car's sides, doors, windows, underframe, end walls and roof unit;
    a wagon's by its body (a box wagon's ribs and its sliding doors on their rails, a hopper's sides falling in to its
    gates, a tank's barrel on its cradles with its dished ends, dome and walkway, a flat wagon's deck, stanchions and a
    container in a seeded colour); its ends' gear (a gangway's bellows and its bar coupler, buffers and a screw coupler
    on their beam, an articulation's bellows ring) as deep as their kind (`END_DEPTH`); its bogies from the bogie shelf.
    The cab car now carries the same gear at its rear, by its kind.
  - **The train** (`composeTrain`, `TRAIN_PLANS`): a family's composition, its cab at the front, its cars, and a unit's
    cab turned end for end at its tail; laid out nose to tail with the gap its ends' gear needs; its laws: ends couple
    only kind to kind, every car valid, a unit's cars its own family's (a locomotive hauls anything its buffers meet).
    `scripts/render-rail.mjs` takes a car's kind as a preset and `train:<family>` for a whole train (its side, a
    quarter, a coupling, its tail; under a catenary when it carries pantographs).
  - Held (`car.test.js`): each bogie arrangement and each wagon body within its laws; a passenger car's section its
    cab car's; the bogies two, one or none where they belong, the wheels on the rail; the doors and windows between the
    ends; a wagon's end gear as far out as its kind's depth; a train's cars nose to tail with the gap their ends need,
    its rear cab turned with its nose at the tail; unlike ends refused, a unit's foreign car refused; the same brief and
    the same plan the same bytes.
- **The cars' insides** (`solveInterior`, `compileInteriorSurface`, `cutAway`): a car's or a cab car's inside solved from
  its design into a plan held to laws, drawn inside its shell when asked for (`interior: true`, or `{ plan, pitch, trim }`,
  on `compileCarSurface`, `compileCabSurface` and `composeTrain`; absent, the shell's bytes are unchanged and nothing of
  it is emitted).
  - **The plans** (`interior-odm.js`, `INTERIOR_PLANS`, a family's by `INTERIOR_FAMILY_PLAN`): benches along the walls
    with poles, rails, draft screens and a wheelchair bay (a metro's); seats across in facing pairs, two and one abreast
    (a streetcar's); facing bays two and two with tables, racks, vestibules behind partitions and a washroom (a
    regional's); airline rows facing the car's middle with headrests and a table bay where they meet (a high-speed
    coach's); a side corridor and compartments off it, two facing benches and a door each (a hauled coach's); a
    locomotive's machine room, its cabinets down the middle and a corridor down each side. Its capacity: seated,
    standing on its free floor, wheelchair bays.
  - **The lining** follows the body's own section in from its skin and is cut by the body's own openings (the windows,
    the doors, a cab's side window: `openings` in `body-shell.js`, which the body's sides now read too), each opening's
    reveals back to the skin; a dado, the floor and its door zones and thresholds, the ceiling and its lamps; the end
    walls and partitions with their doorways framed.
  - **A low floor** (a streetcar's, under its bogies' tops) is raised over each bogie on a podium, a step up to it, its
    seats standing on it. The cab car's and the car's designs now keep a low floor's doors off its bogies (a law, and
    the doors spaced over the clear span between them), so the streetcar's cab car has one door between its bogies and
    its centre module, on its own bogie, none.
  - **The cab**: the driver's raised floor (over a bogie, on a low floor), the desk as far forward as the nose lets it
    stand, its displays and controller, the seat set back so the seated eye is the eye its screen was drawn for, the
    partition behind (a locomotive's with a second seat, its door onto a corridor).
  - Its laws: headroom, the aisle's width, no seat in a door's zone, everything inside the lining, knee room for the
    pitch, a passage through every partition, the bogies covered, the podium's step; a cab's driver's eye in the
    screen, the desk inside the nose, headroom over the eye. `cutAway` opens a compiled thing's near half (its shell, and
    its lining, ceiling, lamps, displays and racks there) so its inside reads from outside. `scripts/render-rail.mjs`
    draws a car's or a cab car's inside: cutaway, saloon, aisle and cab.
  - Held (`interior.test.js`): each seating procedure within its laws; no seat in a door's zone and a passage through
    every partition; on a car with long runs seats across seat more and stand fewer than benches, a plan too wide for
    its body refused; a pitch too short for knees refused, a wagon without one; the lining at the section in from the
    skin and everything inside the skin; no wall across a window or a door; absent, the shell the same bytes; a
    cutaway's near half gone and its seats kept; a low floor's podiums under its seats, a step to each; a driver's eye in
    the screen, the desk inside the nose, a low floor's cab over its bogie; the same brief the same bytes.

### Destructible physics: whole buildings break, and stand at minute zero

A physical level (`destruction: 'physical'`) now breaks its big things by blocks too, not only its walls and props.

- **Towers and temples** (fractal structures): solid tiers, plinth steps and column shafts in courses no wider or taller
  than 3 m; hollow tiers and ring beams filled from their outlines with wall-thick cells that hold each other; a ring
  beam hung across its columns, seated on their capitals. Take a column and the beam over it sags or falls; take a
  course and what it held comes down.
- **A town's houses**: each is wall panels to its eave and a roof resting on them, breaking as the settlement they were
  built from: the style's facade word for the walls (adobe, hand-brick, limewash over rubble…), its roof word for the
  roof at a roof's weight. A settlement with no style of its own takes the cube's walls.
- **Towers and temples are stone**, as the cube paints them, unless the cube's `matter.structure` says otherwise.
- **Raised ground**: a building on a hill stands on its footing instead of dropping to the level's floor.
- **The load at minute zero**: what was built is checked by the page's own laws before anyone touches it (what falls at
  once, what is crushed, what sags), stamped on the world and never refused. Every structure preset stands.
- **Lighter pages**: blocks of one size share their pre-cut pieces; an arena's go from 1.7 MB to under 100 KB.
- **The load pass** finds supports through a grid, with the same answers, so a structure of hundreds of blocks stays quick.
- A level not physical changes no byte.

### Destructible physics: a geocity's near buildings break, the rest stays the skyline

- **A geocube's geocity takes play** (`entities`, `camera`, `pilot`, `play`, `destruction`, `matter`, `scars`, `wind`).
- **Under `destruction: 'physical'`** its buildings within a city block of where the walk starts, the nearest two dozen,
  break by blocks: walls and a roof, each as its finish is drawn (brick, stone, precast concrete, a tower's concrete
  frame), a flat roof a slab, coarse panels so a tower stays a few hundred blocks. They stand at minute zero.
- The rest of the city stays massing. A city not physical is drawn byte for byte as before.

### Destructible physics: combustion that spreads by its heat, and the flame on what burns

A burning block now burns with a real flame, and its fire reaches what is near it the ways heat does.

- **The flame on what burns**: every block that can burn carries a flame from the flame library, sized by Heskestad's
  law from the heat its burning gives (a pine log's under a metre, an oak trunk's a couple of metres), kindling when the
  block catches, moving with it, leaning in the level's wind and dying back when it is doused or burnt out. Its smoke is
  destructible physics' own.
- **Fire spreads by its heat**: a burning block radiates a share of its heat from its flame to what faces it, by the
  solid angle it fills, so a crate catches across a gap; its plume heats what hangs over it, so a beam above a fire goes
  before one beside it; and it heats what it touches, as before.

### Destructible physics: plastic matter dents, squashes and is punched through

Under destructible physics, matter that flows before it breaks now keeps the shape a blow leaves.

- **Yield is one dial across matter**: the stress where a stuff starts to flow, from a liquid's 0 through mud, dough,
  putty and lead to mild and armour steel. A matter with a yield is plastic; glass, masonry and timber break as before.
- **A dent is a crater in a solid**: a blow's work over the matter's hardness (three times its yield) is the volume it
  pushes aside, a bowl as sharp as the blow (a round deep, a swing broad, a burst a dish) with that volume kept in its
  rim. The work comes off the block's budget, so the budget still decides whether it stays.
- **Powerscaling punches through**: a dent that reaches the far face is a hole. The plate pays only for the plug and
  the rest carries on, so a strong enough round goes through a plate into what is behind it, and a blow past twice a
  block's whole budget tears it apart outright.
- **Soft stuff squashes**: a dent wider than the face it strikes flattens the whole block at constant volume, so dough
  spreads under a blow.
- **Plates strip**: a plastic plate hung on a wall by its weld comes off whole when its budget is gone, so focus fire
  strips one panel and leaves its neighbours.
- **A strike carries its tool** (`strikeTool`: sword, axe, knife, bat, metal-bat, hammer, fist, or its own numbers):
  a tool can't press harder than it is strong, and its force caps how wide it bites, so a hammer barely marks a steel
  block and a wooden bat never dents one.
- **Thin panels dish**: past the force that bends it, a panel gives in a broad dish, so a wooden bat dents a car-thin
  sheet a few centimetres and leaves a centimetre plate whole, and a heroic swing dents that too.
- **Edges cut**: an edge harder than what it strikes cuts a groove on the plane of its stroke where it lands; cut through,
  the block parts into two blocks that keep their matter, and what no longer holds falls. Timber cuts as metal does.
- **Trees fell**: a level groove leaves the stack above it on its hinge, and once the hinge is too thin to hold what
  leans past it, the trunk and its crown turn about it and land lying, clear of the stump. The notch decides the fall,
  and a block sawn level with its weight over its seat stands.
- **On the page**: a dented block is drawn displaced by its dents, dishes and grooves, holes dark through; a cut block's
  halves wear its skin, a felled tree turns as it falls, and a stripped plate falls.
  A page whose blocks have no yield keeps its bytes.

### Destructible physics: dust and smoke drift on the wind, each by its own script

Under destructible physics, the dust a break raises and the smoke a burning block gives off are carried by the level's
wind, rise or settle by their own physics, spread as they mix and fade as they thin.

- **Their own scripts**: a puff's path is a formula of time, as a leaf's is: it moves at the wind of its height with
  the gusts' sums, smoke rises on its heat by Briggs' plume rise to its final height, and dust settles at the speed of
  its grains (Stokes for the fine, Newton's drag for the coarse). It spreads by the wind's turbulence, rougher terrain
  mixing faster, and it fades as the same mass spreads thinner, so a fire's smoke is as thick as the fire is big.
- **A solver decides each source**: a fire is a plume, a break's dust or a burst of steam a puff, and each size of dust
  hangs on the air or falls out at once by whether it settles slower than the air's own stirring, every decision with its
  reason in numbers.
- **On the page**: dust in the colour of what broke, soot-dark smoke over what burns, white steam where water meets fire.

### Destructible physics in the geocube: a cube says what its world is made of

A physical world asked of a geocube now breaks by what the cube's style says things are made of, so a thing's matter
agrees with how it looks.

- **The cube's `matter`**, by role (wall, floor, accent, trim, roof, ground, wood, metal, glass): each a matter or
  `{ matter, fill?, porosity? }`. Where the cube names none, it is read off the cube's own look: its surfaces' tiles (a
  stone-brick wall is stone, a flagstone floor stone, rock stone, wood timber), its interior kit (a research lab is
  concrete and steel), and the material words its styles use (ashlar and rubble stone, hand-brick and wire-brick brick,
  adobe, boards and thatch pine, slate stone, precast concrete). Each role says why it is what it is.
- **A physical level in a cube** breaks its walls, pilasters and set pieces by the cube's matter; its props keep their
  own classes'. A level not physical, or in no cube, changes no byte.
- The geocube manual names the facet.

### Destructible physics: the land itself is ground that craters

- **A physical stage's land** is now a soil grid laid from the land it draws, facet by facet the ground the substrate
  says it is: soil, sand, scree, wet ground, a path, bare rock, each over bedrock at its own depth.
- **A blast near the ground digs the crater** its energy would in that soil (sand wider than loam, bare rock nothing),
  stopping at bedrock, throwing a rim and slumping to the soil's angle of repose.
- **The land on the page sinks and rises** with it, and a walker stands in the crater.
- **What stood on dug land comes down**: a house's or a tree's footing drops into the crater and what it carried
  settles.
- A level not physical changes no byte.

### Destructible physics: craters throw their dirt, the shovel digs, rivers run

- **A crater on the land throws its dirt**: clumps from loam and clay, none from dry sand, spray and a hanging dust
  cloud, as much as it dug, landing on the dug ground.
- **The shovel**: a cue's `dig` takes a scoop (a hand shovel's, a bucket's, an excavator's) out of the ground in front of
  a character or at a place and piles the soil beside them at its angle of repose. Bound to a key, a player digs; dig
  after dig the hole deepens, to bedrock and no further, and water finds it.
- **Rivers run**: a physical stage's river is moving water, held at its levels at both ends; a dam ponds it, a crater
  fills from it.
- A level not physical changes no byte.

### One wind: plants, grass, cloth and destructible physics feel the same air

- **A physical level's** blocks, dust, smoke and drifting leaves now take the level's own `wind`, the one its trees,
  grass and hung cloth sway in. The two profiles are matched exactly at 2 m and 10 m (within 2% between); the level's
  `matter.wind` still overrides it for the physics.
- **A geocube's `wind`** is its outside levels' wind when the recipe names none, its specimen worlds' too. Its dunes
  lie across it, and dunes that name their own way give the wind its direction.
- **A geocube's trees** are read by their biocube leaf form: an evergreen spire is a conifer, every other crown a
  broadleaf.
- **Trees in the wind solver**, by species, sized by geometric similarity: the wind that snaps one is the same at every
  size, about 39 m/s at a broadleaf's crown and 31 for a conifer, near the 42 m/s storms break trees of every size at.
  A stand stands still in a breeze, bends in a fresh wind, and goes to the physics in a storm. Bamboo is hollow.
- A level without a wind, and every world not physical, changes no byte.

### Destructible physics: metal panels on objects dent, hole and come off

- **Panels**: an entity under `destruction: 'physical'` can carry `panels`, thin metal plates on its faces (a car's
  doors and bonnet, a mech's armour, a locker, a drum): each a face, a place, a size, a thickness and a metal.
  `panels: true` on a box body plates every face but the bottom.
- They take the world's blows by the same law the blocks do: a round dents a thick plate and holes a thin one, a bat
  dishes a car-thin panel and rings off a plate, a blast pushes the whole panel in, and a panel worn out by its dents
  comes off and falls.
- The page draws each panel as the sheet it is, riding its object: the bowls, the dishes and the holes in its colour,
  lit as the dented blocks are.
- A world with no panels changes no byte.

### Destructible physics: matter that breaks by what it is made of (opt-in)

Walls hold and objects break stays the default; a game that asks for destructible physics now gets it.

- **`destruction: 'physical'`**, the top rung above `world`: everything `world` breaks, broken by its matter rather than
  counted hits. The words that ask for it ("destructible physics", "realistic destruction", "structural collapse",
  "craters", "destructible terrain") name it in a composed stage. Without it nothing changes: every page keeps its bytes.
- **Matter** (`lib/graph/rupa/matter.js`): concrete, reinforced concrete, brick, stone, sandstone, adobe, glass, ice,
  steel, sheet metal, timber, pine, drywall, and soils (sand, loam, clay, gravel, snow), each as density, stiffness,
  compressive and tensile strength, the bond between blocks, failure strain and toughness, from the strength table where
  the two overlap. A thing or a terrain ask takes `matter: '<id>'`; a class has a default (a wall is brick, a crate
  timber, glass glass).
- **A blow is joules, a block holds joules**: capacity is toughness × volume × fill. A swing, a round, a burst (its
  energy from its splash radius by cube-root blast scaling, reaching a block by the solid angle it fills) and a landing
  (½mv²) each spend it; a world's `power` tier (human, heroic, super, titan, cosmic) scales every blow by orders of
  magnitude, so a foot of concrete takes a cannonball and a foot of steel does not.
- **Brittleness picks the cut**: glass and ice shatter, masonry blasts apart, steel and timber chip.
- **What holds it up**: weight is carried down to the supports, and a block crushes past its compressive strength (less
  as it is damaged); a block hung sideways (a lintel, a slab's tiles) is checked in bending at its bonds, so an
  unreinforced overhang past its span snaps and falls.
- **Heat, its own numbers**: melting and softening points, specific and latent heat, and for what burns its ignition
  point and heat of combustion. A block warms by the joules it takes; at its melt it takes its latent heat and melts;
  past its ignition timber burns at the char rate (a world's `fireTime` compresses fire time), losing strength as its
  fuel goes, heating what it touches so the fire spreads, and ending as ash. Heat weakens: a block keeps half its
  strength at its softening point, so a steel frame in a fire comes down by the load. A burst's fireball heats what it
  reaches; `heatBlock` heats from a fire, a beam or a script.
- **Matter meets matter**: a collision dissipates the closing energy of the reduced mass, less what the lower of the two
  bounces (a new number per matter) keeps, and each side takes it inversely to its stiffness, so the softer takes more.
  Density is the mass behind the speed: at the same size and speed a steel ball punches through a brick wall and carries
  on slower, paying only what each block cost, while a pine ball breaks on it. Landings use the same rule instead of
  charging the full ½mv² to both blocks, and `throwMatter` puts bodies of matter into the world (a cannonball, a
  hurled boulder), stepped finely enough not to pass through a block.
- **Liquids are cohesion at its end**: water, seawater, oil, honey, mud and lava hold no shape at rest (cohesion and
  friction angle 0), so their weight is pressure in every direction; `viscosity` says how fast they flow and `yield`
  lets mud and lava hold a low heap. On the ground grid (`lib/graph/rupa/fluid.js`) a fluid layer flows downhill,
  levels, fills a crater's bowl and keeps every drop; inside, tanks and tubs are joined by pipes whose flow viscosity or
  the opening limits, joined tanks meet at one level, an overfilled masonry cistern bursts by the hoop stress at its
  foot and floods the ground, and a hydrant, a pump and a hose make a nozzle's jet. Archimedes falls out of the pressure
  on a body's faces: in a level's pools pine floats a third under, ice nine tenths, a hollow steel hull a sixth, and
  solid steel sinks. A spray (`spray`) throws water that pushes on what it hits and cools it by its heat and its boiling,
  so a hose puts out a burning block.
- **Air and wind**: air joins the matter table as a gas, 800 times lighter than water. It holds things up a little and
  slows what moves through it. Wind is air moving (a level's `matter.wind`: its speed at 10 m, its direction, the
  terrain that slows it near the ground, seeded gusts): it carries light things, bends the hose's spray, and pushes on
  walls with ½ × air density × speed². A stack its weight and mortar can't hold against that push tips or slides and
  falls as loose pieces: a 70 m/s gale tips a dry pine pile while a mortared brick wall stands. A wall casts a wind
  shadow; thin things tumble and catch a quarter of their surface (a leaf falls at about 2 m/s); and the wind moves what
  lies on the ground once its drag beats friction, so leaves skitter while a brick stays.
- **The wind script** (`lib/graph/rupa/wind-script.js`): leaves, litter and ash drawn without simulating them. A
  leaf catches up with the air in a quarter of a second, so it moves at the wind while sinking at its falling speed,
  and its whole path (the wind's rise with height, the gusts, a wall's calm lee, skittering on the ground once the wind
  beats friction) has an exact formula of time. A GPU runs the same formula (`GLSL`), so thousands of leaves cost one
  number a frame; its tests hold it to the full simulation.
- **The wind solver** (`lib/graph/rupa/wind-solver.js`): a scene's wind-moved elements are read by their physics and
  handed their depiction, each with its reason in numbers: drift for what catches up with the air in under half a second
  (leaves, litter, ash), bend for what flexes from its foot (grass, reeds, saplings: a cantilever's curve and its first
  mode), hang for what swings (flags, lanterns: drag against weight, a pendulum), still for what the strongest gust can't
  move, and simulate for what it moves but can't carry, or snaps. Like kinds batch into one GPU draw; each kind is a row.
- **Blocking, flow's opposite**: a barrier is its porosity, and how flow gets past it follows by law instead of a tuned
  share: its resistance (the perforated-plate loss), what bleeds through, the drag it takes (so a slatted fence feels
  less of the wind than a solid one), and the wake behind it recovering as a plane wake does (a solid wall stills the
  air at its back; a hedge shelters less deeply). The runtime's wind, the wind script and the wind solver share it. On
  the ground grid, water pools behind a barrier and pours over its top, seeps through its open share by Bernoulli, and
  breaches it where its push beats the barrier's weight and joint: a thin adobe wall gives way, thick concrete holds.
- **Water and air share one set of fluid functions**: pressure (from a fluid's weight and from its flow), turning a
  pressure back into a speed, and the lift and drag on a body in any fluid. The tanks, pipes, nozzles, pools, spray,
  grain settling and wind all call them.
- **Debris, deterministic in the force** (`lib/graph/rupa/debris.js`; every break on the runtime carries it): a breaking
  opens new crack surface against the matter's fracture energy, so a harder blow leaves more, finer and faster pieces
  and more dust, the same joules shatter glass and split timber, and the pieces take the matter's shape (shards,
  chunks, splinters, torn plates, clods) and fly away from the blow with an exact share of its energy. A crater's ejecta
  flies by the cratering ejecta law as clumps where the soil's cohesion beats the stress of being thrown (none from dry
  sand; lumps from the rim; a clump landing too fast crumbles), spray of grains whose size sets their drag, and a dust
  cloud of its fines; a body meeting a liquid splashes by inertia against surface tension
  and viscosity, so water splashes and lava plops. A burn leaves ash, a melt its liquid.
- **Ground** (`lib/graph/rupa/ground.js`): a soil heightfield over bedrock: craters from energy, ejecta thrown into a rim
  with the volume kept, slopes that slump to their angle of repose while a cohesive soil holds a cut face up to its
  critical height, and dig, deposit and shovel. The kernel and its laws land here; the page's deformable floor is next.
- Internal name: rupa. Map: `docs/rupa.md`.

### Cosmetic damage: a map that may not change still shows its blows

A level's `scars` (`true`, or `{ ground?, wall? }`) keeps every wall, the floor and the footing as they were, and paints
what each blow would have done, by the same laws as destructible physics.

- **A burst near the floor** paints the crater its energy would dig in the ground's soil (less the higher it went off)
  and throws its dirt as clumps, spray and a dust cloud.
- **A wall in a burst's reach** is scorched on the face toward the blast: its share crushes a bowl of its joules over the
  wall's crushing strength, the soot covers the disc the burst's radius cuts on the face, and the bowl spalls off as
  chips. A steel wall dents by its yield strength instead.
- **A round** that stops on a wall chips it by the same law (centimetres out of brick, less out of stone); one that stops
  on the floor leaves a pock.
- The ground and the wall come from the world's geocube unless named, else loam and brick. Outdoors a crater is dug
  in the land's own ground (its commonest off the path: soil, sand, scree, bare rock); a stone floor digs by its
  toughness and throws chunks. Scars go with any degree (crates still smash under `objects`).
- A game's `mechanics.scars` rides onto every level it makes; a stage's words ("cosmetic damage", "scorch marks",
  "bullet holes") ask for it. The systems card names it.
- The page paints each mark once as a decal and flies its debris on sim time, seeded, so a capture stays the same. A
  level without `scars` changes no byte.
- The crater, settling and dirt laws now live in the page's physics, so the ground kernel and the page dig the same
  crater from the same joules.

### Destructible physics: trees that break, burn and fall in a storm

- **A physical stage's trees** built near the trail are now blocks: a trunk of green wood in courses and a crown of
  leaves and air resting on it, standing on their roots on raised land. The stamped and far trees stay scenery.
- **A blast breaks a tree, fire burns it, an axe fells it**, and **a storm throws it**: when the gust at its crown passes
  its break speed it turns downwind about its foot and lies along the wind, its crown beyond its trunk.
- **The level's `wind`** is the storm. A tree is never toppled as a loose pile: the storm is its only wind law.
- **Rain and snow** lean with the wind in a physical level, or under a geocube's wind. Every other world's weather keeps
  the heading it had.
- `breached` and `fell` speak for a building or a tree (a group of blocks); a block restored at the start says nothing.
- A level not physical changes no byte.

### Triggered breaks: the game or the player sets off what a world can break

A level's cues can now break the world, and wait on what breaks.

- **`blast: { at, radius?, hurt? }`**: a charge at a place, breaking what the world lets break in its reach as a
  grenade would (by its energy under destructible physics, one blow a block otherwise), hurting the bodies in it.
- **`collapse: { group, how?, storey?, stagger? }`**: a building comes down. Its foot goes and the rest falls by the
  world's gravity (under destructible physics the fall breaks what it lands on), or every block goes, paced bottom up.
- **`break: id`**: one block, or a whole group.
- **`when: { breached: group }`** and **`when: { fell: group }`**: a building's first block breaks; half of it is down.
- Set off by anything a cue hears: a zone, a lever (`use`), a timer, a boss's fall. A group is a structure's or a
  house's id, or a block's. Only a page whose cues use them carries them; every other page keeps its bytes.

### Destructible physics: the stage's water floods, pools behind levees and fills with rain

- **A physical stage's lake and sea** now lie on its ground as water: laid level, and the physics' pools, so what falls in
  floats or sinks and a fire is doused in it.
- **It moves when something moves it**: a crater dug at the shore floods from the lake, a broken levee lets it through,
  and it runs until it is still. No water is made or lost.
- **Levees**: what stands on the land holds the water back and is overtopped when it rises past; the water's push breaks a
  board, a concrete wall holds.
- **Rain** falls at the weather's rate (drizzle to thunderstorm), real time by default; the level's `matter.rainTime`
  speeds it.
- The page draws the water the physics moved. A level not physical changes no byte.

### The mecha shelf: ridden walkers on real-robot principles

In progress. A new shelf, `control/lib/graph/mecha-shelf/`, for legged machines a rider sits in, built from the ground
up. It starts with the all-terrain walker, the base of its bipedal locomotion, and grows a general-purpose work frame
on it: the utility walker, the heavy walker drawn larger from it, and the giant arm walker carrying a giant arm pack.

- **The all-terrain walker** (`mecha-archetypes.js` `allTerrainWalker`): a pelvis, two legs and the rider's cabin.
  - **The legs:** six joints each, like a real biped's: hip yaw, roll and pitch, the knee, and the ankle's pitch and
    roll. The knees bend backward, digitigrade like a bird's.
    - The hip ram works behind the thigh, the knee ram in front of it, and the ankle ram behind the shank to a heel
      horn, like a tendon.
    - The ankle's arc sits toward pointing down: a backward-bent leg folds its ankle further than a human's.
  - **The rider sits astride, as on a sport motorcycle.** A saddle on a spine, a tank with knee grips and a chest pad,
    pegs set back under the hips, and clip-on bars ahead and low. The rider leans onto the bars, its head tilted up to
    look ahead (the cycle shelf's new `walker` posture card).
  - **The cabin evokes a convertible.** A tub's sides round the rider, their beltline swept low beside the saddle, with
    a door seam and a sill to hold. A low framed windshield with quarter panes is raked over the dash. A roll hoop
    stands behind the saddle, and it is open above.
  - **The front is one nose.** It starts where the cabin ends, as wide as the tub and as high as the windshield's
    foot. It is drawn down and in to a narrow rounded leading edge, with flush lamp strips along its flanks.
  - **The mass:** the battery sits low in the keel between the hips, and the hydraulic power unit under the tail.
  - **Its palettes:**
    - `proving`, the default: warm white over graphite;
    - `fieldOlive`;
    - `rescueOrange`;
    - `desertSand`;
    - `arcticWhite`.
- **The utility walker** (`utilityWalker`): a general-purpose work frame on the walker's locomotion.
  - **Its operator sits at the controls** (the cycle shelf's new `operator` posture card): belted into a suspension
    work seat on a platform over the pelvis, with a rail round it at the waist. The arms are worked from a stick on
    each armrest's console, and the walker by the pedals at the feet. It is boarded by a two-rung ladder at the back,
    and the torso frame's hoop is over the head.
  - **Its legs bend at the knee forward**, as a person's do (the shelf's legs take either bend). The rams are bored up
    and the feet enlarged for its weight and its load.
  - **Its arms are for assistive strength work.** Each has a shoulder yaw drive on the torso frame, a shoulder pitch and
    an elbow on rams, a rotary wrist, and a two-fingered claw. Their poses (`rest`, `carry`, `raise`) are solved by the
    arm's own inverse kinematics: the wrist's place from the shoulder, and the claw's angle.
  - **The mass:** the battery sits low in the keel, and the power pack on the torso's back as a counterweight to the
    arms.
  - **Its stances:** the walker's, plus `carry` (a load held ahead in both claws, the forearms level) and `reach` (the
    claws raised over the head).
  - **Its laws add the arms':**
    - each arm joint's actuator holding half the carry's load;
    - `reach`: its claws' farthest ahead, level with the shoulders;
    - `lift`: its rated load at the carry, 75% of the load that first tips it or overruns an arm's actuator, as a crane
      or a loader is rated.
- **The heavy walker** (`heavyWalker`): the utility walker's frame drawn larger for heavy construction, in the site's
  yellow (the new `siteYellow` palette).
  - **Drawn larger.** Its legs, pelvis and arms are the utility walker's designs at 1.4 times their lengths. Its feet
    are at 1.6 times, for its weight on soft ground, and its power pack at 1.5, as a counterweight to the arms.
    - A part at another size is another row's design scaled whole (`dims.scale`, its `from`), as the construction
      shelf's are: its pins at k times, its mass at k³, a drive's rated torque at k⁴.
    - Its rams scale with their pins, so every joint keeps its design's arc.
  - **Its operator stays a person's size, in a closed cab:**
    - an angled shell: the windshield raked back under the roof's visor, the upper sides drawn in to the roof;
    - a falling-object roof with guard bars, on its pillars;
    - framed glass all round, the side windows' top rear corners cut on the slant, and a low window in the front
      panel to see where the feet go;
    - guard bars along the windshield's rake, against what flies off the work;
    - a door on the left, reached by a four-rung side ladder;
    - mirrors, work lamps and a beacon;
    - a harnessed work seat, the arms' sticks on its consoles, an emergency stop at the right hand, and the pedals.
  - **Its laws add `cab`:** the operator's space held inside the cab's glass and under its roof, the nearest margin.
- **The manipulators' ODM** (`mecha-shelf/mecha-tools.js`, `mecha-tools-parts.js`): the heavy walker is modular, its
  arms fitted for the task rather than built for it.
  - **Its tools** go on the wrist's quick coupler (every tool carries the same coupler plate) in the claw's place. Each
    is an inventory row for its geometry and a card for its work: what it does on a site, the load it holds as rated
    (none for a breaker or an auger), what drives it, and the hydraulic flow it draws.
    - the grapple, its own;
    - a digging bucket;
    - a hydraulic breaker;
    - a concrete crusher;
    - pallet forks;
    - an earth auger;
    - a vacuum lifter;
    - a lifting magnet;
    - a lifting hook.
  - **Its arm kits:** the standard arm and a long-reach arm (a forearm a third longer on the same elbow, so its ram
    keeps its arc).
  - **Its tasks**, each a loadout per arm:
    - demolition: a breaker and a crusher;
    - high-reach demolition: a crusher and a grapple on long arms;
    - trenching: a bucket and a grapple;
    - pipe laying: two grapples;
    - material handling: two pairs of forks;
    - glazing: two vacuum lifters;
    - piling: an auger and a grapple;
    - steelwork: a magnet and a grapple;
    - rigging: a hook on a long arm and a grapple.
  - **A frame's `mount`** says the tools and arm kits it takes, and its own loadout. `composeFrame(id, { task, tools,
    arms })` fits it under its own key (the construction shelf's `composeMachine` is the model), refusing what its mount
    does not take. The laws re-read it as built: its mass, its reach to the tool's working point, its lift, its flow.
  - **Its lift is rated as a lifting machine's is** (ISO 10567's shares): the least of 75% of the load that tips it,
    87% of the load its arms' actuators hold, and what its tools hold as rated. A loadout whose tools hold nothing
    reads no lift, and a load is shared only by the arms whose tools hold. The carry is read at its stance's load, no
    more than it is rated for.
  - **A new law, `flow`:** both arms' tools working at once, their flow as a share of the power pack's pump.
  - **What the laws asked of the build:**
    - the heavy hip roll ram was bored up past its design's, for the heaviest tools' sway on one foot;
    - the heavy wrist is a heavy-duty rotary actuator, rated past its design's, so its arms' rams, not its wrist,
      set what it lifts, and a long arm trades lift for reach.
    - An arm's poses are shares of its length, the same pose on a standard arm and a long one.
  - **On the studio grid** the door takes the words beside the vehicle: `task` ('demolition'), `tools` ({ r, l }) and
    `arms` ({ r: 'long' }), and a pack's `packTask` and `packTools`. The review render takes `--task`, `--tools
    r:breaker,l:grapple`, `--arms r:long`, `--pack-task heavyLift` and `--pack-tools r:spreader,l:giantHand`.
- **The giant arm walker** (`giantArmWalker`): a frame built to carry a giant arm pack. It keeps the heavy walker's
  closed cab, its station and its modular arms.
  - **A more robust pelvis and legs:** the utility walker's designs at 1.6 times their lengths (the heavy walker's are
    1.4), its feet at 2.2 times. Its hip roll and knee rams are bored up past their design's. The laws asked for each:
    the crouch overloaded the knees, one foot overloaded the hip's roll with the heaviest pack tools on, and the sole's
    pressure was over the band before the larger feet. Its side ladder reaches lower, for the taller frame.
  - **The giant arm pack** (`gap-gw`), a backpack for work: a frame against the cab's back, its own power unit and
    cooler, a yoke across its top, and two towers up and out to the giant arms' shoulders over the cab's roof. Its pump
    feeds every arm's tools.
  - **The giant arms:** the utility walker's arm drawn twice as large, on the same factory as the frame's own (a second
    arm set, `packArms`, named under `giant`). Their shoulders are armoured blocks round the joint, the arm coming out
    from under them. Their wrists are heavy-duty rotary actuators, and their own tool is a new three-fingered giant
    hand.
  - **Its stances:** the giant arms `stow` folded (the hands ahead at the chest), `heave` a load ahead in them, and
    `hoist` them overhead.
  - **Its laws read the pack's arms as the frame's are read:** `packReach`, and `packLift` at the heave, rated the same
    way.
    - A stance's `loadOn` says which arms hold its load.
    - The flow law sums every arm's tools against the pump.
    - The clearance and tip-over laws take the giant arms with the rest.
- **The pack's tools** (on the giant arms' larger coupler, `packMount`), each with its card:
  - the giant hand, its own;
  - a giant grapple;
  - a rescue spreader;
  - a shoring prop (it holds a slab up from the ground, not from the arm: it reads no lift);
  - a shear (a felling head, a steel shear);
  - a vibratory pile driver;
  - a clamshell grab;
  - a giant hook.
- **The pack's tasks** (`MECHA_PACK_TASKS`; `packTask`, or the operator's own `packTools`):
  - heavy lifting (two giant hands);
  - disaster response (a hand and a spreader);
  - shoring (two props);
  - forestry (a shear and a grapple);
  - pile driving (a vibratory driver and a hand);
  - debris clearing (a clamshell and a hand);
  - heavy rigging (a hook and a hand).

  `composeFrame` fits the frame's arms and the pack's together under one key.
- **Giant arm packs by design house** (`mecha-shelf/mecha-gap-makers.js`, `mecha-house-parts.js`; `packMaker`): a
  house is a philosophy card, solved into its own pack and giant arms. Four generic houses, none a real maker's:
  - forge: strength first. Short, deep plated arms, armoured shoulders, hydraulics, a four-fingered hand.
  - aero: reach first. Slender tube arms, a long forearm, electric screw actuators, faired shoulders on one mast.
  - truss: service first, built like a crane. Open lattice towers and arms, a parallel gripper.
  - sealed: protection first, for hazardous sites. Every joint under bellows, closed shells, electric actuators.

  The solver, for each house:
  - proportions the arm from the card's size, forearm share and section;
  - places each ram's pins by a fixed search, so the joint turns the whole arc the arm's poses ask. The search keeps
    within the house's spread off the beam and takes the largest least moment arm;
  - sizes each actuator by statics at the heave for the house's rated load: a ram's bore at the system pressure, or a
    screw actuator's rated force;
  - dresses the parts in the house's construction and livery.

  The house's rows are solved the first time one is read. `composeFrame` swaps the pack, the giant arms' parts and
  rams, and puts the house's hand in the giant hand's place; a pack task's other tools stay as they are. The laws then
  hold the frame as built. The houses trade reach for lift, and every house passes every law at every pack task. A
  screw actuator is rated by its force both ways (`ramForce`). The pack's reach band is widened to 4.5 m for a long
  forearm with a prop.
- **The field walker** (`fieldWalker`; registry row `field-walker`, role `scout`): the all-terrain walker hardened as a
  military all-terrain transport. It carries no weapons. Its knees bend backward and its rider sits astride, as on the
  walker.
  - Its frame (`mecha-field-parts.js`) is the walker's drawn 1.2 times larger for clearance and step:
    - its thigh and shank beams carry a bolted guard plate down their outer flank;
    - its belly sits under a skid plate raked up at both ends, with four recovery points;
    - its feet are drawn at 1.5 times and cleated, the lugs never below the sole the legs are solved to;
    - its cabin is behind a brush guard, a second bar across the hoop;
    - its power pack sits in a cargo rack;
    - its saddle's boarding step hangs lower for the taller frame.
  - Against the walker it measures steadier (its standing margin 0.17 m against 0.10), presses softer ground (34 kPa
    against 46), and steps higher and farther. A new law, `belly`, reads how far its lowest carried body stands off the
    ground.
  - Its dress (`mecha-military.js`) is the military styling library's (car-designer), applied to the frame's faces as
    to a field vehicle's hull:
    - the frame is assembled unlit and its faces read back by colour;
    - its kit is fitted on anchors its parts declare: pioneer tools, an antenna, a jerry can each side, a tarp roll,
      shackles at the recovery points;
    - its number is stencilled each side;
    - a `livery` (any camo or mono) is cut into its paint, its structure a shade down;
    - its `wear` (used unless asked) cakes mud low on its legs, dust, fade and grounding;
    - it is baked under the studio's light.
  - **An optional closed armoured cabin** (`cabin: 'armoured'`; the open cabin stays the default). It is a shell of
    plates round the rider in the open cabin's place, with no glass:
    - vision slits at the rider's eye level across the glacis and at each side, each under an armoured lid hinged at
      its brow, swung up as a visor over the slot or shut flush (`slits: 'open' | 'shut'`, the part's state);
    - a camera unit on the roof's front is the main vision: a pan ring, an armoured housing, twin lenses under a hood,
      on a monitor inside before the rider's face. A small camera watches behind;
    - a door on the boarding side and a hatch in the roof; armoured lamps behind grilles; the brush guard round the
      nose as before;
    - the field kit's anchors are on its plates.

    A frame's `cabins` name what it may carry (`mecha-archetypes.js`): the closed cabin's mass is added to the class's,
    and the `cab` law holds the rider's space inside its walls. It holds every law with the rider 4 cm inside its back
    at the nearest.
  - It is olive drab by default (a new palette, `oliveDrab`, the field's olive). `livery` and `wear` are words of a
    dressed frame on the door, the figure and the render script (`--livery`, `--wear`); a frame with no dress refuses them.
- **Backpacks** (`mecha-shelf/mecha-backpacks.js`, `mecha-backpack-parts.js`; `backpack`, `weapons`): the giant arm
  pack's functional cousin. A frame's back is fitted for a job, with no heavy arms. A backpack card names:
  - its frame in the power pack's place, and its mounts each side, each a traverse ring and an elevation cradle on
    rotary drives;
  - the payloads they take, and a spare magazine racked each side;
  - a service tail;
  - the parts it asks the frame to carry heavier (a sku for a sku);
  - its mass on the class's, and its laws.

  A frame offers the backpacks it takes (`backpacks`); the field walker takes the weapons backpack and the functional
  ones below.
  - **The weapons backpack:** the power pack sits under a magazine bay, with a pylon each side out to a weapon mount
    beside the rider. Its payloads (`MECHA_WEAPONS`, generic and invented) are a rotary machine gun with its
    ammunition box and feed chute, and a launch rail under a five-round rocket pod. The pod is the launcher's magazine
    and is swapped whole. The gun takes the right mount and the launcher the left by default; `weapons: { r, l }`
    swaps them.
  - **The service tail, a scorpion's:** a yaw drum on the bay's top, two armoured segments and a gripping head with
    its own camera, each joint an electric rotary drive. It stays tucked down the bay's back, folded against it, until a magazine is to be switched.
    It is solved by its own inverse kinematics (`mecha-ik.js tailAt`): yawed toward a service point, its root segment
    raised past the line to it, the outer segment bent back down, the head straight down onto the magazine's lug.
    Its service points (`TAIL_POSES`): each weapon's magazine (reload), each spare in its rack (fetch), and the drop
    behind, where a spent magazine is let fall. Swapping a magazine from behind is the sequence of stances:
    reload, drop, fetch, reload.
  - **New stances:** the tail's service stances, and `brace` (crouched, a foot set back) to fire from.
  - **New laws** (`mecha-laws.js`):
    - `tailTorque`: the tail's hardest-worked drive holding the tail and a magazine still at every service point.
    - `recoil`: a payload's sustained recoil at muzzle height against the frame's weight on its lever to its heels,
      braced. Standing, the gun would push it over; braced, it holds.
    - `backblast`: the rockets' backblast behind the breech, clear of the rider.
    - `fireClear`: each payload's line of fire at either end of its traverse, clear of the rider.
    - The clearance law now keeps the tail and the payloads out of the rider's space.

  Carrying it, the field walker stands on heavy-duty hip roll rams, and its laden step's band starts lower. Every law
  holds, with the open cabin or the armoured one.
- **Functional backpacks and roles** (`mecha-backpacks.js`, `mecha-backpack-parts.js`; `backpack`, `weapons`, `role`):
  - **Functional payloads** on the same mounts, each with a magazine the tail hot-swaps and a spare racked:
    - a sensor mast: three telescoping tubes, an electro-optical ball, a radar panel, and a battery cassette;
    - a four-drone launcher: a cassette of cells raked up toward ahead, a folded rotor drone behind each door;
    - a smoke discharger: two rows of cups, raked up and fanned out;
    - a four-cell anti-air launcher, its pod the magazine;
    - a cargo carrier: a tray, posts and a rail round a strapped supply crate, the crate the magazine, handed down to
      the drop behind by the tail;
    - a recovery winch: its drum of cable between cheeks, its motor, a fairlead ahead and a hook; the cable reel is
      the magazine.

    A payload that fires nothing (`fires: false`: the mast, the carrier, the winch) has no line of fire, and the
    `fireClear` law skips it. The weapons backpacks also take the smoke discharger.
  - **Backpacks on the weapons backpack's frame**, each offered by the field walker: reconnaissance (a sensor mast and
    drones), logistics (cargo carriers, a winch) and air defence (anti-air missiles, a sensor mast, a rotary gun).
    A backpack whose weight rides behind leans the frame (`lean`): it stands with its hips carried ahead of its feet,
    its centre of mass over them, as one leans under a heavy pack.
  - **Roles** (`MECHA_ROLES`; `role`), as the civilian worker's tasks are its site's: a loadout each, a backpack, its
    payloads by mount and the cabin it asks. They are assault, escort, fire support, reconnaissance, screening, air
    defence, resupply, recovery and bombardment. A frame takes a role whose backpack it offers, or whose payloads its
    own backpack takes: the rover walker is fitted for assault or escort by rearming its heavy weapons backpack, and
    the siege walker is fitted for bombardment as built. The operator's own `backpack`, `weapons` and `cabin` override
    the role's. A role a frame cannot carry is refused, naming what it takes.
  - Every role holds every law on every frame that takes it.
- **The rover walker** (`roverWalker`; registry row `rover-walker`, role `armour`): the field walker on four wheels,
  more heavily armed. It walks, or collapses its legs and rolls as a small armoured car.
  - **Its size:** its own legs and pelvis at 1.35 times the walker's designs (the field walker's are 1.2), with
    shanks a wheelbase long, an armoured car's wheels, and rams and drives rated up for its weight.
  - **Its hull:** its armoured cabin is its own, the open one the option (`cabin: 'open'`, lighter, its cab law off).
    Each shank carries an armour skirt outboard of its wheels, over their upper halves and the gap between, its lip
    turned in over their tread. Collapsed, the skirts are the hull's sides and fenders; walking, they are shin armour,
    short at the ankle so they clear the ground.
  - Collapsed, its legs stand plumb, their roll undone, so the wheels stand upright. Its feet are tall enough that,
    walking, on one foot with its leg rolled under it, nothing but its feet comes near the ground.
  - **Its legs:** a wheel on each knee's axis and one on each ankle's, outboard, each coaxial with its joint and on its
    own hub motor, skid-steered each side. Its shanks are longer for a four-wheeler's wheelbase, its ankle rams
    re-sized with them, and its feet taller so the ankle wheels ride clear when it walks.
  - **Its knees are rotary drives, not rams.** The field walker's knee ram bottoms out near 130°, which no backward
    knee can fold past into a collapse. A drive folds the rover's knee to 165°.
  - **Collapsed** (its `roll` stance, solved in `mecha-ik.js`): the thighs rake back toward level, and the knees fold
    until the shanks lie level, so both wheels stand on the ground. Each foot pitches, across its ankle's range, to hold
    its sole highest: folded up ahead as a fender. It is boarded collapsed, as a four-wheeler is.
  - **Armament:** it carries the heavy weapons backpack as built (`MECHA_BACKPACKS.heavyWeapons`): an autocannon right,
    its box magazine on the side and a muzzle brake, and the five-round rocket launcher left, with the service tail.
    `weapons` swaps its payloads; another backpack is refused. It fires collapsed on its wheels, its longest and lowest
    footing (its `fireStance`).
  - **New laws:**
    - `rollContact`: all four wheels on the ground;
    - `rollClearance`: what the wheels carry clear above the ground;
    - `rollStability`: the centre of mass inside the wheels;
    - `rollActuators`: the legs' rams holding it, its wheels' loads on them.

    Stability, recoil and boarding read the wheels' contacts when a stance is collapsed, and the crouch's actuator
    check skips a collapsed boarding.
  - **The dress:** the field walker's (any camo livery, its wear). A cabin is previewed alone on the frame that offers
    it, a backpack's parts on the frame that offers backpacks.
  - Every law holds as built, with the armoured cabin, and rearmed with the rotary machine gun.
- **The siege walker** (`siegeWalker`; registry row `siege-walker`, role `armour`): the rover walker's principles at
  2.5 times its size, some 33 t and 10.8 m standing.
  - **Its legs:** at 3.375 times the walker's designs; knees on rotary drives; shanks 3.6 m long, each carrying a
    third wheel between the knee's and the ankle's. Collapsed, it rolls on six, its footprint reaching far ahead of and
    behind its hips: a 3.6 m wheelbase and a 4.4 m track.
  - **Its cockpit, human-sized, rides out ahead on a keel** (`mecha-field-parts.js` `keeledPelvis`): a V-bottomed
    armoured prow off the pelvis, its deck railed, a ladder down its side. The rider's space is carried out to it, and
    the cab law holds it there. The armoured cockpit's camera is augmented by a radar dome, half a sphere on a collar, on the hull's top. A rotary
    machine gun sits on its own ring and cradle on the cockpit's side.
  - **Its siege backpack** (`MECHA_BACKPACKS.siege`): the weapons backpack's frame at 2.5 times.
    - A howitzer right: its long barrel, fume extractor, muzzle brake, recoil cylinders and breech, and its autoloader's
      six-round shell cassette (the magazine). Its recoil is what a long-recoil mechanism leaves, read with the frame
      collapsed on its wheels.
    - An eighteen-cell missile launcher left: three six-cell pods side by side, the outermost the magazine.
    - A spare of each racked.
    - **Twin scorpion tails**, one each side (`twin`). Each serves its own side's payload, spare and the drop behind,
      while the other stays tucked (`mecha-ik.js tailAt`). The tail law reads both.
  - **Its side profile, reshaped:**
    - A hull fills the gap between the backpack and the cockpit: an armoured superstructure on the keel, its sides
      sloped, its top stepping down to the cockpit, with hatches, vents and rails.
    - Its weapons are mounted lower and wider on their pylons beside the hull, which lowers its profile and its
      recoil's lever.
    - Its thighs are heavier, with overlapping front armour plates and a knee cop (`platedThigh`).
    - Its shanks are shorter, standing deeper bent as a T-rex balances, its three wheels in line along each shank, the
      front one well above the ankle.
    - Its feet are long, pushed forward of the ankle, their toes ahead on the ground for its balance.
  - **Its feet clawed, its sides a tank's:**
    - Each foot is a short, low palm on a cleated sole, a heel spur raked back behind it and two thick toes ahead
      (`clawedFoot`), their knuckles close ahead of the heel. Each toe sits on its own knuckle (`knuckle-sw`), whose
      yaw splays it out in a V walking (`TOE_SPLAY_SW`) for its footing and draws it in straight in tank mode (the
      joint's `when: { roll: 0 }`; a rolling stance now sets its flagged joints too). Its stance is wide enough that
      the two feet's toes stay clear of each other. Each toe is two segments, a root and a claw, their own bodies (`mecha-toe`,
      `toe1-sw` and `toe2-sw`) on knuckle drives, with a joint line between them. Walking, the toes lie flat, their pads on the
      ground, and the sole's outline runs out to their claws. Collapsed, they clench down and under the palm's front.
    - A clenched toe hangs below the sole. Each shank's ankle is therefore cranked forward of its axis (`ankleFwd`),
      toward its front, which points straight up when it lies level: rolling, the ankle stands a crank's throw higher
      over the ground, and its clenched toes clear it. The leg's inverse kinematics solve the line from knee to ankle
      and turn the knee back by the crank's angle (`mecha-ik.js` `legGeometry`'s `e2`). If they still would not
      clear, the foot is tilted up from level, the nearer way, until they do (`foot: 'level'`, `clear`).
    - Walking, the crank brings the shin's lower end nearer the ground: its front wheel rides higher up the shin, its
      skirt stops shorter of the ankle, and its ankle ram was sized again from its length curve.
    - A sponson each side of the hull: a box of plates out from the hull's side over the hip and the top of the thigh,
      open below for the leg to swing in, its ends raked, its deck the weapons' shelf, with a belt of armour along its
      middle, a stowage bin, bolts and a lip along its foot. Collapsed, it rides over the wheels as a tank's side does.
  - **Collapsed**, each foot is laid level out ahead of its front wheels (`foot: 'level'`), crawling forward on its toes.
    Its ankle ram runs down the shin's front to a horn ahead of and above the cross. The ram was sized from its length
    curve over the ankle's working arc: a first horn put its dead centre right at the level foot.
  - Every law holds, its bands set for its class from what was measured.

    - Its legs reach well out to their feet, spread fore and aft of the hips. Each leg `aim`s, turned at its hip to

- **Every joint is an actuator's** (the construction shelf's chain, `construction-shelf/con-chain.js`).
  - A pitch or roll joint is driven by a hydraulic ram across it. Its range is where that ram lies within its stroke:
    derived, never stated.
  - The hip yaw and the ankle roll are rotary drives with stops and a rated torque.
  - Each ram's barrel is on the body nearer the hip, so the leg's mass stays high.
- **A stance is solved by where the feet are** (`mecha-ik.js`). The leg's inverse kinematics is closed form, with the
  ankle a cross: any foot within reach is set at any heading, sole flat. A stance names its pelvis height (or the knee
  bend that sets it), its track, the feet's places, lifts and headings, and a sway. A sway carries the centre of mass
  over one sole for a static step.
  - The named stances are `stand` (knees bent 45°, clear of the straight leg's singularity), `board` (crouched to be
    climbed into, the feet set back under the folded knees), `stride`, `lift` (on one foot, the other raised) and
    `turn`.
  - A pose may also be a stance of the operator's, or joint values.
- **The laws** (`mecha-laws.js`) are measured from the frame as built and posed:
  - each ram's arc;
  - every stance held within its joints' ranges;
  - the standing knee's bend;
  - static stability on both feet (the centre of mass's margin inside the soles' polygon);
  - the sway on one foot;
  - each actuator's share of its rating holding the frame still (a ram's force from its moment arm at the pose, against
    its push or pull at the system pressure);
  - ground pressure on one sole;
  - the step-up height and the stride reach;
  - the saddle's or the seat's height standing and crouched, and the boarding step's;
  - the tip-over (fallen on its side, it lands on its cabin and legs, never on the rider);
  - the legs' clearance from the rider's space at every stance;
  - the parts' mass against the class's, and the share of a leg's mass below the knee.

### The test suite, once

CI ran the whole suite four times a run, on node 22.14.0, 22 and 24 and on macOS, and the realistic hero's body was
rebuilt in every test file that asked for one. Nothing a user sees changes.

- **The whole suite on one leg.** Node 22 on Ubuntu runs the whole suite, the deep sweeps and the bundled recipe book,
  in three shards. The other legs (the engines floor 22.14.0, node 24, macOS) run what can differ by runtime: the
  critical tier, which carries every byte pin (node 24 still without them), the database and its native module, the
  MCP surface and the install scripts. Geometry is pure JavaScript; its byte pins still run on every reference leg.
- **The realistic body built once per run.** A realistic hero's slice and head cost tens of seconds and were kept in
  memory, but each test file starts with an empty memory. Under test the keeps now have a second shelf on disk
  (`lib/util/kept.js`): the runner names a folder for the sources' hash, a miss in memory reads it before building and
  writes what it built, serialized as the structured clone the keeps already read, so a kept body is the built one bit
  for bit. Without `MOJULO_KEPT_DIR` (every install) nothing touches the disk. `MOJULO_KEPT=off` turns it off under
  test.

### A game's hero runs, and walks by the stick or with Z held
