- **The keys run; the walk is held.** A hero on the animation library (`playerWorld`, every game's player slot) runs on
  W / S at the game's speed (the feel's, or 3.6 m/s) on the library's jog (`Jog_Fwd_Loop`). Holding Z walks, on the
  library's walk (`Walk_Loop`) at 1.6 m/s, its cycle about 2 m, so the feet keep the ground. The legend says it:
  W / S run · Z walk; the pause sheet lists the walk (hold) for a person and no boost.
- **A pad walks by the stick's travel.** Tilted, the stick walks, the pace rising with the push to the walk's; past 60 %
  of its travel (`runAt`) it runs, from the walk's pace up to the game's speed at full travel, the walk and the run
  meeting where the stick crosses. The pad's legend says it: tilt to walk, push to run.
- **F no longer boosts a person.** It was a mech suit's thruster on every hero: held, the hero skated the ground at three
  and a half times its speed in the jump's flight pose. The platform rule's `walkSpeed` (and `walkStride`, `runAt`)
  marks a person: no thrust, no gauge, no boost pose, and F is nothing of its own. A suit, a space suit, and a hero whose
  F is its gear's (the swing and the zip) keep the boost as they had it; a rule without `walkSpeed` plays
  byte-identically. The walk is the pilot scheme's `walk` action (Z, held; remappable), the input's `walk`.
- **The library's walk and jog play over the hero's own door gaits** (`playerStates` with a library): the hero's own
  jog and walk play where no library is named (`library: false`).
- **A side lane and an endless runner only run** (`playerWorld({ walk: false })`), as does a mascot pilot.

### The main quest: a game's beginning, middle and end, its core loop, and the first session's goalposts

A long game had no spine. The game book could make every stretch of one: a walled-core dungeon, a quest open world's
regions, errands, wave gauntlets, a tactics book's epochs, the story's moments, quests. Nothing said how the stretches
add up to a game, how long it is, or what comes first. The main quest is that spine. It is not a game type: its outcome
is the flow and the sequence, and the levels and maps are laid from it.

- **The main quest** (a gameworld's `mainQuest`, `gameworld/main-quest.js`). Its acts, each a beat at a time, and each
  beat what it is played as: a level, a walled-core dungeon's space, a quest open world's quest, a gauntlet, an errand,
  an epoch, or a story moment. A beat may be planned and not built yet (`built: false`). The quest also takes its
  length, the periods it spans and how loose its side quests are, and an ending if it has one; a quest still being built
  may have none.
- **Acts or chapters: two progressions.** A quest is shaped as acts, the arc (a beginning, a middle and an end), or as
  chapters, a long game told chapter on chapter that runs past an arc. Each chapter turns the world: its `turn` is what
  a happening changes, carried on (the time facet's chapter overlay), or a new period. Every law holds both shapes to
  the same progression. A chaptered quest is also held to its own two laws: more than three chapters (three or fewer
  read as an arc, and acts tell it), and each chapter after the first turning something.
- **Its laws map it into the book** (advice, never refusing): a beginning, a middle and an end; every power the hero's
  actions name gained on a beat, in the act its progression stage puts it (early, mid, late); foes that rise in rank act
  on act; acts that vary; a first beat that can be built now; a period past the first drawn as the time facet can draw
  it.
- **The core loop** (a gameworld's `loop`, the intent chapter's): what the player does from moment to moment, what an
  encounter is made of, what it rewards, and what one sitting of play is. Written, or read from the book (the hero's
  verbs, the levels' goals, the beats' gains), and held to what the hero can do.
- **Its levels are laid from its beats** (`gameworld/main-quest-lay.js`). A beat played as a structure is played on the
  level that holds it: a dungeon space's level, the open world's level, an errand giver's, a story moment's. A beat with
  only a goal is laid its own level at a run, composed from its words, named by its goal, and standing the foes it fields.
  It is laid once, into the recipe, and is the creator's from then on (edited in place; the beat finds it by its id). The
  game plays the beats' levels in the quest's order, then the world's others. A planned beat is laid and made nothing:
  the pre-compile check prices it apart (`estimate.planned`). The readout says what each beat is played on, and what
  the next run will lay.
- **The main quest on the time facet** (`cosmos/facets/time.js`). Three settings say a long game's shape, so the sweep
  prices what it still waits on:
  - `arc`: none, acts (built), chapters (partial: a chapter's turn is said, not yet lowered to its world overlay);
  - `periods`: one, new maps (built), the same maps at another period (absent: it waits on eras);
  - `sides`: none, tight, loose, free (partial: the quest records how loose its side quests are; nothing yet places them
    by it).

  A world's main quest sets them in its cube (`gameworld/intent.js` `cubeOfWorld`), so its intent's verdict says what it
  waits on. A long-RPG probe (a hero's main quest told in chapters, the world turned between them, side quests loose on
  a big map) reads blocked on the same maps and gapped on the chapter turns and the side quests. Two new work packages
  price those gaps, `quest-turns` and `side-quests`; on the regenerated hillclimb page, the side quests lift eleven
  swept worlds.
- **The first session's goalposts** (`gameworld/goalposts.js`, the readout's `goalposts` while any is open). A game is
  not done at the end of a session, but a good first session leaves seven things, each read from what the book already
  says:
  1. what game it is (its intent, and its core loop);
  2. how long it is, where it is set and where its story goes (the main quest and the world);
  3. the hero's look and the world's (the cast and the foes when there are any);
  4. how it feels to play, and the hero's powers;
  5. a plan of what to build (the quest's beats, its first buildable, nothing blocking the build);
  6. a plan of the first level (the first beat's level, written or laid, and settled);
  7. the first level made and proved by the machine gate (whether it plays as the game is the creator's, the eyes gate).

  Each is met, partial or open; an open one says what is missing and asks the question only the creator answers. `next`
  is the first not met, with its chapter and the move to make: where this session goes on, and where the next one
  picks up, read from the recipe. The build chapter's view carries them, and the studio card lists them.
- **A first session, measured** (machine gate, real headless Chrome, the default budget). The book was a long RPG: a
  wind-walker, three wind powers, a main quest told in five chapters (the first chapter's beat built, a climb with its
  ladder; the other four planned), intent `long-rpg`, a feel, and its loop written. It took seven `design_game` calls
  and about six minutes:
  - writing the book met five of the seven goalposts;
  - the levels chapter's proof made the first level's three stages ahead of their approvals;
  - the build kept those three stages and made the hero, the systems, the gear and the game;
  - two checking runs walked all three stages, the climb up its ladder among them: three of three proved, and three
    first frames passed;
  - the last readout left nothing open.

  The quest's laws caught a real slip in the book: its mid-stage power was gained in chapter 2 of 5, which is still
  early. The session also found a bug. The first level's goalpost counted only its first stage, so it read met after
  the first check, which had stopped at its budget before the climb was walked. It now counts each stage of the level.
  Whether the level plays as the game is the eyes gate's, and the creator's to say.

### Natural knockback: an impact's energy split between the ground and what stands near it

- **Knockback is its own channel, apart from damage.** A blow carries energy as well as hp:
  - a direct hit's **kinetic** energy pushes what it strikes along the blow;
  - an **impact** where it meets the ground spreads as a shock. The ground takes its share, and each body near takes its
    share by how much of the shock it fills, falling off with distance.
- **What holds, and what flies.** A body holds by its footing (friction on its mass over a short slip; none in the air).
  Past that it is thrown, an arc and then a slide friction stops, held to the play cap. Light things fly, heavy things
  only stagger; a hard throw knocks down, and a wall stops it with a stagger. A body's mass is its `body.mass`, or its
  hitbox's size (a person about 75 kg).
- **Splash damage by proximity.** In a level with knockback, a burst's damage and poise fall off with distance from it
  (`splash: 'flat'` keeps the old way).
- **Magic attacks with kinetic and impact settings:** a weapon's `knock`, a strike's `strikeKnock`, a power's `kinetic`
  and `impact` (its beam pushes its target and releases its impact where it lands).
- **Natural:** a level's `knockback` (true, or `{ scale, hero, cap, splash, min, slam, natural }`) gives every burst an
  impact from its size and makes a hard landing a slam. The hero is thrown too, unless `hero: false`.
- **The juice is vayo's:** the impact's air on the fires near it, a dust ring where it lands, dust under what slides.
- A level without knockback, and attacks without kinetic or impact, change no behaviour.

### Requisitions: one chapter or one level at a time, to quality, and then again

The design for producing a game one unit at a time. A unit is a chapter of the game book or one level. The director
(the person's agent) raises a **requisition** for the next unit, and it goes to the department that owns that unit's
chapter. Units are authored one by one, so a mistake stays inside its unit and an accepted unit is settled ground for
the next. Subagents work inside a unit rather than across units: **diverge** orders make alternatives of the same unit
and keep one, and **critic** orders review it with a fresh context. A unit is **received** when its machine gate holds
and **accepted** when the person approves it (for a level, once they have played it). The person's notes on what they
sent back carry into the next requisition. The game is built up to its last accepted level as each level lands, and it
ends when the last planned level is accepted. A quick game is one unit, made by a single author. The ledger is kept
apart from the recipe and adds nothing to any render or export. The design is in progress; its first piece, below, is in the code.

- **Fixed: a run no longer reverts what was written while it ran.** A `design_game` run read the world once and wrote
  its whole copy back at each checkpoint, on a failure partway and at its end. So a page another chapter wrote during
  the run, or the creator's verdict, was quietly undone. Each write now lays only the run's own changes (its record, a
  pinned hero base and the approval kept with it) onto the world as it is stored at that moment
  (`gameworld/rebase.js`). A run with nothing written beside it writes what it always wrote.
- **One level is a unit of its own** (`design_game({ ref, chapter: 'level:<id>' })`, `chapters.js` `unitOf`). It is the
  levels chapter narrowed to one level: its review part, its page, the links in and out of it, and its next moves. Its
  state is its part's stamp. On the meadowmark reference book that is 1.7 KB, where the levels chapter is 2.6 KB and the
  whole readout 7.0 KB. Its run (`run: true`) makes that level's stages and what their orders name (the level's pilot),
  never a sibling level's. A level the world does not have is refused before anything is made. A write past the level
  is written and reported (`outside`), never refused. The id mirrors the level's review part, so `tools/list` is
  unchanged.
- **The studio card works one unit at a time.** The chapters are listed in the order they read each other, worked one
  at a time to quality so a mistake stays in its unit, and each level is a unit. A subagent is handed the next unit once
  the last one is settled. Before, the card said a wave's chapters could be worked side by side.
- **The requisition ledger** (`design_game({ ref, req })`, `gameworld/reqs.js`, the `gameworld_reqs` table). The director
  asks for one unit at a time: `req: { unit, remit?, staffing? }`, where a unit is a chapter or `level:<id>`.
  - **Pull-through.** Asking for a unit first raises, each as its own req, the chapters upstream of it that the book
    holds and has not settled, in book order. A chapter that is settled, already asked for, or has no review of its
    own is not raised.
  - **One at a time.** The first live req is the current one; the rest are queued. A unit asked for while another is
    open is queued after it and the readout says so; it is never refused. A unit asked for twice is asked for once.
  - **Status is read from the book, never stored.** A unit is accepted when the creator approves every part of it, and
    goes stale if a part changes after. It is "sent back" when a part is sent back. A unit with no review part is
    accepted on the creator's word (`req: { id, accept: true }`), against the print of its pages. A req can also be
    cancelled, and a level that leaves the world is gone.
  - **What a unit reads besides its chapter.** Its view (`{ ref, chapter: unit }`) carries its `req`: the remit, the
    staffing and its budget, and the precedent. The precedent is the last accepted unit of its kind with its remit (a
    level's is the last accepted level), plus the creator's notes on everything they sent back so far. Those notes are
    kept in the ledger the first time the door reads them.
  - **A level's remit** names its way in and out, how hard it is, the one new idea it teaches, its foes and its beat.
    What it leaves out is advised, never required.
  - **Staffing** is `soloist` (one author: the quick path) or `studio`, each with a budget of what the server can count.
    The jobs that spend it come next.
  - The readout's `reqs` gives the current unit, the queue and the counts, and its next moves gain `req`. The ledger
    never touches the recipe: a world reads, renders and exports the same with or without it (tested). The
    `gameworld-next` card's ceiling moves from 4096 to 4352 bytes for its one `req` line.
- **Fixed: a run's first-frame record no longer reverts a page written while it rendered.** It was the last
  whole-world write after a run; it now uses the same rebase as the run's own writes.
- **The jobs inside a req** (`gameworld/jobs.js`, the `gameworld_req_jobs` table). Each job is the size of one agent's
  turn: the exact call it reads with, the pages it may write, the call it reports with, and the tier of judgment it
  needs. Starting a req (`req: { id, start: true }`) issues its authors, by its staffing.
  - **A soloist** gets one author. Its report applies its patch at once.
  - **A studio** gets its diverge authors (`budget.diverge`), each given a different angle on the remit: the plainest
    reading, the boldest, and the one furthest from the precedent. Their patches are held. The director (or the
    creator) keeps one with `req: { id, keep: 'j2' }`: that patch is applied, and the others are declined and kept on
    record.
  - **Critics** are issued once a proposal is kept (`budget.critics`). Each reads with a lens (design against the
    remit, play as a player, look as a viewer), never the maker's reasoning, and reports findings.
  - **A report goes through `design_game` itself:** `req: { id, job, patch, decisions }` for an author,
    `req: { id, job, findings }` for a critic. A decision with no `because` is counted as uncited: a choice the seed
    made. A patch past the unit's pages is applied and reported, never refused. A job reports once.
  - **The budget bounds what is issued.** Every job counts, a reissue among them (`req: { id, reissue: 'j1' }`). A job
    past the budget is not issued, and the readout says so.
  - **What the director does next** is in the unit's view and the ledger's current req (`does`): start, work, keep,
    critique or review. The unit's view lists each job: an issued job's brief, or a reported job's report (what it
    wrote, its cited and uncited decisions, its findings).
  - **No new listed tool:** a job's whole allowlist is `design_game`. The ledger's own card (`gameworld-ledger`, the
    build chapter's) teaches the reqs, the jobs, the received gate and the composite; the studio card points to it.
  - **An author's report can say what it could not make:** `asks` lists what the remit wants that no word of the recipe
    reaches. It is kept on the job and reported to the director, so a gap is said, never faked.
  - **A level's author is handed a level page's manuals.** A level unit's view names the world card (a level's walk,
    goal, places and style) and the foes card (a level's own foes) before its chapter's own cards. A test holds that
    each key a level page writes is taught on one of them.
  - **Tried with a live agent.** A fresh agent given only one author job's brief read its view, authored a level of the
    reference book and reported. It was refused once with a readable error and corrected itself. Its job was kept,
    with every decision cited. It found the two gaps above: the view pointed it at neither of the cards that teach a
    level page, so it missed a level's own `foes` key; and the remit's tide (a passage that opens and closes) is a
    capability no word of the recipe has, which it could only say in prose.
- **The received gate** (`gameworld/reqs.js` `receiptOf`): a unit's machine gate, before the creator's verdict. It
  holds when a proposal is kept, every decision in it is cited, every critic has reported, and no law of the machine
  gate advises on the unit's parts. A level also needs its stages made and played by the probe as they stand, after
  the proposal was kept. What it does not hold on it reports: the kept proposal's asks and the critics' findings. A unit
  whose gate holds is **received**, a status between open and accepted. Received is not accepted: the creator's
  verdict still decides. A unit's view carries its `receipt`.
- **The play probe** (`game/level-probe.js`, `req: { id, probe: true }`, a machine gate). Each of a level's stages is
  played on its World page, in an installed browser (never a download), for 17 seconds of simulated time under a simple
  script: forward the whole time, fire, jump and interact now and then. It says four things:
  - **loads:** no uncaught error while the page loads and plays;
  - **not lost:** the level is not over after a second standing still;
  - **opposed:** a level whose goal is to survive, fight, sneak or race has a foe, a hazard or a rival in it, read from
    the stage's own manifest;
  - **clean:** no debugging text on the page (`0 events → store`, `NaN`, `undefined`, `[object Object]`).

  It keeps a frame at 5, 11 and 17 seconds for a look critic, under the outcomes folder. It cannot aim, so it says
  nothing of balance. Its verdict is kept as the req's ride job: the server's own work, which spends none of the
  budget. With no browser it is skipped, and the loop goes on to the creator. Each check is tested against the starter
  that failed it in play.
- **What the director does next** gains `probe` (a level whose stages have not been played as they stand) and `fix`
  (the probe does not hold: back to its author), before `review`.
- **An accepted unit goes stale when a chapter it reads moves.** The ledger keeps the prints of a unit's upstream
  chapters the first time it reads the unit accepted. If one moves, the unit is stale, and the creator can accept it
  again on their word (`req: { id, accept: true }`) once they have looked.
- **The game is built up to its last accepted level** (`gameworld/runner.js` `composedStages`). When a world's ledger
  asks for levels one at a time, its game is made of the levels the creator has accepted, as they stand: their stages in
  the book's order, the gates chained over them alone, and the links and a map's exits between them only. So the game is
  always playable to its last accepted level, and it ends when the last planned level is accepted. A stale level stays
  out until it is accepted again.
  - **A composite build** (`run: true`) makes the accepted levels' stages and everything they share (the hero, the
    casts, the foes), never a level no one has worked yet: a level's stages are its own unit's to make. Only the
    accepted levels are walked after the game. With none accepted there is no game yet.
  - **The readout asks for it.** Once an accepted level is missing from the game as made, `next` gains `composite` (the
    levels it would be made of; `first` when no game exists yet), and the ledger's `reqs.composite` says whether the
    game holds them. The pre-compile check, the run and the proofs all read the same composite.
  - **A world that asks for no level is unchanged.** With no composite the runner's steps are byte-identical (tested on
    a book with its hero and on a world before its people).
- **The main quest is the queue** (`gameworld/quest-reqs.js`).
  - **A req can name a beat:** `req: { unit: 'beat:<id>' }` asks for the level the beat is played on, found as a run
    finds it. A beat with only a goal has its level laid now, the same lay a run makes, so the req has a level to name.
    Everything after that (the level's view, its jobs, the probe, the composite) is a level's as before.
  - **Its remit is filled from the quest,** and the director's own words win, key by key: the act (its name, its place
    among the acts, its stage of the hero's progression) and the beat's goal; the band from that stage; the beat's foes;
    the powers the hero gains on it as its one idea; the beats before and after it as its way in and out; and the core
    loop's moment and encounter.
  - **`req: { quest: true }`** asks for every built beat's level in the quest's order, each its own req, the first open
    and the rest queued. It says the planned beats, and asked again it raises nothing twice.
  - A planned beat (`built: false`), a beat the quest does not have, or a beat played on no level is refused, with what
    the quest holds.
- **The goalposts read the ledger.** With a req for the first level, the first level's plan (goalpost 6) is met once its
  proposal is kept with every decision cited, and the first level (goalpost 7) once it is received or accepted. Each
  partial one says the req's failing checks, its move is the req's next step, and the goalposts' `next` names the req.
  With no such req the goalposts read as they did.
- **While a req is open the ledger leads:** its move is first in `next`, after only a run its budget stopped.
- **The production ledger: asks and traces** (`gameworld/asks.js`, the `gameworld_asks` and `gameworld_ask_links`
  tables). A long session's decisions can now be read back without its turns.
  - **An ask is a ticket for the intent the agent acts on,** in the agent's own words: its inference of what the person
    wants, never the person's message. No column holds their words, and a call that tries to give them is refused.
    Acting on an inferred intent is the consent the record stands on.
  - **A ticket is cut only when intent becomes work.** `ask: { intent, units? }` goes with the req, the verdict
    (`approve`, `revise`), the patch or the run it causes; an ask with no work is refused. `ask: 'a3'` adds to an
    existing ticket. Intent is capped at 1 KB.
  - **What an ask caused is linked to it,** one row per link: the reqs it raised, the verdicts it gave, the patch it
    wrote and the run it made, each at the recipe's revision. A job keeps the revision its kept patch made.
  - **A trace** (`design_game({ ref, trace: 'a3' | 'r2' | 'r2.j1' })`) reads the chain from any ticket: the intent, its
    reqs and their jobs (each decision with its because, what no word reached, the critics' findings, the revision a
    kept patch made), its verdicts, patches and runs. The correlation path (`gw·a3·r2·j1`) is derived, never stored, and
    a trace never shows a patch's values.
  - **The intent reaches the next unit.** A unit's view carries the intent it was asked for with, and its precedent
    carries the intent behind the last accepted unit of its kind.
  - The ledger never touches the recipe (tested). The ledger card teaches the ticket and the trace.
- **The play probe also checks that the camera sees something** (`sees`). At each kept frame it reads the world's own
  canvas (never the HUD or the legend) and fails a frame that is one colour over the first-frame check's threshold, by
  the first-frame check's own measure (`first-frame.js` `dominantColour`). A camera inside something, or turned to an
  empty sky partway through a level, now fails here; the first real probe had passed one.
- **The impact preview** (`design_game({ ref, patch, preview: true })`). The patch is applied in memory, as
  `update_sketch` applies it, and nothing is written. The answer says what the patch would reach: the chapters it
  touches, the approved parts that would come back for review, the accepted units that would go stale (their own parts,
  or a chapter they read), what a run would make, remake or drop, and the accepted levels the game would lose. A patch
  the door would refuse is refused with the same words. The studio card says to preview a change that may reach far.
- **The production: crews, the assistant director and the director's call** (`gameworld/production.js`, the
  `gameworld_production` and `gameworld_req_notes` tables, new columns on the req and job tables). It follows how a game
  studio runs: the creator is its creative director and publisher; the director (the person's agent) is its game
  director.
  - **The director's style** (`production: { style, checkpoints? }`): yeoman, auteur or avant-garde, auteur when unset,
    overridable per req. It sets the assistant director's posture: assistive ("is it done, and done well?"), strict
    ("is it ours?") or elevating ("what would make it memorable?", within the world's laws). The first goalpost's
    question now asks for it.
  - **A crew per beat** (`req: { unit: 'beat:<id>', crew: true }`): the beat's level and the departments it brings (its
    foes when it fields any, the story when it names its cast or is a story moment), worked as one req. Starting it
    issues an author per unit, each writing only its own unit's pages. The crew shares a notebook
    (`req: { id, job, post }`), shown in every unit's view, and its critics come once every author is kept.
  - **Every job has a stable role** (`<world>:<kind>:<department>`, the assistant `<world>:assistant`), so a host can
    keep one agent in a seat beat after beat, its precedent in its own context and its stable prompt cached.
  - **The assistant director** (`req: { id, assist: true }`, a judge-tier job) reads what was made in its posture and
    recommends pass-up, rework or elevate, with reasons (and fixes, or a bolder angle). It never decides.
  - **The director decides** (`req: { id, direct }`): `settle` makes the unit **directed**, the director's own call and
    never the creator's accepted, which still wins when they approve it; `rework` reissues its authors with the note in
    the notebook and the precedent; `creator` shows it to the creator. The director may settle only after the creator
    accepts the vertical slice (a level), and never a pillar (what game it is, the main quest, the hero's direction and
    look) or a checkpoint (`act`: each act's last level; `every`: every unit). A directed unit goes stale when what it
    was settled on moves, and is played in the game like an accepted one.
  - The readout's `production` says the style and posture, whether the slice is accepted, and how many units the
    creator accepted against how many the director settled. What the director does next gains `assist` and `decide`.
- **Fixed: the ledger reads the parts' real stamps.** It had read the readout's projection of them, which carries no
  prints and names the laws `advises`, so the received gate's laws check never saw a law, and a directed unit was
  recorded with no prints. The ledger, the receipt, the views and the impact preview now read the same stamps.
- **A job's agent works from its seat.** A brief's read carries `as: '<req>.<job>'`, and `design_game({ ref, as })`
  is that job's view: its own unit (the crew's, for the assistant director), its own brief and nothing of its siblings',
  and a call that may only report its own job. Anything else beside `as` (a patch, a run, a verdict, another unit, another
  job's report) is refused with what the seat may do; a reissued job and the probe are no agent's seat.
- **A brief names its agent.** A host that declares `capabilities.jobAgents` (Claude Code) and runs the Claude plugin
  sees each brief name the plugin's agent for its job (`agent`: `mojulo-author`, `-critic`, `-assistant`, from
  `job-words.js`). The agent definitions themselves ship in the plugin with the next release, whose version bump they
  need (an installed plugin updates only when its version moves).
- **A level's laws reach its received gate.** The receipt's `laws` check had read only the parts' own stamps, which
  carry no level law, so a level's req was received over laws that advised. It now holds a level to its intent laws
  (`lay-concerns.js`, as the run plans them) and to the scene composer's (`focus`, `way-on`, `lit`, `palette`), which the
  play probe keeps from the build it plays (`composed`, by stage, played by a browser or not) and the receipt reads while
  the probe is current. The first of the expertise the composer holds to be read by the req layer.

### Effects on the flow: blasts and power-ups moved by the world's air (rupa-vayo)

- **`fxStyle: { flow: true }`** (any look, any flavor): a blast and a power-up drawn as the world's air moves them.
  When an effect goes off, the air round its spot is solved once: the ways it can go (rays against the level's walls,
  ceilings and floor), the wind, a pool it is in. Every puff then follows a formula of time, so the same blast differs
  by where it goes off. Against a wall it runs up the face; in a corridor it shoots down it and out of the open end;
  in the wind its smoke leans downwind; under water it is a pulsing bubble.
- **A blast in stages**: a fireball that races out and holds, then lifts and rolls into a ring (a mushroom needs no
  stem), its white-hot heart inside a coloured shell; a plume of smoke; debris thrown along the open ways; a third as
  many sparks, as embers that cool from white to red to dark; and the ground ring as a dust skirt running along the
  ground. Fewer, larger, bolder puffs.
- **A power-up**: flame tongues rising and turning round the body (a new tongue-shaped sprite), a white-hot core,
  motes drawn in on a spiral, pebbles lifting off the ground, and a gust of dust pushed out along it, in place of the
  spinning onions and rings of spikes.
- **The combat page on the flow**: a grenade's, a death's or a scripted blast's burst goes off as the flow's blast in
  place of the additive spheres, and a hit is a soft flash and a ring of air in place of a sphere, a torus and a star
  of lines.
- **Fixed**: a world whose play cues make its events now keeps its `fxStyle` and `fxLight` (they were laid on the
  events before the cues rebuilt them, and lost). Such worlds now draw the composed effects they ask for.
- A world without `flow` changes no byte.

### A blast's air fans a fire, or blows it out (rupa-vayo)

- **On the flow (`fxStyle: { flow: true }`), a blast's air reaches the world's fires.** Its wind at a fire is the blast
  wave's (its overpressure at the distance scaled by its charge, Kinney–Graham, and the air behind the front,
  Rankine–Hugoniot), sheltered by a wall between them. What it does depends on the fire's size: a bigger flame takes
  more air to strip (a candle goes out at about 3 m/s, a torch at 10, a campfire at 43).
  - **Fanned** (under half that): the flame leans away from the blast and flares, and with destructible physics it
    burns faster for a couple of seconds, so it spreads sooner.
  - **Straining** (half to all of it): the flame lifts off its bed and gutters, the sign it is about to go.
  - **Blown out**: the flame goes in a fifth of a second, a wisp of smoke rises off the hot bed, and the bed glows dull
    red while it cools. A burning block blown out stops burning (`blowout` on its hits), cooled to just under its
    ignition, so a neighbour still burning relights it within a second or two, and a lone one stays out. A torch, a
    candle or a brazier blown out stays out.
  - Inside the blast's own fireball the heat wins: what it reaches catches, and only what lies beyond feels its air.
- The world's own wind fans and strains a block's fire the same way, and a gale past a fire's limit blows it out.
- A world not on the flow, or with no fires, changes no byte.

### Vayo moves: special abilities that move a hero on its own air

- **A dash and a flight as special abilities** (`rule.vayo`, or a power's `vayo-dash` / `vayo-flight`), moved by one law:
  a push against the air the hero moves through, so every vayo move is a curve, never a line. It eases in toward its
  speed and eases out as the air bleeds it, the same at any frame rate. The physical moves (the dodge, the tackle, the
  boost, the charged leap, the cleave step, the zip) keep their laws and their bytes.
  - **The dash** pushes to its peak in its `rise`, then carries its `carry` and hands back to walking at the run speed.
    In the air its own air bears the hero while it pushes. Invincible frames only where it names them.
  - **The flight** rises, hovers when let go, cruises and dives at will, steered by the stick and the jump and kneel
    keys, a boost on the boost key. It never stalls, and it lands when it comes down.
  - **The jetpack** (a power's `vayo-jetpack`): less controlled than the flight. It thrusts along the body's axis and
    goes where the hero leans: the stick tilts the body toward its way and turns it to face it, late, and its momentum
    carries. Its startup spools the thrust and leans the body into the launch before it lifts. The jump key is full
    thrust, nothing held a slow sink, kneel cuts it; its fuel is the meter, and empty it sputters out. Its exhaust blows on
    a fire under it.
  - **The air dash** (a power's `vayo-air-dash`): a dash only in the air, its `count` before the ground again, in its
    element's dash shape. V in the air dashes first; held a quarter second on, by a hero that flies, the dash carries on
    as flight at its speed.
  - **The jump** (an air jump, a power's `vayo-jump`): the jump key in the air, after the physical air jumps. Its air
    catches the hero and pushes it up, then gravity takes it: the same height from wherever it fires, and letting go of
    the key does not cut it. `count` of them before the ground again.
  - **Its own key:** V, or the pad's D-pad down. On the ground it dashes, in the air it air-dashes (while its count
    lasts) or takes flight, in flight it lets go; the vayo jump is the jump key in the air. No physical move's key is
    taken.
- **Elements tune the shape:** wind carries far, earth stops hard, lightning snaps, fire pushes hard, water rises
  smoothly. The game's feel card tunes it (its dash and jetpack), and the hero's own numbers come last.
- **Power sets the fiction, the cap the play:** a move's speed scales as the square root of its tier (a super's dash's
  fiction is 380 m/s), and the hero moves at most 40 m/s (`cap`). What the cap holds back shows in the trail, a boom past
  sound, and the wake.
- **No speed passes through a wall:** a vayo move sweeps its footprint along its path.
- **Its trail and its wake:** a ribbon of its element's colour behind the hero, and on the flow its wake pushes the
  world's air, so a super's dash past a fire puts it out and a human's fans it.
- A world whose hero has no vayo move changes no byte.

### A 3D creative studio: the pieces it makes, from an object up to a game

Supersedes the person-facing frame of "An agent game studio" before it ships. "Game studio" boxed mojulo into one
outcome; the person now reads that it makes 3D objects, characters, environments, interactive worlds and even
playable games, exported to their desktop. The departments stay how the agent works, and "3D compiler" stays the
agent's word.

- **The READMEs** (the repo's and npm's) open on "A 3D creative studio for your agent" and show what it makes piece by
  piece, from the easy to the hard: 3D objects, characters, vehicles and props, rooms and buildings, environments and
  levels, interactive worlds, playable games. Each piece says what the person gets, never how: no tool calls or
  recipe code, no departments or production machinery, no install weight. Where it goes (the browser, a desktop app,
  the engines, 3D tools, a printer) stays.
- **The one-breath answer** (`get_substrate`): "it turns your agent into a **3D creative studio**", with the order to
  open broad, ladder up from an object to a game, and say what the person gets; the departments are named as how the
  agent works, not what it sells.
- **The manifests** (`package.json`, `server.json`, `glama.json`, the marketplace entry, the Claude plugin's
  `plugin.json`), the plugin's README and the dashboard's page description say the same. The plugin's change ships
  with the release that raises its version; its install, fetch and privacy sections are unchanged.
- **`CLAUDE.md`**: "What this is" opens on the 3D creative studio; the copy rule says the person-facing pages open
  broad, ladder up and never say how.

### Figure grades: one to pose, one to play

- **A character at two grades.** A character is made once and baked twice from the same recipe: the PLAY grade a
  game walks and the POSE grade the cinematics act with, the same skeleton and bone ids, the same clips, palette and
  height (`figures/figure-grades.js`: the two words, a grade's triangle budget by role, its advice when a figure is over,
  never a refusal, and `crossGradeErrors`, what keeps two bakes from being one character). The play grade
  (`heroFigure(…, { grade: 'play' })`, a figure's own `grade` over its world's `figureGrade`) lowers what a play camera
  cannot see: the body's rounding split (the one that quartered every body triangle), the anime head's coarse sampling
  and game lenses, its hair's rings and sides (a spike four-sided, half as many rings) and its cap's grid. Chapter 1's
  hero goes from 171k triangles to 32k, a party member from 72k to 35k, a townsperson from 55–76k to 20–26k; the town's
  people from 1.45M to 0.53M. A game's levels (`design_game`'s) play the play grade; every other page keeps its figures
  as they were. A hero on another head (the landmark, the realistic) keeps its head's sampling at both grades for now.
- **The pose grade cut in for a close shot.** A play-grade world bakes the figures its close shots reach again at the
  pose grade (`poseCast`: its party, its battles' foes, the figures its scenes frame close or set talking), `<name>@pose`
  in the bank when the two bakes are one character. On the page (merged-figure.js `__poseFrame`) a figure a close shot
  is on shows its pose twin, a second skinned mesh on the same bones built the first time it is wanted, so the clips never
  change hands: a scene's close, over-the-shoulder or two-shot, and a battle's film (rpg-channel.js: the actor close as a
  skill begins, behind it at its target, the target landing); off the shot, its play grade. A world without twins
  carries none of it.
- **A party RPG's chase pulled back.** A world that fights in party battles plays its hero from `PARTY_CHASE`
  (hero-chase.js `chaseFor`, the hero's own chase built the same way): the eye about twice as far and higher, the hero a
  tenth of the frame across instead of a fifth, the road and the town round it read; every other world's chase as it was.
- **The party walks again, and the chase comes in a little.** A party RPG's party walks the map behind the hero (the
  world's `battles.followers`, the default): each member finds its way round walls by the navmesh, never fights on the
  map (the arena holds the fights), and stops at its own distance, so the party trails in a file; the bodies pass through
  each other. A member walks in the hero's FOOTSTEPS (mind.js `rule.trail`): the hero leaves a crumb every 30 cm, and the
  member's goal is the point its distance back along them, ground the hero has just walked, so no wall stands between
  them however the hero turned; one woken or left more than 8 m from its point is set down on it. The party walks in a
  FORMATION (levels.js `PARTY_FORMATION`), not a file: each member its slot, so far back along the steps and so far
  across them (`rule.flank`), the hero a corner of a slanted parallelogram the next three stand at the other corners of. The party's chase is pulled in to 7.5 m behind and 4.4 m up, the hero an eighth of the frame across.
- **The grass is laid round what the camera frames.** A follow camera's eye stands back from its subject, and the live
  field measured every distance from the eye: on a chase 12 m back the hero's own ground was already past the field's
  near and thinned, and the field ended a few metres ahead of it. The field, the far grass and the static cards now
  measure past the chase's stand-off (its eye to its look point), the contact bed lies round the subject, and the field
  is laid again every 40 cm, not 75, so a tuft at a share's edge grows a step at a time. A walker's eye stands off
  nothing: first person reads as it did.

### The Game Brief: what the game is about, ordered as maps and set pieces, joined as a mandala

- **A game-motif-narrative above the genre.** The genre says how a moment plays; `gameBrief.gmn` says what the game is
  about, as a mix of MOTIVATIONS (the why: stakes, ending, the acts, the cast's relations, the palette's arc and the light
  act by act) and LABOURS (the how: the world's shape, its climax, what a beat is played as, its side content, the genres it
  suits), each a row (gameworld/gmn.js). The mix is read once at authoring and stored: the largest labour decides the
  structure, the others at a tenth or more bring their side content; the largest motivation decides the stakes and the
  colour script, the others add cast and flags; less is said and dropped.
- **The brief orders the game's key places.** With a labour said, it lays its orders for the scene composer, each with
  the colour theorist's notes (how far along the script, its light): the first level, which sets the tone, and the climax,
  a citadel or the labour's own set piece; a hub's home where its shape has one. A list already there is the operator's;
  `orders: 'reroll'` lays them again.
- **A pillar, in conversation.** The brief is the intent chapter's: its mix and orders are in the part the creator
  accepts, so a change sends it back. The pitch stays in `brief`, the creator's words. The readout says what it decided and
  offers the main quest's spine and the labours' genres, never writing either (`gameworld-brief`, the asks in order).
- **The megaworld: maps joined as a topology, the loaded map the current map.** `megaworld: { shape, rings, gates? }`
  (gameworld/megaworld.js) writes a game's zones in rings (a mandala's last its core, a chain's one a ring, a hub's home
  alone in the first, an open world's one ring, each zone joined to its neighbours), lowered at authoring into the links a
  map world already walks, its laws WCD's at the world's scale. A glyph map is a zone: its ends carry its ways, and one with
  no way on keeps its goal, reaching it the level's win; a mandala's core is the game's final level.
- **The current map.** A megaworld's store keeps where the player is (`atlas`, a flags slice), so a save resumes on the map
  it left, arrived at by the way it was come in by. Leaving a map by a way is travel and completes nothing; a zone is found
  by having been next to it. What is won stays won, the world's flags carried from map to map. The shell's home is a travel
  screen, the zones on their rings, the core at the centre, a found one travelled to by a touch.
- **A door carries the store as it stands.** A door handed the next level the session's starting params; what was gathered
  before it reached the store but not the level on the other side.

### The gen-7 sky hides the painted cloud cards outdoors too

- **Fixed: big flat clouds over a gen-7 landscape.** The gen-7 sky (`channels/form-sky.js`) replaces what the stage
  painted for the sky, its cloud cards among them, and finds them by their group name. A textured mesh was given its
  group name only when the indoor form render, a sway, the grass, the tone curve, a preview, the view cone or an arena
  clip was on the page, so on an outdoor gen-7 page (the form land, or the gen-7 sky over a geocity) the painted cloud
  cards kept no name, stayed up, and covered the sky's own clouds with large flat shapes. Those pages now name their
  textured meshes as the others do (`scene-three.js`), and the cards go with the rest of the painted sky. A page
  without the form land or the gen-7 sky emits the same bytes as before.

### The interface department, and the game UI runtime every game will share

- **The studio has a seventh department: interface and UX.** A game's menus, its front (the title, the menu, the
  options, the credits) and its screen were the build's, so nothing owned how a game is worked by hand. The
  `interface` chapter now owns the recipe's `/front` and `/screen`, reads the intent, the world, the systems, the
  battles and the cast, and the build reads it. Its first work is the runtime below.
- **One runtime for game UI (internal name mana-ui), so a screen is built once and not game by game.** The UI was drawn
  by a dozen surfaces, each with its own sheet, colours and focus handling (the HUD, the menus, the RPG's battle and
  party menu, both game shells, versus, the hangar, the board games). `control/lib/mana-ui/` is the implementation
  playscape's words will run on: components with props passed down, three owners of state (the game's, read through
  bindings and never copied; the screen's own focus, tabs and stack; and the appearance drawn from both), a form that
  is a tree of data, and a function that is the cue effects playscape already speaks, emitted and never a callback. It
  ships as one closure through `toString()`, imports nothing outside its folder, and adds no byte to a page that does
  not use it. Nothing emits it yet: the library is built out in greybox first, then styled, and then the surfaces move
  onto it one at a time.
- **The library, in greybox: the components games are built from, and the screens they share.** Before any style and
  before any game runs on it, every part works and reads in values only (focus a shape, bar kinds told by their
  pattern, placeholders crossed boxes), so its structure, the data it reads and the effects it emits are settled
  first.
  - The components: layout (screens with a cursor per couch seat, splits, tabs fixed or from data, a row per item),
    values (bars with phase ticks, pips, counters, timers, compares as ▲ ▼), inputs (long lists that scroll, grids moved
    in two directions, skill trees laid in tiers by what each node requires, carousels, sliders, keybinds, a field
    chosen by data, points spent as a draft, a name typed from a grid), the in-game layer (the nine screen regions, and
    parts placed over things in the world), and the enemies' states (what one knows of you as a shape, its statuses).
  - The screens as compositions, each saying what it reads and emits: attract, title, loading, mode, character and
    arena select, pause, options, controls, confirm, results, save; the party, a skill tree, a level up, a loadout, the
    inventory, a shop, the quest log, a talk; and in game the vitals, objective, compass, minimap, ammo, score, a
    prompt, the feed, the crosshair, a moment, the party strip, plates over the enemies, a boss bar with its phases, a
    target frame and damage numbers.
  - A wireframe board draws every one of them live on one sample game, each a 1280×720 screen in its frame, driven by
    keys (a second seat beside the first) with the effects it emits written under it.
- **Styles are a layer over the greybox: themes, fonts you own, and the world's guide.** A theme is closed words and
  colours (a frame, a corner, a plate, how the focus shows, motion, ornaments such as brackets, scanlines or a stitch,
  and the four colours it needs, the rest derived from them), written over the greybox without touching what a screen
  holds. A game brings its own fonts as their bytes, inlined, so a page still loads nothing. A theme's colours are
  measured for contrast and advised, never refused. A world's UI guide becomes a theme, its tint, dials, border and
  font shelf faces carried over, so a game's menus wear the look its world was directed in. The board switches between
  the themes over the same live screens.
- **Couch players each get their own detail panel, and a list and its detail are one move apart.** On a select screen,
  each seat's panel shows the fighter that seat is on; left and right cross between a list and its detail; a list's id
  belongs to its screen, so two screens can use the same idiom.
- **The live game in each kind of game, in the one style.** What shows during play is drawn by the same components, sheet
  and theme as the menus: a fight's mirrored bars with the chip of the last hit, rounds and clock, super meters and the
  combo; a race's place, laps, times and speedometer; a firefight's damage direction, off-screen markers, lock-on and
  ability bar; survival's hotbar and names over the world; strategy's resources, unit card, attack forecast and wave;
  a match's score bug and lower third; a cutscene's cinema bars and subtitles; a detection meter; quest words; a phone's
  touch controls. The menus that come up mid-play are screens laid out over the held game: a turn-based battle's
  commands, targets, turn order and party, a unit's actions beside its forecast, the scoreboard, a strategy game's
  orders. A test holds every component to the one style: its rule in the sheet, no colour of its own, and every colour
  it reads set by every theme, so a HUD can never drift into a second look.
- **A sport's menus and its broadcast are one production.** The broadcast covers the play (the bug, the calls, the
  closeups, the board); the menus around it (the title, the pause, the results) now take its look and its kits: a
  package becomes a menu theme, and a row, a table row or a badge with a side wears that side's kit, kept apart by the
  broadcast's own colour science. The screen after the results board reads the match's stats in the contest's own
  words, formats and leads, so it continues what the coverage showed (won or lost, the score by side, the head to head
  with each lead marked), instead of a generic "cleared". The parts the coverage already draws are flagged so a covered
  page never shows two score bugs, and a menu now holds the keyboard while it is up, so Enter on a pause never also
  serves the ball.
- **Selection that follows the player's hands, and screens made for a phone.** With keys or a pad the focus is a modern
  ring (a theme may lift it, fill it, make it glow or keep a console RPG's ▶). With a finger or a mouse there is no
  cursor: nothing shows selected until a tap, a tap does what it lands on (a row with a detail beside it is selected
  first), a slider follows the finger, a stepper's ends are their own targets, a toggle is a switch, a swipe turns a
  carousel or the tabs, and the HUD's pause, map and skills are taps. A touch screen's targets grow to 48 px, its long
  lists scroll whole, screens keep out of the notch and the home bar, a phone-width screen stacks its panes, and a
  phone's menus rise from the foot of the screen in reach of a thumb. The board shows phone-sized frames driven by touch.
- **The UI is driven by the game's own controls, and says them back.** The screens are a view: they never read a key
  or a pad themselves. The game's controls (its control schemes, their drivers and who is which player) drive them:
  the keyboard, every connected pad in its own printed layout (each player's pad moving that player's cursor, by the
  seats the game assigned), and any other device through a driver; a remap moves them too, and while a menu is up the
  game never sees its keys. Prompts and legends print the control in the player's hands ("Enter", "A", "✕", the B on
  a Nintendo pad's right) and switch as the player picks up another device; a touch screen shows none. The controls
  screen lists a scheme's real bindings with a clash marked, and a remap reports the conflicts it makes.
- Motion that means something, taken from the broadcast. A number that changes in a menu or on the HUD flashes and pops
  once, a score or a gold count floating its gain off; a row just added rings once, the last move stays marked, and
  the side whose turn it is is lit in its colour. Screens fade in and their rows rise staggered, a moment's banner
  slams. Each theme moves its own way (none, ease, snap, stepped), the greybox only fades, and a player who asks for
  less motion (the system's setting or the game's option) keeps the fades and loses the travel. A hit-stop holds the
  HUD with the game.
- One moment on screen at a time: a goal outweighs a corner, a quest finished outweighs a step done. A weightier one
  takes the screen at once, an equal one waits until the first has been read, a lighter one waits its turn, all on the
  game's clock so a pause holds them.
- A team colour that would vanish into a dark panel (a black kit on dark glass) is outlined so its chip still shows.

### The map, whole: planned as one, written in segments, consolidated into one page

- **A map's tiles are built with the world's whole context.** The map kind handed its sections the page's title alone,
  so a tile never had what a stage page has: the live sun's share (an actor's shadow darkened baked shade twice), the
  form render's read, and the unshaded export (a map handed to an engine was built shaded). Each section is now built
  with the context the stage kind is.
- **What a tile's page says beside its faces reaches the map's.** The groups walked through (`soft`, a bush's, an
  arrangement's) of every tile; the cloud deck (`effects`), one a map; the fauna of every tile on the level's frame (its
  swarms laid together kind by kind, its birds one flock over the whole map, its herds each named for its tile); and the
  live wind's trunks and the petals' crowns of every tile, so the wood on every tile is held by its own trunks and not
  swayed as leaves (`oneGrass`).
- **One hero tree a region, one horizon a map.** Every path tile grew the card's hero tree near its north seam, and
  every tile built its own far ridges for the map to drop. A tile now lays a hero only where its map names one (a
  region's straight or bending path tile nearest its middle: `tile.hero`, beside its path's middle and clear of its
  seams, `heroSpot`), and its far layers only on the first tile and on a place's (`tile.backdrop: false` on the rest; a
  building is seated on the land they lay). The first tile's horizon rings the map with its heights scaled as it is,
  so the skyline stands at the angle its stage drew it at, over the map's rim.
- **Snow on a map is refused by name.** Snow lies on a polygon land (a stage's `shading`), which no tile of a map is
  built on yet; a level's or a region's `snow` says so, where the stage threw from inside its kit.
- **A map planned as segments, written in them.** A glyph map may be written as a PLAN (`grid.plan: { size, rows,
  route, key }`: its segments laid out, the walk through them, each segment's name, role, rise and words) and its
  SEGMENTS (`grid.segments.<S>: { rows, key }`, each size × size), in place of one grid's rows (level/plan.js). The plan
  fixes where the way crosses each seam before any segment is written: a GATE at the middle of each border the route
  steps across. A segment not yet written is laid from the plan (gate to gate by its middle; the first from an end, the
  last to its goal place), so the map is one whole level at every moment. A written one is held to its law: a path at
  each of its gates and none on a side a neighbour lies beyond but there, every path reached from its gates, the plan's
  goal held. `readGrid` stitches them into one grid, each segment its region and a place glyph two segments share
  renamed, so the page, its ends, the game's battles and its quest all read one map; a quest's beat plays a segment by
  its letter. The roles are the scene composer's: the route's first segment the arrival, its last the climax, the rest
  passages, a segment's own pinned. A grid written as rows is read as before.
- **A planned map written by a crew, an author a segment.** `req: { unit: 'level:<id>', segments: true }` raises one req
  for every segment of a planned map: its first segment the unit (`level:<id>/<segment>`), the rest its crew, an author
  each in its own seat. A segment's author is handed its plan's remit (its role, its words, its gates and the neighbour
  each joins, the quest beats played on it, the floor the plan's fill lays, its law) and writes its segment only
  (`/levels/<id>/glyphs/segments/<S>`): a write past it, or a segment its law refuses, is refused before anything is
  stored, the job issued to report again. The map stays whole between reports (the rest laid from the plan), is
  played once by the probe however many segments its crew writes, and a segment's precedent is its own kind's.
- **A glyph-map level is a section of the world's graph.** The world's graph read every level as a walk, so a patch to
  any world holding a glyph-map level was refused at the door; it is now one section, the map.
- **A planned map's pieces: the composer's set pieces at the map's scale.** Each segment's role places its piece on the
  map as stitched (level/map-items.js): a pack on each passage's way, the boss on the climax's way before its goal, the
  hero tree beside the landmark's way (the arrival's, without a landmark). Read from the map's own structure, so a
  segment rewritten by its author still holds its pieces; the plan pins any piece by its id (`plan.props`: moved to a
  tile of its segment, or none), a pin off its ground refused. The page stands its hero tree there and the battles
  their packs; its laws say every passage holds its pack and the climax its boss, and it reads its pieces out.
- **A world's writes one at a time.** A crew's authors report at once, and each kept patch is applied onto the recipe as
  it is stored; the update reads the recipe and awaits its gates before it writes, so two kept together could write
  over each other. design_game now takes a world's writes (a req's reports, the director's patch) one after another.
- **A planned map sets out from its arrival.** A glyph map's walk starts at its path end farthest from its goal, else
  at its first path tile in reading order; a map whose ways all end at doors set its hero down wherever that tile lay
  (in the demo, the woods' lookout, heading into the map's edge). A planned map's walk sets out from its route's first
  segment (its path end farthest from the goal, else its path tile farthest from it), facing the next tile on the way.
- **A path's grade across a seam.** A map's laws measure where a path crosses between tiles whose regions rise apart
  (`path-grade`: the rise eased between tile centres climbs at most 1.5 × its step over a tile), walkable to 30%.
- **A loader for a world still being baked.** A big map takes minutes before the route has a byte to send, so a world
  opened in a tab sat blank with nothing said. A tab that asks for a world not yet baked is now answered at once with a small
  page saying so and counting, which asks for the bake (`built=1`, under the same cache key) and then opens the world
  (worlds/world-loader.js). A frame, a download, a script and a bake already held are answered as ever, and the world's
  own page is untouched. In a game, the shell's veil holds until its level's frame has loaded and says why, where it
  used to lift at 45 seconds onto a blank frame.

### One map: a chapter is one level

- **A level laid as a map.** A level's graph may now branch: the `map` layout (level/map.js) lays it as sections
  PLACED on one ground, each with a position and a heading, where `sequential` laid one walk, a page a section. A new
  section, the JUNCTION (`junction: { radius, gates: { <gate>: <bearing°> } }`, level/graph.js), is a hub whose gates
  stand on its edge at compass bearings; an edge off it names its gate. A trail off a gate heads out along its bearing,
  its path's first point on the gate; a trail after a trail carries its frame on by its depth (its recipe `after` the
  one before, as a chain is laid); a trail may arrive at a junction, which is set past its far end with the gate turned
  back to meet it. The ground each section owns (a trail's whole site, a junction's disc) may not lie over another's:
  the layout refuses gates too close for their junction's radius, an arm folded back, and a loop, naming them. A chain
  is a map whose placements all point one way; `sequential` refuses a junction.
- **A map built as one page.** The `map` world kind (level/map-scene.js, `{ kind: 'map', level }`) builds every
  section as its own stage would and places it on the level's ground: its faces, repeats, lights and anchors turned to
  its heading and moved to its place, its heights met at the gate it leaves from (a trail after a trail keeps its
  parent's lift, its seam built in heights already), its walls on a turned frame laid as runs of short boxes so every
  reader of colliders reads them as before. Each trail keeps its band only (the apron its own page lays past it is
  dropped); the junction is a flat disc of paving; THE LAND BETWEEN is filled on a 4 m grid over the whole map, its
  heights from the bands' own edges (the nearest ruling), lying under each band where it reaches into it so a seam has
  no gap and no flicker; and the root's horizon rings the whole map. The sky, light and walk are the root's.
- **The glyph grid.** A map level may be written as a small grid of glyphs, one square tile each (level/grid.js
  `readGrid`: `grid: { tile, rows, key }`, north row first; `#` a path, `.` open land, a letter a place the key names: a
  town block, a building). Every tile is the same square, so tiles sit side by side, never over each other, and a path
  crosses a tile's edge at its middle, so two tiles' paths always meet. A path tile's SHAPE is solved from its path
  neighbours, never written: one edge open an end, two opposite an I, two adjacent an L, three a T, four an X; a place a
  path reaches opens toward it. The paths must be one network, walked end to end.
- **A glyph map built as one page.** Each tile of a glyph grid is built by the kit's own builder from a TILE SITE
  (era/out-tile.js `outTileSite`, a stage's `tile` in place of its `trail`): its square of the level's ONE land (the
  level's height read in the tile's own place, so tiles agree along every shared edge), its path's solved shape from
  each open edge's middle (an I straight through, an L a quarter arc round its corner, a T or an X meeting at the
  middle, an end stopping there), the path's bed eased level as a trail's. The kit's builder lays it as it lays a trail:
  the ribbon along each of the path's polylines (nature.js `trailFaces`), the boulders, gate stones and pebbles along
  the path wherever it runs (`pathAlong`; a trail's stones exactly where they were), grass, rocks and trees round it; a
  tile with no path gets no path. The map's page (level/grid-scene.js, the `map` kind with a `level.grid`) sets every
  tile at its square, clips it there, writes every tile's grass into ONE field over the map, rings the map with the
  first tile's horizon, and spawns at the first path end.
- **Places and edges on a glyph map.** A place's key may name a building (`{ use: <program>, door? }`: a dwelling, a
  shop, a tavern, a temple…, era/stage-buildings.js): it stands on its tile with ONE door, the side its key names, else
  toward its main road (the path with the most paths round it), and a path opens toward a place only where its door
  faces it, so no road runs into a building's back. A tile clips only its outdoor dress to its square; a building is
  kept whole. The map is closed: walls along its border, and beyond it a rim of land rising 18 m over 70, from the
  land's own height there, so the world's edge reads as the valley's sides; its horizon rings past it all.
- **A glyph map's laws.** A map built from a glyph grid measures itself (`map.laws`): `one-page` every tile in one
  payload; `seams` each shared edge's ground at one height from both tiles (each tile's own corners on the edge line);
  `paths-clear` no collider on any path (sampled every half metre at a walker's height); `doors-clear` every place's
  door clear; `one-network` the paths one network. A whole map built through the kit's builder is held to them in the
  e2e tier (level/grid-scene.e2e.test.js).
- **Regions on a glyph map.** A grid may carry a second layer of glyphs the map's own shape, `regions: { rows, key }`
  ('.' the level's own): each region names a part of the map (the town, the meadows, the larch woods, the pass) and
  dresses its tiles with the stage's own words (`style`, `biocube`, `shrubs`, `grass`, `wind`, `snow`, `palette`) over
  the level's, and RISES over the level's land (`rise`, metres, −24 to 60), each tile's rise at its centre eased to its
  neighbours' between (era/out-tile.js `riseAt`), so the land stays one height across every seam however the regions
  climb. The page reads them back (`map.regions`: each its name, rise and tiles; each cell its `region`).
- **A glyph map's ground runs on across its seams.** A tile's ground patches are the level's, read on the level's
  frame, never its own; a tile's shadows include its neighbours' trees and boulders within reach (placed first, as
  their own builds place them, `isekaiTileCasters`; a place's tile built first and its grown things handed on as
  built), and its own casters are only those standing in its square. Bushes on a tile stand beside its own path,
  whichever way it runs. A law holds it: `seam-shade`, the share of points along the seams whose baked shade steps.
- **A glyph map's open land is lighter.** A tile with no path and nothing standing on it lays its ground at a 1 m cell
  (LAND_CELL), twice the kit's, where nobody walks; the one grass field takes it on the finest spacing (a coarser tile's
  heights and cells written into it). On a 48-tile map: about a fifth fewer faces, the page about a quarter lighter.
- **A level as one glyph map.** A gameworld level may be written as a glyph map (`levels.<id>.glyphs: { rows, key?,
  regions?, tile?, kit? }`, beside nothing else: the map is the level): it is ONE stage, the map kind's page, and its
  ends are read from the grid and the level's land without building it (level/grid-ends.js): the hero set down at the
  path end farthest from the goal (a place whose key says `goal`), the exit at the goal's door, the tiles between as
  beats, each side way's end a pocket, each place by the way a landmark, each beat in its region; the places' doors are
  the town's, where the folk stand. The page and its ends set the walk down at the same end (grid.js `mapStart`).
- **A walk is compiled without drawing.** The capture bridge every page carries steps without drawing when asked
  (`draw: false`), keeping the scene's transforms as a draw would; the audit's walk compiler asks it for every leg, and
  a replay that keeps no frame asks it too. A walk's ticks are the rules', not pictures, so a big level is walked at the
  rules' speed on a machine with no GPU (an export's audit, CI, a laptop's software renderer).
- **A chapter on one map: its quest and its battles by region.** A main quest's beat may play a REGION of a glyph-map
  level (`as: { level, region }`, the region by its name or its glyph; one the map does not name is refused), so a
  chapter's beats (the town, the meadows, the switchbacks, the shrine) are parts of one level, not levels. A glyph map's
  stage takes `per` packs in each of its regions past the first (the town the party sets out from), laid along its way
  in the order it is walked, none in its home region and none at a door, the boss last, before the goal.
- **A desktop export's smoke runs on a box with no GPU, as root.** The gate launches the app with Chromium's flags before
  its folder: no sandbox as root (a container, a CI box), and a software WebGL allowed where no GPU answers (one that
  does is still used); the smoke checks the pages load, and neither flag reaches the app a player runs.

### A platformer's first level, made from its hero's tuned motion

- **The hero plays its own jumps.** A feel written with `takes: true` (`feel: { pole: 'jumping-giuseppe', takes: true }`)
  plays the hero's own jumps on the feel card's flight, in place of the animation library's held leap: its standing jump
  from a stand or a walk, its jump forward out of the run, and its double jump's second push for an air jump. Each clip
  plays its gather over the card's wind-up, its air over the flight (the rise to the apex its first half, the fall its
  second, read off the body's vertical speed, so a jump cut short carries its clip on and never skips), and its landing
  over the card's landing frames; walking off an edge plays the standing jump's fall. The run picks its stride cycle up
  where it left it. The jumps are compiled onto the hero's rig at play, beside its clips, so a hero made by a run and one
  made with `create_character` both play them; the library's run and walk stay.
- **Squash and stretch on a rigged hero.** The card's `look.squash` (Jumping Giuseppe 0.28, Galaxy Boy 0.22) scales the
  hero about its feet with its volume kept: sunk into the gather, stretched by the flight's speed (none at the apex),
  squashed on landing and sprung back over the landing's frames. The readout says the look is partly carried (the
  smears are not).
- **The card's moves, with its takes.** A feel with `takes: true` also plays its card's wall and dash, as the action lab
  tuned them. Falling against a wall with the stick into it slides down at the card's speed; a jump on it (or a few
  frames after leaving it) kicks off it, up and away, the stick locked out for the kick, so a single wall is climbed kick
  after kick with the stick held back to it. A person's F dashes, and a dash is a burst, not a run: the card's frames
  long whatever the button does, it gets up to the card's speed over its first quarter, holds it, and eases back to the
  run's by its end, the hero holding a lunge (the running jump's gather) rather than taking strides. In the air an air
  dash is the same burst, the fall stopped while it is at speed and given back as it eases, once an airtime, given back
  by the ground and the wall; a jump in a ground dash is a dash jump that keeps the burst's speed to the touch-down, and
  a kick with the dash held kicks at the dash's speed. A card's held dash is not carried. Jumping Giuseppe has no dash
  (a mascot platformer runs faster on a held button). The level's legend names F as the dash. The readout says the
  dash is partly carried (its invincible frames and its cancel are not).
- **The reach of a feel.** `feel/reach.js` measures what a feel's hero can cross by playing the rule its game ships
  (the card over the hero's own) in the runtime on scripted presses: the tapped hop, the jump from a stand, the running
  jump, and the air jump at the apex where the card has one. Each move's arc, its height, the widest gap of level ground
  it clears and its air time; `reachAt(move, up)` is the farthest ledge it lands on at a height above or below the
  take-off. Jumping Giuseppe's running jump clears 4.4 m and rises 1.8 m, his air jump 7.7 m and 3.4 m; Galaxy Boy's
  running jump 3.8 m and 1.6 m, with no air jump. With the takes, the dash jump and the air dash join (Galaxy Boy's dash
  jump clears 5.7 m), and the wall's kick and climb (about 1.6 m a kick for Galaxy Boy). The level's segments are sized
  by it.
- **Enemy density, a trail's.** A level's foes take `density`: foes per free beat of a stage (0 to 4, or none, sparse,
  even, dense, swarm), or one per trail node (`{ meet: 'sparse', gauntlet: 'dense' }`), a node it does not name standing
  the even rate. Below one the beats are skipped evenly along the trail; above it the rest stand round the beats, as a
  count's do. A count is a total and a density a rate: a level names one. A level that names neither stands one foe a
  beat, as before.
- **A 3D platformer's cameras.** The world's `camera` takes `follow` and `orbit`, both a chase the hero runs by: W A S D
  move the way the camera looks. `follow` turns by itself, easing behind the hero's run and holding while the hero
  stands, turns fast or runs back at it; `orbit` is the player's to turn (a drag, the right stick, its yaw and its
  pitch), the legend saying the look. Both hold their height through a jump and follow a drop past their band. The
  third-person chase is the one it was.
- **Absent `takes`, nothing moves.** A feel without it lowers to the rule it did, and the page's renderer carries the
  squash only when a rule asks for it; the platform rule's source in the page gained the takes' branch (re-pinned).
- **The course: a platformer's level over a trail.** A level takes `course: { teach, verticality? }` over every trail of
  its walk, or one a trail node: its floors and the gaps between them laid along the trail's own line, each gap sized
  by the hero's reach and tagged with the move it teaches. `basic` widens gaps and steps the running jump clears;
  `meet` is one long flat floor for the first encounter; `advanced` teaches the card's moves in turn, each just past the
  running jump and then tested (the air jump's higher step, the dash jump's wider gap, a face kicked up the wall);
  `gauntlet` lays basic gaps between floors long enough to fight on; `boss` one long floor. Verticality is flat,
  rolling, climbing or towering. The floors are walkway tiles that follow the trail's turns, stairs lead up onto the
  course and down to the exit, and a fall into a gap puts the hero back on the floor it left. The course's floors are
  the stage's beats, so its foes (at their density) stand on them. Its laws join the level's readout (each gap's width,
  rise and what its move reaches), and a card teaches it (`gameworld-course`). It plays from the side or in 3D, on the
  same level, lit and dressed as every game's.
- **A course seen from the side is a side strip.** A side camera's course is no longer laid on a whole trail: the
  geocube's `show: 'side'` (`era/geocube-side.js`) builds what a side-scroller shows. The course is the level, on a
  straight lane the trail's length: its runs drawn as columns down out of the frame in the cube's layers, a terrain run
  a turf cap over a dirt band over the rock's beds and joints (the beds level across the level, so a gap shows the same
  strata on both sides), a built run (the floor up a wall, the stairs) the cube's structure, a trim cornice over ashlar
  in running bond; only the faces the camera sees. Behind it a strip of land a little below the floors, the hills with
  their trees and a far range at their own depths, so the parallax is the perspective's; before it a few low hummocks
  held under the hero's feet line (a law). Front-lit as a side-scroller is, in the cube's key colour, ambient and air;
  the level's `style.geocube`, else the meadow's valley. A trail of Jumping Giuseppe's first level ships about 0.3–0.4 MB
  of geometry where its trail shipped 4.3–6.7 MB, and the level designs in half the time. The ground before the first
  step and after the last is the strip's own (`sidePads`); the course's catch zones and laws hold on it as on a trail.
- **A first level played as one.** A level whose trails are all courses a side camera plays is one side strip: its
  trails the strip's segments end to end along one lane, each at its own length with its own course (what it teaches,
  its verticality), the course coming down its stairs to the ground between segments and up again into the next; one
  page from the first step to the exit. Each segment's floors are beats that name their node, so its foes stand at its
  own density (foes.js `foePlacements` by node); its catch zones and laws name their segment. The level is titled by
  its own name (`stageTitle`). Giuseppe's first level: one 410 m run, the game 3.6 MB where its four trails were 7.1 MB.
- **A side-scroller's pace.** A strip's segments are sized by their courses, not their trails' walks: each the least
  line its gaps and floors fit on and a fifth more, its course standing on the ground (no stairs up to it, `coursePlan`
  `lift: 0`), so the hero is on the first floor at once and a beat comes every couple of seconds. Giuseppe's first level
  runs 157 m where it ran 410. The first level stands more foes: a few on the runs (a stomp to learn from the start, none
  on the floor the hero is set down on), dense to meet, a swarm in the gauntlet.
- **Lives and coins.** Two mechanics (`game/mechanics.js`, their cards): `lives` (a hit through its mercy and each fall
  into a course's pit cost one, a `oneup` gives one back, none left fails) and `coins` (each a coin glyph that pops when
  touched, in the air too, counted on the HUD; every `oneup` coins, 30, says `oneup`). A world's `mechanics.lives` puts
  its levels on lives (no `fail-on-death`, the hero's body binds no hp, no hp bar or level badge on the HUD) and
  `mechanics.coins` lays coins along a strip's course: a row along each floor at the feet's height, an arc over each gap
  where a running jump carries them.
- **The side camera on a course.** Its height is eased while the hero stands and held through a jump (`band`), so a
  stair's risers no longer jolt the frame, and the frame holds in from the lane's ends (`ends`, along the lane's chord),
  turning square to the chord near them. Absent a course, a side world lays and frames as it did.
- **Foes on the rail.** A side strip's foes fight in the hero's plane: each waits off the rail, on the land behind the
  lane, and leaps in on an arc to its place on the floor when the hero comes within its wake; on the rail everything it
  does (its own move, the mind's chase, a blow's knockback) is held to the lane (`rule.rail`, worlds/controllable/foe.js;
  laid by gameworld/foes.js hostileCast). A foe without one moves as it did.
- **The run button.** A feel with its takes whose card runs faster than it runs (`ground.sprint`) and has no dash gets a
  run button: F held while running builds the run up to the sprint over a second (Jumping Giuseppe's 6 to 8 m/s), as
  a mascot platformer's run is earned, and eases back over half a second let go; the air keeps it. Momentum, not a
  move: the dash is the burst. The legend and the pause menu say F as the run.
