- **F is the feel's.** A hero with a feel's dash or run button owns F whatever its walk pace: a side lane's hero, laid
  with none, fell through to the mobile suit's boost thrusters, so its dash was a held boost at three and a half
  times the run. The pause menu's rows say the dash and the run where the hero has them.
- **Controls in the menu.** `mechanics.legend: 'menu'` keeps the controls off the play screen (taught only in the pause
  menu, as a game ships); absent, a level shows them for its first seconds as before. A side camera's level has no
  radar: its screen is the lane.
- **A merged foe can be targeted.** The target rim and the i-frame shimmer read a merged figure's one skinned mesh (its
  bone list holds bones, not meshes); the rim was throwing on it and stopping the page the moment a foe was in reach.
- **A platformer's first level.** `gameworld/first-level.js` lays it as the team's output unit and the production's
  slice: four trails in teaching order, basic (rolling, no foes), meet (one flat floor, foes sparse), advanced
  (climbing, no foes) and gauntlet (foes dense), each its course and its foes' density, every gap sized by the hero's
  reach. Laid in a world, every trail's course holds its laws as built, and the foes stand on the floors.
- **A boss when the creator asks.** A fifth trail, its course one long floor, and the level's `goal: { boss: { win } }`:
  the boss's fall is a win of one of three kinds, a jobber (thrown away), a rival or a boss (each a story hook). The kind
  changes nothing in the fight, its reward or its exit; `storyWins` reads the story so far in the book's order, for the
  next level's build. A level's boss goal is still `true` where no kind is said.

### An RPG made one level at a time: what its vertical slice needed

- **The core loop reads the battles.** A world that fights in battles (written, or a `jrpg` or `tactics` world's, laid
  at the run) read its loop as a platformer's: move and jump to the level's exit, the next level its reward. Its
  encounter is now the battle (a pack met on the trail, a boss at the end; a tactics battle on a board), its reward the
  battle's spoils (experience, gold and gear for the party), and its moment gains `fight`. Every remit carries the loop.
- **A beat's crew brings the battles.** A beat asked for with `crew: true` in a world that fights in battles brings the
  battles chapter beside its level, as it brings the foes a beat fields: a jrpg's level is fought with its packs and boss.
- **A critic reads the crew's work whole.** A critic's seat (`as`) on a crew's req was held to the req's own unit, so a
  critic of a level never saw the battles its crew wrote beside it. Its view may now be any unit of the req, as the
  assistant director's is; an author's stays its own.
- **The play probe loads a page from a file.** It pushed each stage's whole page through one DevTools message, and a
  party RPG's stage (its figure bank inlined: the hero and three party members, past 100 MB) closed the target before
  it loaded: the stage was said not to load. It writes the page to a temporary file and opens it.
- **A party's figures weigh a sixth of what they did on a level's page.** A party RPG's stage inlined four layered
  figures and its foes at 73 MB (90 to 124 MB a page). The page's bank now leaves out what the page never reads (a
  layered figure's skin joints and weights, kept for the engine exports, which read the figure's own row), packs a layered
  part as unit rigs' are (shared corners, positions on a uint16 grid, `packRigMesh`), writes its clips' frames on 16 bits
  (decoded once to a Float32Array), and names a figure byte-identical to an earlier one again instead of writing it
  twice: 11 MB, pages of 33 to 37 MB. A bank with none of these is emitted byte for byte as before.
- **A brief names the patch's ops.** An author's submit shape said `op` without its words; both authors of the slice's
  first round sent `replace` and were refused. It says `set | add | remove`.
- **A refused report writes nothing.** An author's patch was applied before the world was read, so one the door then
  refused (a level node given an `hour`) was stored and its job marked kept: the job could not report again, and the
  world read refused until the patch was undone by hand. The patch is now read first, every level's walk with it
  (`gameworldGraph`), and a refused one leaves the recipe and the job as they were, the job issued to report again.
- **A rework names the authors it sends back.** `req: { id, direct: 'rework', jobs: ['j2'] }` sends back only those
  authors, the rest of the crew's work kept as it stands (every author without it); the critics and the assistant read
  again only once an author has gone back. A req's `reissues` budget counts its authors sent back: a critic or the
  assistant reissued to read the work again had spent it, so one rework round left none.
- **The battles card says what a foe's row does.** A row in `battles.foes` replaces its preset whole, its skills and
  drops with it unless named again: the slice's battles author wrote a shaman's stats alone and lost its `mend`, the
  skill its boss taught by. (The battles card's ceiling is 5120.)
- **A packed page carries its plain groups packed too.** A page laid with `pack: true` (an isekai level, a stage) packed
  only its textured groups; its plain ones (the ground chips, the rocks, the land's core) rode as float32 positions and
  float32 colours, 18 MB of a party RPG's stage. Their positions now ride a uint16 grid over each group's own bounds and
  their colours sRGB bytes (`packGroupArrays`, packTex's colours), decoded by the page to the same Float32Arrays, the
  same triangles in the same order: 8.8 MB, a stage's page without its figures about 15 MB. A page laid without `pack`
  is as before.
- **No NUL byte in a page.** The event bus joined a saga's id and scope with a raw NUL byte written into its source, so
  every page carrying the bus held one, and an artifact host refused the page. It is written `'\x00'`, the same string
  at run time.
- **A beaten pack leaves the map.** A won fight's foes were felled where they stood (`kill`: they lie down, held), so a
  pack the party had beaten still stood on the trail, fallen, as one to fight. They leave in a puff of smoke (`vanish`,
  `with: 'smoke'`).
- **A party that fights but does not walk the map** (`battles.followers: false`). A party RPG stood every member of its
  casting's party on the map behind the hero, each a rigged figure as heavy as the hero's; with `followers: false` the
  hero walks alone, as a classic party RPG's leader does, and the party still fights beside it (the battles' party is the
  cast who join, as before). A member who joins on a story flag still stands where the story puts it. The default is
  unchanged.
- **A party joins one a chapter.** A party RPG's rolled party (its casting page) stood with the hero from the first
  level; by default now, when its book gives none of it a `joins` flag, the first member joins for the first chapter's
  last quest (an act of the main quest: its dungeon, the quests before it to the plains and the woods walked solo), the
  second for the second's, and so on: one a level where
  the world has no main quest (`casting.js` laidJoins: each its flag `join-<id>`, carried on; said as a toast). A member
  past the game's chapters waits for its flag; a book that writes its own `joins` keeps them. With
  `battles.followers: false` a member who has joined fights and does not walk the map.- **A fight on its own stage** (`battles.rules.stage: 'backdrop'`; `'live'`, the default, as before). A party battle was
  staged on the map where it was met, a camera fitted round the fighters wherever the ground let it stand. On the
  backdrop stage the fighters are moved to an arena of their own, seen from the side with the party on the left, before
  the map drawn once from that view where they met (`__mojCtrl.backdrop`, the controllable channel's, emitted only for a
  page whose fights ask for it), and put back where they stood when it ends: a party RPG's battle background, the way
  the genre has drawn them. The encounter, its transition in and its scene out stay the same on either stage, so an
  action game keeps its fights live on the same map.
- **A fight solved onto the map** (`battles.rules.stage: 'arena'`). A place near where the pack was met is solved for
  the fight: candidates round the meeting along several fight lines, each scored by how level its fighters' ground is,
  what stands on their places (the world's colliders), how far from the meeting, and whether a camera on the party's side
  (the party on the left) sees every fighter past the ground. The party stands in an echelon and the pack in a wedge on
  the map's own ground, facing across, under a fixed camera; what stands in the arena and in the corridor from the camera
  to it (trees, rocks, grass: every group but the land) is cut away for the fight (`window.__mojClip`, emitted only for
  such a page) and back after. The scene is the background: no arena is drawn for it.
- **Battles in a building: the dungeon fights.** A building level is fought (`FOUGHT`): its packs stand in the rooms its
  way passes through to its goal room (one spot a room, two in a long one, none at the goal room's threshold, none in a
  room off the way), and its boss in the goal room, met before the room's exit is reached (`levels.js buildingEnds`,
  the building's ends as a trail's). The packs' ladder is walked in the order the main quest plays its levels (the plains
  before the woods before the dungeon), not the order the world writes them. An encounter met in a room carries it
  (`encounters[].room`), and an arena stage holds the fight to it: along the room's length, its places drawn in between
  its walls, its ground read from the floor (never the roof), and the room's contents, its near wall and its roof toward
  the camera cut away, its far walls the fight's background. The clearing reaches a group's textured faces (a room's
  brick walls are those), the camera stands on the room's side with no one else behind it, and whoever is not in the
  fight and stands in what is cleared (a pack still to meet, a marker) is out of the shot till it ends.
- **A chapter asked for as one.** `req: { unit: 'act:<id>' }` raises ONE req for a main quest act: its first level the
  unit, its other levels (in the order its quests play them: the town, the outskirts, the dungeon) and the departments
  its beats bring (battles, story, foes) its crew, an author each; its remit from the quest (the act's place, its quests
  in order, in and out, the loop), the director's words winning. Its received gate waits on every level's stages, its
  probe plays each level (`mergeVerdicts`: a check holds where it holds on every level, said level by level), and once
  accepted every level it holds is in the game.
- **A party's dungeon is laid larger, its exits unmarked, its arches laid in stones.** A world that fights in party
  battles lays its building levels' rooms twice a walker's (`DUNGEON_SCALE`; a program's new `scale`: the template's
  rooms that many times as long and wide, taller by its root, the recipe's own sizes its own; a core-plan building
  keeps its plan), so the fight's camera stands back inside a room rather than cutting its way to it. Its exits carry
  `marker: false`, and the decoration leaves them without the flag and beacon: the road or the door shows the way on.
  An archivolt (`arches.js archRing`) is laid as voussoirs, an odd count of wedge stones about 45 cm round the ring,
  mortar joints between them and the keystone at the crown standing prouder and higher, where it was one band.
- **The boss's fall sets a flag.** `battles.sets: '<flag>'` names the story flag the boss's pack's win sets (a cue on its
  `rpg-won`), carried on as every flag is: a quest's last step done by it, a moment after it. The story's `unset` counts
  it. Three of chapter 1's authors asked for it (the shrine quest's last step had nothing to complete it).
- **A won pack stays won; a way the story opens.** Chapter 1's critics found the map forgot its fights: a pack's win was
  the page's alone, so a way walked back stood every pack again. On a page that carries flags, a won pack sets
  `won-<pack>` as it falls, and a page it is carried into clears that pack at once (`rpg.js wonFlag`). And a link may
  take `needs: '<flag>'`, a quest's flag: the way is shut until the story sets it, in the shell (the exit's flag gate)
  and on its page (the exit's reach waits on the flag's var), so a dungeon is not walked into before its quest is given.
- **A member joined by the story is not joined twice.** The default arrival (the dungeon's quest's member, as its level
  starts) waits for the carried flags and plays only if the member has not joined yet: one the story joins as the quest
  is given in town is not toasted again at the dungeon's door.
- **One draw a figure, culled as a whole; a pixel budget.** Chapter 1's town drew 8,680 calls a frame: each person a
  rigid rig of 59 bone meshes, each its own material, drawn in the frame, the shadow map and the occlusion prepass, and
  never culled. A plain rigid rig (`merged-figure.js mergeableFigure`: indexed parts, nothing that reads a bone's own
  mesh) is now drawn as one skinned mesh, each part's corners bound wholly to its bone, posed as the bone meshes were,
  and culled by a sphere round its height (a figure outside a render's view, the shadow's box included, is not drawn
  there): the town's frame 676 calls, its shadow pass a third of its triangles. Off where a part's own mesh is read (the
  toon ink's hulls, a headset's hands); a wreck of a merged figure goes as it falls. A page played live caps the
  screen's density at 1.5 and holds it to the frame's time (`__mojBudget`: a second over 24 ms takes it down a quarter,
  to 0.75; quick frames give it back). Tried and not kept: far levels welded by vertex clustering (a clothed body's
  layers tear at any grid that saves much); a figure's own density is the next lever, at its mint.
- **A run is smooth; a town's people are never statues.** A hero on a clip library ran the library's jog, whose hips
  drop a quarter of their height every stride (Quaternius's crouched jog: 23 cm on a person, a bounce on screen). A run
  is now held to `RUN_BOB` (12% of the hip height): a library run past it gives way to the hero's own calibrated jog (9
  cm, its stride measured so the feet stay planted), the library playing the rest (its walk, its idle, its jump);
  `LIBRARY_BOB` holds each library clip's measure, checked against its hub. And a town's folk potter by default: each one
  nobody comes looking for (not a shop's keeper, a service's first, one met in every town, anyone in a sidequest, one
  crouched at its work) steps out to a spot before its door and back at a stroll, lingering at each on its own heartbeat,
  talked to wherever it stands (`folk.life: false` keeps them still; `folk.day` still gives the households a day).
- **Rays by grid: no frame spent near a building.** Every walker found its feet by a ray straight down, and the camera
  kept off the walls by a ray from the hero's head, each through three's raycast, which tests every triangle of a mesh
  its box meets: the town's stone, its chips and its ground are one mesh each of tens of thousands, so near the houses
  the frame went on rays (16 ms a ray on a slow machine). A big static mesh (`ground-grid.js`: a thousand triangles or
  more, standing where it was built) now answers by a 2D grid of its triangles built at the first probe, its cells halved
  where it is crowded (`gridFit`): a ray straight down tests the triangles over its point, any other ray those of the
  cells its line crosses, each face as its material shows it, the same hits three's raycast finds.
- **A meadow is drawn once.** The creases' and the occlusion's prepass drew every solid a second time, grass blades
  among them (in chapter 1's town a fifth of the frame). A mesh marked `blades` (stage-grass.js: its fields, its tufts,
  the static cards) is hidden for it: a blade carries no crease and casts no contact.

### WebGPU for gen-7: the spike

A gen-7 page (the form render, the era the renderer lights) is to try three's WebGPU renderer first and fall back to
today's WebGL page; a gen-6 page is not touched. This entry is the spike that tests whether it holds, before any of it
reaches the World page.

- **The spike** (`scripts/spikes/webgpu/`): a geocube island read in gen-7, emitted as today's World page, and the same
  page with its renderer swapped for three's WebGPU renderer (r184's, the release the vendored build is), drawn side by
  side in headless Chromium on SwiftShader's WebGPU adapter. Nothing in the emitter or the vendored tree changes.

### The workshop: where a game is made and seen, said ahead of time

- **Where a big game is seen, said before it is built.** A cloud box builds any game and runs its machine gates, but a
  level reaches the creator from it only as a page under the host's limit, it draws WebGL in software, and it forgets
  its data when the session ends. `design_game`'s readout now carries a `workshop` step, first in `next`, when a level
  is estimated over the host's page limit and the creator is not on their own machine: the estimate is made from the
  recipe before anything is built (a glyph map's tiles by kind, at measured weights; game/workshop.js), the surface is
  the declared one, never sniffed. Its card, `gameworld-workshop` (served by id), gives the agent the words and the
  paths: carry the work to the laptop (recommended), download a desktop export for each look, or keep each level small.
- **The work packs into one file.** `npx mojulo script pack-data` (the repo: `node scripts/pack-data.mjs`) writes the
  database whole, checked and gzipped, to carry it from a cloud box to the laptop; the storage folder is named when it
  holds anything. Claude Code on the web's box row says it has no GPU (`gpu: false`). docs/workshop.md says it all for
  people.

### The World page's light: one record, the sky in every reflection, a finished frame

- **Under way.** The World page keeps its baked light and gains, opt-in and adding no byte to a page that does not
  ask: one light record (sun, sky, ambient) every lit channel reads (built, below); one capture of the page's own sky
  as what specular faces and water reflect, and rooms that reflect the room; and a frame with headroom finished in
  the frame pass (bloom, exposure that adapts), with the grade laid over it as today. All of it is asked for by
  `light.finish`.
- **One light record a page** (`scene/page-light.js` `pageLight`). Where the sun stands is resolved once from a
  payload, from the first that holds: the form render's land (the cube's solved sun), a town's or a city's baked
  buildings, a stage under a sun or a moon, the payload's baked light, the polygonizer's default. Every channel that
  shades by the sun (specular, liquid, shallows, jets, the seaway, crystal, metal) and every one that casts along it
  (the cast shadows, the live light's actors' and hour's maps, a vehicle's form body) reads that record
  (`scene/scene-three.js`), where each took its own argument with its own fallback. A shadow keeps its own rule
  (`shadowToLight`): the world's own direction where it names one, and the shadow's default under a sun on the
  horizon or on a page with no light of its own, so a minted page's shadows stay where they fell. What changes: on a
  gen-7 page whose land, buildings or stage are drawn as form, the shading channels now follow the solved sun as
  the shadows already did (a metal or a specular face there took the baked light's direction). Every page without
  the form render keeps its bytes; the channel pins hold. The record replaces the one-off that set a form page's
  `shadows.toLight` in `worlds/world-scene.js`: the payload no longer carries it, the page's shadows fall where
  they did. A page the form render draws says its record (`window.__mojSun`), and a test holds a shading channel and
  the live shadows of one emitted page to one sun (`lightAgrees`).
- **On a page the land lights, live water brings no light of its own.** The shallows and the seaway each added a
  sun and a sky fill of three's when no light stood in the scene yet; on a gen-7 page whose land is drawn as form
  they ran before the land brought its own, and their fill then lit the land as well, brighter than its solve. There
  they bring none now (`pageLit`): the land's sun and ambient, the record's, are the page's. Elsewhere they are as
  they were.
- **The record on the page.** A page the form render draws carries the record as `__LIGHT` (and `window.__mojSun`,
  the machine gate's probe); a page without it carries neither, and its bytes are as they were.
- **The finish is asked for** (`light.finish`, `scene/page-light.js` `readFinish`): `true`, a curve's word
  (`neutral`) or `{ curve, reflect }`. It is the opt-in to everything laid over the bake; a world without it, every
  minted one, resolves and emits as it did. An unknown word or key teaches.
- **A specular face reflects the sky** (under the finish, on a page with a painted sky; `channels/specular.js`).
  Beside its highlight a spec face now takes the sky along its reflected view, the dome from horizon to zenith and
  a dark ground under it, weighted by Fresnel from a dielectric's 4% and by the face's own strength. The sky is the
  record's, as an environment (`skyEnv`, `envAt`: the same dome and ground a metal's studio already reflects), stated
  once in JS and held to the shader by a test. A room under no sun reflects none of it.
- **A change to the plan's second step.** The plan captures the page's sky into a cube for every reflective
  surface. A metal already reflects that sky analytically from its zenith and horizon, and a capture of the same
  two colours would add a render at load and no new picture; so outdoors the sky's environment stays analytic (no
  render target, the same frame every time), and a capture is kept for where it shows what the analytic sky cannot:
  a room reflecting the room. That, water under the finish and exposure that adapts are not built yet.
- **Bloom, over a frame with headroom** (under the finish; `channels/frame-pass.js`, `scene/page-light.js`). The
  plan drew the frame in linear light and finished it in the pass. That would put every painted colour through the
  curve's inverse, in every custom shader a page has (sky, water, panes, sprites), and one missed is a colour moved.
  Instead the frame stays as it is drawn, display-referred, in the pass's half-float target, where an emitter may
  write past white. What is past white is the bloom (`bloomBright`): drawn down a chain of halves, the first with a
  Karis weight so one hot pixel does not flicker, and back up through a tent, each wider level counted a little more
  (`FRAME_PASS.wide`), then laid over the frame by `strength` under the grade. A pixel at or under white gives
  nothing, so no pixel of a page changes but round an emitter. The chain is five levels, four at the half tier,
  none at off (`BLOOM_LEVELS`). Under the bloom a glow sprite is its emitter's core, smaller and past white
  (`channels/glow.js` `GLOW_HOT`), and the bloom draws its halo from its light. `light.finish` takes
  `bloom: false` or `{ strength, radius }`. What this gives up: a tone curve chosen a page (it stays each
  material's own). Measured in Chrome on a lamp against a dark wall: with the finish the core clips to white and
  its light spreads past the sprite, where the same page without it is the painted halo. The probe is
  `window.__mojFrame.bloom`.
- **A page's emitters are drawn past white** (under the finish's bloom). A face that says it emits, a lit window's
  pane or a sign (`emissive` with its strength, what the lit export already reads) and a fixture's face (`glow`), is
  drawn once more over itself in the frame's headroom, one mesh a page a hair toward the eye
  (`channels/hot-faces.js`), so the bloom draws its light from the face itself and a lamp's face no longer sits cold
  inside its glow. The sun's disc on a painted sky (`channels/sky-dome.js` `SUN_HOT`) and a fire's halo
  (`channels/fire.js` `FIRE_HOT`) go past white with them. The chain's levels are laid back over the root of their
  weights' sum, between a wide emitter, which their sum would multiply, and a point, which the chain thins. Seen in
  Chrome: a lit window, a lamp and a neon sign each with its own halo on a test wall; on an island plaza at night
  the lit window over the square glows. Not past white yet: a lantern's flame (a fixture with no emitting face), the
  form sky's sun, and an emitter inside a repeat.
- **A torch's flame is live in the form render** (a room read in gen-7; `scene/channels/flames.js`). The sixth
  generation draws a torch's flame as two crossed polygons, and the fire channel draws real fire at a real cost: a
  ray marched through every flamelet, embers, smoke, and every material on the page patched for its light. Between
  them: every flame on a page is one instanced quad turned to the eye, its shape a formula of the clock in its
  shader (a teardrop that sways more toward its tip, eddies rising through it, white at its root to orange at its
  tip), added over the frame. One draw call for all of them, no state, no render target; the light they give is
  the bake's, as it was. A torch keeps its iron and a bed of coals in its bowl, which carries its glow and what an
  engine reads as its light (`era/stage.js` `torchFaces`). Under a world's bloom a flame is drawn past white. A
  room with live fire (`fire`) keeps the fire channel's; gen-6 and an engine's read keep the polygons. Seen in
  Chrome on a gothic-stone room, beside gen-6 and under the finish.
- **Left as they are, and said**: on a page with no light of its own the shading channels take the polygonizer's
  default sun and a shadow the shadow's default, two directions, as minted pages have them; unifying them would move
  every such page's shadows. A water surface's own sun (`channels/surface.js`, a kind's argument a surface) is not
  the record's yet.

### The game UI's keyboard: the keypad, the usual keys and typing into a name

- **The keys a player reaches for anyway drive a mana-ui menu.** Past the two remappable slots of each menu action
  (arrows or W A S D, Enter or Space, Esc or Backspace, `[` `]`), the menu scheme carries what every player has learnt
  (`also` on an action in `controls/schemes.js`): the keypad (8 4 6 2 move, 5 and the keypad's Enter accept, 0 backs
  out, + and − turn the tabs), Tab and Shift+Tab to move down and up, and Page Down and Page Up to turn the tabs. They
  are never remapped and never listed on the controls screen; a slot's binding on the same key wins
  (`controls/mana-controls.js manaControls`).
- **Sane defaults in the host** (`controls/mana-host.js`). A held key repeats a move (a long list scrolls, a slider
  runs) and never a pick or a back, so a held Enter buys once and a held Esc leaves one screen. A chord (Ctrl, Alt or
  Meta held) stays the browser's and the system's: a reload, a tab switch and a copy still work over a menu.
- **A held stick or d-pad repeats its move** (`controls/mana-host.js`), as a held key does: a press steps once, then
  after 0.4 s the move repeats every 0.1 s until it is let go, so a long list scrolls and a slider runs from a pad. A
  pick or a back never repeats, and what was held as a screen opened neither acts nor repeats in it. A headset's sticks
  repeat the same way (they are a driver of the same host). `connect`'s `repeat: { delay, every }` (ms) tunes it,
  `repeat: false` turns it off.
- **A name is typed straight in from a keyboard.** With a text entry in focus, the keys type into it (W types a W and
  does not move the cursor), Backspace and Delete erase, Enter is done, and the arrows, Esc and Tab still move and back
  out. A pad still types from the letter grid. The runtime takes text, never keys: `rt.typing(seat)`,
  `rt.type(text, seat)` (the entry's charset and max kept, a lower-case letter read as its capital), `rt.erase(seat)`
  and `rt.submit(seat)`.
- **The previews agree.** The board and `manaUiPage` without a host drive their frames with the same keys
  (`PREVIEW_KEYS`, held to the menu scheme by a test) and type into a name the same way (`previewKey`).

### The game UI in a headset: mana-ui's screens and the controllers as game controllers

- **A snapshot of a mana-ui view, as the screen draws it** (`mana-ui/snapshot.js`). A headset shows no DOM, so what a
  view looks like this instant is made an image another surface can draw: the view's own elements under the sheet they
  were drawn with, rendered by the browser into an SVG image. Layout, theme, the focus's words, ornaments and
  pseudo-elements carry over by construction, never drawn a second time. Whatever is moving (an entrance, a change's
  flash, a moment's slam, a turn breathing) is baked at the value it holds this instant, so a snapshot each frame plays
  the screen's motion. It is a data: URL, which Chromium (the Quest's browser) lets a WebGL texture take; Safari does
  not, so a headset on Safari draws none of it.
- **The transfer gate** (`mana-ui/snapshot.chrome.test.js`, the e2e tier): a view's screenshot against its snapshot,
  pixel by pixel, on a screen in a theme that leans on every feature of the sheet, on a frame caught mid-motion, and on
  one box alone. They agree to within the half pixel a centred box is anti-aliased across (the screen's compositor
  snaps it); the same view snapped without its theme is far outside it.
- **mana-ui's screens on a panel in the headset** (`scene/channels/xr.js`). Every mounted mana-ui view registers on the
  page; in a session, while one has a screen up (a fight's commands, the party menu, a shop), its snapshot is drawn on
  a panel at eye height ahead of the player, set where they look as it opens and left there, never riding the head. It
  is drawn again as the view changes, and up to thirty times a second while something on it moves, so its motion plays
  in the headset as on the screen. The HUD panel no longer mirrors a level's HUD that a fight has set aside.
- **The controllers work a menu as a game's controllers do.** Either stick moves, A or the trigger accepts, B backs
  out, the grips turn the tabs (the menu scheme's new headset rows), read through the view's own input owner like any
  pad, so the legends print the controller's buttons. While a screen is up the world, the walk and the turn hold, and
  the player's body stays on the hero (a fight that stages its party takes the player with it). No laser pointer.
  mana-host takes a device that arrives after it connected (`drive()`), and lets it go with the session.
- **A fight's marks stand in the world.** An anchor's row may name its point in the world (mana-ui's `world`); in the
  headset each such anchor is drawn as a card over that point, square to the eye and as large to the eye as on the
  screen, instead of where the screen's camera would put it: the RPG's bar over each fighter's head, the target
  marker, and the numbers rising where blows land. On the screen nothing changes.
- A page without a headset, or without a mana-ui surface, is unchanged byte for byte. Gates: machine (the transfer gate;
  the headset block against a fake session: the panel, the controllers on a real runtime and mana-host, the world held,
  the cards). Eyes: the operator's Quest, not yet run.

### Variations in passes: a kaleidoscope over any design (internal name mangekyou)

- **Ask for variations of anything made, in words, and get real variety back.** The variations door
  (`run_experiment_sweep`) takes a concept and a count over a stored design (`{ ref, concept, n }`): "darker, corrupted
  versions", "faction liveries", "bigger and spikier". It reads the design generally, whatever its kind, and varies
  only what is seen: colour, size, silhouette, surface treatment, detail and the procedural roll. Ids, kinds,
  positions and gameplay numbers are never touched. The variants are minted into one folder, so the gallery is the
  contact sheet, and the source is unchanged.
- **Every order is new.** The dice are rolled when the order is authored, never in a builder, and the roll is stored
  with the order, so a pass replays exactly but two people's first passes do not look alike. Each candidate commits to
  its own few axes at heavy-tailed strength, the pool is oversampled, and the most dispersed n are kept.
- **Passes, the way a designer works.** `keep` (one or more variants) makes the next pass from them, crossing kept
  variants when there are several and narrowing the spread; `reject` pushes the next pass away from what was turned down.
- **Principles, when the design has them.** `principles` locks paths, holds colours to a palette, bounds values,
  weights the axes and carries notes.
- **Routed to the team that owns it.** Each order says which department it went to (a game's foes to foe design, a
  prop to characters, props and vehicles, a place to worlds), with that team's vocabulary as context (oozes, finishes,
  colourways, outlines, registers). `mint: false` answers the patches alone, for a department to hold as proposals.
- **Departments ask for variations too.** `design_game({ ref, chapter, vary: { concept, n } })` turns the kaleidoscope
  over a chapter's own pages (the equipment, the hero, a game's foes) for the department that owns it, and proposes:
  nothing is written until a variant's patch is taken with `patch`, and a pass is carried by the patches kept and
  rejected. A proposal the game would refuse is never offered: the game's own reader gates every candidate, and the
  next is taken in its place. The studio card teaches a chapter's session the move.
- **Scales stay scales.** A whole-number scale (an ornament 0–3) moves in whole steps, its ladder of tiers shifting
  together so early stays below late; values under one key move together, so a pair stays a pair.
- **Agents find it.** A routing card (`variations`) and two phrasings in the routing fixture send "do me four takes on
  this axe" to the variations door; `run_experiment_sweep` leaves the list of doors with no fixture row.
- **An arm varies by its parts and its finish.** The arms' slot words (optic, muzzle, stock, barrel, underbarrel,
  magazine, a knife's blade and guard) are the house's silhouette words, each swapped only for another its slot takes
  (a barrel's short, standard, long a scale), and a finish card is read where an arm names it, its `style`. A step
  swaps about half of an axis's words and a leap nearly all, so a variant reads as a take, not a reshuffle.
- **Furniture varies as it is stored.** A piece's forms (arms, back, cushions, legs) and its finish (fabric, timber,
  wood, board) are the house's words; its millimetres are whole quantities moved by a ratio and kept whole, where a
  small whole number (an ornament, a count of drawers) is a step on a scale. A measure named by its last letter (a
  seat's `seatH`) is a size; a box's bare `w` and `h` are not.
- **More of the house's words.** A creature's grafts (`chimera`, pure to chimera, a scale), what a hero wears on the
  head (`headgear`, by its card), a vehicle's wear (pristine to battered), its livery and its pattern, its paint by name.
- **Did the shape change, or only the coat?** For a made thing (a prop, a layered body, a scad part) the variations door
  reads each minted variant's outline flat from three sides, each in its own frame so a shape is compared and not a
  size, and answers `outlines`: each variant against the design, the pair most alike, and what it says (two variants
  above the silhouette gate's ceiling read as one outline). Advisory: it stamps, it never refuses.
- **The same ask twice is two kaleidoscopes.** Each order's variants are filed in a folder named for the design, and
  the next order on it looks away from everything shown before (what is kept or rejected now aside); a replay (`roll`
  given) is the order it replays. A concept that names an axis is heard by every variant: "different shapes" never
  answers with a new fabric alone. "Different" asks for difference, not for a reroll.
- **Shape is picked by shape.** When a made thing is asked for shape, the door draws a pool twice as wide, draws each
  candidate's outline and keeps the ones farthest apart in shape from the design and from each other (`outlines.steered`).
  A silhouette move now re-proportions the sizes too, each on its own (a sofa deeper and lower), so an outline moves in
  its own frame where a scale alone would not; on a chesterfield asked for "different shapes" the pair most alike went
  from 0.99 to 0.68. A variant is said to keep the design's outline only when it all but does (0.95).
- **Takes, not everything at once.** Farthest-point picking favours the candidate that moved every axis; a candidate
  turning a mix of axes no pick has turned yet now stands a quarter farther, so a set is a kaleidoscope of takes.
- **An outfit and a car vary by their own words.** An outfit's language (family, sleeve, hem, leg, cut, fit, cloth,
  pattern, collar, lapel, front, shoulder, waist, pockets, feet: `outfit/styles.js` OUTFIT_WORDS) and a car's body,
  decade language, trim, paint by name and parts slot by slot (lamps, grille, wheel, roof, spoiler …) are the house's
  words, each swapped only for another written under the same key.

### The RPG's battles, party menu and shops on the shared game UI

- **A party battle, the party menu and a shop are drawn by the game UI runtime (internal name mana-ui), the first
  surface to move onto it.** The RPG channel drew each of them its own way: its own sheet of about fifty rules, seven
  cursors of its own (the command, the member, the tab, the row, the shop's tab and row, the slot), its own keyboard and
  pad handling, and markup written by hand. Now the screens are a spec of mana-ui's components (`playscape/rpg/rpg-ui.js`)
  and the page is their host: it reads the battle kernel's state to them each frame and answers what they emit (a
  command, a skill, a target, a class, a slot, a ware), and the kernel still says yes or no. Which list a member is on,
  its row, the open tab and the way back are the runtime's; the look is the theme's.
- **The stack is the menu's depth.** A member's commands, then the skill or the item it chose, then whom: each is a
  screen, so back steps out of each one as it does everywhere else, and back from the commands is the member before. A
  round playing out is a screen too, so accept skips ahead, and cuts a long film short, from the keys, a pad or a tap.
- **Fights wear the world's look.** A world with a settled UI guide lowers it into the battles as a mana-ui theme (its
  colours, frame, plate, border, motion and stop: a console stop keeps the ▶ cursor), the greybox until the guide is
  settled, and the console RPG's look where a world has no guide. The guide's old CSS for the battle window is gone.
- **The controls layer drives the menus.** The keyboard and every connected pad in its printed layout come in through
  mana-host from the menu scheme, so the RPG reads no key or pad of its own beyond P and a pad's select, which open the
  party menu. Legends print the control in hand ("Enter", "A", "✕"). The tabs of the party menu and a shop now turn
  with `[` `]` or the bumpers, as on every mana-ui screen; left and right cross between a list and its detail.
- **What a fighter shows, in the runtime's motion.** Each fighter's bar over its head, the one picking marked, the
  target in focus marked where it stands (over a member's head, or over the pack's figure and in the foes' box). A blow's
  number rises once over whoever it lands on, each its own, told by its word (crit, weak, resist, heal) and sized by
  the juice's `pop` (its colour now the theme's). A change in a bar flashes and pops as mana-ui marks every change,
  which is what a row's `jolt` now does; the window's jolt and the screen's flash are the channel's as before. A foe's
  health in the foes' box is a bar without numbers, as it was.
- **mana-ui grew what the RPG needed, for every game:** an anchor whose row has an id is its own element and a
  passing anchor rises and fades once (the damage numbers idiom replays each number now); a HUD region's place may be
  bound, so a game moves a box to the corner its scene leaves clear; a bar can be drawn without its numbers; and the
  runtime's state says which tab is open.
- A page with party battles is larger by mana-ui's runtime and sheet (a page without them carries none of it), and the
  phone layout's rules for the old battle markup are gone: mana-ui lays its screens out for a narrow screen itself.

### The action RPG: a hero with a sword on an open world map, sprinting on a stamina gauge

- **Stamina, lifted from the mobile suits' boost.** The platform rule's boost gauge (seconds of thrust, a refill, a
  dodge's cost, run dry and locked until it refills) is a hero's stamina when its rule says `sprint: true`
  (worlds/controllable/rules-platform.js): the boost held is a sprint on the ground, a walking hero's too, at `boostSpeed`
  along the stick, never with the stick at rest or in the air, on the run's own legs (the run's clip, faster), never a
  thruster's lean; a jump costs none of it unless `jumpBoostCost` says; run dry, the hero is WINDED, back to the run until
  the gauge is full again. A feel whose sprint outruns its run lowers to it (gameworld/feel/lower.js): its sprint speed,
  and its `stamina: { seconds?, refill?, winded? }` (STAMINA: 6 s of sprint, 4 s back, 6 s winded). The page reads the
  gauge as stamina, a green bar and WINDED in place of OVERHEAT, only where its hero sprints; the hero's controls say
  `F  sprint (stamina)`. A rule with no `sprint`, every boost as it was.
- **An orbit camera: the action game's third person.** A gameworld's `camera: 'orbit'` (cameras.js, the cosmos's
  space.camera): the mouse turns the camera round the hero and tilts it, never the hero (rules-basic.js follow `orbit`,
  6 m back over its shoulder, looking at its chest); W A S D run the hero the way the camera looks and the hero turns to
  face its run (rules-platform.js `moveYaw: 'camera'`, the world-frame pilot the overhead camera already drives). Its
  controls: `W A S D  run · mouse  turn the camera`. The `third-person` chase behind the hero's heading is as it was.
- **Seamless: segments walked as one page.** A level's `zone` may be a list of segments (level/zones.js): one page, its
  apron round their whole outline, the gates between them road on it, walls along its outline's every tile edge (a run
  where they line up) open at the gates to the rest. A gameworld's `glyphs.zoned: [['A', 'B'], …]` lays such pages, the
  segments no page names a page each; a page's exits on a grouped page are named by segment and side (`gate-a-s`), as
  two of its gates may face one way. Refused with words: a page of segments no gate joins, a segment on two pages.
- **The far view: the rest of the map on the horizon.** A zone's page with `far: true` (a gameworld's `glyphs.far`;
  level/far-view.js) lays every tile it does not build as greybox on the level's one land, its approved sketch's heights
  lowered: its ground tinted by the sketch (a forest darker, rocks grey, scrub dry, water), a wood's trees as cones, a
  cliff's slabs, its places as blocks, the walk's goal taller; the rim and the horizon ring the whole map, so the land runs
  on past the apron to the map's edge. Never walked: the zone's walls stand inside it. Absent, a zone's page as it was.
- **The sketch's fights are the level's.** A glyph map's level may stand foes (`levels.<id>.foes`, as a walk's trails
  do). Where its page holds an approved sketch, its foes stand round each encounter mark (grid-ends.js `encounters`,
  gameworld/foes.js foePlacements), as many as the mark says, of the bestiary entry its kind names; a mark of a kind the
  bestiary has not is left a mark, and a page whose sketch marks no fight stands none. A page with nothing approved stands
  its foes on its walk's beats, as before.
- **A quick intro and the way on.** A sketched level's page says what the level is and where to go (level/guide.js,
  drawn by scene/channels/guide.js): the concept's pitch held in the middle of the screen as the walk's first page opens,
  then the journey's beats on that page one at a time, at the top of the screen in words, an arrow turned the way it lies
  from where the camera looks and the metres to it, a pillar of light where it stands. Each beat stands where it is
  played: an encounter at its mark (reached once no foe stands about it), a find at its loot or secret, the walk's end at
  the goal's door, a traverse or a climb at the gate on to the walk's next segment. Drafts guide as approved segments do:
  directions are not a build. A page with no guide emits none of it.

### An action hero's combat stance, its weapon sheathed out of it

- **Combat is a state.** An action hero (the orbit camera and a blow: `camera: 'orbit'` with a strike in its right
  hand) enters combat when a foe stands within 10 m (held to 15 m once in it), a lock is held or a blow is struck, and
  leaves it 3 s after the last (the platform rule's `combat`, opt-in). In combat it walks a deliberate guard, its own
  walk at 2.4 m/s (`guard`), unless the sprint is held.
- **Sheathed out of combat.** Where its hand holds a blade, the run makes the SHEATHED HERO beside the equipped one
  (`hero-sheathed`: the same hero, the blade on its back, hilt up over the right shoulder, the hero door's `back` slot),
  and the level carries both: out of combat the sheathed figure plays, in combat the drawn one (the page builds both and
  swaps them, as a loadout's figures are swapped).
- **Pose layers.** A body's `layers` lay a pose over the clip a state plays, each a pivot bone turned and its chain
  carried round the pivot's head, eased in and out with its state: the run's legs set apart (out of combat, running), and
  combat's guard (leaning in, the weapon arm up and forward, the off arm raised, the feet wide; never over a strike, a
  dodge or a stagger, whose clip owns the body).
- **The HP at the bottom left** under the adventure look.
- **Fixed: the sheathed hero struck with nothing.** The held strike (worlds/world-scene.js) armed only the body whose
  figure was the hero being baked, and an action hero starts sheathed (`<hero>-sheathed`), so the drawn hero was baked
  with no swing clips and its rule had no strike: a click did nothing. The body whose combat draws the hero wields it
  too (worlds/held-strike.js). Measured on The Old Keep's rebuilt town page: the pilot strikes (contact on frame 14 of
  a 34-frame swing) and the drawn hero carries its five swings; before, neither.

### Mojulo Fighter: a fight on any level, by its lane

A fight's arena is now any level that can say where its fight lane is. The lane (`versus/versus-lane.js`) is
`{ at, heading, half, floor, back? }`: where the lane's centre stands, the way it runs, its walls, its floor and the open
room on the camera's side. The fight level loader (`versus/versus-levels.js`) turns each kind of level's own words into
a world recipe and its lane, one row a kind: `stage` (the arena as it was, its recipe unchanged) and `greybox`. The
runtime draws the whole fight in the lane's frame (bodies, the ring, the fighters' lights, the camera and the overlay),
so a lane turned and off the level's centre plays as the old one did; a stored arena reads as a lane at heading 0 and
keeps its place.

- **The greybox world kind** (`level/greybox-scene.js`): `{ kind: 'greybox', blocks: [{ at, size, turn?, tone? }] }`,
  boxes shaded by value under one sun (floor, wall, prop, edge), no kit's look. A level of boxes, for blocking out.
- **Greybox fight levels**: presets that stress the lane (`flat`; `alley`, walled behind with little room for the
  camera; `rooftop`, on a raised floor; `turned`, off centre at 35°), each overridable by words.
- **A quick fight's arena may name a level**: `arenas: [{ id, level: { kind: 'greybox', preset: 'turned' } }]`; an arena
  without one is the stage as before.
- **The anime register in the fight**: a character drawn in the character light (the anime head's) is played in it.
  Its tones are the light's own (each group's shade swatch, the eyes unlit as drawn), baked twice, every group lit and
  every group in shade, and the arena steps between them by its own key as the body turns, so both fighters are lit
  from the camera's side whichever way they face. No outline is drawn on them. Every other body is lit as before.
- **The training ground** (`greybox` preset `training`): a fight's graybox stage, its middle the focus. Between its
  walls the floor is the light tone, ruled a line every metre (every fifth lighter), the centre a bold band on the floor
  and up the back wall; past the walls the floor falls dark and unruled. A wall stands at each of the lane's ends, a
  body's width past the sim's, banded light up its front edge, along its foot and on the floor where it stands, so
  where it is reads from the camera. The camera is near. A fight made now is fought there, stamped at mint
  (`arenas: [{ id: 'training', level: { kind: 'greybox', preset: 'training' } }]`) when it names no arenas; a fight
  minted before keeps the ring, the plaza and the nave.
- **A level's view**: a greybox level's `view` (`genre` | `near`, its preset's by default) says how near the camera
  frames the fight; `near` is the ring's framing (a fighter near two thirds of the picture), now any level's.
- **Attack priority** (`versus-library.js` PRIORITY): two strikes landing on the same frame, the higher level's lands and
  the other's does not (a `priority` event, PRIORITY on the overlay); equal levels trade as before. It scales with
  strength (light 1, medium 2, heavy 3, punches and kicks alike), a special's is its own (a rush 2 · 3 · 4 by strength, a
  spinning kick 2 · 2 · 3, an overhead 3, a fireball 1), a super's 4, and a reversal's (the DP, `rps: 'reversal'`, and
  the rising super) 0: its invincibility is how it wins. Any move takes `tune: { priority }` (0 to 5). Two laws keep it
  a balance: `priority-pays` (no grounded normal outranks one that starts no slower than it) and `reversal-yields` (a
  DP's priority is 0).
- **Joint limits**: a pose is held within the bends a body makes as it becomes joints (`versus-rig.js` RIG_LIMITS: a knee
  one way and not past 155°, the ankle from a pointed toe to the foot drawn up, the head 55° off the trunk, an arm no
  further than 45° behind the back), and the body in the round within its own (`versus-figure.js` FIG_LIMITS: no elbow
  past 150°, no knee past 155°, the spine twisted no further than 60°, the hips turned with the chest; a foot never folded
  up into the shin as it is drawn). A knee bends toward its own thigh's front (up when the thigh is raised),
  never sideways.
- **The body keeps out of itself** (`versus-figure.js` FIG_BULK, from the body's own skeleton): a hand, a forearm or an
  elbow that would pass into the trunk, the head, a thigh or the other arm is moved across the plane (the hand's depth,
  the elbow turned out), or the chest turned until the arm clears it (a rear straight squares the shoulders); a leg into
  the other is moved out. All in depth, so the side view, and the boxes, stay the sim's. `scripts/spikes/fighter/
  joints.mjs` reads every pose of every fighter against the limits and the bulk.
- **One look a game: the fight's register** (`register: anime | western`, stamped at mint from the setting's drawing
  tradition, western when it names none): every fighter is rolled in it and drawn its one way, under one light, on every
  arena of the game. `western` lit as an engine lights it (its albedo, relief and roughness), the shadows soft; `anime`
  cel, three tones stepped from the same light, the shadows stepped and the shade cool. The rig: a warm key from the
  camera's side and above that casts, onto the floor (a shadow catcher over the lane) and across the body itself; on a
  greybox it is the level's own sun (`GREYBOX_SUN`), so the room and the bodies share one light; a low cool fill so the
  shadows stay deep; a rim from behind; a sky over a dark ground. The key follows the fight, its shadow's box tight round
  the fighters. Every body is baked as the lit export under a register (the stick figure lit the same way). A fight minted
  before carries none and draws each body as it always did. `styles.mjs --register` bakes a matchup in either look.
- **The fight's effects** (`versus-fx.js`, drawn by `versus-fx.client.js` in the arena under a register): what happens
  told apart at a glance, kept to a fighting game's impact (not a spell's), one library for every art style. Each event
  has its card, parts the register skins its way (anime cel, hard bands round the white core and on twos; western
  material, a soft falloff and a glow standing in for bloom): a hit's small white-hot core, shock ring and rays; a
  counter's gold double ring and a faint blink; a block's striped shield arc bowed toward the blow; a parry's ring
  snapping in; a clash's starburst; a guard crushed in shards; a KO's bloom. A heavier blow is a little bigger, brighter
  and longer. All in shaders (the page has no bloom pass), timed by the fight's own clock, so hitstop holds an effect and
  slow motion slows it; a brief real light at the contact lights the fighters by the rig they stand in. The overlay keeps
  its words; its 2D sparks stand down under a register.
- **The figure coated, not drawn over** (`bodyCoat` in the arena): every fighter's material carries a fresnel coat, light
  on its own surface over the whole figure or a portion of it. A blow coats the one it lands on, round where it landed
  (a block rims the guard blue, a counter gold) or whole (a parry, a crush, a KO), fading with the moment.
- **A blow says what it was**: hit, counter and block events carry where they landed (`at`, the hitbox's overlap with
  the hurtbox), how heavy (`w`, light … super), what struck (`limb`: fist, foot, knee, elbow, head, blade, shot) and the
  move's kind.
- **The spark** (system `spark`): a counter hit struck on the strike's very first active frame, the blow and the
  opening met in one frame. Half again the damage, the moment held (`rules.sparkStop`), meter (`rules.sparkMeter`);
  drawn as a black spark: the picture turned negative for two frames and held, black currents with a red edge crackling
  out of the contact, the one struck darkened with a red rim, a red light, then it lets go.
- **Elements on the limbs** (`element: 'fire' | 'lightning' | 'frost' | 'void' | { kind, on: fists | feet | limbs |
  weapon }`, on a recipe or a roster entry), as a coat of light gathered round the limbs that carry them: fire a warm
  licking rim (flaming fists), lightning a fast white-blue flicker, frost a slow cold breath, void a darkening with a red
  rim; flaring as the limb strikes, and a blow struck with it coats the one struck in the element. Drawn only: the sim
  never reads it, and the same fight is the same fight. `styles.mjs --elements --systems spark` bakes them.
- **The fight's language in mana-ui** (`idioms-fight.js`, shelf `fight`; `docs/mana-ui.md`, "The fight's language"):
  a fighting game's own UI, quiet and side against side, grown from the shared templates and held to ten principles
  (two sides and one centre, health the frame, the fight never covered, a callout a word, the round's ritual, meters in
  stocks, the hit-stop holding it, quiet, the bars lit and moving, picked by their look). In the fight: `fight-health` (the bars meeting at the clock, read by length,
  a guard line under each, each side's tag on its own line over its bar), `fight-meters`, `fight-combo`, `fight-callouts`, `fight-announcer`, and training's
  `input-display`, `frame-meter`, `training-stats`; around it: `versus-splash`, `fighter-select` (each seat's fighter
  at its own edge, the roster between them), `fight-pause`, `command-list`, `training-settings`, `fight-results`. Its
  words are the runtime's (`WORDS`: the round's ritual, the callouts, the meters, the frame data), so a fight ships in
  every language its game does. The elements do their talking: the frame says no word but the names, training's
  readouts carry no headings; the versus screens give each fighter its art at full height (`portrait` `size: xl`,
  `caption: false`), and the select shows style and figures only with `stats: true`, so a fighter is picked by their
  look. The bars are lit and move with what happened: over the round the track sinks and each fill is glossed with a
  bright leading edge; a hit drops the fill and flashes the slice it took once (a new mark on the track, `mana-moved`,
  keyed by the change), the chip holds what the combo took and drains after a beat (drawn from the start under the
  fill, so it drains rather than vanishing), a gain glows, a super with a stock ready runs a sheen (`data-ready`), its
  stocks a whole numeral; less motion, less flash and a hit-stop each have their say. The second side is the first's reflection, part for part (held by `fight.test.js`): a row set at its end
  runs from that end, and over the round a row's parts are centred across and figures take even widths. A bar takes `size: large | thin` and `figures: false`; a region takes `variant: bare`
  (no plate, its parts their own frame); a filling row whose children say `fill` shares its width among them alone.
  Its looks are new theme cards of the family `fight`: `fight-clean` (the default), `fight-cel` (anime) and
  `fight-lit` (western), none leaning, stacking or slamming. The board draws a fight HUD, a training HUD and every
  fight screen. A table's column labelled by a word now reads as the word (it printed the object).
- **Non-human fighters, in the game's look**: a roster's character may be any stored body that stands on two legs and
  fights with two arms: a hero, a xeno (`xenoSpecies`, `xenoHeaddress`), beastfolk (the hero's `beast`: a kin, its tail,
  a second pair of arms, a naga on its serpent's coil), a mascot or a two-legged creature, each measured off its own
  skeleton (a non-hero's girth from its trunk's widest ring, its colour from its palette); a four-legged body or one
  without arms is refused with the reason, and a fighter's own strikes (`moves`) stay a hero's. A body's face bones
  (lids, lips, brows, ears, a snout, horns) ride its head, and a serpent's coil its hips, the rest planted on the ground.
  Beastfolk with a snout carry their heads low: a stance's `stoop` (degrees, 0 … 30) sinks a fighter's rests (the knees
  bent, the trunk hinged over hips sat back), so the standing head comes down about 5 cm and the crouched about 20 at a
  long muzzle's 26 (a short muzzle or a beak 16, a snake's head or mandibles 10, by the head's own word), the hurt box's
  front where it was; the trade is the jabs thrown from the rest, about a tenth shorter. A head is posed over its own
  carriage, so a beast's skull seated crown-forward keeps its snout on the fight (it pointed at the sky). A posed body under a fight's register is drawn in it, as a played one is: the register's
  material, casting and taking the key's shadows, its coats, no ink hull.
- **The fight's sounds, from the SFX shelf** (`versus/versus-sfx.js`): a fight game under its register sounds its blows
  from the library every game hears (merged in from the SFX shelf), each cue built from the shelf's families at their
  dials: a fist by its weight (a jab, a body blow over its flesh, a haymaker), a foot, a blade, a shot, a counter, the
  spark, a block, a clash, a guard crushed, a grab and a throw slammed down, a body hitting the floor, a burst, a super,
  a projectile and the knockout. The arena's page carries them on its audio channel (one room, ten voices, each hit its
  own variant), joining what audio the level has; the runtime plays the cue for what landed (`fightCue`) and starts the
  sound on a first key or touch. An arena made before the register beeps as it did.
- **The move primitives** (`versus-library.js`, a fighter takes the ones it wants; one that takes none fights to the byte
  as before): command normals (forward + a button, `commands`) with the overhead families `axe` and `hammer`, slow and
  blocked only standing, their priority a heavy's; traversal specials, a `slide` (low, it trips, under a fireball), a
  `roll` and a `blink` (through the opponent, untouchable on the way, striking nothing) and a `hop` (over a low); charge
  motions (`[4]6`, `[2]8`: the hold kept only on a fighter with one) with the charged shot `boom` and the flip kick
  `flash`; a `rekka` (three stages, the same motion again on hit, block or whiff, typed through hitstop on its last
  direction and a button); and air blocking (system `airblock`: holding back in the air blocks an air attack or a shot).
  Throws, the fireball, the DP and the sweep's trip were there already.
- **The move list** (`versus-movelist.js`): a fighter's moves by kind, each its input in the player's scheme (the
  classic's motions and charges, the modern's special button), what it is for and its frame data, in mana-ui's command
  list; a tab's label and a table's cell may be one of the runtime's words, said in the game's language.
- **The lab**: training is fought on the game's training ground (its arena marked `lab`; a game minted with arenas of its
  own gets one beside them), straight from character select (you and your training partner) with no stage to pick.
  Under the register the arena carries mana-ui over the fight (`versus-lab.js`, in the register's look): the first
  player's inputs along the foot, each a run with the frames it was held; the frame meter of the last move over them on
  F (startup, active, recovery, what it left); and the move list from the pause, in the pausing player's scheme.
- **CI**: `design-game.vary.test.js` pins its order's roll (it drew one at random each run, and about one roll in
  four hundred lifts most of a late tier's ornaments past their 0–3 scale, the gate leaving two variants of three).

### An action quest's first zone, taught by its land

- **Controls taught at the beat that needs them.** A journey beat of a sketched map takes `teach`: the verbs the hero
  learns there (look, strike, sprint, dodge, lock, jump). The guide shows that beat's keys under its line while it is
  the way on (the arrival's under the intro, its seconds counted from when the world is up); with the world's `mechanics.legend: 'menu'` the controls leave the play screen for the pause menu, so
  nothing is taught as a list up front. A law, `teaches-before-tests`, says when a fight comes before the strike is
  taught, or a fight of several before the lock-on.
- **The first look.** An arrival beat that `faces` another sets its page out facing where that beat stands (a climax
  at the goal's place), not down the road. A law, `first-look`, says whether that place is seen from the start over the
  land as planned (its tiles' heights, the eye at 1.7 m, the place's top 6 m up), and which tile hides it if not. The Old
  Keep's first run of it found the keep's own rocky corner hiding the warden's gate from the town by 2.5 m. What grows
  on the land the plan does not know (a tile's trees and rocks stood in front of the hero in the page), so the start's
  page OPENS on that place: the chase camera's `vista` (rules-basic.js follow, opt-in) stands it 16 m higher looking at
  the place's top for its first six seconds of play, eased back down behind the hero over the last two.
- **One foe before the pack.** A law, `foes-ramp`, says when the walk's first fight is more than one foe.
- **Leaving is graduation.** A concept that `hold`s its pages holds each page's ways out, never the way it was come in
  by, until the foes standing on it are down (a reach-exit's `holds: { who?, count }`, the downs counted as a defeat-all
  counts them); at a held way the guide says it stays shut while foes stand. A page with no foe standing holds nothing.
- **The first zone, laid.** `level/first-zone.js` `firstZone(plan, { foe?, pack?, pitch? })` lays a planned map's journey
  in teaching order, as a platformer's first level lays its trails: the arrival facing the goal (look), the lone foe in
  the walk's first segment (strike), the second segment crossed (sprint) and its pack (lock, dodge), the climb and the
  climax in the last, a secret in each segment off the walk; held. It says the fight marks each segment wants (`wants`),
  placed by its planner. The Old Keep is re-laid on it: a lone bandit at the town's east edge, then the three at the bend.

### A walked world that holds, and a HUD that reads as a game

- **Trees and rocks are solid.** A glyph map asks each of its tiles for its flora solid (`tile.solid`): the meadow kit
  stands a collider on each tree's trunk (about its foot, to 3.5 m) and each boulder (its faces' box drawn in a little;
  a stone the feet step over left out), so the hero walks round them. The map names the groups that are no footing
  (`footless`: a tree's crowns, its leaves and blossom, a stamped tree), and the page takes them out of the ground probe,
  so walking into a crown no longer lifts the hero up through its leaves (the float). A tile not asked is unchanged.
- **The adventure look (mana-ui).** A theme takes a new word, `hud: panel | bare`, and a new preset, `adventure`: an
  action game's HUD on the scene itself, never a card. `gameHudCss(theme)` writes the in-game HUD's sheet for a bare
  look: the HUD's parts with no plate, their words outlined; meters slim and framed in a hairline with cut ends, their
  numbers left to the status page; the pilot's hp up at the top left and its stamina a slim gauge under the hero; banners
  and toasts in the display face.
- **A world names its HUD's look.** `hud: '<mana-ui theme>'` (the interface chapter's `/hud`): its levels' HUD wears it
  (`events.look`), a bare look drops the level badge (the level stays on the status page and in the level-up banner),
  and its game's play shell leaves the menu button off under a mouse (the pause is Esc; a finger keeps the button).
- **The guide, one thing at a time.** The way on, a beat's keys, its line, the intro and a held way's word share one
  place at the top of the screen and never stand together: a line just said, the opening (the pitch, then the arrival's
  keys), a held way, the lesson at hand when the hero nears a beat that teaches (its keys as caps), else the way on. Its
  words sit on the scene, outlined. A meet's way on names who is met; what they say is said on reaching them.
- **Fixed:** the stamina gauge's green and its WINDED read the platform rule's `stamina` again (the 1105-rc merge had
  renamed it, so the bar fell back to the mobile suit's cyan).

### A level's scenario, beat by beat, and how much happens in it

- **One list, each beat whole.** A sketched map takes `scenario: { pitch?, beats }` in place of a concept: each beat its
  segment and its tile there, its kind (arrival, vista, meet, fight, traverse, find, rest, secret, climb, climax), its one
  line, its foes (`{ <bestiary id>: how many }`) or its find (`item`), what it teaches, how it feels (`pace`: calm,
  tension, peak, rest) and whether winning it opens its page's ways out (`opens`). It is read into the concept and a
  mark a beat on its tile (the mark names its beat), so the guide, the fights, the first look and the laws read it as
  they read a concept, and nothing pairs a beat with a mark by its kind or its order. The segments' sketches keep their
  land and scenery. A beat that is not whole is refused with words (a fight with no foes, a find with no tile, `opens`
  with nothing to win).
- **Every beat does something in play.** A fight stands its foes on its tile; a find or a secret that names its item is
  picked up there into the bag (a `collect`; the store carries the bag); a meet's or a rest's line is said on reaching it,
  and a find says what was found; a beat that opens holds its page's ways out, and a page holding the walk's goal holds
  that too, so the climax is won by its fight, never walked past.
- **The pace.** `level/pace.js` walks each beat from the last along the map's own paths at a hero's run (7 m/s): each
  beat's metres and seconds, each segment's beats a minute of walking, the longest stretch with nothing in it. Three
  laws join a scenario's: `dead-air` (no stretch over 30 s), `pace-shape` (tension before the first peak, a breath after
  each peak, the walk ending on its peak) and `segment-interest` (each segment on the walk 1.5 beats a minute at least).
  The Old Keep, rewritten as one scenario of nine beats, holds them all, and the measure says what the miniature hid:
  the town and the fields are crowded (a beat every 3 or 4 seconds at the run, 24 m tiles), the woods and the keep a long
  run between beats.

### The world map: maps linked at their borders, each loaded as it is walked into

- **A planned map built a segment a page.** `level.zone: '<segment>'` (level/zones.js) builds one segment of a planned
  glyph map as its own page: its tiles stand where they stand on the whole map (the level's frame, its one land, the same
  seeds), so the ground at a border is the ground the neighbour's page lays there. An apron of the neighbours' tiles
  (`apron`, one by default) is built round it and never walked, so the land past a border reads as the next zone's; the
  rim rises past the apron. Walls stand on the zone's square, open only at its gates; the page reads out its ways (each
  gate's crossing, an exit just inside it and an arrival further in, facing in), and a law, `zone-ways`, says each is open.
- **Joins: a world map with loops.** A plan may join neighbours its walk does not step between (`plan.joins: [['A',
  'C'], …]`), each a gate on their shared side like the walk's; a segment off the walk, reached by joins, is a pocket. A
  planned map is still walked along its route (its pieces, its start and its goal), a join never its way on.
- **A zoned level is a game's world map.** `glyphs.zoned: true` on a gameworld's planned glyph level (a world travelled:
  `topology: 'interconnected'`) makes it a stage a segment: the walk's first first, the segments off it last. Each zone is
  left by its gates (`gate-<side>` reach-exits on its border, toward the zone across) and arrived in by the zone come from,
  set down at that gate's arrival; the shell's travel, keys and flags work as they are. A zone holding the walk's goal keeps
  it beside its gates: reaching it is the game's win.
- **A test bed with no game round it.** `node scripts/worldmap.mjs` builds a world map (the sample: four 3 × 3-tile zones
  of 24 m round a square, or `--world <file>`) straight to a folder with no database and no design loop: a page a zone,
  the play shell over them. `--serve` to walk it by hand; `--walk` walks every gate in headless Chrome, timing each swap and
  measuring where the walker is set down against the gate's arrival; `--shots <dir>` a picture at each arrival. On the
  sample: a zone of 16 tiles (9 its own) builds in 3-5 s and is 10-13 MB; each crossing loads in about 2-3 s, set down on
  its gate's arrival.
- Not yet: an arrival sets the walker's place, not its facing (a zone's page sets out facing in from its way in along the
  walk; arrivals by its other gates keep that heading); a crossing is at a gate, not anywhere along a border (the zones'
  shared frame makes carrying the walker's place along the border the next step); each crossing is a whole page swapped
  behind the veil, never streamed or fetched ahead; a megaworld's rings do not yet take a zoned map as one of their zones.
- **The world map in miniature.** `level/worldmap-view.js` draws a zoned map from its recipe alone, no page built (a
  moment, against seconds a zone): the WORLD (each zone's square on the shaded land, its name and role, the walk and the
  joins, every gate), a ZONE (its tiles, its apron veiled, its paths, places and pieces, where its page sets out and where
  each gate sets one down, each gate a link sideways to the zone across) and a TILE (its ground, its path's shape, its
  place and door, what of the game lies on it, its gate), each a view drilled into by its address and back out by its
  crumbs. HTML and CSS alone, as the game book's pages are, so it can join the book as it stands. The test bed writes it
  beside the game (`map.html`, each zone's walk a link to its page); `--map-only` writes it alone.
- **The world map as a model.** `level/worldmap-model.js` lays the same recipe as a greybox diorama on a plinth (the
  land's rise lifted to read at table scale and lit in its colours, each zone's ground faintly its tint, its border broken
  at its gates, the paths, the places as blocks, a post either side of every gate, the pieces, where each page sets out),
  orbited on its own page with a bookmark over the whole and one over each zone, each zone named. The test bed writes it
  as `model.html`, linked from the miniature's world view.
- **The map sketch: a level decided in miniature before it is built.** `level/map-sketch.js` writes a planned map's
  CONCEPT (its pitch and its journey, beat by beat: arrival, traverse, encounter, find, secret, climb, climax…, each on a
  segment) and, a segment at a time, its SKETCH: each tile's ground (forest, grove, meadow, rocks, cliff, water, scrub),
  its height in steps over its region's rise, and its marks (an encounter and who, loot and what, a landmark, a secret, a
  rest, a hazard, someone met), each segment a draft until the creator approves it. Laws advise: the journey covers the
  walk and follows it, a path climbs a step at a time, a gate's two sides stand within a step, no path on water or a
  cliff. Each segment's SUBTASK is its brief (`segmentBriefs`): its beats, its fixed paths and places, its gates and the
  ground across each in metres, what to decide and its laws. Not an RPG's: any action quest's map. A gameworld's zoned
  glyph level carries it as `glyphs.sketch`; the build does not read it yet.
- **The miniature reads the sketch.** The world view numbers the journey over the zones and says each zone's status
  (approved, a draft, not yet planned), lists the journey and the sketch's laws; a zone shows its ground drawn (trees,
  boulders, a cliff's hatching, water, meadow and scrub), its heights, its marks with what each is, its notes and its
  brief; the land is shaded with the sketched heights. The model lays the same in greybox: trees, boulders, a cliff's
  slabs, water, the ground's tints, and a coloured post a mark, told on hover. The test bed writes the briefs
  (`briefs/<segment>.md`), writes the sample out to sketch on (`--save-world`) and approves a segment in a world's file
  (`--approve <segment>`). The sample is a quest to an old keep: the town approved, the fields and the keep drafts, the
  woods not yet planned (its laws say the woods' east gate must rise to meet the keep's).
- **The segments' crew plans in miniature.** `req: { unit: 'level:<id>', segments: true }` raises every segment of a
  planned map, those reached only by joins too, an author each. Each author's brief now carries its segment's sketch
  brief: the level's pitch and the journey's beats here, its land's height and the ground across each gate in metres, what
  to decide (ground, height, marks), the sketch's laws and which of them fail as it stands; its gates say the joins too
  (each a path the segment's law holds it to). An author writes its segment's sketch beside its glyphs
  (`/levels/<id>/glyphs/sketch/segments/<S>`, laid for it when the req is raised), and nothing else; a malformed sketch is
  refused by the world's read with nothing written, and a sketch its author marks approved is refused: the approval is the
  creator's (the director's own patch).
- **Found by the first crew to plan in miniature.** A segment already written is handed what is written there (its
  `written` rows and places), not the plan's default fill as its floor. A law, `beats-marked`: each sketched segment
  stages its journey's beats on marks (a fight on an encounter, a find on loot or a secret, a secret on a secret, a rest on
  a rest; any other beat on some mark).
- **A segment geocubed: its approved sketch lowered into the build.** `levelGrid` (level/map-sketch.js), read by the map's
  page and its ends in place of the plain grid: an APPROVED segment's heights go into its tiles' rise in the level's one
  land (so a zone's apron and its neighbour's own page lay the same ground); its ground into each tile's flora (forest,
  grove, meadow and scrub as the kit's own presets: forest, grove, meadow, upland); its rocks into more boulders on a path
  tile (`tile.boulders`, era/out-tile.js); its marks onto the page, a post each, told on hover, read out on `map.sketch`. A
  cliff, water, and rocks off a path are not laid yet, and the page says which (`unlaid`). A draft is never lowered, and
  a level with no approved segment builds byte for byte as before. The test bed builds one segment's zone alone
  (`--zones A`) and says what of the sketch it lowered.
- **A town's houses are homes inside, not crypts.** A glyph map's places asked nothing of their insides, so a house, a
  shop or a tavern was built in the stone room kit's crypt dress (rubble, cobwebs, moss, niches). They now ask for a
  homely inside (`homely: true`, era/stage-buildings.js HOMELY_USES: a dwelling, a shop, a tavern, a workshop, a hall, a
  barn, a library, a guardhouse): the town's vernacular register in the kit's own palette, as a town street's walked-in
  houses are (`town.inside`). A temple, a crypt or a keep keeps its stone; a place's own kit or look wins.
- **Still trees and untouched grass, by word.** `grass.sway: false` on an isekai stage: the trees' crowns stand still in
  the wind the live grass moves in (absent, they sway as before). With `grass.contact: false` (the walker never lays the
  grass) it is a map's to say for every tile (`glyphs.grass`). A sketched ground's flora presets bring the live grass,
  and with it the sway and the contact, where an unsketched map had neither.
- **The grass is walked through, never stood on.** The live grass's blades, its far grass and the cards it takes over
  (and a sakura's petals) take no ray (channels/stage-grass.js): a walker's ground probe stood on the tufts it was in, its
  eye riding up to half a metre over the land. Measured walking a meadow in the town: the eye 1.70 to 2.19 m over the land
  before, 1.70 m throughout after. A page with no live grass is unchanged.

### The artillery range: one turret, every big gun

- **Planned.** The firing range's sibling at a big gun's scale: cannons aimed by hand, ordnance of each kind fired into
  matter of each kind. Its primitive is the turret: one mount, stepped by one piece of the runtime, so a tank's, a
  tower's and a field gun's are the same thing on a different base, stationary or rolling.
- **The turret.** A gun on a mount, aimed by hand on any base: an entity's opt-in `turret: { mount, gun }`, stepped by
  `worlds/controllable/turret.js`. The hand (the mouse's look) moves where the gunner asks the gun to point; the mount
  slews to it at its traverse and elevation rates, accelerating and braking onto it, within its stops; a hand slower
  than the mount is tracked, a quicker one lagged (the mount's weight, the feel). A stabilized mount holds its line in
