  the world while its base turns (a gyro loop, up to its rate); an unstabilized one is carried, as a crank-laid gun is.
  The weapon fires from the muzzle along the barrel. A page without a turret is as it was.
- **The mounts** (`gameworld/combat/mount.js`): a battle tank's turret, a light tank's, a field gun laid by hand, a
  self-propelled howitzer's and a fortress tower's, by class; measured on the runtime (a quarter turn, the elevation's
  whole range, a flick's settle, the lag behind a sweeping hand, the drift on a turning base) and held to their laws.
- **The ordnance and its flight** (`gameworld/combat/ordnance.js`): a tank gun's long rod (APFSDS), its shaped charge
  (HEAT) and its high-explosive shell, and an indirect shell for the high arc, by class: caliber, mass, muzzle velocity,
  drag, dispersion, fuse, filler. Each lowers onto a travelling round; measured from a turret on the runtime: at 250,
  500, 1000 and 2000 m the elevation to hit (° and mils), the time of flight, the speed it arrives at, its drop below
  the bore; the indirect shell's high arc onto 2 to 5 km, its apex and its long flight; a dozen rounds' scatter. At 2 km
  the long rod flies 1.24 s and keeps 93% of its speed, the HE shell 2.44 s laid 13 mils up; the indirect shell lands
  at 4 km on a 69° arc after 47 s.
- **A shell's drag and its gun's dispersion on the runtime.** A travelling round takes `projectileDrag` (quadratic: it
  sheds speed as e^(−k·x)), and a weapon's seeded cone scatters its shells as it does its bullets. Absent, a round
  flies as it did.
- **The matter answering** (`gameworld/combat/terminal.js`): what each round does to what it strikes, seen as it is (a
  hole, a breach, a spall, a dent, a crater, a scorch), computed from the round's numbers and the matter's, drawn
  plausibly and never broken physically. A long rod by a simplified Lanz–Odermatt law (calibrated to about 650 mm of
  rolled armour at the muzzle and 600 at 2 km; a plate at an angle its thickness over the cosine); a shaped charge's jet
  the same at any range, scaled by density; a blast holing only thin steel, breaching a wall when its filler is the
  engineers' breaching charge for it (by its thickness cubed and its material, untamped) and spalling it otherwise,
  cratering earth by its dig energy. The range's stands: armour plates at 100 to 700 mm and one sloped at 60°, mild
  steel, reinforced and plain concrete, brick, granite, timber, sandbags, earth. Held to laws: a thicker plate stops what
  a thinner one stopped, the rod slows and cuts less, a jet does not, a shell holes no thick armour and breaches no
  metre of reinforced concrete, more filler digs a wider crater.
- **The artillery range, played** (`gameworld/combat/artillery.js`, `artilleryOf` / `artilleryHtml`; the spike
  `scripts/spikes/combat-tester/artillery.mjs`). A game's big gun given as its mount (a class, or its fields over one),
  its rounds (up to four, keys 1 to 4), its base (a concrete plinth, or a hull on the range's track: W / S drive, A / D
  turn, the stabilizer holding the aim), its reload and its sounds. The range: the gun on the firing line, a row of each
  stand at 250, 500, 1000 and 2000 m on its own bearing so no near row hides a far one, the sloped plate laid back at its
  angle, white posts taller the farther; with the indirect shell (a mount that elevates past 45°), a bunker's roof and a
  ring of sandbags at 3, 4 and 5 km. The gunner looks through the sight beside the barrel (right click zooms it wide, 4×
  and 10×; O steps outside behind the gun): the bore's cross and, under it, a mark for each band of the loaded round,
  from that round's own flight measured on the runtime, where the target must sit for the round to drop onto it. The
  indirect shell's chart (its elevation in mils and its flight for each range) is on the gunner's readout. Each round
  that bursts on a stand or the ground is marked by the same law the measures run: a hole (and its exit through), a
  breach and its rubble, a spall, a dent, a scorch, a crater and its rim. It sounds from the SFX shelf: a cannon, the
  breech worked over the reload, a large blast where the shell went off. In the browser: a long rod laid by its 1000 m
  mark goes through 300 mm of armour, the HE shell breaches a brick wall at 500 m, the indirect shell laid off the chart
  lands 12 m from 4 km after 47 s.
- **The turret's rounds by key and its view on the page.** A turret's opt-in `rounds` are loaded by the slot keys, the
  breech empty until the reload is done. A page whose world has a turret draws its gun in graybox, its sight, its marks
  and its readout (`channels/controllable/turret-view.js`); every other page keeps every byte.
- **A mix heard farther.** The SFX mixer's opt-in `reach` (metres, with its distance): a cue as far off as the arena's
  distances times its reach is heard as one at them, so a shell bursting 4 km off still sounds. Absent, as it was.
- **The turret on its bases.** The range's `base` takes a vehicle of the library (`{ vehicle: 'light tank', livery?,
  wear?, seed? }`, any word the vehicle registry knows): its realistic build drawn as itself (its camo, its wear), driven
  on its own class's rule (W / S, A / D steer), the mount laid where its gun is (the trunnion, the barrel's length) at
  its class's rates; its turret bone turned by the mount's traverse and its gun bone by its elevation, the stabilizer
  holding the gun's line in the world while the hull steers. A road car, or a field vehicle with no turret, is refused by
  name. The graybox bases gained their own looks: a fortress tower (its shaft and parapet, the gun on its roof) and a
  field gun's carriage (its wheels on their axle, its split trails spread to their spades, its shield on the top
  carriage). In the browser: the light tank's turret laid 40° left and its gun 8° up turn its bones; steered through
  45° the gun's world aim is held within a degree; back on the line, its long rod holes the 100 mm plate at 500 m.
- **A field vehicle's gun on a bone of its own** (`car-designer/military.js`, opt-in `gun`, also through
  `compileRealistic`): a turret's gun and mantlet split off onto a `gun` bone, its head the trunnion (the mantlet's back
  on the barrel's axis), and `gun: { trunnion, muzzle }` said, so a turret runtime can elevate it. Absent, the figure is
  as it was, byte for byte.
- **The mecha shelf's frames on the range** (`gameworld/combat/frames.js`). The range's `base` takes a frame of the mecha
  shelf by its library word (`{ frame: 'rover walker', stance?, palette? }`): the work frames (utility, heavy and
  giant-arm walkers), the walkers (all-terrain, field), the transforming walkers (the rover walker, the siege walkers,
  the brood walker) and the big walkers, standing at a stance (braced to fire where it braces, else standing; `roll`
  its tank form, its legs folded onto its wheels). None walks on a page yet: no frame's gait is built. A frame with
  guns fires from its own backpack mounts (the rover walker's autocannon and rocket pod, the siege walkers' howitzer and
  missiles); one that takes a gun backpack is given it (the field walker's rocket pod); one with none is fitted the
  shelf's own traverse ring, cradle and autocannon on its roof, a field conversion. The frame is lowered body by body
  into a rig: each mount's ring and its cradle with its weapon a bone, turned by the one turret, both mounts following
  the gunner's aim and the loaded round's mount firing (a round's own trunnion and reach, opt-in in the turret runtime).
  The mounts slew at a backpack's rates, a siege backpack's slower and high enough for the indirect arc. The outside
  view stands back by the base's size.
- **A walker's rounds.** A 30 mm armour-piercing core and a 30 mm high-explosive shell for the autocannon, an unguided
  70 mm rocket for the pods, a launcher's missile fired unguided; the howitzer fires the HE and indirect shells. Held to
  the same laws: the 30 mm core goes through about 120 mm of armour at a kilometre; its HE shell spalls a brick wall and
  does not breach it, where a rocket's or a missile's warhead does. Two laws were found too narrow and restated: the
  long rod's 650 mm calibration is the 120 mm round's own (a round that carries a calibration is held to it), and at the
  far band it is the round that arrives sooner, not the one that leaves faster, that is laid lower (a blunt 30 mm shell
  leaves faster than a 120 mm one and arrives later). A wide cone's scatter is measured from a gun stood high, so its
  low rounds are not lost to the ground short of the band.
- **The frames walk** (`mecha-shelf/mecha-gait.js`). Each frame of the mecha shelf now walks, its gait read from its
  structure and scaled to its size. Its structure: two legs step in alternation, four in a lateral sequence (hind then
  fore on a side, three feet always down); the farthest each foot reaches ahead and behind within its joints' ranges,
  through the shelf's own IK, at the height its knees bend to for the longest reach. Its size: dynamic similarity, a walk
  at Froude number 0.25 on its hip's height, its stride by Alexander's relative-stride law, so a bigger frame strides
  longer and steps slower (its cadence as 1/√L) and goes faster over the ground; where its legs reach less, the stride
  is theirs at the same cadence. The swing is shaped to the leg: a knee-forward work frame's flat foot cannot lift from
  behind within its ankle's stop, so its foot comes forward before it rises. From the utility walker's 1.7 m stride at
  112 steps a minute to the siege walker's 7.4 m at 56 and the brood walker's four legs at 51. Held to laws: every key
  within its joints' ranges, a planted foot still on the ground, a swinging foot clear, a foot (a biped) or three (a
  four-legged frame) always down, a walk and not a run. On the range a frame walks at its gait's pace (W / S, A / D
  turn), each body a bone keyed at each step by the IK, its gun laid as it goes; in its tank form it stands. O steps
  through the sight, the view behind the gun and a view beside the base, watching it walk.
- **The transforming walkers drive in their tank form.** The rover walker, the siege walkers and the brood walker are
  one body with two forms on the range: they walk, and B folds them into their tank form and they drive on their wheels
  (the runtime's forms: a beat, then the tank form's rule), B again unfolding them. The fold is solved by their chain,
  their joints and their pelvis carried from standing to rolled in even steps, so the legs stay joined as they fold; the
  tank form's bodies are a pose of the same rig, its wheels turning a full turn every 2πr driven. Its drive from its
  structure and size as its walk is: a wheeled machine's off-road pace at Froude 4 on its wheelbase (the rover walker
  6.1 m/s, the siege walker 9.2, its Mk 1 11.9, the brood walker 16.1), its turn no quicker than keeps its grip within
  half of what would roll it over. Its gun fires from where its mount is in each form, and its sight carries each form's
  range marks. A base transforming on the range stays solid (the beat's shimmer is a game's tell).
- **A four-legged frame's feet pass clear.** The brood walker's legs aim their hips at their ankles, so each foot (its
  bay, its petals, its wheels) turns as it reaches, and in a lateral sequence a hind foot swung into the fore foot still
  planted ahead of it. A four-legged frame's gait now takes the order of the six that keeps a side's two feet farthest
  apart, sets its feet as much wider fore and aft as lets it walk fastest, and shortens its stride until each foot's
  outline in plan, turned with its leg, passes its neighbour's clear: a new law. The brood walker walks a diagonal
  sequence, its feet 15% wider, a 2.6 m stride at 1.1 m/s (from 5 m at 2.1, its bays meeting); no two of its legs'
  bodies touch at any key.
- **Steered wheels** (`worlds/controllable/steer.js`, opt-in; emitted only into a page with a steered body). A
  transforming walker's tank form steers its front wheels: A / D steer them toward their lock at their rate, and it
  turns as a wheeled machine turns, about a point on its fixed axles' line, at v · tan(δ) / its steering wheelbase:
  standing it does not turn (its wheels do), reversing it turns the other way. At speed its lock is what its grip allows,
  so its wheels point along the circle it drives and never scrub; slow or standing, its full lock (30°, steered more
  slowly the bigger the machine). Each steered wheel is drawn at its own angle, the inner one more (Ackermann: the rover
  walker's inner wheel 52° at full lock, its outer 20°); the brood walker steers its front bays' wheels. Held to laws on
  the runtime: the circle at full lock, no turn standing, the other way reversing, the steering rate, the lock at speed.
- **A chase view to drive from.** O now steps through the gunner's sight, a chase view behind the hull (a driver's
  third-person view: behind and over the base by its size, following its heading eased so a steered curve swings the world
  and not the camera, the gun's aim a pip on the glass), the view behind the gun and the view beside the base. The mouse
  lays the gun in every view; W / S / A / D drive in every view.
- **The walkers heard.** A frame's footfalls sound as each of its feet is planted (its legs' phases in its gait, four a
  cycle for the brood walker), weighted by its mass (a heavy footstep, a mech's, a giant's), never in its tank form; its
  hydraulics follow its walking pace and its diesel power pack its speed, idling as it stands. A light tank or a tracked
  carrier rumbles on its tracked engine, a truck on its diesel. The SFX shelf gains the rows: `diesel-engine` and
  `tank-engine` (the engine family's new `diesel` and `tracked` kinds: a slow knock and a sub-rumble, the turbo; the
  tracks' links clanking faster with speed) and `walker-hydraulics` (the servo family's `walker`: a pump whining up, the
  valves chuffing with the steps). A world's own held voices are an opt-in `audio.sustains`.
- **The other military vehicles drivable.** Every field vehicle of the library is a base: the utility vehicle, the heavy
  utility vehicle, the cargo truck, the armoured personnel carrier, the tracked carrier and the missile launcher, each
  driven on its own class's physics (W throttle, A / D steer). One with no turret is fitted a remote weapon station (the
  shelf's ring, cradle and autocannon, stabilized, all round) on the ring it has for one (the carriers' mount rings, the
  heavy utility vehicle's roof ring, the truck's and the launcher's cab hatch ring) or else on its roof. A wheeled one
  steers its front axle (an eight-wheeler its front two), each wheel drawn at its own angle from the drive rule's own
  steering. The views stand back by a vehicle's size (its height, or a long one's share of its length).
- **The aircraft.** The craft shelf's armed aircraft fly the range (`base: { aircraft }`: the warbird, the naval
  warbird, the jet fighter, the delta interceptor, the carrier fighter, the attack jet) on the fly rule the civilian
  trainer and jet already flew, each at its class's envelope in the skyscape's `CRAFT` from its type's published figures
  (stall, cruise, top speed, ceiling, bank, sink, mass and thrust: a P-51D's, an F4U-4's, an F-16's, a Mirage III's, an
  F/A-18C's, an A-10's; a transport's and a stealth jet's beside them). Each is drawn as its shelf rig, gear up, banked
  and pitched as it flies, its propeller spinning. Its gun is fixed along its nose (the turret's new `fixed` mount: the
  mouse flies it, the gun pitches with the airframe), fired at its calibre's rate from its load: a heavy machine gun, a
  20 mm rotary cannon, a 30 mm revolver or rotary cannon (`AIR_GUNS`, with their rounds), a pair of wing guns from
  between them. Its rounds leave at the gun's speed plus the craft's. It starts aloft behind the firing line at its
  cruise, its lever set where its cruise holds, kept to the range by the rule's bound; mouse pitch, A / D bank, W / S
  throttle, a chase view with an aim pip, a prop or jet engine heard by its throttle. Each envelope is its registry row's `sky` handle, so the
  flight door's `craft` word flies them too. An aircraft with no gun on the range (the transport, the stealth jet) is
  refused by name. Not yet: bombs, landing, a crash.
- **Helicopters and drones.** A rotorcraft is a base by its word too (`base: { aircraft: 'attack helicopter' }`, `'camera
  drone'`, `'fpv drone'`), flown on a new opt-in `hover` rule (`worlds/controllable/rules-hover.js`): its rotors' thrust
  along its disc, the disc tilted to move it, quadratic drag; the collective (Space / Shift) asks a climb or holds its
  height, the cyclic (W / S, Q / E) a helicopter's disc's tilt (let go it levels and coasts) or a drone's speed (its flight
  controller: let go it brakes to a hover), the pedals (A / D) its turn, at speed a coordinated, banked turn that holds its
  height. Each flies at its type's published figures (`skyscape/rotor.js` ROTOR, a registry row's new `rotor` handle: a
  Bell 206's, a UH-60's, an AH-64's, a CH-47's; a Mavic-class camera quad's, a five-inch racing quad's, an enterprise
  quad's, the heavy lifters'), so full cyclic comes to its top speed holding its height and the collective to its best
  climb. Armed as such machines are: the attack helicopter's chin chain gun on its turret, aimed by the hand and
  stabilized (a 30 mm dual-purpose round, `hedp30`), its rocket pods and missile rails fired along its nose; a utility or
  heavy-lift helicopter's door gun on its pintle in the right door (a 12.7 mm door gun); a light helicopter's gun pod
  along its nose; a multirotor drone lets go below it what it lifts (a 30 mm grenade, a 60 mm mortar bomb, a
  shaped-charge bomblet on its drogue: rounds that are released, `drop`, measured falling from 10 to 100 m to the speed
  their drag allows), its chase view's ring where it will land; a racing quad is itself the munition, an RPG warhead
  released on its path when it is flown into the ground or on the click, and the next one launched where the first
  started. Two fixed-wing drones join the aircraft: the long-endurance drone (MQ-9 class) with its missiles along its
  nose, the loitering munition (Switchblade 300 class) flown into what it strikes. A helicopter's weapons and a drone's
  stores are each a store of its own (the turret's `store`): switched to at once, its count kept. Every round fired from
  a rotorcraft carries its velocity. The rotors turn on the rig, the helicopter's chin gun turns with its turret, and
  the engine heard is the helicopter's or a new multirotor buzz (`drone-motors`). Every rotorcraft is armed; the
  fixed-wing recon drones (hand-launched, twin-boom, quadplane, flying wing) are refused by name. Not yet: a model for
  the door gun and the pod, bombs from the fixed wings, landing on a pad, a crash.
- **Boats driven on the water.** A boat of the craft shelf is a base (`base: { boat: 'combat rhib' }`, `'center
  console'`, `'patrol boat'`, `'navy patrol boat'`, `'landing craft'`, `'destroyer'`, `'aircraft carrier'`,
  `'submarine'` on the surface), driven on a new opt-in `boat` rule (`worlds/controllable/rules-boat.js`) at its class's
  figures (`craft-shelf/boat-drive.js`: its shaft power, its top speed, its turning circle, a 20 hp skiff's to a
  carrier's 260,000 shp): its throttle a lever that stays where it is set; its thrust its power over its speed, capped
  standing at its bollard pull (a ship's big screws pull less a watt than an outboard); its hull's resistance set so its
  power holds it at its top speed, a planing hull's hump below its planing speed (it climbs onto the plane bow up and runs
  flatter on it) and a displacing hull's wall past its hull speed; its helm on its turning circle slow and no tighter
  than its hull's grip fast (about 0.6 g planing, far less for a ship), an outboard's or a jet's thrust turned so it
  turns standing, a rudder needing way; it slides out of a fast turn; it floats at its waterline on the swell, heaving,
  pitching and rolling with the water under its ends and sides, banking into a turn on the plane, heeling out of it
  displacing; the bottom within its draft runs it aground. The range is laid at sea for it: the water up to a shore 150 m
  out, its bottom 8 m down, a beach to the land, the stands inland. The water is drawn live about it
  (`scene/channels/controllable/boat-water.js`): one sheet fine near the hull and widening to the horizon, its swell the
  rule's own, its Kelvin wake at its speed now (its wake's numbers at a ladder of its speeds, `boat-wake.js`), the white
  water near the hull, a trail of foam where its stern has been (so a turn leaves its curve), spray off its chines and its
  rooster tails on the plane. Its gun is its own, turned on its mount's bone (the RHIB's and the riverine boat's bow
  machine gun, the landing craft's ring mount, the navy patrol boat's 30 mm cannon, the destroyer's 127 mm gun with its
  high-explosive shell and its high arc onto the far field, the carrier's close-in gun) or a heavy machine gun fitted at
  the bow of a boat built unarmed (the submarine's on its sail); its rounds carry the boat's way, and a round that comes
  down on the sea short of the shore splashes, its column by its calibre and its charge. A gun stood high on a ship is
  measured laid down onto its near targets. Not yet: a model for a fitted gun, the boat's wake felt by another boat,
  rowing and sail, a submarine under the water.
- **Cars and motorcycles on the land.** A car or a machine ridden astride is a vehicle base too (`base: { vehicle:
  'sports car' }`, `'sedan'`, `'pickup'`, `'motocross bike'`, `'sport bike'`), driven on the drive rule at its class's own
  row (`roads/vehicles.js`: its power, mass, drag, grip and turning radius, a 911's, a Camry's, an F-150's, a 450
  motocross bike's, a litre sport bike's). A car is the car shelf's own build when the row names a card (its body, its
  language, its trim and paint), else its class's realistic loft; its front axle steers, each wheel at its own angle, and
  it is fitted the weapon station a truck is, on its roof. A motorcycle is the cycle shelf's machine ridden: its rider
  astride (the realistic hero, built once a process: `artilleryReady(spec)` awaits it before the range is laid, or
  `rider: false` rides it riderless), its front turned about its steering axis, the machine and its rider leaning into a
  turn by the drive rule's own lean; its rider aims a 12.7 mm light gun fitted for the range, all round but behind, held
  on its aim while the machine turns under it (`gameworld/combat/roadsters.js`; the shelf's ridden figure built at once
  from a rider already solved, `cycle-figure.js` `riderOf` and `rideFigureOf`). Both start in the chase view; a car is
  heard by its engine, a motorcycle by its own. A site machine is refused by name.

### Game UI that reads, moves and sounds like a game, not an app

- **Research behind it: how game UI differs from app UX.** `docs/game-ui-research.md` sets game UI against the SaaS look
  generated UIs default to (a 4 px rhythm, gentle type steps, grey hierarchy, one radius on everything). It covers the
  style schools, how each kind of screen is built, the type, hierarchy, spacing, motion and sound, and what studios
  hold to, then maps it onto the game UI runtime (internal name mana-ui) as a sequence of work. This is the first step
  of that sequence.
- **A screen is a frame, sized by the screen and by how far away the player sits.** Every length in the runtime's sheet
  is now in units of 1px at a 1080p reference, scaled by the stage's height, so a screen keeps its proportions at any
  resolution instead of reflowing like a page. A theme's new `distance` word says where the player sits: `desk` (the
  default), `couch` (everything larger by the ratio of Xbox's console and PC text minimums) or `hand` (a phone, in CSS
  px). Screens and the HUD's places sit inside a title-safe frame, 5% in from each side. The player can set text up to
  twice its size.
- **Fewer type sizes, bigger jumps between them.** Captions and labels sit at the floor, body text a step above it,
  titles at twice the body and the display role near four times. Headings are in the main ink colour instead of small
  grey uppercase labels, and an option's own name is body text.
- **Text over the world keeps a halo.** Text with no window behind it (a title screen's menu, a screen's own title, a
  banner) gets a halo in the panel's colour so it reads over any scene. A theme's new `halo` word picks an outline (the
  default), a glow, a hard shadow, a plate behind it, or none. Subtitles sit on their own plate, and the player sets its
  opacity. A theme's ornaments are no longer drawn on transparent (ghost) windows.
- **What the buttons do is a bar at the foot of every screen.** A screen's legend is pinned to the bottom right of the
  safe frame. A screen that names none gets one drawn from what it holds: select, change, tabs, and back where back
  leaves something.
- **The UI makes sounds, as effects.** The runtime now emits a sound effect when the cursor moves, a pick is made, a
  value turns, a screen opens or closes, a tab turns, or a disabled row is pressed. The host plays them; the runtime
  ships no audio. A theme's new `cues` word says how many: none (the default), the cursor's only, or all. A world's UI
  guide carries its register's sound setting across, and the wireframe board logs each sound.
- **The focus is the console's ▶ by default, and a highlight bar is a new focus.** The default focus (the greybox)
  marks the focused item with a ▶ at its left, a shape rather than a colour, and it pops as it lands under a theme that
  moves. A theme can still choose a ring, or the new `bar`: a solid block at the item's leading edge with the accent
  fading behind the words.
- **Title and attract screens look like a game's.** The title screen puts key art behind, the game's name and a large
  menu in the left third, and the version in a corner. The attract screen puts key art behind and a "press start"
  prompt that breathes slowly; any face or shoulder button starts the game, and the effect says which player pressed.
- **Menus lean, and a cover passes between screens.** A theme's new `slant` word leans tabs, bars, banners, keys and
  buttons (never a window), the diagonal energy most game UI schools share. A new `transition` word draws a cover over
  the screen as one screen gives way to the next: a wipe, a diagonal slam, an iris, a shutter or a stepped wipe, mirrored
  on the way back. The `modern` preset is now clean glass (a cool translucent plate, a light lean, a highlight bar)
  instead of a dark dashboard card. A heavy frame now makes the inner parts heavier too, and a window inside a window is
  drawn lighter.
- **A world's UI and a sport's broadcast carry their energy across.** Passing a game's juice register to the guide
  bridge makes an anime game's menus snap, lean and slam between screens, and a western one's wipe. A broadcast whose
  plates lean now leans its menus and wipes between them.
- **Numbers count up, and a results screen plays in sequence.** With the game's clock, a number that changes counts to
  its new value, with a tick sound. The results screen slams its outcome in, counts each figure up from zero one after
  another, then stamps the rank on; pressing confirm while it counts lands every number at once.
- **Damage numbers, toasts and feeds read like a game's.** Damage numbers sit bare over the world with a halo, pop in
  large and rise, coloured by their kind, a critical hit larger. A rare toast is held longer, gets an accent edge, a
  sheen and its own sound, and a toast can show an icon. A new achievement toast slides in at the bottom right. A feed
  merges a line said again in a row (×3). Fighting games' health bars are thicker.
- **Grey means unavailable.** Labels are now in the main ink colour at a lighter weight; grey is kept for disabled items
  and captions.
- **A held direction on a pad repeats, and flashing is the player's to turn down.** The controls host repeats a held
  direction after a short delay, as a held key does. A new less-flash option (separate from less motion) drops the
  cover between screens, the sheen and a change's flash. Every repeating animation runs under three times a second,
  checked by a test.
- **A window sits on a thing that sits on a thing.** Five new theme words build game UI in depth. `material` lays a
  surface on every plate: parchment with fibre and burnt edges, paper, a blueprint grid, a CRT's phosphor lines,
  halftone, brushed metal, or blurred glass, all drawn in the page with nothing loaded. `backing` puts something under a
  window: a slab offset in the accent, two slabs at an angle, a torn darker sheet, or a riveted plinth. `crest` rides an
  ornament over a window's top edge: a Victorian cresting of scrolls, a hatched tech tab or a ribbon. `breakout` lets
  words out of the box: a window's heading as a tab across its edge, and a title echoed huge and hollow behind itself.
  `overlay` lays a still filter over the whole screen while the UI is up: scanlines, a CRT, a grid, a vignette or grain.
  The presets wear them (storybook on torn parchment under a cresting, arcade on slabs with breaking-out titles, console
  on a riveted plinth, terminal on a grid under a CRT); the greybox stays flat.
- **More room, and one more layer behind.** A screen's own window takes more of the screen, rows are taller, a pause
  menu's rows are set at title size, and body text is a step larger. A new `stage` word draws a shape behind everything
  a screen holds (a huge band, a sunburst, shards, stripes or rings) that sweeps in as the screen opens, and the button
  legend sits on its own band over it.
- **The party look is a design language with variations.** The arcade preset's look is written down as principles
  (everything leans; planes stack on planes; words break out; two colours punch against one neutral; print texture; hard
  edges; motion slams; a shape behind; a click under every sound), and four new presets vary it: `rebel` (red, black
  and white with a huge band behind), `idol` (pink and cyan with a ribbon crest and a sunburst), `street` (yellow and
  black with shards and grain) and `mecha` (orange and teal on riveted metal with hazard stripes). A test holds every
  variation to the principles.
- **The focus snaps in from the way you moved.** Moving down, the item you land on snaps in from above with the theme's
  overshoot (from the left when you move right), and the focused item stands out with a small nudge. The cursor's
  sound says which way it went and a stepper's which way it stepped.
- **The UI has a sound library, made with the beats tool.** Six sound sets (glass, console, chip, terminal, paper and
  party) give the cursor click, confirm, cancel, the stepper up and down, tabs, opening and closing, a refusal, toasts,
  counting and skipping. Every set follows one interval plan (confirm rises a fifth to the octave, cancel falls back
  to the root, the stepper goes up a fifth or down a fourth), so the sets belong together, and they are level-matched
  so changing theme does not change loudness. Each theme names its set. Pages and the wireframe board play them through
  the beats engine when handed the library; a page without it stays silent and carries no audio. Each set is also a
  beats sound-effects recipe the beats tool mints and plays cue by cue. A new script, `scripts/mana-board.mjs`, writes
  the board with real controls and sound.
- **Heavy sounds, and bombastic ones.** Four more sound sets join the library. `hydraulic` is servos, pneumatic hiss
  and clamps landing (the mecha preset's). `clack` is hardwood blocks, with a clapper's double clack on confirm, for
  serious games. `crypt` is stone, iron and a tolling bell: a dungeon door that creaks open over grit and slams shut
  with a boom and a falling latch, for grim and souls-like games. `jackpot` counts in coin clinks, confirms with a brass
  stab, and pays out a rare toast with a riser, a boom, a held fanfare chord, bells and a shower of coins. They follow
  the same plan and the same loudness on confirm; the door and the jackpot are allowed to be louder. Three presets wear
  them: `grim` (aged gold on black, a serif, a vignette, nothing that leans), `tactician` (paper and ink with an offset
  sheet) and `jackpot` (a party variation in gold on purple with a sunburst).
- **What appears, leaves and shuffles is choreographed, and heard.** A screen now builds in order: its title slams in,
  its windows rise, then its rows fill in reading order after a short lead, and the cursor lands last. Everything comes
  from the side the screen sits on. Screens, toasts and banners that leave now play an exit instead of vanishing:
  faster than they arrived, accelerating away and never bouncing. Rows that change order glide from their old place to
  the new one instead of jumping, and a row that moved past others shows whether it rose or fell. Opening a screen plays
  its sound plus a soft rising ripple of ticks timed to each row as it lands; rows that come, go or reshuffle are each
  heard once, however many. Every sound set gains these cues. The principles are written down in the game UI runtime's
  design doc.
- **Pressing something is seen, and a pause blurs what it covers.** Confirming squashes the item, flashes it in the
  accent and throws a ring off it; pressing something unavailable shakes it on a red edge. A confirm that opens or
  closes a screen still shows on the screen as it leaves. Two new transitions join the others: a fade (a dip to black
  and back) and a blur-through, and a new `backdrop` theme word makes a pause dim, blur or frost the game and the HUD
  behind it. The grim theme now fades between screens.
- **A game can ship in several languages.** A game's spec can now carry its words in each language it ships, and
  the player can change language as they play. The game UI's own words (a legend's Select and Back, Loading, Rank,
  Turn order, an empty list's Nothing here) come from one table the game's languages can say too, and the shared
  screens and legends use it throughout, so a game's translations reach every screen. A word a language lacks reads in
  English.
- **A language picker, looks as cards, and the game's UI styled in the studio.** The options screen now has a
  language row when a game ships more than one language, naming each in its own words; turning it changes every word
  on the screen. A new look for a game's menus is now a theme card, a small file of words saying only what it changes
  over a look that already exists (the way a WordPress theme is a file), so a model or a person can add one without
  code; three ship to start (Ink and Gold, Blueprint, Neon Rebel). Styling a game's UI joins the studio: a game's
  `ui` takes its look from the register its genre sets and its colours from the world's palette, and the game's
  review says where the look came from and what its colours read like.
- **The words come first.** Wherever a menu has text to read, every look now holds back: a panel's texture (a grid,
  halftone dots, scanlines, parchment fibre) shows at its edges and fades out before the words; screen filters such as
  scanlines and CRT lines cover the picture behind a menu, never its words; words on a coloured highlight or tab take
  whichever colour reads; buttons and tabs lean no further than italic type; glass panels are thick enough to read
  through; words with no panel of their own over a theme's backdrop shapes (a title menu, a loading screen) get a soft
  band behind them; and a preview picture shrinks rather than push a mode's description off its panel. Titles and
  big display words can still perform.
- **Loading screens that behave.** The progress bar never jumps backwards, and when the game cannot say how far along
  it is, the bar sweeps instead of showing a made-up number. Something always moves so the game never looks frozen,
  and a load that stalls says it is still loading. Tips turn on their own or by hand. A quick load never flashes its
  screen; a slow one stays long enough to be read. A button held through the load does not skip the continue prompt.
  A failed load says why and offers retry or a way back to the title. Back does nothing unless the game allows
  cancelling. The screen covers what is half built behind it.

### Matter in the science views: one ladder from a walkable place down to a cited sentence

- **A science page is a ladder of scales, and each rung says what it is.** A rung is simulated (a model the solver
  runs and the gates examine), depicted (drawn at true proportions from sourced numbers and held to them) or explained
  (a cited sentence, where nothing can be drawn honestly). What is too far out of scale to show gets its own rung, never
  a silent approximation. A classical body made of a matter carries its ladder, from the body down through its grains
  and its crystal cell to its atoms and its nuclei, each rung with its size, its step from the one above and its
  source; where nothing below is sourced, the last rung says so. A demo standing at true size in a world has the place
  above its bodies. `dress.ladder: '<body>'` draws a body's depicted rung beside the demo (steel's iron cell, aluminium's,
  lead's), its atoms where the lattice puts them, and the `ladder-depicted` gate holds the drawing to the lattice
  constant.
- **A classical body can say what it is made of.** `matter: 'steel'` (any row of the destructible-physics matter table,
  or `{ is, …overrides }`) gives a body with a radius its mass from the matter's density, and a collision or a plane
  with no `e` its bounce: each pair takes the lower of its two, as the games' impact law does. A plane can name its own
  `matter`; drag and buoyancy can name a `medium` (`'water'`, `'honey'`, `'air'`) for its viscosity and density. The
  table is read, never changed, so a ball on a bench and a brick in a level have one source for their numbers.
- **The readout says what each contact did.** A model with matter reports, body by body, its mass and where it came
  from, the energy it holds before it fails, and the worst any contact did to it (holds, dents, breaks), by the games'
  own impact law: the lost energy shared inversely to stiffness. The `bodies-intact` gate advises when a body would
  have broken, because the run keeps every body whole. A model that names no matter is unchanged, byte for byte.
- **A science world's page is one picture.** The classical, microscopic, quantum and relativistic pages no longer show
  the view-camera and wireframe buttons or the corner hint; the readout and the honesty panel stay, and `?hud=1` brings
  the buttons back. Every other page is unchanged.
- **Heat in the classical worlds.** A body can start at a `temperature` (kelvin, `'20 °C'` or `'68 °F'`), and the
  `heat` law moves it: each body with a matter is one temperature, losing heat to the air or water round it
  (convection), to its surroundings (radiation, each surface's emissivity from the matter table) and through a contact
  spot to the bodies and the planes with matter it touches; a plane with a `temperature` is a hot plate. A body takes
  its latent heat at its melting point before it rises past it. The checks: every joule lost is a joule that leaves
  (`heat-conserved`), one temperature is fair for each body (`lumped-holds`, its Biot number), cooling by convection
  alone matches Newton's law (`closed-form:cooling`), and an advisory when a body would melt (`bodies-solid`). A hot
  body struck is weaker, by the games' own heat factor. The page's readout shows each body's temperature, and
  `temperature` can be observed. The destructible-physics matter table gains a `TRANSPORT` table beside it
  (conductivity and emissivity), read only by the science worlds: no game page changes. Heat is stepped along the run
  after the motion, so a model with no heat law is unchanged, byte for byte.
- **Spin and rolling in the classical worlds.** A body given `spin` (`[x, y, z]` in rad/s, or `'300 rpm'`, `'8 rev/s'`)
  is a sphere that turns, its moment of inertia a solid ball's or, when its matter fills less than all of it, a shell's.
  On a plane with friction it rolls: a ball rolls down a ramp at 5/7 of the slide, a skid settles into a roll, a
  backspun ball comes back, and a rough bounce trades speed for spin. The new `magnus` law lifts a spinning ball in the
  air (topspin dips, backspin floats, sidespin curves). The checks: `closed-form:rolling` against the textbook ramp, and
  `spin-held` (nothing in flight turns a spin); `spin` can be observed and shown on the page. `rpm`, `rev/s` and `rad/s`
  join the units, and `'Hz'` is refused for a spin as ambiguous. A body without `spin` slides as before: every existing
  model runs the same steps, byte for byte.
- **A liquid that sets.** The classical `gelling` law puts bodies in a liquid from the matter table whose viscosity and
  yield stress move along a `curve` the recipe writes (`[{ at, viscosity?, yield? }]`). A body in it sinks at Stokes's
  speed, stepped exactly so a near-set liquid needs no tiny step, and is held once the yield carries it (Beris et al.'s
  sphere criterion, τy ≥ 0.048·Δρ·g·D): a falling-ball viscometer slows and stops as the liquid sets. A `layer` of it
  on a `slope` flows as a Bingham film and holds once its yield passes ρ·g·h·sinθ (the tube-tilt test). The checks:
  `yield-holds`, `closed-form:bingham-film`, and `closed-form:viscometer` for a liquid that does not set; the page shows
  η and τy along the run.
- **Aggregation in the microscopic worlds.** The `aggregation` law counts a species binding to itself: nucleated growth
  (Oosawa: a nucleus, then one monomer at a time), whose S-curve's lag shortens as the monomer gets richer, or
  coalescence (any two clusters merge, Smoluchowski's constant kernel, held to its closed form). The readout gives the
  share aggregated over time, the lag and half time, and the sizes at the end; the page shows the free monomer and the
  share aggregated, and says the spheres stay single because the aggregation is counted, not placed.
- **A classical demo under a tenth of a metre is drawn magnified** by a power of ten, with the magnification on the
  panel: at its true size it sat inside the camera's near plane and could not be seen. Larger demos draw as before.
- **One scale feeds the next.** A setting liquid's state can be read from a lower rung instead of written: the classical
  `gelling` law's `from` runs a microscopic model and reads the share its aggregation assembles, and `relations` turns
  the share into the liquid's yield and viscosity through cited rows, never a formula of the recipe's own: `percolation`
  (the yield grows from the gel point with the percolation exponent, de Gennes 1976) and `krieger-dougherty` (the
  viscosity of a liquid filling with assembled matter, Krieger & Dougherty 1959). A glass bead in water is held once a
  protein assembling in it has made a gel that carries it. The checks: `handoff-held` (the lower rung held its own),
  and `stokes-regime`, which now advises whenever a body in the liquid moves too fast for Stokes's drag. The panel says
  what was read and through which rows; the page shows the share assembled beside η and τy.
- **The experiment is the page's name.** A science page that names only its scale (a mint's default) is titled by its
  experiment instead, from its subjects and what acts on them ("Bead of glass: gravity, buoyancy and a setting
  liquid"), and the panel cites the matter table plainly rather than by an internal name.
- **A ladder of scales on one page.** `create_view` with kind `ladder` lays rungs top down, each at its own scale and
  saying what it is: simulated (any science world's model, run and checked), depicted (a metal's crystal cell, drawn
  from its lattice constant and held to it) or explained (a sentence that cites a work and its year). Each rung stands in
  its own case, magnified and saying by how much; a breadcrumb across the top steps the camera from one rung to the next
  and shows each rung's size, its step from the rung above and its source. `below: { rung, body }` expands a body into
  its matter's ladder, down to its nuclei, and a lower rung can feed the one above (a gelling law's `from: { rung }`).
  The checks: every simulated rung's own, `ladder-depicted`, `ladder-cited` and `ladder-ordered`. The derived matter
  ladder's sources now carry their years, and one that has none is marked unsourced.
- **The old one-off science views fold into the worlds that compose them.** The orbit, double-slit, wavepacket and
  black-hole kinds leave the listing and search: their experiments are an orbit in the classical world, the slits and a
  wave packet in the quantum world, a black hole's light in the relativistic world, each run, checked and measured, and
  each card says where it went. They keep rendering every stored recipe and still answer a call by name (the recipe
  book's black-hole and double-slit recipes, and a spinning hole, which no law table holds). The mechanics card's
  motions (a projectile, a pendulum, a spring, a collision, a ball curling in flight), the fluid card's floating and
  sinking, and the atom card's hydrogen orbitals point at the worlds the same way; those kinds keep their machines,
  flows and many-electron atoms. The numerical-experiment notebook sweeps a classical world now.
- **Things the studio makes can stand in an experiment.** A classical body can be `as: { vehicle: 'sedan' }` (any word
  people say for a vehicle: its mass with its driver and its true size from the road tables, drawn as its true-size
  loft, or its box where it has none) or `as: { part: 'crate', size }` (a building or prop part by its
  destructible-physics class: its matter and solid share from the class table, its mass from both). Its contacts are a
  sphere as wide as its box's diagonal, it is drawn resting on its base without turning, and the panel says so; its
  matter feeds the impact verdicts, and heat reads its box's own surface and volume. A sedan can roll into a crate on a
  concrete road and the readout says what the crate took.

### The practice room: an action game's swings, strings and weapons measured on the runtime it ships

- **Fable of Artesia, the Zelda-like template.** A new pole (`gameworld/feel/cards.js`) between Ebon Spirits (the Souls
  knight) and Fallen Angel (the stylish action game): an action-adventure's sword and shield.
- **The measures, headless** (`scripts/spikes/practice-room/measure.mjs`): a game's melee played on the runtime it
  ships (scripted presses at 60 Hz on `stepWorld`, as `feel/reach.js` measures a jump) against a foe that never dies,
  each beside what its feel card asks for, carried, partly or lost: press to contact, the swing to rest, when the next
  press is taken, the string mashed and with its sides alternated, the hitstop, the foe's stun and the advantage, the
  lunge, the reach, the dodge's frames and invincible frames, the guard. A template's rule (`--feel`, with a held
  weapon's class) or a built game's own pilot (`--page`). Machine gate only.
- **What it found** (the sword, normal class): every template swings the held weapon's 0.5 s whatever its card says (a
  card of 23 to 27 frames plays as 33 to 36), so Fallen Angel, Fable of Artesia and Ebon Spirits swing alike; the next
  press is taken only once the swing has ended (frame 34 to 37, where the cards cancel at 11 to 19); a string is the
  opener and one follow-up in another direction, then 2.5 s locked (alternated: hits 36 frames apart, then 186); mashed
  on one direction, an opener every swing and never a string. The hitstop is carried; the lunge, the card's hitstun
  (the world's combo rule is never set) and the guard and parry are lost; the dodge is invincible all through where the
  card opens a window. The foe reels 80 frames a hit, so every hit leaves the hero a second of advantage.
- **The room** (`scripts/spikes/practice-room/room.mjs`): a game's hero and one of its foes (or a pack) in a greybox
  ring, on the runtime the game ships: a `controllable` manifest from the game's first level (its pilot, its figures,
  its orbit camera and lock-on), resolved and emitted as `export_game` emits a level. The foe never dies and stands
  still until P switches its AI on; R sets it back. A HUD reads the live world: the last move's frame data beside the
  card's, and every press, taken or dropped with its reason. Checked headless: real clicks strike, the foe takes them
  and stands, each dropped click says why. Nobody has played it.
- **The combo manifest** (`gameworld/combos.js`): an action game's attacks and the strings that chain them. A move is an
  attack primitive: the swing it plays (the hero's cut, the thrust, the cleave, the rising cuts), its role (opener,
  filler, finisher, launcher), its length and its cancel in frames, how it covers ground (none: in place; step: a step
  into it before the blow; lunge: the swing carries the body through it, stopping at the body it strikes), its damage,
  impact, topple and launch. A combo is its beats, L (light), H (heavy), S (special) and `.` (a pause), one move a
  press; combos sharing their openings are one tree. The timing forgives: a press with a move to chain into is held to
  the live move's cancel however early, any other press is remembered a buffer's frames, a press just after a move ends
  still chains (`late`), a pause beat is a press in its window. Held and mashed beats are named and refused for now.
  The starter: L L L (two cuts and the cleave, which lunges and topples) and H (the thrust, a lunge). `readCombos` says what is
  wrong in words; `lowerCombos` is the platform rule's `moveset`; `comboList` the director's list.
- **The moveset in the runtime** (`worlds/controllable/combat-melee.js`, opt-in `moveset` on a platform rule with a
  melee strike): each press a beat, each move a swing of its own (its clip, length, travel and blow), chained at the
  cancel, every press saying what became of it (taken, and how; dropped, and why). Absent, the strike as it was.
- **L, H and S.** The pilot scheme's `melee` context: light on the left click and the pad's left face, heavy on the
  right click and the top face, special on the mouse's forward button and the right face; the bottom face jumps. Read
  only on a page where a body carries a moveset.
- **The room plays combos.** All combos unlocked; the HUD lists them, lights the beats of the string being played,
  shows the last move's frames, travel and hits, and logs the runtime's verdict on every press. The room writes the
  manifest it played beside the page (`combos.json`), the list a game's director takes; `--combos <file>` plays your own.
  Checked headless with real clicks: L L L plays the cut, the rising cut and the cleave, each chained at its cancel,
  three hits.
- **Fixed: the dodge rolled the wrong way under the camera's movement.** A hero that runs where the stick points (the
  orbit camera's `move: 'camera'`) faces its run, so S held turned it toward the camera and the dodge read S as a
  backflip, away from the camera. Under world or camera movement the roll goes along the stick, the body turned to face
  it (`beginDodge`'s `moveH`).
- **A swing carried by the whole body** (`polygonizer/hero-swing-body.js` `swingBody`, opt-in: a hero whose rule plays a
  moveset, baked through `world-scene.js` `swings.body`): the arm's arc on the strike solver's principles, on the
  structured core's left-forward stance, so the sword hand is the rear hand and a forehand cut drives through as a cross
  does. The hips lead the chest (turned back at the coil, coming forward at the cock while the chest is still wound),
  the weight moves back then onto the lead foot (`shift`), the rear foot pivots (its heel up, its toe in), the off hand
  counters a one-handed swing (out at the cock, home at the hip through the blow; a two-handed swing keeps its own), and
  each key sinks the body as little as lets both planted legs reach their feet on the rig. A backhand turns the other
  way. Absent, every swing as it was. Seen on the body study (the cut at its cock, strike and follow, with and without);
  nobody has played it.
- **The arsenal** (`gameworld/combos.js`): the weapons a hero steps through, each its own moves and strings, and the
  figure it shows (drawn: the blade in hand; sheathed: on the back). A move may play a body's strike (`strike`: the
  punch solver's jab and cross, the boxing solver's hook and uppercut) with its own contact window. The starter: the
  sword (L L L, H) and the fist (L L L the jab, the cross and the hook; H the uppercut). Not yet wired to the runtime.
- **The room's hero** (`--hero anime | tiered | <spec>`): another body on the game's rig and clips, its sword in hand and
  on its back; the room bakes its figures at the pose grade (one hero up close), `--grade play` for the game's.
- **Footwork: no foot teleports or skates through a string** (`polygonizer/hero-swing-body.js` `moveClip`, the law in
  its test). Each move of a moveset is baked as its own clip (`mv_<id>`): its travel is its footwork, every planted
  foot held where it stands on the floor while the runtime carries the body. A STEP is an advance (the lead foot out,
  then the rear, both down before the blow; at most 0.4 m). A LUNGE is not an advance: the lead foot drives out and
  lands with the blow while the rear foot holds, the rear leg extending behind as the body drops, then the rear foot
  recovers forward after the blow (at most 0.7 m, one stride). The body sinks as little as lets both legs reach. Every
  move ends in the stance it began in; a move blends into the next in four frames (the manifest's `blend`) and its
  travel waits that out, so the outgoing pose never rides the body. A move steps in only where all of its travel fits
  before the body ahead (else its `_still` clip, in place). In combat the hero idles in its fighting stance
  (`mv_ready`), so standing and striking share their feet. The law plays a string as the page does (the runtime's
  travel, its crossfade between clips) and measures each planted foot: through stand, L L L, stand, and through the
  thrust's lunge, no planted foot moves more than a centimetre a frame (the plain swings skated over half a metre).
  Seen headless in the room: the moves play their own clips, the thrust in place when the foe stands too close.

### The combat tester: a game's gym for its weapons, movement, feel and destruction

- **A spike, measured on the runtime a game ships.** `scripts/spikes/combat-tester/measure.mjs` mints a shooter through
  the real handlers, takes the rule, weapon and kit its level gives the player and the foe it stands, and measures them
  on the controllable runtime at 60 Hz: how fast the body reaches its run, stops, reverses a strafe and jumps; how many
  rounds and seconds each carried gun takes to drop the game's foe at 5, 15 and 30 m, standing, strafing, aimed and at
  the head, and the cone it fires in; the marks ten rounds leave on a wall of brick, concrete, pine, sheet metal or
  steel (destruction as it is seen, rupa's scars: nothing breaks); and each switch from one carried gun to another and
  each reload. Each game is measured as it plays (its feel, its kit, its camera), and what its feel's card asks for that
  the runtime does not carry is named beside both numbers. Nothing registers yet.
- **What it found** (its README): the sprint is carried by no game; the hero-less first person cannot play its
  template (no acceleration, jump or walk); no automatic gun blooms or climbs at its own rate of fire; every gun leaves
  the same mark on a wall; F boosts the shooter pole's hero-less player at 3.5 times its run. Switching and reloading
  are carried in the arm's own times.
- **The gym page.** `scripts/spikes/combat-tester/gym.mjs` draws a game's gym in graybox, played as the game plays (its
  player, kit, figure and camera, and the other camera beside it): a range with the game's own foe at 5, 15 and 30 m
  that stands back up after it drops, five walls of brick, concrete, pine, sheet metal and steel each marked as its own
  matter, and a lane whose stop box, step, ledge and gap are laid from the game's measured reach, green where it is
  meant to be made and red where it is not. Its gate drives the game's rule at each station, and `--check` drives each
  page's own runtime in headless Chromium. It found that a jump reaches further on boxes than on a floor: the step lifts
  every jump onto a ledge, and a jump pressed at a lip finishes its gather in the air, past the edge.
- **Walls of their own matter.** A level's `scars` takes `walls: [{ min, max, matter }]`, so walls side by side are each
  marked as their own matter (steel dents beside a brick chip); any other wall is the world's. Absent, nothing changes.
- **The arena, grown from the gym.** `scripts/spikes/combat-tester/grow.mjs` tunnels a match arena from a few words
  with its size from the game's run (eight seconds of it across), and holds it to laws in the game's own numbers: cover
  over its eye within a second's run, sightlines its guns drop the foe across, stairs its rule climbs, and no perch its
  jump reaches that sees a spawn. A crate that fails the last is stacked over the jump and every law runs again. The
  arena is drawn and played as the gym is. It found that a high jump turns cover into high ground the arena's own laws
  never looked from.
- **A person's sprint.** The platform rule takes `sprintSpeed`: Shift held with the stick forward runs at the sprint,
  never while firing or with the sights up. A feel with `takes` carries its card's sprint and walk, and the legend says
  "Shift sprint".
- **A spray that builds.** A weapon's spread and recoil take `wait`: they settle only once the trigger has rested that
  long. The arms kit's automatic rifles and SMGs wait 0.15 s, so a held spray blooms and climbs.
- **A round's mark is its gun's.** A weapon's `blow` (the joules a round carries) and `pellets` ride its shot to what it
  stops on, so a sniper chips brick wider than a pistol and a shotgun leaves a pattern of pellet chips; with physical
  destruction, a round breaks by its gun's energy. The arms kit gives each gun its round's energy.
- **No thrust for a person.** A shooter-pole player without a hero walks as a person (Z walks; F no longer boosts at a
  mech's multiple of its run; its dodge stays).
- **A first person that plays its feel.** A first-person game without a hero, with a feel, stands on the platform rule
  at its eye, so it accelerates, stops, jumps and sprints as its card says.
- **The combat book.** A made game that fights with guns has a combat book (`/api/sketches/<ref>/bible?book=combat`,
  `&view=other` for its other camera): its first level's player and foe measured on the runtime the game ships (how it
  runs, stops, sprints and jumps; how many rounds each gun takes to drop the foe at 5, 15 and 30 m, still, strafing and
  aimed; its cone and climb; the marks each gun leaves on brick, concrete, pine, sheet metal and steel; each switch and
  reload) and set in a graybox gym laid from those numbers, with what the game's feel asked for beside what it does.
  `design_game`'s readout links it (`combatBook`), and its equipment chapter reads it. The measures and the gym live in
  `lib/graph/gameworld/combat/`.
- **Fixed: a shooter's hero over the shoulder was not seen.** A hero carrying an arms kit was never drawn: the page built
  a body for each loadout slot's figure, and a kit's guns name none. It is drawn as its own figure now. And the
  over-the-shoulder camera stood its eye 3 m nearer than its numbers (the stand-off a chase camera keeps), on the hero's
  head with the hero under the frame and the crosshair off the rounds' line; it stands where its numbers say now (a
  camera's `standOff`, 0 for the shoulder), the hero in the frame from behind, off its right shoulder.
- **A shooter over the shoulder plays with the mouse.** Its camera turned on A and D and only a pad's trigger fired,
  though its legend said "click fire". A third-person hero that shoots now looks as first person does: a click captures
  the mouse, the mouse turns and pitches the hero, A and D step aside, the left button fires and the right one aims, and
  the legend says "A / D  step aside · mouse  look". The combat book's shoulder page plays the same way.
- **A shooter's gun in its hero's hands.** Over the shoulder the gun was drawn nowhere. The hero now carries it: the
  chest side-on to the line, a long gun's butt in the right shoulder and a pistol out at arm's length, pointed where it
  looks and dipped at a low ready until it aims or fires, lowered through a switch and rolled through a reload, each
  hand closed on the gun where its model says a hand goes. A kit's guns carry those places (`view.hands`).
- **Small arms look like small arms.** A gun's `round` (`gameworld/rounds.js`: its round's speed and its muzzle flash's
  length, by cartridge class) draws its shot as a sim draws one: a flash about a hand's length gone in a frame or two,
  a wisp of smoke, the round a faint thin streak at its own speed, a pinch of dust where it strikes. The arms kit's guns,
  the quick shooter's guns and the realistic half of the shooter pole carry it; without one, the glowing bolt and burst
  a mech's beam rifle wants, as before. A carried gun flashes at its own muzzle.
- **Fixed: rounds over the shoulder flew backwards.** The crosshair's point was searched from the camera, so a wall at
  the shooter's back (the page pulls its camera in front of one) caught it, and every round went into that wall, toward
  the camera. It is searched from the shooter's depth along the ray now.
- **Hands in first person.** The eye's view drew the gun alone. Gloved hands and sleeves now hold it, closed where the
  gun's model says a hand goes; through a reload the support hand takes the magazine out and seats a fresh one; a pickup
  or a use is a reach and a grab. A kit's body carries a quick knife in its free hand (`rule.knife`, the arms kernel's
  combat knife): V from the eye draws it and cuts, a slash then a thrust by turns, the gun carried aside, and the cut is
  a melee strike the runtime adjudicates (two drop a body; its legend says "V  knife").
- **The firing range, for a game being designed.** `gameworld/combat/range.js` takes the weapons a game needs, each a
  kit word, a fire type and its numbers (`hitscan`, `projectile`, `melee`; what is not given, a typical gun's) or a
  runtime weapon row, and optionally a skin for each (a kit word or an arm's build words: the look, never the numbers;
  absent, a graybox of its fire type). A person carries them into the gym from the eye, and the range measures each on
  the runtime the game will ship: rounds and seconds to drop a body at 5, 15 and 30 m, a rocket's flight, a blade's cuts
  and its reach, cones, climb, marks, reloads and every switch, with the laws beside (an automatic given no climb
  fails "a held spray climbs"). Travelling rounds and melee are measured now, in the combat book too.
  `scripts/spikes/combat-tester/range.mjs --spec '<json>'` prints it and writes the page.
- **The firing range is heard.** Each weapon sounds from the SFX shelf by what it is: a gun's shot by its cartridge, a
  launcher's launch, its reload as one cue over its own reload time (the magazine out, a fresh one in, the action
  racked), a round landing on a body, the draw on a switch, the knife's swing and its connect, a rocket's blast where it
  bursts, footsteps on the range's concrete, all on a mix in the open. A game names its own sound for any of them
  (`sounds: { <weapon>: { shot, reload, hit, draw } }`, a shelf word each); `quiet` is silent.
- **Gunshots on the SFX shelf.** A `gunshot` family voices a small arm by its cartridge (a pistol, a submachine gun, a
  magnum, a rifle, a shotgun, a sniper rifle) and suppressed: the report, the blast and its overtones, a sub under the
  heavier rounds, a rifle round's supersonic crack, the action cycling, the casing, the shot rolling off; each in the
  realistic register, the heavier the longer. Seven rows (`pistol shot` to `suppressed shot`).
- **Two sounds a world's audio takes.** `audio.weapon.switch` (a gun drawn; a weapon's own `sfx.draw` wins) and
  `audio.burst` (a travelling round's burst, where it went off). Absent, a page is as it was.

### Level design, its own department: the play layer a block at a time

- **The play layer.** A planned map's level takes `play: { <segment>: { pieces, suggestions? } }`: what level design
  places on a block to make its walk interesting, saved in pure vector space (a point in world metres and a yaw), so a
  terrain rebuilt under it never loses a piece. A piece is a foe (of the bestiary), an obstacle (a crate, a barricade, a
  log, a wall, a pillar, a ledge, an arch), cover, a pickup, a gate, a hazard or a marker, each with the beat it serves.
  The map builds the obstacles in the world's own style (its kit's palette), each a collider; the foes stand where they
  are placed (in place of the encounter marks' rings); the pickups are found where they lie.
- **Pieces that drifted.** A law, `pieces-fit`, says when a piece no longer stands on the land (the land rebuilt
  under it), stands outside its block or inside something solid, and names the nearest spot that fits: the piece is
  dragged there, never lost.
- **Authority.** A block takes the other departments' `suggestions`, each `must` (not overridden), `should` (overridden
  only with a reason, the block's `overrides`) or `may` (a hint); a suggestion `about` a kind of piece is kept when a piece
  of the block has every field it names. Laws: `suggestions-kept` and `casting` (level design recasting the scenario's
  foes is said, and refused only against a must).
- **The department.** Level design is the studio's own department (`level-design`), its chapter the play layer
  (`/levels/*/glyphs/play`: a chapter path's `*` stands for any level), a block its unit (`play:<level>/<segment>`).
  The build reads it.
- **The brief.** `level/play-brief.js` hands a block's level designer everything: its square in world metres, its path
  on the land, what already stands solid on it, the scenario's beats there, the hero's kit (pace, sprint, jump, moves,
  abilities and when they come), the roster it may cast from, the suggestions with their authority, and what it writes
  back.
- **The Old Keep through it.** Four level designers (one a block) worked from their briefs and their tickets (each block's
  suggestions: the town's lone bandit a must, the barn's cache a must, the ambush from the north rocks a should, the
  woods' shrine key a must, the warden a must and the guarded climb a should): 47 pieces, every must kept. The fields'
  ambush is three bandits behind a barricade, a ruined wall and a second barricade round an open bend; the woods gained an
  optional bandit camp on a pilgrims' trail to the shrine; the keep's climb is guarded by two bandits under a rockfall,
  its court framed by columns. Three of the keep's pieces stood under the land (their z guessed): the law named the
  spots, and they were dragged there.
- **Held as the scenario says.** A scenario holds only the page whose beat opens it (its ways out) and the page whose
  climax it is (its win, not its ways): an optional fight elsewhere holds nothing. A pickup level design places stands in
  for the scenario's find of the same item. A gate is drawn but not yet solid (a gate that opens in play comes next).

### The SFX shelf: a library of game sound effects

- **A library of game sounds** (`lib/graph/sfx-shelf/`, `docs/sfx-shelf.md`): one row per sound under the words
  people say (`clang`, `grenade`, `swish`, `skid`, `heal`, `match three`, `chess move`, `shovel`, `jump scare`,
  `trebuchet`, `suplex` …). Each row has a category, the slot a level plays it in, the palette sound it stands in
  for, and what voices it. Game effects only; a menu's sounds are the interface's.
  `sfxSound(word, { style, dials })` gives its cue, or a held voice's spec.
- **Recipes, not samples.** Nothing is stored as audio:
  - a **cue** is a stack of gesture layers;
  - a **held voice** is a set of layers whose every setting runs with one control in 0..1;
  - a **family** builds either from dials, so a designed variation is a dial point.

  Builds are pure (seeds hashed from the family and its dials) and pinned.
- **The styles are kept.** The four palettes (arcade, foley, orchestral, synth) are styles of the shelf, frozen behind
  it: every palette cue id is exactly one row, so no recipe changes by a byte. `realistic` is the shelf's own style,
  several voices sounding as one, and falls back to foley where it has no voice yet.
- **Thirty-eight families, 477 dial points, 217 rows.**
  - **Combat and its world:** explosions by size, impacts by material and weight, footsteps by surface and body,
    melee, weapon handling, projectiles, breakage, the elements, shields, a launch.
  - **Held voices:** boosters, engines (car, motorbike, jet, prop, kart, boat, helicopter), beams, a servo, fire, a
    charge, a crowd, tyres, cooking, a heartbeat, breath.
  - **For each game type mojulo makes:** sports (ball, sport, crowd), racing (tires, crash, motoring), adventures
    (magic, bow, interact), platformers, puzzles and tables (platform, puzzle, tabletop, dice), life sims (work,
    cooking), horror (heartbeat, breath, horror), strategy, flight and brawlers (build, siege, flight, brawl).
  - **Sets of fixed cues** where a sound is better written than built: `mecha` (mech combat) and `mecha-layered`, its
    realistic voice.
- **The SFX mixer** (the kernel feature `sfxmix`, opt-in). Any gesture can be a layer with its own `chain` (filter,
  drive, compress, crush, delay), `pan` and `send`. A world's `audio.sfx.mix: { space?, send?, voices?, distance? }`
  puts its cues on an SFX bus in one shared space (`open`, `interior`, `hangar`, `cavern`, or `vacuum`: the bus dulled,
  no tail). A `duck` gesture dips the score under a big hit, on both scores of an adaptive pair. `voices` caps the cues
  sounding at once: a quieter new cue is dropped, a louder one steals the quietest. `distance` (on unless false) places
  a combat cue by its source's distance from the pilot: duller and roomier, not only quieter. A beats-sfx row takes
  `mix` too, and its WAV takes `?far=`.
- **Held voices** (the kernel feature `sustain`, opt-in): `engine.sustain(spec)` returns `set(x)` and `stop()`, gliding
  on ramps it plans itself. The spec is noise and oscillator layers with ranges for pitch, cutoff and gain, and an LFO
  on the gain, the cutoff or the pitch (a sawtooth on the gain is a train of chuffs). A beats-sfx row's `sustains`
  holds them, and its WAV renders them along a control lane. A world's `audio.thruster.voice` and
  `audio.jump.charge.voice` play one in place of the channel's own synth. The shelf's `booster` `jet` and `servo` are
  ports of that synth.
- **One yardstick** (`measure.js`): a sound rendered as an export renders it, measured by its layers, length, attack
  brightness, crest, energy by band, `spread`, `heard` (bands as the ear weighs them, A-weighted) and `width`. The laws:
  - every realistic one-shot is in the register (`register.js`: at least 4 layers, 1.31 bands heard, 8 dB of crest
    unless it swells);
  - every held voice follows its control (`meetsHeld`);
  - ordered dials move their measures (bigger blasts and heavier blows longer and darker);
  - a set that names a `floor` meets it cue for cue (`meetsFloor`).

  A deep sweep renders every dial point; `npm run sfx-baseline` writes the sets' numbers and, with `--wav <dir>`,
  their WAVs. These are machine gates; the ears are the operator's.
- **Fixed: ramps re-set mid-glide.** A held voice or a duck re-set while a ramp was running lost that ramp, and
  offline the part already played went too. The partial ramp is laid again up to that moment.
- A recipe that uses none of the mixer or the held voices emits the same kernel and the same page, byte for byte.
- **A katana** (`families/blades.js`). Its swing is a stylized slash, light or heavy: an approach whoosh crossing the
  stereo field, a bright noise cut falling from the top of the band, the edge ringing (struck metal and a noise-excited
  plate), a spray of grit, a push of air underneath, and no held tone, which reads as a whistle. With a draw, a
  sheathe and a jostle at the hip (`katana-swing`, `katana-heavy-swing`, `katana-draw`, `katana-sheathe`,
  `katana-jostle`). A heavier cut is longer and darker.
- Nothing in a level reads the shelf by its words yet: the wiring comes next.

### A walked map's hero climbs only what it means to: never a tree, never the map's edge, never by walking

- **Fixed: the hero rode up trees and walls as it walked.** A hero with the wall move (`actions.moves: ['wall']`, the
  city stalker's, worlds/controllable/wall.js) takes hold of any collider face at least 1 m wide and taller than it,
  pressed into from the ground. On a glyph map that was a broad tree's trunk (its collider past the wall's `minFace`,
  mantled onto its 3.5 m top into the crown), a house's wall and the map's own invisible walls. Driven headless on The
  Old Keep's town page, walking only: a 1 m trunk climbed from three sides of four, up to 6.6 m; houses and the zone's
  walls up to 9 m.
- **A map's edge is not a wall to climb.** A glyph map's edge walls, a zone's walls and its apron's are `hold: false`
  (level/grid-scene.js), as a city level's edge is.
- **Nor is a tree.** A solid tile's trunks are `hold: false` (era/isekai.js), slim or broad; a boulder is still held, a
  rock climbed.
- **An action hero climbs from a jump.** The orbit camera's hero with a blow (gameworld/levels.js `actionWall`) takes
  hold of a wall only from a jump (the wall's `ground: false`): walking into a house stops at it, a jump at it climbs.
  `ground: false` now means what it says, a leap since the body last stood (its own, or off a wall): a step off a lip
  beside a face, a frame in the air, no longer takes hold of it. The city stalker's wall, taken from the ground, is as it
  was. Measured on the same page and the same 70 walked approaches: 16 took hold of a wall before, none after.

### The brawler's practice room

- A practice room for brawler-style games (`brawl/brawl-practice.js`), the street's own blocks under a practice mind and
  apart from the fighting game's training: a yard with one to four players and up to eight dummies, each a thug of the
  street's types (or any fighter) in a mode: stand, walk back and forth across the street (lining up on a moving body),
  swing on a slow beat (reading a blow), crowd (the street's own crowd mind, its tokens and its ring) or grab (walks in
  to take hold, knees and throws). A player never dies; a felled dummy is back on its spot three seconds later (its
  health a few of the player's chains), or never falls under refill; a reset puts everyone and every thing back.
- Every press has its verdict: taken (how late) or dropped, and why (the blow before missed, too late, reeling, the
  hitstop, landing); the room reads the line to each dummy (how far across, lined up or not, in reach or not), the chain
  (its blows landed, the finisher or dropped and why), the clinch (knees left, the hold's time, from behind), the last
  combo, the attack tokens, a power-up and a weapon held; and a brawler's move list by kind (the chain by its style, the
  air, the clinch, the desperation and its price, the special, the street's things).
- The yard (`brawlPreset('yard')`): one long open screen ruled a metre along and every half metre across the street,
  its band's edges and middle bold, a back wall and a rack.
- Found by the press log: a press made during a blow's hitstop ran out before the freeze ended, so a chain only carried
  by mashing; the brawler's press is now kept through the freeze, as the fight's is. And a chain's next press made
  while the blow before missed starts a fresh chain once the body is free, never the chain's second blow from a stand.
- The brawler's readouts in mana-ui (`mana-ui/idioms-brawl.js`, a shelf of its own beside the fight's): marks at each
  body's feet saying how far across the street it stands and whether a blow can land, marks over the heads of the crowd
  that may close in next, the chain's blows lit as they land and how the last chain ended, the clinch's time and knees,
  and the press log; the yard's screen over them (`brawl/brawl-yard.js`: the HUD, the move list, the practice settings)
  in a brawler's look (the `brawl-yard` theme card); the board draws them as the brawler practice HUD.
- The brawler's page, its first the practice yard: a world's `brawl` block with its `practice` (`brawlLevel(level, {
  practice })`) is played by the page's brawl channel (`scene/channels/brawl.js`, `brawl/brawl-page.js`,
  `brawl/brawl-yard.client.js`): the room stepped at 60 a second from four seats (the controls layer's new `brawl`
  scheme: the stick, attack, jump and special; a second controller drops in), each body drawn in the round as the fight
  draws its fighters (its move's or its reaction's pose, `brawl/brawl-pose.js`, jointed by the fight's rig), each
  player's line on the floor, the street's things, a flash where a blow lands and the fight's sounds by event, under the
  belt's locked camera; the yard's screen in mana-ui (start the practice settings: the fighter, the dummies' mode, type,
  number and health, the marks and the log; back the move list; R a reset). Absent, a page carries none of it.
- The spike `scripts/spikes/brawler/practice.mjs` plays the yard on a virtual clock as a person would and shoots it.
- Characters in the yard: a practice's `roster` is who can be played and fought, each entry a character by ref
  (`{ hero: { ref }, style? }`: a hero, beastfolk, a xeno or a mascot, measured from the store as a fight's roster is) or
  a fighter's intent; the players and every dummy pick from it (`dummies: [{ mode, fighter: <roster index> }]`), the
  street's crowd types still there beside them; each character drawn in its own body, its parts riding the fight's figure
  as the fight draws a posed character, relit by the yard's key and inked. The settings offer the roster as the fighter
  and as the dummies' type. The spike's `--characters` mints a wolf-kin and a mascot bear and plays one against the other.
- The yard's characters PLAYED and its REGISTER's look: a character is played in its own body by its own clips (its
  blows, a blow taken, its knockdown, its guard; the brawl's own states, walking the street, a hold, being held, a
  pick-up, a throw, posed on its body by the figure, its hands kept as its guard holds them), as the fight's arena plays
  them; a yard with a `register` (`brawlLevel(level, { register: 'anime' | 'western', practice })`) draws every body the
  fight's one way, cel or lit, under one key from the greybox's own sun that casts onto the street and across the body,
  the key following the camera along the belt. The spike's `--register` shoots it.
- The brawler's buttons on the face's diamond with the JUMP ON ITS WEST (the controls' `brawl` scheme): a pad's X jumps, A
  attacks, B the special; the keyboard's diamond under the right hand the same (I J K L: J jumps, K attacks, L the
  special). The stick never jumps: up walks away across the street, down toward the camera.
