- The yard reads the strong: its press in the log (a strong on its cooldown dropped, saying how long is left), a chain
  ended by the breaker or the blowout said so, one opened by the strong too; the move list's Strong tab (each blow, its
  frames and its cooldown); on the move list the stick turns its tabs.
- The yard's move list gains the Dash tab (the run, the running blow, the long jump, the back-step, with the run's
  speed and the back-step's frames) and the Air tab every air blow (the air punch, the flying kick, the stomp, the dive
  kick); the spike plays each.

### The brawler: the belt

- A brawl's ground, the fight's lane opened up (`brawl/brawl-belt.js`): a straight BELT along a level with a depth band
  across it, cut into screens the camera scrolls through, a gate holding the camera at a screen's end until its wave is
  beaten, the last screen the boss's. The camera follows the body furthest on, never goes back and never shows past
  what is held; a body stays inside the view and the band. The camera's angle is locked per stage, a recipe word
  (`classic`, `high`, `low`, `ahead`), and never orbits.
- The levels a brawl is fought down (`brawl/brawl-levels.js`), a new kind a row: the greybox `street` (a road between
  kerbs, building fronts with framed doorways, lamps and things on the far pavement, the near side open to the camera,
  each held screen's line on the road), its belt's words over the preset's; `brawlLevel` gives the greybox world and its
  `brawl` block. A greybox takes a `brawl` block as it takes a fight's `versus`.
- The spike `scripts/spikes/brawler/belt.mjs` shoots the street from each angle.
- The brawl's sim (`brawl/brawl-core.js`): many bodies down a belt, two sides, each body a compiled fighter, so a thug's
  jab and a player's are the fight's frame data (the same frame, the same damage, the same recovery as in the fight,
  checked frame by frame). A blow lands only on bodies lined up across the belt, on every one of the other side its box
  meets; no block; a thrown body knocks down the bodies of its own side it flies into; a body rising from the floor is
  untouchable a moment; bodies push each other only when lined up; each faces its nearest foe. The camera goes on with
  the players and holds at a gate. Deterministic and hashed like the fight; the fight's own core is untouched.
- A brawl laid in the indoor level's rooms: the `stage` brawl level builds the belt on the stage kind building levels are
  made in, on its kits (the plaza's sunlit street, the nave, the stone hall, the catacomb, the lab): a room a screen,
  open to the camera, each into the next through a doorway the band runs through, deep enough before the band for the
  locked angle to see the floor; the open-air plaza one long street; a kit whose furnishing would stand on the fighting
  floor left undressed unless asked. It opens framed by the belt's angle. The spike shoots every kit.
- Timed states, one shelf for both games (`versus-library.js` STATES: power, haste, iron, fury): a body hits harder,
  moves faster or takes blows without flinching for a while. In the fight an INSTALL super grants one as it starts (the
  `super-install` row: no blow, a moment powering up, then ten seconds of power; a recipe's own install takes another
  state); in the brawl a thing on the floor will. A body holding none carries nothing of it.
- The desperation (`whirl` in the specials): an invincible spin at shoulder height that strikes behind as far as in
  front and knocks down, costing its thrower a slice of health the first time it lands, never the last of it. Any
  fighter may take it as a special; the brawler's attack and jump together throw it.
- The brawler's moves (`brawl/brawl-moves.js`): attack, jump, special and the stick. Attack runs a CHAIN, each press on
  a connect the next blow, the last knocking down, the stick toward the foe on the last press a different finisher; a
  whiff starts it over. In the air, a jump straight up and attack is a stomp, a jump with a direction a jump kick.
  Attack and jump together is the desperation. Special throws the fighter's signature special. A fighting style per
  archetype: the rushdown's longer, quicker chain, the grappler's heavy chain and its strongest grabs.
- The clinch, in the brawl's sim: walk into a foe lined up in front to take hold of it, then knee it (the third knocks
  it down), throw it forward into the crowd or behind, or, taken from behind, suplex it. A held body breaks free after a
  while, a holder struck lets go, and the desperation breaks out of a hold. A power-up's state works in the brawl as in
  the fight.
- The crowd's mind (`brawl/brawl-crowd.js`): a crowd that fights like one. Only two close in on a player at once, lining
  up across the street before they swing, and only one swings at a time, so a player always gets a moment to act
  between two attackers' blows; the rest circle in view, half of them working round to the player's back; a thug that
  is hurt backs off and waits before it comes in again. Its types are fighters: the thug, the knife, the charger (a
  rush from range), the jumper (a leaping overhead), the heavy (a big body that grabs, knees and throws).
- Waves: each held screen's crowd waits offstage until a player walks into the screen, then comes in from the right
  edge, the left and the street's back, six at most at once, and the gate opens when the last falls. A scripted player
  beats them all.
- The boss: any of the fight's characters at the stage's end, played by the fight's own opponent (its moveset, its
  reads, its combos), stepping onto the player's line before it swings and keeping the crowd's turn. It comes in first
  with its bar, its crowd behind it; beaten, the rest flee and the stage is clear. A held screen with no wave is open
  from the start, and two attackers can no longer start on the same player on the same frame.
- The street's things (`brawl/brawl-things.js`): food (an apple, a roast chicken, a joint of meat) gives health back,
  power-ups grant the fight's timed states, weapons (a pipe, a knife, a katana: the fight's own, the pipe new to its
  shelf) are picked up and swung by the chain, thrown with special at the first foe lined up ahead, and dropped when
  knocked down; barrels, crates and phone booths give way to a player's blows and leave what they hold. A player stands
  over a thing and presses attack to take it. A level places them along the street.
- The STRONG, a fourth button on the face's north (a pad's Y, the keyboard's I): one heavier blow of the style's
  (`BRAWL_STYLES[…].strong`: its slot, its air slot, its cooldown), slower than the fast attack and on its own cooldown
  (`cool`, frames from its start: the core starts no move with one while its body's `cd` runs), its effect by when it is
  thrown: from a stand the OPENER (it staggers long and the chain follows on from its second blow: St, A, A …), after a
  fast blow that hit the BREAKER (the chain ended early, the body knocked down: A, A, St) or, toward the foe, the BLOWOUT
  (a blow whose `knock` is 'fling': the body flung down the street as a thrown one, bowling over the crowd behind it),
  and in the air the DIVE (it knocks down). The rushdown's comes back soonest, the grappler's last.
- The fight's movement in the brawler: the stick tapped twice along the street runs the way it points (the fighter's
  forward dash's speed, held as long as the stick is: across the street too; attack from it the RUNNING BLOW, carried on
  by the run and knocking down; jump from it the LONG JUMP, `runJump` % further) or, away from the way the body faces,
  BACK-STEPS (the fighter's back dash: its distance, its frames, untouchable as it starts, still facing the foe). In the
  air every height of the fighter's: attack on a jump straight up the AIR PUNCH, on a jump with a direction the FLYING
  KICK; strong straight up the STOMP (straight down), with a direction the DIVE KICK (down at a slant: an air move's
  `dive` sets its flight), both knocking down. A move that passes THROUGH (the fight's roll, its blink) has no push box
  while it travels, so it goes through the crowd it would bump.
- Foes are bodies: a thug is a brawler as a player is, with every move a player has (the chain, the strong and its
  enders, the run, every air blow, the desperation, its specials), only its own TIMING AND DAMAGE and its REPERTOIRE.
  `brawlFighter(recipe, { tune })` lays a body's tune (`BRAWL_TUNE`: damage %, startup and recovery ± frames, the
  strong's cooldown %) on every normal, special, the throw and the desperation through the fight's own per-move tune, so
  its frames are re-laid; a crowd type (`CROWD_TYPES`) carries its tune and its `plays` (`CROWD_PLAYS`: chain, strong,
  break, blowout, run, kick, dive, grab, a special by direction, desperate: held, it breaks out). A body given a token
  picks one of its plays (by its own hash; a strong one only off its cooldown) and closes to where it starts: in reach
  for a blow (stopping as it touches, or its walk would take hold), a jump away for a leap, the ring's edge for a run.
  The token and one-attacker-at-a-time rules hold for every play. The thug sometimes breaks its chain off with a
  knockdown or leaps in; the knife runs in; the charger blows the player away; the jumper flying-kicks and dive-kicks;
  the heavy, slow and hard-hitting, swings its strong and breaks out of a hold.
- The boss is a body as every other: a wave's `boss` takes a `tune` (its own timing and damage, as a crowd type's) and
  `plays` (`BOSS_PLAYS` by default: the strong and its enders, the run, the flying kick and the dive kick, the
  desperation when held; a boss's grab stays the fight's throw). The fight's CPU still fights it; every while
  (`BOSS_REST` frames after its last, and its own share of a second more) it throws a play of its own once it stands
  where the play starts, under the crowd's one-attacker-at-a-time rule. Its chain runs to the blow before its last, so a
  breaker or a blowout has a place.
- The ARMED brawler (`brawlLevel(level, { armed: true })`): a brawl where every hero carries its own weapon the whole
  game (a roster entry's `weapon`, any of the fight's; absent, the armed roster: the all-rounder's katana, the
  rushdown's claws, the zoner's staff, the grappler's axe) and the street lays none. The blade is the fight's: disjointed
  (no hurtbox while it swings), hurtable where its weapon says. In the brawl's core, blades that meet clash (two bodies
  of the two sides lined up, their armed blows' blades crossing on a frame: neither lands that blow, both recoil), and a
  body with its own weapon keeps it (it picks no other up and is never disarmed). The yard draws a held blade along the
  line the sim strikes with, in a played character's own hand.
- The armed crowd and the armed boss: four crowd types each with its own weapon the whole fight (`sword`: two cuts and a
  strong one, or a leaping cut; `spear`: pokes from far off and runs in on its point; `axe`: a big slow body, its strong
  a chop to the floor, a dive from the air; `staff`: three blows, a sweep that blows the player down the street, its wood
  struck as it swings), each its own tune and plays; a wave's boss takes a `weapon` (any of the fight's) for the whole
  fight, its CPU's blows and its own plays swinging it. As in the fight, only the weapon hand's blows are the blade's (a
  kick stays a kick). An armed brawl's yard sets swordsmen as its dummies unless it says.
- The WEAPON ARTS (`BRAWL_ARTS`, one for each weapon on the fight's shelf): a weapon's own chain, every blow one of its
  hand's so every one swings the blade, laid into the fighter's slots from the fight's families (the lead hand's blades
  thrust, cut across, cut rising and cleave from overhead; the spear pokes, thrusts, thrusts low and lunges; the staff
  butt-strikes, swings wide and strikes from overhead), each with its finisher, its strong, its air strong and its blows'
  own names (the katana: thrust, cut, rising cut, cleave; forward on the last, a rising slash). A fighter with a weapon
  fights in its weapon's art (`brawlFighter(recipe, { art })` names another, `art: false` keeps the style's chain); the
  style keeps its grabs. The crowd's armed types, the armed boss and a weapon picked up off the street fight in theirs.

### What to build next now counts cutscenes, game flow and acting

- **The planning map knows about the new story features.** The internal map the studio uses to decide what to build
  next now includes a game's whole order of play (its title, cutscenes, levels and ending), cutscenes shot by a
  director's rules, slow motion and freeze-frames inside scenes, and characters who act their lines. Games that need
  these now count as makeable, and the one missing piece next to them, holding the game world still while a cutscene
  plays, is priced and ranked so it can be weighed against other work.
- **The planning map knows about combos, beat-em-ups and horses.** It now tells a hero's single swing apart from strings
  of moves chained into combos (the weapon kits and their practice room), and counts horses a hero rides. Beat-em-ups
  down a street are listed as built but not yet reachable when designing a game, priced as one piece of work so they can
  be ranked against the rest.
- **Two new kinds of game to check against.** A stylish action game (combos, launchers, a gun) reads as makeable today;
  an open-world adventure on horseback waits on one seamless open land, which the map now describes more accurately: the
  world map's regions load as you walk into them, but by swapping the page at a gate, never streaming. The co-op street
  brawler now asks for the real beat-em-up street, so it shows the gap it actually has.
- **The scrolling shared screen is counted as built, where it is.** The beat-em-up's street already scrolls one view on
  as the players go, never back, holding at each wave; the map now says so, and that the co-op scrolling shooter waits
  only on that camera reaching its kind of level.
- **The planning map knows about realistic gunplay, big guns and crewed machines.** It now tells simple gunplay apart from
  small arms played as small arms (spread and recoil that build and settle, rounds by cartridge marking what they hit,
  the gun in the hero's hands), which shooter games already get. The artillery range's big guns and the tanks, trucks,
  walkers, boats, helicopters and fighters it drives and flies are listed as built but not yet reachable when designing
  a game, priced together as one piece of work. A thrown body, which the beat-em-up's clinch already does, is counted
  the same way.
- **Two more kinds of game to check against:** a military sim (rifle, armour, its gun crewed) and tactical espionage
  (guards, a grab and a throw, a silenced pistol), each showing the gap it has today.

### A game's flow, from boot to credits, as one thing a game can say

- **A game can say its whole flow.** What plays when, from the first screen to the credits, is now something a game
  can describe in one place: its screens, its cinematics, its levels and short holds, and where each one leads. The
  checker explains every mistake: a step nothing reaches, a step with no way out, a level the game does not have, or
  cinematics that would loop forever with nothing for the player to press. A game that says nothing gets the flow it
  has always had, worked out from its title screen, its levels, its runs and its ending.
- **Games now run on their flow.** Every game that uses the light shell (every game the studio designs) now moves
  between its screens and levels by following its flow, so a game that describes its own order plays in that order:
  a beat between screens, a level that goes straight on to the next, a title that moves on by itself when left alone.
  A game that describes nothing plays exactly as before. Two small fixes come with it: the loading veil now lifts once
  the level has drawn its first picture rather than while it is still building, and after a level ends the game
  moves on as soon as its end card has been read, at once when the level shows no card, or early when the player
  presses a key.
- **Cinematics between screens.** A game's flow can now play a cutscene on any of its levels as a step of its own:
  an opening before the title, or a prologue after New Game that hands straight over to play on the same level with
  no reload. A cutscene can be made unskippable. If the level has no such scene, the game simply moves on.
- **Scenes no longer get lost.** When two cutscenes are triggered at once, or one is triggered while another plays,
  they now play one after another instead of the later one being dropped. A scene that should open a level now waits
  until the game has handed the level its saved progress, so it can no longer start too early.
- **A game's story can have an opening, a prologue and an ending.** A moment in a game's story can now be its
  opening, its prologue or its ending, staged on one of its levels. The opening plays before the title on the first
  launch and again when the title is left alone, like an attract loop. The prologue plays after New Game and, on the
  first level, hands over to play without a reload. The ending plays after the game is first completed, before the end
  card. A game whose story has none of these is unchanged.
- **The flow is a page in the studio.** When a game's designer wants a different order, they can now write the
  game's flow for the whole game, naming its levels as the world names them. The review shows the flow as a
  storyboard: each step, which part of the studio it comes from, what it waits for and where it leads. If the main
  quest's ending is played as a story moment, that moment now becomes the game's ending cutscene, unless the story
  has an ending of its own. The studio's guidance makes the flow the main agent's own page, never handed off.
- **A game's menus can now be drawn in its own look.** A game that sets a look for its interface now has its title,
  press-start, level list, options (with its language picker), credits, end card, results and loading screen drawn
  in that look, and they work with a keyboard or a gamepad. The studio carries the look over from the game's design.
  A game without one keeps its screens as before. The pause menu, menu sounds and cover art on the title are not
  drawn this way yet.

### The metro's details: industrial windows, transformer cans, rooftop antennas, cell towers and blinking aviation lights

- **Industrial windows.** A works' hall is glazed in a ribbon high along its long walls. A warehouse is glazed along its
  back and its ends, and a works' office, a substation's control house and a storage yard's gatehouse each have a row
  of windows a storey on every side. The glazing is drawn proud of the wall with the glass's sheen. Past dusk some of it
  is lit (a pane over the glass, so a night metro is still its day's faces plus its lit panes).
- **Transformer cans.** Every fourth wooden pole along an outskirts or industrial street carries a pole-mounted
  transformer (`kit.js` `can`): its drum and lid below the crossarm, hung off the side away from its lamp, with a
  bracket, two bushings and a drop wire up to the crossarm. Like the street's other tall kit, it is taken out from
  under a highway's deck.
- **Rooftops** (`geocity/rooftop.js`). Each flat roof of a low or mid-rise building (mid-rises, slabs, podiums,
  walk-ups, low-rises, shops, schools, control houses, 7 to 75 m tall) is dressed by its own dice: air handlers on their
  curbs, a cell site's three sectors of panel antennas and their cabinet, a microwave dish at an edge facing out, a mast
  with its yagi booms, and on the lower ones a satellite dish, all turned one way. They are drawn near the camera.
- **Cell towers.** A 30 m monopole with its triangular head and three sectors stands in a corner of some car parks and at
  the back of some works and storage yards. It is seen across its district.
- **Aviation lights** (a new page channel, `scene/channels/beacons.js`, the payload's `beacons`). Red lights blink
  together on the world clock (1.6 s, on a third of it), so a capture at a clock and the live page agree. They sit at
  two opposite corners of the roof of every tower over 120 m, the other two half way up one over 220 m, and on top of
  every cell tower. Each is a round soft dot with a faint glow that keeps its size on the screen however far off it
  is. Without beacons the page adds not one byte.

### The metro's highways: expressways on piers over its arterials and its shore, driven by its traffic

- **Highways join the far neighbourhoods.** A metro now runs its expressways (`geocity/highways.js`, a new metro
  setting `highways`: `count`, `lanes` each way, `height`, `along`; `false` none). They are elevated on piers, so they
  cross the street grid without touching it. By default it runs four, after a lake city's:
  - a **lakeshore expressway** along its shore over the water's edge, on single piers in the water;
  - a **crosstown** over the arterial farthest from the shore, out to the country at both ends;
  - two **cross highways** over its outermost arterials the other way. Each flies over the crosstown where they meet,
    risen clear of its deck, and joins the shore's deck at its level where it reaches it.

  `along` names their lines (an arterial's id, or `'shore'`). Without a shore, the metro's long way takes the crosstown's
  part.
- **The deck.** Three lanes each way between shoulders and a median by default. Its deck follows the ground smoothed
  along it, its height over it, held to 4.5% between its stations both ways. It is drawn as asphalt over concrete fascia
  and underside, with a barrier at each edge and down its median, lane lines and shoulder lines, and lamps down its
  median. Its piers are a pair of columns in its arterial's kerb lanes (clear since the kerbs carry no parked cars)
  under a cap beam, never in a crossing; a column is a walker's collider.
- **Under it.** The street's lamps, its wooden poles and their wires and its trees are taken out where a deck is lower
  than they are. Signals, signs and the streetcars' overhead stand under its underside.
- **Driven.** Each highway's lanes join the metro's traffic (`geocity/flow.js`): each way on its own side of the median
  by the metro's hand, faster than the streets (24 m/s), through no signal, on the deck's own height. The page steps and
  draws them near the camera like the rest.
- **Laws and readout.** Two laws: `highway-grade` (no steeper than 4.5%) and `highway-clear` (5.2 m under every deck
  over the land and under every flyover). The readout carries `highways`: each one's role, line, length, lanes, the deck
  it joins and the one it flies over.

### The metro's industry: industrial neighbourhoods in its outskirts, their kit, the grid, and clad sheds

- **Industrial neighbourhoods.** A metro now builds a share of its outskirts' neighbourhoods as industry (`industry`,
  a new metro setting: `share`, its blocks' `segments` by weight, the `block` length; `false` none). The land's edge to the
  country and the shore are chosen first, far from the seat, and each next one is drawn toward those already chosen, so
  they gather into districts (`design.js` `industryOf`). Their blocks are big, their streets a collector's width for
  trucks. Each block is one of five new segments (`segments.js`):
  - a **works**: a corrugated-steel hall under a low gable with a lantern along its ridge, an office in block at its front,
    roller doors on its yard, trucks, a chimney on some, containers out back;
  - a **warehouse**: a long clad box, its docks down one side under a canopy, trucks backed in, its people's cars;
  - **storage**: shipping containers stacked two to four high in rows, in their own colours, a bank of silos and its
    headhouse on some;
  - a **tank farm** (`tanks`): storage tanks in bunded rows, a pipe rack down the middle, gas spheres on their legs at one
    end, or a gasholder in its guide frame where there is room;
  - a **substation**, one in each industrial neighbourhood (its civic block): outdoor transformers in a row, a gantry over
    each bay, breakers between, its control house in concrete block.

  Every block is fenced with chain-link and barbed wire, a gate's gap at its front. The `segments` and `pitch` laws read
  industry as its own ring, its substation as its civic block.
- **The industrial kit** (`geocity/industry.js` `industryTemplates`): a storage tank with its wind girder, cone roof,
  winding stair and roof rail; a gas sphere on braced legs; a gasholder; a silo bank; a shipping container with its ribs
  and doors; an outdoor transformer with its radiators, bushings and conservator; a substation gantry and a breaker with
  their insulators; a lattice pylon with three crossarms each side and its insulator strings; a banded chimney stack; a
  chain-link fence panel; a pipe rack. Each is baked under the scene's light, each way it lies its own template. The tall
  pieces are seen across their district, the rest near the camera.
- **The grid.** Each substation is fed by a high-voltage line on lattice pylons from beyond the land's edge, a pylon every
  85 m or so, stood clear of its halls and off its streets. Six conductors sag between each two pylons and come in to the
  switchyard's gantry. The wires are footless, so no walker or hover cast stands on them. The industrial streets keep the
  outskirts' wooden poles and their wires, and are planted with maples rather than cherries.
- **Clad sheds.** Four new material words (`era/arch-style.js`): `corrugated`, `cladding`, `cmu` and `standing-seam`,
  on the dressed tiles' made cuts, each with its matter for destruction (`rupa/look-matter.js`). A yard's shed is now
  corrugated steel under a standing-seam roof, an emergency station brick, and a works' or a warehouse's hall and its
  control house each its own. A works' yard is concrete, a tank farm's bund and a switchyard gravel.
- **Readout.** The page counts its `industry` (its blocks, its pieces by kind, its pylons and lines), and a neighbourhood
  built as industry says `industrial`.

### The industrial and waterfront materials: rust, sheet piling, decking, membranes, and finishes by family

- **New cuts in the dressed tiles** (`matte-paint/dressed.js`, made class):
  - `sheetpile`: steel sheet piling, deep trapezoid pans interlocked at their clutches, a heavy coat chalked by the
    weather, rust run down through it at grit;
  - `decking` (a floor): timber boards, gapped, a butt joint each, a screw pair at every joist, the grain along them,
    gone silver at grit;
  - `membrane` (a floor): a flat roof's pale sheets welded at their laps, rings where ponds dried at grit.

  Corrugated sheet takes an opt-in `rust` (0 to 1): its coat failing, rust run down from the lap's fasteners and bloomed
  through it, heaviest in the troughs. Absent, not one byte of an existing sheet changes. The tile-spec rails, the form
  render's roughness and the matter each new cut breaks as (`rupa/look-matter.js`) carry them.
- **New material words** (`era/arch-style.js`), each with its matter:
  - walls: corrugated sheet in red oxide (a little rust at its laps), works green, cream, works blue and let go to rust
    (`corrugated-red`, `-green`, `-cream`, `-blue`, `-rusted`); cladding in grey and logistics blue (`cladding-grey`,
    `cladding-blue`); `tilt-up` concrete; `factory-brick` (an old works' darker, sooted brick); `sheet-pile`;
  - roofs: `membrane`;
  - grounds: `granite` pavers, `hardstanding` (a yard's big saw-cut slabs, oil-stained), `ballast` (a switchyard's
    crushed stone), `decking`, `armour-stone`.
- **Finishes by family** (`geocity/industry.js` `INDUSTRY_FINISHES`, `finishOf`). Each industrial building draws its
  wall's word and its roof's from its family by its block's dice, so no two neighbours need match:
  - a works: sheet in one of its paints, rusted, or brick, under standing seam;
  - a warehouse: cladding or tilt-up under a membrane;
  - a control house: block or brick;
  - a shed (a yard's, storage's, a pier's): sheet in its paints or rusted.

  Each variant is its own group, `geocity:<family>-<variant>`, with its finish.
- **The grounds re-laid.** A works' yard is hardstanding, a switchyard ballast, a warehouse's roof a membrane. On the
  waterfront the quays are granite, the decks and the park and step promenades timber decking, the revetments armour
  stone, and a marina's and a pier's quay wall steel sheet piling.

### The metro's traffic: its arterials driven, a signal at every crossing, drawn near the camera

- **Traffic, not parked kerbs.** A geocity parked a car in most stalls along its arterials' kerbs. Now its kerbs are kept
  clear and its arterials are driven (`geocity/flow.js`). This is the old fractal city's "ants"
  (`scene/channels/cars.js`) at a metro's scale:
  - **Lanes.** Every travel lane is a ring its vehicles drive round: out at the land's edge, back in at the other. A
    streetcar's lanes are kept to its tracks.
  - **Signals.** Every crossing has a signal: two exclusive phases and an all-red clearance. The clearance is derived
    from the longest vehicle across the widest box. Vehicles stop at a line behind the crosswalk, queue behind the one
    ahead and pull away on green. This is the shared signalised model (`traffic-model.js`), its numbers in metres.
  - **Vehicles.** Each is one of the fleets' (`fleets.js`): the family cars mostly, a taxi, a delivery van or truck, a
    bus, a works pickup or a garbage truck now and then.
- **Only what the camera sees.** The page's flow channel (`scene/channels/flow.js`) gives each lane its own model and
  steps it only while the camera is within reach of it. A lane far off waits. One that comes into reach starts from the
  last turn of its signals' cycle: all of a metro's signals share one cycle, so a lane's pose at a clock is the clock's.
  Its vehicles are instances, written each frame only for those within reach and in front of the camera. A camera high
  over the metro steps and draws none.
- **One template a model.** They are drawn on the parked vehicles' own templates. A repeat may carry `pool`, a key the
  flow channel instances it by, and is packed even with nothing parked (`geotown/cars.js` `carRepeats({ pool })`).
  Without a flow the page adds not one byte.
- **Laws and readout.** Two laws, `flow-holds` (every lane within what it holds) and `flow-clearance` (the all-red long
  enough). The readout carries `flow`: lanes, vehicles, signals, cycle, clearance. `flow: false` drives none.

### The metro's vehicles: civilian, city service and construction, each in its yard

- **A metro keeps its vehicles, each in its yard.** A geocity parked box cars in its car parks and none elsewhere. Now its
  vehicles are the vehicle registry's (`geocity/fleets.js`), each fleet by its role in the city. Every row is read
  through the registry to the realistic body it stands as:
  - **civilian**: the car shelf's family cars (a sedan, a hatchback, a crossover, an SUV);
  - **bus**: the bus;
  - **delivery**: vans and box trucks;
  - **utility**: works pickups and vans, each with an amber beacon;
  - **garbage**: green box trucks;
  - **construction**: the construction shelf's mixer and tipper trucks.

  The taxi, police car, ambulance and fire engine have no realistic body yet. Each stands for now as the nearest that
  does (a sedan, a van, a box truck), in its livery, marked by its roof: a taxi's sign, red and blue or red light bars.
- **Yards by role.** The metro's design gives each parking block a yard by its own dice (`yards`). Each role takes its
  yards from the parking blocks out of the core first:
  - a bus depot, one for every thirty neighbourhoods or so, its buses in rows under a shed;
  - a works yard, as many, its garbage trucks and works pickups and vans;
  - an emergency station for every dozen, a brick station with its bays, its fire engines, ambulances and police cars;
  - the rest car parks, the registry's cars in their stalls, nose to the aisle.

  The vacant block nearest a neighbourhood's construction sites becomes its contractor's yard, its mixers and tippers in
  rows behind the fence, a shed at its end. A new law, `yards`, holds a metro with car parks to a depot, a works yard and an
  emergency station.
- **Kerbs and sites.**
  - Every arterial's parking lanes are parked (an evocation's where it draws its neighbourhoods, not along its skyline):
    a car in most stalls, each nose the way its side drives. In the core and the frame there is a delivery van or truck
    now and then; in the core, a taxi.
  - A construction site's mixer stands on the band along its back, with its excavator and tipper as before.
- **How it is drawn.** All of them are drawn near the camera as instanced repeats, each model once (`geotown/cars.js`):
  - a model may now be a realistic loft by its class (`loft:bus`) as well as a card, its paint split from its trim;
  - a roof's extra stands on the same transforms (`ROOF_EXTRAS`).

  A repeat may say `occlude: false`, and the ambient bake then makes no occluders of its instances, on the page and in
  the GLB. The metro's vehicles, its machines and its frontage say so, since a parked car or a window darkens nothing
  the bake needs; a metro's page otherwise ran out of memory expanding them. The page counts its `vehicles`, `machines`
  and `yards`. A default metro parks about 10,000 vehicles and 350 machines.
- **The walk gate's walker keeps a huge triangle off its grid.** `network/walk-gate.js` indexed every triangle into
  2 m cells; a geocity's sea quads, out past the map, filled millions of cells. A triangle over 4,096 cells now sits on
  its own list, asked by every query: the same answers, and a subway town's walk peaks at 1.4 GB, not 1.9.

### The metro's waterfront: its shores reclaimed, a harbourfront of quays, piers, parks, a beach and a marina

- **Reclaimed shores.** The water no longer stops at a wall at the city's edge. A metro now reclaims a strip of new
  ground out into the water along each of its shores (`geocity/waterfront.js`, a new metro setting `waterfront`, true by
  default, `false` none).
  - Its **main shore** (the one its land falls toward) is 170 to 230 m deep, with a **waterfront boulevard** along its
    back. Its arterials run on across the land's edge to the boulevard. The lakeshore expressway now stands over the
    boulevard on piers in its median (as a lake city's expressway stands over its lakeshore boulevard), and the
    boulevard carries two lanes of traffic each way. Along it stands a row of the waterfront's own mid-rises, shops
    facing the water.
  - Its **other shores** are shallower (70 to 110 m): parks, beaches, steps, a marina, a restaurant row.
- **Segments**, each its own way of meeting the water, cut along each shore by the metro's dice (never the same twice
  running):
  - a **quay**: a granite plaza and rows of trees, a terminal pavilion, a long rink (a reflecting pool in summer), a quay
    wall with its coping and mooring bollards, a tour boat moored;
  - a **pier**: the quay's plaza and finger piers out over the water on timber piles, railings down their sides. On each
    a corrugated pier shed, or a restaurant at its head with patios, and boats moored along them;
  - **dining**: restaurant pavilions along the promenade, their patios out front (tables under parasols in their
    colours), planters, a kiosk;
  - a **park**: a lawn under trees, its path, the edge a rock revetment down into the water, a railing;
  - a **beach**: sand from a boardwalk down into the water under pink parasols, loungers in their colours;
  - a **marina**: a clubhouse and its lot of cars, pontoons combed out into the water at the water's own level, a
    gangway down to them, sailboats and motorboats in their slips;
  - **steps**: timber steps down to the water to sit by it, a lawn, its trees and chairs behind.
- **Elevation.** The strip's ground falls from the land's edge to its promenade, a quay's height (1.4 to 2.2 m) over the
  water. Its edges go down to the water by their kind: a quay wall, rocks, sand, timber steps, pontoons at the water's
  level, piers on piles at the promenade's. Where its edge steps from one segment to the next, a wall runs down to the
  water across the step.
- **The promenade** runs along the whole edge: granite, or timber in a park and on the steps. It has lamps and benches
  facing the water, a railing where it drops, and bollards on a quay.
- **The kit** (`waterfrontTemplates`): parasols and loungers (pale, for their tint), patio sets, mooring bollards,
  railings, timber piles, planters, and boats (a sailboat, a motorboat, a tour boat). They are drawn near the camera.
  New finishes for granite, timber decking, the promenade, rock revetment and sand, the last a new material word
  `sand` on the dressed tiles' sand cut, its matter sand.
- **Laws and readout.** A new law, `waterfront`: each shore met end to end, its ways of meeting the water more than
  one. The readout carries `waterfront`: each shore's segments, whether it has the boulevard, and the area reclaimed.
- **Natural shores.** A beach's and a park's edge need not be straight (`shoreAt`, a segment's `shore`, on its own dice
  so the strip's segments are the same whatever their shores). A beach is a crescent bay cut 25 to 60 m into the strip,
  its sand following the water's line down into it, its parasols and loungers inside the curve, its boardwalk straight
  behind. A park is a headland out into the water or a cove into it, its line wavering. Its timber boardwalk and its
  rock revetment follow the curve, and its trees, lamps and benches keep to its side of it. Each is flush with its
  straight depth at its ends, so it meets its neighbours as before. None comes closer than 60 m to the strip's back.

### Geocube sharpening: the joined map's terrain, its ways and its shores

The geocube's terrain, reoriented on the joined map (the glyph map: tiles of one land, built a zone a page). This theme
makes the main world rich, so the level design department's play layer lands on a composition that reads as the map
asked: the cube's look on every tile, ways told apart by what they carry, and water whose edge is a beach or a cliff.

- **The cube paints the joined map.** A glyph map's level may name a `geocube` (with its `terrain`, `hour` and `clouds`).
  Every tile is lowered under it as a trail is (era/geocube.js withGeocube's tile branch): the cube's look on the tile's
  square of the level's one land, its land drawn as the cube's (its shading), its biocube and its wind where the map
  names none. The page's era, contrast and register are the level's cube's (`cubeSpecOf` reads a map's level), so a
  sixth or seventh generation cube paints the map as it paints its trails. A gameworld's glyph level takes its style's
  geocube, terrain and hour (and is lit by it: no `unlit` advice), unless the level names its own kit. `terrain`, `hour`
  or `clouds` without a cube is refused with words. A map with no cube is as it was.
- **A seventh generation map is the form render's.** A glyph map a geocube paints, read in a form era, takes the land
  read a geocube page takes (form/land-read.js: its land as material under the cube's light, the ways' dress, the
  biocube's moss and grass) and its plants grown as form (form/flora-read.js: trees with branches and leaves, bushes,
  shrubs) in the painted ones' place: the map page carries its tiles' plants on the level's frame (`plants`), and the
  land is read framed from the south over the map's middle, as an island's camera frames it. Before, a gen-7 map drew
  the sixth generation's painted trees and land under the live light. The page says what it got (`map.form`: the form
  read, its plants and its far range); a map no geocube paints, read in gen-7, is drawn as paint and says why and how to
  have the form's (name its level's geocube). The era's own record (era/eras.js) names the glyph map among what the form
  render draws.
- **Real mountains round a gen-7 map** (level/far-range.js). The far ring a map took from its first tile (painted
  curtains, scaled out round the whole map) read as the sixth generation's impressionistic backdrop, washed near-white by
  the distance. A map read in the form render is ringed instead by a range of real ground: rising out of the rim at its
  height (the rim is its foot, drawn as the same far land), ridged peaks on the level's frame growing outward over a slow
  lift, out to 800 m past the map. They are the form's far land (`isekai:ridge`): lit in facets, the grass's colour low
  and the stone's toward the peaks. Its own haze (`haze` on the land read: the page's fog at 0.3 of its density, and less
  of the sky's air) lets them read through a morning's air; the haze is emitted only on a page whose land read asks for
  it, so every other gen-7 page is byte for byte as it was. A painted read keeps its ring.
- **A gritty cube's tiles build.** A tile on a polygon land with grit (the cube's `grit`, at 0.35 and over) failed:
  its solid flora read an item off the gritty land's strewn stones, which carry none (they are skipped, as pebbles
  are). And its edge stones were strewn by the trail's line by depth, which a tile's ways do not follow, in rows across
  the tile and over the water: on a tile only those at a way's edge are kept, and none on the map's water or its
  beach.
- **A tile's casters are grown in its own look.** The trees and stones a tile hands its neighbours to cast across a seam
  were grown from `manifest.style`, which a tile never names: under a cube whose card is not the meadow's, the casters were
  the meadow's trees, not the tile's. They are grown in the kit's style, as the stage builds the tile
  (level/grid-scene.js).
- **Ways of rank** (level/path-ranks.js, `ways: 'ranked'`, the default). Each path tile's rank is solved from the
  network, never written tile by tile:
  - a **road** is the trunk through a town (a tile beside a building) or on a way joining two places door to door: 4.2 m,
    setts beside the houses, a stone road out of them, a narrow verge;
  - a **track** is the rest of the trunk (every shortest way between the doors, the start, the gates, and with no goal the
    far end): 2.4 m of beaten earth;
  - a **path** is a branch that leads on (to a door, to a fork, or back to the trunk: a loop round a pond): 1.5 m;
  - a **trace** is a branch to nothing, a game trail: 0.9 m.

  A region says its own (`path`: a rank, or `{ rank?, surface?, width? }`). Widths meet at every edge: an edge is as
  wide as the wider of its two tiles (a road runs on into a track at its own width and narrows inside the track's tile),
  and a way wanders a tenth of its width on the level's frame, so both tiles read one width at their edge
  (era/out-tile.js `way`). The walk's tests against a way's edge stay true: a tile's `trailDist` stands nearer or
  further by how much its way is wider or narrower than its middle, and the stones, shrubs and hero tree set along a way
  read its width where they stand (`pathAlong`'s `h` and `f`). A boulder set off one branch onto another at a fork's
  middle is no longer laid. `map.ways` reads the ranks out. `ways: 'one'` keeps every way the kit's one width.
- **Water across the tiles, its edge a beach or a cliff** (level/map-water.js, era/out-tile-water.js). A grid's `~` (a
  planned segment's too) and an approved sketch's `w` on open land are water tiles, gathered into bodies:
  - **its level**: each body stands under the lowest of the land along its outline, so no shore is under it;
  - **its shoreline**: the water tiles' outline, rounded over a 4 m disc, wandered by two octaves of noise and set in,
    so a lake is never a square;
  - **a beach**: the land eased down to a strand of sand from the waterline to its berm, a shelf falling away under the
    water;
  - **a cliff**: the land held up at least 3.2 m over the water, a sheer face of the cube's stone down to a toe under it;
  - **which edge**: each land tile beside water says it: its region's `shore` (`beach` | `cliff`), else its sketch (a
    cliff `c` or rocks `r`), else its drop (land standing more than 2.6 m over the water a cliff, else a beach); weighed
    along the shore so a beach turns into a cliff and never steps at a seam;
  - **a place beside the water** keeps its land as it lies, so its building stands on the ground it was planned on.

  Every height is a function of the level's frame, so each tile cuts its own square and two tiles meet at one height on
  every seam. The sheets lie only on the water's side of the shoreline (a hollow inland is dry land), each corner over
  dry land clear, so the water's edge is where the land meets it. The bed is sand under any edge, and nothing grows on
  the beach or on a cliff's lip. The rim rises from the water's surface where water runs to the map's edge. `map.water`
  reads the bodies out (their level, tiles and shore). A sketch's `w` and a `c` beside water are laid (`laid.water`,
  `laid.cliffs`); a cliff away from water is still named as not laid.
- **The map's laws read the land as it lies.** `seams` reads a beach's sand and a cliff's rock beside the ground (a shore
  across a seam was read on one side at the lip and on the other at the foot); `seam-shade` reads the soft land (a
  cliff's rock is baked a facet at a time) and, on a map with ranked ways, not the ground under a crossing way's ribbon,
  which is covered and never seen. A new law, `paths-dry`: no way's line lies under a water sheet.
- **Advisory, measured:** under a cube with a contrasty ground ramp (valley-morning's grass), `seam-shade` reads 9 to 11%
  on a wooded map against its 8% tolerance. Traced: a shadow's edge crossing a seam steps a whole ramp stop on that
  ramp, where the meadow's closer stops stay under the 4% a point is counted at; seen from above, the seams read
  continuous. The law advises; the tolerance is the meadow's.
- **The game book's world card** (`gameworld-world`) says the water, the ways and the style's geocube; its ceiling moves
  5248 → 5376.
- **A composed town stands on the metro's land.** A geotown composed into a geocity (a neighbourhood or a block, geocity
  /towns.js) took the metro's natural ground and blurred its own streets' ground from it inside its frame, its edges
  clamped: along its frame it differed from the metro's by 0.05 to 0.09 m on average and up to 0.23 m (lakeshore and
  harbour-island, 56 to 60 m of relief), a step against the metro's walks round it. Its streets' ground is now the
  metro's own (`streets`, geotown/design.js geotownLand, threaded through the town's design and scene), equal to the
  millimetre. A new law on the page as built, `town-seams`, reads each composed town's street-level ground (its roads,
  walks, verges, lanes and margin; never a house's pad, stepped on purpose and closed by its own bank or wall) just inside
  its outline against the metro's green just outside, within 0.3 m (a kerb's): 0.19 m at most now, 0.62 m before.
- **A seventh generation metro is the form render's.** A gen-7 geocity was painted massing and drapes under the form's
  sky: its builder was never told the read was a form read, and none of its ground was the land the form reads. Now
  (ctx.form, worlds/world-kinds.js) its soft ground (parks, medians' lawns, the green round its towns, its lawned pads:
  `FORM_GROUND`) is the form's land, its street trees the form's plants (`plants`, grown as form, form/flora-read.js), and
  its composed towns are built in the form too, their trees, bushes and shrubs carried into the metro's (a block town's
  on its block, its bushes' kinds merged into one list). Its land is read as a town's (lawns mown, no trail's rubble), and
  it says what it got (`geocity.form`). Its buildings keep their own tiers (detail, massing, skyline) under the live
  light: the far structures' cards (channels/far-structures.js) are not baked for a metro (`structures: false` on the land
  read, emitted only when a page asks), since a card reads a painted fill a metro's textured faces do not carry, and they
  stood in black. The form's land read takes a face without a fill at its first corner's colour, where it threw. A
  gen-6 metro is as it was.
- **Uphill and downhill streets: a geotown's streets on profiles.** A geotown's streets rode its land blurred 24 m, so on
  hills a crossing tilted (1.3 m across one on the default hills, 4.5 m on 25 m over 400 m, 13 m on 40 m over 200 m) and
  each block rose and fell with every hummock under it. With `profile` (geotown/profile.js, opt-in: `true` or
  `{ walkable, curve }`) each street is laid as a hill town lays it: its crossings held level at the land's height there,
  each block between two crossings graded on one ramp (the hummock between cut and filled) with its ends eased in vertical
  curves, and past the outermost streets each runs on level to the frame's edge. The streets' ground is the profiles
  filled over each cell of the grid (a Coons patch, its shares eased over each crossing), so every street's line is its
  profile and every crossing is level corner to corner (0.00 m on all three). The town says its profiles (`profile`: each
  street's crossings and stretches, rise and grade), and a new law, `walkable`, names every stretch steeper than a street is
  walked at (20 % by default), too steep to walk (a street's stairs are its buildings' front steps, never the street's
  own): none on 25 m over 400 m (19.5 % at most), two on 40 m over
  200 m (48 % and 31 %). Graded blocks step their pads more than draped ones (25 m over 400 m: 1.47 m against 0.94), so
  `pad-step` advises there. A town composed into a geocity keeps the metro's streets' ground. A town without `profile` is
  laid as before.
- **A geotown parks the registry's cars.** Its parked cars were two painted boxes each (a body and a cabin). They are
  now the vehicle registry's family cars (geotown/cars.js: a sedan, a hatchback, a crossover, an SUV, an estate, a
  minivan, a supermini, each word read through its row to its car shelf card and compiled realistic), at the kerbs (each
  nose the way its side of the street drives), on the front pads, the forecourts, a walk-up's lot, a shop's yard and a
  school's or sports field's lot. A town parks hundreds, so each model is drawn once as an instanced repeat: its painted
  body baked pale and tinted per car by its paint, its trim (glass, tyres, wheels, lamps) a second repeat on the same
  transforms; the town's dice that placed and painted its cars are as they were, a model chosen by its own. A town's
  counts say its `cars` and `carModels`. A page carries about 24,000 faces of templates more, and its box cars' faces
  fewer. In the seventh generation the cars are the studio's bake, not lit by the form's light.
- **Drives and one-car garages: a houses block's `access`.** A geotown's houses blocks reached their cars by a rear lane
  (garages off it for a share), mutual drives between houses, or neither, by the pattern's dice. Now a town may say
  which (`access`, every houses block's) and a block its own (`blocks: { A1: { access } }`), and two more are laid:
  `compact`, each house its own drive from the walk, across its boulevard to the kerb, to a one-car garage beside the
  house, its door a little back of the house's front (its lot a garage's bay wider, a semi's garage on its outer side,
  no mansion on the block, the drive cutting the kerb's stalls, a car on a share of the drives); and `alley`, a rear
  alley, every house a one-car garage at its yard's back off it, behind an apron ramped from its door down (or up) to the
  alley, its sides retained, a car on a share of the aprons and the street's front yards whole. Each garage is solid
  (`<plot>:garage`). The ledger closes over the new drives and garages; the laws read a compact lot's frontage and
  coverage without its bay (a compact row laid to scale fills tight, a building at its least where its roll did not fit,
  and stretches its fewer, wider lots up to a tenth), and the parking law counts a single garage and its drive or apron.
  The pattern's dice take `compact` and `alley` shares, none by default: a town that asks neither is laid byte for byte
  as before (its layout's hash unchanged on seven towns across the evocations, streetscapes and patterns).
- **The slope word: this climbs.** A geotown may say how it climbs (`slope`): `{ toward, grade }` its land rising toward
  a side at a grade over its hills (its streets and its houses' pads with it), and `streets: { 'ns-1': 0.12 }` streets
  that climb at their own grade toward their north or east end (one axis, so no crossing is set twice), laid on their
  profiles (a profile on whether asked or not): each such street's crossings set at its grade from its first, its cross
  streets graded to meet them, and the land under it and its lots lifted to its climb (geotown/profile.js `climbLift`),
  full a third of the way to its parallel neighbours and eased out there, so its houses climb with it; where it outruns
  them its cross streets are too steep to walk, and `walkable` says so (a 14 % climb beside level streets: its cross
  streets at 33 %).
  A town composed into a geocity takes no tilt of its own (its land the metro's).
- **A geocity's streets on profiles.** A geocity may lay its streets as a hill town does (`profile`): its arterials'
  crossings level at the land's height there, each block between them graded on one ramp, the land's edges kept on the
  land's own ground (the shore where it falls to the water, the beyond where a town joins); then inside each
  neighbourhood its collectors and locals the same, the neighbourhood's edges kept on its arterials' ground; and every
  geotown it composes profiled too, unless its recipe says, its perimeter streets kept on the metro's ground so its
  seams hold (`town-seams`: 0.20 m at most on a hilly lakeshore, against 0.27 m draped). A profile keeps lines given as
  the edges it must meet (`keep`), names its lines (`ids`) and climbs the streets asked (`climb`). Arterials that climb at
  their own grade: `slope: { streets: { 'ns-2': 0.04 } }`, the land under them lifted with them. On a hilly lakeshore
  (30 m over 900 m) the arterials' crossings tilted up to 0.77 m and the neighbourhoods' up to 0.47; profiled, 0.00 and
  0.03. The stretches past the walkable grade are said by a new law, `walkable`, the profiles by the page (`geocity.profile`).
  Two crossings whose reaches meet are a step between them, their grade read on the run between their middles. A metro
  that asks neither is designed byte for byte as before.
- **Too steep to walk, said; every street's grade by its rank.** A profile's stretch past its walkable grade is `steep`,
  and the law naming them is `walkable` (in the geotown and the geocity): too steep to walk, never a stair wanted (a
  street's stairs are its buildings' front steps and stoops). The `grade` laws read every street by its rank: a geotown's
  local streets against the pattern's `grade`, its main and major streets against its gentler `grades` (6 % and 5 %; the
  old town's 8 % and 6 %), naming each street over its own most and the steepest; a geocity's arterials against its
  `grade` and, newly, each neighbourhood's collectors and locals along their runs against its `grades` (a recipe's
  `grades: { collector, local }`, by default the gentler of 10 % and 12 % or the arterials'), each measured every 4 m on
  the streets' ground as built (profiled where asked), naming each street over and the steepest of each rank.
- **The metro at a person's height: storefronts, windows, doors.** A geocity's buildings were massing at street level
  (grey and brick boxes without a window, lit panes past dusk only) and an evocation's detailed facades met the walk with
  blank ground floors. Now near a person's eye (each camera within 25 m of the ground) every building's walls are
  dressed (geocity/frontage.js), as the street kit is, by templates the light is baked into (each way a wall faces its
  own) stamped as instanced repeats drawn near the camera: WINDOWS in frames with a stone sill and head on every storey
  (a block of four bays by two storeys where it can be, its windows stretched to the wall's bay and storey, a template
  once each frame's paint); STOREFRONTS on its shopping streets (arterials and collectors in the core and the frame, main
  streets, avenues): glazing over a stall riser between pilasters, a door, a transom, a fascia sign in its shop's colour,
  an awning on nearly half, a band over them; APARTMENT ENTRIES on its residential streets (a pair of doors in a stone
  surround under a canopy, a step), every 18 m or so among ground-floor windows; an office's LOBBY under its canopy among
  shops; BALCONIES on nearly half its residential buildings; a cornice. A mid-rise's courtyard walls and its wings' joins
  are left bare; a tower's shaft takes its ground floor (its skin over it is its own); an outskirts house its windows and
  its door on its street; an evocation's detailed lots their ground floors, stood proud of their piers. The page says how
  many walls and pieces (`counts.fronts`, `frontPieces`): a core neighbourhood about 400 walls in 30,000 pieces, its page
  4.4 MB heavier (36 to 40 MB).

### The hover bot: a world's tester that flies

- **A tester that samples a world as a person sees it.** The hover bot (`lib/graph/scene/hover-bot.js`) holds an eye a
  height over whatever surface a capture page draws. It flies a path at a speed (`crawl`, `walk`, `jog`, `cycle`,
  `drive`, `fly`, or metres a second: the faster, the coarser its samples, every speed × 0.5 s) or teleports to a
  coordinate to take a shot.
  - Each sample says the ground under it: its height, its group, which way it faces.
  - Each next ground is cast from 3 m over the last, so a tree's crown or an awning is passed under.
  - A flight's report names its holes (where nothing is drawn), its steps (where the ground jumps more than 0.35 m),
    its steepest slope, the groups under it and the frame's triangles.
  - It has no body's physics: the walker stays a level's completability audit.
- **The capture page's bridge** gains `ground(x, y, from?)` (the highest surface the world draws under a point, cast
  down past what cannot be stood on) and `hover(spec)` (the eye stood over it, looking where told, rendered). Both are
  named in `capture-contract.js` and emitted on a capture page only. A capture page tags its textured meshes with their
  groups too, so the cast can say what it stands on. A live page is unchanged.
- **Its CLI**, `node scripts/hover.mjs <tour.json> [--out dir]`: a world's recipe (or a written page), then teleports
  with shots, flights along a path or the world's own route, and the page's cameras; its shots and a `report.json`.
  Guide: `docs/hover-bot.md`.
- **Tests:** its plans and reports (`hover-bot.test.js`), and a live run over a little world of a slab and a step in
  headless Chromium (`hover-bot.live.test.js`, the e2e tier).

### The run & gun on the belt: bullets that fly, its practice range

- The run & gun's guns (`brawl/brawl-guns.js`): a gun as its ROUND's flight, never a hitscan: its speed (mm a frame), its
  rate, its fan (pellets, spread) and its stream's wander (a fixed cycle of its shots, no dice), its damage and
  stagger, its life, how many bodies it passes through, the line across the belt it lands within, a knockdown, a burst
  where it lands, a lob, its ammo, the warning a foe aims for before it fires. The shelf: the players' sidearm (never
  out), machine gun, spread, flame, rocket and grenade, and the foes' rifle, burst, bazooka and lob, their rounds slow
  enough to see and step off. A gun passed into a practice room is its dials over a row (`readGun({ from, … })`).
- In the brawl's core a body with a `gun` fires rounds that fly along the belt and across it (eight aims on the floor,
  the across ones shallow so the depth reads under the side camera), land only within their line (step off it: dodged),
  pierce as their gun says, burst where they land (a rocket, a lobbed grenade), and never re-stun a body already reeling
  (a stream cannot pin it; its damage is whole, not scaled by its own count). A pick-up gun's ammo spent, the body is
  back on its sidearm; firing, it walks slower and faces its aim; `roll` is the gunner's dodge, untouchable as it goes.
- The gunner's buttons (`brawl/brawl-gunner.js`), no melee: the stick walks and aims (eight ways) while attack is held
  (auto-fire at the gun's rate), strong held plants the body so the stick only aims, special lobs a grenade, jump
  jumps (it fires in the air too), the stick tapped twice any way rolls.
- The shooting crowd: the rifleman, the gunner (a burst of three), the grenadier and the bazooka, each its gun and the
  `shoot` play: it holds its range along the belt and, given a token (its fire token), aims for its gun's warning (the
  aim fixed as the warning starts: the round goes where it pointed, so a player who steps off it is missed), then fires
  its volley.
- THE RANGE, the run & gun's practice room (`practiceOf({ …, range: { guns?, grenades? } })`): the guns passed in to be
  tried (names, or dials over one: `{ from: 'machine-gun', rate: 3 }`), the player holding the first over its sidearm;
  dummies that stand, walk, crowd as the shooting crowd, or SHOOT back on a slow beat (`{ mode: 'shoot', gun? }`); it
  never runs dry (a spent gun loaded again, the grenades back); it reads the rounds fired and landed, their damage, the
  rounds taken and each press's verdict (a shot taken, by its gun; a press while rolling dropped as rolling); its move
  list each gun's numbers (its round's speed, its rate, its reach, its burst, its ammo).
- The range on its page (`brawlLevel(level, { practice: { range: { guns, grenades }, dummies } })`): each round drawn as
  it flies (a tracer along its flight, warm a player's, hot red a foe's, its shadow on the street so its depth reads; a
  rocket's or a grenade's a ball on its arc), a foe's warning a thin red line along its aim, the gun out in both hands
  along the aim, a flash at a burst; the settings' Gun (the guns passed in) and a dummy's Shoot mode; the move list's
  Guns (each gun's numbers) and the gunner's moves; the gun meter on mana-ui's brawler shelf (`gun-meter`: the gun, its
  rounds left, the grenades, rounds landed of fired, their damage, the rounds taken). Rounds landing and bursts sound
  from the fight's shelf; a gunshot of its own is not there yet. The brawl yard's special in play no longer opens the
  move list (the back key does). The spike's `--range` plays it.
- A gun reads as a rifle held in both hands: every gunner's hold is the genre's, a rifle of sorts at the chest, always
  ready (`brawl-pose.js` RIFLE: the lead hand forward on the foregrip, the rear on the grip by the chest, on one level
  line; the arm angles found on the rig, each body type's hands landing within a centimetre or two of it), drawn
  through its own hands: its stock behind the rear hand, its barrel on past the lead hand along the aim, a magazine
  under the grip, inked, each gun its length and girth (`gunShape`: a carbine for the sidearm, a long barrel for the
  machine gun, a fat tube for the rocket). A round leaves where the drawn barrel ends (`GUN_MUZZLE`, out along the aim),
  so a tracer leaves the muzzle; a character holds it as the figure poses it (its reactions still its own clips).
- Shot sounds, impact frames and hitstun by poise. Each gun names its voices on the SFX shelf (`sound`, `hit`: the
  machine gun's round and a body hit, the rocket's and the bazooka's shot and burst, the grenade's throw and blast, the
  flame's whoosh), a gun passed in bringing its own (`brawl/brawl-sfx.js` gunAudio, onto the range's page); the range
  adds a foe's round whizzing past close, a gun run dry and a magazine seated. A gun's weight: its `hitstop` (the body
  it makes flinch frozen), its `freeze` (a burst holds the whole street still) and its `impact` (IMPACT FRAMES: the
  picture flashed a few frames as a burst or a heavy round lands, inverted under the anime register, white otherwise).
  HITSTUN BY POISE: a light round staggers a body (its damage summed, drained a frame) and nudges it back; only past
  the body's poise does it flinch (a big body soaks a stream: the bazooka, the axe, the heavy carry more; a rifleman
  flinches almost at once), a flinch cuts short a foe's aim (its shot never comes), a heavy round floors; the range
  reads each dummy's stagger on its line mark.
- The range's WAVE TESTER (`brawl/brawl-waves.js`; `range: { waves, loop? }`, `waves: true` its sampler): a wave a
  group of the crowd's types (each `{ type, n, hp?, poise? }`) with its FORMATION (line, column, stairs, pincer,
  surround, back: where it comes in from and the stations it takes round the player as it starts, on the street and in
  the view) and its ATTACK PATTERN (tokens: the street's crowd; volley: all together on the beat; sweep: one after
  another down the formation; alternate: by halves, half a beat apart; pincer: by sides), its `beat` and its breath
  before (`after`). One wave at a time: its bodies come in from the view's edges or the street's back to their
  stations, its shooters fire to the pattern (each volley warned of, the aim fixed from its start, a flinch cutting it
  short), its brawlers fight as the street's crowd; cleared when its last falls (its time and the rounds taken kept),
  the next after its breath, the set over again. Its page: the wave meter on mana-ui's brawler shelf (`wave-meter`:
  which wave of how many, its name, its formation and pattern, the bodies left and its clock, the last clear) and the
  settings' Waves; the spike's `--waves` plays the sampler.
- How the crowd comes in and where it hides, for both games (the brawler's and the run & gun's). ENTRANCES
  (`brawl-core.js` enterBody): walking in from the view's edge, out of a door on the street's far side, DROPPING from
  above onto its spot, DIGGING up out of the ground (untouchable until it is out) or VAULTING the back fence in an arc.
  HIDING: a body ducks (`hide`: its crouch at 60% of its height, so a round at the chest passes over it) until a command
  brings it up. COVER (`THINGS.cover`: sandbags, a stack of crates, a low wall, each its size, health and the voice a
  round makes on it): a round meeting it is stopped and wears it down, unless its shooter stands right behind it (a body
  fires over its own cover); a grenade goes over it, a burst reaches behind it and breaks it, blows break it, no body
  walks through it. In the waves: a range wave's (and the brawler yard's own, `practice.waves`) `entrance`, `cover`
  (a piece between each station and the player: its shooters down behind it between volleys, up to fire over it) and
  `ambush` (hidden at its stations until the player comes near); a street wave's crowd entry `entrance` and `ambush`.
  The sampler gains dug in, from above, out of the ground and lying in wait; the page draws cover, a dig's dirt and the
  crouch, and sounds a round on cover and a body digging out; the spike's `--waves --melee` plays the brawler's.
- MOUNTED FOES, for both games. A body RIDES in (`enterBody` how 'ride', on a mount of `MOUNTS` in brawl-things.js: the
  motorcycle, fast with a hard ram, and the scooter, slower and nimbler) along the street from where it is put, steering
  onto its target's line while it comes at it, running over a body in its way (knocked down, once a pass; a body in the
  air clears it) and turning past the view for its `passes`. Knocked off (a blow, a flying kick the genre's answer, or a
  stream of rounds past its poise), it flies on and its mount skids into a WRECK, cover on the street (`THINGS.cover`
  motorcycle and scooter); `onFoot`, it gets up and fights on, else the crash knocks it out. Its passes done, it brakes
  in the view and steps off (on foot, its mount left standing) or rides away. Nobody takes hold of a rider; a rider
  with a gun fires from the saddle. In the waves: a range wave's (and the brawler yard's) `entrance: 'ride'` and its
  `mount` (kind, passes, onFoot), riders coming in one behind another; a street wave's crowd entry the same. The
  sampler gains the bikers. Its page: the mount drawn under its rider sat astride it, the wreck a mount on its side, the
  crash's flash and impact frames; the street's own sounds (a crash, metal, the ground dug out of) voiced on any brawl,
  with guns or without (`streetAudio`). Its engine and its tyres are held voices on the shelf, not played yet.

### Cutscenes in a game written as a screenplay, shot by the director's rules

- **Write a cutscene the way a script is written.** A scene in a level can now be written as a short screenplay: who
  speaks and what, a feeling in brackets, who crosses to which place, who turns to whom, a pause. The studio's
  cinematics side then stages it on the level itself. It works out where everyone stands and whom they face, and
  shoots it the way a director would: a wide shot to open, over the shoulder for the conversation, a close-up on a
  line said with feeling, the wide again when someone moves, and the camera always on one side of the conversation so
  left stays left. The writer writes only the words; the shots are chosen for them.
- **The scene sets itself up.** Before the first line, the hero walks up to the person it is meeting and everyone turns
  to face as the scene begins, so the shots frame what they were planned to. When the scene ends, the hero is the
  player's again and the camera is its own.
- **Everything a scene could already do still works.** A written scene can be skipped, can carry a choice between two
  stretches of script, can set and read story flags and quests, and can be played by the game's flow as an opening, a
  prologue or an ending. A script that names someone or somewhere the level does not have is caught when the game is
  built and reported by name, while the rest of the game builds.
- **A blocked walk no longer stalls a scene.** A scene that waits for someone to walk somewhere now goes on if the walk
  is stopped by a wall, instead of waiting for ever.
- **A written scene keeps its own timing while the player reads.** Each line of a script now carries how long it
  takes to say, and the scene keeps that time while the line is on screen. A press shows the whole line at once while
  the moment plays on; a line left alone plays out and then waits, the cast listening, for the press. However quickly
  or slowly the player reads, the next line starts on its own beat, so the acting that follows in a later step stays
  in step with the words.
- **Characters act their written scenes.** In a scene written as a script, the characters now perform it in the
  level: their bodies move with the lines, gestures land on the stressed words, and the listener nods and stays alive
  while the other speaks. A realistic character's face plays too: the eyes and brows lead the words, and the eyes find
  whoever they are talking to. When a line has played out and waits for the player, or once the scene is over, everyone
  goes back to standing and breathing as normal. Characters whose faces the game doesn't animate yet still act with
  their bodies.
- **Slow motion and freeze-frames in a written scene.** A script's "Slow motion." now slows the world in the level,
  people walking and everything moving, until "Real time." brings it back; "Freeze." holds everything still for a
  moment. The camera, the text box and the characters' speech stay at normal speed, so the action slows and the words
  never drag. Skipping a scene in slow motion puts the world straight back to normal speed. A hand-written scene can
  call on a game's own slow-motion moments the same way.
- **Say how each character acts.** Each character, the hero included, can be given an acting style, a role (such as
  someone who holds their head high, or one who keeps glancing away) and a way of speaking, and their written scenes
  are played that way: the timing of the lines, the gestures and the faces follow it.
- **The director's notes.** When a game is built, each written scene gets the notes a director would give after a
  read-through: a shot held too long, a speaker turned away from whom they're talking to, a long talk with no
  close-up, a line slowed by slow motion. Each note comes with a suggested fix to the script, and none of them stops
  the build. They appear in the game's design readout and its book. The game's flow storyboard also marks which
  cutscenes are written scenes.

### Battle city on the game UI runtime: the table's language, and the pages' own house

The board games (`lib/graph/tabletop/`) and the strategy boards (`lib/graph/board/`) each draw their UI by hand: five
board-game pages with their own header, side panel and sheet, played by pointer only; a tactics, tower defence and
skirmish client of monospace text panels with three key listeners of its own. This theme moves them onto the game UI
runtime (`lib/mana-ui/`, [docs/mana-ui.md](../../../../docs/mana-ui.md)). Planned, in order: the pages' own house; what
the runtime lacked for a table; the board-game pages on one spec; the strategy boards on one spec with one input
owner; the table's broadcast furniture folded into the same parts; the holo arena. Built so far: the first two, and
the board-game pages on one spec, the strategy boards (a tactics battle, a tower defence, a skirmish) on another, and the holo arena.

- **A board game's page drawn by the runtime: `tabletop.ui`** (`{ theme?, languages?, language? }`,
  `tabletop/table-ui.js`). One spec and one host for the tabletop pages. With `ui`, a page's header and side panel are
  gone: the prompt and what can be done now are the table's action bar (each action on a key), the game so far its
  log, new game, undo, the level and the view its menu, and a promotion or a drop one question at a time.
  - **One coverage.** The seats, the calls and the result are the table's own parts too: seat plates along the top
    (the seat to play alight, a score that rose popping, a running clock), where the game stands under them, a call
    (check, a promotion, the dice, a new round, the end) one at a time by weight there and never over the play, and
    the places by points a beat after the end's word, ties sharing a place, with see the board and play again. A
    page's client says them in the calls it always made; with `ui` the runtime answers, and the page no longer carries
    the broadcast's DOM client or its sheet. The broadcast's data still makes the look's sides and the pieces' kits.
    The result is now moved through by keys and a pad (it had no focus).
  - **Keys and a pad.** The tabletop pages were played by pointer only. With `ui` the board has a cursor moved by the
    controls layer's `board` scheme (arrows or a stick, confirm, back), the menus and questions by the `menu` scheme,
    and back from the board opens the menu. A key pressed while a screen is up is that screen's: it never also acts
    on the board.
  - **A card game is one screen of grids**: the supply, the market, the hand, what was played, each seat's piles as
    backs and counts, moved through with the cursor; what can be bought or played has an edge alight.
  - **The look** is the game's (`ui.theme`: a preset, a theme card or its own words), else the table's own materials
    (`table-wood`, or `table-felt` for a card table), its sides the broadcast's kits so a chip here and a plate there
    agree. A game's `languages` reach the table's own words.
  - **The euro game**: its build modes, the dice, buying and ending the turn are actions; what you hold (resources and
    cards) a row of counters; the cursor moves among the places that can be taken now; a trade is the offer screen,
    each resource a count turned, the kernel saying why an offer cannot be made.
  - **The round games** (worker placement, sealed bids, drafts, duels): the spaces, the supply, the lot, the chain, the
    field and the hand are zones of the same screen; a bid is an action on its digit; a card with several targets asks
    for one among the actions.
  - Built for every tabletop page but one: a round game played on a board (a duel of summons on cells) takes `ui` and
    still draws its own panel, since its board and its cards want the cursor at once.
  - **With `ui: false` a page plays as it did** and carries no runtime, sheet or host. Its client's source gains the
    branches that choose between the two, and a page drawn by the runtime is about 220 KB larger (the runtime and its
    sheet).

- **The default: a table, a board and an arena are drawn by the runtime.** A tabletop game, a board (a battle, a map,
  a defence, a skirmish) and a holo arena that name no `ui` are drawn by the game UI runtime in their own look
  (`table-wood` or `table-felt`, `tactician`, `modern`). `ui: false` keeps a page's own panels and carries no runtime.
  - **This changes what a game already minted draws**: its recipe is the same, its page regenerates with the runtime's
    parts, keys and a pad, and is about 220 KB larger. A game that must keep its old page says `ui: false`.
  - The pages' own panels are kept, not deleted: `ui: false` uses them, a round game played on a board still draws its
    own under any `ui`, and a skirmish's key rebinding panel is only there.
  - The tabletop's card says `ui`.
- **The holo arena drawn by the runtime: an arena's `ui`** (`tabletop/holo-ui.js`). The overlay it drew on a canvas is
  the runtime's parts: the two duelists across the top, mirrored, each its light's chip, its life points and their
  bar, the one to play alight; the title between; the status at the foot; the duel's words (DUEL!, CHECK!, the end)
  while they are said. A promotion is one question, put off by back. The board has a cursor on the controls layer's
  `board` scheme (a ring on a cell, stepped over the cells as the camera shows them), so a duel is played by keys and
  a pad; confirm duels again once it is over. The look is the game's, else `modern`; its sides the duelists' lights.
  A world's `ui` reaches its board game's arena. With `ui: false` an arena's block carries no runtime.
- **The strategy boards drawn by the runtime: a board's `ui`** (`{ theme?, languages?, language? }`,
  `board/board-ui.js`; a level's `board.ui`, or the `board` kind's own). The board page still plays the battle; its
  text panels become the runtime's parts, read from what the page stands at each frame it changes:
  - **The battle**: the turn order (each unit its side's chip, the one acting alight), the unit in focus (its bars,
    how far it goes, what is on it), the action menu as a screen beside the board (Move, Act, Wait; the attack, the
    skills, the bag), an aim's forecast as a table, the end's word and its spoils as a banner, the numbers over a blow
    toned by their kind.
  - **The tower defence**: the wave, the lives and the purse; each tower on its digit with its cost, the one in hand
    marked; sell, the next wave and where a tower may stand on their keys. The cursor moves by the controls and the
    view follows it, so a defence is built from a pad.
  - **Keys and a pad through the controls layer**: the `board` scheme's intents (cursor, confirm, back, turn, zoom,
    tilt) for the board, the `menu` scheme while the action menu is up. The board page says what a control means once
    (`intent`); its own keys go through it too. Under the UI a defence's sale is R, since the board scheme's S moves
