    the cursor.
  - **The look** is the game's, else `tactician`; its sides the board's own side colours. A gameworld's `ui` reaches
    its battle, map and defence levels. Nothing covers the board as the menu comes and goes.
  - **The skirmish**: the purse along the top (gold, the second resource, supply, workers, army, tier), the clock and
    what the next click does, what is selected (a building's queue and research, a unit's figures, many units as
    tiles that pick one), and the command card as slots on their keys, the armed one marked, one that cannot be done
    saying why. A match's lobby is a screen of rows turned, its results the figures side against side with each row's
    lead marked and each side's army over the match. Its orders stay on its own keys and the pointer (the drag box,
    the right click), so the board scheme is not connected for it; the lobby and the results take keys and a pad.
    Rebinding its keys is not offered under the UI yet.
  - With `ui: false` a board's block carries no runtime.
- **Fixed: the server could not be loaded once the fight's cast rig met this line.** The fight's channel, inside the
  page's emitter, imported the cast rig's card to fill in an arena handed to it without one; the rig's solver reads the
  era's cubes, whose buildings reach back to the emitter, so the CLI, the stdio server and the install smoke stopped at
  `FLOORPLAN_DEFAULTS` before initialization. The channel takes the card it is handed (the world's resolver already
  hands it), and imports none.
- **Fixed: back from an aim left the keys with the cursor.** The action menu was drawn again and could not be moved
  through; it has the keys again.
- **The runtime gains a table's parts.** Three components, each with its rule in the sheet and no colour of its own:
  - `card`: a card's face (a band in its side's kit, the name, the cost, what it does, its tags, its power and guard,
    how many lie under it). Its state is a shape: playable an edge alight, picked lifted, spent turned on its side;
    face down it is a back and a count. A tap plays it from the HUD; a spent card is not tapped.
  - `log`: the whole of what happened, kept: the last rows shown, pinned to the newest, the rest counted above,
    numbered from the first.
  - `spark`: a small series as bars against its largest value, the last said as a number.
- **What cannot be done says why.** A disabled button, slot, list row or grid cell takes `why`; its reason shows under
  it while it has the focus or the pointer, and as it is pressed. A slot takes `disabled`, and a disabled one is not
  tapped.
- **The table's language** (shelf `table`, `idioms-table.js`), held to six principles (the board is never covered;
  whose turn it is is a shape and a place; one question at a time; the hand is at the foot; history is kept, never in
  the way; what cannot be done says why): `seat-plates` (flagged as coverage, so a table its broadcast covers is not
  drawn twice), `card-hand`, `card-row`, `action-bar`, `game-log`, `choice-prompt` (back leaves it only where the game
  gives a way out), `trade-offer`, `table-results`.
- **Strategy's parts filled in** (shelf `live`): `turn-order` (lifted out of the turn-based battle's menu, which now
  uses it), `selection-grid`, `skirmish-lobby`, `skirmish-results`.
- **Two looks**, theme cards of a new family `table`: `table-wood` and `table-felt`, from the tables' own materials;
  the board draws three new frames (a board game's table, a tactics HUD, a skirmish HUD). Contrast advice measured on
  both cards: none left.
- **The board-game pages share a kit** (`tabletop/page-kit.js`): the escapes, the levels and their picker, and the
  table view's cameras and faces were written in each of the five pages.
- **The strategy board says things once.** Its grid-to-world point and its bus push were written twice and its banner
  three times; the tower defence and the skirmish are handed them.
- **Fixed: a tower defence's S sold the tower under the cursor and panned the camera down in the same press.** A
  defence's letters are its own; the arrows and the screen's edge pan.
- **Fixed: a skirmish's pause banner named the wrong key** ("P to play on"; P is patrol). It names the key pause is
  bound to.
- **Fixed: a promotion or drop picker had no way out.** On the move page a click outside it or Escape puts it away; in
  the holo arena a press on the board or Escape does.
- **Fixed: a player's id went into the euro, tile and move pages' logs and seat rows unescaped.**
- **Fixed: the tile game's table view was fitted to the laid tiles only on a move**, never as the window was resized.
- Pins: the `holo` fixture a third time, for the default (it names no `ui`, so it now carries the runtime); before it,
  the `holo` fixture for the arena client's hooks; the `board` fixture again, for the board page's hooks and its `intent`; before it, the `board` and `holo`
  fixtures of the World page's byte pin, for the board page's fold and the holo's picker; `brawl`, the one
  fixture that inlines the runtime's kernel, for the kernel's new parts (the yard draws as before).

### Buildings as material: a town's and a city's walls in the form render

- **A town's tiles are material.** A detail tile (`matte-paint/detail.js`: a wall or a roof dressed by a word, a land's
  rock) is read by the form render from the dressed cut it was painted from (`form/room-form.js` `formMaterialOf`: its
  normal, its occlusion, roughness and height, by its own metres), where it was read back from its paint's light as any
  stock tile is. A room that wears one draws its true relief; a bonded-brick floor's detail is read from its paint as
  before.
- **The sun as a baked light** (`form/sun-light.js` `sunLitFaces`; nothing reads it yet). A building's faces baked as
  a room's are, their colour and their light apart, under the light a cube solves in the place of lamps: each corner
  its base (its paint's colour shown square to the sun under the whole sky, the land's own reference, over the light
  there) and the light the day lays on it, the sky by how much of it the face sees, what the ground throws back onto a
  face turned down, and the sun by its cosine where a shadow test says the sun reaches the corner; beside it the share
  of that light the sun gives, by which a live shadow darkens it.
- **A town's buildings are drawn as form** (a geotown read in gen-7, by day; gen-6, a town at night, and the engine
  handoff's read are as they were). Its buildings, its street's furniture and its paved ground (the `town:` and
  `geotown:` faces) carry their paint as it shows lit, never darkened by their turn to the sun, and are baked with
  their colour and their light apart (`geotown/scene.js`, `form/sun-light.js`): the sun's shadow is tested against the
  town itself, so an eave shades its wall and a house the one beside it, which the paint never drew; a wall in shade
  takes the sky and what the town's paving throws back. The page's form channel draws them (`scene/channels/form.js`,
  the payload's `form.town`): the sun is its one lamp, set far off along its way, and lights the tiles' relief and
  sheen near the eye only by the share of the bake the sun gave, so nothing shines in a baked shadow. They are toned
  with the land. A live shadow darkens a face by its sun share, so a tree no longer shades a wall the sun does not
  reach. A detail tile's material keeps the colour the page already draws (set to the detail's mean), its hue the
  face's. A room's page is byte for byte as it was. Seen in Chrome on an island-noon town, beside gen-6 and the
  gen-7 read before it.
- **A town's first read in gen-7 is quicker, and its relief whole.** A detail tile's material brings no colour of its
  own (the page's tile stays, never painted a second time), and a town's maps are read once at full size, with no
  byte budget and so no second, smaller read of every tile: an island-noon town resolves in about a minute where the
  first cut took a minute and three quarters (a little over half a minute before its buildings were form; what is
  left is the tiles' relief being painted, once a process). Its page grows by the maps (49 MB against 30).
- **Buildings and land shade each other.** Measured on the page: every `town:` and `geotown:` mesh casts into the
  land's sun map, so a house's shadow lies on the grass; a paved face takes a tree's by the live light, by its sun
  share.
- **A patch of grass ends on a ragged edge, not on squares** (every gen-7 land). The far blanket (the grass drawn in
  the ground past the blades' reach, `scene/channels/far-field.js`) read the ground map a cell at a time, so from
  above a lawn's edge and a bare patch's were stair steps half a metre wide; the cell is now found at a place that
  sways and scatters in a fine grain (`FAR_FIELD.edge`), and the blades themselves read their cover between the map's
  cells along a wandering line (`scene/channels/form-grass.js` `GRASS_EDGE`), thinning out toward it. Inside a patch
  nothing changes.

- **A city's massing is drawn as form** (a geocity read in gen-7, by day; gen-6, a city at night and the engine
  handoff's read are as they were). Its towers, podiums, blocks, roads, walks and walls (the `geocity:` faces; the
  glass, a lit window and a detail lot's skin are left as painted, the land's ground is the land's) carry their paint
  as it shows lit and are baked with their colour and their light apart, as a town's are (`geocity/scene.js`,
  `form/sun-light.js`); a town composed into a metro comes baked by its own hand. The sun's shadow is the page's:
  where the page takes live shadows, no shadow is baked and the hour's map takes each face's sun share away to the
  pixel, a tower's shadow lying sharp across the block beside it; a read with no live light bakes it, tested against
  the massing. Seen in Chrome on a small and a mid valley-morning
  lakeshore city, beside gen-6 and the gen-7 read before it.
- **One sun a page.** On a page whose land is drawn as form, the live light's maps (the actors' and the hour's) are
  drawn along the land's solved sun where the world names none of its own (`worlds/world-scene.js`,
  `shadows.toLight`). A gen-7 geocity named none, so its buildings' live shadows fell along a default sun while its
  land was lit and shadowed by the cube's: the two crossed, and a wall turned to the land's sun stood in the other's
  shade. Every gen-7 page with a form land and live shadows moves to the land's sun; gen-6 pages are as they were.
- **A city with no industry district is made.** A small metro whose plan lays no industry threw while its payload was
  assembled (`geocity/scene.js`, its wires' word read from a count that was not there).
- **A city's street frontage is drawn as form** (the windows, shopfronts, awnings, lobbies, entries, balconies and
  bands a street repeats; gen-7 by day). A piece's template is one a facing and never turned, so it carries its paint
  under no light and the day's light on its own corners, the sky and the sun by its facing (`geocity/frontage.js`
  `frontageTemplates` `flat`, baked by `form/sun-light.js`); the page hangs that light on the one geometry a repeat's
  instances share and draws them with the form material (`scene/scene-three.js`, `scene/channels/form.js`), toned
  with the land, the hour's map taking each piece's sun share away where a tower shades it. No shadow is baked a
  piece, so a read with no live light draws its frontage unshaded by its neighbours. Its glass is lit as its frame
  is. A page with no baked template carries none of this. Seen in Chrome at street level on a small valley-morning
  city.
- **A stage under a sun or a moon is drawn as form** (a sunlit plaza, a street set, their night; gen-7). It was the
  one room the form render left as paint. It is baked as a room is, its colour and its light apart, with the sun
  beside its lamps (`era/stage.js` `formLightFaces` `sun`; `form/room-light.js` `solveDayLight`): the reference is
  the sun itself, so a surface square to it and unshadowed shows its paint; a corner takes the ambient, the sun by
  its cosine where the paint bake's own shadow test reaches it, what the ground throws back onto a face turned down,
  and each lantern, torch and pool in the sun's share (what it adds at the reference's metres as the paint lays it
  there). At night the moon is the sun. The page lights the tiles' relief by the sun as a lamp set far off, always
  in its live set whatever lamp stands nearer (`scene/channels/form.js`), and a plaza's dress beside its stage reads
  its tiles as material (`worlds/world-scene.js`). An engine's handoff of a sunlit stage is paint, as it was; gen-6
  and a room under no sun are byte for byte as they were. Seen in Chrome on an island-noon plaza by day and by
  night, beside gen-6.
- **The records.** The seventh generation's world note says what is drawn as form now (a stage under a sun or a
  moon; by day a town's buildings, a city's massing and its streets' frontage) and what is still planned
  (`era/eras.js`). A page read in gen-7 no longer lists its repeats as approximated where every template is baked,
  and names the ones still paint where some are (`era/era-marks.js` `eraReading`).
- **An engine gets a town's relief.** In the engine handoff a detail tile (a town's wall or roof dressed by a word)
  leaves with the normal, the occlusion and roughness and the height of the dressed cut it was painted from, its
  colour the tile it already carried (`scene/handoff.js` `dressedMaterials`); before, only a room's dressed tiles
  did. An export with no detail tile is as it was.

### The cast channel: one light for every body, in both eras

- **The light a cube solves agrees with the sky it paints** (the form render's; a painted page reads none of it).
  The sky's share of a cube's light was its look card's alone (its ambient against its ambient and key), written for
  paint that mixes its light in display units: taken to linear light, an overcast look's sky gave a tenth of the light
  the sky it paints would. A jungle-haze scene read in gen-7 drew a near-black sky over land lit almost wholly by a sun
  the look does not have (a frame's mean luminance 47 against its gen-6 paint's 116). Now the share is read against the
  painted sky (`era/cube-light.js` `skyShare`): where the dome is more than 1.5 times (`SKY_OVER`) the ambient the
  card's share gives, the share rises to meet it, to at most 0.9 (`SKY_SHARE_MAX`: a sun is still a key); past that the
  light's level is the sky's and the materials fall dark under it, no base at the brightest a material may be. The
  jungle path's mean is 108. `cubeLight` returns the read (`skyLight`: the rule, the card's share, the dome's level
  and the ambient's) and says it in its checks.
- **A cube states its own**: `light.skyShare` (between 0 and 1), kept as written, the sky only read against it.
- **What moved, measured**: jungle-haze's share 0.13 to 0.85, theatre-grey's 0.13 to 0.50, limestone-crags' 0.38 to
  0.53, gothic-night's 0.06 to 0.10, city-night's 0.03 to 0.04. island-noon, valley-morning and upland-morning keep
  their look's share: their payloads are byte for byte as they were, in both eras and at another hour. Every gen-6
  payload is as it was.
- **Far ridges stand in the look's haze, not in a clear horizon's.** A form page's far land and its fog took the air
  at the horizon, about twice the look's own haze under an overcast sky: with the sky's share raised, a jungle-haze
  scene's ridges drew near white against a grey sky where the paint draws them dark. A look whose fog is darker than
  its dome's horizon by more than a tenth (`form/land-read.js` `HAZE_UNDER`) now carries that share (`form.land.sky.air`)
  and the form sky lays its haze at it (`channels/form-sky.js`). A clear noon's fog is its horizon's, so island-noon
  carries none and its page is as it was; at dusk its ridges darken against the horizon's glow.
- **The cast rig, as data** (`color-theorist/cast-rig.js` `castRig(cube, { hour, register, palette })`; nothing in a
  mint or a page reads it yet). The one light a body is drawn under, solved from the world's own: the key is the
  cube's solved sun at the level's hour (the light the land is lit by), the hemisphere that solve's sky light over
  what its floor throws back, the rim the horizon's hue. Only the key is a light a page owns; the hemisphere and the
  rim are for a body's own material, so they light nothing else. Two gains are the body's alone, as a fight lights its
  bodies: its key raised (to 3× at most) where a sky-lit level turns a figure less than 1.6× from its key side to its
  shade, its fill raised where a moon over a dark sky leaves the shade more than 6× under the key. The rim is raised
  where the shade side sits on the horizon's value. `register` (`western` | `anime`) is the body's, the light the same:
  the cel carries its three tones. With no cube it is the card, the fight rig's own lights in the solve's units, kept
  as written. Read on the cube presets: the clear and morning looks need no gain; jungle-haze's body key is raised 3×
  and still turns 1.57× (its level is the sky's); city-night's fill is raised 2.6×; both night looks' rims are raised.
- **The cast material** (`scene/channels/cast-rig.js`; no page builds a body with it yet, so no page changes). The rig
  laid on a body's own shader, so it lights nothing else: the hemisphere in the place of the page's ambient (the rig's
  sky on a face turned up, its ground on one turned down), the body's own key gain on its direct light alone, and the
  rim as a fresnel edge on its surface, stepped for the cel. `western` is three's standard material, `anime` its toon
  material over the rig's ramp; `patch` lays the rig on a material a client already has, after its own patch. Only the
  key is a light, one a page (`key`): a form page's sun is taken as it is; on a painted page, whose world is unlit, the
  page's shadow-casting light takes the key's colour and level and every other directional light is put out; a page
  with none gets one along the rig's key. On a form page the renderer's curve tones the body with the land; on a
  painted page the body tones itself with the same curve. The kit is page source by `castKitSource()`. Its tests hold
  it against the vendored three's own standard and toon shaders. Proof on real pages
  (`scripts/spikes/cast/proof.mjs`, headless Chrome): on the island trail and the jungle path in gen-7 the page's
  lights read the same before and after a body is added; on the island in gen-6 the page had no light and has one.
- **A fight game's bodies are drawn under the cast rig** (Mojulo Fighter under a register; an arena made before the
  register is as it was, not a byte). The arena's rig (`versus-arena.client.js` `fightRig`) keeps its one key, its
  shadows and its catcher over the lane's floor, the key's colour and level now the rig's; its fill light, its rim
  light and its sky light are gone from the scene and are the bodies' own, laid on each body's material by the cast
  kit after its coat (`castKit.patch`): the sky over the ground with the low fill in it, the rim a fresnel edge. A
  lit body tones itself (the room is painted, the renderer tones nothing). The ring's pieces take the rig as the bodies
  do. The page carries the rig as the arena's `cast` (`versus/versus-cast.js` `fightCast`: the card in the game's
  register, a fight's levels being a stage or a greybox, neither painted by a cube) and the kit beside the fight's
  modules. Seen in Chrome on the training greybox in both registers and on the ring: bodies lit and shadowed, the
  coat and the ink as before, no page error.
- **The brawl yard's bodies are drawn under the cast rig** (a brawl under a register: the brawler, the run & gun, their
  practice yard and range; a yard with no register is as it was). The yard's rig (`brawl-yard.client.js` `yardRig`)
  keeps its one key (the greybox's own sun where the yard carries it), its shadows and its catcher over the street;
  its fill, rim and sky lights are gone from the scene and are in the material every body, limb, prop and gun is drawn
  with, laid on by the cast kit. The page carries the rig as the yard's `cast` (the same card a fight takes) and the
  kit beside the brawl's modules.
- **The hero a player pilots is lit by the land's sun on a form page.** On a level whose land is drawn as form (a
  glyph map a geocube paints, read in gen-7), the body a player pilots is read as the lit export reads it (its colour
  under no light; each corner's normal where its form writes one) and carries the cast rig solved from the land's own
  cube at its hour (`figures.<name>.cast`, `worlds/world-scene.js`): the land's one sun is its key, the sky over the
  floor's bounce and the horizon's rim its own. The page draws it with the cast material by whichever builder draws
  it, the merged one or the per-bone one, its normals the read's or its mesh's own
  (`scene/channels/controllable/`), toned with the land, taking the land's shadows, and with no baked rim over it. Its
  rig, its clips and its playback are as they were. Every other figure (a walker, a foe, a crowd), every page without
  a form land, and every gen-6 page are as they were: a bank with no such figure carries none of the kit. Its register
  is the level's `fxStyle.register` where that is `anime` or `western`, else `western`. Seen in Chrome on a small
  valley-morning map with the Saikyo body, beside its gen-6 read.
- **A vehicle's form body takes its sky from the rig, and no longer lights the land.** A body in the form render (a
  supercar, a racer, a craft: `scene/channels/controllable/`) added a sky light of three's to the scene, which on a
  page whose land is drawn as form lit the land as well, brighter than its solve. Its sky over its ground is now in
  the body's own shader, laid on by the cast kit from the body's own setting, and no sky light joins any page. On a
  form page it asks for no light and no curve of its own (the land's sun lights it, the renderer tones it with the
  land); over a painted world its key and its own curve are as they were. Seen in Chrome: a supercar on a painted
  gen-7 lot, its frame as before; on a valley-morning map, the land back at its own light.
- **One tone rule an era.** On a form page the renderer's curve tones every lit body with the land; on a painted page
  (the renderer tones nothing) a lit body tones itself.
- **The records.** The seventh generation's cast conventions `albedo-unlit` and `material-by-response` read partial,
  each saying what is built and what is not (`era/eras.js`), and the cosmos reads them (`reality.cast=gen-7`). A page
  read in gen-7 no longer lists its figures as approximated where every one is under the cast rig or a form body, and
  names the ones that are where the rest are paint (`era/era-marks.js` `eraReading`).
  [docs/hero-form-light.md](../docs/hero-form-light.md) says what draws a hero now and what is not built.
- **The WebGPU spike is retired** (`scripts/spikes/webgpu/`, removed): mojulo's pages are WebGL, and the cast and form
  materials are laid on three's own shaders.
- **The rig's core is its own module** (`color-theorist/cast-rig-core.js`: the laws, the card and the rig's making,
  with the solve passed in; it reads none of the era's modules). `castRig` is that under the cube's light solve, and a
  fight's card (`versus/versus-cast.js` `fightCast`) reads the core alone. The fight's and the brawl's channels, inside
  the page's emitter, read the rig's card through the cube's solver at first, which put the era's cubes in the
  emitter's import graph and stopped the CLI, the stdio server and the plugin profile from loading their tools; the
  candidate's own fix took the card out of the fight's channel, and with the core split both channels take the card
  again for an arena or a yard handed to them without one, importing nothing of the era's.

### Catalyst molds: a mold joins a chapter, and an ask says which kind of gap it is

The design for bringing the catalyst shelf into the studio. A making catalyst is a mold: it teaches an agent how to
press a want into a mojulo-shaped thing. The studio works a game one unit at a time, and a unit's author is handed its
chapter's cards; the molds were not among them. Designed, not built: nothing below is in the code yet.

- **A mold names its chapters** (`chapters` in a catalyst's frontmatter, checked against the chapter registry; `[]`
  for one that molds for no game chapter). Every curated catalyst states it.
- **A unit's author is handed its molds.** A unit's view lists the molds of its chapter beside its cards, the
  operator's own among them, and a job reads one from its seat through `design_game`.
- **A job's ask says which gap it is:** a mold makes it, mojulo cannot yet (named in the cosmos registry where a value
  names it), or the remit is off. The agent sorts; the server only looks up what the ask names.
- **The readouts sort them,** and the director's next move follows the kind. A build ask moves nothing: the unit is
  received over it, as before.

### What to build next now counts November's work, and says what that work made

- **The planning map caught up with what November built.** The internal map the studio uses to decide what to build
  next had fallen behind the work merged since the start of the month. It now counts as built: blows that knock
  things back, worlds that break (from a few crates up to matter that breaks by what it is made of, with fire, craters
  and floods), breaks the game or the player sets off, the special moves that carry a hero through the air, guarding
  and parrying, a hero's motion tuned from a card, levels written as maps, a platformer's course sized by its hero's
  jump, a world map crossed zone by zone, worlds joined in rings, a level's scenario and the things level design
  places on it, the screen a game is made for, a mascot as the hero, the kinds of body a game puts in it, a game's
  title screens and menus in its own look, the colour grade over a game, and a big moment taking the camera as well as
  the clock.
- **Things that were wrongly listed as missing are corrected**, and notes that had gone stale now say what is true:
  the fighter is fought on any level that names a lane, an RPG's party has its menus and shops, a vehicle comes from
  the registry by its word, and a flight's aircraft is still a placeholder shape although the real airframes exist.
- **Four gaps are now priced so they can be ranked.** Seventh-generation looks (the world, and the cast, which needs
  the world first) had no price and so could not be compared with other work; they have one now. Sound for a designed
  game is listed as a gap: a quick game can say its music and effects, a designed one cannot, and no level uses the new
  sound-effects library yet. A level's own HUD, talk menus and pause do not yet run on the shared game UI. Playing in
  a headset works for stage levels and is listed as part done.
- **Four more kinds of game to check against:** a 3D platformer, an action RPG on a world map and a destruction
  sandbox all read as makeable today; a headset adventure shows the gap it has.
- **The page now says what recent work made.** Each capability on the map can say the day it was built. The page
  counts, over the same rolled games it always uses, how many are makeable only because of what the last fortnight
  built, and for the games that use a new capability and still cannot be made, which missing piece they wait on most:
  the other half of a combination, and so a good next build. It also lists pairs of new capabilities that now work
  together in one game.
- The comic hero pack's game types now ask for knockback and breakable streets directly, since both are built.

### Drawn plates: a book's illustrations, drawn from solid forms in curves

- **A book can now carry drawn illustrations, not only diagrams.** `drawnPlate(spec, { style, caption, span, id })`
  (`lib/graph/book/drawn-plate.js`) returns the press's figure holding an SVG of curves in the book's own paper and
  ink. A plate is said the way a draughtsman is told, and no pixel is placed: the forms (field terms, what
  `mint_solid` reads, standing on the ground in metres; `formsOfSolid` takes a minted workbench solid's own `fields`),
  the station (a level eye, so two-point perspective: the vanishing points follow from the turn and the lens), one
  light, and a finish. Each sample of the picture plane is lit where the eye's ray meets a form, each tone step is the
  closed outline of "darker than this" laid over the lighter one, a hatch line is a slice of the form by a plane square
  to the light, and the contour is heavier on the side away from the light. Three finishes: a wash, an engraving, a
  woodcut. Round and blended forms, a shadow cast from one form onto another and inner edges are drawn; the plate is
  framed on what it holds. Deterministic: the same spec gives the same bytes.
- **From the shell:** `node scripts/drawn-plate.mjs <out-dir>` draws the examples (or a plate's JSON) in each finish;
  `--book <out.html> [--pdf out.pdf]` sets three of them in a sample book on the press.
- **Not yet:** no door mints a plate and no book calls for one on its own (a book's builder adds the block); a
  line-only finish, texture, transparency, a second light, a surface other than the ground, and solids that are not
  field terms are not drawn. The sketch expander (`neo-rembrandt`, `rendrant`) is unchanged: stored sketches still
  regenerate through it.

### Exhibits: interactive pieces for a museum, a classroom or an encyclopedia

Built on this branch: one door for exhibits, the tour, rooms with a kiosk, the expert's brief, prepared states,
narration, and two exhibits to start from.

- **One door for exhibits, arranged in halls.** The science, space, earth, life and mathematics study objects, the
  science demos built from laws and the historic cities at their period are all asked for in one place, by hall:
  `science/fission`, `earth/hydro`, `life/dna`, `math/derivative`, `history/pompeii`. A hall lists what it holds, an
  exhibit's card is its manual (a historic city's entry still says what is known, reconstructed or conjectured), and a
  made exhibit's measurements are read back in real units from the same place. The separate tools for making a study
  object and for measuring one give way to it, so the list of tools your agent reads gets shorter; their old names
  still work for a release. The Claude plugin's helpers keep the old names until the release that updates the
  plugin, since an installed plugin changes only then. Kept setups in your cookbook are recalled by their hall too. Everything already made looks
  exactly as it did. The manuals for building a world (its bases, stage kits and looks) stay where they were.
- **A tour you step through.** An exhibit, or any world, can carry stops. At each one the camera glides to a view, a
  caption explains, and the part being talked about is lit while the rest dims; the stop can say how sure it is
  (known, reconstructed or conjectured for history; simulated, depicted or explained for science) and where its claim
  comes from. A panel along the bottom has the way back and on and a dot for each stop; the arrow keys and a swipe step
  it too, and a link can open on any stop. A toured page looks like an exhibit rather than a workbench: it fills the
  window, a phone's or a kiosk's, its title stands quietly in the corner, the camera and wireframe buttons step aside,
  and on a plain background the subject glows softly in the colour of the part each stop is about. Give the stops when you ask for the exhibit, or add them to one you have; a stop that names a
  camera or a part the exhibit does not have is refused, with the ones it does. A historic town can name its parts
  when asked, each monument and each kind of building (its theatre, its houses, its walls, its fountains), so a stop
  lights the one its caption is about; asked for nothing, it is drawn exactly as before. On a town you can walk
  through, the panel's arrow keys and its camera moves work as they do anywhere else (they were held back until now),
  and a science exhibit's own readout moves to the top so the panel never covers it.
- **Rooms and a kiosk.** Several exhibits join into one gallery, with no score to win and no way to fail: a lobby
  with a card for each room (its hall, its title, how it opens, how many stops), and each room its exhibit, with the
  way back and on to the next. A gallery remembers its rooms, not copies of them, so improving an exhibit improves
  every gallery it stands in. On a kiosk, a single exhibit or a whole gallery plays itself when nobody is touching it,
  each stop held as long as its words take to read, a gallery walking from room to room, and it hands itself to the
  next visitor the moment they touch the screen, in large type with nothing to select by accident. A gallery saves as
  a folder that opens with no internet and no server, the form a kiosk wants. Asked for the web form, the folder's rooms fetch their 3D
  engine from the web instead, so the gallery and its prepared states also run on a page host that refuses code built
  into the page (a downloaded gallery ran; the same gallery published to the web showed only its background).
- **Told where it runs.** Saving an exhibit as a page or a folder now says which form you got, in words your agent
  passes on before you open it. When every page fits a web page, the web form is written beside the download and is
  the one to show; when a page is too big for one (Pompeii with all its people is about 41 MB), it is a download, to
  save and open from your computer, and you are told why. A download opened on a web page shows only its background,
  so nobody is left thinking the exhibit is broken.
- **A check made for exhibits.** An exhibit has nothing to win, so it is checked the way a label wall is: does it tell
  a story, does each stop say how sure it is, does a claim taken from the historical record say where it comes from
  (a warning when it does not), can each caption be read in the time a visitor gives it, and does every stop show its
  subject on the screen. It advises and never refuses; whether the exhibit looks right is yours to judge, and whether
  a claim is true is the expert's.
- **The expert's brief.** A curator or teacher says what a visitor should leave understanding, whom it is told for, and
  each fact the exhibit states, with its sources and how sure it is. A stop can say one of those facts and take its
  sources from it, and can tell its caption three ways: for everyone, for young visitors, and in depth. The visitor
  picks with a switch on the panel, a gallery remembers the choice from room to room, and a kiosk's next visitor starts
  with everyone's words. When the expert signs off, the sign-off keeps a copy of every fact as they read it; if a fact
  is changed afterwards, the exhibit says so and asks for the expert again. Nobody but the expert signs, and the
  studio never says the facts are true. Every exhibit has a printable catalogue: what it sets out to teach, each stop
  in every audience's words, each fact with its sources and whether the expert has signed it.
- **Prepared states.** Show one exhibit at several settings and let visitors switch between them: a dam at three
  water levels, a cell before and after it divides, a city in two different years. A toggle, a slider or a carousel
  picks the version, a caption says what is different about it, and the view stays exactly where the visitor turned
  it, so the difference is all that changes. The arrow keys work too, and on a kiosk it steps through the versions by
  itself. Each version is made ahead of time, so it looks the same every time; it saves as a folder that opens offline,
  and it can be a room in a gallery.
- **Narration.** Each stop can be read aloud: give it a recording of its caption, made by the optional local voice, by
  your assistant if it can speak, or by a person, and the exhibit keeps it, so it plays on any machine with no voice
  installed. Visitors turn the sound on with a button (a browser plays nothing until someone touches the page); each
  stop speaks in the words they chose, for everyone, for young visitors or in depth, and when the exhibit plays itself
  on a kiosk it waits for the voice to finish. The caption always shows, so nobody needs the sound, and a stop without
  a recording is simply quiet. The check notices a quiet stop among spoken ones, and a recording that seems to belong
  to another stop.
- **An exhibit in a lesson plan.** Add an exhibit to the material for a lesson plan and the plan carries it: the
  exhibit travels inside the lesson's folder (it opens from there, with no internet), the learners' handout lists its
  stops in words for their age (the young visitors' captions for primary classes, the in-depth ones for university
  and professional groups), and the teacher's plan adds what the exhibit sets out to teach, about how long it takes,
  each fact with its sources and whether the expert has signed it, and how to show it on the web. Before, an exhibit
  in a lesson plan came out as an empty picture.
- **Two exhibits to start.** Pompeii in 79 CE: the town before the eruption, its people in that year's dress, a walk
  of nine stops from its walls and forum to its theatre, houses, water and painted election notices, told for
  everyone and for young visitors, every fact taken from the town's own cited record (and graded by how far that
  record checks it), with the expert's sign-off left open. And hydroelectric power, from water to wire: five toured
  rooms (the dam, the falling water, the turbine, the generator, the whole plant) and a room where the visitor changes
  the water's height, every number quoted being the one the exhibit computes. Ask your agent for either, or for one
  made the same way from your own notes and sources; the orientation gallery tours the first.

### The gun rooms: a shooter's practice before its levels

- The practice door now opens the gun rooms for a game that shoots, the way it opens the action room for one that
  fights hand to hand: the firing range (its guns tried on a range, measured) and the artillery range (a big gun on its
  base). Each is its own page, controls and HUD; nothing of the melee room's model is forced onto them.
- A world's guns are read from what it already carries (`gameworld/loadout.js` `loadoutOf`): a quick shooter's `arms`,
  the guns its hero holds, else its feel template's own loadout (Conscription a rifle, a handgun and a knife; Cogs of
  Combat a rifle, a shotgun and a handgun; Infinity Crisis a rifle and a launcher; Steel Serpents a handgun and a
  knife). No new recipe key.
- The door routes by how a game fights. A shooter's template (Conscription, Cogs of Combat, Infinity Crisis) has the
  firing range; so does any world whose hero carries a gun. Steel Serpents has the range (its pistol and its knife on V)
  and no longer the action room, which taught launchers and juggles its stealth game does not have. Galaxy Boy keeps
  the platform room: its buster is a platformer's.
- Mech Battle Kai owns its machine: a transforming biped of the mecha shelf, the rover walker (`TEMPLATE_FRAMES`). Its
  room is the artillery range on that frame: it walks on the walker's own gait, folds its legs into its wheeled form and
  drives, and fires its own mounts.
- Served at `bible?book=practice&room=range|artillery`, listed by design_game's readout and the rail, each with its
  icon (a crosshair, a shell).
- The firing range is measured before any level, on the world's own guns: each gun's laws from the combat book's
  measure (its cone widening on the move and tightening aimed, a spray blooming and climbing, the rounds to drop a body
  at each band), tallied in design_game's readout as `practice.measured.range` beside the feel's own measure. A law
  lost is advised as a `feel` step, never a refusal. The measures are kept by the guns they were taken on, so a
  readout does not measure the same guns twice. The readout's `practice` now lists its rooms under `rooms`.
- The run & gun joins the cube: a probe of its own (a street the game scrolls, guns in eight directions, slow rounds
  stepped off, friends dropping in), its gunplay a value of its own (`arcade`: rounds that fly, lobs and bursts, poise),
  both local until the brawler's door makes one from a gameworld; that door now says it opens the run & gun too. A
  brief that names it ("run & gun", "contra-style", "metal slug") reads as this genre; "run and gun" alone, which also
  says a platformer that shoots, only leans toward it.

### The lorecube: from a setting's lore to a power system the game can play

Planned on this branch. The first piece is built (the table of what opposes what); the lines after it are still
plans, and each is rewritten as it lands.

- **One table of what opposes what.** The studio already knew many element words, in several separate lists: the
  ones a character is coloured by, the ones that shape a hero's air moves, the ones a party's spells and a monster's
  weaknesses are written in, the ones a beast is grown by. None of them said how two elements stand to each other.
  Now one table does, over those lists and not beside them: two poles (light and dark), opposites in pairs (fire and
  water, wind and earth), a ring where each beats the next (the five phases; fire, ice and lightning), and a wheel
  where each is allied to its neighbours and opposed to the two across. You can name one or write your own, and it is
  checked so every element has a weakness and none stands over the rest. It also gives a monster of any element the
  weaknesses and resistances a party game reads. Nothing in a game uses it yet.
- **One description of a reserve of power, and which of the game's gauges can carry it.** A game already has several
  separate meters, each built for one job: the points special moves draw on, the meter air moves fly on, the stamina
  for sprinting and dodging, the stamina for guarding, the resource a hero's powers spend, and a party member's magic
  points. A setting usually has one idea ("an inner energy that drains as it is used"). You say its name and what
  empties it; later passes add how it comes back, what happens when it runs out, and its numbers. It then tells you
  which meter can carry it, what that meter cannot do, when one idea would end up as two separate bars on screen, and
  what nothing can do yet: pouring the reserve into an ordinary attack is named as a gap, with the smallest change
  that would close it. Nothing in a game uses it yet.
- **Who holds a share of the power, and what can be theirs alone.** A setting gives powers to sides: four factions, a
  light side and a dark side. A game has four kinds of thing a share can belong to: the hero, a class in a party, a
  monster, and a faction of the world. Each can have some things to itself (its element, its powers, its look), shares
  others with the whole game (there is one set of combos, one feel, one menu style per game), and cannot have the
  rest at all. This is now written down as one table, so when a setting asks two sides to differ by something a game
  has only one of, you are told before anything is built. It also says when a side's weakness has nowhere to land (a
  party member has no weaknesses today; a monster in a party game does) and when a side's reserve has no meter of its
  own. A faction, as things stand, is only how its things look. Nothing in a game uses the table yet.
- **A monster manual from a few lines.** Say which creatures a region has, what element each is of and what part it
  plays (the bulk, a quick second threat, a tougher test, the boss). The manual works out the rest so the set holds
  together: each creature is weak to whatever beats its element and resists its own, a boss soaks up its own element,
  and each is as strong as its part and how far into the game it is met. You can overrule any of it. It tells you
  when an element has no creature, when there is no boss, or when a tougher part is worth less than a lesser one. The
  result is written in the words a party role-playing game already uses for its monsters and their attacks, and is
  checked by that game's own rules. An action game's monsters cannot carry elements or weaknesses yet, and it says so.
- **A skill tree from a list of techniques.** Name a school, its element, and what each technique does (a bolt, a
  storm, an elemental blade, a ward, a rallying surge, a mend, a hex, a weakening). Then say how each is come by:
  learned as the class ranks up, or bought with points after the techniques it builds on. Costs follow from how deep
  a technique sits, and deeper ones hit harder; you can set your own. It warns when nothing is learned at the start,
  when techniques require each other in a circle, when one cannot be reached, or when one costs less than what it
  builds on. The result is a playable class and its skills in a party role-playing game's own words, checked by that
  game's rules. This is the first piece that reaches levelling.
- **Your setting's story, written down as it is, and carried into the game book.** Hand over the lore of a setting in
  whatever form it is in, and it is laid out without anything being added: who is in it, what happened in order and
  what each event came from, how the world stands where your text stops, what each side wants, where they stand against
  each other, what you planted and never came back to, and what the text does not say. Anything read between the lines
  is marked as such, with the reason. It does not name your eras, pick your protagonist or decide where the story
  starts: those are yours to say, and it records them only when you do. When you answer a question, only what you
  answered changes. It then reports, without deciding: events with no stated cause, stretches where nobody could act,
  conflicts two sides' wants imply that the text never states, and how much material there is for one story or
  several.
- **More lore can be added later.** A setting is rarely told in one go. When you come back with more, what you add
  (new sides, new places, events that belong earlier in the story) is set in where it belongs and everything that
  referred to the old order still points at the same things; nothing already there is reworded. When your text does
  not say when something happened against the rest, it is placed after what it must follow and marked as "when: not
  said", so the gap is visible and not papered over.
- **When you later say when something happened, it moves there.** An event first marked "when: not said" is set where
  you now say it belongs, and stops being marked.
- **Who leans on whom.** From what the text says passes between places (power, ore, goods, demand), the backdrop
  counts for each side what its places give and need, whom it draws from and whom it supplies, and which open
  conflicts it is in. It is a count from your own text, never a judgement of who is stronger.
- **What a side believes, and a disagreement nobody is fighting over.** Two more things a setting says: what a side
  takes to be true, which may not be (kept apart from what is true and from what it wants), and a difference the
  parties live with, which is neither settled nor an open fight.
- **A game can keep it.** The backdrop is saved on the game itself, shown in its game book (the events in order, where
  play begins, what is open and unsaid), and each chapter of the book is handed only its own part: the world chapter
  gets the places as history left them, the cast chapter the people and what they want, the story chapter what
  happened before play, the main quest the open conflicts and loose threads. A game without one is unchanged. It feeds
  the story's timing and the world's starting state, never a game mechanic.
- **Pictures of these relationships, drawn from the same data.** Each arrangement of elements and each reserve can be
  drawn as a diagram: the elements round a circle in their own colours with who beats, opposes and is allied to whom,
  and a reserve with what empties it and the meters that carry it. The drawings are made from the data and checked,
  so they cannot drift from it. A set is kept under `docs/lorecube/`.
- **Made in passes, so the first one stays small.** A piece of lore is made in two kinds of step. The first only
  commits to what the thing is (which elements, in what arrangement) and stops there, however much is asked. Every
  step after that deepens what exists (the reasons, later the numbers and the moves) and may not change what was
  already settled. So a first sketch is quick and stays yours, depth is added as many times as you want it, and a step
  that tries to do everything at once is told so.

- **Describe how power works in your world and get a system a game can play.** A magic system for four factions built
  on the elements; one energy with a light side and a dark side; a reserve that drains as it is used and can be poured
  into an ordinary attack; a faction's technology; a book of monsters. You say it roughly, in detail, or not at all,
  and the studio answers with a system that holds together.
- **Your idea stays yours.** Said roughly, the gaps are filled in. Said in detail, it is followed as written, and
  anything that cannot be built yet is named instead of being dropped.
- **You say what should be true, not how.** "The dark side hits harder and costs you something each time." The game is
  built to that, and you are told, outcome by outcome, whether it was delivered.
- **It starts where the story starts.** The system is first sketched when the game's premise is decided, in your
  words, and filled in when the game is made: the moves, their timing and cost, how each side looks and sounds, and
  how its menus are styled.
- **Sides that are different on purpose.** Factions, colours or poles are given their own share of what a game can do,
  so each plays differently, each has a weakness and none is simply best.

### The practice room's arsenal reaches the game: a world's `arsenal`, laid on every level's hero

- **A world's `arsenal`** (`gameworld/arsenal.js`): the weapons and strings the practice room plays, written once on the
  world. A template's kit by name (`'fallen-angel'`, `'fable-of-artesia'`), the kit with edits over it (`{ from, … }`:
  `art` and `ranged` replaced, `timing`, `mp` and `juggle` merged, weapons and their combos edited by id, `{ id, drop:
  true }` dropping one, a move merged field by field or `null` dropping it), `'auto'` (the kit of the feel's template, the
  nearer one that has a kit; none where neither has one), `false`, or a whole arsenal. Read with the world: a wrong word
  is said, a combo left on a dropped move is the combo manifest's own refusal.
- **Laid on every level** (`levels.js`, `armLevel`): the hero that strikes (a right-hand item serving `strike`), and each
  seat's copy of it, takes the weapons, the first one's moveset and the sidearm; the foes take the juggle's rules where
  they write none of their own. A weapon shown on the sheathed figure (the fist) is laid only on an action hero that
  sheathes its blade. Nothing written, or no hero that strikes: the level as it was, byte for byte.
- **Suggested, never laid** (`design_game`'s readout): an `arsenal` step suggests `'auto'` for a striking hero whose feel's
  template has a kit, with its patch; one written for a hero that strikes with nothing is said. The readout's `arsenal`
  names the kit, the weapons, the combos and the sidearm. The feel card says the key.
- **The room plays the game's arsenal** (`scripts/spikes/practice-room/room.mjs`): the world's `arsenal` when it writes
  one, `--kit` over it.
- **The practice room from the recipe, before any level** (`gameworld/practice-room.js`, its page
  `practice-room-page.js`): a world that writes a feel that fights hand to hand (or any feel with an arsenal) has a
  room. It is built from the world alone:
  - the feel template's own stage, greyboxed (the floor the stick view plays on), or the ring;
  - the hero: the run's own (its sketch and its sheathed twin) where made, else a stand-in on the template's body with
    the world's blade, sheathed out of a fight;
  - the foe: the bestiary's first, its sketch or a person of its class standing in, two metres ahead;
  - the arsenal: the world's, else the template's kit, else the basic one.
  
  The page measures the foe's health on the resolved bodies and lays the HUD (frame data beside the card, the combos,
  every press taken or dropped and why). It is served on read as `bible?book=practice` (`cast=female` for the stand-in)
  and linked from design_game's readout (`practiceRoom`) and the rail. `room.mjs` is its CLI (`--kit`, `--combos`,
  `--art`, `--hero`, `--cast` over the game's). Checked in headless Chrome: a template's room comes up with no error,
  and three clicks play its L L L string, each press taken and all three blows landing.
- **The feel measured: the feel chapter's machine gate** (`gameworld/feel/measure.js`). The room's hero is played
  headless on the runtime the game ships, each number beside what was asked: carried, partly or lost.
  - The kit: every ground combo of every weapon as written, each move's contact in its window, its chain at its cancel
    or its length, less its own hitstop, and its travel.
  - The card: the hitstop, the foe's stun, the dodge's frames and invincible frames, the parry window.
  - Not measured, and named: air strings and the sidearm's press.
  
  design_game's readout carries it as `feel.measured`: the tally, and the lines that fell short or were lost; a loss is
  a `feel` step in `next`. `measure.mjs` is now its CLI (`--feel`, `--game`, `--page`). What it found on the templates'
  rooms: every kit carried move by move. The card's stun falls short on every template that asks it (13 or 14 frames
  where it asks 27 or 30: its hitstun is not lowered onto the foe), and the dodge is invincible all through where the
  card opens a window.
- **The practice door** (`gameworld/practice.js`): which practice rooms a game's play has, chosen by how it plays, each
  built from the world alone before any level.
  - The action room (`room=practice`): a template that fights hand to hand, or any world with an arsenal.
  - The platform room (`room=platform`, `gameworld/platform-room.js`): a platformer's template. Its course has steps, a
    gap, the double jump's ledge and the wall kick's chimney, with walkers and a hopper to stomp. The hero stomps and is
    touched as a level's hero is.
  - The mount lane (`room=mount`, `gameworld/mount-lane.js`): any world with `mounts`. The world's horse stands at the
    start of a posted 200 m lane, with a timed 100 m split, three fences at the horse's jump heights and a ring to turn
    in.

  The run's hero and foes play where they have been made, stand-ins (the template's body, a person of the foe's class)
  where they have not.
- **Templates whose fights are another runtime's have no action room.** The fighting game is practised in its own lab;
  the RPG's fights are its battles. The door says so.
- **Mounts suggested for a template that rides** (Fable of Artesia, after Zelda's horse): design_game's readout has a
  `mounts` step with its patch, never laid.
- **Served and linked:**
  - `bible?book=practice&room=…`: the first room by default; a room the world lacks is a 422 saying which it has;
  - design_game's readout `practice` (each room's link);
  - the rail's exits (one per room, each its icon).

  The platform room's and the mount lane's spikes are now CLIs over their pages.
- **Checked in headless Chrome** (`practice-room.live.test.js`): each room comes up with no error. The action room's
  string lands; the platform room's hero jumps, its four foes standing; the mount lane's hero gets on and rides the
  horse on down the lane.

### Publications: the books a world keeps, printed and read in play

- **A grimoire, a bestiary, a manual or a notebook is now one small recipe, and it is read three ways.** Printed as a
  book on the press (with a PDF), opened as a book held in the hands (two pages side by side, turned with the arrows,
  a click or a swipe), and found in a level. The pages are the same in all three, so the book a player reads is the
  book that prints. A recipe is words and blocks, never html: paragraphs, headings, notes, remarks in the margin,
  numbered entries, a creature's numbers, tables, drawn plates, and figures another tool made.
- **A level can keep a library.** `play.library: [{ id, book, found? }]` puts books on a shelf the player opens with L.
  A book is there from the start, or joins the shelf when a flag is set (a scene, an answer or a cue sets it), and a
  word shows at the top when it does. The shelf holds the world as a menu does; a cover opens the book, the arrows
  turn it, Escape closes it. A level without a library is unchanged.
- **Illustrations without writing forms by hand.** A shelf of small things already built (a still, a vial, a cup, a
  candle, a book, an orb, a crystal, a sword, a shield, a skull, a toadstool) can be stood up to four in a row as a
  still life, each in a tint, and drawn as a plate with its viewpoint and light set for what it holds.
- **The lorecube's parts can be published.** A monster manual becomes a bestiary (a chapter an element, an entry a
  creature, with what it fears and its numbers once those are settled); a skill tree becomes a grimoire (the school,
  then a chapter a tier, each technique with how it is come by and what it costs). Both are written from the lore's
  own data, with its diagram set in, and leave out whatever a later pass has not yet said.
- **Three forms brought over from the studio's publisher.** A **comic** is a new kind of publication: each page is
  a grid of panels (seven layouts, from one full panel to a splash over three), each panel a picture with a caption
  box and up to three balloons, and a comic can be set to read right to left. A **specimen** is a field guide's entry:
  the picture, its number and name, a second name, its marks and a description; a bestiary is now made of them, one a
  creature. A **cover** gives a book a front: the studio's cover layouts with a drawn plate where the illustration
  goes, on a cloth of its kind's colour. The cover is the book's first page in print and in the open book, and it is
  what a level's shelf shows; a book without one keeps a plain binding.
- **From the shell:** `node scripts/publication.mjs <out-dir> [--pdf]` writes the examples (a notebook, a handbook, a
  comic, the sample bestiary and grimoire) as press pages, open books and PDFs.
- **Not yet:** no door mints a publication (a recipe is written into a level or handed to the functions); the game
  designer, the bibles and the table RPG's game book do not make one; a book is found by a flag, not as an item or a
  place in the world; publications are not a department and join no chapter of the game book. A level's page carries
  each book whole, so a book of engravings adds a megabyte or more to it.

### The SFX shelf by intent, and a game's sounds solved from the game

- **Mouth foley's bodies join the shelf** (`sets/mouth.js`, traced by `scripts/mouth-foley/bake.mjs`). A new
  renderer (`scripts/mouth-foley/body.py`) builds a sound from syllables cut once, then held, layered or struck
  under ~150 ms. It renders the takes the operator passed by ear sample for sample. Eighteen new rows in its first
  round, all voiced only by the mouth:
  - creatures (a new category, `creature`): `growl`, `snarl`, and `roar-lion`, `roar-bear`, `roar-monster` (a
    first vowel opening into A, rising; the monster's I starts high and ends higher);
  - martial arts: `staff-swing`, `staff-twirl` ("whop whop"), `nunchaku`;
  - the ch sounds: `sword-guard` チャキッ, `latch` カチャ, `armour-clank` ガチャ, `spark` パチッ,
    `electric-crackle` バチバチ, `drip` ピチャ, `scissors` チョキン, `ticking` カチカチ;
  - `wade` バシャッ and `fire-crackle` パチパチ.

  The mouth also voices five rows already on the shelf: `step-grass`, `punch`, `kick`, `ricochet` and `coin-drop`.
  A second round adds:
  - new rows: `slide`, `stab`, `shuriken`, `sparkle`, `eat`, and two short lion roars (`roar-lion-short`,
    `roar-lion-rough`);
  - a mouth voice for `jump`, `bounce-pad`, `land`, `dodge`, `hit`, `uppercut`, `down`, `katana-draw`,
    `katana-sheathe`, `blade-clash`, `arrow-hit` and `potion-drink`.
  A third round adds:
  - new rows: `power-up-rings`, `power-up-glass`, `bubbles`, `bubbling`, `button`, `rattle`, `bucket-splash` and
    `horse-neigh`;
  - a mouth voice for `power-up`, `door-creak`, `lever`, `wood-impact` and `metal-impact`;
  - the giant monster's roar, now traced as air: one voiced trace carries one pitch and lost the screech.

  A whistle is stored as its cue, the kernel's own tones, with nothing traced: `bird-chirp`, `sparrow`, `bird-trill`
  and `bird-warble`. `step-wood` and `step-metal` gain a heel-and-toe mouth voice. Each ring is placed from the
  trace's onset, not its time in the file, so a ring sounds with its click (it had sounded about 0.1 s late). A
  `tone`'s `to` takes Hz, as `hz` does. `dog-bark` and `cat-hiss` are two bird calls the operator heard as those.
  `traceSound` takes `maxHz`, the highest pitch it looks for a hum at (500 by default, a voice's, so every existing
  trace is unchanged). A recipe raises it for a bird's buzz, which as air traced as band noise and sounded like
  sandpaper.
  A ring is never traced, since the tracer would hear it as hiss. The bake traces the dry part and strikes each ring
  with the kernel's own `ring` gesture, at its modes, time, level and length. The round 5 traces are byte for byte
  as they were.
- **Searchable by intent** (`sfx-shelf/facets.js`, `sfx-shelf/find.js`):
  - **Facets:** what a sound is made of (`matter`), how big it is (`weight`) and which games use it (`genres`, the
    cosmos genre ids). Each is set once on a family, read off the dials a row is built at, or written on a row
    where neither says it.
  - **Sound words:** a row's `say` holds its onomatopoeia, in kana with romaji and in English, so カチャ, kacha and
    clink each find their sound.
  - **`findSounds`** ranks by words and filters by facets. A word that names two things is read by the rest of the
    phrase: "a crackling fire" is the fire, and "fire" alone is still the shot.
  - **`solveSound`** sets a family's dials from the words: "heavy footsteps on gravel" is `step-gravel` at
    `body: heavy`.
  - **`suggestSounds`** gives the shelf's rows as a refusal's tail.
  - Ties go to the newest voices.
- **The sound sheet** (`gameworld/sound-sheet.js`, the game book's new `sound` chapter in the play department). A
  game's sounds are solved from what the game is:
  - its first weapon by its words (a staff's `staff-swing`, nunchaku, a katana's swing, a blade's, a fist's);
  - its level's ground (grass on a nature or jungle stage);
  - its beasts' voices by species (a wolf's `snarl` when it spots the hero);
  - a door's `latch`.

  The newest voices come first: the sheet's style is `mouth` unless the game says otherwise, so a sound the mouth
  doesn't voice plays realistic. A game overrides any of it with `sound: { style?, slots?, on? }`, each a shelf word.
  A quick game hears it with `sfx: 'sheet'`. `beats-world.js` voices `sfx: { sheet }`, wiring the level's mechanics'
  events as `auto` wires a palette. `auto` and the palettes are unchanged, so every game made before this sounds as
  it did.
- **A bird's call in the kernel** (feature `syrinx`, opt-in, absent from a page that uses none). A `syrinx` gesture
  synthesizes a call whole: a sawtooth on a pitch path, its period jittered, an octave under it for a caw's
  harshness, a rattle, and a breath of noise, through the bird's moving resonances (`beats-sfx` manual). A tonal
  call traced through the vocoder sounded like sandpaper or a trumpet; this one is played as it was built. The birds on the shelf are syrinx cues: `crow`, `raven`,
  `eagle`, `goose`, `geese`, `duck` and `chicken`. A game's sound sheet voices a fielded animal by its species (a
  dog barks, a horse neighs, a crow caws, a snake rattles). What a game's environments need most:
  - footsteps on gravel, snow, dirt, sand, mud, a puddle and dry leaves;
  - a raindrop, thunder near and far;
  - a cricket, a frog, an owl and a fly;
  - a siren.

  A sound sheet reads a stage kit's ground from its name (a snowy stage walks on snow).
- **Played as a performer plays them.**
  - **Per-hit variation reaches traces and the syrinx.** Each hit's noise, bands, hum, pace and level move a
    little, seeded per hit, so a combo or a walk never repeats one sound. An older page's kernel is unchanged.
  - **Beds** (`sfx-shelf/beds.js`): rain, night, forest, cave, swamp and farm, as patterns of the shelf's one-shots.
    Every hit is a variant, and so is every loop pass.
  - **One breath across a sheet game's hits** (`audio.breath`): a fast combo lightens and a rest refills it. A level
    without a sheet carries none of it.
  - **The firing range and the practice rooms vary every shot and swing** for a game on the sound sheet, or one whose
    `sound.vary` says so: a sword combo, a burst of fire, a beam rifle's shots. A game made before is unchanged.
  - **A level plays its environment's bed under its score** (`audio.bed`, on its own engine). A game on the sound
    sheet lays one from its stage, by the stage kit's name, its weather and its hour: rain, a cave, a swamp, a farm,
    night, a forest.
- **The voice protoform** (`families/voice.js`): a person's efforts composed for any voice from its dials (body,
  sex, age, rough, breathy), never recorded voice by voice. A glottal buzz goes through the vocal tract's formants,
  scaled by its length, with its breath through the same tract. Rows: a jump's hup, a grunt on a hit, a heavy hit's
  cry, a landing's oof, an attack's shout and a strain. The kernel's `syrinx` takes `buzz` (0: breath alone, a pressed
  effort's hiss).

### Mouth foley: sound effects traced from a voice

- **The `trace` gesture** (kernel feature `trace`, opt-in): a noise vocoder. Fixed bands each follow a lane of levels,
  frame by frame, over seeded noise (`air`) and a sawtooth following a pitch lane (`hum`), with a pan lane (`side`).
  It is how a voice's sound becomes a recipe: numbers traced from it, synthesized on play. The kernel stays
  synthesized, never sampled; a page that uses no trace gets no new bytes.
- **The tracer** (`sfx-shelf/trace.js`, pure): a rendered sound in, a trace gesture out, quantized to whole dB.
- **The `mouth` style and set** (`sfx-shelf/sets/mouth.js`): swishes, swooshes and swings made the way a vocal
  sound-effect performer makes them. Kokoro says a sound word (Japanese manga words: シュッ, ザシュッ, ヒュン, ブン,
  スパッ …), the vowel is cut out, the air is swept, panned and layered, and the result is traced. Voiced: `swing`,
  `blade-swing`, `katana-swing` (the katana's own synth with the traced voice under it), `net-swish`, and a new row,
  `swell-in` (a reversed swish). The katana has no heavy cut here (cut air sounds the same light or hard):
  `katana-heavy-swing` is the swing's sound. Falls back to `realistic`.
- **The bake** (`scripts/mouth-foley/`): renders the recipes through the local voice worker and traces them into the
  generated `sfx-shelf/sets/mouth-traces.js`. Kokoro is needed only to re-bake; playing and exporting never need it.

### The game studio says what a first session needs before the gate

One brief run through `design_game` twice showed the door let a game of several departments be built with no intent
on record, refused wrong words without naming the page's manual, and kept a run's advice inside each step. Three
changes to what the door says; nothing refuses that did not refuse before.

- **A book that stands on an intent says when it has none.** A gameworld with a hero, a main quest or a bestiary a
  hand wrote, and no ask on its ledger, carries `advice.intent` and leads `next` with `{ step: 'ask' }`. The call
  that cuts the ask answers it at once. A quick game and a composed world are one call by design and are left alone.
- **A game built with no ask is stamped.** A run that makes the game with no ask on record writes `unasked: true` on
  the game's entry in the gameworld's build ledger (`made.game`), and a run an ask links lifts it. The stamp is the
  ledger's alone: the game's row, its levels and everything that renders or exports are byte for byte what they were,
  and no game made before this is touched.
- **A refusal ends with the card its page is written from.** A refused gameworld page (`characters: hero.actions…`,
  `gameworld: foes.<id>…`) now ends `read first: get_game_vocab({ id: '<card>' })`, the card of the chapter that owns
  the path (`chapters.js`); a path inside a level names the level page's cards; a refusal that already names a manual
  is unchanged. The guide card says the book starts from a ticket (its ceiling re-pinned for the one line).
- **A run's advice is read whole.** Each distinct line a run's steps advised is lifted into `advice.run` as
  `{ says, steps }`, in the full and the changed readout; each step keeps its own.

- **A level's plan is verified before anything is walked.** `lib/graph/gameworld/level-plan.js` reads the recipe and
  the stages a run would make, with no browser. A beat that is one boss alone is a duel: its level stands one and is
  won by clearing it. A beat that fields foes is played on a level that stands them. A stage lays a win that can be
  reached (one won by clearing it has something stood to clear). What it finds is `advice.plan`, with the write that
  would lay it offered in `next` (`{ step: 'plan', patch }`); the level stays the creator's.
- **A check that walks no level says why.** The walk stays all or nothing, and no longer runs while a level's plan is
  known wrong. With `check: true` and nothing walked, `audits` is `{ gate, proved: 0, of, plan?, unwalked? }` where it
  used to be absent: the plan's findings, and each stage the walk cannot prove with its reason. The `first-level`
  goalpost quotes the first of them instead of asking for a check that was already run. `compile.walk` carries the same.

New: `lib/graph/gameworld/routing.js` and `lib/graph/gameworld/level-plan.js` (both pure). Still to come on this theme:
a beat's place words reaching the level laid for it.

### Design and code rails aligned: a game made from a sentence is one a player can win

Two action games were made end to end from a sentence (a stylish action game and an anime action RPG), exported and
played by a scripted player on the shipped pages. Every level built and loaded and every action piece ran, and no level
could be won: the rails wrote what the runtime does not play, and the hero, its blows and its foes were numbered in three
scales. The player gate is built, the page binds what its legend says, the sentence door reads the action genres and
lays their camera, a world with an arsenal numbers its foes in its kit's strings, and the casting call reads the kit; the
rest below is designed, not built yet.

- **The playthrough: a made level played by a scripted player** (`gameworld/playthrough.js`). A level is resolved as its
  page resolves it and played headless on the runtime it ships, in about a second: the BASIC player fights the foe in
  its face first, turns the sidearm on a shooter within its range (the lock cycled until it holds that foe; closing on it
  when the lock will not take or it stands too far), locks on, closes, plays the light string at a person's pace, guards
  between strings, hops when it gains no ground and leaves a foe it cannot reach for another (it has no pathfinding),
  and walks to the way on once no foe stands; the STILL player holds no input. It reports won or lost, when, the hero's
  hp, the foes downed, who hit the hero most and what it could not reach. A level passes when the basic player wins it
  and the still one does not. Machine gate only; nobody has looked.
- **Where it runs.** `node scripts/playthrough.mjs <world ref> [--level <key>]` plays every made level of a game (PASS /
  FAIL a level). `design_game` with `run: true, check: true` plays each level where foes stand and the hero plays a
  moveset, in order while the run's budget lasts (the first always; the rest named `unplayed`): the readout's
  `playthrough` (each level's verdict in a line), and a `playthrough` step in `next` naming the levels the basic player
  lost (advice, never a refusal; the `gameworld-next` card says it).
- **The level sim runs what the page runs** (`game/level-sim.js`). The stats kernel steps as the page's watch loop steps
  it, and the stats bound to bodies (the hero's hp) reach them; the world's own options the page hands its runtime (the
  lock, the minds' tuning, a match, the seats, the tempo, the knock) reach it when given (`world`). Absent, every sim as
  it was.
- **Fixed: a killing blow left a body with no poise standing** (`worlds/controllable/combat-hit.js` `armReaction`). A
  hero whose hp the stats bind carries no poise, and a blade or a round that took it to 0 left it up at 0 hp: its level
  never failed (only a foe's touch or a beam downed it). It is now downed, as the ranged path's own comment meant. Every
  page that inlines the runtime changes its bytes (sixteen emit pins re-pinned).
- **Fixed: a moveset's mouse never struck under a camera that does not capture it** (`scene/channels/controllable`). Its
  beats (the light, the heavy, the special, the weapon cycle) were bound only under a mouse-look camera, so on a follow
  camera a click did nothing while the legend said "click strike" (only a pad struck). On such a camera a press now
  strikes at once; a drag still looks. A page whose hero plays no moveset is byte for byte as it was.
- **Fixed: a page with both rims threw on load.** The target rim (the foe the hero targets) and the effect rim (the cast
  lit by its effects) each declared a page-level `__rimMat`; a hero whose power has a look, on a level with lock-on,
  threw "Identifier '__rimMat' has already been declared" and every level stayed blank. The target rim's is its own now.
  The fixture matrix gains that combination (`action-hero`: a moveset's hero, its lock on a foe wearing the target rim,
  a rimmed cast), so the parse gate holds every page that carries it, and a live check (`action-hero.live.test.js`)
  brings it up in headless Chrome with no error and strikes with the mouse on both kinds of camera.
- **Fixed: a styled moment's halo threw where nothing explodes** (`scene/channels/moment-channel.js`). A styled floor
  rings any moment that flashes with a halo in the air (`scene/effect-style.js`), and the air's sprite was declared only
  on a page with an explosion: on a page whose moments flash but nothing explodes, the first such moment threw
  "__moAir is not defined". The sprite is declared wherever moments are; a page with an explosion is byte for byte as
  it was. Found by the channel contract lint on the new `action-hero` fixture.
- **The sentence door reads the action genres** (`gameworld/intent.js`). "Stylish action" and "character action" name
  the stylish action game, "action rpg", "action-rpg" and "arpg" the action RPG; and a name said inside another genre's
  longer name is that one's: "an anime action rpg like zelda" composed a turn-based party RPG (whose name is "rpg"), and
  composes the action RPG now; "an open world rpg", a tie read as nothing, is the long RPG. "An rpg" is the party RPG,
  as it was. A world of either genre that writes no feel is suggested its template (`feel/suggest.js`: Fallen Angel for
  stylish action, Fable of Artesia for the action RPG), never laid.
- **The sentence door lays the camera the genre asks** (`gameworld/genre-forms.js`). The orbit camera (and the 3D
  platformer's follow) were missing from the cameras a genre's frame writes, so both action genres were laid on the
  default chase: tank turning, no mouse look, no lock-on. A stylish action game or an action RPG composed from a
  sentence now writes `camera: 'orbit'`, and its levels' striking hero runs where the camera looks, turns it by the
  mouse and locks on (C). A genre whose hero takes the default chase writes none, as before.
- **One scale: a world with an arsenal numbers its foes by its kit** (`gameworld/arsenal.js`). A foe's health came from
  the foe shelf's frame, a hero blow of 20, while a blade deals about 2: an elite took some 120 cuts and a boss 300. A
  world that writes an arsenal now gives each foe the strings its rank takes (`STRINGS_BY_RANK`: a grunt one, an elite
  three and a half, a boss eleven) times what the kit's first light string deals on a normal blade (`stringDamage`):
  with either template's kit a grunt carries 8, an elite 28, a boss 88 (were 40, 240, 600). The hero's own health is
  as it was: it already takes ten hits. A world with no arsenal keeps every byte. On the Zelda-like game made from its
  sentence and armed with Fable of Artesia's kit, the crossing is now won (46 s, 14 of 20 hp left); the other fight
  levels fall to the archers and the boss's counter, the casting call's to fix.
- **The playthrough plays as a person would, a little more**: arrows that do not tell (six loosed with the foe's health
  unchanged) give way to closing in; a level where no foe stands is no fight (the walk audit's), said, never failed.
- **The casting call reads the hero's kit** (`gameworld/foe-casting.js`). A hero that plays strings (the cube's moveset,
  or the kit its world or its feel's template carries) meets its foes blade to blade: the grunt, the elite and the boss
  are cast from the classes that come within the blade's reach on the ground, never a flier and never a mind that
  stuffs every swing it sees with a charge (the opportunist's counter, beaten only by a roll: the stalker the action
  RPG's boss used to be), and the boss is cast before the elite, the heaviest such body its own. A foe that shoots is
  cast only where the hero's sidearm answers a shot as a shot does, straight and at once (an automatic: Fallen Angel's
  pistols), and stands where it is; with a bow (an arrow's flight and drop is no answer to a rifle at thirty metres) the
  harrier is a flanker on foot. Every other game is cast as before, and the roles are said in their order of record. The
  Zelda-like sentence now casts a charger, a guard, a patrol elite and a brute boss (was a charger, a rifle hunter, a
  brute elite and a stalker boss), and its first two stages' fight levels are won, three of six in all.
- **What the gate found first, on the anime action RPG** (no level won): in the town square the basic player downs two
  of four foes and goes down at 87 s; on the crossing it shoots the archer down, downs the first charger, then needs
  about two minutes and 278 presses for the 240-hp elite and goes down at 168 s; on the boss's heights the boss's counter
  (the opportunist mind's tackle, which beats any swing it sees) answers every string and the sword never lands. The
  still player goes down at 22 to 45 s wherever foes reach it.
- Found and not fixed here: a foe climbs the forest's foliage (the ground probe stands a body on the `spray` faces, the
  page's as the sim's), so the boss can end up on a canopy five metres over the hero, out of the blade's reach.
- **The hero a player pilots runs the engagement run, sword sheathed** (`worlds/world-kinds.js` the pilot's run,
