  `polygonizer/hero-swing-body.js` `carryArm`). Out of combat the hero ran its gait with a layer setting its legs 6°
  apart, which flicked the folded shank out sideways each stride, both forearms pumping high across the chest: it read as
  a mincing run. In a fight it ran the same gait with no such layer and its sword arm carried low. Now every game's
  piloted hero runs that way out of combat too: the legs as the gait sets them, the right arm held relaxed by the hip
  (an empty hand is held, not solved: `CARRY.empty`), the other arm swinging; a hand holding a blade is carried as it
  was. The walk, foes and walkers are as they were. Every page with a piloted hero changes its bytes.
- **The sentence door lays an action RPG as a world map** (`gameworld/world-map.js`, `gameworld/compose.js`). The action
  RPG's cube asks for one map travelled zone to zone (`worldMap: 'zones'` on `levelForm: 'map'`), and the door laid a
  run of trail walks joined by roads instead (and, tried by hand, a platformer's course of raised walkways: an action
  RPG walks the land). It now lays one planned map: its first zone the first three blocks on one page (a village, a
  road, old ruins), a zone a block after it, the last a castle's heights holding the goal; topology `interconnected`. Its
  scenario stands each beat on a tile of the default ways in the first zone's teaching order (the first look, a lone
  foe and the blow, the road and the sprint, a pack with the lock-on and the dodge, a breath, the zone's captain held as
  its way out), each further zone a fight held as its way out and a breath after it, then the climb and the boss; its
  laws hold for a first zone alone and for one with zones after it. The casting call fields the map's roles. Every other
  genre is laid as before.
- **The readout says the first slice and the map's work** (`design_game` `next`, the `gameworld-next` card): `room`, the
  combat room to play before any level is made, for a hero that fights hand to hand; `worldmap`, a map whose blocks are
  still the floor: the segments req (each block's ground, heights and marks), then its play layer from each block's
  brief.
- **The playthrough reads what a person sees.** Two things the basic player did that no person does, found on the two
  games made from their sentences on the merged tree:
  - It shoots only down a clear line. On the stylish action game's first level it loosed a burst into the hero's own
    cover (a wall five metres ahead), judged the pistols told nothing, never drew them on that shooter again and walked
    down its lane to it: down at 16.5 s. A shooter behind a wall is now closed on until the line opens, then shot; rounds
    loosed into a wall say nothing of whether the sidearm tells.
  - It raises the guard to a charge it sees coming. A rushing foe braces before it charges (its telegraph) and the
    runtime stops a charge on a guard up in front of it (`worlds/controllable/foe.js` `guarded`); the player walked into
    each one. It now turns to a foe braced or on its line and holds the guard until the charge is spent; in the blade's
    reach a braced foe is cut down instead.
  Still the floor of play: no dodge, no specials, no air strings.
- **A boss's phases never step into the counter a string cannot answer** (`gameworld/arsenal.js` `bossPhases`). A boss
  steps its temper up as its health falls, and one step up from bold is the opportunist, whose counter stuffs every swing
  it sees: the mind the casting call keeps away from a hero that plays strings came back at two thirds of the boss's
  health, a 4.5 s shove answering each press. In a world armed with a kit the boss's phases are written out, each to the
  next temper that answers a string by being cut. A boss that writes its own phases, one that never meets the counter,
  and every world with no arsenal are as they were.
- **Measured on the merged tree, each game made afresh from its sentence and armed with its feel's kit** (machine gate
  only; nobody has looked): the stylish action game, six of six fight levels won by the basic player and none by the
  still one (was one of three); the action RPG's world map, three of three fight zones (was one of three). On the
  action RPG the basic player ends every zone at full health: its foes can be won against, and do not yet press.
- **The verdict is kept and the bible says it** (`gameworld/made.js` `play`, `gameworld/bible-html.js`). A check's
  playthrough is kept in the run's record beside each level it judged, as its opening frame's verdict is, and the
  world's bible says under each level how its stages played: won by a player who fights and not by one who stands
  still, or not yet, with what each player did. A level remade drops it with its record.
- **Fixed: a world laid as a map had no bible.** The world's bible drew a walk, a building, a city, a town, an airspace
  and a roadway, and threw on a map level: every action RPG made from a sentence since the map was laid had none. A map
  level is drawn in plan: its blocks in their places by name, the walk through them, the blocks one page shows together,
  the goal, and who each block's fights stand.
- Found and not fixed here:
  - a mind's ground snap is cast from its head (`worlds/controllable/mind.js` `standOnGround`), so a body stands on
    whatever is lower than its head: a boss of 3.4 m steps onto a tomb's lid and then the storey above it, out of the
    blade's reach. The forest's canopy, said above, is the same seam. The fix is the runtime's (every page that carries a mind
    changes its bytes), so it is left for its own step;
  - the brute's blow is written as one that cannot be blocked (the lab's red zone) and the runtime blocks it: the boss
    is won with the guard alone;
  - the stylish action game's shooters open fire at fourteen metres and the hero's pistols reach thirty.
- Designed, not built yet: a changed genre answered with what it left behind; the loop's encounter from the terminals.

### The crypt in ashlar: the dungeon room, graver

- **A second crypt, `gothic-ashlar`** (`era/stage.js`, `era/style/crypt.js` `CRYPT_SOBER`): the gothic-stone vault and
  its dressing in a graver register, for a room that should read as built stone at its own scale and not as a pattern
  of blocks. Gothic-stone outlines every stone (a deep black joint round a pillowed, bright face, each block its own
  value), frames its niches in pale stone, carves a key along its plinth and stands a barrel in its corner. The new
  card lays dressed ashlar (long low courses a third of a metre high and over a metre long, thin joints, a tooled
  face, each block's tone close to its neighbour's), which the form render reads as its true relief; a floor of large
  worn slabs; pilasters of one plain monolith's stone, slimmer, over a lower plinth and under a lighter cornice;
  arches, niches and the vault cut in more than twice the pieces, so a curve is a curve; its motif a low band of
  dentils under the cornice in the wall's own tone; torches set
  higher with a longer reach, so a tall wall is lit up its height and the vault is lost above them. Its dressing is
  the crypt's with the same principles, sober: thin dark-backed niches, a grey tomb that takes the candles' light
  and never burns white, fewer and lower candles, the accent wall in large calm blocks of the same dressed stone,
  moss and grime a stain and not a stripe, and the corner things a vault holds (stones, a boulder, planks, debris).
  It is made for tall rooms: give it height.
- **The seventh generation's laws, written down** (`era/laws.js`, the laws marked `form`). The rooms are placed by
  principles, not by hand: a style card states them, the laws table counts each as a shared law, and the dressing
  applies them by seeded dice. Those laws were the sixth generation's, and read again several were limits of its
  frame and its light, not tastes: detail sized to be read at 640 by 448, contrast drawn into the tile because the
  light could not make it, shapes faceted because a curve cost vertices, shade lifted because black was a hole. The
  form render answers each: `built-scale` (an element is the size it is built at), `relief-is-material` (a joint is
  relief the light finds, no line is drawn), `value-by-light` (a surface's elements close in tone, the contrast the
  light's), `true-curves`, `dark-is-a-place`, `live-emitters`. The composition laws (focus, the repeat, the accent
  wall, corners, causes, height) hold in both eras and are untouched.
- **The design pass stated as principles, and held to them.** The ashlar crypt's card states its form register's
  principles (`CRYPT_SOBER.form`, counted as `crypt/form`), and a kit is measured against the laws a card's numbers
  can answer (`era/form-laws.js` `readFormKit`: a course's height, a slab's size, what stands proud of a wall, the
  generator, a block's tone against its neighbour's, the pieces a curve is cut in, the torches' height, the
  vault's tint). The ashlar crypt keeps every one; gothic-stone, read the same way, is told which of its numbers
  are its era's (its blocks drawn and each its own value, its curves faceted). Writing the principles down
  corrected the pass itself: the first cut had dropped the crypt's motif, which its own principle keeps (a motif
  is small, in a band), so it is back as cut stone and not as paint.
- **More in the kit, each as a law first.** Three things the ashlar crypt gained, each stated as a principle, counted
  as a law and measured on the card:
  - *Nothing is a box on its first pass* (`no-voxel-first`, a craft law of both eras). Its torch is turned: a cone
    of iron, point down, with a rolled lip, held in a ring on an arm that is a rod (`era/stage.js` `torchFaces`, a
    kit's `torch.form: 'cone'`). The sixth generation's read stands its flame's two cards in the cone; the form
    render's its live flame.
  - *A column is worked, never a flat strip* (`pillars-are-worked`, both eras). Its pilasters are cut in parts as
    a column is (a base, a ring, a capital, each a little proud: a kit's `pilaster.bands`) over a fluted shaft
    (the dressed `fluted` cut as the pillars' own tile).
  - *A wall has layers* (`layers-stand-proud`, the seventh generation's). Its walls wear a coat of lime render
    over the ashlar, fallen away in patches to the courses behind (the dressed `render` cut). The coat stands
    proud, and in the form render its broken edge casts its shadow on the stone and takes the torch's light.
  Gothic-stone, measured by the same reader, is told its torch is boxes and its pilaster a flat strip; it is not
  changed.
- **A wall keeps a rhythm** (`wall-rhythm`, a craft law of both eras; `era/wall-rhythm.js`). Along one wall at most
  two neighbouring bays look alike, and a pair is never followed by the same pair: four bays are ABBA or BAAB, never
  AAAA or ABAB; five are AABAA or BBABB. The rule is local, two checks on what stands side by side, the same on a
  wall of two bays as on one of ten (a pair alike is allowed anywhere, so a short wall is solved as it stands), and
  that a wall needs two kinds follows from it. A mirrored order is taken where the length has one: a wall is built
  from its middle. Three is its own case: a wall of exactly three bays is ABA or BAB alone, the odd one in the
  middle (AAB keeps both checks and still reads lopsided). The second kind of bay is derived, the first with less on it: in the ashlar crypt a bay with one
  niche where its neighbour has two, and nothing in it (`era/crypt.js`, a card's `niches.rhythm`). The rhythm is
  what a wall reaches for unasked. A wall all alike is a stated choice (a stage's `rhythm: 'same'`), and then every
  bay is drawn clean and repeatable: no urn, no sealed niche, nothing that marks one bay from the next.
- **A wall's tile by the bay** (a kit's `tiles.wall.perBay`, as a floor's). Seen on the first render of the rhythm:
  the coat's patches were the same stamp in every bay. Each bay now takes its own variant of the wall's tile.
- **A floor is laid, not tiled** (`floor-is-laid`, a craft law of both eras; a kit's `floorPlan`, `era/stage.js`).
  The ashlar crypt's floor is no longer one field of tile. A border course runs round the room along its walls, its
  slabs' long side along the wall, a tone darker: nobody walks there. The walk runs down the room's long axis to
  the tomb, in larger slabs laid along the way, a tone lighter: worn. The fields either side are laid bay by bay,
  their joints on the pilasters' lines, and along the room they keep the walls' rhythm, the second kind of bay the
  same slabs turned a quarter. A stage's `rhythm: 'same'` lays every bay alike.
- **A threshold and an apron** (`floorPlan.threshold`, `floorPlan.apron`). Inside each doorway a threshold: larger
  slabs laid across the way in, worn by everyone who comes through. Round the tomb an apron, its dais and a walk
  round it, laid across the walk and darkened by its candles (`era/crypt.js` `tombSite`: where the tomb will stand,
  before it is built). Both are laid over the rest, which is cut round them: no part lies on another and none is
  missing (a test holds the floor's parts to the floor's whole).
- **Why a floor is not one shade** (`era/floor-shades.js`). The same stone laid the same way is seen in different
  shades across one room, and each shade has a cause, said in words beside its numbers: `worn` (feet polish stone:
  the walk, a threshold; lighter), `unwalked` (dust lies where nobody steps: the course along a wall; darker),
  `soot` (flame blackens what stands under it: the apron; darker and warmer), `damp` (water darkens stone and
  cools it; darker and cooler), `relaid` (a repair: newer slabs, paler and a little cooler), `plain` (the floor as
  laid). A part of a floor names its cause; a field bay now and then is relaid or damp by the room's dice. A floor
  meant all alike (`rhythm: 'same'`) is laid clean, every bay the floor as laid.
- **Above.** The room was designed to about three and a half metres and stopped: over the niches one sheet of
  plaster to the cornice, and a vault that was only black. Three things answer it, each a principle first:
  - *A wall has storeys* (`wall-has-storeys`, both eras; a kit's `storeys`). A string course runs at three fifths
    of the wall's height, and over it an upper register derived from the lower by the same rule as a bay's second
    kind, the same with less: one large blind arch a bay, shallow where the niches are deep; a full bay's springs
    from an impost, a lesser bay's is the arch alone.
  - *Plaster tells the height* (`layers-stand-proud`, by cause). Damp rises from the floor, so the coat is ragged
    under the course and nearly whole over it (a second wall tile, `tiles.wallUpper`, laid over the course), and
    the upper wall is the paler and carries the light further up.
  - *The air above is furnished and lit by a cause* (`air-is-furnished`, both eras; `era/crypt.js` `cryptAbove`).
    A ring of candles hangs on chains over the walk of a room tall enough for one (iron, turned: a band, cups, a
    hub, rods), one baked light a ring, so the upper wall is lit from below; and a slit of cold sky stands high
    in the wall behind the tomb, its light a pool on the tomb: the second, cooler light the room lacked.
  Seen in Chrome in gen-7, looking up the hall and along a wall. Not done: the vault's own work (ribs from the
  capitals, a ridge rib, a boss), and soot above the torches.
- **The new kit joins what reads a kit**: its starter rooms and the words people ask for it by (`era/entries.js`),
  and the place a level's score is suggested for (`beats/score-suggest.js`); the tier found both missing. The
  generated tool-surface pages name it.
- **Gothic-stone is as it was, byte for byte.** A kit's numbers are a promise over every room already made with
  it, so the pass is a new card, not a change to the old one. Two small openings were cut for it, each the old
  value where a card names none: a niche's head takes its card's `seg`, and the accent wall's stone may name its
  own generator (`era/crypt.js`).
- Seen in Chrome in gen-7: a 12 by 22 metre hall nine metres high, beside the gothic-stone room and the hangar.
  Still chunky, and said: the candles' glow; a column is fluted and cut in parts but not yet tapered or round.

### Hydraulics: flowing water as a solved circuit, for a fountain or any water that runs

- **A fountain's water as a circuit** (`materials/hydraulics.js` `solveHydraulics`). Three things mojulo already had
  are joined, none of them simulated on the page. The hydraulics (`rupa/fluid.js`): a basin, a riser with a pump, a
  nozzle; the pump's head, less the climb to the nozzle, is the pressure behind it, and that is the jet's speed and
  the flow. The falls (`materials/jet.js`): the jet rises and falls as a closed-form stream, and each tier spills
  what it receives over its lip as sheets at critical depth (at rest every tier passes the pump's flow). The air
  (`rupa/vayo.js`): where water lands, mist is carried by the air round that spot, solved once when the world is
  resolved (the faces it meets, the wind), so each mote's place is a formula of the clock. One dial moves it all: the
  pump's head. A circuit that cannot run teaches (a pump too weak to reach its nozzle, a tier above the jet's rise).
- **Any world may carry one** (`hydraulics`, a circuit or a list: `{ basin, pump: { head }, nozzle?, tiers }`, or a
  given `flow` with no nozzle: a spring, a channel). Its falls join the world's jets and its mist goes to the page
  (`worlds/world-scene.js`), the air solved against the world's own colliders. The page's channel
  (`scene/channels/hydraulics.js`) is a few dozen points a landing, moved by the clock: no state, no render target,
  the same frame at the same time. Its probe is `window.__mojWater` (the mists, their points, the solve's report:
  litres a second, the jet's speed and rise, the pump's power, each tier's sheet).
- **The island plaza's fountain runs on it** (a stage's `water: 'works'` or `{ works: { head?, nozzle?, mist? } }`).
  A jet rises from the finial, falls into the bowl, and the bowl brims over to the basin in sheets whose flow is the
  pump's; mist stands where they land. `water: true` is the live water it was, and a stage with no `water` its
  painted strips: both byte for byte. Seen in Chrome on the island plaza by day in gen-7.
- **Water landing on water.** Where a circuit's water strikes water the solve says how (`impacts`: the place, the
  ring it lands on, the speed of its fall, its flow): a tier's sheets a little out from its lip on the water below,
  the jet's own fall back on the water under it. The page draws the strike (`channels/hydraulics.js`
  `WATER_IMPACT`): rings running out from where the water lands and dying away, a broken line of foam where each
  sheet comes down and none between them, and drops thrown up to a share of the landing's own head and falling
  back. All of it is a formula of the clock: one disc and a few dozen points a landing. `impact: false` leaves it
  out. Seen in Chrome on the island plaza: rings across the basin under the bowl's sheets, and in the bowl round
  the finial.
- **A fall ends on the water it lands on.** A circuit's sheets and its jet were given a fall a little past their
  water, as the plaza's live sheets are, and through clear water they were seen running on to the floor. Each now
  falls exactly to its water: a sheet to the pool below (a tier's own `level`, a little under its lip where it names
  none), the jet back to the water under its nozzle.
- **The mist's air meets the world's solids.** A circuit a kit lays is solved before its world has its colliders, so
  its mist's air was the open air. Where the world is resolved the air is solved again among its solids
  (`mistAir`, `worlds/world-scene.js`): the world's walls, and the kit's own stone (the plaza's fountain gives its
  bowl and its pedestal, so the mist under the bowl spreads out from under it).
- **A second shape of circuit, and a circuit that draws itself.** A spout thrown from a wall into a trough that
  pours forward into a floor basin, in a stone room, from the world's `hydraulics` key alone. What it took: a nozzle
  that points any way (the jet is thrown along it for as long as it is in the air, and the solve says where it comes
  down, `report.lands`); a lip that pours over an `arc` of itself, not all the way round (a trough against a wall);
  and the circuit's own vessels as plain stone and standing water where the world brings none
  (`hydraulicsFaces`: the basin a walled ring, each tier a bowl on a stem; `stone: false` for none). A jet thrown
  past the water meant for it teaches, with how far it missed: the first three tries at this very demo were
  refused that way. Seen in Chrome in a gothic-stone room in gen-7.
- **Named apart from a trail's `waterworks`** (the land's own rivers and falls, `era/water-live.js`): that is a plan
  the land draws; this is a circuit a pump runs.

### The tool list, trimmed: the research book and the stash links

Ten tools leave the list your agent reads, and nothing you have made stops working. Built on this branch:

- **The research book is retired for the stash.** Starting a research book, binding items into it, reading and listing
  books, sketching one and synthesizing an abstract were the gathering tools from before the stash, and their own
  guidance already said to prefer the stash: it checks every item's type as it comes in, and it is the only thing a
  cook reads. The seven tools are no longer listed or routed to. They stay callable by name, so a book you already
  have, a compiled plan that names one and a delegate key granted the research pack keep working, and the Research
  page still shows your books. To gather now: `mint_stash`, `gather`, then `cook`.
- **The stash links are retired.** Linking a stash to a plan or a cook, unlinking it and listing the links wrote rows
  that no build, cook or page ever read, so an agent could spend calls on them for nothing. The three tools are no
  longer listed and stay callable by name; a cook names its stashes in its own `slices`.
- **Variations no longer need a research book.** `run_experiment_sweep` moves beside the plan tools (plans and sweeps),
  and its mechanics experiment (`base`, `param`, `values`) now puts the runs and the plot of the outcome in one folder
  and answers the table of outcomes, with no book to start first. Passing the `research_ref` of a book you already have
  still binds the runs into it as before.
- **The numerical experiment notebook keeps its notebook in a stash.** The catalyst poses the question, sweeps, gathers
  each run by its ref, and cooks the finding. One thing is given up: synthesizing an abstract with `review: true` used
  to re-check every bound experiment against its stored copy automatically. The notebook now holds a pointer to each
  run instead of a copy, so there is no copy to drift, and the catalyst has the agent re-read each cited run with
  `get_exhibit({ ref })` before it writes the finding. That re-read is a step the agent takes, not a check the server
  runs.
- **A shorter list.** The flat tool list goes from 212,165 to 199,558 bytes (ten tools fewer) and the packs list to
  31,771 bytes; both pins are lowered. The research and link code, their tables and the Research page are
  untouched.
- **Machina's manual moves to a card.** `verify_machina` (can this mechanism move this load within these limits?) had
  the longest description on the list for a tool few sessions call. Its description now says what it is for and when
  to reach for it, and the full manual (every machine and its parameters, the units, the limits, what comes back, a
  worked example) is the `machina` card, read with `get_solid_vocab({ id: 'machina' })` and found by
  `semantic_search` from a question like "how many pulleys do I need". The tool takes the same recipe and gives the
  same verdict; a malformed recipe is sent to the card. The flat tool list drops again, to 195,837 bytes.
- **Three small reads fold onto the tool they served.** The list of host adapters is `get_adapter({ list: true })`, the
  author's guide for writing a catalyst is `mint_catalyst({ guide: true })`, and a world's theme packs are
  `get_view_vocab({ themes: true })` (or a family: `themes: 'scifi'`). The old names (`list_adapters`,
  `custom_catalyst`, `list_world_themes`) are off the list and still answer by name with the same result.
- **The tools that record your other MCPs say less.** Declaring which MCP servers you have, and recording and reading
  what one of them can do, keep working exactly as before and stay on the list, because a catalyst that reaches
  Blender or another MCP is matched through them. Their descriptions and argument notes are cut to what an agent needs
  to pick the call; the shape of a capability body is taught by the `research-mcp-vendor` catalyst, as it was.
- **The always-listed orientation tools say less.** The glossary and refusal legend, the dashboard map, the worked
  examples, the update check and the tool-call ledger are listed for every host in both list modes, so their wording is
  paid on every connect. Their descriptions and argument notes are cut to what an agent needs to pick the call; each
  returns what it did. The packs-mode list, the default for most hosts, drops from 31,771 to 29,805 bytes.
- **A delegate key keeps its reach.** With the roles pack on, a key is granted packs by name. A tool that folds or
  retires moves to another pack, so a key granted its old pack would have been refused the old name; it now still runs
  it. Nothing changes for a key that was never granted that pack.
- **An old name works wherever it used to.** A folded or retired tool still runs when called through the pack it used
  to be in (`pack_stash({ tool: 'list_cooks' })`, or `mojulo pack_stash list_cooks` from a shell), and a stored plan
  that names one still counts its steps by tier.
- **The plan tools say less, and the inbox is one read.** `get_plan` with no `plan_ref` lists your plans (by
  `status`, nothing marked read), so `list_plans` is off the list and still answers by name. Forging, revising,
  sketching, compiling and executing a plan work as before; their descriptions and argument notes are cut to what an
  agent needs to pick the call.
- **The stash tools say less, and each list is one read.** `get_stash` with no `stash_ref` lists your stashes and
  `get_cook` with no `cook_ref` is the outcomes inbox, so `list_stashes` and `list_cooks` are off the list and still
  answer by name. Minting, renaming, drawers, updating and archiving items, ranking kinds, proposing a stash and
  cooking several candidates work as before, with shorter descriptions.
- **Where the list stands.** Over this theme the flat tool list goes from 212,165 to 179,797 bytes (117 tools to 101)
  and the packs-mode list drops to 29,796. Every tool that left the list still answers by its old name.
- **The Claude plugin's helpers keep the released names.** An installed plugin changes only at a release, so its
  helper agents go on naming the tools the released server lists; every one of them still answers. They take the new
  names at the release that updates the plugin.

### Reflections: built things under a live sun, a wet ground that mirrors

- The sun's shadow on a built thing outdoors is live, never baked into its corners. A building's shell and its yard's
  containers carry the sun's share of each corner's light, and the page's hour map takes it away where the sun is
  hidden. Open: under a strong sun a container's faces draw in uneven bands. The cause is the live shadow map: the
  bands go when the containers are kept out of it (`shadows.noCastGroups`), so they are shading themselves in error.
  The map's fit and bias on a land page are the next thing to set.
- A sun for rooms indoors. A room kit's recipe takes `daylight: { elevation, azimuth?, color?, gain? }`, and the form
  render takes it live: every corner turned to the sun carries its share, and the page's hour map (which a room's page
  did not have) takes it away where a roof or a wall hides it, so the sun comes in at a window as its own shape on the
  floor. Glass, sky cards and the painted sun patches let it by, and the painted patches give way. A painted page lays
  none, and a room without the word is as it was. `alone: true` turns the lamps off: the room lit by the day alone.
- A daylight's `gain` stands the sun over its paint: the solve lays a sunlit surface as painted, and the sun is then
  that many times it.
- Samples: a recipe's `samples: [{ of, at, size? }]` sets a material down in a room to be looked at: a liquid (`oil`,
  `water`) a pool on the floor, a metal (`chrome`, `steel`) a cube, each with its own roughness and metal to the form
  render. What they show today: a room gives a mirror nothing to hold but a plain gradient, so a pool is dark and a
  chrome cube a dark box; neither holds the windows, the sun on the floor or each other.
- A room's capture. Where a room's page asks for reflection with a `probe`, the form render takes one cube of the room
  as it stands lit, a few frames in (after the hour's map is drawn), and a glossy surface looks it up along its
  reflected ray where that meets the room's own box, down its mips by its roughness. A pool holds the wall's lamps and
  a chrome cube the floor's markings; a rougher metal holds them blurred. A room with samples asks for it.
- A liquid stands proud of what it lies on: a pool's face is its `thick` over the floor (oil 14 mm, water 9 mm), its
  edge a rounded lip down to it, so the lip turns the light and the pool reads as lying on the floor.
- A pool's outline is a smooth one (slow waves round it by its dice, no corner). A liquid may be seen through
  (`clear`): square on it keeps a share of its own colour and the floor shows under it, darker where it is wet; the
  lower it is looked along the more it mirrors. Water is so. A fuel carries a thin film on its face (`film`): what it
  gives back is coloured by the film's thickness and the eye's angle. `gasoline` joins the samples.
- A liquid is seen as what it is. `rupa/liquid-look.js` reads a liquid's look off its matter: its thickness from the
  puddle its surface tension holds against its weight (and what a yield stress holds over that), its smoothness from
  whether it flows; its colour, clearness and film beside (`LIQUID_OPTICS`, a row a liquid, held to the matter table's
  own list). A room's samples take any of the table's liquids and draw them from it. `gasoline` and `crude` join the
  matter table.
- Footfalls in a liquid (visual cues, no solve). A step that comes down inside a pool's outline rings it: the rings
  bend what the pool holds and die as its liquid lets them (`liquidLook().ripple`: water rings, honey barely, mud not
  at all). The steps after it, past the pool's edge, are wet: a dark print each, fainter step by step, drying away
  (`print`, the liquid's own count). A step is a piloted figure's gait or the walk's own stride.
- Wet with no depth (`wet-hugs-the-surface`). A room kit's `wet: true | 0 to 1` wets its floor as a state of the
  surface: no thickness and no edge of its own, the relief kept, the water lying by the tile's own height (its joints
  fill first and lie mirror-smooth, its faces darken and take a sheen), thinner and thicker over the floor by the
  world's place. It holds the room's capture and, under lamps alone, each lamp's highlight. Past brimming it is a
  pool, which has a thickness. The form render's; a painted page lays none.
- On a wall a wetness runs: streaks down the face by the wall's own length, heaviest at its foot and thinning up it;
  a ledge or a joint still holds it. A wet room's walls, plinth and trim take it with its floor.
- Out of doors a wet recipe wets every built thing with no depth: the apron, the walls, the roofs and a yard's
  containers, each by the same law (the slab's joints full and its faces dark, the walls and containers run with it).
- Degrees of wetness (`era/wetness.js`). A recipe's `wet` is true, a degree (`damp`, `wet`, `raining`), 0 to 1, or
  `{ degree?, amount?, spots? }`. The rules: water finds the low ground first (joints, then hollows, then faces); a
  wetness has a cause (rain is everywhere and shows no edge; a leak or a spill is a spot that fades from its heart and
  may stand as a pool there); a wall is wet by what runs down it and never wetter than the ground under it; while it
  rains the standing water is struck with rings. Out of doors `wet` and `raining` stand pools in the ground's hollows;
  under a roof no rain falls and only a spot pools.
- Floodlights: a building's `yard: { floods }` stands masts along its yard's edge. Each is a lamp no bake holds, laid
  whole by the page with its highlight (the nearest four, apart from a room's own lamps).
- A yard's slab is laid in bays three metres square with a sealed joint (`yardSlab`, a floor's dressed cut), as a
  room's flags are, so its joints hold water.
- A built thing out of doors casts into the shadow map by its far faces only (it is closed and drawn both sides), so
  its lit faces no longer shade themselves in bands: the fault on the containers and the slab.
- What a floodlight lays is not the sun's or the moon's to take: the hour's shadow leaves it standing.
- Open, on a wet yard at night: a floodlight casts no shadow of its own; standing pools and rain rings are faint; the
  slab is plainer than a room's worked floor.
- While it rains every face out of doors that is not a floor is wet all over (darkened and smooth as a film of water),
  its runs only the heavier part.
- A floodlight's head is turned down (a cone under it, soft at its edge), and a yard's floods may stand down its
  middle (`yard.floodsAt: 'middle'`).
- Splatter patterns (`rupa/splatter.js`): the shapes a liquid leaves on a flat, as primitives that join (a disc, a
  capsule; where two meet they run into one). `blot`, `splash` (a body and the drops flung off it), `drips` (a trail),
  `run`, `seam` (held in a line), and `puddles` (rain over a rect by the share that stands, none with its heart in a
  box kept out); `join`, a field, and a raster for a page.
- Puddles on a flat. A wet place whose degree stands pools lays `puddles` over every slab apron, rastered once, and
  the form render stands water where the pattern's depth passes its edge: level with the slab, no thickness, a soaked
  rim round it, struck with rings while it rains.
- While it rains the whole ground wears a film: a skin of water over every face that looks up, thin enough that the
  joints show through, and struck everywhere with small rings (each cell on its own beat), larger and slower where
  water stands deep.
- A downpour (`wet: 'downpour'`): water stands over nearly all the ground, in a few wide sheets, and the rain strikes
  hard (more of the ground struck at once). A ring's crest catches a faint line of the sky, so rain reads on water that
  holds no lamp; standing water is darker than the film round it.
- A yard's containers wear corrugated steel sheet (`containerSkin`, a made cut as a shed's wall is): its flutes upright
  on the sides and across the top, the line's colour its tint, read by the form render as relief, so light and wet
  work on them as on any wall. The painted rib stripes give way to it.
- A container has its frame: a square rail round its foot and its head and a post up each corner, a hand proud of the
  sheet (`geocity/industry.js`, the one builder: a metro's containers and a yard's alike).
- A weather and its wetness are one thing said once: a geocube recipe with buildings that names a weather and no `wet`
  is as wet as that weather leaves a place (`wetOfWeather`: rain raining, a downpour or a thunderstorm a downpour,
  drizzle wet, mist damp), beside the weather's own falling rain and sky.
- Rain's rings are one system: on a page whose wet surfaces are struck in their own material, the weather channel
  stands none of its own (they lay at the camera's height, in the air beside a raised eye). A place with buildings
  under a wet weather and no clouds named takes the weather's own sky and its dimmer light.
- While it rains no puddle shows apart from the sheet (`raining` and `downpour` stand no pools; they stand out once it
  has stopped, `wet`); a downpour's sheet is deeper.
- Nothing falls under a roof: a building's footprint up to its roof is kept dry of the weather's falling drops, so it
  rains outside the door and not within.
- A net under a building's ground: one unseen level face a hand under its apron and a stride past its edge, so a
  walker who finds a gap lands on it and never falls through.
- An apron's skirt: the kerb round its edge goes down to the land wherever the land lies (the lowest land at the edge
  and a stride out, and a hand further), stretch by stretch, so no part of it hangs over ground that fell away where
  the site was filled. A test walks the skirt and finds none hanging.
- A night's weather takes a third of the light a day's does (a night is dark already), on a page lit by the form
  render; a yard's floodlights are brighter and reach further.
- Rain's film on what stands: while it rains a wall's and a crate's side sheet, thin runs of the sky's own light
  sliding down the face by its length, of no thickness, as the floor's film is; and the land wears the film too
  (`form.land.rain`, from the recipe's wetness): darker, smooth, the sky held in it, running in streaks where it
  stands steep, so a cliff reads wet. A land it does not rain on is as it was.
- A walker stands parked: a level's `parked` takes a vehicle word for a mecha shelf frame (a field walker, a siege
  walker), standing at its stance, fitted for a `role` where it names one, solid over what it takes up; a geocube's
  level carries parked vehicles as a stage's does. A building's `look` takes a `dressing`, and the `garage` dressing
  leaves a tall room's height and its middle clear for what is parked there: no crane, no great object.
- The sun indoors, in a building on a land: a room's faces turned to the land's sun carry its light and its share of
  theirs, no shadow baked, and the page's hour map takes that share away wherever no opening lets the sun in. A window
  lays its patch on the floor and the far wall, what stands outside it its shadow in the patch; the lamps stand lower
  by day beside it; the painted patches at the windows give way to the real ones. A face turned from the sun takes
  none of its cast (a tree outside drew its shadow on the inner face of the wall it stood behind).
- What lies loose in a wet room is wet with it: the debris's heaps and the vessels join the room's wet surfaces, each
  by its own group, in the form render (its instanced repeats take a surface as its faces do).
- A parked walker under its world's light: read in the form render, a dressed frame carries its faces' materials and
  is lit as a field vehicle is, by its world's sky and sun, wet when its weather is. A body that stands still for the
  whole level is the static world's: it casts into the hour's map wherever it stands, not only near the player.
- A body under the land's sun stands in its building's shade: the land's sun's map is drawn with the static world in
  it (at the hour's pass and whenever the land asks for it again), so a hero or a vehicle indoors takes the sun only
  through an opening (it took it through the roof).
- The hour's map fitted to the built place: on a land whose own sun shades it, the map covers its buildings' aprons
  and a margin for what stands by them, not the whole land, so its texels are centimetres: a tree's leaves read in its
  shadow on a wall, a window's patch has an edge.
- A floodlight's shadow: a yard's first two floods each carry a map of their own, drawn once with the static world in
  it, so what stands under a flood (a container, a parked walker, a building's corner) throws its shadow across the
  slab and up the next thing.
- A wet yard gives back the place: where a land's buildings are wet, a capture of the yard as it stands lit, taken from
  the widest strip of slab beside them, is what its wet slab, walls and containers hold (the buildings, the containers,
  the land), corrected to that strip's box and read along the ray past it. Standing water out of doors gives back more
  than a film does, so what stands by a puddle reads in it.
- The light of where a body stands: on a land with buildings, a body under the cast rig (the hero, a parked walker, a
  foe) carries its own light and takes the light of its place, eased as it walks: a room's lamps overhead and its
  floor's bounce indoors (lower by day, as the room is), the sky out of doors, a flood it stands under. A form body
  gives back less of the sky indoors.
- The whole cast under the land's one sun: on a page whose land is drawn as form, every body an entity wears (a foe, a
  walker, one that stands still) is read lit and carries the rig solved from the land's cube, as the piloted hero did
  alone.
- Fixed: a person's shadow was lost on a land with buildings. The hour's map was fitted to the built place only on a
  page with no entities (the fit was asked before the land was read), so with a cast it stretched over the whole land
  again and its bias swallowed anything a person's size; the fit is asked once the land is read. A whole level's test
  holds it (`worlds/built-light.e2e.test.js`).
- A yard's floods are dark by day: lit when the sun is down or low, so what stands under a mast by day wears the
  sun's shadow.
- The land's own casters (its ground, its trees) stay in the maps drawn with the static world, so its trees shade
  what is built.
- The form render takes the finish by default: a page drawn as form (a land, a land's buildings) wears the default
  `light.finish` (its tone curve, its bloom) where its recipe says nothing of one, so its lamps, its floods and its lit
  windows spill their light; `light.finish: false` says otherwise.
- Day and night for a land's buildings are told by the land's light (a sun clear of the horizon under a sky that gives
  light, or the moon): by night the floods are lit and their heads glow, the rooms' lamps stand at their full level and
  the moon's patches through the windows are faint; by day the floods' heads are dark.
- The cast's materials told apart by how they answer the light (`color-theorist/cast-response.js`): a hero read lit
  says each of its palette's groups' class (skin, hair, an eye, cloth, leather, metal: a roughness and whether it is
  metal), and under the cast rig each corner takes its class off its own colour: cloth is matte, skin takes a soft
  highlight, an eye a wet one, leather a worn sheen, a metal the rig's sky in its own colour. No map, no new geometry;
  a body with a painted texture, and the cel register, are as they were.
- A realistic hero's relief under the cast rig: the lit read asks for the body as the skinned export gets it, so a
  realistic hero brings its normal map (its skin's relief, its clothes' creases, seams and grain) and its roughness
  (each cloth's own, a leather's satin, wool's dullness: `epidermis/cloth-relief.js`), and the page's cast material
  reads both on the paint's atlas. The tangents, the parallax's depth and the correctives stay the engine export's.
- A geocube's level takes `fxStyle` (its effects' style and the cast's register: `register: 'anime'` draws its cast in
  cel), as a stage's does.
- Page pack (`scene/page-pack.js`, `scripts/pack-page.mjs`): a World page made smaller with nothing cut. Its module
  script is gzipped and the page carries a few lines that inflate it (the browser's own `DecompressionStream`) and run
  it as the module it was. One file (the script as base64 in the document) for a page a person opens, or parts (a
  small `index.html` and the script in binary files beside it, each under a size) for a host that limits a file. The
  day facility's page goes from 38 MB to 25 MB as one file and 19 MB in parts; with a realistic hero, 129 MB to 40 MB
  and 30 MB. The packed page was run in a browser both ways and draws as the page it was.
- Page pack's text form (`bundlePage({ form: 'text' })`, `pack-page.mjs --parts --text`): the script as it is, in
  `.txt` parts that each end on a whole character, for a host that serves only a web page's file types. A Claude
  artifact refused the binary parts by their extension (`.bin`, `.gz`) and took the text parts of the CDN build. A
  packed page whose host refuses a blob as a script now writes the script into the document as an inline module; seen
  to run that way under a policy that allows only inline and CDN scripts.
- Said once: two parked vehicles that are the same vehicle in the same dress are one figure stood twice.
- A face's blend shapes said once and only where they move (`figures/morph-sparse.js`): a faced part carried a row a
  corner, every target at every corner; now the corners that share a row share it, and each target's column holds only
  the rows it moves, in the same 16-bit steps, exactly (sparse then dense is the input byte for byte). A dressed
  realistic hero's face goes from 36 MB to 2.5 MB. The page's two players read it (`__mz`); an export keeps its floats.
  The lit read's face rows, which came as an export's floats, are written the page's way too: the facility's page with
  a realistic hero goes from 129 MB to 59 MB, 25 MB packed in parts.
- A realistic hero's geometry as the page reads it (`pageFigures`, `full: 1`): a part that carries its paint's place,
  its normals or a face's rows was a corner a triangle, every number a float32; it is now welded (the corners that are
  the same corner are one), its places and its paint's places on 16-bit grids over their own range, its normals signed
  bytes, and its face's rows named by the welded corners. A part with an engine's tangent, corrective or metal stays as
  it came. The facility's page with a realistic hero goes from 59 MB to 48 MB, 22.7 MB packed in parts; the hero itself
  from about 21 MB to about 10 MB.
- The far lift, in progress (`scene/channels/far-lift.js`, a land's `farLift`, opt-in): the grass past the view
  cone's reach given its height. The ground is drawn a second time where grass grows, pushed up to the sward's height
  × its cover (so it comes down to the ground where the grass ends), in the far field's colour, rising from nothing at
  the reach. Rendered on the island trail with it on and off: the far grass stands over the bare ground behind it and
  hides the feet of far trunks. It replaces a first attempt drawn as a wireframe box.
- The grass's economy, in progress: the tall and medium swards a fifth shorter (their width kept, so the cone's reach
  is unchanged) and about a fifth denser, thinning sooner (from 0.42 of the reach), so the density is spent near the
  eye; the far lift stands over the blades' tips (× 1.3). A change to every gen-7 page's grass; its change-reach tests
  pass.
- The grass lines, in progress (`GRASS_LINE`, `form-grass.js`): between the thinning and the reach half the clumps
  stand (`POV_GRASS.keep`); past the reach a share of them stand again on a crest (the ground behind falls below the
  line of sight) and at a patch's near edge, out to three reaches, wider and taller with distance, on the far lift
  where there is one: the land's layers and the lift's side read by a line of blades, solved from the camera each
  frame. A tile's rows are ordered by their dice and it draws only those that can stand at its distance. Not yet seen
  drawn; its tests not yet run.
- The far lift's seam, in progress: the lift begins where the blades begin to thin and is whole at the reach, rising
  among them and filling in as a stipple of blade-sized cells, so there is no stretch where the blades have gone and
  the lift has not come. The grass lines' patch-edge clumps are removed; the crest lines stay. Not yet seen drawn.
- The far lift's walls, in progress: a raised plain stands at its full height to a patch's edge and comes down to
  the ground there as a steep side of the same triangles and material, drawn where no grass is mapped too (the
  grass's own colour), so it is closed all round; the side's lower part fills in with the seam's stipple. Not yet seen
  drawn.
- The grass lines are removed: past the reach the far lift alone stands for the grass, one switch between real blades
  and the lift. The halved clumps between the thinning and the reach, and a tile drawing only the rows that can stand,
  stay.
- The far lift stands where the grass is, in progress: its place and height are read from the far map (a strand a
  cell where a clump stands, its height its own) as the mean of the strands within a metre, the empty cells counted as
  nothing, × 1.5: high where the grass is tall and thick, low where it is short or sparse, none on the trail, in a
  claim or on bare ground. It no longer reads the cover and a height per sward. Not yet seen drawn.
- The form grass on a gen-6 stage, in progress (`stage-grass.js` FORM_FIELD, a live grass's `form`, opt-in, in the
  field's place): the form render's grass and its far lift drawn in the stage's look. The grass script takes a `ramp`
  look (blades unlit, the stop their height picks from the lit or the shade window); the stage's landform and mask are
  read as its ground map; the lift is a sheet over the landform raised to the mean of the clumps that stand, in the
  ramp's upper stops. The field, the far clumps and the cards are not drawn; a blade is not pressed by a foot. A first
  lift written into the old field is removed, and the old field is as it was. Not yet seen drawn; tests not yet run.
- A stage kept clean (`hats: false`): no grass cap on a rock and no fringe over a cliff lip; absent, the stage as it
  was.

### Room craft: the reasons behind a worked interior, as questions a room is asked

The ashlar crypt's craft laws said what to build (a turned torch, a fluted shaft, a blind arch, a candle ring). Carried
to another interior as they stood, they would have placed the crypt's things in a lab. `era/room-craft.js` carries each
law back to its reason and puts it as a question to the place being built: what its fixtures are made of and what holds
them, what carries the roof and in what material, what a wall's full bay is and what it is with less, where reach ends
on a tall wall, what covers the structure and what has taken it off, where the floor's edge, way and centre are, what
the height is for, and what gives light above. Each row has its why, what the answer is derived from, how a crypt, a
lab, a hangar and a chapel each answer it (no two alike), and the answer that is not one.

- `readRoomCraft(kit)` reads which questions a room kit's card answers and by what; `roomCraftLedger` reads the room
  kits together. It reads what a card declares, never a kit by name; whether an answer reads on the page is the eyes
  gate's.
- The agent reads it: a generated card, `room-craft`, and a `CRAFT` line on every room kit's card naming what the kit
  answers and what is open for whoever builds with it (answered with `items` and `lights`).
- The craft laws' wording no longer names the crypt's things.
- The bay kits' service boxes follow a wall's rhythm (`services.rhythm`, `era/wall-rhythm.js`) where they stood on
  every second bay; the everyday register boxes the fewer of a wall's bays. A bay room already minted draws its boxes
  on other bays.
- The catacomb answers every question in its own things, each by its own cause: a clay lamp on a corbel of the rock
  (`torch.form: 'lamp'`, its live flame a wick's); piers splayed at the foot with an impost; loculi in a rhythm; a
  ledge at the first diggers' floor with the oldest tombs sealed over it (`storeys.loculi`); plaster within reach and
  sooted bare rock above; a floor laid by its use; shoring logs wedged wall to wall with a lamp hung from each
  (`above.span`) and a light shaft's mouth over the ossuary. A catacomb already minted renders differently.
- As read now: the ashlar crypt, the catacomb and the bay kits (but the vernacular, which has no services) answer all;
  the research lab lacks a rhythm and a coat; the nave a made fixture, a rhythm and a coat; the first crypt
  (`gothic-stone`) answers none and is unchanged.
- An opening has depth (`openings-have-depth`, a craft law and a question of its own): a niche is cut into the wall
  and built behind it (a back, a floor, a head, two sides), and what it holds stands inside it. `era/carve.js` cuts a
  wall's faces round a convex hole, carrying the wall's texture across the cut; a card's `niches.depth` asks for it.
  The catacomb's slots and the ashlar crypt's niches are cut in; the first crypt's are as they were.
- The coat is optional: a recipe's `coat: false` lays a kit's bare wall (the same stone, nothing over it) on every
  storey that wore render; a kit without a coat is unchanged. A wall bare by intent answers the coat's question. A room
  kit's card lists `coat` and `rhythm` among its options where the kit has them.
- A tall research lab is lit in the form render. It drew black: the room's light is solved under its median lamp at a
  reference distance, and in a tall lab the median was a lamp that does not reach that far, so the solve divided by
  nothing. The reference is now a lamp that reaches it (`form/room-light.js` `referenceLamp`). The lab's troffers also
  hang no higher than `hang` over the floor, on longer chains, with a reach of at least twice their height.

### Skandart: debris that has a cause, laid where it would come to rest

A room gathers what has happened to it. Skandart asks a room what falls, wears off, is dropped or grows there and where
it comes to rest, and lays the answer as clumps: each built once in its own frame, stamped where the room's structure
puts it, and lit where it lies. What is too small to be read where it is seen is left out; the rest is built at the
size it would be.

- A recipe's `skandart` (`true`, a number from 0 to 1, or `{ amount }`) asks for it on a kit that answers the question
  on its card. The ashlar crypt (`gothic-ashlar`) is the first: at each wall's foot a heap a bay long, its render's
  flakes, the ashlar's spall and a fallen block, filling the gutter and spilling over its lip, the bays in the wall's
  rhythm (the full heap and the lesser one, the same heap lower with less on it); a deeper heap in each corner against
  the pilasters' feet, a block or two at its toe; the tomb's candles' wax poured on the dais and pooled at its foot; the
  webs within reach swept, those over it left. A kit that answers no debris question says so. Without the key every
  room is as it was, byte for byte.
- A heap is a body and the pieces on it. The body is the fall's fines standing at their angle of repose (rupa's `phi`:
  sand's for the fines, gravel's for loose stone), a wedge along a bay with a hip at each end or a quarter cone in a
  corner, clipped where it meets the ground so its toe runs as a contour. The pieces lie on its face, square to it and
  part buried, sorted as a fall sorts them: the bigger, the farther down, so blocks come to rest at the toe and chips up
  the face. The amount raises the body and deals the next of the same pieces: more is always the same heap with more on
  it.
- The debris shelf (`era/debris-shelf.js`): the things that pile up, one row each under the words people say, with its
  matter, its sizes, its shape and how it comes to rest (it rolls, or it lies): spall, a fallen block, brick, render
  flakes, slate, roof tile, sherd, plank, beam, splinter. Its shapes are a broken chip, a dressed block with a broken
  arris (never a box), a plate flat or bent, a length of timber broken off on the slant. A kit's card names a heap's
  pieces off the shelf; a new thing that piles is a row.
- Asked for, it replaces the crypt's gutter rubble and the fallen stone among its corner things (stones, a boulder,
  debris); every other corner thing stands where it stood (`cornerThings`' `leave`: a kind placed by the dice and not
  built).
- A new law, `too-small-to-read` (`era/laws.js`, the builder's in both eras): what is too small to be read where it is
  seen is not made, neither built nor painted in. A thing under the eye spot (12 pixels of the frame its era reads at)
  at the distance the player meets it is left out; `eyeSpot(distance, screenPx)` beside `EYE_SPOT_PX` in
  `playscape/objects/laws.js` measures it. The debris is its first reader, as filler (met at six metres): in the sixth
  generation's 640×448 a piece under about 19 cm goes, in the form render on its target's lines (1080 by default) one
  under about 8 cm. The dice fall for every piece first, so the coarser frame keeps the same heap with fewer of its
  small pieces; a flake that lay on a stone left out lies on the ground instead.
- The debris rides to the page as instanced repeats, one geometry a clump and one transform a stamp: a two-room crypt
  in the form render lays 39 heaps from 8 clumps, about 13,500 triangles in all (35 from 7, about 6,500, in the paint),
  its worst view 61,387 triangles against the room's 53,235 without it, the page no larger. Each stamp takes
  the room's light at the middle of its mass and a share of the grime of the ground it lies on (a fresh fall has not lain
  there as long as the floor), in the paint and in the form
  render; a clump is shaded only by how its faces turn up, so a stamp may turn and still be lit where it lies.
- The form render lights instanced repeats in a room under no sun when they carry their light (until now only under a
  sun). A page without them is as it was.
- The form render's bake answers the light at points that are no face of the room and the base a paint takes in it,
  when asked; asked nothing, it is as it was.
- A room's condition (`condition`, `era/condition.js`): one word for its state of repair sets its debris, its grime and
  whether anyone still sweeps, together, on a ladder: `kept`, `worn`, `neglected`, `derelict`, `ruined`, or a word for
  one ("abandoned" is derelict, "crumbling" is ruined). From neglected up nobody sweeps, so the webs within reach stay.
  A kept room is one where nothing has come down: it lays no heap and keeps none of its kit's fallen stone. A recipe's
  own `skandart` or `grime` stands over the word's. On a kit that answers no debris question the word sets the grime
  and the room says what it could not (`condition.unanswered`); every room asked in a condition says it (`condition`:
  its step, the dials it set). A room kit's card lists the word among its options, and a kit that answers the debris
  question lists `skandart` too.
- The cavern answers the debris question too (`era/skandart-land.js`), asked by the same keys (`skandart`, or a
  `condition` word): talus heaped against each wall's foot, a heap a stretch of wall in the walls' rhythm, and
  breakdown, the slabs a ceiling lets go, standing free on its floor off the walk and its rocks. A land's floor rises
  and falls, so each heap is laid on the land where it lies (its body draped over the ground, each piece on the ground
  under its own middle) and joins the cavern's boulders: its rock banded and tiled as every rock of it is. A ruined
  cavern lays 32 heaps, about 18,000 triangles. The shelf gains the breakdown slab; the heaps a cone, standing free.
  Asked nothing, or kept, a cavern is as it was; open ground asked for debris says it has none to give yet.
- Every heap's face holds its fines' repose however tall it stands: a long heap's crest waves stretch with its height,
  a round heap's slope varies only gentler than its repose, and where a bay's face meets its hip the two round into one
  another (a soft minimum), never a crease steeper than either; and no heap stands taller than its reach lets its face
  fall to the ground.
- The research lab answers the debris question in its own things: a lab sheds no stone, so at each wall's foot, in the
  bays it lays between its columns, its upper boards lie fallen and the draughts' papers and broken glass are carried
  past a skin of dust; deeper in its corners; and where its roof came down (its `decay`'s collapse), the slab in pieces
  heaped under the hole on a low bed of dust, the deck's sheets across it, chunks rolled out over the floor. The old
  pile there keeps only the bay's fallen troffers. A card may size its own heaps (`heights`), carry what lies past the
  body (`spread`) and paint its own matters (`matters`). The shelf gains what a lab drops: slab chunk, concrete chunk,
  deck sheet, board, paper, glass shard (the word "board" is the lab's wall board now; a plank is "plank").
- A room's condition reaches a kit's own story of decay: on a kit whose style card tells one (the lab's abandonment,
  blackout, leak, broken set piece and fallen roof), neglected abandons it, derelict abandons it in the dark with a
  leak, and ruined brings its roof down too, so its debris has a hole to lie under. A recipe's own `decay` stands over
  the word's.
- Fixed: a wall without pilasters split into strips read a length `Array.from` never passes (it threw).
- Any room answers the debris question, not only the kits with a card: what it sheds is read from what it is made of
  (`era/skandart-derive.js`). Each wall, upper wall and ceiling tile names its matter by its generator's settings, its
  key or its family's name (a recipe's own tiles included); each matter sheds its own (stone its spall and a block,
  render its flakes, brick its bricks, concrete its chunks, boards their boards, timber its planks and splinters, metal
  its sheets, glass its shards; a ceiling's under a hole in it), heavy things heaped at their repose and light ones
  drifted; a room's use leaves its own (an office its papers, a store its sherds, a workshop its splinters). A kit's card
  is the art direction over that answer, and a recipe may give its own over both (`skandart: { foot | corner |
  collapse: { pieces: { <shelf row>: n } } | false, heights, spread, reach, matters }`, each piece checked against the
  shelf). The room says whose answer it laid (`skandart.from`: recipe, card or derived) and what it read. Only a room
  made of nothing that sheds, asked for debris with no answer of its own, is refused, and is told how to give one; a
  `condition` on it sets the grime and says the debris was unanswered.
- A room's bays are read the same way for every room: between the pilasters it lists, else between its own bays (a
  lab's columns, a bay kit's pilasters), else the wall cut in stretches a heap fits in; the bay kits' wall feet were
  getting none.
- Weathering is one scale (`weathering`, `era/weathering.js`): how far the causes have worked on a room's surfaces, an
  axis apart from its debris (`skandart`: how much of what came off still lies). A room can stand weathered and swept,
  or fresh with a fall in it. The scale is 0 (fresh) to 1, the kit as drawn at its middle; each cause is a weight on it
  (`{ amount, damp, water, fire, time }`) and acts where it acts: damp loses a render wall's coat low and brings the
  damp band, moss and fungus; water from above loses its coat over the string course and streaks it; fire soots over
  the lamps; time ages the dirt, wears the stone and cracks the floor. It fills the dials it tells (`grime`, `dirt`,
  `cracks`, `growth`, the coat's loss on the kit) wherever the recipe set none; the room says what it set. A
  `condition` sets weathering and debris together (its old grime dial is weathering now), and either turns on its own:
  `condition: "derelict", skandart: 0` is a derelict room swept clean.
- `skandart: 0` is a room where nothing lies, the kit's own fallen stone gone too; only an absent key or `false` leaves a
  kit as it was drawn.
- Weathering reaches every made surface by the cause that acts on it: a dressed tile's wear (`grit`: paint off the
  arrises and rivets, dents, scuffs, stains) by `use` on a floor and by time elsewhere, a corrugated roof's rust by
  water, a render's coat as before; and its baked dirt reaches a bay's own surfaces (its base band, columns and crown as
  walls, its floor band and hazard paint as the floor), asked by weathering only. A new cause, `use` (traffic), wears
  the floor and the walk. A hangar weathered and kept (`kit: "bay-military", weathering: 1, skandart: 0`) shows its
  roof rusted through, its floor stained and scuffed and nothing lying on it.
- Snow answers the debris question on open ground: a stage's or a geocube path's `skandart` under its snow lays drifts
  (`era/skandart-snow.js`), the wind's piles in the lee of each rock and trunk, the wind the recipe's (`wind.dir`) or the
  default's. A drift leans on what slowed the wind, highest at it, its tail running out downwind to a tongue, its back
  and sides no steeper than snow stands (rupa's `snow` repose) and easing out onto the ground; it rises with the amount
  and with the snow's depth, never past what it leans on, is cut where the snow ends or the walk begins, and is not made
  lower than the eye spot. It is the cover's snow: painted in its colour, and in the form render the ground the snow's
  map covers, the map filling the hollows the cover's patches opened under it. Walked over, never a collider. The level
  says what it laid (`skandart.drifts`) and any law it broke. Debris words on open ground without snow are still refused.
- The fall heaps its leaves (`era/leaf-piles.js`): a level whose biocube is in the fall (`flora.autumn`) gives each
  tree that turns its own leaf piles, drawn by the form render (gen-7) as heaps of that tree's turned colour, not as
  single leaves. Blown along the ground, leaves bank against the windward face of what stops them: one against the
  tree's own trunk, one against the nearest rock downwind within its reach, and on some trees a loose heap blown out past
  the crown. A pile is laid in SHEETS, as wind lays leaves: each a little smaller than the one under it, sharing its
  wobble, with a matted edge; the page draws the lower sheets browner, each edge a shade darker and the crease under it
  darker still, so it reads in layers, with a leaf-sized grain near and a heap's colour far. The pile as a whole stands
  no steeper than dry leaves (34°), a matted edge no steeper than 55°; it rises the further into the fall, a bank never
  past three fifths of what it leans on; none on the walk, in a rock or lower than the eye spot, and the grass keeps off
  it. A needled or a far tree lays none, nor a level in snow, nor a painted (gen-6) page. The level says what it laid
  (`leafPiles`: each pile's role, place and height); a page with none carries none of the code. A dozen piles add about
  a megabyte to a page, most of it the grid their edges need.
- Open ground answers the debris question (`skandart` on a stage's trail or a geocube path, no snow): its rockfall
  (`era/skandart-land.js trailSkandart`). What a cliff lets go comes to rest by its size, so cones of fallen rock lie
  past its talus apron's toe, and the biggest blocks of each, rolled farthest, lie alone at the walk's edge on the cliff's
  side, sunk where they stopped; every big stone beside the walk sheds a ring of spalls round its own foot. A new shelf
  row, `talus-block` (a cliff's own rock, broken, no face squared). More falls the more is asked; nothing lies on the
  walk, and the grass keeps off each heap and block. Read at the form render's frame (1080 lines) when it reads them, so
  its spalls are made. The level says what it laid (`skandart`: its cones, runners and rings). A `condition` on open
  ground is still refused, now saying why: a condition word is a room's or a cave's.
- A trail's debris takes in its trees and its rain. DEADFALL (`era/deadfall.js`): each tree near the walk lets fall its
  dead branches and now and then a limb, lying under its crown where they fell, mostly pointing out from the trunk, each a
  curved, tapered stem with its forks, one propped up off the ground as a fallen branch lies; never across the walk's
  middle, never in a rock, none too thin to be read where it is seen. Drawn as its own wood (`isekai:deadwood`, a new land
  class: the cube's floor, weathered paler than a standing trunk's bark, so the form render's own trees do not hide it; listed in a land's
  payload only where its faces stand, so a land without deadfall is byte for byte as it was), on a polygon land. WASH (`era/wash-fans.js`): where rain running down a trail slows (its dips and the foot of each
  descent) it drops its load: a fan of washed sand opening off the trail on the side lower at its toe, or, where the
  trail is sunk in its banks and the water stays in it, a lobe of sand across its tread run on down it; centimetres deep,
  so drawn by its colour (the land cut as sand, as a shore's is, no grass on it), and it never climbs. Both with the
  trail's rockfall under the same `skandart`; the level says what each laid (`skandart.deadfall`, `skandart.wash`).
- A room's debris answer keeps its VESSELS (`era/skandart-vessels.js`): what it stored and left, pots, urns, jars,
  crates and barrels standing in groups against its walls, a share of its bays holding a group in a heap's place (taken
  out before the wall's heap rhythm, so the heaps keep theirs). The room's amount says how they were left: the further
  gone, the more lie tipped on their sides, fallen away from the wall, and the more are already broken where they stood
  (a clay one's lower part still standing, open at the break, its sherds about its foot; a crate's planks). Each standing
  or tipped vessel is a solid thing of its own, so a game that lets objects break (`destruction`: objects and up) slashes,
  shoots and blows it apart like any crate or pot, and under `physical` it breaks as fired clay or pine. The crypt's card
  keeps urns, pots and jars, the lab's crates and barrels; a room's use keeps its own (a store, cellar or kitchen pots
  and jars; a workshop, warehouse or hangar crates and barrels); a recipe names its own (`skandart.vessels: { kinds,
  every }`) or none (`vessels: false`). New prop forms on the shelf (`pot`, `urn`, `jar`, each one turned vessel) and a
  breakable class, `urn` (fired clay, one blow). The room says how its vessels were left (`skandart.vessels`).
- The wooden things join them: a `chest` (long along the wall, a lid proud, two iron straps), a `keg` and a woven
  `basket` on the prop shelf, breakable as `chest` (timber, two blows), `barrel` and `basket` (wicker, one). A standing
  crate may carry another, no bigger than it, each its own thing: break the one under and the top comes down (the
  runtime drops what nothing holds). The crypt keeps a chest of grave goods with its urns, the lab crates and kegs, a
  store baskets with its pots, a workshop or warehouse crates, barrels, kegs and a chest.
- Vessels take the look of the room they stand in. A card names ROLES (crate, barrel, keg, chest, basket, pot, urn,
  jar) and the room's look gives each its form: `old` wood and clay (a room of stone, render or brick: a crypt's
  barrels, crates, chests and urns), `industrial` painted steel (a room of metal or concrete: a military bay's steel
  crates on skids, drums with their rolling hoops, footlockers with latches, in olive, grey, navy or red), `clean`
  moulded plastic (a room of board: a lab's totes, plastic drums and hard cases). The look the card names
  (`vessels.look`), else read off the room's walls. Every vessel a flat colour, no grain: it reads by its shape and its
  colour, never by a texture that pulls the eye. Steel and plastic do not break where they stand (a gone room tips them
  instead), and each breaks as what it is made of: sheet steel dents, and a new matter, moulded plastic (polycarbonate's
  numbers, a shell round air, softening and burning), cracks into plates. The room says which look it took
  (`skandart.vessels.look`).
- Debris can be struck and gone. A level that lets things break (`destruction`, any degree) turns a room's debris heaps
  into LOOSE things (`worlds/controllable/loose.js`, an opt-in builder emitted only where a world has them): each heap
  its own faces in its own render group (its instance's turn and light baked in, so it looks as it did) and a
  walk-through breakable. A loose thing is never a collider: the walker wades through it, sight and rounds pass over and
  through it. A blow still finds it: a round strikes every loose thing its line crosses on the way to where it stopped,
  a burst everything in its splash, a swing what is in its reach and in front; struck, it bursts into many small bits of
  its own colour (`SKANDART_BURST`), which settle and sink away. It leaves the same break record a block does, so the
  page hides it and plays it with the same break player. A page without loose things keeps every byte. A land's debris
  is loose the same way (each named on its faces, `skl-`): a trail's cones, runners and rings, its trees' fallen
  branches and limbs, its snow's drifts (a round through a drift bursts it white), a cave's heaps. The fall's leaf piles
  are not yet: they lie only on a geocube's path page, which no played level is.

### Sun in buildings: a building on open ground seated clean and lit by the land's one sun

A composed building standing on an outdoor map (the hangar, a barracks) is read by the form render as its land is.

- The land is cut at a building's footprint. It was dropped by each face's middle, so a face straddling a wall stayed
  and stood inside the room over its floor; a face is now cut to what of it lies outside, its corners' heights and
  colours carried along its edges. What the form render grows from a seat (trees, bushes) is cleared there too.
- The geocube kind takes `buildings` on a land a trail is laid over (`show: 'path'` or `'town'`), so a building's map is
  read with the cube's land, light and flora.
- A building's rooms keep their light when it is seated: the form render's record of its lamps comes with it, moved
  into the world's frame. It was dropped, and the rooms drew as their colour under no light.
- A building's shell is baked as a town's is (`form/sun-light.js`), its colour and the day's light apart, under the
  cube's light at the hour; the sun joins the page's record as its live light.
- A painted page is as it was: no record, no baked light on a shell.
- A composed building lays its own ground: it levels a place on the land a margin wider than itself (deeper before its
  front), lays an apron of poured concrete there with a kerb at its edge, and the land eases back to its own height
  round it; the land under the apron is cut away and nothing grows through it. First pass: not yet seen rendered.
- The building asks the land for its site: its level is the land's own mean across its ground (cut on the high side,
  filled on the low), the bank round it three metres out for each metre cut or filled (5 to 18 m), and the building's
  record says the level, the cut, the fill and the bank; a cut or a fill past 1.5 m is a finding. The floor is never below the land at its door.
- The apron is a slab or the ground: a building's `apron: 'ground'` levels its site and lays nothing on it, so a
  building on rock or sand stands on rock or sand. Left out, the land decides: the ground where a sixth of its site is
  already sand, bare rock or scree (read off the land's own faces), else a slab. Its record says which, and the share.
- The shell is baked with the sun's shadow of the building on itself (`era/sun.js`), and the page's record says it
  stands under a sun, so the page draws it as it draws a town's buildings. The building's shadow on its apron and on
  the land is the page's live one: a page of rooms seated on a land keeps the hour's shadow map, which a room's page
  on its own does not have.
- A dock's first parts. A building's `yard: { containers }` stacks shipping containers on its apron before its front
  (the city's container, `geocity/industry.js`), one to three high, each in a line's colour, lit as the shell is, each
  stack a collider. A recipe's `wet: true` (it has just rained) darkens the apron's slab and lays the wet film over it
  that gives the sky back (`channels/wet-road.js`). The geocube kind passes both.
- Built surfaces give the sky back. The form render's material takes a page's `reflect` (`scene/channels/form.js`): the
  sky by Fresnel, blurred by each surface's roughness, and the sun's highlight where the bake says the sun reaches; a
  metal's base colours both. A building on a land asks for it: painted steel and a container's enamel sheen, poured
  concrete barely. A page that asks for none carries none of its code.
- Wet is a state of the material. Where a recipe is `wet`, the form render lays one field of water over the apron by
  the world's own place and the recipe's seed: standing water, a soaked band at its edge, damp past that; each darkens
  the slab, smooths it and flattens its relief, so the sky lies in a puddle and only sheens on damp concrete. The
  painted page keeps its film.

### The animation studio: a scene written as a screenplay, filmed in Blender, from the agent

In progress. The first step of a sibling studio to the game studio, whose outcome is a directed film rather than a
game.

- **Ask for a short film of your characters.** Write a scene as a screenplay (who says what, a feeling in brackets,
  who crosses to where, who turns to whom, a pause) and name who plays each part. Your agent now hands it to the
  cinematics department directly. Before, that took a command run by hand. The characters act it (their faces and
  bodies on the words, listening and nodding while the other speaks). It is shot the way a director would shoot it.
  It comes back as a Blender film: each actor with its performance, the cameras cut together, and a film look
  (Cycles) or an anime look (EEVEE), ready to render to video in one command.
- **Cast a persona and it plays itself.** A persona you made is the actor: its character, its way of speaking, its
  acting style and its role come with it. Anything the scene says for that part wins.
- **The director's notes come back with the film**, such as a shot held too long or a speaker turned away from whom
  they're talking to. Each comes with a change to the script that answers it. They never stop the film.
- **See the film before it is made: a storyboard.** Ask for a scene and the first thing back is its storyboard, in
  seconds, with nothing rendered. There is a panel for each shot the director would take, drawn as a sketch with
  stand-in figures where the actors stand and seen from that shot's camera. Beside each panel is a plan of the room
  from above, showing where everyone stands, the path they walk and where the camera is. Under it are the shot's name,
  how long it holds, its lens, whether the camera moves, the lines spoken in it and any director's note about it. Look
  through the cut there before the film is made: the film is made from the same plan, so what you approve is what you
  get.
- **An animatic.** Ask for a video and the storyboard is played as one: each panel held for as long as its shot lasts,
  with the line being spoken shown under it. Several scenes' animatics can be stitched into one cut.
- **Your recordings set the scene.** Give the scene a recording of any line, from the voice worker or from a person.
  - That line now lasts exactly as long as the recording.
  - The character's face, gestures and mouth are fitted to the recording, and whoever is listening nods on its
    stressed words.
  - The storyboard's animatic plays the recordings with captions. The Blender film carries the voice and plays it
    under the render.
