  - A recording that was made for different words than its line is pointed out.
- **Dubbed versions.** Give the same scene in other languages, one recording per line. The picture stays exactly the
  same and only the mouths change to match the new language.
  - The animatic carries each language as its own audio track and subtitles.
  - The Blender film switches between languages with one command.
  - A dubbed line that runs into the next one is pointed out, with how far over it goes.
- **A set.** Put a scene in a world you made (a room, a hall, a trail, a level).
  - Its rooms and doorways become places the script can send the actors to.
  - Anyone not placed stands in the biggest room.
  - The world comes into the Blender film under the actors.
  - A shot whose camera would be behind a wall is pointed out.
- **A whole short film: the animation studio.** Write a film as a set of scenes that share one cast, with the places
  they are set, one look and the order they play in. It is kept as one piece of work, and its page is the film's book.
  - **Departments.** It is made the way a studio makes one, in departments: the script, casting, the sets,
    performance, the camera, voice and dubbing, the look, the edit and the render. Each says how its part stands and
    gives its own advice, such as a part nobody plays, a wall in a shot, or a scene where nobody looks at whom they
    talk to. The film also says what to do next.
  - **Boards and approval.** Board every scene in seconds, then look at the boards and approve them one scene at a
    time. Change a scene afterwards and its approval is marked as out of date.
  - **The animatic.** Cut every scene into one animatic, with the voices and each dubbed language as their own tracks
    and subtitles.
  - **Blender.** Send the whole film to Blender, scene by scene. A long film is made over several calls, each picking
    up where the last stopped, and a single script joins the rendered scenes into one cut with their sound.
- **Rendering the film in Blender.** A single command renders a scene, or the whole film, in Blender on your machine.
  - **Stop and go on.** It works through the film a short piece at a time and can stop whenever you like. Run it again
    and it carries on from where it stopped, never redrawing a frame it already has.
  - **The finished film.** It finishes each scene with its voice, then joins the scenes into the finished film.
  - **Progress.** The film's book shows how far each scene has got.
  - **Change a scene and only that scene is rendered again.** Edit a scene after it was rendered and the next run
    renders that scene afresh, keeps the others and joins the film again. Before, the old render was taken for the
    new scene.
- **A bare stage for a scene with no set.** A scene that is not set in one of your worlds now plays on a plain stage:
  a floor, a soft sky and a light. Before, the film opened on Blender's own starting cube, with the actors standing
  inside it, and each actor brought a second floor and spare cameras of its own.
- **A set is lit as you made it.** A scene set in one of your worlds now takes that world's light into Blender: its
  sky, its sun, or indoors its lamps at their strength. Before, a room came in dark, its torches barely glowing.
- **Each language has its own picture.** A dubbed version is now drawn on its own, so going from one language to
  another, or back to the original, always shows the right mouths. Before, a dubbed render kept the original's mouths
  under the new voice, and the frames of whichever language was rendered first were used again for the next. A scene
  with no dub in a language plays its own voice in that language's cut.
- **Film a scene in a room you decorated.** A room fitted out by the interior designer can now be a film's set.
  Before, a scene set in one was refused: the room named nowhere to stand.
  - **Places a script can name.** Each piece of furniture, the fireplace, the door and each window is a place:
    "Ada crosses to the fireplace.", "Jon crosses to the door.", "to the sofa". The place is the clear floor nearest
    the piece's front, so nobody is stood inside a table.
  - **Where the cast stands.** With no marks of their own, the cast stands on the room's open floor with the most room
    left for a camera, not in the room's middle where the coffee table is.
  - **The camera stays in the room.** A real room has four walls, so each camera stands inside them on a wider lens,
    and stops in front of a bookcase or a chimney breast rather than in or behind it. Before, a wide shot stood
    outside the wall and saw only its back.
  - **Walking round the furniture.** A cross goes round the sofa, the table and the other actors by the shortest
    clear way, turning at each corner. Before, it was a straight line through whatever stood between.
  - **The storyboard shows the room.** Each panel now draws the room's walls and furniture as plain blocks round the
    stand-in figures, seen from that shot's camera, with each door and window as an opening in its wall. The plan
    from above shows each piece of furniture, the doors and windows, and the way a walk goes round the furniture.
    Before, the panels showed the figures on empty ground, so a shot blocked by a sofa could only be seen by
    rendering it in Blender.
  - **House lights.** A room with no lamps of its own is lit by a soft light under its ceiling. Before, it rendered
    black.
- **A scene anywhere, with anything in it.** A scene can now be set in anything mojulo made, and anything mojulo made
  can stand in it. Neither has to be prepared for filming.
  - **Any world is a set.** A city, a landscape, a house, a level, or a single object such as a table or a vehicle.
    Before, only worlds that named places to stand could be a set, and the rest were refused. A world with no named
    places puts the cast on the clear ground nearest its middle.
  - **Things in the way are respected everywhere.** Whatever the set is, a walk goes round what stands in it, and
    each camera is moved to where it can see the actors. Before, this worked only in a decorated room.
  - **Props.** Name any object and where it stands, and it is in the scene: "Ada crosses to the car." sends her to
    it, walks go round it and the cameras see past it. A scene needs no set to have props.
  - **The storyboard draws it all.** Buildings, furniture and props are drawn as plain blocks round the stand-in
    figures, in each panel and in the plan from above.
  - **Props are in the Blender film.** Each prop comes into the film as itself (the car is a car, not a block),
    standing where the storyboard drew it and at the same size. Before, a prop was in the plan and the storyboard
    only.
  - **Dress a scene by naming things.** Say "a sedan", "a city bus", "a motorcycle", "a chesterfield", "a crate" or
    "a barrel" and where it stands, and it is in the scene at its real size. Nothing has to be made first: the
    vehicles, the furniture and the props mojulo already has are all there to be named. Before, every prop had to
    be an object you had made, and a vehicle needed its scale given. A word mojulo has nothing for is refused, with
    what it does have.
  - **A thing can arrive, and leave.** Say where a prop comes from and it drives or moves in to its place during
    the scene: a car that pulls up at the kerb. Say where it goes and it drives off. Say both and it pulls up,
    waits, and goes. Time it by the script ("as line 2 starts", "when line 4 ends") or in seconds. It faces the way
    it came, and stays on the ground along its way. In the storyboard it is drawn where it stops.
  - **It can follow a route.** Give a moving thing the points of its way and it goes through them in turn, facing
    the way it is going and turning into each corner: a car that comes along one street and turns into the next.
  - **Not yet:** a house does not name its rooms, so its cast stands outside it. A moving thing's route is the one
    you give it: it is not found for it, and it is not kept clear of the cast.
- **Film outdoors: hills, fields and streets.** A scene can be set on land that rises and falls, and in a town.
  - **The cast stands on the ground.** On a hillside each actor, camera and prop stands at the height of the ground
    under it, and a walk keeps its feet on the land. Before, everyone stood at one height, so on a slope they floated
    or sank.
  - **A hill is not a wall.** Rising land is no longer treated as something in the way. Before, a storyboard on a
    field drew the land as stacked slabs round the cast.
  - **A house is a place to stand in front of.** Send the cast to a town's house and they stand before its front
    door. Before, they were stood inside it and the first shot was a blank wall.
  - **Nobody is stood inside a thing.** A place a scene uses that is inside a rock or a building is moved to the
    clear ground beside it.
  - **The storyboard shows the slope.** The land is drawn as low steps the cast stands on, so someone up the hill
    is drawn up the hill. Before, the storyboard drew the ground level and a slope showed only in Blender.
  - **A hill between the camera and the cast is pointed out,** with where it rises and by how much.
  - **More places to send the cast.** A landscape, a town or a city now has a `start` (where its walk begins). A
    town also has its streets and the crossing where two meet. A city has the street corners nearest its centre.
    Before, a city named nowhere and its cast was stood near the middle of the map.
  - **A walk follows the path.** Send someone from one place on a trail or a sidewalk to another and they go along
    it. Before, they walked a straight line across country.
  - **Street trees and parked cars are part of the set.** The cast walks round a tree's trunk and a parked car,
    the camera avoids them, and the storyboard draws them. Before, anything a town or city placed by repeating one
    model was invisible to the scene and the cast walked through it.
  - **Faster on big places.** Only the part of the world near the scene is read, and a film whose scenes share a
    place reads it once. A city still takes about a minute the first time.
  - **Not yet:** a town's park, school yard and lot, and a city's waterfront and squares, are not places.
- **The written build steps keep the cast.** The steps a scene's Blender folder gives for building it by hand now
  save the actors into the film. Before, followed as written, they left the film with its set and cameras and no
  actors (rendering with the one command was not affected).
- **Say where a scene is, in words.** A film's set no longer has to be a world you made first. Say "a grassy field
  by a lake at dusk" and the film makes that place and plays the scene there. Or name a style of town or city and
  it makes the street.
  - **Made once, and kept.** The same words give the same place every time. Edit the film and the place stays as
    it is. Change the words and the place changes with them.
  - **It says what it understood.** The film lists which of your words shaped the place and points out any it
    could not use, such as a thing or a person, which belong in the scene's props.
  - **An ordered cutscene can ask the same way,** so whoever orders it need not hand over a world for every place.
- **Shoot a place at any hour.** Give a scene its hour (dawn, noon, dusk, night, or a time) and the Blender film is
  lit for it, whatever time of day the place was made at. One street can be a noon scene and a night scene in the
  same film, with no second copy of the street. Before, a scene could only be lit as its place was made.
  - **Street trees and parked cars take the light.** In a world sent to Blender, anything placed by repeating one
    model (a street's trees, its parked cars) is now lit like the rest of the place, and casts its shadow. Before,
    those kept their own flat colour whatever the light, so at night they glowed white against a dark street.
  - **Not yet:** street lamps that a place lights only at night.
- **The film suggests where a scene should be.** A scene with no place plays on a bare stage. When its words name
  one, the film now suggests it, ready to accept: a street of houses for "outside her house", a city for "a street
  corner downtown", a landscape in the scene's own words for "a field by a lake", and the time of day it mentions.
  For an ordered cutscene it reads the notes on each event, so an order can arrive with no places at all.
- **Ask for a room.** A film's place can be a living room, a bedroom, a dining room, a study or an entry, in a
  named style, with no room made first. The film has it designed and furnished, and the scene can send the cast to
  its sofa, its bookcase or its door. Ask for another style and the same room is redecorated. A scene set
  "in the study" or "inside" is offered a room the same way an outdoor scene is offered a street.
- **Choose how a street is built.** A place asked for as a town or city can name its building style (a Tudor market
  town, art deco, brutalist, a brick streetcar suburb and others) and how its streets are laid.
- **Weather.** Give a scene its weather and the Blender film is shot in it: clear, haze, mist, fog, dust, overcast,
  drizzle, rain, a downpour, a thunderstorm, snow, a blizzard or a dust storm.
  - **Cloud dims and softens the light.** Under an overcast or stormy sky the sun barely gets through, shadows go
    soft and the sky is grey.
  - **Mist and fog fade what is far.**
  - **Rain and snow fall** round the cast for the whole scene.
  - It combines with the scene's hour: the same street can be a bright noon, a foggy morning and a rainy dusk.
  - **Not yet:** rain falls through a porch roof or a ceiling; the ground does not get wet and snow does not
    settle; no lightning, and the trees do not move in the wind.
- **Street lamps come on at night.** A scene shot at night, dusk or dawn has the set's street lamps near the cast
  lit in the Blender film, each a warm pool of light under its own head; shot by day they are dark. It follows the
  scene's hour, whatever hour the place was made at.
- **Clouds.** Give a scene its clouds and the Blender film's sky has them: clear, fair, overcast, storm, haze or high
  cloud, as thick or thin as asked, lit for the scene's hour, with the sun dimmed and softened by how much they cover.
  - It combines with the hour and the weather: fair cloud at dusk, a storm sky at night, overcast with rain.
- **Wind in the trees.** Give a scene a wind (still, a breeze, fresh, a gale, or the weather's own) and the trees,
  bushes and hedges near the cast lean and sway in the Blender film, their leaves quivering.
  - **Not yet:** only plants move; cloth, hair, rain and dust are not blown.
- **A city's traffic in the film.** A scene set in a city can ask for the city's life, and the Blender film has
  the city's own traffic driving past the cast: family cars, taxis, vans, trucks and buses in their lanes, stopping
  at a red light and pulling away on green, exactly as the city's own page drives them.
  - The scene can start at any second of the city's clock, so the same corner can be shot with the lights red or
    green.
  - The film says so if a vehicle would drive through where an actor stands, and if the scene's place has no
    traffic of its own.
  - A city that has people of its own has them walk through the film too: round their blocks, waiting at the
    crossings, each stepping as far as it goes. Its cars drive through as well, turning at its junctions.
  - The storyboard and the animatic show the traffic and the people too, as plain stand-ins where they are at
    each shot's moment, so a car in the back of a shot is seen before the film is made.
  - **Not yet:** people walking in the street, animals, and vehicles turning at a crossing. The storyboard and the
    animatic do not show the traffic.
- **The film, made in mojulo.** Ask for the film and you get a video, with no other program to install or run.
  The characters act the scene on the place itself, and the camera work is the same as the storyboard's.
  - **The place is alive without asking.** In a city the traffic drives, the lights change and people walk past
    behind the cast, because the film is shot in the world as you would walk it.
  - **The weather is the world's own:** ask for rain and it rains on the street. A landscape or a street of houses
    made for the film is also shot at the hour and under the clouds the scene asks for.
  - **It has the scene's sound:** the recorded lines, each dubbed language as its own track, and the captions.
  - **A whole film is one video.** Each scene is shot and they are joined in order. A long film can be shot over
    several goes: scenes already shot are kept, a scene stopped halfway goes on from where it stopped, and only a
    changed scene is shot again.
  - **It takes minutes:** about a minute to get a character ready. A city street then films quickly; a landscape
    with grass and trees takes about a minute for each second of film.
  - **Games play it.** A cutscene ordered as a film is ready once it is shot this way, and a game plays it.
  - **Blender is now the high-end version** of the same film: the same acting and camera work, lit and rendered by
    Blender, for when that finish is wanted.
  - **Not yet:** the characters are not lit by the place's sun and cast no shadow on the ground; things placed in
    a scene (a parked car, furniture brought in) are missing; anime-style faces blink but do not speak their lines;
    another hour or sky is only read on a place made for the film as a landscape, a town or a city.
- **Order a cutscene.** Another part of mojulo (the game studio, for one) can order a cutscene from the animation
  studio by handing over what it already has: its characters, its places (a landscape, a street, a level, a room) and
  notes on what happens in each event.
  - **The order becomes a film.** The characters are the cast, each place is a set, and each event is a scene, in the
    order given. The film's book opens with the order: who asked, what for, and each event's notes.
  - **Notes are enough to start.** An event given as notes with no dialogue is marked as not written yet, with the
    notes beside it, until its scene is written. An event that came with its dialogue plays it as given.
  - **It says how far the order has got:** each event as not written, written, storyboarded, approved, cut into the
    video, filmed, or rendered in Blender, and which events are still to go.
  - **The cutscene is handed back** to whoever ordered it: the video, the film and each event's storyboard. Handed
    back early, it says what is still missing. Changed afterwards, it says the hand-back is out of date.
  - **Whoever ordered can ask what it ordered** and gets every cutscene with its progress.
  - **The game plays it.** A game can name the returned film as its opening, its prologue, its ending or any
    cutscene in its flow. The video plays over the game and can be skipped. The game points at the film, so when
    the cutscene is made again the game plays the new one, and an exported game carries the video with it. A film
    with no video yet is passed over, and the export says which.
  - **Not yet:** the game studio fills the order in by hand (naming a story moment does not fill it in), and a
    cutscene cannot yet take the place of a story moment by its name.
- **Walk up to someone.** A script can send a character to another character ("Ada crosses to Jon."), not only to a
  place. They walk up and stop at a conversation's distance.
- **Lighting each shot like a film crew.** Ask for it and every shot gets its own lights, placed from where that
  shot's camera stands and which way the actor faces: the main light on the far side of the face, a softer fill
  across from it, and a rim light from behind that lifts the figure off the background. The lights change on each cut,
  as a crew relights each setup.
- **Focus and motion blur.** The camera can focus on whoever it is looking at, with the background softly out of
  focus, and fast movement can blur as it would through a real lens.

### A course's walls and its backdrop, designed with the way and the asks as one dress

In progress. A rolled course's dress (`gameworld/course-dress.js`) gains its two outer layers, so the whole screen is
one design: the way and its asks (as before), the WALLS beside it, and the BACKDROP behind its far end.

- The walls (`gameworld/course-scenery.js`): the flanks beyond each kerb, laid a slice a segment. A slice is data: boxes
  in the slice's own measure (along it, off the kerb, up), each in a role of the dress. Two kinds a course: A, the
  complex one, and B, the plain one, ordered along each side by the walls' rule (never three alike, never a pair
  repeated), the two sides differently. The rail yard's: a goods shed, a fence before an embankment, stacked
  containers. A slice may be named or written in place.
- The backdrop: the sky from its horizon to its zenith, a far skyline of silhouettes, and the land beyond the way. It
  stands far past the course's end, so it stays in the top third from the first step to the last.
- New roles in a dress: flank, flank2, trim (the walls), land, far, horizon (the backdrop).
- One gate across every layer (machine; it advises): the asks are read against the walls and the backdrop as against
  the way; nothing in either is as vivid as an ask; `receding` (the further a layer, the nearer the sky: the skyline
  nearer the horizon's colour than the walls are); `interest` (A is the more complex slice); `rhythm` (each side
  keeps the walls' rule, and the sides differ); `banded` (the skyline is seen at the start and still inside the top
  third at the end).
- A level's `obstacles.dress` is a theme's name or the dress written out: `{ theme?, palette?: { <role>: '#hex' },
  walls?: { a?, b?, order? }, backdrop?: { skyline?, bands? } }`, each part falling back to the theme's.
- The course sheet (`gameworld/course-sheet.js`): the design book's page where the layers are seen together without
  running the game. The screen as the course's camera frames it, drawn from the course's own faces, with its thirds
  ruled across it; each slice in elevation; the palette by layer; every law. Served at
  `bible?book=practice&room=roll&view=sheet`, for a level by `&level=<id>`.
- The design loop: `design_game`'s readout carries the dress's laws for each course level; the roll room wears the
  first course level's dress; the agent's card (`gameworld-course-dress`) says the layers, the words, the laws and
  who works which, read by the world's and the levels' chapters.
- A dress has a PREMISE: one sentence every thing on the screen answers to, and what each thing is in it. A dress of
  parts chosen role by role (a brick wall across a track, a shed whose door opens onto the rails, a skyline that
  could be anywhere) does not cohere, however well each part reads. New law `premise`: the theme states one and names
  its lanes, its asks, their tells, its walls, its backdrop and its end; a slice or a backdrop written in place
  carries its own name. The rail yard, which has none, now loses that law and says so.
- Last train (`last-train`, now the dress unsaid): a kid late for the last train home runs down the tracks into the
  terminus at dusk. The three lanes are three running tracks. A hurdle is a striped crossing barrier, a block a row of
  crates, posts two wagons stabled on two of the three tracks (the open lane is the clear track). A jump's window is
  hazard hatching between two lines; posts' arrows gain a lit indicator on each kerb where the change must begin. The
  walls are a station platform under an iron canopy (A) and the brick cutting between stations (B). The backdrop is
  the city, the terminus's roof and its lit clock where the tracks meet the horizon. The end is a signal gantry
  showing clear over every track, buffer stops, and the train with its doors open. Brick for what is built into the
  ground, iron for what stands on it, lamplight the one accent (new roles `iron`, `lamp`).
- What a thing is drawn as (`gameworld/course-things.js`) is drawing over the box the course was measured with: one
  box a thing, one collider, its tell where it was sized. A themed ask is a single box (the plain themes' asks stay
  walls laid in courses). A thing the theme draws longer than the ask was measured with (a wagon, 3.2 m) is met all
  along it, and each segment grows by as much, so the rest after it is still the rest: found by the reaction bot,
  which a slow hero's 7 m segments failed on 10 seeds of 12 before it.
- A skyline silhouette may be a light (`role: 'lamp'`): set near the top of the silhouette it stands on.
- The course sheet opens with the premise and what each thing is in it.
- Last train, three things seen on the game's page and put right. The crates read as crates: each a framed panel
  with a brace, every other one a shade deeper, wide gaps between. The end is seen from the start: a train shed over
  the end of the line, its ribs taller than anything on the way and a lit departure board under the first. The top
  of a tall frame is not the far sky alone: the overhead line (a theme's `overhead: 'line'`), a portal at every
  slice's end and a wire over each outer track, running to the vanishing point, all of it over any jump.
- Last train's palette, again, for contrast and colour: an indigo sky over a rose horizon, violet ballast, red brick,
  near-black iron, and brighter asks (amber, orange, a stronger blue). Every colour of the way is now about as rich
  as the gate's `quiet` lets it be beside asks this bright (the way's chroma was near grey before); the values are
  spread to the dark side, since anything on the way as light as an ask stops the ask being read. Holds every law on
  200 seeds' shades.
- The test game asks for its juice and its grade (`juice: 'auto'`, `grade: 'auto'`, the world's own words): the
  effects' floor in its register (anime) and its game type's movement juice (pinball: a trail at the feet past
  running pace, the air streaking by near top speed, speed lines on a surge), and the frame graded vivid.
- Last train in daylight. The look was too much a diagram of a runner: flat boxes, paint that explains, a dark
  scene, a small hero. Against what works in this kind of game it is now late afternoon with the sun low ahead: pale
  ballast, dark soot-brick stations with cream stone and green ironwork, a gold horizon under a soft blue sky, and
  the asks read ON a light way by their colour and their shadow (an orange-red to go over, a blue to go round), where
  before the way was kept darker than the asks. The gate is unchanged and holds on 200 seeds' shades.
- Three tones and a shadow (a theme's `sun: 'ahead'`): every box of the walls is lit on top, as it is toward the way
  and in shade toward the runner; an ask's top is lit and its face shaded, and it throws its shadow toward the runner
  as long as it is tall; each overhead beam lays a bar of shadow across the way, a segment apart.
- A jump's tell may be its window's two lines alone (`edges`): the coins say the rest.
- THE COINS (`gameworld/roll-course.js`, a platformer's `coins`): five with each ask, laid only where that ask
  stands. Over a jump an arc in the middle track from where the jump is pressed to where it lands; beside wagons a
  line down the clear track. They trace the way through and are what a map is scored by.
- A roll's `with` (`game/roll.js`, the runtime's roll): `{ '<pickup id>': '<block id>' }`, a pickup that lies only
  where that rolled block stands. No dice of its own, so every pick a roll made before is the pick it makes now. A
  roll may name a coin as it names a collect's pickup.
- A course's camera stands nearer (`course-view.js` `COURSE_NEAR`) and a tall frame uses a longer lens
  (`COURSE_TALL_FOV`, 32 degrees across): the hero is about a fifth of a phone's height, where it was a ninth, with
  the three bands where they were.
- The sky is mixed straight through OKLab: a gold horizon under a blue sky passes through cream, not green.
- Chunky, specific things (`course-things.js`). An ask is drawn WHOLE as the thing it is, inside the box that is met
  (a block may be `bare`: met, and not drawn as its box, `playscape/terrain.js`). Things are built of bevelled chunks
  in three tones. A barrier is a striped board on three feet with a rail under it. Crates are five, with daylight
  between them, every other one lower and set back. Wagons are two, round-shouldered on an underframe and wheels,
  each with a face toward the runner: a windscreen with the sky in it, two headlamps, a number board, a buffer beam.
- Denser sides. The platform gains stout columns with feet, a deep canopy, a name board hung over the edge, a clock,
  a kiosk, a door and lit windows, a bench, a luggage trolley; the cutting gains piers, dark arches, a relay cabinet
  and a signal on its post. Behind the walls (a theme's `beyond`, the new `mid` role): two houses a slice a side, of
  the seed's heights, their windows toward the way, so the sides are three layers (the wall, the town, the far
  skyline) and not one row.
- Movement. A viaduct runs along the left behind the wall, and a train of four cars crosses it the other way to the
  runner, round and round: the page's mover slides its group (a level's `sceneryMovers`). Seen in Chrome at two
  places six seconds apart with the hero held still.

### Emergent gameplay: a game that plays a different map each time

In progress. A level's `roll`: what the session's seed picks on it. The recipe and the page never change; the seed the
game's shell already sends with `game-init` picks, and seed 1 is the reference roll (what a page with no shell, a
capture and the level played in Node show).

- `roll.cover` (`game/roll.js`): groups of the level's `blocks`, named by each block's `id`, of which the seed stands a
  number or any number in a band: `roll: { cover: [{ of: ['wall-a', 'wall-b', 'crate'], stand: [1, 2] }] }`. A rolled
  block is one thing: one render group and one box. Left out, it is gone whole, as if never built: out of the
  colliders, the sight, the nav grid and the scene, with nothing broken and nothing said on the bus.
- `roll.items`: groups of the level's pickups, named by each pickup's `id` in its `collect`, of which the seed lays a
  number or a band: `items: [{ of: ['gem-a', 'gem-b', 'gem-c'], lay: [1, 2] }]`. One left out is not there to be
  found: its zone is no source on the bus, and its glyph and its sparkle are not drawn.
- `roll.start`: the places the pilot may set out from, each written as the pilot's own transform is
  (`start: [{ pos: [x, y, z], heading? }, …]`); the seed picks one. A fall's respawn and a level's doors stay where
  the level wrote them.
- `roll.pattern`: a LINE of slots, one of each slot's blocks standing, picked one after another so the line is paced,
  where a group's picks know nothing of each other. `kinds` says what each block asks of the player; never more than
  `run` (2) of one kind stand running and a pair of kinds is never repeated (ABAB), the rule the dungeons' walls keep;
  `never` names two forms that may not stand one after the other; `ramp` weighs a form by its place in the line
  (`{ hurdle: [4, 2], block: [1, 4] }`: it opens easy and tightens). A slot the rules leave nothing is filled all the
  same. `rollWays` counts the lines that keep the rules.
- The rolled course is one such line. Rolled slot by slot with no memory, 83 % of its courses ran three or more asks of
  one kind and 96 % broke the walls' rule (2,000 rolls); as a pattern, none does. Its audit gains `paced`.
- The dice keep their order (the cover, then the items, then the start, then the patterns), so a roll that gains a kind
  keeps every pick of the kinds it had.
- The runtime's roll (`worlds/controllable/roll.js`): whole-number dice, so every runtime rolls the same from the same
  seed (the page's against Node's: 305 seeds, none unequal). Emitted only into a page whose level has a roll; a level
  without one keeps every byte.
- A rolled level says `game-shown` only once it has started, so the shell's veil never lifts on the level as it was
  before its roll.
- A level played in Node rolls too: `simLevel` / `levelSim` take the session's `seed`.
- The seeds audit (`game/roll-audit.js`), a machine gate: a level with a roll is many maps, so a sample of its seeds
  (24, from 1) is walked in Node, each rolled by the same dice and held to four laws: the pilot has a body, the way is
  open (from the start the seed picked, through the contract's own walk, and to every pickup it laid), the sample is not one map, and the seeds played through
  (led corner to corner on the nav grid) reach the level's success. It says how many seeds it walked and which failed,
  by seed; it never refuses. `create_game` answers with it (`rolls`) for each level that rolls, and a `design_game`
  run's level audit carries it.
- The browser's walk of a rolled level proves its reference roll: its one-leg plan is led round what seed 1 stands.
- The roll room (`gameworld/roll-room.js`), a practice room: a world whose levels roll (`roll: true`) tries a roll before
  any level, on its own hero and feel template. A flat walled yard whose cover, gems and start a seed picks; R rolls
  the next seed. Its measures are read by `design_game` (`practice.measured.roll`): the seeds audit of the yard, and
  which forms of cover stop this hero, each form laid across a lane and the hero run at it jumping. A hero on its feet
  is stopped by a crate; one with an air jump goes over a 2 m wall. Served at `bible?book=practice&room=roll`.
- The rolled course (`gameworld/roll-course.js`): a hero that runs on momentum (a feel on the pinball base) has an
  obstacle course for its roll room, seen from behind on three lanes. Three asks: a hurdle and a block to jump, posts
  that leave an outer lane open. It is sized by time, measured on the rule the game ships (`paceOf`): each jump's
  window in seconds, a lane change steered as a player learns to. A slot stands every (the neediest ask + a rest) of
  the hero's top speed, and each slot is one group of the level's roll, of which exactly one thing stands, so every
  roll is fair by how it is laid. Its audit is the reaction bot: it sees only so far ahead and acts a reaction time
  after; the laws are fair (a 0.4 s reaction with the sight the course asks runs every sampled seed clean), finishes
  (a 0.8 s one still does) and apart. The sight a course asks is (its need + the reaction) x the hero's speed.
- The course's dress (`gameworld/course-dress.js`): a rolled course is coloured by ROLE (the way: ground, sleeper,
  rail, kerb, wall, sky; the asks: go over, go round; the tells; the exit) from a theme card, the rail yard first
  (ballast, sleepers and steel rails; amber barriers and orange crates to jump, blue wagons to go round). Its own
  machine gate, measured in OKLab: every ask is read against the way, the two kinds of ask are told apart by hue,
  nothing on the way is as vivid as an ask, and each tell is in its ask's hue. A game's seed gives it its own shade of
  the theme. `obstacles: { dress }` names one; the greybox loses every law, and says so.
- Where a course is read (`gameworld/course-view.js`, the principles in `docs/course-dress-principles.md`): the
  screen in thirds from top to bottom, the vanishing point on the line between the first two. The top third is where
  stuff comes from (its key: readability and distinction by the game's intent), the middle where it comes to view
  (readability of form: where a thing is made interesting), the bottom where you react (the character). A course is
  followed by a camera that frames them (`courseCamera`): the way's far end on the upper line, the place the reaction
  begins on the lower, the hero in the bottom band; `viewBands` says where the bands fall for any camera, and the roll
  room's readout whether its own frames them. The practice rooms' usual follow camera frames none of the three.
- The course map (`gameworld/course-map.js`): the diagram a design book draws a running game's course with. The course
  from straight above, turned on its side, read left to right a row at a time: each segment numbered and named, its
  ask in its role's colour with its tell before it, a run drawn through it (the reaction bot's, dashed in the air), a
  ruler in metres and in seconds at the hero's top speed, and the flanks as cells lettered A or B by the walls' rule
  (`era/wall-rhythm.js`): where a designed slice is placed. One map a roll. Served for the roll room's course at
  `bible?book=practice&room=roll&view=map`. A lane is drawn as a guide: a place to be, not a thing on the ground.
- The tells: paint on the way that carries what the course was measured by, rolled with its ask. A jump's window is
  painted as a strip (jump while on it); posts' arrows point at the open lane from where a two-lane change must begin.
- A level's `blocks` may carry their own colour (`tint`) and flat paint that goes with them (`marks`).
- A level that is an obstacle course: a gameworld level's `obstacles: true | { slots?, rest? }`, in place of `walk`. A
  run lays the lane for the world's hero (sized by its measured pace), its things as the level's blocks and a roll
  over them, the exit at its end; every play is another course. `create_game` answers with the reaction bot's audit
  for it (the made level read back as a course: its things are jumped and steered round, never walked round).
- The roll room's stand-in hero wears the body its game reads (`game-bodies.js`): a mascot's big head on a small body
  for a runner, a platformer or a game to collect. The rail runner's feel (the one on the pinball base) joins the mascot
  rail, so its hero reads as a mascot wherever a game's body is read from its feel.
- A world's `roll` reaches its levels (`gameworld/roll-lower.js`): `roll: true | { cover?, items? }` on a gameworld, and
  each walking level a run lays on a trail takes a roll on its recipe over what it already holds: its cover (the cover
  concern's own walls and crates by the trail's beats, laid for the roll when the level's concerns laid none), of which
  half or more stand and never all, and its pickups, of which half or more lie and never all. A pilot with no body (a
  first-person walker's) is given one, since no cover stops it without. A level that is no trail walked on foot, and a
  world that does not roll, are as they were.
- A run over levels that roll (`game/game-manifest.js`, the play shell): `run: { length, repeat: true }` lets a run draw
  a level more than once, so a run may be longer than its pool: one level that rolls is a run of its maps. Each draw
  has its own seed (the run's number and step), never the same level twice running when there is another.
  `create_game` says so when a repeated level has no roll. A level that rolls says which map was played on its result
  (`map 202`), and played again is the same map.
- A rolled level opened with no shell takes its seed from the page's own `?seed=` (1 unsaid: the reference roll).
- The door: the agent's card for it (`gameworld-roll`, in `get_game_vocab`): what a roll is, the two ways to ask (a
  world's `roll: true` over its walking levels; a level's `obstacles` for a course), the run that repeats one level,
  what each audit says and what none of them sees. The game design routing card answers "a different map every time"
  and "an obstacle course"; `design_game`'s roll steps point at the card; the levels chapter owns it.
- A made course's camera is solved for the game's own screen: on an upright frame it is found again at that frame's
  field of view (the table's pull-back would have moved every third). A world that names no hero runs its course from
  the eye, and its level says so (`followed`): the tells and the thirds are laid for a chase.
- A made course is played as it was measured: its hero is steered across the lanes in the camera's frame and the
  camera is held behind the lane (the chase the player turns), where a hero turned as a tank is and a chase easing
  round behind it swung the course off the screen at the first lane change. Its exit is the lane's whole width, kerb
  to kerb (a disc on the centre line let a run that ended in an outer lane go past the end of the course; the roll
  room's too). Its controls legend is said at the top of the screen: the bottom is the character's.
- One rolled game, end to end (`scripts/spikes/roll/game.mjs`): designed, approved and run through `design_game`, made
  as a run of three maps by `create_game`, exported, and played in headless Chrome through its shell by the reaction
  bot's policy on the page's own frames. Three different courses, each run clean in about the time Node's audit said,
  the shell carrying the run to its result. It is how the four faults above were found.
- Not yet: the foes a seed picks, the level's book, and the room layout itself rolled in the
  page from a kit of rooms.

### Game audio: the sound sheet on every level, and a score by request

- **A game on the sound sheet hears it on every level** (`gameworld/sound-sheet.js` `levelSheet`, `onSheet`). A game
  that writes a `sound` of its own, even an empty one, now gets the sheet's sounds and its stage's bed on every level
  it builds: the designed game's levels and a world walked before its people, which were built with no audio at all,
  as well as a quick game's. A quick game that names another `sfx` keeps that. A stage that wrote its own soundtrack,
  `sfx` or bed keeps each. A game with no `sound` builds the levels it built.
- **The whole arsenal on the sheet.** A game with an arsenal (its own, or its feel's kit) hears every weapon on its
  levels, not its first: each weapon's swing and blow by the move's weight, the guard's block, parry and break, the
  bow, the weapon cycle, a foe's swing and fall, a blow taken. The words are the practice room's (one table,
  `MOVE_SOUND_WORDS`, read by both), and a weapon is read by its words where the shelf has its own. A game overrides a
  weapon with `sound.weapons` and an event with `sound.moves`. A game with no arsenal keeps its two slots.
- **Guns by cartridge.** On a sheet game's shooter levels (the shoot and deathmatch goals), each gun the player
  carries sounds as what it is, by the firing range's procedure: its shot by its cartridge, its reload over its own
  reload time, a round landing, the draw. A game overrides a gun with `sound.guns`. Not on the sheet yet: a
  dogfight's craft, guns picked up off the floor, the bots' guns, and a rocket's blast.
- **Foes sound on what they do.** Each foe of a sheet game's bestiary sounds on its attack, on a blow taken and as
  it falls, placed where it stands: a beast in its species' voice (a big cat grunts when struck), a foe drawn as a
  person with a shout, a grunt and a cry. A pack's attacks are held apart. A game overrides a foe with `sound.foes`;
  a foe with no voice of its own is listed as owed. Before this a foe's voice played only when it spotted the hero.
- **A ride's engine.** A sheet game's driven level hears its vehicle: a held voice of the shelf by what is ridden,
  following the ride's speed from an idle up to its top (a level's new `audio.engine`, and the page's engine
  channel). `sound.ride` names another held voice, or `false`. A transformer's forms are not on the sheet yet.
- **The sound book** (`/bible?book=sound`, `gameworld/sound-book.js`). A game's sound sheet as a page: every sound
  it plays, the shelf word and why, each with a button that plays it on the game's own kernel; the beds by level
  and what is owed. A game on no sheet sees the sheet it would have.
- **The music department and the audio direction** (`gameworld/audio-direction.js`; the book's new `music`
  department, its chapters `audio-direction` and `score`; the recipe's new `music` key). The direction is the
  game's taste in sound, what the art direction is to the picture: `music.direction: { style?, identity?, cast?,
  sfx?, space?, ui? }`, solved from the game's words where it writes none (the orchestra unless they say
  electronic). Play keeps the SFX and reads it: the sound sheet speaks the direction's `sfx` where `sound.style`
  says none, and each level of a game with a `music` is heard in a space (the direction's, else its place: a cave a
  cavern). Taste is advice: the department says where the sheet sits badly with the score (the sound book shows
  it) and changes nothing. A game with no `music` builds what it built.
- **The cue sheet** (`gameworld/cue-sheet.js`, [docs/game-audio.md](../../../../docs/game-audio.md)). Every
  department that needs music asks for it (the flow's title, menus and credits; each level's place; a level's fights
  and its boss; each cinematic the flow plays; the outcomes) and the music department answers each on the game's
  one score identity, in the direction's style and cast. `music.cues` names another mood for a request, or `false`
  for silence. A game with a `music` has every level it builds scored from the sheet: its place, with its fight or
  boss coming in on the tension. A quick game's own `quick.music` still wins. The outcomes' stingers play: a run
  mints each as a step of the score's chapter (`cue-victory`, `cue-defeat`) and the game names them, a changed
  answer remaking its cue in place. The flow's cues are on the sheet and not yet played; the title, menus, credits and cinematics are stand-ins, listed as owed, until
  the title theme and a cue that ends are written.
- **The score book** (`/bible?book=score`, `gameworld/score-book.js`). The audio direction said once, then every
  request for music, who asked, the cue and why, each with a button that plays it on the game's kernel.
- **An agent is told.** `design_game`'s readout suggests a `sound` and a `music` to a game that writes neither (a
  `next` step each, with its patch, its book and its card), and two cards, `gameworld-sound` and `gameworld-music`,
  are the manuals of the `sound` and `audio-direction` chapters.
- **Fixed: a composed game's ground and bed.** A composed game's stages carry no stage kit (the world's style
  holds it), so the sheet gave a forest stone footsteps and no bed. A level's place is now read from the world's
  kit and weather, the level's climate and its look's title: grass in a grove, sand in a desert, snow in the alps,
  the night or the wood as its bed.
- **Fixed: a game's `sound` reached no level.** The world reader checked `sound` and did not carry it, so a quick
  game on the sheet played the solved sheet and ignored the game's own style, slots and cues.
- Planned, not built yet: the flow playing its cues (the play shell scores no screen or cinematic); a title theme
  (the menu and the credits the same tune at another energy) and a cue that ends, written to a cinematic's length;
  the ground changing within a level.

### The game room: one room composed for the game, tried in the practice door

A game that needs a single setting gets one good room, composed from what the game needs out of room primitives and
played in the practice door, which reconfigures itself into the game's room. It is not a geocube and not a
roguelike's rooms: one seeded, editable composition. Design notes: [docs/game-room.md](../../../../docs/game-room.md).

- **Room primitives** (`lib/graph/gameroom/primitives.js`): a closed table, as the board rail's kernel is. Low and tall
  cover, a pillar, a platform with its step, a crate, and a shift's counter, bin, shelf and pass. Each is its blocks,
  its plan and what it affords play (cover, screen, hop, vantage, climb, station, source, store, hand-in). A new kind of
  room is a new composition; a new primitive is a row.
- **The brief** (`needs.js`) reads the room from the game, each need saying why:
  - **size:** a crossing of about four seconds at the hero's run;
  - **cover and pillars:** for a fight hand to hand;
  - **decks:** where the jump makes them worth having;
  - **foes:** the world's count, else three where it fights;
  - **a shift:** its card tuned for one player;
  - **the camera:** the world's own.

  Shooters and platformers are left to the firing range and the platform room.
- **The composition** (`compose.js`, seeded): bands for the entry, the field and the goal, a clear lane down the spine,
  pairs mirrored across it, everything kept a metre apart. Decks stand against the side walls, foe spots behind cover,
  and a shift's line runs down the middle with the pass as the goal.
- **The room laws** (`laws.js`), on a quarter-metre grid of the floor, advice that never refuses: reachable, a 760 mm
  walkway (clearance), climbable decks, room to move, and nothing too tall for an overhead camera.
- **The practice door's game room** (`gameworld/game-room.js`, `room`), offered to a world that fights hand to hand,
  works a shift or has foes:
  - the conceptual plane, its primitives as blocks, the spawn and the goal ringed, a shift's recipe on the floor;
  - the hero, its own or a mascot, on the feel;
  - the foes on their spots, still until Shift+F;
  - a chase pulled back to read the room, or overhead for a shift.

  Its page says the brief, what was laid, the laws and the shift's proof. It has its own rail icon.
- **The dress** (`gameroom/dress.js`): the second pass, which never moves what stands. Each place keeps its box and
  collider, and its thing is drawn into that box, fitted to it. The things are the stage dressing's pieces, the
  furniture door's builds, and a few of the room's own (a range, a field plot, a leaf pile, a wheelie bin). A trade
  maps places to things:
  - kitchen, farm, site and chores for the shifts;
  - the hall for a fight.

  A shift wears its card's trade (its own `dress`, else its starter's) and a fight the hall. `dress: false`, or
  `&dress=none` on the practice pages, keeps the greybox, and the pages offer every trade.
- **The area** (`gameroom/area.js`): what the room stands in, designable. The dress draws the places and the area
  draws everything else, moving nothing:
  - **the floor:** a pattern in its colours (plane, tiles, boards, concrete, earth, lawn, flags);
  - **the walls:** a style with its height and colours (plain, tiled with windows, a fence, hoarding, stone between
    pilasters, a hedge, none), cut to a dark section on the south, where either camera starts. The wall colliders take
    the height drawn, so a chase pulls in off a full wall;
  - **the surround:** static things outside (a dining room, a street, fields, a barn, trees, a frame going up, a tower
    crane, a materials yard, the neighbours' houses, a colonnade);
  - **the ground and the sky.**

  Each trade has its own area. On a roof card, the deck is drawn as the house in a garden. A world designs its own with
  the new gameworld key `room: { dress?, area? }`, where the area is a name or an object over one (`like`, `floor`,
  `walls`, `surround`, `ground`, `sky`, `cut`); a malformed one is taught. `area: false`, or `&area=none` on the
  practice pages, keeps the conceptual plane, and the pages offer every trade's area. Seen in headless Chromium for
  each trade and the hall; the work proofs are unchanged.
- **The rooms' menu on mana-ui** (`gameworld/practice-mana.js`): the work room's and the game room's readout and
  choices leave their page panel, the H key and Shift+F for a menu drawn by mana-ui and driven by the controls layer.
  The keys, every pad layout and a finger work it alike, and each control is named as the controls kernel names it.
  - **It is the shell's pause, kept on the page.** The pilot scheme's `pause` (Esc, a pad's start) opens it, and the
    scene is held on the shell's sidecar, its clocks stopped. It opens as the page loads, as the room's briefing.
  - **Its screens:** the room's readout in tabs; set up (the movement, the worker, the dress, the area and the foes),
    the room reopened with them; and the controls this world answers to, its live rows.
  - **The foes** are woken on the shell's AI switch or the pilot's own G.
  - **The hint line** names each action by the key the scheme binds it to.

  - **Its look is the shift family** (theme cards `shift`, `shift-kitchen`, `shift-farm`, `shift-site`,
    `shift-garden`, `shift-hall`), chosen by where the room stands. It is a couch co-op work sim's look: order tickets on
    paper over an offset slab, rounded faces, a heavy outline, the floor's shovel and bucket colours as its accents,
    and each trade's own tint (the kitchen's tomato and the awning's stripes, the farm's stitched feed-sack, the site's
    hazard yellow and stripe). The HUD's counters, its hint line and the use prompt wear it too. Every card's words read
    on its focus and its tabs (the contrast advice measured).
  - **The screen keeps to the game.** The explaining moved off it into the menu's How to play, a tutorial in tabs
    (the goal, moving, the work, the floor; for a fight, moving, the foes, the room). Each key is drawn as a cap in the
    glyph of the device in hand. In play, the screen shows the counters, the use prompt and one "Esc menu" chip in the
    corner. The prompts lose their tags: the station's verb is said by its colour, and a shelf's count by its pips.
  In headless Chromium, the shift's clock held at 240 through the briefing and ran once resumed. Esc reopened the menu,
  and set up reopened the room with the movement and the area picked.
- Played in headless Chromium: a sword fighter's hall (28 m, two decks, pillars, low cover, three foes) and a shift's
  room (its line on counters, the proof won). Machine gates only: whether the room plays well is for someone in it to
  judge.

### Highlight: a thing indicated by a rim light

A primitive of the game UI language's fx channel: an entity lit at its silhouette (a fresnel: bright where its
surface turns from the eye, nothing face on) in a colour, so the player's eye finds what can be taken, what is next,
what to use. The same idea as the rim light the characters wear, on things.

- An fx state: `{ highlight: true | '#rrggbb', pulse?, power?, k?, as?, when? }` on an entity by its id
  (`game/highlight.js`). `pulse` breathes it; `power` is how narrow the rim is; `as` keeps a motion under it (float,
  spin, pulse); `when` names a bus var, and it is lit only while that var is truthy (the quest's next thing).
- A level's switch: `game.highlight` (true, a colour, or `{ color, pulse, power, k }`) lights every thing its
  mechanics lay to be taken (a collect's pickups, coins, supplies, an escape room's keys, a trade) under its float,
  and its exit and its delivery point.
- It is the game's own rim. Drawn as a status's coat is, from one shared source (`scene/channels/coat-src.js`: the
  status channel's pages are byte for byte what they were), so it holds the page's logarithmic depth and stands a hair
  off the surface; a mesh with no normals is given smooth ones. Where its `power` and `k` are unsaid it takes the
  juice floor's rim, as the characters do: a soft fade under isekai, a hard cel band under cel, a thin line under
  material, at the game type's strength. A world with no juice keeps a soft rim of its own.
- Spliced only when a state is a highlight: an fx world without one emits the bytes it did (the `fx` pin holds).
- Seen in Chrome on a quick collectathon's gems, with no juice and under each look (`scripts/spikes/highlight/level.mjs`). Not done: a skinned body
  (a character keeps its own rim), a highlight on a level's static scenery (a block, a door: not an entity), and a
  default colour taken from the game's look.

### A level always hears its shell: the game's params and seed are no longer dropped on a slow build

A level page under a game shell waits 1.5 s for the shell's `game-init` before it starts on its presets. The shell
shares the level's thread, so its answer is queued behind the level's own build; when the build ended near the 1.5 s
mark, the presets ran first and the shell's params (the loadout, the door entered by, a staged scene) and its seed were
dropped for that session.

- The wait is counted in time the shell could have answered in (`scene/channels/game.js` `awaitShell`): a tick the
  thread was busy through counts for nothing. A shell that never answers still gets the presets after 1.5 s.
- Measured on a 15.9 MB level in headless Chromium: 4 of about 17 loads started on the presets before; 0 of 13 after.
- The emission pins of the three fixtures whose page carries the game channel are re-pinned.

### mana-ui grows: pictograms, and four more families of looks

In progress. The game UI runtime had a place for an icon and drew a name's initials there, and its looks were mostly
dark and serious. The plan: pictures and icons, one HUD host for every level, layout that adapts, touch as a device,
the parts every game composes by hand, more motion, a layout law, and a handoff to engines.

- PICTOGRAMS (`mana-ui/icons.js`): fifty of them (what is counted and kept, what a body has and meets, where things
  are, what a menu does, what a hand does), one outline each on a 24 grid, with the other words a game says for one
  (`coins`, `time`, `hp`, `settings`). A theme's `icons` word says the style they are all drawn in: `solid`, `line`,
  `chunky` (filled and fattened), `badge` (on a round plate of the accent), `duo` (the outline over a pale fill of
  itself). Nothing is loaded: an icon is a mask in the theme's sheet, in the ink of the words beside it.
- The runtime names an icon and the sheet draws it: an `icon`, a counter's `icon` and a prompt's glyph carry
  `data-icon`. A name with no pictogram keeps its initials; a theme that says no style (every preset) is as it was.
- FOUR FAMILIES of looks, two cards each (`playscape/ui/theme-cards/`): `broadcast` (matchday, floodlight: read from
  across a room), `cosy` (picnic, knit: made by hand), `clean` (lightdeck, orbit: exact and airy), `dread` (dread,
  static: restraint). Each has its icon style and its stages. The shelf's README names every family and what it
  holds to.
- The toybox draws its pictograms chunky; the runner's HUD counts coins beside a coin.
- The pictograms take more of the theme. Three more styles, each a hand of its own inside the icon's picture:
  `sketch` (a pencil line that wobbles, gone over twice), `stencil` (the silhouette with a bridge left across it),
  `glow` (the line and its light round it). `iconTone: 'meaning'` draws each icon in the theme's colour for what it
  means (a heart the health's, a bolt the stamina's, a skull the harm's, what is won the accent), where `ink` keeps
  the words' colour. A badge's plate is the theme's corner (round, soft, square, cut), its silhouette the ink the
  theme reckons reads on it. `iconSwap: { coin: 'ticket' }` is a look's own picture for a word.
- The cards say theirs: matchday stencil, picnic and dread sketch, orbit glow, knit badge, floodlight and lightdeck
  line, static solid, toybox chunky; matchday, picnic, knit, lightdeck, static and toybox in the colours of meaning.
- One HUD host for every level. A world that says a `ui` has its levels' own HUD rows (`events.hud`) drawn by the game
  UI runtime, in the game's look: `game/hud-mana.js` lowers readouts, bars, counters, clocks, banners, toasts and
  legends to one composition, and the page's host (`scene/channels/mana-hud.js`, the course's, made general) reads the
  level's bus into it each frame, gates a row by its part and its phase as before, and draws the pilot's health and
  sprint beside them. The host is laid over the scene's own frame. A world without a `ui` emits the bytes it did;
  carved titles stay the title channel's. A level whose pages change: one of a world with a `ui`.
- Layout that adapts. The frame a view is drawn in is state the runtime holds (`rt.frame`, measured by a mount from
  its own box and again when it changes), and a spec branches on it: `{ frame: 'portrait' | 'landscape' | 'narrow' |
  'short' | 'hand' }` in a `when` or an `unless`. A `stack` says what it does out of width (`fit: 'wrap' | 'stack'`).
  The runner's HUD is one composition for both frames now, laid again when a phone is turned, where it was two specs
  chosen at emit. A page with a course HUD emits different bytes; a spec that names no frame draws as it did.

### A world's inhabitants: a goblin kin, foes that carry arms and stand as their game draws them

An action RPG made from a sentence fielded green-skinned villagers who charged like boars, drawn smooth-shaded beside an
inked hero, in a book that counted them on another scale. Its foes are now a people of their own, armed, cast to trade
blows, drawn in the game's style, and said so in its books. Machine gate throughout; nobody has looked but in passing.

- **The goblin, a kin of its own** (`egocube/ancestry.js`, `beast/cards.js`, `creature-heads/relational.js`). A lineage
  below the hero door, built the seventh generation's way on the game's own rig:
  - its HEAD a skull of the relational creature head: a small round vault under a heavy brow, a short broad muzzle that
    is all mouth with its corners back under the eyes, a chin drawn to a point, a long nose of its own carried over the
    mouth to a point, big forward eyes with slit pupils, long thin ears set low and swept back past the skull;
  - its BODY a card: a narrow chest over a round pot belly, thin arms hung forward with big hands, thick thighs on
    short bent legs with the knees forward, big feet, a deep hunch it keeps in its walk; sea green, bare.
  It joins the foe shelf's peoples (`foes/people.js`), so any class that stands on two legs can be skinned as one.
- **Four measures the creature head lacked** (`creature-heads/relational.js`): `earSweep` (the ear laid back toward the
  back of the skull, its length kept), `noseLength`, `noseWidth` and `noseDrop` (a nose of its own, a cone out past
  the muzzle to a point), `chinPoint` (the chin drawn to a point). Each is nothing at its canon value: a skull that
  names none is as it was.
- **A kin's card names its own head and where it stands** (`beast/cards.js` `head`, `stands`; `beast/head.js`). A kin
  whose head is not a library skull's wears the relational head its card names, at the size the card gives it on the
  body (`scale`, a new word of a relational head: a small body under a big head). `stands` is its share of a person's
  height in its rest; the foe shelf measures it by that (`peopleBody`), and a lineage of one build stands at it.
- **A hero that plays strings meets foes that swing a blow, from the first one on** (`gameworld/foe-casting.js`). The
  grunt, the flanker and the elite are cast from the classes that strike (a wind-up, a contact, a recovery the hero
  reads and trades with), never one that braces and charges down a line or hurts by a touch: those are a beast's
  lessons, and a person who charged like a boar read wrong. The elite is such a class a rank up, the grunt's own where
  no other is left, never the boss's body.
- **A people's rank and file stands at its lineage's smallest build**, its elite and its boss at their own roll grown
  by their rank. A person dressed as a crew takes its build from its dress, as before.
- **A people that swings a blow carries its lineage's arm** (`PEOPLE_ARMS`, from the armory's own builds,
  `equipment/armory.js`): the goblin and the orcish rank and file a cudgel, their elite and boss a spiked club, in the
  right hand. A lineage with no row carries what its own roll gives it; a new people's arms is a row.
- **The meadow's era fields goblins first** (`ERA_PEOPLES`): the action RPG's sentence now casts a goblin guard, a
  goblin patrol, an elite guard and a brute boss, each armed (was an orcish charger, a guard, a patrol elite and a
  brute boss, bare-handed).
- **A held weapon never takes the fist guard** (`polygonizer/hero-gesture.js`). The guard is a boxer's, both fists
  before the face, so a blade or a club in the hand stood across the head. A figure asked for the guard with a weapon
  in a hand stands ENGAGED instead, a new stand: the weapon arm carried low and out, the point ahead and clear of the
  body, the off hand open. The record keeps the word it was given, so the guard comes back when the hand is empty; a
  shield on the forearm keeps the guard. Every figure that holds a weapon and was asked for the guard changes its stand.
- **A beast-kin is drawn as its game draws its people** (`egocube/plan.js`, `mcp/tools/create-character.js`). A kin
  rolled in an anime game's setting takes the character light, flat tones stepped once and inked; it was smooth-shaded
  beside an inked hero. The light rides in a beast's spec, where the hero door reads it: beside the spec the door
  dropped it, which the anime head's own default hid for a person. Any other setting, and every person, as they were.
- **The books say it** (`gameworld/foe-cast.js`, `foe-cast-html.js`, `gameworld-cards.js`, `docs/foes.md`):
  - a foe's card says what it carries, by the armory's name;
  - the lineup stands a kin at the height its card gives it (a goblin a little over a metre beside the hero);
  - in a world armed with a kit the book numbers each foe on the kit's scale, the strings its rank takes and the
    health that is, where it counted the foe shelf's blows (two for a grunt that falls to one string, sixty for a boss
    that takes eleven), and writes a boss's phases as its levels carry them;
  - the agent's foes card names a people's `gear`; the foes doc says the kin, the arms and the casting.
- **One body, many foes, and no gear designed by hand** (`foes/packs.js`, new; `egocube/outfit.js`, `egocube/plan.js`,
  `foes/people.js`, `gameworld/runner.js`). A kin's foes are told apart by what they wear and how big they stand, and
  what they wear is what the FRAME-ADORNED PRINCIPLES give them (`adornFromSheet`: role, station, archetype, anatomy,
  concept, restraint; each piece with its reason). Those principles were written for the creature biped and their answer
  was dropped on the tiered body, the ledger saying so.
  - **The bridge.** A kin on the tiered body made with a designed dress (the cube's default) now wears its adornment: an
    outfit with no cut, the pieces on its bare frame (`heroAdornOf`). A kin character made from a sheet is adorned from
    here on; one already made is as it was.
  - **Three words on a kin foe's skin.** Wild: neither, bare (the run's order says so, since the cube would now adorn
    it), a rabble told apart by `body: { size?, coat? }` (runt, lean, squat, big; a lineage swatch or a hex).
    `adorned: true`: each by its own sheet. `pack: { style, colourway?, motif? }`: the same principles with what a band
    shares pinned.
  - **The pack is the principles, not a design.** A pack style names no piece: it pins the character every member is
    read as (the raiders a hero's: one great shoulder plate the focal, a warrior's trophies and paint), its order, its
    cloth (short breeches and a cloth hung front and back, the chest left bare for the pieces), its colourways and its
    marks. A member's class gives its role's gear and its rank its station and how many pieces it keeps
    (`adornFromSheet` takes a `station` and a `room`). So two of one class and rank wear the same whoever they are, a
    fighter is told from a caster, and a leader wears all the rank and file does and more. The laws are read again in
    the pack's colours, and the colourways (rust, bone, moss) were set to keep them; a caster of the rank and file, at
    three pieces, carries the trim once where the law asks twice (its belt's fittings, which the law does not count,
    are the second).
  - A kin whose card is one body is rolled at its lineage's one build (a goblin rolled a brute stood 1.7 m).
  - **The casting call reads which a kin's cast is off the game's minds** (`gameworld/foe-casting.js`). Creatures of
    the place (they guard a ground, they wander): WILD, sized by role where the lineage has one build. A force come for
    the hero (the cube's motivation hunts) or one that hunts as one (`squad: 'pack'`): a PACK in one rolled colourway,
    and a band of two kins is led by the bigger (`KIN_BANDS`: the goblin under the orc), its elite and its boss that
    kin where the style is cut for it and the class fits. So the action RPG made from a sentence fields goblin raiders,
    a guard and a lean patroller, under an orc elite and an orc boss, one pack; it fielded bare goblins of four sizes.
  - A kin's collider now stands at its card's height (`stands`) and its size: a goblin's was a person's.
- **The orc is its own creature** (`creature-heads/relational.js`, `creature-heads/dentition.js`, `beast/cards.js`,
  `egocube/ancestry.js`). A lineage `orc`, a kin card and a skull: a deep jaw square at its front and set ahead of a flat
  nose (an underbite), two tusks standing up out of the lower lip, a brow over small eyes, short ears laid out to the
  sides; on a wedge of a body, the head sunk between sloped shoulders, long heavy arms, short bowed legs. The head gains
  `jawSquare` (the jaw's front a bar across) and `tusk` (the lower canines drawn out, on the jaw's bone, the one tooth
  that stands outside the shut skin); both nothing at their canon value, so every other head is as it was. The meadow's
  era fields the orc where it fielded the orcish, with the same arms. `orcish`,
  the near-human on the hero door, is as it was and still what the word "orc" in a character's brief rolls.
- **The books say it**: a foe's card in the foes book has `body` and `pack` rows and its line says wild, adorned or
  which pack; the agent's foes card names the three words (its ceiling re-pinned, with the reason); the foes doc has
  the principles as a table and the three words.
- **Brows, as form** (`creature-heads/relational.js`, `creature-heads/worn.js`, `beast/head.js`). The relational head
  gains `browRidge` and `browSlant`: a bar over each eye from beside the nose out past the eye's corner, its beads
  marched out to the skin and left standing proud of it, its inner end fallen for a scowl. It is a volume, so the
  character light steps on it and the ink finds its edge; its faces are painted a shade under the coat so it tells from
  the forehead at a distance. The goblin and the orc both carry one; nothing at the canon value, so every other head is
  as it was.
- **A kin's hands sized to its arms** (`beast/cards.js` `hands`, `polygonizer/hero-form.js` `heroPlan({ hands })`). A
  card's `mass.hand` only thickened the hand; `hands` sizes it whole, the palm and the digits with their joints. The
  orc's are half again a person's, under arms half again as thick. One at 1, the default, is exact.
- **A kin's headgear, a first shelf** (`creature-heads/headgear.js`, new; `headgear/wear.js`). A person's headgear is
  drawn on a person's cranium; a kin's head is one skin netted from a field, any shape. So a kin's helmet is that
  field set out by a pad and a plate, kept above a rim from over the eyes to the nape, the ears' feet left clear, a
  card's own masses joined on: a skull cap, a helm with a nasal, a horned helm, a spiked cap. One card fits any skull.
  Worn by the hero door's `headgear` word, which on a kin (a new body the word knows, `kin`) lowers to its head's word;
  a person's card is refused on a kin and a kin's on a person, by name. The raiders' leaders wear them by rank (an elite
  the cap, a boss the horned helm).
- **The hero is designed, as everyone else in its game is** (`gameworld/hero-design.js`, new; `gameworld/compose.js`,
  `egocube/outfit.js`, `gameworld/hero-looks.js`, `gameworld/cast-setting.js`). A game laid from a sentence rolled and
  dressed its cast, its folk and its foes by principle and left its hero the door's stock body in plain clothes: the
  one figure nobody designed. Where no body rail designs it (the action RPG, the stylish action game, the party RPG),
  the sentence door now rolls the protagonist as a person of its world (the Egocube, in the game's own setting; a game
  with a casting page takes its cast's anchor, so the hero is the person the party was rolled against) and writes the
  looks pages from its sheet, each in the page's own words: its build, its face, its hair, its colours, and as its
  underlayer the cut and the pieces the outfit principles design (the role's gear, the one focal, the trim repeated).
  - **The protagonist reads against its ground.** The outfit designer takes a garment colour given it
    (`outfitFromSheet({ garment })`); the hero's is the world's accent, the colour its palette keeps apart from the
    land, and every other role of the outfit's palette still follows from the garment by the palette's own rules. A
    world with no palette keeps the archetype's colour. Before, the hero's shirt was a stop of the grass ramp.
  - The base wears its cloth at ornament 0, which took the belt a cut closes on: the belt is worn as a piece.
  - The brief keeps what was decided (`brief.hero.design`: the roll, the garment, the pieces, the reasons) and the
    character bible's base page says it ("How it was designed"); the agent's looks card says the pages come written
    and are rewritten like any other. A hero with pages of its own, an adopted hero and a railed one are untouched.
  - **A painted world keeps its setting's clothes** (`hero-looks.js` `underlayerFor`, `cast-setting.js`
    `quickFigure`). A palette or a look repaints a kit under an id of its own, and the underlayer rail was looked up
    by that id: a painted world's hero, and a quick game's rolled figures, fell back to plain casual clothes. The rail
    is the stock kit's the world was painted from.
- **The game's colour, chosen with the colour theorist** (`color-theorist/figures.js`, `color-theorist/directions.js`,
  `gameworld/colour.js`, `gameworld/colour-book.js`, `gameworld/world-palette.js`, all new; `docs/colour.md`). The
  theorist solved a palette for a world and nothing coloured the people in it against that world: the goblin, the orc
  and the old hero each sat within a hair of the grass they stood on. Colour had been decided spike by spike (a coat
  taken to the kit's ramps here, a hand-picked colourway there); this is one bridge and one aid, the same for any game.
  - **Figures on a ground.** A figure is measured by its distance from the ground it stands on and the foliage behind
    it, and solved clear of them and of the figures before it, for every eye. A creature keeps its hue family: its
    value and chroma move, its hue turns last and never past its family (a goblin stays green, an orc olive). A mark
    wears the world's second accent, or the protagonist's complement where the two accents are neighbours. Laws
    advise: figures clear, figures apart, colour vision, families kept, the protagonist the loudest.
  - **Colour directions**, rows the same for every game: a quiet land (three bands of value, low in chroma, colour
    spent on who matters) and a colour script across the levels. A direction never picks a hue.
  - **The options, and the colour book** (`/bible?book=colour`). For any gameworld: what its colour is now, measured,
    and each way it could go (the same land with the cast painted clear of it; each direction the world can take with
    the cast solved against the land that makes), every one a patch and every one painted into the same small landscape
    with the cast on its ground. The machine names its pick; the choice is the eyes gate's. `design_game`'s readout says
    when a figure sinks (a `colour` step), the agent's card is `gameworld-colour`, and `pick_palette` points at both.
  - **Who is read**: the hero's garment, a kin foe's skin, a pack's mark. A crew's dress and a beast's coat are said
    unread; a new kind of figure is a reader.
  - **A pack's mark takes a colour given it** (`foes/packs.js` `pack.accent`), and a kin's coat was already a colour
    (`body.coat`): the two words the options write.
  - **The sentence door colours a game once, when it is stored** (`mcp/tools/design-game.js`, `gameworld/compose.js`):
    the cast painted against the ground the world is stored with, what moved kept in `brief.colour`; and a genre with a
    direction chosen for it laid in it (`GENRE_COLOUR`, a row per decision: the action RPG in a quiet land). An existing
    world is untouched until an option is taken.
- **How a game starts: the controls, then an enemy trail** (`gameworld/world-map.js`, `level/guide.js`,
  `scene/channels/guide.js`, `level/map-sketch.js`; `docs/game-flow.md`). The action RPG's world map opened on a first
  zone of three blocks and five foes, its controls shown only as each came up and its first frame a look at the far
  ruins with the hero out of it. The opening sequence is the flow's own step (a cinematic before play), so the level
  no longer does its work. The map now starts on an OPENING: its first block alone, a page of its own.
  - **The controls first, with the hero in hand.** The arrival teaches moving, looking, the jump and the sprint, and
    the guide explains them as LESSONS: one at a time, each staying up until the pilot does it (walks a few metres,
    turns the camera, leaves the ground, runs at its sprint) or its patience runs out. An arrival that teaches one
    verb shows its keys as before.
  - **Then the enemy trail**: a lone foe on the way through the block (the blow), then two at its way out (the
    lock-on and the dodge), each fight's keys shown where it stands; the way out is held until both are won.
  - **No bigger than its tasks**: one block and three foes. The first zone is the next two blocks on one page and
    teaches nothing new: it tests what the opening taught.
  - The brief says it (`brief.worldMap.opening`); the hand-laid first zone (`level/first-zone.js`) is as it was.
- **Foes that come at the hero** (`foes/classes/pursuer.js`, new; `level/map-sketch.js`, `gameworld/foes.js`,
  `level/guide.js`, `scene/channels/guide.js`, `gameworld/playthrough.js`). Every blade on the shelf either held a
  post (a guard, a patrol) or was a boss's body, so a game whose minds hunt still fielded a rank and file that waited
  to be walked up to, and could be walked round.
  - **The pursuer**: a class that hunts by what it sees, from a fair way off, at an even pace, and holds no post. The
    casting call takes it for the grunt of a game whose minds hunt by its own score (its motivation is the game's);
    a game whose minds guard their ground is cast as before.
  - **A fight that comes after another** (a scenario beat's `after`): its foes are minted asleep and woken when every
    foe of the fight before it is down, a banner saying so. The stage's cues do it (the play layer's own `down`,
    `add`, `spawn`); a stage with no such fight lays none.
  - **The opening's trail comes to the hero, one fight at a time**: the lone foe is posted at the far end of the way,
    beyond its sight of the start, so the controls have their room and it comes down the trail once the hero heads up
    it; the pair come from the same way out only when it has fallen.
  - **The guide follows the fight**: a scenario's fight is won by its falls, wherever it was fought, and its keys show
    when its foes have come within a few strides, not only near its mark; the controls lessons give way to a foe at
    hand. The scripted player no longer walks at a foe that is not there yet.
- **A game starts in play, its opening a cutscene** (`game/flow.js`, `game/play-shell.js`, `gameworld/game-flow.js`,
