  `gameworld/runner.js`, `gameworld/compose.js`). The opening sequence was a cinematic before the title on a first
  boot, a prologue after New Game and an attract loop, so a made game stood behind a press and a menu before anyone
  moved.
  - **The `cutscene` step**: a sequence made elsewhere and played whole. A `video` plays over the shell and the game
    goes on as it ends (or cannot play); a directed `scene` is staged as a cinematic is; with neither, the slot is
    empty and is passed at once. Skipped by a key or a click once it has been up a moment, unless `skip: false`.
  - **`flow: 'play'`** on a gameworld: the default flow started in play (`startInPlay`): that cutscene, then the
    save's level, else the first, with no attract, title or prologue before it. The story's opening moment fills the
    slot where there is one; the title stays, where quitting goes. The storyboard says the slot and that an empty one
    waits on nothing.
  - **A game laid from a sentence says it**, and its brief says how it starts. A game that says no flow plays as it
    did.
  - **A gameworld's flow reaches the game made of it** (`lib/mcp/tools/design-game.js`, `create-game.js`). The run
    ordered a game with its flow (its own, the story's cinematics placed in the default, now the start in play) and the
    door made the game without it, so a made game always played the default. The flow and the front go with the
    game, made or remade; `create_game` carries a `flow` it is handed (unlisted: the flow is the gameworld's page).
- **The opening level as a place** (`level/grid-scene.js`, `scene/channels/guide.js`, `gameworld/compose.js`).
  - **No designer's posts in a played level.** A sketch's marks (a post and a tooltip a beat: "encounter: …") were drawn
    on every page; on one a player pilots they are left out, the marks themselves read as before.
  - **No pillar of light on a fight.** The guide's pillar marks a place to go to; a fight's stood on its foe.
  - **A world map grows.** A cube's land takes grass only where a biocube brings it, and the map's cube named none, so
    it was bare ground. A meadow kit's map takes the meadow's own flora unless the cube or the sentence names what
    grows; the brief says so.
- **The meadow card's colours as the action RPG's world, each place derived from it** (`color-theorist/directions.js`,
  `gameworld/world-palette.js`, `world-map.js`, `colour.js`, `level/grid-scene.js`). Supersedes the quiet land the
  action RPG was laid in: a choice made again at the eyes gate.
  - **`kit-card`, a colour direction**: the land given back to its kit's card, as a palette the theorist solves to the
    card exactly and can move. The action RPG's row in `GENRE_COLOUR` is now this; any game on a kit with a row is
    offered it in its colour options.
  - **Each place its own light** (`PLACE_LIGHT`): the village and its road are home, unmoved; the ruins, the towns
    between and the castle heights are the same palette shifted, a row and a sentence a place. A region's
    `palette: { shift }` moves the level's cube for its tiles.
  - **The cast is painted clear of every place** (`landsOf`): the figure solver sees each place's land at once, so the
    sentence door's cast and every colour option hold across the whole map.
- **The action RPG's protagonist, designed at the eyes gate** (`gameworld/hero-rows.js`, new; `hero-design.js`). A genre
  may have a protagonist kept as a row (`GENRE_HERO`): its looks pages whole, given to a game of that genre laid from
  a sentence in place of the rolled person. The action RPG's is a young swordswoman in red and gold under a short plum
  cape, blonde, every colour on her the meadow card's. A creator's own pages still take it away.
- **Clothing words the design needed** (`polygonizer/outfit-plan.js`, `body-garment.js`, `outfit/styles.js`,
  `outfit/expand.js`). Each is an option on the outfit any hero can wear; absent, a piece is built as before.
  - **A drape panel's `hem: 'petal'`**: its corners drawn up in a curve, the middle the longest.
  - **A cloak's `lining`** (the cape's own inner face in its own colour: one cloth, where a second cape inside the
    first crossed it whenever the figure moved; `polygonizer/body-garment.js` `insideGroup`, `station-loft.js`
    `mirrorGroup`), a `hem` given as a place between the length words, and **`arms: false`**: a cape hung from the
    trunk alone, where one carried by a swinging arm was dragged through the cloth beside it. A cape's inside now
    skins as the outside over it.
  - **`crest`** (a six-sided plaque with a gem standing proud of it, on the breast or on the centre line at the
    waist), **`bands`** (lines of braid across the front of the chest), **`midriff`** (the belly's cloth in another
    cloth's colour).
  - **A waist belt of pouches on the torso** (`on: 'torso'`, with one pouch alone at the front or the back), a belt
    with no buckle of its own, a belt or a sash worn lower (`drop`), a hip belt's `window` and `standoff`.
  - **A plain shoulder cap in any colour** (`plain`), its `size`, `crown` and `standoff`; **anklets** anywhere on the
    shin (`window`: a boot's rim), on a hero's shank as on a creature's shin.
- **The action RPG is heard** (`gameworld/compose.js`). A world map's game laid from a sentence is put on the sound
  sheet and given a score (an empty `sound` and an empty `music`): its sword, its ground underfoot, its foes' voices
  and a bed a place solved from the game, every level scored from the cue sheet. Play's sounds only: the interface
  keeps its own sound set. The brief says so; a game with no map is laid silent as before.
- **The made game reads as a game** (the action RPG's, each change opt-in so no other game's bytes move):
  - Her sword is cut short and worn at the left hip out of combat, never on the back under the cape (a genre hero
    row's `carry`: `gameworld/hero-rows.js`, `levels.js` sheathedSpec).
  - She runs the move library's run, the hero's standard (a genre hero row's `run: 'library'`: her own calibrated jog
    is not handed to her levels, `hero-rows.js` rowGaits).
  - She fights with her feel's kit (`arsenal: 'auto'`, `gameworld/compose.js`): the sword's strings and specials and
    the bow as the sidearm, where a game laid from a sentence had the one blow.
  - Her foes never lock blades with her (the row's `foes.clash: false` → `rule.clash: false`,
    `worlds/controllable/combat-melee.js`): a swing that meets their swing lands. The row's alone: every other game's
    foes clash as they did.
  - Her foes are harder (a genre hero row's `foes`, `hero-rows.js` rowFoe): never floored by a string's finisher
    (`rule.topple: false`, `worlds/controllable/combat-hit.js`: a knockdown reels a living body), a temper up
    (relentless), quicker to answer (veteran), half again the health and a little faster. A boss keeps its own mind.
  - A step is played at a share of a cue's level on the sound sheet (`sound-sheet.js` STEP_GAIN; a game's own:
    `sound.steps`): it sounds twice a stride, and at a blow's level it was all a player heard.
  - A zone's page is titled by its places ("The village", "The meadow road and the old ruins"), where it showed the
    map's id and the zone's letters (`gameworld/levels.js`).
  - The hero's health is a bar labelled Health, where it was a chip reading "HP 20" (`fail-on-death` `bar: true`,
    `game/mechanics.js`; set where the genre has a hero row).
  - On a page a player pilots, the rim's near rings stay the land's colour under a far range (`level/grid-scene.js`):
    a hero who starts by the border no longer stands over a slab of far haze.
- **The input map** (`gameworld/input-map.js`): what each of a hero's actions is on each device, read from the pilot
  scheme and never written by hand. A hero with an arsenal says its attacks, its sidearm, its specials and its guard in
  the level's legend (it said "click strike" alone), and the pause sheet lists them (`controls/schemes.js`: a moveset's
  rows, on keys and on a pad). The wireframe board has an adventure HUD frame (`mana-ui/board.js`): vitals, the action
  cluster, a compass, the objective, one prompt, one card at a time. The first step of the action RPG's interface,
  designed from its inputs.
- **The HUD grammar** (`scene/channels/hud-grammar.js`, `gameworld/hud-grammar.js`): the action-adventure's HUD on
  mana-ui, in the greybox, where its genre's row asks (`hud: 'grammar'`). The hero's health as hearts (two hits a
  heart), a compass strip with the goal's bearing and the objective under it, and the actions on their controls (the
  weapon in hand, the sidearm, what is collected with its count; keys, or a pad once one has spoken). The page hosts
  it: each frame it reads the bus's vars and the pilot. The health chip, the item chip, the legend line and the radar
  and the stamina gauge are not shown beside it. What the level says is one lane: its guide gives its one thing as
  data (`scene/channels/guide.js` `view()`) and keeps its own line down, and the HUD draws it: the current beat as the
  objective with its distance and its bearing on the compass, a lesson's keys as a prompt (no counter), the opening,
  a line said and a way held as cards on mana-ui's moment queue; the stamina under the hearts while it is spent. A place card as the hero comes into each named place of a planned map (`gameworld/hud-grammar.js` mapPlaces: the plan's key, each segment's square). A moveset's special is on Q too (`controls/schemes.js`: not every mouse has a forward
  button), and Q never strafes a hero with a moveset.
- **Her items and her bag** (`gameworld/inventory.js`, a genre hero row's `items`): playscape's own inventory wired
  onto each level. A healing draught restores two hearts (an item's `hearts` lowered to hp on the level's health,
  never past its full), used on X from the bag; the bag opens on I (an inventory menu); a new game starts with one
  and the bag is carried from level to level (the `bag` mechanic, the store's slice). The HUD's item slot is the
  quick item, its count the bag's own var, greyed when there is none.
- **The interface's look on the HUD** (`playscape/ui/interface-look.js`: the action RPG is `storybook`): the HUD
  grammar is drawn in the game's look, the world's palette on it (`events.grammar.theme`), the hearts large in its
  accent on no plate, each slot its thing's icon (`playscape/ui/item-icons.js`).
- **Its screens in the same look** (`gameworld/compose.js`: a world map's game has an interface, an empty `ui`): the
  play shell's screens (the levels, a result, the options, the loading) are mana-ui's in the game's look, as its HUD
  is. And **the pause is one of them** (`game/play-shell-mana.js` `pause`, any game with a `ui`): resume, restart, the
  controls the level lists (each a control and what it does), the options, the way out; backing out of it resumes.
  A game without a `ui` keeps the shell's own panel.
- **The HUD after a play** (the operator's notes): the actions are one row of icons at the bottom (the weapon, the
  sidearm, the item, the guard, the sprint, the lock, each on its control), and no reminder text is drawn: a lesson's
  line and a fight's keys are what the row shows. The compass has no box: its marks and the objective stand on the
  world, white with a dark edge. A step is softer again (STEP_GAIN 0.15). Her blows leave no trail (a genre row's
  `juice: { trail: 0 }`). Her game fills its window whatever its shape (a row's `screen: 'fill'`: no frame written, so
  no bars). The viewer's strip (the view cams, wireframe, fly and walk, reverse view, the AI switch) and its corner
  hint are not shown on a page with a HUD grammar, however the page is opened. The game's `ui` is carried into the made game (`mcp/tools/create-game.js`, `design-game.js`: it was
  dropped at the mint and at a remake, so a world's interface never reached its shell).
- **Her build is a heroine's** (`gameworld/hero-rows.js`, the row's body page). On the anime frame alone she stood 8.7
  heads tall on thighs narrower than her calves (10 cm against 13), a stick figure at the play camera's distance. Her
  tune stands her about 7.4 heads: a larger head, thighs and calves that taper (17 and 16 cm), fuller arms, hips and
  shoulders a little wider, legs a little shorter. Measured off the mesh; the look is the operator's to judge.
- **Esc opens the pause** (`game/level-contract.js` MSG_MENU, `scene/scene-three.js`, `game/play-shell.js`): a level a
  shell plays tells it when Esc is pressed there, or when the captured mouse is let go by it (the browser takes that
  press itself); Esc on the shell's own page does the same. With the pause up, Esc is the menu's back. Not while one
  of the level's own menus is up (its Esc closes that). The pause's controls list is the level's own rows, filled as
  they arrive (it showed the stock three).
- **The fantasy dressing branch merged.** A cape minted before keeps its bytes: its inside skins as its outside only
  on a cape that says `arms: false` or a lining. The hero's cloak is wool by the cloth law and swings in her clips on
  a new mint; a shared corner is placed by its weights on the page, so her cape and skirt no longer split in a stride.
- **Merged with the release candidate.** Its pause on mana-ui (`game/play-shell-mana.js`) is the one kept: this
  theme's own was dropped for it, and Esc (MSG_MENU) opens it. Its level HUD on mana-ui (`game/hud-mana.js`) draws a
  level's rows in the game's look; a level with a HUD grammar keeps the grammar alone, so nothing is drawn twice. The
  game's `ui`, `screen` and `hud` are carried into the made game by the candidate's own fix.
- Not here yet: a scabbard is not drawn (the blade
  hangs bare at the hip); the HUD grammar is its own page layer, not yet a composition on the level HUD's host (`game/hud-mana.js`), so its cards and the level's banners are two lanes; the pause menu still says "quit to levels"; the HUD grammar's marked slot is always the weapon; the bag's menu is still the old menu layer's (not mana-ui's, not in the game's look) and the quick item and the bag have no pad control; the lessons' keys are still written by hand (`level/map-sketch.js` TEACH), not read from the input map; a cape does not drape over what is worn on a belt (a pouch at the back shows through it); the hero's
  cloth takes no texture on the anime body; the back of
  light hair shades brown; the bell bob is the stock bob's clumps moved (no hair form of its own), its lined strands
  blocky at the sides; a crest's and a band's place are offsets tuned on one body; a cutscene's video has no file carried into the export by the game's own door (it names a path the
  page can reach); the land beside an opening's path is still walkable (its fights hold the way out; a solid gate that
  opens on a win is not in the level kit); a pursuer gives up a hero it can no longer see (it hunts by sight, not by
  memory); the lessons name the keyboard's keys only; a crew's dress, a beast's coat and a quick
  game's rolled people are not read as figures; the colour
  book paints the theorist's small landscape, not the game's own level; the options are not yet a `pick_palette`
  argument (the readout and the book carry them); a hero on a body rail (a comic hero, a fighter, a mascot) is still dressed plain; the hero's dress
  rides in its underlayer, though the book calls dress a later page (the adornment page holds equipment only); the
  party battles' own "goblin" and "shaman" (`gameworld/battles.js`) are still orcish people, and the
  word "orc" in a brief still rolls the near-human; a kin's headgear has helmets only (no hood, no mask, no cloth) and no row in the
  agent's foes card yet; the brow ridge is a round bar (no arch, no thinning to its tail); the foes book does not yet list a pack member's pieces and their reasons (the principles give them);
  a row for the action RPG in the pose rails, so its hero stands as its game shows it; the goblin's hips, boxed where
  its thighs thicken; ink on what a hand holds.

### A running game's UI on mana-ui: the in-play HUD, themed from the premise

In progress. On a course game nothing shown in play was mana-ui's: the controls as a line of text, a bare gauge, the
shell's own markup. The plan: a HUD host on the level page, a runner HUD as one composition, the shell's screens, the
phone, and a theme that comes from the dress's premise.

- A HUD host on a level page (`scene/channels/mana-hud.js`): one mana-ui runtime over a state the page feeds each
  frame. A level's `manaHud: { spec, theme, feed }`; a level without one carries not a byte of it.
- The runner HUD (`gameworld/course-hud.js`), carried by every course level: how far along the course and how many
  metres are left; which map of the run this is, as pips (the shell hands a level its place in the run,
  `params.__run`); stamina as a themed bar; a start cue that holds the hero (3, 2, 1, then GO); on a run's first map,
  what to do in the device's own glyphs. Laid by the course's thirds: nothing in the bottom band, the character's.
  The text legend and the runtime's own gauge are not shown on such a level.
- A dress names its UI theme (`ui`). A look is chosen by the game's style (who the hero is, its tone, where it is
  played), not by an object of its setting. Last train wears the toybox (`playscape/ui/theme-cards/toybox.json`, the
  first card of a toy family for light games with a mascot hero): round glossy blue plates with a pale rim on a
  plinth, white rounded letters, yellow for what matters, sized for the hand. The departure board
  (`departure-board.json`) is on the shelf for a sober railway game.
- On a tall frame the HUD is one plate in the top's middle (the run over the stamina, the progress beside them),
  clear of the shell's menu button in the corner. The metres left are said as words the host writes, so a number that
  falls every frame is not marked as news every frame.
- The HUD begins when the game's channel has started, which on a game's level is some frames after the page: the
  shell's params, the run among them, are in hand by then.
- The HUD counts the coins taken (the level's own, off its bus) and the page's old widget rows stand down beside it.
  On a tall frame the metres and the coins sit under the progress, so the plate stays clear of the menu button.
- The shell's screens on mana-ui for a course game. A world of obstacle courses that says no `ui` still has its
  game's screens drawn by the game UI runtime, in its first course's look (the dress's `ui`); a world's own `ui`
  wins; a course whose dress names no look keeps the shell's own screens.
- A run's title says its rules under the name, how deep the best went in the corner, and "start a run" / "new run".
- The pause is mana-ui's pause menu over the held level (resume, restart, controls, sound, quit; back resumes), with
  the level's own controls on a screen of their own. The shell's panel stays down for such a game.
- A map cleared in a run is a moment over the play, with its seconds, and the loading screen on the way to the next
  says what was cleared and which map is next.
- A run's result says the map it ended on, the seconds played (the shell's own clock: from a level's first frame
  shown, its pauses taken out), and what its maps kept that adds up (coins), and stamps a rank on a run cleared.
- A course level keeps its coins (`score`, counted high) so a result can say them.
- `create_game` carries a game's `ui`, `screen` and `hud` into its manifest. A gameworld's run handed them over and
  they were dropped at the mint, so a world's `ui` never reached its made game; a remake keeps them, its `front` and
  its `run` too.
- The image component's placeholder marks are not shown on a game's screens (a backdrop keeps its ground).
- A course in the hand (`scene/channels/controllable/touch.js`, a level's `courseTouch`). On a touch screen the hero
  runs by itself; a swipe left or right takes the next track over (the layer steers to that track's middle and brakes
  into it, so a flick is a whole lane, where the hero is otherwise steered freely); a tap or a swipe up jumps, held
  through the leap so it is the full jump. Nothing is drawn: no stick, no button. The pause's controls say so, and the
  HUD's first-map hint shows "tap" and "swipe". Only a level made for a screen carries it; a page told `?touch=1` plays
  so on a desk.
- Played by touch alone in headless Chrome (`scripts/spikes/roll/touch.mjs`): a bot whose hands are the touch
  layer's own pointer events (swipes and taps, never a key) clears three maps with no hit, in about the seconds the
  keyboard bot takes, taking the same coins.
- More than one kind of excitement behind a screen (`mana-ui/theme.js`). A theme's `stage` had one lively shape, the
  burst, so every screen of a lively game wore the same rays. Six more: `chevrons` (speed: bars leaning in to meet
  down the middle), `dots` (print pop, two grids), `confetti` (scattered pills and dots), `tunnel` (wide rings
  opening from a point), `streaks` (thin and thick lines on a slant), `zigzag` (rows of teeth). And a `stage` may be
  a LIST, a show: each kind of screen takes its own in order (the title, a screen in the middle, a full one, a
  result, a count over the play), round again when the list is short, `none` leaving a kind bare. A theme that names
  one stage is as it was.
- The toybox is a show: chevrons behind the title, dots behind the pause, streaks while it loads, confetti on a
  result, nothing over the start count.

### Shovels & Buckets: a work-sim primitive, its difficulty solver, and a shift to play

A primitive for work sims (cooking, farming, construction, chores). Each card's labour is shovel work or bucket work:

- **Shovel work** is active processing. The hands are on it, it may then run alone, and it burns if left.
- **Bucket work** is sorting, to storage or to the next step: fetch, collect, combine, shelve, carry, serve.

A solver tunes a card to a challenge, and the `work` mechanic plays it on a level. Design notes:
[docs/worksim.md](../../../../docs/worksim.md).

- **The card** (`lib/graph/worksim/card.js`) is stations, a crew and a demand, in seconds of play. Its difficulty
  levers are capacity (workers, slots, storage), output (batch, work) and demand (pace, patience, mix, rushes, a
  chore's backlog), and nothing else. Several stations may give one item, its routes (a hoe or a leveller): the
  cheapest is preferred, and the crew takes another when that one is busy. A malformed card is taught, never guessed.
- **The closed form** (`analyze.js`) reads the card as a network of queues: each order's labour as shovel, bucket and
  travel, the loads, the bottleneck, the critical path and each route's labour a unit.
- **The simulator** (`sim.js`) plays a seeded session:
  - The crew rescues, then hands in, then collects, then runs: what runs alone first, then the step nearest an order.
  - Stock is allotted by due time.
  - The crew's foresight is the player the session is measured against.
  - Its orders are rolled once (`arrivalsOf`), and the page plays the same list.
- **The solver** (`solve.js`) has three presets:
  - beginner, measured against a newcomer;
  - intermediate;
  - advanced, measured against an expert.

  A challenge number from 0 to 1 sits between them. The solver bisects pace and patience for its bands, adds a slot
  where a station is full, and records every move with its family and reason. When the bands cannot all be met, it
  returns the closest result and says so.
- **The `work` mechanic** (`lib/graph/game/work-mechanics.js`, a terminal) lowers a card onto the bus's verbs alone.
  Crates are taken with E. A station is worked by standing at it, and its progress is kept when the worker walks off.
  What runs alone burns past its hold. Shelves have a put pad and a take pad. Orders take a ticket at a hand-in, and
  one press serves one order. At the bell, the goal (four fifths of what one player who knows the card serves) wins
  or loses it. It has a mechanic card, sounds for each event, and a date in the cosmos registry
  (`power.mechanics=work`).
- **The quick door:** `design_game({ quick: { goal: 'work', card?, challenge?, serve? } })` tunes the card for one
  player, lays the line on flat ground beside the trail, and makes the game.
- **The work room** (`gameworld/work-room.js`, the practice door's `work`) tries a shift before its level, the way the
  action rooms try a feel. It stands the line as greybox counters coloured by verb. The hero is the world's own or a
  stand-in (male or female), and its movement is a feel template: the world's own, or the everyday walker (the
  realistic template that runs slowest). Every template and both bodies are offered on its page, and each reopens the
  room. The shift is measured by the work proof at the template's run, and the movement shows: the kitchen at advanced
  serves 13 of 25 at the slowest template's run (its goal 13) and 19 at the fastest; at beginner every template serves
  10 of 11. The room has its own rail icon.
- **The work room is a conceptual space.** The fidelity is in showing the work, not the characters:
  - **The view:** a pale plane ruled every two metres under the ¾ overhead camera, the work flowing up the screen.
  - **The floor is the recipe:** arrows from each crate, shelf and station to where its thing goes next, coloured by
    the work they feed (shovel work warm, bucket work cool).
  - **Pips show the work:** they fill over a station as it is worked, fill again as it runs alone, and go out toward
    the burn. A shelf shows a pip a unit (the mechanic's `show: true`; absent, nothing of it is laid).
  - **The worker is a mascot** of a form chosen on the page (orb, sprout, toon), piloted by its own body.
- **The quick shift looks like the room.** A quick work game is seen from overhead and worked by a mascot (unless the
  creator names a camera, a hero, or `hero: false`), its line laid facing north so the work flows up the screen. It
  stands a counter under each place, each place's marker a dome on top (`counters: true`), and shows the work: the pips,
  and what is in hand on the HUD, a counter an item that stands only while one is held. Made through `design_game` and
  exported, the level played in headless Chromium: the mascot at the crates, the chopping board's pips filling, the
  fish and lettuce in hand on the HUD.
- **The work room wears its trade.** Each starter's line is drawn as its trade's things, fitted to its counters, with
  the colliders kept (the game room's dress): a kitchen's range, workbenches, counters and shelving; a farm's field
  plots and carts; a site's mixer drum and sandbags; a chore's leaf piles, sacks and bin. `&dress=none` keeps the
  greybox.
- **An inline character.** A figure may carry its layered recipe inline (`layered`) instead of a stored ref, a
  mascot's plan or a hero, regenerated on read and held to the same pilot check. Absent, nothing changes.
- **A site, a real climb.** A card may stand its line on a deck: `site: { up, climb? }`, a roof `up` metres high with
  the hand-in on the ground below, joined by the playscape's ladder (a lean ladder, rungs, a rope or a net). The card
  reads the climb's seconds from the ladder object and walks them both ways on every hand-in. The work room builds the
  deck, the ladder (its rails, rungs and climbable surface, climbed by the hero's own rule) and the bin below. The hero
  starts on the roof, and the proof walks the route through the ladder at the climb's own speed. The roof starter is
  4 m up on a lean ladder in place of a fixed 8 s trip. On the page, the hero climbed from the foot to the roof in
  about two seconds, and the advanced roof serves 9, 10 and 11 of 12 bags at three templates' runs.
- **The work proof** (`worksim/work-proof.js`, a machine gate) plays a level on the page's bus as a player who knows
  the card would. The kitchen, the farm and the roof are won near what the simulator serves. The site, a crew's job
  played alone, falls short, and the proof says so. On the exported page in headless Chromium, one whole order was
  played by hand and served. The proof walks a route when one is given (a room's climb), each leg at its own speed.
- **Starter cards** (`scenarios.js`): a sushi counter, a wheat farm, a building site (a spade or an excavator) and
  leaves off a roof (4 m up a lean ladder). The board `scripts/spikes/worksim/solve.mjs` solves each at each preset.
- The gates are machine gates only: whether a shift is fun is for someone playing it to judge.

### Aerospace vehicles: modern launchers and the winged orbiter

Today's launch vehicles on the craft shelf, at their classes' figures, in a realm of their own (`launch`), and named in
the vehicle registry. Each is a class, not a replica, and wears no agency's or company's markings.

- **The launch parts** (`craft-shelf/rocket-odm.js`, `rocket-parts.js`): a stage (a painted core with its interstage
  and raceway, a side core's nose; a foam tank with its intertank's ribs, its ogive and spike, its orbiter's struts; a
  stainless hull with its welds, chines, hot-staging ring, and a ship's nose and heat-shield tiles); solid boosters (their
  segments, attach rings, flared skirts and nozzles); engine clusters (one, the octagonal nine, a square of four, rings of
  thirty-three, a ship's three and three); a fairing; capsules (a crew capsule's trunk, heat shield, windows and escape
  pods; a deep-space capsule's service module, boost cover and abort tower); grid fins and flaps; folded landing legs;
  the winged orbiter (its fuselage and flight deck, double-delta wing, split rudder, manoeuvring pods, three main
  engines, body flap, tiles black under and white over, its gear).
- **Seven launchers** (`rocket-archetypes.js`): a reusable two-stage medium launcher, the same with a crew capsule, a
  three-core heavy, a stainless super-heavy booster and its ship, the winged orbiter's stack on its external tank and two
  solid boosters, the orbiter alone on its gear, and a heavy-lift crew rocket with its abort tower. Each stands on its
  tail (an archetype's `stand: 'vertical'`). Their grid fins and legs are stowed until posed out (`pose.fins`,
  `pose.legs`).
- **The older launchers**: a three-stage moon rocket (its roll pattern, its five engines under their fairings and four
  fins, its third stage's adapter over its lander, its command module under its escape tower), an early single-seat
  capsule rocket on its finned stage, a two-seat capsule rocket on its two-chamber stage, a four-booster cluster rocket
  (its waisted core between four tapered strap-ons, its fairing under its tower and grid finlets) and a winged orbiter
  without main engines on a heavy core's side among its four strap-ons. A stage takes a radius profile, black rings and
  a roll pattern, a tapered top, named sides and an orbiter's fittings; a strap-on may be tapered; tail fins and their
  engine fairings; an escape tower over a fairing or a capsule's nose. Each absent adds nothing.
- **The registry**: a `launch` role and rows for the rocket, the crew rocket, the heavy rocket, the super heavy rocket,
  the space shuttle, the winged orbiter, the heavy-lift crew rocket, the moon rocket, the early capsule rocket, the
  two-seat capsule rocket, the cluster rocket and the side-mount orbiter stack. A level parks one on its tail; nothing flies one
  yet. Review: `scripts/render-rockets.mjs`.

### The city's working trucks: medium-duty, Asian city trucks and delivery, realistic

The trucks that carry a city's goods, at their true numbers in the hull kit's language, as the haulers are, and named in
the vehicle registry. Each is a class, not a replica: no maker's face, badge or livery.

- **Six classes** (`car-designer/road-city-truck.js` over `city-truck-kit.js`, `roads/vehicles.js`, [E]):
  - `mediumTruck`, a medium-duty conventional (the haulers' bonneted cab) on its stake bed; `dump` gives it a tub that
    tips about its tail (`tipping`), `flatbed` a bare deck;
  - `lightCabover`, the Asian 2-ton cab-over: a narrow flat-faced cab over its front wheels, its door's low window, on
    small wheels and duals; its drop-side deck behind a gate guard, or by word a wing body (`open` lifts its wings about
    the ridge on its load), an aluminium box, a reefer, a dump tub or a knuckle-boom crane;
  - `wideCabover`, the 4-ton wide cab-over on its wing body, the same words;
  - `miniGoods`, a mini goods carrier, its deck and fixed sides, a tilt over bows `canvas`;
  - `cubeVan`, a cube van: a cutaway van's nose and cab, its box out over the cab's roof, its roll-up rear door
    (`unloading`);
  - `beverageTruck`, a side-bay beverage truck on the wide cab, its shutters rolled up `delivering` on stacked crates.
- **The registry**: rows for the medium duty truck, the 2-ton cab-over, the wing body truck, the mini goods carrier, the
  cube van and the beverage truck. Review: `scripts/render-haul.mjs`.

### Fantasy character dressing

Fantasy clothing on a hero, then armour: the breaks mended, one cloth law (a material's rigidity read at rest, in
motion and in the drawing), the flow wired into the clips, and a fantasy wardrobe on every body.

Built so far: the mends, the cloth law as data, the flow in the clips, and the first drape at rest (the chest, the
sleeves, the hood).

- **A robe's skirt no longer tears down its centre on the World page.** The rig preview moved each bone's triangles
  rigidly with its bone, and a triangle rides the bone its corners vote for; a skirt's centre seam (its corners half on
  each thigh) voted for one leg and the other in turn, so the page showed a sawtooth slit front and back at rest (the
  idle clip a hero with no stand opens on) and tore it open from the waist to the hem in a stride; a cloak's hem, a
  realistic skirt's lower half and every joint cracked the same way. A corner the skin shares between bones is now placed
  by its weights, as the skinned GLB places it, then taken into its bone mesh's frame (`rig-preview.js` `rpBlend`; the
  ink a part wears follows its moved corners), so two triangles meeting at a corner meet in every frame. The recipe, the
  pack and the GLB are as they were: the mesh never had the seam. A bank whose parts carry no skin emits the channel
  byte for byte as before.
- **The realistic body wears the ranger's kit and a mantle.** A fold ring the cloth's folds insert between two rings
  (`body-relational-folds.js`) mixed its neighbours' weights without holding them to four, so where the kit's belt or a
  mantle moved a fold onto rings weighing different bones a ring carried five and the rig gate refused the hero
  (`top_body blend at st29f1 must be ≤ 4 …`). It is held to the four strongest and made whole, as every other mixed
  ring is; a mix of four or fewer is as it was, so no minted hero moves.
- **A piece the outfit already wears is said and left off, never refused.** A `belt` piece over a card that wears one
  (the adventurer's) was `adorn (belt).id: 'belt' twice` at the rig gate. The card's is kept, as a kit's belt keeps over
  an outfit's, and the readout says `the belt is not worn: the outfit already wears a belt …`.
- **A piece built on a creature's landmarks says so plainly.** The medallion (a necklace hung from a creature's neck
  chain) is still not worn on a hero, whose neck is a loft it does not read; the readout now says so in those words
  (`the medallion is not worn: its medallion hangs on a creature's landmarks … so it is left off`).
- **The chest lies flat, and the mantle is a shoulder cape (outfit laws 2).** A robe's, a gown's or a tunic's bodice
  showed a roll at each of its rings from the waist to the shoulders: each ring's lift over the shirt beneath came out
  apart from its neighbours', and the rounded body puffed every dent between them. From a short band above the waist
  (where a sash or a belt holds the cloth) up, the bodice now bridges those dents along its length (`body-garment.js`
  `lie`, never in, so nothing beneath shows through); below the band it gathers as it did. The MANTLE was a band round
  the upper chest with a buckle on its front, which read as a belt across the collarbones, and the realistic tailor,
  which makes a belt of every wrap round the trunk, made it one (the shirt bloused over it up there too). It is now a
  short cape from the neck's root over the shoulders and the arms' tops (the cape fit, its dents bridged the same way),
  closed at the throat by a round clasp; `drop`, `open` and `clasp: false` shape it. A hero minted before keeps its
  look: its outfit is stamped with laws 1 (`outfit/principles.js` OUTFIT_LAWS_VERSION 2; the cut's own bytes unchanged).
- **The cloth law as data.** What a piece is made of is one table, `polygonizer/cloth-law.js` `MATERIALS` (silk, linen,
  wool, leather, fur, mail: each a rigidity on the rigidity scale and a weight against plain linen), and how a register
  draws cloth in motion is another, `CLOTH_REGISTERS` (strings round a curtain, links along each, the share of the
  body's travel the cloth feels as headwind, keys a pose is held for), a row for each hero register and for the anime
  and realistic lanes. A piece says `material` beside or instead of `rigidity` (its own rigidity wins); the weight slows
  the cloth's pull to its skin and the air it catches, never the gravity it feels. The rigidity words stay valid, and
  `docs/garment-principles.md` points at the table where it listed a second fabric scale. The numbers are a starting
  tuning from published spring-bone and cloth defaults, not measured. The solver's angles, exponentials and powers now
  run on the deterministic math, so a baked swing is the same on both CPUs.
- **A hero's loose cloth swings in its clips (hero laws 23).** The flow solver (`hero-flow.js`), until now called only by
  its own test, hangs every piece that says how it moves on its register's strings: a cloak (wool), a robe's, a wizard's
  robe's or a gown's skirt (wool, wool, silk; a tunic's linen), a card's drape panels, a bow's tails. Each string is bones
  appended after the body's, so the body's bones keep their indices and keys, and every clip's swing is simulated between
  its keys and baked into those bones (`hero-cloth.js`, the mount's hair bake's pattern), so the World page's player and
  the skinned GLB both play it as bone keys. The skirt hangs from the hips and is pushed out by the leg capsules (on the
  robed round and anime heroes a knee no longer shows through the front at mid-stride), the cloak by the arms; the
  hem's embroidery and other trims worked on the cloth ride the flowing vertex nearest them. An open curtain (a cape) now
  spreads its strings over the arc it covers, so its open edges are its own: laid round the back from a seam at the
  centre, a cloak had split up the middle in the walk. Read where the rig is packed: no plan or recipe moves, a hero
  minted before keeps its clips (its stamp, laws 22 or under), and a hero with nothing that flows packs byte for byte as
  before. A card's panels under a flowing cloak keep their skin (the two layers do not collide with each other yet, and
  a panel swung on its own came out through the cloak). Not yet: the hood (locked to the head), wide sleeves, the hair,
  and the realistic body's tailored skirt (the tailor's `robe_pelvis` declares no material, so it rides its weights as
  before; the realistic cloak, a cape, flows). A heel still shows out of an ankle-length hem's back mid-stride (the
  foot is not in the collision form), and the bake adds a few seconds to a flowing hero's page.
- **The chest and the sleeves lie as one surface (outfit laws 2, refined).** The bodice still showed ledges from the bust
  to the shoulders after the first pass. Its rings were bridged off each ring's own middle, and on the game body those
  middles jump forward at the bust and back at the shoulder blades, so a straight line in that frame was no straight
  line on the figure. The cloth is now read off one straight axis from the band to the collar. Each slot's line is
  bridged, rounded a little (never closer to what lies beneath than a third of its ease), and bridged again. The
  yoke's sideways cap, which holds the cloth in at the shoulder, now comes on over the rise from the armpit to the
  collar rather than at one ring, so it no longer steps in round the chest. A robe's, gown's or tunic's sleeves lie the
  same way down the arm, so the upper arm is no longer a stack of rings. A bell cuff keeps its widening to the wrist. On
  the tiered body, the box and the anime hero, the deepest roll the drawn bodice shows from the front or the back is
  now under 3 mm, where laws 1 drew up to 12 mm. The yoke's sides above the armpit, under the sleeve, still dip where
  the cap holds them, and the realistic body's bodice still stands in under its bust. Laws 1 are byte for byte as they
  were.
- **The hood is cut and falls as cloth (outfit laws 2).** It was a smooth bell over an ellipsoid sized from the head's
  joints. That ellipsoid was too big on the landmark head and far too small on a chibi, whose hood vanished inside its
  hair. The hood is now fitted to the head this figure has, read from its own parts: the skull, the face, the ears and
  the hair, on the landmark, anime, realistic and chibi heads alike. Its crown lies on the skull and the hair with a
  little slack, more as the cloth stiffens: soft wool lies close and stiff leather stands off. It never passes through
  either. From the head the cloth falls straight onto the shoulders, as a tent rather than a tube dropped onto them,
  and gathers into a few large folds at the neck. Its foot sits on the cloak's or the robe's collar. The opening frames
  the face from the chin to a rolled brim that clears the cheeks. The brim stands above the brow as far as the cloth
  is stiff, and `depth` sets how far it comes forward of the face. The back of the hood draws out to a `point` behind
  the crown. A short point is a peak with a seam ridge down the back. A long point is a liripipe hanging down the back,
  its own part, which flows on a strand of the hood's cloth in the clips. None keeps the back round. `worn: 'down'` lays
  the hood collapsed on the back as a loose ring at the collar over a soft sack, narrowing to its point, with the head
  and the hair bare. The words are `hood: { worn, point, depth, open }`. An unknown word is said and the piece left
  off, as a hem word is. The register sets the budget: a few planes on the box, facets on the low-poly body, smooth
  elsewhere. On the hair I chose clearance over tucking. A ponytail or long hair under the hood is enclosed, so the back
  of the hood stands out over it. The hood's body stays locked: up, to the head and the neck; down, to the shoulders.
  Laws 1 keep the bell byte for byte.
- **The open items, cleared where they fall out (outfit laws 2, hero laws 23).**
  - A clip played at two speeds. A clip that carried no seconds played over three seconds on the World page and over
    one in the GLB, and its cloth was simulated for the page's three, so the exported swing was the slow one played
    fast. A hero whose cloth flows now plays every clip over one duration on the page and in an export, the one its
    swing is baked at: a clip with seconds keeps them, the hero's own clips take the anime hero's timing (an idle in
    four seconds, a wave in two, a walk in one), a compiled clip one second, and an act its own clock. A hero with
    nothing that flows is as it was.
  - The realistic body's cape keeps its skin. On strings its open side edges sheared into angular flaps where the arm
    carries the cloth draped on it and the strings swing the rest, and the shirt showed through between them. No
    tuning of the strings made that clean, so the cape rides its weights as it did before the hero laws 23. A hood's
    liripipe still flows.
  - A heel still shows out of the back of an ankle-length robe in a stride. The cause is that the strings collide at
    their joints only: a heel kicked up behind the leg sits between the knee's joint and the hem's, mid-link, where no
    joint can meet it, which is why adding the foot to the collision form did nothing. Colliding the links as well,
    with the foot in the form, moved the hem but let the heel through between the strings and opened holes in the
    cloth, so it was not kept. The solver is as it was.
  - The medallion is worn. The necklace read the neck's radius as a chain's, and the hero's neck is a loft, so its
    chain came out with no size and the piece was left off. Under outfit laws 2 it reads the lofted neck by its lowest
    ring and hangs from the nape to its pendant on the chest. Laws 1 leave it off with the line that says so. The pendant
    is laid on the body's chest, so a tunic's or a robe's bodice over it still hides it.
  - A hood worn down lies flat on the back. It stood the hood's whole ease and a deep sack off the cloak, a hump in
    profile; it now keeps a share of the ease and a shallow sack, and its liripipe lies on the sack it hangs from.
  - The mantle is wool, so it hangs on strings and swings a little in the clips.
  - On the realistic body a robe's, a gown's or a tunic's bodice is the outer layer. The pieces named their part as a
    bare word where a card's pieces name a list of one, and the realistic body's tailor reads only the list, so it
    passed the bodice and the sleeves by: the game body's kernel drew them on the bare skin and the tailor's shirt came
    out over them. Under outfit laws 2 they name a list, the tailor makes them as its own cloth, a layer over the card's
    shirt and its sleeves, and the shirt shows only at the collar. The game body reads either form alike, so the
    tiered and anime bodies are unchanged; laws 1 keep the old look.
  - The realistic bodice under the bust. With the bodice now the tailor's close cloth, the 14 mm roll the game body's
    kernel drew there is gone from the realistic body. Over a 6.4 cm chord the tailor's bodice still goes in about 7 mm
    under the bust, where the card's shirt went in about 6; it was not brought under a few millimetres.
  - Not changed. The tunic's and robe's shoulders keep their bulbous caps: they are the game body's own shoulder forms
    (its deltoid ball, the trapezius cone and the web) standing out of the bodice's yoke. Wearing the bodice over them
    raised a ridge round the neck and left the caps, so it was not kept. The neckline is still the torso's top turning
    in to the neck. The embroidery that floats off a skirt mid-stride is placed at the skirt's waist ring rather than its
    hem (its window counts the skirt's rings from the top), and much of it lies too far from the cloth to ride it; it is
    left as it was. The box register's cloak reads its row as written (four strings of two links, held on twos); it moves
    little because two long links follow the skin closely. The hood still clears big hair rather than tucking it, so the
    chibi's hood stays large and the anime hood's back stays boxy over long hair. The chamfer noble's green shirt still
    shows at the back waist at mid-stride, where the skirt's top swings off it.
- **The open items, second pass (outfit laws 2, hero laws 23).**
  - A long skirt is carried by the legs. The strings kept their joints out of the legs, never the cloth between them, so
    a heel kicked up behind in the stride came out through the back of an ankle-length robe. Now a skirt that hangs as a
    ring of strings knows the shins, the feet and the toes as their outermost points, carried by their bones; each pose
    its target is pushed out round them, and what is shown of it is pushed out too: each string straight out from the
    ring's axis by what the cloth between it and its neighbour needs to pass outside every shin or foot point at that
    height, the push shared with the neighbours so the ring bulges instead of creasing, the links' lengths kept, so the
    trailing leg lifts the back of the skirt. The simulation's own state is untouched by that last pass, which is what
    flung the cloth when the push was made a constraint inside the solve; the last link runs on a little past its joint
    to the cloth's own edge. Through the walk the shin and foot points outside the skirt's surface fell from thousands
    to a few dozen on the round, anime and low-poly robes and the round noble's (the chamfer's eight strings leave a few
    hundred mid-chord at the back), and the ring keeps its order. The bake is two to three times slower. The realistic body's robe skirt is the tailor's shell on the legs' weights, not
    strings: hung on strings it tore and creased, so it was left as it was and its heel still shows.
  - Work on a flowing cloth rides it by the cloth's surface. It took the skin of the nearest cloth vertex, and on a coarse
    register the hem work lay farther from any vertex than it may lie to ride, so it stayed put while the skirt moved and
    was hidden or floated. It now takes the blend of the nearest triangle of the cloth's outer face (never the hem turned
    up inside a skirt).
  - A skirt's hem work lies on its hem. Its window was read as shares of every ring of the skirt, the turn-up inside
    counted too, so it landed on the lining at the knees, two to twenty centimetres off the cloth that shows. Under outfit
    laws 2 it is addressed on the skirt's outer rings, waist to hem, in the skirt's own measure, and lies within a
    centimetre of the cloth near the hem. On the realistic body, which read any band on a skirt as a belt at its waist,
    the hem work is a band of the trim's thread at that height of the tailor's skirt.
  - A hood worn up tucks the hair. The hood was cut round the whole head of hair. Now the hair behind its brim (the crown,
    the back, long back hair) is pressed in toward the skull to within a centimetre of it before the hood is cut, and
    the fringe and the locks that frame the face are kept whole; worn down, the hair is as it was. The anime hood's back
    is rounder and a little smaller. The chibi's hood is only a little smaller: its hair stood little off its head, and
    the hood's size there comes from its own ease, the brim drawn forward and the point behind the crown, scaled to the
    head, which this does not change.
  - A medallion hangs over the bodice. The chain was laid on the body's own chest, so a tunic's or a robe's bodice hid
    the pendant. Under outfit laws 2 it clears the close cloth already worn on the chest, and lies low and close round
    the neck's root behind, where it stood off the nape over a mantle. Over a mantle's shoulders the chain still shows on
    top of the mantle rather than under it.
  - Not changed. The tiered body's tunic and robe shoulders keep their bulbous caps and the shelf neckline: no different
    approach was tried in this pass. The chamfer noble's green sliver at the back waist mid-stride is the shirt's tail,
    skinned to the thighs, passing out between the skirt's strings at the top of the thighs; the legs' clearance covers
    the shins and the feet only. The light sliver at one shoulder with the hood down and the shirt's cuff at the
    realistic noble's forearm are as they were.

- **A fantasy wardrobe (phase 5).** Six outfit cards, one per archetype, each a seeded sample the hero door already takes
  as `outfit: { type: 'outfit', style }`: `ranger`, `mage`, `peasant`, `noble`, `cleric` and `rogue`
  (`outfit/styles.js` FANTASY_OUTFITS). A fantasy look was the modern `adventurer` card with pieces over it, and that
  card's green shirt showed at every collar and cuff. Now each card carries its own underlayer (its cut: a linen shirt,
  legs, boots or shoes) and its designed pieces over it, listed in the order a costume is worn: the over-garment (a
  tunic, a robe, a wizard's robe, or the cut's own coat or jerkin), a girdle at the natural waist, the outer layer (a
  cloak or a mantle, hoods by the draped hood's words), then what hangs over all (bracers, a medallion, a satchel, a
  thigh pouch).
  - Each card names what its cloth is made of (silk, linen, wool, leather, fur), so it hangs and flows by the cloth
    law. Its values run dark at the feet and light at the chest, and neighbouring layers differ by a value step or by
    their cloth.
  - Every card has a belt at the waist, never on the chest: the girdle piece carries an id of its own, and the cut
    spends no belt beneath the over-garment.
  - On the realistic body the cards wear what that body can: the cloak keeps its skin and does not flow, and a robe's
    skirt is the tailor's shell.
  - Make one your own as an inline card.
- **Fantasy headgear.** Three headgear words, each a card over the existing builders: `circlet` (an eyegear cast pushed
  up to the brow, its strap the band round the head, a gem on its front; it keeps the hair), `travelerHat` (a soft
  helmet shell with the brim fitting round it) and `wizardHat` (the same with a cone ornament leaning back off the
  crown). They fit the game body only. On the anime head the circlet is hidden under the hair.
- **A skirt's hem binding lies on its hem.** Under outfit laws 2 a robe's, a gown's or a tunic's `trim.hem: 'binding'`
  is painted on the skirt's last outer band. Before, it was painted on the last share of every ring, the turn-up inside
  counted, so it showed as a band at the waist. Laws 1 keep their band.
- **The shoulder under cloth (the tiered body).** A top worn on the game body ended in a flat shelf at the shoulders,
  and the body's own shoulder forms (the ball, its cone and its web, painted as the shirt) stood over it as balls: at a
  sleeveless tunic's armholes, through a cloak at the side and the back, beside a robe's sleeve. Under outfit laws 2
  every piece on the trunk (the cut's shirt, coat and waistcoat, a robe's, a gown's or a tunic's bodice) names its
  `shoulder`, sleeved or sleeveless (`body-garment.js`), and on a body with shoulder forms:
  - the forms are laid under the shoulder's line, from the neck's root down to the shoulder point and rounding over the
    arm's root; they keep their weights, so they move as before, under the cloth;
  - the piece's cloth runs on over them as pieces of its own, copies of the forms that skin as they do: over the
    trapezius from inside the neck to the shoulder point, then into the sleeve's head when sleeved, or ending there as
    the armhole's edge when not;
  - each layer stands off the cloth another layer wears there, so a shirt's shoulder lies inside a sleeveless tunic's,
    and a cloak, a mantle or a hood hangs over it.
  On the round, low-poly, chamfer, box and anime bodies the shirt's shoulders stood 3–5 cm over the over-garment's top;
  they now lie inside it, and the outline's rise at the shoulder (the ball on the shelf) went from about 2.5 cm to a few
  millimetres. With the arm raised, a shirt's sleeve head still comes up through a sleeveless armhole with the arm.
  Still open: the bodice's front still turns into its top at a level line across the upper chest, and the peasant's
  tunic is still boxy below the shoulders. Outfit laws 1 and the realistic body are unchanged.
- **A top's front is one surface to its neckline, and a belted tunic is a tunic (the tiered body).** The tiered torso's
  top is a box: its front and back stand up to the shoulder line and its last rings turn in over a flat lid to the neck.
  A top copied off those rings turned over the same lid, a level edge across the upper chest with a shadow under it, the
  shirt showing in a sliver along it, a little V at the neck, and a fold across the shoulder blades. Under outfit laws 2,
  on a body with shoulder forms (`body-garment.js`):
  - every piece on the trunk that names its `shoulder` RISES: from the chest's fullest ring up, each of its lines is one
    curve to the neckline, which is the neck's root carried out over what is worn there (a shallow round, lower at the
    front than at the sides). It is lifted over the layers beneath it, over the body, and over the shoulder's cone by its
    yoke's own ease, so the yoke lies under it at rest and comes out with a raised arm;
  - a sleeveless piece is an armhole: under the arm its side runs up from the chest's own width, never held out by the
    arm's root or by the shirt there, which now shows in the armhole; over the armpit it goes on over the shoulder's
    corner to its own yoke, so the shoulder point is narrower and rounder;
  - a robe's, a gown's or a tunic's bodice worn under a belt or a sash at the waist is taken in under it (the new garment
    word `cinch`), blousing a little above it, and ends just under it, where its skirt now hangs from (before, from the
    top of the hips, a ledge under the belt).
  The game body's jacket fit reads a risen ring at each point's own height, so a jerkin's front is no longer pulled in
  to the neck at the front (on the rogue that showed as a dark chevron of the shirt). Measured from the front on the
  peasant, ranger, mage, cleric and rogue cards (round) and the peasant and mage cards (low-poly, chamfer, box, anime),
  the largest step down the front's middle line from under the neckline to mid-chest went from 26–94 mm to 1–2 mm, and
  its sharpest turn from 48–80° to 9–20°, on the eleven heroes that had the lid, at rest, in a walk and with an arm
  raised; the fold across the back is gone. The peasant's chest is 2–4 cm narrower a side, it comes in a further 4.5–6 cm a
  side to the belt, and its skirt starts under the belt. The anime body shared the defect and takes the fix. Outfit laws 1
  and the realistic body are unchanged.
  Still open: the tunic's cross-section at the chest is no rounder (its front corners stay while its side came in);
  with an arm raised, the shoulder's cloth that follows the arm still meets the chest at an edge at mid-clavicle; the
  neckline rides 1–2 cm up the neck on some casts; the peasant's hood worn down still covers the shoulders; on the box
  and low-poly registers a small chip of the shirt shows at the top of a sleeveless armhole.
- **The fantasy wardrobe on the realistic body (gen-7).** The six cards were minted on the realistic body under the
  gen-7 cube, both sexes, and shot still, in the walk and with an arm raised. Under outfit laws 2 (the hero laws 23):
  - a tailored robe's skirt (the tailor's rings carried down from its body) that names its cloth hangs on the realistic
    register's strings from its first ring below the hips, its bodice and hips kept on their skin (`hero-cloth.js`
    `tailoredSkirts`, a curtain's new `top` in `hero-flow.js`), so the legs' clearing carries it: the shin and heel
    points above the hem that stood outside the mage's and the cleric's skirts through the walk went from 48–55 % to
    0.1–0.6 %. The tunics' short skirts hang on them too;
  - the cape sways instead of riding its skin: six stiff strings rooted below the hanging hand (`CAPE_FROM` of the way
    from the knee to the hip), its shoulders and sides on their skin, so the edges the arm carries are never sheared;
    its hem swings about 7 cm behind the stride and its turns down the cloth are as on its skin (95th percentile 45°);
  - a skirt's hem work is a motif: a thread of its colour in peaks over a plain rule, lying on the skirt where it flares,
    each a thread along its path rather than a band (whose ends were a disc across the open skirt) (`hemMotif`);
  - a medallion is worn: its chain, bail and pendant were each read as a belt round the waist (three gold bands over the
    girdle); they are laid on what is worn instead (`layNecklaces`), the chain on the cloth at the front and out of it
    elsewhere, round the neck's root, the pendant on the chest.
  Outfit laws 1 and the game and anime bodies are unchanged. Still open on the realistic body: the fur mantle stands
  off the shoulders as a stiff box and a raised arm tears its side; the arm swinging back comes through the cloak's side
  (as before); the hood is faceted, and worn down it stands proud of the back in the robe's own colour; the shirt's
  shoulder pokes white through a sleeveless robe's armhole; the hats and the circlet still fit the game body only (the
  relational head has no cranium kit to carry them).
- **The fantasy wardrobe on the realistic body, second pass (outfit laws 2, hero laws 23).**
  - The circlet and the hats are worn on the realistic body. They were refused there: the relational head has no
    cranium kit. Each card now has a realistic side, which lowers to a `headwear` word, and `headgear/realistic.js`
    builds it on the head the hero has. It reads the head's skin, its hair and a hood worn up, as the draped hood does.
    The circlet is a band traced round the head on a line from just under the hairline to the back of the skull. It
    sits over the hair, rides the hair's crests (it never dips into them), and widens to a setting and a cabochon at
    the front. A hat's crown is fitted over the hair: each meridian is bridged, then cleared crest by crest by half its
    ease. It has a ribbon at its foot, a brim turned up at the front and let down at the back, and, for the wizard, a
    cone leaning back off the crown. Each is one part per colour, pinned to the head's skin where the head bone alone
    carries it. The hair is kept under it. The card's colours sit under the operator's palette. A hero minted under
    hero laws 22 or earlier still refuses these words, by name. On the six heroes shot, no point of the head or the
    hair lies outside what covers it (`headwearGaps`).
  - A cloak on the realistic body takes the nearer arm out to 24 cm from it (`capeArm`). The cloth behind a swinging
    arm now goes back with it. In the walk's back view, the ranger's forearm and hand had shown through the cloak's
    side (0.7–0.8 % of their points, in 3–6 of 12 keys); now none do.
  - The mantle's clasp rides the shirt. Every shell worn on a body segment under outfit laws 2 (a clasp on the torso,
    a bracer on the forearm, a satchel on the hips) now stands off the tailor's cloth on that segment. Before, it
    searched for that cloth by the segment's own name and missed it. The noble's clasp points inside the shirt went
    from 7 of 52 to 0. The mantle's shoulder is rounded (a quarter ellipse from the neck to its widest ring) and its hem
    is rolled by 1 cm. It still stands about 3 cm off the shoulders, and a raised arm still draws its side out along the
    arm.
  - A draped hood on the realistic body is eased round (`hoodRound`). Worn up, each ring is smoothed round its
    directions and down its rings, then cleared again. The arch springs from the cheekbones, and a deep hood's brim
    comes forward as a soft fall rather than a visor. Worn down, it is a cowl gathered at the nape: a thicker roll, the
    cloth heaped under it with folds at the back, shorter down the back, and in its lining's shade (the cloth's colour
    × 0.72).
  - The peasant card's shirt is lighter and its tunic darker (`#e4dccb` over `#7a6440`, from `#d8ccb0` over
    `#9c8a66`).
  Outfit laws 1, the hero laws up to 22, and the game and anime bodies are unchanged. Still open on the realistic body:
  the shirt's white sliver at a sleeveless armhole, the skirt's centre-back crease and the facets at the hips, the
  rogue's pale ring at each boot top (it is the shank's skin seen between the blousing and the boot's cuff; turning the
  blousing's hem in did not close it, so that change was reverted), the bodice's dip under the bust, and the medallion
  chain's beads.

### The game turn: one level session in named phases

In progress. Built so far: the turn's shape, its reader and its kernel (`lib/graph/game/turn.js`), and the play
shell running it ([docs/game-flow.md](../../../../docs/game-flow.md), "A level step is a turn"). A game whose level
steps say no turn carries none of it. The arena shell and versus still keep their own set-up. The rest below is what
the theme will hold.

- **Built: the play shell runs a turn.** The picks are drawn by mana-ui, one screen a pick, in the game's `ui` or
  the greybox; back unwinds one. The level is handed the game's own words as `params.__picks` and, of a consumed
  slice, the members picked. A retry and the pause's restart keep the picks. A start trigger's scene is staged on
  the level's page, or its video plays over the held level, once a save, with no pause while it plays. An end
  trigger's video plays after the level's end card. Not yet: an end trigger that is a scene, a locked row, a quit
  from the pause recorded.
- **Built: the pick screen** (`mana-ui/idioms-front.js` `pick-screen`), an idiom on the board, and what the play
  shell draws a pick with. The question and a line under it, how far along the choices it is, what was chosen
  before, and the rows beside the one in focus: options as a list with what each means, a party slice as a grid of
  faces with each member's tags, level and figures, a carried thing with its count. A row that cannot be taken says
  why; a pick of several marks its rows and is confirmed. On a tall frame the face is drawn once and the figures
  give way to the words. A pick says `ask` and `hint`; an option may be `{ id, name?, about? }`.
- **Built: a world's set-up** (`lib/graph/gameworld/setup.js`). A gameworld says `setup: { difficulty?, picks? }`
  once, and `design_game` asks it before every level that asks nothing of its own: the run lowers it into the level
  steps of the flow the game is made with (the default, the world's own, or the one started in play). `difficulty`
  is the engine's tiers (easy, medium, max) in default words or the game's; the play shell hands the level the pick
  as `params.difficulty`, the dial its foes' minds already read. The review's `flow:sequence` says what each level
  asks; the flow's card teaches the set-up and a level step's turn; `/setup` is the flow chapter's. A world that
  says none hands its game the order it did.
- **Streamlined after playing a made game through a turn:**
  - A pick says how long it lasts (`keep: 'level' | 'game'`). One kept for the game is asked once, held by the save
    and never asked again; a set-up's difficulty is kept for the game unless it says `level`.
  - Back on a turn's first pick goes to the screen it came from, or home when it came from a cutscene or a level.
  - A game with a `screen` has its mana-ui shell screens drawn in its levels' frame, centred (a phone game's menus
    are a phone's on a monitor).
  - A level's title that is only an id is said in words on the shell's screens (`sayTitle`).
  - The results screen draws no rank row without a rank, and no window with neither figures nor a rank
    (`results-screen`'s `bare`).
- **The pause button is mana-ui's.** A game whose shell screens are mana-ui's draws its pause button in the HUD's
  top-right corner, in the game's look and inside its frame, only while a level is the player's (not over a screen,
  a trigger or a held level); a tap or a click opens the pause. The shell's own button stays in the page, unseen, as
  the shell's word for whether a level is in play. A bare HUD look still draws none under a mouse.
- **Fixed in mana-ui's defs:** a `when` or an `unless` on a param a def was not given was no condition at all, so
  the play shell's loading screen drew its failure's Retry and Quit buttons while a level loaded (and Enter landed on
  Retry). A param not given is now a condition not met. Found by playing a made game through a whole turn. The brawl
  and holo pages are re-pinned for it.
- **Fixed in mana-ui's mount:** a view mounted on an element with no box of its own (the play shell's, the preview
  page's) never measured its frame, so a spec that branches on the frame always drew wide. It measures its root's
  box there now. The brawl and holo pages, which inline the kernel, are re-pinned for it and for two new words.
- The play shell's cutscene video and the triggers' share one player; every play shell page's inlined code changes
  by that and by the turn's hooks.

- **Built: a level step's turn.** A level step takes `picks` (what the player chooses before it loads, from the
  game's own options or from a slice the level consumes), `start` and `end` (a scene or a video as play starts and
  as it ends). `readFlow` teaches each fault, a pick's slice checked against what the level consumes. The kernel
  steps the phases: a choice that cannot stand keeps the pick and says why, back unwinds one pick, a failed load
  goes back with its reason, a retry keeps the picks and never replays the start, the pause is legal in play only.

A game's level session becomes a turn with named phases, so that setting up, loading, playing, pausing and the
results are one path every game shares, where today the play shell, the arena shell and versus each keep their own.
The names are internal; the agent and the person read plain words (set up, loading, play, pause, results).

- **The phases:** `turn:untap` (the player picks: mode, difficulty, character, loadout, level), `turn:upkeep` (the app
  checks the picks against the level's contract, seeds, loads and starts the level), `turn:main` (play),
  `turn:cleanup` (the outcome applied to the store, the save written, the unlocks worked out) and `turn:end`
  (results and what next). `interrupt` is the pause over the held game, legal in play only, and is not a phase.
- **The load's screen:** `turn:upkeep` is the app's work, and the loading screen is all it shows.
- **Main's triggers:** a level may name a scene or a video for the start of play and for its end (by outcome: won,
  lost, left). Each plays on the level's page with control held, can be skipped, and the start plays once a save. A
  level that names none waits on nothing.
- **Where it runs:** in the flow kernel and the store kernel (`lib/graph/game/`). The flow strings turns together;
  the title, the options and the credits sit outside a turn.
- **mana-ui stays a view:** it draws the picks, the load, the pause and the results, owns cursors and drafts, and
  holds no pick once it is confirmed. The picks are a session record the shell holds and hands to the level.
- **Exits:** a retry starts again at the load with the same picks; a level with nothing to pick passes its set-up at
  once; a quit from the pause is recorded as a level left.
- **Nothing changes for a game with nothing to pick:** its flow and its page are as they were.

### Industrial vehicles: the highway's haulers and the farm's machines, realistic

The trucks that move freight and the machines that work a field, built at their true numbers in the hull kit's
language, as the city's utility vehicles are, and named in the vehicle registry. Each is a class, not a replica: no
maker's grille, badge, colours or livery.

- **The highway's haulers** (`car-designer/road-haul.js` over `haul-kit.js`, five classes in `roads/vehicles.js`, [E]):
  - the eighteen-wheeler, `semiSleeper`: a long-nosed aero tractor (its one-piece hood falling to a chrome grille, swept
    lamps, a wraparound bumper; the cab and its sleeper under a roof swept up from the screen to the trailer's height;
    twin stacks, saddle tanks, chassis fairings, quarter fenders over its drive tandem, the fifth wheel) and its 53 ft
    trailer on a tandem, five axles and eighteen tyres. Its trailer by word: a dry van (its posts, rails, swing doors,
    skirts and conspicuity tape), a reefer and its fridge unit, a flatbed and its tarped load, a tanker (its rings,
    walkway, hatches and ladder), a container on its chassis, a curtain-sider; `bobtail` leaves it off;
  - the European articulated lorry, `semiCabover`: a tall cab-over (its step wells, roof spoiler and side deflectors) on
    two axles, its 13.6 m curtain-sider on a tri-axle of wide singles;
  - `straightBox`, a straight box truck on a bonneted medium-duty cab (its roll-up door rolled up `unloading`, a fridge
    unit when refrigerated), now the box truck row's realistic build;
  - `flatbedTruck`, its timber deck, headache rack and strapped load (`empty` takes it off), the flatbed row's;
  - `logTruck`, a day-cab tractor and its log trailer, bunks, stakes and a strapped bundle of logs.
- **The farm's machines** (`car-designer/road-farm.js` over `farm-kit.js`, three classes):
  - `farmTractor`, a row-crop tractor: its narrow hood and front weights, steering fenders, the glasshouse cab between
    tall rear fenders, its stack and steps, the three-point hitch and PTO; `loader` fits a front loader whose bucket is
    held level at a reach (a parked tractor takes one), `plough` a four-furrow mouldboard plough, in the ground
    `ploughing`. The tractor row, a concept until now, takes it;
  - `combineHarvester`, its grain platform (cutterbar, auger, reel) or a corn head (`corn`), the feeder house, the cab
    high at the front, the grain tank and its extensions, the unloading auger swung out `unloading`;
  - `cropSprayer`, a high-clearance self-propelled sprayer, its poly tank, its booms folded along its sides or out to
    36 m `spraying`.
- **Wheels a body says itself.** A hull-kit body may give its wheels axle by axle (`wheelSet`: radius, tyre width,
  duals, lugs, rim) and its own axles (a tractor bobtailing); `military.js` draws them, and a body that says neither is
  drawn as before. That gives the haulers their duals and the farm machines their small fronts and tall rears.
- **The registry**: the semi truck row takes the sleeper (its fleet loft stays the traffic and the recipes minted
  before), the box truck row the straight box truck; new rows: cab-over lorry, log truck, combine harvester,
  self-propelled sprayer. Review: `scripts/render-haul.mjs`.

### The metro's trucks: rigs on its highways and at its docks, small trucks on its streets

The metro now keeps and drives the new trucks.

- **Its fleets** (`geocity/fleets.js`). The garbage trucks, fire engines and ambulances are the city's own realistic
  bodies; they were stand-ins. The deliveries take a cube van and a 2-ton cab-over among their vans and box trucks. Two
  new fleets: `freight` (the eighteen-wheeler, its tanker and a cab-over lorry) and `industry` (wing bodies, flatbeds,
  box trucks). A fleet row may give its body's words (`brief`: a semi's trailer).
- **Its industry** (`geocity/industry.js`, `scene.js`). The rigs back onto a warehouse's docks, their tails at the dock
  and their length out into the court (a vehicle op's `back`). They wait at a storage yard's gate. The working trucks
  stand in a works' court.
- **Its traffic** (`geocity/flow.js`). Each road has its own mix: a street's small trucks among its cars, an arterial
  along an industrial neighbourhood's working trucks, and a highway's rigs. A rig never takes a signalled street, so the
  signal boxes are sized to the streets' longest vehicle.
- **Its models** (`geotown/cars.js` carModel). A hull-kit body is compiled in a pale livery, so its own paint takes the
  fleet's tint. Its width is its body's, without its mirrors. A key may carry a brief (`loft:semiSleeper|tanker`). The
  front-third search was quadratic in a model's corners: a rig cost seconds, now milliseconds. The memo holds a
  metro's whole fleet.

### Side-scroll action starter: the beat 'em up

A beat 'em up as a game, on the brawl library's own kit (`lib/graph/brawl`, over the fighting game's fighters: the
chain and its finisher, the strong blows, grabs and throws, the running blow, the desperation, weapon arts, thugs
from the fight's archetypes). The library's street (screens held by a gate until their wave is beaten, a boss's
screen) is now played on a page; before, only its practice yard was.

- A street fought down on the World page. A brawl level's `street` (`{ players?, roster?, waves: [{ screen, crowd,
  boss? }], things? }`, `brawlLevel(level, { street })`) is played by the brawl channel in the yard's place: the room
  a street (`brawl-crowd.js` streetOf / stepStreet), the players' buttons read by the brawler's own reader, the camera
  scrolled on and held at each uncleared gate by the belt. A level is a yard or a street, not both.
- Its screen (`brawl-street.js`, on mana-ui in the brawler's look): the player's name and health, the held screens as
  pips, the crowd left on this one or the boss's bar while it stands, GO as a screen is beaten and the boss's name as
  it comes in, and the two ends (the street cleared, the player down) with the time, the health left and a button
  that fights it again. What it reads is `brawl-street-read.js` streetRead, pure off the street's state.
- Measured with no page: `scripts/spikes/brawler/street-sim.mjs` plays a street on the brawl's sim with a bot on the
  native kit. On the page: `scripts/spikes/brawler/street.mjs` (a virtual clock, the keyboard): a lighter street is
  cleared through its boss to its end screen, a full one beats a button-masher on its second screen; fight it again
  returns to the start; no page errors.
- Its sound, from the SFX shelf by word (`brawl-sfx.js` BRAWL_SOUNDS, brawlAudio): the brawler's sound sheet. The
  cues a blow already played (a fist by its weight, a foot, a blade, a grab, a throw, a body landing, a knockout) are
  voiced by shelf word in the sheet's style, the newest voices first (`mouth`, falling back to realistic where the
  mouth voices none; `brawl.sound.style` says another), over the fight's family cues. And what a brawl never
  sounded: a blow thrown (a fist's swing, a strong blow's whoosh, a blade's), a jump, a thug's shout as it attacks
  (one in three, so a crowd is not a chorus), its grunt on a heavy blow and its cry as it goes down. The practice
  yard hears the same sheet. A probe reads what was asked for (`window.__mojBrawl.heard`): on a street played
  through, every cue asked for has a sound on the page.
- `brawl` re-pinned: the one fixture whose page inlines the brawl's client.
- A world that is a brawler: the quick goal `brawl` (`design_game({ quick: { goal: 'brawl', roster?, streets?, register? } })`).
  Its players are made as a fight's are (each a character through the character loop; the first plays), its streets
  are its levels (`quick.js` brawlStreets: a brawl level with its waves, and the hosted level's contract), and the
  game runs them in the play shell, its screens the game UI runtime's in the brawler's look unless the world says
  its own. Unsaid, one greybox street: a crowd a held screen, each a body more than the last, a knife among them from
  the second, a boss on the boss's screen. The agent's card for the goal says its levers; the character roll has a
  `brawl` genre (street fighters, never a bystander).
- A street in a game's shell: it says it is ready, takes the keyboard's focus as it starts, and sends its end up the
  level wire (cleared or down, the seconds and the health kept) in place of its own end screen, so the shell shows
  the result and what comes next. The greybox kind takes the level's contract (`game`).
- Through the doors and Chrome (`scripts/spikes/brawler/game.mjs`): design_game makes the player's character, the
  street and the game; export_game writes it; in the shell the title starts the street, the keyboard plays it, a
  masher beaten on its second screen is shown the shell's FAILED with try again, and a street cleared its CLEARED
  with the time and the health; no page errors.
- A street's rank: S, A, B or C by the health it is cleared with (three quarters, a half, a quarter), sent with its
  end and stamped on the shell's result; a result with no rank shows no rank row (the results idiom drew an empty
  one). The boss's bar runs along the foot, clear of the corners' readouts. The keys go back to the shell as a street
