  ends, so its result is driven from the keyboard, and "play again" fights the street from its start.
- The crowd has faces: a street's `cast` (`{ <crowd type> | boss | *: a roster index }`) draws its crowd and its boss
  as the roster's characters, their fight still their type's. A quick brawl makes two beside its players (a thug,
  the boss: `quick.js` BRAWL_CROWD), so its street is fought against made characters, not stick figures.
- A street of the GEOTOWN (`brawl-levels.js` the `town` kind): a block of the town's pattern with its main street along
  one side and the belt down it between its cross streets. The shops stand on the far side, the town's bare margin is
  open to the camera, and the road, the kerbs, the walks, the lamps and the fronts are the town's own. A quick brawl
  is fought down it unless it names another level (a stage kit's rooms, the greybox street). A street longer than
  the block is refused, saying how long the block is.
- The brawler's look: a brawl's one register is the western (lit) unless it names another, and every body it makes is
  one of the anime frame's muscular bodies in its muscular form (the muscle shirt) under the WESTERN head (`quick.js`
  brawlBody): the base pair for the players and the crowd, the hulking pair for the heavies and the boss. Never the
  anime head, never the realistic one.
- The crowd is a crew of the comic pack's: a brawl's `crowd` is a faction (`cosmos/packs/comic-hero/grunts.js`: the
  street gang, the crime family, the shadow clan, the motorcycle club, the private military, the cult, the punks,
  corporate security) or `{ faction, colourway?, size? }`, the street gang when none is said. `quick.js` brawlCrowd
  casts a grunt of each of the faction's kinds in ONE colourway and its boss (its heaviest kind, on the hulking body),
  each minted by the hero door as a dressed foe is, out of the pack's own light, on the brawler's body under the
  western head. A grunt fights as what it carries (crowdTypeOf: a drawn knife the knife, a machete or a katana the
  sword, a staff or a sceptre the staff, a pistol the gunner, a long gun the rifleman; bare-handed, a big body the
  heavy and any other the thug); a blade is the street's to draw, so only a gun stays in the hand. A street that names
  no waves draws them from those types, no more than two of a wave shooting. A cast's kind may name several
  characters, taken in turn body by body.
- The street is dressed (`brawl/brawl-dress.js`): what stands along a belt beside the band, laid on the belt and never
  on the level under it. Three shelves, each a table: the PIECES (a crate, stacked crates, barrels, a pallet, sacks, a
  market stall under its striped canopy, a cafe table under its parasol, a sandwich board, a planter, a pot, a bench, a
  paper box, a skip, tyres, a hand cart, a bollard; on the wall posters, the crew's tag and its banner), the SETS (a
  screen's theme: market, cafe, yard, turf, plain: what its far side draws from and how close, what its wall carries)
  and the seeded layout (a piece and a gap at a time against the fronts, the wall's marks at their stride). A town
  street is dressed unless its level says `dress: false`; `dress: { sets, colour, seed }` says a set a screen and the
  crew's colour (its tags, its banners, the boss's corner). A quick brawl's street wears its crowd's colourway. The
  dress collides with nothing: it stands outside the band.
- The street's angle: a belt angle `street` (further back, looking over the bodies' heads: the band in the frame's
  lower half, the fronts, their awnings and the first floor over it), the town street's own unless it names another.
  An angle carries the height it looks at (`look`; a body's chest for the others, as before).
- The street spike tours: `scripts/spikes/brawler/street.mjs --tour` walks the camera down an empty street and takes a
  still every 12 m, so a dress is seen in a couple of minutes without a fight.
- The street's fronts broken up: a geotown's `fronts: 'broken'` (opt-in; unsaid, a shop row as it was) gives each shop
  of a row its own house over the shop, from the row's `broken` table (`geotown/pattern.js`; the old town's: nine
  fronts): its render and its shutters' paint, each at its own lightness, its height (two to four storeys, so the eaves
  step), its shutters' form or none, its roof (the tiled hip, a steep slate one, a flat parapet), and on some narrow
  balconies from the second floor up (a front's `balconies` may now say its own size, and may hang over a shop's door).
  The brawl's town street asks for it.
- Alleys and setbacks: a shop row broken up (`fronts`) now breaks in plan too, by the row's `breaks`
  (`geotown/pattern.js`): an alley beside some buildings (as wide as its plot can spare, never two running, never on a
  corner) and some set back from the walk behind a paved forecourt, on their own dice, so a row not broken up is laid
  as it was.
- A rough quarter: `fronts: 'rough'` is the same row gone to a working street (the row's `rough` table): red, brown,
  yellow and dark brick tenements and walk-ups on the main street's brick with sash lights and flat roofs, between
  renders gone grey and grimy, shutters missing, a concrete front. The brawl's town street is rough unless its level
  says `fronts: 'broken'`.
- The dress gone urban (`brawl/brawl-dress.js`): new pieces (rubbish bags, dumped cardboard, a vending machine, a fire
  in an oil drum, litter and a stain on the walk; on the wall a steel shutter rolled down and sprayed, a big sprayed
  piece, a boarded window, an air conditioner, a drainpipe, a lit blade sign, a fire escape with its landings and
  ladders), a new set `strip` (a shuttered strip), rubbish and marks in the other sets, and the turn a street takes
  unsaid: the way in a strip, the held screens a market, a strip, a yard, the boss's the crew's corner (a cafe terrace
  is said, never fallen to). A dress may be told its `fronts` (the buildings' own lines along the belt): a wall's mark
  then stands on one building, at that building's line, and a gap between two is an alley with something left in it.
  A town street says them from its shops.
- The rough quarter's ground: under `fronts: 'rough'` the old town's setts are tarred over and its flags replaced in
  poured concrete (the pattern's `grounds.rough`: the road, lanes, drives and yards asphalt; the walks, the furnishing
  strip, paths and steps pavement).
- Skandart on the street (`era/skandart.js`'s shelves, used as they are). Its VESSELS (`era/skandart-vessels.js`) are
  the dress's crates, barrels and kegs (the old look) and its steel drums, steel crates and footlockers (the
  industrial look, a new piece `drums`), standing in groups, some tipped, some already broken, by how far gone the set
  is. Its DEBRIS SHELF (`era/debris-shelf.js`) is the street's debris: `rubble` at a wall's foot (bricks, spall,
  flakes of render, concrete), `wreckage` (broken concrete, bricks, planks, a roof sheet), `shards` (glass and
  papers), in the rough sets and in the alleys; a piece too small to be read from the street's camera is left out.
- The street's breakables: a street that names no `things` now has two boxes on each held screen (a barrel, a crate,
  a steel drum in turn: `quick.js` defaultThings; a new box `drum`), every other one holding food. A box is drawn as
  its skandart vessel (`brawl-dress.js` boxModels, carried by the page only when a box is laid) and, broken, leaves its
  wreck where it stood (its form's planks and splinters, a drum's sheet).
- The side-scroll map, for any contemporary place (`brawl/brawl-dress.js`,
  [docs/side-scroll-map-principles.md](../../../../docs/side-scroll-map-principles.md), the agent's card
  `gameworld-side-scroll`). What made the street work is said as principles and measured as laws (`dressLaws`, which
  advise): the band low and the backdrop over it, nothing tall between the camera and the fight, the dress outside
  the band, a screen a place of its own, the boss's screen held, things on the floor AND marks on the wall, no long
  bare run, variety inside a set. A map now has a SETTING, the kind of place it is, a row each with its sets, the turn
  it takes unsaid and what stands in its band to be broken:
  - `street` (as before), `facility` (a dock, a store of racking, a process hall, its heart), `base` (a gate, a depot,
    a motor pool, the command post), `office` (a lobby, an open floor, a break room, the corner suite);
  - their pieces: pallet racking, a tank, a cable reel, cones, a barrier, a forklift, a generator, lockers; sandbags,
    footlockers (skandart's vessels), jerry cans, a radio table, a floodlight; a desk, cabinets, a cooler, a copier, a
    sofa, a cubicle screen, a reception counter; on the wall pipes, a cabinet, a hazard board, an extinguisher, a duct,
    a stencilled unit number, a map board, a gun rack, a camouflage net, a whiteboard, a clock, pictures, glazing, an
    exit sign.
  A map's `sets` may name a set, leave a screen bare, or say A SET OF THE AGENT'S OWN from the pieces
  (`{ far, wall, gap, marks, near }`), read against them and held to the same laws.
- A building's bays are brawl levels: the stage kind takes the contemporary bays (`bay-military`, `bay-utility`,
  `bay-science`, `bay-everyday`) beside the arena kits, a kit with a setting of its own is dressed as it unsaid (its
  `dress` an object: `{ setting, sets, colour, seed, kit }`; true or false is still the kit's own dressing), and a
  dressed stage is framed by the belt's `street` angle. A quick brawl's boxes are its setting's.
- Vertical motion: a belt may RISE (`brawl-belt.js` `rise`: the floor's height along it, `[[s, z], …]`, no steeper
  than a stair between two points; `beltFloor`). The map still scrolls side-on: the camera rises with the floor it
  looks at, and the simulation is untouched (it plays on a level floor; the page draws every body, shadow, round,
  thing and wreck that much higher, its shadow catcher a ribbon along the floor). Across the belt the floor stays
  level. A town street CLIMBS by a word (`{ kind: 'town', climb: 0.06 }`, rise over run to 0.1, under 0 it falls): the
  town's own slope, its main street on a profile and its buildings stepping up beside it, the belt's rise read off its
  ground. A greybox street that rises is terraced (a ramp cut into steps, the road grown down to the ground). The
  dress stands on the floor under each piece. Three principles join the doc (the ground).
- The road turns: a belt may TURN (`brawl-belt.js` `turn`: `[[s, degrees], …]`, how far the camera is turned down the
  street at each point, to 55° either way, eased between points, no faster than 12° a metre; `beltTurn`). The walk is
  still along the belt and the band still across it, so the map scrolls sideways and heads up the screen (or down it),
  as an arcade brawler's diagonal stretch does; the camera swings round the point it looks at, and the simulation and
  the controls are untouched. A town street and a building's bays take it by word (`turn`), a greybox street on its
  belt. Three principles join the doc (the turn).
- The band drifts: a belt's band may slide ACROSS its line as it is walked (`brawl-belt.js` `drift`: `[[s, n], …]`, m
  across, north of the line over 0, no faster than 1.2 m a metre walked; `beltDrift`). The camera stays square to the
  street and follows the band up or down the screen, so the walkway runs on a diagonal, as an arcade street does where
  it leaves the straight line; the simulation is untouched (it plays a straight band; the page draws everything that
  much across). A greybox street moves whole with it, smooth: each block cut at the drift's own points
  and the piece on a diagonal TURNED onto it (its length the diagonal's, a little past each end so a bend closes),
  road, kerbs and fronts along the band's line. A town's street runs on it too (`{ kind: 'town', drift: […] }`,
  `brawl/brawl-warp.js`): the finished town is sheared across its belt by the band's drift where its page is made, a
  face that crosses a bend cut there first (so a wall and its windows stay together), its instanced things (lamps,
  trees) moved whole; its dress follows its ground (`follows`: a thing on the floor moved across, a mark on the wall
  sheared with it). Where a dress's ground stands still, what would be left in the drifted band is left out. Three principles join the doc (the drift).
- The walk bends, in any place: the three bends (rise, turn, drift) are said of the walk and the place round it, never
  of a street as such ("here is how a room turns"). The principles doc's three sections are one, `The walk bends`
  (what each bend keeps still, that the walk always scrolls sideways, that a bend is eased and is where the map turns a
  page, that the place goes with the walk), and the card teaches the three words as a level's own. A building's rooms
  take them as a street does (`{ kind: 'stage', kit, rise, turn, drift }`): `brawl-warp.js` placeWarp shears any place
  that already stands, across by the drift and (rooms, whose ground does not climb of itself) up by the rise, a face
  cut at a bend first, its lights, rooms, colliders and anchors moved with it; its dress follows its ground.
- Each street a turn (the game turn, `game/turn.js`, merged from the release candidate): a quick brawl's game now
  carries a flow whose every street asks the brawl's set-up before it loads (`quick.js` brawlSetup, lowered by
  `gameworld/setup.js`): how hard it fights, asked once and held by the save, and who plays, asked before every street
  when the roster has more than one player (the pick is the roster entry's id). The play shell draws the picks on
  mana-ui, loads the street, and takes its end to the results and the next street, so the shell stitches the game. A
  hosted street reads its session when the shell starts it (`brawl-street-read.js` streetSession: the fighter picked
  plays, to four seats; STREET_DIFFICULTY: the tier's crowd rules over the street's and its bosses' minds; the middle
  tier is the street as written). A world's own `setup` is kept, the fighter pick added unless it asks one.
  Proven on test streets (`scripts/spikes/brawler/turns.mjs`: three blockouts, one straight, one that rises, one that
  drifts, two fighters; designed, made, exported and played through the shell in headless Chrome).
- A brawl is made for a wide screen: a quick brawl's world says `screen: 'screen'` unless it or its quick says
  another (a new game's default is the upright phone, and the shell now draws its screens in the game's frame: a
  side view in a phone's column). Found by playing the turn through.
- A street's scenes, in its turn (`brawl/brawl-scenes.js`). A street names its scenes (`street.scenes: { <id>:
  [beat…] }`), a beat one of a card (`title`, `sub`), a line someone says (`say`, `who`), the camera travelling the
  belt (`pan: [from, to]`) or cut to a place on it (`look`), or a rest (`wait`); read against its belt, stepped by
  frames, a line or a card put away by accept, the scene ended by start where it may be skipped. The game calls them:
  a quick brawl's street step says `start: { scene: 'arrive' }` (every street its own, never on a retry) and `end:
  { scene: 'leave', when: 'won' }`. The page plays a staged scene with the fight held under the cinema bars and says
  when it ends; an end scene is played once the street is over and BEFORE its outcome is told, so the save and the
  results come after it. A street that names none is given a starter pair (`quick.js` defaultScenes: its name and who
  holds it, the camera brought back to the player; a card and the way out); its own are kept whole; `scenes: false`
  plays none.
- A hosted street says when its first frame is drawn (the level wire's `shown`), so the shell's loading screen lifts on
  it and the turn's start scene begins then, never under the loading screen. Found by playing the turn through: the
  arrive scene had played hidden.
- The play shell hands a level its end scene (`game/play-shell.js`): an end trigger that is a scene is named to the
  level as it loads (`params.__end: { scene, when, skip? }`) for the level to play on its own page; a video still
  plays over the shell as before ([docs/game-flow.md](../../../../docs/game-flow.md)).
- A composed world makes a brawler: a level walked SIDEWAYS (`gameworld/sideways.js`, `sideways-read.js`). A level
  of the game book says `sideways: true | { ground?, cast?, waves?, things?, scenes? }`: `ground` a brawl level's
  words (the place and its belt: its screens, its dress, its rise, turn and drift; the town's street unsaid), `cast`
  who of the world's bestiary the crowd is drawn as (a foe under a crowd type, under `*` for the rest, under `boss`),
  the rest a street's own, the starter's when not said. The level is alone on its level, read where the world is read.
  The run lays its street with the world's own: the hero (as the book equips it) and each of its cast who joins are
  its players, its cast's foes (fielded for it, each made as the bestiary makes a person or a crew's grunt) the
  crowd's faces, in the world's tradition; the level is a hosted level like any other, and the game the world's
  (its store, its links, its own `setup` and `flow` kept). Its turn asks the set-up, who plays when more than one can,
  and calls the street's scenes where every level is one. A world with no sideways level is made as it was.
- A map is played by a PLAY TYPE (`brawl/brawl-play.js` `PLAY_TYPES`, a row a type: the kit, what the turn asks,
  the screen, what stands in the band, how the map is held, what the end reads back): the same belt, bends, dress,
  scenes and turn, another set of idioms. `play: 'brawl' | 'gun'` on a quick brawl, on one street, or on a composed
  world's `sideways` level. A RUN & GUN (`gun`) plays a street with the gunner's kit, until now the practice range's
  alone: the players hold a gun over their sidearm with their grenades (`guns`, what they may start with; the turn
  asks which when there is more than one, the pick reaching the street as `__picks.gun`; `grenades`), the screen
  shows the gun held, its rounds and the grenades, the end reads accuracy. Unsaid, its map gets shooters on every
  screen with a rush between them (a crew's own shooters where it has them), cover across the band (the setting's:
  sandbags on a base, crates in a facility), a crate holding a gun on each held screen and food before the boss.
  A brawl is made as it was.
- A gun to take up (`things`: `{ kind: 'gun', what }`, in a box or lying; `brawl-things.js` `THINGS.gun`): a gunner
  takes what it walks over, in its stride (a gun, food, a power-up), and holds the gun over its sidearm until it is
  spent; a brawler leaves it lying.
- A wave on an OPEN screen (one with no gate) is fought on the move, in either play: it comes in as the player walks
  in, the camera is not held, and it is let go once a player is on the next wave's screen (those still standing left
  behind). A wave on such a screen was refused before.
- THE FIGHT, MEASURED (`brawl/brawl-measure.js`): a map's encounters have a machine gate. A street is fought down on
  the brawl's own simulation, no page, by a bot that plays the player's kit through its buttons (the masher, the floor:
  it walks up and attacks; the careful one: off a round's line, food when hurt, crates opened, a roll away from a
  brawler when it holds a gun), at each difficulty, over several takes (the middle one is the run), and each wave says
  how long it lasted, what share of the health bar it took and how many fell. The runs are read against the FIGHT LAWS
  (the floor finishes on easy, care is rewarded as written, max can be won, no spike, no slog, it opens gently, it
  ends); a law lost names the wave and what to change. `design_game`'s readout measures each sideways map (a quick
  brawl's streets, a composed world's sideways levels: `gameworld/fight-measure.js`) and adds a `fight` step where a
  law is lost. The whole table: `node scripts/spikes/brawler/measure.mjs`. It advises; the bots and the player are
  stand-ins, and it is not the eyes gate.
- The starter's own fights were set against it, and a deep test holds them to it. A brawl: a held screen opens with
  two bodies (three before), every box holds a roast chicken (an apple in every other before), the boss's screen a
  joint of meat at its door. A run & gun: two shooters and one rushing in on a held screen (a shooter more each), and
  its boss is a shooter (below), not the brawler it first ended on: a gunner had no answer to one, measured. The difficulty tiers (`STREET_DIFFICULTY`): easy and medium send one body at a time (medium with a breath
  between them; it was the crowd's own two at once), max is the crowd's own pace with a boss on its sharpest mind.
- A BOSS OF THE CROWD'S OWN KIND: a wave's `boss` may be `{ type, name?, hp?, volley? }` in place of a fighter's
  recipe: a crowd type's body as the boss, on its type's mind (a shooter holds its range and fires its volleys), with
  a boss's health (four times its type's unless said), its bar on the screen and the street won when it falls. A run &
  gun's starter boss is the crowd's rocket with two shooters beside it.
- A player's round breaks a box open (it stops there): a gunner has no blow to open a crate with.
- COVER FROM THE DRESS: a place's cover is of the place. A cover row named for a dress piece (`brawl-things.js`
  `THINGS.cover`: a barrier, footlockers, steel drums, barrels, a pallet, sacks, a skip, a planter, tyres, a cable
  reel, a desk, cabinets, a sofa, a reception counter, beside the sandbags and crates there were) is that piece stood
  in the band: drawn by the dress's own builder, fitted to the box that stops a round, leaving its matter's debris
  when it breaks (`brawl-dress.js` `coverModels`; the sandbags and crates are drawn so too, a low wall and a mount's
  wreck as they were). A run & gun that names no things takes each screen's cover from the set that screen wears
  (`dressCover`), its setting's where the set has none (`settingCover`, read off the sets: the table by setting is
  gone), each piece stood clear of the band's edges. A map with no dress keeps sandbags and crates.
- Fixed: what stands in the band (a breakable, a piece of cover, what either leaves broken) was drawn paler than the
  same piece against the wall: its colours reached the renderer unconverted. They are brought to linear light on the
  page, and a thing in the band now matches the dress it comes from.
- A BOSS'S PHASES: a boss of a crowd type takes `phases: [{ at, type?, volley?, calls?, says? }]`. As its health
  falls to `at` (a share of it, each lower than the last) it turns: it fights as another crowd type (that type's gun
  and plays) or with more rounds a volley, the bodies it `calls` come in (held off the street until then; never, if it
  falls first), and the screen says its word (`says`, or the phase's number). Its bar carries a pip a phase. The run &
  gun's starter boss throws its rocket down for a burst gun at half its health and calls two more, measured against
  the fight laws.
- A SECOND PLAYER SITS DOWN MID-STREET, in either play: a street makes a body for each spare seat (the playable
  characters no one picked, never one the crowd is drawn as; two seats at least, four at most) and keeps it off the
  street (`streetOf` a player `away`; `joinStreet`). A controller that presses attack or start takes the next seat and
  walks in beside the first, whole and armed as it, the street going on. Before, a second controller began the street
  again, and could be handed a crowd's grunt to play. Its name, health and gun stand under the first player's; the
  street is lost when every seated player is down. Checked on a page: `node scripts/spikes/brawler/street.mjs --coop
  --play gun` (a pad the page reads as any sits down, walks in and fires; exit 0 only if it held).
- THE SCREEN of a side-scrolling action game in play, redone for both plays: FOUR SEATS across the top, a quarter of
  the screen each, so a seat never moves when another is taken. A seat taken shows its tag in its own colour (the
  look's sides; the mark its player stands on wears it too), its name, its health read by its length, and for a run &
  gun the gun in its hands as two letters (`gunCode`: MG, SP, FL, RK), its rounds (marked LOW at a fifth of a
  magazine) and its grenades. A seat open says how to sit down; a seat the game has not leaves its quarter empty. The
  way through and who is left moved to the foot's corners, the boss's bar between them: the middle of the screen is
  the fight's. A new look, `brawl-street` (a theme card: the brawl yard's asphalt and hazard yellow with stencilled
  pictograms coloured by what they mean), on the street's screen and on a brawl's shell; the practice yard keeps
  `brawl-yard`. Two pictograms joined the icon shelf: `bullet` (also said ammo, rounds) and `grenade`.
- ONE STREET, TWO DOORS IN (the street's design door merged in: the `brawl-doors` theme beside this one). A street
  written at its DESIGN (a designed game's `levels.<id>.street`, a quick `brawl` or `rungun` that says `street`,
  `waves`, `lives`, `players`, `armed` or `guns`, a game made from a sentence: its stops and its boss, its crowd the
  game's own cast by role) and one written by its STREETS (a quick brawl's `streets`, `crowd`, `play`: a place of
  its own, its dress, its bends, its scenes) are both played on the one street: the
  seats, the fight laws' numbers, cover, pickups and the turn are the same under either. The page reads a design's
  street (`brawl.practice.street`) as it reads a street's block. What the design door brought onto the street:
  LIVES (`lives`: the falls its players share; a player knocked out is back on its feet where it fell, whole, until
  the last one allowed; hearts at the foot of the screen), a TUNING (`tune`: its players' health, the crowd's as a
  share of its own, the crowd's guns and rules), a crowd body drawn as the cast member its wave names, a fighter boss
  in STAGES (beside a crowd-kind boss's phases; either turns the boss's marks and says its word), and DUCKING and
  JUMPING a round. A quick brawl or rungun that says none of the design's words, in a world with no `foes`, is the
  starter's (the dressed town street, a crew of the comic pack's; a rungun played with guns).
- `sideways` IS FOLDED INTO `street`: a designed game has one key for a street level. `levels.<id>.street` takes a
  `ground` (a place of its own in a kit's stead: a town's street, a stage, a blockout, with its dress and its rise,
  turn and drift; the stops laid along it), its own `things` and `scenes`, and may be `true` or say no stops (three
  that build to the cast's boss). On a ground its play's things (breakables with food; a run & gun's cover from the
  dress, its gun crates) and the starter's scenes are laid unless said, and a world whose every level is such a street
  has each level's turn call them. The fight measure reads a street level as its page does (its cast's waves, its
  lives, its tuning). `levels.<id>.sideways`, its `cast` by crowd type and its raw `waves` are gone: who comes is
  written at the street's stops, by role or by a foe's name.
- A game whose every level is a street wears the street's look (`brawl-street`) on its menus when it says no `ui`,
  as a quick brawl does: its level list, set-up, pause and results are the game UI runtime's, driven from the keys.
  A blockout takes the game's `screen` word, as a stage does (a street on a blockout ground was refused for it).
- Not yet (the two doors): the design door's scripted player and this theme's fight measure both read a street (one check would do); the
  practice room that ends (`stakes`) is still its own path for a wave set with no street.
- Not yet (run & gun): one-hit play, a boss's own attacks (a pattern only it has), the turn asking each
  seat its fighter and gun (a second player takes the next playable and the first's gun), the fight measured with two.
- Not yet (sound): footsteps, a street's bed, the score and its stingers (the cue sheet), the screen's own sounds.
- Not yet: a crowd of its own per street, a boss with a fight of its faction's own, a street of more than one
  block, the town's page under a host's size limit (a town street's page is about 18 MB and slow where a box draws in
  software), the realistic jacked body's wrist (its forearm ends wider than its hand), lives and continues, a rank on the result, two players checked on a page, a brawler from a composed
  (non-quick) world.

### The touch controller drawn by mana-ui

In progress. A game that moves on W A S D already plays on a phone: the touch layer is a virtual gamepad read through
the same bindings as a real pad. It drew its own stick and buttons, though, beside a HUD that is mana-ui's. The plan:
mana-ui draws them, the controls layer keeps reading the thumbs.

- **Built: the view half.** On a level made for a screen whose HUD is mana-ui's, the HUD draws the virtual pad and
  the touch layer draws nothing (`touchScript(L, { view: 'mana' })`): the same zones, the same pad arithmetic, the
  pads found from the view's own elements, what it knows said as `window.__mojTouch.view()` and copied into the
  HUD's state each frame.
- mana-ui's `touchpad` takes `lane`, `held` (where the stick rose and where its nub is) and `down` (the controls
  pressed). A stick at rest is seen through, a held one stands out where the thumb landed, a pressed pad is filled.
  The pad is as wide as its frame allows (it ran off a tall frame's side).
- A level with no mana-ui HUD, and a runner's or a course's swipe layouts, emit the touch layer they did.
- **Built: its look.** A pad named for what it does wears its pictogram inside its round where the theme draws
  icons (`use`, `interact` and `talk` are the tap's). The pads fill from the screen's edge inward. The HUD's bottom
  corners stand over the pad while it is drawn. A level's hint line says the thumbs while the pad is up
  (`hudToMana({ touch })`), its keys otherwise. The board draws `touch-controls` with a held stick and a pressed pad.
- **Fixed in mana-ui, seen on a phone frame:** a glass theme blurred the world behind every HUD region, the bare
  ones too (a slab behind the pad); bare regions and the ones that are their own frame are no longer blurred. A
  region whose every part is gated off left an empty plate; it draws nothing now.
- Played in headless Chrome on a phone-sized touch screen, a made game in the toybox look: the stick rose under the
  thumb and the hero walked; a touch on the jump pad pressed the pad's control and the hero jumped.
- **Built: a game's own button.** A level's HUD takes a button row, `{ press: '<event>', label, slot? }`. Pressed
  (a tap or a click), it raises that event on the level's bus as a key bound to it would, so a touch screen gets a
  control the virtual pad has none for. The mana-ui HUD draws it as a button and its host carries the press; the
  page's own HUD draws it too. Only a level with such a row carries the bus's way in. The HUD guide card teaches it.
  Tapped in headless Chrome on a phone frame: the event reached the bus and a banner listening for it showed.
- **Built: a screen level never asks for a key a thumb cannot press** (`lib/graph/game/screen-keys.js`). The pad
  already stands for the keys that move, look, jump, fire and use. Every other key a level made for a screen
  listens for gets a HUD button by itself, drawn only on a touch screen: its own key inputs (`events.inputs`), the
  journal (J), the library (L), the party menu (P). Pressed, the button is that key pressed, so the channel that
  listens for it hears what it always did. A HUD button row may say `key` (and `code`) in place of `press`, and
  `touch: true` to stand only while the touch layer is up. A level with no screen, or no such key, emits what it
  did. Seen in headless Chrome: a level that binds Q grew a button on a touch screen, a tap fired its event, and on a
  desk no button was drawn.
- Not covered by that rule: a physics toy's action keys and a mover's key (they are a world's, outside a level's
  events), and a level walked with the tour's walk camera in place of a pilot.
- Not yet: the pad's size and place tuned by hand on a real phone; a world with no `ui` and no course (it keeps
  the driver's own drawing); a gameworld's own word for such a button (today it is a level's `events.hud` row).

### What to build next now counts a world's people, its colour and how a game starts

- **A second pass over the same merges, for what a game can now ask for.** The first pass over the work merged since
  November 10th dated a few things and left the rest in its notes, as plumbing the planning map does not count. This
  one counts the parts of that work a game can ask for, each with the day it was built: a game that starts in play
  behind an opening cutscene, a level session that asks its set-up first (difficulty, picks) and then loads, plays,
  pauses and shows its results, a world map that opens by teaching the controls and then sending foes at the hero, a
  fight that comes when the one before it is won, an obstacle course run at speed that is different every play,
  goblins and orcs as peoples of their own, a people's foes left wild, each geared by its own role, or dressed alike
  as one band, the cast coloured so it stands clear of the land it walks on, two ways a game's land can be coloured (a
  quiet land that leaves colour to the cast, a day that turns to night across the levels), a setting's history kept
  on the game, and a hero designed as a person of its world.
- **Six things that are made but cannot yet be asked for in a designed game are priced**, so they can be ranked
  against other work: a power system from a setting's lore (what opposes what, a reserve of power, who holds a share,
  a monster manual, a skill tree), a room's state of repair in one word (kept, worn, neglected, derelict, ruined),
  books a player finds and reads in a level, one composed room as a level of a game, a finished frame (bloom, the sky
  in shiny surfaces), and a story moment filmed by naming it. The first of these is now named for what it would be:
  orders from lore.
- **The count of makeable rolled games went down, and nothing broke.** Naming those gaps means more rolled games ask
  for something that is not finished: 43 of 500 read as makeable where 69 did, and 288 of 500 near the kinds of game
  people ask for (was 294). Nearly all of the 43 are games that could not be made a fortnight ago. No kind of game
  changed its verdict.
- **Cutscenes made to order are counted.** A game can now play a cutscene the animation studio filmed for it, and an
  exported game carries the video. What is left is priced: the order is still filled in by hand, so a story moment
  cannot yet be filmed just by naming it. The animation studio itself makes films, not games, so it stays off the map.
- **Left off the map on purpose.** Exhibits, galleries and the kiosk have nothing to win, so they are not games. The
  new trucks and launch vehicles are rows of the vehicle library. The work on light, wet ground and reflections is
  already described where the seventh-generation look is.
- The page's notes say which of the joins they list are now priced, and no longer call the game room "not a level
  form": it is one that only the practice door plays.

### What to build next: the planning map caught up through 1114, and says where the rails stop

- **The planning map counts the last merges.** The internal map the studio uses to decide what to build next now dates
  the ashlar crypt and the foe that comes at the hero, and its notes say what is true since: the practice door opens the
  firing and artillery ranges from a designed game, the boards, the tables and the rooms' menu run on the shared game
  UI, and a game can start in play behind its opening cutscene. The co-op kitchen is now described by the work a shift
  does. The totals did not move: what merged was mostly rails (the playthrough, a world's arsenal, the casting call, the
  rooms), which the map does not count as values.
- **Counted from 1113 and 1114:** a game that plays a different map each time is now a thing the map can ask for and
  date. A level's own HUD, its pause button and its touch pad now run on the shared game UI, so what is left of that gap
  (talk menus, the quest log) is priced smaller. The notes say that every level session now runs as one turn, with a
  game's set-up asked before each level. The new trucks and launch vehicles are library rows and change no count.
- **A check for the action games made from a sentence.** The suite that asks "what does a person get from one
  sentence" gains the action games, held at "not yet": the sentence lays the camera and the foes and writes no weapons
  kit, so the hero plays no strings and no level is played by the scripted player until the kit is written by hand. The
  check turns over the day the sentence door lays the kit.
- **The board's notes say the joins in order**, rails before shelf rows: the kit from a sentence, one won-gate for
  every kind of level (five separate checks answer that today), a made room as a level, a room's condition on a designed game's levels, sound from a designed
  game.

### Shops you can walk into

- **A town's shops can be entered.** Ask for it on a town (its `shops` setting) and each shop on a main street gets a real
  doorway and a furnished interior behind it, taken from the same store designs the shopping mall uses: clothing,
  electronics, a bookshop, homewares (a cafe or a food hall when you name them). A town made without it is unchanged.
- **Interiors are drawn only when you are close.** Each inside appears as you approach its door and is left undrawn
  from further away, so a street of shops costs little until you walk it.
- **You can see into an open shop from the street.** Its windows are now real glass: the shelves and racks inside show
  through from the pavement, and the street shows through from inside.
- **A city's shop rows can be entered too.** The same setting on a city opens every shop along its main streets and
  neighbourhood edges, and any town built into that city follows. Shops of the same size share one interior, so a
  city of dozens of shops carries only a handful of them. In a city the shop windows are still painted, not glass.
- **Five new kinds of shop for a street.** A convenience store, a pharmacy, a diner, a pawn shop and a gun store join
  the store designs, and each can also be made on its own or placed in a shopping mall.
- **A street decides who rents its shops.** A main street leans to clothing, books and homewares, a busy avenue to
  electronics, convenience stores and pharmacies, an old town to bookshops and clothing. No two neighbours are the same
  kind, and each shop's sign takes its store's colour. You can still name the kinds yourself.
- **A city shop has a real door and a step up to it.** Its doorway now clears a person's height, and where the shop
  stands above the pavement a short flight of steps leads up to it. Where the shop stands far above the pavement its floor is set
  lower than the block around it, so the flight is never more than three steps and every shop on a sloping street opens.
- **An errand can send you into a shop.** An item on an errand's list can name the kind of store it is bought in (a
  pharmacy, a convenience store, a diner). Where the level's town has its shops open, you walk in and make the trade at
  that store's counter; where it does not, the trade is placed as before.
- **A game's hero can walk into an open shop.** In a level set in a town with open shops the hero has floor to stand on
  inside, the fixtures block the way, and the level no longer swaps to a separate interior for a shop that is already open.
- **A shopkeeper behind the counter.** In a game whose level is a town with open shops and townspeople, each open
  shop's keeper now stands behind its counter facing the till, and you can talk to them there. The town's other
  people stand by their own doors, as they do in other towns.
- **Shop interiors are standard sizes and much lighter.** Every open shop is now fitted from a small set of standard
  units, so shops across a town or a city share the same interiors. Parts no one can see are left out, floors and
  brick walls use the surface textures the street already has, and the interiors are stored in a compact form. In a
  test district of 88 open shops the interiors went from about 15 MB of the page to about 2.5 MB.

### A city district as a game level

- **A game's level can be a district of a city.** A level can now be one neighbourhood of a city, drawn in detail
  with the rest of the city as its skyline, and walked by the game's hero from its streets. Where the city's shops
  are open the hero walks into them, and an errand can be traded at a shop's counter there.
- **A city page is lighter.** A city's cars, cranes and site machines are now stored in the same compact form as the
  shop interiors. A test district's page went from about 72 MB to about 43 MB in the painted look (from 149 MB to 120 MB
  in the default look, where the land and plants are most of the weight).

### Geocube refinements: a trail library, an open world map, cliffs that make sense

- **The trail library** (level/block-fills.js). A block of a planned map (level/plan.js) was laid one way before its
  author wrote it: a line from gate to gate through its middle. A plan may now name a template for each block
  (`key.<S>.fill`), each a procedure over the block's size and gates, turned to whichever sides its gates are on:
  `through` (the way it always was, and still the default), `round` (the way goes round the middle by one side),
  `loop` (a ring round the middle, every gate on it: two ways round), `spur` (through, and a dead end off the middle
  toward a side with no gate), `crossroads` (through, a branch toward every such side) and `switchback` (lanes back and
  forth between two opposite gates). A ring lies a tile in from the border, so a template never joins a neighbour where
  the plan did not. A template the block has no room or gates for is laid as the nearest that fits; a goal still stands
  at the block's middle with a way at its door. A plan that names no template is laid byte for byte as before.
- **The game door's world map is an open world** (gameworld/world-map.js). It was blocks in a snake, each a corridor.
  Now its blocks are 5 × 5 tiles laid by the library (the village its street, the road a ring, the ruins and the town
  crossroads with dead ends for their finds, the zones after in turn, the goal ringed by a way), and wherever two blocks
  lie side by side off the walk a side way joins them (the plan's `joins`), so the map has loops and the goal is reached
  two ways. The opening keeps its one way out. Fights stand at each block's heart, on its ways; finds beside them. The
  walk itself (map-items.js `mapWay`) keeps to its route where a join would shortcut it, so every block still holds its
  pack and the guide leads the long way. The world's bible draws the side ways, dotted, on its map.
- **A shortcut costs more.** A side way that skips blocks of the walk is held: a band stands at its gate in the block
  it comes out in (five of the rank and file and two elites by default, `WORLD_MAP.shortcut`, against a block's own
  fight of three), off the walk, so only a player who takes the short way meets them. The long way stays the taught way.
- **Cliffs that make sense** (level/map-cliffs.js, era/out-tile.js `riseAt`). A sketch may say `cliffs: true`: where its
  approved heights stand 6 m or more apart between two tiles side by side and no way crosses that edge, the land no
  longer eases from one to the other across both tiles (a long ramp nobody asked for): each holds its height to their
  shared edge and steps there, a rock face 2.4 m wide whose line wanders, drawn as the kit draws any steep ground. Where
  a way crosses, there is never a cliff: the way keeps its eased climb. So a cliff is always the edge of somewhere
  higher that nobody walks over, and a trail is where it is passed. The scarps ride in the level's rise, so the page,
  its ends, its zones and its far view read one land. The world map lays its blocks as terraces that climb a step a
  block to the goal's heights, each way a step a tile at most (cut down into the higher terrace where a side way comes
  up from low ground), and asks for the cliffs. A sketch that does not ask, or whose heights never step that far, is
  read as before.
- **A terraced land rolls less.** The level's own hills (about 5 m either way) lost a 3 m terrace in their roll: on the
  world map the ruins' high ground stood over the river town's low ground a step above it. A map that asks for its
  cliffs lays its hills at 2 m (`MAP_CLIFF.hills`, riding in the rise), so each terrace reads as one: the blocks' land
  now stands in order with little overlap (ruins 1.2 to 4.6 m, river town 3.7 to 7.2 m, castle heights up to 9.3 m).
- **Fewer bushes by a tile's way.** The world map asks five bushes a tile (`WORLD_MAP.shrubs`) where the kit's card
  gave a tile a whole trail's fourteen.
- **The map designer draws the cliffs.** The world map in miniature and its greybox model (level/worldmap-view.js,
  worldmap-model.js) read the same scarps the pages lay, so a map is looked at with its cliffs before it is built.
- **A map is looked at before it is made.** A gameworld's planned map is served in miniature as a book
  (`/api/sketches/<ref>/bible?book=map[&level=<id>]`, gameworld/map-designer.js): its blocks, ways, side ways, heights,
  cliffs and beats from the recipe alone, no tile built. `design_game`'s `worldmap` step carries it as `look`, and the
  next-moves card says to open it and show the creator first, before a block is written or a page built, and after each
  change; the card's ceiling moves 4864 → 5120.
- **The world map test bed walks a page of several blocks.** Its gate walk (gameworld/worldmap-bed.js `crossings`)
  read a page's gates by side alone and stopped at a page of two blocks, whose gates are named by block and side.
- **Measured:** a zone's page of the world map is heavier for its bigger blocks, as payload: the opening 40 MB, the
  first zone (two blocks) 70 MB, the goal's zone 52 MB (42 tiles, 25 its own, about 162,000 faces), where the goal's
  zone was 34 MB (20 tiles, about 89,000 faces).

### Shooting rails: the firing range stretched into a first mission

A shooter's practice is the firing range: the agent writes the game's guns and the creator plays them. Nothing carried
that into a level: a quick shooter laid a trail with posts, a book shooter got one fixed gun, and a template's loadout
reached the range and nowhere else. A world with a firing range now has a **mission**: the range stretched into a first
level with sections and tasks, briefed, played and debriefed on mana-ui. Design notes:
[docs/missions.md](../../../../docs/missions.md).

- **The mission, composed** (`lib/graph/mission/`, pure). Sections are a closed table (staging, contact, lane,
  overwatch, emplacement, holdout, extract): each is what it teaches, the band it is sized from (the range's 5, 15 and
  30 m bodies) and the task that ends it. The brief reads the world's guns to their bands and chooses the sections: a gun
  for the mid band gets the lane, a long gun the long line too, close guns alone a room and a yard held across a room.
  The composition lays them down one line out of the room primitives, a doorway between each on alternate sides, each
  fight's foes at its band from its firing line behind cover of their own. Seeded; the same seed lays the same mission.
- **Its laws** in the game's own numbers, advice never a refusal: walkable, sealed (no way round a task), banded,
  covered within a second of the run, entry-safe, in order (it teaches before it tests), armed, paced.
- **Tasks on the bus** (`game/objectives.js`, the mechanic `objectives`): take, reach, clear, man and hold, done in
  order. A task begins as its section is walked into and wakes its own foes then; met, it opens the way on; the last met
  wins. A sealed way puts a body back. It keeps the tasks met, the foes downed and the seconds taken for the result. It
  has its vocab card and its sounds.
- **The level** (`gameworld/mission-level.js`): the range's own body (its slots, sights and knife), hunters of the
  range's health dormant on their spots, the level's hp, rounds and health on the floor, a greybox ground. With no hero
  it is aimed from the eye; a hero seen from behind aims over its shoulder.
- **Three doors:**
  - the practice door's `mission` room (`bible?book=practice&room=mission`), played from the world alone, with its
    icon on the rail;
  - a level's own form, `levels.<id>.mission: true | { seed?, sections?, foes?, hold?, waves? }`, in place of `walk`;
  - a quick shooter's `mission`, its level in place of the trail, laid from its carried `arms`.

  `design_game` proposes it (a `mission` step with its patch) for a world with a firing range and no mission level. A
  run makes the foes' figure (a gunner rolled in the game's setting), the level and the game. Its card is
  `gameworld-mission`.
- **On mana-ui, end to end** (`gameworld/mission-mana.js`, the page channel `mission`): the briefing over the held
  scene, the HUD (the level's hp, the gun in hand, the objective tracker, the yard's clock) read each frame off the
  scene, the pilot's pause and, on a page played alone, the debrief. Inside a game's shell the shell's own result screen
  is the debrief. A world with a mission and no `ui` of its own gets its shell on mana-ui in the mission's look, so the
  front, the briefing, the HUD, the pause and the result are one runtime. The look is a new theme card, `field-brief`; a
  look with an overlay across the screen is read without it.
- **The damage ring.** Taking fire, a mark stands on a ring round the aim where each hit came from: the top of the
  ring ahead, the bottom behind. It stands for a moment, follows its attacker and turns with the player, so turning
  until it is at the top faces the shooter. Read off the scene (the pilot's hits and who dealt the last), drawn by
  mana-ui's `damage-direction` idiom only while a mark stands; said in the briefing's How to play (Under fire).
  It is its own concept (`gameworld/damage-ring.js`), so a level whose HUD is the page's own has it too: a quick
  shooter's level on foot and a deathmatch carry `damageRing` and draw the same ring through the page's damage ring
  channel. A level nobody shoots in carries none; a level minted before keeps its bytes until it is made again.
- **Two machine gates**, read by `design_game` after a run as `mission_proof` (`gameworld/mission-proof.js`):
  - on the bus: every task done in the order written, every sealed way put the walker back, the last task won;
  - played: the level stepped headless on the runtime by a gunner that walks the laws' grid, aims, raises the sights,
    fires in bursts, takes the gun the range asks for and reloads; a still player must not win. A mission the gunner
    loses says where, with the dials that move it.
- **The arms library's guns in the hands.** The first-person view drew a gun as its parts' boxes, on every shooter
  page. A slot may now ask for the arm itself (`gunplay.view.detail: 'arm'`, `gameworld/arms-kit.js` `armDetailed`): the
  page's resolve builds the arm as the arms library builds it (`equipment/arms/handling.js` `armMesh`: every part's
  quads, each wound outward, in its lit colours) and the view draws it on the same stations, sights and hands, each face
  shaded by the way it looks. The optic is drawn from the hip and gives way to its hood at the sights; the magazine
  still leaves through a reload. The recipe carries the ask and the build words, never the mesh. The mission and the
  firing range ask; a page that does not ask draws as before (no page pin moved). A skin's arm goes with its skin.
- **Fixed: a world's `ui` never reached its made game.** The runner wrote it and `create_game` dropped it, on a make
  and on a remake, so no game made through `design_game` had its shell on mana-ui. It is carried now, as `flow` is.
- The range's body is its own module (`combat/range-body.js`, re-exported by `range.js`), so what carries the same guns
  elsewhere reads the body without the page's emitter. The shooter's foe and its tune are exported from `quick.js`.
- Checked in headless Chromium: the practice page is briefed, begun, paused and debriefed; a sealed way puts the body
  back; the tracker moves on as the rounds are taken. An exported game goes from its mana-ui title into the mission and
  to the shell's result. The gunner wins every feel template that shoots and kits of a rifle, a long gun with a close
  one, and a shotgun with a sidearm, in about a minute; an SMG alone is lost in the yard, and said. Machine gates only:
  nobody has played one.
- Designed, not built yet, each named a gap: the emplacement's mounted gun (its section is in the table with what it
  waits on, and asking for it is refused with that, never laid half), a machine as the hero for a template that owns a
  frame, a dressed mission.
- **Arena maps: the principles as laws** (`lib/graph/arena-map/`, pure; design notes
  [docs/arena-maps.md](../../../../docs/arena-maps.md)). A fighting map is not a trail, so the map is its own thing: a
  closed table of blocks on one grid (floor, wall, low wall, solid, ramp, ladder; a drop is an open upper edge), the
  principles of line-of-sight combat as measured laws in four groups (structure, access, sight, economy), sized from
  the firing range's own numbers (the run, the bands the guns are for), and a generator that grows a template a block
  at a time and keeps only what the laws hold no worse.
  - **Ramps and ladders run into nothing.** A ramp wants a landing at each end that leads on, its cells clear of mass,
    no floor over them, no wall across its line at the height a body is, a slope a body walks; a ladder a floor at its
    foot, an open shaft, a ledge that leads on and no wall along it. A way with a fault joins nothing and says what it
    ran into.
  - Spawns and things are read off the map's own shape, never placed by hand.
  - Four templates (a court under a gallery, two rings sharing a middle, three rooms with a bridge, a tower round a
    well), sized for a kit of close and mid guns. Each grows to every law held in one to three seconds, on every seed
    tried: a law not held names what mends it (a line to break, an edge to rail, a floor no ramp reaches) and the
    generator's repairs do that where the dice fall.
  - Not built yet: a geocube building or town read against the laws.
- **A mission fought on a fighting map** (`mission: { map: true | '<template>' }`, on the practice door's spec and a
  level's own form). The firing range decides the rules, the map is grown under the arena laws for the kit's bands
  (`true` picks by the longest band: close guns a tower, the mid band a court, a long gun the figure of eight) and the
  phases are placed from its own measures (`arena-map/phases.js`): set down on a spawn far from the heart, arm up at the
  small thing nearest it, a clear a band with its foes woken out of sight at that band's distance over different
  approaches and levels, hold the heart (the most seen place) against waves from the quiet places by more than one way,
  get out at a far spawn by a way not walked yet. Its laws, advice: placed, unseen, two ways, in order, banded; the
  map's own ride beside them.
  - **The map laid as ground** (`arena-map/ground.js` `mapGround`): floors (an upper one a slab walked under and stood
    on), walls and rails, solids, ramps as slopes the platform rule walks up and down (sliced colliders under them stop a
    body at their sides), ladders as the runtime's own climb (`rungs`, plumb in the foot cell, mounted at the ledge).
    Walked headless on the runtime: up a ramp and down, off an open edge, stopped by a wall and a rail and a ramp's side,
    up a ladder, under a slab.
  - **Recipes, not renders:** the level carries the map as grown (`mission.plan.map`: its template, seed and blocks)
    and is rebuilt from those blocks; it is never regrown on a read, so a change to the generator cannot move a minted
    level. The greybox mission (no `map`) is as it was.
  - The bus proof reads a task done as the mechanic's var moves past it (a task with no zone begins as the one before is
    met, and may be done in the same breath). The headless gunner walks a map on its own graph (the shortest way cell to
    cell, up its ramps and ladders, off an edge where the way drops) and finishes a climb before it fights. Machine gate:
    with the shooter feel it wins the practice room on every template; as a level on two seeds it won six of eight (it
    stalls on a ladder taken from above, and once went down in the lane), said, not tuned away. Nobody has played one.
- **Buildings designed as fighting maps** (`building.fight: true | { rings?, stagger?, stairs?, gallery?, cover? }`,
  opt-in; an unasked building is byte-identical). Five dials on the plan, each the answer to an arena law the geocube's
  buildings fail: rings (a second doorway for every room), stagger (the core's side doorways offset), stairs (a stair
  room at each wing's far end), gallery (the tall annex overlooked from the upper storey), cover (the hall broken by its
  own stock). The arena reader reads the gallery. Read against the laws, every core building but one improves; what
  still fails is said in the design notes.
- **A mission is read in the seventh generation.** Its page named no cube, so it had no era and was drawn flat. It now
  carries its world's cube with the era `gen-7` unless the cube names one: the actors' shadows, the hour's shadow map
  and contact occlusion are on, on the practice room and on a level. Its greybox and its figures are still paint under
  that light, and the era reading says so.
- **A mission in a building, drawn by the form render** (`levels.<id>: { building: { use, fight? }, mission }`,
  `gameworld/mission-building.js`). The building's plan, designed as a fighting map unless it says otherwise, is read
  onto the arena grid, the phases are placed there from its way in to one of its doors, and each place is held to the
  real plan (in its room, on its floor, clear of the walls, the stairs and the stock: moved where the grid's snap put it
  in one, left out and said where nothing is free). The level is the building's own lowering with the mission's cast,
  tasks and page; the pilot climbs its stairs on the platform rule. It is read under the world's cube in the seventh
  generation, its bones the building's kit, so its rooms are `form.room`; its figures are still paint (no cast rig
  indoors yet). `design_game`'s `mission` step carries the building by the kit's band beside the greybox. Proved on the
  bus; played on its resolved page, where the gunner wins a warehouse and an armoury and the hold's waves never come.
  Fixed on the way: a gallery's doorway over a ground-floor doorway on the same span was walled by the lower one's lintel
  and walled the lower one with its own sill, so neither could be walked through.
- **A hold's waves come to the fight.** A hunter knows a target by sight and memory, so a wave woken out of sight had
  seen no one and stood where it was put: on a map or in a building the hold was a clock. The foes a hold wakes are now
  sent: a mind with no perception knows where the body is and paths to it. A clear's foes keep their sight and memory.
  Measured headless on the court map: none of nine moved before, all nine after. They keep to the floor they wake on.
- **A ladder between a map's floors is climbed by holding jump.** Stood under it, facing any way, holding the jump key
  takes hold of it and goes up it rung by rung while the key is held; let go and the body hangs there; back goes down.
  It is an opt-in on a climbable (`hold`, `holdReach`; `worlds/controllable/rules-basic.js`), set on an arena map's
  ladders; walking into a ladder still climbs it, and any other ladder is as it was. The seventeen page fixtures that
  inline the controllable runtime are re-pinned for the runtime's text; its trace holds.
- **A wave crosses a map's floors, and a mind's path keeps to its ground.** The pathfinder takes an opt-in `ledges`
  (`worlds/controllable/nav.js`; a mind asks with `rule.navLedges`): a cell with no ground at the body's height is shut
  as a wall is, so a path goes round a well and along a gallery, never out over a drop. A map mission hands a hold's
  wave the map's upper floors and the ramps up to them (`arena-map/ground.js` `mapFloors`) with the mind that crosses
  them. Measured headless with a still body on the upper floor: the court two of nine before, all nine after; the three
  rooms none before, all nine after. Played through, the gunner still wins three of the four maps and now goes down in
  the three rooms' hold: said, not tuned. Minds keep to ramps (no ladder, no floor over a floor); a building's waves
  still come on their own floor. The seventeen runtime fixtures are re-pinned for the runtime's text; no path already
  made changes, since no mind already made asks.
- **A wave crosses a building's storeys.** Two things kept a building's wave off the storey over the ground, each
  found by tracing one foe. The gallery's doorway had no floor through the wall's thickness (`era/bay.js`: a sill
  opening now takes its reveal, its floor at the deck's height), so a body on the gallery stopped at it. And a storey's
  floor stopped no sight: a foe under the pilot saw it through the slab and fought from below, so a mission's building
  now lays its rooms' ceilings as colliders (the stage's opt-in `ceilings`). With those, the building mission hands a
  hold's wave the storey over the ground and each stair up to it, and a mind walks a flight that turns by its own points
  (`rule.floors` `flights[].way`, `worlds/controllable/mind.js`). Measured headless in a warehouse, a still body in two
  upper rooms out of sight of the ground: none of nine within 8 m before, all nine after; the gunner still wins the
  building. One storey only (the floor over the ground). The seventeen runtime fixtures are re-pinned for the runtime's
  text; no fixture's flight carries a `way`.
- **A town or a city, cut as a fighting map.** `arena-map/read-town.js` reads a window of a designed geotown (a block:
  its buildings on its streets, alley and yards) or geocity (an industrial block's halls, tanks, containers and fence;
  a shore's ground, piers and water) onto the arena grid, named or picked by the most edge between ground and what is
  not. Water is a cell with no floor: nothing stands in it and a line crosses it; the map's ground draws it and keeps a
  body out. As read every cut fails the sight laws (real ground is open); the generator now takes a given map
  (`growArenaMap({ map })`), keeps what the place is made of and grows cover on its open ground, never cutting it in
  two: of eight 36 m cuts three reach all fourteen laws and the rest twelve or thirteen, what stays unheld being the
  place's own shape (a pier is a dead end). A mission takes a place as its map (`mission.map: { town } | { city, on }`):
  played headless, the gunner wins the quay, the pier, the container yard and the main street and goes down in the hold
  on the houses block and the beach. Greybox only; a place's hedges, cars and pavilions are the scenes' and are not read.
- **Maps and places in the seventh generation.** A mission on a grown map or a place's cut is drawn by the form render
  (`arena-map/ground-form.js`): the greybox's geometry, each face in a tile by what it is, baked under the cube's sun
  with the blocks' own shadows, handed to the page as a town's buildings are (`form.town`; a controllable manifest now
  carries an opt-in `form`). The era reading no longer lists its faces and tiles as approximated; figures, water and
  ladders are still paint. A first dress of generic tiles: a place's house is a brick mass.
- **A radar and a map.** `gameworld/radar.js`: a round scope in the mission's HUD, the pilot at its middle and ahead at
  the top, the foes awake within its range and the task in hand pinned to its rim; and a map screen (M, and in the
  pause menu), the level's plan north up, drawn on the page from the scene's own colliders and water, with the pilot,
  the task and the foes awake. A foe asleep is on neither. Each task that is a place to go carries its place.
- **Glass and glows no longer show through walls from the eye.** The gun in the hands clears the depth to lie over the
  world, but an opaque material is drawn before every transparent one whatever its order, so the depth was cleared
  under the world's panes, sun patches and hot faces and they were drawn through every wall in front of them (seen in
  a building mission: white bars across the view). The gun's materials are now marked transparent, so it sorts after
  them (`channels/controllable/gunplay-view.js`). The form render's glass shader also takes the page's logarithmic
  depth (`channels/form.js`), which it did not.
- **A mission fills its window.** Its HUD and screens are laid over the window, so its page fills it where its game
  names no screen of its own (a screen holds its own frame); before, the view kept the studio's size beside them.
- **Room to fight in.** A sixth fight dial, `room` (`era/programs.js` `FIGHT`, `program-core.js` `ROOMY`): every storey
  a metre taller, the corridors six metres wide, the lobby with them, the core given more floor so its stair still
  finds its run. `fight: true` asks it, so a mission's building is roomier; a building that asks no fight is as it was.
- **The gun and the hands in the seventh generation.** On a page drawn as form the gun in the hands and the hands
  themselves are lit by the room's own light (`channels/controllable/gunplay-view.js`, the form channel's
  `probe.light`): the live lamps nearest the eye, reaching what is held from further than the relief's few metres, and
  the ambient mostly by its level, each face by the way it looks, a metal's highlight on the gun and a cloth's on the
  hands, through the page's own tone curve. On a painted page they are the paint they were. The hands sort with the
  gun, after the world's glass.
- **An industrial yard, designed.** `arena-map/facility.js` `designFacility`: windows over a geocity's industrial block
  read in turn, the ones that are a yard grown under the laws with what the place is made of kept (the most varied
  first), the one that holds the most answered with where it stands; a mission's city cut names it (`map.at`). The
  reader keeps the block's plan (`read.things`). The default metro's tank farm at 48 m holds all fourteen laws.
- **A mission on a place as the geocube builds it.** `gameworld/mission-site.js`: a base building on its land with its
  yard of containers under floodlights, by night in the rain, a siege walker parked in its hall, all of it the
  geocube's own recipe (`era/stage-buildings.js`, the form render's floods and wet, `parked`); the mission is laid on
  it as it stands, its page's colliders read onto the arena grid (`arena-map/read-colliders.js`: a mass a solid, a thin
  wall an edge wherever no body's width is clear, one ground), the phases placed from that map and the laws said. The
  geocube kind carries a level's page channels (`events`, `audio`, `mission`, `game`, `parked`) and a camera that is
  the page's. The headless gunner walks a site as it walks a building, on the place's colliders. A builder with a
  script (`scripts/spikes/shooter/facility.mjs`), not yet a level's form. A first attempt drew a yard itself, in
  flat-painted pieces under a bake of its own: retired for this, which uses what the geocube already does.
- **Fixed:** the mission's brief read the geocity's tables as it loaded, a ring of imports that failed two geocity
  test files; it reads them when asked.
- **An industrial level.** `levels.<id>: { industrial: true | { use?, depth?, hour?, weather?, wet?, tower?, walker? } }`
  (`gameworld/mission-industrial.js`, its words in `industrial-words.js`): a fenced yard before a base building, at
  sunset on wet ground, a tower to climb in its middle (or a walker parked there, by its word). Its blocks are the
  geocube's, its layout the laws': `arena-map/yard.js` designs a yard piece by piece (a forty-foot container, a
  twenty-foot one, a barrier on a line), keeping a change only when the yard holds its laws no worse and stays one
  ground, the floodlights over its prizes, the building's door its way out. `era/stage-buildings.js` takes a design's
  placements as a yard's words (`depth`, `fence`, `stacks`, `barriers`, `masts`, `towers`, in the plan's metres), the
  height a floor is asked to stand at (`at.floor`), and says a building's seat before it is built (`buildingSeat`), so
  the level is planned with nothing resolved and is a stage as any is. A tower is a railed steel deck a level up, a
  body walking under it, with stairs in steps a body climbs; on the map it is an upper floor with a ramp a stair, two of
  them since the laws ask two ways onto high ground, and the mission's minds and its proof are told its stairs. A
  world's run proves the level; `design_game` offers it beside the first mission. `bounded` asks for a wall or a rail.
  The default yard holds twelve of fourteen laws; built, the headless gunner wins it in 78 s.
- **A wave no longer stalls the industrial level's page.** A mission with floors sent its waves' minds with
  `navLedges`, and a ledge is asked of the page's ground a cell at a time, a ray through the scene each: on a place
  the size of the yard, with a few minds pathing at once, the page spent about a second a frame on it. A mission whose
  upper floors are railed all round says `ledges: false` (the industrial level does) and its minds ask the ground
  nothing. Measured in headless Chrome with every foe awake: script time over fifteen seconds from about 5.5 s to 0.3 s.
- **The industrial level is heard.** Its guns carry the range's own sound (a shot, a reload, a draw, a hit for each,
  chosen by what the weapon is); `industrialManifest`'s `quiet` asks for none.
- **Supplies are a medkit and an ammo crate.** Two forms on the glyph shelf (`medkit`: a first-aid case, a red cross
  on its faces; `ammo-crate`: a drab steel box with a stencil band), and the `supplies` mechanic's decoration wears
  them: health is a medkit where it was a heart, rounds an ammo crate where they were an orb.
- **The range's jump is a body's.** Its feet had a step and a landing and no jump, so a jump played the gait's default
  chirp. Now a jump is the boots pushing off the concrete and the kit shifting, and a landing is both feet and the
  weight under them (`combat/range-sound.js`).
- **The view's hands are the figures' own.** A first person's hands on a gun were boxes: a palm, a finger slab, a
  thumb. They are now the hero's hand (`polygonizer/hero-hand.js`: a palm and five jointed digits), one mesh built at a
  run of curls from open to a fist by the hand's own rule (`equipment/arms/view-hand.js`; `heroHand` takes a `curl`),
  which the page blends between as the hand closes on a grip, a magazine or a knife. A little over life, the cuff no
  wider than the wrist, so the hand reads past its sleeve and the gun.
- **The yard is held by a crew.** An industrial level's foes are dressed as one (`crew`, a faction of the grunts:
  private military where it names none; `false` for the plain stand-in): three of its rank and file, each rolled on its
  own seed, in the hero door's own words (`foes/dress.js`), so a contractor stands in a tactical rig with a carbine in
  hand where a bare figure stood. `missionCast` takes a `crew`; a made figure given still wins.
- **The crew is masked.** An industrial level's crew wears the headgear shelf's masks, a body each in turn (a tactical
  mask, a gas mask, a respirator: `CREW_MASKS`); `masked: false` shows their faces.
- **The yard is heard whole.** Over its guns an industrial level carries effects, an ambient bed and a score
  (`industrialAudio`, on the world's audio channel). Its own events each sound: a task begun, a task met, the mission
  done, the pilot down, a supply taken (the rounds a magazine seated and racked), a wave an alarm; the foley palette
  in the score's key, on the range's mix in the open, so a shot across the yard is quieter than one at the ear. The
  wind's long bed is its air. Its score is two states: a held tension while the yard is crossed, the fight's score in
  on the bar line as hits, downed foes and waves raise the meter, and out as it settles. `score: false` leaves the
  music out.

- **Sounds that belong to a place, and the ground by place.** Two words on a world's audio channel
  (`beats/beats-world.js`, `scene/channels/audio.js`), each opt-in and not a byte where it is absent.
  `audio.emitters: [{ at, cue, every, reach, level? }]`: a cue of the level's own sounded again and again from a point,
  after a wait rolled between two bounds on its own dice, heard by the listener's distance and not past its reach.
  `audio.surfaces: [{ box, step, land? }]`: the cues a step and a landing play where a body's feet stand in a box.
  The industrial level uses both: water drips off the tower's deck and its tallest stacks, the hall hums at its door,
  the fence rattles along its runs, and the tower's deck and stairs ring as steel under a boot.
- **The crew shoulders its guns.** A crew's body carries the hero door's own holds for what it has in its hands (a
  carbine: the aim and the low ready; `CREW_HOLDS`), and the page plays them: a figure with a `fire` clip brings its
  weapon up while its trigger is down and for a breath after a round has gone, standing or on the move, and stands at
  the low ready between (`scene/channels/controllable/index.js`; a hold is a clip played once and held, so it runs on
  its own count and not on the gait's phase). A page whose figures carry no `fire` clip has not a byte of it.
- **The yard's score is electronic.** A half-time drift while the yard is crossed, a driving techno for the fight
  (`club:drift`, `club:drive`), in place of the orchestral cues.
- **A round that lands is seen.** A crew's body flinches when it is hit: the figure library's hit clip, once through,
  over whatever it was doing (`flinch`, beside `fire`). Seen only: the body is not stopped by it.
- **Every shooter wears the new HUD.** The shooter's HUD (the gun in hand as a belt of rounds, the health strip, the
  screen's edge, the scope, the damage ring, the map and the pause) was the mission's alone. A quick shooter's level, a
  deathmatch and the firing range now wear it too, as the mission's page with no mission in it (`shooterHudUi`,
  `mission: { tasks: [], plain: true }`): no order, no briefing, the level's own end; the level's counters stay and
  stand clear of the scope, and the page's own health row and old radar give way. Its principles are set down as the
  baseline for every shooter, and the look over them is the game's: a world's `ui` themes the same parts
  ([docs/mana-ui.md](../../../../docs/mana-ui.md), "The shooter's HUD is the baseline").
- **A bout's arena and a push's cover are the arena laws'.** The two shooter modes that laid their ground by a recipe
  now grow it under the arena's laws, each for its own means (`arena-map/bout.js`). A DEATHMATCH's floor: the arena's
  words still say where the laws start (lanes, or a court), the laws grow it for the bout's sight (close quarters the
  near band, long sightlines every band), and the half they liked best is turned half round onto the other, so every
  panel has its partner; what is the bout's own stays (spawns out of sight, supplies by risk, towers stood first on the
  bare floor with the panels giving way, crates), and where the grown floor leaves one way between spawns the tunnel
  takes the panels beside it and says so; a sparse arena stands ungrown. A QUICK SHOOTER's cover: the fixed wall, crate
  and wall at each post give way to a strip grown for a push, from where a body comes on to the post that holds it, the
  post's cover a sidestep away, its cell and the way on clear, always a way up. The firing range is a measuring room
  and is laid from its guns' numbers as before. Said: growing is slow (a new arena takes seconds, the arena tunnel's
  own tests about a hundred), and cover is counted as crates and grown panels together.
- **The map is of the floor it is fought on.** The map screen and the radar's plan are drawn at the height the pilot
  stands at and boxed on the ground a level says it is fought on (a bout's arena), where they assumed a floor at zero
  and the whole site: a yard on its land and an arena on a hill were blank.
- **A campaign's opening mission.** The first level of a shooter's campaign as a run of places, each a beat of one
  loop and a level of its own (`mission/campaign.js`): the loop and its seven beats set down (cold open, kit check,
  insertion, first contact, push, set piece, run out), each built from what a world already has (a mission's sections,
  the ground the arena's laws grow or read, the level played as a turn). `openingMission` lays the legs as one world's
  levels in order: a staging yard, a street, a building where the kit asks for one, the works. A leg is a checkpoint.
  `design_game` offers it beside the first mission, with its patch
  ([docs/missions.md](../../../../docs/missions.md), "A campaign's opening mission").
- **Orders are spoken, and someone goes with you.** A mission's section carries the line its task is given in, and the
  HUD stands it for a few seconds as the task begins, under who gives it. A mission takes a `squad` (0 to 2): a body
  at the pilot's shoulder on the pilot's side, an escort's mind (it keeps by the pilot and fights whom it sees of the
  other side), the pilot's first gun at a share of its harm; neither harms the other and no task counts it. A
  campaign's legs each ask one.
- **Bigger maps.** Each kind of fighting ground is larger by its own measure: a bout's arena (small, medium and large
  are 32, 44 and 56 m across where they were 26, 36 and 48; one that names none is 44), a push's strip (seven cells
  across and up to ten deep where it was five and eight), a place cut from a town or a city (48 m a side where it
  named none, from 36), the industrial yard (36 m deep), and the campaign's first leg (three rooms in a row where it
  was one court). The grid's cell stays 3 m: a wider cell was tried and broke what is designed on it (a ladder's
  climb, where a mission's phases stand, a fight building's loops), so it is not changed here.
  A bout's arena is grown on twelve cells a side at most: a bigger one is the same grid drawn larger, so its ways are
  wider (near 4 m at 44 m across, 4.7 m at 56 m) and it grows no slower. Long sightlines clear a lane end to end.
- **One radar.** A page wearing the shooter's HUD showed two: the HUD's scope and the page's own round radar, which the
  runtime draws whenever there are other bodies. The HUD's sheet now puts the page's own away on every such page (the
  missions, a quick shooter's level, a deathmatch, the firing range), by the class the runtime gives it.
- **The radar is a minimap.** The shooter HUD's scope is a third larger, reaches 40 m (from 30), and carries the level's
