  plan under its marks (the same plan the map screen draws, from the scene's own colliders), at the scope's scale and
  turned so ahead is up, the pilot at its middle; it fades out before the bezel.
  A grown floor's panels are snapped to 5 cm with their sign kept, so a panel and its turned partner stand on exactly
  opposite places wherever the arena is laid; and the peek law reads a square block (a grown mass) the same way on
  both sides of the middle, where float noise had it lie one way on one side and the other way on the other.

### Stylish action: fights settled in the room, laid into levels

In progress. Built so far, all in the practice door's game room
([docs/game-room.md](../../../../docs/game-room.md), "A fight"):

- **Built: the brief reads the kit** (`gameroom/needs.js` `kitAsks`). Each move asks something of the place and
  says why: a ring, headroom, a run-up, a perch, a gap, the lock. A kit without the move asks nothing.
- **Built: a fight composed** (`gameroom/fight.js`), in four kinds (a duel, a melee, a gallery, a boss fight), from
  new room pieces (a rift, a perch, an urn, a font, a dais), with its ways, rifts and ring named, and held to its
  own laws beside the room's (ring, headroom, run-up, seen, lock, put-back, asked).
- **Built: a fight played.** The room's menu has a Fight choice (`&fight=<kind>`, `&seed=<n>`). Waves are written
  by role or by a foe's id; the foes stand asleep at the rifts, on the perches and on the dais; the hero is armed
  with the kit. The fight begins when the hero steps into the ring, every way is sealed until the last wave is
  down, and a death begins it again.
- **The wave gauntlet takes two more settings**, each adding nothing where it is not said: an arena that waits to
  be walked into (`enter`) and other ways sealed beside the way out (`seals`).
- **Measured:** the scripted floor player wins a duel, a melee and a boss fight on the stand-in bestiary; one who
  does nothing wins none. It does not win the gallery (it has no answer to a shooter on a perch). Nobody has played
  them yet.
- **Built: a game's own fights.** `fights: { <name>: { kind, seed?, waves? } }` keeps a fight on the world by name;
  the room plays it by that name, and `design_game` says what is kept, the laws each loses and whether together
  they answer everything the kit asks. A world that keeps none is offered one of each kind, never laid unasked.
- **Built: the loadout's first part** (`gameworld/carried.js`). `loadout: { slots?: { melee }, start?: { melee,
  sidearm } }` says what the hero carries of the game's weapons: two melee weapons at once unsaid, in the order
  the weapon switch steps through them, and the sidearm or none. It is laid on every level's hero and in the game
  room's fights. A world that writes none carries its whole kit, as before. Choosing it at points in the game is
  not built yet.
- **Built: the switch cancel.** An arsenal says `switch: 'cancel'` (the stylish kit does): the weapon switch
  pressed mid-swing is held to the move's switch point (its cancel, or the end of its blow for a move with none, a
  finisher), the rest of the move is cut with no rest and no cooldown, the next weapon is in hand, a press that was
  waiting opens its string at once, and the string's count carries on. One weapon's string chains into the
  other's. An arsenal that does not say it switches between moves only, as before. Every page that embeds the
  runtime is re-pinned for the lines this adds.
- **Fixed: a swing trail from a weapon that is put away.** A hero that switches to the fist keeps its other figure,
  blade in hand, animated out of sight, and that hidden blade still left its trail. A body that is not drawn leaves
  none now. Every page that carries swing trails has that one line more.
- **Built: a building to fight through** (`era/programs.js` `citadel`). A pathed plan of four rooms in a chain, each
  sized for a fight of a kind as the stylish kit asks it: a gate court (a duel's), the great hall (a melee's), the
  long gallery (a gallery's), the sanctum (a boss fight's), with the route through its doorways. A new law, `fits`,
  says whether any room a level gives holds a fight (its ring, the way round it, the headroom a launch asks). It
  is built on the seventh-generation basis: the ashlar kit (`gothic-ashlar`), read in `gen-7`.
- **Built: a level's tasks** (`gameworld/tasks.js`). A building level says its fights in order,
  `goal: { tasks: [{ fight, at }] }`, each a fight the world keeps, laid in a room: composed on the square the room
  holds, turned to the doorway the hero comes in by, its pieces standing as the stage's props (new pieces: a pillar,
  a perch, an urn, a font, a dais), its foes asleep until their wave. A fight begins when the hero steps into its
  ring and seals its own room's doorways until its last wave is down; a death begins that fight again at its
  doorway; the last one down ends the level. The wave gauntlet takes an arena's own `seals` and `start` for it, and
  arms the next entered arena at the clear.
- **Built: the action game's first level** (`gameworld/action-first-level.js`): the citadel with a duel, a melee, a
  gallery fight and a boss, against zombies and armed skeletons (the slow dead, the armed skeleton, the archer, the
  armoured dead, the knight).
- **Measured:** the scripted floor player walks the citadel's rooms in order and wins all four fights; one who does
  nothing wins nothing. The scripted player now walks a level that ends on its fights point by point. Nobody has
  played it. Not yet: the task said on the HUD.
- **Made through `design_game`:** the first level as a whole game, Fallen Angel, with made figures: Lucien on the
  realistic body (long dark hair, a long dark coat), the five undead, the citadel, the game; the recipe and how
  to rebuild it are in [docs/examples/fallen-angel](../../../../docs/examples/fallen-angel/README.md). The door's
  own check played it: the floor player won, one who does nothing did not.
- **Built: a fourth sword art, `wild`** (`polygonizer/hero-swing-body.js`): a brawler with a blade. The anime
  sword's reach with none of its composure: the hips spun until the back is to the target, the weight and the off
  arm thrown furthest, a taller, looser, longer stance, the anticipation and the finish held least, the cut
  fastest. Held to the laws every art keeps (the legs reach, the blade clear of the head and the floor). Lucien's
  kit is Fallen Angel's swung in it.
- **Fallen Angel in the seventh generation:** its citadel is dressed by a gothic night cube read in `gen-7` on the
  ashlar bones, and Lucien's coat is pale so he reads against the dark.
- **Built: the style meter's runtime** (`worlds/controllable/style.js`, a game's `styleMeter`). How well the hero
  fights, read off the world each step: it rises on blows landed, more for a move not just used, a blow in the
  air, a launch, a switch mid-string, a parry and a foe felled; it falls with time once nothing lands and drops a
  whole tier on a hit taken. Tiers are letters (D to S) unless the game says its own words. `styleMeter: 'auto'`
  lays it on a game whose feel is the stylish template; a game that writes none carries none, and its pages keep
  every byte. The page says where it stands (`window.__mojStyle`), and the scripted player's readout says the tier
  it peaked at and its longest combo.
- **Built: the style meter on the HUD** (`game/hud-mana.js`, the page's HUD host). A level that carries the meter
  draws it at the right on the game UI runtime, in the game's look: the tier's name and, under it, the combo's count
  while there is one; it stands only while there is style to show. Such a level's own rows are drawn there with it,
  whether or not the world writes a `ui`. A level with no meter keeps every byte of its HUD.
- **A principle: a stylish action game's HUD draws no box.** What stands on the screen is letters and figures over
  the play, on no plate; what changes is said by effects and motion on them, never by a frame; and nothing is
  explained in words the play shows (a legend row is not drawn; a mark or an arrow says where to go). The level's
  HUD holds to it wherever the meter is carried: every region sits on no plate, the meter is its letter and its
  count alone. Seen on an action hero's page in a headless browser (the letter, the count rising blow by blow);
  nobody has played it.
- **Built: the meter's motion** (the HUD host, only on a page whose level carries the meter). The tier's letter fills
  from its foot as the tier is climbed; a tier gained slams it in, a tier lost shakes it; the top tier glows. The
  combo's count is struck by each blow and grows heavier as the combo runs. In the theme's colours and display face,
  and still for a player who asks for less motion. Seen in a headless browser at three tiers; nobody has played it.
- **Built: the rank on a level's results** (`game/rank.js`, a level's `game.rank`). A level of a game that carries
  the meter is ranked as it is won: one letter of the meter's own tiers, the mean of three marks (the time against a
  par, the highest tier reached, the hits taken). Its figures (the time, the style earned, the longest combo) join
  the level's kept numbers, so the results screen shows them and the play shell keeps each one's best. The par is
  counted on paper from the level's tasks (a fight's walk in, and each of its foes); a level with no tasks is
  ranked on style and how clean it was alone. A level that is not ranked keeps every byte. Seen on a page ended in a
  headless browser (its result carried the rank and the three figures). Not yet: the par a level writes itself,
  the best rank kept as a letter.
- **Built: the immersive UI on the game's screens** (`game/immersive-ui.js`, a game's `ui.immersive`). A game that
  carries the style meter has its title, pause and results drawn on the game UI runtime with no box, whether or
  not it writes a `ui`: a window, a banner and the legend sit on no plate and in no frame, no veil is laid over the
  play behind a screen, and what is chosen is marked by its arrow alone. The letters carry the look: a light rim
  and a light shadow in the theme's own accents (cut one way, lit the other), a soft glow of the same, then the
  dark that keeps them read. A rank is its letter, stamped large, with no caption. The HUD's meter and readouts wear
  the same letters. A game that does not say it keeps every byte. Seen in a headless browser: the results screen
  (the outcome, three figures, the rank's letter, the menu and its arrow, nothing framed) and the meter. Nobody has
  played it; the key chips in the legend still draw their own small frames.
- **Built: the way on, as an arrow** (a level's `manaHud.ways`, the HUD host). Between a level's fights an arrow,
  and no words, points to the next fight's ring: over the place while it is in view, at the screen's edge turned
  toward it while it is not; gone once the hero steps in. It reads the gauntlet's own word for the arena waiting to
  be walked into. A level without it keeps every byte. Seen in a headless browser at the screen's edge, turned to a
  place out of view; the arrow over a place in view was not caught there, and nobody has played it. Not yet: an
  arrow to a level's way out.
- **Lucien's coat redesigned** (Fallen Angel's recipe, `docs/examples/fallen-angel/world.json`). The coat's body to the
  hip and its long skirt as drape panels from the waist: two long tails at the back, a panel at each side, so a
  raised knee passes between them where it went through a skirt that was one tube round both legs. The dark top
  painted on the body (a second skin) under it, so there is no shell of it to come through, and the coat at its full
  wearing ease. Read in both canons; the advice left asks for a waist return, declined so the coat clears the body.
- **Lucien dressed over his seams.** Where the coat still shows its joins in play, it is dressed over them: a leather
  harness crossed on the back with small strapped shoulder caps over the shoulder blades, the coat's sleeves rolled
  to the elbow so no cloth crosses its bend, and flared leather gauntlets. Two words new to an outfit card for it:
  an outer layer's `cuff: 'rolled'` (the sleeve's end turned back on itself, a band of its cloth a layer out and a
  shade down) and `hands: '<a glove card>'` (gloves worn from the card, as a word list's glove word is: a game's
  hero, whose clothes are one card, wears gloves so). A card that says neither keeps every byte. Seen on the level in
  a headless browser: the shoulder blades and the elbows covered; the small of the back and the hip hem not yet.
- **Lucien's shoulders, again.** The crossed harness gave way to the coat's own shoulder straps (`epaulettes`) over the
  small caps, and a STOCKING under the coat (`outer.stocking: true`, a word new to an outfit card): a second skin of the
  coat's own colour on the upper arms and the yoke, so what a bent arm opens under the coat's shoulder shows the coat's
  pale and not the dark top. Measured on the body, the arm overhead: the dark top shown at the shoulders down by three
  quarters. Found on the level: the sawtooth left is the page's, not the cloth's. A hero is drawn there as rigid parts,
  each vertex carried by its one strongest bone, so at every joint the layers step past each other in teeth; the
  fauna are drawn as one skin where it holds, a hero not yet.
- **A realistic body keeps the realistic head.** A game in the western tradition drew its hero with the landmark head
  even on the realistic body, whose own head is the realistic one. Now a hero on the realistic form wears it,
  with a face (the world's seed unless the head page writes one, so the hair grows: the realistic head grows its
  hair from a face). The head page takes the face's `skin` too (its beard, the hair's colour on the brows). Lucien:
  the realistic head, a western face, clean-shaven, light-brown hair cut to the jaw (`angled`), the face clear.
- **Built: a hero drawn as one skin** (realistic laws 17, the realistic body's doc, "One skin on the page"). A realistic
  hero minted under them is drawn on the page as skinned parts on one skeleton, every corner carried by its own bones,
  keeping its paint, normals, face and light; the page's bank keeps its weights. The sawtooth where the cloth's layers
  met at a joint is gone from Lucien at rest and in a swing (seen in a headless browser on Fallen Angel's level). A
  hero minted before, and every page without such a hero, byte for byte as it was. Its page carries the weights, a byte
  each: Fallen Angel's export went from 39.6 MB to 48.6 MB.
- **Built: the transformation seen.** Transformed by the Halo Meter, the hero grows a pair of black angel's wings on
  his back behind the coat (feathers in rows along each arm, unfolding as it begins and beating slowly while it lasts),
  a golden halo stands tilted just over his head, his hair turns white and his skin dark grey. The hair and the skin
  are told apart by marks the level asks of the piloted hero's figure (`packLayeredRig` `marks`: each corner its
  triangle's class), and, where a realistic head's hair is painted into its skin, by the hair's own colour on the
  page. Only a game whose meter carries a halo; every other page as it was. Seen on Fallen Angel's level in a
  headless browser; nobody has played it.
- **Fixed: a coat's shoulders under a raised arm** (realistic laws 17, the realistic body's doc, "The correctives").
  The tailor's cloth now carries the skin's correctives: each of its points moves as the skin nearest it moves. A
  raised arm had pushed the shoulder's skin out through the coat (the marks on the shoulder blades, the deltoid
  showing). Measured: of what the coat covers at rest, an arm raised overhead now shows under half. A hero minted under
  laws 16 or before keeps its bytes. Left: the bare forearm at a bent elbow, a little.
- **Built: the Halo Meter** (`worlds/controllable/style.js`, a meter's `halo`). The power a stylish hero builds by
  fighting, in stocks: blows landed fill it (more in the air), a hit taken fills it a little; it does not fall
  while it is not spent. The stylish template's meter carries one (`styleMeter: 'auto'`); a meter that does not say
  it has none, and its pages keep every byte.
- **Built: the transformation the Halo Meter buys.** With the stocks it takes full (three unless said), the transform
  press (B, a pad's left stick) transforms the hero: its blows hit harder and it runs faster while the meter drains,
  its own health heals, and it ends when the meter runs dry or on a second press, everything given back. While it
  lasts the meter fills no further. It is seen: a ring of light over the hero's head and its light on the hero, a
  burst as it begins; the HUD says it without a word (the meter breathes when it is ready, the figure glows while
  it lasts). Measured on the runtime and seen on Fallen Angel's level in a headless browser (the meter full, B held,
  the ring over Lucien's head). Not yet: the level's own health (the fights' row on the bus) is not healed by it,
  and no new body, moves or sound come with it. Nobody has played it.
- **Built: the vitals** (the HUD host; a meter's `vitals: { look, hp, halo }`). The health and the Halo Meter
  drawn as one figure, no box: a crest at their root, each bar drawn at its share of the length it reaches by the
  game's end (the health twice its start unless said, ten stocks), so a short bar at the start reads as composed as
  a long one at the end; one end cap at any length and one rhythm of stocks however many. A hit's chip is held a
  moment, then drains. The sprint rides as a hairline over the health. Three looks for how the forms answer:
  `overlap` (one slant, the gauge riding over the health's lower edge, both under the crest), `contrast` (the
  health a thin pointed blade, the gauge heavy blocks, the crest round), `echo` (one form twice, the gauge a step in
  and down). Lit as the letters are. Seen in a headless browser at a game's start, mid-hit, late and fully grown,
  each look; nobody has played it.
- **Fallen Angel remade with all of it**, through `design_game`, and its level's own page seen in a headless
  browser: Lucien in the gate court with the health bar, the weapon's count and the meter (its letter and its
  count) standing over the play on no plate. What that showed, and what was put right: the wave's banner and the
  cleared toast are not drawn on an immersive HUD (passing words; the banner's figures were never filled in either),
  the page's own weapon panel loses its plate there, and the letters are light whatever ink the theme's plates
  were written in (the world's palette had made them dark on a dark hall). The door's check played it again: the
  floor player won in 122 s, all 18 foes down; one who does nothing did not. Nobody has played it.
- **A building level has its action hero.** A world played under the orbit camera with a hero that strikes now
  gets, in a building as on a trail, the orbit that locks on, movement in the camera's frame and its sheathed
  twin, so the fist is in its hands and the weapon switch has two weapons to switch between. Before, a building
  level's hero carried the blade alone.
- A prop's surface a kit does not carry is painted in the kit's nearest of its own (a pillar in a gothic hall is its
  pilasters' stone); a kit that carries the surface reads as it did.
- Not yet: urns that pay and fonts that heal in play, a fight approved on its own or edited piece by piece, and
  everything below.

What the theme will hold:

- **The room settles the fight.** The practice door's game room reads the hero's kit: a launcher asks for
  headroom, a pack of foes for open floor, a dashing thrust for a run-up, the pistols for a foe out of the blade's
  reach. New room pieces answer them (a place waves come in, a high perch, an urn that breaks and pays, a font
  that heals, a boss's dais), new kinds of fight are composed from them (a duel, a melee, a gallery, a boss
  fight), and the room laws check each. A fight is played there with its waves and its ways sealed, and one the
  creator approves is kept on the world by name.
- **The loadout.** What the hero carries is chosen from the game's weapons: melee weapons switched in play, a
  switch chaining one weapon's string into the other's, the choice made at points in the game (before a level, at a
  rest between fights, when a weapon is earned).
- **Levels stay the geocube's.** A level's fights are laid by the same rules into a building's rooms (a dungeon,
  sealed at its doorways) and onto a trail's ground, in order, the task said on the HUD, a boss in the goal room.
- **Style.** A meter in play that rewards varied strings, the air and a clean run, and a rank on a level's
  results, its best kept.
- **From a sentence.** A stylish action game asked for in a sentence gets its kit, its set-up and a first level:
  an approach that teaches the string on one foe, then a dungeon that tests it.
- **A bigger dungeon.** A walled-core dungeon's fights grow heavier with depth, and its gates are played.
- **Built: the transformation mends the level, and its ready moment.** A level that keeps its own health on the bus is
  mended while the hero is transformed (`halo:heal`, the whole points healed, added up to the level's starting health;
  `game/level-synth.js`), as his own body's health already was. The bus hears `halo:ready`, `halo:on` and `halo:off`,
  and the HUD marks the instant the gauge comes full once (a ring off the vitals' crest, the gauge struck white) before
  it breathes. A level without the Halo Meter, or with no health of its own, gains no rule.
- **Built: tenebrae, a room's shade asked.** A stage asks its `shade` (0.02 to 0.6, a geocube's `light.shade`): the
  share of the light a surface turned from every lamp keeps, asked of the form render's solve (`era/stage.js`,
  `form/room-light.js`, which now says the contrast its paint would take, `own`), so its shade falls to black and its
  lamps light pools. Its air is lit as its shade is (the fog and the void darkened with it), and its figures, drawn
  unlit, take the room's light where they stand (`scene/channels/form.js` `lightAt`, the controllable channel's room
  light): a body walks out of the torchlight into the dark. A grade word, `tenebrae`, joins the grades. Fallen Angel's
  citadel is lit so. A room that asks none, and every other page, as it was. Machine gate only: seen in headless
  shots, nobody has played it.
- **Built: the citadel raised.** Fallen Angel's citadel takes the height its seventh-generation kit was drawn for
  (`building.rooms`: the gate court 10 m, the gallery 14 m, the great hall 16 m, the sanctum 18 m, from 7 m and
  10.5 m). The law checks (`era/law-checks.js`) fold a building's faces for its crown and its darkest corner instead
  of spreading them into one call, which overflowed the stack on a stage this size.
- **Built: the chase sees a tall room.** The follow camera takes `tall: { rooms, from?, span?, back?, rise?, look? }`
  (`worlds/controllable/rules-basic.js`): standing in a room over `from` (7 m), it eases back and up and lifts its look,
  by how far the ceiling stands over it, never through the ceiling. A building level played with the action orbit
  asks for it (`tall: true`, `gameworld/levels.js`); the page fills in the stage's rooms over the threshold
  (`worlds/world-scene.js`), and a building with none so tall keeps its page as it was.
- **Built: the figures lit and shadowed by the room.** In a room that asks its shade, a body is no longer tinted by
  one number: each surface is lit as the room is (the ambient, the six lamps nearest the pilot each by its falloff and
  how the surface turns to it, a cold rim where it turns from the eye), on its own material, so a body has a lit side,
  a shade side and an edge against the dark. And each throws its shadows on the floor it stands on: from the two lamps
  that light it most, its silhouette laid flat away from each flame, as dark as that lamp's share of its light and
  fading with its length, and a dark at its feet; one plane each pixel darkens once (the floor never moves: the
  projection is the shadow). The form probe hands the lamps over (`__mojForm.lit`). Walls take no actor shadow yet.
- **Fallen Angel's citadel lifted.** With the figures lit and shadowed by its lamps, the room no longer has to be as
  dark to read: its shade keeps a little over a third of the torches' light (`shade: 0.38`, from 0.06), and its grade is
  `tenebrae` with the vignette eased and a quarter stop more exposure.
- **A body's shade kept deeper than the room's.** A body lit by the room takes a share of its fill (a third), not the
  whole: the room can be lit to be read and its cast still modelled hard by the lamps, a lit side against a dark one.
- **Built: a room's light designed.** A stage's `plot: { <room>: { torches?, fill?, key?, lead? } }` (a building's
  `plot`, carried to its stage) lights a room by design rather than by the kit's rhythm: how many of its wall torches it
  keeps, spread round it (the rest taken down, fixture and all); what each gives; the gain on what hangs over its floor
  (the candle rings: its key, a pool over the fight); and its way on, the doorway on the shortest way to the building's
  goal, framed by a brighter pair of torches. The form render's bake is solved against its median lamp, so a plot's
  contrast is its lamps' strengths against each other. Fallen Angel's great hall is lit so; its other rooms keep the
  rhythm. A room the plot names none of, and every stage without one, as it was.
- **Built: variety in a room's light.** A plot's room takes `vary` (each flame its own strength and colour, from an
  ember's low red to a bright one's, by where it hangs) and `cold` (a moonlit lancet high on the wall facing its way in,
  its slit drawn and its cold light falling into the room: a second colour with a cause). A toned room solved for a plot
  keeps its lamps' hues against its reference lamp (`form/room-light.js` `hued`: the median lamp neutral, so its ramps
  stand), so an ember and a moon read as such; every other toned room's lamps stay without hue. Fallen Angel's four
  rooms each take their own.
- **Built: a weapon held as its own item, and Fallen Angel's bo.** An arsenal's weapon takes `held` (an item's build
  words: a staff, a spear): the run mints a hero of its own for it (`hero-held-<weapon>`, the sheathed hero with the
  item in its right hand, the blade on the back), the level names it (`combat.held`), the runtime shows it in combat
  while that weapon is up and the sheathed hero out of it (the item manifested, never holstered), and its moves are baked
  on that hero. Fallen Angel's second weapon is a bo in the fist's place: two wide sweeps and a spin, a poke, and a string
  that ends on the heavy in a ground slam all round with a toppling knockback.
- **A coat's storm flap** (an outer layer's `stormFlap: true`): a layer of the coat's own cloth hung from the yoke over
  its upper back to below the shoulder blades, the trunk's alone so an arm swings clear, its hem free and standing proud
  of the coat behind it, toned a shade down (`Flap`) so its edge reads on the back. Lucien's coat is now one coat from
  the shoulders to the knee, the back the sides' length and flared evenly round the hips (`hem: 'knee'`, `cut: 'aline'`,
  the tails and panels gone), with the flap over its back.
- **The posed coat** (an open coat's `posed: true`, on the realistic body): the long open coat that fights, by the
  compromise action games made for it. Its skirt is split at the back from the hip into two halves meeting at the vent
  (`body-relational-jacket.js` `ventBack`), each hung on three hinges at the hip (front, side, back) carried by the
  pelvis, not the thighs; every clip sets them by its family (`polygonizer/coat-poses.js`): standing, at rest, the coat
  open over the thighs, its fronts turning back from the hips so no cloth lies on a leg; walking, behind the hips, its
  fronts swept round past the sides so the legs stride through; running, streaming back behind the legs and lifted off
  them; in
  action (a strike, a guard), open at the back from the hip, the halves hung behind and beside the legs, their hems
  kicked out a little; in the air or a whirl (a jump, a spin, the slam), flared, each half swung out and up. A posed coat
  is cut away below the hip (each skirt ring opened to just short of its side seam: tails at the sides and the back,
  never cloth over the front of a leg), worn wide open above it, its back hung straight from the shoulder blades past the seat (the small of the back bridged, no
  bump over the seat), and its hem's lining is hinged as the hem it is sewn to. The hinges ride the pose's `flow`, so a turn
  of the hips carries them and the page's blend between clips blends the coat. Absent, the coat, its rig and its clips
  as they were. Lucien's coat is posed, to mid-calf, and his build a V: shoulders broad, waist and hips narrow, legs
  long, lean and defined (the body's `tune` and `physique`).
- **The figures' shadows unified with the room's.** A body in a room that asks its shade threw two black shadows, one
  from each of the two lamps lighting it most, as dark in a lit room as in a dark one and hard at every polygon of its
  silhouette. It now throws one, as the room's own are: from its key lamp, as dark as the share of the light there that
  lamp gives (the light it takes away: deep under a lone torch, faint in a lit room), its edge a penumbra (laid from
  points of the flame a little apart, each copy darkening a part); the dark at its feet by the same share, its own.
- **A stylish hero parries, with no shield.** A drawn weapon's guard defaulted to the shield's pose with a shield on the
  off arm, so a stylish hero guarding (Shift) showed a round shield. A weapon's guard takes `parry` (`combos.js`: the
  shield's pose, the off forearm braced, no shield), and the stylish template's sword parries.
- **A sealed doorway is a barrier.** The seals a fight raises on its room's ways (`game/wave-gauntlet.js`) were drawn as
  the bus's marker, a red sphere half sunk in the floor at the doorway. A seal now knows its doorway's facing (the way
  back into the room) and is drawn across it as a veil of its colour, glowing from the floor and fading up, breathing
  (`scene/channels/events.js`; the event bus keeps an entity's `facing`, `worlds/event-bus.js`); a marker without one is
  its sphere, as before.
- **A blow that meets a blade or a guard only clangs** (an arsenal's `clang: true`, the stylish template's: `combos.js`,
  laid as the hero's `rule.clang`, `arsenal.js`). Met blades no longer lock the pair face to face: they ring (a spark at
  the cross) and the blow lands, either's swing going on, since a foe mid-swing is not defending; a guard up before the
  hero only blocks with the clang, never parries, so the string is never broken (`worlds/controllable/combat-melee.js`).
  Without it, the clash as before.
- **A guard never struck comes down when let go** (`worlds/controllable/combat-melee.js` stepGuard): its blockstun is
  unset until its first block, and the guard waited on it, so a guard raised and let go before any blow stayed up, the
  body held still under it. The citadel's playthrough found it: its player raised the guard against a skeleton's string
  and stood held after the fall back to the way on.
- **A stylish hero runs in combat with nothing held** (`combat.run`, laid on a stylish game's action hero,
  `gameworld/levels.js`): in combat a hero walked at the combat pace unless the trigger was held; the trigger is now its
  sprint, never its run (`worlds/controllable/rules-platform.js`).
- **Face strands** (`face-strands`, a realistic groom's move: `epidermis/dermal-hair.js`): a loose strand let down at
  each temple, falling before the ear to the cheek, claimed before a ponytail's tie gathers the rest; Lucien's bangs.

### The stylish-action starter: a game of one's own from the rail

- **Built: a stylish rail lays its starter** (`gameworld/pitch-start.js`, by `'action'`). Locking a stylish rail's pitch
  (`rail: { from: 'fallen-angel', locked: true }`) lays, beside its genre's reading, the citadel fought room by room as
  its first level (`action-first-level.js` `actionStarter`: the undead cast, the four fights, a task a room), the rail's
  template kit (`arsenal: { from }`), its style meter (`styleMeter: 'auto'`, the Halo Meter with it), the orbit camera,
  and a look (`CITADEL_LOOK`: the rooms raised to the heights the ashlar kit was drawn for, each room's light designed,
  the gothic night read in the seventh generation with its shade deep, the tenebrae grade). Each a default the creator
  changes by name; every key they write wins. Before, the rail laid a generic composed level, and the citadel's first
  level had no caller. Other rails lay as they did.
- **The meter offered.** design_game's readout offers a `styleMeter` step to a stylish feel's game that writes none
  (written, never laid).
- **Taught: the stylish game's card** (`gameworld-stylish`, pointed to by the rail's card and the meter's step): what
  the starter lays and every word that changes it, the kit's moves and combos, a second weapon in the hand (`held`),
  knockback, the meter and the Halo, the vitals, a room's heights and light (`plot`, `shade`, `grade`), and the coat that
  fights (`posed`, `stormFlap`); the worked example named as one to read, never to copy.
- **Built: the weapon shelf** (`gameworld/weapon-shelf.js`). Second weapons as rows a game names in its kit,
  `weapons: [{ shelf: '<row>', …edits }]`: the bo, the spear, the scythe, the hammer and the greatsword, each its held
  item (manifested in the hand while it is up, the blade on the back), its reach and weight, its moves and its strings
  (sweeps and a slam all round, thrusts and a launching rise, reaping arcs, toppling blows and a quake, committed cuts),
  any field written laid over the row's as an edit is. A new weapon is a row first.
- **Built: light moods** (`action-first-level.js` `LIGHT_MOODS`). A building level's light as one word, written as its
  rooms' `plot`, its cube's `light.shade` and the world's `grade`: tenebrae (fire in the dark, the starter's), moonlit,
  hellfire, cathedral. design_game's readout offers a stylish game's first building level each mood as a patch (a `mood`
  step), the creator's pick, then theirs word by word.
- **Built: the duelist** (`outfit/styles.js`, `ACTION_OUTFITS`). The character action wardrobe's card: the long coat that
  fights (to mid-calf, open, cut away in front below the hip, its tails set by the pose, a flap over the back) over close
  dark clothes and boots. The stylish starter dresses its hero in it, on the realistic body (where the coat is cut away
  and moves with the pose; on another body it is a long open coat), the composer's cast, hair and colours kept.
- **Fixed: a hero remade onto another body keeps nothing of its old head.** A hero stored with the anime head and remade
  on the realistic body (a stylish starter's, or any) carried its anime cast (`animeStyle`) and its anime face's words
  over, and the hero door refused both. The cast is kept only while the order keeps the anime head (`hero-mint.js`), and
  the face never from a hero that had the anime head (`layered.js` `withRolledFace`).
- **Built: the action level plans** (`gameworld/action-levels.js`). Where a stylish game's level is fought, as rows: the
  citadel, a cathedral (one long tall nave fought down its length), catacombs (tight, low and dark), a keep (its solar
  and treasury up the stair), a tower (a fight a floor to the lookout) and a jungle temple. Each is a building's use from
  the era's programs with its fight rooms sized for their fights, the fight each room holds in order, its kit and cube,
  and its light mood; every one lays each fight in its room by the game room's laws and assembles lit (a deep sweep).
  The stylish starter lays the plan its pitch's words name (a cathedral, catacombs, a tower; else the citadel), and the
  readout offers a stylish game's level each other plan as a patch (a `place` step), so a game's levels need not all
  be the same place. The card teaches the plans and the sizes a fight asks (a melee 18 m a side, a boss 22, a launch 6 m
  of headroom).
- **Fixed: a storeyed building's rooms' light.** A stage with storeys and a `plot` lit each storey with the whole plot,
  and refused a room upstairs as one it did not have; each storey now takes its own rooms' (`era/storeys.js`).
- **Said: a step the run finds taken.** A row at a step's ref the run has no record of making is kept as it is
  ('taken'), and was said only in the run's log: a pass cut off between a mint's row and its record (a hero refused
  mid-mint) left Reaper Knight's sheathed hero the old anime one while the rest were remade realistic, unseen. The
  readout now advises each such step by name, with the way to remake it (`force: true`).

### From an idea to a first level: how a game is started

- **A new visitor is offered four ways to start.** When someone opens the studio with nothing in mind yet, the agent
  now offers to make a character, design a game, design an object or make a 3D exhibit. Someone who arrives knowing
  what they want is taken straight there.
- **A game starts from what you bring.** Choose a game and the agent asks whether you have drawings, plans or
  documents to turn into the game's plan. It uses what they say, sets aside what it cannot place, and asks only about
  what is still missing.
- **The first session aims at a first level, and you decide whether it is the game.** The studio checks the level
  itself (it loads, it can be won); you approve it by playing it. The studio's guidance to the agent now says plainly that
  the work of a first session runs from the idea to its first level: who is in it, what the player does again and
  again, the level built, how it feels, and a game that loads it and leads to the next one. Most games are made of
  levels played this way; an open world is made differently, and the guidance says so.
- **What you brought is kept on the game.** When a game is started the agent is now asked, once, what you brought.
  Each drawing, map, document, piece of lore or set of rules is recorded with what it says and where it went, or why
  it has no place yet; nothing is quietly dropped. The game then says which of its first decisions your material
  already answered and which are still open, so you are not asked again what a document already said. Bringing
  nothing is an answer too. A quick one-level game and a game made from one sentence are not asked.
- **A book of monsters becomes the game's enemies.** Hand over the creatures of a setting (each one's element and
  the part it plays: the bulk, a quick threat, a tougher test, the boss) and a party role-playing game now fights
  them: what each is weak to and resists, how strong each is, which groups are met in what order, and the boss last.
  Anything you write yourself wins over what was worked out for you, and the game says which parts were worked out
  so you can make them your own. Each creature also stands on the map as a creature: a body by the part it plays
  (the bulk a small beast, a quick threat one that flies, a tougher test a big one, the boss the biggest), changed by
  its element, so a fire one and a frost one are told apart at a glance; give any of them your own look and yours is
  used. An action game's enemies cannot carry elements yet.
- **A school of techniques becomes a class your party can be in.** Name a school, its element and what each technique
  does (a bolt, a storm, an elemental blade, a ward, a rallying surge, a mend, a hex, a weakening) and a party
  role-playing game now has it as a class beside its own: each technique a skill, learned as the class ranks up or
  bought after the ones it builds on, stronger and costlier the deeper it sits. Say nothing of the order and they are
  learned one rank after another as you wrote them; the game says so, so you can set your own.
- **A producer beside the director.** The agent's guidance now names three seats on a game: the director decides,
  the assistant director holds each piece of work to what was asked, and the producer runs the work (what was
  brought, what is open, what is next). The producer never chooses between two looks: what is unclear is listed and
  asked.

### Beat-em-ups and run & guns: two new games you can ask for

- **Ask for a beat-em-up and you get one to play.** A street seen from the side, and wave after wave of its crowd
  coming at your hero, fought hand to hand: you line up across the street to land a blow. One to four players on one
  screen. Clear the last wave and the level is won; fall too many times and it is lost. You can say how many
  players, how many falls are allowed, which waves come (who is in each and how they arrive), the look, and whether
  your heroes carry their own weapons.
- **Ask for a run & gun and you get the same street fought with guns.** It is the same kind of game with a different
  way of hitting: rounds that fly and can be stepped off or rolled through, grenades, and a crowd that shoots back
  after a warning. You can say which guns your heroes carry.
- **Your heroes are characters, made for the game.** Each player's hero is rolled and made as a character, the way
  a fighting game's fighters are, and drawn in its own body on the street. You can describe them, or bring ones you
  have already made.
- **The crowd is your game's own cast.** Say who the enemies of your game are (a street gang, goblins, a rival
  school and its boss) and they are who comes down the street. You write each wave by the part someone plays (the
  rank and file, a shooter, a tougher one, the boss) or by name, and each enemy fights the way it is: a big one
  grabs and throws, a quick one cuts and runs, a shooter keeps its distance. Enemies that are people are made as
  characters and drawn in their own bodies. In a run & gun everyone on the street carries a gun.
- **You design the street.** Say how far it runs, where it holds your players and who waits at the end. It opens
  on a quiet stretch where nothing comes, so the controls can be learned. Then come its stops: at each one the view
  holds until everyone who came there has fallen, then the street opens again. At the end is the boss, with
  whoever stands with it. Beating the last of them wins the level. The same street works for a beat-em-up and a
  run & gun.
- **The studio says what a street is missing, and builds it anyway.** A street with no boss, or a stop that meets
  fewer enemies than the one before it, is pointed out for you to decide on.
- **A street can be a level of the game you are designing.** A game designed page by page (its intent, its
  enemies, its hero) can now say that one of its levels is a street. It is reviewed, built and checked with the
  rest of the game: its enemies are the game's own, made once and used wherever they appear, and the hero is the
  game's hero. A game that has no hero yet is played by a stand-in, and the studio says so.
- **Up to four can play a street.** Say how many play from the start. The seats go to your game's hero and then
  to the companions who join the party, each in their own body, and anyone with a body can drop in on a second
  controller. A seat nobody fills is played by a stand-in, and the studio says how many.
- **A game can have more than one street.** Each is a level; clearing one opens the next, and the game's menus
  (choosing a level, the result, going on to the next) are drawn in the game's own look.
- **The studio warns when the screen is the wrong shape.** A street runs across the screen. A game made for an
  upright phone shows only a sliver of it, and the studio now says so and how to change it.
- **A street shows the game, not the practice room.** While you play a street you see each player's name and
  health, the falls you have left, which stop you are at, the boss's health while it stands, and a banner when a
  stop clears and the street opens again. The practice readouts and the practice settings no longer appear in a
  level.
- **A street is played through before you get it.** When the studio checks your game it now plays each street
  with a simple player that lines up, closes in and attacks (or fires, in a run & gun), and with one that does
  nothing. A street passes when the first can win it and the second cannot. If the simple player loses, the studio
  says where it ran out of falls and what would ease it: more falls, a thinner wave at that stop, or an easier
  boss. It tells you; it does not change your design.
- **The street a game gets by default can be won by one player.** Its boss now fights as a novice. Measured: at the
  usual level one simple player lost at the boss with all three falls gone, while two players won.
- **Ask for one in a sentence.** "A beat em up in a port town" or "a run and gun through a factory" now gives you
  that game: streets for its levels, a hero made for it, a wide screen. Before, the studio answered that these kinds
  of game could not be made yet. A "side-scrolling shooter" is read as a run & gun. A sentence that names a game
  whose feel the studio knows ("a Mega Man style run and gun") still gets that feel, not a street.
- **A first street forgives more.** The street a sentence lays allows five falls. Measured with a hero made from a
  sentence: the simple player lost it at three falls and won it at five.
- **A run & gun now plays like an arcade one.** Soldiers fall to two or three rounds, your hero falls to a
  few hits, the enemy fires sooner and its rounds fly faster, and each stop sends about twice as many, dropping in
  from above and coming out of doors as well as walking in. The street is narrower, so it reads as a side view, and
  you have five falls. This is one word on a street, its tuning, and you can ask for the older, slower fight
  instead. A beat-em-up is unchanged.
- **The tuning is held to what it claims.** The studio's simple player must still win the default street alone,
  while taking hits. Measured: at a weaker hero it lost at the boss with every fall gone, so the hero was set to
  survive one of the boss's blows.
- **Jump over fire, duck under it.** In a run & gun an enemy's round flies at chest height. Jump early enough and
  it passes under you; jump late and you are caught in the air and knocked down. Hold duck (strong and down
  together) and it passes over you, and you can fire back from the crouch, low. Enemies notice: they aim low at a
  ducked player, and the way out of a low round is a jump. Stepping off a round's line still works as before.
- **Ducking is a move, not a hiding place.** Measured on the default street with three kinds of simple player: one
  that only ducks and fires was hit the most, one that jumps incoming rounds was hit the least, and the plain one
  sat between them.
- **A boss can fight in stages.** In a beat-em-up or a run & gun, say how many stages the boss fight has, or
  write each one: the point in its health where the stage begins, how hard it fights from there, what the stage is
  called, and who it calls in to help. As a stage begins the boss cannot be hurt for a moment, a banner names the
  stage, and its bar across the top shows the stages as segments.
- **A game made from a sentence gets a three-stage boss.** It fights harder at each stage and calls two of its
  rank and file in at the second and third. Measured with the simple player: won in a beat-em-up with two of five
  falls, and in a run & gun with three of five.
- **Not yet:** an enemy that is a beast is drawn as a plain jointed figure, and the game says so; only a person's
  body stands on the street today. A game that names no enemies of its own still meets the stock crowd, drawn as
  plain figures on one open screen: that path is kept for testing. The things that lie on a street to pick up or
  break are not laid, and the number of players is set by the game, not chosen on the screen before a level. No person
  has played these: the studio's simple player has, and it does not jump, throw, use a strong blow or a special, so
  it shows a street can be won, not that it is fun.

### Camera: the frame read, framing by words, the named moves, camera styles and the contact sheet

- **The frame read** (`shoot/frame.js`): what each shot of a shoot plan frames, in a cinematographer's words: the
  subject it is about, its shot size by where the frame cuts the figure (extreme close-up to extreme wide, a row each in
  `SIZES`), its headroom, its eyes against the upper third, its lead room against the way it faces, and at each cut a
  jump cut (the same subject within 30° and one size) or a mover's screen direction flipping. The shoot door answers
  with it as `composition`, advice with a fix, never a refusal.
- **Framing by words** (`shoot/framing.js`, the shoot op `frame`): a camera placed from `size`, `angle`, `side`,
  `place`, `lens` and `dutch` on a subject, riding it when it moves; the frame read of the key gives back the words.
- **Named moves** (`shoot/moves.js`, the shoot op `move`, a key's `move`): push in and pull out, the dolly zoom, the
  arc, the crane up and down, the tracking shot (a truck on a still point), the whip pan and the crash zoom, each laid
  as keys framed in words on its subject, so a move on a walker rides it and reads back as its sizes. Framing from
  where a camera stands (`solveFromStand`): a pan and a zoom, the lens the distance asks for.
- **Shake** (`shoot/shake.js`, a camera's `shake`): handheld, steadicam, run and rumble, a style a row, seeded and
  laid over the keyed path by the sampler, so the render, the page's track and the Blender frames shake alike.
- **Camera styles** (`actor/camera-styles.js`, a screenplay's, a film's or a scene's `camera`): how a scene's coverage
  shoots its cuts, a card each: classical (the coverage as it was, byte for byte), verite, planimetric, still, oner,
  kinetic and observational. A card says the opening, what a line, the turn and a move are shot as, the singles' size,
  lens, angle, side and place, the least a framing holds, a reaction beat, a one-camera long take, its shake and the
  director's notes it answers by design. Its shake rides the Blender pack's and the native film's cameras.
- **The contact sheet** (`shoot/contact.js`, `motion/contact-sheet.js`, the shoot door's `contact`): each shot of a
  shoot plan at its start, middle and end, captured on the world's own page and laid a row a shot, the rule of thirds
  over each frame and the frame read under it, one PNG in the world's outcome folder. Seconds where the film takes
  minutes: what an agent looks at before it renders. The skill `/direct` is the director's loop round it: the shots in
  words, the why, the read, the sheet, three rounds of words at most, the eyes gate the person's.
- **A scene's frame and its contact sheet** (`actor/frame-read.js`; a screenplay's `shot.params.contact` with `export:
  'film'`): a scene's coverage read as a shoot plan is, its actors the subjects, rides the screenplay's answer as
  `framing` beside the director's notes; its contact sheet is the film shot in mojulo at each cut's start, middle and
  end. A style's framings are solved in the film's 16:9 frame, its singles say whom they frame, the same actor within a
  size is no cut, a two-shot is framed in words, and a long take's glides are read as on their way.

### Ask for a hooded mage: the character loop knows the wardrobe

- Asking for a character now reaches the ready outfits by name. The hero card the agent is routed to for "a character"
  names the fantasy six (`ranger`, `mage`, `peasant`, `noble`, `cleric`, `rogue`) beside the everyday cards, says that
  any outfit's cloak or robe takes a hood (worn up or down, a point, a depth), and that headgear takes a circlet and two
  hats (`circlet`, `travelerHat`, `wizardHat`). "A hooded mage", "a ranger in a cloak", "a noble with a circlet", "a
  cleric's robe" and "a wizard's hat" are phrasings the card answers (`routing-cards/hero.md`).
- Changing a character you already made reaches the same words: "put a hood on her", "give him a wizard's hat", "dress
  my hero as a rogue" (`routing-cards/revise-character.md`).
- The hero loop's dress and adorn steps teach them: pick a ready card, name each piece's cloth so it hangs and flows,
  set the hood up or down, add headgear, then read back the pieces the body did not wear and look at the cloth on a
  walk frame and the hood from the side (`catalysts/create-hero.md`). Detail and adornment still come last, each
  earning its place.
- The routing fixture carries the new phrasings, and a guard fails if the hero card stops naming a card of the fantasy
  wardrobe or names a headgear word that is not a card.
- Gates: machine (the routing card tests, the changed and critical tiers, both asks minted through the CLI). Eyes: not
  claimed.

### The open city's sound: ambient beats, the street, and a car you hear

- **Ambient beats under the streets** (`cue-sheet.js` `cityScore`, a played city in a game with `music`): the club's
  `chill` (boom-bap with a swing, tape and dust, keys in sevenths and ninths) on the game's one identity, in place of the
  land's orchestral cue; where the law or a faction can come for the player, a chase (`drive`) the level changes to as
  the tension rises (a star, a fight, blows), held while any star is on (the wanted level's calm raises it each second).
- **The street** (`sfx-shelf/beds.js` `city`): horns far off down the blocks, a truck, a dog, a siren somewhere, the wind
  between the towers, sparrows; and under it the city's **traffic far off** (`traffic-hum`, the new `ambience` held family,
  the audio channel's `ambience`), quieter from inside a car.
- **The car's sound design** (`sound-sheet.js` `citySounds`, the audio channel's cab): the door opened as the driver
  reaches it and shut as they sit, the starter cranking and the engine catching a moment later (`car-ignition`); the
  engine through its gears, its **growl under the pedal** (`road-car-load`, silent coasting), its **tyres' roar and the
  wind** by the speed (`road-roar`), their **screech** past their grip in a turn or under hard braking, the **brakes**
  squealing as it stops hard (`brake-squeal`), a **gear** changed up under the pedal; getting out, the engine stopped
  (`car-engine-off`), the door opened and shut. The audio read takes an engine's `drive` (held voices beside it) and a
  level's `ambience`.
- **Fixed**: the city's engine never started. While a car is driven the pilot is the car, which rides nothing: the sound
  now finds the driver as the car's rider.

### The open city's UI, drawn as an open-world game's

The open city's screens worked, but they read as an app. The radar was a square picture in a yellow frame, money was a
boxed "coin 0", and a strip of every key sat along the bottom of the screen at all times. The map, phone, bag and
journal were huge solid-yellow panels over a striped backdrop. They now read as a city game at night. This work is UI
only: nothing about how the city plays has changed.

- **A city look.** A new look, Downtown: near-black glass, white words, a taxi's yellow for what matters and a
  banknote's green for money. Nothing is drawn across the screen, so the city shows through the map, the phone, the bag
  and the journal. A game made as a city game starts from it.
- **The radar** is round, with a rim and a shadow, and fades toward its edge. The opened map shows the city at night
  with water in blue, and names only where to go and where you are (every stop's long label at once was unreadable).
- **Money** is a coin and a large figure, with no box and no word. The bag shows it the same way.
- **Keys appear when they matter.** The strip of keys speaks when what you can do changes (a car in reach, the wheel
  taken, a call on the phone) and steps away after a few seconds.
- **The car's name.** Getting into a car says its name large at the bottom right ("MID SUV"), then it is gone.
- **The objective** is one line with a mark and the distance.
- **The phone is a phone.** It is a handset held at the bottom right, with the city still visible around it. It has the
  hour and the signal along its top, its apps as tabs, and the contacts above the open conversation.

### Driving in a town and a city district

- **A hero can get into a parked car and drive.** In a game whose level is a town or a city district, the cars the
  town already parks are yours to take: walk up to one near where the level starts and press the interact key to get
  in. It is the same model in the same colour that was standing there. You drive it with the usual driving keys, and
  press again when it is nearly stopped to get out beside it and carry on on foot. Nothing has to be asked for.
- **A district with no car near its start has some at the kerb.** A city district keeps its cars in lots that can be
  blocks away, so where none stands within a short walk of the start, up to three cars of the city's own everyday
  fleet are parked at the kerb there.
- **A car stays on the street in a city district.** A driven car no longer climbs a building's raised ground, cars are
  parked only where the road is open from nose to tail, and a level that starts under an elevated highway now starts
  on the street below it rather than up on the highway.
- **Cars are solid to each other and to people.** A car you drive into a parked car stops against it and loses its
  speed instead of passing through, and you can no longer walk through a car on foot.
- **A city's traffic reacts to you.** The traffic already driving a city's main streets now brakes and queues behind
  your car, or behind you on foot, when you are in its lane, and drives on when you leave. Its vehicles are solid:
  drive into one and you stop against it. Cars parked for you at the kerb are kept out of the traffic's lanes.
- **Street paint lies on the road.** On a sloped city street the lane lines, streetcar rails and crosswalk bars used to
  sit level, each piece floating at one end and sunk at the other, so a hill read as a flight of steps. They now lie
  flat on the road's own slope, and every crosswalk sits on the road where it is rather than at its crossing's height.
- **Shops on a hill are entered on the level.** Where a row of walk-in shops in a city stands well above its sloping
  pavement, the pavement is now raised to the shops' floor along the whole front, so each door opens straight onto it
  instead of into a notch cut in a wall. The raised stretch meets the street at its uphill end, and at an end that
  stands above the street it has a ramp down where there is room, or a flight of steps beside it with a landing at
  the top. It is two metres wide, room for two people side by side, and railed wherever its edge stands over the
  street: along the front, across a closed end and down the steps. Rows more than three metres above their pavement
  are left as they were.
- **An errand can be driven: a fare.** In a town or city-district level with cars, an errand's pick-up and hand-in
  now stand well apart along the streets instead of a few steps from each other, and each is reached from the kerb:
  pull up beside it in a car and it counts, without getting out. A single-level world can now carry an errand on a
  town or a district, so a one-fare taxi run (pick up a passenger, drive, set down, get paid) is a game on its own.

### An open city in gen 7: half the page, half the textures, its tiles read again

A town or city exported at `era: 'gen-7'` (the form render: its buildings lit by the sun's bake, each dressed tile a
material with a normal and an ORM beside its paint) was measured against the same city at gen 6, the commuter's story
city: the page was 51.5 MB against 4.8 MB, its textures on the GPU about 226 MB against 101 MB, its draw calls the same
(about 1,300) and its materials nearly double. Almost all of the difference was the dressed tiles' relief: 39 tiles, each
a normal and an ORM at 512, in pairs that were one tile at two seeds.

- **One reading of each tile** (`matte-paint/detail.js` `firstReading`): a town in the form render draws each dressed
  tile at its first seed (`-a`); its second (`-b`), a second seed of the same tile laid by where a face stands, is drawn
  as the first. The page's resampler (`scene/channels/resample.js`) already reads every tile again at seeded shifts, so the
  second seed added nothing the eye keeps, and on this page it doubled every tile's paint, normal and ORM.
- **The resampler kept under the form render** (`scene/channels/form.js`): the form's material took each mesh's paint
  over and dropped the resampler's patch, so on a gen-7 page a wall's tile repeated as it does nowhere else. It now reads
  the tile through the resampler where the parallax landed; the plans shift by whole courses, boards and units, so the
  joints stay where the relief has them. A room in the form render whose tiles carry plans is read the same way.
- **A town's relief at the smaller size** (`worlds/world-scene.js`, `form/room-form.js` `formRoomMaps({ reliefSize })`):
  the relief is drawn only near the eye (`pom` to 8 m, `relief` to 22 m), so a town reads it at `ROOM_MAPS.small` (256)
  outright, once.

Measured on the story city's district at gen 7 (headless Chrome, software GL): the page 51.5 → 25.4 MB (under the 25 MB
per-file note it carried before), the relief 29.8 → 3.7 MB of it, the textures on the GPU about 226 → 126 MB (gen 6:
101), textures 122 → 68, draw calls and triangles unchanged. A frame's time is not measured here: software GL varies by
two times from one frame to the next, so the frame rate on a real GPU is the person's to see. A gen-6 page is as it was.

**What a frame draws, with the shadows and the light kept.** Gen 7's look is its sun (a shadow map over the land, drawn
once), the actors' live shadows, the static world's hour map, the baked sun and sky on every building, the relief near the
eye, tone mapping and contact occlusion; all of it stays. What it drew around them was counted per draw on the same
district (two frames, by shader): about 3,700 draw calls and 7.4 M triangles a frame, against gen 6's 2,200 and 2.5 M.

- **Passers-by culled and one draw each** (`scene/channels/walkers.js`, `WALKER_DRAW`): a walker is drawn only in the
  camera's view within 80 of its own heights, or within 12 all round (where its shadow may fall into view); one unseen
  walks on but is not posed. A blended walker's parts are one mesh (one skin, one material, its bones the material's), so
  a passer-by is one draw and one shadow draw. A capture draws them all, as before. Walkers' draws: about 910 a frame,
  and as many again into the shadow map, to 5 and 6. Every era's page takes this.
- **The occlusion's prepass leaves out what it cannot show** (`scene/channels/creases.js`, `OCCLUSION_FAR`): a mesh wholly
  past 240 reaches of the camera (120 m at the default half metre), where a contact spans under two pixels of the pass,
  is not drawn into it again. Only a page with occlusion alone; the creases' ink and outline read the far.
- **A town's flora** (`form/land-read.js` `TOWN_FLORA`): a geotown's or a metro's lawn draws its blades to 0.4 of the view
  cone's reach (about 12 m), its impression past that; its street trees lay no litter.

The district at gen 7 now: about 950 draw calls and 5.5 M triangles a frame, the walkers 5 of the calls, the grass about
0.6 M triangles (was 1.26 M), the litter none (was 0.28 M), the prepass about 300 calls (was about 940).

### The open city's guns: drawn or put away, and the police armed from the third star

- **A holster** (`rule.holster`, laid on the bare hands' pistol where a city sells rounds: `arsenal.js`): the pistol is
  drawn or put away on R (the weapon cycle) or by number, 1 the hands and 2 the gun. Put away, the click punches and
  the gun fires not at all; drawn, the click fires it at the foe before the hero and swings nothing (Q held too). The
  page's reticle and ammo panel show its rounds. A sidearm with no holster fires on Q as it always did.
- **Armed police** (`law.armed`, the third star unless said, or false): from that star the police come as the tactical
  unit in black, a pistol each (`LAW.gun`, a loadout slot before their blow), firing at the player in sight; their
  rounds are blows on the street's health.

### The open city as a game: its title, continue, and its end

- **A level's own save** (`level-contract.js` `MSG_SAVE`; the level's game block `save: { vars, on }`, opt-in, the game
  channel's): a level that is one long game (a played city with jobs: `levels.js` `CITY_SAVE`) sends what it keeps (the
  jobs' and factions' flags, the bag, standing, a one-off handed in, a mission passed) to the shell as it is earned (a
  job taken or done, a mission passed, a side joined, a gun's rounds bought, a respray), with "Progress saved". The shell
  (`play-shell.js`) keeps the newest in the browser; CONTINUE goes to it and hands it back, the level setting it again
  and raising `resumed` (a mission taken and not passed picks up); START is a new game, what was kept forgotten.
- **A story city's front** (`runner.js` `STORY_FRONT`, a world with missions and no `front` of its own): the title in
  the lower third, CONTINUE (once there is a save), START, OPTIONS and CREDITS; the last mission's win is the end card,
  GAME COMPLETE · THE END, then the credits.

### The open city's shops: a respray and a gun shop

- **A world's `shops`** (`gameworld/shops.js`: `{ respray?: true | { price }, guns?: true | { price, rounds } }`), laid
  on a played district with a bag to pay from and marked on its map.
- **The respray** (`game/shop-mechanics.js` `respray`): a garage at a street junction a drive from the start, clear of the
  parked cars. Driven into with stars and the price, the car comes out a new colour (the cast's `repaint`) and the law
  loses the player (`cleared:wanted`); with no stars, nothing to hide.
- **The gun shop** (`gunshop`): at a shop front a walk from the start; the price buys a box of rounds for the pistol the
  hero carries empty (`arsenal.js` `cityPistol`, the bare hands' sidearm: Q held, it fires at the foe before the hero).
  A sidearm takes `reserve` and `loaded` (a gun carried empty), and a weapon `loaded` (the runtime's).
- **Bare hands strike**: a hero whose moveset is only its fists is armed with them on the page (`held-strike.js`
  `FIST`); before, its clicks swung nothing. A city the law watches, or where guns are sold, has a hero who fights.

### City sound: the open city heard

- **The city has a sound of its own.** A game on the sound sheet (`sound: {}`) hears a played town or district as a
  street: sparrows and birds on the ledges (a new `city` bed, also asked for as street, town or downtown). It has no
  cars in it: car sounds come only from the car you drive. Footsteps, the punches, a crew's shouts and grunts, and the score (`music: {}`) with the fight cue coming
  in as a fight starts all come from what the game already is.
- **The cars are heard, but only at the wheel.** A car's engine rises and falls with the speed of the car you are
  driving, and is silent on foot. A car door sounds as you get in or out, H sounds the horn, and hitting something at
  speed sounds a crash.
- **The jobs are heard.** Taking a job from someone, a call with the next one (two pips, until the shelf has a phone
  ring), a TaskFu task, subscribing, joining a faction, taking a posting, finishing it, a fight starting and going
  down each have a sound.
- **Lighter street people.** Each passer-by is now packed (each corner once, weights a byte each): a person is about
  a quarter of the size, so a street of them costs less than it did before they were cleaned up.
- **Footsteps on a street are a heel's click.** A played town or district is walked on its pavement whatever the rest
  of the world grows, so its steps are a new pavement footstep (a clean click and a knock, barely a scuff) in place of
  the grass rustle it was getting. No footsteps sound while you are in a car (or riding anything); the car's engine
  is what you hear, and it is louder than before. The engine runs only while you are in the car: it starts as you get
  in and stops as you get out, with no idle hum while you walk.
- **You can hear the car.** The car's engine was pitched like a real car's, too low for a laptop's or a phone's
  speaker to play. Cars in the city now have an engine voiced for small speakers (a new road-car engine: its note
  higher, a burble, the tyres' hiss growing with speed), and it changes up through its gears as you pull away instead
  of one long rising whine.

### The open city's story: missions with ways to fail

- **A job told as a story mission** (an errand's `mission`: `{ heat?, clean?, time?, final? }`, and its `name`;
  `game/mission-mechanics.js`): it starts as the job is taken (its name as a banner, a clock when it has time), its goods
  can bring the law's stars (`heat`), its hand-in can ask for none (`clean`: lose the police first), and it fails when
  the player is wasted, busted or out of time: MISSION FAILED, then it starts again a few seconds on. Handed in, MISSION
  PASSED; the story's last (`final`) ends the level, the game won. A contact's missions come one after another by phone.
- **A one-off's hand-in is quiet once done**: coming back to a giver who has had it asks nothing more of it.

### Designing a game: the next question leads, and an early build is a draft

- **The studio asks the next design question instead of pushing to build.** When you are designing a game and
  something is still undecided (what game it is, how long, who the hero is, how it plays, the plan), the agent's
  list of next moves now carries that question. For a game you are designing page by page it comes before the
  build; for a game you asked to be made from a sentence it comes right after it.
- **An early build is a draft, and is said to be.** Building is fast, so the agent can build whenever there is
  something worth showing. A game built while those decisions are still open is no longer announced as complete
  with an offer to share it: it is shown as a draft, the next question is asked, and sharing waits until you ask
  for it. A one-level quick game is unchanged.
- **Designing a game starts as quickly as a one-level game.** Tell the agent you want to design a game and it can
  now begin with nothing written: it answers at once with what to ask you (what you brought, then what game it is,
  how long, who the hero is, how it plays), and builds nothing until there is something to build. Before, a design
  could not begin until a first level had been written.
- **A quick game can grow.** A one-level game made the quick way is still made at once and offered to share as
  before. It now ends with the question that would turn its one level into your game, for when you want to go on.
- **What you brought comes first.** When you hand over drawings, plans or documents, the next question is asked
  before the build even for a game you asked to be made in one go.
- **The studio's guidance to the agent leads with the designed game.** It names designing your game first and the
  one-level path as the choice when one level is all that was asked.
- **The first instructions an agent reads now agree with each other.** The studio's opening guidance, the game
  tool's own description and the game guide all say the same thing: for a game of your own, ask what you brought
  and begin from just a name; for a one-level game you asked for outright, make it at once. Before, one said to ask
  first and another said to make one call, and an agent starting a design had to invent a level to begin.

### Hijack City: the open city's crime game as a rail and a starter for a GTA-like

The open city this branch built (a district of a metro, cars to take, a contact's missions, the law, the shops, the
street's health, the sidearm, crews, the phone's fares, a title, a save and a score) is now a game type an agent can
start a person's own from, named for it and offered by the producer.

- **The rail** `hijack-city` (gameworld/rails.js): Hijack City, an open city crime game; designed; seen in the round;
  its first level a district. Found by a brief's words (a GTA-like, steal cars, a wanted level, police chases).
- **The genre** `open-city-crime` (cosmos/fixtures.js, gameworld/intent.js): the city as a sandbox on foot and at the
  wheel, the law answering what is done in it; makeable today. It joins the tables a genre is read by: the interface's
  look (downtown), the sound shelf's city group, the feel's action flavour, and the sentence door's forms, which lay it as
  a district (gameworld/genre-forms.js).
- **The starter** (gameworld/hijack-city.js): `design_game({ world: { name, rail: { from: 'hijack-city', locked: true } } })`
  lays it whole under the person's own words (gameworld/pitch-start.js, `laid.by: 'hijack-city'`); `HIJACK_GROWS` names
  what is changed first. Built in gen 7 by default.
- **Its card** `gameworld-hijack-city` and the game-design routing card's word for it; [docs/hijack-city.md](../../../../docs/hijack-city.md).
- **The game's interface on the candidate's mana-ui** (merged from 1116-rc): the health in cells under the radar, corners
  on scrims, the rc's pause. The gun's readout stands only while the sidearm is drawn (scene/channels/mana-hud.js), and a
  gun empty with nothing in reserve says "No ammo", not "Reload" (mana-ui kernel.js). A district's level is titled by its
  own name (the pause said "district · district").

### A new game fills its window: no phone frame unless one is named

- `design_game` no longer writes `screen: 'phone'` into a gameworld it starts (`game/screen.js` `NEW_GAME_SCREEN` is
  now none). A new game is framed for no screen and fills the window it is given; a game meant for a phone names it
  (`screen: 'phone'`), as a tablet or a monitor game names theirs. A gameworld already stored with a screen keeps it,
  and a genre form that names its own screen (the endless runner's phone) still does.
- The action RPG's row, whose game fills its window (`screen: 'fill'`), writes that as `screen: null`
  (`gameworld/compose.js`), the world's word for no frame, where it used to leave the key out. Left out, the key read
  as "none named" and took the default, so the game from a sentence stood upright in a strip on a desktop with its
  hearts outside the frame.
- The action RPG's land as the meadow card draws it (a genre hero row's `land`, `hero-rows.js`, laid by
  `gameworld/compose.js`). Its rocks and cliff lips are bare: `hats: false` is now a glyph map's word and a region's
  (`level/grid.js`, `gameworld/world.js`), carried to each tile's stage (`era/isekai.js`). Its sky and air are the
  card's own (`land.sky: 'card'`): the card's dome and haze colour written as the cube's `light.sky`, its thin haze as
  `light.outsideFog`, where the cube's solved sky was a dull blue-grey under nearly three times the haze. The sun
  stays the cube's reference's. Any other genre's world, and a map that says no `hats`, is as it was.
- Gates: machine (the screen, row and design_game tests). Eyes: not claimed.

### An open city

- **A job that can be done again.** An errand can now be a standing job: its hand-in pays every time and no longer
  ends the level, and what it asks for can be picked up again straight after. A taxi fare, a delivery round or any
  repeatable job in a town or city district is one setting on the errand, and the city stays open around it.
- **Any parked car can be taken.** Every car a town or city district parks is now one you can get into and drive,
  wherever it stands, not only the few nearest the start. Vans and trucks from the city's fleets are included; a
  vehicle carrying something on its roof (a taxi's sign, a police light bar) is not yet.
- **A car can be taken out of traffic.** Walk up to a vehicle that is stopped or crawling in a city's traffic and the
  same prompt offers it; press and you are in it, and it is yours to drive. Up to six taken vehicles are kept at once;
  after that the one left standing farthest away is given up for the next.
- **People on the pavements.** A played city district now has pedestrians walking round the blocks near you on their
  pavements, some one way and some the other, following the ground up and down the hills. They are scenery for now:
  they do not react to you or to cars.
- **The people are made the way your hero is.** Each pedestrian is a person from the same character generator as the
  hero, rolled from the game's own seed in its setting, so they share its body, proportions, clothes and palette
  rather than being a separate stock figure. A handful are rolled for a district and shared among everyone walking,
  each at a slightly different height, and each is re-sampled to about a quarter of a played character's detail so a
  street of them stays light.
- **Cars sit on the road.** A car now pitches and leans with the ground under it instead of standing level on a
  slope, both parked and while you drive.
- **The city tells you what to do.** A town or city-district game with cars now opens with a line saying what it is,
  teaches the keys one at a time with your character in hand (walk, get in and out of a car, drive), and then keeps
  one instruction at the top of the screen with an arrow, the distance and a pillar of light where to go: get into
  a car, pick up the job, deliver it. A job that repeats sends you round again; with no job it says the city is open.
- **Your earnings stay on screen.** A repeating job's pay is shown as a running count in the corner, and the key hints
  now mention the car key.
- **Jobs send you across the district, to its own shops.** In a city-district game with cars, an errand's stops now
  stand at the district's shops rather than along the starting street, each chosen far from the start and from the
  others so a job is a drive. A stop you pull up to is at a shop's door; one bought over a counter is at the till
  inside a shop of that kind, so you park and walk in. The on-screen guide names the place ("Buy the gadget in the
  electronics shop", "Deliver the gadget to the gun store") and takes a job with a price in its right order.
- **One-off jobs and repeating jobs share a city.** Where a level has a repeating job, finishing a one-off job pays
  and the level carries on, so a district can hold a quest or two and a standing job at once.
- **Jobs are quests in a journal.** Every errand in a level is now also a quest: press J for the journal, which lists
  each job with its steps ticked as you do them, in the same words the on-screen guide uses. A line appears as a step
  is done and when a quest is complete.
- **The journal and its messages wear the game's look.** In a game with an interface look, the journal and the quest
  messages are drawn by the same interface system as the rest of the game's screens and HUD, instead of a separate
  plain panel. A game without one keeps the journal it had.
- **A map.** A played city now has a map. A small radar sits in the corner showing the streets and blocks around you
  with the way you face at the top, and M opens the full map: the whole place with its blocks, parks and water, your
  position, where to go next, each job's stops, the shops and the cars. V turns it between a straight-down plan, a
