  tilted miniature with the buildings standing up, and a view that follows you; + and - zoom. A key beside it says
  what each icon means. The world pauses while it is open.
- **The map belongs to the game's interface, not to itself.** It is a new part of the game interface system, so it
  takes the game's theme like every other screen and has no colours of its own. What it shows is a setting on the
  game's interface: whether there is a radar and which way up, which views it turns through and which opens first,
  how far the radar sees, whether shops and cars are marked, and which icon stands for each kind of marker.
- **Three new icons**: a car, a shop and a parcel, in every icon style the themes offer.
- **An inventory.** Press I to see what you are carrying: a grid of items, each with its icon and how many you hold,
  and beside the one in focus what it is and which job it is for. Money is counted at the top and has its own tab.
  It lists only what the level's jobs can put in your hands, and pauses the world while open.
- **The inventory is the game's interface too.** It is drawn by the same interface system and theme as the map and
  the journal. Its title and the icon for any item are settings on the game's interface; an item with no icon named
  is drawn by its own word where there is a picture for it, otherwise as money, a person or a parcel.
- **One screen at a time.** The journal, the map and the inventory no longer open on top of one another.
- **Menus name the real keys.** The map, the inventory and the journal now show the keys that work them along the
  bottom (V to change view, + and - to zoom, Q and E for tabs, the key that closes each) instead of internal action
  names.
- **Lighter pages.** A level that has the journal, the map or the inventory alongside its HUD now carries the game
  interface system once instead of once for each, which takes about 0.7 MB off the open-city level page. Levels
  with only a HUD are unchanged.
- **One interface, top to bottom.** In a city game with an interface look, the on-screen guide is now drawn by the
  game interface system too: a compass strip that turns with your view and marks where to go, the instruction with
  its distance under it, each key lesson as key caps with its place in the run, and the opening line and "passenger
  aboard" style messages as cards. It takes the game's theme like the map, the inventory and the journal.
- **Key hints that match what you are doing.** The strip of key words along the bottom is replaced by key caps for
  the keys that work right now: Move and Jump on foot, with Get in when a car is in reach; Drive, Brake, Steer and
  Get out at the wheel; and Map, Bag and Journal throughout.
- **Jobs have a giver and a start.** In a city game each job is now taken from someone: a person standing outside a
  shop near where you begin. Go to them and they say what the job is; only then do its stops work and only then does
  it appear in your journal. The on-screen guide leads you to them first, and an errand can carry the words its
  giver says.
- **The people you work for call you.** Whoever gives you jobs is now a contact: you meet them once, where they stand,
  for the first job. After that they are on your phone (P): what they said, what to do next, each step as you do it,
  what you were paid, and a count by the key when there is something new. Their next job comes as a call when the
  last one is done, so there is no going back to ask. A one-off job is brought back to them to be paid, which is the
  only time you return; a standing job (fares) pays where it ends. Jobs belong to one contact unless an errand names
  its own (`contact`), and each contact is their own person on the street. The phone can be retitled or turned off
  (`ui.phone`) and wears the game's theme like the map and the inventory.
- **TaskFu: jobs from an app, not a person.** The phone has a TaskFu tab. Subscribe to it there and it lists paid
  tasks; take one and it becomes a quest in your journal with its reward, paid where the task ends. Nobody is met
  and nobody is gone back to, so an open world can offer ride-hailing style work with no character standing for it.
  A world's maker puts any job on the app by naming it on the errand (`app: 'taskfu'`; another word is another app,
  with its own tab). Jobs from people and jobs from apps sit side by side: the phone opens on the app when you have
  met no one yet, and on-screen guidance tells you to take the task on your phone.
- **More than one fu in a game.** Tasks carry tags (ride, food, courier) and the phone can have several apps, each
  with its own name, its own tab and the tags it carries (`ui.phone.apps`). A tagged task shows up on every app that
  carries one of its tags, and taking it on one takes it on all. Each app is subscribed to on its own. A game that
  names no apps still has TaskFu, which carries every tag.
- **Factions: the city has sides.** A game's maker writes its factions: a name, a colour, the part of the district
  that is its turf, its rivals, and what its board posts (`factions`). Each has a contact standing on its turf;
  walking up to them joins it, and you are with one faction at a time. Its board is a tab on your phone: your
  standing with it, and the jobs it posts at that standing. A posting is something to do rather than something to
  carry (an act, on a rival's turf when it says so); it is taken on the board, becomes a quest, and pays money and
  standing when done. More standing opens more of the board. Turf shows on the map in each faction's colour, with
  where to join. What actually performs an act is not built yet: a posting completes when its event is raised.
- **Joining a faction is a choice, not an accident.** You join by walking up to a faction's contact only while you
  are with no one, so passing a rival's contact changes nothing. You leave from the phone (the first row of your
  faction's board); your standing is kept. A posting's place is now kept clear of anyone who stands on the street.
- **Fights happen in the city itself.** A faction's posting can be a fight (`act.fight`). The rival faction's crew
  (`crew`: one of your game's own enemies, dressed in its colours) waits out of sight at the posting's place. Arrive
  with the job taken and they appear and come at you, there on the street, with the traffic and the people still
  going. You fight as yourself, with what your character carries. Put them all down and the job is done and paid;
  go down yourself and they are gone, your health is back, you are returned to your own faction's contact, and the
  job is still open. Your health shows while there is a fight to be had.
- **The car no longer wobbles when you get in.** A car tilts to the ground under it, and while driven it was
  measuring its own body as if it were ground. It now ignores itself.
- **Nothing stands in the road of a level you play.** Trees along outskirts streets grow on the pavement by the kerb,
  where before they stood a metre into the carriageway, and any lamp, hydrant, pole, signal, bin, bench or sign found
  on road surface is left out.
- **Fists are the default weapon.** A hero who has to fight and carries nothing fights bare-handed: a jab, a cross,
  a hook and an uppercut on one button. Carrying a blade or a gun still replaces them.
- **An athletic run.** A hero's movement can be called `athletic` (or `bounding`): the legs open wide and a stride
  takes a lot of ground, with a longer flight. It is meant to look fast, not to be measured. Behind it is a new
  `reach` dial for how far a stride goes.
- **Cleaner people on the street.** Passers-by and the people who give you jobs were cut down from the full character
  in a way that broke them into loose pieces at the joints, smeared their colours into flat patches and let the shirt
  under a jacket show through in triangles. They are now cut down as one closed body that bends at the joints, each
  part keeps its own colour (a face, a collar, a scarf stay crisp), and anything a garment covers is left out first,
  so a street of them carries about twice the detail it did for the same cost. A person's shown surface now fits
  whole, so each is drawn exactly as the character was made: faces, eyes, a belt's buckle, a neckline, and nothing
  opens where a sleeve or a belt ends.
- **Jobs are driven.** The person who gives you work now stands a short drive from where you start, not across the
  street, and every stop of a job is a real drive from the one before it: the shop you pick something up from is no
  longer the shop next door to the counter you buy at. Stops are placed in the order you drive them, each the place
  that keeps it far from the last stop, the next fixed one (a shop's counter, the giver's door) and every other stop.
  In the demo city the legs run from about 300 to 550 m.
- **An athletic hero runs further.** A hero whose run is `athletic` (its legs opened wide) now covers the ground its
  longer stride covers: it runs about 60% faster at the same cadence, so its feet still keep pace with the street.
- **Joining a side is your choice, and it comes later.** A faction's contact says nothing until your first job is done;
  then you hear the faction has heard of you, and its contact is on the map. Walking up to them only asks ("Y to join,
  or walk on"); you join by pressing Y there, never by passing by.
- **Everyone runs faster in the city.** Every hero in a played town or district runs at least 5.5 m/s (the streets are
  long). An athletic hero gets there on its longer stride; any other on quicker legs, its feet still keeping pace.

### The platformer's rail in two dimensions: a 3D Jumping Giuseppe, the side-scroller as it was

- **One rail, two games.** `gameworld/platformer-game.js` lays a mascot platformer from its feel to a game whose first
  level is laid and whose flow is said, each level a turn (set up, load, play, pause, results) the play shell runs:
  `platformerGame({ dimension })` answers the words to write on a gameworld. `2d` is the side-scroller: the side camera,
  the first level as `firstLevel()` lays it (one strip, one page, one turn). `3d` is new and opt-in. What the 3D game
  gained, the side-scroller has too: a flow of its own, a start menu, a screen on its side, the look.
- **The 3D platformer's first level.** `firstLevel({ dimension: '3d' })` lays the same teaching order as courses up a
  hill, each trail its own page and its own turn: the grounds (the yard movement is learned in, no foes), the meadow
  (the first foes), the climb (the advanced moves, each floor a tall step up), the ridge (movement and foes together)
  and, when asked, the summit (the boss). Foes stand thinner than a strip's: in the round a foe is walked round as well
  as jumped, on a walkway three metres wide. Absent the word, `firstLevel` lays what it did.
- **One flow shape.** Both say a flow of their own (`platformerFlow`): the title, a level played, its result (on to the
  next, again, or home); a level quit goes home with no result. The 3D platformer's home is its courses screen (the
  place every course is entered from and left to; each one won opens the next); the side-scroller's is its title (its
  first game is one level, so it has no levels screen yet). The front is the start menu the flow is entered through
  (continue, play, and the 3D game's levels): a plain title offers play alone, so a save could not be continued. Both
  are made for a screen on its side (`screen: 'screen'`).
- **Hilltop, a look for a mascot platformer.** A theme card of the toy family
  (`playscape/ui/theme-cards/hilltop.json`), the rail's `ui.theme`: cream sticker plates in a thick cocoa outline with
  a hard drop shadow, round letters, tomato red for what matters, grass green for what is going well, coin gold for
  what is won; a sunburst on warm yellow behind the title, dots behind a full page, confetti on a result, nothing
  behind a menu laid over play (a pause leaves the level in sight); screens open and close on an iris; chunky
  pictograms in the colour of what they mean. Its contrast advice is empty.
- **The hero is a mascot by default.** The rail's patch writes the mascot's body (`characters.direction.body:
  'mascot'`, chibi-sized: a big head on a small round body) on a character book that names no body; a body the creator
  named is kept, and a world with no book is told the words to write.
- **A course in the round is skinned.** A 3D course's floors and stairs were grey boxes; they are now drawn as part of
  the place (`gameworld/course-skin.js`), as the side strip's are. A floor is the land it stands on lifted up: a turf
  cap over a dirt band over rock, in the stage's own kit colours. The stairs and a floor reached up a wall are masonry,
  a trim cornice over stone, in a geocube's colours. Which cube is read from what the level needs: the level's
  `style.geocube`, else the world's, else the cube made for the kit the stage stands on, else the meadow's valley, so a
  world that names a cube restyles its course's masonry with everything else. Every box keeps its footprint, its top
  and its foot, so the course's laws hold as built. Every 3D course world gains the skin on its next run.
- **A course is sized by what its hero clears.** The course's lift over the ground and a floor's thickness are shares
  of the hero's running jump (`course.js` `liftOf`, `slabOf`), no longer fixed metres: the lift a little over a jump,
  a floor in the round a slab about two thirds of a jump thick where it was a column down to the ground. A floor still
  reaches down past a lower floor beside it, so a step's or a wall's face is whole. A climbing course's floors are
  under half the height they were drawn at; tops, footprints and the course's laws are as built. The side strip draws
  its own columns and is unchanged.
- **A platformer's hero holds nothing.** The rail writes no item, and a book whose hero carries some is told
  (`advise`): a platformer's hero runs, jumps and stomps with empty hands. The items are the creator's to take off.
- **Two geocubes for a mascot platformer.** The existing cubes are places with a history (limestone, red roofs, a
  stone night): none is light in weight and none is active. `sherbet-orchard` is the platformer's own, the rail's
  `style.geocube` in both dimensions: warm pastels solved by the colour theorist (a peach floor, plum blossom, cream
  blocks), one mint accent, the only cool colour on the land, the values in three masses so a platform reads at a
  glance; rounded land with no far cliff, quiet surfaces. `toy-hill` is its sibling: clean greens, cream blocks and a
  bright clear sky, one tomato red. Both palettes hold every law of the theorist. The rail writes the orchard on a
  world whose style names no cube; a cube the creator named is kept.
- **A cube that paints the land colours the course's floors.** Where the level or the world names the cube, a course's
  turf, dirt and rock are read from the cube's own outside, as the side strip reads them, so a floor is the same land
  as the ground round it. A stair is stone alone (a tread is about as tall as a cornice), and the trim is a stop
  lighter than the stone.
- **The side strip's land is dressed.** The land behind a side-scroller's lane was a bare terrace and one row of like
  trees. It is now dressed by principles lifted from a running course's dress and turned on their side
  (`docs/side-strip-principles.md`): the terrace in slices, A a grove (trees of unlike sizes, a bush, a stone) and B
  open ground, ordered by the walls' rule (never three alike, never a pair repeated); the grove at the terrace's back
  and only low things at its front, so the band the hero runs in stays the hero's; tufts on the nearest land, where
  speed is read; clouds set low, since a side camera looks down; a small tower in the cube's accent past the lane's
  end. Three laws join the strip's (`rhythm`, `behind`, `quiet`). Every side strip gains the dress on its next run.
- **Scoops: a shape family for a side strip.** A geocube describes a place to walk round in; a side-scroller shows a
  stack of silhouettes, so a strip may now be drawn in a shape family (`era/geocube-side.js` `SHAPE_FAMILIES`), named
  by its cube or by the strip (`side.shapes`). `scoops`, the sherbet orchard's: every shape a dome or a circle. Hills
  in three rows of domes, each about 1.6 times the one before it and a step further into the air; round crowns; puffed
  clouds; a domed tower; turf that hangs over a floor's edge in scallops; all flat and facing the camera. A shaped strip
  is framed by a camera nearly level and a little over the hero, so the sky and the far rows are in the frame (the
  default looks down and shows mostly ground). A law joins the strip's (`one-family`). A cube with no family is drawn as
  it was.
- **Light as shapes, and a more vivid orchard.** A shaped strip is flat, so the seventh generation's lighting
  principles are drawn as silhouettes: one key every shape agrees on (a lit cap on each dome and each crown toward
  it), air with a colour (a far row goes toward the sky's own hue, not toward white, and mist pools at its foot),
  contact (a soft shadow under each tree and bush, the turf's lip shading the dirt), and a lit line along a floor's
  edge. A law joins the strip's (`one-light`). The sherbet orchard's palette is more active and its blossom is locked
  pink (the solve's own foliage was a dark plum; the lock loses the value-groups law, said on the palette), and the
  rail grades the frame `vivid`.
- **The orchard is drawn in the seventh generation.** `sherbet-orchard` names `era: 'gen-7'`: its levels take the live
  light (what moves casts a shadow each frame, the land its own shadow map at its hour, contact occlusion), in both
  dimensions. A world that wants the lighter render names the cube with `era: 'gen-6'`.
- **A side-scroller's foes stand on the rail.** Every foe of a side strip waited on the land behind the lane and leapt
  in as the hero came near, so a player could not see what a jump was being timed on. A foe now stands on the rail
  from the start, in the hero's plane (a swarm's extra foes are brought onto the lane and spaced along it, no two in
  one spot). An ambush is rare: one foe in six, never one of the first four, still waits off the rail and comes in
  (`foes.js` `RAIL.ambush`, `railAmbush`).
- **Lives and coins are pictures.** The `lives` and `coins` mechanics say their HUD readouts as counters, so a look
  with pictograms draws a heart and a coin beside the numbers.
- **Coins along a 3D course.** `mechanics.coins` laid coins on a side strip only; a trail's course (a 3D platformer's)
  now carries them too (`trailCoins`): a row of three along each floor where the feet pass, an arc of three over each
  gap, on the trail's own line. A world without the word lays none, as before; a 3D course world that already said
  `coins` gains them on its next run.
- **Offered by the design door.** A world that plays a platformer's template (its feel, or what its brief or genre
  points at) and has no course is offered the rail in `design_game`'s readout: `next: first-level`, a ready patch that
  keeps what the world already says (its lives, its camera, its levels) and starts it on the level it lays. 2D unless
  the camera (`orbit`, `follow`) or the brief (3D, Mario 64) says the round, the other dimension beside it as `or`
  (the round is Jumping Giuseppe's; a run-and-gun stays on its lane). A book with no level yet gets the same in the
  start readout, as the words its first write takes. It says what it cannot lay: a platformer watches its hero, and a
  world with no character book is walked first person until it has one; a stored world's upright phone screen is
  advised, never changed. Offered, never laid.
- **A world without a book keeps its flow.** A gameworld with no character book dropped a flow of its own when its
  game was made (only `flow: 'play'` was carried); it now carries it, its levels the refs of their first stages, as a
  world with a book does.
- **The course card** teaches the two dimensions and the step.

Not yet: the machine gate walks no level on lives or coins (a platformer's first level is the creator's to play, in
either dimension); courses are titled `<level> · <node>`; lives start over on each course; the card's context jumps
(the long jump, the backflip, the triple jump) and a hub that is a place rather than a screen; the shell's own words
(levels, Modes, Players) are not the game's to rename yet, so the courses screen says "levels".

### The producer's rails: the size and the template picked before anything is built


- **The rail roster** (`gameworld/rails.js`): one row per game type mojulo builds, under the name the producer says:
  the house titles (Fallen Angel, Fable of Artesia, Jumping Giuseppe, Steel Serpents, Mech Battle Kai, Mojulo Fighter
  and the rest of the feel templates) and the types that have no title yet (racing, sports, the board game simulator,
  the side-scroll beat-em-up, the run and gun, the work sim, farming, tower defense, strategy, rhythm, puzzle, flight,
  the table RPG). A rail is a template, never the game: a
  person's game starts from it and is theirs. A row names into the tables that measure it (its feel template, the genre
  cubes it starts a designed game from, its quick goals, its pixelizer games) and copies no number; it says how much of
  mojulo makes it (a pixelizer game, a quick game, a table game, a designed game: `SIZES`, least first), what its first
  level is, and what it lacks. `railShape` is the producer's one line a rail; `seenOf`, `railWords` and `railLacks`
  read the rest from the tables. `NOT_YET` names what is built apart and makes no game yet (the shared kitchen),
  with what it waits on. The side-scroll beat-em-up and the run and gun are rails: they were listed as not yet until
  the street genres were made from a sentence, and the roster's guard failed until each had its row.
- **Held to what is built** (`rails.test.js`): every feel template, quick goal and pixelizer game belongs to a row, a
  row's sizes are what the tables say (a designed size only where the book lays one of its genres today), and a type
  listed as not yet fails the day it can be made, so it moves. A new game type is a row first.
- **The size call** (`sizeCall(rail, wants)`): how much of mojulo an ask needs, the producer's first decision. From a
  rail and what the agent infers the person wants (`levels`, what is theirs to design: `OWN`, `simple`), it calls the
  least size that answers it, with that door and the rail's keys for it (its quick goals, its pixelizer games, the
  genres a designed game starts from), why, and the next size up the rail reaches. A designed game is the only size
  the Game Brief is asked for (`brief`). It never refuses: an ask for more than a rail reaches (a fighting game of
  many levels) is called at the rail's largest, and what the larger one waits on is said (`short`), before anything is
  built. With no rail it calls quick or designed by the wants alone.
- **The two depths** (`railShapes`, `railSheet`). The shape is a line a rail and a line a type not made yet: the whole
  of what the producer holds before an ask. A rail's sheet is pulled once it is picked: its sizes with their doors and
  keys, its four tunings read from its tables (level: the cube's space; action: its feel template and the cube's
  power; character: the cube's soul; world: the cube's reality), what the cube asks of a world, the Game Brief's
  labours that suit it, the chain of tools that builds it at each size with the card to pull at each step, and what it
  does not do yet. Nothing is copied: a sheet is a fresh read of the tables.
- **Two cards served by id** from `get_game_vocab` (not listed): `gameworld-rails`, the shape and the size call's
  rule, and `gameworld-rail-<id>`, one rail's sheet. Both generated from the roster; both the intent chapter's.
- **One reader of a brief's words** (`nearestRails(text)`): the rails whose words the text uses, most first, over a
  rail's own words, its feel template's and its genres'. A heuristic, said to be one: the agent picks or asks.
  `notYetFor(text)` names a type not made yet that the text asks for, so it is said before anything is built.
- **A rail may be seen more than one way** (`seenOf` is a list, the template's way first, then its cubes'). More than
  one is a choice the producer asks (side-on, or in the round?), so a template and its cube never disagree unsaid.
  A rail's first genre is its OWN cube, what the template is: its tunings are read from it, built or not, and the
  sheet says what of it is not built yet (`gaps`) and the cube a designed game starts from today (`starts`). Steel
  Serpents' own cube is `tactical-espionage` (seen from above, as its template is; a designed game starts from
  `stealth` today). Fallen Angel is stylish action and no longer claims the arena brawler's words.
- **The pitch** (a gameworld's `rail`, the intent chapter's): `{ from, size?, departs?, locked? }`. The template the
  person's game starts from, the size the producer called, where their game leaves the template (a line a tuning:
  level, action, character, world) and whether the structure is agreed. A record, never a page: it lays nothing on a
  level, and a world without one is unchanged. `design_game`'s readout says it back (`rail`): the template, what the
  game keeps of it and where it departs, the cube it starts from, what its own cube lacks, its sheet's card. It never
  refuses: a size the rail does not reach is said (`short`), and a locked pitch moved to another rail is a re-plan,
  said to the creator (`replanned`).
- **Nothing is asked twice** (`goalposts.js`). A picked rail makes "what game it is" partial and its question "where
  does their game leave the template?"; its move is the cube the rail starts from, and the play goalpost's move the
  rail's feel. A written Game Brief has decided the stakes and the structure, so the shape goalpost says what it
  decided and asks only its length and whether its spine reads right. The start readout (a book with no level yet)
  says the pitch back with its rail's sheet to pull.
- **Steel Serpents is seen in the third person.** A rail row may say how it is seen outright (`seen`) where its
  tables' cameras are not the game's (its template's lab view is from overhead); its own cube is `stealth`, which the
  book lays today, with `tactical-espionage` beside it.
- **A locked pitch is kept** (`gameworld/pitch-start.js`). A gameworld begins with its first level, so a pitch the
  person agreed to used to live only in the session that made it. `design_game({ world: { rail: { from, locked: true },
  … } })` on a book with no level now lays the rail's STARTER first level under what the creator wrote (every key of
  theirs wins) and stores it, saying so (`pitch: { stored, by, levels, says }`): the platformer's own first level and
  the flow that plays it for a platformer's rail, else one level of the genre the rail starts from, read by the
  sentence door's composer without its review, mode or brief. Nothing is built. Only the lock asks for it; a rail
  with no starter yet, or a pitch of a smaller size, is answered and said (`pitch: { stored: false, why }`).
- **The producer leads the readout** (`goalposts.js` `producerSteps`, `producerSays`). The client talks to the
  producer: a book with no level is answered with the producer's steps before the goalposts, each with the ONE
  question it asks: `intake` (what was brought), `rail` (what kind of game and how big, with the templates the book's
  own words point at and any type not made yet), `lock` (the pitch said back: is this the game?), and for a designed
  game `brief`. The readout's `producer` says the seat and the one question this turn asks; the rest of `next` waits.
  A stored game with a pitch carries its `lock` and `brief` steps ahead of its goalpost and the same `producer` word.
  A stored game with no pitch reads as it always did.
- **The hand-off** (`gameworld/hand-off.js`): where the producer's work ends and the director's begins. Once the pitch
  is locked and a designed game's brief is written, the readout offers `next: hand-off`: the chain's first unit as a
  req the ledger takes, ready to raise. Its unit is the main quest's first built beat, else the world's first level;
  its remit is filled from what the producer settled: the template it starts from and that the game is theirs, what
  it keeps and where it departs, and for a level with no quest behind it its place (the game's start, early), what it
  shows (the rail's first level) and the brief's first order. It proposes and raises nothing: the agent raises it
  with its own ticket (`ask: { intent }`), and the ledger runs as it always has (what the unit reads and has not
  settled is asked for first). It leads ahead of a goalpost, and is gone once the ledger holds a level.
- **The producer's card, rewritten around its loop** (`gameworld-producer`): the seat that faces the creator, one
  agent in both seats (as producer it asks and shapes, as director it builds), one question a turn. Five steps, each
  the readout's own step: hear (the intake, its rows the table's), place (the rail, a template never the game, and
  the size called), lock (the pitch said back; a lock on a book with no level stores it on the rail's starter), deepen
  (the rail's sheet and the Game Brief, a real plan recommended only here) and hand off (the first level's req, raised
  as the director). Its intake example now patches with the door's own op, `set` (it said `add`, which the door
  refuses). The studio card's seats line says the same.
- **Said where an agent first meets a game.** The `initialize` preamble: for a game of their own the agent is its
  producer first (a one-level game asked for outright is still made at once),
  `design_game({ world: { name } })` builds nothing and answers the one question to ask, the game is placed on a rail
  (a template their game starts from) and its size called. The `game-design` routing card points at `producer.ask`
  and the `gameworld-rails` card, inside its byte ceiling.
- **Docs**: `docs/zero-to-level-one.md` says the producer's steps as the path's first step; `CLAUDE.md` says the
  rails and the producer's loop and points at their modules.

### A shooter's HUD that reads as a game, not an app

The first mission's HUD tracked every value it needed, but it read as a dashboard: a box per readout, "HP" and
"Ammo" written beside the numbers, a checklist of tasks, and the radar in a square frame. It is now drawn as modern
shooters draw theirs. The game UI's design notes gain the principles behind this, so other games' HUDs can follow them
([docs/mana-ui.md](../../../../docs/mana-ui.md), "A HUD that reads as a game"). This work is UI only: nothing about how
a mission plays has changed.

- **The gun in hand** (bottom right): the rounds in the magazine are the big figure, the reserve is small beside it,
  and the magazine is drawn as a belt of rounds that empties as you fire. The gun's name and fire mode (auto, burst,
  semi, launcher) sit small above it. Low on rounds, the figure and the belt turn red and say "Low ammo"; empty, they
  say "Reload"; while reloading, the belt refills. A shot kicks the figure instead of flashing it, because firing is
  not news. A gun with an endless reload shows ∞ for its reserve.
- **The gun at a glance.** Over the figure, the gun in hand is drawn as a wireframe of its side: its stock, grip,
  magazine, barrel and sights, and the few lines that tell one gun from another (a rifle's rail, a shotgun's pump, a
  marksman rifle's scope and bipod). A rifle, carbine, bullpup, submachine gun, shotgun, marksman rifle, sniper rifle,
  pistol, revolver, rocket launcher and knife each have one, and the other words for them (a handgun, a PDW, a DMR) draw
  the same. A gun with none shows its name alone.
- **Ammunition you can see.** The belt is a row of cartridges, the round the gun feeds: a rifle's bottle-necked round,
  a pistol's short round-nosed one, a shotgun's shell, a rocket. A spent round is its empty outline. A knife counts
  nothing and says nothing about reloading.
- **Health** (bottom left) is one long bar in cells, read by its length, with no label and no number.
- **No boxes over the world.** Both corners sit on a soft shade that fades out before any edge shows, and each one
  fades back while it has nothing new to say (a full magazine, full health). It comes forward the moment that changes.
- **Danger is felt.** Below half health the screen's own edges close in, tinted red, and near the end they beat slowly.
  They beat less than three times a second and stay still for players who turn down motion or flashing.
- **One order, not a checklist** (top): a mark, the task in hand, which of how many it is, and how far away it is (in
  metres to a place, or how many foes still stand in a room to clear). A place you have to hold drains its clock under
  the order. The full list of tasks, ticked as you meet them, is on the map screen.
- **The radar is an instrument** (top left): round, with a bezel of ticks, the wedge you are looking down, and north
  riding the bezel as you turn. Its face fades into the world.
- **Hits come from somewhere.** The damage ring's marks are arcs round the aim that taper at their ends and fade as
  they age.
- **For every game, not only the mission.** These are new parts of the shared game UI: a magazine readout, the screen's
  danger edge, a radar scope, arcs for the damage ring, a soft shade behind a corner's readout, and a readout that
  rests while it holds no news. The shooter HUD idioms (weapon readout, health strip, objective order, radar scope,
  danger edge) are built from them. The wireframe board's shooter HUD now lays these out together.
- **What is next on this road** is listed in the notes: a compass strip, a waypoint over the objective in the world, a
  kill confirm and a feed of icons, and grenades as counted slots.

### The open city's street: health, wasted, and passers-by who react

- **The street's health** (`game/vitals-mechanics.js`, the `vitals` mechanic, laid on a played city where something can
  hurt the player: its law, a faction's fight): each blow costs health, a few quiet seconds mend it, and at none the
  player is **wasted**: out of any car, a hospital bill paid when they hold the coin, set down at the start, whole again.
  The law lets a wasted player go; a faction's fight leans on the street's health (`fight.wasted`) and is lost with it.
- **A police car's hold is no wound**: boxed in by one, the player is held (`held:<player>`, counted toward the bust),
  not hurt.
- **Passers-by who react** (the walkers channel's `react`, a played district's people): trouble near (a blow, a fall,
  mayhem, a fight begun, a car bearing down) sends them running away along their own walk; struck by the player or run
  down by a car they fall, lie a while, then get up and run. Downing one is mayhem (`mayhem:assault`,
  `mayhem:runover`): a star from the law.

### Underwater: who lives there

- **The sea's animals, called** (`control/lib/graph/marine/fauna.js`, a biocube's `fauna.sea`, a gen-7 geocube page under
  a `sea`). Nothing new is modelled: a row names an animal the encyclopedia already builds (the fish, sharks, rays,
  whales, seals, turtles and cephalopods of `fauna/`, the lobsters and crabs of `bugs/`) and says how it lives in a sea:
  the depth of water it lives under, its habit, how many go together, and the compositions it belongs in. A swimmer was
  refused as a herd ("a level's water holds no animals yet"); it is now the sea's, and the refusal says so.
- **Habits** (`MARINE_HABITS`), each the rule an animal's path is laid by: circling close over an anemone it never
  leaves, round a rock at the rock's height, on the sand, hanging nearly still by a rock, a school on one loop in open
  water, a cruiser on a long loop over the whole place.
- **The laws of the call** (`castMarine`, `MARINE_CALL`), each said where it leaves an animal out, never a refusal:
  *depth* (it lives under its own water); *room* (the water holds it, an open-water animal needing more: no whale in a
  lagoon); *habitat* (an anemone fish needs anemones, a reef fish a rock: the seats the flora laid); *salt* (a
  fresh-water animal is not a sea's, an extinct one comes only when named); *the pyramid* (one kind a habit, two round
  the rocks, one large cruiser at most, kinds and bodies under the page's budget, the largest groups thinned first).
- **Asked for**: `fauna.sea` is `true` (who its flora's mix calls), words (`'sharks and rays'`), or `{ cast: { <species>:
  true | a count | null }, find, density, seed }`. An animal the words name is asked for (the longest name first, so "a
  whale shark" is not also "a shark"); what they only describe, a family or a habit, is preferred where it fits.
- **Searched** (`searchMarine`, `node scripts/marine.mjs search <words> [--depth m]`): what grows and what lives, by the
  words people say (a name, a family, a habit), each row saying whether it fits the depth and why not;
  `marine.mjs cast` shows the call for a mix and a depth, `marine.mjs list` every row.
- **On the page**: each animal is its species' own rig with the one gait it moves by, built where the world is resolved
  (`worlds/marine-fauna.js`) and swum on a closed loop by the walkers channel (no mind, no collision, the same loop every
  load), over the bed and under the surface; the sea's light takes it as it takes the land.
- **Said back**: the geocube's readout carries `marine` (what was laid, the cast, what was left out and why, and who else
  lives there), so the next ask can name them. The `seabed` biome calls its animals; the `seabed` biocube alone calls none.
- **One skin for a body that bends** (`scene/channels/walkers.js`, a walker's `blend`). A rig is packed in parts, each
  triangle handed whole to the bone its corners vote for; ridden rigidly, a fish's parts opened in a sawtooth along its
  length. Asked for, a figure is now drawn as one skin: each corner placed by the bones it is weighed to (the weights
  every layered pack already carries, until now read only by the preview and the exports), in the vertex shader, the
  bones posed by the same clip as before; the depth prepass is told the same move. It is the drawer's, so any looping
  figure can ask; no walker asking, the channel is byte for byte as it was.
- **A skin is measured before it is asked** (`walkerSkinStretch`, `WALKER_BLEND.holds`): the most the blend stretches
  one of a figure's own edges over its gait, against the body's size. A species whose binding sets neighbouring corners
  on bones that part (some sharks and whales, the pufferfish) would show a spike as one skin, so it swims in rigid parts
  and the readout's `rigid` names it with its measure: a defect of its family's binding, found by the measure.
- **Fixed: a shaped body was bound to the wrong bones** (`fauna/rig.js` `stationsOf`). A loft names its whole stations
  `st0…` counted apart from its shaping rings, which it names by their address (`st1_st2_50`); the binder counted every
  ring alike. So on any species whose body has shaping rings (the sharks, the whales, the pufferfish, and land animals
  too: found by a count over the roster, not a list), each whole ring took the bone of the one before it and each
  shaping ring, named by nothing, fell to the part's first bone: a ring at the shoulder rode the tail. Rigid parts hid it
  as a ragged seam and one skin showed it as spikes. The binder now names rings as the loft does; the worst edge stretch
  of a great white's skin over its gait fell from a quarter of its length to under a hundredth, and every sea animal now
  holds the blend. A minted animal with motion binds differently from before on those species: its skin weights and the
  parts its triangles ride change, its shape and its clips do not.
- **One skin for a herd's animals** (`worlds/fauna-units.js`). The controllable drawer already draws a figure that asks
  for it as one skinned mesh (`skin: true`, the path a ridden mount takes); a herd's animal now asks where its skin holds
  the blend over every clip it carries (its gait, its eating, its flinch, fall and rise: `walkerSkinStretch`
  `{ clips: 'all' }`), so a crocodile's or a lizard's back bends as one skin and a knee no longer cracks. A page with a
  herd carries the figure's joints and weights, which a rigid figure's page drops. A skin that does not hold rides its
  bones in rigid parts, as before.

### Underwater: what grows on the bed

- **A seabed laid as an aquarium is** (`control/lib/graph/marine/`, a biocube's `flora.marine`, drawn on a gen-7 geocube
  page by `scene/channels/marine.js`). The surface world is taken out and the bed's own flora laid in its place: the
  hardscape first (reef rock in lumpy mounds), then what grows on it, what sits round its foot, what stands apart in
  groups, and what carpets the sand in drifts, with open sand left between. Nothing that swims or crawls: those are the
  fauna's.
- **The primitives** (`marine/forms.js`, one import-free kernel run by the laws and inlined into the page, so a page
  carries only where each copy stands): forking branches, a plate on a stalk, a ribbed dome, upright fingers, a fan in
  one plane, whips, a barrel, open tubes, an anemone's column and crown, tube worms and their plumes, a sea pen, kelp's
  stipes and hanging blades, a tuft of seagrass, sea lettuce, and reef rock. Each is a mesh at its true size with its
  colour (no light in it) and how far each vertex moves in the current: nothing in the bed moves.
- **The roster** (`marine/roster.js`): a kind is a row (the words people say, its primitive, its size, its sway, its
  colours, where it sits in a composition, and the depth it lives under); a composition is a mix (`reef`, `kelp`,
  `meadow`, `wall`, `deep`, `vents`). `flora.marine: true` grows the mix its sea's zone grows; a kind that does not live
  at the depth is left out and named in the readout (nothing that needs the sun in the dark), never refused.
  `{ mix, density, kinds: { <kind>: weight }, seed }` tunes it.
- **The lay** (`marine/place.js`): read off the land as built (its ground and its trail), along the walk; the trail kept
  clear; a fan set on a rock's flank facing out; a drift wholly one kind; thinned evenly to the page's budget with the
  rocks kept. The same lay from the same seed.
- **On the page**: each template is grown there and drawn as one instanced mesh, lit in the vertex by the cube's sun and
  sky (a blade lit through from either side), swaying by where it stands so a stand of kelp leans together, then taken
  by the page's fog: under a `sea` its reds go with the depth as the land's do. `window.__mojMarine` is the probe.
- **The `seabed` biocube and biome**: the desert's baseline with no tree, grass or bush and `marine: true`; the biome
  lays it with the desert's sand and palette and locks the land's grass role to sand. With `flora.marine` and no grass
  the gen-7 land grows none.
- **Words**: a scene's `underwater`, `undersea`, `seabed`, `seafloor`, `reef`, `coral`, `abyss` lay the seabed biome on
  low dunes, open, under a `sea` at the word's depth. In a game these words lay the bed without its water yet.
- `scripts/spikes/sea/aquarium.mjs` shoots a bed from words or by zone and mix, and `--sheet` stands every kind in its
  colours. Absent `flora.marine`, every page is byte for byte as it was.

### The wanted level: the law answers mayhem

- **A world's `law`** (`true`, or `{ police?, stars?, per?, calm?, busted?, fine? }`; `gameworld/law.js`): an open city
  the law watches. Its police are a bestiary entry, the maker's or a patrol in uniform (the new `police` grunt style: a
  uniform shirt and duty belt, a sidearm; a tactical unit). The law is no faction: it gives no work.
- **The `wanted` mechanic** (`game/law-mechanics.js`): mayhem raises a star (a street fight started, a police officer
  downed, a car taken from its driver, a crash into traffic), up to five; each star brings more police, set down near
  the player and out of reach, who chase and strike. Keeping clear of them and of trouble for a while takes a star off
  and sends its police away; taken down by them, the player is **busted**: fined and set down where the level began.
- **Police cars** (`law.cars`, 3 unless said, one with each star): the city's police car (the fleets' patrol car in its
  livery, a red and blue light bar flashing on its roof, its siren heard near the player), set down at a street junction
  out of sight and driven after the player on the district's streets (`gameworld/cars.js` patrolCar; the runtime's
  `chaser` rule: routed over the junctions of every street, arterial and local, straight at the player near, braking to
  stop beside one who stands, backing off a wall it stalls on). Holding a player who stands, in a car or on foot, it
  counts a blow each second; caught in a car, the player is taken out of it (the cast's `dismount`) before being set
  down. A street's runs come from the district itself (`geocity/scene.js` `ctx.streets`).
- **Stars on the HUD**: a readout `as: 'stars'` (mana-ui's pips in a new `star` shape).
- **A spawn near a body** (the cast's `spawn` with `near` and `ring`, on one of `among`'s points when given).
- A city level lays its police and the mechanic only when its world has `law`; absent, not one byte.

### Boss fights: gimmicks, phases and patterns; vehicles won by mechanics

A boss is no longer a foe whose phases only change its temper. `lib/graph/boss/` holds the pieces a boss fight is made
of, each held to laws a body facing it needs.

- **Attack patterns** (`boss/patterns.js`): an attack as a timeline. Its tell (the wind-up, and each hazard's mark on
  the ground from the moment it is shown), its hazards (a line, a cone, a sweep, a ring, discs, charged tiles, a
  strafing run; a lock that follows the body and holds before it fires), and its opening, the recovery a boss can be
  hit hard in. Each hazard says how it is escaped: out of it, through it in a dive, under it in a crouch, or behind
  cover. The shelf: sweep, fan, charge, ring, rain, lock, strafe, grid, scythe.
- **The laws** (`boss/laws.js`), measured on a quarter-metre grid of the ground each hazard touches:
  - told: shown at least a reaction before it lands;
  - escapable: every place it lands is left in time, dived through or crouched under, or else marked as wanting cover
    the arena must stand;
  - survivable: a body standing still anywhere in it loses half its health at most;
  - opening: a recovery follows it.
- **Human bosses** (`boss/bosses.js`): a gimmick read off a name and a design, with moves of its own over the patterns
  (said in its words, tuned to its idea), and phases. Each phase gives the moves' weights, the tempo, the mind's temper
  and an arena event at the crossing (the floor burns, it changes perch, it tears cover out, the tiles go live, its crew
  comes in). The shelf: Cinder the flame trooper, Glint the marksman, Breaker the demolisher, Lineman the high-voltage
  man.
- **Vehicle bosses** (`boss/vehicles.js`): event driven and won by mechanics. A vehicle is parts, each a box saying the
  hits it takes (a round, an explosive, a mine), how many break it, and what it hides until then. Its states drive the
  encounter and move on when parts break, a run is flown, or time passes. The shelf:
  - the tank: mines under its tracks strand it, then launcher rounds go into its engine grille;
  - the gunship: attack runs met behind cover, launcher rounds into its rotor hub while it hovers to turn;
  - the walker: launcher rounds strip its leg plating and its bared knees break, and kneeling, its cockpit is in reach.
  Its laws hold it winnable with the arms in hand: no tank without mines, no walker without a launcher.
- **Played** (`worlds/controllable/boss.js`):
  - A human boss fights with its mind between moves. It takes a move at its phase's tempo and is planted through the
    move's tell and hazards; a charge carries it down its lane.
  - Its hazards land on a body standing in them, never through a dive, under a crouch, or behind cover from their
    origin.
  - Its opening takes half again.
  - A phase crossed runs its event: the rim burns, it changes perch, cover is torn out, the floor goes live, the crew
    is woken.
  - A vehicle is driven by its state: along its route, on its runs and hovers, stranded. Each hit on it is judged by
    part after the step.
  - `E.bossHit` judges a hit another module lands.
  - Emitted only where a world has a boss.
- **Land mines** (`worlds/controllable/mines.js`, the kit's `mine`): laid at the feet on the trigger, armed after a
  moment, tripped by a person of another team near it or a vehicle over it. A vehicle it goes off under is told, and
  its track breaks.
- **Seen** (`scene/channels/controllable/boss-view.js`):
  - each hazard's mark on the floor, filling as its landing nears, then the landing itself;
  - the mines arming and armed;
  - a vehicle's dress and parts, with its weak spot beating red while it can be hit and a broken track wrecked.
  - The HUD draws the boss across the top: its name, its title, and its health with a tick between its phases.
- The spike `scripts/spikes/mission/boss.mjs` stands each boss in an arena laid for what it wants, the operative
  carrying the kit that beats it. Craft in `docs/boss-fights.md`.
- **Counters** (`boss/bosses.js` `counters`): how a human boss is beaten other than by rounds poured in. A `part` counter
  is a piece of its own that breaks under the hits it takes, only from where it shows and only while it is bare, and its
  breaking makes the boss reel, costs it health and shortens a move. Its law holds it reachable: the move that bares it
  comes in every phase, and its opening is long enough to react and land the hits. Cinder is the first: every arc of
  flame ends with him turned away to vent, and four rounds into the tank on his back rupture it. He goes up in his own
  fire, and his arcs reach a share as far for the rest of the fight.
- **Looks by phase** (`looks`, a phase's `look`): a phase can swap the boss's figure. Cinder's mask cracks open in his
  last phase to show his face. The page builds each look's figure up front, under the same light as the body.
- **Cinder's look**: a heavyset welder minted through the character door (`scripts/spikes/mission/cinder.json`) in
  canvas coveralls, a leather chest plate, bracers and kneepads. He wears a new realistic headwear, the WELDING MASK
  (`headgear/realistic.js` `shield`): a strap on the band line and a plate stood off the face, convex across and down,
  with a slot of dark glass at the eyes. Its cracked twin is split open across the eyes. The tank and its hose are
  drawn by the page on his torso bone (`boss-view.js`), so the tank can glow while it is bare, flash as each hit lands
  and burst when it breaks.
- **Glint** (the `flash` counter): his eye is at the scope through every lock, and a glint flares there so you always
  know where he is. A stun grenade bursting in front of him then, with a clear line to his eyes, blinds him for four
  seconds where he stands: his shot is called off and he takes double. A flash is never used up. His mind is a
  sentry's, so he holds his perch and fires from it. His phases move him on from the perch he stands at to the next:
  in his arena, three gantry decks 1.8 m up, low enough that a stun out in front sees his eyes, high enough to want
  climbing. A boss is never knocked out by a stun (`knockout.js`); what one does to it is its counter's.
- **Glint's look**: tall and lean, minted from `scripts/spikes/mission/glint.json`: an oilcloth duster to mid-calf
  over a sand shirt and a shooting vest. On his face a new realistic headwear card, the SHOOTER'S WRAP: mirrored glasses
  wrapped temple to temple, built as a lens band (the shield's `span`), over a scarf wound high round the lower face
  (its `wrap`).

### Room to move: buildings laid larger for a third-person camera

A building's plan was sized for a walker (corridors three metres, five-and-a-half-metre rooms, three-and-a-half-metre
storeys, a two-metre stair with two of floor at each end), and under a third-person camera it read as cramped.

- **A core building's `scale`** (1 to 2, opt-in, `era/program-core.js`): its rooms, bays, corridors, core, lobby and
  annex laid that many times larger, each storey the root of it taller. Scale 1 is the plan as it was, byte for byte.
  A level's building, a geocube's or stage's building and a complex's building take it.
- **The `hall` stair** (`construction/circulation.js`): a building laid larger climbs flights three metres wide on a
  shallower going, with three metres of floor at the foot, the head and the landing, and a wider well.
- **Facilities are laid at 1.5**, and no longer ask for the fighting map's wide corridors on top of it. The Steel Serpents
  interiors (the holding block, level 1's barracks and hangar) are laid at 1.5, their laws still holding.
- **The room layouts' widths** are a body's with a camera behind it (aisles 2.2 m, lanes 2.2, pods 2, rows 1.6, a centre
  aisle 2.4), and a room is held to a hall's laws from 100 m², ten metres square.

### Cinematic action game: guards that keep their eyes on you and fight with the gun they carry

- **Once seen, it keeps you** (`rule.alert`, worlds/controllable/alert.js, opt-in): a watcher that sees the pilot is
  alerted. Alerted, its sight is wider and longer (`cone`, `range`), so a body that steps out of a patrol's narrow beam
  is still followed; it remembers where it last saw the pilot for `hold` seconds, goes there at a quicker pace (`pace`)
  when the line is broken and searches round it for `search` seconds before it lets go and takes up its round. It
  follows farther from its post (`leash`). A fresh sighting calls the watchers of its team within `call` metres, who
  come to where it was seen and look there with their own eyes. The weapon comes up before its first round (`raise`
  seconds), so the first shot is never from the hip. A watcher whose way to the spot is walled off searches from where
  it stands rather than walking into the wall. Its state is `e.alert` ({ level: calm | combat | search, up }), read by
  the page. It only changes what the rule says and holds the trigger until the gun is up: what is seen, chased and shot
  is the mind's own, so a pilot behind cover is still not seen. It wraps the world's step: every other page keeps every
  byte.
- **The gun in a watcher's hands** (`rule.armHeld`, scene/channels/controllable/gunplay-view.js, opt-in): a body with a
  mind carries the arm its slot's `gunplay` view draws, its hands closed on it as the hero's are, its posture read off
  its alert: on its round the patrol carry (the butt in the shoulder, the muzzle down and across the body, the chest
  little turned, over the walk); searching a high ready; in combat the attack stance, shouldered, the chest side-on, the
  gun on the mind's own aim and kicking with each round, which leaves from its muzzle. A body without an alert raises
  it while it fires. Emitted only into a page that has such a body.
- **The fan says it is looking** (sight-view.js): amber while its watcher is alerted and does not see the pilot (its
  search, or a call it came to), and the fan it draws is the alerted one, wider and longer.
- **The infiltration yard's guard** carries its carbine (the arms library's, as the hero's kit draws it), keeps the
  hero once it has seen it (`alert`: a 1.3 rad cone, 1.6 times its reach, 12 s of memory, 6 s of search, its pace 1.8
  times, called guards within 14 m, the gun up in 0.45 s) and fires its carbine in bursts of three, a round 6 of the
  hero's 100, where it fired one round a pull. The level-1 yard and hangar stand the same guard. Played headless:
  patrol carry on the round, the gun up and the first burst half a second after the sighting, the hero followed as it
  stepped aside, searched for where it slipped away; nobody has played it.
- **A world without a watcher steps as the engine does** (startle.js): the pilot's pace over the ground was written on
  every world's pilot by the startle step, so a world without one no longer stepped byte for byte as the engine
  without it (foe, knock and vayo-move's opt-in pins were red). It is written only where some body has `startle`.

### A cinematic action game's HUD, item select and pause, drawn as a game's

The shooter's first mission was redrawn to read as a game rather than an app (the theme `shooting-rails-ui`). The same
principles now reach the three screens of a cinematic action game, and of every level that draws its HUD in the game's
look. This work is UI only: nothing about how a level plays has changed.

- **The HUD.** The boxed "HP 35 / Down 0" panel and the page's own ammo box, radar and damage marks give way to one
  look:
  - **Health:** a strip in cells at the bottom left, read by its length, with no label and no number. Where a level
    counts health itself, its count fills the same strip, so the screen shows one health. Sprint is a thin bar under it.
  - **Bullet time:** a ring round an hourglass beside the health. It fills as the slow motion comes back, glows when
    it is ready, says what sets it off ("Dodge"), and drains while the world crawls.
  - **The gun in hand** sits at the bottom right with its wireframe and its rounds as cartridges.
  - **The radar** is a round scope at the top right with north on its bezel. Hits are arcs round the aim.
  - **Danger:** the screen's edges close in, tinted red, below half health.
  - Corners sit on soft shades and nothing is boxed. A full magazine and full health fade back until they change.
- **Item select.** Holding RB opens a weapon wheel in place of the old list panel. Each weapon sits at the button that
  picks it (Y at the top, B right, A at the foot, X left, as on the pad), drawn as its wireframe with its name, its
  button and its rounds. The one in hand is lit and named large in the middle. The world shows through, with no box.
- **Pause.** The world blurs behind. PAUSED stands large at the left with the level's name under it, and the menu is
  set large. Which level of how many and the time played sit at the right. The controls screen shows each key as a key
  cap beside what it does. The first mission's pause takes the same layout.
- **For every game.** These are parts of the shared game UI: a charge ring, a weapon wheel, a pause with where you are
  beside it. The wireframe board gains a cinematic action HUD and the wheel.
- **The radar a game asks for.** A world's `ui.radar` (game/hud-mana.js `RADAR_LOOK`) names its look:
  - `shape: 'square'`: the scope in a square, still turning with the player, translucent, with an inner square.
  - `size: 'large'`: about a third larger.
  - `floor: true`: the plan and the guards of the floor the player stands on alone. The level's floors are read off its
    slabs (gameworld/radar.js `planFloors`), and each floor's plan is drawn the first time it is stood on
    (`floorPlanSvg`): its slabs as ground, what stands at it on them, the rest dark. On a stair, the radar keeps the
    floor left until the player is all but up.

  Absent, the round scope as it was, byte for byte. Steel Serpents asks for all three.
- **Crouch on the pad.** The operative's south face is its stance: a press crouches and stands, held it lies down, as C
  does, and the left stick's click still does too. The dive moves to the north face. On a touch screen its pads read
  crouch and dive.
- **The roll drawn whole.** A dive rule's `blink: false` (worlds/controllable/dive.js) keeps the dive invincible and
  stops the page flickering the body through it; every other i-frame still shimmers. The operative's dive says so.

### Cinematic action game: a mission spiked on Steel Serpents' first level

A spike of one primitive, the mission: an encapsulated sortie with a preset loadout, a walled-core dungeon infiltrated a
layer a page, cutscenes between and inside its layers, and one result. Nothing registers a kind, a mechanic, an MCP tool
or a recipe key; the spike mints through the real doors and measures.

- **The probe** (`scripts/spikes/mission/`): Steel Serpents' base written through `design_game` as it stands, to say
  what builds, what is refused and what is dropped. In progress.
- **A bandana** (`headgear: 'bandana'`, headgear/cards.js): a cloth band tied round the brow over the hair. On the
  realistic head it is the circlet's band wide and without its gem, a knot at the back and two tails hanging from it
  (headgear/realistic.js `tails`; a wide band takes one support over its whole height, so nothing stands through it);
  on the game body the band alone. Held to the headwear law beside the circlet and the hats.
- **The aim held** (`rule.aimView`, worlds/controllable/aim-view.js, opt-in): a third-person body moves under a free
  camera; while its aim is held the camera stands behind its shoulder, the body turns with the look and the trigger
  fires (it does not with the aim down, unless `hip`); from the aim, an edge goes to the eye and back (the body hidden
  while the camera rides it), another to the other shoulder. Let go, the free camera again, looking where the aim left
  it. It wraps the world's step, so every other page keeps every byte.
- **The operative's controls** (`SCHEMES.operative`, controls/schemes.js): the pilot's actions laid out as a stealth
  action game lays them. The aim on the left trigger and the right mouse, fire on the right trigger, the eye on the
  right shoulder and Tab, the other shoulder on the right stick's click and Q, the sprint on the left stick's click
  and Shift, the action on the west face, reload on the east, the dive on the north, the weapon in hand on the D-pad's
  up. A page whose pilot aims this way reads it in the pilot scheme's place. The stance, the binoculars, the radio and
  the item slots have no action yet.
- **The infiltration yard** (gameworld/infiltration-room.js, `scripts/spikes/mission/room.mjs`): a practice room for
  this kind of game. The world's hero on its feel, its template's kit in its hands (Steel Serpents: a handgun and a
  knife), a walled yard of cover and a person's box at 5, 15 and 30 m and behind a corner. Not on the practice door
  yet. Played headless on real key and mouse presses: the run, the sprint, no round unaimed, the aim, a round, the
  other shoulder, the eye, the free camera again, with no page error; nobody has played it.
- **A practice room's hero under the cast rig** (`castLight: { cube, hour? }` on a world that is no form page,
  worlds/world-scene.js): its bodies are read as a level's form page reads them, the skinned body under one light, where
  a greybox page drew the painted figure, whose skin showed through its cloth at the shoulders, the collar and the
  joints. The infiltration yard asks for it (the `theatre-grey` cube) and bakes its hero at the play grade. Absent, a
  page is as it was.
- **The camera back from the eye** (the aim held's pages only): a follow camera is no longer pulled in on what is not
  drawn. The eye's own hands and gun, hidden once the aim leaves the eye, pulled the chase into the hero's back.
- **Getting over things** (`rule.freeRun`, worlds/controllable/free-run.js, opt-in): the runtime's half of the free-run
  library, whose vault clips (polygonizer/hero-vault.js) nothing on the runtime played. A body running at a thing no
  higher than its hip and no deeper than a table goes over it on an arc that clears the top and lands running, with
  nothing pressed; the jump at a taller thing (to a standing reach) climbs onto its top, or over it where the top is
  too thin to stand on. Refused where another thing stands at the landing or over the top. A wall laid in courses or
  crates stacked are one thing. The page plays `vault` and `mantle` (`TRAVERSAL_FALLBACK`: a figure without the clip
  plays a state it has). It wraps the world's step: every other page keeps every byte.
- **The infiltration yard runs by default and goes over its cover**: the stick's push is the feel's fast gait with
  nothing held; its low walls are vaulted out of the run and its stacked crates climbed on the jump. The operative
  carries the solved clips (`motion: stepVault, speedVault, hurdle`) and the vault plays its step vault; the climb has
  no clip of its own yet (it plays the jump's start).

  carry it; level 0 sends two guards down the trail from the base as backup.
- **The play grade held** (figures/figure-lod.js, worlds/world-scene.js): a play-grade world's figure that no player
  pilots and that bakes over its budget (a hero on a head that does not lower its own sampling: the realistic body, its
  garments, its gear) is simplified part by part under the foe's budget: each part welded where every corner buffer
  agrees (a seam stays a seam), its open edges locked (a hem, an opening keeps its line), quadric edge collapses
  (polygonizer/skin-net.js), and a soup again, each surviving corner keeping its own colour, joints, weights, uv and
  normal. The face's morphs go with the face, never framed close at this grade; the bones, clips and height stay. The
  starter's guard goes from 130k triangles to 36k and reads the same at play distance. The figure a player pilots, and
  every other grade, as it was. A level on a geocube place may ask for the grade (`figureGrade`, geocube.js), and
  every segment of the starter does; they had not, so their guards were baked at the full grade.
- **Level 0 starts forty metres back**: its trail is laid longer (`run: 20`), and its places are said along the trail
  (`{ trail, off }`: metres up it, metres to its side), set down on the trail's own line as it is laid (level0-plan.mjs
  `spineFrom`, `placeRecipe`), so a longer or another trail carries the layout with it. The first forty metres are
  quiet: the controls are told there a few at a time (moving, aiming and the menus, the crouch and the prone, the dive
  and the vault, the radar's wedges, the alarm), before the convoy. The planner holds both places to their laws on the
  new ground. `--no-occlusion` builds a page without the seventh generation's contact occlusion, for its cost.
- **Level 0 built rather than parked**: one truck, and the rest of the cover a patrol builds where it stands, as the
  static world's own faces (a few boxes each, drawn with the land, never a body): sandbags a metre high (they hide a
  crouch), wire on stakes (it stops a body and hides nothing: the route search reads a box `sight: false`), and two
  watchtowers whose lookouts stand on the deck and see from four metres up, over what a guard on the ground cannot
  (a box `walk: false` is walked under). The convoy is now a checkpoint: sandbags with a gate on the trail, wire either
  side, a tower over the gate, a slot beside the truck; the camp sits behind sandbags under its tower. The planner
  holds both places to all four laws; a second way now keeps off the first one's middle third only, since two ways to
  one goal meet near their ends.
- **What the page may cost** (level0.json `performance`): its shadows at the half tier (`light.tier`), no contact
  occlusion, real grass out to 20 m (the view cone; [ and ] move it live). The figure a player pilots is held to the
  hero's budget too, its face kept whole (the operative 160k to about 70k). The spike's pages carry a frame readout
  in a corner (frames a second, milliseconds a frame, the pixel budget's density), for the person to report.
- **One draw a body.** A layered body (the realistic operative and guard: painted, lit, 64 parts) in a play-grade world
  is drawn as one skinned mesh a material (controllable/merged-figure.js `oneDrawFigure`, `__oneDraw`), where only a
  plain rigid rig was before: its bone meshes are built as ever and kept, hidden, as the bones the sync poses and every
  reader reads (the aim, the held gun, the target rim, a hit), and a face's morphing parts stay their own. The world marks
  such a figure `oneDraw` (world-scene.js, the play grade); none marked, not a byte.
- **Bodies cast no live shadow** where a level asks (level0.json `performance.bodies: 'blob'`): no body in the live
  light's map each frame, a soft pool at each one's feet instead (suit-shadows.js `feet`: no ray through the scene a body
  a frame, the pool where the runtime stood the body). The land's own hour shadows stay.
- **The level fills its window**: a geocube level takes the game's `screen` (era/geocube.js, a level's word beside `events`
  and `mission`), and level 0 asks for a monitor's (16:9, grown wider before it bars; its HUD inside the frame, not a
  1120×780 box at the top of the window). The spike's other pages take the same where their payload names none, and
  hide the World page's orbit hint.
- **Thinner air**: level 0's `air` a light haze (visibility 450 m, clear to 40 m, no far blur) in place of the land's
  distance haze (about 130 m).
- **The map under the radar** (gameworld/radar.js `radarPlan`, mana-ui's minimap `plan`): the level's plan, from its own
  colliders and its tall grass, drawn once on the page and laid under the scope at the radar's scale, the pilot at its
  middle and ahead at the top, turning as the pilot turns. `planSvg` takes `rel` (each thing by its own height, a land
  that rises and falls) and `veils` (tall grass). Level 0's radar reaches 25 m (the pilot's `radarRange`).
- **The radar's map topographical** (a geocube level's `radar: { map: 'topo' }`; gameworld/radar.js `radarLand`, planSvg's
  `relief` and `trail`): the land's heights and its trail's mask read when the level is built (its grass map, every
  1.5 m; its path mask), the page drawing them under the plan once: contours a metre apart and a brighter one every five
  (the gorge's walls a crowd of lines), the trail in its own colour. Level 0 asks for it. Bench: no frame cost.
- **No zoom onto the body on a stair** (channels/controllable/index.js, the follow camera's stair rule): a building's stairs
  reach the page with their footprints (era/storeys.js anchors carry each flight's `rect`; the page's `__STAIRS`, absent
  without stairs), and on one, where the ceiling or the flight overhead would pull the eye in to the body, the camera
  looks for a clear line nearby instead.
- **Nor at a wall: the clear line** (a follow camera's `clear: true`; the infiltration room's camera, both of the starter's
  levels, asks for it): the stair rule's search wherever a wall, a crate, a column or a ceiling would pull the eye in onto
  the body. Lines a little flatter, steeper, all but overhead or swung up to about fifty degrees aside are read from the
  look point, each eye stood short of the wall its line meets (the pull-in's floor no longer stands a steep line's eye
  through it) and taken only if the body is in sight from it; rising is cheaper than swinging, the line held is kept
  unless another is clearly clearer, the eye eases onto it (cutting where the way between would lose the body) and aims
  back toward the body as it turns off the rule's line. It looks again eight times a second, only while pulled in.
  Measured in the hangar, the operative backed against each of the hall's walls and into a corner: as it was, the eye
  stood 0.3 to 0.4 m from the head at three of them; now 2 to 6 m, the head and the waist in frame and in sight at every
  one, and at every point up both flights (the stair rule alone had come to 0.44 m on one). Absent, every byte as it was.
- **A played building's top floor stands taller** (a stage's `headroom: { top }`, era/stage.js `withHeadroom`; not `ceilings`, which lays a room's ceiling as a collider; carried
  by a level's building, gameworld/levels.js): metres added to every room of its highest storey, so its ceiling clears
  the follow camera. The hangar asks for 1.5 m.
- **Things to find, drawn as what they are** (a mission item's `look`, channels/controllable/mission-view.js): a keycard
  (the card, its access stripe, chip, photo and lanyard), a document (a folder with its papers showing, a stamp, typing
  and a photograph clipped on), a ration (a foil pouch, crimped, its label), an ammo can (its lid, handle, latch, stencil
  and rounds stood by it) or a case, each a few boxes at twice a thing's size, a little lit from within, turning low over
  a ring the colour of its kind; never hit by the camera's or the ground's rays. Until now each was a yellow diamond.
  The hangar's keys and intel, and the yard's key, wear theirs.
- **Supplies** (a mission item's `gives: { hp?, rounds? }`, worlds/controllable/mission.js): used as they are found,
  health back to the body (to its most) and rounds into the reserve of the gun in hand (else the first gun carried that
  keeps one); one that would give nothing (health full, no such gun) stays where it lies and the player is told why.
  Rations and ammo laid in the hangar (by the parts store, in the shops above, in from the hall's doors, both corners of
  the hall below, a storeroom on the way out) and on level 0 (behind the truck in its grass, by the camp's crates, behind
  the south log: the level's `supplies`, laid on the trail).
- **The crawl crawls** (the operative's `proneIdle` and `proneCrawl`, scripts/spikes/mission/operative.json): the keys
  were posed for a body standing, so lying, a drawn-up leg crossed the other (its yaw pulled it in), the reaching arm
  swept its forearm over the head and the resting hands floated over it. Now a low crawl: the forearms flat before the
  face, one arm reaching as the other elbow draws in and the opposite knee comes up and out along the floor (the hip
  turned out), every channel keeping its side through the cycle, so nothing sweeps through the body between keys.
- **The radar a glass** (mana-ui css.js, a scope minimap): its face a third of the panel's colour at its middle (seven
  tenths) and the map under it at 0.55 (0.8), so the world reads through it and it never stands over the play as a disc.
- **A trail as wide as it is said** (a stage trail's `width`, era/out-trail.js; a geocube scene's `trail`): the walked way
  in metres, 1.2 to 8, wandering along it as the kit's footpath does; absent, the kit's own (about two), so every trail
  that says none is laid as it was. Level 0's is 4.5 m: a track a jeep fits at its narrowest, the stands of trees kept
  six metres off its line.
- **A trail's dirt brought together** (a trail's `match`, 0 to 1, era/trail-dress.js, color-theorist/ground.js
  `soilTones`): the colour theorist lays a dirt trail in two dirts about the floor, a lighter powder toward the light at
  its edge and a darker clay toward red in its worn core; on some floors the two read as a red strip in a grey verge.
  `match` brings the core's clay to the powder's hue, fullness and light (at 1, the powder a worn shade darker), so the
  track reads as one ground worn down the middle. Absent or 0, the tones are as they were. Level 0's trail at 0.85.
- **A wide trail's middle is on the trail** (form/land-read.js, the path map's signed distance): the depth inside a
  trail was stored in a byte that held three metres of verge and a metre and a half of trail; deeper than that it ran
  under the byte and wrapped to the far verge's value, so a wide trail's middle read as off it (the land's own colour
  and grass down its middle, a hard zigzag where it wrapped). Now held at its deepest. A trail no deeper than that (most
  of every footpath; a rest's widening could pass it) draws byte for byte as it did.
- **Trees back on level 0** (the level's cube: the upland's lone trees grown into a dozen stands of two to four, seven
  to twelve metres): the gorge wooded again without the jungle's cost; the sneak's laws hold as before (each way still
  seen first, an unseen way and a second one at both places).
- **The checkpoint's left side is a takedown** (level 0, `west-sentry`): a sentry paces from the cut in the west wire
  out across open ground and back, slowly, looking wide, and turns all the way round at each end of his beat; one end is
  in the cut itself, where no body gets past him, and the far end is in the open, where a body that followed him out is
  found wherever it lies. So the west way is passed only by taking him down: wait in the grass by the cut while he looks
  round in it, follow him out as he walks away, and E behind him before he turns. The line's patrol keeps to the gate
  and the slot; the grass that ran through the cut is gone (on his line it hid no one), a clump beside the cut and one
  on the approach in its place; the takedown's hint is said where the west way begins. The planner proves it (below):
  the straight way is seen, no way passes him standing, and a way opens with him taken down from behind.
- **A patrol's look round** (foe.js `patrol.look: { secs? }`, opt-in): at each end of its round it stands and turns all
  the way round, one way, and on to face back (540° in `secs`, 6 unless said), then walks back. One that looked to one
  side and back would leave a sector unswept to lie in; all the way round, a body behind it would have to keep pace
  round it. Absent, a patrol turns on the spot as it always did.
- **A guard's reach at arm's length** (mind.js and foe.js `rule.near: { r?, back? }`, opt-in): a body within `r` metres
  is seen whatever way the guard faces, unless it stands in the `back` degrees square behind him (the arc a takedown
  comes from), and that only while he walks: stopped to look round, he feels it all round. A body can no longer circle
  a guard at his elbow out of his cone; one coming up square behind a walking guard still can.
- **Level 0's patrols walk the rounds the planner proved**: a patrol was laid with its round's length and no ends, so the
  runtime walked a round centred where it stood (the gate's patrol, planned from 64 m up the trail to 77, walked from 57
  to 70); its ends are now given, `at` to `to`.
- **The planner knows a takedown** (gameworld/stealth-routes.js): a way may come up on a named watcher from the arc
  behind it, within reach and never seen, standing or crouched, and put it down (the runtime's own numbers, takedown.js);
  from then on that watcher sees and hears nothing. A place that `needs: 'takedown'` is judged by three laws, the
  straight way seen, no way past standing and a takedown that opens it, each with room to spare (every watcher wider by
  a margin, so a way along a cone's edge at the instant a guard turns, which no player can find, is said and not
  counted). A point may be searched in a lane, a band of the field to one side of the trail (`off: [lo, hi]`). And the
  search is truer for every place: two bodies never share ground (a way no longer slips through a guard as it turns),
  a move that takes more than a tick is unseen at every tick of it, and a patrol's look round and a guard's reach at
  arm's length are read as the runtime has them.
- **No body's shade side is black** (color-theorist/cast-rig.js, a `value` law): the cast rig held a body's lit side
  over its shade side and its shade side against the horizon, but never asked how dark the shade side was, so a dark
  suit under a weak sky (level 0's evening haze, the operative's near-black top) went to black on every face turned
  from the sun (a third of the operative's pixels under 20 of 255, where the land's darkest are over 60). The rig now
  reads the body's bulk (its palette's `Top` and `Bottom`) and, where its shade side would fall under the floor (an L of
