  0.27: dark, never black), raises the body's own key and fill together, at most 6×, so its form keeps the turn it had.
  A form page now hands each hero's palette to its rig (it was read as a middle grey, which never falls under the
  floor); a body with no palette, and a light one, is lit as it was.
- **Level 0's guards keep their pools** (`performance.bodies` 'pilot'): every body casting was benched (no dearer than the
  operative alone), but under the level's low, hazy evening sun a body's shadow is a thin streak seen nearly edge-on from
  the follow camera, and a guard without the pool at his feet reads as floating; the operative casts his own.
- **What moves shades a form page** (scene/channels/cast-shadows.js, the live light on a form land, `formLand`): on a seventh-generation
  land the land's sun is the one light and every other directional light lights nothing, the actors' own included, so
  the actors' shadow map, drawn every frame, darkened nothing three lights: no body's shadow fell on the land or on
  another body (level 0's operative included, and every guard once they cast). Each lit surface that receives (the land,
  its grass and plants, a body under the cast rig) now takes the actors' light's own shadow, three's getShadow on its
  map at its place among the casting lights (its depth convention three's: a reversed depth buffer's compare runs the
  other way, which a hand-rolled sampler read as lit), on the sun's light in three's own loop: a guard's shadow on the
  trail and on the operative, the sky's fill kept; a normal offset keeps a body from shading its own skin. Emitted only
  where actors cast on a form land; every other page keeps its bytes.
- **Floodlights on a form land** (a geocube's `floods`, scene/channels/form-floods.js): up to four, each where its lamp
  hangs and the point on the ground it shines at, with its colour, power (its light at ten metres in the land's own
  units, a noon sun's about 1), cone, reach and whether it casts: real spots that light the land, its grass and plants
  and the bodies as the land's sun does, falling off by the square of the distance, their heads burning with a glow the
  haze does not eat; the first two cast what stands in their beam, drawn every frame. Level 0 tried at night (the moon
  the key) with one hung over each tower's deck, aimed at the ground a body crosses.
- **A body's key gain is its key's** (scene/channels/cast-rig.js): the cast rig's own gain on a body's direct light
  multiplied every light's, so a flood or a lamp would have lit a body many times brighter than the ground beside it; it
  now multiplies each directional light's colour alone, in three's own loop (three's chunk laid out in place, and the
  actors' shadow spliced into the same text, so either patch may run first). A page whose only direct light is its key
  is lit as it was.
- **A flood on a mast** (`floods[].mast`, the height its pole stands on, drawn from there up to the lamp): level 0's
  floods first hung a metre and a half over their towers' decks, and each deck's metre of rail stood in the beam from
  17° to 47° below the level, so its shadow lay over the whole near pool and the ground under them stayed dark; hung on
  a mast 3.2 m over the deck, the rail is under every ray of the beam. And the land shades no flood's light itself: a lamp
  skims the ground, so the least rise by a trail laid its shadow over the whole pool (measured on the page, a pool as
  dark with the floods' shadows as without the floods); the land's shadow depth is left out of every perspective map, a
  spot's, and kept in the sun's orthographic one, where it still shades itself.
- **Level 0's structures in the level's light** (scripts/spikes/mission/level0.mjs): its towers, sandbags and wire were
  painted with fixed fills, lit as daytime paint at any hour (at night they glowed); each face's colour is now its fill
  under the land's own light at the hour, the sky's and the sun's or moon's by how it faces it, as the stage bakes its
  painted groups. And the night's air a night blue (`air.colour`; the jungle haze's own hue carried into the dark is a
  muddy olive).
- **An air with its own colour keeps it** (channels/atmosphere.js, channels/form-sky.js): a recipe's `air.colour` was laid
  on the fog and then overwritten a few frames in, when the gen-7 sky is built and sets the fog to its own haze; the air
  now says its colour on its probe and the sky leaves the fog (and the far blanket's air) to it. And the colour is read as
  the eye sees it, sRGB decoded to the fog's linear light, as its own manual says (read raw, a night's dark blue was shown
  a pale grey-blue). No recipe in the library sets one.
- **Level 0's night sky a night blue** (the level's cube `light.sky` and its `air.colour`): the jungle haze's own sky hue
  is green, so its night, carried to the night's value, was olive.
- **Level 0's watchtowers built, with stairs** (scripts/spikes/mission/level0-plan.mjs `towerFaces`, `towerStair`): a tower was
  four leg boxes, a deck box and four rail boxes; it is now drawn as it is built: four posts up to the eave, an X of
  bracing on each side but the stair's, a deck of boards on joists, a rail and a mid rail on posts, open where the stair
  arrives, a straight flight of open treads on two stringers with a handrail, and a pyramid roof over the deck. Its boxes
  stay what the search, the colliders and the walk read, and gain the stair's treads: each a block from the ground to
  one riser under its tread (a tread is shallower than a body is wide, so a block at its own height stood two risers
  over the feet of a body on the tread before it, past its 0.35 m step), a quarter metre a riser, so the operative walks
  up to the deck on the drawn treads; and the deck's frame, a box from over a standing head up to the boards (a guard
  walks under it, the search's band never meets it), so the flight and the deck are one thing to a runner: without it
  the free-run took the last treads for a low box and vaulted the operative off the top of the flight, down under the
  deck (measured on the page, frame by frame, at tread 10 of 15). A tower's `stair`
  names the side its flight runs out from (the gate tower's north, away from the gorge's wall; the camp's south,
  down the trail's side toward the camp: east, its flight ran into the north log). A flight runs down to the land at its foot
  (`seatStairs`, read off the relief the plan reads): a tower on a rise has a longer flight, so its first tread is a
  step off the ground wherever it lands (the camp's, on a slope, 21 risers to the gate's 16). Each was run up on the page, from the land to the deck, where
  the rails held the operative. The sneak's laws hold with the stairs standing.
- **A body at night sits in the dark the land sits in** (color-theorist/cast-rig-core.js `CAST_RIG_LAWS.night`, read off
  the sky's height at the hour, era/geocube-hours.js `hourLight`'s `s`): under the moon the value floor (0.27 L) had a
  dark suit's key and fill raised six times, and the rim, as bright as that raised key and raised again to carry the
  outline, drew every body as a glowing blue edge on a moonlit land. From the twilight into the night the floor falls to
  0.17 L and the lift to 3× (2× and 0.12 L, tried first, left the operative a black cut-out), the rim is as bright as the
  world's own light on the body (never its lifted key's) at half its strength, and no rim is raised to carry an outline: a silhouette lost in the dark is the night's, and a
  floodlight still lights a body as it lights the land. The day and the golden horizon are as they were.
- **A realistic night** (era/geocube-hours.js `REALISTIC_NIGHT`, a cube's `light.night: 'realistic'`): the night every
  cube took was its reference's, a gothic game's (dmc3): a saturated blue moon, a blue-violet shade, a navy sky, which
  read as a fantasy game's. The realistic register keeps each at the stylized night's value and drains its hue to a
  cool grey (the eye sees colour poorly by moonlight): the moon a pale light barely cool, the shade and the sky
  near-neutral, the twilight before it drained to a whisper of blue; so the dark reads as a real night's and the floods'
  warm light is the only colour in it. `stylized`, unless said, is every other cube's night as it was; the day is the
  same either way. Level 0 takes it, its sky and haze near-neutral greys.
- **A night grade** (scene/channels/grade.js `GRADE_PRESETS.night`): a film's night over the frame, the colour drained
  further (0.72), a little harder round the middle grey (1.08), the corners dark (0.3), a little grain (0.08), and no
  hue of its own, so a realistic night's greys and a lamp's warmth stay what they are. Level 0 takes it (`grade:
  'night'`, laid on its geocube scene by the spike); every list of the grade's words names it.
- **A geocube world takes a grade** (era/geocube.js): the frame's `grade` is any world's (the controllable vocab says
  so), but the geocube kind refused it as not its setting; it is let through to the world scene that reads it.
- **Level 1's barracks past the hangar's door, its key past a sentry** (scripts/spikes/mission/level1.json
  `segments.perimeter.barracks`, yard.mjs): the barracks stood across the trail from the hangar's side door, its key in
  the first room off its lobby, six metres on. It is now one storey at the trail's far end, twenty metres past the door,
  rooms both sides of a corridor each way off a stair core; the key is in the first sergeant's office at the far end of
  the south corridor, and a sentry walks that corridor end to end, looking round at each end and feeling a body at his
  elbow. The only way to the office is past him: slipped by from room to room while his back is turned, taken down from
  behind, or darted. The outside's second guard walks the trail between the door and the barracks.
- **Level 1's yard at night, as level 0's approach** (scripts/spikes/mission/level1.json `segments.perimeter`, yard.mjs):
  the perimeter was built at 17:00, so its bodies wore the golden hour's warm rim, inside the barracks too. It is now the
  same night as level 0's: the realistic night, its sky and haze near-neutral greys, the night grade; and the base is
  lit by four floodlights so it reads in the dark (over the hangar's side door, at the barracks' front, on the apron and
  at the gate; the first two cast), seated on the land where it was laid, on masts where they stand free. `--hour`
  still sets another hour.
- **The crawl seen from the eye** (worlds/controllable/stance.js `prone.view: 'eye'`, the infiltration room's operative):
  lying flat, the camera rides the body's eye a third of a metre over the ground, the body hidden, and the body turns and
  pitches with the look, so the crawl goes where it looks; up again, the chase camera and the body's own turning are given
  back, looking where the eye left them. The aim held while lying takes its own camera, as before.
- **Crawling under things** (vehicle-registry/parked.js `crawl`, worlds/controllable/veil.js `under`): a parked road
  vehicle that says `crawl: true` and rides high enough (its wheels' radius `CRAWL_LEAST`, 0.5 m, or more: a truck, a bus,
  never a car) stands on a box at each wheel and its body from its chassis up, so a body lying flat (0.45 m) crawls under
  it between its wheels while one crouched or standing is stopped at its side; and the space under it is a CRAWL SPACE,
  a veil the runtime's sight reads (with the guards', the alarm's body found and the knockout's wakers): a body in it,
  under its ceiling, is hidden from an eye over that ceiling outside it beyond arm's reach (a guard standing over the
  truck does not see who lies under it; one lying, or beside it, does). Level 0's cargo truck is one, its boxes and its
  space seated on the land; the route search keeps its boxes (a line low enough passes under it) and its laws hold.
- **The meadow drawn to 70 m on the stealth levels** (level0.json `performance.cone`, level1.json
  `segments.perimeter.cone`, read by yard.mjs): the view cone's reach is the screen's by default (about 25 m at a
  desktop window), so the meadow's blades ended partway up the trail and a band of flat grass colour lay past them; a
  player planning an approach read the land past an edge. At 70 m the blades run on to the far field, the edge out of
  the view up the trail. Measured on the software renderer: the frame's draw 27.7 → 35 ms (the tall grass, the cover,
  was drawn at every distance already).

### A lived-in city district

- **Back yards behind every row of houses.** In a city district you play or look around, the wide empty lawn behind
  each row of houses is now a back yard for every house: a patio or a deck off its back door, a vegetable garden, a
  play set or a trampoline, a shed, a shade tree, chosen so no two neighbours have the same yard. Fences of board,
  lattice, slats, chain-link, pickets, brick, stone or hedge run between the yards and along the back where two rows
  meet. On a hillside a yard that crosses a terrace's step is split into two, with a fence along the top of the wall.
- **Service yards behind shops, a car park beside a low-rise.** The land behind a row of shops is a paved yard with
  bins by each back door and a car now and then; a low-rise apartment block has its residents' car park.
- **Little parks are parks.** A block given over to a park now has two paths across it, a playground, a pavilion,
  benches along the paths and trees on its lawn, as a town's park does.
- **Vacant lots and fields.** A fenced vacant lot has a few young trees that seeded themselves near its fence, and a
  school's field has a pitch with its goals where it is big enough for one.
- **Grass everywhere it belongs.** In the most detailed look, vacant lots, school fields and the courtyards of
  apartment blocks grow the same grass as the lawns round them instead of showing as a flat green colour. No grass
  grows up through a patio, a deck, a shed or a path.
- **Lawns that look kept.** A town's or a city's lawns in the most detailed look are bare in only a few worn places,
  and those places are irregular. They used to run in long straight stripes north to south across every lawn and park,
  which read as a pattern rather than as wear. Islands and trails are drawn as they were.
- **Houses are house-sized.** A pair of semi-detached houses along a main road stood as tall as the five- and
  six-storey buildings beside it. A house is now three storeys at most.
- **Street paint lies on the street.** Lane lines, centre lines, crosswalk bars, streetcar rails, parking-space lines
  and tree pits were placed by the lie of the land, but the road and pavement are drawn in flat panels, so on a hill
  a piece could float up to half a metre over the road or sink into it. Every piece of paint now sits on the road
  that is actually drawn under it, following its slope from end to end, a centimetre over it (it used to be five, enough
  to cast its own shadow). Lamps, signals, poles, hydrants, bins, benches, bike stands and street trees stand on the
  pavement drawn under them in the same way.
- **Site fences follow the ground.** The temporary fences and hoardings round a building site or a vacant lot stood at
  one height for the whole block, so on a terraced block some panels hung in the air and others were buried. Each
  panel now stands on the terrace under it.
- **Smaller, faster-loading city pages.** In the most detailed look a city district's page is about a third smaller
  (158 MB to 101 MB for a played district). Buildings and grounds that are finished in the same material now share
  one texture rather than each carrying its own copy, and the large maps behind the land (where grass grows, the
  ground's shape) are compressed in the page and unpacked by the browser as it loads. Smaller lands are unchanged.

### The exhibit's producer: a concept fitted to its people and its time before anything is made

In progress. Each line is added as its phase lands.

- **The producer faces the person with a concept to display** (an educator, a curator) and asks only what they alone
  can answer, one question a turn: what people should leave understanding, who it is for and at what degrees of
  learning, how long they have with it, and what material they bring.
- **The fit, said back before anything is made**: what their time and people hold (one exhibit, a toured one, one at
  several settings, a gallery of rooms; how many stops). A plain request to see something is still made at once.
- **Their knowledge stays theirs**: the producer records what they said and lists what is open; it never writes a
  claim or a source for them.
- **The fit** (`exhibit/fit.js`, `exhibitFit({ time, people, wants })`): what a span of time and its people hold, as
  the size of what is made and a budget of stops. Time is a word a person says (`TIMES`: a glance, a visit, a sitting)
  or seconds or minutes. The size is the least the time holds: one exhibit with one sentence, a toured exhibit, or a
  gallery of rooms once the time is longer than one room holds a visitor (`ROOM_SECONDS`); an exhibit at several
  settings rides beside it when they want to show what changes. People (`AUDIENCES`) are a caption each at every
  stop: words to write, no time added. It names three depths of attention it serves (the glance, the visit, the
  study) and says the fit in a line. Its arithmetic is the tour's own (`holdSeconds`), so a fit's stops played as the
  exhibit's audit plays them fit the time they were called for: a test holds that. A stop count is a ceiling, read
  end to end. Advice, never a refusal.
- **The start** (`exhibit/producer.js`; the door: `create_exhibit({ start: { concept?, people?, time?, brought?,
  scales?, wants? } })`, asked alone). A person with a concept to display is answered before anything is made: the four
  questions only they can answer, in order (what people should leave understanding, who it is for, how long they have
  with it, what material they bring), each dropped once answered, and `producer.ask`, the one to ask this turn. With
  their time, the fit. When all four are answered, `make`: the fit's door, said back first, the stops and claims
  written from what they said and never for them. A plain request to see something (a concept and nothing of people,
  time or material) is marked `plain` and made at once. It builds and stores nothing; without `start` the door reads
  as it always did.
- **The exhibit is made new.** The agent composes it from the primitives a world is made of, for this person's
  concept. The halls' exhibits are samples of what one is like (how a tour steps, how a part is lit, how a claim is
  graded), read for their form (`like`) and never offered as the thing to make: nothing matches a concept's words to
  the catalog. A fit's sizes say how each rides a world made new: a tour and a curation are opt-in keys of any
  world's recipe, a prepared state and a gallery's room are any world.
- **The intake** (`exhibit/intake.js`): what the person brought, read before they are asked anything it already
  says. Each thing is recorded with what it says and where it went (`EXHIBIT_PLACES`: the aims, the claims, the
  stops, the rooms, reference) or why it has no place yet; nothing brought is dropped. Its kinds (`EXHIBIT_INTAKE`:
  learning goals or a lesson plan, label text, sources, a list of topics, pictures, a programme) each say what takes
  it and the questions it usually answers; a new kind of material is a row. The start reads it as `brought`: a
  question their own material answered is never asked, its step says `read` (the agent writes the answer from the
  item and calls again), and `intake` reads back what was placed, what was set aside and what is still open. A
  source is never a claim until they say what it shows. It records and never authors.
- **Kept with the exhibit**: a curation may carry `brought`, the record as read, so the next session knows what was
  brought. A curation without one is as it always was.
- **The scales** (`exhibit/scales.js`): the first primitive of an exhibit, the size of the thing it shows. The human
  point of view is the base (what a person could stand beside); below it the micro, the atomic and molecular, the
  subatomic; above it the macro (the bigger view from above), the geo (a geocube: terrain modelled), the planetary
  (its own views), outer space. The two ends are conceptual. Two things stand beside the ladder with no rung: a
  place in history (the historical views: a real place at its period, where the historic cultures are the primitives
  of what can be shown, Pompeii and Sumer among them) and an idea, which has no size. Each
  rung says what it shows naturally (the tour's own shapes: a structure, a process, a quantity), how a world at it is
  made new, the law tables that can compose it where there are any, and the samples in the halls that are like it.
- **The exhibit determines its scale.** The agent reads the concept and names the rungs it lives at (`start.scales`,
  its home first): never a question for the person. A concept that spans rungs is a room a rung, and the fit's rooms
  are the rungs unless they asked for a number of their own.
- **The map** (`map` on the start, once there is a fit): a spine and its sequences. One page stepped through, or a
  lobby of rooms each stepped through in order, each room's scale and stops, and between rooms at different scales
  the way the visitor zooms (in, out, or aside to an idea). Nothing branches.
- The tool list's payload pin is raised for `start` (an argument on the door that owns the exhibit intent), with its
  reason beside the pin.
- **The camera's own words** (after the camera work landed). A rung says how a room at it opens (`view`: a size by
  how much of the frame the thing fills, an angle: the macro is the wide view from above, the geo a map of the place
  from overhead), and the zoom between two rooms names the camera's move for it (a push in, a pull out; a crane up to
  a view from above, a crane down from one; aside is a cut). The words are the shoot plan's own tables; a test holds
  them to those tables.
- **The hand-off** (`exhibitHandOff`, the `make` step's `steps`). Once the four are answered and the fit is said
  back: the steps that make it, a room at a time. A room's world made new at its scale (how it is made, how it
  opens, the samples like it, its parts named so a stop can light them); its tour and curation set on it (how many
  stops the time holds, the first standing alone, each caption said again for each audience); the states where they
  want to compare; the rooms joined, with the move between each two; then the machine gate and the person's look. It
  proposes and runs nothing. The curation it carries is what was said (the audiences, what was brought); the aims
  and the claims are marked theirs: none is written for them.
- **Said where the exhibit option is chosen.** The start is an argument of `create_exhibit`, the door that owns the
  intent of making an exhibit (it began on `get_exhibit`): its first call builds nothing and says what to ask, as
  `design_game`'s does. `forward_context`'s WORLD row sends someone's own people to its `start` first; the exhibit
  form says an exhibit is made new at its scale and that the halls hold samples; `create_exhibit`'s line in the tool
  index says the start. A routing card of its own, `exhibit-producer`, takes the exhibitor's phrasing (a class, a
  gallery's visitors, a lesson plan brought) and carries the producer's steps: ask, scale, fit, make. The plain
  "show me" ask stays the `exhibit` card's and is made at once. `forward_context`'s body ceiling is grown for the
  row, with its reason beside the pin.
- **`CLAUDE.md` kept light**: a pointer to the exhibit producer's modules, and the game producer's paragraph and
  architecture entry cut to pointers. The steps live in the routing cards and the readouts.
- **A tour's contact sheet** (`create_exhibit({ contact: '<ref>' })`; `exhibit/contact.js`, `motion/tour-contact.js`):
  every stop of a made exhibit's tour as a visitor meets it, a row a stop, on one PNG in the exhibit's outcome folder.
  The exhibit's own page is opened, each stop seated and photographed (its view, the part it lights, its caption on
  the plate), the rule of thirds over each frame, and under it how long the stop is held and how much of the view its
  lit part fills, in the camera's own words; the page audit's findings ride beside the stop they are about. The page
  is the truth: it already seats and measures each stop, so nothing is solved a second time. It is what the agent
  looks at first and what the person with the concept is shown before the tour is finished; whether it reads is the
  eyes gate, theirs. The hand-off carries it as a step (`sheet`) between the machine gate and the person's look.
  A gallery or a states page is asked for a room at a time.

### Facility pieces: buildings to move through

A building laid from its use alone was a corridor of five-metre rooms, each stocked along its walls: hallways and empty
boxes to a sneaking body. Two new pieces make it a ground, and a walled-core dungeon's layer can name one.

- **Room layouts** (`era/room-layouts.js`): a room's floor laid in a figure from the dressing's own pieces: `aisles`
  (rack rows, cross aisles aligned or staggered), `machines` (plant on a staggered grid), `islands` (desk or bench pods),
  `stockpile` (crate clumps stacked by the dice), `chicane` (blocks against a corridor's walls by turns, each slid to a
  stretch no doorway takes) and `rows`. A program's `layouts: { <room or role>: <layout> | { layout, …dials } }` asks for
  them; compose-dress.js lays them in place of the room's stock, keeping a body's way through each doorway (not the
  dressing's whole approach, nor a doorway's sightline), and falls back to the stock where nothing fits.
- **Their laws** (advisory, the stage's `compose.layouts`): doorways joined, a way round, the gaze broken (from a hall's
  doorways; down a corridor's length), cover in reach. A room smaller than a hall is held to its doorways and cover.
- **Facilities** (`era/facilities.js`): `depot`, `power-plant`, `motor-pool`, `research-wing`, `field-hq`: a use, its
  fighting dials (rings, wide corridors, a catwalk), its layouts and its own construction and palette (utility, bunker,
  military, science, everyday). A level's `building: { facility }`, a WCD space's `facility`; the recipe's own look, fight
  and layouts over it. A complex's buildings take `layouts`.
- **Proved**: `scripts/spikes/mission/facilities.mjs --plan` crosses each hall by the route search under a watcher
  walking it: the depot's shed and the power plant's generator hall have no way across unseen bare and one laid.
  `--svg` draws each ground storey; `--out` builds the page. docs/facility-pieces.md; the `gameworld-wcd` card names them.
- **In the game book**: the facility maps, `/bible?book=facilities` (`gameworld/facility-maps.js`): this game's
  building levels and the whole shelf, each storey from above (rooms, doorways, ways out, stairs, every piece by what it
  hides) with its laid rooms' laws, its materials, its moves and the recipe line that names it. `design_game`'s readout
  offers it to a world with a building level, a dungeon or a rail of interiors; the world book draws a facility level
  the same way, and the spike's plans are drawn by it.
- **Nothing on a stair**: a gallery's stairs (the catwalk's way up from a hall's floor) join the dressing's keep-outs
  (`compose-dress.js keepOuts`), so the stock, a room's layout and the cover all keep off them; a depot's racks and a
  power plant's machines stood on them before.
- **Racks that are not copies**: a rack a room's layout lays carries a load of its own (`load: true`, seeded from its
  id): a pallet of cartons of mixed sizes, a wrapped load, a row of totes or a gap, level by level, each box in a
  surface and a variant of its own. A rack stocked along a wall keeps its one fixed load, byte for byte.

### Superhero beat-em-ups: a team of heroes, each with a power, against an army and its villain

- **Ask for a superhero beat-em-up and you get one.** A team of heroes fights down a street seen from the side.
  Each hero has one signature power on its own button and a few uses of it each life. The street throws an army at
  them that drops in from above and comes out of doors as well as walking on. More of them come at once, and each
  falls to a few blows. At the end waits a villain who has a power of its own and fights in stages. You have five
  falls. "A superhero beat em up in a port town" now lays its streets this way. A plain "beat em up" is unchanged.
- **Powers, each a card.** A beam from the eyes or the hands that passes through everyone lined up on it. A
  great slow ball of force. A barrage of darts. A gout of flame. Lightning called down all round you. A berserk
  rush through the crowd. A step through space. A strongman's grip that slams a body down. Each is drawn in its own
  colour as it flies, and each hero's uses left show as pips under its health. Using one spends one; falling fills
  them again. A new power is a new card.
- **The team and the villain come from the comic hero pack.** Unless you say otherwise, the team is the pack's
  leader with the beam, the rival with the storm, the sidekick with the phase and a strongman with the grip. Each is
  rolled as a character from its member's sheet and drawn in its own body. You can name the powers, swap in another
  of the pack's cast or rename a hero. The villain is the pack's mastermind with the ball of force unless you pick
  another (the brute with the grip, the rival with the beam). It is made as a character too and stands at the end
  of every street. The army is the pack's shadow clan, with blades and a staff, unless you name another crew.
- **Design your own heroes and powers.** When you ask for this game, the studio now asks first who your heroes
  are and what each one's power is, and offers the defaults if you have none in mind. A hero can be your own,
  described in a sentence with its build, age and whether it is a man or a woman. It is rolled from your words and
  made as a character. It can also be a character you have already made, or another of the comic pack's cast. A
  power is one of the kinds made yours: give it a name and a look (any beam, a laser or lightning or a ball
  of fire), how many uses it has each life, and how strong it is. A power thrown down the street also takes how
  fast it flies, how big it is and how many enemies it passes through. Each setting has limits. The villain can be
  chosen too, with a name and a power of its own. The hero picker shows each hero's power by name. A power far
  stronger or weaker than the ones the street was tuned with is pointed out for you to decide on, never refused.
  A designed power is not measured by the studio's simple player.
- **A designed game's street can be a superhero one.** Give a street level `tuning: 'heroes'`. Your game's hero
  then plays its own power: the first attack its actions page throws is played as the street power of that kind and
  drawn in that beam. The cast who join the party and any stand-ins take the team's powers in seat order. A street
  can also name each seat's power itself, one of the shelf's or one you designed. The street's enemies are still your
  game's own.
- **A power is a super moment.** When a hero calls up a power, the whole street holds still for an instant, as a
  fighting game's super does: longest for the ball of force and the storm, a blink for the phase. While it holds,
  the screen marks the hero. The air round them goes to its negative like a comic's impact frame (the ball of force,
  the storm), lights up (the beam, the flame, the barrage), bends (the phase) or darkens (the frenzy, the grip). The
  hero's own body is left alone; the effect is in the air round it. A villain calling up its power gets the same
  moment against you, and so does a fighting-game super thrown on the street. You can choose a designed power's
  moment (`screen`: lift, ring, shade, ink or none). Only a street whose heroes have powers carries this layer.
  Every other street's page is unchanged. Measured with the freeze in: one hero still wins the default street alone
  with each power, losing two or three of five falls, and four heroes lose one. Seen in headless Chrome: the street
  held, and the air round the hero inked as the ball of force was called up.
- **The whole game, from the first screen to the end.** A superhero beat-em-up is now a campaign rather than one
  street. You fight down the city street the army has taken, then the works it runs from, then the villain's lair.
  Each opens once the one before is cleared, and your progress is kept. The army's own boss holds the first two
  streets and the villain waits at the end of the last, where the army also comes harder. The game opens like an
  arcade: an attract screen to press start, then a title saying who fights whom, with continue, play, a street picker,
  options and credits. When the villain falls, an ending card plays, then a roll of the heroes and the villain, then
  back to the title. Name your own streets and they are the campaign instead. A world's own title screen and credits
  win over these. Measured with the simple player that uses its power, each street played once by each of the four
  heroes alone: every street was won by every hero. The streets get harder in turn: on average 1.3, 1.5 and 1.8
  falls of five, 27, 33 and 37 blows taken, and 60, 62 and 77 seconds. A single run is too chaotic to judge by
  (one hero took 49 blows on the city street, another 11), so the climb is measured as the average.
- **Supervillains, and the foe idioms on the street.** The villain at the end of a superhero game is now one of a set
  of supervillains, each with a way of fighting you learn and beat:
  - **The mastermind** keeps back behind drones it summons out of the ground a few at a time. Cut it down and every
    drone it called falls with it.
  - **The juggernaut** is an armoured suit that grabs and slams; break it and the fast, frail pilot comes out.
  - **The twins** fight as one, one firing while the other rushes. Drop one and the other is enraged.
  - **The warlord** calls reinforcements in at every turn.
  - **The speedster** never stops running you down.
  - **The tempest** becomes the eye of a hurricane when hurt.

  Each fights in acts that begin as its health falls, with its power on its special. The pack's mastermind is the
  mastermind, its brute the juggernaut, its rival the twins; name another kind for any of them. The streets on the way
  end on lieutenants: an enforcer who calls its thugs, then a conjurer who summons drones. The army gains henchmen: a
  caster that summons, the drones it calls, and a blaster that fires a bolt of its own.

  These are the studio's foe idioms, played for the first time on a beat-em-up's street: a summoner and its summons, a
  pair that shares a fate, and a boss defeated into another form. A designed game's own foes play them too. Its
  summoner calls its summons, which before stood as a plain thug. A boss's partner stands beside it, and each form a boss
  becomes is one of its acts. A pair that revives each other in other games enrages here instead, and the game says
  so. On the page a summons rises in a ring of dust, one cut down goes up in a puff, an enraged partner flashes red
  under a banner, and a new form bursts into view.
- **Design your own supervillain.** A villain can be a kind with your own words over it (`design`): how it fights,
  its power, its health, who it summons and how many at once, its partner, its acts and what each calls in or turns it
  into, and the henchmen beside it. A new villain on the shelf is a row of the same words. Every word is checked as
  the game is designed, and a wrong one says where it belongs. The studio's villains card lists each villain, what it
  does, how it is beaten and every word.

  Measured with the simple player, one hero alone beats each villain at the end of the lair. Against the mastermind,
  the juggernaut, the twins, the warlord, the speedster and the tempest it fell 0, 1, 1, 1, 0 and 1 times of five. Each
  fight's way was seen: the mastermind's drones were summoned and cut down, the juggernaut and the tempest changed
  form, and one twin enraged. Seen on the page in headless Chrome, in a game built from scratch: in the lair, Doctor
  Umbra (the mastermind) under its bar of three acts called two drones that stood on the street; cut down, both drones
  fell with it and the street was cleared, with no page errors. The drones are drawn as the army's own soldiers, so on
  the page they do not yet look summoned. Nobody has played the villains by hand yet.
- **The producer knows the superhero variant.** Asking for "a superhero beat em up" now picks the beat-em-up's heroes
  variant by name, with its own plan of steps. That plan asks who the heroes are, each one's power and the villain
  first, before anything is made, for a quick game and a designed one alike. A designed game started from it gets
  the heroes' tuning on its first street. The plain beat-em-up's plan lists the variant and is otherwise unchanged.
- **Powers throw bodies by their weight.** Some powers now carry energy as well as damage, by the studio's own
  destruction physics: a blow is measured in joules and a body holds by its footing. What gets past the footing
  throws it, so a light grunt flies and a heavy brute only staggers under the same blast. The beam and the flame shove
  whoever they hit along the line. The ball of force and the storm strike the ground: the ground takes most of the
  blow, shown as a ring of dust where it landed, and the rest throws everyone near, harder the nearer they stand. A
  body thrown down flies, lands and slides to a stop. An enemy a power has just finished off is thrown with the rest.
  A villain's power throws your heroes the same way. The motion plays at a beat-em-up's pace, so nobody is thrown
  off the screen. The other powers move bodies as before. Measured: each power still wins the default street alone,
  losing two or three of five falls, and four heroes lose none.
- **An earth power: summon a wall, then push it.** A new power, the wall. The first press wrenches a slab of the
  street up out of the ground in front of the hero, rising in a ring of dust. It stands as cover: enemy fire stops on
  it, and nobody walks through it. Press again while it stands and the hero shoves it down the street. It is a few
  tonnes of stone, so the shove's force gives it its speed, and the ground's friction slows it. Every enemy it meets
  is floored and thrown ahead of it. It slows a little with each, so it bowls through a line until the ground and the
  bodies have taken its speed. A slab that has nearly stopped only nudges. It crumbles into dust when it stops, or
  after a few seconds if nobody shoves it. It has three uses a life, and only raising the slab spends one; the shove
  is free. A designed wall's strength makes both the shove and the blow harder. Measured: one hero with the wall wins
  the default street alone, losing two of five falls (with two uses a life it lost four, so it has three). Seen on the
  page in headless Chrome: the slab standing between the hero and two enemies, then sliding into them and throwing
  them.
- **Heroes who float, and a wind power.** A weather hero is carried on the air instead of walking, as the weather
  witch of the comics rarely touches the ground. It hovers off the street with a slow bob, never walking, in the
  comics' pose of power: carried upright with the chin up, one knee drawn up near level with its shin tucked back under
  it and the foot drawn in by the other knee, the other leg let down long and straight with the toe pointed, the fists
  clenched at the waist with the elbows bent. Gliding, it leans into the way it goes and the long leg trails back. It drifts rather than walks: it eases up to speed and glides on for a moment after you let go, by the same law the studio uses for a
  hero's air dash. With no footing under it, a blow knocks it further than a hero standing on the ground. The storm
  power's hero now floats, and so does the new gale power. The gale calls a hurricane of wind down the street. How hard
  it pushes each enemy is the wind's drag against that enemy's footing: a grunt is blown off its feet and carried away,
  a heavy brute braces and holds, and a floating body is swept away hardest. Enemy fire caught in the gale is blown out
  of the air. The gale is drawn as streaks of air down the street. A designed power can carry its hero too
  (`float: true`), and its strength makes its wind stronger. Measured: one hero with the gale wins the default street
  alone, losing three of five falls. The four-hero team now loses two falls (it lost none before its storm hero
  floated, since a floating hero is easier to knock about). Seen on the page in headless Chrome: the hero hovering,
  the streaks of the gale, and the enemies in it braced and pushed back.
- **Long hair and loose cloth move with the air.** On a street, a character's long hair (what hangs below its neck)
  and its loose cloth (a skirt, a coat's tails or a cape's hem hanging below its hips) now swing with the air it moves
  through. Walk or run forward and the hair streams back, more the faster you go. Stop and it swings forward past
  where it hangs, then settles. A floating hero is borne up on its own updraft, so its hair and cape billow and stream
  behind it even while it hovers still, and further as it glides. In a gale the wind blows them the way it blows, hard
  enough to stand the hair out level. A knocked-down body's hair rests. Cloth swings less than hair for the same
  air. How far it hangs is the air's drag against its weight, eased by a spring, so a strand swings and settles
  rather than snapping. A bent strand keeps its length. This is drawn only: the fight itself never sees it. Hair
  that ends at the neck and trousers do not move. The street's bodies carry no hair bones yet, so the whole lock
  bends as one about its root rather than strand by strand. A cape on the street hangs from the shoulders only: its
  edges no longer follow the arms, so it is not pinched in to the fists while the arms strike or hold them at the
  waist. Seen on the page in headless Chrome on a hero made with long hair and a cloak: the cloak and the hair swept
  back as it glided, the cloak blown across it in a gale at its back, and a slow billow as it hovered still.
- **Describe how your hero looks, and it looks that way.** A hero you design used to take only who it is from your
  sentence: its hair and clothes were rolled, so "long white hair and a flowing cape" could come out a short brown
  bun. Your sentence now sets the hair and what hangs loose on the hero. That covers the hair's style (long, a
  ponytail, a braid, a bun, a bob, a buzz cut, bald), how far it falls ("down to her waist", "to the shoulders") and
  its colour ("white hair", "silver-haired"). It also covers a cape or cloak, a gown, dress or skirt, and a robe, each
  falling as you say ("a long cape", "a short skirt"). You can also say it outright: `look: { hair, length, colour,
  cape, gown, robe }`, whose words win over the sentence's. Everything else (the face, the build, the rest of the
  clothes) is still rolled. A cape or gown is added to the hero's rolled outfit, so nothing it was wearing is taken off.
  The look is laid in the words each head wears, the anime one or the western one. A hero you made already keeps its
  own look, and a look given with one is turned down: change it with the character's own edits. The studio now asks
  for each hero's hair and cape along with who it is. A hero whose look nobody described is made as before.
- **Every word the character maker takes, on a designed hero and on the villain.** A hero you design can carry
  `spec`, the same words `create_character` takes for a person. That means the hair with all its controls, the face,
  the expression, the whole outfit, the palette, headgear, gear, the build and the rest. They are laid over what its
  sheet rolled, word by word, the way `create_character` lays words over a rolled sheet, and they win over the look
  read from its sentence. The villain takes the same `spec` and `look`. The villain can also now be a character you
  made with `create_character` (`villain: { hero: { ref } }`), drawn as you made it, as a team hero already could be.
  The words are checked by the character maker itself as soon as the game is designed, each hero's as it will be
  made, so a word it does not take is pointed out then, with where it belongs or the word it is near, before anything
  is made.
- **A power's round can floor what it hits.** A special's projectile now knocks down when its move says so, and a
  power's round passes through as many bodies as its card says. Before, a projectile knocked nobody down and
  stopped at the first body.
- **Projectiles are seen on a street.** A fighter's thrown special (a fireball, a villain's power) used to be
  invisible on a street's page. It is now drawn as a glowing shape the size of its hit box, in its thrower's power
  colour. A hero calling up a power flashes in that colour.
- **Measured, by a simple player that presses its power.** The studio's simple player now has a `hero` version.
  It uses its power when two or more enemies are lined up with room before the nearest, or three are around it.
  On the default street with the heroes tuning, one hero won alone with each power, losing two to four
  of its five falls (two or three with the super moment in). The plain player, which never uses a power, lost four.
  Four heroes together won with no falls (one with the super moment in),
  and a player that does nothing cleared no stop. On the street a superhero sentence makes, the hero player won with
  one fall. The plain player won there with none, so on that street the power is not yet shown to make the game
  easier. Seen on the page in headless Chrome: the beam flew in its colour down the line and hit, the storm flashed
  around the hero, the pips went from three to two, the heroes card's five hearts showed, and the page had no
  errors.
- **Fixed: a beat-em-up in the anime look could not be made.** Its heroes were drawn from an anime character
  sheet (anime hair, face and expressions) and then given the western head, which turned those words down, so making
  the game stopped with an error. An anime beat-em-up's heroes now keep the anime head on the brawler's body. A
  western one is unchanged.
- **Not yet:** the coin-op's foot soldiers were robots, and only a person's body stands on a street, so the army
  is people. The team is four, the street's seats, not six. A power has no fallback when its uses run out (it
  simply does not fire). Nobody has played it: the simple player shows a street can be won, not that it is fun.

### Invisible mode: walk a level unseen

A designer's walk, never a game's: a pilot whose rule carries `ghost` (`true` or `{ on }`) is seen by no guard while it
is on (`worlds/controllable/ghost.js`), so a level's layout and its watchers are read on foot without setting them off.
The guards walk their rounds, look round, call to each other, see a fallen teammate and wake a sleeper as they would.
On the page, I toggles it, and a badge at the top says which it is (`scene/channels/controllable/ghost-view.js`).

- It wraps the step just outside the patrol, so both the patrol's sighting and the mind's fail while it is on, and the
  alert's calm and hot sets, the alarm and the knockout's waking all read the guards' own sight. A guard toggled back
  to seeing sees at once.
- Emitted only into a page whose pilot carries `ghost`; every other page keeps every byte.
- The facilities spike's page (`scripts/spikes/mission/facilities.mjs`) starts invisible (`--seen` to start seen) and
  stands a sentry in each ground corridor beside the hall's guard; a chicane's corridor, with no straight line down it,
  is walked along its longest clear stretch.

### Racing: a track's design language, the runner's segment on a track, the race on the game UI

In progress. Built so far:

- **Built: a track's design language** (`roads/track-language.js`, a roadway's `language`). A card names a small family
  of materials (what each is, its finish, its colour) and the parts drawn in them: the way, its edge, the corners'
  kerbs, the rail, its posts and their caps. Two cards: `candy` (a kart track of moulded plastic: a pale way with a
  cream bead at each edge, striped pillows on the corners, one glossy tube rail on round posts with a ball on each)
  and `grand-prix` (a circuit: the look's own road and painted kerbs, a W-beam guardrail on steel posts). A rail wears
  its tell in stripes round the outside of a corner. A track from words takes its class's language; a track given none
  is drawn as it was.
- **Built: the language's laws** (machine; they advise): a premise said, a small family every part draws from, the
  rail and its post of one stuff, two finishes at most, the kerb read against the way, a tell that is not the rail's
  colour, a class it suits, and nothing drawn outside the family.
- **Built: the chunky look** (`roads/chunky-look.js`, a kit's `pole: 'chunky'`): smooth rounded polygons under a soft
  light, a gloss on plastics. A kart track from words is drawn so unless a word says otherwise ("voxel", "blocky" and
  "cubes" still give the cubes; "chunky", "rounded" and "plastic" name it). Its light is baked: not yet lit by the
  page as the kart is.
- **Built: a language's sky and what is seen to move.** The candy card says its own day (a blue sky over a pale
  horizon, a sun) and its clouds, built as the track is: puffs of rounded chunks in a ring round the course. Its way
  is laid in bands of two tones with a cream dash down the middle, and its verge is mown in stripes across the way,
  so the pavement and its sides are seen to move at speed.
- **Built: a corner told on the way, flags down a straight, trees built as the track is.** Chevrons on the way before
  each corner, pointing into it, on the outside half. Bunting on tall poles down one side of a straight, the side by
  turns. On the chunky look the land's trees are a stout trunk under a crown of balls set off-centre, no two alike, a
  share in blossom. The two sides of a track never mirror.
- **Built: the trackside in the language.** A language names a stand-in for each set piece and paints every surface
  group in its own materials, so the arch, the braking boards, the castle and the bumpers are of the track's family.
  Candy's: a fat hoop on two balls with a stripe and a banner hung off-centre, a lollipop board counting down in bars,
  a cream tower with a band, balls for battlements and a berry roof, a castle whose tall tower stands off its middle,
  bumpers of three rolls. The venue's own buildings take the family's paint too. Two primitives join the block library
  for them: a ball, and a ring with a round section (a square one, as before, unless it says).
- **Built: a kart track lit by the page, its sun casting** (the seventh generation's form render). A chunky track's
  faces are built in their colours alone, every part's normals kept, then baked as the gen 7 town's buildings are
  (`roads/track-form.js`): each corner its base and the day's light apart. The page lays the sun's shadow live: the
  static world into a map fitted to the track, drawn once, and the karts into a map that follows the action, each
  darkening only the sun's share of a corner's light, so a shadow is a soft blue. The sun stands at 36° so the rail,
  the posts, the balls and the arch lay shadows that read from the kart. The palette is held on what lies flat: the way,
  the kerbs and the verge show the card's own colours. A kart track from words is drawn so; "baked" bakes its light as
  before. The outdoor bake (`form/sun-light.js`) gains two opt-ins for it: a normal a corner for what is drawn smooth,
  and a reference face the colours are held on. A world's page keeps a builder's own fitted shadows, the live
  defaults filling what it leaves unsaid. The page weighs more with its per-corner light (about half again).
- **Built: the race's HUD on the game UI runtime** (`gameworld/race-hud.js`, hosted by the level page's HUD channel).
  Every roadway level raced by laps wears it: the place, large, over the field; the lap of the laps, this lap's time
  and the best; the track's map with you and the field on it; the speed on a dial; the final lap and the finish as
  moments. It keeps to the corners and the right edge, the way ahead and the kart left clear. The start is five lights
  on a plate, one a beat, out together for GO: the karts held and the world frozen with the race's clock until they
  go out (the race's time was counted from the page's first frame before). Read off the laps mechanic's own vars; the
  raw widget rows (Time, Lap, Place) stand down beside it. A tall frame lays the place and the lap on one plate at the
  top. Two looks for racing on the theme shelf: Candy Kart (`kart-candy`, the toy family, the candy track's own
  palette) and Pit Wall (`pit-wall`, the clean family: a timing tower, near-black and quiet), worn by a race by its
  track's language or class unless the world names a theme. The minimap gains a `route`: a way drawn under its markers
  as a dotted line, in the place of the blank map.
- **Built: a street circuit, a kart race through a toy town** ("a kart street circuit", "downtown", "through the
  streets"; the course preset `city-blocks`). The lap runs round a few blocks of a grid grown from one, its corners
  square (`roads/course.js` `designStreets`, its blocks kept on the course). Its town is laid from the geocity's ideas
  in the track's design language (`roads/street-frontage.js`, the `candy-city` card's `city`): rows of buildings face
  the way down each side of every straight, past the rail and a sidewalk; they rise toward the town's middle (shops at
  the edge, flats, a few towers at the core), never three of a kind in a row, each in a colour of the family by turns,
  never the one beside it, none standing in another. Lamps down the sidewalks by turns, a signal at the outside of
  every corner, a zebra across the way at each straight's start. The town is planned before the land round it, which
  keeps clear of it; a street circuit has no venue beside it, and its side pieces give way to its fronts. New blocks
  for it: a toy shop, toy flats, a toy tower, a lollipop lamp and a signal of three balls, each held to the block laws.
  A realistic street circuit ("a street circuit") gets the square course and no town yet: only the kart language has
  one.
- **Built: a split and an underpass on a street circuit** (`roads/street-features.js`, the language's `city.split` and
  `city.tunnel`). Before a corner a cobbled alley leaves the way and cuts across the corner's inside to the straight
  after it, leaving and rejoining along the way's own line; either way is the lap: the alley is drawn in the language
  (cobbles in two of its colours) and driven as road (its points join the drive surface), the rail opens at its two
  mouths, and no checkpoint stands between them. It is shorter than the way round but its cobbles drag (a new drive
  surface, `cobbles`), and two lemon boost pads with berry arrows lie down it: a racer over them gains on the turn, one
  who misses them loses (measured: a kart round the corner 11.8 s, down the alley over the pads 10.5 s, down it bare
  12.7 s). **Boost pads** are a track feature any drive can read: the drive rule gains an opt-in boost
  (`rules-drive.js`, through the world's `padAt`: a wheel on a pad lights a boost, its top and its pull past the kart's
  own while the throttle is held), the drive surface table carries a track's pads (`roads/surface.js` `padAt`), and a
  page wires the hook only when its track lays pads: a drive on a track without them is as it was.
  Down another straight a toy building spans the street, the way passing under its ground floor (the `toy-tunnel`
  block: two piers, a deck, the building over it, a berry band and a row of balls over each mouth, lamps along its
  ceiling); the page's shadow darkens it. The town gives way to both: its rows stop at the mouths and the underpass, and
  the alley has fronts and a sidewalk down its far side.
- **Built: a mine, a kart race inside a chocolate mountain** ("a kart race through a gem mine", "underground",
  "tunnels", "caves"; the `candy-mine` card's `mine`, `roads/mine.js`). Laid from what mojulo knew of the underground,
  the trail's caves and caverns (`era/cave.js`, `era/cavern.js`), in the track's family. The whole arena is
  underground: the lap runs round the floor of one great cavern (`mine.cavern`). Its outline is a ring round the lap
  as far out as the lap reaches and a margin, its walls lumpy up to a domed ceiling. Stalactites hang from the ceiling,
  stalagmites stand clear of the way, and the floor is the track's own ground repainted in the family's dust. Lantern
  posts lean over the rail down the lap, crystal clusters glow on the floor each in its own colour, and one skylight
  lets the day down a shaft toward the yard. A language may now lay its verge in one of its materials
  (`verge.material`): here the rock's colour, mown. No meadow, farm or lake surrounds it; the page's haze is the
  cave's dark, and the karts are lit dimmer than the open day. Through rock masses on its floor the lap runs into
  galleries bored under the rock, rising toward each gallery's middle and falling to its mouths as a hillside. A gallery is laid only where the way bends gently enough for its walls, never over the
  grid: the longest first, a short one after it. Each mouth is a biscuit-timber portal with a lemon board of gems. Inside:
  - the miners' sets (log posts and a cap with knees, every eight metres), marking the speed
  - lantern pairs over the kerbs
  - berry, lemon and cream gems glowing in the walls
  - a boarded floor past the way
  - a narrow-gauge cart line on the ledge, with carts heaped with gems

  Outside the longest gallery is the yard: a headframe with a berry wheel, carts and a heap of spoil. It is lit as a
  cave is lit. Under the hill a corner sees the day only through the mouths, less the deeper it is, and the lanterns
  lay warm pools in the cave's torch register and falloff, scaled to the bore's width as a big cave's lamps are. A light
  pass after the bake does it (`mineLight`), on the page-lit track and the baked one alike, with the gems and lanterns
  kept as their own light; in the cavern every corner's sky is the cave's dark and the sun reaches only down the
  skylight's shaft, where a kart casts its live shadow. The rail and its posts are the mine's timber. A mine
  has no venue beside it: the land, the set pieces and the trees keep clear of the hill and the yard.
- **Built: items, and the boxes that drop them** (`roads/kart-items.js`, a track's `items`; a kart track from words
  lays them, a level's roadway may say `items`). Rows of mystery boxes across the way on the straights, never on the
  grid. Each is a rounded golden core with a "?" on every face, inside a glassy shell lit at its rim in colours that
  run round it (a fresnel), turning on a tilted axis and bobbing: a thing to drive at. Driving through one takes an
  item if the kart holds none; the box pops and grows back. Three items in the candy family's words:
  - a sugar rush: a boost, the drive rule's own
  - a toffee: dropped behind, it slows and spins the kart that drives over it
  - a gumball: rolled ahead along the track's line, it knocks the first kart it meets

  What a box hands out depends on where the kart stands (catch-up): the race ranks the field by each kart's progress
  round the lap, and the last mostly draws sugar rushes while the leader mostly draws toffee (`catchup: false` draws
  flat). The pilot uses its item on F (or right Shift, or the pad's left face; the pilot scheme's `useItem`, on the pause
  sheet's controls), and rivals use theirs by judgement. The pause sheet lists the key on a race with boxes, and no
  longer lists the thrusters' F in a vehicle, where they never ran. The race HUD's held item is one large slot at the
  top's middle, there all race and in no words: dashed while empty; holding one, the item's pictogram fills it, its
  frame the accent, its key in the corner. The kart's juice pulses while one is held. Run by one step inlined on the page as the boost pads' is
  (`scene/channels/controllable/kart-items-view.js`), emitted only on a track with boxes. The roadway contract carries the rows.
- **Built: a pictogram for each item.** Three join the game UI's icon shelf (`mana-ui/icons.js`): a wrapped sweet with
  a bolt cut through it, a toffee splat with its droplets and shine, a gumball with its shine. The items name them,
  and the item ids alias them. The held-item slot is the pictogram, filling it. mana-ui's `slot` draws its
  pictogram where the theme has one (it drew initials) and takes a `size` (`l`, a slot read at a glance). Candy Kart now draws its
  pictograms in the chunky style, each in the colour of what it means, each readable on the berry plate: the sweet in
  the accent's lemon, the gumball in the second accent's sky (the gumball rolled on the track is sky now too), the
  splat in the cream ink.
- **Built: screen effects on the game UI** (mana-ui's `effect`, a HUD layer): confetti (falling from the top, popped
  from the centre or fired from the bottom), streamers, sparkles, a burst of stars, petals and a flash. Each plays
  once on a new trigger, or holds while it loops. Its pieces come from its own dice, in the theme's colours. It is pure
  CSS and never touches play: it catches no pointer, is laid out alone, moves transform and opacity only, pauses with
  a held clock, and plays only a fade under reduced motion. A race lays confetti on the finish and sparkles on a lap
  better than the best.
- **Spike: boxless UI** (`scripts/spikes/boxless-ui/`, not shipped). The race HUD drawn with its plates stripped and
  the decoration moved onto the letters, in four letter dresses (candy, sticker, chrome, extrude): a fill, rings, an
  extrusion and a drop, as one SVG filter a size. It covers about a third of the screen the boxed HUD does (18.1% to
  5–7% at the busiest moment). The rings scale with the type, or a small number reads as a chip. The README says what
  shipping it would take: a theme word `letters`, `hud: 'bare'` read by mana-ui's regions, the filters laid at mount,
  and a ring-contrast law.
- **The principles a new map starts from** ([docs/track-design-principles.md](../../../../docs/track-design-principles.md))
  and the agent's card for them (`gameworld-track-language`, read by the levels chapter): a premise first, a small
  family, a quiet way, a corner told three times, things seen to move, asymmetry, chunky, the track's own sky.
- **A roadway level's gate says more.** Its laws now carry the language's and the trackscape's beside the track's
  own, for a kart track and a circuit alike.
- **Fixed:** a world made from a track's words lost the track's drawing (its kit carried no pole).

The plan for the rest:

- A track's design language: one card says what a track is made of and how its parts are shaped (the way, the kerb,
  the rail, the post, the span, the sign), so its rails and its furniture are one family. A card a tuning to start:
  a candy one for a kart track, a grand-prix one for a circuit.
- A kart track's default look in the seventh generation: chunky, rounded, smooth polygons lit as the kart is. The
  voxel look stays, by word.
- The forward runner's segment on a track: the screen's thirds, the slice and its rhythm, the three depths, and a law
  for the least a segment must hold to be interesting.
- The race on the game UI: a race HUD (place, laps, times, speed, the track's outline, the start lights), results
  with the field, kart and track picks, and looks made for racing.
- The gate a made racing game is read by says the language's laws and the segment's, for a kart game and a realistic
  one alike.

### KO and kill: the sleep dart, knockouts, waking and dragging

- **Two ways down** (worlds/controllable/knockout.js, opt-in on the pilot's `rule.knockout`): a guard is KILLED by a
  gun's round (it falls and fades, as before) or KNOCKED OUT by stun. What stuns: the pilot's melee blows (fists, the
  knife), its takedown (takedown.js: with the knockout it knocks out where it killed), and a round from a slot whose weapon
  says `stun` (the sleep dart). What a stunning blow hurt is given back and stun taken in its place: a blow stuns
  `melee` (30) per point it would have hurt, so a jab, a cross and a hook knock a guard out; a dart stuns its damage, a
  body's whole most, and puts it to sleep after `drowse` (3 s; half a second in the head), the guard looking round
  meanwhile (startle.js). A stun short of a knockout ebbs once the guard has been left alone a while.
- **A sleeper sleeps for good**: on its back where it fell (the page's `e.tumble`), never stepped by its mind, never
  faded (its disposal put by), never counted by the alarm as a body found. A live teammate that SEES it (its reach, its
  cone, a clear line to the body lying there, past the colliders and the tall grass) walks to where it saw it, kneels over
  it (its gesture) for `wake` (2.5 s) and wakes it: it gets up, both search round there, and the team's alarm is raised.
  A sleeper gone from where it was seen when the waker gets there is searched for there instead; a waker that sees the
  pilot drops it for the pilot.
- **Dragging a body** (the action, near a sleeper, where no takedown is to be had): it trails a metre behind, its head
  to the hands that hold it, the pilot slowed to 1.4 m/s and holding its fire; the action again lets go. Dragged into
  tall grass or behind a wall, no guard finds it, so none wakes it.
- **The alarm's body found needs a clear line** (alarm.js): a downed body behind a wall or in tall grass is not found.
- **The sleep dart gun** (gameworld/arms-kit.js `dart`, shown as `dart gun`): a service pistol firing one quiet dart a
  load, four base rounds of stun (twice in the head), on the stealth rail's loadout before its handgun
  (gameworld/loadout.js `steel-serpents`). The operative of the infiltration room carries the knockout.
- **Shown** (scene/channels/controllable/knockout-view.js): z's drifting over a sleeper (growing over a drowsing guard), a
  waker's progress under them, and at the foot of the screen what the action does: drag the body, or let go.

### Level kinds: a rail's primitives, and the holding block

- **A rail's level kinds** (gameworld/level-kinds.js `LEVEL_KINDS`; rails.js `railSheet` carries them as `kinds`, the
  rail's card says them): the kinds of level a game of a rail's type is built from, each a primitive an agent picks by
  name with its shape, the verbs it teaches, what presses on the player there, the laws that prove one of it good, its
  status (built, a spike, or proposed with what it waits on) and where a level of it is made. A game is kinds in an
  order, and the order is its Game Brief's, never the rail's. Steel Serpents names seven: the approach (level 0), the
  compound (level 1's yard), the interior (the barracks, the hangar), the holding block (a spike), and, proposed, the
  gauntlet on alert, the moving checkpoint and the overwatch. A new kind is a row.
- **The kit taken** (worlds/controllable/carry.js `locked: '<item id>'`): until the mission holds that item, the weapon
  menu offers bare hands only and nothing is in hand; the moment it is held, the kit is back, its first slot in hand.
- **The holding block** (scripts/spikes/mission/holding.json, holding.mjs): a level of the new kind on the `cell-block`
  program, its design in the building's own room names. The operative wakes in the last cell of the east wing with the
  kit taken; the kit is on the processing desk; a turnkey walks the cell corridor end to end and a desk sergeant crosses
  the sally port, each looking round at its ends; the front door, reached holding the kit, ends it. Its laws are proved
  by the route search over the building's own walls (`--plan`): the straight way out is seen (by the turnkey at once), a
  way out unseen exists by the round alone (53 s, crouched behind the turnkey), the kit is on a way out, and so no way
  out needs a kill.

### The beat 'em up, the run and gun and Fable of Artesia, drawn as games

The shooting rails' and the cinematic action game's way of drawing a game's screens now reaches three more kinds of
game. This work is UI only: no rule, number or system has changed.

- **The HUD stays inside the game.** On a page whose world is a fixed frame, the beat 'em up's and the action
  adventure's HUD used to land in the dark margin around it. Every game's HUD is now laid inside the frame.
- **The street: the beat 'em up and the run and gun.**
  - **The players:** each player across the top is a name and a health strip in cells in that player's own colour,
    on one soft shade instead of a box each.
  - **The run and gun's gun:** shown as a drawing of the gun, with its rounds as a large figure over a row of
    cartridges (∞ for the sidearm) and its grenades as dots. The machine gun, spread gun and flamethrower have new
    drawings, and the counter no longer flashes red with every shot.
  - **Danger:** alone, the screen's edges close in red as health runs low; in co-op, the low player's bar beats.
  - **The fight:** the foe you are hitting is named, with a short health bar, and a combo count grows at your side
    with a word at each step ("Nice", "Great", "Wild").
  - **The way on** is a pulsing "GO ➜" at the right edge instead of a word over the fight. The boss's name stands as a
    title over its bar, its phases as ticks inside it, and the stages and foes left are marks without labels.
  - **Scenes:** the HUD clears the screen while a stage's title card plays.
  - **The end of a street** no longer reports "health 0" on a loss, and the rank is stamped.
  - **Choosing a gun** before a street shows each gun's drawing beside its name.
- **Fable of Artesia (the action adventure).**
  - **Hearts** empty by quarters, so a hit that takes part of a heart shows it.
  - **The sword, the bow and the item** sit small at the top right. Guard, sprint and lock are no longer drawn as
    items; their keys are on the controls screen.
  - **Stamina** is a ring by the hero's shoulder, shown only while it is used and red when nearly gone.
  - **Lock-on** draws brackets over the locked foe's head, with its health under them. Before, the lock sat at the
    foe's feet, and a second bar was drawn above it.
  - **A round map** at the bottom right turns with the hero and shows the foes and the way on.
  - **Messages** like "No healing draught left" sit at the bottom left, off the middle of the screen.
- **The cinematic action game's work comes with it:** the bullet-time ring, the weapon wheel and the redesigned pause
  arrive in the same change.

### People talking, drawn in the game's own look

The first step toward talking heads that any game can use: portraits, people talking, scripts played through talk
boxes, or the same scene acted out in the world.

- **The talk box is drawn as part of the game's interface.** In a designed game, a level's scenes now show their lines
  in the same look as the game's menus and HUD, instead of a plain box of their own.
  - The speaker's name is a nameplate on the box.
  - The line types on, and a ▼ shows once it is whole.
  - Choices are numbered, with the one in hand marked.
  - The bar at the foot says which keys do what; a touch screen shows none.
  - The level's HUD steps aside while a scene plays, as it always did on pages without the game's interface.
- **Whoever speaks is shown in the box.** Their own character, head and shoulders, appears live beside their words:
  what they do in the world (standing, breathing, acting a scene) is what the picture shows.
  - A level's speakers sheet can show someone by the box alone, for a scene that is already close on their face.
  - Someone with no body in the level, or the player seen from their own eyes, has no picture.
- **Faces say their lines.** A character with a realistic, an anime or the default (landmark) face now moves their
  face as they speak: their mouth follows the words, their face takes the line's expression (worried, determined and so
  on), and they blink as a speaking face does. The default face opens its jaw on the words. It shows in the world and
  in the talk box's picture. Lines written as a script keep the acting they already had.
- **Recorded voices, if you want them.** A line can carry a recording (a WAV from the voice worker, another speech
  engine or a person). It is saved with the world, the level plays it as the line begins and stops it when the line
  moves on, and the speaker's lips follow the recording. A level can also note which voice each character is cast in.
  Lines without a recording stay silent, as before. A browser plays no sound until the player has clicked or pressed a
  key, so a line that starts before then is picked up partway through.
- **Nothing else changes.** Advancing, holding to skip, Esc and picking a choice by number, arrows or a click work as
  before. A world without the game's interface keeps its box as it was, though its characters' faces now talk too.

### Offshore rigs: a level of open decks over the sea

A stealth level of no walls. A rig (`lib/graph/offshore/`) is decks stacked over the sea, laid from three tiles and the
modules on them, held to the laws a sneaking body needs, and built as a played page. Craft in `docs/offshore-rigs.md`.

- **The tiles** (`offshore/tiles.js`):
  - Floors: plate, grating and the helideck, a glyph each in a deck's map.
  - Rails: a guard rail stops a body and no gaze, a bulwark hides a crouch, a wind screen hides a standing body.
  - Pillars: a leg runs from the sea bed through every deck; a column carries one deck from the next one down.
  - Modules stand on the tiles. What each hides is read from its height.
- **The plan** (`offshore/plan.js`): decks as maps of glyphs at their heights, with legs, stairs and modules. The rails
  and the columns are found, not written:
  - A rail runs along every open edge except a stair's head: the deck's own kind, a wall kind on the side it faces,
    an inner kind round a hole.
  - A column stands at every n-th node, on the deck under it or the sea bed. It never drops through a moonpool and
    never stands in a flight.
  - A stair is a switchback of three cells by two, with its well cut through the deck it climbs to.
- **The laws** (`offshore/laws.js`): railed, joined, carried, stairs-clear, modules-placed, sight-broken and
  cover-in-reach.
- **Built** (`offshore/build.js`): faces shaded once under the sun, each deck shadowing the ones under it. Decks,
  pillars, walls and modules are colliders. Guard rails and a stair's sides are barriers. The sea is a sheet of ocean
  water. A tread's box stands a quarter metre under the tread drawn over it, so a body's footprint spanning two treads
  climbs.
- **The drilling platform** (`offshore/rigs.js`) has four decks:
  - The boat landing.
  - The cellar deck, a forest of columns under the main deck.
  - The main deck's yard, its quarters, and a hall of columns under the drill floor.
  - The drill floor under its derrick, with the helideck beside it.

  Each deck has rounds watching it, and the route search finds a way across unseen on every one.
- **In the game book**: the facility maps book draws the rigs after the facilities: each deck from above
  (`offshore/map.js`) with its rounds, and the rig's laws beside them.
- The spike `scripts/spikes/mission/rig.mjs` proves the plan (`--plan`) and builds the page (`--out`), starting in
  invisible mode.
- **Night, floods and rain.** A rig names its `hour` (day or night), its `weather`, its `floods` and its `fittings`:
  - Floods stand on a deck at a height, aimed, drawn as a pole and a burning lens. Fittings hang under a deck over
    another.
  - Every face is baked under the hour's sky and moon plus each lamp that reaches it, never through a deck's floor.
  - Rain wets the tiles open to the sky: darker, with the page's wet film throwing the floods back.
  - The rain falls nowhere under a deck. Each deck's floor is a roof to the weather channel, which now keeps its
    landing rings out from under a roof too, as it did its falling drops.
  - The drilling platform is now a rainy night lit by eight floods. The dark between the pools is a look, not yet cover:
    a guard's sight does not read light.

### The reactive top layer: screen effects that act on the picture (spike)

In progress. Built so far:

- **Spike: what a layer of CSS can do to a game's own picture** (`scripts/spikes/reactive-layer/`, not shipped). Over
  a world drawn by the World page's own emitter, sixteen screen effects are laid by CSS alone, after the page draws:
  - harm: hurt
  - impact: a blow at a point, chroma, a shock ring, lightning
  - power: gather, level up
  - state: a blackout iris
  - status: poison, frozen
  - place: under water
  - time: slow motion
  - focus: a scope, an x-ray lens, night vision

  There are four ways to reach the world's pixels: a blend, a backdrop region, the canvas filtered or moved, and a
  point the game projects. Each was probed in Chrome, with its relative cost measured. The finding that decides the
  design: a layer that blends with the world must not be its own stacking context (the HUD's root and the confetti's
  are), or every blend mixes with nothing. `FINDINGS.md` says what works, what does not (refraction round a point
  through an SVG image map), what each costs, and the primitive it argues for: a screen layer beside the HUD.
- **Built: the lens, mana-ui's screen layer, for turn-based fights.** A spec's `lens` is a second part of the runtime
  (`rt.lens()`, mounted apart with `part: 'lens'`), laid beside the world's canvas and under the UI, its root never its
  own stacking context (`lensCss`), so its regions act on the world's own pixels.
  - **Its first effect, the `strike`:** the air round a figure on the screen bent and lit (`ring`), lit (`lift`),
    darkened (`shade`) or turned to its negative for a beat (`ink`; a lift under less flash). Each row may name its own
    kind. Each strike is a region the band's size, at most a few at once, held with a held clock, and fading in place
    under less motion.
  - **For still figures, so never in an action game.** A region is drawn where the figure was last projected: a figure
    that stands while the round plays is where it says, and one that runs outruns it. An action level's hits are
    answered by the world already, so the level HUD carries no lens.
  - **In the RPG's battles, a juice step:** `{ lens: ring | lift | shade | ink, at?: target | actor }` draws round the
    figure for the beat. By default a miss bends the air round its target and a cast lights the air round its caster.
  - **It never overlaps the world's own effects:** its mask's hole is the figure's body, and a lens step yields where
    the beat's world answers (a flash over the field, a puff on the same figure, a beam landing on it).
  - **Proved in Chrome** in a party fight (`scripts/spikes/reactive-layer/lens-proof.mjs`): each kind round the struck
