    figure, and nothing on a hit that flashes the field.

### Glass and mesh: barriers a gaze goes through

Every wall stopped sight, so a guard was only ever read through a doorway. Glass and mesh now stand in a body's way and
not in a gaze's.

- **Barriers in the runtime** (`worlds/controllable/barrier.js`, opt-in): a world's `barriers` are kept apart from its
  colliders, so every sight test runs through them, and after each step every body standing in one is put back out of
  it, as a wall would hold it. A round goes through. Emitted only into a page whose world has barriers.
- **Inner windows** (`era/inner-windows.js`, a program's `windows`): glass between a room and its corridor, on the
  longest stretch its doorway leaves, sill to head, cut in both walls, glazed by the kit's own glazing with no daylight
  beyond it, its pane a barrier.
- **Mesh** (`compose-dress.js` `mesh-panel`, a piece that is `see`: its anchor a barrier, never a collider) and the
  **cage** layout (`era/room-layouts.js`): a ring of mesh inset from a room's walls, each side drawn in until it stands
  clear of the doorways' approaches and the vents' hatches, a gate in its long side, its stock in rows inside. A room's
  laws and the route search count mesh and glass as in the way and stopping no gaze.
- **The armoury** joins the facilities: its cage rooms and its vault caged, its magazine in crate clumps, its issue and
  cleaning rooms windowed onto the corridor; the research wing's labs and the field HQ's offices are windowed too.
- Each storey's crawl spaces, vents and barriers now reach the page lifted to their storey (the ground's alone did).
  The facility maps draw windows as pale bars and mesh as dashed grey lines.
- **Cages closed and roofed.** A piece can be stretched to a length of its own (`w`, `d` on an item: `footprintOf`
  and its parts follow), mesh abuts mesh, and the cage tiles each side edge to edge, its long sides run out over the
  corners and its end sides fitted between them, so the ring is closed but for its gate. A roof of mesh tiles
  (`mesh-roof`, laid overhead: an item's `over`, taking no floor and stopping no gaze) covers the whole ring at the
  panels' head, so no body climbs in over it.

### The side map's HUD: Galaxy Boy read as an 8-bit action platformer

Galaxy Boy's side map level gets its own look and a HUD on mana-ui. Before, it showed the level page's generic HUD: a
lives box, the boss's name with its figures, a radar, a melee ring and a strip of key hints.

- **The `galaxy` look** (`playscape/ui/theme-cards/galaxy.json`, from `console`): navy plates with a square edge,
  energy in yellow and cyan, a boss's in red, a monospace face in capitals, stepped motion, screens that shutter. The
  platformer's rail writes it on a side map game (`SIDE_MAP_LOOK`); the mascot platformer keeps Hilltop.
- **The side map's HUD** (`gameworld/side-map/hud.js`, given as a side map level's `manaHud` when the game has a `ui`):
  - the hero's energy is a column of fine ticks at the top left, split into one block a life;
  - a special weapon's energy stands beside it in the weapon's tint, while the hero holds a gun with energy of its own
    (there are none yet: the column is ready for them);
  - the boss's column stands at the top right, opposite, once the boss is awake and near, and its name is said across the top;
  - READY flashes as the level starts and after a life is lost;
  - the keys show as key caps for the first seconds;
  - the radar and the melee ring are put away.
- **The HUD host** (`scene/channels/mana-hud.js`) takes a HUD's own `css` laid over the sheet, and feeds `sm.*` from
  the level's `lives` and `boss_<n>`, the held gun's energy and the boss's waking and distance.

### A stealth level's sound: music that follows the alarm, the garrison and the mission heard

- **The alarm on the bus** (worlds/controllable/alarm.js, castFacts wrapped): `alarm:detected`, `alarm:found` and
  `alarm:clear` as its phase turns, `alarm:call` as a guard starts the radio call, `alarm:cut` as the caller is put down
  first, `alarm:sweep` each time the searchers spread again, `alarm:backup` as backup is sent. A bus that has not yet
  heard an alarm hears it from rest, so its first turn is never lost.
- **The mission on the bus** (worlds/controllable/mission.js, castFacts wrapped): `mission:item`, `mission:clue`,
  `mission:reveal`, `mission:ride`, `mission:hint`, `mission:exit`, `mission:done`.
- **Any bus event voiced by a shelf word** (beats-world.js, the sound sheet's `events: { '<event glob>': '<shelf word>' }`):
  each word a cue of the level's (`ev-<word>`), over the mechanics' own.
- **A page whose audio listens carries the bus** (scene-three.js): where its sfx's `on` or its tension's `on` names an
  event, the events channel is emitted to carry the cast's happenings, even on a page with no reaction of its own; until
  now such a page's music never heard a sighting. Never on a capture run. Every other page byte for byte.
- **Level 0 scored** (the spike's `audio`): the field's `tension` while sneaking and its `battle` once the garrison has
  found the player, the alarm's turns and sweeps raising the score's tension and a glimpse a little, the gorge's wind and
  a low forest bed; a guard's glimpse the alert's sting, a threat detected the dread, the radio's call a click, a threat
  found the siren, a guard put down a thud, a thing taken the pickup, an exit the door, the steps on grass, the pistol.
  Proved on the page: spotted, the combat score comes in on the bar; hidden, the alarm falls to detected and the
  tension leaks back toward the explore score.
- **The first sighting, once** (`alarm:spotted`, alarm.js): said as the garrison leaves calm because a watcher saw the
  intruder, never at each glimpse after; level 0's sting plays on it (a glimpse still raises the score's tension a
  little).
- **Less of the land, more of the game**: level 0's wind at -40 dB (the default's -30) and the forest's birds at 0.12 (they
  were 0.35), so the score and the game's own sounds lead.

### Tall grass: cover a body hides in

- **A geocube's tall grass** (`tallGrass: { patches: [{ at, r, h? }], elsewhere?: 'none' | 'grass' }`, form/tall-grass.js):
  grass in tight clumps only where the level lays it, standing to its height (1.2 m), drawn at every distance; no blades
  anywhere else, so a gen-7 land keeps its look at a fraction of the grass's cost.
- **It hides** (worlds/controllable/veil.js, an opt-in runtime module; the engine hands minds a world's `veils`): each patch is a VEIL, a column of grass a watcher's
  sight reads. A line from a watcher's eye to a body's that runs `through` metres (1.2) of grass under its top does not
  see it, so a body crouched or lying in a patch, or low behind one, is unseen; standing, its eye is over the grass; within
  `near` (2 m) it is seen whatever; a lookout on a tower looks down into the grass and sees a crouch, not one lying flat.
  The world carries `veils`; the minds' `perceive` asks them.
- **The route search reads them too** (gameworld/stealth-routes.js `place.veils`), so a sneak's level is proved with its
  grass.
- **It stands where it grows.** The land read says how each patch stands (its share of level green ground, where its
  grass grows, and that ground's height); the veil stands on that ground, and a patch with under half of it grown is no
  veil, so the page never hides a body where it shows no grass.
- **Level 0 laid with it** (the spike's `level0.json` `grass`): a practice patch by the trail with its hint, a belt
  along the checkpoint truck's south face and behind it, and one down the camp's west side; no grass anywhere else. The
  checkpoint's second way now crouches through the grass at the truck. The build says each patch's share of level
  ground, and the plan draws the land's relief (a bank's cells lit and shaded) so a patch is not laid on one.
- **The geocube card** (`sketch-vocab/geocube.md`) teaches `tallGrass`.
- **Thinner**: the stand's clumps set 0.336 m apart, not 0.26 (three fifths as many a square metre).
- **A road whose rocks are drawn** (a geocube's `path.rubble: 'parallax'`, era/trail-dress.js): no stone stood up on the
  trail or its verge (none strewn by the stage, none of the form render's, its scree's kept off it too:
  form/land-stones.js `offTrail`); its pebbles marched in the ground's parallax instead, in clusters over a third of it
  (form/land-read.js ROAD_PEBBLES), the verge's scree texture lighter. Level 0's trail is laid so.
- **A lean ground** (a geocube page's `parallax: false`, channels/form-land.js): none of the ground's height marched near
  the eye (the scree's, the clay's, the undergrowth's and the rock's parallax, the procedural pebbles' and cracks'), the
  pebbles and cracks on the trail alone. Measured by hiding each kind of thing on level 0's page in turn, the ground was
  over half its frame (the jungle a tenth); lean, the frame fell about a fifth. Absent, every byte as it was.
- **A page's pixel density** (a geocube page's `density`, 0.75 to 2): the pixel budget's cap, 1.5 unless said (the same
  bytes). Level 0 asks for 1, so its full window on a high-DPI screen shades fewer pixels than a boxed page at 1.5.
- **Level 0 on open ground**: the jungle haze's look over the upland's flora (lone trees, short grass) with no cliff walling
  the trail, so the land is a field both sides and every patch of tall grass stands wholly on level ground. Its laws hold;
  the checkpoint's first unseen way now crouches through the truck's grass.
- **The spike's bench** (scripts/spikes/mission/bench.mjs): pages timed side by side in headless Chromium at one window
  and one density, a relative yardstick. Hangar 229 ms a frame; level 0 as it was 283, open and lean 199.
- **Tall grass among a field's grass** (`tallGrass.elsewhere: 'grass'`): the patches the tall sward and the stand, the land's
  own grass round them the short sward, thinned (six bristles a cell, no dark twin: form/tall-grass.js `fieldOf`), so grass
  that hides nothing is never drawn as grass that does. Until now the field took the stand's clump at every distance.
- **Level 0's checkpoint a line** across the whole field (wire to both edges, sandbags and a gate on the trail, the tower,
  the truck on the line) with two ways through besides the gate: the slot by the truck, screened by grass both sides and
  in it, and a cut in the west wire behind its grass, the line's patrol walking past it. All eight laws hold. The field's
  grass back, real out to 10 m (the view cone), painted past it: bench 246 ms a frame against the hangar's 236.
- **A lean ground keeps its cliffs plain** (`parallax: false`): no relief cut into a cliff's faces (each steep triangle
  was cut into 36) and a third of its scree's stones stood up (form/land-read.js `stones`, a share of them). Benched at a
  quarter of the window, a cliff's cost was its geometry more than its pixels.
- **Level 0 boxed in a gorge** (the spike's `gorge`: a cliff face down each side of the field, 14 m, the high side out,
  as the trail's ground edits): the field between them as it was, every law holding. Bench: hangar 231 ms a frame, the
  open field 237, the gorge 248 (with relief and the full scree it was 345).
- **The bench** opens each page in a browser of its own (one opened after another ran slower) and counts draws only
  after the frames are timed.
- **Level 0 cut again** (the spike's `performance`): its real grass out to 6 m, not 10 (painted past it), and its pixel
  density 0.85. Bench, each page its own density (`bench.mjs --dpr page`, new): 219 ms a frame as it was, 195 now; the
  hangar 259 on the same run. The live light off was tried and bought nothing (its bodies cast blob shadows, so the map
  draws next to nothing). The opening view side by side reads the same. `level0.mjs --perf '{…}'` tries a setting over
  the recipe's without editing it.
- **Grass is cover, and only cover** (a geocube's `tallGrass.elsewhere: 'paint'`, form/tall-grass.js): the land's own grass
  kept as its colour on the ground from the eye out (the far field's blanket brought to the feet, channels/far-field.js;
  the short sward's tier built no blade, channels/form-grass.js), so the field reads as grass and only the patches, the
  cover, stand. Level 0 laid so: no short grass anywhere (`none` left the field bare earth, dark under where the blades
  had been).
- **Far figures** (a geocube level's `farFigures: { at?, budget? }`, worlds/world-scene.js, controllable/merged-figure.js
  `farFigureScript`): each body no player pilots baked a second time coarse (figures/figure-lod.js `loose`: welded by
  position alone, no edge locked, so a dressed figure's seams and hems no longer hold it: the guard 39070 triangles to
  4498) and drawn past `at` metres from the eye (24; two metres' grace back), the same bones posed each frame, shown only
  while its body is. Level 0 asks for it, and its haze drawn in (visibility 180 m, clear 30) so the far land and what
  stands on it fade and the far flora is culled. Bench, all at one density: 199 ms a frame (the last cut) to 176, its
  triangles 0.95M to 0.60M; in play the six guards past 24 m are drawn at 4498 each.
- **Level 0's middle** (after level 1 was measured beside it: the yard 372 ms a frame, the hangar 251, level 0 171): what
  the cut had overdone given back where it shows. The gorge's walls rock again (a geocube's `parallax: 'cliffs'`: the
  ground lean, its rock kept: the fractured plates over it, `wK2`, the blocks a wall reads by; the rock's own march near
  the eye; its cliffs' relief at a 3 x 3 cut, not 6 x 6, a quarter of its triangles: channels/form-land.js,
  worlds/world-scene.js). Found by elimination: the relief alone at any cut and the march alone left the walls plaster;
  the plates are the look. The operative's own live shadow, every guard a pool at its feet (a page's
  `shadows.actors: 'pilot'`: scene/live-light.js, controllable/index.js `__pilotCasts`, suit-shadows.js `others`).
  Density 1; the haze out to 250 m, the base seen at the trail's end. Bench at one density: 247 ms a frame (172 lean,
  264 with the whole ground's relief), the hangar 265.
- **The bench corrected** (scripts/spikes/mission/bench.mjs): a page runs several animation loops (the game's, its
  HUD's, its readouts'), each called with the frame's one timestamp, and the bench counted every call a frame, so every
  page read faster than it ran and a page with more loops faster still. Frames are now counted by their distinct
  timestamps. Read again at one density: the hangar 2.66 s a frame in software, level 0 lean 3.67, the yard 4.61, level 0
  as committed 6.17 (the middle above read 247 ms against the hangar's 265: wrong). Taken apart, the ground's material is
  about three quarters of level 0's frame; the plates and the rock's march about a twentieth; the live shadows' passes,
  the figures' light and the grass next to nothing.
- **Layers** (scripts/spikes/mission/layers.mjs): a built page with a panel that takes it apart on the machine it is played
  on: each layer of the scene on or off (the ground, the grass, stones and plants, trees and far sheets, structures,
  characters, the rest, each with its triangles), the ground as plain paint, the live shadows' passes, the haze, the HUD,
  the pixel density, and a frame readout that counts each frame once; a line to copy back. The level is not changed.
- **What made level 0 slow was its rays, not its pixels** (channels/controllable/index.js): with every layer of the page
  off (the layers panel, played on the person's own machine) it still ran at 8 frames a second. Profiled, seven tenths of
  its time was rays tested against triangles: the ground probe under each walker every frame, the camera's pull-in.
  The ground grid (ground-grid.js, a straight-down ray testing only the cells it crosses) indexed the big static meshes
  once, at the first probe, before the gen-7 land was built, so the land the walkers stand on (43k and 32k triangles)
  took three's own raycast, every triangle, every probe; it now indexes again whenever the scene's top changes and every
  120 probes (ray time over eight seconds 242 ms to 27). And every ray through the world leaves the bodies out
  (`__rayRoots`), whose hits each threw away after testing their every triangle, a skinned body's posed by its bones
  first. What each ray finds is as it was.
- **What a frame costs, by side** (`window.__mojCost`, channels/controllable/index.js, scene-three.js's frame loop): a page
  with controllable bodies keeps the game's logic a frame (its step), its rays alone (the ground probe, the camera's) and
  the render call's own time, each a running mean; the spike's corner readout, the layers panel and the bench say them
  (a level slow with nothing drawn is its logic, not its looks). And each big mesh a ray tested triangle by triangle, by
  name (`slow`: the grid's slow path, only where a ray reached the mesh).
- **The ray budget, guarded** (controllable/ray-budget.chrome.test.js, the e2e tier): a walker on a gen-7 land in headless
  Chrome; no ray may test a big mesh triangle by triangle. With the grid indexed once, as before, it names the land's two
  meshes and fails.
- **The ground's index** (channels/controllable/ground-index.js): the ground probe under each walker reads the surfaces over
  its own 4 m cell and tests those alone (a big static one through its own triangle grid), never a ray through the whole
  scene. Every mesh a world ray would test is baked into the index with the grid, and again when the scene's surfaces
  change; one wider than the index (a far land's ring) is in every cell; a surface that moves after the bake is noticed
  once a frame and tested wherever it stands. What it finds is what the full-scene ray found (tested point by point
  against it in three: a floor on its grid, a deck by a transform, instanced steps, a decoration that is no footing, a
  body, a far plane, the deck moved).
- **The grid for every big mesh** (controllable/ground-grid.js `__gridRaycast`): a mesh placed by a transform, or moved
  since, takes its grid (the ray carried into its own frame, a distance along it the world's), and one of several
  materials too (each face its group's side); three's own raycast had taken them triangle by triangle. Tested ray by ray
  against three on a placed, a mirrored and a two-material mesh. The hangar's columns and painted walls were its rays'
  slow meshes (`__mojCost.slow`), 11.7 ms of a frame's 16 in rays.
- **A meadow round the cover** (a geocube's `tallGrass.elsewhere: 'meadow'`, form/land-read.js): the land's own grass as
  level 1's yard has it, real blades at their full clump in its own short and medium areas, never tall: the tall sward
  is the patches' alone, the cover. Level 0 laid so, its grass at the page's own reach again (the cut to 6 m and the
  painted field were the ray cost misread as the grass's).
- **The grid for every mesh of two hundred triangles** (ground-grid.js `__gridMeshes`, a thousand before): an indoor camera's
  rays crossed many smaller walls and props, each tested triangle by triangle; the hangar's rays a frame 3.7 ms to 1.8.
  And the grid is built by the camera's first ray too, so none of its rays before the first ground probe goes slow.
- **One far grass** (a geocube's `farGrass: 'lift'`, worlds/world-scene.js; channels/far-field.js `farBlanketGlsl`,
  far-lift.js, form-grass.js): the far grass was three at once (the blanket's painted colour with its flecks, flowers
  and weeds; the tall cover's blades standing out of it at every distance; and, where asked, the lift), so the eye read
  them apart. Now, past the view's reach, the far lift alone (the ground raised to the grass's mean height, taller over
  tall cover, filling in as the blades thin, so they are never seen to stop), coloured calm (the blanket's colour, no
  speck), and the near blades, the cover's included, end at the reach. The lift was a land's opt-in no recipe could ask
  for; the word wires it. Level 0 asks for it.
- **The camera in on the body** (gameworld/infiltration-room.js, every level of the starter): four fifths of the feel's
  distance and height, its angle kept, so the operative is more of the frame and less of it is ground to paint.
- **One far grass, tuned** (`farGrass: { as: 'lift', blades?, raise? }`): `blades` the share of the view's reach the
  blades are drawn whole to (0.42 to 0.9; 0.42 before, where each tile dropped to half its clumps and the rest shrank
  away, the band where grass is seen coming and going), the lift beginning there; `raise` the lift's height over the
  grass's mean (1 to 4, 1.5 before), so far off it reads as a raised platform. Level 0: blades 0.7, raise 2.5.

### The traditional side-scroller map: a level as the camera's path, Galaxy Boy's first

Built through its render benchmark: the principles, the strip's seams, Galaxy Boy's game body, the side map from its
words to a game's level its bot plays, and the benchmark that measures its frames. Lit by its lamps and the cube's sky. Not yet: a foreground and things that
move beside the way, the hero under the cast rig, the boss's fight in its room, the hero's climb seen from behind, a metroidvania's rooms on a grid.

- **The principles, written first** (`docs/side-map-principles.md`): the map as the camera's path, the screen as a
  measure, teaching by stakes, going up earned, falls and ladders, the closed parts painted, the look, and who makes it
  (a level form of the cube's space, its look reality's through the geocube).
- **The side strip's seams, mended.** A rolling trail on a strip rolls and no longer sinks: a drop that would take a
  floor under the strip's ground is taken only as far as it, its gap sized from the hero's reach at that height
  (`course.js` `coursePlan`'s `floor`); every default 2D first level's basic trail ended 1.5 m under the ground, its
  floors lowered to boxes upside down. A course's floor is never lowered to a box whose bottom stands over its top. A
  strip's segments are held to a JOIN law where they meet its ground (`joinLaw`: a drop is free, a step up one the
  running jump makes); the strip's laws gain a `join-in` and a `join-out` a segment.
- **Galaxy Boy's body: the toy hero robot, a game body of its own** (`game-bodies.js` `herobot`, the soul facet's new
  body word): too real for the mascot's chibi. The herobot proportions under the anime form's bare head (a head cast's
  body tune undid them: the door's default, Shonen High, stretched the figure to 4.9 heads; bare it stands about four
  and a half, 1.75 m), on the game body at the current laws. Galaxy Boy's feel and the metroidvania genre read it, and
  the platformer's rail writes it on a Galaxy Boy book (`platformerBody`); Jumping Giuseppe stays a mascot.
- **The toy hero robot dressed from the libraries.** Its helm a headgear card (`heroBotHelm`: a face window, cheek
  guards curled under the jaw, ear domes, a raised V over the brow round a gem), worn in the robot's own armour groups so
  the hero's palette paints it with the suit. Its body armour a fourth armour family beside plate, lamellar and hardsuit:
  **toy** (`armor/toy.js`), moulded volumes whose read is girth contrast (balls on the shoulders, a barrel chest,
  forearms swelling to a flared cuff, boots widening to half-egg soles, a brief, knee caps, a collar, and at ornament 2
  the chest's plaques and the thigh rims), `mass` how far each swells past its limb; its seeded card `herobot`. The

- **The hero collides as tall as it stands.** Every level's hero collided as a 1.7 m person whatever its body. A hero's

  through anything; let go, the highest level reached fires, on the lab's beat (a level's frames after the press; a frame

  the charge's colours, its charge lighting the hero juice's sparks; composed into a page only where a body carries one.
- **The arm cannon** (`cannon: 'R' | 'L'`, the toy family's): one form with the forearm, the forearm's line carried on
  past the wrist over the hand to a muzzle with its lip and the bore dark in its face, on a BONE OF ITS OWN
  (`polygonizer/hero-buster-rig.js`: wrist to knuckles, riding the hand, appended after every other bone at pack time,
  every clip keying it). The hand becomes the cannon while the buster is out: on the page the cannon's bone grows to
  whole and the hand's shrink away (charging, or a shot just fired), and the skinned GLB carries the same swap as

- **A level seen as an elevation.** The course map's sibling: a side-scroller's level as the camera's path through the
  along × up plane, a chain of zones (runs one screen thick, rooms that scroll both ways, full-screen corners), built
  only where the camera can see. Across develops, down is free or a commitment, up is earned.
- **Keyed in the cosmos cube**, so the studio can lay one for any game: the side map a level form of space
  (`space.levelForm=side-map`, partial: written and read, not yet laid; priced as the `side-map` package, requiring a
  side camera and the platform rule) and its closed parts' fills reality's (`reality.fill`: none, or rock, built,
  machine, padded, a row each in `side-map/fills.js`; the painting absent). The words a map writes
  (`gameworld/side-map/zones.js`): a chain of runs (across, up, down; a length in screens) and rooms (a size), each with
  what it teaches (the first level's words) or a beat (rest, reveal, landing, commit), an up run's climb (ledges, a
  switchback, a chimney, a stair, a ladder; `rises`: the screen from below), a down run's drop (a cascade, or a chute:
  a commit), its place and fill, its spawners, pillars and ceiling; refused with teaching.
- **The layout** (`gameworld/side-map/layout.js`): a zone chain laid on the along × up plane in screens and the hero's
  reach, each zone from where the walk left the last. An across run is the course for what it teaches at its length
  (its gaps open to the frame's bottom: pits; `pillars` a pit crossed on tops a jump apart; `ceiling` a held one); an
  up run a shaft narrower than a screen, its walls closed out to the frame's edges, climbed as a chimney (rests on
  alternate walls within three kicks, a pickup on each), ledges, a switchback, a stair or a ladder; a down run a
  cascade of steps or a one-way chute shut at its foot; a room its size, a boss's shut behind its door. Each zone says
  what the camera sees (its swept area, one screen thick on its locked axis), what the play moves in and what is
  closed, its checkpoint, and what it could not fit (a run too short for what it teaches is laid as one floor, and
  says so).
- **The dress** (`gameworld/side-map/dress.js`): the design that makes a side map look good, dealt over the layout as
  data the build paints from and the laws read, placing nothing. A premise names its setting (a plant, a mountain, a
  temple, a base; a new setting is a row), and the setting deals a place a zone by its role (an across run, a climb, a
  drop, a room), never the same place twice running, each a material family and a key colour, the places' order the
  story. The closed parts lighter than the dark open space; play and place on opposite hues; the boss's colour unused
  until the zones that lead to its room, growing toward it, its mark across its room's back wall. A run's back wall in
  bays a screen and a quarter wide by the walls' rule, a pillar between, a lamp an A bay, a hatch at each spawner; the
  next place's family and key at a zone's last half screen; the setting's pipes, cables, roots or channels threaded
  from zone to zone; a shaft's railings stepping up its back wall, its top lit, a chute striped; what the stage is about
  shown small, then large, then whole in the boss's room; an outdoor zone's backdrop by the height it stands at; wear one
  dial a place.
- **The screen as a measure** beside the hero's reach (`gameworld/side-map/screen.js`): what one screen is in metres for
  a side camera at 16:9, the camera that holds a hero at an eighth of the frame's height with the lane two thirds down
  it (for the toy hero robot's 1.67 m, 22.8 m back and a screen 13.4 m by 23.8 m), and a distance read in screens.
- **Going up, earned.** Climbs in their forms (ledges, a switchback, a chimney with rests, a stair, a ladder, pillars
  over a gap), light at the top of every climb, a backdrop that knows how high the hero is, and the screen from below:
  a climb's frame that rises on its own.
- **The path, designed from the top down** (`gameworld/side-map/path.js`), considered and never scattered: an across
  run's floor shaped on its own BAY GRID, the one the back wall's pillars and seams stand on (`bayGrid`, the dress lays
  them on it too), so the floor keeps the walls' rhythm. Its PROFILE says what happens at each pillar and at each seam
  and gives the whole run one step HEIGHT, a share of the hero's jump, as a stair's steps are all one rise: a rest's low
  terraces walked up, never jumped (under what the body steps up by itself: nothing asked), the basics rolling up at each seam and down at each pillar, a fight's raised block centred on every seam,
  the dash's runways level between steps at its pillars, a gauntlet's blocks on its seams and steps at its pillars, a
  landing's one rise, a boss's floor one floor; toward a climb its steps go up, toward a drop down, inside the frame the
  camera holds; never at a pit's lip or on a dash's runway. A new law, `varied`: no run (but a landing's and a boss's
  floor) more than a screen and a quarter of one smooth floor; `reach` reads every step up. The bot hops them and still
  plays Galaxy Boy's first level to its end without a fall. Measured on it, a light bug mended: a face lit as the zone
  it is part of, not the first whose camera area holds it (a boss's floor had been lit as the chute before it).
- **The cap** (`paint.js` `SIDE_CAP`): every top a hero stands on is a designed surface, never one smooth band of the
  zone's colour. Its band down the lit edge and the walking surface itself are cut in segments on the fill's own module
  and grid: a built run's coping in half bond with its courses and a pier cap where each back-wall pillar stands, a
  machine's deck plates on its panel grid with their seams and rivets and a hazard band at every pit's lip, a padded
  run's cushions on its block grid, a rock's slabs on one rhythm of lengths, chipped every third joint; each segment a
  tone of the zone's own in a fixed cycle. `painted` holds every top capped; the benchmark's `top-segmented` reads the
  tops' lightness varying on the page.
- **The jamb** (`paint.js` `SIDE_JAMB`, `wallSurfaces`): every wall a hero kicks off or runs into (a shaft's, a chute's,
  a room's: a closed part's face on open space a body tall or more) is the cap turned on its side, so walls and floors
  are one terrain: a band down its edge and its face into the open, the kicking surface itself, cut on the fill's own
  module and grid (built quoins long and short in turn, machine plates with seams and rivets, padded cushions, rock
  slabs on one rhythm) in the cap's tones, joints and lit edge. Chunky: the edge steps in and out on that rhythm, a notch
  the open shows through, never deeper than 0.15 m and never past the plane the hero kicks off (the climb is the
  collider's, untouched); a string course every few courses as a floor has its pier caps; a bracket under each rest in
  the wall's own matter. `painted` holds every wall jambed; the benchmark gives walls a role of their own and reads
  `walls-segmented` on the page.
- **The cake** (`gameworld/side-map/cake.js`, `texture.js`, `doodads.js`): every wall or floor segment is a slice of
  cake. Its icing is the cap and the jamb; under it, its layers are its world's MATERIAL, a row each, never bricks
  everywhere: techno kibble in a plant (a conduit on its brackets, panels with vents or a status light, ribbed machinery),
  bolted plate in a base, the built and padded fills as they were, rock's strata (soil, a band of rubble on one rhythm,
  bedrock on the level's beds, a copper vein in a works), snow on a cold cube's open land or a mountain's heights (a
  snowpack under an icing of snow, a band of ice, rock below). Its strata hang from each slice's own top, so a pit shows
  the same layers either side.
  The material is baked with the light: each its finish (specular, gloss, metal, the share of sky it reflects), the
  side camera's view fixed so a glint and a metal's sheen bake truly, and a procedural texture tile (rock's grain,
  snow's sparkle, brushed metal, stone, cloth) on world uvs, multiplied by the baked light (`textures`, `textureLit`).
  On the icing stand things that block nothing, none a collider, at three depths that parallax against the lane: a
  material's set on its A bays (pipes, vent stacks and crates on a plant's rear; urns and column stubs on a temple's;
  boulders, tufts and pebbles on rock; snow lumps, and icicles hung under snow's lip), and a dark foreground
  silhouette in front (a girder's frame, a stepped hummock, a fallen block, a drift) under the hero's feet line. The
  `doodads` law (none sunk in a closed part or at a pit's lip, the lip's things low, the foreground under the feet line);
  the benchmark reads `reflective` (a metal or snow lane's glints over its flat twin) and, in a run's frame, the
  `foreground` under the feet, which it had said missing. On Galaxy Boy's first level and the volcano stage both hold.
- **The map is a geocube** (`gameworld/side-map/scene.js`, the geocube's `show: 'sidemap'`): a zone chain laid for the
  hero it names (a feel and a stature, Galaxy Boy's unsaid), dressed in the cube's hue (its stone the place's, play the
  other side of the wheel) and built where the camera sees: the closed parts in their zone's key, every top a lit edge;
  an indoor zone's back wall in its void carrying the dress (pillars and seams, a lamp an A bay, a hatch at each spawner,
  the next place at the edge, a shaft's railings, a chute's stripes, the boss's emblem), an outdoor zone's back the
  cube's sky; shutters, ladders and pickups in the play's colour; lit by the cube's key from behind the camera, framed
  by the side map's camera. A zone's solids are cut where they would stand in another zone's space (a shaft's near wall
  hung into the run before it, a chute's far wall into the room after it), and the `swept` law says so where one does.
- **The map drawn** (`gameworld/side-map/drawing.js`, `scripts/side-map.mjs`): the elevation the studied maps are read
  as, the camera's area on black, read left to right: the zones outlined and numbered with their places, rulers in
  screens, metres and seconds at the run, the bot's line (an arc over a pit, a chimney's kicks counted between its
  rests), checkpoints, doors, ladders, pickups and a rising frame's pace, the dress's cells (bays, pillars, seams, lamps,
  hatches, the next place's band, the boss's emblem), and the laws: each lost one named, or all held. The script writes
  the drawing and, asked, the page seen from the side map's camera at every zone.
- **The closed parts painted** (`gameworld/side-map/paint.js`), what the strip never did: every closed part the camera
  sees drawn as its place's fill, as marks on its face. Rock in beds level across the whole level (one datum: a pit shows
  the same strata either side), joints along them, roots under an outdoor lip; built in courses of running bond with a
  trim under every lip; machine in panels on one grid; padded in framed blocks. Cut along the way in slices a quarter
  screen wide, A and B by the walls' rule, an A slice carrying its fill's motif (a pocket, a niche, a lamp panel, a bolt
  plate); a big mass something toward its middle (a vein of ore, a recessed panel, a window into the works behind, a
  great block); an end toward open space lit, an end at a pit bitten out; the dress's thread (pipes, cables, roots, a
  channel) carried through them from the first zone to the last, under the way, up a shaft's wall, down a chute's. The
  `painted` law now reads the paint: no closed face plain, no zone's slices repeating. The reality facet's fills are built.
- **The backdrop by height** (`paint.js` `backdropOf`): an outdoor zone's hills and range at their depth behind the lane,
  sized for the side map's camera to see them where the frame should and wide enough for anywhere along the zone; at the
  foot both in the frame, higher the hills gone and the range lower, at the top only sky over a low horizon.
- **Galaxy Boy's first level, a side map** (`side-map/first.js`; a world's `levels.<id>.sidemap`, `side-map/level.js`):
  the first level's teaching order seen from the side, with the beats a strip never had: a rest with no pit, the

  frame, a landing, a gauntlet, a chute and a one-screen boss's room. The platformer's rail writes it for the run and
  gun (`SIDE_MAP_POLES`); Jumping Giuseppe's strip is as it was. A world refuses one with no side camera or beside

  its goal the far side of the boss's room.
- **The bot** (`side-map/bot.js`), the machine gate's player: a laid map played on the shipped rule as a player who
  knows it would (a jump at each pit's lip, a dash jump for the dash's gaps, the stick let go over a narrow top, a
  chimney kicked up the wall across from its next rest, a ledge jumped to from within reach of it, a ladder held up), and
  what it took said: the time, each fall, each climb's kicks and the least its feet stood over the rising frame. It
  plays Galaxy Boy's first level to its end in about two minutes without a fall, and every climb form under a rising
  frame; played on a level resolved as its page resolves it, on the level's own bus, the goal is reached and no life is
  lost, and a frame that rises five times too fast costs lives.
- **Played, the map was mended**: a run carries no wall face (the wall kick is a climb's: `coursePlan`'s `walls`); a
  shaft's near wall rises from a doorway at its foot, so a chimney has both walls from the floor up; a ledge stair's
  first rest is on the far wall, away from the doorway; a stair's steps leave a standing hero room under the next; a
  switchback's floors are a hero apart with a step under each opening (it was a stack of floors no one could stand
  between); the reach law reads the room over every rest; the camera never lets a drop down a chute outrun its frame.
- **The map's laws** (`gameworld/side-map/laws.js`), advisory, measured on the layout and its dress: a run one screen
  thick across its held axis; a shaft's two walls in the frame; every pit crossed by the move that teaches it and every
  stand up a climb a jump away; no more than three kicks between a chimney's rests, its top counted; a rising frame
  slower than the bot's climb on the shipped rule by a margin; every climb's top opening into the next zone's space and
  lit; no pit in the first zone and climbs that lengthen; a checkpoint in every zone; ladders on floors; the teaching in
  its order and no zone the one before it again; nothing built outside the camera's path and nothing it sees left
  unbuilt but a pit; the boss's room shut behind and marked. The dress's: a place a zone, solid lighter than void, a lit
  edge on every top, play against place, the boss's colour its own and growing, bays by the walls' rule with a pillar or
  a seam in every frame and spawners a screen apart, the next place at the edge, the thread unbroken, every closed part
  named its fill. Laid to them: a cascade's steps go as deep as the frames that see them, a climb's rests are spaced
  evenly with the last on the way out's wall, a pit between pillars is a pit, a room's doorway is open, and a rising
  frame's pace is set from the bot's climb.
- **The map's camera** (`worlds/controllable/sidemap.js`, the camera rule `side-map`, opt-in): the hero's zone holds
  the frame inside its rectangle, its locked axis fixed and its free axis followed (a run's height held as the hero runs
  it, a shaft's side held as it climbs, a room both ways); the zone is the next one along as soon as the hero is in it,
  so a corner turns toward the way on, eased and never snapped; a zone a door shuts behind (a chute's foot, a boss's
  room) is never left backward; a rising zone's frame climbs on its own at the layout's pace: the screen from below.
  `side-map/play.js` hands a laid map to it: the camera's zones with their checkpoints, the ladders as climbables, the
  level's solids.
- **Falls and ladders.** A hero wholly under the frame's bottom has fallen out: it is taken to limbo, where a catch
  zone stands that the lives mechanic counts a fall in (`side-fall`), and a beat later it is back at its zone's
  checkpoint with the camera cut to it. Under the side map's camera, up or down at a ladder takes hold of it (the lane's
  hero never walks into a ladder's face), the climb owns the body from there, facing into the place with its back to the
  camera, and its top steps it off onto the floor; no shot leaves on a ladder unless the body's rule says so. The hero's
  climb clip, seen from behind, is still to come: on a ladder it plays what it has.
- **The render benchmark** (`side-map/benchmark.js`, `node scripts/side-map.mjs <manifest> --bench`): a run, a climb and
  the boss's room shot on the page as the side map's camera frames its hero, each rendered twice (as the page draws it,
  and as a role pass: every face its role's flat colour, a stand-in where the hero stands), so every pixel of the page
  knows what it shows, and measured by role against the frame's principles: the hero an eighth of the frame's height,
  the top under it two thirds down, play and place on opposite hues, the tops lit, the closed parts painted, the lane's
  layer the sharpest and each layer behind it quieter, a lamp in an indoor run's frame, the boss's mark in its room. A
  contact sheet (`bench.html`: the page beside its role pass, each law's reading) and `bench.json`. Missing and said
  so, never claimed: anything moving beside the way (the foreground under the feet came with the cake, below). On Galaxy Boy's first level and a
  volcano stage every law the map builds holds. Measured, the look was mended: an outdoor zone's hills and range no
  longer stand over the next zone's at one depth (they flickered), and a shaft's climbing rails are a guide behind the
  lane, quieter than it.
- **The light** (`gameworld/side-map/light.js`, the default; `light: 'flat'` keeps the one baked key it was): the map lit
  per corner and baked as the page's vertex colours, so the page draws it as cheaply. Each face's colour is its base. An
  indoor zone is lit by a quiet ambient, the camera's fill on the lane alone (the lane the lit layer, the back a step
  down) and each of the dress's lamps with the house's falloff (`form/room-light.js`) and its bounce, so an A bay glows
  and a B bay falls to its shade; an outdoor zone by the cube's sky and sun (`era/cube-light.js`), the sun from the side
  map's key. A closed face darkens under its own lip and the back wall under a top over it; a climb's top screen takes
  the next zone's light and a chute darkens as it drops; the zones leading to the boss take its colour in their light.
  What gives light (the lamps, the boss's emblem, the far layers) is left as it is. Large faces are cut into cells two
  and a half metres across for a lamp's pool to fall over (the first level about three times the flat build's faces).
  The benchmark measures it: a lamp's falloff on the back, a ledge's shadow, the lane lit a step over the back, a climb's
  frame lighter at its top; on Galaxy Boy's first level and the volcano stage every one holds lit and the flat build
  loses the falloff, the shadow and the climb's light. Not yet: the hero under the cast rig on a side map's page.
- **The shot light** (`worlds/controllable/shot-light.js`, `scene/channels/controllable/shot-light-view.js`): what moves
  lights the baked map live, over its bake: a buster's round in its level's colour, a foe's shot in its own, a burst as
  it goes off, a muzzle's flash, and the hero's charge at its chest growing as it fills. The strongest few near the
  camera each frame, added over the baked colour in the surface's own hue by how it turns to the light, no shadows.
  Only a side map's page carries it.
- **The shot's look** (`gameworld/feel/round-look.js`): a buster's round drawn as the anime register draws a charged
  shot: a white-hot core, its colour saturated in the falloff and deeper at the edge, all of it additive under a halo
  in its hue; the ball always at its head, where it hits, and everything else behind it (streaks along its flight and
  a tail from the ball back, never ahead of it, sparks trailing); at the firing point, rings in an accent hue far round
  the wheel (the cel look's), one more a charge level, their near arc bright, left there growing and fading as the
  round flies on; the full charge's ball round, white-hot and as big as it hits. Its light on the map is
  spill, not flood: its hue on the edges near it, the world kept in its key.
- **A round's hitbox is its own** (`gameworld/feel/lower.js` `BUSTER_HIT`, `worlds/controllable/buster.js`): the tap and
  the first charge meet a body with less than their drawn size; the full charge is a tall capsule, so it catches what
  stands anywhere in its height (a crawler under the line a tap shot sails over) and bursts at the height it met it.
- **What a shot destroys is lit by it** (`worlds/controllable/shot-light.js`, `shot-light-view.js`): a block that breaks
  (rupa's matter, a breakable) and a body destroyed (dismantle, a cleave) flash as they come apart, in the colour of the
  round that burst there, fading like a burst; and the shot light reaches every piece of matter as it comes into the
  scene, so a crate's chunks and a wreck's pieces take its light as they fly. Glows stay as they are.
- **Impacts and explosions in the shot's light** (`gameworld/feel/round-look.js` `blastLook`): on a page with a buster, a
  round's impact, a hitscan hit, a block blown apart (rupa) and a body destroyed (dismantle, a cleave) are drawn as the
  shot is: a white-hot core flashing first and fading fastest, the hue saturated round it and deeper at its edge, a halo,
  shock rings in the accent with their near arc bright, sparks flung out; an impact quick and small, an explosion longer
  with more rings and sparks; each in the colour of the round that did it (a full charge's hit an explosion), drawn in
  front of what it struck. Every other page keeps its effects as they were.
- **Crates** (`gameworld/side-map/crates.js`, the chain's `crates: true`): breakable crates on a side map's runs, the
  buster's other target. Each stands across the lane's middle in a resting bay (the bays with doodads left to them),
  clear of every pit, step, door, ladder and checkpoint, as tall as a hand over the buster's muzzle (so a tap shot meets
  it) and under the hero's jump (so it is hopped or shot apart), with room to stand on it. The scene names its faces and
  anchors it as a crate, the play makes its collider its own, and the level breaks `objects` where its game names no
  degree, so a world's breakability makes each a block that breaks: one shot and it bursts in the round's light, its
  chunks lit as they fly. A law (`crates`) holds them to it; the bot hops them. Galaxy Boy's first level has four.
- **The cel body**: a `cel` body register, a body's light and not its face's, picked by the side scroller's and the run
  and gun's rails: their characters keep the character light while they play (each piece's lit tone and its shade tone,
  metal drawn by its dark and its gloss), stepped by the side map's own light, so the hero and the land agree. A
  dark navy line, never black, runs round each of a cel body's parts (the land takes none: the toon ink's new
  `only: 'bodies'`), so the forms that adorn it read as its segments; and on a side map a body turns its head toward the
  screen, its face seen, most when it stands. The toy hero robot's helm ends its cheek guards at the jaw line instead of
  making a chin of them. Where a zone is lit by lamps, each body is lit from its nearest lamp's side and height (its face
  still toward the camera's side), and a shot or a blast cuts a hard rim in its colour down the edges that face it While
  the hero charges its buster its body, limbs and helm are lit up by the charge (its face never, only edged), all over and on
  their fresnel, brightest at the silhouette, from a white-hot heart at its chest, in the level
  reached's colour, more as the charge fills, pulsing slow and deep (faster once a level is reached), and its energy
  gathers over its whole body: a bloom wrapping it head to foot, sparks drawn in from all round onto it and motes
  circling it, a burst at its middle at each level reached, the charge's light pulsing round it.
- **The side map's foes**: a side map stands its own foes (`levels.<id>.foes` beside a `sidemap`), on its spawners and
  its runs, on the side strip's rail, drawn in cel like its hero. The side scroller's bestiary is the toy hero robot's
  design language carried to animals (the herobot ooze: helmets, ear domes, gems, antennae, ball joints, their faces
  their own, never a person's) and the game's critters (the mascot ooze).
- **A body fit to a height** (`body.fit: { least, from? }`): the world resolver stands it at least that tall by its figure's
  own bounds, its hit egg and collider with it (a beast's skeleton is shorter than its flesh). A rig body drawn at a scale
  of its own now has a cel line as wide as every other body's.
- **The bosses**: robots of the hero's own family whose faces are never a person's. The hero alone keeps the open face;
  a boss's face is its theme (a mask, a visor, a grille, one eye, a screen, a beast's head, an object), it always has
  eyes, and it lights up as the boss winds up an attack.
- **Crucible, the first level's boss**: a robot on Galaxy Boy's own body and suit, broader and a head taller, whose head
  is a crucible of molten metal with two lit eyes. It stands in the last room of Galaxy Boy's first level, in the colour
  that level holds back for its boss, and lobs at where the hero stood. Bringing it down ends the level. Its eyes and its
  metal glow as it winds up a shot and flash as it fires, lighting the room round its face.
- **The terrain's shadows**: a side map's blocks are shaded as a 3D run and gun's stage is: each face bright under its
  icing, with a crisp shadow line beneath it, and falling into shade deeper in the block. Ledges, ceilings, props and
  crates throw hard, crisp shadows onto the back wall and the floors beside them.
- **The drawn relief**: a side map's painted details are drawn with their depth, as a pixel artist shades relief. Panels,
  labels, conduits and the icing are lit along their top and left edges and drop a crisp shadow down and to the right.
  Vents and niches are sunk under a shadowed lip. Brick and stone courses read raised from their mortar.
- **Zero Boy**: a second playable hero for the side scroller, Galaxy Boy's body and suit in red with a yellow ponytail,
  a saber in place of the buster, and a three-hit string that stays in place, lit like the shots and on the buster's
  damage scale. The saber's blade is a strand of the charged shot, its white-hot core and its bloom, and each cut sweeps
  a slash of it. Each cut plants his feet as his body swings into it, one leg forward and one back, holding the split
  from cut to cut while he never leaves his place. A move in any string can now do the same (a move's `plant`).
- **Galaxy Boy's controls and jump**: on a pad, the left face fires (beside the right trigger) and the top face dashes
  (beside the left trigger), from his feel card's `pad`; a card can now lay out a pad's faces of its own. His jump goes
  1.4 times higher (2.24 m), and the side map lays its gaps and ledges by it. His jump is his own: one pose held the
  whole flight, the knee away from the buster drawn up so he is balanced to fire, the legs reaching down only before
  the floor (a card's `jumps`, the poised jump). A side map's hero now plays its own jumps at all (before, the air
  played the run), and a cel-lit hero keeps the jumps its game gives it.
- **Galaxy Boy's dash**: his dash is his own pose, leaning hard into it and streamlined as he is driven along, the knee
  away from the buster driven forward with its foot swept back and pointed, the buster side's foot pushed back on its
  toes, and the arms a pair on a clock face (facing 3 o'clock): the buster arm's elbow down, its forearm aimed at 4
  o'clock with the buster tipped up, the free arm's upper arm straight back and its forearm aimed at 7 o'clock (a card's `jumps.dash`, the poised dash, played over the burst, in the air
  dash too). A ground dash throws a wisp of dust and grit back off his feet; an air dash raises none.
- **A pointed foot**: a free foot can be pointed, its toes turned down about the ankle (the rig's `point<S>`), as a
  dash's streamlined front foot is.
- **Galaxy Boy's shot**: as he fires, his buster arm comes up level along his facing over whatever he is doing (a run,
  a jump, a dash) and eases back down; the shot leaves from the cannon at the end of that arm, not his chest. It is his
  right arm whichever way he faces (the body turns, never a mirror), so facing left the shot leaves from his far side.
  Walking, dashing or jumping, the shot leaves from where that arm is in the move (a dash's lean and sink lower it).
- **Galaxy Boy's arm cannon and hands**: the buster runs flush on from the forearm, straight, its end rounded and a short
  nozzle standing out of it with the bore dark in its face (an armour volume can now end in a dome and a nozzle). The
  hero robot's gloved hands are a little smaller and stand on a longer wrist (a hand can stand further off its wrist).
- **Zero Boy, caught up**: he jumps, dashes (its pose and its dust) and takes the pad's faces as Galaxy Boy does. His
  saber cuts in the air too: a cut at what is ahead while the jump goes on under it, never holding him up. The saber is
  a fifth longer (its light runs past the blade it springs from, its reach and its slash wider) and cuts a fifth harder.
- **On the wall**: jumping up to a wall, the hero faces it; caught on it and sliding down, he turns his back to it and
  faces out, so a shot or a cut goes out from the wall (where the stick moves him in the world's frame, as on a side
  map; a stick read off the facing keeps facing the wall).
- **Vistas behind the play**: a zone whose back should say "somewhere else" opens it into a frame (a parapet up to a
  little over its lowest floor, a header down from its top, its pillars between) and stands a vista beyond: a few

### Underwater: the sea a gen-7 geocube is seen through

- **A land put under water by its light alone** (`scene/channels/sea.js`, the recipe's `sea` on the `geocube` kind, every
  gen-7 show). Nothing is built for it: the land is the land the cube makes, and the water is what the light does on the
  way down and on the way back to the eye. A zone's word (`shallows`, `reef`, `blue`, `twilight`, `midnight`), `true`
  (the reef), a depth in metres (its measures taken between the zones it lies between), or `{ zone, depth, water,
  visibility, level, caustics, shafts, snow, lamps, torch }`. It is three's own fog chunk, patched once before any
  material compiles (as the air's: the two are not asked together), so every surface that took the page's fog takes the
  water. A painted (gen-6) page and the unshaded export are as they were; the word is read on any geocube.
- **The light at a depth, colour by colour.** A water (`ocean`, `coast`, `murk`) is its diffuse attenuation per metre
  for red, green and blue and a visibility: red goes in the first metres, green next, and the last light keeps the
  water's own deep colour, never a primary. The eye adapts: the light at the walk's ground is laid at the zone's level,
  never black. Along the view the water takes each colour by Beer-Lambert (its absorption and the scattering its
  visibility sets) toward the water's own body colour, lighter looking up and darker looking down.
- **What each depth reads by.** Shallow: caustics on what faces the sun (the surface's ripples as a net of light whose
  mean is 1: light is moved, never made), shafts where the sun's rays pass, and the surface from below (the sky through
  Snell's window, a mirror outside it). Deeper: value alone, shapes as silhouettes against the lighter water over them.
  Where the sun does not reach: `lamps` (up to the page's limit, each `{ at, colour, power, aim, cone }`: a pool on
  what it faces, falling by the square of the distance and by the water, so a warm lamp greens with reach, and a glow
  in the water round it), `torch` (one at the eye), and marine `snow` that shows in their beams.
- **Under the water there is no sky and no waterline**: the page's dome, clouds and sun are hidden, the land's own sea
  sheet with them, and what stands over the surface is not seen from under it.
- **Inside** (a flooded hall, room or cavern) no sun reaches: the room's own light stands, seen through the water.
- A bare, duned land is a sandy bed (`biocube: 'bare'`, a trail's `ground.dunes`): grass reads as seagrass.
  `scripts/spikes/sea/depths.mjs` shoots a land at every zone. `window.__mojSea` is the probe. Absent `sea`, the page
  is byte for byte as it was. How it is built and tuned: `docs/underwater.md`.

### Vents: crawl spaces through a building

A building's `vents` (`era/vents.js`, opt-in: a program's, a level's building's, a geocube's or a complex's) lays a duct
along the back wall of each row of rooms off a corridor: through a hole in each wall the rooms share, under a lid a body
lying passes beneath and one standing does not, with a hatch into each room. A body goes in at one room's hatch and comes
out at another's, never in the corridor the guards walk; a guard cannot follow it, nor see it from over the lid.

- **The stage** cuts the holes, draws the ducts in the services' finish, makes their walls and lids colliders, keeps every
  piece off their floors and their hatches (`compose-dress.js keepOuts`), and gives the page their insides as crawl
  spaces (`veil.js` `under`). A building with vents rings its rooms by doorways at the corridor's end and the middle of
  their shared walls, by turns, so the back walls stay the ducts'.
- **Headroom** (`worlds/controllable/stance.js`): a body lying rises only where nothing hangs lower than it would stand:
  under a lid, a truck's chassis or through a hole in a wall it stays down, whatever the key says.
- **The route search** (`gameworld/stealth-routes.js`) passes a cell under something higher than a body lying, lying
  only, so a level's laws read a crawl as a way.
- **Facilities** have vents; the holding block's operative starts on the processing room's row, and its law
  `a-vent-to-the-kit` holds: with the corridors shut, the duct is a way from the cell to the kit (a 20 m crawl, never
  nearer a guard than 9.5 m). The facility maps draw each duct's floor and its hatches.
- **A duct is dark.** A room's shade level and its lamps' bounce reach every surface of it alike, so a duct read as lit
  as the floor round it (inside 0.22 to 0.30 against the room floor's 0.25, measured). Now each duct is lined (a plate on
  its floor and on the back wall under its lid, its own faces, so the room's floor and wall do not blend their light
  through), what lies inside it keeps 0.3 of its baked light (`vents.js shadeDucts`), more within 1.4 m of a hatch's
  mouth, and no lamp is seated on the wall over a duct under 2.5 m. The depot's first duct reads 0.07 to 0.09 inside;
  the lid's top and the front wall's face to the room keep the room's light.

### The co-op kitchen: seats work the shift, in a kitchen of their own

The work shift (the Work Sim rail's kitchen, farm stand, site and roof) learns its seats, the first step toward the
co-op kitchen the cosmos registry refused: two to four cooks in one kitchen on one screen, an order carried from
station to station and handed between them.

- **Every seat works with its own hands.** A level with seats (`seats.bodies`, a cube's `soul.seats`) lowers the work
  mechanic once a seat: seat n's hands are the holder `hands<n>` (seat 1 keeps `bag`), its presses `s<n>:use-<place>`,
  its zones watching its own body. Stations, shelves, tickets and the clock stay shared. A station slot remembers who
  works it: walking off pauses only that cook's work, and what a run with no wait makes comes into that cook's hands.
- **The pass.** A shelf is put on from one pad and taken from the other by anyone, so a kitchen laid with the shelf
  between two cooks can only be worked by handing things across it.
- **The page.** Seats 2 to 4 each get their own reach and interact press (seat 1's is as it was), emitted only for a
  world with seats and a shift.
- **The proof.** `proveWork` plays several cooks, each its own spawn and reach, on the page's bus; a split kitchen is
  won only through the pass (machine gate). Whether it plays well together is the eyes gate, the operator's.
- **Opt-in, byte for byte.** A level with no seats lowers and emits what it did.
- **The kitchen, a designed arena** (`worksim/kitchen.js`). A card's places are read by role (crates, prep that takes
  only raw things, assembly that takes a made thing, shelves, the hand-in) and laid in a kitchen: `split` (prep on one
  side of a counter, assembly and the hand-in on the other, everything that crosses on a pass set in the counter) or
  `island` (one floor round an island of shelves). A new kitchen is a row. Its laws, measured on its floor and advised,
  never refused: every place reached from its side, the sides sealed (no way round, a counter the cooks cannot jump),
  every order crossing the pass, a pass for everything that crosses, a 760 mm walkway, the whole room on one screen.
- **Tuned to its cooks.** `tuneKitchen` tunes the card for that many hands, then plays the kitchen with its cooks on
  their sides and slows the orders until they keep up; the goal is four fifths of what they served. The simulator alone
  counts four cooks as four times one, and they fall short of that in a real kitchen.
- **The quick door.** `design_game({ quick: { goal: 'work', cooks: 2 | 4, kitchen?: 'split' | 'island' } })`: the
  cube's seats, and the level a kitchen room of its own (`gameworld/kitchen-level.js`), never laid by a trail: the game
  room's area (the trade's floor and walls, cut away on the camera's side), its places dressed as the trade's things,
  no recipe on the floor (the practice room's arrows teach; in the game the cooks work out what comes next), each cook
  on its own side, a seat nobody sits in held still, one fixed overhead
  station framing the whole room. One cook and no kitchen named is the line by the trail, as it was.
- **Each cook's corner.** Seated, each other seat's hands and what it holds stand in its own corner in its colour (P2
  bottom right, P3 top right, P4 bottom); seat 1's are where they were.
- **Made, not refused.** The registry marks `soul.dependence=handoff` (the work mechanic's kitchen) and
  `soul.frame=fixed` (the kitchen's fixed station, besides the versus fighter's) built: the co-op kitchen probe is
  makeable. The shared kitchen joins the Work Sim rail (its words point there; the not-yet list is empty), a quick work
  goal with cooks reads as the co-op kitchen genre, and a sentence asking for one is told the quick door that makes it,
  with its cooks. Proved through the real door: `design_game({ quick: { goal: 'work', cooks: 2 } })` made the game in
  one call, `export_game` wrote it, and in headless Chromium its shell's play button opened the kitchen, two pads sat
  down and a fish crossed the pass into the second cook's corner.
- **The kitchen, seen.** The open orders run along the top of the screen (the work mechanic's opt-in `rail`: each
  ticket in its order's colour, what it wants said, its bar the patience it has left; the 3D ticket markers and the
  order toast give way to it). A tag over every seated cook names its seat in its colour and what its hands hold, so a
  handoff is seen where it happens. The kitchen's dress has pieces of its own: plating stations a stainless counter with
  a plate and a board, a pass between cooks a stainless hatch with a warm lit top, the hand-in a servery with its bell;
  the counter between the sides stainless. A seated shift's seat strip sits at the bottom, the top being the rail's.
- **The food** (`control/lib/graph/food/`). What a card handles is drawn as it is read off the card, never modelled
  item by item. A dish's words compose its parts on its plate or bowl (nigiri, maki rings, a salad heaped in a bowl). An
  ingredient's words give the thing, in the state its words or its station give: worked by hand it is prepped (a fish
  becomes a fillet), run alone it is cooked (rice becomes a bowl of rice), packed by a bucket it goes in a crate or a sack.
  A produce grown from another thing is itself. A thing no row names is a block in a colour from its name. Ingredients,
  states, dishes and vessels are rows (`food/roster.js`); the forms are face lists from the lathe, box and prism, built
  at glyph scale and placed at a size: every round shaded smooth (each corner lit along the mean of the normals meeting
  there, creases over 50° kept sharp, carried as `cornerFills`) and every box chamfered (its faces set in, its edges and
  corners cut, each face lit as it faces). Laws, advised: every thing drawn, a card's things told apart, made unlike what it
  was made from, each in its box. Review: `node scripts/render-food.mjs <dir> [card|all]`, a captioned sheet raw → made
  → dishes. The kitchen's eyes gate is the operator's; the food is not on the page yet.
- **More recipes.** The kitchen gains menus beside the sushi counter, each a recipe shape (`worksim/scenarios.js`):
  `pasta` (pasta and sauce in two pots met on the plate; a tray layered and baked again), `wok` (fried rice and chow
  mein tossed in a wok that burns), `ramen` (a long stock, noodles and eggs boiled, pork sliced, a bowl of four),
  `diner` (a grill, a fryer, a burger stacked; a meal wants a burger and fries), `pizzeria` (dough kneaded and rolled,
  sauce, cheese, topped and baked). The food shelf draws them: arrangements for pasta twirled under its sauce, a toss, a
  bake in a tray, a curry beside its rice, a fold, dumplings, skewers, a soup with its noodles, egg halves and slices, a
  pizza in layers; a thing several things are cooked into that names its base is that base with the rest mixed through
  (fried rice); a dish put through an oven comes out browned; an ingredient's finer method is a row (an egg boiled is
  halved); poultry, pork, dough, bones, tofu and fries are rows. Every starter's food holds every law (a deep sweep).
- **The kitchen, lit as a studio set.** A warm key from high in front and to the left and a cool fill from the right
  shade each of the room's faces as it faces the camera; ambient occlusion is baked (the floor subdivided, so a counter
  darkens round its foot); the counters' shadows are cast once from the key and the cooks' each frame (the camera's
  side, cut low, and the surround cast nothing in); contact occlusion and inked seams live; a warm grade with a vignette.
  The tiled floor is quieted to two near tones. Each crate shows its raw thing sitting on it, drawn by the food shelf.
- **The map changes as the levels go on.** A kitchen is a level of its own (`levels.<id>.kitchen`: its layout, its
  menu, its challenge, `mirror` and `obstacles`, `gameworld/kitchen-shifts.js`), and `quick.shifts` makes a campaign of
  them: `shifts: n` the progression's first n (an island for the sushi counter's opening night, then splits, mirrored,
  with a counter island in each side's floor, each shift a new menu and the challenge rising), or a list of shifts. Each
  shift is a level of the game, named for it, laid and tuned on its own map; every kitchen law holds on a mirrored map
  with islands. The proof walks straight lines, so an island's cost to real cooks is the eyes gate's.

### Realistic trees and the raised ground (era flora)

- **Grass:** a new trail scene's grass is gen-7's raised ground in both eras (`grass: { form: true }`), with dark
  strands in the far grass. Rows minted before it draw as they did.
- **Realistic trees (`crowns: 'realistic'`):** a tree drawn from its structure, for a scene that asks for it. Its limbs
  grow from its crown's masses back to a leader, in proportion to the tree (`form/tree-form.js` EVOKE). Structural
  branches are bare, and its leaf-holding twigs carry clouds of puffs (CLOUD). Far off it is a card baked full in
  pixels. It stays within the plain tree's triangles, and its lowest limb is 3 m up at least.
- **A habit per kind of tree** (`form/flora-read.js` REALISTIC_HABITS, a row a species): a single, Y (forked high)
  or V (forked low) trunk and its girth; its limbs' girth and climb; its twigs rising or drooping; its crown widened,
  narrowed or flattened; its clouds wide or tall, sitting on their twigs or hanging under them. Rows for the library's
  broadleaves, and three new kinds reached by a kind's `species` word (`REALISTIC_KINDS`: birch, poplar, acacia), with
  their scene-solver cards. Each holds to its plain tree's triangles, its smallest puffs given up first.
- **Realistic trees in gen-6 too:** a gen-6 trail's `crowns: 'realistic'` draws the trees the form render keeps
  (`realisticPlan`: the same species, places and heights), each painted from its template's own structure
  (`era/isekai.js` REAL_BANDS): the trees near the trail built whole, the rest stamped from a few turned variants, the far
  casting as their coarse selves. One stand of trees in both eras; a trail without the word draws as it did.
- **No grass hats on rocks in new gen-6 scenes:** a stage's `hats: 'lips'` keeps its rocks clean (no grass cap, no
  fringe on a boulder) and its cliff lips' fringe; a new level's trail stage is written with it (`gameworld/levels.js`),
  and a geocube path takes the word. `hats: true` and `false` and rows already made draw as they did.

### The JRPG starter: a party RPG from a town to its first boss

A party RPG made the way an RPG Maker game is made, from mojulo's own pieces (`docs/jrpg.md`).

Built:
- **A JRPG intent lays its world round its town.** The words name a party RPG with a castle and a dungeon, and the
  world is laid as:
  - the town at the centre (the hub, where the game starts);
  - the wilds;
  - the castle's level;
  - the dungeon, last, with the boss at its end.

  Before, a dungeon named turned every level indoors and the town was lost.
- **The town's trades: an inn, a temple and a smithy.** A street's `enter` may name a trade where it names a use
  (`era/town-trades.js`). The lot keeps its shape, and its door, its inside and its keeper become the trade's:
  - the inn's innkeeper at its taproom keeps the world's inn;
  - the temple's priest stands at its sanctuary (the rite that raises the fallen is a gap the folk sheet says).

  A party RPG's town keeps an inn and a temple on its street.
- **The castle walked.** A level that raises a castle and names no town of its own stands the castle's ward on its
  trail:
  - its curtain and gatehouses are the castle's fortification;
  - its ranges are the ward's houses;
  - its keep is entered at its door: the gatehouse, the great hall, the chapel, the solar and the treasury.

  Before, a castle was drawn only in the bible and the atlas.
- **The folk talk in the talk box.** In a world with the game's UI, each townsperson's lines are a scene they speak:
  their name over the box, their own body drawn live in its portrait, played each time they are spoken to. A party
  RPG's world carries the game's UI. Built on the talk box (`1117-mana-ui-talking-heads`, merged here).
- **The round travelled as a mandala.** A round of three levels or more is laid in rings (the megaworld,
  `gameworld/megaworld.js`); a town and one stretch of wilds stay a plain hub:
  - the town is the first ring, where the game starts;
  - the wilds and the castle are the second, each a road from the town;
  - the last level is the core, reached from the farthest wilds through a gate its key opens: the key lies in the
    castle when the castle is not the core (`crypt-key`), else in the farthest wilds (`castle-key`).

  The travel screen draws the rings with the core at the centre, a fight won stays won when a place is gone back to,
  and the core's first win ends the game. A world with a book (its battles) now carries a megaworld's atlas and its
  core into its game too; before, only a world without one did.

Planned next, each said in words on mojulo's own pieces rather than an editor's:
1. The wilds as a zoned world map in their ring: battles met on the map's marks, a rest on the road.
2. Talk that follows the story: a townsperson's lines keyed to what has happened.
3. Save slots and save points.
4. Travel by ship or airship, opened by the story: the crossing played while the next place is built.
5. The battles' depth as rows: foe patterns, states, troops.

### The JRPG starter, continued: the wilds as a world map

- **The wilds are a world map in the round's second ring.** A party RPG's wilds are now the world map's blocks
  (`gameworld/world-map.js` `wildsLevel`), not a trail walk:
  - three blocks walked out from the town: a road, then ruins, then the far wilds, each laid by its template of the
    trail library;
  - a page a block (zoned), crossed at the plan's gates;
  - the first block has the road back to the town;
  - the far block has the way on to the core, gated by its key;
  - a pack stands on each block's way past the first, met as a battle by walking up to it, and none in the block the
    town opens on.

  A second stretch of wilds reads as its own place: the same blocks under other names. A megaworld's ring now takes a
  zoned map as one of its zones.
- **The wilds' ground is quiet.** The round's grit is the town's stone. Painted over open ground it set every tile in
  relief, and a block's page weighed about four times its quiet weight (128 MB against 36 MB), so the wilds' cube
  wears none (`grit: 0`, said in `brief.round.quiet`). The town and the castle keep it.
- **A JRPG wears the console RPG's plain blue windows.** Its battles, its talk box and its HUD are drawn in a new theme
  card, `classic-rpg` (`playscape/ui/theme-cards/`): the console RPG's blue, a double white rule and a gold marker, with
  nothing behind or over the windows (no brushed metal, no plinth, no heading tab). A composed party RPG names it
  (`ui: { theme: 'classic-rpg', colour: 'theme' }`), and a JRPG's world look by its intent is the same card
  (`playscape/ui/interface-look.js` `INTENT_LOOKS`). A battle whose level names no UI guide of its own now wears the
  level's look, so the battle, the talk box and the HUD are one game's windows; with neither, it draws as before.
- **The battle's command window beside the one acting.** While a member picks, their window (commands, then a skill or
  an item, then a target) stands beside that member's own bar over their head, follows them to wherever the view
  puts them, and is held inside the screen, clear of its bottom; with their bar off the screen it keeps its corner
  (`playscape/rpg/rpg-ui.js` `pick`, `scene/channels/rpg-channel.js` `besideAt`).
- **Picked, the window goes and the action plays.** A member's commands no longer stay drawn under the round while it
  plays (the channel closed only the top screen; it now closes them all).
- **A JRPG fights one turn at a time.** A composed party RPG's battles are on the timeline (`rules.turns:
  'timeline'`): each member picks when their turn comes and acts at once, the foes between them, never the whole
  party choosing before a round plays.
- **A bar over every fighter, up when it matters.** A foe now has the same bar over its head as a member (its HP as a
  bar, its numbers kept back, where the book shows foes' HP: a JRPG's `rules.foeHp: 'bar'`), and the foes' box and the
  turn order are gone. The bars are up on the player's turn; while a round plays they are down, but for a fighter whose
  numbers just moved (a blow, a heal, a spell's cost), shown for as long as it takes to read.
- **Townspeople who follow the story: a person's pages.** A person's `characters.folk.say` may be a list of pages,
  `[{ if?, say }]` (`folk/pages.js`), RPG Maker's event pages in words: read top to bottom, the first whose `if` holds
  is what they say, and a page with no `if` always holds. Its conditions are a scene's (`flag`, `not`, `has`, `done`,
  `chapter`, `var`). In the talk box each page is a scene on the person's one talk, held to its own `if` and to every
  page above it failing, so exactly one is said each time. In a talk menu (a world without the game's UI), the default
  page. A level whose folk read the store carries the story's flags and reads the bag and the campaign for them, as
  its story's scenes do.
- **A JRPG's priest follows its gate.** A composed party RPG's priest says where the core's key is kept until it is
  held, then that the way is open (`brief.round.talk`); the operator's own `say` takes its place.
- **Save points: saving steps out.** A megaworld may name the zones that keep a save point (`megaworld.saves`). Where
  the party comes into such a zone, a press asks "Save your journey here?", and yes takes a way out to the same map
  (`reach-exit`'s new `by`: a way taken by an event, never walked into). The store is written as at any crossing, so
  a save keeps the rule that the store is written only when a level is left, and the map loads again with the party
  set down beside the save point. Saving completes nothing. A composed party RPG keeps one in its town and in each
  stretch of its wilds, none in the castle or the core.
- **Save slots.** A game may offer its title several saves (`slots`, 2 to 4, `game/game-manifest.js`): in the play
  shell's mana-ui front, start or continue first asks which slot, each said by where its party stands, the one in use
  marked. Each slot keeps its own store, the flow's steps it has seen and a level's own progress; slot 1 is the game's
  own keys, so a game saved before it had slots continues as its first. Starting in a slot begins it anew; continuing
  an empty one starts it. A game's runs and bests stay the game's. A game whose megaworld keeps save points offers
  three.
- **A foe's action pattern.** A foe may say what it does and when (`play.rpg.foes.<id>.pattern`, and so a world's
  `battles.foes`): rows of `{ use: 'attack' | 'guard' | '<skill>', when?: { hpBelow?, hpAbove?, turn?, every?, after? },
  weight?: 1-9 }`. On its turn, a row whose `when` holds and that it can pay for, chosen by weight on the battle's own
  dice; with none holding, the rule every foe keeps (a skill by chance, else an attack). A guard it takes lasts until its
  next turn. A foe without one fights as it did.
- **A fight's own pages (RPG Maker's troop events).** An encounter may carry `pages` (`play.rpg.encounters[].pages`, and
  a world's boss fight through `battles.bossPages`): `{ when: { start: true } | { foe?, hpBelow } | { round }, say, who?,
  sets? }`, each said once in the message line the first time its moment holds; the page channel says `rpg-page:<fight>:<n>`
  on the bus, and the flag it sets.
- **A JRPG ends on a boss battle.** A composed party RPG's boss is a party battle (`battles.boss`: the Ember Drake, the
  core's last pack, no escape from it), with a line as the fight begins and one at half its HP; before, the words' boss
