  was a real-time goal's and stood in the crypt without a fight.
- **A battle's opening says all it has.** The opening played only its first beat and went to the picks; it now plays
  each in turn, so a fight's opening page, and on the timeline the foes who act before the first pick, are seen.
- **States as a table.** A fight's states are no longer only poison, sleep and silence: a world may name its own
  (`play.rpg.states`, and a world's `battles.states`), each by what it does: `skip` (its turns held), `noCast` (no skill
  that costs MP), `miss` (a share of its blows go wide), `wild` (its blows at anyone at all), `tick` (a share of its HP
  each turn, hurting or mending), `wake: 'hit'` (a blow ends it), lasting its `rounds`. The starter book's: paralysis,
  blindness, confusion, burn, regen (`presets.js` STATE_PRESETS), pulled in where a skill or an item names one. A skill
  inflicts one and an item or a skill cures one as the three were; a fallen fighter is rid of them; the bar over its head
  says them; a member held by one is not asked to pick. A fight that meets none rolls the same dice as before.
- **Crossings: travel by ship or airship.** A megaworld may name ways taken aboard beside its rings' own
  (`megaworld.crossings: [{ from, to, by: 'ship' | 'airship', needs? }]`): each a link (`links[].by`) shut until its
  story flag where it names one (a quest's, or the boss's `battles.sets`), out and back, and an exit's `crossing` in the
  game. Leaving by one, the play shell shows the trip while the next map is built in place of the loading veil: a ship
  bobbing on drifting waves under a low sun, or an airship over drifting clouds, "Sailing to" or "Flying to" the place,
  for 2.6 s at least and until the map is drawn. A crossing can join the world further than its rings: an isle, or
  another mandala.
- **The screen and sound as words.** A cue's (or a scene's `do`) `screen` effect: `{ fade: 'out' | 'in', tint:
  '#rrggbb' | 'none', flash: '#rrggbb', for? }`, a fade to black and back, the world washed in a colour, a flash,
  undone after `for` seconds or when the cue ends, drawn by the page's screen layer (`scene/channels/screen-fx.js`,
  emitted only where a level uses it). A cue's `sound: '<word>'` plays a sound off the SFX shelf by its word as it
  fires (`sfx:<word>` on the bus, voiced by the level's sound sheet). A composed party RPG is sounded and scored (its
  `sound` and `music`), as the action RPG's world map is.
- **Battle music.** A world of party battles asks its cue sheet for a fight's score on every level it fights on (not its
  hub) and the boss's on its last; the level's score turns to it while a battle is up and back after, the meter held
  full by `rpg.battle` however long the picks take (`audio.tension.held`, `beats/adaptive-music.js`: a bus var that pins
  the meter while it is set). A building level of a sounded game (a dungeon, a keep) now has its sounds and score as a
  trail's level does; before, it was silent.
- **The party menu's Item and Formation.** Two tabs beside Status, Class, Equip and Skills:
  - Item: a battle item from the bag used outside a fight, on the member in focus or, an item for allies, on all the
    party (a heal, MP, a revive, a cure); one that would do nothing is not spent (`kernel.js` fieldUse).
  - Formation: the member in focus traded for the one picked, the order the party fights in and, where it fights fewer
    than it has (`rules.size`), who is at the front and who in reserve (`kernel.js` swap). The order rides the party's
    save once it is set; a save that never set one is as it was.
- **The conversation's path to a JRPG.** A party RPG's pitch, locked with no level yet, is laid as the round (the
  `isekai-party` rail's own `starter`, `gameworld/rails.js`: a walled town, the wilds, a castle and a dungeon with a
  boss, four levels), not one plain level of its genre. Its designed chain teaches the round's steps before its first
  level (a rail's `steps`): the round (the mandala, its save points, a crossing), the battles (the party, the boss with
  its pattern and pages, the states) and the talk (the townspeople's pages), each on the card that owns it; its first
  level is said as what is laid. The cards teach the new words: the world card the megaworld's `saves` and
  `crossings`, the folk card a person's pages, the battles card and play.rpg's (PARTY BATTLES) a foe's pattern, a
  fight's pages and the world's own states.
- **Traits on classes and gear.** A class or a piece of gear may carry `resist` (elements taken at half), `immune`
  (elements taken not at all) and `ward` (states warded off): a member takes its class's and what it wears as it
  stands. A world that names none fights as it did.
- **The temple and the smithy keep shop.** A party RPG's town with a temple on its street has the temple's rite (a
  shop's `raise`: each fallen member raised, healed and cured, for its gold; `rpg-raised:<shop>` on the bus), opened by
  its priest; one with a smithy, the smithy's arms and armour, opened by its master. A keeper whose say is paged says
  their page, then opens the shop as the talk ends. A trade's shop is laid only where its lot's door is on the town's
  stage (a small town's square may leave one without frontage). The folk sheet's shrine is built; the smith's mending
  and bettering stay a gap.
- **A fight's page that acts.** A fight's page may give a foe back a share of its HP (`heal`: the foe its moment names,
  else every foe standing) and call foes into the fight (`summon: [foes]`, six fighting at most), fought and counted in
  the spoils like the rest. A summoned foe's figure is the next in the encounter's `who`, minted dormant and woken in
  smoke where it stands. A fight whose pages only speak is as it was.
- **A change of music from an event.** A cue's (or a scene beat's `do`) `music`: a mood of the score (a field mood, or
  a club's) played in place of the place's, `stop` for silence, `place` for the place's own again. Each mood a level
  names is a piece of its audio in the soundtrack's identity (`audio.pieces`, `beats/beats-world.js`), faded in on an
  engine of its own as the score fades out; while it plays, a fight's change of score waits. A level that names none
  emits not a byte of it.
- **A number put in.** A menu of kind `number` (`ask`, `var`, `digits` 1 to 8, `min`, `max`, `then`): its digits turned
  up and down and moved along, accept writing the number to its var, held to its bounds, before its effects; a cue that
  reads the var after the pick is a code lock or a count.
- **A walk that finds its way.** A cue's walk may say `find: true`: each leg walked round what stands in the way (the
  runtime's pathfinder, `worlds/controllable/nav.js`), arriving only at the places it named, by an opt-in builder
  (`worlds/controllable/route-find.js`) composed into a page only when a cue of its world walks so. Without it, a walk
  is as it was: straight lines, stopped at a wall.
- **The fights acted out, and varied.** The member picking steps out of the line; one who attacks runs up to its target,
  strikes and goes back; one who casts or uses an item steps out; a foe lunges the same way (the page's stepping,
  `rpg-channel.js`, played by the controllable channel's battle acts with the run clip on the way in). Every party
  member and a battles world's hero are made with a party battle's repertoire (`egocube/moves.js` `battleMovesOf`):
  three attacks by role, a cast and an item gesture, three recoils beside the stagger, a ready stance held through the
  fight and a win pose the whole party strikes. The page plays a figure's strikes and recoils in turn, so no blow
  repeats the one before. The acts reach the page by name (`fig.battle`), not as second copies of their clips. Before,
  the hero had no strike at all and each companion one move.
- **Weapons in hand by class.** In a world of battles, each party member who is a person, and the hero, is made holding
  its class's weapon (`egocube/moves.js` `WEAPON_OF_CLASS`: the fighter a greatsword, the knight a sword and a shield,
  the rogue a dagger, the mage a short staff, the cleric a mace; the monk its fists; a long staff is swung from the
  wrong end, so a caster's is on an arm's haft), passed to its mint as the hero door's `gear`.
  Its three attacks are the held swings (the cut, the thrust, the cleave) that the page bakes on its own rig at the
  weapon's weight, so the fists are not minted for one who holds a weapon. Before, the party fought with fists, its
  swords and staves numbers alone.
- **The foes' own repertoires.** A party battle's foes on the field are made with their own moves (on a board, as
  made):
  - A beast has its lunge and its other ways at a foe (`fauna/behavior/strike.js`, each a clip of its own built from
    its posed body): the **snap** (barely gathered, a quick bite), the **maul** (reared up, brought down low and far;
    a body on legs only) and the **roar** (up tall, the head high, held). It plays the lunge, the snap and the maul in
    turn (`egocube/moves.js` `beastMovesOf { battle }`). The animal door takes them too, as words (`snap`, `maul`,
    `roar`) or `motion.strikes`. A body that cannot strike yet (a bat, a swimmer) has none.
  - A people or a person foe carries a member's repertoire by its role and a roar (`foeBattleMovesOf`; a people's
    sheet made with `moves: 'battle'`).

  Before, a beast in a party battle had no blow at all, and a person foe one.
- **A boss's roar and heavier lunge.** A boss's fight opens with its foes' roar (the `boss` juice: `act: roar, at:
  foes`). A boss runs up slower, strikes longer, and the camera shakes as it lands.
- **A summoned foe's entrance.** A foe a page calls in roars as it appears out of the smoke (the `summon` juice).
- **Everyone channels.** A new pose, `channel` (`polygonizer/hero-aura.js`, the `spell` family): feet set broad, both
  hands drawn up from below to cup a gathering power before the chest, palms to each other, the eyes on it, swelling as
  it fills. Any hero takes it as a motion word. In a party battle every fighter has one: each party member and the
  hero (`battleMovesOf`), each person foe, and each beast that can strike (its own way, `channel`, in
  `fauna/behavior/strike.js`: drawn in, then hunkered low, the head down and still). A skill used channels first and
  then casts: the `cast` juice is `act: channel, then: cast` (an act's new `then`: an act it goes on into, the beat held
  while the first plays). One without its own channel stands in its ready stance while it gathers.
- **The foes armed by their kind.** A party battle's people foe is made holding its kind's arms (`gameworld/battles.js`
  `FOE_ARMS`, rows of the armory): the goblin a cudgel, the shaman a bone club, the skeleton a rusted sword and a
  cracked round shield; the zombie claws, bare. Its three attacks are then the held swings, as a party member's are, and
  so are a person foe's that holds something (the bandit's dagger). A look the world writes with its own `gear` holds
  that. Before, every people foe fought with its fists, and the bandit punched with a dagger in its hand.
- **Victory poses by class.** Seven new poses (`polygonizer/hero-aura.js`, the `victory` family) and a starter for each
  class (`egocube/moves.js` `WIN_OF_CLASS`): the fighter's champion (its blade thrust up), the knight's salute (its hilt
  before the chin), the rogue's ease, the mage's triumph (its staff planted, a hand to the sky), the cleric's thanks
  (palms pressed), the monk's martial salute (a fist in the palm, a bow); one with no class cheers. The party strikes
  them when a fight is won, the hero and each member by its class (a member's class read from its facets, as the
  casting reads it: `classOfFacets`). A world names its own per class, any pose of the hero door's (`battles.wins`),
  and the hero and that class's members are made with it. Before, a member struck its archetype's showcase pose and the
  hero a fist to the sky. A `motion` laid over an egocube character's sheet (`create_character { egocube, spec }`) now
  adds its words to the moves the sheet gives it, where it replaced them.
- **Treasure chests.** A book's battles may keep treasure off the path (`battles.chests: n`, 0 to 4 a fighting stage;
  a composed party RPG keeps two), each on a beat the packs leave free, a step aside from the way
  (`gameworld/chests.js`). E opens one: everything in it goes into the bag at once and the find is said ("Found 2
  potions and an ether!"), its loot by how far on. Opened again it is empty; emptied, its shut body gives way to an open
  one; and the store keeps what each still holds (the bag's `holders`, the `chests` slice), so it stays opened. Built
  from a chest menu looted whole, new: `play.menus` `{ kind: 'chest', loot: 'all' }`, which any level can stand by hand;
  and two new forms on the glyph shelf, `chest` and `chest-open`.
- **Game over.** A composed party RPG ends a lost fight in a game over (the game's `gameOver`, `game/game-manifest.js`):
  the fight lost is never kept (the store stays as it was last written), and the game over screen offers continue, from
  where the journey was last kept (the map the party was on at its last way taken or save point), or quit to title. A new
  flow screen, `gameover` (`continue`, `home`), where a lost level goes in place of the result (`game/flow.js`); drawn by
  the play shell, and by its mana-ui front in the game's look. Any play-shell game may ask for it (`gameOver: true`).
  Before, a lost fight showed the result with try again, and its defeat was written into the save.
- **A fight's results.** A fight won ends on a results window (`rpg-spoils`, `playscape/rpg/rpg-ui.js`) once its last
  beat is told: its XP, its gold and what it dropped; each member standing with its level and an XP bar to the next; a
  level gained with a Level up! badge and each stat it raised, before → after; a class rank risen; the skills learned.
  Continue closes the fight. A level beat now carries the member's stats before and after (`kernel.js` `gain`). Before,
  the spoils were only lines told one after another in the message line.
- **A party RPG is about something: its brief from its words.** A composed party RPG now carries a game brief
  (`gameworld/gmn.js`): a motivation and a labour read from its words (`GMN_WORDS`, the words people say for each:
  princess, citadel, sea, sister…, `gmnOfWords`; the first named the lead), a JRPG's own where they name none (save the
  world, storm the citadel). It is stamped as any brief is (stakes, ending, acts, colour script, light, the first level's
  and the climax's orders) and said in `brief.round.brief`. The round's shape is read from its labour: the mandala, as
  before; a labour asking for a chain, a hub or an open world is laid as the mandala for now, and the brief says so.
- **The citadel: a labour's climax as a walled core.** Where a party RPG's labour climaxes in a citadel (storm the
  citadel), its core is a walled-core dungeon (`wcd/wcd.js`) over its level: a guardhouse (an outer), its vault (the
  dungeon the words name, else a crypt) and its sanctum (the `citadel` program), the complex's buildings on its critical
  path, the packs fought through them and the boss in the sanctum. A citadel the words name is always laid, with its boss
  (before, "save the princess from the citadel" laid no dungeon and no boss); the JRPG's own labour, unnamed, builds it
  where the words lay a dungeon. The WCD's gates are its design's words, not locks: the way in stays the mandala's key.
- **The round's quest in the journal.** A party RPG laid as a mandala keeps a quest (the journal, J), named for its
  brief's motivation and walked as the round is: find the core's key where it is kept, go into the core, bring down its
  boss where it has one. Each step is raised by what happens: the key's pickup, the core begun, the boss's fall
  (`battles.sets`). For this a world's quest step may now be raised by any bus event or by its level's start
  (`{ log, done, on, at? }`, `gameworld/story.js` `questRaises`: a cue a stage lays for it), beside a moment's or an
  answer's flag.
- **The round in its era.** A party RPG's round is reskinned in its setting's era (`gameworld/round-eras.js`), the
  presets' numbers kept so its ladder, shops, chests and packs compose unchanged: a future round's foes are machines in
  an animal's shape (the `techno` and `transmetal` oozes), the hive's insect people and troopers, its items Med-kits and
  Energy Cells, its boss the Core Sentinel, its citadel barracks, a lab and command, its levels named for a colony; a
  modern round's strays, thugs and First-aid Kits. "Sci-fi", "space", "futuristic", "galactic", "starship" now name the
  alien world's kit (the composer's `LEXICON`, for any genre). A chest says its find by the world's names. A kind's arms
  go with its own look only. Before, a sci-fi party RPG was a meadow of slimes and potions under an Ember Drake.
- **The round in its labour's shape.** A party RPG's round is laid in the shape its brief's labour asks for
  (`gameworld/megaworld.js`): the mandala (storm the citadel), a CHAIN of maps one way on (cross the great sea), a HUB
  joined to every zone (be the very best), an OPEN ring of neighbours (conquer the map); in each the town sets out, the
  core is gated by its key and its first win ends the game, with the save points, the game over, the chests and the
  quest. The megaworld's game end is now a chain's last zone, or a hub's or an open world's `end` (a new key), where
  only a mandala's core ended a game before; the travel screen draws each. Before, every party RPG was a mandala.
- **The boss, measured, and its telegraphed blow.** A foe's action pattern row may `charge` (`true`, or the line said,
  `{name}` the foe's): it spends that turn gathering, said in the message line and played as its channel (the juice's
  new `charge`), then lets the blow or the skill go on its next turn at twice its power (`unleash`); a guard takes half,
  so the turn between is the party's to brace. A foe may take **phases** (`phases: [{ below, say?, pattern?, traits,
  numbers }]`): under each share of its HP, once and in order, it takes that form on that fight's foe alone, said and
  roared (the juice's new `phase`). The Ember Drake breathes a charged blast every third turn, and under half its HP
  its scales blaze: it absorbs ice and is weak to thunder, hits harder and charges every second turn. It is retuned
  (800 HP, atk 26, mag 24, from 160, 17, 13) against a new law, `gameworld/boss-law.test.js`: a party walks the
  round's ladder for real on sixteen seeds (its levels, class points and spells earned), then meets the drake four
  ways, held to a boss's shape (a careful party wins nearly always, a careless one mostly falls, one that skipped the
  ladder's last fights wins less, bracing and reading the second form are each worth winning, 8 to 20 rounds).
  Before, a careless party at level 3 beat it seven times in eight.
- **The story's bosses, starters to edit.** A party RPG's boss is the one its story calls for
  (`gameworld/round-bosses.js`, by the brief's labour): the Ember Drake (a citadel, the innermost cave), a Leviathan (a
  sea voyage's far shore), the Champion (a tournament's final hall), the Warlord (a conquest's last stronghold), the
  Thunderbird (catching them all) and the Colossus (once every task is done). Each is a new preset foe with a
  telegraphed blow and a second form that turns its weaknesses round, a look, its kind's arms (the champion's
  longsword and kite shield, the warlord's great axe), a height, lines for its fight and its era's versions; four new
  skills carry them (Tidal Wave, Gale, Quake, War Cry). A composed world writes its boss out whole in its battles
  (`foes`, `looks`, a new `heights` key, `bossPages`), so every part is the person's to change, or to replace with a
  boss of their own; a people foe's arms now follow its look written out as well as its preset. A story the words named
  now always lays its boss (a sea voyage had none before). Each starter is held to the boss law by a new deep sweep,
  `gameworld/boss-law.deep.test.js`, on the law's harness, `gameworld/boss-law.fixture.js`.
- **Not everyone wears a necklace; bosses are named whole.** The character designer's focal piece by archetype
  (`egocube/outfit.js` `FOCAL`) gave eight of twelve archetypes a medallion, so a crowd was all pendants. A necklace is
  now the emblem only of those who keep one (the ruler's chain of office, the sage's and the magician's amulet); the
  others are told by a piece of their own: the innocent's and the caregiver's sash, the lover's arm rings, the
  explorer's satchel, the everyman's belt (its buckle in the accent), the jester's collar, the creator's pouches, and an
  unarmoured hero its belt (bracers where the cut already draws its own belt, so no figure wears two). A belt's buckle in the trim now counts toward the outfit's repetition law, as a sash's knot
  does. The beast-kin body's designed pins moved with its default dress (the body itself unchanged). The people bosses'
  looks name their facets, so neither rolls a child or an elder: the Champion an adult hero of heroic build, the
  Warlord a seasoned outlaw of brute build (its baldric and cloak); their era versions alike.
- **The people bosses in every tradition and era.** A people boss is drawn in each tradition (the anime head in an
  anime world, the landmark head in a western one) at the age its look names, and an era's version holds none of the
  fantasy armory: the modern and future champions' looks say `gear: {}` (bare-fisted; write `gear` to arm one), since a
  look written out like the preset's now carries the preset kind's arms. Held by a new case in `round-bosses.test.js`.
- **RPG primitives, step 1: traits.** A class's or a piece of gear's traits (`playscape/rpg/rpg.js` `readTraits`) gain
  the RATES, shares added to the fight's own: `hit`, `eva` and `crit` (the kernel's MISS and CRIT were constants); what a
  plain blow carries: `element` (a flame sword strikes fire) and `inflict: { is, chance?, rounds? }` (a status left only
  where the blow lands); and the skills a piece `grants` while worn or a class while held. A foe names its rates,
  element and inflict as its own fields; a state may carry rates. The rates move the fight's own dice and add none, so a
  world that names none fights byte for byte as it did (the boss law and the kernel's pins unmoved). Five starters
  (the Venom Dagger, the Flame Sword, the Hunter's Charm, the Shadow Cloak, the Ember Ring), in the second and third
  shops, named in each era.
- **RPG primitives, step 2: effects.** A skill may strike more than once (`hits`, 2 to 8), deal its damage in another
  form (`damage`: `gravity` a share of the HP as it stands, `fixed` its power exactly, `pierce` through the guard, `mp`
  from the MP), take a share back (`drain`, HP or MP) or steal (`steal`: a foe's first drop into the bag, once a foe; a
  mug with power); an item may leave a `status` or give a `buff`. None rolls where it is unused, so the boss law and the
  pins are unmoved. Starters on the class trees, bought, never learned unasked (Steal, Mug, Armor Pierce, Twin Cut,
  Drain, Osmose, Gravity: the bosses immune to it), and three items in the shops (Power Tonic, Sleep Powder, Smoke
  Bomb), named in each era; a theft has its juice (`steal`).
- **RPG primitives, step 3: what a state does.** A state (the world's own, or a preset's by name) may now scale its
  bearer's numbers (`stats`), the damage it takes (`takes: { blow?, spell? }`), fight in a frenzy past commanding
  (`berserk`), turn a spell aimed at it alone back on its caster (`reflect`), draw the foes' aimed blows to itself
  (`taunt`), fell it as it runs out (`doom`), and say what a second cast does (`stack`: refresh, keep, add). Eight preset
  states (haste, slow, barrier, shell, berserk, reflect, taunt, doom) and the skills that cast them, a world's to put on
  a tree or grant: none sits on a preset tree, so a world naming none carries no states table and fights as it did. The
  bosses are immune to Doom. Petrify is not yet a behaviour.
- **RPG primitives, step 4: reactions.** What a fighter does on another's turn, a trait on a class or gear, a foe's own
  field or a state's: `counter` (a chance to strike back at a blow aimed at it alone; never a counter countered), `cover`
  (it steps before a badly hurt ally a foe's blow is aimed at) and `revive` (it rises once a fight with that share of its
  HP; a state's, Reraise, spent with it). Only a counter rolls, and only for its bearer, so a world naming none fights as
  it did. The Riposte Ring, the Guardian Crest and the Phoenix Charm in the shops, named in each era; the Reraise state
  and its cast opt-in; their juice (counter, cover, rise).
- **RPG primitives, step 5: costs.** A skill may cost HP (`hpCost`, its user needing more), be a limit break (`limit`:
  used only on a full gauge, which the blows a member takes fill, emptying it; a world with none keeps no gauge, and
  `rpg.<member>.limit` is on the bus where it does) or rest after use (`cooldown`, 1 to 9 of its user's turns). The skill
  list shows each cost (MP, HP, LIMIT n%, wait n); a foe pays as a member does and never uses a limit break. Starters:
  Blood Blade and Meteor bought on the fighter's and the mage's trees; Braver and Healing Wind, limit breaks, opt-in.
- **RPG primitives, step 6: rows and scan.** A world that asks for rows (`rules.rows`) stands its party in a front and a
  back row (`party[].row`): the back deals and takes half from blows, never from spells or ranged blows (a skill's or a
  weapon's `ranged`), the Row command moves a member, and a save keeps it; a world without rows has neither. `scan` on a
  skill or an item reads a foe's HP, weaknesses and guards into the message line. The mage's Scan on its tree, the Scan
  Lens and the Hunting Bow in the shops, named in each era. The six steps' primitives (traits, effects, state behaviours,
  reactions, costs, rows and scan) leave a world that names none fighting byte for byte as it did.
- **Openings: the party strikes first, or is ambushed.** `rules.openings` (true, or the chance of each) rolls a fight's
  opening: the party first (the foes sit out the first round; on the timeline the party's gauges start full) or
  ambushed (the reverse, the rows turned about where there are rows), never at a fight with no escape; an encounter may
  script its own (`opening`). Each opens with its line and juice (`start:first`, `start:ambush`). A composed party RPG
  asks for them; a world that asks none opens every fight as it did.
- **Key items, locked chests and mimics.** The party menu gains a Key tab: what the bag holds that is no battle item,
  gear or gold (the map's keys, a chest's, a quest's piece), named by `play.items` of kind `key` where the world names
  them. `battles.chests` may be `{ n, locked?, mimics? }`: a locked chest's Iron Key is won from one of its stage's packs
  (never the boss), the bag holding it opening the chest; a mimic is a fight the chest stands for (`mimic`, a new preset
  foe; a Trap Drone, a Booby Trap in the eras), sprung as the party walks up, its treasure had when it is won. A
  composed party RPG asks for both (one in four, about one in seven); a book asking none keeps its chests as they were.
  The citadel's inner gates are not yet doors met in play.
- **The citadel's locks, met in play.** A new non-terminal mechanic, `lock` (`game/mechanics.js`): a seal in a doorway
  that opens for good where the bag holds its key (kept), else says what opens it and puts the party back. A party RPG's
  citadel lays its walled core's gated doors as locks across the building's route (`battles.js` `citadelLocks`), each on
  the last doorway between a guard and what lies past it, its key (named for the space it opens: the Vault Key) carried
  by that guard and given as its fight is won. A door with no doorway there is not laid, never a lock whose key lies past
  it; the composed citadel meets one lock (its last guard stands in the boss's room).
- **Joint techs.** `play.rpg.techs` (a book's `battles.techs`): a skill two or three members make together, each
  knowing one of its `needs`; listed in a member's skills with whom it is made (or no partner), each maker paying its
  part's MP, the partners' turns spent on it (reserved as a round is picked, so none moves first; on the timeline their
  gauges emptied), made with their stat summed; never started by a familiar. Five presets (Fire Strike, Frost Strike,
  Holy Cross, Venom Flame, Trinity, a triple), their juice (`joint`, `joined`); a composed party RPG asks for them, a
  world asking none lists none.
- **Dialogue and cutscenes that play.** A spike (`control/scripts/spikes/story-play/`) played a composed round's talk and
  story on the page in headless Chromium and found three gaps, now closed: a story moment binds to a building's stage
  (`levels.js` buildingSpots: its start, goal room, boss's spot and rooms), so a citadel keeps its ending; a composed
  party RPG is written a starter story from its brief's motivation (`gameworld/round-story.js`: its opening in the town,
  a line as the core begins, its ending in the core, staged by the flow on their pages); and a level won or lost while a
  scene is up ends as the scene closes (`scene/channels/game.js`: a quarter second's grace on a page with scenes, then
  held), so a moment at an exit is no longer cut short.
- **A building's page carries the world's interface, and the story's live test.** A building level now takes the
  world's HUD on mana-ui as a walk does (`levels.js` buildingLevelOrder), and with it the talk box its scenes are said in:
  the citadel's lines were said in the page's plain box before. `gameworld/jrpg-story.live.test.js` (the e2e tier) plays
  the composed round's story in Chrome: the opening staged on the town's page, a moment at the way out holding the
  level's end until its line is closed, the citadel's line as it begins and its ending staged there.
- **What a member wears, minted.** `battles.wardrobe: true` (or the book's own table over the presets) mints a figure
  per party member per armour its class may wear, the member's own body and dress under the armour's `adorn`
  (`gameworld/wardrobe.js`): leather armour a laced jerkin, chain mail a hauberk. The looks are run steps
  (`hero-look-<armour>`, `cast-<id>-look-<armour>`) beside the base figure; the page swapping them in on equip is the
  next step.
- **Leather and mail in the armour library.** Two families beside plate, lamellar and the hard-suit, each its own
  construction rather than plates: `leather` (`armor/leather.js`: a jerkin laced up the front or a boiled cuirass
  buckled at the sides, welted edges, a yoke and rounded caps on the shoulders, laced bracers and greaves, a belt and
  hanging strips, studs in rows: `language: { cut, studs }`) and `mail` (`armor/mail.js`: a byrnie, then a hauberk's
  slit skirt and belt, long sleeves, a coif and chausses, every piece worked in courses of rings by a new `courses`
  signature, a surcoat on request: `language: { coif, surcoat }`). Four cards: `jerkin`, `studded`, `hauberk`,
  `surcoat`. Worn over a designed outfit, a period armour leaves off the outfit's outer layer and its own armour
  pieces (a mantle, pauldrons, a chest plate, bracers, wraps), which hid it.
- **What a member wears, shown.** Each level lays the wardrobe's looks on its members' figures (`wardrobe.js`
  `wearLooks`, the hero's from the figure that holds its weapon); the page builds every look up front, as a loadout's
  bodies are (only where a figure has looks: none, not a byte), and the RPG channel shows the look the member's armour
  slot names (`rpg-channel.js` `dress`), on the map and in a fight, equipped from the menu or loaded from the store.
  `gameworld/wardrobe.live.test.js` (the e2e tier) puts armour on and takes it off in Chrome.
- **What a member wears, in the book and the handoff.** The world bible's battles section has a wardrobe card: each
  member in its own clothes and in each armour, photographed where made (`lib/mcp/tools/wardrobe-portraits.js`, the
  bible route); an engine handoff's level record gives each member's marker its looks, each armour's figure and the made
  body behind it. A run may now record a hero's look (`made.js` `MADE_KEY`: `hero-look-<armour>`), which it refused.
  The world bible no longer fails on a party RPG whose hub is a street (`battles-page.js` read it as a level graph).
- **The wardrobe played with its real bodies.** `control/scripts/spikes/wardrobe-play/` makes a party's members and their
  looks as a run does and plays a wilds block in Chrome: loaded in the starting gear's looks, taken off and put on, and
  fought in them by all four. It found mail refused on the anime head (its coif's head pieces are not fitted there): mail
  on that head is now worn without them, its drape kept (`hero-dress.js`).
- **A fight's shot kept clear.** A party battle on the map now clears what stands in its shot while it lasts: its
  footprint and the corridor from its camera to it, as wide as the frame (`rpg-channel.js` stage). Props there are cut
  away, the land kept (`scene-three.js` `__mojClip`, now on every page with party battles, not only an arena's; its cut
  now places an instanced group's copies where they stand), trees whose crowns reach it are left out (`form-flora.js`,
  only on such pages), and whoever is not in the fight is hidden. Found on the starter's wilds, where a crown filled half
  the frame, and on a town level, a wall's roof before the camera. `gameworld/fight-clear.live.test.js` holds the frame
  to at most 5 % covered; `control/scripts/spikes/fight-clear/` measures it.
  The clearing is patched into the materials as the page settles, not at the first fight. And a bar's news is drawn
  for at least three frames as well as 1.8 s: on a slow renderer, a frame longer than that, the struck foe's bar was
  never drawn (`rpg-channel.js` TOLD_FRAMES).
- **The command window opens beside the one acting, clear of the party.** The window beside the acting member's bar
  (its HP and MP parked over its head) now tries the places beside the bar, the right first, and takes the one that
  covers the acting member least, then the rest of the party, then the foes (`rpg-channel.js` besideAt). It was laid to
  the bar's right at the bar's top whatever stood there, and covered about half the hero beside the one acting in every
  fight of the starter's first three fighting levels; now none, and 14 % on a town level's tightest frame.
- **Only the one acting has its bar up.** On a member's turn only its HP and MP are over its head; choosing a target,
  only the target in focus shows its bar, moving with the cursor (`rpg-channel.js` battleModel `onAim`, `rpg-ui.js`
  HEAD); a round playing keeps its news. Every fighter's bar was up on the player's turn and hid the cast.
- **Each level its battle scene; no fights in a settlement.** A party RPG's fights are now fought at one place a level,
  solved at its first fight and kept (`rules.stage: 'scene'`, the battles' default, `rpg-channel.js` arenaStage): the
  level's most open place round its fights and where the party set out, scored by its level ground, what stands in its
  places, the plants round it (`form-flora.js` `__formFloraNear`) and what is built within 12 m. No pack is laid on a
  whole town or a street, nor within 30 m of what a stage has built beside its trail (`battles.js` SETTLED). The
  starter's castle heights fought in front of its church, the camera cut through its wall; it fights on the open hill.
- **RPG dungeon kits.** Four room kits for RPG dungeons, none of them built stone as the gothic kits are: `deep-forge`,
  `fungal-grotto`, `drowned-shrine`, `arcane-vault` (`era/stage.js` STAGE_KITS, their style cards
  `era/style/dungeon-kits.js`), each a chamber and its halls (`KIT_STARTERS`). One data-driven dressing,
  `era/dungeon.js` `dungeonDress`, reads each card's set piece, floor feature, walls, corners, halls and ceiling and
  places twenty-three new doodads (a forge hearth, anvils, ore carts, chain hoists, a molten channel; a mushroom grove,
  glowcaps, bracket fungi, roots, spores, a still pool; a drowned altar, coral, kelp, jellyfish lanterns, a flood; an
  orrery, a rune circle, bookcases, a lectern, crystal clusters, floating crystals) at the props' places
  (`props.js` `wallSpots`); their glow is self-lit and lays its light. A kit may light no lamp (`torch.none`).
  [docs/dungeon-kits.md](../../../../docs/dungeon-kits.md).
- **A town with a story carries its bag in again.** Once a level has story scenes (the round's opening in the town),
  what it carries in was read off the story's scenes alone, so the townsfolk's own pages that read the bag (the
  priest's crypt key) lost it (`levels.js` storyPart); both are read now.
- **The dungeons' principles counted, and one measured.** Each dungeon card's principles map to the shared laws
  (`era/laws.js` PRINCIPLE_LAWS, its cards in `statedPrinciples`; a card's `id` now its kit's, `dressing: 'dungeon'`
  sending it to its dressing). They add a law, `light-has-a-source` (every light is something in the place that gives
  it), measured by `era/dungeon.js` `sourceless`: each kit's starter lays no light away from its own glow.
- **A name typed in game.** mana-ui's text entry grows a name's keyboard (`charset: 'name'`): capitals, small letters
  and marks on pages of one size, turned by the shoulders or their tabs, with Space, Delete, Done and Cancel (when the
  entry answers `cancel`); `min` holds Done back. A pad types from the grid and its back erases what it typed; a
  computer keyboard types straight in whenever the entry has the focus, its case and marks kept. The RPG's party menu
  uses it: Status, Rename opens `rpg-name`, the kernel's `rename` names the member in every line after, and the store's
  new `rename` event (a party slice's, produced by the party mechanic) carries the name into the next level. The page's
  P key no longer closes the menu while a name is being typed.
- **A name asked as a game begins.** Any play-shell game may ask the player a name (`naming: { slice, id?, label?,
  max?, min? }`, a character slice's or a party member's): the flow gains a `name` screen (`withNaming`) before the
  first level wherever a new game begins, from the title's play or, for a game started in play, after its opening on a
  first boot. It is mana-ui's keyboard (the greybox where the game says no `ui`), and done keeps the name in the store
  (`rename` on a character slice too, marked `named`). A level with a party hands its page the names given
  (`window.__mojNames`), so story lines say them. The party RPG asks the hero's name unless `battles.naming: false`.

### Galaxy Boy's screens: energy, game over, the intro card, the start menu

The side map gets its own screens, drawn in the galaxy look over the held level, and a hit now costs energy, not a
life.

- **Energy** (the lives mechanic's `energy`, opt-in): a hit takes `hit` ticks of `max`, and a life goes when they run
  out. With `down`, the hero is dropped to fall out of the frame, and the fall takes the life and brings them back.
  A side map's hero has 28 ticks and a hit takes 4 (`SIDE_ENERGY`, `SIDE_DOWN`). The mascot platformer keeps a life per
  hit.
- **Continues** (the lives mechanic's `continues`, opt-in): none left waits on the player. `continue` on the bus gives
  the lives back, and `giveup` fails the level. A side map level of a game with a `ui` turns it on.
- **The HUD:** the hero's column is the energy, and the lives show under READY when they change.
- **The intro card:** as a level with a boss starts, a band with the boss's name in its hue, its world, its tell and
  what it gives. Any button or three seconds, then READY.
- **The start menu** (Enter): the weapons in the order earned, the buster first and the slots not yet won locked, the
  energy columns and the lives. Accept equips a loadout's weapon.
- **GAME OVER:** the gate reached, then Continue (from that gate, the lives back, weapons kept) or Give up.
- **The HUD host** (`scene/channels/mana-hud.js`) opens a side map HUD's screens over the held level, drives them with
  the keys and the pad, and raises their choices on the level's bus.

### Cinematic action game: the weapons in hand, and the round where the crosshair is

Tuning what it is to use a gun over the shoulder, found by playing the infiltration yard headless with the operative
(the hero door's words, `scripts/spikes/mission/operative.json`) and photographing the aim from behind, beside and in
front, a tick at a time.

- **The sights at the eye** (scene/channels/controllable/gunplay-view.js, the gun in the hero's hands): aimed, the gun's
  rear sight is brought onto the strong eye's line along the look. A pistol is pushed out along it to the arms' reach
  (the sights 0.6 m from the eye, nearer only where the strong arm would not reach), both hands on it; a long gun is
  lifted from its shoulder pocket to the line, its depth kept. Before, aiming held the pistol at the belly with the
  elbows bent, so over the shoulder no gun was in the frame. The raise follows the sights' own `aimTime` (a service
  pistol's is 0.16 s from the low ready); a round flips the muzzle up as well as back (a pistol's more), settling as the
  kick does. It is every carried gun's hold off the eye (a quick shooter's over the shoulder too); the first person's
  viewmodel is its own and unchanged.
- **The arm itself in the yard's hands** (gameworld/infiltration-room.js): the hero's kit asks for each gun as the arms
  library builds it (arms-kit.js `armDetailed`), as the mission and the firing range do, where it drew the parts'
  boxes (a pistol read as a dark slab). About 55 kB a pistol on the page. The guards' carbines keep their boxes: each
  guard would carry its own copy of the mesh (140 kB).
- **What is seen is hit** (worlds/controllable/combat-ranged.js, a converging round's: `weapon.converge`, an
  over-the-shoulder camera): the round is resolved along the crosshair's own ray, from the shooter's depth on it, its
  cone and climb round that ray; the muzzle's line to what that ray meets is still what cover is read on, and a round
  that misses stops where the ray meets a wall, or short of it where the muzzle's line meets cover first. Down the
  muzzle's own line to the crosshair's point, a body half a metre beside the crosshair at 5 m was hit (the camera stands
  that far off the hand), and the round struck it low and to one side of where the crosshair was.
- **The shot blocked, said before the trigger** (combat-ranged.js `shotBlocked`; the reticle, controllable/index.js, the
  aim held's pages only): the camera sees past what the gun does not (a low wall under its eye, a corner beside it).
  While the muzzle's line to the point under the crosshair meets cover first, the crosshair dims and a small cross marks
  where the round would stop. Before, the crosshair sat on a guard behind a low wall and the round went into the wall,
  with nothing said.
- **A rifle on the cheek** (gunplay-view.js, a long gun aimed): its butt stays in the shoulder's pocket and rises only a
  quarter of the way to the eye's line; the head comes down and over onto the stock for the rest (to a limit), so the eye
  looks down the sights. Brought up to the eye whole, the rifle floated before the face with its stock through the head.
- **The crosshair climbs with a spray, and a ring is its cone** (controllable/index.js, the aim held's pages): a round
  leaves up the crosshair's ray raised by the climb, and the view rises only part of it, so the crosshair is drawn where
  the climbed ray points and settles back as the climb does; round it, a ring is the cone the next round leaves in (its
  base as the sights have scaled it, the move's share, the bloom). An aimed rifle's spray stays inside what is drawn.
  Before, the crosshair stayed small and still while a spray's rounds climbed 2.6° over it and opened to 4°.
- **An aimed spray opens less** (worlds/controllable/gunplay.js, arms-kit.js `ADS.bloom`): a held trigger's bloom, a
  round's and its most, is the sights' share of the hip's (half); the hip's is as it was. An assault rifle's aimed spray
  opens to 2°.
- **The scope carries the whole climb** (gunplay-view.js): through a scope the view rises with all of a round's climb,
  so its crosshair is where the next round goes while the rifle settles; neither the drawn crosshair nor its ring is laid
  over the scope's picture. A bolt rifle's climb settles in a second (arms-kit.js, its `recover` 2.5 to 4 a second),
  inside its 1.3 s cycle: the scope is back on the mark as the next round is chambered, where it drifted back over 1.6 s
  and the next round left 0.75° over the scope's crosshair.
- **A kit in the yard** (`scripts/spikes/mission/room.mjs --arms rifle,sniper`): the arms kit's words carried in place of
  the feel template's, to try a gun there.
- **The launchers in the arms library** (equipment/arms/launchers.js, item `launcher`): the GRENADE LAUNCHER (`grenade`,
  the default), a 40 mm revolving launcher: a fat barrel out of a breech block over a six-chamber cylinder on its axis
  (its chambers' mouths dark in its front face, bands along it), a strap over it carrying the rail and the sight, a
  raked grip and its guard behind, a stock, a vertical grip under the barrel; and the ROCKET LAUNCHER (`rocket`), a
  bazooka: one tube flared to a venturi at its back, a pad under it where the shoulder takes it, a raked grip ahead of the
  pad, a vertical grip forward, and the sight on a bracket off the tube's left side, where the eye is beside the tube on
  the right shoulder. Both held to the arms' laws in each line (the future's conduit, the near's seam and counter), their
  stations and handling read off them (handling.js: a sight off the bore's side carries its `x`), a hero's long gun
  (hero-gear.js). `render-arms.mjs launcher,launcher-od` draws them.
- **A grenade launcher and a bazooka in the kit** (gameworld/arms-kit.js `launcher`, `bazooka`): their rounds travel
  (combat-ranged.js the lob). The grenade launcher six a load at 45 m/s under gravity, bursting 3 m round for four base
  rounds; the bazooka one a load at 38 m/s and straight, bursting 4 m round for six, its tube reloaded in three seconds.
- **Launched through the crosshair** (combat-ranged.js `lobAim`; a converging lob's): over the shoulder a travelling
  round is launched from the muzzle on the flight that passes the point under the crosshair (a grenade's low arc, a
  rocket's straight line; past its reach, the farthest arc toward it), its cone and climb round that. Where it was
  launched along the look, a rocket flew beside the crosshair by the hand's offset all the way.
- **The arc and the landing ring before the trigger** (combat-ranged.js `lobPath`; the aim held's reticle): while a
  launcher is aimed, its round's flight as it would go now is drawn, a dashed line from the muzzle, and where it goes
  off a ring the size of its burst laid there, red where the flight ends on a body. Not while it reloads or is drawn.
- **The crosshair stops at the ground** (combat-ranged.js `crosshairPoint`): the crosshair's ray ends on the ground
  plane a travelling round bursts on, where it ran on under the floor to its range; a grenade aimed at open ground came
  down 3 m short at 90 m. A rifle's round is unchanged by it (it flies the ray either way).
- **What a launcher's round looks like** (a round's `look`, gameworld/rounds.js `grenade`, `rocket`; the controllable
  page): a 40 mm shell a hand long, dull, no glow, eased out of the drawn gun's muzzle onto its flight; a rocket finned
  on a flickering flame, dropping smoke behind it, the tube's backblast thrown a few metres back at the launch. Its burst:
  a white flash, a ball of fire billowing and gone in a third of a second, grey smoke rising and spreading for two, chips
  thrown out and falling, a ring of dust running out along the ground to the burst's reach and a scorch left there for
  nine seconds, sized by the reach, every scatter golden-angle. Soft sprites, each born at its first size. Before, a
  travelling round was the mecha's glowing cone and its burst a translucent sphere. The explosion library
  (playscape/elements/explosions.js) draws on the moment channel, which a page without events does not carry: not yet.
- **Hand grenades: frag, stun and chaff** (gameworld/arms-kit.js `frag`, `stun`, `chaff`, `GRENADES`, `THROWN`): weapons in
  hand from the weapon menu, three to a slot (one in hand, the next in it 0.6 s after), thrown at 16 m/s under gravity,
  quietly (no shot is heard). Aimed, the arc and the ring are drawn as a launcher's are, the ring its burst's reach: a
  frag's 4 m (red on a body), a stun's 6 m (white), a chaff's cloud's 15 m (a cold blue).
- **The throw** (worlds/controllable/throw.js, `weapon.throw: { dur, release, clip? }`, inside the aim): the press starts
  the throw and the round leaves the hand at its release (half of its second), launched on the arc through the
  crosshair; a switch, a reel or a fall before the release throws nothing. The body plays its `throw` state for it: the
  infiltration yard's `toss` (`room.mjs --throw throwOverhand`) the hero's own solved overhand (the operative carries the
  motion word `throwOverhand`), its ball the grenade in the hand.
- **What each does where it goes off** (combat-ranged.js burstProjectile, the round's `effect`): a FRAG hurts all round
  it, whole inside its reach (four base rounds); a STUN knocks out (knockout.js E.knockOut; staggers, where a world does
  not knock out) every body inside its reach with a clear line from it to the eyes, and hurts no one; a CHAFF hurts and
  knocks no one and lays a cloud that jams round it for 15 s (`state.jams`, `E.jammedAt`): a guard inside it radioing the
  alarm in gets nothing through while it is jammed (alarm.js: the call waits, `jammed` its seconds), and the radar reads
  nothing while the pilot stands in it (the page's own radar and mana-ui's: static and JAMMED, no blips).
- **A burst's hurt stays a hurt** (knockout.js): a world that knocks out took every hurt of the pilot's that was not a
  gun's round for a blow, so a frag or a launcher's burst knocked guards out where it should kill. A burst marks what it
  hurt (`burstHitAt`) and the knockout leaves it.
- **What they look like** (the round's `look`, rounds.js `frag`, `stun`, `chaff`): a frag a round body with its fuse, a
  stun's and a chaff's a can, dark and pale, each tumbling end over end on its arc. The frag's burst the blast. The stun's
  a white flash metres wide gone in a quarter second, a cold glow after it, a ring of air along the ground to its reach,
  a little white smoke, and the eye within one and a half its reach whited out, the more the nearer, thinning over a
  second and a half. The chaff's a pop of grey and its cloud: foil strips thrown a few metres out, slowing, drifting down
  and swaying, each glittering in its own time, the cloud thinning at the end of its seconds.
- **Getting into a vehicle and riding it** (worlds/controllable/board.js, a vehicle's `board: { reach?, out?, form?, climb? }`,
  inside the takedown and the knockout): the action within a vehicle's reach (3.5 m), with no takedown or sleeper nearer,
  climbs in (half a second, the climb's clip, carried onto it), and then the vehicle is the pilot: its pilot rule, the
  stick, the trigger and its turret's look, the camera following it where it followed the rider; the rider is aboard,
  out of sight, never hit, carried with it. The action again halts it and lets its rider out, in its boarding form first
  (a walker folds onto its wheels), set down at its left side, the pilot and its camera given back. A vehicle downed
  throws its rider out where it stands. The guards see, chase and shoot the vehicle while it is ridden: it is the pilot.
- **The rover walker to ride** (gameworld/ride-machine.js `rideVehicle`, `RIDE`; the yard's `ride`, `room.mjs --ride
  'rover walker'`): the transforming walker parked in its tank form, low on its wheels as it is boarded, and got into.
  Driven on its wheels at its drive's 6 m/s, steered; B unfolds it onto its legs and it walks at its gait's 2.2 m/s (the
  artillery range's frame, combat/frames.js: its rig, its gait, its tank form, the fold between them, its steered wheels).
  Its backpack's guns, laid by the mouse on their mounts (the turret's chase view, its aim a pip): the autocannon
  automatic, four rounds a second from a belt of 40, each bursting 1.8 m round; 2 loads the rocket pod, a salvo of six at
  60 m/s, each bursting 4 m round; drawn as the launchers' rounds are. It takes 1200 before it is downed.
- **A frame to ride resolved from its words** (worlds/world-scene.js, a figures-map entry `{ frame: { frame, stance?,
  palette? } }`): rigged as the artillery range rigs it, so a level's manifest carries the words and never the bodies;
  combat/frames.js `frameBase` keeps a few by their words (the machine's numbers and its figure read the same frame).
- **The gunner's readout only for a gunner** (turret-view.js): its panel and its sight's glass hidden while no turret is
  the pilot's (a rider got out), the small arms' reticle and card back.

### Start screens as a game's launcher: its cast as graphic design, type that performs

In progress. A game's start screen opens at once, before any of the game's engine loads, and today it shows little: a
title over the theme's ground, or a heading and a play button. The plan: a start screen made like a high-end motion
website, composed from the game's own characters, vehicles and props, never a level or a set.

- Two modes of one composition. The default draws stylized pictures of the game's subjects (cut out, duotone, halftone,
  inked) laid out with large type and motion, with no 3D on the screen. The high-end mode puts the same subjects in live
  3D, idling under the game's light, loaded only after the first picture has shown.
- A layout per kind of game, each a card: a hero posed, two fighters facing off, a car in a showroom, a gun or an
  operator as hardware, a party, pieces on a table.
- The game's name performs (letters that rise, slam or draw themselves on) while the menu stays plain words with
  no boxes, and a player who turns down motion gets fades.
- While the start screen is up, the first level starts loading, and the loading screen keeps the start screen's look.
- In the guided design, the start screen is offered near the end, once the first level plays; the person can ask for
  it at any time.
- **Begun: the recipe and the first layout.** A game's front takes a `stage`: which layout, which of its subjects stand
  on it (its hero, a friend, a foe, its vehicle, a prop, or a sketch named), pictures or 3D, and how a picture is made
  graphic. It is checked like the rest of the front and drawn by nothing yet, so every game's start screen is as it was.
  A game's subjects are read from what its design runs made and the hero it adopted, and a game with something to
  show can be offered a stage that suits its kind of game. The first layout is the hero pose: one figure large and off
  centre, the game's name huge behind it, the menu as words on the open side, laid out for a wide screen and an upright
  phone (`playscape/ui/front-cards/`).
- **The start screen drawn, in pictures.** Exporting a game whose front has a stage now pictures its subjects: each
  is posed a moment into its first animation, seen from the angle its layout asks, cut out cleanly (a soft edge, no
  floor, nothing behind it) and drawn in one of six looks in the game's own colours: cut out with a rim of the accent,
  a flat silhouette, two-tone, a few flat bands of its own colours, a dot screen, or inked lines. The game's start
  screen then shows the hero pose: the game's name set huge behind the figure and entering letter by letter, the
  figure rising in, the menu as plain words with no boxes, for a wide screen and an upright phone, whether its screens
  are the plain ones or drawn by the game UI. The pictures are kept between exports, so a second export takes no time,
  and a game whose subject could not be pictured (no browser where it is exported) still gets its name and its ground,
  with the reason said. A player who turns motion down gets fades. Only an export draws it: the game page in the
  dashboard is unchanged.
- **Every game UI title performs.** A game whose screens the game UI draws now brings its name in letter by letter on
  its title and its attract screen, in its look's way: rising, slamming in, wiped on or tracking in. A look says which
  with a new word, `title` (`still` keeps the name whole), and one that says none rises. The entrance follows the look's
  own motion, so a look with none shows the name at once, and a player who turns motion down sees it fade. The name is
  still read aloud as one word. On a start screen drawn as a picture, the menu is now words with no window or band
  behind it, drawn so by the game UI itself. The wireframe board shows the entrance on its title and attract screens.
- **The high-end start screen: the figure comes alive.** A stage in `mode: '3d'` opens on its pictures as before;
  then, once they have shown, the page loads the 3D engine and each subject's model and fades the living figure in
  over its picture, framed by the very camera the picture was taken with and starting its idle where the picture
  caught it, so the picture seems to begin to breathe. The figure turns a little toward the pointer and sways, keeps
  its accent rim (or its silhouette), and stops drawing while a level is played. The engine comes beside the game in
  its folder, or from the pinned CDN when the game is exported with `cdn: true`. Without WebGL, with a model that will
  not load or is too heavy for a start screen, or for a player who turns motion down, the picture stays and nothing
  else changes. Looks that remake a picture's colours (two-tone, dot screen, posterize, ink) stay pictures, and the
  export says so.
- **From the start screen into the game.** While a staged start screen is up, the game quietly starts fetching its
  first level in the background (not on a connection that asks to save data, and not past 30 MB), so pressing start
  plays from what is already there. Pressing start then turns the start screen itself into the loading screen: the
  figure stays where it stood, the big name gives way to a small one in the corner, and the place being loaded is named
  over a thin bar, with a note if a big map is still being built. When the level's first frame is drawn, the loading
  screen fades away over it. Both screen kinds, the plain ones and those drawn by the game UI, hand over this way; a
  game without a staged start screen keeps its loading screen as it was.
- **Offered near the end of the guided design.** Once a game's first level is proved and it has something to show,
  `design_game` offers its start screen as a next move, `front`: the layout its kind of game suits, who stands on it,
  and the change that lays it, which the person takes or leaves (it is never a goalpost, and nothing is laid unasked).
  Before then it is theirs to ask for in the interface chapter. A start screen is reviewed there as its own part, the
  start screen: its layout, who stands on it, pictures or 3D and their look, and what it lacks. The interface card
  says what a start screen is, when it is offered, and its layouts and looks.
- **One character a start screen, and the other shells' starts.** A start screen stands a single character on its
  ground, never a cast: a layout that names more is refused (a cast is the select screen's). A new layout, the
  champion: one fighter squared up to the player across a hard diagonal, its side of the cut in the game's accent,
  sliding in from its side, the game's name huge across the cut. It is the start screen offered to fighting games,
  brawlers and arena shooters with a hero to show, and a layout can now say which way its figure turns. A versus
  game's title, drawn on its own canvas, is laid out by the same layout: its first fighter on its colour, the name
  entering letter by letter, press start as plain words, on a wide screen or an upright phone, and whole at once for
  a player who turns motion down. An arena game's start screen takes a stage too (`menu.stage`, its subject named by
  sketch), pictured at export and drawn behind its start screen alone, its words moved where the layout puts them;
  one without a stage is as it was, byte for byte. A contest's start stays its broadcast's opening; the tabletop, the
  pen-and-paper game and the pixel games keep their own starts.
- **The character, or a picture of the person's own: never both.** A start screen is the character on a graphic
  ground, unless the person brings a picture for it: `background` on the stage, a picture uploaded to a stash on the
  dashboard, or a file the agent has, which the game design's patch files into a stash first, so the recipe names the
  picture wherever it goes. A picture stands on its own with the game's name and its menu, and no character is drawn
  over it (it may well show the character already). The export copies it beside the game and fills the screen with it
  under a wash of the game's own ground colour so the name and the menu still read; a picture that is gone or is not a
  picture is said, and the character stands on the graphic ground instead. The review's start screen says which it is.

### The aerial ground: a pilot's country of fields, woods, roads, towns and a metro

A flight level's land was the terrain kernel's ramp coloured per vertex: from altitude, flat paint over rolling hills,
and its city plain boxes on a plinth. `airspace.ground.country` lays settled country on it, drawn at a pilot's grain:
what reads from the air (a block's buildings at their heights, their windows, the streets as paint, a highway on its
piers, a tank farm, a pylon line), never a walker's detail. See `docs/flight-games.md`, "The ground from the air".

- **The country** (`skyscape/country.js`): every settlement is the geocity's design laid on the map's own natural
  ground, at a card by its size: a metro (a geocity metro card; sited on the coast where the sea allows, its water side
  turned to the sea, its harbour dredged, its shore expressway and waterfront the sea's), a market town and a village
  (the same generator at smaller cards: a low core, houses outward, nothing over seven storeys in a town or three in a
  village). Each is graded onto its streets' ground with a kernel grade layer. A minimum spanning tree of roads joins
  them and the airfield, each road routed across the land on the map's grid (grade a cost, the sea and the pads walls;
  a metro's link to a town a highway, a village's a lane). A pylon line runs from a substation out to the reach, away
  from the field. Water towers stand on the settlements' high edges and a lit mast on the field's highest ground. Ask:
  `country: true | { metro?, towns?, villages?, settlements?, roads?, power?, landmarks? }`.
- **The land's cover** (`skyscape/cover-kernel.js`): woods, crops, heath and sand read off the land (woods on slopes
  too steep to plough, on high ground and in woodlots, cleared round the settlements; crops on the flat low ground
  near them; pasture the rest). It is self-contained, like the terrain kernel; the page inlines it and bakes it.
- **The page** (`scene/channels/aerial.js`, carried by the terrain channel as `aerial`, packed by `skyscape/aerial.js`):
  - The ground's shader draws the cover per pixel: field systems turned with the land, their parcels hedged, furrowed,
    cropped or grazed; woods as a canopy; heath; sand. The settlements' plans and the roads are painted from a canvas.
    Each pattern fades to its mean under a pixel, and all of it is lit as the land is.
  - Every building is an instance of a unit box under a facade shader, its windows a storey and a bay by its skin
    (curtain wall, office, flat, hall's ribbon, house), its glass catching the sky as the eye grazes it. Houses and
    halls have gables. Tanks, spheres, stacks, water towers, highway decks and their piers stand too, and pylons as
    lattices of lines with their conductors sagging.
  - A map without a country carries none of it: the terrain channel's script is byte for byte as it was.
- **The craft's ground**: the settlements' roofs, the water towers and the mast join `roofs`, so a craft can hit them.
  A settlement's approach is a bookmark.
- **Exports** carry the buildings as faces. The cover stays the page's.
- **Pilot School**'s island airfield is farmed country now: a market town, two villages, the lanes between them and the
  field, a line of pylons and a mast.
- The flight card (`gameworld-flight`) names `airspace.ground.country`.

### The airfield: a taxiway, its lights, the PAPI, and runways sited for their approach

- **A taxiway** beside every runway (`skyscape/ground.js`, `TAXIWAY`, `taxiwayOf`): parallel to it 85 m off its
  centreline, on the side toward the field's middle, joined by a connector at each end and one at its middle.
  - It lies on the runway's graded ground, with the strip between them painted the cover's pasture, the field it is cut from.
  - It is asphalt with a yellow centre line.
  - At night (`skyscape/night-lights.js`) its edges are lit blue every 30 m and the connectors' centre lines green.
- **The PAPI** (`papiOf`, the page's `night-lights.js`): at each runway end, four lamps beside the touchdown aim
  (`RUNWAY_AIM`, 150 m past the threshold) on the left as the runway is landed on.
  - Each is white seen from above its angle and red from under it (3.5°, 3.17°, 2.83°, 2.5°), so the 3° path shows two
    of each.
  - The page colours each by the eye's elevation from it, seen only from its approach.
  - They are lit by day as well as by night, so a map by day carries the lights channel with the PAPI alone.
- **Runways sited for their approach** (`APPROACH`): a runway's site now keeps the ground beyond the end it is landed
  over under a 3% (about 1.7°) surface, as it kept its departure's under 5%. Pilot School's island runway moved to such a
  site.
  - A clear departure still comes first: an approach is weighed only between sites that can be flown out of.
  - Only a powered craft's runway is held to it; a glider lands from whichever way its course brings it in.
  - Earthwork past 15 m now costs steeply, so a runway is not sunk into a cutting to find a clear approach: its walls
    would be obstacles of their own.
- **The lesson pilot** aims at the runway's aim point, the PAPI's. On its way in it comes down toward the slope's height,
  never under 90 m until lined up, and tracks the glide path more tightly. The night circuit is still flown to gold, and
  the flight proof checks that its final reads two red and two white.
- The night circuit's words name the PAPI and the taxiway lights.

### Recorded sound library

- **In progress.** Games and worlds can play recorded sound effects alongside the synthesized ones: a library of
  realistic sounds recorded with ElevenLabs, installed on demand and never part of the npm package. A sound keeps its
  synthesized voice, which still plays wherever the library is not installed.
- The SFX shelf plays its recordings: where the library is installed, a realistic one-shot it records (a gunshot by
  its cartridge, a footstep by its surface, an impact, a creature) plays one of its recorded takes per hit, and a
  creature the realistic style had no voice for gets one. A page carries only the recordings its level plays, as MP3.
  Other styles, sounds asked for at their own dials and machines without the library are unchanged.
- Cars sound recorded: an engine is a set of loops recorded at steady revs, crossfaded and bent in pitch as it revs, so
  it climbs smoothly; tyres screech and the road roars from recordings too. The open city's car and a racing car share
  the recordings and drive them their own ways (the city's through a small speaker, short of its redline; the racer's
  over the whole range). Recorded engines: a hatchback, a V8, a V12, a race car, a sportbike, a V-twin, a scooter, a
  kart, a diesel truck, a locomotive, an electric motor, an outboard, a propeller plane and a jet.
- Every vehicle in the registry has its sounds: its engine, what it runs on (tracks, rails, a rotor, a freewheel,
  hooves, sails) and the events it is known by (sirens, horns, bells, air brakes, a reverse beeper, a car's alarm and
  its lock, a flyby, a liftoff), by its kind or its own. A ride a game names is heard by its vehicle: a helicopter by
  its rotor, a supercar by its V12.
- In the open city (Hijack City), the car you take is heard by its own engine where the library is installed: a muscle
  car's V8, a luxury saloon's V12, an electric car's whine, a stolen van's or truck's diesel, each heard from the
  driver's seat; every other car keeps the city's hatchback. It is heard by its own events too: a V8's start, a truck's
  air horn, air brakes and reverse beeper, a bus's folding doors, a backfire as a muscle car or a hot hatch comes off
  the pedal, the lock's chirp as you walk away; an electric car starts without a crank.
- The horn (H) sounds at the wheel of a car in the open city again: it only answered while getting in.
- Racing games hear their car the same way where the library is installed: its start as the race begins, its revs
  climbing through the gears with each change heard, its brakes, its horn on H, a backfire as a muscle car comes off the
  pedal, and its tyres roaring on the road and screeching in a slide. A ride named in plain words ("a car", "muscle
  car", "rally car") is heard as the vehicle it names.
- Music can play recorded instruments. A recorded piece plays one of its takes per hit and falls back to the
  synthesized piece it stands in for where the library is not installed; recipes without recorded pieces are
  unchanged to the byte. The first recorded drum kit lost to the synthesized 90s rock kit by ear, so no recorded
  instrument is offered yet.
- Galaxy Boy sounds like itself where the library is installed: its arm cannon's tap, charged and full shots and the
  charge building, its small robot hero's dash, wall kick, wall slide, jump, landing and the hits it takes, its robot
  foes firing, sparking, glancing rounds off their armour and blowing apart, its bosses going up in a chain of blasts,
  the stomp, the boulder thrown, the boss room's blast door. A game's own sounds are its flavor: they never reach
  another game, which keeps the shelf's.
- Jumping Giuseppe sounds like itself where the library is installed: a springy cartoon hero's steps, jumps and
  landings, its coins, extra lives, checkpoints and goal, its bumps and falls, and, heard for the first time, its wall
  kick, its slide down a wall, its double jump and the foes it stomps.
- Steel Serpents sounds like itself where the library is installed: an operative's quiet steps on concrete and steel
  catwalks, a vault, a drop and a roll, a knife and a takedown, keycard doors and security doors, and the guards'
  shouts, grunts and falls; being spotted sounds an alarm stinger and the extraction a success stinger.
- Game menus have themed sounds where the library is installed: the title, set-up, pause and results screens click,
  confirm and open in the game's own voice. Fallen Angel's are gothic (bells, iron and heavy doors in a high stone
  echo), Galaxy Boy's clean, app-like chimes, brighter and quicker than Steel Serpents' subtle ones, every other game's light and
  bouncy. The recordings belong to the game UI's sound sets, so any page drawn in a set (a menu, a preview, the
  wireframe board) hears them. A new sound set, robot, joins the others.
- A recording can be reused: one take can voice several sounds and menu cues (Steel Serpents' extraction chime is also
  its checkpoint and its menus' notification).
- Mobile suits can be designed to sound apart (Mech Battle Kai's sounds): a suit is heard by its weight (a light
  suit's quick footfalls and electric servos, a medium one's heavy metal step, a heavy one shaking the ground, each with
  its own landing), its drive (rocket, jet or ion boosters held by the thrust, their ignition and their quick boost)
  and its loadout (beam rifle and its charge, beam cannon, railgun, head vulcan, machine gun, bazooka, missiles, beam
  saber, heat axe), with a roll, a jump, an overheat alarm and its vent, the transform both ways, a lock-on and a power-up
  every suit shares. A game designs its suit with `sound: { suit: { weight, drive, arms } }`; Mech Battle Kai's own is
  heard where the library is installed. The firing range's walkers are heard by their weight the same way. Without the
  library every suit sounds as mech games did before.
- Magic has sounds: every element (fire, ice, thunder, water, wind, earth, light, dark, poison, nature, arcane) as a
  spell gathering and landing at three sizes (a bolt, a burst over many, a cataclysm), the statuses (poison, burn,
  freeze, paralysis, sleep, silence, confusion, blindness, stun, petrify, doom, regen, haste, slow, berserk, a barrier)
  with a stat raised or lowered, a cure and a status wearing off, the spells (heals great and small, a revive, a drain,
  mana, a dispel, time stopped, a teleport, a summoning), and what magic does to a world: a quake, the ground cracking,
  stone rising and sinking, lava erupting, a flood, ice spreading, vines growing, portals, a ward over the land, the sky
  darkening and dawn breaking, with lava, a portal, an aura and a poison bog held. Party battles (Isekai Party's) are
  heard by them where the library is installed: each spell at its size, the statuses, the heals, a critical hit or a
  weakness ringing over the blow, a foe dissolving, a level gained, a skill learned, the fight's start and a boss's
  entrance. `sound: { battle: false }` keeps a game's battles silent. Without the library battles are silent as before.
- Animals have voices: every animal mojulo makes (the 144 of the fauna roster, the insects, the sea's creatures, the
  bestiary's and the RPG's monsters) is heard as one of its kind, a big cat, a canine, a bear, a horse, a bird of prey,
  a songbird, a buzzing or chirping insect, a crawler, a whale, a dinosaur, a dragon, a slime, a golem, the undead and
  others, each with a call at rest, a threat, a cry of pain and a dying cry, and wings, slithers, splashes and a swarm
  for what moves without a voice. Where the library is installed, a game's foes are heard by them: a wolf snarls as it
  attacks, yelps when struck and whimpers as it falls, an unskinned brute is a bear, a party battle's foe falls in its own
  voice. Without the library foes sound as before.
- The mount lane's horse is heard where the library is installed: its hooves keep its pace from the walk to the gallop
  and fall silent when it stands, it neighs as the hero settles in the saddle and snorts when urged into the gallop.
- A field sounds alive where the library is installed: a flock of crows calls over the site about as often as one
  crosses, gnats buzz at their clouds, ducks quack on the stream, mice squeak and roaches skitter by the walls, and each
  herd calls from its own ground, a heavy animal heard farther off than a small one. Fireflies and butterflies stay
  silent. Without the library a field is as quiet as before.

### Cinematic action game: the brood walker, beaten with its own drones

- **A carrier on the boss director** (boss.js, a vehicle row's `carrier`): a boss that fights through what it carries and
  is beaten through it too. Its GUNNERS (bodies of their own, `rule.bossCrew`, carried at their places on it) each lay a
  burst on the pilot in their arc and in sight (cover as a burst's: the line to its chest and to its head), or on a
  hacked drone near them; a gunner is a person, killed by rounds or knocked out by the dart (knockout.js), and down for
  good. Its DRONES (`rule.bossDrone`) are endless: launched from its bays, shot down, reprinted. A hunter patrols round it
  and drops a grenade on a pilot it sees (a hazard disc marked from the drone: a roof between them is cover); a courier
  laps round it and goes home. The RF gun (a loadout slot whose weapon says `jam`) held on a courier HACKS it (let go, the
  hack drains; a gunner's burst on the pilot shakes it off): it fetches the nearest package, carries it home into a door
  whose gunner is down (one whose gunner stands shoots it) and goes off inside, an explosive hit on its hangar. From the
  second delivery its hunters chase the hacked courier and shoot it: shot down, its package is lost and comes back to its
  pallet. A dart in a drone does nothing. `state.bosses[id].carrier` says its gunners, drones, packages, deliveries and
  hack; a state that holds its ground and its heading says `turn: false`.
- **The brood walker as the boss** (boss/vehicles.js `brood-walker`, boss/stand.js `carrierEntities`): the mecha shelf's
  brood walker standing on its hung eggs, a gunner on its roof facing ahead and one in each hangar door facing out of its
  side, eight drones two to an egg's bay (two of them couriers), its hangar the weak spot what goes off in its doors hits.
  Tuned as an on-ramp: slow bursts, rare drops, two chasers at most and two pistol rounds each, a courier every twelve
  seconds, a two-second hack, three deliveries. The vehicle laws read a carrier as won by what it carries home.
- **The page shows it** (boss-view.js): the drones flown with their rotors spun, shown only out of their bays, a mark over
  each (a courier's green, the hacked one's blue with its health, a chaser's red), its packages on their pallets and under
  the drone that carries one, the RF gun's beam and the hack's ring filling round the courier, each gunner's gun turned on
  what it fires at and drooped once its gunner is down, the bursts' tracers; under the boss bar its gunners and its
  deliveries, and what it last said.
- **Played with the operative** (scripts/spikes/mission/boss.mjs `--boss brood-walker`): the drone yard, barriers,
  containers and roofed shelters, three pallets; the dart, the pistol and the RF gun in the kit.
- What lifting it onto the rail would take: the siege walker's list, and the drones as a foe of the foes shelf in their own
  right (a hunter is a flying guard: its patrol, its sight and its drop would serve a stealth level's sky as well).

### Cinematic action game: the siege walker, fought as a boss on the boss director

- **The siege walker as a vehicle boss** (boss/vehicles.js `siege-walker`): the mecha shelf's siege walker on the boss
  director (worlds/controllable/boss.js). STANDING it lays a BARRAGE on you (a new pattern on the shelf, boss/patterns.js
  `barrage`: four shells and six missiles round where you stood, every landing marked as it is fired, a wall between the gun
  and you its cover; held to the pattern laws), then RELOADS with its tails (a window: no move), then WALKS its round.
  Mines on its round break its LEGS (two under one foot); a leg gone, it FOLDS onto its wheels and is a TANK, fought as the
  tank is (its states, its gun's lock and its coaxial fan are the tank row's own: a body that becomes a tank is beaten as
  one), its wheels mined to strand it and its engine open from behind then, and its folding opens its HIPS, bare between
  its folded legs, from its sides. Its RELOADERS, shot from behind, slow its reload (1.8 times for one, 2.6 for both).
