- **The ground's index sized to its items** (`ground-index.js`). The walker's ground probe buckets every surface at 4 m
  over the plan of them all, and is rebuilt when the set changes; a flight's chunks spread over 16 km made it millions of
  cells, rebuilt as each chunk streamed in, and it held hundreds of megabytes. `indexBuckets` now doubles its cell while
  it would hold more than 64 cells an item or list its items more than 256 times an item.
- Each of the three only chooses which surfaces a ray tests, so what a ray finds, and every page's play, is as it was.
  The flight level's heap, collected, sits near 60 MB where it climbed past 3 GB; the kart race's near 40 MB.
- **Pinned.** The grid's and the index's tests build a 16 km land of 341 m triangles, a 12 km backdrop and a flight's
  quadtree of chunks, and hold them within the limits with every ray and probe finding what it found before; a browser
  test on the e2e tier (`big-ground.chrome.test.js`) loads a flight level and a kart oval in headless Chrome and holds
  each one's collected heap under a ceiling (it fails on the old code: the page never comes up). The world pages that
  embed the controllable runtime carry the new code by its source and were re-pinned.

### The speed's look: speed lines in the air, dust in space, for Wolf Squadron and Rebel Storm

A flown craft's speed, and when it is driven hard, now reads off the world round it (`scene/channels/speed-fx.js`, a
page's `speedfx`). It is laid on every airspace level whose pilot flies a rail stage or a cockpit; absent, it emits
nothing.

- **In the air: speed lines.** Thin streaks of air rush past the camera on a tube round its line of sight, born far
  ahead and gone behind it, kept wider than the craft so they never cross it. At cruise there are a few and they are
  faint. Boosted they lengthen, grow in number and brighten; braked they thin away. Wolf Squadron's ground stages have
  them.
- **In space: dust.** Motes are held still in space round the camera, in a block that wraps as the camera moves. Each is
  drawn as a streak along the way it is passed, as long as the craft's speed makes it. At cruise they are a drift of
  short specks; boosted or with the throttle wide open, the streaks lengthen and brighten. They show which way the craft
  is turning. Wolf Squadron's space stage and Rebel Storm's cockpit missions have them.
- **Read off how the craft moves** (its position over the world's clock), so it is one cue for every rule that flies:
  - the rail's boost and brake;
  - a cockpit's throttle and its engines' power.

  Its drive runs 0 at cruise to 1 at the boost (`window.__mojSpeedFx`: mode, speed, drive). A jump in place is not
  speed.

### A mixed fair-weather sky: wide cumulus with volume (not popcorn), of several kinds, altocumulus patches under the cirrus

The flight sky's cumulus read as popcorn: heaped clusters of small round puffs, about as tall as they were wide. Seen
from under them, their bellies stacked into horizontal slabs. They now read as fair-weather cumulus, wide and flat-based
with a heaped dome, across every game under the flight sky (Wolf Squadron's ground stages, Pilot School, any airspace
level).

- **Wider, still deep** (`skyscape/sky.js`): fair weather's are 900–2200 m across and 450–1100 m deep, where they were
  450–1300 and 350–800, so there are fewer, broader clouds for the same cover, each with its height. A hazy day's small
  cumulus are widened alike.
- **One domed body, not a heap** (`scene/channels/flight-sky.js`):
  - each cloud is a dome: a broad low body over its base, then puffs heaped toward its middle as it climbs, a rounded
    crown;
  - it is drawn out a quarter longer along the wind;
  - its puffs are larger and overlapping, and softer at the rim;
  - it is lit as one body by the sun and its height (bright up its sunward tops, shaded under its belly), so the volume
    reads and the puffs do not read as balls.
- **No slabs under them.** Each puff is a camera-facing card, and the flat base cut each card where it crossed the base
  height. Seen from below, the tilted cards met the base at different heights on screen and stacked into slabs. A fair
  cloud's low puffs now sit higher over the base and fade into it over 45 m, and the belly's shade is the cloud's own
  depth, not each puff's.
- **Of several kinds** (`skyscape/sky.js` `CUMULUS_KINDS`): each fair cloud is one kind, by its own dice, so the sky is
  mixed rather than one cloud repeated:
  - humilis: flat and wide;
  - mediocris: the domed heap;
  - congestus: the odd one climbing, kept under a thunderhead's height for its width;
  - fractus: small ragged bits.

  Each kind is the same builder at its own proportions.
- **Altocumulus at mid level** (fair weather's new middle layer, the deck primitive's altocumulus at 4200 m). A few
  fields of small cells sit between the cumulus and the cirrus. An altocumulus deck is now one sheet at its middle, not a
  base and a top 180 m apart that showed its pattern twice from under it. From below it is pale with the sun through it,
  each cell's middle a little darker, not a thick deck's dark belly (a high-cloud day's too). A fair day's report says
  it: `FEW036 SCT138`.
- A storm's towering cumulonimbus keeps its shape: its puffs stay round, its foot cut flat.

### Wolf Squadron's ground stages: laid in segments, under the flight sky, a sci-fi colony, terrain on the holo table

Wolf Squadron's Canyon run is now a long route down Moon IV in three stretches, open dust flats, the Red Canyon colony
on the way, then the canyon to the gunship, under Pilot School's flight sky and over ground laid at a pilot's scale.
Its briefing is told over the moon's real ground.

- **A route map** (`skyscape/map.js`, `map.route: true`). A rail stage's long field:
  - its reach is the field and a narrow band (the rail keeps the craft on its way);
  - its haze sees ahead rather than corner to corner;
  - its one grid spends the same cell budget along its length (about 50 m cells on a 15 km route, where a square map of
    its length is about 130);
  - its laws are its own (`way-seen`; no turn-room).

  Every other map plans as it did.
- **Ground in segments** (`skyscape/ground.js`, `ground.segments`). The field's length is cut into stretches about the
  gorge's line, eased over 600 m at a join:
  - `canyon` keeps the walls;
  - `open` is a broad valley with no walls;
  - `colony` stands a settlement on the line.

  A route's line weaves by the metre. The rail stage keeps its hazards out of a colony, checks its walls only down a
  canyon, and sweeps its box over the roofs (`topIn`), so the way rises over a spire rather than through it.
- **The colony style** (`skyscape/country.js`, `country.style: 'colony'`, a new `colony` settlement card: a town's grain
  round a core of towers). The same generator's masses dressed as a sci-fi colony:
  - composite panels with one lit band of glazing, not a grid of windows;
  - teal glass, spires with a crown set back and a lit mast (in the roof grid, so a craft can hit them);
  - habitat modules under domes and flat-roofed halls (no gables);
  - radar domes for water towers;
  - a colony's plan: dark roads, landing aprons, hydroponic greens, no garden trees;
  - the cover leaned to its world's colours.

  It is data only: the page's facade shader is unchanged, and an earth country is byte-identical.
- **A stage's route in segments** (`campaign/stage.js`). `route.segments` (each `canyon`, `open` or `colony` and its
  seconds) and `route.sky` (a flight sky, an afternoon's fair-weather cloud by default) lay one long route
  (`routeGround`). Its stretches sit at their shares of the way, and its ground is coloured for its world
  (`worldGeocube`: a rust moon's dust and red rock, not an island's grass). It has no airfield.
- **Terrain on the holo table** (`campaign/stage-ground.js`). A ground stage's table is drawn over the level's real land:
  - a heightfield sampled along the way, its heights stretched three times so a canyon reads;
  - the way as flown;
  - each wave where it is posted and the boss where it waits;
  - the pillars and the colony's masses.

  It works on the level page and in the game's briefing book once the level is built. A space stage's table, and a
  mission's, draw as they did.
- **The Canyon run redesigned**: 25 s open, 25 s colony, 50 s canyon, four waves across them, its briefing in six steps.
  The flight proof's attentive pilot wins it; a still one loses it.

### Wolf Squadron flown close: an arcade chase camera, the gear up

A rail stage's craft was followed by the free flier's long chase: about a quarter of its top speed behind (about 100 m
for Wolf Squadron's fighter), plus the chase's lag at speed, so a 12 m starfighter filled a sliver of the screen. A rail
stage now has its own close chase (`skyscape/rail-stage.js` `RAIL.camera`, laid by `gameworld/levels.js`):
- 30 m behind and 7 m above the craft;
- looking 60 m down the way.

The ship sits large just under the sights, with the way ahead and what comes at it in view. It is flown in, never off a
runway, so its landing gear is up. Other flight levels keep their chase.

### Wolf Squadron's foes: real ships in its waves, a sci-fi ground force on the moon

An arcade stage's fighters were red boxes. They now fly ships, and a ground stage has a ground force to shoot down.

- **Its fighters fly ships off the craft shelf** (`gameworld/flight-goal.js`, as a Rebel Storm sortie's foes do: a rigged
  craft, flying, gear up). A design's wave names its ship (`craft`: a dagger or arrowhead interceptor, a faceted raider, a
  twin-panel, tri-wing or bent-panel fighter, `campaign/stage.js` `FOE_CRAFT`). Absent, it flies its formation's: a line
  the dagger interceptor, a vee the arrowhead, an echelon the faceted raider, a swarm the twin-panel. The holo table
  stands each wave as its own ship's miniature.
- **The ground force** (`groundforce/`, a new library). A sci-fi army's units as cards of a few big chamfered shapes
  (the workbots' primitives, now shared as `WORKBOT_PRIMITIVES`), in a military register of their own:
  - composite grey armour, graphite running gear and guns, one foe-red stripe;
  - a red sensor slit and a drive's glow, lit;
  - drawn 2.5 times life so they read from a fighter going past.

  There are three units:
  - **the gun emplacement:** an armoured dome on a dug-in ring, twin long barrels;
  - **the hover tank:** a sloped wedge on four glowing pads, a flat turret with twin barrels;
  - **the personnel walker:** an enclosed cab on two backward-kneed legs, a red visor, twin chin guns.

  A page stands one by a figures-map `unit: { kind }`; absent, nothing changes.
- **Laid by the rail** (`skyscape/rail-stage.js`, a plan's `ground`). Each group is placed from its mark on, a unit every
  1.1 s of the way, on alternate sides across the box, never on its line. Each stands on what is there (the ground, or
  a roof in a colony) and faces back up the way. Cast as static minds that turn to the craft and fire up at it in short
  bursts while it is in reach.
- **A stage's ground groups** (`campaign/stage.js` `ground`: `{ id, name, kind, count, at }`, a ground route's only).
  Each is read with its faults said, shown before launch (the `every-wave-shown` law reads them), scored by kind (a gun
  emplacement 150, a hover tank 200, a walker 150, into the medals' shares) and stood on the holo table where its units
  are. The build list and the orders say them.
- **The Canyon run's ground force:**
  - gun emplacements on the flats;
  - hover tanks at the colony's edge;
  - walkers in its streets;
  - more guns down the canyon.

  Its briefing shows each. The flight proof's attentive pilot wins it with 38% of its shield; a still one loses.

### Wolf Squadron's stages designed whole: the holo table, arcade score and medals, mana-ui

Wolf Squadron's game now runs like Rebel Storm's: on mana-ui in its own look, each stage designed whole, told on the
holo table as it loads, and approved there. It is tuned for arcade play, not a sim.

- **Its look** (`playscape/ui/theme-cards/squadron.json`, a new card in the `party` family). Night-blue plates cut at
  the corner, a cyan hairline, an amber call for what matters, capitals, menus that slam in on chevrons. Nothing is
  drawn across the way ahead during a stage. The rail's starter dresses its game in it (`ui: { theme: 'squadron' }`);
  the creator's own `ui` wins.
- **A stage's design** (`campaign/stage.js`), the arcade sibling of a mission's. It says:
  - its place;
  - its route (a canyon on a moon or rocks over it, its speed, its hazards `none` to `many`);
  - its waves (up to eight, each 1 to 6 fighters at a share of the way, in a `line`, `vee`, `echelon` or `swarm`);
  - its boss (1 to 6 guns round a core, light or heavy armour, a capital class for its miniature);
  - its medals (in points; by default shares of all the stage holds);
  - its briefing's steps.

  `readStage` says each fault by its field. `stageLaws` (advisory) checks five things: every wave and the boss shown
  before launch, the waves spaced, gold reachable, and a briefing short enough. `compileStage` lays its level.
- **The designer takes stages** (`campaign/designer.js`). A design that names a `route` is a stage, and a world's
  `missions` hold both kinds. Both are read, held to their laws, compiled and approved the same way. `design_game`'s
  readout names each one's kind, and its briefing is served at the game's books
  (`?book=briefing&mission=<id>`). A stage has no table editor: its table follows from its design.
- **The rail stage lays a design** (`skyscape/rail-stage.js`, `airspace.rail.plan`). The plan does four things:
  - puts its waves at their marks in their formations (a vee trails back from its point, an echelon steps back and up,
    a swarm is loose and weaving);
  - sets its hazards' spacing (or none);
  - rings its boss's guns round its core, heavy armour taking more;
  - carries its score.

  A stage without a plan is laid as before.
- **Arcade score and medals** (`gameworld/flight-goal.js`). A designed stage scores every fighter, gun and core it
  downs (the `score` mechanic, on the HUD). Its medal is read off the score as the boss goes down (the `grade`
  mechanic), and the shell remembers the best.
- **Told on the holo table** (`stageBriefingData`, the table's own data shape). It opens on the orrery (the system, the
  cluster, the moon), then the theatre: the route as a ribbon, the waves at their marks with their formations, the boss
  past the route's end, the orders with the points and the medals. It is held until Launch.
- **A level's briefing takes the keyboard as it opens** (Rebel Storm's too), so Enter steps the table from inside the
  game's shell without clicking into it.
- **Wolf Squadron's two stages are designed and approved** (`STAGE_DESIGNS`), so the rail lays them from their designs:
  - the Canyon run, down Red Canyon to a gunship;
  - the Debris field, through the Varn Shoals to a carrier.

  Both are won by the flight proof's attentive pilot and lost by a still one (the machine gate).

### The castle in segments, joined by the megaworld

- The castle can now be played a segment a map: each box (the bell tower, the courtyard, the keep) is its own map, with
  the bridge and the gatehouse as the ways between them. Walking out through the far door of a connector loads the next
  part of the castle, and Erina stands just inside the door she came through. `vampireSonataGame({ castle: 'segments' })`
  lays the three on a megaworld chain; a level names its box with `segment`.
- What Erina gains carries across, through a new `journey` save: her powers and keys, the relics she has taken, the
  bosses she has felled, the gates she has opened, the rooms she has explored, the skills she has learned and the souls
  she has won. The pause map stays the whole castle's.
- `design_game` starts it: Galaxy Boy's rail has a new variant, Vampire Sonata: the castle in maps
  (`rail: { from: 'galaxy-boy', variant: 'vampire-sonata-castle', locked: true }`). A sentence such as "a castle of
  maps" finds it, and its starter lays the three maps on the gothic night cube.
- The metroidvania box is in the hill-climb's registry as a level form (`space.levelForm=box`), and the metroidvania
  genre probe asks for it.

### The cinematic action probes: Steel Serpents' core, its adventure, and bullet time apart

- **Cinematic action is the core Steel Serpents is made on** (cosmos/fixtures.js `cinematic-action`): a hero seen over
  the shoulder works through a linear run of set pieces, with a gun aimed off the eye and a knife, objectives laid as a
  mission, getting over and onto things, and cutscenes cut into play. The probe was the world clock's (11-02) and
  waited on a replay. It is now makeable. Steel Serpents' rail names it among its genres and is still a stealth game first: its own
  cube, which its tunings are read from, is `stealth`, the espionage and cinematic action cubes near it (as Artesia is an
  action RPG near the top-down and open adventures).
- **The same core as an adventure** (`cinematic-adventure`, "Cinematic action adventure"): a treasure hunter climbing
  between gunfights behind cover that breaks, a vehicle chase for a set piece, the story told in acts with banter on
  the way. It is the direction the core grows toward, and the probe says what that waits on: the hero getting into a
  vehicle in a level (`soul.mount=vehicle`, the `crewed` package).
- **Bullet time is its own probe** (`bullet-time-action`, "Bullet-time action"): the world clock's slow, ramp, freeze
  and bullet time, and the finisher shown again, which still waits on `replay`.
- A brief's words are read the same way (gameworld/intent.js): "cinematic action" and "third-person shooter" for the
  core, "uncharted" and "treasure hunter" for the adventure, "bullet time" and "kill cam" for bullet time. The
  interface look and the SFX shelf's facets read the two new probes as they read the core.

### Keying in play: characters on twos, the camera on ones

- **A level's bodies drawn on twos or threes** (`worlds/controllable/keying.js`, a level's `keying`). Limited animation
  in play: each animated body (a rig or a baked figure) is posed on its key and holds that pose between keys, at 24
  drawings a second's grain (twos: 12 poses a second; threes: 8), while the world steps, the bodies move through the
  level and the camera turns on every frame. Its clips keep their time: a held key catches up with the time it held.
  `keying: 'twos' | 'threes'`, or a layer each: `{ hero, cast, fps?, root? }` (the hero the player pilots, the cast
  every other body; `ones | twos | threes`). `root: 'held'` steps a body's place with its pose, the old cartoon's
  stride; absent, the place and the heading run on ones. A level without `keying` draws every frame, every byte as it
  was.
- **A game says it once** (`gameworld/keying.js`, a world's `keying`, laid on every level as its `tempo` is).
  `'auto'` reads the juice: the cel look (the anime fighter's and the brawler's, its effects already drawn on twos)
  keys its bodies on twos; the anime isekai look and the western register draw every frame. Read in the motion chapter.
- **The registry**: the time map's grain on twos, on threes and mixed (each layer its own) is built in play; the
  `sound` values are marked built (the sound sheet on every level and the score by request, 11-13; a played city's,
  11-16), where the registry had them waiting.

### The home's producer: a house or a room offered as a start, produced before it is made

- **A fifth start.** A visitor with no ask is offered five starts: a character, a game, an object, a 3D exhibit, and a
  home or a room. The `initialize` preamble and `forward_context`'s line for a visitor with no ask say it; for
  someone's own home the agent is its producer first, and a plan or a photo they send is read, never asked for.
- **The rails** (`home/rails.js`): what a home starts from, one row each, least first: a room redone, the home you
  have (your plan built to the inch, every room you name designed, walked through), a house from nothing, the set to
  build from (drawings, frame, schedules, IFC), and a shop or a café fitted out. A row names into what is built (its
  doors, the house's outcomes, its vocab cards, the questions it asks, the first look the person approves) and copies
  no number. What no rail does is said before anything is made: no prices, no permit or code sign-off, no structural
  engineering. Where a made home can go next (a game level, a piece made to build, an engine) is offered once, after
  the first look.
- **The start** (`home/producer.js`; the door: `mint_building({ start: { what?, place?, living?, look?, brought? } })`,
  asked alone). It builds and stores nothing. First what they want to make (the agent reads their words as the rail),
  then the rail's own questions in its order, one a turn, each dropped once answered: their place (a plan,
  measurements, a photo, or a house already made here), who lives there and how (bedrooms, a room's jobs, the rooms
  that matter), what it should feel like (their words; the agent names the style card), and what else they bring. A
  café's question is who comes, not who lives there. A plain ask (a rail and a look, nothing of their place, their
  household or their material) is made at once. When the rail's questions are answered, `make`: said back first, then
  the steps.
- **The hand-off** (`homeHandOff`, the `make` step's `steps`): the calls that make it, in order, with what was said
  filled in: the house from their plan (never a room the plan does not have), its `next` read as its machine gate,
  each room they named by `design_interior` in the style read from their words, the review's refusals and gaps
  mended by piece id, the walkthrough (`forge_motion` a room each, then `stitch_motion`), their look, and the offers.
  It proposes and runs nothing. The home you have is the README's decor session: a test holds the hand-off's calls to
  the calls that session made.
- **The intake** (`home/intake.js`): what the person brought, read before they are asked anything it says. Each kind
  (`HOME_INTAKE`: a floor plan, measurements, a photo of the room, pictures they love, furniture they keep, what
  cannot change, a budget) says what takes it and the questions it usually answers; a new kind is a row. Each thing
  is recorded with where it went or why it has no place; nothing brought is dropped. A budget has no place: mojulo
  prices nothing, and the furniture schedule is what they price from.
- **Said where a house is chosen.** A routing card of its own, `home-producer`, takes the phrasing of someone with a
  home of their own ("we just moved in, here is our floor plan", "I want to redo our bedroom but don't know where to
  start"); the plain asks stay the `interior` and `house` cards' and are made at once. `mint_building`'s description
  and its line in the tool index name the start; the interior card and the HOUSE row send someone's own home to it;
  the building form says it.
- The tool list's payload pin is raised for `start` (an argument on the door that owns the house intent, `required`
  emptied so it may be asked alone), and `forward_context`'s body ceiling for the fifth start, each with its reason
  beside the pin.

### The metroidvania map: a spiralling box, greybox first

- **In progress.** A metroidvania's map laid as one box entered from the left, its way spiralling inward ring by ring
  to a core: along the floor, up the far side, back along the top, down the near side, then a gated step into the ring
  inside. Each ring is a region of its own; the core holds the last boss. Every ring lies against the one outside it,
  so a power found deep in the box opens shortcuts back out and pockets in rooms already walked.
- The gates are rows: a grate passed in a small form, a sill reached on a double jump, a cracked wall broken by a
  special strike, a locked door and its key, a boss's seal. Each has its own shape in the greybox.
- Vampire Sonata is its template: a storm-the-castle metroidvania with no stomp and no wall kick, the outer wall, the
  halls and the inner ward walked to the keep.
- The greybox is measured (the box filled, the spiral turning one way inward, both axes travelled, every gate opened
  by what was found before it, the way back shorter than the way in) and drawn as an elevation
  (`node scripts/metroidvania.mjs`).
- The box plays. A world's level can be a metroidvania box: it is built for the hero's height and measured jump, and
  played on the side-scroller's runtime with a camera that holds each room as the walk reaches it. Gates hold until the
  hero has what opens them. A key opens its lock as she reaches it, a boss's fall breaks its seal, a cracked wall falls
  to her blows once the special strike is hers, and an opened hatch is fallen through. Picking up the second leap gives
  her the double jump. Bosses are stand-in blocks until the foes join.
- Erina, Vampire Sonata's hero: a monster hunter drawn as a grown woman in the traditional anime register. She fights
  with Zero Boy's three-cut saber string, with no wall kick, no stomp and no buster. Her sword is a hunter's longsword, a
  new look on the equipment shelf: a silver blade under a winged guard, with nothing on it lit. A saber hero can now play
  the string with a steel sword (`blade: { steel: true }`): no light over the blade, and its slash in steel.
- The castle theme: a box can be dressed ring by ring. Vampire Sonata's castle stands under a moonlit night. Its ramparts
  are open to the sky, with merlons and torches. The great halls have arched windows, candles and a crimson runner. The
  inner ward is cold and mossy under pale lamps, and the keep has gold-trimmed stone, banners and braziers. Its stone is
  coursed and its light is baked from its lamps; the gates keep their colours so they still read.
- The castle is closer on its hero: Erina stands a fifth larger on screen than a side-scroller's hero, and the box is laid
  round her at that scale. She is drawn in mojulo's own anime look (her own face, shading and light), not the
  side-scroller's cel bands and outline.
- The castle plays as an action RPG, with no lives. Erina has health and MP, shown as bars. Walking into a save room
  refills both and makes it where she wakes. When her health runs out she wakes in the last save room she visited, full,
  keeping everything she has found and opened.
- Each castle room is dressed by principles of its own, the craft a dungeon's walls have in 3D carried to a side view's
  back wall. The wall is ashlar, block by block, with a plinth or wainscot, pillars, and a vault or beams under the
  ceiling. Every glance at the wall finds some detail, and the band behind the play stays calmer than the wall above it.
  Bays alternate by the wall's rhythm, and each room has one focal piece: the lord's portrait, a broken statue, the
  house's arms, a gargoyle. Columns and chains stand between the lane and the wall. The mood is dark: light falls in
  pools from candles, braziers and cold lamps whose flames glow, and dust hangs in their light. Each principle is
  measured.
- A box can take other shapes besides the spiral. A **serpentine** is climbed row by row, each row run back the other way.
  Its regions are bands of rows, and a chute down its middle drops back to the bottom: a bell tower walked through from
  its foot to its spire. A **hub** is a centre column reached up an approach. Its wings are walked out from it and back,
  each wing's prize opening the next, and a wing's boss sealing its way back: a courtyard. Each region is given its save
  rooms, key, boss and pockets the same way whatever its shape. Both are held to the box's laws, each to its own form, and
  Vampire Sonata has a bell tower and a courtyard drawn and played beside its spiral castle.
- The castle's rooms are drawn to Erina's scale. Books, swords, shields, candles, ladders and the wall's stones keep their
  true size against her, statues and portraits are life-size to heroic, and furniture stands on its floor. A tall hall is
  filled with more things at their size rather than the same things blown up. The library is now a case twice her height
  with a gallery and a second tier above it and a ladder between, in place of a shelf of metre-tall books. Each piece's
  size is measured against hers.
- The castle's walls are drawn with depth. They are laid stone rather than a grid of blocks, each course its own height
  and each block its own length. Piers stand at every bay with a base and a capital that the vault's ribs spring from. In
  the vaulted halls, slender shafts rise from carved corbels over the hero's head to the ribs, and the columns in front
  of the lane are round. The light is baked smoothly across every surface and shows the relief: columns are lit round on
  the side of their lamp, each stone is lit domed, and what stands out of the wall casts a shadow across it from each
  candle, torch and brazier, with the dark gathering around it and under the ceiling.
- A castle of boxes. Several boxes can be joined into one level through their ports. Every box is entered on its left. A
  climbed tower is left where its top row runs to, and a courtyard at its top right. A keep wound to its core is where the
  castle ends. The boxes are joined by connectors: a bridge open to the night, or a gatehouse with a save room and a gate,
  its own boss standing in it. Powers are found once across the castle and open things in the boxes after them. Each box
  is checked against its own shape, and the castle as one walk through all of it. Vampire Sonata's castle climbs its bell
  tower, crosses the bell bridge to an open courtyard, and passes the Gatekeeper into the keep. It is drawn as one
  elevation and played as one level.
- A game can have trees: a skill tree on how its hero moves and a tech tree on its spells and attacks. Movement skills
  turn the hero's own numbers: a second and a third jump, a higher jump, a glide, a faster run, a longer dash, an air
  dash more. Techs add to the hero's own strings: a lunging thrust, a cleave forked off its string, a launcher, a
  plunge from the air. Spells cost MP: a burst all round, a dashing cut, a spiral. A node is bought with points that
  bosses and prizes give, after the nodes it builds on, or is given when a power is found. Pressing T opens both trees as
  one screen to learn them in play. Erina's trees hold more than the castle's points buy, so she grows one way or
  another.
- The castle has an explored map, a tile for every screen, revealed tile by tile as Erina walks it. A map room's lectern
  shows its region's tiles before she has walked them. The map marks save rooms, map rooms and bosses (crossed out once
  felled), along with what is left to pick up. It draws an unexplored doorway as an opening into the dark. A gate shows
  in its own colour, ringed once she holds what opens it, so a power found tells her where to go back. The map also
  shows how much of the castle and each region she has walked. A minimap stays at the top right, and M opens the
  whole map.
- The castle is haunted. Each region names its foes from the game's bestiary: rats and crows on the walls, ghouls in the
  halls, wolves in the ward, undead armour in the keep. Walkers spread along corridor floors and flyers hold the shafts.
  The fight thickens toward the core, and the rooms where she rests, reads a map or meets a boss stay empty. Felled foes
  give souls, and souls become points to spend on her trees. Until their figures are made, the foes stand as blocks of
  their size and class. The castle checks that the foes stand clear of doorways and holes, and that between two save
  rooms she meets no more than her health can bear.
- The castle's bosses stand as real foes once its foes have joined. Each boss is read by name from a shelf of the
  castle's bosses: the Gate Warden, the Bellkeeper, the Great Bell, the Crypt Lord, the Lord of the Keep and the rest,
  each a foe class at the boss's rank, taller than Erina by its tier, its health a count of her blows. It stands in its
  room facing the way in and never follows her out. Its name and health show as a long bar across the bottom while she
  is in its room. Cut down, it gives what its room gives: its seal breaks and its power is hers. Until its figure is
  made, it stands as a tall block. The castle checks that every boss is on the shelf, has room to fight, and that the
  bosses never get easier going in.
- A boss's room shuts behind Erina once she is inside: an iron portcullis drops across each doorway and a grate covers
  each hole, until the boss falls. If she dies in the fight, she wakes at her last save, the room opens, and the boss is
  back where it stood at full health, so the fight starts over when she returns.
- The castle's bosses fight with telegraphed attacks. Each boss has three or four moves in its own words (the Gate
  Warden's halberd cleave, haft slam and thrust; the Bellkeeper's cracked bells; the Crypt Lord's pounce and howl; the
  Lord of the Keep's bat swarm and blood wave), in phases that come quicker as its health falls. Each attack is marked
  before it lands, and a pause follows it. Seen from the side, an attack is drawn upright along the floor as high as it
  reaches. A low one, like a front rolling along the floor or a low spring, can be jumped; a tall swing must be backed
  away from. A boss attacks only while Erina is in its room. The castle checks that every boss's attacks can be seen
  coming, escaped along the floor or jumped, survived and answered, measured with Erina's own run and jump.
- The boss pattern shelf learns the side view: a hazard can say how high it reaches, a jump clears it, and the pattern
  laws measure a body that can move only along a lane, with a jump among its escapes.
- The castle's bosses have their own figures, made through the character door like Erina: the Gate Warden as a death
  knight with a halberd, the Gatekeeper in crimson plate under a horned skull helm, the Bell Ringer and the Bellkeeper
  as dead monks, the Warden as a horned, tailed devil in a crimson robe, and the Lord of the Keep as a pale, silver-haired
  vampire noble. The Crypt Lord is a great shadow wolf from the animal door. Each stands in its room, grown taller than
  Erina. The Great Bell stays a block until a bell can be made.
- Their attacks have their own looks: a glint on the blade and a crimson crescent for a swing, glowing cracks and rolling
  dust walls for a slam, rings of shimmering air and a wall of ripples for a toll, a falling bell or a swarm of bats for
  a throw, and speed streaks for a lunge.
- The castle's bosses wind up with their bodies. Before a swing, a boss draws its weapon back over its shoulder; before
  a slam, it raises both hands high; before a throw, it draws its arm back low; before a toll, it spreads its arms and
  throws its head back; before a lunge, it sinks low on bent knees. As the attack lands it strikes through, then eases
  back to its stand. The great wolf does not wind up yet.
- The Great Bell is a bell now: bronze gone green at its waist with a gilded lip, hung from a timber yoke on chains. It
  swings back before it tolls and swings through as the toll rolls out, its clapper lagging behind.
- The Crypt Lord winds up like a wolf: it crouches with its head down before it pounces or mauls, then springs, and
  drops low with its head thrown up before it howls.
- The two knights lose the extra shoulder cape that sat over their armour like a roof, and carry heavier weapons.
- The castle's bosses trade their big shoulder plates for capes and grim details. The Gate Warden wears a black cloak to
  the floor lined in dried blood, a standing collar, a chain and a skull at its hip. The Gatekeeper's ragged cloak hangs
  with bone charms and skulls. The bell ringers carry bells and chains, and the Lord of the Keep wears a high collar and a
  floor-length cloak lined in crimson.
- Armour can leave pieces off: `adorn: { type: 'armor', without: ['pauldron'] }` wears a plate suit with its shoulders
  bare, so a cape can hang from them.
- The knights' cloaks are torn at the hem into ragged tongues, and rags hang off their plate at the hips and the
  shoulders: grave-cloth grey on the Gate Warden, rust red on the Gatekeeper. The Lord of the Keep's cape is lightly torn.
- A cloak can be torn (`{ kind: 'cloak', torn, tongues }`): its hem cut into tongues, the gaps torn up, the same cloak
  torn the same way every time. A new outfit piece, `rags`, hangs torn strips from the hips and the shoulders, draped over
  whatever is worn there.
- The Lord of the Keep is a woman now, androgynous: a slim body squared at the shoulder, a sharp, cool face and short
  swept-back silver hair, in the same crimson coat, high collar and torn crimson-lined cape.
- The Lord of the Keep has a second form. Cut down, she does not fall: she becomes the Lord Unbound, a black dragon on two
  legs, 2.5 times Erina's height, horned and spined, with crimson wings on bone swept back along it and gold at its throat
  and arms. Its health bar fills again under its own name, and it fights with its own moves: it rears with its wings
  flung wide, charges low, beats its wings into a storm of bats, and roars. Only its fall opens her seal; lose to it and she is back in her first form when Erina returns.
- A boss can be built with a second form (`second` on its row): a foe mode of its own figure, health, fight and size; a
  mode may stand at a height of its own (`body.fit` on the mode).
- Characters can wear wings: an outfit piece, `wings`, a pair of membrane wings on bone off the back, spread out or swept
  back along the body (`sweep`) so a side view sees them whole.
- The Lord Unbound's wings beat as it attacks, up and down through every wind-up and down with every blow, and it takes
  to the air: it dives out of the room's height to rake the floor (jump it), or rises over Erina and drops onto her (get
  out from under its shadow, then jump the shockwave). It flies only as high as keeps its head on the screen.
- Wings flap: each wing rides a bone of its own, beaten by its own clip word (`wingR`, `wingL`), which a character's clips
  can key.
- A boss's attack can fly (`flies` on a pattern: a path of keys through the move), lowered under its room's ceiling and
  the air the screen gives it (`sky`); two new attack patterns, `swoop` and `dive`.
- Four more boss fights in the castle: the Carrion Abbess in the belfry (a crow-nun who fights from the air on beating
  wings and throws her quills into the floor), the Siege Ogre in the lower keep (it rolls a boulder the length of the room:
  jump it), the Armiger in the armoury (an empty suit of gilded plate that bursts lances out of the floor under marks)
  and the Serpent Countess in the upper keep (a lamia whose tail sweeps the floor and whose venom burns where it lands).
- Five new boss attacks: `volley`, `lances`, `coil`, `venom` and `boulder`, and a hazard that rolls (`roll`), harming
  only where it is as it passes.
- A boss kept to its room stands on its floor: a tall boss no longer climbs a room's ledges between its moves.
- The new bosses' looks: the Siege Ogre is an oni (red skin, ivory horns, a loincloth of ochre and black), the Carrion
  Abbess a crow tengu (a mountain monk's whites, a red sash, a ringed staff), the Armiger's helm has a wing swept back
  off each ear, and the Serpent Countess has a crimson coil, a gold circlet and a black corset laced up her back with
  skulls down it.
- Characters can wear a corset (an outfit piece, `corset`), laced up the back with skulls set down the lacing
  (`skulls`); and a winged helm, the `wingedTVisor` headgear (its `earWings` ornament).
- The castle's HUD draws each thing once: one map (the corner map with how much is explored) and the boss's bar across the
  bottom of the screen; a boss's name shows alone as Erina enters its room, then fades.
- No map over the play: the map is on the pause screen and in the map rooms.
- Boss chambers are plain rooms fought in on their floor: no ladders, stairs or shafts. A boss whose room climbed moved to
  the nearest plain room of its region, and the Siege Ogre moved from the barbican (all shafts) to the lower keep.

### Recorded instruments, note by note

- An instrument can be played note by note from recorded takes. The sound library measures each take's real pitch to
  the cent (the generator gets a note's letter right but its octave by chance) and, for an instrument that holds, a
  seamless loop on a whole number of its periods. A page then plays each note on the take nearest it, bent the rest of
  the way, and holds it on its loop for as long as the note lasts. The synth's modulators carry over: its unison
  detune, its pitch lanes and vibrato, a pitch LFO, and, as before, its filter, envelope and tremolo.
- The first is a recorded electric drawbar organ (`organRec`, played as the organ with its own chain), heard beside the
  synthesized organ; on a machine without the library it is the synthesized organ, byte for byte. It is not on the
  instrument shelf until it is chosen by ear.
- A recorded grand piano (`pianoRec`, played as `grand-piano-3` with its soundboard and room): notes struck once and
  left to ring, each played on its nearest take across F#2 to F#5 and damped when the key is let go; asking each note's
  register in words (a left hand's low notes, a bright treble) lands most takes in their octave. Without the library it
  is the tuned grand, byte for byte; not on the instrument shelf until chosen by ear.
- The robot band's pitched instruments recorded the same way: the celesta, the vibraphone (recorded with its motor off,
  the synthesized one's tremolo laid over it), the steel drum and the picked bass, struck once and left to ring; and the
  organ's low register asked again, reaching down to F#2. Each part matches its synthesized one's loudness and falls back
  to it, byte for byte, without the library. `RECORDED_TWINS` names each synthesized patch's recorded twin, so a band is
  heard recorded by naming the twins as its parts' patches; none is on the instrument shelf until chosen by ear.
- The pitch converter reads a struck note while it rings, not the silence after it: a celesta's bell, gone in a second,
  is measured over that second.
- A song plays its whole band on its recorded instruments with `recorded: true`: every part whose patch has a recorded
  twin is heard on it with its instrument's chain, and a part says `recorded: false` to stay synthesized. Without the
  library the song is exactly the synthesized one. The rest of the robot band is recorded for it: one clean guitar under
  the rhythm and the lead (the amp is each part's chain, its level the amp's makeup), the brass and the strings held on
  their loops (the brass brighter the harder it is played, the strings with the string machine's swell and vibrato), and
  the slap bass. The kit stays synthesized.
- More of the instrument shelf recorded and twinned, each matched to its synthesized one's loudness: the steel-string
  and nylon-string acoustic guitars (the classical guitar on the nylon), the electric guitar (on the band's clean
  guitar), the Rhodes, the harp, the marimba, the xylophone and the glockenspiel, the upright bass, and, held on their
  loops, the violin, the cello, the flute and the trumpet: recorded with no vibrato, the synthesized vibrato laid over
  each as a pitch lfo. A fretted instrument's low notes are asked by string and fret, the way a player names a pitch:
  the guitar now reaches its open low E (E2), where its low asks in words never came below C#3.
- The orchestra recorded: the French horn, the trombone and the tuba, the viola and the bowed contrabass, the clarinet,
  the oboe and the bassoon held on their loops (their synthesized vibrato laid over them), the timpani and the tubular
  bells struck. Every orchestral patch's second and third tiers are heard on their first tier's recording, each matched
  to its own patch's loudness, so a score written on any tier of the orchestra is heard recorded with `recorded: true`.
- The setting colours recorded: the harpsichord, the music box, the banjo, the harmonica (held, its vibrato laid over it),
  the shamisen and the pedal steel. The erhu was recorded too but stays synthesized: its takes came back as a drone.
- The pitch converter reads every recorded instrument better: it searches round the note asked (a hum or a bell's odd
  partial no longer reads as the note), reads six stretches of the sounding note and keeps the largest agreeing group
  (one slipped read no longer throws a good take away), and loops a held note inside the part that still sounds. Nearly
  every instrument now keeps all its takes: the music box went from 2 to 40, the glockenspiel from 15 to 47.
- The recorded piano and Rhodes have velocity layers: each note recorded soft and hard beside the medium takes, so a
  note played gently is a gentle note (darker, rounder) and one struck hard is a hard one (brighter, its hammer heard),
  not the same take turned down or up. Each note plays the take nearest it in pitch and in strength; its level still
  follows its velocity. An instrument without layers is played exactly as before.
- A recorded instrument now moves as its synthesized one does: a glide in from the previous note, a portamento, a
  glissando that slides (a struck one still runs the scale), and a legato run, one take whose pitch walks its notes with
  no retrigger. The take's playback rate rides the same ramps the oscillator's frequency would.
- A key let go is heard on the recorded piano and organ: the piano's felt damper falling back onto its strings (low,
  middle and high registers) and the organ's key click, played when the note's key is released, under the note's level
  and softer the softer it was played. The harpsichord's and the Rhodes' recorded releases came back with a buzz at one
  fixed pitch, so their notes still simply fade.
- The recorded violin reaches its upper register: its notes asked "on its upper strings" had all come back an octave
  low (nothing above B4, so a melody at E5 was a lower take stretched up as much as an octave, thin and screechy). Asked
  again by string and position (up the E string, up the A string), it now reaches A#5, every note of a high melody within
  a few semitones of a real take. The erhu, asked the same way, still came back on its open strings, so it stays synthesized.
- The recorded violin is one violin: its takes from separate passes in different words played as different violins side
  by side (a high run heard as another instrument). It is recorded again as one set, every note asked the same way up its
  four strings, and its earlier passes are kept but set aside.
- The Rhodes' release is heard: its recorded key-off carries a tick at one pitch, so it is tuned to each note let go
  (a release with a pitch of its own is measured, and a patch can ask for it to follow the note).
- The harp, the marimba and the vibraphone have velocity layers, soft and hard beside their medium takes.
- The shelf has saxophones: `soprano-sax`, `alto-sax`, `tenor-sax` and `baritone-sax`, synthesized (a conical bore's
  full row of harmonics, a reed's breath and drift, a singer's vibrato, a horn's body) and recorded note by note, each
  matched to its synthesized one's loudness. The casting table reads them as smoky, late-night woodwinds.

### Trees as flock

- Realistic trees' crowns are drawn as a model maker's clump foliage is cut: a porous sponge the sky shows through and
  the sun lights from behind, its edges breaking into the tree's own leaves at their real size (an oak's lobed leaf,
  a beech's oval one). It is the realistic crown's look from now on; a scene can turn it off, leave the leaves off, or
  choose its shadow: dappled, solid or none. Far trees are the same sponge, so a tree keeps its look as it
  recedes; exported models keep the crown as it was.
- Leafy bushes on the same scenes are flock too: a box or laurel dome stands as clumps of sponge, and a forsythia's
  fountain as runs of sponge along its arches, each with its own small leaves on the skin and the light through it, near
  and far. Hostas, ferns and the needled
  bushes keep their own look.
- A spike compares the crown as it was with the sponge and the sponge with leaves from the same cameras
  (`scripts/spikes/flock`).
- In the fall, the trees shed as they turn: each its own way, its crown opening onto its limbs from the top and the
  outside in, its last leaves catching the sun, more light reaching the ground, a wood never one density.
- Geotowns and geocities take the same trees: their street trees and their gardens' bushes read as realistic flock
  when the scene asks for realistic crowns. Street trees grow away from the houses, over the street, so a town keeps its
  trees; and a residential street is a mix of maples, flowering cherries and birches at a street's sizes, not a forest.
- A town's hedges are clipped hedges, flat on top and straight along their line, and its gardens are filled with small
  plants: a bed along each house's front and companions round each bed's plant, box balls, heathers, hostas and little
  flowering shrubs.
- A city's streets and parks look planted over the years: about a third of its trees are young, short and airy, among
  the grown ones; a vacant lot's self-sown trees are all young.

### The metroidvania box on its geocube

- A geocube can say a metroidvania box's look: its `box` names a library (the castle, XenoJager's planet), and the
  cube supplies the rest. Its colours tint each ring toward the cube's ramps, keeping the library's lightness so the
  light still pools and the walk still reads. Its crystals give the gem and its glow, and `rock` gives the boulders.
- A box level whose words name no theme now takes its look from its world's geocube. `gothic-night` builds the castle,
  and XenoJager's cube (`XENOJAGER_CUBE`, a document over gothic-night) builds the planet. A cube without a box keeps the
  greybox, and a box whose words name a theme is drawn exactly as before.
- The planet's crystals are drawn in centimetre paths, as the land's are, so a sapphire reads blue rather than black.
- The game book has a page for a box level, read off the box as its level builds it:
  - the plan: rooms in their ring's colour, the closed parts, ledges and ladders, the doorways and holes, each gate in
    its colour, pockets, saves, bosses, keys, the powers and the way in;
  - a card for each ring: its look, locales, what it is built of, its hazard, light, climbs, what it holds and the gate
    on inward;
  - the powers and what each opens;
  - every law the box is held to, labelled as the machine gate.
- The game book opens for a metroidvania level and a side map level. Both used to stop the book before its first page.
- A box game starts from a template on Galaxy Boy's rail: its variants `vampire-sonata` (the castle on the gothic night)
  and `xenojager` (the planet on its own cube). Locking the pitch lays the template's box with no theme, on the world's
  geocube, so the cube dresses it. The rail's sheet, the readout's pitch report and the variant's rail card each name
  the box and its cube. Each variant asks first for the person's box and its cube, and a sentence finds it by its own
  words. A new card, `gameworld-box`, teaches the box's words, its templates, the look a cube gives it, and its page in
  the book.
- XenoJager's handle now has its feel wired: the run and gun's, its wall kept. Its hero and its hazards are still the
  next builder's.
- The interface card lists theme cards a family at a time, a re-key counted on its parent. The world card's ceiling
  rises for a side strip's `scenery`.

### Blaze Gunner: a scrolling shooter in space, left to right

Blaze Gunner is an original horizontal scrolling shooter: a small, agile ship over a screen that scrolls on its own,
waves of foes, a hull flown along and a capital-ship boss. Its game is its weapons:
- pods taken from the foes that carry them, each giving the ship a different hurtbox, a shape in time;
- two pods at once, switched with a press;
- a held eject that launches the live pod as a timed bomb that never harms the ship.

Offence and dodging matter more than shielding. The ship moves on an eight-way d-pad, and damage comes off its HP.

It is a rail (`blaze-gunner`). Its words are a shmup, a shoot 'em up, bullet hell or a scrolling shooter, and its
starter lays the first stage as a designed game's level. A "side-scrolling shooter" stays the run and gun's.

**The scroll stage.** A stage is an airspace's `scroll`, built and played by `gameworld/scroll-stage/`:
- **The frame.** Play is written in screen axes, so a vertical stage seen from above is the same stage turned. The
  screen is set from the ship's own length.
- **The runtime.** The screen is carried down a track: legs, holds, and a hold until a boss is down. The ship moves on
  the d-pad. Its lives respawn it at home on the screen. Pods are hurtboxes in time, and foes fly their paths and fire
  told patterns.
- **Space in layers.** Dust lies in front of the play, stars at three depths behind it, and plated fleet hulls hazed by
  depth, all under the space map's sky. They parallax under the perspective camera, as a side map's layers do.
- **The ship.** The hero gunship is a new row on the craft shelf and in the vehicle registry: a classic hero fighter
  in profile, with a keel blade and a gun rail.
- **A hull on the play plane.** Rebel Storm's procedural enemy is broken by its systems and blown apart in rupa's chain
  in zero g. Its guns become turrets, and its outline is terrain.
- **Effects.** Rebel Storm's space blast plays where a craft dies. What is fired lights the hulls it passes, through
  the side map's shot light with an opt-in hook. Rounds are drawn in the shot look, and muzzle flashes, impacts and a
  guard ring show.

**The HUD.** The stage's HUD runs on mana-ui. It is drawn as a ship's console in the `orbit` look, which is now Blaze
Gunner's look for its menus too: hairlines, dark glass and a soft glow, with nothing drawn across the play. It speaks
in pictures and leaves the play clear between its corners:
- a star and the score, a ship for each life left, a heart and the hull as ticks, and the speed as lit chevrons at the
  top left;
- a card for each pod at the bottom left: the pod's own picture in its hue, its ammo as a count and a bar, and the
  eject's hold filling under the live one;
- a skull and the boss's systems at the top right while its hull is on the screen, its name said as it comes in;
- READY at the start and after a life is lost, then GAME OVER or STAGE CLEAR with the score;
- hints with the controls at the bottom right, as key caps or as the pad's own buttons. They show for the first
  seconds and again when a pad or the keyboard is picked up, then fade out.

A pod scores its kills.

**The menu.** Enter opens the stage's menu over the held stage, and so do Esc and the pad's start on their own page.
In a game, the shell's pause keeps Esc and start, and the stage's menu is on select. It is mana-ui's pause:
- resume;
- a controls sheet, with the keys and the pad side by side;
- the control hints on or off, remembered.

**A controller.** A pad plays the stage as a shooter's pad does: the d-pad or the stick flies, A or RT fires, X or LB
switches the pod, B or LT held ejects, and Y or RB changes speed. Each pad's buttons are printed as that pad names them
(Xbox, PlayStation or Nintendo), and the HUD's controls follow the device in hand. The game shell's controls panel
lists the same layout.

**Interiors.** A stage can fly inside a station or a facility: its `interior` lays a run of sections from its mouth:
- a mouth that closes in from the hull's face;
- a hall wide enough to fight in;
- a duct that is narrow and bends;
- shutters, bulkheads from the ceiling and the floor in turn;
- a core, the wide room at the heart.

Its floor and ceiling run as ramps between the middles of its steps, so the corridor climbs and narrows at an angle,
never in stairs. Guns stand on its walls facing the open. The walls are terrain: touching one costs a hit and pushes the
ship out (back off the hull's face at the mouth), and rounds end on them (a grenade bursts there, a bomb blows on one,
a beam stops where the corridor closes over it).

The corridor is drawn as a section through the station, seen from its open side:
- its cut face is plated with the hull kibble the fleet's capital ships wear;
- its bevelled edge catches the light;
- its decks are in bands that go darker deeper inside;
- ribs frame it every other stretch, conduits run along the back over the floor and under the ceiling;
- the back is in bays with lamp strips;
- the hull's face stands at both ends with docking lights;
- dark struts slide past in front.

Things live inside:
- guns stand on its walls, aimed at the ship;
- hatches in a hall's deck launch drones that rise out of the wall and run back across the screen;
- crushers shudder before they slam out of the ceiling or the floor, hold, and draw back, and even fully out each
  leaves the passage;
- locks close right across the way, two leaves meeting in the middle, and open again often enough and long enough to
  cross.

A crusher or a lock where it stands is terrain and stops rounds, as a wall does. Each sets its place in the wall: a
hatch's opening, a slot through the deck and the cut with warning lamps, a lock's frame. Laws hold them: a crusher out
leaves the passage, a lock opens long enough and twice while it is on the screen, and every mover is told before it
moves.

It is lit as the ship is, by the ship's own light in space: one key from the stage's star, the galaxy's faint fill, a
cool rim, the same tone curve. There are two looks:
- a station: steel plate, cyan lamps, windows out to the stars;
- a facility: dark steel, amber lamps, rust-brown conduits, hazard stripes on what crosses the way.

It is held to laws: the open is never narrower than
four ship breadths, each step overlaps the last by as much, a bend asks no more than the slowest gear can follow, the
open stays on the screen, and every gun stands on its wall.

**The reactor and stage 2.** The core room holds the station's reactor, a boss fixed in the room that throws a spiral
all round, behind shields that open and shut ahead of it; once it falls they stay open, and the run goes on out
through the far face. The HUD names it and reads its hp as the bar. Stage 2, "infiltration", is a short approach in
space with a carrier bringing the vulcan. Then it goes into the station by its mouth:
- a hall of guns and hatches;
- the duct;
- the crushers;
- the locks;
- the shutters;
- the reactor, the screen held until it falls.

The rail lays both stages. The bot reads the corridor, the bulkheads and the movers where their cycles will have them,
follows a bend before it is in it, and clears stage 2 end to end.

**From nothing to level one.** Blaze Gunner is made through the game book from nothing to a first level a person can
play. A shmup's words (or a station infiltration's) place it on its rail, and a locked pitch lays both stages as the
game's levels. It also writes the game's front (a press-start, its tagline, the end card "The reactor is down") and its
look (`orbit` in its own colours, no overlay across the play). Its play is the stages' own, so the play goalpost is met
by them. A run with `check: true` proves every stage the way a fight level is proved: the bot clears it and a still
ship that neither moves nor fires does not, and that meets the first level's goalpost. The shell plays the whole game
on mana-ui: press start, the title, a stage under its HUD, CLEARED with the next stage offered, the second stage, the
end card.

**Its screens.** The game is named Blaze Gunner where the person gives it no name of its own. Its menus are drawn
over a new mana-ui stage, `starfield`, in place of orbit's rings: scattered stars drawn short along the way the stages
scroll, drifting on in parallax, with a world's lit rim low in a corner. It holds still under less motion. The title,
the result between stages and the end card all wear it.

**Laws.** The arsenal and the bullet patterns are held to laws:
- no pod is better on every measure, and every pod is worth taking over the base gun;
- a bullet is seen coming, a volley always leaves a way through, and every volley is told;
- a stage stays under a density of bullets on the screen.

**Checks.** A bot plays a stage to its end on the shipped rules. Stage 1 is cleared as an end-to-end gate.

`node scripts/scroll-stage.mjs` shoots a stage on its page.

### More to do in the city

- Four new driving jobs on Jobsified. **Ambulance calls**: take one of the emergency station's ambulances, pick up the
  patient waiting by a red cross sign and drop them off. **Fire calls**: take a fire engine to fires burning at the kerb
  and hold to hose each one down. **Courier run**: a courier van from the dock, a parcel handed over at each of four
  doors. **Mail round**: a mail truck emptying four post boxes, the mail taken back to the yard. The stations' jobs show
  up where a district has an emergency station.
- Each job's screen line speaks its own words (a patient aboard, "hold F to hose it down") instead of a bus's.
- Fixed: the heavy vehicle call, street sweeping and the new mail round could be silently missing when their yard had
  no kerb nearby; their vehicle now waits at a kerb near the start instead. A street with a streetcar line no longer
  loses all its kerb parking. The courier's van never parks in a bay another truck already stands in.
- Two more buildings to walk into near the start: an **arcade** behind a lit pink-and-cyan sign, its games floor with a
  blocks cabinet, and a **public library** with a small portico, a reading room with a match table, the stacks and the
  archive in plaster and oak. Each opens on a page of its own, like the museum, and you walk back out onto its steps.
- An **aquarium** behind a deep blue sign: glass tanks of water down its three wings, The Reef, Life on the Bed and Open
  Water, with clownfish, angelfish, a pufferfish and a cuttlefish, an octopus and a moray eel on the sand, and a sea
  turtle, a manta ray and squid in the big tank at the end.
- A **zoo** behind a gate with a lit sign and a ticket booth: open to the sky, three wings of pens fenced in mesh,
  The Savanna (zebras, ostriches, a giraffe and an elephant in the big enclosure), Big Cats and Bears (lions, tigers, a
  brown bear and a polar bear) and Around the World (kangaroos hopping, flamingos, penguins, meerkats and camels).
- **Hidden stars**: ten stars tucked round Hijack City where nobody walks on the way anywhere (a park's far corner,
  the back of an empty lot or a building site, beside a highway ramp's foot, the corners of the dock and the yards),
  spread far apart and picked up into the bag. Any world can hide some (`hidden: true | { stars, item }`).
- **Fishing off the quay**: Hijack City's dock keeps a fishing stall at its water's edge past the crane, its keeper
  facing the water. Any world's minigames can be kept there (`where: 'quay'`), and beside the way where no city keeps a
  dock.

### A museum in the city

- Hijack City has a museum: a stone building with columns and banners on a block near where you start. Walk up its
  steps and through its door and you are inside, on its own page, without the city loaded behind it; walk back out and
  you are on its steps again, the city as you left it.
- Inside: a lobby and three gallery wings, each with its own name: plaster walls (mostly white, an oxblood or a
  grey-blue room here and there), oak and pale stone floors, daylight from the ceiling and warm lights. Each piece stands
  on a plinth, and one piece per wing stands full size in the hall at the wing's end. Nothing to win, just a place to
  look around.
- The museum is filled with things made in mojulo: cars and a tram, a digger, swords and a shield, animals from a
  wolf to an elephant, and furniture.

### The Claude plugin for 3.2: Claude Code installs mojulo, and a skill for each way in

The 3.1 plugin was held by the plugin directory and never published; the plugin returns with 3.2, shaped to what the
directory reads.

- **Claude Code installs the server.** The plugin's root carries `package.json` and `package-lock.json` (one exact
  dependency, `mojulo`, every package hashed and from registry.npmjs.org). Claude Code installs them itself when the
  plugin is added or updated, into its own copy of the plugin, and the plugin runs
  `node ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/node_modules/mojulo/scripts/mcp-stdio.mjs`. The 3.1 launcher (`server/launch.mjs`, an
  `npm ci` of ours at first start) is gone, so the plugin runs no installer of its own, needs no npm at start, and the
  first session starts at once. Claude Code installs with scripts off; no package mojulo needs has an install script
  (better-sqlite3 and sharp arrive prebuilt), and the lockfile is refused when one does.
- **The plugin declares the host it reaches** (`network.hosts`: registry.npmjs.org, for `check_for_updates` and the
  dashboard) and passes `claude plugin validate --strict` with nothing to report.
- **A skill for each way in.** `make-character`, `design-game`, `design-object`, `make-exhibit` and, for a home or a
  room, `design-building` (the home producer first, `mint_building({ start })`) and `design-interior`: the five starts
  the `initialize` preamble offers, each loaded on the person's own words and carrying its start's steps, the routing
  cards it goes to and the entry tool to load (Claude Code defers MCP tool schemas). They are generated from the routing cards (`scripts/plugin-skills.mjs`, written by
  `node scripts/plugin-agents.mjs` with the subagents), so a skill and the server's routing say the same thing; the
  main `mojulo` skill names them.
- **The checks follow.** `plugin-lock.mjs` writes the plugin's root package; `check-plugin-version.mjs` holds the
  server command, the one exact dependency, the lockfile (version 2 or 3, no install scripts, no overrides) and the
  directory's limits (under 512 files, each under 256 KiB).
- plugin.json is 3.2.0, the release the plugin ships with; at the release `plugin-lock.mjs` locks mojulo 3.2.0.

### Warlords of Mars: the hangar and the garage

- **The frame builds in the page** (`assault-frame/kernel.js`): the parts, the assembly, the body, its clips and the
  pilot's entity as one page-runnable kernel, so a level can stand any build the player chose. Its packed figure is
  the server's, byte for byte (a tripwire test).
- **A frame level stands the save's build** (`assault-frame/hangar.js`, the store's `hangar` slice): the build kept as
  a flag a slot (`frame.<slot>`: a part's id, `-` for none). Every frame level consumes the slice, a world with frame
  levels declares it, and the page builds the frame it says with the kernel and stands it in the pilot's place: its
  figure in the light the level's own pilot was made under, its numbers, its weapons, its HUD.
- **The hangar** (`scene/channels/controllable/frame-garage.js`, a frame stage's `garage: true`): every operation opens
  with the frame on its pad in a hangar bay (the field put away behind a render layer of the bay's own), the camera
  swaying slowly across its front, the operation held behind it. Its
  words are mana-ui's, three new campaign idioms (`mana-ui/idioms-campaign.js`), read as tables on solid plates for
  fitting: `garage-slots` (the slots and their parts, then Sortie), `garage-parts` (a slot's parts in a list, the one
  in focus said in a line, and one table of every part's figures, each with its change from the fitted part; a column
  only where the parts differ, its labels said once) and `machine-sheet` (the frame's load as a bar against its legs',
  its figures in two columns, its laws). A part fitted is stood at once; Sortie keeps the build in the save and lets
  the operation go. While it is up the field's HUD (its radar, banners, legend and readouts) is put away.
  - The bay is dressed: panelled walls (inset plates, vents, lamps), cable trays and loose cables sagging between the
    ribs and down the gantries, steel crates stacked in the corners and along the walls, drums in clusters; the
    turntable's deck is plate drawn in the page (ring and radial seams with their bolts, a hub, a hazard band at the
    rim). Laid by fixed dice: the same bay every time.
- **Parts won** (an operation's `reward`, frame-goal.js; the store's `parts` inventory): each operation's win adds its
  parts to the garage, emitted as it is won (the game channel's `wins`, a level's grants on a success; a level with
  none carries nothing). Warlords of Mars rewards a ladder: a conventional biped kit at Landfall, the close and long
  FCS, the Scatter, the Gatling and the Lance, the light and heavy arms, heads and legs, the Falcon and the Ox, the
  Shear blade, the Arc after the Thunderhead and the Citadel core after Vermilion.
- **The operation's briefing** (`campaign/operation-brief.js`, a frame stage's `briefing: true`): an operation is told
  on the holo table before the drop, as Rebel Storm's missions and Wolf Squadron's stages are. The table is the field's
  own ground (its height grid the hologram's terrain; a works' field its machines, decks, furnaces and racks stood up as
  masses), the drop, every group of the operation where it stands as a miniature with its count, and each beacon. The
  steps are the operation's own design (an operation's `briefing`: a region and its steps, each a title, its words, what
  it lights and the routes it draws), else a step for the field and one a task. The briefing channel holds the operation
  behind it; Launch hands it to the hangar. The table's roster is headed in the design's word (`rosterTitle`: an
  operation's Forces; a squadron's Flight groups, as before). The ground force's other cards stand on the table as the
  nearest miniature (a frame, a drone and a gunship join the unit minis).
- **Two designed operations.** The Siq (the gorge massif, Valles Marineris): guns on the high ground over a slot canyon,
  Wasps raking its length, two Bastions shutting the narrows, then out to the beacon at its mouth. Furnace Row (the
  smelter hall, Pavonis Works): walkers on the operating decks, the crane controls reached and held while the main
  ladle is cut loose, then the foreman's pack of two Jackals and their Rhino.
- The hangar's idioms (`garage-slots`, `garage-parts`, `machine-sheet`) have a hangar in mana-ui's sample state, so the wireframe board and the idiom sweep draw them full.

### A city at street level

- A town's or a district's level can now ask for its sky and air in its style, the same way it asks for its hour:
  clouds, haze or mist lying over the streets, the far blocks softened in it, and a finish (one tone curve, the sky
  reflected in glass, light that blooms). It can also ask for the view cone, which draws the street's kit and trees
  only as far as they read. Hijack City asks for all of them.
- The camera behind a vehicle you drive is framed by its size: a car is seen as before, a van, a box truck or a rig
  from further back and higher, so the road ahead shows over its roof; and the camera comes in front of a wall rather
  than standing inside the building behind you. A vehicle taken from the traffic is framed by its own size too.
- Suburbs can be a West Coast tract or a tropical coast, not only a northeastern streetcar suburb or a European old
  town. A West Coast street is one-storey stucco ranches and Spanish revival bungalows on wide lots, each with its own
  drive and garage, palms along a grass parkway, pools out back, and stucco shops behind their parking on the boulevard.
  A tropical street is pastel block houses raised a step under white tile, louvred shutters, low walls and iron gates,
  and coconut palms. A city's outskirts carry the same look out to its edge, with its houses, shops, flats and street
  trees all in it, while its downtown stays its own.
- Their shopping streets are a Rodeo: two-storey boutiques of cream and white stucco over limestone, tall display
  glass in black frames, crisp canopies and gold lettering, under palms. The tropical coast's are the same in pastel.
  The strip malls stay on the boulevards.
- San Francisco, in two neighbourhoods. A Victorian one: narrow wooden houses touching up steep streets, each painted
  its own three colours (Italianates and Stick houses under flat false fronts and cornices, Queen Annes under gables,
  bays up their fronts, stoops to their doors, Edwardian flats among them, corner stores). And the Avenues: rows of
  two-storey pastel stucco houses each over its own garage, a picture window above it, a car on every apron, few
  trees. A hill city to set them in, on a peninsula with water on three sides and cable cars up its streets.
- Hijack City by locale: Los Angeles (ranches and palms in a low gold sun and a warm smog), Miami (pastel houses
  and coconut palms under a high noon sun, a bright sea haze, vivid colour), San Francisco (the hill city in its
  morning fog under a grey sky, cool), Boston (a brick inner city on an overcast afternoon, filmic) and Toronto (its
  streetcar suburbs on a fair morning). Each is one word that sets the suburbs, the part of town, the light, the sky,
  the air and the colour grade together; any of them can still be named over it.
- Each locale builds its city its own way, from the old metro city's flavours: Los Angeles low and wide in cream and
  sand stucco with few towers on a nearly flat basin; Miami's slender white and glass condo towers with stacked
  balconies on flat land by the water; San Francisco's pale stone and glass on its steep hills; Boston's brick and
  brownstone without New York's fire escapes and water tanks, on low hills.
- Hijack City's suburbs are the West Coast's now; one word makes them a tropical coast, the northeastern suburb they
  were, or a San Francisco district in its fog.
- No building floats off its ground any more: where the land falls away under a wall (a slope, a terrace, a
  waterfront ramp), that wall is carried down to the ground on a plinth, and a door level with its plaza keeps its
  threshold. The hill city's land eases down to its water instead of standing on a cliff over it.
- The city's glass gives back the sky: windows, shop fronts and glass towers mirror it by angle and catch the sun's
  highlight, where before they were painted flat and dark. Parked cars wear a clear coat; the traffic and the car you
  drive gleam the same way, the sky in their roofs and doors and the sun glinting off their panels.
- Roads, walks and plazas keep their own colour under a low sun instead of turning navy, and a highway's underside is
  textured concrete instead of a dark flat slab.
- Highways no longer run into buildings: every elevated highway now has its own corridor, the deck plus 3 m of
  clearance each side, and the arterial under it is laid that wide before any block is cut, so nothing is built under
  or against a deck (a wider sidewalk runs under it instead).
- The city has places now: some neighbourhoods have a church, a mosque or a temple on its forecourt and lawn behind a
  railing; some have a cemetery with rows of headstones, crosses and ledgers, gravel walks, trees and a chapel at the
  gate. Which faiths a city has is a setting (`civic.faiths`), and `civic: false` turns them off.
- Big city parks are no longer bare lawn: promenades cross at an obelisk, each quarter has a playground, a pavilion,
  benches and trees, and the park is railed along its streets. Park blocks are railed too, and car parks are lined with
  bollards along their streets.
- Places of worship are part of the city downtown too: in the core and the inner city a church, mosque or temple is
  built into a block on a street corner among its neighbours, or fills a small downtown block of its own on a paved
  plaza, instead of standing on a lawn behind a railing (that churchyard form stays for the suburbs).
- Downtown streets are dressed: dashed centre lines, zebra crossings at every junction, cars parked along both kerbs
  with parking meters, trees in their pits between the lamps, hydrants and newspaper boxes at the corners.
- Hijack City's downtown is the city's core now: its towers, podiums and square, with the inner city round it (the
  suburbs are their own district).
- A side street no longer dead-ends into the main road's sidewalk: where it meets an arterial the sidewalk is opened
  across its mouth and the road runs through, and no bench, lamp, bin or tree stands in the way.
- Downtown shops hang blade signs over the sidewalk, and the roofs are dressed: towers carry a mechanical penthouse
  and cooling towers, flat roofs a stair bulkhead, a row of air handlers and, on the big ones, a cooling tower.
- The city's ground level looks lived in: some windows have blinds drawn or curtains, some homes have a window air
  conditioner, a few shops are shut behind roller shutters (some tagged with graffiti), and open shops put things out
  on the sidewalk: sandwich boards, planters by the door, a cafe table under an umbrella, crates, bags out for
  collection. Downtown streets get manhole covers, oil stains where cars park, utility cabinets, mailboxes and the odd
  vendor's cart. Each is placed by its own position, so nothing else in the city moves.
- Buildings no longer share one wall colour: each building's walls are a little lighter or darker and warmer or
  cooler than its neighbours', and some wear brick where their neighbours are stone (or the other way round).
- About a third of open shops show a lit interior through their glass (a shelf, a counter, someone behind it), lit by
  its own lamps, so it glows the same at noon and at night.
- Roadworks: some streets and main roads have a crew's works pickup or van (or a delivery truck) standing in the kerb
  lane, a barrier behind it and cones tapered round it.
- Alleys: more than half of the inner city's blocks are now split down the middle by a service alley running street to
  street, with the backs of buildings on both sides (windows, balconies, no shopfronts), dumpsters and bags along the
  walls, oil stains, a manhole, wires strung across overhead and sometimes a car or a delivery van. The sidewalks open
  at each alley's mouth, and nothing is parked or stood across it. `alleys: false` turns them off.
- Night scapes: Hijack City can be played at night (`hour: 'night'` or `'dusk'`), each locale with its own night (LA's
  sodium-amber lamps in a lit smog, Miami's white lamps, San Francisco's fog, Boston's cold white, Toronto's warm). The
  city falls dark so what is lit stands out: windows, lit shop interiors, a pool of light under every street lamp and
  alley lamp with a glow at its head, and the traffic's headlights and tail lights. Alleys now have wall lamps.
- Pedestrians, in sixes: the played district's sidewalks are walked by groups of six different people (two pairs side
  by side and two on their own, each at its own pace and some going the other way round). Busier blocks (a square,
  towers, a main street) get more sixes than quiet residential ones, filled nearest the middle first. A level's
  `crowd` sets how heavy it is: `quiet`, `busy` or `packed` (one, two or three rolls of six different people, up to
  four, eight or twelve sixes walking); downtown and the inner city are busy and the suburbs quiet by default.
