- Fixed: a hero starting downtown could find no car to take at the kerb, since a downtown parked car nearby kept the
  kerb cars from being laid; the kerb cars are laid now, never on a bay already taken.
- Realistic heroes' hands fit their bodies: a hand is now as long as an adult's for the body's height (about a ninth of
  it) and as broad across the knuckles as a man's or a woman's, where it had been a fifth short and narrow. Heroes made
  before keep their hands; a new one, or one remade, gets the new size.
- Athleisure outfits, drawn for women (any outfit dresses anyone): `yoga` (a matching long-sleeved crop and leggings),
  `jogger` (a running tank and brief shorts in runners), `bikeShorts` (an oversized tee over bike shorts), `tracksuit`
  (a zipped track jacket with ribbed cuffs and waist over a tee, tapered joggers), `studio` (a zip-up left open over a
  crop and leggings), `tennis` (a collared knit top and a crisp short skirt) and `lounge` (a loose cropped sweatshirt and
  wide sweatpants). Street people wear them now and then.
- Realistic faces look more like their own people (new heroes; existing ones are unchanged):
  - Eye colour now comes from ancestry: mostly brown, with blue, green, grey and hazel mainly for European ancestry.
    Every face used to have the same blue-grey eyes.
  - A hero in clothes keeps their own hair, brow and lash colour. Dressing used to turn everyone's hair the same dark
    brown.
  - Women's faces read as women's: larger eyes, a smaller and finer nose, a narrower jaw, a softer, smaller
    chin, a flatter brow ridge and fuller lips. Bold features (a square jaw, a strong chin, heavy brows) are rarer, and a
    woman's overall character leans soft and delicate while still reaching the full range.
- Street people mix ancestries (no more than two of one in a six) and their faces vary more than a hero's do.
- Realistic women's bodies have a flat belly and a navel: the six-pack is now a smooth toned front, the pouch under the
  navel and the mounds at the front of the hips are gone, and the navel shows (it was too small for the body's mesh to
  carry). Heavier builds keep their belly. New heroes only; existing ones keep their bodies.
- Realistic people's heads and necks are their own: head size varies a little person to person (it was one size for
  every woman and every man of a height), neck length varies, and the neck's width follows the head on it. Heavyset
  necks are thick but no longer wider than the head. New heroes only; existing ones keep their bodies.
- Hijack City can be walked by realistic people (`people: 'realistic'`, opt-in): the street's cast of realistic men and
  women in everyday clothes, their ancestries drawn from the city's own mix. Each person is drawn in full detail near the
  camera (their face kept) and simplified further away, and a level's people are baked once and kept on disk, so a
  level opens quickly after the first time.
- Realistic pedestrians are lit by the city: shaded by the sun by day, brighter under street lamps and dimmer between
  them by night (they used to glow at night and look flat by day).
- Pedestrians in a group no longer walk inside each other: partners walk side by side and the groups along a block
  are spread out. Before, each pair was drawn on one spot, so two people's clothes showed through each other in
  patches.
- Hijack City builds again: since its district moved downtown, the contact's jobs had no shops to stand at and the level
  could not be laid. Downtown's shopfronts are now the jobs' stops (the kerb before each shop).
- A big level's loading screen no longer disappears before the level is ready. Exported games' levels now say how their
  download is going (the percentage and what is loading: the world, the people, then building the world) and the
  loading screen stays up until the first frame is drawn. Before, it was taken down after 45 seconds, leaving a blank
  screen while a large level was still loading. The level's files also download at the same time instead of one after
  another.
- The loading screen also covers a level's warm-up: it stays up, saying "warming up", until the game runs smoothly,
  instead of lifting on the first frame and leaving the game frozen for a while. Realistic pedestrians' detailed
  figures are built during that warm-up (one body shared by everyone wearing it), so walking up to someone no longer
  hitches the game.
- Realistic pedestrians really walk now, with planted feet. Before, they took steps in place while sliding along the
  pavement. Each walks the main character's own walk in a gait of their own, chosen by age and build: easy, brisk,
  stroll, heavy, weary, graceful, swagger or shy, from about 0.7 to 1.55 m/s. Each group walks at its members' own pace,
  so a pair stays side by side, each stepping in their own rhythm.
- The city's buildings, trees, lamp posts and parked cars now cast shadows. Before, only characters did, because the
  city's shadow map stretched over the whole metro and its water, about 3 km across, too coarse to draw anything in the
  street. It now covers only the district you play in. Shadows are strong at noon; at a low sun, like Los Angeles's
  golden hour, they are long but faint, since the sun then gives the street only about a quarter of its light.
- Parked cars, benches, hydrants, trees and street furniture now cast shadows everywhere in the district, not only near
  where the level starts, and moving traffic casts them around the player. The static objects cost nothing per frame,
  because the city's shadows are drawn once while the level loads. Moving traffic adds about 1% more draw calls and 7%
  more triangles per frame on a downtown street.
- Hijack City has one streetcar line instead of track down several main streets, and streetcars now run on it: one each
  way along every track, stopping at the traffic lights with the cars. Other cities keep their own amount of track.
- Driving is smoother. The car you drive was drawn one step behind the camera following it, which made it judder; it is
  now drawn exactly where the camera sees it, and its tilt over bumps in the road is eased instead of snapping. Traffic
  now moves every frame instead of in 20-per-second steps.
- Driving is less jerky. The camera behind your car no longer jumps in and out past lamp posts, trees and bollards,
  it turns with the car smoothly instead of whipping round at each tap of the steering, and your car no longer hops when
  it drives over the spot where a traffic car is.
- Hijack City has its own music. The streets play a darker lo-fi beat with a sketchy edge, and the police chase still
  kicks in over it when you get stars. The title and menus play its mirror, a bright, bouncing "vibrant city" version of
  the same tune. Both are new moods any game can name: `shady` and `vibrant`.
- Hijack City's streets sound like a city, not a park: no more birdsong and wind under the music. Horns, a car alarm and
  a siren a few blocks off, a gate creaking and now and then a bottle breaking. A busy daytime boulevard is the other
  choice.
- Wheels visibly turn. Each moving car, yours and the traffic's, shows a spoked hubcap on each wheel that turns with its
  speed.

### The geocube card: its presets in groups, accurate to what a cube takes

- The geocube card names its presets a group a line (a level's look, a frame's open terrain, a frame's industrial
  interior, the children of Sol), each group described on a card of its own (`geocube/<group>`), so a new preset grows
  its group's card and never the geocube's: the card is back under its ceiling with room to spare.
- It no longer lists each preset's ingredients (its light, bones and land), which read as what a preset is for and
  misled (a smelter hall's "research-lab bones").
- It says what it was missing: every specimen `show` takes (not only room and land), a cube's `light.heavens` and its
  interiors, a field's standing rock (`massif`) and a works' hall over its land (`works`), and the recipe's `sea`.

### Mech Battle Kai interiors: a smelter hall a frame fights through, lit by its own lamps and furnaces

Enclosed fields at a frame's scale. The first is a steelworks' melt shop half a kilometre across. It has no sky: its
light is the place's own and its background a smoky void. It stays in the seventh generation's form render, so its
steel, concrete and slag are lit as materials. Its materials are the field's own floor: the land's layers re-dressed,
so everything the land does (bands, wear, sections, stochastic tiling, rubble) works on them.

- **The land's materials** (`form/land-materials.js`, a geocube's `outside.materials`, opt-in).
  - A set dresses the four natural layers in a works' cuts, each with its tile, its cube colour and how metal it is:
    `foundry` (riveted steel plate, black slag, slabbed concrete, settled ash), `refinery` (tread plate, gravel,
    concrete pads, oily grime) and `hangar` (wall plate, a sealed epoxy floor, grit).
  - The page blends each layer's metalness and roughness by its weights, and the metal reflects the place's
    environment.
  - Absent, the land is byte-identical.
- **The interior's light** (`form/interior-light.js`, a geocube's `light.interior`, opt-in).
  - A land under a roof has no sky: it has a void, a smoke haze, high-bay lamps and the glow of what burns.
  - The lamps are the works' own (hung from the trusses' bottom chords) or rows under the roof. The page hangs the
    nearest the middle as point lights, with the furnaces' and ladles' glows.
  - The cube's sun stays as the high-bay field's overhead key, at a third of a sun, so decks still throw shadows.
  - The metal reflects an interior environment, never a sky: a dark hall, the lamp rows a band overhead, the glow low
    down. World-scene drops the page's sky and sets its background to the void.
- **The works** (`local-meru/works.js`, a local meru island's `works`, a geocube's `outside.works`, opt-in). An
  industrial interior built over the land, everything a height grid cannot draw:
  - the hall's walls;
  - its roof on lattice trusses (top and bottom chords, verticals and Pratt diagonals, purlins between) and the
    column lines under them;
  - a bridge crane on its rails;
  - operating decks on legs with ramps up to them;
  - furnaces under their hoods and stacks, their mouths glowing;
  - tanks on concrete footings, ladles of molten metal, pipe runs on supports.
  - **Wire scaffolds** are towers of tube in bays, with standards, ledgers and braces. Each lift is a floor of open
    grating, a lattice of bars a frame sees through, stacked a frame's height apart, with guard rails and a barred ramp
    up to the first lift. Under each floor lies a plate a frame stands on (`works:floor`), ray-cast and never drawn
    (the land's `ghosts`).
  - Its faces take the land's own classes, so the materials and the light reach them: steel is the rock layer,
    concrete the soil, and what glows (`works:glow`) keeps its own fill.
  - It gives the page its lamps and glows, its decks, and what stops a body.
- **The smelter hall** (`assault-frame/geocubes.js` `smelter-hall`, the field's form `smelter`).
  - The foundry's materials and colours under the interior light, with the smelter works on the `smelter` massif
    card's floor: slag heaps at their repose, concrete plinths, casting pits.
  - Steel is blackened low by soot, panels have their own tones, rust runs from the seams.
  - Slag rubble; stochastic tiling.
- **A frame under a roof.**
  - On an indoor field a frame looks for its ground from a step over its feet (`rule.probe`), not from 60 m up, so
    it walks under a deck or a scaffold floor and lands on one it jumps or ramps onto.
  - The frame rule stops at what the world's colliders stand (`resolveBlocking`, when its rule names a body): the
    works' walls, columns, furnaces, tanks and ladles, and the decks' slabs, walked under and stood on.
  - The level carries the works' colliders (`frameField` `indoor`, `colliders`).
  - A frame that names no body moves as it always did.
- **A refinery superstructure** (`assault-frame/geocubes.js` `refinery-works`, the field's form `refinery`). A place
  built up, not out, under a 140 m enclosure on deep trusses, its new works words:
  - **process frames** (`frames`): heavy steel in 12 m bays, a grating floor at each level a frame's height apart,
    girders, braces, a ramp to the first; lamps hung under each level's corners; the columns stop a body, and every
    level is a deck walked under and stood on;
  - **columns** (`vessels`): distillation columns and reactors on concrete footings, a platform ringing each at each
    height a frame can stand on, its rail and a lamp;
  - **spheres** on their legs, **pipe racks** (`racks`, a bent every 12 m and four pipes on each tier) carrying the
    spine between the units, **walkways** (`bridges`) of grating from a frame's level to another or to a column's ring,
    and fired heaters glowing at the edges.
  - Scaffolds and process frames share one tower builder: a scaffold is the light one.
  - The `refinery` massif card is its floor: gravel between low concrete pads, bunds round the storage, oily sumps.
  - The refinery's materials, sodium lamps, and a fill as warm as its lamps (`HALL_LIGHT` takes a sky), so the floor
    is never shaded blue.
- **Every unit lit, and racks that stop a frame.**
  - A place with more lamps than a page hangs has them pooled, not cut: every lamp joins its nearest pool, and each
    pool hangs at its members' centre with their reach, as strong as their mean grown by the root of their number.
    The outer units and the far walls are lit, not only the middle (`form/interior-light.js`).
  - A pipe rack's posts stop a body, each tier's bundle is a slab a frame walks under below the lowest tier and is
    stopped by above it, and the top tier's crowns are a plate a frame lands on and walks along.
- **The works' floor, designed from above** (`local-meru/works-floor.js`, a works card's `floor`, opt-in; drawn by
  `scene/channels/works-floor-glsl.js` in the land's shader). The floor is a plant's plan, not one tile repeated.
  - Its zones are read off the works:
    - a pad poured under every frame, scaffold, deck, column, tank and sphere, bunded by a kerb round what stores;
    - a footing under each column of the hall's lines and each rack post, a rack's footings stepped along it;
    - steel plate round the furnaces and ladles;
    - a trench along each frame and each rack.
  - Only the lanes and the yard are designed: lanes along the axes and one round the hall `ring` metres in, and a
    gravel or concrete yard.
  - Each zone is drawn its own way:
    - a pad is sawcut at its own spacing from its own corner;
    - an apron is laid in steel plates of three sizes, welded and bolted;
    - a lane is lined in paint, dashed down its middle and worn in two tracks;
    - a trench is grating over a pit seen in parallax;
    - the yard is domed gravel stones, or concrete in long strip pours sawcut at no rhythm (no running bond).
  - Kibble lies over the pads and the yard: manhole covers, drain grates over their own pits (parallax), bolted anchor
    plates, oil stains. One at most per cell, kept off a zone's edge.
  - Near, the floor's relief (joints, kerbs, bolts, plates, stones) turns its normal; far off, only its tones.
  - It is drawn only on the floor, within 1.5 m of the floor at the centre, so a deck's top and a pipe's crown are not.
  - The page reads it as two small textures: the zones, and a grid of cells naming the zones over each.
  - The foundry's and the refinery's concrete layers became a jointless grain, since the plan draws the joints.
  - Absent, the land and its page are byte-identical.
- **The smelter's charge and its metal** (`local-meru/works.js` `rails` and `runners`, `scene/channels/works-melt.js`).
  - **Rails:** tracks along the axes, two rails on sleepers at a heavy plant's broad gauge, ballast under them in the
    floor plan (a lane crossing is paved over).
    - Trains stand on them: hopper wagons on their bogies, heaped over the brim with what is to be smelted. Ore and
      coke are mounded to the middle in lumps; scrap lies in plates and bars every way; `mixed` takes them in turn.
    - Each wagon stops a frame and is cover the height of its hopper.
    - The smelter has two tracks the length of the hall: trains of ore and coke on one, scrap and a mixed train on the
      other.
  - **Runners:** refractory troughs carrying the molten metal from each furnace's tap.
    - Each is level across its furnace's deck, then a spout off the deck's edge (a height at each point of its path),
      on trestles a frame walks under. The metal pours into the ladle at its end.
    - The metal is the page's own, lit by itself: white-yellow down the middle, orange to its banks, and a dark crust
      in plates drifting down the runner with the flow. The stream falls faster than the runner flows.
    - Each ladle's metal is now a pool whose crust drifts in from the rim.
    - Glows along each runner and at each pour light what is round them.

### Mech Battle Kai terrain: sandstone cliffs, gorges, talus and water for a frame's field

The land a frame fights on raised from rolling dunes round a mound to sandstone country: sheer jebels stepped by their
beds, gorges and siqs between them, talus and fallen blocks at their feet, and water the suits hover over. It is pure
terrain with no trail and no seam, since the field is read off its radar and its beacons. It is tied back to the game
book's map: a frame level's plate is now its operation map. Buildings come after.

- **The massif** (`local-meru/massif.js`, a local meru island's opt-in `massif`, a geocube's `outside.massif`). A field's
  standing rock as words: a card (`wadi`, `gorge`, `scree`, `oasis`) or `{ from?, … }`. Absent, a land is as it was.
  - **Blocks** (jebels, buttes, the plateau a canyon is cut through). Each block's plan is a superellipse warped into
    lobes and fluted into vertical ribs.
  - **Beds.** One column of beds runs through the whole massif, so every block's walls step at the same heights and the
    country reads as one rock cut apart. Each riser is sheer at its foot with a rounded shoulder; a bench's run wanders
    along the wall. A cap tops the block: domes, beehive knobs, or flat.
  - **Cuts** (gorges and canyons) take the same wall profile from the other side. **Clefts** are slots cut into every
    block from its edge, Wadi Rum's siqs.
  - **Talus** lies at the angle of repose, lobed into fans, with fallen blocks strewn on it as boulders.
  - **Water**: river beds and pools carved under the floor's datum, so the island's sea fills them with no water of
    their own.
  - **The face** (`face: { beds, bulge, undercut, grain }`): the walls' own relief at a mech's scale.
    - The column is parted again into thin beds 5 to 10 m thick, each with its own hardness.
    - Every wall is cut at those partings and at each bed's middle. Each corner is pushed along the wall, out of the
      rock: a hard bed bulges, a parting recesses, a massive bed's foot is undercut, and a grain of noise in all three
      directions keeps any two walls from matching.
    - The push swings over a few hundred metres, so one jebel stands massive and smooth and the next is ledged bed on
      bed.
    - The push is a function of place alone, so faces that share a corner still meet. It adds no faces beyond the cuts.
  - **The ground in front of a frame**, at its scale:
    - **outcrops**: low ledges of the same rock laid by the dice over the floor, off the blocks and the water, 2.5 to 7
      m high and 15 to 50 m across. Cover and a ledge to step up, stepped by the same beds.
    - **washes**: dry washes wandering across the floor, 1 to 1.7 m deep and never under the sea line, their beds laid
      as gravel (scree).
    - **scatter**: clusters of boulders 3 to 7 m across out on the open floor, off the rock and the water.
  - **horizon**: the field's skyline. Escarpments stand round it just inside its shore, each long along the ring and
    short across it, each its own height, laid by the dice so they overlap into a broken skyline with its gaps. They
    are the same rock as the rest. The battlefield cubes' island rim is now a low far rise, so the pale ring wall it
    was is gone.
  - **craters**: meteorite impacts on the floor. Each is a simple crater: a bowl a fifth of its diameter deep under a
    raised rim, its ejecta thinning as the cube of the distance out to three radii.
    - Sizes follow the impacts' power law (`slope`): many small pits, a fair few of every size between, a few great
      bowls.
    - Each crater has its own age. A fresh one is deep, its rim sharp, its thrown blocks strewn round it; an old one is
      shallow, its rim worn, its floor filled flat with sand. A younger crater prints over an older.
    - They are laid by the dice off the rock and the water, or named in `at`.
    - **Strewn fields** (`clusters`): a meteorite broken up on its way down, its fragments struck together along its
      flight. Each field is an ellipse turned to its heading, all its craters of one age, the largest at the down-range
      end and the small trailing behind. The crater plain has six, the wadi and the scarp two each.
    - A fresh crater's bowl and rim are laid as gravel (`crush`) and small fresh craters throw blocks too, so a young
      field reads as broken, blasted ground; an old one is sand-filled dimples.
  - **Fallen blocks** are mostly small, with a few great slabs: the size's dice are weighted to their low end, up to
    12 m.
  - **Laws**: walls stand (the rise is climbed on faces over 70°), talus at repose, the floor open for a frame.
- **The rock's colour** (`form/rock-colour.js`, a geocube's `outside.rock`, opt-in, read by the form render's land for
  any cube that names it). The colour comes from the beds the rock is made of and the weather that ran down it:
  - **beds**: bands by height, each the stone pulled toward one of the cube's own colours (pale trim for upper beds) and
    lifted or darkened, eased over each contact.
  - **thin**: thin beds, each with its own small tone, so no two ledges are one colour and nothing repeats.
  - **wear**: the rock lit by its own shape. Each corner's standing out of or sitting back in its neighbours, along its
    normal, is read off the land's mesh: edges lifted, creases darkened, so every bulge a massif pushed is its own
    colour.
  - **sections**: the rock in sections, each a cell of jittered points keyed to its own place and never a repeating
    tile. Each takes its own small value and hue toward a cube colour; on a wall their edges are vertical joints.
  - **varnish**: dark streaks down the walls, a function of the plan alone so they run straight down any wall; a slow
    mask leaves some walls clean.
  - It is baked into the land's own corner colours over the rock layer, so a page and an engine handoff get the same.
    Absent, the land's colours are as they were.
  - Each battlefield cube names its column: a dark plinth, the massive red wall, a lighter band, and pale upper beds
    weathered toward its trim (Wadi Rum's Disi over its Umm Ishrin).
- **Rubble at a cube's scale** (a geocube's `outside.rubble: { sizes, density }`, opt-in; `form/land-read.js`): the
  scree's instanced stones at the cube's own sizes. On the battlefield cubes that is 0.8 to 3.6 m across, a frame's
  knee-high rubble where a walker's pebbles would be. Absent, the stones are as they were.
- **Stochastic tiling** (a geocube's `outside.tiling: 'stochastic'`, opt-in; `scene/channels/form-land.js`). The form
  render's natural layers (rock, scree, soil, sand) never repeat in a grid.
  - A slow noise over each tile picks one of eight offsets and the next. Both are sampled with the tile's own
    derivatives, so there is no mip seam, and blended across the noise by their own difference, so the join wanders
    with the texture's shapes.
  - Absent, the page's shader is as it was. The battlefield cubes take it.
- **A massif's rock is bare** (`local-meru/scene.js`, `massif.js` `inside`): anything on the rock itself steeper than a
  near-level bench or top is rock, so its domes and shoulders never wear an apron's soil and scree.
- **The battlefield cubes** (`assault-frame/geocubes.js`, in `GEOCUBE_PRESETS` with their palettes and outposts).
  - `sandstone-wadi`, `sandstone-gorge`, `scree-scarp`, `crater-plain` and `wadi-oasis`, sized for a frame 7.5 to 9 m tall: walls 40
    to 120 m, gorges 25 to 200 m, talus 10 to 40 m out, blocks 3 to 7 m.
  - Each is red sandstone over an orange sand floor under a hard desert sun and a clear sky with no stars by day.
  - `crater-plain` is a stony plain struck all over, with one great fresh bowl 240 m across and one old one worn nearly
    flat. The wadi and the scarp take a handful of craters each.
  - A dry cube's sea lies 60 m under its floor, so a crater's bowl never fills; the oasis and the gorge keep theirs for
    their lake and river.
  - Each cube's outside is a field: an open island with no geology, its floor long low dunes, its rock the massif's card.
- **The field's forms** (`assault-frame/field.js`): `wadi`, `gorge`, `scree`, `craters` and `oasis` beside `plain` and
  `basin`.
  - A massif form is its own cube's unless a world is named; Warlords can lay Mars's dust on a wadi's shape.
  - A frame level's map may name one: the flight map checks the rest (`gameworld/world.js`).
  - The level reads its geocube through `frameLevelManifest` (`gameworld/levels.js`).
  - Its walls are drawn as their bands stand, without the page's rock relief, which cracks walls this tall.
- **Water under a frame.** `frameField` returns the ground a frame stands on: the land, or the water's sheet where the
  land lies under it, since a frame hovers and never goes under. `landAt`, `waterAt` and `sea` are kept for the hover's
  effects to come. The page's ground probe already finds the water's mesh.
- **The operation map** (`gameworld/frame-map.js`): a frame level's plate in the game book, in place of the flight map's
  rectangle.
  - The field from above, shaded from the north-west: rock by its height, walls dark, water blue.
  - The square a frame keeps to, the drop and the exit.
  - Every group of the operation where the level lays it, marked by kind, and each reach task's beacon with its radius
    and its order.
  - The radar's ring round the drop.
- **Lighter fields.** A frame's field was a 67 MB page (30 MB gzipped) that took nearly three minutes to build. The wadi
  is now 25 MB (17 MB gzipped), built in about 40 s. Every saving is scoped to a massif's land; any other page is
  byte-identical.
  - **Lean land** (`form.land.lean`, a massif's). The form render's meshes are the page's only ground: the painted
    groups it hides are no longer sent (`scene/scene-three.js`). A world on the page holds its step until the land has
    drawn (`window.__formReady`, the controllable channel's `landHold`), so nothing falls through it while it loads.
  - **Far walls coarser** (`massif.js` `far`): past the detail's reach, a little inside the horizon's escarpments, a
    wall is cut every 10 m and not pushed. The push eases out before the edge, so a wall cut both ways still meets
    itself.
  - **Rocks.** Only the great boulders are drawn broken, about a twelfth of the faces for the rest. No walker's pebbles
    are strewn (the cube's rubble lies at a frame's scale), and no boulders past the shore.
  - **Build.** The rock's height is kept per point and a cut is read only within its reach. The painted sun's shadow is
    not baked for a land the page lights itself.
- **Fixed on the way.**
  - A wall on a 4 m grid is cut into bands at fixed heights (a massif's thin beds' partings and middles; 6 m
    elsewhere), so the scree at its foot stays in its lowest band rather than smearing up the face. On a massif, every
    face is cut at the same heights, so shared edges agree.
  - The land's layers take even dice (`form/land-layers.js` `even`, opt-in, on for a massif land). Their wander and
    scree patches no longer run in bars along y, which read as stripes from a frame's height. Absent, the dice are as
    they were.

### The castle's climbs: going up is going across, built into the castle

- A metroidvania's rooms are no longer climbed by a hop straight up a column of ledges, nor by runs of floating steps.
  Each room is climbed by its structure (`docs/metroidvania-map.md` "Climbs"): flights of stairs walked up across the
  screen, the lowest built up from the floor as one stepped mass; flights of great steps leapt; landings built out from
  a wall or a tower's pier on their corbels; a ladder at each turn where the way doubles back above itself; and, in the
  rooms on the castle's bottom row, the rock breaking through the floor. Every piece is solid. Rooms take the stair
  tower and the great stair in turn.
- A structure is laid only where it holds: a jump at a time (a ladder's rise excepted), nothing solid within a jump and a
  body over her head, nothing over a hole she comes up through, and nothing before a doorway, a save, a relic or a key.
  A room none fits, or one left through a double jump's sill, keeps a figure of ledges (a switchback, flights, a stair,
  the zigzag last), which no longer folds back over itself against a wall.
- Towers two screens wide: a ring's `towers: true` makes its legs up and down two screens wide. Vampire Sonata's outer
  wall has them, so the castle is 14 × 8. A tower is closed against the night (the outer wall's new `tower` locale),
  with a pier up its middle and its way woven from one screen to the other through archways in the pier. The camera
  follows across both screens. Doors climbed to stand over the end of a bay, so a climb ends on a landing.
- Ladders join the box's play: each is a climbable the level carries (`W` climbs). Three box laws say the climbs hold:
  `climbs-across` (a climb of more than a storey spreads across its screen), `headroom`, and `no-kick`.
- A bot climbs every ungated room of the castle on the runtime, stairs walked, great steps leapt, ladders held, and out
  through its door: the level's e2e.
- The fabric builds the pieces in the room's stone: a flight one coursed mass, a great step in courses, a landing on its
  corbel, the pier quoined with its archways made as doorways are, a ladder's rails and rungs, the rock in boulders. The
  backdrop shots take `--tall` to see a tower whole.

### Northeast suburbs

- **In progress.** A Northeastern US suburb for towns and cities: colonials and Cape Cods on wide lawns with their
  driveways, garden apartments round their courts, towers in the park over their plazas, strip shops on the arterials.
- A town can be a Northeast suburb (`pattern: 'northeast'`): colonials in white, yellow or sage clapboard and red brick,
  Cape Cods under their steep roofs, each detached on a wide lot behind a short lawn with its own driveway and garage,
  no cars on the street; and garden apartments, long brick blocks of flats on their lawns along the avenue.
- Clapboard: painted lap siding, each board lapping over the one below, for any style's walls.
- A city's inner ring can be low-rise: brick walk-ups, four-storey low-rises and main streets of shops among its
  midrises, and its outskirts can hold garden apartments round their shared gardens. A new Northeast metro (a Boston)
  is built that way.
- Hijack City can be played in the inner city or the suburbs, not only downtown: a district is chosen by a word, and any
  city's district can be asked for by its ring.
- A city's street trees stand on the walk, behind the kerb and clear of every crossing, in a game or out of one; none
  were left standing in the road where it is shown rather than played.
- Sidewalk trees are small street trees (flowering cherries, birches, maples of 6 to 10 m), each in a box of soil in
  the walk; an outskirts walk is wider to hold them with a clear way past. Park, yard and garden trees keep their size.
- The outskirts' buildings stand closer to their walks: houses a short front yard back, low-rises and walk-ups on their
  street with their lots behind (no longer in the middle of their blocks), garden apartments a few metres back; less
  grass between the walk and the wall.
- Apartment complexes (low-rises, walk-ups, garden apartments) are fenced along their streets with a low black iron
  fence, a paved path from each front door across the lawn to a gate in it.

### Side-scrollers' backgrounds: contrast, composition, light and motion

- What makes a side-scroller's background nice to look at, written down as principles (`docs/side-scroll-backgrounds.md`):
  the play owns the picture's extremes; distance is told by hue; the rows stand in a stair of silhouettes and leave the
  sky its share; the light's source is in the picture; and something moves on most screens, slowly, a little and
  never in step.
- A new page channel moves a backdrop: `ambient` names render groups that sway, twinkle or blink on the page's clock,
  each phased by where it stands. A page without it carries no bytes of it.
- Jumping Giuseppe's strip: the hill rows lowered into a stair, so the sky takes a quarter to a third of the frame; the
  far rows' lit caps quieter than the near ones'; the big domes cut finer; the terrace a step into the air, so the lane
  reads against it; clouds on a shaded underside, drifting; the blossom stirring.
- Vampire Sonata's castle: the night over the ramparts has stars that twinkle, cloud wisps that drift, a haloed moon,
  far mountains and a forest ridge before the towers' feet. The night's bands no longer lap: lapped bands were lifted
  a step each by the page and stood in front of the towers high up. Every window shows the night, pale at its foot,
  with a moonbeam falling from it to the floor that breathes as cloud passes. Torches, candles and braziers burn as live
  flames, and the cold lamps pulse.
- Galaxy Boy's and Astro Girl's plant: a vista under the sky stands against a dusk glow drawn in bands, so its towers
  and stacks read as silhouettes. Towers carry blinking beacons and masts, and the middle skyline has lit windows.
  Stacks steam and gantries carry amber lamps. A hall's far wall has a row of lit clerestory windows.
- Galaxy Boy's level is drawn in a city by night of its own instead of the mascot platformer's orchard, and each of the
  plant's places has its own colour (teal, azure, indigo, violet), so the stage is no longer one brown all through.
  Two new places, the reactor gallery and the sky bridge, keep the gauntlet from repeating the gate tunnel.
- A future city in the plant's vistas: domed arcologies with lit window bands, glass domes lit from inside, needle
  towers under saucer decks, neon down the near buildings, a skyway whose train runs and craft drifting between the
  layers.
- A giant set piece: the reactor, the machine the plant makes, a wheel larger than the window turning slowly about a
  pulsing core, an inner ring turning the other way, pistons pumping before it. It is seen in the reactor gallery and
  again in the core. The page's ambient channel learned to spin a group about its hub.
- The castle's rooms are dressed as locales by what they are: every save room a chapel of stained glass with a rose
  window over its altar; the great halls' shafts the library's stacks under an orrery whose worlds turn; the inner
  ward's shafts and the Bellkeeper's room a brick clock tower, its gears meshing and the great clock's hands going round;
  every other corridor of the ward the catacombs, rough rock, skulls in their niches and a sarcophagus; the Lord's room
  a throne room. The backs are laid in their own walls (ashlar, brick, rock, plaster), and every backdrop law still
  holds.
- The night's clouds are banks you can see, puffed and lit on the moon's side, and one crosses the moon.
- Jumping Giuseppe's strip runs through sceneries, a trail each: the orchard it starts in, a lake (water in bands,
  the far hills reflected, light glinting, a sailing boat drifting), a forest's edge (a mint canopy behind a blossom
  one, swaying) and the coast (the sea to the horizon, islands, a sand beach). A headland stands where the scenery
  changes. A level names them as its `style.scenery`.
- What made the three backdrops starters, written down (`docs/backdrop-variations.md`): a place is a row, a piece a
  word, and the deal matches them by role; the slots every backdrop fills; the principles of composition, colour
  keying (the cube keys the light, the place its hue within a band set apart from play, the lit things the accent),
  light and motion that let a variation be new words; the pitfalls the page taught; and how to add a scenery, a place,
  a vista or a locale.
- Seeded variations, Giuseppe's: dunes (warm sand hills, a beach, teal cacti in the groves) and a snowfield (the hills
  under snow, a snow terrace, frosted crowns), each a re-key of the orchard's rows with no drawing of its own.
- Seeded variations, Galaxy Boy's: every side map setting's places have their own tones; three vistas built from the
  existing pieces (a neon market, an orbit with stars and a planet rising under the window, a greenhouse of domed
  gardens); two settings dealt from them, a neon city and an orbital colony. Every side map law holds in every setting.
- Seeded variations, the castle's: two re-keys, castle-frost (an ice-blue night, a pale moon, cold lamps) and
  castle-blood (a blood moon, crimson halls), each the same rings and locales in other colours with no drawing of its
  own; two locales from new pieces, the alchemist's laboratory (potions glowing on their shelves, a cauldron bubbling
  under its hood) in every other corridor of the halls, and the armoury (weapon racks, a suit of armour) in the keep's
  other hall. Every law holds in every theme.
- The castle's fabric (`docs/metroidvania-map.md` "The castle's fabric"): the parts Vampire Sonata's hero stands on, runs
  into and passes through are built as what they are, where they were grey blocks. A floor is a path in its room's
  material (flagstones, boards, a checker of tiles, the rock's own beds) over a string course and coursed stone; a
  ceiling a cornice on a corbel table, a timber hoarding over the walks outside, machicolations at the top; a wall
  quoined, with a plinth, an impost and a string course at each storey. Every doorway has an arched head, a threshold
  and the passage's far reveal seen through it; every hole through a floor is framed. A stair's ledges are stone slabs,
  timber platforms hung on rods from what is over them, or iron catwalks on a truss, by the room. The towers on the
  box's edge have an arrow slit each storey; moss and damp weather the stone outside. The box has a crown (a parapet,
  bartizans, corner towers under conical roofs) and stands on a crag. Each is a law (`fabric:*`), and every law holds
  in every theme.
- The backdrop shots frame a castle room as the play does (a cell, the zone holding the frame), and `--whole` shows the
  castle entire.
- Four more of the castle's locales, each from new pieces: the observatory at the top of the outer wall's towers (charts
  of the stars, a brass telescope aimed at a round of night), the ballroom (tall gilt mirrors, a great chandelier of
  live candles), the banquet hall (a stag's antlers, a great hearth burning live under the house's crest) and the
  dungeon (barred cells, chains from the roof, manacles, an iron gibbet). A look may name a list of locales for a kind
  of room, dealt room by room in turn, so the halls' other corridors are the laboratory, the ballroom and the banquet
  hall, the ward's the catacombs and the dungeon. Every law holds in every theme.

### Side-scrollers' UI: the castle's HUD on mana-ui, looks for each place, and the HUD heard

- Vampire Sonata's HUD is drawn on mana-ui in a castle look of its own, the `nocturne` card: aged gold on black, a
  serif, a Victorian cresting, health in crimson and magic in blue. It shows her vitals and the place she stands in;
  a banner across the top for each thing found (a power held longer, with its own bell), "Saved", a waking, a new
  region, a boss's name and its fall; the boss's bar while it stands; and what she holds. A pause (Enter) has the map
  of the rooms walked, her vitals and the castle's relics, found or locked.
- Re-keyed looks: `nocturne-frost` and `nocturne-blood` for the castle under frost and a blood moon, and `galaxy-neon`
  and `galaxy-orbit` for the side map's neon city and orbital colony. A level wears the one for its box's theme or its
  setting.
- A level's HUD on mana-ui is heard in its look's UI sounds: banners chime, a rare one rings, menus open and close and
  the cursor clicks. The castle in the crypt set, the side map in chip. Muted with the game's sound; a silent look adds
  nothing.

### The children of Sol: Mercury to Pluto on one shelf, seen whole, in a space level's sky, under foot and flown

A game or an exhibit that wants Mars, Saturn or the Moon now gets the real one from one place instead of making it
again. The shelf (`lib/graph/sol/`) has one row per body (Mercury, Venus, the Earth, the Moon, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn,
Uranus, Neptune, Pluto) under the words people say for it, with its real figures (radius, gravity, day, distance, tilt,
air, temperature, the Sun's width in its sky) and a handle into each place that draws it. `solHandles(word, { view })`
hands a game all of them at once. The guide is [docs/sol.md](../../../../docs/sol.md).

- **The body whole** (the ray-traced planet study, `saturn-view`). The Moon and Pluto join the eight (Pluto with its
  heart), and `gallery: 'sol'` steps through every child of Sol in order out from the Sun. The eight's own gallery is unchanged.
  There are two close passes. `scenario: 'close'` runs low over the limb: a giant's bands carry weather drawn out
  east–west, with festoons, eddies and white ovals, and its cloud tops are in relief; a rocky world shows its small
  craters. `scenario: 'rings'` passes through a ringed world's rings, a little above their plane, with the ringlets drawn
  in. The extra detail is behind a uniform that the globe views never set, so their pictures are unchanged. A raymarched
  study's camera may now come closer than three units (`minDistance`); every other study keeps three.
- **The body in a space level's sky** (`skyscape/planet-gen.js`). Each body is a kind of world with its knobs fixed to
  the real one. No hue is turned and the dice never draw it. Its axial tilt is its own (Uranus lies on its side), and
  Saturn's rings are at their real radii. A level names one wherever it names a kind of world: `space.backdrop.worlds`,
  a theatre's moon, a ground stage's `route.world`. A ringed world held near is drawn with its rings live, in its
  equator's plane: the Saturn density profile, the planet's shadow across the rings, the rings hidden behind the globe,
  and the ringlets faded before they alias. Pages without live rings carry none of that code.
- **The body under foot**, for the bodies with ground: a geocube preset each for Mercury, Venus, the Moon, Mars and
  Pluto. Each comes with its palette and a colony's building seeds. The airless ones (Mercury, the Moon, Pluto) are the
  airless plain: craters, a black sky with the stars out by day, and a low hard sun at its own width (huge at Mercury, a
  star at Pluto). The Earth hangs blue and white over the Moon and Charon hangs over Pluto. Mars is rust dunes under a
  butterscotch sky with Phobos in it. Venus is dark basalt under a lid of orange cloud, with no sun seen.
  What hangs in a world's sky is a cube's new `light.heavens` (`era/heavens.js`): `void` (no air, or `false` to give an
  airless card air), `disc` (the sun's width, or `false`), and `companion` (a body in the sky, its colour and the spots
  of land and cloud on its face). The island specimen (`show: 'land'`) now draws an airless card's sky too. A card that
  grows no grass no longer breaks the island.
- **The giants, flown**. Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune have no ground, so they get no geocube; they are flown
  over their cloud tops. An airspace's `sky: { world }` (`sol/skies.js`) is the giant's own weather: a deck that closes
  the sky under the pilot, Jupiter's storm towers, Neptune's white cirrus, the haze, and its colours over the deck and
  under it. The ground under the deck is painted as more of the giant's cloud. A craft seated over a giant starts aloft
  above the deck, since there is nothing to take off from. Saturn's rings, and Uranus's faint ones, stand over the
  flight sky as an arch toward the equator, with the planet's shadow across them. A sky with no rings carries none of
  their code.

Not yet: the composer's words (`gameworld/compose.js`) still read "mars" and "lunar" as the generic airless kit rather
than the real body.

### Flight games heard

- A flown level hears its craft. How it is flown picks the kit: a light plane on the fly rule is a trainer, a fighter
  down a rail an arcade fighter, and a starfighter flown from its seat a cockpit. Pilot School, Wolf Squadron and Rebel
  Storm sound with nothing written, where every flight page was silent before.
  - The trainer has its prop engine by the throttle, the air over it and its wheels on the runway by its speed, the
    stall warning while it stalls, a touchdown soft or hard, a crash and a ring flown through.
  - The arcade fighter has its engine from cruise to boost, its lasers and the foes', its boost, brake and barrel roll, a
    shield hit, and fighters, ground guns and the gunship boss blown apart.
  - The cockpit has its engines by the throttle, its laser cannon and the foes', shield and hull hits, the targeting
    computer seeking and locking, a torpedo away, the incoming warning, flares, a fighter roaring past, a fighter and a
    warship blown apart, and a scrape along a hull.
- Sounds are heard by their distance out to a flight's kilometres, not an arena's 900 m.
- A level's own audio keeps its cues over the kit's. `flightSound` changes or silences one event, and `audio: false`
  silences the level.
- The sound library records the kits (`cards/flight.js`): the starfighters' engines at steady throttles, crossfaded as a
  car's are, and every new sound, each heard as a stand-in where the library is not installed.

### Going up in Galaxy Boy and Jumping Giuseppe: storeys and chutes, towers and terraces

- Galaxy Boy's side map has two new climb forms for long climbs, both climbed as a wall-climbing hero climbs (never by
  stairs): a `tower`, a screen wide, and an `atrium`, two screens wide (`docs/side-map-principles.md` "Going up is
  earned"). Each is built in storeys, with a thick floor at every screen of height (`SLAB`), so a long climb keeps its
  middle floors.
- Each storey is risen through a chute in the floor over it: a chimney of the shaft's wall and an inner wall, its rests
  within three kicks, entered under the inner wall and left over it, the last over the far wall's top. The chutes
  stand at the two ends in turn, so every storey is crossed between kicks. A ladder stands only where a wall kick has
  nothing to kick off: an atrium's middle storey is risen by a ladder through a chute in the open (and a hero with no
  wall kick climbs every storey by ladders).
- Galaxy Boy's first level climbs an atrium through the plant's heart after its gauntlet, before the chute down to the
  boss. The side map's bot climbs towers and atriums storey by storey, and the `rests` law holds their chimneys to three
  kicks. A ladder steps off where its floor is.
- Jumping Giuseppe's strip: a face climbed by kicks is a tower of the orchard, with quoins down its ends, string courses
  and round windows under its cornice. A segment that ends high comes back down across terraces, each a share of the
  jump down and a landing long, so going down is going across and each can be climbed back up, never a cliff dropped
  off.
- The castle's climb planner learned to handle more rooms: a ladder whose foot landing would stand low is taken on down
  to the floor; a lowest flight that would wall off the way in is a ladder instead; an exit at a wall's top or a
  doorway is never a ladder's head; and the turns' ladders, the flights' goings and the exit's gallery are tried in turn
  until the turns fall clear of the floor's ways. A room's second climb is a zigzag round its structure, clear of it.

### Warlords of Mars: an assault frame of parts, boosted and fought on Mars

A single-player mech game rail, the Armored Core tuning of Mech Battle Kai taken out of the action lab and into levels.
It is fast, the frame spends much of its time in the air, and it moves by boost and control rather than flight. It runs
on the level path Wolf Squadron and Rebel Storm laid: a rail row, a starter of levels, an operation goal on the
objectives mechanic, and a HUD. It is not the mobile suit arena.

- **The assault frame** (`assault-frame/`). A frame is built from parts, one in each slot:
  - a core, a head, two arms, biped legs, a booster, a generator and an FCS;
  - a weapon in each hand and on each shoulder (`parts.js`). The hands carry a rifle, a shotgun, a gatling, a bazooka, a
    laser or a blade. The shoulders carry a missile pod, a mortar or a plasma cannon.
  - Three stock frames: the medium Vanguard, the light Raptor, the heavy Citadel.
  - The pilot's Vanguard is headless on reverse-joint legs. Its core is a forward fuselage (`cr-prow`): a long
    armoured prow ahead of the shoulders, the cockpit under a narrow canopy, the optics in a chin turret, a chrome
    sensor cone at the nose, so the head slot is empty and the core's sensors lengthen the lock. Its legs
    (`lg-reverse`) bend the knee back as a bird's, the shin and the foot raked forward to a splayed three-toed foot
    with a spur, a crouched stance with its hips at 4.2 m (the frame 7.5 m tall): they jump highest and land lightest. The Raptor and the Citadel keep their heads and biped legs.
  - A new part is a row. The assembly (`assemble.js`) reads a build into the frame's weight, armour, movement, energy and
    lock. It holds the build to laws: within the legs' load, the booster carrying its mass, the generator good for three
    quick boosts. The laws advise and never refuse: an overweight frame is slower, not forbidden.
  - Its body (`body.js`): each part its own look by class, layered armour plate with chamfered edges, panel lines,
    vents and intakes, chrome rams and piston rods at the knees, elbows and hips, joint collars, cable runs, glowing
    optics and stencils. A gun is held forward in each hand and a launcher rides each shoulder; the booster's bells
    and verniers on the shins, shoulders and core are its thrusters, burning as the frame is driven. A medium frame
    is about 9 m tall and 7,000 faces. Palettes: federation (the default), mars, ash; wear: factory, used, battered.
  - Its clips (`clips.js`, its own forward kinematics and a two-bone leg): idle, a heavy walk, the boost's skate and
    its leans left, right and back, the hover with the knees tucked, the fall reaching down, the landing's crouch.
  - Its figure (`figure.js`) is in the form render: chrome drawn as polished metal, the paint as satin plate.
  - Its thrust is layered fire (`scene/channels/controllable/frame-flame.js`, thrusters of kind `flame`, opt-in): each
    mouth three nested cones, each its own scrolling-noise fire shader burning in its own stretch of the plume. A
    white-hot core with shock diamonds at the mouth, a sheath of the exhaust's blue, an amber tail going red, and a
    flare on the bell. The burn follows the frame: full in a quick boost, hard climbing, then boosting; off on its feet.
    It writes its depth for a page with a logarithmic depth buffer, as a flight's is.
  - Its review sheets: `node scripts/render-frame.mjs`.
- **The frame rule** (`worlds/controllable/rules-frame.js`, opt-in `frame`).
  - The mouse turns the frame and aims it. W, A, S and D walk it. X assault-boosts and F kicks.
  - Shift held skates on the booster; C quick-boosts a burst toward the keys (back when none); Space jumps and, held,
    climbs on the thrusters.
  - The generator's EN is drawn by the boost, the quick boost, the climb and an energy weapon's shot. It comes back
    after a delay; emptied, the frame is shut out of its boost until it is back over a third.
  - The FCS locks the foe nearest the aim within its cone after its lock time. Locked, the rounds lead the target and a
    missile homes on it.
  - Four triggers fire four guns: the right hand on the left mouse, the left hand on the right, the shoulders on Q and
    E. Each has its own magazine, reload, cooldown and charge. Their rounds are the world's projectiles and burst on the
    terrain.
  - An enemy frame runs on the same rule with its own mind: it keeps its range, strafes, boosts, quick-boosts out of
    the way as it is hit, climbs and fires while it holds its lock.
  - Its scheme is `frame` (`controls/schemes.js`). Its HUD (`scene/channels/controllable/frame-hud.js`) shows the
    reticle and the lock box, EN, AP and speed, and the four weapons where they sit on the frame.
- **Stability and the stagger: the fight's loop** (`rules-frame.js`, `assemble.js` `stab`). Pressure a frame until it
  breaks, then punish it.
  - Each frame has a stability bar sized by its mass: the light Raptor's is about 0.8 of a standard bar, the Vanguard's
    1.1, the heavy Citadel's 1.5. It recovers on its own, the lighter frames faster.
  - Every round's impact (its weapon's `stagger`, a share of one bar) chips it. The bazooka and the mortar break bars;
    the rifles and gatlings wear them down.
  - Broken, the frame reels for 1.6 s: no boost, quick boost, climb or guns. It is carried on by what it was doing and
    pulled down, and every hit on it lands 1.5 times as hard. A break during a reel does not extend it, so there is no
    lock it cannot leave. The bar then comes back from empty.
  - It rides the engine's poise chip, but the break is taken by the frame itself: the engine's hit reaction would root
    it in mid-air.
  - The HUD shows the locked frame's stress under the lock box, filling as it is pressed, red with STAGGER when it
    breaks, and the pilot's own stability under the armour.
  - An enemy frame punishes a reeling pilot: everything it has, in close, and a kick.
- **Handling: how each weapon fires on the move** (a weapon row's `handling`, the legs' `steady`).
  - Free: on the move at full speed, in an assault boost too. The carbine, the shotgun, the charge laser and the
    missiles.
  - Drag: its sustained recoil holds the boost and the charge to a fraction of their speed while it fires. The gatling,
    to 70%.
  - Brace: firing it stops the frame and cuts a boost or an assault boost. It sticks where it fired, in the air too, its
    gravity off and its drift checked hard, then winds down, its gravity and control coming back. The bazooka briefly
    (0.3 s, then 0.45 s), the plasma cannon and the mortar at length (0.7 to 0.9 s, then 0.8 to 0.9 s).
  - The legs scale the brace: heavy legs settle in about half the time, light legs take a fifth longer.
  - A quick boost in the wind-down cancels it, the skilled way out; the stick itself cannot be cut short.
  - The HUD reads BRACED in the stick and RECOVER in the wind-down. An enemy frame that fires its mortar hangs in the
    air for it: the moment to punish.
- **Closing in: the assault boost, the kick and a blade** (`rules-frame.js`, `assemble.js` `move.ab`, `kick`).
  - The assault boost (X, a toggle) charges along the aim at two thirds again the boost's speed. Its height settles at
    once and it climbs or dives with the aim. It burns a light-up and nearly twice the boost's draw a second, and ends on
    its key, a quick boost, a kick, the generator emptied or a stagger. The HUD marks it.
  - The boost kick (F) lunges onto the locked frame within 80 m and lands the frame's own mass as its blow, heavy on a
    bar: out of an assault boost it opens a reel, and on a reeling frame it punishes one.
  - A blade, the Shear (`bl-shear`, fire `melee`), is a left-hand weapon: its trigger lunges onto the locked foe within
    its reach and cuts, no round fired. Its look is an emitter on the fist and a long white-hot edge. The Raptor now
    carries it in place of its laser, and an enemy Raptor closes on its assault boost to cut.
  - The lunge and the blow are the same for both: met, the damage and the impact on the foe's bar, a break or a kill
    armed as a round's is, a spark where it struck.
- **The fight's look: the flight games' effects, in the military register** (`scene/channels/controllable/index.js`,
  `gameworld/feel/round-look.js` `BLAST_LOOK_MILITARY`). A frame level drew its rounds as plain cones and its bursts as
  flat shells; it now draws them as the flight games do.
  - Every frame's and MT's gun fires its rounds in the shot's look in the gun's colour (the carbine amber, the laser
    cyan, the plasma pale blue), sized by the gun; the enemy units' rounds a hot red-orange.
  - A round's hit is a spark in its gun's light; a splash's or a kill's burst an explosion as wide as its reach. Both
    are kept at least a share of the view, so a blast two hundred metres off still reads.
  - In the military register: no far hue, but the fire's own gone gold, a ring fewer, more sparks, an explosion that
    lingers (0.85 s).
  - A muzzle flash at each gun's muzzle as it fires, sized by the gun (a cannon's the biggest).
  - The page's smoke is on: billows down a bazooka's, a mortar's and a missile's trail, a rolling cloud where each
    bursts, and the dust a boost raises off the land.
- **The Hellas Road: an enemy ladder up to the ace.** One path, each rung teaching what the next leans on.
  - The Gnat drone (`groundforce/` `gnat`, a card that `flies`): a flat armoured pod between two ducted fans burning
    amber, a red eye and a chin gun, some 5 m across. It flies on the AI rule in the air, quick and close, weaving round
    the frame, held at least 10 m over the land (a flier's `floor`, the frame levels' `frame-fliers` pass). Its operation,
    the Gnat Screen, puts eight of them over the road before two emplacements: shooting on the move, holding a lock.
  - The Hammer carrier (`groundforce/` `hammer`): a six-wheeled truck braced on outriggers, a rack of eight missile
    tubes raised over its bed. No gun: the engine's AI launcher (`rule.missiles`) locks and streams homing missiles from
    its standoff far back. Each missile carries its launcher's impact into its burst (the frame levels' `frame-missiles`
    pass), so it chips a frame's bar rather than breaking it as an impact-less burst would; its splash reaches past its
    proximity fuse, so one that bursts passing still lands. Its operation, Long Guns, puts three behind a screen of
    tanks: quick-boost out from under each salvo, charge through on an assault boost.
  - The Bastion walker (`groundforce/` `bastion`): a stocky walker behind a tall slab shield with a lit vision slit and
    red edging, its cannon reaching round the slab. It carries the engine's frontal shield (`body.shield`): rounds from in
    front are eaten until the shield breaks, a flank goes round it. A frame's lunge knocks the shield aside and staggers
    it, and a broken shield is raised again 7 s later (`rule.shieldRaise`, the `frame-shields` pass): the punish window.
    The lock box reads its shield's share, or SHIELD DOWN. Its operation, The Shield Line, puts three before two guns.
  - The MTs (`assault-frame/mts.js`, a frame group's `mt`): the warlord's smaller frames, from the same parts on the same
    rule, drawn smaller (a body's `scale`, `body.js` `scaleBody`: its bones, faces, mounts, thrusters and rig) with less
    armour and a shorter stability bar, their eye and hit volume at their size. The Jackal (0.6, 4.8 m): a carbine and a
    shotgun on light legs, in threes, circling in close. The Rhino (0.72, 6.8 m): a gatling and a mortar on heavy legs,
    hanging back; its mortar braces it, the window. Their operation, the Jackal Pack, puts the pack on the crater road
    and the Rhino behind it, before Vermilion. `node scripts/render-frame.mjs --mts jackal,rhino` draws their sheets.
  - A locked lunge now lasts as long as its reach takes to cross, so a foe at the edge of a kick's reach is met.
  - The ground force's sheets: `node scripts/render-groundforce.mjs --units gnat,walker` draws each card from three sides
    beside a frame's height.
- **The fliers.** Three cards that fly (`groundforce/` `wasp`, `kite`, `harrow`); a frame level's `frame-flight` pass
  flies them by their `flight` while the AI aims and fires.
  - The Wasp: a swept delta strike drone, one engine burning aft, twin guns under a red-eyed nose. A `strafe` dives on
    a mark beside the pilot, rakes past low firing and pulls out to come round. Its operation is Dust Devils.
  - The Kite: three ducted fans round an armoured hub, a missile rack on its back, a sensor ball under it. A `perch`
    holds high and far and lobs homing missiles down. Its operation is High Watch.
  - The Harrow: a gunship twice a frame's length, a long hull on four big ducted fans, a chin gatling, a missile pod on
    each stub wing. A `circuit` orbits the pilot, tighter as it is hurt, and hangs to barrage. It carries a boss bar, and
    its operation, Harrow, comes before Vermilion.
  - The Thunderhead (`thunderhead`): the heavy gunship at the top of the air ladder, a quad drone at a gunship's
    scale, some 54 m duct to duct. A heavy armoured hull (a deep core, side sponsons, a dorsal block, a brow over a wide
    lit visor, a gun bay under it), an X of armoured arms, and four great rotors turning flat inside armoured ducts: a
    thick wall rounded at its lip, eight curved plates round its outside, a grille of bars over its mouth under a hub
    cap, a lit ring deep in its throat. A chin gun and a rail cannon are slung forward under the hull. An `orbit` flies it round the frame at height, its nose on the frame, never stopping; hurt, it
    comes lower and circles tighter. Its rail cannon's slugs barely turn but land hard. Its guns cannot bear more than
    `under` degrees below it (the frame levels' `frame-broadside` action, its `blind`), so a frame right under it is
    safe while it stays there, and the lock box says UNDER ITS GUNS. Its operation, Thunderhead, follows Harrow.
  - Its rotors spin, the pairs opposite ways, a faint disc where the blades blur (`UNIT_MATERIALS.blur`, seen through;
    the form render's alone). Its ducts are lathed sections (`groundforce/` `lathe`: a closed section swept round the
    vertical, whole or a plate's arc). A card's `hubs` make a bone of each, its `turns` their ways; the figure's `roll` clip spins
    them about the vertical (`vehicle-rig.js` `packVehicleFigure`'s new `axis` and `turns`; absent, the wheels' clip as it
    was). A card without hubs packs as one bone, as before.
- **The ground force in the form render** (`groundforce/` `unitFigure(kind, { form })`, a figures map's
  `unit: { kind, form: true }`; a frame level's units ask for it).
  - Its armour is a satin painted metal under a thin clear coat, its structure gunmetal, its eye and drive lit by their
    own colour (`UNIT_MATERIALS`), lit by the world's sky as a frame is: the light runs off them.
  - Its shapes are rounded: the same card built with rounded primitives, each box filleted at its corners and edges and
    each round part twice the sides, its corners' normals smoothed across the faces they join within a crease, weighted
    by area, so a panel stays flat and its edge reads round.
  - The baked units (an arcade stage's) are unchanged.
- **Aces: the frame a path ladders up to** (`assault-frame/aces.js`, a frame group's `ace`, a group's `reserve`).
  - An ace is a row: its name, build, paint, how much more armour it has than its build, and its phases. A new ace is a
    row.
  - Its mind fights in the phase its armour's share is in, each with its reach, press and dodge: a duel keeps its
    reach; a rush assault-boosts in and lunges, but first its optics flare (a tell) for a moment, the window to make it
    miss, and it rests after; a desperate one charges and fires its braced cannon. Crossing into a phase can wake its
    reserve (a group held back dormant) and steady its stability.
  - Vermilion, the warlord's ace: a light-medium duellist on reverse legs in lacquered red over black (the `vermilion`
    paint), with a carbine, the Shear blade, missiles and the Arc plasma cannon, at 1.8 times its build's armour. It
    duels above 60%, rushes with its blade below it, and below 25% calls in four walkers and braces its cannon.
  - Its operation sits between Red Dust and The Warlord, on the crater floor.
  - The HUD carries an ace's name, armour and stability across the top, the line it says as it crosses a phase, and a
    red diamond over it while it tells a lunge.
- **The frame level** (an airspace level's `frame`, `gameworld/frame-goal.js`). The frame is stood at the south of its
  field facing north. The level is fought for its operation:
  - groups of the ground force's turrets, tanks and walkers at a frame's scale, and enemy frames;
  - tasks on the objectives mechanic: a group destroyed, a waypoint reached, a hold.
  - The frame's armour is its life.
- **The field** (`assault-frame/field.js`). A frame's level is fought on the Sol shelf's `mars` geocube's own land, drawn
  in the seventh generation's form render: pure terrain, with no trail (the frame has its radar) and no blocking.
  - It is the geocube's island specimen widened to a mech's field: its shore some 600 m out with the rim raised all the
    way round, a mesa and a rise for its tiers, a painted landscape for its ground, a craggy or eroded relief, the
    geology's rock and scree on everything raised. An operation's map names its form: `plain` (broad country round a
    mesa) or `basin` (a crater's floor under a high rim).
  - Its height is read without building a face (`local-meru/scene.js` `localMeruHeight`). The frame, every foe and
    every waypoint stand on it, and the frame keeps to a square inside the shore.
  - It is drawn under the cube's own heavens and its air thinned for a field a kilometre wide.
  - An island's new opt-in `open` (walk `'none'` only) drops the level apron where a trail would land, so the relief
    runs all the way round. An island that does not name it reads as it always did.
  - A played geocube land takes only its own words from the page (`era/geocube.js` `GEOCUBE_KEYS`), as the geotown
    and the side map do.
  - Fixed on the way: a land as wide as a field overflowed the stack reading its lowest sand (`form/land-form.js`,
    `form/land-read.js`); the walked land's ground cumulus is left out under a Sol world's heavens.
- **Mars's sky** (`sol/skies.js` `THIN_SKIES`, an airspace's `sky: { world: 'mars' }`): a world with ground and a
  little air under its own weather: a butterscotch sky paling to a dusty horizon, a small dim sun, thin ice cloud
  high over a haze of dust. It rides the flight sky's machinery as the giants' skies do, with no deck: a flight over
  Mars, where a frame's field is under its cube's heavens.
- **The rail** (`rails.js` `warlords-of-mars`, `gameworld/warlords-of-mars.js`). Its starter is eight operations:
  - Landfall at Tharsis: a gun line, then a tank column;
  - Gnat Screen: a drone swarm, then its emplacements;
  - Long Guns: missile carriers behind a line of tanks, then the ridge;
  - The Shield Line: shield walkers, then the guns behind them;
  - Red Dust: a pass held by walkers, then a guard frame;
  - Jackal Pack: three light MTs, then a heavy one;
  - Vermilion: the warlord's ace, alone, its pickets held back;
  - The Warlord: an escort of two, then the warlord's heavy frame.
- **Made from words.**
  - The genre reader names a new genre, `mech-action` (armored core, mech game, assault frame).
  - The producer's rail step and the sentence door both lay the starter.
  - A door probe holds the sentence door to a level whose pilot is an armed frame.
  - The cosmos cube names `power.rules=frame` and `soul.hero=frame`.

### Warlords of Mars heard: the recorded library first

- Every operation now has sound. A frame is heard by its parts: its footfalls and landings by its legs, its thrust,
  ignition and quick boost by its booster, each gun by what it is (the carbine's heavy rounds, the gatling's bursts,
  the lance's charge and beam, the bazooka, the Hornet's salvo, the Arc's discharge, the Shear's blade), its cockpit's
  lock-on, EN alarm and vent, and the power-up as it drops. A part fitted in the hangar changes how it sounds.
- Its foes too: turrets, carriers, Bastions behind their shields, drones and gunships humming overhead, each struck,
  each going up; bursts where rounds land; the objectives' stingers; Mars's wind outside and the works' furnaces in.
- Every word is the recorded library's first (Mech Battle Kai's suit kit, the registry's machines, the explosions),
  its synthesized voice where the library is not installed. The sounds the library lacks are new rows heard as their
  stand-ins until they are recorded, and their cards are written (`cards/warlords-of-mars.js`).
- The hangar's and the briefing's menus play the holo table's sound set.
- The recorded `shield-hit` card (a sword on a wooden shield) voices a parry's block now, not an energy shield.

### XenoJager: a dangerous planet in the metroidvania box's idioms

- A new visual library for the metroidvania box: `xeno`, a dangerous planet explored down through its crust
  (`docs/metroidvania-map.md` "XenoJager: the planet"). The box, its rings, gates, pockets, climbs and two-screen towers
  are the castle's own. The planet draws them in a new library:
  - **The crust.** Its walk is open under a ringed planet, a second moon and spires of rock, a crag behind the walk, and
    the explorer's lander in the room she enters by.
  - **The caverns.** A cave's walls in rough beds of rock with wandering seams, stalactites, stalagmites near the lane,
    and crevices glowing with a deeper cavern.
  - **Its pieces.** Boulders, crystals, giant fungi, tendrils, waterfalls and lava falls, the ruins and monoliths of a
    people before, a fossil, a great bloom, egg pods and the nest at the core.
  - **Its light.** Lamps are glowing pods. The water, the lava, the glowing life and the tendrils move on the page's
    ambient channel.
- Nothing on the planet is laid in courses. Its rock breaks as rock does: boulders of every shape with dark cracks
  between them, on the cave's wall, the fabric's floors, walls and roofs, and the walk's top.
- Its boulders and crystals are mojulo's own materials:
  - **Boulders** are real rocks, fractured and grained by their minerals, of each look's rock (basalt, slate, marble,
    granite).
  - **Crystals** are real stones of each look's gem (amethyst, sapphire, tourmaline, ruby, quartz), shaded live by the
    page. Each cluster is a few long stones standing up off the rock, so it reads at play distance; a ruby or a sapphire,
    whose real habit is a short barrel, grows as a cluster of smaller barrels. Grown out of a wall, they throw no print
    onto the room below.
  - A boulder or a druse counts as one piece of detail in the backdrop's laws, however many faces it has.
- The fabric builds a rock look's closed parts as rock, where the castle builds masonry: stairs and landings as
  boulders, doorways as cave mouths, a tower's wall cracked through each storey, metal ladders, and the crust's crags
  along the top.
- `xenoJager()` gives the planet's map words: the crust, the fungal caverns, the flooded depths and the magma core, with
  three powers opening the castle's three gates. Every law the castle holds, the planet holds.
- There is no XenoJager game yet. `XENOJAGER_HANDLE` says what the next builder wires: the hero (an explorer in a suit,
  her arm a cannon), the feel (the run and gun's, its wall kept) and the hazards. The looks' water and lava are recorded
  in each room's plan for a suit's power and a gate kind to come. Its HUD card is wired already: `nocturne-xeno`, a
  re-key of the castle's Nocturne.
- The backdrop shots take `--xeno` to review the planet.
- A look may name a `first` focal piece, the one the box's entry room shows in place of its ring's.

### The metroidvania box's map, revealed screen by screen

- A box's map is now revealed a screen at a time, as the hero enters each screen, the way a metroidvania's map is
  read. A room's screens join; the walls between rooms stand, with the doors through them. A gate is marked at its door
  until she holds what opens it, and a relic is marked where it lies until she takes it. Save rooms found and bosses
  still standing are marked, as is she.
- A minimap in the top right corner follows her through the box, the boss's bar under it in a boss's room. The pause
  shows the whole map walked so far, and counts the rooms seen.

### Secret walls in the metroidvania box

- A box's pocket can be a secret: `pockets: [{ gate: 'secret', holds }]`. Its wall looks like the walls round it and
  is marked nowhere, not in play and not on the map. No power opens it: the hero finds it by striking the wall, and its
  prize appears on the map once the wall is down.
- Destructible terrain where the game asks for it: under `destruction: 'physical'` a secret wall is matter. It is the
  room's own wall stone (the geocube's), calibrated to break in a few blows at the hero's power, and it comes apart by
  rupa's physics, its debris that stone. Without it, a secret wall still breaks by counted blows.
- Vampire Sonata and XenoJager each hide a secret or two. The game book's ring cards say each one.

### Claude flows: the plugin's skills route, so each session reads less

- **The main skill sends a start to its skill.** A start skill that covers the ask (a character, a game, an object, a
  3D exhibit, a home or a room) is used directly; `forward_context`, the routing index, is read only when none does.
- **The plugin's preamble is its own short text.** Under the Claude plugin profile the initialize preamble says what
  mojulo is, that the skills route with `forward_context` behind them, the recipe and gate rules and the secrets rule;
  npm and source builds keep theirs byte for byte.
- **Shorter skill descriptions.** Each start skill's description, read in every session, keeps its lead and the first
  of the person's words that fit half the old budget.
- **The plugin's forward_context leaves the starts to their skills.** Under the plugin profile its character, game,
  object and house rows (and the exhibit's clause) are one line naming the start skills, with what those rows routed
  that no skill carries kept beside it; every other build reads the index unchanged.
- **The repo's own skills describe themselves in a sentence or two**, use case first, their arguments in
  `argument-hint` (`.claude/skills`, read in every session in this repo: 8.6 KB of descriptions to 3.3 KB).
- **CLAUDE.md sheds its architecture map** to `docs/architecture-map.md`, a pointer left in its place.
- plugin.json is `3.2.0-rc.2` while 3.2 is prepared (a change to the plugin moves its version, or an installed copy never
  updates); the release sets 3.2.0.

### The metroidvania box heard

- Vampire Sonata and XenoJager are on the sound sheet with sounds of their own, where a box level heard only its HUD
  before.
  - **The castle.** Erina's longsword cuts the air, cuts into the dead and rings off plate, and her boots strike
    flagstones. A foe felled is unmade, and a boss falls as a great body. Its menus play the crypt's set, as its HUD does,
    no longer the rail's robot.
  - **The planet.** A sealed suit's arm cannon, its servos and boots, its crystal rock; its menus and its HUD on the
    terminal's set.
  - A game's own `sound.flavor` names its recordings (a box variant no longer borrows its rail's robot), and
    `sound.menus` names its menus' set.
- Every boss on the director is heard.
  - Each move's wind-up plays as it is told, and its strike as it lands.
  - Its voice is read from what it is. It roars at its first move and as its phases turn, is hurt when struck, and dies
    as its last form falls.
  - A second form rises with a surge.
  - A game's `sound.bosses` overrides any of these words.
- A metroidvania's held gates are heard. The boss's room is barred by a portcullis and winched open after the fight. A
  cracked wall crumbles, a secret wall falls away into its hollow, a grate scrapes aside, a lock turns and a boss's seal
  shatters.
- Foes drawn as the undead, the orcish or the infernal are heard as their own voices (the dead, an ogre, a demon), never
  as people's shouts. A wolf that braces to charge braces in its own threat, not a motor's rev. The ogre and the demon
  are new voice classes.
- A sheet word the shelf has but nothing voices here (a sound only the library records, where it is not installed) is
  silent rather than an error.
- The sound library records the boss kit, the two new voices, and the castle's and the planet's own sounds.

### The side map in its game book

- A side map level has its page in the game book (`#sidemaps`, with its tab), read off the map as its level builds it,
  so the book and the game agree:
  - the side map's own elevation: its zones, its rulers, the bot's line through it, checkpoints, doors, ladders and
    pickups;
  - a row for each zone: its place and material, its run, its size in screens, what it teaches or which beat it is, its
    climb or drop, and its spawners, pickups and crates;
  - every law the map is held to, labelled as the machine gate.
- The level's own page shows a small plan of its zones in their places' colours, in place of a placeholder.

### Bring your own 3D model: a file from this machine read in, a character rigged onto the vajra as a body or a mascot

A model made outside mojulo comes in from a path on the machine mojulo runs on: a folder the person chose in the desktop
app, or a file uploaded into a cloud session. Two doors, one import: `mint_solid({ kind: 'model', spec: { from } })`
for an object, `create_character({ from })` for a character. Mojulo reads the file; it downloads nothing.

- **One door format.** `lib/graph/import/to-glb.js` turns each file into the GLB the bound-mesh slot stores:
  - a GLB or a VRM, checked as it is;
  - a `.gltf` with its `.bin` and images, from a folder or a zip (how Poly Haven and Sketchfab ship);
  - an OBJ with its MTL, colours and textures;
  - an STL or a 3MF, as before.
  - The same file gives the same bytes. What did not travel is named. A neighbour is never read from above the folder
    the model was found in (`read-path.js`), and a URL is refused.
  - A format not read yet (FBX, DAE, USD, .blend, PLY, Draco- or meshopt-compressed glTF) is refused with the line that
    gets it in: export a GLB.
- **What a model holds, read once** (`inspect.js`):
  - its geometry, materials, textures, skins, clips and morphs;
  - a VRM's licence block, and the author and licence a glTF exporter writes;
  - its rest in the native frame, skinned where it is skinned (a Mixamo export's 0.01 armature no longer reads as a
    two-centimetre figure);
  - its units: a figure whose height falls outside 0.3 to 12 m is read in the unit that makes it one, and the readout
    says so.
- **What it is, from its shape, never its size** (`classify.js`). A body is 4.5 heads tall or more. A mascot's head is a
