  third of it or more (3.25 heads or less: the mascot law). Between the two it is read as a stylized body, and the
  readout says it could be said otherwise.
  - The legs are followed down from the trunk to where they fork.
  - The neck is the narrow run under the head, above the shoulders.
  - A rigged humanoid's chin is its skeleton's.
  - More than two legs: furniture with no skeleton, a creature with one. No legs: a prop.
- **A character's own skeleton, read wider** (`scene/rig-import.js`):
  - by its shape when its names say nothing: the hips are the joint that sends a mirrored pair of chains down and the
    spine up, the chest the one that sends a pair across (CesiumMan's numbered chains);
  - a palm as the hand on a side with no hand;
  - a rigid part hung under a joint moves with that joint (a robot of parts).
  - `ledger.how` says `file`, `name` or `shape`.
- **Fitted onto the vajra when it has none** (`autorig.js`). The figure's landmarks are fitted from its shape:
  - hips over the crotch, knees, ankles, toes forward along the soles (which also say which way it faces);
  - the chin;
  - each arm traced in from its fingertip.
  - A humanoid skeleton is stood on them, each vertex weighted to the bones of its region by inverse distance and
    smoothed over the mesh's own edges (a mascot's sharper), and the whole is written as a skinned GLB with VRM joint
    names, which rig-import reads like any rigged file.
  - A fit needs a T or an A pose with the legs apart; a figure with its arms at its sides is refused, naming the pose.
- **The machine gate** (`rig-gate.js`). A rig either way is posed through the bends a character makes: arms raised and
  forward, elbows and knees at a right angle, a hip flexed, the head turned, the trunk bent. The readout gives the
  share of triangles torn. It advises and never refuses; the eyes gate is the person's.
- **The `model` kind** (`worlds/model.js`). Its recipe is what the import decided: the file and its hash, the files
  read beside it, its units, its up axis, its height, its class, its rig and its licence. Its geometry is the bound
  file, drawn at rest on the measured studio.
  - A world places an object with `figures.<n>.meshRef` and plays a character with `figures.<n>.modelRef` (the
    character's decided height carried when the world says none).
  - Both work under the Claude plugin profile, since nothing is bound through the hidden handoff tools.
- **Measured against open files.** `lib/graph/import/corpus.js` pins open files by hash: Khronos samples, three.js
  examples, three-vrm and Poly Haven. `node scripts/import-corpus.mjs --fetch` fetches them into a cache on the machine
  (never the repository) and writes `docs/import-corpus.md`.
  - The page shows each file's read, class, rig and gate.
  - Its strip-and-score table takes each artist-rigged humanoid's skeleton away, fits it onto the vajra, and measures
    the fitted joints against the artist's and both rigs through the gate.
- **Around it:**
  - the producer's intake takes a 3D model file (`INTAKE_KINDS.model`);
  - the routing cards are `import-model` and `import-character`;
  - the manual is `get_solid_vocab({ id: 'model' })`;
  - `pack-data` names the sketches whose bound meshes must be carried beside the database.
- **The plugin cache rule counts released versions only.** `check-plugin-version.mjs --since` asks for a plugin.json
  bump when the base's version has been released (its `v<version>` tag exists); the plugin waiting on its release
  (3.2.0, untagged) takes changes under the version it will ship as, since no installed copy is stranded. A checkout
  with no tags keeps the rule.

### A plume for a prop's drive, and the frames' score

- A prop's plume (`scene/channels/plume.js` `PLUME`; a frame operation's prop's `plume`, on a card with a `bell`): the
  frames' plasma boost at a ship's scale. As the level's bus says `ignite:<id>` the bell lights: a white-hot core
  inside layers of the plasma's colour, soft (brightest at the bell and fading along it, thin at its edges), flickering;
  pulse beads running up it; a ring of plasma bits thrown out across the ground at the moment it lights, and a flash; a
  light of its colour on the ground round it. Heard: the ignition's roar (a noise swept down over a deep rumble) and the
  burn held under it. The Roman Candle's card has its bell. A page whose level names none carries none of it.
- The frames' score (`gameworld/frame-score.js` `FRAME_SCORE`): two loops in D minor with a Phrygian edge, the fight
  some 3 LU over the quiet. Regolith (84 bpm, half time: Dm, B♭, Gm, A), while the field is quiet, is a heavy band in one
  room: a gated stadium kit, a reese bass kept low and dark under it, a string machine, crotales and a tam-tam. Hardpoint
  (134 bpm: Dm, B♭, C, A) once the shooting starts, a techno machine: a 909 four on the floor (its trance drive the second
  pass), an acid line driven hard in sixteenths, rave stabs on the offbeats, a poly-string pad, and in the second pass a
  sixteenth arpeggio and a supersaw hook. Changed on the bar line by the fight's tension (hits and falls raise it). Every
  frame level plays it. Regolith is recorded (`recorded: true`): its strings are the sound library's where it is
  installed; Hardpoint's machines have no recorded twins.
- A recorded score on a World page (`scene/channels/audio.js`): a soundtrack, a combat score, a boss score or an
  event's music whose `recorded` puts a part on its twin now carries that twin's takes (they had been read only off the
  cues), and every engine that plays a score is handed them, each its own copy. Before this the twin always fell back
  to its synthesized patch on a page. Without the library a page carries nothing of it, byte for byte as before.
- A retry says "Restart at Checkpoint"; a frame stood up again is cleared of its stagger (the frame HUD had flashed
  STAGGER over the restart).

### Couch closeout: the hill-climb caught up, and the seat values still missing

- The hill-climb registry now dates the mechanics the flight and metroidvania rails added without a date: a flight's
  `crash`, a lesson's `grade`, a rail stage's `wake` and the castle's `journey` (all 11-23). They now show in the page's
  "what was built lately". The side map's note now includes its boss room, its towers and atriums, and its page in the
  game book, and points to the metroidvania box for rooms on a grid. The in-game UI's note now includes the box's and
  the side map's HUD, minimap and pause on mana-ui, and the frame's hangar.
- What couch play still waits on is written down: versus beyond the fighter, free-for-all, teams, roles, split, window,
  turns and a lobby. The three couch probes blocked on them are party mash, driver and gunner, and split-screen
  deathmatch.
- The hill-climb prices couch play as one package (`couch`): versus, free-for-all, teams, roles, window, turns and the
  lobby. Each couch genre needs two or three of them at once, so priced one at a time none of them made a world. The
  lobby's old `seats` package is folded into it. Split screen stays its own package.
- A second, third or fourth player whose health runs out no longer lies down for the rest of the level. Their collapse
  plays, then it counts as a fall: a life is spent where lives are counted, and they get up beside the others with full
  health, or are out when none is left. The first player's knock-down still ends the level, as before.
- Each extra player's chip at the top of the screen shows a small bar of their own health, which follows it as they
  are hit. The first player's health stays on the level's own HUD.
- In a level that counts hits, every player now has their own health. Player 1 keeps the level's, and players 2–4 each
  get one shown in their own corner of the screen, in their colour. A player hit to nothing goes down, then a life is
  spent and they get up beside the others, or they are out.
- When the players count lives, player 1 is a player like the others: running out of health costs a life rather than
  ending the level, and the level is lost only when no player is left. Without lives, player 1's health running out
  ends the level, as before.
- Every player now works the level, not just the first. Any player picks up coins and items (into the team's count, once
  each, even when two reach one together) and can take the way out. A hazard hurts whoever steps in, in their own health.
- Players can now play against each other in a third-person deathmatch on one screen. With free-for-all or versus, each
  player is their own side: every player has their own health, frag count and corner of the screen, a fallen player
  comes back at a spawn point as the bots do, and the first to the frag limit wins the match, with the winner recorded
  for the results. In co-op the players are one side against the bots, and a player's hit on a partner scores nothing.
- In a team deathmatch, players split between red and blue: odd-numbered players on the first player's side, even on
  the other. A team deathmatch with a designed hero would not build at all before; it does now.
- The hill-climb marks versus, free-for-all and teams as built. The three couch genres still blocked now wait on the
  lobby, plus the time-window contest (party mash), roles (driver and gunner) or split screen (split deathmatch).
- A game can open each level on a lobby. Every player slot shows in its colour and says whether that player has joined;
  each controller joins with a press. The level waits behind the lobby until player 1 presses Start (or Enter on the
  keyboard), then joining closes for that level. A game that lets players drop in at any time is unchanged.
- A new party round, `mash`: each player's presses are counted over a window, each shown in their corner in their
  colour, and the most presses at the horn wins (a tie is a draw). It can also be a race to a count. With one player it
  is a count against the clock, or a mash to break free. Its end rings the goal cue, and it has its vocabulary card.
- The hill-climb marks the lobby and the time-window contest as built, and party mash is now makeable. Driver and
  gunner waits on roles, split-screen deathmatch on split screen.
- Two players can share one vehicle in roles. On a vehicle level whose game asks for roles with two players, the car
  carries a gun on a stabilized roof turret: player 1 drives, and player 2 turns the turret with the right stick and
  fires with the trigger. With nobody in player 2's seat, the driver works the gun. Players 2–4 on a pad now also have a
  right-stick aim, which the gunner uses.
- The hill-climb marks roles as built, and driver and gunner is now makeable. Of the couch genres, only split-screen
  deathmatch is still blocked, waiting on split screen. Turns (one player at a time) is the last seat value not built;
  the couch package is retired and turns is priced on its own. Over the branch the sweep went from 75 to 79 makeable
  random worlds and from 340 to 355 near the genre probes, with blocked worlds near the probes down from 49 to 32.
- The hill-climb registry dates the values the release candidate's newest rails added without a date: the city museum's
  `bay-gallery` kit (11-24), and the Hijack City activities' `shift`, `forger` and `request` mechanics (11-26). A
  crewed ride (a driver and a gunner) now opens on the lobby when its game asks for one.

### A frame operation's encounter: the alarm, the waves, the split and the duel

- A task's alarm (`goal.operation.tasks[].alarm`, `gameworld/frame-goal.js` `OP_ALARM`): as it begins the enemy is heard
  coming: a warning (the cue's, below in its own theme), its words under the title WARNING. A level cue, not a scene:
  the fight goes on under it.
- A group that comes with a task (`groups[].comes`: a task's number): it stands dormant till that task begins and comes
  then, not that task's to down (a frame that arrives beside the one fought, to be led off in a split).
- An ally that holds its post till a task begins (`allies[].hold`: true, or a task's number): it stands its ground, turned to
  the pilot, until then, and from then fights and keeps by the pilot as a wingman does (the frame rule's cast op
  `unhold`, `worlds/controllable/rules-frame.js`). An instructor who comes to help when the alarm goes.
- A split (`goal.operation.split`, `SPLIT`): an ally and a foe leave the field together for a fight of their own, never
  played (a level's economy). As its task begins, a scene: the foe's group in a wide push (its `title` a banner), the ally
  alone as its `line` is said, then both off toward `to`, the two in one frame as they go, and gone; as task `back` begins the ally comes back
  from there alone, let go of any hold.
- A task's ops (`game/objectives.js` `ops`): the cast's ops issued as it begins, once, beside a clear's own foes woken:
  what the encounter's words above lower to, and any level's own.
- A scene holds the field's minds too: while the pilot's input is held (a scene playing, a menu up), every frame's mind
  stands down with it, its keys idle, and takes up again after (the input's `held`, given on a frame page): a split's
  foes had walked on the pilot through the scene. A scene's own walks still move them.
- A wide shot on big subjects far apart still looks at them: the aim under big subjects (so they ride above the talk
  box) is no more than half their height (`rules-basic.js` shot); it had grown with the distance, and a shot from 200 m
  looked at the ground before them.
- A shot can keep a body out of it (a scene's `shot.away`, `rules-basic.js`): the camera stands past its subjects, well
  off the line from that body to them, so a pilot standing between the lens and a candle being set down is out of the
  frame (it had landed in front of the camera, the candle unseen).
- A shot can pull out (`shot.move: 'pull'`, `rules-basic.js`): opening out from its subjects over its time, eased, to some
  two and a half times as far, the place round them coming into the frame (the candles firing and the rock beginning to
  move under them, as the field shakes).

### A frame's lessons: its controls taught as it is played

- An operation can teach (`goal.operation.lessons: [{ teach: [<word>…], at?: <task> }]`): the frame's controls one at
  a time on the guide's line, each kept up until the pilot does it or its patience runs out. The words are the frame's
  (`FRAME_LESSONS`: move, look, boost, quick boost, jump, climb, assault boost, energy, lock, each hand and shoulder,
  kick), each done by the frame's own state: a boost held, a quick boost, the climb, a slot's rounds gone, the sight
  locked. A group can wait for its task (`at`), so a training level teaches its movement as it starts and its weapons as
  its drones come.
- The guide channel reads them on any geocube level that carries `lessons`; a guide without a frame's lessons is as it
  was, byte for byte.

### A frame's wingman

- An operation can field allies (`goal.operation.allies: [{ id, name, build?, palette?, ap?, lead? }]`, up to three):
  frames on the pilot's side, stood beside the drop. A wingman's mind (the frame rule's `ally`) fights the nearest foe
  awake within its reach; with none, it leads the pilot through the operation's places in order (its reaches' and its
  scans'), waiting at each until the pilot has reached it, and past the last keeps by the pilot. It is hard to lose (its
  armour three times its build's unless it says otherwise), and its frame takes the field's gravity.

### The game's screens: an opening that loads the level, a chapter's card, the end said as a screen

- The results (`scene/channels/game-screens.js` resultsScript, the game channel's): every game's level now ends on a
  results screen, not a card: in wireframe (hairlines, corner brackets, a faint grid, spaced capitals),
  the result's word (a level's noun: "Mission complete" on a frame's operation, "Level complete" elsewhere; `complete.text`
  retitles it as before), the level's name, what it kept on dotted leaders, its rank where it has one, and Play again
  when it is played on its own. Painted in the level's own look: the world's interface theme (`ui.theme`, its ink,
  panel, line, accents and harm, carried on the contract as `game.look`), else the page's tokens.
- An objectives list that retries keeps its retries for the results.
- A level's opening (`levels.<id>.opening`: `{ title?, kicker?, chapter?: { label?, name? }, press? }`): played on its
  own, the level opens on its title screen, which loads it: a bar that fills as the world comes up, the land is laid,
  every object in the scene is drawn once (hidden or out of view, so each material's program is built and each mesh is on
  the card: a camera turned after the opening onto what its shots never saw builds nothing then) and frames are drawn,
  then "Press any key". The level waits for it (its start, its scenes and the
  pilot's keys), so nothing after the opening scene waits on the build. Pressed, a chapter's card on black (Chapter 1,
  the level's name unless it says) fades off as the level begins under it. A hosting shell keeps its own front.
- The level's contract names its game and itself (`game.title`, `game.name`) for its screens.

### Hijack City activities

- **Jobsified, the city's driving jobs.** A new phone app lists jobs done in one of the city's own vehicles. Take one
  on the phone, get into its vehicle and do the job in it; nothing counts on foot. Each pays into the money in hand and
  can be done again.
- **Bin round.** Get into a garbage truck at the works yard. Piles of bags stand at kerbs across the district: pull up
  and hold F to collect one. Four fill the truck; take it to the dump to empty it and get paid, its tailgate swinging
  up as it unloads. Collect every pile and the city puts more out.
- **The dump.** A district can now have a dump (`dump: true` on its city settings): one of its car parks is built as a
  big tipping hall, open to the street, that a truck drives into. Hijack City has one.
- **Heavy vehicle call.** A general call for heavy operators: trucks and construction machines wait at the kerb by the
  works yard, a concrete mixer, a flatbed, a wheel loader, a tipper, a skip lorry, a backhoe, a box truck, a wheeled
  excavator, three at a time. The call names one; drive it across town to its building site to get paid, step out and
  it goes back to the yard, and the next is called. Each handles as its own weight and power.
- **A fake ID.** The city has a forger: walk in with 150 and walk out with a forged heavy machinery licence. The heavy
  vehicle call can't be taken without one; the phone says what it needs and who sells it. A world turns the forger on
  with `shops: { forger: true }`; Hijack City has one.
- **Dig and load.** A side game at a building site, for licence holders: climb into the site's excavator and work it
  with an operator's levers, A/D to swing, W/S for the arm, the arrow keys for the boom and the bucket. Dig into the
  pile of spoil, curl the bucket to scoop, swing over the waiting tipper and open it to tip. Three loads fill the truck
  and pay. The boom, arm, bucket and their hydraulic rams all move as the real machine's do.
- **The materials never came.** Once the dig is done the foreman calls: his building materials never turned up, does
  anyone know a logistics company? The Dockers do. Check in at the Dockers' HQ for delivery orders: trucks of steel,
  timber, fittings and containers wait at the dock, and each driven to a building site pays.
- **A dock, and highways you can drive.** A district can now have a working port on its shore (`dock: true`): a yard
  with a warehouse and truck bays, container stacks and a big quayside crane. Its highways get ramps: at every arterial
  they cross there is a ramp down to the street on each side, and one from the shore highway down into the port, so
  trucks can run from the dock up onto the highway and come off again in town. Hijack City has both.
- **Bus route.** A bus waits at the kerb by the depot. Its stops come in order, each with a sign and people waiting.
  Pull up and hold F to open the doors: the waiting people walk over and board, and the ones who got on at the stop
  before get off and walk away. The last stop pays and the route starts again.
- **Street sweeping.** A street sweeper waits at the kerb by the works yard, and litter lies along the kerb side of
  the streets nearby. No button to hold: drive along the kerb and the sweeper picks each heap up as it passes. The
  screen counts what is swept and calls each quarter; sweep it all to get paid, and the streets are dirty again by the
  next round.
- **Groundskeeping.** The parks' grounds crew keeps falling ill, and the parks office will take anyone with a licence:
  the fake ID gets you this one too. There's no mower left lying around town: it's kept in the groundskeeper's shed by
  the nearest park. Take it out and a round starts on the clock, right there on the park's own lawn: long grass round
  the paths and trees, cut to stubble as you drive over it, striped light and dark by the way you went. Cut enough of
  it before time runs out to get paid; get off and the mower goes back in the shed.
- **A new minigame, Mowing** (for an arcade, later). Beside blocks, match and fishing, a level can put a pixel mowing
  round at a place (`play.minigames`, `game: 'mowing'`): a zero-turn mower over a lawn from above, with a condition
  before it can be started (`if`) and what's said when it can't (`locked`). Nothing in Hijack City uses it yet. The
  book's `minigames: true` stays the three stall games.
- **The ride-on mower** is new on the vehicle shelf (`ride-on mower`, `riding mower`, `lawn tractor`): a low bonnet, an
  open seat with a high back, a cutting deck under it and its chute out to the side, at a mower's own weight and top
  speed.
- **The temp agency.** A new app on the phone, Placeholder Staffing, posts an office temp's job at Synergetics Tower.
  It asks for an office ID badge; the forger happens to have one, lifted off a commuter's lanyard (the forger now sells
  whichever paper the job that turned you away asked for). Walk through the tower's glass lobby into its own building:
  reception points you to your desk, and the desk starts a shift.
- **Deskwork.** The shift is a browser of tabs: an inbox of tickets, invoices to read and file, vendor recommendations
  to make against a memo's constraints, TPS reports to tally, cover with the right sheet and route. Every answer is
  worked out from what the tabs show, the Policies tab most of all. Mistakes bring Quality Assurance; late tickets are
  escalated to a committee; Mandatory Training interrupts. Meet quota and you're paid, recognised (automatically) and
  commended; two commendations make a promotion, and a promotion is more work: more tickets, less time for each.
- **The municipal office.** A parallel track to the temp agency, at City Hall: constituents' requests come in on the
  CityLine 311 app and fill the journal. Buy a city worker ID from the forger (a laminated ID and a hi-vis vest), then do
  each request yourself: get a work order stamped at City Hall's clerk desk (a Deskwork shift of work orders: route it,
  cost it, stamp it), collect the material at the works yard, and fix it where it is. Shovel and tamp a pothole by the
  shops near the start, lift and nail the panels of a building site's blown-down hoarding, and clear the litter off the
  park's lawn: hold F, then tap F, at each spot. Fixed, you're paid and the constituent writes back.
- **City Hall.** A district can now have one (`cityhall: true`): the museum's civic front on the next block over, its
  banners in the city's colours, walked into on a page of its own. Hijack City has one.
- **Issued vehicles stand in their yard.** The heavy call's trucks, the bus and the sweeper are now waiting in the works
  yard and the bus depot when there's room, instead of at a kerb; the streetcar line had taken the kerbs by the yard.
- **The way and the screen.** Taking a job on the phone points the guide at it straight away; the arrow leads to the
  nearest pile still waiting. A line on screen shows the truck's load or the next stop and who is aboard, with a bar
  while F is held. A finished job is announced with a card in the middle of the screen over what it paid, the money in
  the corner counts up to its new amount, and a new task slides into the phone's list.

### A frame level played again: a retry, a scan's ring, drones that are seen, rounds that can be dodged

- A retry (`game/objectives.js` `retry`, `RETRY`; a frame operation's `retry: true`): the player down while a task is in
  hand no longer ends the level on a card with nothing to press. The screen fades, the player stands up whole where it
  fell, the task in hand begins again (its foes up and whole, each fought group put back where it stood: a task's
  `again` ops), and the level goes on from there. A level that asks for none is lost on a death as before.
- A scan's place on the ground (`scene/channels/guide.js` a step's `ring`, `GUIDE_RING`): a frame level's scan place is a
  disc laid on the ground and following it, a hand over the ground under the frames' feet and drawn behind what stands
  on it (never through a frame's legs); its rim marks the place and its surface holds a faint light, and while it is
  stood in the whole surface glows, breathing, brightest at its middle, until its clock is run and it goes. A guide with
  none carries none of it.
- The Gnat drone redrawn (`groundforce/index.js`): no fans; a lens of armour borne up on a ring of plasma round its
  waist, lit all the way round, a red eye in its rim, a chin gun, two fins aft; larger (its ring some 7 m across as
  drawn), and in its own colours (a card's new `livery`: bone white under a hazard-orange dome, a dark stripe), so it
  stands out against black space and grey ground.
- A foe's rounds can be dodged: an enemy frame's guns fire at where the pilot is as they leave the gun, no longer where
  it will be (`rules-frame.js`; a mind's `leadShots` leads them as before), and a drone's rounds fly slower (170 m/s,
  its range in over a second and a half), seen coming. Missiles still home.

### A level's beats let breathe, its foes found before they are fought, its screen the game's

- An objective's `pause` (`game/objectives.js`): the seconds after the one before is met that a task begins, so what was
  found is said, a line spoken and the quiet held before the next is set; a pause on the first waits after the level
  starts. A paused task is never met before it has begun: a place reached in the pause is met as it begins. A frame
  operation's tasks take it too (`goal.operation.tasks[].pause`).
- An objectives list can be `quiet`: no count of the tasks met on the HUD, only the task in hand and its own clock (a
  frame operation's always is: the frame's HUD says what it needs). A hold's clock is shown only while it is in hand, as
  a scan's is.
- A wary group (`goal.operation.groups[].wary`): a unit that goes about its work holding its fire until it is hit (the
  mind's `defensive` temperament), so a survey drone can be spotted and pointed out before it is fought.
- Strict lessons (the guide's `strict`, a frame level's that teaches): each control's lesson waits for the pilot to do
  it, however long, and no count of them is shown; the keys' legend along the bottom is left off, the lessons saying
  each key as it comes.
- A frame's level draws no pilot's strip of its own on the mana HUD (`manaHud.heroBar: false`, `game/hud-mana.js`): the frame's own HUD carries
  its armour and generator, and the strip in the corner was a second health bar.
- A level that teaches by instruction: an objective can be an `act`, met as a bus event says the thing was done while it
  is in hand (`game/objectives.js`), and a strict guide says each lesson done on the bus (`lesson:<fact>`). A frame
  operation's `learn` task is a control shown and met only as the pilot does it (its lesson shown once the task has
  begun, so it is never done in the pause before it); its `act` task waits on any event the level raises (a scene's
  end, `scene-end:<id>`), no clock.
- An ally that holds (`allies[].hold`): an instructor on the range, standing its ground turned to the pilot, leading
  nowhere and fighting only a foe that comes to it.
- A frame's field heard by where each sound is (`scene/channels/frame-audio.js` `FRAME_EAR`): every sound but the pilot's
  own falls away with its distance from the pilot (full within 30 m, silent past 700; the shared rolloff, full to
  250 m, heard a whole fight at once), and the field's effects sit lower in the mix.
- The frame's HUD stands down while a scene plays (`window.__mojScenes.on()`): the letterbox and its lines are the
  screen.
- A frame's level, played, fills its window as a mission's does (`scene/scene-three.js`): its page had kept the studio's
  fixed height, taller than most windows, so the view's middle (where the reticle stands and a scene's shot frames its
  subjects) sat below the window's and the page scrolled.

### A frame's plasma wake: streaks the pilot draws

- A booster names its propellant (`assault-frame/parts.js` `PROPELLANTS`: argon refined from Mars's air, a muted violet; xenon
  shipped in, blue; krypton a cheap mixed fill, white-green). The drive is a pulsed plasma drive, not a fire: a frame's
  plume and its wake take the propellant's colour (the figure's `wake`), and the plume's tail deepens toward the dark
  where it was amber. A booster is read by its streak.
- The wake (`scene/channels/controllable/frame-wake.js`): a ribbon from each main bell, kept in the world where the bell
  has been, so the pilot's movement draws the streaks: white at its heart, the propellant's colour at its edges, thin to
  nothing as it ages. Bright beads along it are the drive's pulses, held where they were thrown, their spacing the speed.
  In air it curls and frays and fades sooner; in vacuum it runs straight and lasts. A quick boost burns it wide and
  white-hot and sheds a burst where it begins: a fine ring of small plasma bits (a tenth to a quarter of a metre, some 7 m across at its widest) thrown out across the dash, each slowing,
  drifting back along the way it came and going out on its own, so the ring frays and scatters as it fades; an assault boost burns it wider while held.
- One mesh a frame, its pulses and its curl in the shader and the ribbon's sampling; emitted only on a page whose figures
  carry a wake, never in a capture.
- A look that fails never stops the game: the wake puts itself out, said once, and the world plays on (a sample past the
  ribbon's end once threw on a boost and a jump and froze the page).
- The frames take longer, heavier steps: each some 0.84 of a leg's reach (`assault-frame/clips.js` `FRAME_STEP`), the
  foot lifted higher through its swing and the pelvis dropping deeper onto it, and the walk's cycle covers the ground
  its own legs do (`frameStride`, the frame rule's `stride`), so a planted foot holds where it landed.
- The walk's cycle runs by the ground covered each step (the frame rule's gait phase had taken the speed for the
  distance, a cycle and more every frame: the legs flickered through their poses, a tiptoe), and a frame off its
  booster keeps its way on in the air: what it carries, and at least its walk, steered by the keys (it had been braked
  to a stand whenever a key was held).
- Sticky feet: a frame on its feet that has not jumped or climbed stays on the ground over a crest or a dip, held down
  by as much as `stick` metres a step (1.2) or its pace over the ground, so a bumpy field is walked, not floated over; a
  deeper drop is a ledge, and it goes over it into the air.
- A quick boost is steered: through its burst it turns toward the keys held, at its own speed (`qbTurn`, 9 rad/s).
- The guns fire where the reticle looks: the page gives the frame's pilot its sight, the camera's ray through the
  middle of the screen (`inp.aim`), and unlocked, every gun fires from its own mount at what that ray meets past the
  frame (a foe's body it passes within, else the ground, else the gun's range: rules-frame.js `sightPoint`), so the
  rounds meet on the reticle; its lock looks along the same ray. A mind's frame aims as it did.
- A frame level's field lays its stones once: on a page whose pilot is a frame, the land's stones are no longer swapped
  in and out as the eye moves (the ladder's coming and going read as stones popping), its `STONE_STILL.most` biggest
  laid as the page opens and held, the rest the ground's own scree and pebbles (`scene/channels/form-land.js`).
- The frame's HUD lets its weapons' names go: shown as the level opens and when a weapon's state turns (a reload, run
  dry, a new one in its slot), then faded out after a few seconds (`FRAME_HUD`), so the fight is the screen and only the
  rounds stay.
- A wake is broken where its body is set down rather than flown (a scene's spawn, a respawn: further in one step than
  `WAKE.jump` m), never drawn across the gap.

### Prospecting: a find revealed, the specimens a prospector finds

- The specimens (`prospect/specimens.js` `SPECIMENS`): what a prospector finds in space and on Mars (carbonaceous
  chondrite, nickel-iron, platinum-group metals, water ice, hematite, olivine, quartz, corundum), each with its name, its
  grade, what it is good for and its colour, and its wireframe drawn by mojulo's own depictors: a crystal's natural
  habit (`polygonizer/crystal-optics.js` crystalPolytope), a native metal's cubic form (a cube cut back by an
  octahedron, or the other way), a rock's creases (`form/land-stones.js` stoneForms). A new find is a row.
- A find revealed (`scene/channels/find-reveal.js` `FIND_REVEAL`): a frame operation's scan that names a `specimen` (and
  its `amount` and `unit`, the yield reckoned) stops the game as it is met (the world frozen, the keys held) and shows
  it: the specimen laid line by line until it stands whole, then turning and glowing in its colour; "Sample confirmed",
  its name, its grade, its yield counted up, what it is good for, logged to the survey; a chime rising as it is laid.
  It stands a few seconds, or until a key, then the play goes on. In the level's look; a page with no finds carries
  none of it.
- The Gnat drone larger still (some 12 m nose to tail as drawn) and tougher (twice its armour).

### A scan objective, and a frame level's way to its places

- The objectives have a `scan`: stay inside a ring while a readout fills (its clock runs only inside the ring and keeps
  what it had when the pilot steps out; `total: false` starts it again), then what it found is said as a banner and as
  an event (`objective:found { task, text }`) a script can answer. An operation names it as a task
  (`{ scan: [x, y], radius?, seconds?, found?, text? }`), its ring a beacon on the holo table as a reach's is.
- A frame level shows the way to each place its tasks name (a reach's, a scan's) on the guide's line, an arrow, the
  metres and a pillar of light where it stands, held back until its task begins and passed as it is met; its line sits
  under the objectives' own (the guide's `top`). The guide reads a step's `when` as a task in hand reached and a
  `from` gate; a guide without them keeps its bytes.
- The operation's briefing lights a place's beacon by its task's number, as the table names it: a reach after a fight
  was never lit.

### A scene inside a frame level: things carried, props stood for it

- A body carried, a new cast effect any cue or scene can use (`glide: { who, to, seconds? | speed?, face? }`,
  `worlds/controllable/glide.js`): straight lines through the air from place to place, its height with it (a point
  `[x, y, z]`, a spot's z), each leg eased in and out; no ground, walls or gait. It holds at the last place and says
  `arrive` at each, so a scene's `until: { arrive }` waits for it, and a skipped scene sets it down at once. A ship come
  in, a pod lowered on its cables, a lift. Opt-in on the page: a world that never glides carries none of it.
- A frame operation's props (`goal.operation.props: [{ id, unit, at, raise?, hidden?, face? }]`): things stood on the
  field for the level's scenes to move, drawn as a card, no mind, nothing hits them, raised `raise` metres over their
  place and asleep while hidden. Each one's place, where it is set down, is a spot of its own id, and each reach's and
  scan's place is the spot `t<n>`, so a scene frames them and sets things down on them.
- The first prop card, the Roman Candle (`groundforce/` `candle`): a tall pusher rocket on a braced, drilled foot, its
  bell to the sky, a thing a mining ship lowers onto a rock. A prop is never a foe a stage fields (`GROUND_PROP_IDS`
  beside `GROUND_UNIT_IDS`).
- A level with no walk (an airspace's, a frame's) keeps its `scenes`, played in its one stage.
- A directed shot on a subject bigger than a person (a frame, a tower) is framed by its size, room round it by its
  radius and looked at by its height (a person's shot as it was); and as it cuts it finds a place whose line to its
  subjects no other body stands in (`worlds/controllable/rules-basic.js` `shot`): the pilot's own frame no longer fills
  the lens of a shot on what it is watching.
- A frame operation's marks (`goal.operation.marks: { <name>: [x, y] }`): named places on the field, each a spot of its
  name for the level's scenes (where a walk ends, a shot's place).
- A foe's intro (`goal.operation.groups[].intro: true | { title?, line?, who? }`, `FOE_INTRO`): the first time a group
  comes (its down task begins, or the level starts for one awake from it), a short scene: the camera pushed in on its
  members, its name as a banner (its title, else its card's label), a line said over it where one is written, then the
  play back. Optional, a group's own; skippable as every scene is.
- A shot on big subjects aims a share of its distance under them, so they ride above a scene's talk box (its lower
  third) rather than behind it.
- A tracking shot looks again each second: the ground it moves over rises and falls, so a ridge come between it and
  its subjects is gone round (aside, then higher), where it had only looked as it cut.

### A level's script, said as comms

- A level's spoken lines are data (`gameworld/script.js`): each `{ id, who, text, on, after? }`, said at one of the
  level's own moments (its start, a task begun or met, a scan's find, a wave, a body down, the win, the loss), a few
  seconds after where it says. Every line has an id, so the game's script can be read whole and voiced line by line.
- A frame operation carries one (`goal.operation.script: { speakers?, lines }`), its allies speaking under their own
  names; each line raised on the bus at its moment (`comms:<id>`) and shown on the page as comms
  (`scene/channels/comms.js`): the speaker's mark in their colour, their name, the words as a subtitle, one line at a
  time and held as long as it takes to read. A page without a script carries none of it.
- The game's script read whole, the script book (`/api/sketches/<ref>/bible?book=script`, `gameworld/script-book.js`):
  level by level in the game's order, each line its id, who says it, its moment in words and its words; the page holds
  the same as data (`script.json`) for whoever voices the game, a recording named for a line's id being its voice.

### The space ground: a frame's gravity by name, and an asteroid in the belt

- A frame level says its gravity (`airspace.frame.gravity`): `planetary`, the frame's own and the default; `space`, the
  space ground (an asteroid, the Moon, a flat orbital platform) at a third of it, a game's and not a simulation's; or
  metres a second squared. Under a lighter gravity a frame's jump reaches the same height, slower, and a landing is
  hard at the speed that height falls to there (`assault-frame/pilot.js` `FRAME_GRAVITY`, `frameGravity`).
- A battlefield cube in the belt, `belt-asteroid` (a frame field's `asteroid` form): charcoal regolith struck by
  craters of every size, low ridges struck up between them, no skyline past a close horizon, a black sky with the stars
  out, the Sun a third of ours and a neighbouring rock hanging in it. Its standing rock is the massif's new `asteroid`
  card.
- An airless field is airless: no wind in its sound, its boost's dust the regolith's own colour, and the gen-7 sky
  over an airless cube (its heavens' void) holds no air, no cloud and no haze, only the stars and the Sun's disc. Every
  other page keeps its bytes.

### A warning: a boss coming, said as its own

- A cue's `warning` (`playscape/ui/cues.js`): `{ warning: '<words>' | { say, title?, ttl? } }`, the moment a boss, or a
  fight that plays as one, is coming. Not a banner among the others: a band across the screen in translucent red over a
  dim of the world, hazard stripes along its edges, its title (WARNING by default; CAUTION, or any word up to 16 letters)
  large and spaced over the words, the band blinking as it comes, gone after its seconds (3.2).
- Its own sound: a two-tone klaxon synthesised on the page (a square wave stepped between two pitches through a low-pass,
  three times; no file), through the page's audio where it has it and silent while it is muted.
- Its page layer (`scene/channels/warning.js`) is read off the bus's vars each frame, as the screen layer is, and emitted
  only where a level's events raise a warning: a page without one carries none of it.
- A frame operation's task alarm (`tasks[].alarm`) is a warning now, where it was a banner, a borrowed missile beep and a
  flash.

### The crag: a rock in the belt broken up, cover from what is overhead

- A frame field's form `crag` (`assault-frame/field.js`; its battlefield cube `belt-crag`, `assault-frame/geocubes.js`;
  its card `crag`, `local-meru/massif.js`): the belt asteroid's charcoal rock and black sky, broken up into tall spurs
  and blocks of rock, benched to climb, clefts between them, ledges and scatter on the floor, round an open middle with a
  crater in it. The cover a frame needs from a ship fighting it from overhead: some nine percent of it stands over 25 m
  above the floor (the asteroid's, under half a percent), its tallest rock near 57 m, its middle open for what is
  defended there.

### A frame operation's crew, the Iron Rose, and aviators on the realistic head

- An operation's crew (`gameworld/frame-goal.js` `CREW`): people off the field for its scenes, each a character from the
  hero door's words (inline, built by the world as any figure is), stood at a place and raised high over it (out of the
  fight's sight), turned, on a bridge set where it has one (groundforce/ `bridge-set`: a back wall of three dark
  viewports in their frames, lit consoles each side, a chair), so the live face the talk box draws as they speak
  (scene/channels/talk-face.js) has the bridge behind it. Each a speaker in the script under its name, and a spot of its
  own for the scenes' shots. Captain Quattro Petersen is the first: the realistic head, long blonde hair, aviators.
- The Iron Rose (groundforce/ `iron-rose`, a prop that flies): the company's mining tender, some 160 m as drawn, an
  off-white hull banded in steel blue, a raised bridge forward with its windows lit warm, two cable gantries amidships
  with their drums and cables, cradles under its belly, radiator fins, three drive bells aft.
- Aviators (headgear/ `aviators`): two broad dark lenses in a thin gold frame, a bridge between them, arms back to the
  ears. On the stylized heads the eyegear kit's (a goggles outline, no strap, arms); on the realistic head a pair of
  teardrop lenses cut from the face shield (headgear/realistic.js, a shield's `lenses`: each at its eye, its foot fuller
  toward the outside, in a rim of the trim, a bridge across between them, the strap its arms). Before this no eyewear
  fitted the realistic head but the shooter's wrap.
- A speaker's portrait (`gameworld/script.js`, a script speaker's `portrait`: a small still of their face, a data URI of
  at most 60 KB carried in the recipe): the comms box draws it in place of the initials on their colour
  (`scene/channels/comms.js`). A captain heard over the radio costs a few kilobytes, not a character's twelve megabytes:
  Captain Quattro speaks so in level 2, his still a screenshot of his realistic hero.

### Defend the asset: a frame operation's props with armour, the foes sent at them, a task that keeps them up

- An asset (`gameworld/frame-goal.js` `GUARD`): a frame operation's prop given armour (`props[].hp`, and its `name` for
  the HUD) is the foes' to hit: it is a ward (`body.ward`), so the pilot's side's rounds and blasts go through it
  (`worlds/controllable/combat-ranged.js`) and the pilot's lock passes it over. The Roman Candles burning on a rock
  being pushed are the first.
- Foes sent at it: a group's `target: <prop id> | [ids]` sets its units' minds on the nearest of them standing
  (`worlds/controllable/mind.js`: a target policy of ids, falling back to the pilot once they are all down), and a flier
  sent at one flies on it (`rules-frame.js` frame flight).
- A task that keeps it up: a task's `guard: [prop ids]` lowers to the objectives' `keep` (`game/objectives.js`, on any
  task): one of them down while the task is in hand loses the level, or, where the level retries, begins the task again
  with the assets stood up whole, the task's foes back where they stood.
- The frame HUD shows what is guarded (`scene/channels/controllable/frame-hud.js`): each asset's name and armour down the
  left, flashing red as it is hit and struck through when it is lost, and a mark over each on the screen.
- The world keeps a frame field's own fields on a body (`rules-frame.js`, a normalizer): an asset's `guard`, so the HUD
  finds it in play (the world drops what no module names, and had dropped it), a ship's `ship`, a part's `perch`, and
  `shielded`.

### Frames that fight as one: the cosmos mind facet's squad on the frame rule

- A squad of enemy frames (`worlds/controllable/rules-frame.js` `squadPlan`; a mind's `squad` { id, way }, the cosmos
  mind facet's squad; a frame group's `squad`, `gameworld/frame-goal.js` `SQUAD_WAYS`): its mates the frames of its id
  standing. A `pack` goes at one foe, the pilot, from both sides of it, the nearer pressing in and the other keeping its
  range, so a pilot that turns on one gives its back to the other. A `team-aware` squad splits the pilot's side between
  it, one to the pilot and one to each wingman. Either way a mate that reels (a broken bar, the stagger build-up) is
  covered: the mate nearest it turns on whoever is closest over it and goes in boosting, everything it has. The pair's
  focus: break one and the other comes for you.

### The patrol ship: a building-sized boss over a frame's field, fought in two steps

- A frame operation's `ship` (`gameworld/frame-goal.js` `SHIP`): a Rock Hydra patrol ship, some 110 m long as drawn,
  hanging on four lift pods over the field (`groundforce/` cards `patrol`, `patrol-pod`, `patrol-gun`: parts of one
  boss, never on a stage's shelf). Its pods and its gun turrets are bodies of their own perched at their places on the
  hull and carried with it (`worlds/controllable/rules-frame.js` `frame-perch`, a body's `perch`).
- Fought in two steps, each a task's, by its two groups `<id>-pods` and `<id>-guns`: its pods first; with them all down
  it sinks, listing, to a fraction of its height over `fall` s (crippled, `frame-ship`); then its guns, shielded until
  the task that downs them begins (the cast's `expose` op) and each rebuilt after the ship's `regen` s unless every one
  is down together. It comes with its task (`comes`), asleep till then. Its bar on the HUD under its name, its armour
  the sum of its pods' and guns' standing, falling with them and rising as a gun comes back; the pilot's lock never
  takes the hull (a body's `noLock`), only its parts.
- A clear's `regen` (`game/objectives.js`, on any clear): each foe it downs comes back whole after its seconds while the
  task is in hand, its count taken back, so the task is met only by every one of them down together.
- Heard: a lift pod's drive held under it, a turret's heavy rounds, each a wreck as it goes (`sfx-shelf/frame-sounds.js`).
- The frame HUD's boss bar reads a body with no rule of its own (the ship's hull).
- The holo table's briefing knows the ship's two groups (`gameworld/frame-map.js`: a part group's bodies by its ship's
  names) and draws them, a lift pod as a gunship and a turret as a turret (`campaign/holo-minis.js`); a spider bot has its
  own miniature, a low body on six splayed legs.
- The hull's hover over the field is a body's `overfield`, not `ship`: a starfighter carries its systems as `ship`
  (rules-starfighter.js), and the hover had pinned a flown level's craft over the ground (a cockpit sortie's foes out of
  its pilot's reach).

### Spider bots: a crawler on the ground of a frame's field

- A spider bot (`groundforce/` `crawler`): a low armoured crawler on six high-kneed legs, a red-eyed wedge of a head
  with mandibles and a lit plasma cutter between them (the end it leads with), an orange abdomen behind so it reads on
  grey rock. Each leg is its own bone; the figure's stride clip swings them about their hips in two tripods half a
  stride apart and lifts each as it comes forward (`CRAWL`, `crawlClip`): a card with `legs` walks.
- On a frame operation (`gameworld/frame-goal.js` `OPERATION.units.crawler`, the group kind `crawler`): quick on the
  ground, closing right in to cut at what it is sent at (a group's `target`) with short hot plasma, cutting upward at a
  tall thing's middle from under it (a unit's own `fireArc`). Kept on the land under it as it goes over the hills, its
  legs walked by the ground it covers (`worlds/controllable/rules-frame.js` `frame-crawl`).
- Heard (`sfx-shelf/frame-sounds.js` `FRAME_UNITS.crawler`): its cutter crackling as it cuts, its legs' servos whining
  as it comes, a small blast as it goes.

### Stagger build-up: a frame's bar kept under pressure, and two seconds of a frame stood still

- A frame's stability bar builds under fire (`worlds/controllable/rules-frame.js`, `STAB`; a built frame's
  `stab.hold`, `assault-frame/assemble.js`): it comes back on its own only once the frame has gone `hold` s unhit (1 s),
  so fire kept on a frame breaks it where scattered hits never did (the bar had come back the moment a round landed,
  faster than a rifle could chip it).
- Broken, a frame reels for 2 s (it was 1.6) stood still: braked where it broke (`stab.brake`, its way checked by 8 a
  second), no keys, no guns, no dodge, still coming down if it was in the air; every hit on it lands 1.5 times as hard
  as before. Two seconds of a target that neither moves nor dodges, the moment to land everything.
- How a weapon hits (`assault-frame/parts.js` `IMPACTS`, a weapon's `impact`): ballistic rounds (rifle, shotgun,
  gatling, bazooka, mortar, missiles) build the bar fastest, a rifle or a gatling kept on breaking a medium frame in two
  to four seconds; energy weapons (the laser, the plasma cannon) build a fraction of that for their damage; a blade's blow
  shoves (melee); `stun` is reserved for weapons made to break the bar. The shelf's numbers are retuned to it.
- Every frame on every level plays by it: the pilot's, an enemy frame's, an ally's, a level 1 survey's and a Warlords
  operation's.

### Couch doors: the couch games asked for by name

- A party round is a quick game of its own (`goal: 'mash'`): two to four players in an arena, each mashing to out-press
  the others before the horn.
- `players` (2 to 4) on the quick door seats a couch game on one level: a deathmatch for several players on a split
  screen, a ride with a driver and a gunner, a party round.
- A sentence asking for a party game, a driver-and-gunner game or a split-screen deathmatch is answered with the one level
  the quick door plays of it today, as a co-op kitchen's is; laying a whole game of each waits on its level form in the
  book.
- The producer's rail roster has a Party Round row for the new quick game, and the hill-climb page's genre probes now
  each have a sentence probe: party mash, driver and gunner, and split-screen deathmatch answer with their one level, as a
  co-op kitchen does. "Split screen deathmatch" and "couch deathmatch" now read as split-screen deathmatch, not the arena
  shooter.

### Couch forms: whole games from a sentence

- A deathmatch is now a level form of the game book (`levels.<id>.deathmatch: { bots?, frags?, seconds?, mode? }`, on a
  walk and its arena): the quick deathmatch's match (its frag limit, its supplies, its bots and the damage ring), from the
  level's own words.
- A sentence asking for an arena shooter now lays a game of three matches against bots, and one asking for a split-screen
  deathmatch lays three matches for four friends on a split screen, each player a hero. Both were answered with one level
  of the quick door before. No foes stand on a match beside its bots.
- The hill-climb page now reads "yes" from a sentence for the arena shooter and the split-screen deathmatch, and the arena
  shooter's rail (Infinity Crisis) is offered as a designed game as well as a quick one.
- A party round is a level form of the game book too (`levels.<id>.mash: { seconds?, to? }`, on a walk). A sentence asking
  for a party game now lays three rounds for four friends in a lobby, each against each: a mash, a race to a count, and a
  mash. The hill-climb page reads "yes" from a sentence for party mash, and the Party Round rail is offered as a designed
  game as well as a quick one.

### Hijack City movers: a house emptied into a moving truck

- **Movers**: a removals job on Jobsified in Hijack City. Take the moving truck from the dock to the Hendersons' house on
  the block, go in, and empty it: any piece (a couch, a fridge, a box) is lifted whole with E and carried in your hands,
  through any door, up and down the stairs, out of the basement, nothing it would hit stopping it. Carried to the front
  door it goes on the truck; twelve fill it, and it pays. (docs/movers.md)
- A family's house to walk into (`house`): two storeys over a basement, furnished as a home is (a sofa and armchairs in
  the living rooms, a fridge and a dining table in the kitchen-diners, beds and wardrobes upstairs, boxes in the
  basement), and new household pieces on the furniture shelf: sofa, armchair, coffee and dining tables, bookcase, media
  console, chest of drawers, nightstand, fridge, wardrobe, moving box.
- Lifting is a runtime piece any stage can ask for (`heave`): a held piece's box leaves the world while it is carried,
  and its drawing rides in the hands.
- A stage over a basement now puts its front door, the arriving walker and its drop zone on the floor its way in is on.

### Ride form: the hero a ride in the game book, and races from a sentence

- A designed game can make its hero a ride (`ride: { ride, vehicle?, tier?, livery?, wear? }`, the quick door's ride
  words): the ride is made once and every road and trail level is driven in it.
- A race is a level form of the game book (`levels.<id>.race: { laps?, rivals? }`, on a roadway): the quick door's race,
  its laps and checkpoints the roadway's, its rivals on the grid.
- From a sentence: a kart racer lays a cup of three kart races, a racing game three races in a coupe on city circuits,
  and a driver-and-gunner game three runs in a car with a roof gun for the second player. Each was answered with one level
  of the quick door before.
- The hill-climb page now reads "yes" from a sentence for the kart racer and driver and gunner, and the racing rail is
  offered as a designed game as well as a quick one. Every couch genre probe now lays its game from a sentence.

### Split screen: a view for each player

- A game whose players each need their own view (a first-person deathmatch, a chase) can now split the screen: two
  players side by side, three or four in quarters. Each player's view follows their own body with the level's camera,
  and in first person each player's own body is hidden in their view and seen in the others'.
- A game whose cube asks for a split screen lays it: each player's view is their own camera, the level's own kind of
  camera on their own body, and the shared camera that held every player in one shot steps aside. A first-person game
  now seats more than one player when the screen is split. The hill-climb marks split screen as built: split-screen
  deathmatch is makeable, and every couch genre probe is now makeable.
- Not yet: in players 2 to 4's views a third-person camera does not pull in against a wall, the HUD is the whole
  screen's rather than one a view, and post effects show in player 1's view only.
- Turns, the alternating two-player game: players take turns at one hero. Only the player whose turn it is drives; a
  fall, or the hero knocked down, spends that player's own life and passes the turn to the next player with lives left,
  and a game can also pass the turn on a clock. The chip strip marks whose turn it is. A game whose cube asks for turns
  lays it, and a turns game can open on the lobby. With turns built, every seat value in the hill-climb is built.

### The READMEs say the studio as it now works: five starts, a few questions first, a game to its first level

- **The README opens on the way a session goes.** You say what you want or pick one of five starts (a character, a
  game, an object, a 3D exhibit, a home or a room); you bring what you have (sketches, a floor plan, a document, a
  photo, a 3D model); for a game, a home or an exhibit the agent asks a few questions first and says back what it will
  make; then you look, play and change it by asking.
- **Games have their own section**: from an idea to a first level you play in one session, started from a kind of game
  you already know, delivered as a game (a start screen, menus, a HUD, pause, results and the next level), whole games
  from one sentence, and couch play for up to four on one screen or split screen.
- **The Claude Code plugin is the first way in for Claude Code**; `npx mojulo init` stays the way in for every other
  agent. The npm page and the plugin's README follow the same order, and the plugin's "Try it" starts from the starts.
- **Shorter.** The military-base walkthrough moved to the long tour (`docs/tour.md`); the README keeps one
  line for it.
- **Agent-facing docs follow.** `docs/AGENT-REFERENCE.md` opens on the starts and their producers, then the game
  rail; the retired surfaces are one paragraph. `AGENTS.md` says the starts and the producer-first rule.
- **Retired pages archived.** The README working outline is deleted; the contextmap, composer, app-runtime and an old
  clothing hand-off page move to `docs/archive/`, with a stub left where code still names the old path.

### The plugin's last 3.1 leftover goes, and 3.2's size is said before it is measured

- **The Claude plugin drops its `inference-worker` skill.** It answered the parked inference tasks of mojulo apps, a
  surface retired from the tool list in 3.1; the `run-inference-worker` catalyst and the agent-task queue stay for any
  host that drives them. plugin.json moves to `3.2.0-rc.3` so an installed copy updates.
- **The 3.2 package is about twice 3.1.1's**, and the plugin README and `docs/tech-requirements.md` say so beside
  3.1.1's measured figures (a pack from source: 22.3 MB tarball, 68.7 MB unpacked); the published 3.2.0 is measured at
  the release.
- **A 3.2.0 release summary is drafted** (`changelog/release-3.2.0.draft.md`, read by no tool and not shipped), with
  the release-day checklist: the parked engine-handoff plan to delete, the detailed log to move to
  `CHANGELOG-3.2.md`, the version pins, and the plugin agents' release lists to empty.
